Visualizing linguistic performance across diagnostic groups
To explore patterns in linguistic performance across diagnostic groups, we conducted an unsupervised dimensionality reduction analysis. We standardized all linguistic variables (mean = 0, SD = 1) to ensure equal weighting. We applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA)79 to identify the main axes of variation in the data and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)80,81 to generate a nonlinear, two-dimensional embedding that preserves local similarities. UMAP was configured with n neighbors = 15 and min dist = 0.1, and both methods used a random seed for reproducibility. To enhance interpretability, extreme outliers (beyond 1.5 × IQR in the reduced dimensions) were excluded from visualizations (retaining 8,927 and 9,791 participants for PCA and UMAP, respectively). The resulting embeddings were colored by clinical diagnosis to assess the degree of separation or overlap among groups.
We designed a machine learning pipeline to classify a speaker’s diagnosis into one of six categories based on statistical features derived from language productions on tasks, namely patient with LHD, RHD, dementia, MCI, TBI, and HCs. The pipeline is designed to manage speaker-dependent data, address class imbalance, and a provide comprehensive, comparative evaluation of multiple machine learning (ML) models, namely include Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting, and a Deep Neural Network (DNN). The entire process, from data preparation to model evaluation, was conducted in a Python environment utilizing pandas for data manipulation82, scikit-learn83 and imbalanced-learn84 for machine learning algorithms. The deep learning component was build using Tensorflow85.
The core of our methodology is built upon the principle of speaker-independent validation, which is crucial for developing models that can generalize to new, unseen individuals rather than memorizing characteristics of specific speakers in the training set. To facilitate this, a designated speaker identifier column was used to group data points belonging to the same individual. The dataset was then partitioned into features and the target variable.
To ensure that the model evaluation provides a realistic estimate of performance on new individuals, a strict speaker-independent splitting protocol was enforced. The dataset was divided randomly into a training set (80%) and a hold-out test set (20%) using the GroupShuffleSplit strategy. This method guarantees that all data points from any given speaker are confined to only one of the sets (either training or testing), completely preventing data leakage between them. This approach is critical for assessing the model’s ability to generalize beyond the specific speakers it was trained on.
A multi-step preprocessing pipeline was applied sequentially to the data. Crucially, all preprocessing steps were fitted only on the training data to prevent information from the test set from influencing the training process. The same fitted transformers were then used to transform both the training and test sets.
Missing values in the feature set were managed by imputing them with the mean of their respective columns, calculated from the training data.
To reduce multicollinearity and model complexity, highly correlated features were removed. A Pearson correlation matrix was computed on the training set, and for any pair of features with a correlation coefficient and we evaluated various threshold features, for correlations greater than 0.90, one of the features was discarded.
The features were standardized by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance using the StandardScaler83. This transformation ensures that features with larger scales do not disproportionately influence model training, which is particularly important for distance-based algorithms like SVM and regularization models like Logistic Regression.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was employed as the final feature engineering step. PCA transforms the standardized features into a smaller set of uncorrelated principal components. The number of components was chosen to retain 95% of the original variance in the training data, effectively reducing noise and the dimensionality of the feature space while preserving most of the relevant information.
We have evaluated five distinct classification models to explore a range of algorithmic approaches: Logistic Regression (LG), Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM) with an RBF kernel, Gradient Boosting, and a feedforward Deep Neural Network (DNN). We selected these models to allow for a comprehensive analysis of the dataset and selection of a model that explain the data. More specifically, the following models were selected:
LG is a fundamental linear classification algorithm. It works by fitting a linear equation to the features and then applying a logistic function (or sigmoid function) to the output to return a probability between 0 and 1. This probability is then used to predict the class. LG serves as a baseline model86.
RFs is an ensemble learning method; it constructs many individual decision trees during training. It can capture complex, non-linear relationships in the data without requiring explicit transformations. It is generally robust to overfitting, especially when compared to a single decision tree as it averages the predictions of many trees87.
SVM models detect the optimal hyperplane (or decision boundary) that best separates the classes in the feature space. SVM can model both linear and non-linear boundary by mapping the data into a higher-dimensional space, with good generalization performance on unseen data88.
GB is another powerful ensemble technique like the RFs, which builds models sequentially. It starts with a simple model and then iteratively adds new decision trees that are specifically trained to correct the errors made by the previous ones. RFs, however, build trees independently and in parallel whereas GBs are sequential with an error-correcting approach leading to more powerful and flexible model86.
DNN consists of an input layer, multiple “hidden” layers of interconnected nodes (neurons), and an output layer. The network learns to detect complex patterns and features by adjusting the connection weights between neurons during training. The DNN approach can uncover patterns in the data than the other, more traditional machine learning models might miss89.
The data exhibited an imbalanced class distribution as there are fewer patients with MCI, RHD, and TBI, than patients with dementia, LHD, and HC. To mitigate the risk of models becoming biased towards the majority class, we integrated the SMOTE directly into our modeling pipeline90. For each model, a pipeline was constructed with SMOTE as the initial step. This approach ensures that over-sampling is performed correctly within each cross-validation fold: SMOTE is fitted and applied only to the training data partition of a fold, generating synthetic samples for the minority classes before the classifier is trained. The validation partition of the fold remains in its original, imbalanced state, providing an unbiased evaluation of the model’s performance. This in-pipeline application of SMOTE is crucial for preventing data leakage and obtaining a reliable estimate of model generalizability. We defined a custom DynamicSMOTE class to automatically adjust the k neighbors parameter, preventing errors in cross-validation folds where a minority class had very few samples.
To identify the optimal set of hyperparameters for each model, we employed a hybrid search strategy using a participant-aware data partitioning with GroupKFold cross-validation (with 5 folds) to maintain speaker independence. For the traditional models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Gradient Boosting), we used HalvingRandomSearchCV. This efficient method starts by evaluating many hyperparameter combinations on a small subset of the data and iteratively prunes fewer promising candidates, allocating more resources to the best-performing ones.
For the computationally intensive Deep Neural Network (DNN), we used RandomizedSearchCV to sample a fixed number of hyperparameter combinations from the search space. The performance of each combination was evaluated based on its default scoring metric. The best hyperparameters for SMOTE’s k neighbors parameter were also determined during this search. The DNN architecture was also part of the hyperparameter search. Key parameters tuned included the number of hidden layers, the number of neurons, the dropout rate, batch size, and the learning rate for the Adam optimizer. An “early stopping callback” was used to prevent overfitting by halting training when performance on the loss function stopped improving.
After hyperparameter tuning, the best-performing version of each model was evaluated on the completely unseen hold-out test set. Model performance was assessed using a comprehensive set of metrics to provide a holistic view of their classification capabilities:
Accuracy is the percentage of predictions that were correct out of all predictions made. If your model correctly predicts 85 out of 100 cases, your accuracy is 85%.
Balanced Accuracy solves this problem by averaging the accuracy within each class. It calculates the recall (true positive rate) for each class separately, then takes the average. In other words, the balanced accuracy is defined as the average of sensitivity (true-positive rate) and specificity (true-negative rate) for the two classes in a binary classification “Patient vs. Healthy Control (HC)”, the Specificity (HC Recall) (1) and the Sensitivity (Patient Recall) (2) is calculated. Then the Balanced Accuracy is the sum of the Specificity and Sensitivity divided by two (2), the number of classes in a binary classification.
F1-Score (Weighted) addresses the trade-off between recall (2) and precision (3). The F1-score is the harmonic mean of these two, giving you a single number that balances both concerns. The weighted version calculates F1-scores for each class and then averages them based on how many samples each class has, making it appropriate for imbalanced datasets.
Cohen’s Kappa measures how much better your model performs compared to random chance. It is particularly valuable because it accounts for the possibility that some correct predictions might just be lucky guesses. Kappa values range from − 1 to 1: 1.0: Perfect agreement beyond chance and 0.0: Agreement is no better than random chance; Negative values mean worse than random
AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve). The ROC curve plots your model’s true positive rate against its false positive rate across all possible classification thresholds. The AUC-ROC tells you how well your model can distinguish between classes. AUC = 1.0: Perfect classifier.
AUC-PR (Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve). ROC curves can often be optimistic on imbalanced datasets, precision-recall curves focus specifically on the positive class performance. This makes AUC-PR especially valuable when you care more about correctly identifying the minority class. The PR curve plots precision against recall at different thresholds. AUC-PR is particularly informative for imbalanced data.
Confusion matrices were generated for each model to visualize the distribution of correct and incorrect predictions across the different classes. For tree-based models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting), feature importance scores were calculated and visualized to provide insights into the most influential principal components for classification. Finally, the best overall model, along with the fitted preprocessing transformers, was saved for potential future deployment.
To assess the influence of clinical diagnosis on each linguistic outcome variable, we utilized an automated mixed-effects modeling pipeline. This analysis included participants from the five diagnostic groups (LHD, Dementia, MCI, RHS, TBI) and the Healthy Control (HC) group. The pipeline, developed in R91 was designed to be flexible, data-driven, and robust to violations of statistical assumptions common in linguistic data.
For each linguistic variable, a mixed-effects model was implemented. Diagnosis was specified as a fixed effect to determine its influence on the outcome.
As discussed earlier there is variation in the subgroups within the participants and the tasks they perform, to appropriately account for the non-independence of data arising from the study design, and given the complexity of the databases, two random intercepts were included in the model:
The (1 | Speaker) term addresses that multiple observations (i.e., linguistic measures from one or more tasks) originate from the same individual. By including a random intercept for each speaker, the model accounts for individual-specific baseline differences in linguistic performance, thereby modeling the repeated measures dimension of the data.
The (1 | Task) term addresses the inherent variability across different elicitation tasks (e.g., “Cinderella,” “Flood,” and “Cookie Theft,” as listed in Table 1). Given that the study design involved diverse groups of participants undertaking varying subsets of these tasks, this random intercept allows the model to estimate an average deviation from the overall mean for each specific task. This effectively controls for baseline differences in how tasks might elicit certain linguistic features, regardless of the speaker or their diagnosis.
These random effects structure is robust to the unbalanced nature of task administration (i.e., not all participants completed all tasks, and tasks were not fully crossed with participants). It allows for the estimation of the fixed effect of ‘Diagnosis’ while simultaneously partitioning out variance attributable to individual speakers and specific tasks. The general model structure was:
The analytical pipeline systematically selected the most appropriate statistical model based on the distribution of each dependent variable. This adaptive process involved fitting Gaussian Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMMs) for continuous variables, using robust LMMs if residual diagnostics (via the DHARMa package92) indicated violations of model assumptions, and employing Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) with appropriate distributions (e.g., binomial, Poisson, or negative binomial) for binary or count data, including checks for overdispersion and zero-inflation. If a suitable model could not be fitted through these steps, a rank-based LMM was applied as a robust fallback. When a significant main effect of ‘Diagnosis’ was found (typically p < 0.05), post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted between all diagnostic groups using estimated marginal means (via the emmeans package95). Tukey’s method was applied to adjust for multiple comparisons. Group means and confidence intervals are reported to aid in the interpretation of these differences.

To investigate the global structure of linguistic variations across diagnostic groups, we performed a Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) analysis80,81. Figure 3 displays the two-dimensional embedding of the comprehensive linguistic profiles (derived from the extracted linguistic features) for all participants. Interpretation of the UMAP Projection Unlike linear projections (e.g., PCA), the axes in Fig. 3 (UMAP 1 and UMAP 2) do not correspond to specific, single linguistic variables. Instead, they represent non-linear, dimensionless coordinates that preserve the local neighborhood structure of the high-dimensional data. Consequently, the proximity between data points indicates the similarity of their overall linguistic profiles: points clustered closely together represent individuals with highly similar speech patterns across the domains of morphology, syntax, lexicon, and phonology. The ‘X’ markers indicate the centroids (geometric centers) of each diagnostic group, illustrating the average location of that group’s linguistic profile in the projected space.
The distribution observed in Fig. 3 is a direct result of the feature selection process, where we retained robust, non-redundant measures across all linguistic levels. This multidimensional approach reveals three primary patterns of distribution. Firstly, the distinct clusters in LHD and Dementia show that the LHD group forms a distinct cluster significantly separated from the HCx. This separation aligns with the severe deficits in syntax and phonology (e.g., reduced complex syllable structures and functional words) identified in our statistical analysis. Similarly, the Dementia group separates from HCs, driven by their specific lexico-semantic impairments.
In contrast, the TBI, MCI, and RHD groups show substantial overlap with each other and the HC group. This visual overlap suggests that while these conditions have unique linguistic markers (as detailed in Table 6), their overall linguistic footprint is less distinct than that of LHD. The wide dispersion of the LHD and TBI clouds relative to the tighter HC cluster illustrates the high variance in these populations—reflecting that brain injury affects language production in heterogeneous ways depending on severity and lesion location. This unsupervised visualization serves as a validation of the supervised ML results presented in subsequent sections, confirming that while LHD and Dementia present strong, separable signals, conditions like MCI and RHD present subtler linguistic deviations that require the high-dimensional discrimination provided by the NeuroScreen models.

is study represents a critical step toward transforming language analysis from a research tool into a scalable, clinically actionable digital biomarker for neurological disorders. By applying automated, computational linguistic analysis to one of the largest and most diverse databases of spoken language, we demonstrate that distinct, quantifiable linguistic profiles can differentiate between individuals with le hemisphere damage, right hemisphere damage, dementia, MCI, TBI, and healthy controls. ese findings not only advance scientific understanding of language impairments but also establish a practical foundation for integrating language-based digital biomarkers into routine neurological assessment. Large-scale serum N-glycomics tracks N-glycosylation dynamics in hepatocellular carcinoma progression and enables early diagnosis
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer mortality, yet the role of N-glycosylation in its pathogenesis remains unclear. We applied a multi-center, large-cohort N-glycomics strategy combining isomer-specific glycan profiling with multi-omics integration to characterize disease-associated glycan alterations and develop serum-based diagnostic models. Serum N-glycomes from 1,074 individuals across health, chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis, and HCC were analyzed using a high-throughput pipeline of N-glycan release, derivatization, enrichment, and mass spectrometry. HCC progression was marked by pronounced increases in branching and fucosylation, elevated bisecting GlcNAc, and reduced galactosylation. Machine learning models built on these glycan signatures achieved high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.84–0.93), significantly outperforming alpha-fetoprotein, with performance validated in two external cohorts. Integrative glycoproteomic and transcriptomic analyses further illuminated the regulatory pathways driving these glycan shifts, highlighting N-glycosylation as a promising axis for mechanistic insight and early HCC detection.
The workflow of this study is summarized in Fig. 1. The study included three independent cohorts (discovery cohort Guangzhou-I, GZ-I, n = 744; external validations Guangzhou-II, GZ-II, n = 186 and Xuzhou, XZ, n = 144) covering healthy controls and liver disease stages (detailed demographics in Supplementary Data 1 and Supplementary Data 8). In total, 1,074 participants were recruited. Serum N-glycome profiles were collected for all individuals by MALDI-TOF MS. Identification was done using in-house tool GlyHunter and quantitative information was obtained by applying median quotient normalization to peak intensities after removing N-glycans with over 50% missing values (see Methods for details). A subset of GZ-I cohort (n = 120) was used for LC-MS based N-glycoproteomics and proteomics analysis. Another subset of GZ-I cohort (n = 186) was used for sialic acid linkage specific N-glycomics analysis. We used GZ-I cohort for bioinformatic analysis, model training, and internal model validation, and used GZ-II cohort and XZ cohort for external model validation. Detailed schematic of sample allocation is in Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1. Quality control (QC) assessments demonstrated the high technical reproducibility of our analytical workflow. Median coefficients of variation (CVs) were 0.08, 0.07, and 0.11 for the GZ-I, GZ-II, and XZ cohorts, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2a). QC samples exhibited strong correlations, with a median Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) of 0.98 and a minimum of 0.91 (Supplementary Fig. 3). Furthermore, median inter-plate and inter-cohort correlations were both 0.98, indicating consistent performance across plates and cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 2b–c). These results collectively confirm the robust stability and reproducibility of our analytical workflow, enabling reliable analysis of the serum N-glycome.
The GZ-I cohort serves as the main study population, as all downstream bioinformatics analyses apart from diagnostic model evaluation were performed on this cohort. In total, we detected 201 N-glycan compositions (Supplementary Fig. 4a–d, Supplementary Data 2), of which 121 were detected in all four groups (Supplementary Fig. 4b). After rigorous filtering (detection in >50% samples, literature structural validation22,23), 64 annotated N-glycans were retained for analysis (Supplementary Fig. 4d, Supplementary Data 2), with >80% detection rate in most cases (Supplementary Fig. 4e). Liver function tests (LFTs) are essential clinical tools for evaluating liver health and diagnosing liver diseases. We investigated the associations between serum N-glycome profiles and LFTs, as well as two established liver function scoring systems (LFSSs), the Albumin-Bilirubin (ALBI) stage and Child-Pugh class (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Data 4). Significant correlations were observed between N-glycome profiles and both LFTs (Fig. 2b, top panel) and LFSSs (Fig. 2b, bottom panel). Notably, the ALBI score, a modern indicator of liver function and hepatopathy prognosis24, exhibited strong correlations with multiple N-glycans (Pearson’s r ≈ 0.5, FDR < 0.05). To characterize the N-glycome comprehensively, we calculated derived traits related to biosynthetic pathways, including branching, bisecting GlcNAc, fucosylation, galactosylation, and sialylation (Supplementary Data 3). Poorer liver function was associated with increased branching, bisecting GlcNAc, and fucosylation, alongside decreased galactosylation and sialylation (Fig. 2c, d, Supplementary Fig. 5). To account for the confounding effects of different hepatopathies, we conducted subgroup correlation analyses within each disease cohort. These analyses confirmed robust associations between serum N-glycome profiles and liver function, particularly in patients diagnosed with liver cirrhosis (LC) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Supplementary Fig. 6). Correlation patterns were consistent across global and subgroup levels, with notable concordance in LC and HCC cohorts, as demonstrated for the ALBI score (Fig. 2e, f). This suggests that N-glycans can serve as reliable markers for assessing liver function. A random forest model developed to predict ALBI stages from N-glycome profiles further supported this, achieving an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.892 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). The predicted probabilities closely mirrored actual ALBI scores (Pearson’s r = 0.734, P < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 7b). These results indicate that serum N-glycome profiles can effectively reflect liver function deterioration.
Differential abundance analysis identified 48 out of 64 N-glycans significantly dysregulated across disease groups (Fig. 3a–c, Supplementary Data 5). HCC exerted the most pronounced effect on serum N-glycome profiles (Fig. 3c), followed by a more moderate impact in liver cirrhosis (Fig. 3b). In contrast, few significant N-glycosylation alterations were observed in chronic hepatitis (Fig. 3a). In cirrhosis, downregulated N-glycans were predominantly tri- and tetra-antennary, multisialylated structures lacking fucosylation (Fig. 3b). Conversely, HCC was characterized by upregulation of similar tri- and tetra-antennary, multisialylated glycans bearing fucosylation (Fig. 3c). Notably, these fucosylated, multisialylated tri- and tetra-antennary glycans were uniquely upregulated in HCC, while remaining largely unaltered in cirrhosis (Fig. 3d). The 48 significantly dysregulated N-glycans were grouped into five Glycan Co-expression Modules (GCMs) based on their expression patterns (Fig. 3e). Each GCM exhibited distinct expression profiles (Fig. 3f) and enriched structural features (Fig. 3g), with little expression similarity (Fig. 3h). For instance, GCM1, comprising fucosylated, fully sialylated tri- and tetra-antennary glycans, was exclusively upregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In contrast, GCM2, consisting of their afucosylated counterparts, was downregulated in liver cirrhosis. GCM3, primarily composed of smaller glycans with bisecting N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), was upregulated in both cirrhosis and HCC. Notably, GCM4, which included two hybrid mono-sialylated glycans, was upregulated across all liver diseases, with a less pronounced upregulation in HCC. Finally, GCM5, consisting of a large number of high-mannose, hybrid, or immature complex glycans, were downregulated in HCC alone. Characteristic structural alterations in serum N-glycome were observed across liver diseases (Fig. 3i, Supplementary Fig. 8). Bi-antennary glycans were downregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), whereas tri- and tetra-antennary glycans were upregulated. Additionally, galactosylation was reduced, while bisecting N-acetylglucosamine and fucosylation were increased in both liver cirrhosis and HCC. Using sialic acid linkage-specific derivatization, we identified a specific downregulation of α2,6-linked sialylation in liver cirrhosis (Supplementary Fig. 9).
To isolate disease-specific N-glycosylation traits independent of liver function, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. By including all liver function tests and scoring systems as covariates in an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA), 30 of the 48 significantly dysregulated glycans retained FDR < 0.05 (Supplementary Fig. 10). These findings demonstrate that, beyond their association with liver function, the modulation patterns of most N-glycans are closely linked to underlying pathological conditions. To further disentangle the contributions of liver function deterioration and hepatopathy to N-glycome alterations, we conducted multivariate regression analysis, incorporating age, sex, ALBI score, and disease group as independent variables. Elevated levels of tri- and tetra-antennary glycans were strongly associated with HCC, although a broader trend linked poorer liver function to increased antennary complexity (Supplementary Fig. 11). Notably, some established N-glycome hallmarks of HCC, such as elevated bisecting N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and fucosylation25, were more accurately attributed to liver function deterioration in advanced liver disease rather than malignancy-specific changes (Supplementary Fig. 11d, i). Nevertheless, these N-glycomic signatures retain diagnostic utility, providing complementary information, as HCC is typically characterized by impaired liver function. Additionally, the two hybrid mono-sialylated glycans, H6N3S1 and H5N3S1, were significantly associated with liver pathology (Supplementary Fig. 12).N-Glycome subtypes with distinct clinical features
Molecular subtyping is a cornerstone of precision medicine26, facilitating the stratification of heterogeneous diseases through biomarkers such as N-glycome profiles. Unsupervised consensus clustering of serum N-glycome data stratified HCC samples into three distinct subtypes (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 13). Each subtype exhibited unique N-glycan profiles (Fig. 4b). Subtype 1 was characterized by elevated levels of small, immature glycans, including those with bisecting N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in GCM3, and reduced levels of large, multisialylated, afucosylated glycans in GCM2 (Fig. 4c, Fig. 3g). Subtype 2 was defined by decreased levels of large, multisialylated, fucosylated glycans in GCM1. Subtype 3 displayed increased GCM1 glycans alongside reduced levels of high-mannose, hybrid, or small complex glycans in GCM5, presenting a glycomic profile partially complementary to subtype 1. Compared with control groups (healthy controls, chronic hepatitis B, and liver cirrhosis), subtype 2 exhibited a serum N-glycomic pattern closely resembling non-HCC states (Supplementary Fig. 14), suggesting an early-stage carcinoma phenotype. Significant associations were observed between the N-glycomic molecular subtypes and clinical parameters (Supplementary Fig. 15). Subtypes 1 and 3 were characterized by poorer liver function compared to subtype 2, as reflected by LFTs including AST, ALT, GGT, ALB, TBIL, TP, ALBI score, and AAR (all p < 0.05, Supplementary Fig. 15a). This aligns with the N-glycomic profile of subtype 2, which more closely resembled the control groups. The N-glycomic subtypes also demonstrated significant overlap with established clinical staging systems, including the Child-Pugh classification (Fisher’s exact test p = 1.54 × 10⁻⁶), ALBI stage (p = 8.50 × 10⁻⁹), and TNM stage (p = 2.08 × 10⁻⁴) (Supplementary Fig. 15b). Importantly, individuals in subtype 2 were predominantly in earlier pathological stages (Supplementary Fig. 15c), suggesting that this subtype represents a less advanced disease state with relatively preserved liver function. Subtype 1 and subtype 3 showed no significant differences in liver function or cancer staging but exhibited entirely distinct glycosylation patterns. This may indicate different underlying disease mechanisms, which warrant further investigation in future studies.
While previous analyses have characterized global N-glycome alterations associated with hepatopathy progression, a critical question remains: how do site-specific glycosylation events collectively contribute to the serum glycome? To address this, we conducted orthogonal N-glycoproteomics and proteomics analyses in DDA accucision mode on a subset of the GZ-I cohort (n = 120, 30 per group) to tackle two key challenges: (1) determining whether glycomic changes result from altered glycosylation enzyme activity (site-level regulation) or shifts in glycoprotein abundance (global proteome variation), and (2) identifying the primary glycoprotein carriers of disease-associated glycans. We identified 3057 glycopeptides, 2824 site-specific glycans, 477 glycan compositions, 276 glycosylation sites, and 168 glycoproteins (Supplementary Fig. 16a). Of the 961 protein groups detected in global proteomics data, 107 overlapped with those identified in glycoproteomics (Supplementary Fig. 16b). Additionally, of the 201 glycans detected in glycomics data, 148 were also identified in glycoproteomics (Supplementary Fig. 16c). Among all site-specific glycans (defined as unique combinations of protein sites, proteins, and glycan compositions), 2083 were consistently detected across all samples and technical replicates.
We generated pseudo-glycome profiles by aggregating the quantitative data of all site-specific glycans sharing identical glycan compositions (Fig. 5a, Supplementary Fig. 17). These pseudo-glycome profiles exhibited high concordance with the actual glycome, with an average Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) of approximately 0.95. It should be noted that the pseudo-glycome represents an estimation strategy by aggregating signals across different proteins and glycopeptides, rather than a strict quantitative approach. While the high consistency with the real glycome is indeed remarkable, this agreement should be interpreted with caution given the potential biases introduced by signal summation. Nevertheless, this approach demonstrates the potential to interpret glycomics phenotypes at the site-specific level, leveraging glycoproteomics as a complementary tool. Notably, glycans displayed diverse site-specific contributions (Fig. 5b–d). For example, the most abundant glycan in the serum N-glycome, H5N4S2, showed uniform contributions from multiple glycosylation sites (Fig. 5b). In contrast, H5N5F1S1 was predominantly associated with IGHM N46 and IGHA2 N92 (or IGHA2 N207) (Fig. 5c). Glycans with similar structural features exhibited similar site contributions (Fig. 5d). For instance, tri- and tetra-antennary, fucosylated, multisialylated glycans were primarily derived from A1AG1 N93, whereas immature, agalactosylated complex or hybrid glycans were mainly associated with IGHG1 N180 (or IGHG1 N299). These findings reveal the heterogeneous site-specific contributions to the serum N-glycome, predominantly driven by a subset of highly abundant glycoproteins27.
Differential analysis of site-specific glycans (SSGs) was conducted, selecting only those SSGs exhibiting significant alterations independent of changes in their corresponding protein abundance (Methods, Fig. 5e–g, Supplementary Data 6). In total, 67, 148, and 114 SSGs were significantly upregulated in CHB, LC, and HCC samples, respectively, while 63, 124, and 73 SSGs were downregulated (Fig. 5h). By integrating glycomics and glycoproteomics data, we elucidated two distinct mechanisms underlying glycomic alterations: (1) glycosylation-dominant mechanism and (2). protein-dominant mechanism. The glycosylation-dominant mechanism indicates that certain glycomic alterations arise from dysregulation of upstream glycosylation pathways. For instance, H5N3S1, a mono-sialylated hybrid glycan elevated in glycomic data across all liver diseases, particularly in CHB (Fig. 3f, g), was predominantly linked to the N869 site on alpha-2-macroglobulin (A2MG) (log₂FC = 7.73, FDR = 0.00032) (Fig. 5i). Further analysis of this site revealed a marked increase in H5N3S1 in CHB, despite only a modest elevation in global A2MG levels across liver disease progression (Fig. 5j). This exemplifies how dysregulation of N-glycosylation itself drives phenotypic N-glycome changes. In the protein-dominant mechanism, on the other hand, alterations in the expression levels of certain highly abundant glycoproteins can exert a non-negligible impact on the observed glycome, even in the absence of changes in the upstream glycosylation regulatory pathways, as demonstrated by the increased levels of tetra-antennary, fucosylated, multisialylated glycans (H7N6F1S2, H7N6F1S3, and H7N6F1S4), primarily driven by elevated A1AG1, an acute-phase immune protein (Supplementary Fig. 18a–d). This highlights an important perspective for future glycomics research, namely that serum glycomic data alone may not be sufficient to provide regulatory insights.
Among the differentially regulated site-specific glycans (SSGs), 27 were consistently upregulated and 22 downregulated across all liver diseases, while 31 were uniquely upregulated and 20 downregulated in HCC (Supplementary Fig. 19a–d). At the protein level, 26 glycoproteins were commonly dysregulated in all liver diseases, whereas only fibrinogen gamma chain (FIBG) and alpha-fetoprotein (FETA) exhibited dysregulated glycosylation specifically in HCC. Glycoproteins with dysregulated N-glycosylation across all liver diseases were enriched in pathways including complement and coagulation cascades (e.g., CLUS, FIBB, A2MG), cholesterol metabolism (e.g., APOB, APOH, PLTP), platelet activation (e.g., VWF, FIBG, FIBB, THRB), extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interactions (e.g., VWF, VTNC, TSP1), fibrinolysis (e.g., FA12, HRG, APOH), and lymphocyte-mediated immunity (e.g., IGHA2, IGHM, HEMO) (Supplementary Fig. 19e–f). Additionally, certain dysregulated glycoproteins in HCC and liver cirrhosis were associated with negative regulation of hemostasis and coagulation (Supplementary Fig. 19e).
Protein N-glycosylation is a highly regulated process that includes sequential steps of initiation, trimming or processing, branching and elongation, and capping, which are controlled by the ordered actions of a variety of glycosyltransferases, glycosidases, and other regulators in the ER and Golgi compartments28. To understand whether alterations in these enzymes and regulators are involved in driving the N-glycosylation changes observed in HCC, we analyzed gene expression data from TCGA-LIHC dataset, focusing on 307 genes annotated to involve in human N-glycosylation pathway in Reactome database (Supplementary Data 7). A global upregulation of glycogenes was observed in tumor liver tissues (Fig. 6a). We also found that a small portion of the tumors exhibited glycogene expression patterns similar to those of healthy tissue, implying the heterogeneity of glycosylation in HCC tumors.
Differential expression analysis (DEA) revealed 118 upregulated glycogenes (FDR < 0.05, log2FC > 1) and only two downregulated glycogenes (FDR < 0.05, log2FC < −1) (Fig. 6b), indicating an overall enhancement of N-glycosylation in tumor cells. Notably, DPAGT1, a critical enzyme catalyzing the transfer of GlcNAc to dolichol phosphate, the initial step of N-glycan biosynthesis, exhibits a significant upregulation (1.9-fold). Similarly, multiple ALG family genes (e.g., ALG1/3/5/6/12), responsible for assembling the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor, also display increased expression levels (1.5 to 2-fold). The oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, essential for transferring glycan precursors onto nascent polypeptides, is notably upregulated. The catalytic subunit STT3A exhibits a 2.3-fold increase, while other OST subunits, including DDOST, RPN1, RPN2, and TUSC3, also show significant overexpression. This suggests that tumor cells might enhance the efficiency of N-glycan attachment, facilitating the glycosylation of a broader range of glycoproteins. In parallel, the ER-resident molecular chaperones calnexin (CANX) and calreticulin (CALR), which mediate glycoprotein folding quality control, are upregulated (~2-fold). Collectively, these findings indicate that HCC cells augment both the initial glycan biosynthesis and transfer steps, reinforcing an enhanced N-glycosylation landscape.
Further supporting this trend, multiple N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases (GnTs) involved in N-glycan branching and elongation are substantially upregulated. MGAT1 (GnT-I), an important enzyme catalyzing the conversion of high-mannose glycans into hybrid or complex structures, is upregulated (~1.4-fold), which is consistent with its known association with dedifferentiation and malignancy in HCC29. More strikingly, MGAT4A/B (GnT-IVa/IVb), responsible for adding β1,4-GlcNAc to form tri- and tetra-antennary glycans, are upregulated ~2-fold, while MGAT5 (GnT-V), the key enzyme generating β1,6-GlcNAc branching, a hallmark of tumor progression30, is highly upregulated by more than 3-fold (log₂FC = 1.73). This is in accordance with our glycomics results that tri- and tetra-antennary glycans were upregulated (Fig. 3i). MGAT3 (GnT-III), which catalyzes bisecting GlcNAc addition and has been proposed to counteract MGAT5-mediated branching thus being an anti-metastasis factor31,32, also exhibits substantial upregulation (~5-fold). This is also consistent with our glycomics results (Fig. 3i). Additionally, β1,4-galactosyltransferases (B4GALT2/3/4/6), which catalyze terminal galactosylation, are all significantly overexpressed (~2-fold). It is worth noting that B4GALT1, the predominant β1,4-galactosyltransferase in human liver, was not significant in TCGA-LIHC dataset but has been reported elsewhere to be downregulated in HCC tissues33. Therefore, despite the observed upregulation of B4GALT2 and B4GALT3, their more restrictive substrate specificities and narrow organ distributions may not fully compensate for the loss of B4GALT1 activity, which is consistent with the overall decrease in galactosylation observed in our glycomics data (Fig. 3i).
HCC tissues exhibit substantial dysregulation in fucosylation and sialylation, both of which are crucial for modulating glycoprotein stability, receptor signaling, and immune evasion28. Core fucosylation, catalyzed by FUT8, is markedly increased (~1.7-fold). Additionally, FUT3, which mediates Lewis antigen fucosylation, is highly upregulated (~4-fold), suggesting a shift towards an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment34. This agrees with our findings in glycomics (Fig. 3i) that fucosylation was upregulated. In the context of sialylation, multiple α2,3- and α2,6-sialyltransferases (STs) exhibit significant upregulation. ST3GAL2/3/4, which catalyze α2,3-sialylation, are upregulated (1.7–3.3-fold), whereas ST6GAL1, the dominant α2,6-sialyltransferase, remains highly expressed in HCC, although its expression does not show a significant increase. Notably, ST6GAL2 and ST3GAL6, which participates in α2,6- and α2,3- sialylation respectively, are both downregulated (~50% and ~1.6-fold decrease, respectively). These findings suggest that HCC cells preferentially upregulate α2,6-sialylation via ST6GAL1 while selectively reducing certain minor sialylation pathways, which is consistent with our glycomics results (Supplementary Fig. 9). The glycogene expression pattern was further validated in seven GEO datasets (Fig. 6c, Supplementary Fig. 20a–h), indicating highly conservative disease-related N-glycosylation dysregulation across populations.
Finally, we conducted a survival analysis to identify glycogenes with prognostic potential. Of the 307 glycogenes assessed, 158, 141, 145, and 109 were significantly associated with overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-free interval (DFI), respectively (Supplementary Data 9). Notably, galactosyltransferases emerged as key prognostic indicators. For instance, B4GALT2 was significantly linked to overall survival (Fig. 6d, e), whereas B4GALT3 was strongly associated with disease progression (Fig. 6f, g). Additionally, other critical glycogenes, including ALG3, DDOST, MAN1B1, MOGS, and UGGT2, exhibited notable prognostic relevance. These findings suggest that glycosylation may play a crucial role in modulating disease progression and prognosis, offering potential therapeutic targets for future interventions.
Twenty-six N-glycans with a missing proportion less than 1% were selected for training machine learning-based diagnostic models (Methods). Of these, 20 exhibited significant differences across the four groups, with 14 differing between healthy controls (HC) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), 17 between chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and HCC, and 13 between liver cirrhosis (LC) and HCC. All 26 glycans with reliable detection were included in the models to capture potential non-linear interactions. The GZ-I cohort was randomly divided into a training set (n = 526) and an internal validation set (n = 218). Two external validation sets (n = 186 for GZ-II cohort; n = 144 for XZ cohort) were used to assess the models’ generalizability (Fig. 7a). Three models were developed to classify HCC versus HC, HCC versus CHB, and HCC versus LC samples. This approach supports a pre-screening strategy, enabling tailored HCC diagnosis for patients with pre-existing chronic liver diseases (Fig. 7b).
Optimal algorithms and hyperparameter configurations were selected using state-of-the-art AutoML techniques, guided by cross-validation performance on the training set (Methods). All three models demonstrated high classification performance across the internal and two external validation sets (Fig. 7c–e). On the internal validation set, Model 1 (HCC vs. HC) achieved an ROC AUC of 0.93 (95% CI 0.892–0.975), Model 2 (HCC vs. CHB) an ROC AUC of 0.90 (95% CI 0.838–0.955), and Model 3 (HCC vs. LC) an ROC AUC of 0.84 (95% CI 0.770–0.907). Notably, all three models maintained consistent performance in the external validation cohorts (GZ-II and XZ), with only a slight decrease (Fig. 7c–e, Supplementary Fig. 21a), despite potential differences in population characteristics and medical facilities, demonstrating robust generalization and resilience to distribution shifts.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), the most widely used biomarker for HCC, is limited by its low sensitivity. In contrast, our N-glycome-based machine learning models demonstrated superior diagnostic performance, detecting up to 80% of AFP-negative HCC cases (Supplementary Fig. 21b), highlighting their potential as a robust and sensitive alternative for HCC diagnosis. Compared to AFP alone (Supplementary Fig. 21c), all three models exhibited significantly superior performance (DeLong test, P = 0.001, 0.005, and 0.026 for Models 1, 2, and 3, respectively). Combining glycans with AFP did not enhance performance (Supplementary Fig. 21d), indicating that the N-glycome alone captures all diagnostic information provided by AFP for HCC detection. These results highlight the high diagnostic performance and robustness of our N-glycome-based models, which not only outperform the current clinical biomarker AFP but also demonstrate consistent effectiveness across two independent external validation cohorts.
We then evaluated the diagnostic performance of N-glycome profiles when no pre-screening is available, i.e., differentiating HCC and all non-HCC samples. The model, Model 4, had comparable performance (ROC AUC: 0.87, 95% CI 0.818–0.915) (Fig. 7f), better than AFP (Supplementary Fig. 21c–d). To further assess the potential for early diagnosis, we evaluated the performance of the four models across different TNM stages (Supplementary Fig. 21e). All four models achieved ROC AUCs above 0.80 for stages II, III, and IV, and they retained acceptable diagnostic power even for stage I HCC patients, with AUC values reaching 0.859 (HCC vs HC). These findings demonstrate that our models hold strong promise for the early detection of HCC.
We also evaluated the clinical utility of predicted probabilities from Model 4 (PP4), for patient stratification (Fig. 7g–l). PP4 exhibited significant differences across all groups, including the three control groups (healthy controls, chronic hepatitis B, and liver cirrhosis; Fig. 7g), indicating its potential as a reliable marker for monitoring liver disease progression. Furthermore, PP4 demonstrated significant associations with ALBI stages (Fig. 7h) and Child-Pugh classifications (Fig. 7j), with consistent patterns observed within HCC samples (Figs. 7i, k). These findings highlight PP4’s robust capacity to reflect liver function status. Additionally, PP4 showed significant variation across TNM stages, with higher values corresponding to more advanced cancer stages (Fig. 7l), underscoring its utility in cancer staging.
We utilized the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) technique to assess feature importance across the four diagnostic models (Fig. 7m–p). Three glycans—H6N5F1S3, H5N4F1, and H3N4F1—consistently ranked as the top three features in all models, maintaining the same order. Additionally, three other glycans—H5N2, H6N5S3, and H5N4S1—consistently placed between the 4th and 6th ranks, though in varying orders. The significance of these six glycans was corroborated by permutation feature importance analysis (Supplementary Fig. 21f). Furthermore, the importance of these glycans was validated by training ML models using only the six most informative glycans (Supplementary Fig. 22). The models maintained nearly the same performance across all three cohorts, with only a slight, non-significant decrease (DeLong test, P > 0.05). Individually, these glycans exhibited modest classification performance compared to the models (Supplementary Fig. 23), suggesting that their collective contribution arises from synergistic, non-linear interactions. These glycans originate from diverse glycosylation sites: H5N2 is predominantly linked to IGHM N46, H5N4F1 and H3N4F1 are primarily associated with immunoglobulins (e.g., IGHM, IGHG1, IGHA2), while H6N5F1S3, H6N5S3, and H5N4S1 have varied site origins (Supplementary Fig. 24a–f).
Collectively, these results demonstrate that serum N-glycome-based machine learning models not only outperform traditional biomarkers like AFP but also provide valuable insights into liver disease progression and cancer staging through robust stratification and feature importance analyses, paving the way for precision diagnostics in HCC.
The comprehensive multi-cohort and multi-omics investigation presented here elucidates the intricate relationship between serum N-glycome dynamics and liver disease progression, particularly in HCC. Our findings not only validate the clinical relevance of N-glycosylation alterations as functional biomarkers but also provide mechanistic insights into how hepatic pathophysiology reshapes the N-glycome landscape. The integration of glycomics, glycoproteomics, transcriptomics, and machine learning approaches offers a paradigm shift in understanding liver disease heterogeneity and opens new avenues for precision diagnostics. The strong correlation between serum N-glycome patterns and LFTs (e.g., ALBI score, AAR, and ALB) underscores glycosylation as a sensitive marker of hepatic synthetic capacity. Interestingly, the reported elevation of bisecting GlcNAc 19,35 (catalyzed by MGAT3) and core fucosylation 36,37 (catalyzed by FUT8) in advanced liver diseases were found to be mainly associated with deterioration of liver functions, regardless of concrete hepatopathy. Notably, the inverse relationship between galactosylation/sialylation and disease severity may reflect impaired hepatocyte Golgi function, as β1,4-galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases require intact cellular trafficking machinery 38 . These findings extend the concept of liver function tests (LFTs) beyond conventional protein biomarkers like albumin, suggesting that N-glycome could enhance existing prognostic models such as ALBI. The conserved glycome-liver function relationship across subgroups argues against mere epiphenomenal associations, supporting a direct role of hepatic metabolic stress in driving glycosylation remodeling. While HCC-enriched tri-/tetra-antennary fucosylated glycans (GCM1 cluster) align with the malignancy-associated "β1,6-branching surge" typically driven by MGAT5 (GnT-V) upregulation 30,[39][40][41] , our glycoproteomics analysis attributes the observed elevation of serum tri-/tetra-antennary glycans primarily to increased A1AG1 levels. As an acute-phase response protein, A1AG1 enhances macrophage immunosuppressive functions 42 and likely contributes disproportionately to serum glycome alterations. Notably, this interpretation does not exclude concurrent global changes in N-glycan branching: there might still be a global up-regulation of tetra-antennary glycans across glycosites, though not valided in this research. The apparent coexistence of site-specific glycoform enrichment and systemic glycosyltransferase activation reflects the multi-layered regulation of protein glycosylation in malignancies. Furthermore, the hybrid glycan H5N3S1 elevation across liver diseases, traced to A2MG N869 site, exemplifies how acute-phase response proteins acquire distinct glycosylation during chronic inflammation, a phenomenon potentially facilitating immune evasion through lectin receptor modulation 43 . By applying sialic acid linkage specific derivatization, we also observed a decrease of α2,6-linked sialylation. This is in line with the global manifestation of sialylation decrease for serum glycoproteins predominantly carry α2,6-linked sialic acids 44 , as well as the downregulation of ST6GAL2 at gene expression level. The transcriptomics and glycoproteomics analysis revealed two distinct pathogenic axes: 1) Global glycosylation pathway activation (e.g., OST complex upregulation) enhancing glycan diversity supported by a systemically upregulated glycogene expression, and 2) Site-specific regulatory events modulating individual glycoprotein functions involved in immune response and hemostasis. This is particularly relevant to hepatocellular carcinoma, where alterations in immune function and hemostatic disorders are common [45][46][47] . Specifically, unique glycosylation changes in proteins such as fibrinogen and alpha-fetoprotein are observed in HCC, underscoring the importance of these site-specific events in the disease. These findings bridge bulk glycome changes with precise molecular pathobiology. While global shifts in glycan types offer valuable biological insights, their diagnostic utility is limited; the true diagnostic strength emerges from integrative machine learning models that leverage the full multi-dimensional glycan profile. The machine learning models' superior diagnostic performance over AFP, particularly in AFPnegative HCC, addresses a critical unmet need in surveillance programs. Two external validation cohorts ensured a robust evaluation of our models, circumventing the "illusory generalizability" common in machine learning based medical models 48 . In the current era of precision medicine, multimodal molecular diagnostics are poised to become a prevailing trend 49 . Among the array of emerging noninvasive circulating biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we believe our glycomic model holds significant potential to enhance the accuracy of HCC surveillance and management. We have demonstrated that our glycomic model complements AFP, suggesting that integration with other non-invasive biomarkers and surveillance procedures like imaging could establish a more accurate diagnostic pipeline, potentially reducing reliance on invasive biopsies. Notably, the diagnostic performance for distinguishing HCC from cirrhosis (Model 3) was lower than for other comparisons, reflecting the welldocumented clinical challenge of separating malignancy from its cirrhotic background 1,49 . While this study advances hepatic glycomics significantly, certain limitations warrant mention. The Chinese cohort focus necessitates validation in Western populations with differing HCC etiologies. Technical constraints in distinguishing isomeric glycans may underrepresent structural diversity. Future single-cell glycotranscriptomic studies could resolve intra-tumoral heterogeneity, and functional validation of key glycosites is needed. Another limitation of our study is the lack of longitudinal follow-up data, which prevented us from directly assessing the utility of PP4 for risk monitoring in cirrhotic patients. In conclusion, this work establishes serum N-glycome profiling as a powerful tool for liver disease management. By decoding the "glycosylation language" of hepatic pathophysiology, we move closer to personalized monitoring frameworks and enzyme-targeted therapies for HCC.

Leveraging medical imaging and deep learning for diagnosis of breast cancer using histopathological images
Globally, breast cancer is one the life-threatening diseases among women. Breast histopathological image (HI) investigation is the most effective method applied for the recognition of cancer malignancy. Manual breast HI investigation is, still, time-consuming, abstract, and susceptible to human errors. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) became a possible and popular solution for medicinal image investigation owing to current developments in computer memory and power. Still, the CAD methods performance required to be enhanced to apply for practical reasons. In recent times, deep learning (DL) like convolution neural networks (CNN) have proved reliable in identifying BC targets from pathological images. This paper proposes a Leveraging Medical Imaging for Early Breast Cancer Detection Using Deep Leaning (LMIBCD-DL). The LMIBCD-DL approach presents a reliable tool for supporting automated breast cancer diagnosis in medical applications. Initially, the LMIBCD-DL method applies wiener filtering (WF) for the image preprocessing step to effectively reduce noise while preserving important tissue structures. For feature extractors, the squeeze-and-excitation ResNet (SE-ResNet) model is employed to capture rich and discriminative representations from complex histopathological patterns. Finally, the bi-directional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) is utilized for the BC detection process. The comparative results demonstrated a superior accuracy value of 98.72% over the existing methodologies under dissimilar measures and the BreakHis dataset.
In this manuscript, a novel LMIBCD-DL approach is introduced. The LMIBCD-DL approach presents a reliable tool for supporting automated BC diagnosis in medical applications. To accomplish that, the LMIBCD-DL model has image pre-processing, feature extractor, BC detection, and parameter tuning. Figure 1 specifies the overall workflow of the LMIBCD-DL model.
Initially, the LMIBCD-DL method applies WF for the image preprocessing step to effectively reduce noise while preserving crucial tissue structures32. This method is chosen as it effectually mitigates noise without blurring significant tissue information that are considered crucial in histopathological assessment. Additionally, this model adapts to local image discrepancy, unlike median filter (ML) or simple smoothing technique. Furthermore, WF ensures that meaningful patters are captured by WF and also efficiently preserves edges and fine structures that carry diagnostic data. WF also provides a balanced trade-off between noise removal and structural fidelity, compared to more intrinsic denoising models. Thus, it improves the reliability of downstream DL methods by giving cleaner, high-quality input.
WF is a great noise reduction method applied in image preprocessing, mainly efficient in improving the quality of medical images like CT scans, MRI, and mammograms for cancer recognition. It works according to statistical valuation, targeting to reduce the mean square error (MSE) among the new and the restored image. Unlike simpler filters, the WF adjusts to the local image modification, maintaining edges and fine details while eliminating Gaussian noise. This is important in cancer imaging, whereas correct visualization of smaller anomalies like microcalcifications or tumors is important. By increasing image clarity, WF advances the performance of the following classification and feature extraction phases. It additionally aids in decreasing false negatives and positives in the diagnostic procedure. Generally, it plays an important role in constructing a strong and noise-resilient BC detection pipeline.

Additionally, the BiLSTM network is employed for the BC detection process34. Machine learning application in colon cancer treatment outcome prediction
Colon cancer represents a significant global health burden, accounting for a substantial portion of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. Many studies have been conducted to predict survival outcomes; however, most of these analyses have been performed predominantly via basic statistical methods. The aim of this study was to perform machine learning techniques to build models for survival prediction in patients with colon cancer. A retrospective review of 764 colon cancer patients treated over a 10-year period facilitated the construction of a detailed dataset containing 44 predictor variables and one dependent variable, the survival status of the patients (alive or dead). The data were randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing sets. Prognostic features from the database were used to build machine learning algorithms, including random forest, logistic regression, XGBoost, gradient boosting, categorical boosting (CatBoost), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), multilayer perceptron (MLP), and one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) to predict progressive disease outcomes. Models were validated for sensitivity, accuracy and specificity, with predictive ability assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and area under the curve (AUC) calculations. In terms of model accuracy and precision, almost all algorithms produced similar outcomes; however, among the evaluated models, CatBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 0.813, and the random forest model demonstrated the best precision of 0.727, whereas the logistic regression model exhibited the highest recall of 0.658 on the test set. Machine learning for predicting functional outcomes in acute ischemic stroke: insights from a nationwide stroke registry
Accurately predicting the prognosis of patients with acute ischemic stroke at discharge remains highly challenging after active treatment. The aim of this retrospective nationwide registry-based study was to identify key predictors associated with favorable outcomes and to develop machine learning models for patient outcome prediction. Analysis of a comprehensive dataset of 40,586 patients revealed younger age (odds ratio [OR]: 0.975; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.972-0.977; p < 0.001), lower initial National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score (OR: 0.862; 95% CI: 0.855-0.868; p < 0.001), mechanical thrombectomy (OR: 2.617; 95% CI: 2.185-3.134; p < 0.001), and rehabilitation therapy (OR: 2.765; 95% CI: 2.530-3.022; p < 0.001) as significant predictors of good functional outcome. We developed three machine learning models-random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and logistic regressionto predict favorable functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale score, ≤ 2) at discharge. Among these, the RF model revealed superior predictive performance, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.87, compared to the SVM and logistic regression, each achieving an AUC of 0.80. This study underscores the transformative potential of machine learning in stroke management, predicting and improving patient outcomes and streamlining healthcare delivery.

Missing data related to onset-to-image time and onset-to-door time variables accounted for less than 3% of the total patient dataset. ese missing values were replaced using the median value before analysis.
This retrospective observational study analyzed data from the Korean National Stroke Registry collected over a 5-year period. The nationwide ASAR was established in Korea to control the quality of acute stroke care. Data for this registry are collected for 6 months each year, with the selected period determined by the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) to assess healthcare quality. In Korea, ASAR has been established, examined, graded by the HIRA, and analyzed. These ASAR data are collected once every 2 years from approximately 220 hospitals nationwide, providing a comprehensive dataset of 40,586 patients diagnosed with acute stroke. Patients first diagnosed with acute cerebral infarction within 7 days of symptom onset and admitted to one of the 220 nationally certified stroke centers were included. Patients were excluded if they had a prior history of stroke, had been previously hospitalized at another institution for the same event, or if the diagnosis was related to trauma.
This study was conducted in partnership with the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service under the National Registry Research Project. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Catholic University Hospital (IRB No. UC23Z1SE0023). The requirement for informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Uijeongbu St. Mary’s Hospital, The Catholic University of Korea, due to the retrospective nature of the study. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations.
Clinical and demographic data, including age, sex, medical history (atrial fibrillation, smoking, and comorbidities), NIHSS score at admission, laboratory results, stroke management interventions (intravenous thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, stroke unit admission, rehabilitation therapy, and dietary adjustments), and time metrics (onset-to-door and onset-to-imaging times), were retrieved from the electronic medical records. Rigorous data-cleaning processes were implemented to ensure the inclusion of complete, high-quality records, which were essential for conducting robust statistical and ML analyses. All data were anonymized using encrypted personal identification numbers in partnership with HIRA under the Joint Project on Quality Assessment Research in Korea. Variables with more than 5% missing data were excluded before analysis whenever possible. Functional outcome data with incomplete descriptions were removed entirely. Missing data related to onset-to-image time and onset-to-door time variables accounted for less than 3% of the total patient dataset. These missing values were replaced using the median value before analysis.
Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient demographics and baseline clinical characteristics. Mean values and standard deviations were used for continuous variables, while frequencies and percentages were calculated for categorical variables. Outcomes, including the rate of favorable functional outcomes (mRS score ≤ 2), IVT, mechanical thrombectomy, and surgical interventions, were analyzed to understand treatment efficacy and prognostic factors. A multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to determine the association between independent variables—age, sex, initial NIHSS, CCI, atrial fibrillation, smoking, stroke management interventions, and hospital characteristics—and good functional outcomes. ORs and CIs were calculated for each predictor variable. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.42).
The predictive modeling process was designed to follow a structured and systematic approach. Initially, data preprocessing steps were performed, including the removal of unnecessary columns such as “ID” and “year” to streamline the dataset. Categorical variables, including antithrombotic medications, were translated and encoded using one-hot encoding techniques to ensure compatibility with ML algorithms. The dataset was then divided into training and testing subsets, with 70% allocated for training and 30% for testing, while maintaining the distribution of the target variable, which was the achievement of a good functional outcome. Subsequently, feature selection focused on clinically relevant variables, including NIHSS scores, age, and specific time intervals, such as onset-to-image time. These features were prioritized based on their well-established influence on stroke outcomes, as highlighted in the existing literature.
For model development and evaluation, three distinct ML algorithms were implemented: RF, SVM, and logistic regression. Hyperparameter tuning was conducted to optimize model performance, with key parameters adjusted for each algorithm. Model performance was comprehensively evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC. Threshold optimization was performed for all models to enhance their predictive performance. The optimal decision threshold for each model was determined using Youden’s index, which balances sensitivity and specificity to maximize diagnostic performance.
Finally, the results were visualized and interpreted to provide a clearer understanding of the model outputs. ROC curves were plotted for all models to provide a comparative assessment of their performance. Additionally, variable importance was analyzed within the RF model to identify the most influential predictors and their relative contributions to the predictions.
