Sleep stage classification from ECG using machine learning: Evaluating the impact of signal duration
Sleep stage flagging is critical for diagnosing conditions like insomnia, sleep apnea, and narcolepsy. Traditional methods rely on time-intensive manual scoring by experts, limiting scalability and accessibility, especially in resource-limited settings. Automating sleep stage classification through signal processing and machine learning could improve diagnostic efficiency and reduce healthcare burdens. While prior studies have utilized multiple signals such as electroencephalogram (EEG), electromyogram (EMG), and electrocardiogram (ECG), this study focuses solely on ECG to provide a simpler, more accessible solution. By simplifying signal input, the approach enhances feasibility in resource-constrained environments. Features based on heart rate variability (HRV) and Poincaré plot descriptors were extracted and used to train machine learning models for five-stage sleep classification. The approach was evaluated using two publicly available datasets, the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum Sleep Staging Database and the MIT-BIH Polysomnographic Database, which were chosen for their varied recording environments and subject diversity. Neural Networks, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), XGBoost, and Random Forest were employed to assess performance. The highest classification accuracy of 67 % was achieved with long-duration ECG recordings, outperforming models trained on shorter segments by 12 %. These findings emphasize the impact of signal duration on classification performance and suggest opportunities to refine sleep stage prediction. The study demonstrates the feasibility of ECG-only systems for portable, low-cost, and scalable sleep monitoring. The insights gained may facilitate the development of more accessible and efficient sleep disorder detection, particularly in low-resource settings.
This study consists of three independent experiments conducted to evaluate the performance of sleep stage classification using only ECGbased features. The aim was to assess how different feature sets and signal durations influence classification outcomes. In the first experiment, features were extracted from 5-min ECG segments, aiming to reduce computational complexity compared to deep learning models applied directly to raw signals. The second experiment explored 30-s segments, with a broader set of features to account for reduced temporal context. The third experiment utilized 30-s ECG segments from a different dataset, incorporating additional geometric, statistical, and heart rate variability (HRV) features. A range of machine learning algorithms was evaluated across these studies. Each experiment is described in detail in the following sections. Instead of directly applying deep learning models to raw ECG signals, which typically require significant computational resources, this study focused on classifying sleep stages using features extracted from ECGderived signals. In particular, heart rate variability (HRV) and Poincaré-based representations were used as compact, interpretable alternatives. Each healthy ECG signal comprises three phases: P, QRS complex, and T, with the R peak typically used for heartbeat detection. HRV signals were derived from ECG using the Pan-Tompkins algorithm (Tompkins, 1985) to detect R peaks and calculate the time intervals between successive R peaks (Shaffer and Ginsberg, 2017). This resulted in a sequence of RR intervals forming the HRV signal. In addition to HRV, the Poincaré plot, another visualization method derived from HRV, was employed to extract additional dynamic features (Moharreri et al., 2010). It was defined as: where RR n is the interval between successive R peaks and n is the total number of intervals in each axis of Poincaré plot. This study used two datasets. In the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum dataset, 30-s epochs were merged when labeled with the same sleep stage, resulting in 5-min segments. In contrast, the MIT-BIH Polysomnographic dataset was used without merging, preserving the standard 30-s interval. HRV and Poincaré features were extracted from both, and statistical and geometrical features were added to enrich the input space. Across all studies, feature counts ranged from 11 to 52 depending on the interval and dataset. Shorter signal durations are more commonly used in clinical sleep studies. However, when the window size was reduced from 5 min to 30 s, a substantial decrease in classification accuracy was observed. To mitigate this decline, the number of extracted features was increased by incorporating geometrical measures (e.g., ellipse area and co-occurrence matrix-based metrics), statistical descriptors, and additional Poincaré-related features proposed by Moharreri et al. (2010). Three distinct classification studies were conducted: one using 5-min segments and two using 30-s segments. The first relied exclusively on a neural network, while the others explored additional models including K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), XGBoost, and Random Forest. To address class imbalance, a weighted loss was applied in neural networks. For the traditional classifiers, sampling techniques such as SMOTE, undersampling, and random oversampling were tested. For implementation, TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2015) was used for neural networks, while Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) handled conventional classifiers and cross-validation. All experiments were accelerated using an RTX 2060 GPU. The features utilized for classification are summarized in Table 2, categorized by type: statistical descriptors, HRV-based measures, Poincaré plot-based metrics, and geometrical features. Study 1 employed a subset of statistical and Poincaré-based features on longer 5-min signal segments. Study 2 expanded the feature set for 30-s segments, introducing several geometrical descriptors to capture temporal variation. Study 3, based on the MIT-BIH dataset, utilized the complete feature set, including ten novel features proposed by Moharreri et al. (2010) to further evaluate model performance under different conditions. This structured comparison highlights how feature selection varied across studies based on segment duration and dataset characteristics, supporting a more nuanced analysis of classifier effectiveness. In this study, classifier performance was assessed using commonly applied metrics in sleep-stage classification, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These metrics were computed from the confusion matrix based on the number of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), and false negatives (FN). Accuracy, which indicates the proportion of all correctly classified epochs relative to the total number of evaluated epochs, is computed as defined by Equation (3): Precision was calculated to reflect the proportion of correctly identified epochs among those assigned to a specific sleep stage, following the formulation in Equation (4): Recall (sensitivity) was employed to quantify the proportion of true epochs of a given sleep stage that were correctly recognized by the classifier, as mathematically expressed in Equation ( 5): Finally, the F1-score, defined as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, was used to provide a balanced measure of performance, particularly in the presence of class imbalance commonly observed in sleepstage datasets. This relationship is governed by Equation ( 6): To provide a clear overview of the entire pipeline developed in this study, the complete workflow is visualized in Fig. 2. As illustrated, the process begins with raw ECG signals, which are passed through a series of pre-processing filters, including a notch filter to eliminate powerline interference, a high-pass filter at 5 Hz to remove baseline wander, and a low-pass filter at 15 Hz to reduce high-frequency noise. The cleaned ECG signal is then fed into operational blocks, where R peaks are detected using the Pan-Tompkins algorithm. These R peaks are used to compute the HRV signal and subsequently generate the Poincaré plot. In the next phase, various features, statistical, HRV-based, Poincaré-based, and geometrical, are extracted from the processed signals. These features are then normalized and, if necessary, refined through feature selection techniques. Finally, the prepared feature sets are passed to the prediction stage, where models are trained, optimized, and tested to classify sleep stages effectively.
This research explored various algorithms for sleep stage prediction using solely ECG signals, a non-traditional input for sleep scoring. To evaluate model performance, two datasets were employed across three consecutive studies. Study 1 used longer ECG segments (5 min) from the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum dataset and served as a baseline for assessing model feasibility. A neural network trained for 250 epochs using the Adam optimizer achieved 67 % accuracy (Fig. 3). To prevent overfitting, dropout layers (0.3 and 0.2) were incorporated (Kingma and Ba, 2014;Srivastava et al., 2014). While this performance was promising, it lacked clinical robustness, prompting further exploration in Study 2. The training curve demonstrated a consistent upward trajectory, while the validation curve exhibited moderate fluctuations before stabilizing. Although the resulting accuracy indicated a fair level of generalization, it remained below thresholds typically considered sufficient for clinical deployment. This outcome, while encouraging, emphasized the limitations of using ECG-derived HRV and Poincaré features alone for sleep staging and motivated further investigation in Study 2, which employed shorter signal intervals and a broader feature set. For context, the 67 % accuracy obtained in Study 1 for five-stage classification using 5-min ECG segments is broadly consistent with, though slightly lower than, performance reported in recent HRV-based approaches evaluated on public datasets and wearable sensor data. Several episode-level deep learning methods have achieved accuracies in the range of approximately 65-88 %, depending on the number of classes and sensing modalities employed (Pini et al., 2022;Fonseca et al., 2023). Studies using PPG-or HRV-based wearables that integrate heart rate with movement or respiratory surrogates typically report 68-78 % accuracy for three or four class classification tasks, often under conditions involving longer training durations or multimodal inputs (Silva et al., 2024). By comparison, ECG-derived HRV studies targeting full five-stage classification have generally demonstrated lower accuracy than EEG-based approaches, although they consistently show that multi-minute windows enhance HRV discriminability (Radha et al., 2019). Accordingly, the 67 % accuracy achieved here using purely ECG-derived HRV and Poincaré features in combination with a compact neural architecture is aligned with prior literature and reflects the expected trade-off between signal simplicity and stage-resolution capacity. In Study 2, the neural network achieved 40 % accuracy on the test set, despite the inclusion of more complex features. Training was conducted for a maximum of 50 epochs and was halted early using an early stopping criterion. Consistent with Study 1, the Adam optimizer and dropout regularization were applied. To validate these results and explore alternative models, classical machine learning algorithms, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), XGBoost, and Random Forest, were also evaluated under the same experimental conditions. In Study 2, traditional machine learning models were introduced to benchmark classification performance against the neural network baseline established in Study 1. Using 30-s signal segments and an expanded feature set, the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm achieved a modest average test accuracy of 27.64 %. Table 3 presents a summary of classification accuracy across all three studies, each of which employed a distinct combination of signal length, engineered features, and machine learning models. Signal features were progressively expanded and refined, while both traditional classifiers and neural networks were evaluated to assess performance trade-offs under varying experimental conditions. Interestingly, KNN showed a notable improvement in Study 3, achieving 34.83 %, which may be attributed to the addition of Co-Occurrence Matrix (COM) features that enriched the textural diversity of the feature space. Other classifiers presented mixed outcomes. XGBoost yielded the lowest performance in Study 2 with 18.21 % accuracy, indicating poor generalization under high feature complexity and limited signal length. In contrast, Random Forest demonstrated relatively strong results, achieving 42.27 % accuracy on the same dataset. These findings (summarized in Table 4) underscore how feature interaction and model architecture significantly impact classifier performance, especially under the constraints of short input duration and class imbalance. Despite various optimization efforts, including feature augmentation, undersampling techniques, and neural architecture tuning, the accuracy gains across models were limited to approximately 5 %. Fig. 6 presents confusion matrices for all classifiers, offering insight into stage-wise performance variability and modelspecific misclassification patterns. Fig. 5a-d presents the correlation heatmaps for both raw and engineered features derived from the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum and MIT-BIH datasets. These visual tools offer crucial insights into interfeature relationships, redundancy, and the impact of feature engineering on the model's input space. In Fig. 5a, representing the HMC dataset's 41 raw features, clusters of moderate to high correlation are visible, particularly among geometric and temporal descriptors. This pattern suggests potential multicollinearity, which could hinder model generalizability if not addressed. By contrast, Fig. 5b, which displays correlations among the 81 engineered features (created via pairwise feature multiplication), shows a more diverse and dispersed correlation pattern. While some new clusters of correlation appear, the matrix remains relatively structured, suggesting a controlled increase in complexity that could enhance discriminative power without overwhelming the classifier with noise. A similar trend is observed in the MIT-BIH dataset. Fig. 5c illustrates structured correlation clusters within the 52 raw features, again reflecting underlying physiological relationships. Fig. 5d, however, demonstrates that the 131 engineered features have lower overall inter-correlations, suggesting that the feature selection process successfully reduced redundancy and introduced complementary information. Overall, the transition from raw to engineered features, when guided by correlation structure, helped create a more orthogonal feature space. This likely contributed to improved model robustness and reduced overfitting by minimizing feature overlap and enhancing the classifier's ability to detect subtle differences across sleep stages. The confusion matrices presented in Fig. 6, encompassing both Study 2 (HMC dataset) and Study 3 (MIT-BIH dataset), provide a detailed account of the classification performance across the five sleep stages using three classifiers: KNN, XGBoost, and Random Forest. These matrices offer a granular view of stage-specific classification outcomes, particularly highlighting the strengths and limitations of each algorithm under varying dataset characteristics. In Study 2, the KNN model demonstrated high classification accuracy for the Wake and N2 stages but exhibited difficulty differentiating transitional stages like N1, which was frequently misclassified as either Wake or N2. This underscores its limited sensitivity to transitional stages. XGBoost showed improved separation across most stages, particularly for N2 and REM, although persistent confusion between N1 and N2 was observed. Random Forest delivered the most balanced results across all classes in Study 2, notably improving predictions for N3 and REM. Its robustness to both feature noise and class imbalance was evident, though N1 still proved challenging to classify accurately. In Study 3, the MIT-BIH dataset presented additional challenges. KNN again favored dominant stages like Wake and N2, while showing even greater misclassification for N1 and N3. XGBoost performed less effectively here than in Study 2, particularly in distinguishing REM from light sleep stages, likely due to reduced physiological contrast in this dataset. Random Forest once again emerged as the most stable classifier, achieving higher precision and recall for REM and N3 while still underperforming in N1 classification. These results emphasize both dataset-dependent variability and classifier-specific trade-offs in ECG-based sleep staging. While Random Forest consistently outperformed other models in handling class imbalance and subtle feature patterns, transitional stages like N1 remain a key limitation across all models. Interestingly, the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm demonstrated a measurable improvement in Study 3 compared to Study 2, as shown in Table 5. In Study 2, average validation accuracies across ten folds hovered around 27 %, with minimal variance between folds, reflecting the limitations of KNN when applied to short 30-s ECG segments and a basic feature set. In contrast, Study 3, which utilized the same segment duration but introduced a significantly expanded feature This improvement suggests that the enriched feature space, particularly the inclusion of textural and geometrical attributes, enhanced the model's ability to capture subtle differences between sleep stages. Fold-wise accuracy ranged from 32.6 % to 38.9 %, indicating more stable and improved generalization across the MIT-BIH dataset. While still below clinically acceptable thresholds, these results highlight the impact of feature diversity on even simple classifiers and suggest that certain engineered features may increase the separability of challenging classes when high-complexity models are not used. In Study 3, the KNN model employed a 10-fold cross-validation approach, achieving an average accuracy of 34.83 % on the test set. This reflects a noticeable improvement compared to Study 2, highlighting the value of incorporating Co-Occurrence Matrix (COM) features. However, despite this improved performance, the model's reliability remained limited. The XGBoost model recorded an accuracy of 31.94 %, showing only a marginal increase from Study 2 and continuing to struggle with distinguishing certain sleep stages, particularly N3 and REM. Random Forest, on the other hand, produced the highest accuracy among the non-neural classifiers in Study 3 at 48.73 %, nearly matching the performance of the neural network. These results are summarized in Table 4, and the detailed classification outcomes are visualized in Fig. 6. To assess generalizability and robustness, the models were tested on a completely independent dataset in Study 3. In this investigation, the dataset was enriched with 52 features, derived through feature multiplication and correlation filtering. A neural network trained on this feature-enriched dataset achieved a test accuracy of 48 %, marking a modest improvement over the results obtained in Study 2. However, this level of performance still reflects the inherent limitations of relying solely on ECG-derived features for fine-grained sleep stage classification. As shown in Fig. 4, the model was trained for a maximum of 50 epochs, with early stopping applied to prevent overfitting. The validation accuracy plateaued around 48 %, suggesting that, despite feature expansion, the model's ability to generalize across unseen subjects and sleep stages remained constrained. These results further underscore the challenges of ECG-only approaches, particularly when applied to more complex classification schemes involving short-duration segments. When comparing performance across datasets, Random Forest emerged as the most stable algorithm, maintaining consistent performance despite class imbalances. In contrast, XGBoost exhibited notable difficulty with the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum dataset, delivering lower accuracy and poor generalization. The MIT-BIH dataset further revealed model limitations, particularly its failure to correctly classify any N3 sleep stages, even after multiple runs. However, REM, Wake, and N2 stages were identified more reliably, which aligns with the general sleep distribution where N2 dominates the sleep cycle. Table 6 presents the precision values across individual sleep stages (N1, N2, N3, REM, Wake) for each classification algorithm in both datasets. The data reveals that precision varies notably not only between classifiers but also across datasets. In Study 2 (HMC dataset), XGBoost achieved the highest precision for REM (0.52) and Wake (0.51), suggesting its relative advantage in detecting these physiologically distinct stages. However, both KNN and Random Forest showed moderate precision, particularly struggling with N1, where all classifiers recorded values below 0.20. In contrast, Study 3 (MIT-BIH dataset) showed a marked improvement in N1 precision for Random Forest (0.36) and KNN (0.26), indicating a dataset-specific variation in classifier sensitivity. Across both datasets, N2 consistently exhibited the highest precision, especially with XGBoost (0.57 in Study 3), reflecting the robustness of this stage's physiological signature in ECG-derived features. REM and Wake stages also maintained strong precision, particularly under XGBoost and Random Forest. Despite slight variability, Random Forest emerged as the most consistently balanced model across sleep stages and datasets, highlighting its generalizability. Notably, N3 presented the greatest instability in precision, with a drop to 0.11 for KNN in Study 3, underscoring the inherent challenge of detecting deep sleep from short, single-lead ECG segments. By comparing the results, Random Forest showed the most stable results in terms of data imbalance and predicted consistent results across both datasets. In contrast, XGBoost struggled with the Haaglanden Medisch Centrum dataset, particularly the overall accuracy. The MIT-BIH dataset failed to predict any N3 sleep stage correctly and misclassified all despite multiple tests but consistently classified the REM sleep stage and performed well on the Wake and N2 stages. As indicated by this research findings and mentioned by Sun et al. ( 2020), in the time-series analysis, longer-duration time windows return more robust results. The model's performance generally declined for the N3 and REM stages due to their distribution (Radha et al., 2019), while most people spend half of their sleep in the N2 stage (Sun et al., 2020). The Random Forest-based feature importance analysis revealed that several Poincaré-derived descriptors, along with non-linear geometric indices, were among the strongest contributors to model discrimination. Ratio, Skew, EI, Kurtosis, GI, and the Poincaré-derived Ptri and Area emerged as the highest-ranked predictors, each demonstrating importance values above 0.034. Classical HRV metrics such as SD2, SD1, SDSD, RMSSD, SDRR, and CVR also appeared prominently within the upper portion of the ranking, indicating that both linear and non-linear measures contributed meaningfully to stage separation. Additional geometric features derived from the ellipse or rectangular Poincaré approximations (vRect, pRect, sRect) were similarly influential, suggesting that shape-based variability captured by second-order interactions plays a notable role in distinguishing sleep stages. Consequently, the distribution of importance values supported the relevance of both traditional HRV measures and engineered interaction features in capturing physiologically meaningful distinctions across sleep stages. To better understand the discriminative power of the extracted features, a statistical analysis of p-values was conducted using one-way ANOVA for each pairwise comparison of sleep stages. The results, presented in Table 7 through 9, reveal important trends in feature relevance across different datasets and segment durations. In Study 1 (Table 7), the Haaglanden dataset with longer segments showed clear statistical separation between stages, with several features yielding low p-values, thereby supporting their use in feature selection and dimensionality reduction. In Study 2 (Table 8), which utilized 30-s segments from the same dataset, significant differences were still observed for many stage pairs. However, shorter segment duration introduced more overlap, illustrating the trade-off between temporal resolution and feature separability. Study 3 extended this analysis to the MIT-BIH dataset (Table 9), using the same 30-s segment duration. Consistent with earlier findings, specific stage comparisons such as N2 vs. Wake produced multiple features with p-values below 0.0001, indicating strong discriminative potential. In contrast, comparisons like N2 vs. REM yielded higher p-values, suggesting weaker separability. The consistency of low p-values across datasets for certain features points to their crossdataset robustness, offering valuable insight for future model generalization. While Study 3 achieved better classification performance overall, the p-values from Study 2 were more consistently low, especially among geometrical features derived from Poincaré plots and HRV analysis. These features often demonstrated strong discriminative capability, even when overall classification performance was lower. Interestingly, some features, such as variance, performed inconsistently. Although variance typically produced low p-values, its comparison of N1 and Wake stages yielded unusually high values, implying limited utility in those specific cases. These findings underscore the importance of careful feature selection, as performance can vary significantly depending on the specific stage comparison. Features that perform well overall may still underperform in critical pairwise scenarios, thereby reducing their effectiveness in multiclass classification. The aggregated confusion-matrix metrics across the three studies provide a clearer view of how each classifier handled the five sleep stages. As shown in Table 10, performance varied substantially across algorithms, with the Random Forest model exhibiting consistently stronger macro-level precision and recall relative to KNN, XGBoost, and the neural network baselines. In particular, Random Forest demonstrated more stable precision for N2, N3, and W, whereas KNN and XGBoost showed larger drops in minority stages such as N1 and REM, especially in Studies 2 and 3. The neural network models displayed the widest performance variability across datasets, with lower macro-averaged precision and recall. Overall, the confusion-matrix summary highlights that Random Forest not only reached the highest average accuracy but also maintained comparatively balanced stage-wise discrimination, particularly for N2 and wake segments, where many of the other models struggled. Collectively, these three studies evaluated a range of machine learning models and ECG-derived feature sets to classify sleep stages under different time constraints and dataset characteristics. Study 1, which used 5-min input segments and a smaller feature set, achieved the highest accuracy (67 %), highlighting the benefit of longer temporal context. In contrast, Study 3 adopted a more complex feature space, employing 52 engineered features, and yielded a moderate accuracy of 48 %. This suggests that richer feature representations can partially offset the limitations imposed by shorter input windows. Despite multiple refinements in Studies 2 and 3, including dropout regularization, feature engineering, and classifier tuning, overall classification performance remained modest, with neural networks and Random Forest models demonstrating the most consistent results. These findings underscore the inherent limitations of ECG-based sleep staging, particularly in distinguishing between overlapping stages such as N1, N3, and REM. Statistical comparisons further revealed that certain features, while generally discriminative, failed to differentiate effectively between key stage pairs in multiclass settings. The limited gains observed from advanced feature extraction suggest that more transformative improvements may necessitate integrating additional modalities such as PPG, actigraphy, or simplified EEG, or adopting architectures capable of modeling temporal dependencies more effectively (e.g., transformers or attention-based networks). Moving forward, efforts should prioritize targeted feature refinement, improved handling of class imbalance, and leveraging sequence-based models to better capture the dynamic structure of sleep. These directions offer the most promising path toward making ECG-based sleep staging feasible for real-world applications, especially in wearable and home-monitoring contexts.
Sleep stage classification using non-invasive signals has been extensively studied, with varying results depending on signal types, feature engineering strategies, and model complexity. While polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard, its reliance on multiple electrodes and complex equipment makes it impractical for routine or ambulatory monitoring. This has led to growing interest in leveraging ECG-or PPG-derived signals, such as heart rate variability (HRV), which can be captured using simpler, less invasive devices like smartwatches and fitness trackers. Several studies have demonstrated the feasibility of sleep stage classification using alternative physiological signals. For example, Casal et al. (2021) employed pulse oximetry, using heart rate (HR) and SpO2 as inputs to a recurrent neural network with bidirectional gated recurrent units (GRUs), choosing this architecture over LSTM to manage computational load. Their work illustrates a common trade-off between model performance and resource efficiency, an issue that also was encountered in this research. Similarly, Song et al. (2023) combined actigraphy and heartbeat signals using CNN-LSTM architecture to achieve 68 % accuracy across four sleep stages. Notably, they reported that relying solely on actigraphy reduced classification accuracy to 55 %, reinforcing the importance of multi-signal input. These observations underline a central challenge in sleep staging from wearable signals: whether acceptable performance can be maintained when constrained to a single, easily measurable input such as ECG. Ganglberger et al. (2023) further demonstrated that HRV and respiration data in ICU patients could achieve 60 %-81 % accuracy in sleep stage prediction under clinical settings using deep neural networks. Likewise, Silva et al. (2024) and Aghaomidi and Wang (2024) explored deep learning approaches with synthetically generated ECG-based features, reaching accuracies of up to 80 %, though often by simplifying the classification task (e.g., combining N3 and N4). Zaman et al. (2024) reported high accuracy for W and N3 stages using EEG and deep models, but only 51 % F1 score for N1, again illustrating its ambiguity. In this context, the present study offers a meaningful contribution by systematically investigating the limitations of ECG-derived temporal features across different time windows and modeling strategies, highlighting their potential and constraints in real-world, wearable-oriented scenarios. Experiments conducted across three studies and two datasets showed that while longer ECG segments (e.g., 5-min windows in Study 1) offered moderate performance, reducing the signal duration to 30 s (Studies 2 and 3) caused accuracy to decline sharply. These findings are consistent with observations by Sun et al. (2020), who noted that longer time windows tend to produce more stable results in time-series analysis. Even with the application of feature engineering and advanced models, including neural networks, KNN, Random Forest, and XGBoost, the highest test accuracy in Study 3 was found to plateau at approximately 48 %. Notably, XGBoost performed poorly in Study 2, especially when classifying the N3 stage, while Random Forest remained the most stable across datasets. These inconsistencies mirror observations in the literature. Lyu et al. (2023) struggled to classify N1 due to its transitional nature and limited data representation, and Aghaomidi and Wang (2024) found similar performance drops for N1, citing overlap in signal features with adjacent stages like Wake and N2. Zaman et al. (2024) reported excellent performance for Wake and N3 stages using EEG and complex deep models (92.7 % and 91.4 % F1 scores, respectively), but only 39.8 % correct classification for N1, underscoring the challenge posed by that stage. Interestingly, some studies have reported high classification accuracy using HRV and respiratory signals under specific conditions. Ganglberger et al. (2023) achieved 60 %-81 % accuracy in ICU and clinical environments using deep neural networks. However, these settings typically allow for cleaner signals and more extensive preprocessing, unlike wearable use-cases where signal quality may degrade due to motion or sensor limitations. This distinction underscores an important contextual gap that is directly addressed in the present study, as model performance is evaluated under conditions that closely approximate consumer-grade, ambulatory environments, where constraints related to signal quality, recording duration, and computational resources are more pronounced. These challenges also reflect broader physiological patterns. As reported in the literature (Gottesman et al., 2024) (Ganglberger et al., 2023), deeper sleep stages like N3 and REM often decline with age or illness and are associated with greater signal stability in healthy individuals. The findings of this study align with this: despite the use of advanced models, reliable classification of N3 in Study 3 was not achieved, particularly when the XGBoost model was applied. Conversely, REM and N2 stages were predicted more consistently, likely due to their greater representation and clearer signal patterns. Importantly, this consistency across signal-derived patterns, even in the face of reduced model performance, reaffirms the physiological relevance of the present ECG-based features and underscores the value of investigating sleep staging in real-world, signal-constrained contexts, an area this study helps illuminate. Beyond these physiological observations, it is also valuable to consider how developmental and autonomic mechanisms influence sleep-stage dynamics. Although this study did not include neuroimaging or affective measures, the developmental trajectory of sleep architecture provides an important physiological framework for interpreting ECGbased classification. Across adolescence and early adulthood, REM and slow-wave sleep proportions undergo gradual reorganization, reflecting maturation of both cortical and autonomic systems involved in sleep regulation (Zandieh et al., 2023). Recent evidence indicates that cardiac autonomic modulation during sleep captured through heart rate variability (HRV) is closely associated with sleep quality and continuity in adolescents (Lins-Filho et al., 2023). Moreover, nocturnal HRV studies have revealed distinct sympathetic-parasympathetic interaction patterns during REM sleep, suggesting that ECG-derived features can indirectly reflect developmental and regulatory processes in sleep physiology (Ucak et al., 2024) (Mateos-Salgado et al., 2025). Systematic reviews further confirm that sleep deprivation and poor sleep quality significantly alter HRV dynamics, reinforcing the sensitivity of autonomic markers to both physiological and behavioral states (Zhang et al., 2025). These findings imply that developmental variability in autonomic regulation may partly influence classification performance in ECG-based sleep staging. Future work could benefit from age-specific or development-specific analysis to clarify how maturation of autonomic control affects the discriminability of REM and NREM features in wearable applications. From both clinical and technological perspectives, one of the most significant implications of this work is that robust classification performance was difficult to achieve when relying solely on ECGderived features, particularly when shorter analysis windows suitable for wearable devices were used. Even with advanced models like onedimensional convolutional neural networks, the improvements were marginal. This suggests that temporal ECG features, though informative, are insufficient on their own for high-fidelity sleep staging, especially when compared to EEG or multimodal systems. Nonetheless, this work contributes meaningfully to the growing body of literature exploring the viability of ECG-based alternatives for sleep monitoring. By systematically evaluating signal duration, model types, and feature engineering strategies across multiple datasets, this study offers one of the more comprehensive assessments of the strengths and limitations inherent to such approaches. The correlation heatmaps presented in Fig. 5 provide compelling evidence for the importance of thoughtful feature engineering and selection in ECG-based sleep staging. In both datasets, the initial raw features exhibit noticeable clustering patterns, implying a degree of redundancy that could dilute model effectiveness if left unaddressed. By contrast, the engineered features, particularly those refined using correlation-based filtering in Fig. 5d, demonstrate substantially lower inter-feature dependencies. This sparsification of correlations reflects a more orthogonal feature space, critical for reducing multicollinearity and improving classifier stability. The strong influence of Poincaré-based geometric indices (GI, EI, Ptri, Area) suggests that shape-derived variability encodes subtle dynamical patterns that are not fully captured by conventional HRV descriptors alone. These features likely capture non-linear fluctuations characteristic of REM and wake, where autonomic activity becomes more irregular and fragmented. In Study 1 (5-min windows), traditional HRV measures such as standard deviation (Std), variance (Var), Poincaré plot standard deviation perpendicular to the line of identity (SD1), Poincaré plot standard deviation along the line of identity (SD2), and root mean square of successive RR interval differences (RMSSD) consistently showed statistically significant differences (P < 0.0001) in comparisons involving deeper sleep stages (e.g., N3) and wake states. This suggests that longer ECG segments effectively capture parasympathetic dominance and cardiac deceleration patterns characteristic of slow-wave sleep, making these features particularly robust for assessing sleep depth. In contrast, Study 2 employed shorter 30-s segments from the same dataset. Although some features retained discriminative power, overall statistical significance declined. Features that were previously strong discriminators exhibited higher p-values across multiple sleep stage comparisons, especially involving transitional stages like N1 and N2. This reduction in statistical power highlights a critical trade-off in temporal granularity: shorter segments may fail to capture the necessary variability or stability in ECG signals required to distinguish between physiologically adjacent sleep states. Study 3 expanded on this by analyzing the MIT-BIH dataset using a broader and more heterogeneous set of 52 features, including geometrical, morphological, and statistical descriptors. Despite also using 30-s segments, this enriched feature space helped restore statistical robustness in many comparisons. Several engineered features such as Power, rRect, xC, yB, and non-linear combinations demonstrated strong statistical significance, particularly in distinguishing N2 and REM, and N3 and Wake. These results suggest that increasing feature diversity can partially offset the limitations of shorter signal durations, offering a compelling case for moving beyond conventional HRV metrics. Several heart rate variability (HRV) and Poincaré-based measures employed in the present work are established indicators of autonomic balance and have been consistently linked to physiological variations across sleep stages (Eddie et al., 2022). Deep non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (stage N3) is generally associated with parasympathetic predominance and a concomitant reduction in heart rate and overall variability, as reflected by lower mean HR and SDNN values. In contrast, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is characterized by relative sympathetic activation and pronounced phasic fluctuations, often resulting in increased heart rate and elevated variability within specific frequency bands (Ghorvei et al., 2025). Metrics such as the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) and high-frequency (HF) power primarily capture beat-to-beat vagal modulation and therefore tend to assume higher values during sustained NREM periods. Similarly, the Poincaré plot descriptors SD1 and SD2 represent short-and long-term variability, respectively, with SD1 reflecting tonic parasympathetic activity and SD2 capturing slower, trend-related components of heart rate dynamics. In cases where the present models identified lower SDNN yet higher RMSSD during REM relative to N3, several mechanistic explanations may be considered. The shorter analysis epochs and transient phasic bursts characteristic of REM can elevate short-term variability (increasing RMSSD), while leaving long-term variability (SDNN) comparatively reduced. These observations may account for the differential discriminative capacity of HRV-derived metrics across sleep stages and align with prior evidence from aggregated HRV reviews and task-specific HRV-sleep investigations. Across studies, N3 and REM were consistently distinguishable from Wake, whereas N1 showed substantial overlap with adjacent stages such as N2 and REM. This pattern reflects the limited ability of ECG-derived features to capture the subtle physiological transitions characterizing light sleep and indicates that stage indistinctness, rather than model performance alone, contributes to misclassification. These findings parallel model performance patterns and confirm that stage-specific physiological indistinctness, rather than model inadequacy alone, contributes to classification challenges. Taken together, the P-value analyses provide a statistically grounded framework for prioritizing features during model development. Features that demonstrate consistent separability across datasets and segment durations should form the core of classification models, particularly in real-time or wearable applications where computational constraints exist. By aligning physiological insight with data-driven analysis, these results support hybrid feature engineering strategies that combine temporal, geometric, and morphological descriptors to better capture the complex dynamics of sleep. Furthermore, the results highlight the need for temporally adaptive models and multimodal signal integration to address persistent challenges in distinguishing transitional stages like N1. These insights not only reinforce the feasibility of ECG-based sleep staging but also outline a clearer path toward enhancing its robustness and generalizability. The results of this study confirm that ECG-derived features can provide a viable basis for sleep stage classification, especially when using longer time windows, but their effectiveness drops sharply as signal duration decreases. This limitation was most apparent in classifying transitional (N1) and deep (N3) stages, even with advanced feature engineering and tuning. Among the models evaluated, Random Forest consistently proved to be the most stable across datasets, while KNN showed modest gains when enhanced with co-occurrence matrix (COM) features. However, none of the tested approaches yielded sufficient reliability for real-world clinical or consumer-grade deployment using short ECG segments alone. To contextualize the findings of this study within the broader body of literature, Table 11 summarizes a selection of prior research efforts focused on automatic sleep staging. These studies span a wide range of input modalities, including EEG, ECG, PPG, and actigraphy, as well as diverse algorithmic strategies such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), random forests (RF), and deep neural networks (DNN). Classification schemes also vary, covering problems from two to six classes, and reported performance metrics include accuracy, kappa scores, and F1 scores. While several EEG-based approaches have achieved high classification accuracy, many rely on multi-sensor setups or longer input durations that are not suitable for wearable applications. In contrast, only a limited number of studies have addressed the five-class classification problem using ECG alone, particularly under short-segment conditions. The present work contributes to this underexplored space by evaluating ECG-based sleep staging models within the practical constraints of segment duration and signal modality, offering benchmarks that are more representative of real-world, wearable-compatible systems. An ECG-based approach utilizing HRV and Poincaré-derived metrics has the potential to facilitate remote sleep monitoring, longitudinal screening, and triage in environments where full polysomnography (PSG) is impractical or unavailable. Potential applications include (i) detection of coarse alterations in sleep architecture, such as reduced proportions of N3 or fragmented REM periods; (ii) preliminary screening for probable sleep-disordered breathing when integrated with simple respiratory surrogates; and (iii) longitudinal tracking of sleep-related trends to inform clinical referral decisions. Nevertheless, the use of single-lead ECG should remain restricted to screening and triage contexts, as its temporal and spatial resolution does not provide the diagnostic specificity of EEG-based assessments. Prospective validation in clinically defined populations, such as individuals with obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia, or REM behavior disorder will be essential to establish the clinical reliability and translational applicability of this method. Nonetheless, even with these promising results, certain limitations must be acknowledged. The experimental evaluation in this study was conducted using two publicly available datasets acquired under controlled clinical conditions. Both datasets primarily comprise healthy or mixed cohorts and therefore may not adequately represent the full range of clinical populations, such as individuals with severe obstructive sleep apnea, heart failure, or cardiac arrhythmia. Because HRV dynamics are known to differ substantially in the presence of autonomic dysfunction and sleep-related pathophysiology, model accuracy and generalizability are expected to decrease in such populations. This limitation is explicitly acknowledged, and future validation should be performed on cohorts with confirmed sleep disorders, recordings obtained from ambulatory wearable ECG or PPG systems, and demographically diverse groups encompassing wider age and ethnic variability. Despite these challenges, this study addresses a meaningful gap in literature: few works have focused on five-stage sleep classification using ECG or PPG signals at time resolutions suitable for wearables. The results of this study suggest that while current HRV-based models hold potential, they are not sufficient on their own for fine-grained staging. This underlines the need for hybrid systems that combine PPG with other sensor modalities like accelerometry or simplified EEG, to strike a better balance between accuracy, usability, and wearability. Additionally, future studies should consider enhancements in preprocessing, architecture selection (e.g., attention-based models or transformers), and domain-informed feature selection to improve performance on short segments. Addressing persistent challenges like class imbalance and improving the detection of underrepresented stages such as N1 and REM will be key to pushing wearable sleep monitoring systems toward broader adoption and reliability.
This study was motivated by the growing need for sleep staging methods that are both computationally efficient and suitable for integration into wearable health technologies. Current clinical sleep assessments rely heavily on multi-signal, hardware-intensive systems, most notably those using EEG. While highly accurate, these are impractical for daily home use. To address this, the reliable classification of sleep stages was investigated using only ECG signals processed through machine learning algorithms, including both classical models and those augmented with advanced feature engineering. The results of this study, derived from three investigations across two datasets, highlight a central finding: longer ECG segments significantly enhance the classification accuracy of sleep stages, confirming that temporal context is essential for capturing the physiological dynamics underpinning different stages. While classification using only ECG signals proved feasible, particularly for distinguishing deep sleep (N3) and REM stages, performance degraded substantially when using shorter signal segments, which are more common in clinical annotations and real-time applications. This degradation occurred despite the use of complex features and model tuning, suggesting a fundamental limitation in the information density of brief ECG windows. Among the algorithms evaluated, Random Forest consistently demonstrated the most robust performance, while models like XGBoost showed instability and underperformance. The inclusion of co-occurrence matrix (COM) features modestly improved KNN performance in shorter windows, but not enough to yield clinically reliable results. These outcomes underscore both the potential and the constraints of ECG-only sleep staging under different temporal and algorithmic configurations. Key findings of this research are. • ECG signals can support five-stage sleep classification only when longer time windows (e.g., ≥5 min) are used. • EEG and other brain-derived signals remain superior for fine-grained sleep staging, particularly for light and transitional stages like N1. • Sophisticated algorithms perform better than simpler ones on short ECG segments, but their gains are limited by signal-inherent ambiguities. • Random Forest emerged as the most stable algorithm for ECGderived features, while XGBoost proved unreliable across all configurations. A primary limitation of this study is the reliance on datasets collected in controlled environments, which may not fully reflect the signal quality and variability found in real-world wearable ECG recordings. Additionally, despite exploring a wide range of engineered features, the performance of all models plateaued on short intervals, highlighting a ceiling effect in ECG-only approaches. Future research should prioritize multimodal integration, combining ECG with signals like PPG, accelerometry, and minimally invasive EEG to improve stage discrimination without compromising comfort or portability. Advanced deep learning architectures, such as LSTM and 1D CNNs, show promise for leveraging temporal dependencies more effectively. Incorporating domain-specific signal preprocessing and attention mechanisms may also enhance model sensitivity to underrepresented stages like N1 and REM. By offering a comprehensive, statistically grounded evaluation of ECG-based sleep staging, this study fills a critical gap in the wearable health literature. Valuable insights are provided for developers of sleepmonitoring systems, indicating that although ECG alone shows potential, the achievement of clinically actionable accuracy requires careful feature design, the use of longer time segments, and the incorporation of complementary signals.

Supervised Machine Learning-Based Prediction of In-Hospital Mortality Following Hip Fracture in Older Adults
Background/Objectives: Hip fractures in older adults are associated with substantial morbidity, functional decline, and high in-hospital mortality. Early identification of patients at increased risk of death may improve clinical decision-making and resource allocation. This study aimed to develop and internally validate supervised machine learning models to predict in-hospital mortality among older adults hospitalized for hip fracture using nationwide administrative data from Chile. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using anonymized hospital discharge records from the Chilean National Health Fund (FONASA), covering admissions between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2024, across 72 public hospitals. Demographic, clinical, and care-related variables were included as predictors. Multiple supervised machine learning algorithms were trained and evaluated using stratified train-test partitioning. Model performance was assessed using AUC-ROC, precision, recall, and F1-score. Model interpretability was explored using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results: A total of 40,253 hospitalization episodes were analyzed. The Gradient Boosting model achieved the best overall performance, with an AUC-ROC of 0.885 and a favorable balance between precision and recall. SHAP analysis identified age, comorbidity burden, and surgical treatment as the most influential predictors, revealing nonlinear and clinically meaningful contributions to mortality risk. Conclusions: Supervised machine learning models based on routinely collected administrative data demonstrated strong predictive performance for in-hospital mortality after hip fracture. Interpretable models may support early risk stratification and clinical decisionmaking at a national healthcare level.
This retrospective cohort study developed and internally validated supervised machine learning models to predict in-hospital mortality among older adults hospitalized for hip fracture in Chile. The analysis used anonymized hospital discharge data from the Chilean National Health Fund (Fondo Nacional de Salud, FONASA), which consolidates standardized administrative records from the 72 public hospitals forming the national healthcare network. These institutions deliver moderate- to high-complexity care, including orthopedic trauma and surgical management. The database contains detailed information on patient demographics, diagnostic and procedural codes, and discharge outcomes. Data were extracted from the open-access FONASA repository (https://datosabiertos.fonasa.cl, accessed on 9 February 2026) and included all hospitalizations between 1 January 2019, and 31 December 2024. Each individual was identified using an encrypted unique patient identifier, which allowed linkage of multiple hospitalizations belonging to the same patient. To avoid within-patient clustering and ensure independence of observations, only the first hospitalization for hip fracture per individual during the study period was retained for analysis.
FONASA covers roughly 85% of Chileans aged 60 years and older, representing the public healthcare sector where most hip fractures occur. The dataset undergoes regular audits by the Ministry of Health to ensure internal consistency and coding accuracy. All stages of model development and validation adhered to the TRIPOD-AI reporting guideline, ensuring transparency and reproducibility in the construction of AI-based clinical prediction models. All hospitalizations of adults aged 60 years and older with a principal diagnosis of hip fracture were included. Cases were identified according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes: S72.0 (femoral neck fracture), S72.1 (pertrochanteric fracture), and S72.2 (subtrochanteric fracture). Exclusion criteria comprised: (i) missing information on age, sex, or discharge status; (ii) diagnostic codes not falling within the predefined range; (iii) transfer cases or duplicate admissions; and (iv) records with all predictor variables absent. Exclusions were intentionally restricted to data quality–related issues in order to preserve the representativeness of the national cohort. Clinical variables not captured in administrative records—such as physiological parameters, laboratory values, time to surgery, or frailty scales—were not excluded but were unavailable in the dataset.
To ensure data integrity, validation procedures involved cross-checking unique admission and discharge identifiers to confirm internal consistency and remove duplicates. The final analytic cohort included 40,253 hospitalization episodes of older adults treated across the 72 public hospitals in Chile. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, defined as death occurring during the same hospitalization period. Mortality status was extracted from the standardized discharge condition field within the FONASA database, which documents each patient’s vital status at discharge.
During data preprocessing, the positive class (death) was identified automatically through string matching for terms such as “falle”, “muer”, “defun”, and “dead” appearing in the discharge condition variable. When no direct match was detected, the final label was assigned lexicographically to preserve consistency across the dataset. For clinical coherence and interpretability, death was pre-specified as the positive outcome class in both sensitivity and main analyses.
Only deaths verified at the time of discharge were included; post-discharge mortality data were not available. Each record corresponded to a distinct hospitalization episode, confirmed through cross-referencing of admission and discharge identifiers to avoid duplication. Predictor variables were selected a priori based on three predefined criteria: (i) consistent availability across the national administrative hospital discharge database, (ii) early availability during hospitalization to allow potential clinical applicability, and (iii) prior evidence supporting their association with in-hospital mortality after hip fracture. These criteria were applied to ensure both methodological robustness and clinical relevance while preserving the generalizability of the model to real-world inpatient settings. Based on these criteria, seven routinely collected variables were selected for model development and organized into three conceptual domains:
Demographic variables: Sex (male/female), ethnicity (categorical), and age (continuous, in years) [5,6,7,8].
Disease burden and treatment: Number of comorbidities (count of secondary diagnoses recorded at discharge) and surgical treatment (yes/no) [5,6,7,8].
Care process indicators: Transferring service or first hospital ward (categorical; e.g., orthopedics, internal medicine, intensive care) and length of hospital stay (continuous, in days) [5,6,7,8].
Categorical variables were encoded using one-hot encoding, while continuous variables were standardized before model training. This preprocessing step facilitated comparability among predictors and minimized potential bias related to variable scaling during model optimization. All selected predictors were available for all patients prior to discharge, allowing model application in early inpatient settings. To ensure robustness and reproducibility across heterogeneous CSV exports, a standardized data management and preprocessing workflow was established. The datasets were imported through an automated parser capable of recognizing multiple delimiters (;, ,, \t, |) and character encodings (UTF-8 or Latin-1). Lines containing formatting inconsistencies were automatically omitted to preserve dataset integrity. Column headers were normalized to lower-case ASCII and converted to snake_case notation, while synonym mapping was applied to standardize variable names. For instance, variables such as “cirugia_(0 = no/1 = si)” were unified as “cirugia,” and all variations referring to “days of hospitalization” were consolidated under a single label.
Before model training, variable types were harmonized to ensure compatibility across models. The variable representing surgical treatment was recoded to binary format (0/1, yes/no, or true/false), and both age and length of stay were converted to numerical type. Records lacking outcome data or missing all predictor values were removed. Missing data were handled by imputing the median for continuous variables and the mode for categorical ones. Numerical features were scaled, and categorical variables were encoded using a OneHotEncoder configured to ignore unseen categories. Both transformations were implemented within a ColumnTransformer to ensure consistent preprocessing across datasets.
To prevent data leakage, all preprocessing steps were embedded within the machine learning pipeline using scikit-learn and fitted exclusively on the training data. This design safeguarded methodological transparency, reproducibility, and the validity of model evaluation. The dataset was randomly divided into training and testing subsets using an 80/20 stratified split to maintain the original distribution of the outcome classes (alive vs. deceased). Randomization was performed with a fixed seed (random_state = 42) to allow full reproducibility of the results. Each hospitalization episode was assigned to only one subset, ensuring that no records overlapped between the training and testing datasets and thereby preserving a strict separation throughout model development and evaluation. Eight supervised classification algorithms were developed and trained under a standardized scikit-learn framework to enable consistent comparison across models. The classifiers evaluated were:
Naïve Bayes (GaussianNB),Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) neural network with two hidden layers (64 and 32 neurons, ReLU activation, α = 1 × 10−3, max_iter = 500, random_state = 42),
Random Forest (400 estimators, class_weight = “balanced_subsample”, n_jobs = –1),Gradient Boosting (default parameters, random_state = 42),k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) (k = 7, distance-weighted voting),
Logistic Regression (solver = LBFGS, max_iter = 1000, class_weight = “balanced”),upport Vector Machine (SVM) with radial basis function (RBF) kernel (C = 2.0, gamma = “scale”, probability = True, class_weight = “balanced”, random_state = 42), and
Decision Tree (class_weight = “balanced”).All algorithms were implemented as scikit-learn Pipelines, integrating data preprocessing and model fitting into a unified workflow. This approach minimized the risk of data leakage and ensured full reproducibility of the analytical process. Model training was carried out exclusively on the training subset, and performance was subsequently assessed using the independent test data. Model performance was evaluated solely on the independent test set to ensure an unbiased assessment of predictive ability. Discriminative power was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) for binary classification, and the macro-averaged One-vs-Rest AUC for potential multiclass scenarios. To provide a comprehensive overview of model behavior, additional performance metrics were computed, including accuracy, precision, recall (sensitivity), and F1-score. These complementary indicators allowed for a balanced interpretation of predictive performance across classes.
For each algorithm, individual ROC curves were generated and exported in high-resolution format (600 dpi). A summary figure comparing all ROC curves was also created to visually contrast model performance. When a classifier produced a decision function rather than direct probabilities, a sigmoid transformation was applied to enable ROC curve computation and visualization. This adjustment improved interpretability through probability scaling without affecting the underlying AUC values. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to estimate the contribution of each predictor to the model’s output. For tree-based algorithms, including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Decision Tree models, the TreeExplainer method was employed. In the case of linear models such as Logistic Regression and linear SVMs, the LinearExplainer with interventional perturbation was applied. For nonlinear algorithms lacking native SHAP integration—namely MLP, RBF SVM, kNN, and Naïve Bayes—the KernelExplainer was implemented using a background sample of 100 randomly selected training observations and 200 test instances for visualization purposes.
The interpretability outputs included a series of global and local explanation plots: bar charts of mean absolute SHAP values, beeswarm plots, and dependence plots for the three most influential predictors. Additionally, individual waterfall plots were generated to illustrate subject-specific feature contributions. All figures were exported at 600 dpi resolution. SHAP values were expressed in log-odds, where negative values indicated a reduced probability of survival—reflecting an increased predicted risk of in-hospital mortality, given that the positive class corresponded to survival.For the best-performing model according to AUC, an interpretable risk equation was derived using SHAP values. The model prediction for each individual can be expressed as:
logit(p)=β0+∑iϕi, p=1(1+exp(−logit(p))), RR=pp0where β0 represents the SHAP base value, corresponding to the expected model output (in log-odds) across the entire dataset, and ϕi denotes the individual contribution of predictor i to the predicted outcome. The baseline probability can be obtained as p0 = σ(β0), where σ is the logistic (sigmoid) function.
This formulation allows the decomposition of each patient’s predicted risk into additive contributions from all predictors, providing an individualized and transparent estimation of mortality risk directly interpretable in clinical terms.
Given the relatively low prevalence of in-hospital deaths, class imbalance was managed by setting the parameter class_weight = “balanced” in all algorithms that supported this option. This adjustment automatically reweighted the contribution of each class in inverse proportion to its frequency, reducing bias toward the majority (survival) class. In addition, a stratified train–test split was used to maintain the original outcome distribution across both subsets.
To preserve the empirical characteristics and natural class proportions of the dataset, no oversampling or synthetic data generation techniques were applied in the main analysis. This decision ensured that model training reflected the real-world clinical context represented in the national hospitalization data.
Several pre-specified sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness and clinical interpretability of the developed models. First, the orientation of the positive class was reversed—defining death instead of survival as the reference outcome—to verify the consistency of SHAP values and predicted probabilities. Second, the stability of categorical encoding was examined by consolidating low-frequency categories within the transferring service variable to reduce sparsity effects. Third, the reliability of complex algorithms was tested by varying key hyperparameters, including the regularization parameter C in the Support Vector Classifier and the number of estimators in the Random Forest model.
In addition, several methodological extensions were identified as recommended for future work. These include probability calibration using Platt or isotonic scaling, combined with calibration plots and Brier scores; estimation of 95% confidence intervals for the AUC using bootstrap or DeLong methods; and external validation—temporal or geographic—to assess model generalizability. Decision-curve analysis was also proposed to evaluate clinical usefulness, along with fairness auditing across sex, age, and ethnicity to ensure equitable model performance.
The unit of analysis was the hospitalization episode, with each record corresponding to a distinct patient admission. Records were excluded only when essential variables required for cohort definition or outcome ascertainment, such as age, sex, or discharge status, were missing; missing values in predictor variables were handled using median imputation for continuous variables and mode imputation for categorical variables. Model outputs were primarily descriptive and comparative, and no correction for multiplicity was applied, as all algorithms evaluated the same predictive construct under equivalent analytical conditions. Hospital-level effects were not explicitly modeled, because the analytical focus was placed on patient-level risk prediction and on maximizing generalizability across the national public hospital network. To ensure full reproducibility, the random seed parameter (random_state = 42) was fixed across all stages of the workflow, including data partitioning, model training, and evaluation. Confidence intervals for the AUC were not computed in the main analysis to optimize computational efficiency; however, these can be readily obtained through stratified bootstrap resampling, which yields nonparametric 95% confidence intervals for model discrimination.
All analyses were conducted in Python 3.12.2 using the Jupyter Notebook environment (version 7.1.0). The computational workflow was built with widely adopted libraries, including pandas for data manipulation, scikit-learn for machine learning pipelines, matplotlib for visualization, SHAP for interpretability, and python-docx for automated report generation.
The analytical script was designed to automatically log diagnostic information—such as delimiter and encoding detection or column mapping—while executing all preprocessing and model training steps. It also computed the full set of performance metrics and exported publication-ready outputs, including metric tables (CSV), high-resolution ROC curves and SHAP visualizations (600 dpi), as well as a structured summary report in DOCX format.
To further strengthen reproducibility, the workflow can be containerized (for instance, using Docker 27) and accompanied by the public release of both the source code repository and a synthetic dataset. The latter should retain the statistical structure of the original data while safeguarding patient privacy.
The study included 40,253 hospitalization episodes of older adults with hip fracture. The mean age of the cohort was 81.9 years (SD 9.1), and women accounted for 76.8% of the sample. Regarding disease burden and treatment, the mean number of comorbidities was 6.6 (SD 4.2), with the majority of patients presenting three or more comorbid conditions. Most patients underwent surgical treatment during hospitalization (88.0%), while 12.0% were managed non-operatively. The mean length of hospital stay was 12.7 days (SD 13.9). The Gradient Boosting model demonstrated the best overall performance, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.885, an F1-score of 0.791, precision of 0.738, and recall of 0.849, indicating a strong balance between sensitivity and specificity (Table 1). The MLP neural network and linear approaches-Logistic Regression and linear SVM-reached comparable AUC values (approximately 0.88). However, their calibration between precision and recall was less optimal, which may limit their interpretability in clinical settings. In contrast, algorithms such as Random Forest and k-Nearest Neighbors achieved very high overall accuracies (≥0.96) but markedly low F1-scores (≤0.12), suggesting a strong bias toward the majority (survival) class and poor discrimination of deaths. The Naïve Bayes classifier yielded the highest recall (0.989) but an AUC of only 0.499, indicating near-random predictive performance. Taken together, the Gradient Boosting algorithm provided the most favorable compromise between discriminative capacity and clinical relevance. Consequently, it was selected for interpretability assessment and individualized mortality risk analysis (Figure 1). The beeswarm plot (Figure 3) illustrated that higher comorbidity counts consistently shifted predictions toward lower survival probability (negative SHAP values), whereas surgical treatment was associated with positive SHAP contributions, indicating a protective effect. Age and prolonged hospitalization also produced predominantly negative shifts, aligning with poorer outcomes. Categories corresponding to intensive or high-complexity care (e.g., ICU or internal medicine) showed small but directionally coherent negative effects. Dependence plots confirmed these trends:
The main finding of this nationwide study is that a Gradient Boosting machine learning model achieved excellent discrimination for predicting in-hospital mortality among older adults hospitalized with hip fracture (AUC-ROC = 0.885), outperforming the other evaluated algorithms. In addition to its predictive performance, the model provided clinically meaningful interpretability through SHAP analysis, identifying comorbidity burden, surgical treatment, and age as the most influential determinants of mortality risk. These results demonstrate that interpretable, data-driven models based on routinely collected hospital data can effectively support early risk stratification in real-world inpatient settings. Our findings are consistent with previous research that has applied machine learning techniques to predict clinical outcomes in patients with hip fractures. For example, a recent 2024 study from China reported that an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model achieved an AUC of approximately 0.91 for predicting in-hospital mortality after hip surgery, identifying age, comorbidities, and surgical intervention as the most influential variables. These results closely mirror the patterns observed in our study, reinforcing the robustness and generalizability of tree-based ensemble methods for mortality prediction in this population [20]. Similarly, a Thai study using multiple models reported AUCs ranging from 0.81 to 0.99 for one-year mortality prediction, also highlighting the utility of Random Forest and Gradient Boosting techniques [21]. In contrast, a retrospective analysis in Spain with a smaller sample (~500 patients) failed to surpass an AUC of 0.65, underscoring the need for large, well-curated datasets to build robust models [22]. Additionally, a Swedish registry study involving over 124,000 cases found that regularized logistic regression achieved an AUC of ~0.74, showing that in some contexts, traditional statistical models remain competitive, though with more limited interpretability at the individual level [19]. The SHAP analysis provides important interpretative insights into how established clinical predictors contribute to mortality risk after hip fracture. Although age, comorbidity burden, and surgical treatment are well-known determinants of prognosis, SHAP analysis adds value by quantifying their relative and nonlinear contributions at the individual patient level. In particular, nonlinear age effects, threshold patterns in comorbidity burden, and the consistently protective contribution of surgical treatment across age strata were observed. This patient-level risk decomposition extends beyond traditional summary statistics or conventional mortality scores and supports transparent, individualized risk stratification in real-world inpatient settings. Although SHAP values were used to identify the most influential predictors, the models were not refitted using only SHAP-ranked features, as SHAP was applied for interpretability rather than post hoc feature selection. Restricting the feature set based solely on importance rankings may lead to information leakage or overly optimistic performance estimates and may overlook complex interactions captured by the full set of clinically plausible predictors. Several mortality risk scores have been developed to support prognostic assessment after hip fracture, including the Nottingham Hip Fracture Score and indices based on comorbidity burden such as the Charlson Comorbidity Index. These tools have demonstrated clinical utility and remain widely used in routine practice. Rather than replacing established mortality scores, the present machine learning approach should be viewed as complementary. By integrating routinely collected hospital variables and allowing nonlinear interactions, the Gradient Boosting model achieved higher discriminative performance while providing individualized risk decomposition through SHAP-based explanations. This feature enables transparent interpretation of how traditional risk factors-such as age, comorbidities, and surgical treatment-contribute to predicted mortality risk at the patient level, thereby extending the interpretability of conventional scoring systems. From a clinical perspective, one of the most relevant findings is the negative impact of the number of comorbidities on survival after hip fracture. This is consistent with the geriatric literature, which has consistently shown that a higher burden of chronic diseases worsens prognosis. For example, each one-point increase in the age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index is associated with approximately a 31% increase in mortality risk among hip fracture patients [23]. Likewise, patients with more than three comorbidities experience substantially higher rates of infectious complications and death within the first year after the fracture compared to those with fewer comorbidities [24,25]. Our results confirm the number of comorbidities as the most important predictor, reflecting how preexisting conditions such as heart disease, renal failure, neurological disorders (e.g., dementia), or cancer reduce the patient's physiological reserve and hinder recovery after trauma. In fact, in a study focused on octogenarian patients with hip fracture, the Charlson Index was found to be a better predictor of in-hospital mortality than the ASA scale (BMC Surg), underscoring the importance of quantifying multimorbidity [26]. Our findings reaffirm that high comorbidity translates into greater vulnerability and a higher risk of fatal outcomes; therefore, risk stratification should carefully consider this factor and encourage perioperative interventions aimed at optimizing preexisting medical conditions. Another notable finding is the protective effect of surgical treatment on in-hospital mortality. In our model, patients who underwent surgery had a lower predicted probability of death during hospitalization, a result that aligns with well-established clinical evidence. Most hip fractures in older adults require surgical repair, and numerous studies have shown that early surgical intervention significantly improves survival outcomes. International guidelines, such as those from the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), recommend performing surgery within 48 h of the fracture, as timely intervention reduces both mortality and postoperative complications [27,28]. Conversely, the non-surgical option is typically reserved for extremely frail patients or those with terminal comorbidities for whom surgical risk is prohibitive. Previous studies have shown that non-surgically managed patients have markedly higher mortality rates than those who undergo surgery, although this difference is influenced by the poorer baseline condition of the non-operated group [29].
