In our cohort, the higher mortality observed among patients who did not undergo surgery is likely attributable to their older age, a greater proportion of very elderly men, and a higher comorbidity burden compared with those who were operated on, factors that are well recognized to increase mortality risk following hip fracture. Consequently, the apparent protective effect of surgery reflects not only the intrinsic benefits of fracture repair-such as enabling early mobilization, effective pain control, and prevention of complications like thrombosis or pressure ulcers-but also a degree of selection bias, since only patients deemed clinically stable are typically eligible for surgery. Nevertheless, our findings reinforce current clinical recommendations to provide surgical treatment to all appropriate candidates, accompanied by adequate preoperative optimization. Timely surgery remains a modifiable determinant of survival and should be prioritized as a cornerstone of hip fracture management in older adults. Advanced age also emerged as an important prognostic factor, in line with clinical experience and epidemiological studies. As patient age increases, so does the risk of mortality after a hip fracture; it has been estimated that mortality rates may rise by up to 30% in the oldest groups compared with younger adults [30]. This effect is attributed to the biological frailty associated with aging: very old adults often present sarcopenia, reduced cardiac and respiratory reserve, immune alterations, and higher susceptibility to adverse events such as delirium or infections, all of which contribute to worse outcomes. It is therefore unsurprising that age is included in traditional prognostic scales (such as the Nottingham Hip Fracture Score) and in indices like Charlson, and that it consistently appears among mortality predictors identified in modern analyses [19,31]. In the study by Forssten et al., for instance, advanced age was one of the main factors associated with increased one-year mortality [19]. In our cohort, we observed the same trend: older patients had lower in-hospital survival rates. This highlights the need for comprehensive geriatric approaches for very old hip fracture patients, including full geriatric assessment, nutritional optimization, delirium prevention, and aggressive management of acute comorbidities, with the goal of mitigating the negative impact of age on prognosis. Finally, other findings of our study deserve mention for their clinical relevance, even if they carried a smaller weight in the predictive model. We observed that prolonged hospitalization tends to be associated with worse outcomes. This is consistent with previous reports linking longer hospital stays to higher short-term post-discharge mortality [32]. A plausible explanation is that prolonged hospital stays often arise from medical complications occurring during hospitalization-such as nosocomial infections, pneumonia, thromboembolism, or delirium-or from delayed functional recovery. These complications, in turn, substantially increase the risk of death. Consequently, reducing the length of stay through early rehabilitation, infection prevention, and proactive management of comorbid conditions could have a meaningful impact on survival outcomes. Another relevant aspect is the type of hospital service and care model. The literature has shown that implementing shared-care models between orthopedic surgeons and geriatricians (orthogeriatric units) is associated with lower in-hospital mortality among hip fracture patients [29]. Orthogeriatric collaboration ensures more holistic care: it optimizes comorbidity management upon admission, tailors surgical indication and timing to patient conditions, and promotes preventive interventions (early mobilization, nutritional support, avoidance of inappropriate polypharmacy) that impact recovery. In our setting, adopting a similar multidisciplinary approach could partly explain the favorable outcomes observed and represents an opportunity for improvement where such models are not yet implemented. In summary, these findings reaffirm that mortality following hip fracture in older adults is a multifactorial phenomenon determined by the interaction between patient baseline characteristics (age, comorbidities, functional status), treatment factors (performance and timing of surgery), and the quality of hospital care (prevention of complications, interdisci-plinary management). Addressing each of these components comprehensively is essential to reduce mortality and improve prognosis in this vulnerable population [29,32]. From a clinical perspective, the proposed Gradient Boosting model may have several practical applications in the inpatient management of older adults with hip fracture. By leveraging routinely available hospital data, the model could support early risk stratification at admission, helping clinicians identify patients at higher risk of in-hospital mortality who may benefit from closer monitoring, multidisciplinary care, or early optimization of comorbid conditions. In particular, the strong contribution of comorbidity burden, surgical treatment, and age aligns with current orthogeriatric principles and reinforces the importance of timely surgical decision-making and comprehensive medical management. Moreover, the use of SHAP-based explanations enables transparent, patient-level interpretation of risk, facilitating clinical communication and supporting shared decision-making without replacing established clinical judgment or existing mortality risk scores. This study has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, it relied on a retrospective cohort derived from a single national health system (FONASA), which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other healthcare settings. Although the dataset encompasses a large proportion of the Chilean population, external validation-either temporal or geographic-was not performed in the present analysis due to reliance on a single nationwide administrative database. Second, the set of predictors was restricted to administrative and care-related variables routinely available in hospital discharge records. The absence of physiological measures (e.g., vital signs), laboratory results, and detailed perioperative indicators (e.g., ASA score, time to surgery) may have introduced residual confounding and reduced the precision of individual risk estimation. Third, the outcome definition-in-hospital death at discharge-does not account for deaths occurring shortly after discharge. As a result, time-to-event or competing-risk models could not be applied, potentially leading to an underestimation of early post-discharge mortality. Finally, it is important to note that SHAP-based explanations describe model-derived associations, not causal relationships. Although SHAP enhances model transparency and interpretability, its results should be understood within the framework of predictive inference rather than causal explanation.
In this nationwide cohort of older adults hospitalized with hip fracture, a Gradient Boosting machine learning model demonstrated excellent discrimination for predicting in-hospital mortality using routinely collected hospital data. Comorbidity burden, surgical treatment, and age emerged as the most influential predictors of mortality risk. The integration of SHAP analysis enhanced model transparency by providing clinically interpretable, patient-level explanations. These findings support the potential role of interpretable machine learning models as complementary tools for early risk stratification in real-world inpatient settings. Future studies should focus on external validation and evaluation of clinical impact.

Synthetic Blood Data Generation for Fair Machine Learning
Synthetic data generation is a promising solution to privacy concerns in healthcare analytics, particularly when working with sensitive patient information. This study evaluates the performance and fairness of generative models in creating realistic synthetic datasets derived from blood test and demographic data. Three distinct medical datasets are used, including anonymised clinical data from a public hospital in Ireland, a public UCI medical dataset, and a Korean National Health Insurance dataset from 2002. Seven generative models-CTGAN, TVAE, Gaussian Copula, CopulaGAN, MedGAN, DiscGAN, and FASTML-are applied to generate synthetic records. The quality of these records is assessed using statistical similarity metrics, including the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Wasserstein distance, and Jensen-Shannon Divergence, complemented by visual distribution plots. Fairness is evaluated by examining the representation of sensitive attributes such as gender and age group in both real and synthetic datasets. Results indicate that while some models maintain statistical distributions effectively, they may introduce or amplify demographic imbalances. The analysis further highlights how model performance varies across datasets of different sizes and complexities. This work provides a comprehensive evaluation of bias-aware synthetic data generation techniques and reflects on their broader implications for human-centred AI in healthcare. The findings aim to support the responsible adoption of synthetic data in privacy-sensitive environments without compromising fairness, inclusivity, or clinical reliability.
To evaluate the fidelity and fairness of generative models, we selected three diverse tabular medical datasets that vary in source, scale, and feature composition. These datasets include laboratory blood test results, demographic variables, and clinical indicators. Each dataset provides a unique context for evaluating the models under realistic constraints. This dataset consists of anonymised blood test records from a public hospital in Ireland, collected over multiple months. It includes 9,923 rows and 62 features, covering both continuous laboratory measurements (e.g., potassium, sodium, albumin) and quality indicators such as haemolysis, icterus, and lipaemia levels. These quality fields are essential for assessing fairness, as their distributions are often skewed and underrepresented in traditional datasets. Additionally, patient demographics such as age, sex, and unique identifiers (anonymised) are included. This dataset represents a medium-sized clinical dataset with moderate complexity, suitable for testing models' handling of imbalanced subgroups and medical distributions. The second dataset is sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and contains structured medical data from multiple diagnostic tests [16]. It includes only 319 rows and 39 attributes, such as glucose, cholesterol, vitamin D levels, blood pressure, and gender. Despite its small size, this dataset is useful for examining how generative models perform under data-scarce conditions. One of the key fairness features in this dataset is Diabetes Mellitus (DM), a binary attribute with strong class imbalance. This dataset helps us evaluate how well generative models preserve minority class information and whether preprocessing or rebalancing is necessary for fairness improvement. The third dataset is a large-scale sample from the Korean NHIS 2002 dataset, containing approximately 1,000,000 records and 29 attributes [17]. It includes routine health screening data, covering features like haemoglobin, height, weight, cholesterol, liver enzymes (AST, ALT), and demographic information (age group, sex). Due to its scale and structured nature, this dataset is ideal for testing model scalability and subgroup balance across a population-level dataset. Many attributes are numerical with wide value ranges, making it a good benchmark for evaluating fidelity through statistical divergence metrics.
This study followed a structured experimental pipeline comprising dataset preparation, preprocessing, model training, synthetic data generation, and evaluation. The goal was to compare the fidelity and fairness of synthetic datasets produced by multiple generative models across distinct healthcare datasets. Each dataset was preprocessed to ensure consistency and privacy. Continuous features were normalised, and categorical variables were one-hot encoded. Missing values were imputed using median or mode, depending on the data type. Sensitive attributes such as gender, age group, and laboratory quality indicators (e.g., haemolysis, lipaemia) were preserved to support downstream fairness analysis. Seven generative models were selected for evaluation. Gaussian Copula served as a statistical baseline for modelling feature dependencies in structured numeric data. CTGAN and CopulaGAN extended generative adversarial networks (GANs) to tabular domains. TVAE utilised a variational autoencoder architecture adapted for mixed feature types. MedGAN and DiscGAN were selected for their design focus on healthcare data. Finally, FAST-ML was included as a lightweight generator for benchmarking computational efficiency. Model training was conducted separately for each dataset. To ensure reproducibility and comparability, each model was trained five times using fixed random seeds, generating synthetic outputs at 2×, 3×, and 4× the size of the original dataset. This scaling analysis was performed to observe how model fidelity and subgroup balance change as the quantity of generated data increases. Larger synthetic samples can reveal instability or bias amplification effects that may not appear at smaller scales. Evaluating multiple generation sizes therefore provides a practical stress-test of model generalisation and fairness robustness, rather than an attempt to optimise performance through dataset enlargement. GAN-based models were trained for 300 to 1500 epochs, depending on dataset complexity and convergence stability. Evaluation covered both fidelity and fairness. Fidelity was assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Wasserstein Distance, and differences in mean and standard deviation, which measure how closely synthetic features match real distributions. Visual checks using histograms and KDE plots supported these metrics. Fairness was evaluated through subgroup representation using Jensen-Shannon Divergence and Proportional Difference, with additional checks for class imbalance before and after synthesis, particularly for underrepresented groups. Raw Dataset Selection (Preprocessing) Preprocessing (normalisation, encoding, imputation) Synthetic Data Generation (7 generative models) Fidelity Evaluation (JSD, WD, Mean/Std.) Fairness Evaluation (JSD, Proportional Differ) Results Analysis It captures all key stages of the experimental pipeline -starting from raw dataset selection, followed by preprocessing, synthetic data generation using seven different models, and finally evaluation using both fidelity and fairness metrics. This structured process ensured consistent comparison across datasets of varying sizes and complexities, while enabling insights into model performance, bias behaviour, and mitigation strategies. We selected a diverse set of tabular synthesizers to benchmark performance across data types and fairness contexts. Gaussian Copula serves as a transparent statistical baseline suitable for continuous laboratory variables (Patki et al., 2016). CTGAN and TVAE are widely adopted deep generative models for mixed-type tabular data (Xu et al., 2019;D'Amico et al., 2023). CopulaGAN and discGAN extend these foundations by modelling feature dependencies and subgroup fairness (Fuentes et al., 2024). MedGAN acts as a healthcare-oriented baseline originally developed for electronic health records, while FAST-ML provides a lightweight and efficient reference for rapid generation. Evaluating both classical and neural models remains common practice in healthcare benchmarking studies (Pezoulas et al., 2022) and is particularly relevant in hospital settings where interpretability, reproducibility, and computational efficiency are essential. This combination also creates a stable baseline for comparing newer diffusion and transformer-based methods in future work. This diverse model set aligns with recent benchmarking frameworks for synthetic healthcare data generation, which recommend combining statistical, adversarial, and variational approaches to ensure fair and reproducible evaluation (D'Amico et al., 2023; Fuentes et al., 2024). During initial trials, we experimented with simple subgroup re-weighting and SMOTE-style oversampling to improve class balance before generation, as well as post-generation sampling filters to adjust subgroup proportions. These methods produced minor fairness gains but also reduced distributional fidelity and stability across datasets. Consequently, they were excluded from the final evaluation to maintain consistency and reliability of results.
The experiments were designed to evaluate the generative models on both fidelity and fairness across the three datasets. Each model was trained five times per dataset, generating synthetic datasets at multiple scales. Evaluation metrics were computed across all features, and subgroup fairness was assessed for sensitive attributes. This repeated training ensured robustness by reducing the impact of random initialization and model variance. Scaling experiments allowed us to analyse how models perform when the volume of synthetic data increases, highlighting potential issues with distribution drift or bias amplification. Together, these evaluations provided a comprehensive understanding of both the quality of the generated data and its implications for fairness in downstream use cases. Evaluation metric rationale: To ensure comparability across datasets and models, we applied complementary metrics that capture both statistical fidelity and subgroup fairness. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic quantifies the maximum difference between cumulative distributions, while the Wasserstein Distance (WD) measures overall shape and spread alignment. Mean and Standard Deviation (MD, SD) differences highlight shifts in central tendency and variance. For fairness, the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) and Maximum % Deviation captures how subgroup proportions in synthetic data diverge from real data (e.g., male vs. female, low vs. high haemolysis). This combination provides interpretable yet sensitive indicators of both data realism and representational balance. These expressing the percentage change in subgroup representation. The Maximum % Deviation reports the largest absolute proportional difference across all subgroups for that attribute. For example, if males represent 55% in real data and 52% in synthetic data, the proportional difference is -5.5%, and the maximum deviation for that attribute is 5.5%.These simple measures translate statistical divergence into an intuitive, human-readable fairness indicator. To complement the quantitative metrics, we also provide realversus-synthetic distribution plots (Figures 234) and summary tables (Tables 12). These visual comparisons illustrate how closely the synthetic data matches key features such as Albumin, Haemoglobin, and Age Group. For Dataset 1, Gaussian Copula achieved the best fidelity (KS = 0.045, WD = 0.210), with the albumin distributions showing almost complete overlap between real and synthetic data. Fairness metrics also indicated small subgroup deviations-5% for haemolysis, 2% for icterus, and 4% for lipaemia-suggesting minimal bias amplification. All visual comparisons use KDE or histogram plots to show alignment between real and synthetic data. Although KDE smoothing can introduce minor artefacts, we verified accuracy by checking raw histograms and statistical metrics (KS, WD). For Dataset 2 (UCI), TVAE achieved the highest fidelity (KS = 0.003, WD = 0.332). The haemoglobin distribution closely matched the real data, and gender balance was well preserved (2.2% deviation). The diabetes minority class was initially missing but was recovered after rebalancing the real dataset, which significantly reduced JSD and improved fairness. For Dataset 3 (Korean NHIS 2002), CTGAN demonstrated strong scalability, achieving average KS = 0.041 and WD = 0.879 (excluding the IDV-ID outlier). Age-group distributions were preserved within a 3% margin and gender proportions remained almost identical, indicating good demographic balance. Post-generation filtering further reduced residual drift, highlighting CTGAN's robustness in capturing large-scale population patterns while maintaining fairness across key subgroups. A summary of fidelity results is presented in Table 1, comparing KS, WD, and distributional differences across datasets and models. Table 2 reports subgroup fairness metrics, including proportional difference and JSD for key sensitive attributes. Overall, Gaussian Copula performed well on continuous laboratory values, TVAE was most effective on smaller mixed-type datasets, and CTGAN scaled reliably to population-level synthesis while preserving balance after filtering. In contrast, MedGAN and DiscGAN often amplified subgroup biases, particularly for gender and disease-related attributes.
The results across all three datasets highlight both the strengths and limitations of current generative models for healthcare data. Regarding RQ1, models such as Gaussian Copula, TVAE, and CT-GAN consistently achieved high fidelity, accurately reproducing key statistical properties including means, variances, and feature distributions. These findings indicate that synthetic blood data can reliably support exploratory analysis, prototyping, and privacysensitive data sharing when rigorous evaluation is applied. This aligns with prior studies demonstrating that generative models can match real clinical distributions when assessed across diverse datasets. However, fidelity alone was not sufficient-rare or imbalanced subgroups were sometimes underrepresented . For example, CTGAN required filtering to preserve extreme age categories in Dataset 3, and the minority diabetes class in Dataset 2 disappeared unless rebalancing was performed. For RQ2, our fairness analysis showed that demographic representation varied noticeably across models. Weaker generators such as DiscGAN and FAST-ML amplified subgroup bias by overfitting to dominant patterns, reinforcing the need for fairness-aware evaluation beyond global fidelity metrics. Our mitigation strategies-including preprocessing through class rebalancing and post-generation filtering-improved subgroup representation without substantial fidelity loss. Nevertheless, even small representational gaps in synthetic data may propagate into downstream predictive models, influencing calibration, sensitivity, and reliability across clinical subpopulations. This underscores the importance of subgroup-level validation before synthetic datasets are used in high-stakes applications. These findings align with broader human-centred AI principles by emphasising fairness, transparency, and accountability-requirements reflected in emerging regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and ALTAI. Reliable synthetic data can support clinicians, patients, and data stewards by enabling safer data access, reducing privacy risks, and strengthening equitable research practices. Embedding fairness evaluation into existing institutional ethics and governance processes further enhances trust and compliance. Overall, synthetic data shows substantial promise, but meaningful trade-offs exist between fidelity, fairness, and scalability. No single model excelled in all contexts, highlighting the need for continued research into hybrid, fairness-aware, and robust generative approaches, particularly for imbalanced or low-resource clinical datasets. 7 Limitations While this study presents a comprehensive evaluation of synthetic data generation in healthcare, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the fairness analysis focused on a limited set of sensitive attributes, such as gender, age group, and diabetes status. Intersectional biases-such as combinations of gender and age-were not explored, which may overlook deeper structural disparities in synthetic data representation. Second, the range of generative models was restricted to classical statistical approaches and GAN-based models. Recent diffusion or transformer-based architectures, which have shown promise in other domains, were not included due to resource and time constraints. Their inclusion could offer additional insights and more competitive baselines. Third, the datasets themselves posed challenges. The UCI dataset was relatively small, which limited the strength of statistical conclusions, while the Korean NHIS dataset, although large, lacked rich clinical annotations necessary for downstream clinical validation. Another limitation concerns the fidelity-fairness trade-off. While methods such as rebalancing and post-generation filtering improved subgroup parity, their effect on downstream utility (e.g., predictive model performance) was not assessed. Finally, model hyperparameters were kept constant across experiments for comparability. More extensive tuning, especially for deep learning models, could potentially enhance results. Future research should address these limitations by incorporating broader fairness metrics, exploring state-of-the-art generative models, and evaluating task-specific utility on synthetic datasets.
This paper presented a comprehensive evaluation of synthetic blood data generation using seven generative models applied across three medical datasets of varying size, complexity, and clinical relevance. By adopting a dual evaluation framework that jointly assessed fidelity and fairness, we examined not only how effectively each model replicated key statistical properties of the data, but also how well they preserved the representation of sensitive attributes such as gender, age group, diabetes status, and laboratory quality indicators. This combined perspective allowed us to evaluate synthetic data not just as a statistical product, but as a socio-technical tool intended for responsible healthcare use. Addressing RQ1, our results show that machine-learning models can generate realistic and statistically reliable synthetic healthcare data when supported by rigorous evaluation and appropriate preprocessing. High-fidelity models such as Gaussian Copula and TVAE demonstrated strong capability in preserving distributions, capturing central tendencies, and modelling feature variability even in smaller or mixed-type datasets. CTGAN further demonstrated the ability to scale to population-level synthesis in the NHIS dataset, producing large synthetic samples while maintaining stable fidelity. However, fidelity alone did not ensure balanced representation. Rare subgroups-such as extreme ages or minority diabetes cases-were often underrepresented without fairness interventions, showing the need to prevent subgroup loss in imbalanced datasets. Addressing RQ2, our fairness analysis demonstrated that bias in synthetic data can be effectively quantified using subgroup-based metrics, including Jensen-Shannon Divergence, Proportional Difference, and Maximum % Deviation. These measures revealed that while strong models maintained low subgroup divergence, weaker models such as DiscGAN and FAST-ML amplified dominant categories, distorted demographic proportions, or collapsed minority groups entirely. Pre-generation balancing and post-generation filtering proved effective in correcting these issues with minimal fidelity impact, reinforcing the importance of fairness-aware workflows. These results align with human-centred AI principles and recent regulatory expectations, such as the EU AI Act and ALTAI guidelines, which emphasise transparency, accountability, and equitable performance in high-risk domains like healthcare. Looking ahead, future research should explore more advanced generative architectures-such as diffusion models [24,25] transformer-based tabular generators, and hybrid statistical-neural approaches-to better balance fidelity, fairness, and robustness. Additional fairness dimensions, including intersectional biases, sociodemographic attributes, and temporal consistency, should also be considered for more comprehensive evaluation. Further work is needed to assess how synthetic datasets affect downstream predictive model performance and to better connect statistical validation with practical clinical utility.

Tool-wielding language model-based agent offers conversational exploration of clinical tabular data
Advancing evidence-based medicine requires integrating clinical expertise with data analysis. While clinicians contribute essential domain knowledge, applying modern data science methods often requires specialized training, creating a barrier to adoption. To bridge this gap, we developed ChatDA, an artificial intelligence agent enabling large language model-mediated conversational analysis of de-identified clinical tabular datasets. ChatDA empowers clinicians to extract meaningful insights efficiently and accurately, making data-driven clinical research more accessible and effective.
To enable AI-assisted clinical data analysis primarily through predefined tools, we developed TableMage, a high-level, low-code Python package designed specifically for analyzing tabular clinical data. Our focus on tabular formats reflects their central role in clinical research (Supplementary Note 4). TableMage integrates functionality from widely used packages in the Python ecosystem including NumPy42 and pandas43 for data manipulation, SciPy44 and Statsmodels45 for statistical analysis, Matplotlib46 and seaborn47 for data visualization, Scikit-learn48 and Optuna49 for machine learning and hyperparameter optimization, and Boruta30 for feature selectiot
A core feature of TableMage is its seamless integration of data exploration, transformation, and modeling within a unified framework. It enforces strict separation between training and testing sets by requiring a train-test split prior to any analysis. This guarantees that the test set remains entirely isolated from all transformation and modeling processes, effectively mitigating data leakage and preserving the integrity of model assessment. This design allows users—whether human or AI agent—to freely conduct exploratory data analysis, apply transformations, and train models without worrying about execution order or inadvertently neglecting to persist transformations. By automatically tracking and applying transformations, TableMage ensures consistency across training and testing data, preventing common errors such as applying scaling only to the training set or failing to carry over preprocessing steps to new data. We note that exploratory analyses—summary statistics generation, distribution visualization, statistical testing, and correlation analyses—are still performed on the entire dataset, and the initial train-test split is enforced primarily to ensure proper modeling, as preprocessing-related mistakes are frequent (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html48). Additionally, TableMage enables highly efficient pipelining by automatically converting any sequence of transformations into a custom scikit-learn pipeline. When combined with a fitted model, this pipeline can be serialized for downstream analysis and deployment, streamlining the entire machine learning workflow.
Building upon TableMage, we developed a suite of clinical data analysis tools using LlamaIndex50, an AI agent development framework. These tools were then integrated into ChatDA, a function-calling agent designed to facilitate conversational data analysis. To optimize the use of the underlying LLM’s context window, ChatDA dynamically selects only the most relevant tools for a given query through retrieval-augmented generation13. Once the appropriate tools are identified, ChatDA executes them and synthesizes a response based on their outputs. If appropriate, ChatDA can use multiple tools to respond to a single query. As a conversational agent, ChatDA utilizes a buffer-based memory for short-term recall and a vector index-based memory for long-term retention, ensuring continuity and context awareness in conversations.
ChatDA optionally provides access to a Python interpreter for short-term tasks such as data indexing and generating custom plots. However, because the Python interpreter allows direct access to individual-level data, its use must be restricted to non-sensitive datasets or cases where the underlying LLM is locally hosted to ensure data security. Even without access to its Python interpreter, ChatDA can still perform operations such as categorical variable encoding, value counting, and min/max value reporting using its built-in tools, thereby limiting its applicability to properly de-identified datasets. We provide a discussion of the aggregate-level reporting scheme of ChatDA’s tools and its potential to reduce the likelihood of re-identification in Supplementary Note 1.
ChatDA is compatible with cloud-hosted LLMs (closed-source or open-source) as well as with locally hosted open-source LLMs. If ChatDA is powered by a multimodal foundation language model such as GPT-4o, it can view and analyze the figures generated by its tools. ChatDA’s tools are listed in Supplementary Table 1.
We evaluated the performance of ChatDA, OpenAI Advanced Data Analysis, Open Interpreter, and Data Interpreter on a range of non-machine learning (non-ML) and supervised machine learning (ML) tasks.
To assess text in, text out AI systems (e.g., language model-based data analysis/coding agents) on foundational data analysis capabilities, we developed DataAnalysisQA, a benchmark consisting of 100 question-answer pairs across 10 publicly available tabular datasets. This benchmark was inspired by InfiAgent-DABench18 but addresses several key limitations we observed in its design:
Code-specific technical language. Many questions in InfiAgent-DABench prompt agents to invoke specific Python functions, favoring Python code-writing agents rather than general-purpose data analysts.
Code-specific technical language. Many questions in InfiAgent-DABench prompt agents to invoke specific Python functions, favoring Python code-writing agents rather than general-purpose data analysts.
Dependence on OpenAI Advanced Data Analysis. InfiAgent-DABench was constructed using GPT-4 and OpenAI ADA, making it less suitable for independently evaluating OpenAI’s own tools.
Lack of continuity. All questions in InfiAgent-DABench are independent, limiting its ability to assess whether agents can retain and apply transformations across sequential queries.
To address these limitations, we designed DataAnalysisQA using human-generated questions and ground truth answers, ensuring broader applicability and independence from specific AI systems. For each of the 10 datasets, we curated a coherent sequence of queries covering summary statistics, data transformation, indexing, statistical testing, feature engineering, and regression. This sequential structure enabled the evaluation of each agent’s ability to retain and apply data transformations over multiple interactions. Unlike the code-specific instructions commonly found in InfiAgent-DABench, our benchmark queries were designed to be accessible while maintaining clarity and ensuring unique, well-defined answers. Ground truth results were generated manually for each query, and all question-answer pairs were labeled with one or more topic categories, including indexing, statistical testing, data transformation, persistence (retention of previous transformations), summary statistics, and regression analysis. In total, DataAnalysisQA consists of 100 questions across these categories.
In addition to non-ML tasks, we evaluated all agents on 11 publicly available datasets from a tabular ML benchmark51 on OpenML52. The 11 datasets represent the subset of the tabular data machine learning benchmark with no more than 10,000 rows and no more than 100 columns; larger datasets were filtered out to ensure fair evaluation of OpenAI Advanced Data Analysis, which is the limited by its cloud CPU memory and runtime capacities. Each agent was instructed or preconfigured to perform a 70–30 train-test split with identical random seeds and to report the best-performing model based on evaluation metrics. For regression tasks, we used root mean squared error (RMSE) as the primary metric, while for binary classification tasks, we evaluated model performance using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
For both ML and non-ML benchmarks, ChatDA was evaluated in two modes: (1) normal mode, where it had access to both its custom tools and a Python interpreter, and (2) tools-only mode, where it was restricted to its custom tools only. In normal mode, ChatDA was tested with both a closed-source LLM (GPT-4o) and an open-source LLM (Llama 3.3 70B). While normal mode ChatDA does not reduce data re-identification risk when using a cloud hosted LLM, it does guarantee data privacy when powered by a locally hosted LLM. Notably, Llama 3.3 70B can be deployed on consumer-grade hardware, offering a privacy-preserving alternative. In tools-only mode, ChatDA was tested exclusively with the closed-source GPT-4o. Together, these evaluations assessed two approaches to reducing the risk of data re-identification: (1) local LLM usage (normal mode with Llama 3.3 70B) and (2) a non-coding approach (tools-only mode with GPT-4o). Additionally, normal mode with GPT-4o was tested as an option for non-sensitive datasets.
For both benchmarks, agents return unstructured output. Following InfiAgent-DABench, we employed LLMs to extract structured answers from unstructured output. To assess stability, each agent was tested across 10 replicates in both the data analysis and machine learning benchmarks. For each metric, the mean and its 95% confidence interval were reported. Complete DataAnalysisQA and machine learning benchmarking results are presented in Supplementary Figs. 1–3. For DataAnalysisQA, failure rates, defined as the proportion of questions an agent could not answer, were calculated by category for each agent (Supplementary Fig. 4). For ChatDA, tool-level error rates were determined by manually labeling each question with the tool expected to produce the correct answer (Supplementary Fig. 5). We include ChatDA’s performance on the InfiAgent-DABench benchmark in Supplementary Note 5. In addition to the performance benchmarks, a brief analysis of agent software usability is included in Supplementary Note 12.
ChatDA was evaluated using both GPT-4o, a closed-source model, and Llama 3.3 70B, an open-source model, as its underlying LLM, with model temperatures set to 0.1 to allow for variability in responses. OpenAI Advanced Data Analysis, Open Interpreter, and Data Interpreter were all evaluated with GPT-4o as their underlying LLM. ChatDA, Open Interpreter, and Data Interpreter were assessed systematically using Python scripts, while OpenAI Advanced Data Analysis was evaluated by manually uploading datasets to ChatGPT and obtaining responses through direct queries. To standardize the output for scoring, we used GPT-4o-mini to convert unstructured agent responses into structured formats. Additional implementation details, including system prompts and pre-analysis instructions, are available in Supplementary Notes 6–9.
To assess ChatDA’s practical utility in a real-world setting, we applied it to a proprietary clinical dataset comprising 1419 knee arthroplasty patients. We investigated whether patient-specific anatomical and functional features could predict the surgeon’s choice between TKA and UKA—a critical decision in knee joint reconstruction. The dataset contained 36 variables, including demographic characteristics (e.g., age, sex, height, and weight), detailed quantitative assessments of knee joint morphology (e.g., bone dimensions, joint angles, and alignment metrics), functional range-of-motion measurements (e.g., flexion and rotation), and structural deformity indicators (e.g., varus/valgus alignment, joint line convergence, and tibial slope irregularities). These features provide a comprehensive characterization of knee joint anatomy, biomechanics, and pathological severity, offering key insights into surgical decision-making. A subset of patients was manually annotated by a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon to establish ground truth labels for TKA and UKA. Dataset metadata is provided in Supplementary Note
The primary objective of this analysis was to evaluate whether ChatDA could derive clinically meaningful insights from these features, particularly in predicting surgical decision patterns. Given that many clinicians lack the technical expertise required for advanced statistical modeling, we aimed to assess ChatDA’s ability to bridge this gap by enabling conversational data analysis. Prior to analysis, we ensured compliance with HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification guidelines (https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/de-identification/index.html)53. To further reduce the likelihood of re-identification, we disabled ChatDA’s Python interpreter (tools-only analysis mode), eliminating the LLM’s ability to access individual-level data. This constraint ensured that the LLM processed only structured tool outputs, which were explicitly designed to provide insights at the population level while excluding any patient-specific information (Fig. 2A). To simulate real-world clinical use, all queries were phrased in non-technical language, requiring no prior programming or statistical expertise. The full conversational session was completed without manual intervention and is available in Supplementary Note 11.
The clinical dataset analyzed in this study was derived from preoperative imaging data originally collected for a previously published study29. The corresponding author of that study shared the data with our team. The study from which the data originated had been determined to be exempt from IRB review by Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Our team did not interact with human participants, and upon receipt, we de-identified the dataset in accordance with HIPAA Safe Harbor guidelines.

Towards advanced AI-based solutions for securing IoMT in smart health information systems
The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) refers to the number of interconnected medical objects and applications that are essential in contemporary healthcare. Nevertheless, its dependence on interrelated ecosystems subjects it to high risks of cybersecurity, including data breaches, privacy breaches, and malicious attacks that threaten patient safety and system integrity. This paper resolves these issues by presenting a new and enhanced intrusion detection model, BiGRU/RBWK, which is a combination of Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Units (BiGRU) with a Refined Black-winged Kite (RBWK) optimization algorithm. The RBWK algorithm improves on the BiGRU model by optimizing its hyperparameters, resulting in faster convergence and better classification performance. The model uses a powerful preprocessing pipeline, which includes Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) that is used in conjunction with Support Vector Machines (SVM), which helps to curb the overfitting and lessen the computational cost. The experimental findings with two public datasets, namely WUSTL-EHMS-2020 and ECU-IoHT, indicate that BiGRU/RBWK model displays higher accuracy (95.6% and 93.8% respectively), precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC than all other currently available methods, including Random Forest, LSTM, CNN, Autoencoder, and CNN-LSTM hybrid models. The suggested framework has a high discrimination capability and can be easily used in real-time applications in the resource-constrained IoMT settings
To ensure the proposed model is valid, two public datasets were used: WUSTL-EHMS-2020 29 and ECU-IoHT 30 . e multiple datasets used in this model represent various scenarios of IoMT applications to empower it with robustness through diversity across healthcare-based applications.The WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset was created due to the absence of public datasets that combine network flow metrics with patient biometric data on a real testbed, employing a real-time Enhanced Healthcare Monitoring System (EHMS) testbed. The EHMS testbed framework was composed of four main components, which include medical sensors, a gateway, network infrastructures, and a control system visualization, as shown in Fig. 2. Data is transferred from sensors attached to patients to a gateway, from which it flows to a server through a switch and router for visualization. This architecture is susceptible to potential threats, since attackers can eavesdrop and capture data during transit. One prevalent attack type is simply data injection, where packets are modified as they travel through the network, breaking the integrity of data. The dataset consists of 16,318 samples, as indicated in Table 2. The dataset size is 4.4 MB. It contains a thorough description of both normal and attack instances, and as a result, can be used to reliably evaluate the functionality of intrusion detection systems in the healthcare domain. ECU-IoHT (East Carolina University Internet of Health Things) simulates attacks for identifying the vulnerable scenarios in a specific environment. It targets many different attacks to identify many different vulnerabilities. It enables the healthcare security community to study attack behaviors and develop more robust defensive capabilities. Figure 3 presents the ECU-IoHT testbed. The new anomaly detection framework was proposed using the ECU-IoHT data set, which is unique in this area and can be used for evaluating various degrees of anomaly/manipulation detection algorithms, and revealed that among the investigated nearest neighbor-based methods performs better than clustering, statistical, and kernel-based methods for detecting cyberattacks. Table 3 indicates the description of the ECU-IoHT dataset.
The two datasets were selected for this study because of their high relevance to real-world IoMT environments and representativeness of both normal and attack scenarios in healthcare systems. The WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset was specifically designed to simulate an Enhanced Healthcare Monitoring System in such a manner as to capture both network flow metrics and patient biometric data through a realistic testbed designed to replicate hospital environments where medical sensors engage in communication with centralized monitoring systems.
Thus, evaluation of intrusion detection models specifically aimed toward IoMT paradigms is most amenable here, where data integrity and the timely detection of threats are of intense concern. In stark contrast, the ECU-IoHT dataset provided a wealth of cyberattack types, including ARP spoofing, DoS attacks, port scanning, and Smurf attacks, in a controlled IoHT environment for a thorough examination of the model’s ability to detect both common threats and much more sophisticated ones.
Both datasets reflect heterogeneous IoMT use cases, including wearable health-monitoring devices and networked clinical equipment, therefore ensuring that our approach is generalized across various smart healthcare applications. Furthermore, the fact that they are open datasets means that they lend themselves to reproducibility and comparative study, two conditions that will be very much conducive to the development of research into secure IoMT systems.
Pre-processing of Data is an important step to ensure that data is up to the mark and applicable to ML or DL models. This study explains the preprocessing of the IoMT datasets, which comprise the following: Encoding of categorical features, missing value treatment, class imbalance treatment, and outlier treatment. The model introduces two key innovations: (i) a Trimester-Weighted Wasserstein Similarity (TW-WD) mechanism for adaptive alignment of user and video embeddings under trimester-specific safety constraints, and (ii) a Safety-Aware Directed Graph Convolutional Relational Neural Network (GCRNN) that propagates health-condition and trimester relationships across the recommendation graph. Experimental results demonstrate an accuracy of 98.3% under fivefold cross-validation and over 97.5% trimester-specific safety compliance, highlighting the framework's clinical reliability and effectiveness in delivering personalized prenatal yoga recommendations.this section, we propose a novel trimester-aware yoga video recommendation framework that leverages hybrid deep learning to provide clinically safe and personalized yoga pose suggestions for pregnant women. Unlike conventional yoga or video recommendation models, the framework introduces two key innovations: a Trimester-Weighted Wasserstein Similarity (TW-WD) mechanism and a Safety-Aware Directed Graph Convolutional Relational Neural Network (GCRNN). The TW-WD adaptively aligns user and video embeddings by weighting similarity according to trimester-specific physiological safety, enforcing stricter filtering during early trimesters and progressively relaxed constraints in later stages. Concurrently, the Safety-Aware GCRNN extends conventional GCNs by encoding directed relationships among users, poses, and videos that reflect both trimester and health conditions, enabling propagation of safety information across the relational graph. The workflow begins with preprocessing of video and text data to ensure consistency and quality. Text metadata are processed using stop word removal, tokenization, and lemmatization, while video frames are extracted and denoised using the Fused Probabilistic Wiener Filter (FProbWF) to preserve fine posture details. Features are extracted from text via Boosted Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (BTF-IDF) and from video frames using ResNet152 for deep visual embeddings. These multimodal features, combined with user profile attributes, are integrated and compared using the proposed trimester-weighted Wasserstein similarity. The fused embeddings are subsequently processed by the safety-aware GCRNN to generate trimester-specific, personalized, and medically safe yoga recommendations. To achieve this, we propose a trimester-weighted Wasserstein similarity function that conditions multimodal similarity computations on the pregnancy stage. This mechanism enables stricter filtering of potentially unsafe poses during early trimesters while permitting controlled flexibility in later stages. Preprocessing of both text and video data is a crucial step for ensuring consistency and quality in recommending yoga poses from YouTube videos for pregnant women. Text preprocessing reduces variability in video metadata and is performed through three main steps: stop word removal, tokenization, and lemmatization. Video preprocessing focuses on enhancing frame quality by removing noise from the extracted individual frames. In this work, a Fused Probabilistic Wiener Filter (FProbWF) is applied for denoising, preserving fine posture details and improving the clarity of video images for accurate feature extraction and subsequent recommendation.The three major phases like stop word removal, tokenization, and lemmatization31,32 are discussed below:
Stop words are common words used to connect or complete sentences in textual data, but they generally carry little semantic significance. Since they do not contribute meaningfully to most natural language processing tasks, these words are typically removed to reduce noise and improve computational efficiency. Eliminating stop words does not compromise the semantic content of the original text; rather, it helps focus on the meaningful terms. In the proposed method, stop words are removed by comparing each token in the text against a predefined stop word list, ensuring that only relevant words are retained for subsequent feature extraction and analysis.After stop words are removed, the text is tokenized by separating the significant words from the input. Tokenization is a critical step, as it identifies the key terms that contribute most the semantic meaning of the text. This process can be challenging for languages without explicit word boundaries, as well as for texts containing symbols or special characters. In the proposed method, each sentence is first divided into a list of words, and the meaningful tokens are subsequently extracted from this list to be used in downstream feature extraction and analysis.Lemmatization is the process of converting a word into its base or dictionary form while preserving its contextual meaning. After tokenization, each word is analyzed, and complex or inflected forms are replaced with their corresponding lemmas. Although this step may appear minor, it improves overall system performance by reducing redundancy in the vocabulary, enhancing consistency in textual representation, and increasing processing efficiency for downstream feature extraction and similarity computations.Each collected video was converted into a sequence of RGB frames using FFmpeg for frame extraction and OpenCV for resizing and normalization. Frames were uniformly sampled at a fixed rate of one frame per second to capture representative yoga poses while keeping feature computation tractable. All frames extracted from a given video were treated as a single unit during dataset partitioning. Frames were resized to 224 × 224 pixels to match the input requirements of ResNet152, and pixel values were normalized using ImageNet statistics (mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])33.To enhance frame quality, each image was denoised using the Fused Probabilistic Wiener Filter (FProbWF), which incorporates Gaussian mask kernels, local mean filtering, and sliding-windowvariance adjustment34. This approach divides each frame into smaller pixel groups, processes each group individually, and effectively reduces noise while preserving fine posture details. For videos with fewer than two frames, all available frames were used; for longer videos, uniform sampling at 1 fps was applied to reduce computational costs and eliminate redundancy33. Denoised and normalized frames were then exported as JPEG or PNG files and forwarded To estimate the corresponding Gaussian standard deviation, convolution with a Gaussian mask is applied to the frame image, enabling noise-aware preprocessing prior to feature extraction. A predetermined noise threshold is used to determine the mask size, allowing selection among different kernel options. Subsequently, mean filtering is applied using a local mask via convolution with the selected kernels. A sliding-window subtraction technique is then employed to generate a variance-adjusted image, ensuring uniform distribution by leveraging local variance features to produce balanced outcomes. Finally, a denoised image is obtained by averaging the results from the uniform distribution, effectively reducing noise while preserving important posture details.Before preprocessing, each video was reviewed to ensure that only pregnancy-safe yoga poses were included in the dataset. This screening process followed established prenatal yoga safety guidelines and expert recommendations, ensuring that all retained videos were suitable for pregnant participants.

To address these limitations, the proposed study utilizes efficient techniques to derive meaningful features from preprocessed text. Boosted Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (BTF-IDF)35 enables semantic feature extraction by quantifying the importance of each word in the dataset. High-quality feature representation is achieved by combining unigram and bigram models, which capture both individual words and word-pair relationships. The inverse document frequency (IDF) component provides a global evaluation by quantifying the importance of a term across the entire dataset. By combining TF and IDF, the method assigns weighted importance to terms, enhancing the representation of key textual features for downstream recommendation tasks. Each frame was denoised using the Fused Probabilistic Wiener Filter (FProbWF). The last classification layer of ResNet152 was discarded, and the output of the global average pooling layer was used as a 2048-dimensional feature vector. For each video, a video-level embedding was obtained by averaging the frame-level feature vectors across all sampled frames, providing a compact and robust representation. These embeddings were then fused with textual features and passed to the GCRNN via the Wasserstein distance-based similarity computation module. This approach produces stable pretrained spatial representations even on a relatively small dataset while maintaining moderate training time and memory requirements.
Compared to 3D convolutional networks such as C3D, I3D, 3D-ResNets, or transformer-based video encoders like ViViT, ResNet152 is more efficient for the current task. Although these models can capture spatial and temporal dynamics, they require large annotated datasets, extensive training, and high GPU memory. Given that the dataset comprises 200 videos, which primarily rely on static spatial arrangements of individual frames to represent basic yoga poses, ResNet152 with transfer learning provides stable spatial embeddings, reduces overfitting, and lowers computational demands. Temporal and relational patterns are subsequently encoded using GCRNN-based sequence learning, frame sampling, embedding aggregation, and Wasserstein similarity, eliminating the need for complex spatio-temporal models while effectively capturing both spatial and temporal features.
By computing TF-IDF and Wasserstein distance across modalities, the framework enables cross-modal similarity learning. Textual data, including user search queries and yoga pose descriptions, are represented via TF-IDF, which transforms inputs into sparse vectors that highlight highly informative words. ResNet152 converts video frames into 2048-dimensional embeddings, which are L2-normalized and treated as visual probability distributions. The Wasserstein distance (also called Earth Mover’s Distance) measures similarity between video embeddings and user query representations by computing the minimum cost of transforming one distribution into another. This framework allows TF-IDF to capture semantic similarity in text space and Wasserstein distance to capture visual similarity, providing an effective method to map user queries to corresponding yoga video frames.

is research presents a hybrid, safety-aware recommendation framework that integrates data preprocessing, advanced feature extraction, and relational graph learning to deliver trimester-specific yoga pose recommendations for pregnant women. e proposed system balances accuracy and safety by employing FProbWF for denoising, BTF-IDF and ResNet152 for multimodal feature extraction, and Wasserstein Distance for similarity measurement, while the GCRNN model captures complex relationships among users, videos, and yoga poses to enable personalized recommendations. Vaner2: towards more general biomedical named entity recognition using multi-task large language model encoders
Biomedical named entity recognition (BioNER) serves as the foundation for many downstream tasks, such as relation extraction, question answering, and clinical text analysis. BioNER was previously dominated by BERT-based models pretrained on large biomedical corpora. However, BERT-based models finetuned on specific BioNER datasets exhibit limited ability to generalize to other datasets. With the recent advances of large language models (LLMs), several works have fine-tuned autoregressive LLMs that are not inherently suitable for BioNER tasks, which limits model performance. In this study, building upon our previous work VANER, we utilized LLMs with the causal attention mask removed as a text encoder for sequence labeling. Using 39 BioNER datasets, we trained a multi-task NER model that extracts all entity types with one LLM forward pass. We also proposed a token-wise loss rescaling technique to deal with the data imbalance between different tags and entity types. Extensive experiments on independent test datasets demonstrated that our VANER2 model achieved the best generalization results compared with BERT-based baselines and several recent BioNER methods.
We collected 39 expert-annotated biomedical NER datasets for training and evaluation of our model , representing a diverse range of entity types and domains (Please refer to Figs. 4 and 5 for dataset overview, more details are provided in Supplementary Table 1 and 2), and selected annotations of 8 entity types from them: Gene, Chemical, Disease, Species, Cell Line, Variant, Anatomy, Cell Type. All datasets are converted to PubTator format to ensure consistency and facilitate analysis. To further enhance data quality, we first used the unidecode python package to replace all special characters in text with ascii characters. en we applied entity span correction by matching the entity names in annotations to the text and selecting the entity that is closest to the originally labeled entity span. Annotations that did not find a corresponding match in text were discarded Fig. 3 Our instruction for Llama 3.1 model to ensure consistency and accuracy. Finally, we manually corrected certain format mismatches in different datasets following AIONER [25]. Specifically, we removed the cell(s) suffix for Cell Line and Cell Type annotations, and removed too general annotations, such as "gene" for gene, "animal(s)" for species. Note that for the MedMentions dataset, we used the full version instead of the st21pv version since many valid entities do not appear in the st21pv version, resulting in poor model performance when testing on the MedMentions dataset.
We utilized all the collected datasets (except the test datasets) to train our VANER2 model. We used Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B as our backbone model and finetuned the model parameters together with the classification heads. Since our training dataset is very large, we only conducted MNTP fine-tuning for 1 epoch, then instruction fine-tuning for 4 epochs. Both MNTP finetuning and instruction fine-tuning incorporated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [66]. After MNTP fine-tuning, we merged the LoRA adapter parameters into the base model and initialized another LoRA adapter for instruction fine-tuning. Our work showed the potential of encoder LLM for the BioNER task and marks the first systematic investigation into the generalization ability of LLMs for BioNER. While most existing works evaluate models only on the same datasets they are trained on, which may not be able to reflect the actual performance of the model on real applications, as each dataset has its bias and limited scope. Several works have shown that models that perform well on trained datasets can suffer from a large performance drop when tested on independent datasets [11,26,68]. For this reason, we selected several independent test datasets for each entity type and used the average F-score on them as a more accurate model evaluation. e result agrees with our hypothesis: models leveraging larger amounts of training data exhibit better generalization, as evidenced by improved performance on unseen datasets. On the other hand, by using token-wise loss rescaling, we better balanced different tasks in our MTL model and further improved the capability of MTL. Our work still has several limitations. For example, though VANER2 is fast among LLM based methods, it's still much slower compared with BERT based methods since LLMs have a lot more parameters. Also, Llama 3.1 has not been exclusively trained on biomedical data, so its overall performance may be constrained. In the future, we plan to improve the efficiency of the model using model distillation. In this paper, we proposed an LLM-based bioNER model VANER2. Instead of using LLM for generation, we regarded the LLM as a text encoder and utilized a multitask scheme to train an all-in-one NER model. By applying MNTP fine-tuning and token-wise loss rescaling, we further improved the model's capability. VANER2 is trained on 32 BioNER datasets, supporting recognition of 8 entity types. Compared with VANER, our model runs much faster and generalizes better. We also surpassed several existing SOTA BioNER methods. Overall, our result showed that encoder LLMs can be competitive on BioNER tasks, providing a new perspective to solving BioNER problems.

Brain Latent Progression: Individual-based spatiotemporal disease progression on 3D Brain MRIs via latent diffusion The growing availability of longitudinal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) datasets has facilitated Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven modeling of disease progression, making it possible to predict future medical scans for individual patients. However, despite significant advancements in AI, current methods continue to face challenges including achieving patient-specific individualization, ensuring spatiotemporal consistency, efficiently utilizing longitudinal data, and managing the substantial memory demands of 3D scans. To address these challenges, we propose Brain Latent Progression (BrLP), a novel spatiotemporal model designed to predict individual-level disease progression in 3D brain MRIs. The key contributions in BrLP are fourfold: (i) it operates in a small latent space, mitigating the computational challenges posed by high-dimensional imaging data; (ii) it explicitly integrates subject metadata to enhance the individualization of predictions; (iii) it incorporates prior knowledge of disease dynamics through an auxiliary model, facilitating the integration of longitudinal data; and (iv) it introduces the Latent Average Stabilization (LAS) algorithm, which (a) enforces spatiotemporal consistency in the predicted progression at inference time and (b) allows us to derive a measure of the uncertainty for the prediction at the global and voxel level. We train and evaluate BrLP on 11,730 T1-weighted (T1w) brain MRIs from 2,805 subjects and validate its generalizability on an external test set comprising 2,257 MRIs from 962 subjects. Our experiments compare BrLP-generated MRI scans with real follow-up MRIs, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy compared to existing methods. The growing availability of longitudinal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) datasets has facilitated Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven modeling of disease progression, making it possible to predict future medical scans for individual patients. However, despite significant advancements in AI, current methods continue to face challenges including achieving patient-specific individualization, ensuring spatiotemporal consistency, efficiently utilizing longitudinal data, and managing the substantial memory demands of 3D scans. To address these challenges, we propose Brain Latent Progression (BrLP), a novel spatiotemporal model designed to predict individual-level disease progression in 3D brain MRIs. The key contributions in BrLP are fourfold: (i) it operates in a small latent space, mitigating the computational challenges posed by high-dimensional imaging data; (ii) it explicitly integrates subject metadata to enhance the individualization of predictions; (iii) it incorporates prior knowledge of disease dynamics through an auxiliary model, facilitating the integration of longitudinal data; and (iv) it introduces the Latent Average Stabilization (LAS) algorithm, which (a) enforces spatiotemporal consistency in the predicted progression at inference time and (b) allows us to derive a measure of the uncertainty for the prediction at the global and voxel level. We train and evaluate BrLP on 11,730 T1-weighted (T1w) brain MRIs from 2,805 subjects and validate its generalizability on an external test set comprising 2,257 MRIs from 962 subjects. Our experiments compare BrLP-generated MRI scans with real follow-up MRIs, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy compared to existing methods. The code is publicly available at: . Neurodegenerative diseases represent one of the most pressing challenges in modern healthcare, as these conditions lead to an irreversible decline in brain function and quality of life. With no effective cures available to date, patients and caregivers face prolonged suffering, while healthcare systems struggle with escalating costs and resource demands. Tackling this crisis requires a paradigm shift towards proactive strategies that prioritize early intervention, precision medicine, and comprehensive care. These diseases are notoriously complex, displaying a wide range of neuropathological variations linked to distinct molecular subtypes ( Tijms et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, they manifest unevenly across brain regions, progressing through diverse mechanisms and at varying speeds, reflecting the intricate nature of their pathophysiology ( Young et al., 2018 ). Addressing this issue requires the development of advanced tools to deepen our understanding of disease mechanisms, ultimately facilitating the creation of tailored and more effective therapeutic strategies. Early approaches to disease progression modeling focused on capturing the dynamics of scalar biomarkers ( Young et al., 2024; Oxtoby and Alexander, 2017 ). For instance, in Firth et al. (2019) , the characteristic atrophy patterns observed in subjects with posterior cortical atrophy are studied by modeling the volumetric changes in specific brain regions. Although scalar biomarkers provide a simplified representation, they have significantly advanced our understanding of various neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) ( Vogel et al., 2021 ) and multiple sclerosis ( Eshaghi et al., 2021 ). However, a significant limitation of these approaches is their inability to capture spatiotemporal characteristics that may more accurately reflect the underlying pathophysiology of a disease. For instance, patients with frontotemporal dementia exhibit shape alterations in the thalamus prior to any detectable volumetric reduction ( Cury et al., 2019 ). The growing recognition of spatiotemporal patterns has driven the evolution of traditional disease progression models towards spatiotemporal approaches. Spatiotemporal models ( Young et al., 2024 ) typically leverage high-dimensional data, such as 3D shapes or full medical scans, to represent disease dynamics in a more detailed and holistic manner, enabling the visualization and precise localization of complex structural changes over time. In particular, this paper will focus on spatiotemporal models applied to 3D T1w brain MRIs, with the goal of estimating the structural changes occurring in the brain at the individual level, under both pathological (e.g., neurodegeneration) and non-pathological conditions (i.e., aging). We identify and focus on four primary challenges associated with this task: 1. Individualization. Disease progression is influenced by various individual factors, including demographic and clinical variables. To improve prediction accuracy, models must incorporate and leverage subject-specific metadata. 2. Longitudinal Data Exploitation. Longitudinal data offer valuable insights into individual disease trajectories, such as the rate of progression for each patient. When available, models should integrate this data into the inference process. 3. Spatiotemporal Consistency. Predictions of disease progression across multiple time points should display a smooth, consistent evolution that aligns with the underlying biological processes. 4. Memory Demand. Processing 3D medical images requires significant memory resources, which can limit model applicability in low-resource environments ( Blumberg et al., 2018 ). Enabling such models to run on consumer-grade hardware would support more widespread adoption. Individualization.
