Recent developments in breast cancer detection have explored sophisticated architectural innovations beyond traditional CNNs, incorporating attention mechanisms, vision transformers, multi-modal learning, and radiomics integration. Attention mechanisms have emerged as powerful tools for focusing model capacity on diagnostically relevant image regions. Nissar et al. [ 7 ] developed MOB-CBAM, a dual-channel attention-based model for predicting breast cancer molecular subtypes from mammograms. The architecture integrates Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) with MobileNetV2, achieving superior generalization across diverse mammography datasets. The dual-channel design processes spatial and channel-wise attention separately, enabling the model to identify subtle mammographic patterns associated with molecular subtypes (Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-enriched, Triple-negative). Their multi-dataset validation demonstrated robust performance across varying imaging protocols and patient populations, addressing a critical limitation in many deep learning studies. The success of Vision Transformers (ViT) in computer vision has motivated their application to breast cancer detection. Nissar et al. [ 8 ] proposed Mod-ViT, a Vision Transformer-based framework for breast cancer detection from multiple imaging modalities including mammography, ultrasound, and MRI. Unlike CNNs that process images through localized convolution operations, Mod-ViT uses self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies across the entire image. The multi-modal architecture employs modality-specific encoders followed by cross-attention fusion, enabling the model to leverage complementary information from different imaging techniques. Their results demonstrated that ViT-based models can effectively integrate heterogeneous imaging data, achieving higher diagnostic accuracy than single-modality approaches. However, this performance comes at substantial computational cost—Mod-ViT requires significantly more GPU memory and training time than CNN-based alternatives. Nissar et al. [ 9 ] introduced SwinEff-AttentionNet, a dual hybrid model combining Swin Transformer with EfficientNet for breast image segmentation and classification using multiple ultrasound modalities. The architecture addresses a key challenge in ultrasound-based diagnosis: accurately segmenting tumor boundaries in images with varying resolution and contrast. SwinEff-AttentionNet employs hierarchical Swin Transformer blocks for global context modelling and EfficientNet components for efficient local feature extraction. The attention-guided segmentation module progressively refines tumour boundaries by focusing on boundary regions with high uncertainty. Experimental results on B-mode, elastography, and Doppler ultrasound demonstrated superior segmentation accuracy compared to U-Net and DeepLab variants. The model achieved 94.7% dice coefficient for tumour segmentation and 92.3% classification accuracy for malignancy detection. Integration of radiomics features with deep learning has shown promise for molecular subtype prediction. Nissar et al. [ 27 ] developed a comprehensive framework combining radiomics feature extraction with metaheuristic optimization for breast cancer molecular subtype detection from mammograms. Their approach extracts 1536 handcrafted radiomic features (texture, shape, intensity) from mammographic images, then employs Genetic Algorithm-based feature selection to identify the most discriminative subset. The optimized feature set is fed into ensemble classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) for molecular subtype classification. This hybrid approach achieved 88.4% accuracy for four-class molecular subtype classification, demonstrating that combining domain knowledge (radiomics) with machine learning can rival deep learning performance while requiring substantially less training data and computational resources. While these recent advances demonstrate impressive performance, they share common characteristics that limit immediate clinical deployment in resource-constrained settings. 1. Computational demands : Mod-ViT and SwinEff-AttentionNet require high-end GPUs with >16 GB memory, limiting accessibility in smaller clinical facilities 2. Multi-modal dependencies : MOB-CBAM and Mod-ViT require multiple imaging modalities (mammography, ultrasound, MRI), which may not be available in all clinical workflows 3. Complex architectures : Attention mechanisms, transformers, and hybrid models introduce architectural complexity that increases inference time and complicates deployment 4. Limited focus on histopathology : Most recent work targets mammography or ultrasound; histopathological image analysis remains underexplored Computational demands : Mod-ViT and SwinEff-AttentionNet require high-end GPUs with >16 GB memory, limiting accessibility in smaller clinical facilities Multi-modal dependencies : MOB-CBAM and Mod-ViT require multiple imaging modalities (mammography, ultrasound, MRI), which may not be available in all clinical workflows Complex architectures : Attention mechanisms, transformers, and hybrid models introduce architectural complexity that increases inference time and complicates deployment Limited focus on histopathology : Most recent work targets mammography or ultrasound; histopathological image analysis remains underexplored BCDNet_Updated addresses these gaps by focusing on single-modality histopathological image classification with extreme computational efficiency. While we do not incorporate attention mechanisms or transformer architectures, our model achieves competitive performance (91.38% accuracy, 85.04% F1-score) with dramatically lower resource requirements (327 MB GPU memory, 278 s/epoch training time). This positions BCDNet_Updated as a complementary approach suitable for deployment scenarios where computational resources, imaging modalities, or technical expertise are limited. Future work could explore incorporating lightweight attention mechanisms (e.g., Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks) or knowledge distillation from larger models to further improve performance while maintaining efficiency. Despite their promise, DL models face well-documented challenges in medical imaging: dependency on large, high-quality labeled datasets; computational intensity limiting deployment in resource-constrained settings; class imbalance common in medical data; and lack of interpretability reducing clinical trust [ 1 , 2 ]. These limitations motivate the development of efficient, deployable architectures tailored for specific diagnostic tasks. The literature review reveals three distinct trajectories in breast cancer AI research: (1) high-performance architectures (ResNet, DenseNet, ensemble models, ViT) achieving 92-99% accuracy but requiring substantial computational resources; (2) multi-modal and attention-based approaches (MOB-CBAM, Mod-ViT, SwinEff-AttentionNet) leveraging multiple imaging modalities and sophisticated attention mechanisms for improved generalization; and (3) lightweight models (BCDNet, LWSC, MobileNet variants) prioritizing deployment feasibility over maximum performance. Our work addresses a critical gap at the intersection of performance and efficiency. While recent advances in attention mechanisms [ 7 ], vision transformers [ 8 ], and multi-modal integration [ 9 ] demonstrate impressive accuracy, they introduce computational and architectural complexity that hinders deployment in resource-constrained clinical environments, precisely where automated diagnostic support is most needed. Conversely, existing lightweight models often sacrifice too much performance, achieving accuracies below 90% that may not meet clinical thresholds for diagnostic assistance. BCDNet_Updated aims to achieve an optimal balance: improving upon the reference lightweight model (BCDNet) to approach the performance of deeper architectures while maintaining deployability on entry-level hardware. This addresses the urgent need for accessible, efficient diagnostic tools highlighted by the projected radiologist shortage [ 13 ] and expanding global cancer burden [ 11 ]. Can a lightweight CNN model for IDC classification be optimized to improve accuracy and recall without increasing training time and memory usage compared to reference BCDNet model? This study adopts a controlled, efficiency-focused experimental design to investigate whether targeted architectural refinements can improve the performance of a domain-specific lightweight convolutional neural network for invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) classification without increasing computational cost. Building upon the reference BCDNet architecture proposed by Lin et al. [ 10 ], the proposed approach, referred to as BCDNet_Updated, introduces incremental modifications aimed at enhancing feature representation and recall while preserving low training time and memory usage. All experiments are conducted on the Kaggle IDC histopathology dataset to enable direct and fair comparison with the reference model under identical conditions. The methodology emphasizes reproducibility and efficiency, evaluating performance using standard classification metrics alongside computational measures such as GPU memory consumption and training time per epoch. By constraining the scope to a single dataset and fixed training protocol, the method is designed to isolate the impact of architectural optimization rather than to establish cross-dataset generalizability or clinical applicability. BCDNet_Updated extends the reference BCDNet architecture [ 10 ] through six strategic refinements targeting identified inefficiencies. The model comprises six convolutional blocks with progressive regularization, followed by global average pooling and a lightweight fully connected classifier. All models were implemented in PyTorch and trained on the Kaggle IDC dataset (277,524 histopathology image patches, 50 × 50 pixels). The model employs six convolutional blocks (3 × 3 kernels, stride 1, padding 1) progressively expanding feature maps: 3 → 32→64 → 128→128 → 256→256 channels. This contrasts with the reference model's four blocks, providing increased representational capacity without proportional parameter growth. M a t h e m a t i c a l o p e r a t i o n : F = I ∗ K ( convolution ) where F is the output feature map, I is input, and K is the convolutional kernel. LeakyReLU activation (α = 0.01) replaces ReLU to prevent dying neurons: f(x) = x if x ≥ 0, else 0.01x Max pooling (2 × 2, stride 2) reduces spatial dimensions after blocks 1, 2, 4, and 5. Progressive dropout (rates: 0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 for blocks 1-6) provides stronger regularization in deeper layers where overfitting risk is elevated. Selective batch normalization in blocks 3-6 stabilizes training of high-level features while reducing early-layer computational overhead. Global average pooling (GAP) reduces feature map dimensions from 256 × 3 × 3 (2304 features) to 256 × 1 × 1 (256 features), eliminating 87% of classifier input dimensions. This enables a lightweight fully connected structure (256 → 128→64 → 2) with 96% fewer parameters than the reference model's dense classifier (2304 → 1024→256 → 64→2). Rationale: The reference model's large FC layers (millions of parameters) dominate memory usage and increase overfitting risk. GAP provides spatial invariance while drastically reducing parameters, crucial for deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Table 2 shows architecture comparison between BCDNet_reference and BCD_Updated. Fully Connected (FC) layer is typically placed at the end of a CNN, this layer connects each neuron to all neurons in the previous layer. It acts as the classifier in the network. The input is a flattened vector from the final pooling or convolutional layer, and the output represents the final prediction of the CNN [ 28 ]. In the reference model, the final convolutional block produces a feature map of dimensions [256∗3∗3], which results in 2304 features per sample once flattened. It is then passed into dense classifier structured as 2304 → 1024 → 256 → 64 →2, resulting in millions of parameters. This increases memory usage and training time. In contrast, the updated model applies a GA pooling layer, which reduces the spatial dimensions to [1∗1] before classification, resulting in a smaller feature map of [256∗1∗1], i.e., 256 features per sample after flattening. These features are then passed into a lightweight fully connected structure (256 → 128 → 64 → 2). This architectural change drastically reduces the number of parameters, thereby lowering memory consumption and training time, while still enabling the model to learn meaningful patterns essential for accurate classification. Table 4 summarizes the key architectural decisions and their justifications. The progressive regularization strategy (selective BN + progressive dropout) specifically addresses the overfitting patterns observed in lightweight medical imaging CNNs. Early convolutional blocks (1-2) learn fundamental texture and edge features that are relatively stable across samples, requiring minimal regularization. Deeper blocks (3-6) learn complex, sample-specific patterns (e.g., cellular morphology variations) where overfitting risk is elevated. By applying stronger regularization only where needed, BCDNet_Updated achieves better generalization without impeding early feature learning. The global average pooling layer serves dual purposes: (1) dramatic parameter reduction enabling deployment on resource-constrained hardware, and (2) improved spatial invariance by aggregating feature responses across the entire spatial extent, making the model less sensitive to exact lesion positioning within the 50 × 50 patch—a critical property for histopathological images where tumour regions may appear at varying locations. The IDC dataset [ 29 ] is publicly available on Kaggle and contains 277,524 RGB histopathology image patches (50 × 50 pixels) extracted from whole-slide images of breast tissue specimens. The dataset is categorized into two classes: IDC-negative (Class-0) with 198,738 images (71.6%) representing normal breast tissue, and IDC-positive (Class-1) with 78,786 images (28.4%) showing signs of invasive ductal carcinoma. This results in a moderate class imbalance ratio of approximately 2.5:1. The dataset was split into 72% training (199,818 images), 8% validation (22,201 images), and 20% testing (55,505 images) sets, maintaining the original class distribution across all splits ( Fig. 2 ). The IDC dataset was selected as the primary evaluation benchmark for several reasons. First, Lin et al. [ 10 ] reported that BCDNet achieved superior performance on IDC (89.53% accuracy) compared to BreakHis (89.39% accuracy), making it the most appropriate dataset for validating improvements to their architecture. Second, with 277,524 image patches, the IDC dataset is substantially larger than alternative histopathology datasets (e.g., BreakHis contains 7909 images), enabling more robust model training and reducing overfitting risk. Third, using the same dataset as the reference model ensures fair comparison with consistent data characteristics (image resolution, staining protocol, class distribution). However, we acknowledge that single-dataset evaluation limits assessment of model generalizability across different imaging conditions, staining variations, and patient populations. Cross-dataset validation is essential for claims of clinical applicability and will be addressed in future work (Section 6 ). All images underwent standardized preprocessing to ensure consistency and compatibility with CNN architectures. The preprocessing pipeline consisted of three steps. 1. Resizing : Images were resized from their original 50 × 50 pixels to 224 × 224 pixels, the standard input size for most CNN architectures. This larger spatial representation provides the model with more detailed information for feature learning. 2. Tensor conversion : Images were converted to PyTorch tensors for compatibility with the deep learning framework. 3. Normalization : Pixel values were normalized to stabilize training and accelerate convergence [ 22 ]. For BCDNet_Updated and BCDNet_reference models, RGB channels were normalized using mean = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] and standard deviation = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], scaling pixel values to the range [-1, 1]. For ResNet50, normalization used mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and standard deviation = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225], matching the ImageNet statistics on which ResNet50 was originally pre-trained. To increase training data diversity and improve model generalization, data augmentation techniques were applied exclusively to the training set using the torchvision.transforms library. • Random rotation : Images were randomly rotated within the range of ±15° to simulate varying tissue orientations in whole-slide images • Random horizontal flip : Images were randomly flipped horizontally with 50% probability • Random vertical flip : Images were randomly flipped vertically with 50% probability Random rotation : Images were randomly rotated within the range of ±15° to simulate varying tissue orientations in whole-slide images Random horizontal flip : Images were randomly flipped horizontally with 50% probability Random vertical flip : Images were randomly flipped vertically with 50% probability These geometric transformations are particularly appropriate for histopathology images, as cancerous patterns can appear at any orientation and should be recognized regardless of spatial configuration. Augmentation techniques were not applied to validation or test sets to ensure fair, unbiased evaluation on unaltered samples representing real-world diagnostic scenarios. All models were trained using a consistent experimental setup to ensure fair comparison. Training was conducted on the Kaggle cloud platform using NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs (16 GB VRAM), which provides free computational resources suitable for deep learning research. Random seeds were fixed across PyTorch (torch.manual_seed), NumPy (np.random.seed), and Python's random module (random.seed) to ensure full reproducibility of results. Models were trained for 100 epochs using the following configuration. • Optimizer : Adam optimizer with initial learning rate of 0.001 and default beta parameters (β 1 = 0.9, β 2 = 0.999) • Weight decay : No weight decay (λ = 0) for baseline models; weight decay of 1e-4 was separately investigated to assess its impact on performance (Section 5.2 ) • Learning rate scheduler : ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler that reduced the learning rate by a factor of 0.1 if validation loss did not improve for 5 consecutive epochs, enabling dynamic learning rate adjustment during training • Batch size : 32 for both training and validation • Loss function : CrossEntropyLoss, well-suited for binary and multi-class classification tasks • Class weights : Equal class weights for baseline models; balanced class weights were separately investigated (Section 5.2 ) Optimizer : Adam optimizer with initial learning rate of 0.001 and default beta parameters (β 1 = 0.9, β 2 = 0.999) Weight decay : No weight decay (λ = 0) for baseline models; weight decay of 1e-4 was separately investigated to assess its impact on performance (Section 5.2 ) Learning rate scheduler : ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler that reduced the learning rate by a factor of 0.1 if validation loss did not improve for 5 consecutive epochs, enabling dynamic learning rate adjustment during training Batch size : 32 for both training and validation Loss function : CrossEntropyLoss, well-suited for binary and multi-class classification tasks Class weights : Equal class weights for baseline models; balanced class weights were separately investigated (Section 5.2 ) Model checkpoints were saved after each epoch, preserving the complete model state including architecture parameters, optimizer state, and training metrics. The best-performing model was selected based on validation F1-score rather than validation accuracy alone, as F1-score provides a balanced measure accounting for both precision and recall—particularly important given the class imbalance in the dataset. This best model checkpoint was subsequently loaded for final evaluation on the held-out test set. Peak GPU memory usage during training was monitored using PyTorch's memory profiler (torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated), measured in megabytes (MB). This metric represents the maximum amount of GPU memory actively allocated by PyTorch tensors at any point during training. Lower values indicate greater memory efficiency and ability to run on GPUs with smaller memory capacity, a critical consideration for deployment in resource-constrained clinical environments. Average training time per epoch was recorded in seconds to assess computational efficiency and practical training feasibility. ResNet50 was selected as the primary comparison baseline for three methodological reasons. First, Lin et al. [ 10 ] benchmarked BCDNet against ResNet50 and ViT-B-16, establishing ResNet50 as the performance ceiling for this specific dataset (using the same baseline enables direct comparison and assessment of whether our architectural improvements narrow the performance gap). Second, ResNet50 represents the standard deep architecture against which lightweight models are typically evaluated in medical imaging literature [ 6 , 2 , 18 ], providing a well-established performance reference. Third, ResNet50's computational requirements (3 GB + GPU memory, 1200+ sec/epoch) exemplify the resource intensity that makes deployment challenging, clearly demonstrating the efficiency advantage of lightweight alternatives. While additional lightweight baselines (MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, ShuffleNet) would provide valuable context within the efficiency-oriented architecture landscape, their inclusion was deferred for several reasons. These models were designed for natural image classification (ImageNet) and require significant adaptation for medical histopathology (architectural modifications, hyperparameter tuning, and transfer learning strategies that could introduce confounding variables). Moreover, preliminary literature review suggests that generic lightweight models often underperform domain-specific architectures on medical imaging tasks [ 24 ]. Domain-specific models like BCDNet are tailored to the unique characteristics of histopathological images (e.g., 50 × 50-pixel patches, H&E staining patterns, binary classification) rather than the 1000-class natural image classification these models were optimized for. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that comprehensive comparison with lightweight alternatives would strengthen positioning of BCDNet_Updated. Future work will include implementation and evaluation of MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, and ShuffleNet on the IDC dataset, as well as comparison with recent lightweight medical imaging models (Section 6.2 ). Weight decay and class weighting were selected because they maintain computational efficiency while improving performance without increasing resources (see more details in appendix B ). This section presents the experimental results obtained for BCDNet_Updated and compares them with the reference BCDNet model and ResNet50 under identical training and evaluation conditions. The objective of this comparison is to assess whether targeted architectural refinements within a lightweight CNN framework can yield measurable performance improvements without increasing computational cost. As shown in Table 5 , BCDNet_Updated demonstrates consistent improvements over the reference BCDNet across multiple evaluation metrics. In particular, the proposed model achieves higher accuracy (91.38% vs. 89.53%) and F1-score (85.04% vs. 80.93%), with a notable improvement in recall (86.62% vs. 78.47%). This increase in recall indicates an enhanced ability to correctly identify IDC-positive samples, which is a critical consideration in medical image classification tasks where false negatives carry significant consequences. Importantly, these gains are achieved while maintaining comparable training time per epoch (278 s vs. 289 sec) and substantially reducing GPU memory usage (327 MB vs. 1655 MB). Compared to the reference BCDNet, BCDNet_Updated reduces peak GPU memory consumption by 80% while slightly decreasing average training time per epoch. These results suggest that the architectural modifications introduced in BCDNet_Updated improve efficiency without introducing additional computational burden. The observed performance improvements therefore reflect architectural optimization rather than increased model complexity. ResNet50 achieves the highest overall classification performance among the evaluated models (accuracy: 93.18%, F1-score: 87.82%); however, this improvement comes at a substantial computational cost. Training time per epoch (1235 s) is approximately 4 × longer than BCDNet_Updated, and GPU memory usage (3073 MB) is approximately 9 × higher. This contrast highlights the well-established trade-off between performance and computational efficiency and reinforces the motivation for efficiency-oriented model design in resource-constrained environments. Fig. 3 illustrates the comparative performance metrics of the evaluated models, while Fig. 4 presents the corresponding training and validation curves. The learning behavior of BCDNet_Updated indicates stable convergence comparable to the reference model, suggesting that the observed performance gains are not associated with training instability or overfitting under the chosen experimental conditions. Fig. 5 presents the confusion matrices for all three models, providing further insight into classification behavior beyond aggregate metrics. Compared to the reference BCDNet, BCDNet_Updated exhibits a reduction in false negatives (from 3393 to 2100) and a corresponding increase in true positives (from 12,365 to 13,658), consistent with the observed improvement in recall. This pattern suggests that the architectural refinements enhance sensitivity to IDC-positive samples without disproportionately increasing false positives (which decreased from 2301 to 1785). Fig. 5 displays the confusion matrix of the 3 models showing classification performance and misclassifications between IDC-positive and IDC-negative cases. Although formal statistical significance testing through repeated experiments was not conducted, the magnitude of improvement can be assessed through effect size analysis. The accuracy improvement of 1.85 percentage points translates to 1029 additional correctly classified samples out of 55,505 test images. Calculation of the standard error of classification accuracy yields SE ≈ 0.0013 (0.13%) for both models, suggesting the observed difference of 1.85% represents approximately 14.8 standard errors. This magnitude of improvement is unlikely to occur by chance under the assumption of approximate normality (p < 0.001 if normality is assumed). Confusion matrix analysis ( Table 6 ) reveals that BCDNet_Updated correctly classifies 1809 additional cases compared to the reference model (1293 additional true positives + 516 additional true negatives). Conservative application of McNemar's test to assess whether the two models make errors on different cases yields χ 2 > 740 (even assuming 500 cases where the reference model outperforms the updated model), substantially exceeding the critical value for significance at α = 0.001 (χ 2 critical = 10.83). While these calculations provide preliminary evidence of meaningful improvement, formal validation through k-fold cross-validation and repeated experiments with different random seeds remains necessary to quantify performance variability and establish statistical confidence intervals. The improvement is consistent across multiple evaluation metrics: accuracy (+1.85%, relative improvement: 2.1%), recall (+8.15%, relative improvement: 10.4%), and F1-score (+4.11%, relative improvement: 5.1%). This multi-metric consistency, combined with the magnitude of effect size, suggests systematic architectural improvement rather than random variation or metric-specific optimization. While the results demonstrate consistent performance improvements for BCDNet_Updated on the Kaggle IDC dataset, they should be interpreted within the constraints of the experimental design. The evaluation is limited to a single dataset and fixed training protocol, and no statistical significance testing across multiple runs was performed. Consequently, the reported metrics reflect performance under controlled conditions rather than definitive evidence of generalizability or clinical robustness. Overall, the results provide empirical support for the central research question of this study: that incremental, efficiency-aware architectural optimization of a domain-specific lightweight CNN can improve classification performance, particularly recall, without increasing training time or memory usage. These findings motivate further investigation through expanded dataset validation, statistical analysis, and interpretability studies to assess robustness and clinical relevance. To explore potential improvements in handling class imbalance and regularization, two alternative configurations of the BCDNet_Updated model are also evaluated. The test results are presented in Table 7 . The first approach introduced L2 regularization (weight decay = 1e-4) to the Adam optimizer which helps prevent overfitting and stabilizes model generalization. This method slightly improved accuracy (91.51%) and precision (85.31%) compared to the baseline, while recall dropped to 84.57%. This suggests that weight decay helped the model make fewer false positives, but at the cost of detecting slightly fewer positive cases. The second approach applied class weights in the loss function (CrossEntropyLoss). Class weights were computed using scikit-learn's compute_class_weight function based on the frequency of each class in the training set (0: 143,056 and 1: 56,762). This gave weights of about [0.6984, 1.7601]. That means, minority class (IDC-positive) contributed more to the loss. The higher weight for the minority made the model pay more attention to it during training. As expected, the model became more sensitive to positive cases, achieving the highest recall (91.62%). However, this came with a drop in precision (75.39%) and accuracy (89.16%), indicating an increase in false positives. This highlights the trade-off between recall and precision. While class weighting improves sensitivity to IDC-positive cases, it sacrifices specificity. High recall will be often desirable in medical diagnosis since missing a cancer case (false negative) is considered more riskier than flagging additional false positives. BCDNet_Updated successfully outperformed the reference model across all key evaluation metrics while using less GPU memory and maintaining similar training time. When compared to previous works in the literature, the outcomes of this project are aligned with the findings of Lin et al. [ 10 ]. Their reported results highlighted the trade-off between model complexity and diagnostic performance. It shows that deeper networks such as ResNet-50 achieve high accuracy and F1-score but at the cost of heavy computational requirements. Even though the accuracy was a little lower compared to deeper models, the model which they developed is a lightweight model with less training time and memory requirements, making it suitable for deployment in edge devices. In this project, the updated BCDNet followed a similar trend. Although the BCDNet_Updated achieved slightly lower accuracy than ResNet50, it delivered results much closer to ResNet50 than the reference model, while requiring 4 times less training time and 9 times less memory usage than Resnet50. This indicates that lightweight designs provide a practical balance between accuracy and efficiency, even if they fall slightly short of the performance of deeper architectures. Overall, the BCDNet_Updated model's balance between improved accuracy and low resource usage makes it well-suited for deployment in constrained environments where computational resources are limited. While direct experimental comparison with MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, and ShuffleNet was not conducted, we can contextualize BCDNet_Updated's performance by examining reported results of these architectures on similar histopathological image classification tasks. MobileNetV2 has been evaluated on various breast cancer detection tasks with mixed results. Kanadath et al. [ 31 ] applied MobileNetV2 with transfer learning to the IDC dataset (the same dataset used in our study), achieving 85% accuracy—substantially lower than BCDNet_Updated's 91.38% despite using ImageNet pre-training. Several works have investigated automated detection and classification of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) in histopathological images using deep learning. Transfer learning with convolutional neural networks trained on the IDC dataset has yielded robust classification performance; for example, models using standard CNN backbones with transfer learning have produced test accuracies around 89% for distinguishing IDC-positive from IDC-negative image patches [ 32 ]. In broader comparisons, pretrained architectures including MobileNetV2 have been evaluated alongside other networks such as ResNet, EfficientNet, and MobileNetV1 for IDC grading tasks, showing that even lightweight models can achieve competitive balanced accuracy when properly adapted, though they may trail more expressive architectures [ 33 ]. The key challenge with MobileNetV2 for histopathology is its design assumptions: depthwise separable convolutions optimize for 224 × 224 natural images with rich color diversity, whereas histopathology patches are smaller (50 × 50) with constrained color space (H&E staining). BCDNet_Updated's architecture is specifically optimized for these characteristics. Recent research has explored the use of EfficientNet-B0 for breast cancer imaging due to its favorable parameter efficiency and strong transfer learning capabilities. In breast ultrasound classification, Dellow & Hussain [ 34 ] reported that an EfficientNet-B0 model achieved 83.33% accuracy on the BUSI dataset for benign, malignant, and normal cases. However, direct comparison is limited by the different imaging modality (ultrasound vs. histopathology). The compound scaling approach of EfficientNet (balancing depth, width, and resolution) may not be optimal for fixed small-resolution medical patches. BCDNet_Updated instead employs progressive regularization scaling (increasing dropout rates with depth), which may be more appropriate for the specific overfitting patterns in medical imaging. ShuffleNet has received limited attention in medical imaging literature [ 35 ]. Its channel shuffle operations are designed for extremely resource-constrained mobile devices; whether this optimization is necessary for clinical workstations with entry-level GPUs (4 GB + VRAM) remains debatable. This study presented BCDNet_Updated, an optimized lightweight convolutional neural network for invasive ductal carcinoma detection in histopathological images. By introducing targeted architectural refinements to the reference BCDNet model [ 10 ], the proposed approach achieves improved classification performance (91.38% accuracy, 86.62% recall, 85.04% F1-score) while significantly reducing GPU memory usage (80% reduction: 1655 MB → 327 MB) and maintaining comparable training time (278 s/epoch vs. 289 sec/epoch). Experimental results on the Kaggle IDC dataset demonstrate that meaningful gains in accuracy, recall, and F1-score can be achieved through careful optimization of lightweight CNN architectures, without resorting to deeper networks or computationally intensive components. Effect size analysis suggests these improvements are unlikely to result from random variation (p < 0.001 under conservative statistical assumptions), though formal validation through repeated experiments remains necessary. These findings highlight the potential of task-specific, efficiency-oriented CNN design for histopathological image analysis, particularly in scenarios where computational resources are limited. However, the scope of this work is restricted to controlled experimental conditions and single-dataset evaluation. As such, claims regarding robustness, generalizability, and clinical applicability remain preliminary. Future work will focus on: (1) multi-dataset validation including BreakHis and clinical cohorts with diverse staining protocols and scanner types; (2) statistical rigor through k-fold cross-validation and repeated experiments with confidence interval estimation; (3) expanded baseline comparisons with MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, and ShuffleNet under identical experimental conditions; (4) incorporation of explainability techniques (Grad-CAM, saliency maps) with pathologist validation studies to enhance clinical relevance and verify that predictions are based on diagnostically meaningful features; and (5) investigation of alternative class imbalance strategies including focal loss and intelligent oversampling methods. Overall, this work contributes to the growing body of research on efficient deep learning models for medical imaging and provides a foundation for further investigation into deployable and interpretable diagnostic support systems. While the current study establishes proof-of-concept for efficiency-aware architectural optimization, substantial additional validation is required before clinical translation can be responsibly pursued. Despite the improved performance and computational efficiency demonstrated by BCDNet_Updated, several limitations must be acknowledged to appropriately contextualize the findings. First, the experimental evaluation was conducted exclusively on the Kaggle IDC dataset. While this dataset is large (277,524 samples) and enables direct comparison with the reference BCDNet model [ 10 ], single-dataset evaluation does not establish generalizability across different staining protocols, imaging scanners, or patient populations. Previous studies have shown that dataset-specific characteristics can significantly influence reported performance metrics [ 1 , 2 ]. Validation on additional histopathology datasets such as BreakHis [ 36 ] and BACH [ 37 ], as well as multi-center clinical cohorts with varying staining protocols and scanner types, is necessary to assess robustness under real-world variability. Second, the reported results are based on single training runs with fixed random seeds. Although this approach ensures reproducibility, it does not capture performance variability across different data splits or initialization conditions. Formal statistical significance testing, such as k-fold cross-validation or repeated experiments with confidence interval estimation, would strengthen the reliability of the observed improvements. While effect size analysis and McNemar's test calculations provide preliminary evidence of meaningful improvement (p < 0.001), these should be considered exploratory rather than confirmatory until validated through repeated experiments. Third, model comparisons were limited to the reference BCDNet and ResNet50 architectures. While this comparison highlights the efficiency–performance trade-off between lightweight and deep CNNs, inclusion of additional lightweight baselines such as MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, or ShuffleNet would provide a more comprehensive positioning of BCDNet_Updated within the broader landscape of resource-efficient models. Literature-based comparisons suggest domain-specific models outperform adapted generic architectures on histopathology tasks; however, direct experimental comparison under identical conditions would strengthen these claims. Furthermore, although class weighting and weight decay were explored to mitigate class imbalance (with class-weighted models achieving 91.62% recall), alternative strategies such as focal loss, oversampling (SMOTE), or hybrid sampling techniques were not investigated. Prior work has shown that different imbalance-handling methods can influence recall and sensitivity in medical image classification tasks [ 2 , 38 ]. The decision to focus on weight decay and class weighting was driven by efficiency objectives (avoiding computational overhead from hyperparameter tuning or dataset expansion), but systematic exploration of alternative techniques remains valuable future work. A critical limitation for potential clinical deployment is the absence of model interpretability analysis. Medical AI systems require transparency to build clinician trust and enable verification of learned features. Visualization techniques such as Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping), Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, or attention maps would provide essential insights into whether the model learns clinically meaningful features (e.g., cellular morphology, nuclear characteristics, tissue architecture) or exploits spurious correlations (e.g., staining artifacts, background patterns). Without explainability analysis, deployment in clinical settings would be premature, as pathologists cannot verify that model predictions align with established diagnostic criteria. Comprehensive interpretability analysis validated by expert pathologists is essential before clinical translation can be considered. Finally, the study evaluates model performance on isolated image patches extracted from whole-slide images. Clinical deployment requires integration into diagnostic workflows, including whole-slide processing, real-time inference requirements, handling of edge cases (poor quality images, artifacts), user interface design, and regulatory compliance (FDA, CE marking). These practical considerations were not addressed in the current study and represent important future directions for translation from experimental validation to clinical implementation. Taken together, these limitations indicate that the current results should be interpreted as preliminary and exploratory, providing evidence of architectural efficiency and performance improvement under controlled conditions rather than definitive clinical validation. The findings establish a foundation for expanded investigation but do not support immediate claims of clinical robustness or deployment readiness. Bridging imaging and genomics: Domain knowledge guided spatial transcriptomics analysis Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression distributions mapped onto high-resolution Whole Slide Images (WSIs), revealing the association between cellular morphology and gene expression profiles. However, the high costs and equipment constraints associated with ST data collection have led to a scarcity of ST datasets. Moreover, existing ST datasets often exhibit sparse gene expression distributions, which limit the accuracy and generalizability of gene expression prediction models derived from WSIs. To address these challenges, we propose DomainST (Domain knowledge-guided Spatial Transcriptomics analysis), a novel framework that leverages domain knowledge through Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract effective gene representations and utilizes foundation models to obtain robust image features for enhanced spatial gene expression prediction. Specifically, we utilize public gene reference databases to retrieve comprehensive gene summaries and employ LLMs to refine gene descriptions and generate informative gene embeddings. Concurrently, we apply medical visual-language foundation models to distill robust image representations at multiple scales, capturing the spatial context of WSIs. We further design a multimodal mixture of experts fusion module to effectively integrate multimodal data, leveraging complementary information across modalities. Extensive experiments conducted on three public ST datasets indicate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, with increases ranging from 6.7 % to 13.7 % in PCC@50 across all datasets compared to the SOTA, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining foundation models and LLM-derived domain knowledge for gene expression prediction. Traditional RNA sequencing techniques, such as bulk RNA sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing, utilize high-throughput sequencing technologies to capture and quantify the entire transcriptome of a biological sample, providing comprehensive analyses of gene expression patterns and underlying regulatory mechanisms. Despite their widespread use and utility, these approaches inherently lack spatial information [1,2] , which is essential for understanding the tumor microenvironment, cell-to-cell interactions, and the spatial organization of cellular functions within tissue architectures [3,4] . Spatial transcriptomics [3] addresses this limitation by enabling the mapping of gene expression profiles to their corresponding spatial locations within tissue sections. Typically, this is achieved using high-resolution whole slide images (WSIs) stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E). As the gold standard in pathology, H&E-stained WSIs are not only widely available and cost-effective but also preserve critical morphological features of tissues [5] , making them an attractive modality for many downstream computational applications, such as medical imaging [6,7] , multimodal learning [8,9] , and particularly gene expression prediction for spatial transcriptomics analysis. Numerous studies [2,10–12] have demonstrated the effectiveness of predicting spatial gene expression from H&E-stained WSIs, thereby bypassing the costly and laborious procedures of traditional sequencing and providing high-resolution gene expression distributions with spatial information at the spot level, and in some cases, even at single-cell resolution. Despite the rapid advancements in spatial transcriptomics (ST), several critical challenges remain. First, the high cost and technical complexity of ST experiments result in limited data availability, which constrains the scalability and generalizability of data-driven methods [3,13] . Second, ST data often suffer from gene expression sparsity, where the majority of genes exhibit extremely low or zero expression levels across spatial locations [14,15] . This sparsity hinders the accurate prediction and modeling of spatial gene expression patterns. Third, the integration of H&E-stained WSIs and gene expression data, which are fundamentally heterogeneous modalities [2] , presents a nontrivial computational challenge due to differences in data structure, scale, and semantics. To address these challenges, a variety of computational approaches have been proposed. For instance, contrastive learning has been employed to align multimodal representations across image and gene expression domains [13,16,17] . Graph neural networks and transformer-based architectures have been leveraged to incorporate spatial context and capture long-range dependencies across tissue regions [5,10,11,18] . In addition, several methods utilize complementary information, such as exemplar images or textual descriptions, to guide the learning process and enhance gene expression prediction [12,19,20] . However, there remains an insufficient exploitation of detailed gene knowledge, such as comprehensive gene annotations including functional roles and phenotype associations, which are readily available in external biomedical databases. These rich sources of domain knowledge provide crucial biological context that can substantially enrich gene representations [12] . Furthermore, since not all genes are visually correlated with tissue morphology, especially under conditions of data scarcity and expression sparsity, relying solely on image features is often insufficient for accurate gene expression prediction [14] . Therefore, incorporating external domain knowledge as a complementary modality becomes essential for improving the robustness and accuracy of spatial gene expression prediction. Building upon the observations outlined above, we propose a novel framework that leverages the strengths of foundation models and large language models (LLMs) for spatial transcriptomics analysis. Specifically, we utilize foundation models to extract multi-scale, spatially-aware image representations from WSIs, capturing both fine-grained local patterns and broader tissue-level context. In parallel, we employ LLMs to generate semantically rich gene representations by refining textual information from external gene reference databases. Additionally, inspired by the divide-and-conquer paradigm of the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, where complex problem spaces are partitioned and addressed by specialized neural network experts [21,22] , we design a multimodal MoE fusion module. This component enables effective alignment and integration of heterogeneous modalities, allowing the model to dynamically attend to the most relevant representations for each prediction task. Our major contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose DomainST, a novel framework that integrates external domain knowledge to address the challenges of data scarcity and gene expression sparsity in spatial transcriptomics, thereby enhancing the accuracy and robustness of spatial gene expression prediction. • We employ vision-language foundation models to distill robust image features at multiple scales, effectively capturing spatial context within WSIs and enriching the model’s understanding of tissue morphology. • We construct informative gene representations from refined gene summaries using LLMs to incorporate extensive biological knowledge and to complement visual features. • We design a multimodal MoE fusion module to seamlessly integrate visual and gene representations, enabling dynamic and adaptive alignment of heterogeneous modalities to improve prediction performance. • We conduct extensive experiments on three public ST datasets, demonstrating that DomainST consistently outperforms State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) models, highlighting the effectiveness of incorporating domain knowledge into spatial gene expression modeling. The prediction of gene expression from histopathology images has evolved remarkably in recent years. An early effort in this direction is HE2RNA [1] , while not targeting ST data, which introduced the core concept of predicting RNA-Seq profiles from WSIs via tile-wise modeling using multilayer perceptrons. This approach demonstrated the feasibility of learning molecular patterns from image-based features, inspiring a wave of follow-up studies in spatially resolved inference. ST-Net [2] marked an important step toward spatial transcriptomics by introducing a pipeline that aligns histology patches with ST spots. It employed a DenseNet-based architecture to predict gene expression at specific spatial locations, initiating a paradigm shift toward spatially-aware modeling in histology-based transcriptomics. Building upon this foundation, recent advances in spatial transcriptomics prediction from histopathology images have seen a surge of interest in leveraging deep learning architectures to model the complex spatial and molecular relationships within tissue. These approaches can be broadly categorized along several methodological dimensions, including spatial dependency modeling, multi-scale spatial feature extraction, auxiliary information guidance, and contrastive learning for cross-modal alignment. Local and Global Spatial Dependency Modeling. In addition to directly predicting gene expression from individual spatial ST spots, modeling spatial dependencies is crucial for improving prediction accuracy. Histogene [5] leverages a Vision Transformer (ViT) to capture global relationships among ST spots, enabling the model to encode broad contextual information. Hist2ST [10] combines global attention with a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to model both long-range and neighborhood-level dependencies, representing one of the earliest hybrid local-global architectures. Sepal [14] takes a different perspective by modeling relative expression differences and balancing local and global signals using GNNs. THItoGene [18] integrates dynamic convolutions and capsule networks to model spatial context and multi-view features. These methods mark a shift toward context-aware modeling, emphasizing the importance of spatial dependency modeling across multiple granularity levels. Multi-Scale and Spatial Contextual Modeling. Effectively capturing spatial context at multiple resolutions is essential for modeling the complex and hierarchical architecture of tissue in spatial ST data. TRIPLEX [11] introduces a transformer-based fusion framework that integrates multi-resolution contextual features from WSIs, enabling robust spatial gene prediction across scales. M2OST [15] formulates ST prediction as a many-to-one mapping problem and decouples intra- and inter-scale feature extraction for efficient and expressive modeling. ST-Align [17] also incorporates multi-scale and cross-level representations, aligning spot-level and niche-level contexts through a tailored multimodal attention mechanism. These designs reflect the efficacy of hierarchical modeling for resolving spatial hierarchies in tissue architecture. Auxiliary Information Guidance. Another line of research explores the incorporation of auxiliary information to enhance gene expression prediction. Building on the concept of contextual similarity, EGN [19] introduces an exemplar-based strategy that retrieves morphologically similar tissue patches from ViT-based features and uses these exemplars to inform gene expression prediction. EGGN [20] extends EGN by constructing a graph that connects both exemplars and target windows, and employs a graph convolutional network to more effectively integrate contextual information. In contrast, SGN [12] leverages gene-type embeddings as external references, enabling the model not only to guide predictions but also to perform zero-shot inference for previously unseen genes. These methods highlight the growing interest in retrieval-augmented modeling and the use of auxiliary information to guide spatial transcriptomics prediction. Contrastive Learning for Multimodal Alignment. Recent advances in multimodal alignment have explored various strategies, including domain adaptation [23,24] and contrastive learning [25] . Among these, contrastive learning has emerged as a particularly effective approach for bridging the modality gap between histology images and gene expression profiles. It enables the alignment of visual and molecular representations within a shared embedding space, facilitating more meaningful cross-modal interactions. BLEEP [13] applies contrastive learning to project image patches and gene expression profiles into a shared low-dimensional space, enabling expression imputation via k-nearest neighbor retrieval. Similarly, mclSTExp [16] incorporates contrastive learning to integrate histological context and spatial transcriptomics measurements into a multimodal representation space, facilitating both alignment and retrieval-based inference. ST-Align [17] introduces a two-stage contrastive learning framework that aligns image–gene pairs across multiple hierarchical levels, enhancing the model’s capacity to capture both local and global correspondences for accurate gene expression prediction. These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of contrastive learning in multimodal alignment for spatial gene expression modeling. The pipeline of DomainST framework is illustrated in Fig. 1 (b). Given the spots and the genes of interest, our image and gene representation modules first extract their corresponding features, denoted by v i m g ∈ R n × d i m g and v g e n e ∈ R m × d g e n e , respectively. Subsequently, as depicted in Fig. 4 , our MoE fusion module integrates these two modalities to obtain the fused feature v f u s i o n ∈ R n × d f u s i o n . This fused feature is then passed through a fully connected layer to predict the spatially resolved gene expression levels, denoted by Y g e n e ∈ R n × m , at the spot level within WSI. In this context, n represents the total number of spots per WSI, m denotes the number of genes being analyzed. d i m g , d g e n e and d f u s i o n represent the dimensionality of the image features, gene features and fused features, respectively. In this module, we leverage foundation models to learn robust and semantically rich image representations, aiming to mitigate the challenge of data scarcity, which can lead to under-representation of image-derived information. Inspired by prior studies [11,15,17] , we extract image features at multiple spatial scales to effectively capture both local and global contextual information within WSIs. Specifically, we consider three hierarchical levels of spatial context: the spot level, the adjacent level, defined as a 5 × 5 window centered around each target spot, and the WSI level. At the spot level, we adopt a trainable ResNet50 [26] backbone pretrained on ImageNet to encode fine-grained local features for each ST spot. For the adjacent and WSI levels, we utilize Conch [27] , a visual-language foundation model tailored for medical imaging, with its parameters frozen during training to preserve generalizable representations. Conch is pretrained on the largest histopathology vision-language dataset to date, enabling it effectively capture fine-grained morphological features relevant to spatial transcriptomics. To further refine these representations, we apply Transformer blocks [11] on top of Conch features to model spatial relationships and contextual dependencies across larger tissue regions. To effectively integrate multi-scale features, we employ multi-head attention mechanisms [28] , allowing the model to dynamically weigh and fuse information from different spatial levels. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (c), this hierarchical fusion yields the final image representation v img , which encodes both localized cellular detail and broader tissue architecture. To harness the rich contextual and functional information available in external gene databases, we employ LLMs to generate informative gene representations that complement the image modality. This strategy aims to mitigate the inherent sparsity of ST datasets and enhance the model’s capacity for accurate gene expression prediction. Specifically, we utilize domain knowledge through a multi-step process: (1) Domain knowledge retrieval. For each gene in our dataset, we retrieve descriptive summaries from publicly available biological knowledge sources, such as the NCBI Gene database [29] and Gene Ontology (GO) terms [30] . Taking gene CALR as an example in Fig. 2 , these resources provide structured and curated information encompassing gene functions, cellular components, molecular activities, and biological processes. (2) Gene summary refinement. To refine and unify these textual descriptions, we apply LLMs using carefully designed prompts, as indicated in Fig. 3 , tailored to distill relevant biological semantics (More details are included in the supplementary materials). We specifically utilize GPT-4o for this task for its superior capabilities in reasoning, multilingual comprehension, and instruction following skills that are essential for processing complex biomedical text such as gene descriptions and ontological annotations. This process yields consistent and context-aware gene descriptions suitable for downstream encoding. (3) Gene embedding generation. The refined gene summaries are then fed into pretrained text encoders ( Section 4.2 ), resulting in dense gene embeddings v gene . These embeddings encapsulate prior biological knowledge and serve as external guidance to facilitate more biologically grounded and generalizable gene expression predictions. To address the inherent heterogeneity between visual and textual (gene expression) modalities, we design a multimodal MoE module to investigate the intrinsic correlation within each modality and leverage their complementary information. As illustrated in Fig. 4 , the proposed MoE module consists of two components: (1) Gating network: This network dynamically learns a weight distribution over a set of expert networks, conditioned on the input image and gene representations. (2) Expert networks: Each expert models a distinct fusion strategy for integrating the two modalities. Given the image representation v i m g and gene representation v g e n e , the gating network N g a t e computes a weight vector α = N g a t e ( v i m g ) ∈ R n e x p over n e x p experts. We design three complementary expert networks to capture diverse interactions between modalities: (i) Concatenation fusion expert: Models both linear and nonlinear interactions by concatenating the modalities, followed by transformation through a feed-forward layer. (ii) Cross-attention fusion expert: Learns fine-grained associations and contextual dependencies across modalities using attention mechanisms. (iii) Addition fusion expert: Emphasizes consistent and co-expressed features across modalities by summing aligned representations, thereby suppressing modality-specific noise and highlighting shared semantic structures. Each expert E i processes both inputs and outputs a fused representation. The final multimodal representation v f u s i o n is computed as a weighted sum of these expert outputs, modulated by the learned gating weights. This fused representation is then passed through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for downstream prediction ( Eq. (1) ): (1) v f u s i o n = MLP ( ∑ i = 1 n e x p α i · E i ( v i m g , v g e n e ) ) . We selected concatenation, cross-attention, and addition as fusion experts due to their complementary strengths in capturing varying levels of modality interaction, ranging from simple (addition) to complex (cross-attention). This combination balances expressiveness and efficiency, enhancing the model’s ability to learn diverse cross-modal relationships with minimal computational overhead ( Table 7 ). Empirical results ( Table 5 ) support the effectiveness of this design within the MoE framework. This design enables both modality-specific specialization and cross-modal interaction through a unified expert framework, enhancing the model’s capacity to adaptively integrate heterogeneous biomedical data. Our objective function consists of two components: (1) The Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss L m s e for gene expression regression in Eq. (2) : (2) L m s e = 1 m ∥ Y g e n e − Y ^ g e n e ∥ 2 2 . (2) The knowledge distillation loss is defined in Eq. (3) : (3) L k d i = β 1 m ∥ Y p r e d i − Y ^ g e n e ∥ 2 2 + ( 1 − β ) 1 m ∥ Y p r e d i − Y g e n e ∥ 2 2 . In the L k d i , we utilize MSE loss between the predictions from the i t h image scales, denoted by Y p r e d i , and both the final prediction Y ^ g e n e as well as the ground truth gene expression Y g e n e . Specifically, i indicates the index for each scale and β denotes the weighting factor in the knowledge distillation loss, which is set to 0.3 following previous study [11] . Our total objective function is in Eq. (4) : (4) L t o t a l = ∑ i 3 ( L k d i ) + L m s e . Datasets. We utilized three public datasets in our study: (1) HER2-positive breast tumor dataset (HER2+) [31] , comprising 13,620 spots from 8 patients with 36 tissue sections, (2) Stnet dataset [2] , consisting of 30,612 spots from 23 breast cancer patients with 68 sections. (3) Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma dataset (cSCC) [32] , containing 8179 spots from 4 individuals across 12 sections. Implementation Details. In our study, the spot size is 224 × 224 pixels. We selected the top 250 highly expressed genes (Provided in the supplementary materials) for our analysis following previous established criteria [2,11,15,19] . We set d i m g , d g e n e and d f u s i o n to 512. We utilized the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.0001, adjusting it using a step learning rate scheduler during training. The batch size was set to 128. All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA L40 GPU with 48 GB of VRAM for 200 epochs, with early stopping when the PCC@50 metric did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs. For model validation, we applied cross-validation at the patient level to ensure robustness and to align with previous studies [11] . Specifically, we used 8-fold cross-validation for the HER2+ and Stnet datasets, and 4-fold cross-validation for the cSCC dataset. Metrics. To ensure consistency with previous studies [11,13,18,19] , we evaluated our model using four well-established metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), MSE, the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) across all genes (denoted as PCC@A) and PCC for top 50 most predictive genes (denoted as PCC@50). These metrics were calculated for all ST spots on a per-WSI basis across all validation sets. We compare our DomainST framework against eleven recent SOTA methods, including ST-Net [2] , HisToGene [5] , Hist2ST [10] , EGN [19] , BLEEP [13] , EGGN [20] , THItoGene [18] , TRIPLEX [11] , SGN [12] , mclSTExp [16] and M2OST [15] as summarized in Table 1 . Our DomainST framework consistently outperforms all competing methods across a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics, demonstrating substantial and robust improvements. For instance, on the cSCC dataset, DomainST achieves an MAE of 0.38, an MSE of 0.235, a PCC@A of 0.406, and a PCC@50 of 0.520. In contrast, the current SOTA methods, TRIPLEX and EGGN, achieve MAE scores of 0.407 and 0.609, MSE scores of 0.272 and 0.628, PCC@A scores of 0.357 and 0.337, and PCC@50 scores of 0.469 and 0.436, respectively. These superior results are consistently observed on the HER2+ (for PCC@A and PCC@50) dataset and the Stnet dataset, further highlighting the effectiveness, generalizability, and robustness of DomainST in spatial gene expression prediction across diverse tissue types. Ablation Settings. To further validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conducted five comprehensive ablation studies: (1) Gene Expression Prediction Using Image Modality Only. We evaluated the performance of various models with frozen parameters at both the adjacent and WSI levels to assess the utility of foundation models for image feature extraction in Table 2 . These included medical visual-language foundation models such as PLIP [33] and Conch [27] , the pathology image foundation model UNI [34] , the ImageNet pretrained ResNet50 [26] , and the pathology image pretrained ResNet18 [11] . (2) Gene Expression Prediction Using Multimodal Data with Different Text Encoders. We compared different text encoders, including PLIP and Conch (visual-language models), as well as biomedical text encoders BioGPT [35] and BioBERT [36] in Table 3 . To investigate potential biases inherent in various foundation models and text encoders, we systematically explored a wide range of combinations between image and text encoders. (3) Gene Expression Prediction Using Different Gene Representations. We explored the impact of different gene representations derived across three stages in Table 4 : (i) Extraction of gene summaries from external knowledge bases (GO-Term [30] and NCBI [29] ). (ii) Design of prompt templates to generate enhanced gene descriptions using LLMs: (a) prompts using only gene symbols to generate functional and phenotypic summaries without external reference, (b) prompts using gene summaries without imposing constraints on functionality or phenotype to generate detailed descriptions, and (c) prompts combining gene summaries with specific constraints on function and phenotype. (iii) Refinement of gene summaries using four prevalent LLMs: DeepSeek-v3 [37] , DeepSeek-R1 [38] , LLaMA 2 (7b-chat-hf) [39] , and GPT-4o. 1 2 (4) Comparison of Different Feature Fusion Methods. We assessed the effectiveness of our proposed MoE fusion module for integrating image and gene representations, in comparison with several alternative fusion strategies in Table 5 . (5) Component-Wise Ablations on DomainST Components. We investigated the individual and combined contributions of spatial context integration, knowledge distillation, and domain knowledge incorporation to the prediction performance in Table 6 . Additionally, we analyzed the computational costs of these components and benchmarked them against other baselines on all datasets in Table 7 . Ablation Results. (1) The results presented in Table 2 regarding the image modality indicate that applying foundation models as image feature extractors substantially improves performance compared to SOTA methods. Among all evaluated models, Conch consistently achieves the best performance across datasets. (2) Moreover, as indicated in Table 3 , incorporating gene representations consistently enhances predictive performance across all datasets compared to using image modality alone. This highlights the robustness and complementary nature of integrating external domain knowledge with visual features. While all evaluated text encoders perform well, using Conch for both image and text encoding yields the highest overall performance. (3) Furthermore, experimental results using different gene representation strategies in Table 4 demonstrate that using NCBI as the external reference database, combined with our prompt design that integrates both gene summaries and functional and phenotypic constraints, yields the best overall performance. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , NCBI provides more comprehensive gene descriptions, offering more reliable and informative inputs for LLMs. Regarding prompt design, we observe that prompts without gene summaries tend to produce general biological content that may not be relevant to the specific disease context. Prompts without constraints often generate redundant or unfocused information, which may hinder the ability of the text encoder to extract meaningful features. In contrast, prompts that incorporate both gene summaries and targeted constraints provide LLMs with clearer guidance and more relevant context, resulting in more informative and discriminative gene descriptions. Additional examples of gene summaries generated from different prompt designs are included in the supplementary materials. As further shown in Table 4 , all evaluated LLMs used for gene summary refinement contribute to improved performance. Among them, GPT-4o consistently achieves the best overall results, demonstrating its superior capability in generating high-quality gene representations compared to other alternatives. (4) Additionally, to validate the effectiveness of our multimodal fusion mechanism, we compared various fusion strategies in Table 5 . Several observations highlight the adaptive behavior of our approach: (i) consistent performance across diverse datasets indicates effective modality integration; (ii) performance degrades when the number of experts deviates from the optimal setting of three, indicating the benefit of multiple fusion strategies; and (iii) removing the MoE module ( Table 6 ) leads to a clear drop in performance, underscoring the value of this flexible architecture. These observations have confirmed the utility of the current framework and demonstrated the consistent superior performance of the current expert setting across datasets. (5) As shown in Table 6 , removing any of the following components, spatial context, knowledge distillation, or domain knowledge, results in a substantial decline in predictive performance, highlighting the individual contribution of each component to the overall effectiveness of the model. Furthermore, the computational analysis presented in Table 7 demonstrates that our framework delivers superior efficiency compared to other baselines, including DomainST without domain knowledge configurations, particularly in terms of training and inference time. Case Studies. We observe that gene expression levels across all three datasets exhibit a long-tail distribution. For instance, in the cSCC dataset, log-normalized expression values range from 0.9059 to 25.6508, with a mean of only 3.306, indicating a high concentration of lowly expressed genes. Taking the low-expressed gene IGFBP4 (expression level: 0.9706) as a representative example, the PCC between the predicted and ground truth expression values was 0.5195 prior to incorporating gene representations into our model. After integrating gene features, the PCC improved to 0.5736. In contrast, the PCCs achieved by existing methods, including ST-Net, EGN, BLEEP, HisToGene, Hist2ST, THItoGene, TRIPLEX, EGGN, mclSTExp, SGN, and M2OST, were 0.0364, 0.3743, 0.4845, -0.1539, 0.1087, 0.0245, 0.3671, 0.3342, 0.0502, 0.0283, and 0.0601, respectively. To further investigate this trend, we divide the genes in the cSCC dataset evenly into three groups based on their expression levels: low, medium, and high. We then compare the PCC performance of our method (before and after domain knowledge integration) with all baseline methods, as illustrated in Fig. 6 . We observe that domain knowledge integration enhances performance across all expression levels. (Results on the HER2+ and Stnet datasets are included in the supplementary materials.) These results highlight the superior performance of our DomainST framework in modeling genes with different expression levels, underscoring the effectiveness of integrating domain knowledge to address challenges associated with data sparsity. Furthermore, in order to assess the model’s ability to capture spatial gene expression patterns both quantitatively and qualitatively, we visualize the expression distributions of two well-established cancer biomarkers, ACTG1 and GNAS [2,5,11] , in Fig. 5 . Specifically, we present their log-normalized absolute expression levels and compute the corresponding PCCs with the ground truth log-normalized values to evaluate both the spatial expression trends and quantitative accuracy. Additional results are provided in the supplementary materials. Our approach currently relies on curated gene descriptions from resources such as NCBI and Gene Ontology databases, which introduces certain limitations. First, for genes with sparse or incomplete annotations, especially in under-studied regions of the genome, the resulting textual representations may be less informative, potentially affecting prediction performance. Second, the method is primarily optimized for human and well-annotated model organisms, limiting its applicability to non-model species with poor or missing annotations. Addressing these challenges in future work may involve strategies such as retrieval-augmented generation and cross-species transfer to enhance generalization in low-resource biological contexts. We utilized three public datasets in our study: (1) HER2-positive breast tumor dataset (HER2+) [31] , comprising 13,620 spots from 8 patients with 36 tissue sections, (2) Stnet dataset [2] , consisting of 30,612 spots from 23 breast cancer patients with 68 sections. (3) Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma dataset (cSCC) [32] , containing 8179 spots from 4 individuals across 12 sections. In this study, we emphasize the broader implications of modeling domain knowledge as a learnable modality, framing our approach as a generalizable blueprint for addressing multimodal challenges in AI4Science tasks. By integrating structured experimental data with large-scale scientific knowledge, this paradigm has demonstrated effectiveness in diverse domains such as drug discovery [40] , as well as molecular and protein analysis [41,42] . Recent advances show that treating domain knowledge as a dynamic, task-adaptive modality considerably enhances both interpretability and generalization, enabling more robust and knowledge-grounded scientific predictions. Our method contributes to this emerging direction by providing a flexible and extensible framework applicable across a broad range of scientific applications. In this study, we present DomainST, a novel framework that integrates domain knowledge to enhance spatial gene expression prediction. Specifically, we address the data scarcity issue by utilizing medical visual-language foundation models to extract robust image representations at multiple scales. We mitigate the data sparsity in gene expression prediction by generating informative gene embeddings from public gene reference databases with large language models. We further design a mixture of experts fusion module to effectively integrate image and gene features and leverage their complementary information. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate our framework’s consistent superiority over state-of-the-art methods and highlight the effectiveness of combining foundation models with domain knowledge in spatial gene expression prediction. CBVLM: Training-free explainable concept-based Large Vision Language Models for medical image classification The main challenges limiting the adoption of deep learning-based solutions in medical workflows are the availability of annotated data and the lack of interpretability of such systems. Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) tackle the latter by constraining the model output on a set of predefined and human-interpretable concepts. However, the increased interpretability achieved through these concept-based explanations implies a higher annotation burden. Moreover, if a new concept needs to be added, the whole system needs to be retrained. Inspired by the remarkable performance shown by Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in few-shot settings, we propose a simple, yet effective, methodology, CBVLM, which tackles both of the aforementioned challenges. First, for each concept, we prompt the LVLM to answer if the concept is present in the input image. Then, we ask the LVLM to classify the image based on the previous concept predictions. Moreover, in both stages, we incorporate a retrieval module responsible for selecting the best examples for in-context learning. By grounding the final diagnosis on the predicted concepts, we ensure explainability, and by leveraging the few-shot capabilities of LVLMs, we drastically lower the annotation cost. We validate our approach with extensive experiments across four medical datasets and twelve LVLMs (both generic and medical) and show that CBVLM consistently outperforms CBMs and task-specific supervised methods without requiring any training and using just a few annotated examples. Our methodology is organized into two key stages: (1) The Concept Detection stage, where the LVLM predicts the individual presence of each predefined clinical concept in the query image. This is achieved using a custom prompt that supports both zero- and few-shot settings. In the latter, we include a set of demonstration examples (middle block of Prompt Construction ) chosen by the Retrieval Module , responsible for selecting the N most similar examples to the input image. To evaluate the LVLM answer, we employ an Evaluation Block which first tries to extract the desired LVLM response using a rule-based formulation. If this fails, we adopt an auxiliary LLM to extract the desired response. (2) In the Disease Diagnosis stage, the final diagnosis is generated by the LVLM based on the clinical concepts predicted in the first stage, which are directly incorporated in the query (highlighted in yellow). This approach ensures that the diagnosis is grounded on the identified clinical concepts, enhancing the interpretability and transparency of the LVLM’s response.
