More information on our project page: . The field of medical imaging analysis has witnessed significant advancements through the use of supervised deep learning methods. However, their performance greatly depends on the availability and quality of training samples, which are particularly costly to obtain, as clinician expertise is required. The recent rise of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) has also made its way into the medical field, of which Med-LVLMs such as [1–4] are prominent examples, where pre-trained LVLMs are fine-tuned using medical data. However, despite the improved performance, these Med-LVLMs require even more annotated data. Consequently, a different research direction has emerged, exploring the potential of applying LVLMs to specific downstream tasks with minimal or no supervision, by leveraging their few-shot capabilities [5–7] , particularly the use of in-context learning (ICL) for improving model performance through a short number of examples in the prompt. In addition to the need for annotated data, another major challenge with deep learning-based medical imaging is the lack of interpretability, which is of the utmost importance in high-stakes decision-making scenarios [8] . One way of introducing interpretability into such frameworks is via concept-based explanations. Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide this type of explanations by introducing a layer, the “bottleneck”, that predicts the presence or absence of a predefined set of human-interpretable concepts. The final classification prediction is then based on these concepts. Nevertheless, CBMs still require training and annotated data; in fact, the amount of annotated data actually increases since concept annotations are needed on top of the classification labels. We propose combining the best of both worlds: the interpretability of CBMs and the few-shot abilities of LVLMs to decrease the annotation cost. Our methodology, CBVLM , encompasses a two-stage approach, where, first, the LVLM is prompted to predict the existence/absence of a set of concepts in an image, and, in a second stage, the predicted concepts are incorporated into the prompt such that the LVLM provides a final diagnosis grounded on these predicted concepts. Fig. 1 represents this methodology compared to the common approach where an LVLM is simply prompted to perform classification. Moreover, contrary to CBMs, which require retraining the entire model to incorporate a new concept, CBVLM can easily incorporate additional concepts, requiring only two inference steps. We validate CBVLM on four medical datasets encompassing different imaging modalities and using twelve LVLMs, and show that CBVLM achieves comparable performance or even surpasses task-specific supervised methods, doing so without training, with few annotated examples, and without sacrificing interpretability. Although, individually, the techniques used in CBVLM (e.g., ICL) are not novel, this is, to the best of our knowledge, the first work combining them in a novel methodology exploring the capability of LVLMs to provide concept-based explanations for medical image classification. The emergent capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to the development of LLMs able to process visual inputs, i.e. LVLMs. These models can reason about images in a zero- or few-shot manner (e.g., LLaVA [9] , GPT-4V [10] ), allowing them to tackle downstream tasks without fine-tuning. General-purpose LVLMs have recently been adapted for the medical domain through training on extensive medical datasets, coining the term Med-LVLMs. The generalization capability of these models has prompted researchers to assess their performance in multiple medical data. Royer et al. [11] recently released an open-source toolkit for fair and reproducible evaluation of Med-LVLMs in tasks like classification and report generation. Han et al. [5] evaluated the performance of a general LVLM on the NEJM Image Challenge, as well as the impact of fine-tuning the LVLM. In [12] , Med-LVLMs were evaluated in different specialties and compared with medical experts, with results comparable to the performance of junior doctors. In [7] , the authors benchmarked the performance of GPT-4V against fully supervised image classifiers and found that their performance is comparable. In a different line of research, Xia et al. [13] evaluated the trustworthiness and fairness of Med-LVLMs and found that models often display factual inaccuracies and can be unfair across different demographic groups. CBVLM distinguishes itself from previous studies as it is not limited to prompting the LVLM to provide a diagnosis, but it is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to generate concept-based explanations on which the LVLM response is grounded prior to diagnosis prediction, thus enhancing the performance and transparency of the decision-making process. CBMs [14] are based on an encoder–decoder paradigm, where the encoder predicts a set of human-specified concepts from the input image, while the decoder leverages these predicted concepts to generate the final predictions. Due to their inherent interpretability, these models have attracted particular interest in medical image classification. Several CBMs have been proposed for a wide variety of medical tasks (e.g., melanoma diagnosis [15–17] , knee osteoarthritis [14] and chest X-ray classification [18] ). Nevertheless, CBMs have well-known limitations: (i) they require concept annotations (image-level or class-level), (ii) they tend to have lower performance compared to traditional (black-box) supervised methods, (iii) they struggle to predict concepts accurately, and (iv) incorporating new concepts implies retraining the whole CBM. These challenges are particularly significant in medical imaging, where data availability is typically limited due to the expertise required for annotations. Consequently, LVLMs represent a promising alternative to traditional CBMs, as they are able to generalize to unseen domains with minimal or no supervision. Moreover, incorporating additional concepts becomes trivial and does not require fine-tuning, as happened with traditional CBMs. Given the task of predicting a target y ∈ R from input x ∈ R d , let D = { ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) , c ( i ) ) } i = 1 n be a batch of training samples where c ∈ R { 0 , 1 } l is a vector of l concepts. Traditional (black-box) models learn a function h : R d → R that directly predicts the target y ∈ R from the input x ∈ R d . However, CBMs first map the input x into a set of interpretable concepts c (“bottleneck”) by learning g : R d → R l , and use these concepts to predict the target y using f : R l → R . Therefore, the prediction y ˆ = f ( g ( x ) ) is entirely based on the predicted concepts c ˆ = g ( x ) . In order to generate concept-based explanations with LVLMs, we follow the CBM paradigm and introduce a two-stage methodology, as outlined in Fig. 2 and detailed in the following subsections. The first stage involves predicting the l concepts present in a given input image. For each predefined clinical concept, we start by providing the LVLM with a short description of that concept and then prompt it to answer if that concept is shown in the image (see Fig. 2 on the left). Thus, concept prediction is given by p L V L M ( t a n s | t I 1 , … , t I m , t P 1 , … , t P k ) , where t a n s corresponds to the first generated token, t I 1 , … , t I m correspond to the input image tokens, and t P 1 , … , t P k correspond to the tokens of the prompt (description of the concept and the question). The structure of the (zero-shot) prompt for the prediction of a single concept is as follows: The descriptions for each clinical concept, as presented in the Instruction section shown in Fig. 2 , were generated by ChatGPT [19] with the following prompt: ” According to published literature in {dermatology, radiology, retinal lesions}, which phrases best describe a {skin, X-ray, eye fundus} image containing {concept}?” . Examples of prompts for different concepts related to the classification of diabetic retinopathy are shown in Fig. 2 on the left. The full prompts for all datasets can be found in the Supplementary Material. The second stage involves prompting the LVLM to answer if a certain disease (i.e. class) is present in the image. The concepts predicted in the previous stage are appended to the question, such that when providing an answer, the LVLM not only considers the image and the question, but also takes into account the concepts. Thus, the disease diagnosis is given by p L V L M ( t a n s | t I 1 , … , t I m , t P 1 , … , t P k , t C 1 , … , t C c ) , where t C 1 , … , t C c are the tokens representing the concepts. This approach ensures that the diagnosis is grounded on the identified clinical concepts, enhancing the interpretability and transparency of the model’s response. The structure of the (zero-shot) prompt for diagnosis classification is as follows: An example of the prompt designed for the classification of diabetic retinopathy is shown in Fig. 2 on the right. The full prompts for all datasets can be found in the Supplementary Material. A key factor contributing to the appeal of LLMs, and consequently LVLMs, is their ability to perform ICL. ICL, or few-shot learning/ prompting, is a prompt engineering technique in which the model is provided with examples, known as demonstrations, consisting of: i) questions, and (ii) their corresponding answers. It has been shown to significantly improve the performance of both LLMs [20] and LVLMs [21] . Therefore, our methodology incorporates ICL in both stages, as shown in Fig. 2 . Although the demonstrations for ICL could be chosen randomly, Zhou et al. [22] have shown that this selection policy can decrease the model performance when compared to the 0-shot scenario (when no examples are included in the prompt). Thus, following other works [21,23–25] , we introduce a Retrieval Module to select the demonstrations based on their similarity to the query image x 0 , a method known as Retrieval-based In-Context Examples Selection (RICES). Given the feature vector ϕ ( x 0 ) of the query image obtained from an arbitrary vision encoder, we select the N most similar image feature vectors from the training set D as the few-shot demonstrations to include in the prompt. For each different type of prompt, the question is repeated for every demonstration. The ground-truth answer to each demonstration question is also provided; depending on the stage of our methodology, this can be the absence/presence of a given concept (1st stage), or the disease diagnosis, as well as the absence/presence of all concepts (2nd stage). As LVLMs produce their outputs in natural language (i.e. it is open-ended), it is necessary to process the generated text to compare it with the ground-truth concepts or the ground-truth class labels. To simplify this process and limit the space of possible responses, all questions are posed as multiple choice and the LVLM is instructed to answer by choosing one of the options and not providing additional information (see the example prompts in Fig. 2 ). One way of extracting the LVLM answer would be to select the option with the higher first token log probability, i.e. if token B is the one with the highest probability, then this would mean that the LVLM had chosen option B. However, [26] have shown that there is a mismatch between the first token probabilities and the actual LVLM answer. Thus, we use a Regular Expression (RegEx) to directly find the pattern “option_letter)”, either in lower or upper case. We choose to provide the options as “option_letter” + “)” instead of “option_letter” + “.”, as it would be less probable to find the pattern “option_letter)” in the middle of the LVLM response. If none of the predefined options is found in the LVLM answer (e.g., when the LVLM answers the question but in a more verbose fashion), we follow the approach of previous works [3] and employ an auxiliary LLM 2 2 Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 . to extract the information from the LVLM answer and match it to the predefined list of options. If both approaches fail (e.g., when the LVLM response is just a description of the input image without any actual answer to the question), we mark that instance as unknown and report separately the percentage of instances for which this occurred. In this section, we outline our experimental setup with information about the adopted LVLMs, datasets, and evaluation metrics, as well as the implementation details. We conduct experiments on four publicly available datasets, encompassing dermatology ( Derm7pt [27] and SkinCon [28] ), radiology ( CORDA [29] ) and eye fundus imaging ( DDR [30] ) modalities. The selection of these datasets is constrained by the availability of datasets with annotated clinical features, hereinafter referred to as “ concepts ”. Unless otherwise stated, we use the official train-val-test splits of the datasets. For the Derm7pt [27] dataset, with a total of 827 images, we consider only dermoscopic images of the “nevus” and “melanoma” classes, jointly with the 5 annotated dermoscopic attributes, namely Absent/Typical/Atypical Pigment Network, Absent/Regular/Irregular Streaks, Absent/Regular/Irregular Dots and Globules, Blue-Whitish Veils, and Regression Structures. The SkinCon [28] dataset contains 3,230 images from the Fitzpatrick 17k dataset [31] annotated with 48 clinical concepts. Following previous works, we use the binary labels denoting skin malignancy for the target task and randomly split the dataset into train/val/test with the proportion of 70%, 15%, and 15%, respectively. Additionally, only 22 out of the 48 concepts are used, as the other 26 concepts appear in less than 50 images. From the CORDA [29] dataset, a COVID-19 diagnosis dataset, we use its 1601 chest X-rays. Inspired by the work of Barbano et al. [32] , we use a pretrained model on the CheXpert [33] dataset to annotate the samples with a binary label to denote the presence or absence of 14 radiological observations. Of those 14 concepts, we exclude the “Fracture” and “Support Devices” concepts, as these are not directly related to the presence or absence of the target class. The “No Finding” concept is implicitly included in the remaining 11 concepts given that if all 11 concepts are 0 it represents a healthy case without any findings. The DDR [30] dataset comprises 13,673 fundus images divided into six Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) levels. In our experiments, we focus on the five-class classification task for DR grading, discarding the images belonging to the ungradable class and considering a subset of 757 images annotated with 4 types of lesions correlated with DR, which we use as concepts. We augment this subset with 743 “No DR” images, resulting in a dataset of 1500 samples. Table 1 provides a detailed summary of the statistics for each of the considered datasets. All results ( cf. Section 5 ) are reported on the entire test set of each dataset. In our experiments, we assess the performance of open-source LVLMs that can process both text and multiple images. Specifically, we focus on models trained on general-domain data, such as OpenFlamingo [23] , Idefics3 [34] , VILA [35] , LLaVA-OneVision [36] , Qwen2-VL [37] , MiniCPM-V [38] , InternVL 2.5 [39] and mPLUG-Owl3 [40] . Additionally, we consider models specialized for the medical domain, including Med-Flamingo [1] , LLaVA-Med [2] , CheXagent [3] and SkinGPT-4 [4] . We use their corresponding checkpoints from the HuggingFace library (the full list of checkpoints can be found in the Supplementary Material). We compare the performance of CBVLM against several baselines, including: (i) standard CBM [14] trained on each of the four datasets considered using the official implementation. It is worth noting that, for training the CBM on the Derm7pt dataset, we considered 11 clinical concepts. Specifically, 3 out of the 5 annotated concepts have three options each (e.g., Pigment Network can be Absent, Regular, or Irregular), as described in 4.1 . To address this, and given that the concept layer predicts the presence or absence of each concept, we treated each option as an independent concept. For instance, for Pigment Network, we defined the concepts: Absent Pigment Network, Regular Pigment Network, and Irregular Pigment Network; (ii) CLAT [41] - a concept-based framework specifically designed for retinal disease diagnosis. For DDR, the pre-computed textual embeddings of the clinical concepts provided in the official CLAT repository were used. However, since the original embeddings were obtained from a retinal foundation model [42] , for the other datasets, we replaced it with MedImageInsight [43] , an embedding model for medical imaging trained on a mixture of X-ray, computed tomography, dermatology, and pathology datasets. For Derm7pt, we follow the same strategy described above, i.e. we transformed the 5 concepts into 11 independent concepts; (iii) supervised black-box models , namely ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 [44] and ViT Base [45] fine-tuned on the disease diagnosis task; (iv) task-specific black-box models , namely [17] for the Derm7pt dataset, [46] for the SkinCon dataset, [47] for the CORDA dataset, and [48] for the DDR dataset, reporting classification performance on the respective dataset. For the retrieval strategy used to perform ICL, image similarity is determined using cosine similarity between features, which are extracted from two distinct encoders, namely MedImageInsight [43] and the (vision) encoder of the corresponding LVLM. For both concept prediction and disease diagnosis, we report Balanced Accuracy (BACC) and F1-score, as these metrics are tailored to deal with imbalanced datasets, which is the case in medical image classification. For concept prediction, we measure the BACC and F1-score averaged over each concept. This section presents the key results of CBVLM , comparing its performance against CBMs and task-specific supervised methods in terms of BACC and F1-score across two tasks: (i) Concept Detection ( Figs. 3 , 4 , 5 , and 6 ); and (ii) Disease Diagnosis ( Figs. 7 and 8 ). We start by assessing the predictive performance of CBVLM in the task of concept detection. Fig. 3 presents the results across different datasets under various n -shot settings, n ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 } . For comparative analysis, we also report the performance of CBM and CLAT. The results for n > 0 were obtained considering the best vision encoder, in this case, MedImageInsight, selected after an ablation study with different vision encoders (see Fig. 9 ). The results presented in Fig. 3 and the analysis depicted in Fig. 4 (left) reveals that few-shot prompting significantly boosts performance by incorporating contextually relevant information within the prompts [1] . Notably, there is a consistent trend across all datasets, demonstrating improved performance as the number of demonstrations increases. For example, the performance of CBVLM when adopting CheXagent, LLaVA-OV, Qwen2-VL, and SkinGPT-4 improves by over 15% when incorporating 4 demonstration examples into the prompt compared to the zero-shot scenario ( n = 0 ). Remarkably, CBVLM outperforms both CBM and CLAT across all datasets except Derm7pt, where its performance is on par with CBM. Impressively, CBVLM achieves these results without any training, relying on only four demonstration examples or less. From the results depicted in Fig. 4 (right), in the 0 -shot scenario, generic LVLMs consistently outperform medical LVLMs across all datasets. However, in the few-shot setting, medical LVLMs outperform their generic counterparts in all datasets using only one or two demonstration examples ( n ∈ { 1 , 2 } ). The stronger performance of generic LVLMs in the zero-shot setting can be attributed to their training on large-scale generic image datasets, allowing for better generalization in this setting. As demonstration examples are introduced into the prompt, medical LVLMs improve, benefiting from their pre-training on specialized medical data, which enhances their ability to generalize in these scenarios. However, in the 4-shot setting, generic LVLMs tend to achiever higher concept detection performance than their medical counterparts. This might stem from the fact that generic LVLMs tend to allow for longer prompts and are trained with interleaved image-text data, while medical LVLMs are not. Fig. 5 presents a detailed comparison of the per-concept F1-score for each dataset. The reported results, averaged across all, generic, and medical LVLMs in the 4-shot setting, reveal that underrepresented concepts are the most challenging to detect, as expected. For instance, in the CORDA dataset, none of the models correctly predicts the presence of the “pleural other” concept (which only appears in 4 images of the entire dataset). The concepts “atelectasis” and “lung lesion” are also consistently difficult to detect. The full results per-LVLM can be found in the Supplementary Material. CBVLM outperforms CBMs and CLAT in concept prediction across all datasets, except for Derm7pt, where CBM achieves the best result with a margin of ≈ 5%. This may be due to the fact that in Derm7pt, some concepts have three available options, whereas in the other datasets, each concept is binary, which may make it easier for the LVLM to predict the presence or absence of a concept more accurately. Although CBVLM is able to outperform CBMs with only 4-shots, it should be noted that, in total, more than 4 images are being used, as the same 4 example images will not be the most similar for all query images in the test set. To assess the impact of the number of images per class in the examples set, we progressively reduce the percentage of images per class, limiting the number of available examples for selection for few-shot prompting. This experiment is conducted using the best-performing model for each dataset: CheXagent 4-shots for Derm7pt, and Open-Flamingo 2-shots for SkinCon, CORDA and DDR. The results, shown in Fig. 6 and averaged across 3 runs, demonstrate that even with just 10% of the images per class in the examples set, CBVLM consistently outperforms CBM across all datasets, except for Derm7pt where even with 100% of the images per class, the performance is lower than CBM, as discussed earlier. Nevertheless, the results shown in Fig. 6 underscore a key observation: few-shot prompting with a good example selection strategy can boost performance by up to 20% ( cf. BACC at 0% and 10%), even in situations where annotated data is severely limited, which is the case of medical data. Thus, LVLMs can indeed be successfully used for concept detection with very limited amounts of annotated data, thus reducing the annotation cost inherent to CBMs. Fig. 7 shows the performance of CBVLM in terms of BACC and F1-score for the task of disease classification across different datasets under various n -shots ( n = { 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 } ). Similarly to Section 5.1 , we also report the performance of CBM, CLAT and a Black-box (Bbox) model for comparison. Additionally, we include results for the setting where the CBVLM predicts the disease label directly without prior concept information (“0 w/o” bar in Fig. 7 ). Similar to the trend observed in the concept detection task, the results shown in Fig. 8 (left) confirm our initial assumption and align with findings reported in the literature: few-shot prompting significantly enhances the performance of LVLMs in disease classification as the number of demonstrations increases, across all datasets. The results show that incorporating clinical concepts into the prompt improves both BACC and F1-score compared to the scenario without concept guidance (i.e., “0” vs “0 w/o” bars in Fig. 7 ). Furthermore, grounding the final diagnosis on a set of clinical concepts promotes transparency and explainability, aligning more closely with human reasoning, unlike the concept-free setting (“0 w/o”). The results in Fig. 8 (right) confirm that generic LVLMs consistently outperform their medical counterparts across all datasets in the scenario without concepts (“0 w/o”). This trend is also observed in the 0-shot scenario with concepts, in general. In the few-shot setting, generic LVLMs exhibit superior performance only in SkinCon in terms of BACC, with a marginal average improvement of 1% across scenarios with n > 0 . Conversely, when averaging across all few-shot scenarios ( n > 0 ), medical LVLMs consistently outperform generic models across all datasets, achieving F1-score improvements of 25.74%, 14.48%, 4.62%, and 19.81% for Derm7pt, SkinCon, CORDA, and DDR, respectively. This phenomenon can be attributed to two factors: i) the stronger domain knowledge of medical LVLMs, and (ii) the initialization of their vision encoders from medical-specific CLIP versions, such as BiomedCLIP [49] for LLaVA-Med, or larger improved CLIP architectures like EVA-CLIP-g [50] , used in CheXagent and SkinGPT. CBVLM surpasses CBMs across all datasets. With the top-performing LVLM, we observe F1-score improvements of 7.42%, 39.70%, 7.25%, and 63.13% for Derm7pt, SkinCon, CORDA, and DDR, respectively, compared to the standard CBM. It is worth recalling that CBVLM achieves these results without any kind of training, whereas CBM needs to be trained for each dataset. When comparing CBVLM with CLAT [41] , a method specifically optimized for retinal disease diagnosis, our experiments show that CBVLM outperforms it on the diabetic retinopathy dataset, DDR, in terms of F1-score. Furthermore, CBVLM also outperforms CLAT on the other datasets, achieving an average relative improvement of ≈ 6%. Finally, when compared to black-box approaches, a similar trend is observed. CBVLM outperforms task-specific black-box models by 2.15% in BACC for Derm7pt and achieves comparable performance on CORDA, with a slight decrease of −2.32%. In terms of F1 score, the best performing CBVLM exceeds black-box task-specific models by 0.36% on SkinCon and by 1% on DDR. Thus, CBVLM achieves state-of-the-art results on Derm7pt, SkinCon and DDR. In order to validate the importance of the Retrieval Module ( cf. Fig. 2 ), which employs RICES [24] (i.e. ranks examples based on the cosine similarity between image features extracted from an arbitrary vision encoder), we conduct an ablation study on the task of concept detection for the 1 -shot scenario. In this study, we first compare random ICL example selection with RICES, and then assess different vision encoders to perform RICES. For random selection, we compare choosing only 1 random example against choosing 1 random example per class. The results of Fig. 9 show that, except for Open-Flamingo and MiniCPM-V, using 1 example per class does not improve performance. In fact, in the majority of cases it slightly decreases it, when comparing to simply choose 1 random example. We then explore two different encoders for RICES: MedImageInsight [43] and the encoder integrated within the respective LVLM. Although in some models (e.g., Open-Flamingo and MiniCPM-V), choosing the examples randomly brings better performance, in the majority of cases it improves both BACC and F1-score (especially for Medical LVLMs). More importantly, we are not concerned with the average results, but rather on maximizing them, even if just for one LVLM, to be able to find the best configuration of CBVLM to compete against other approaches like CBM and supervised black-box models. Thus, using RICES beats random selection and using MedImageInsight instead of the LVLM encoder yields the best results on all datasets. As such, all experiments are conducted using RICES (i.e. the Retrieval Module ) with MedImageInsight as the feature extractor. Table 2 presents a detailed comparison of our proposed CBVLM with concept-based models, supervised black-box models, and task-specific models. As highlighted in the results, CBVLM consistently achieves either the best or second-best performance across all evaluations. Notably, this is accomplished without any additional training and by leveraging just four examples, enabling concept-based explanations and enhanced interpretability and transparency in the model responses. In summary, CBVLM using CheXagent with 4 demonstration examples emerges as the top-performing combination for Derm7pt. For SkinCon, CBVLM with the generic Open-Flamingo model and 4 demonstration examples achieves the best results in both disease diagnosis and concept detection tasks. For CORDA, the best performance is achieved by CBVLM with CheXagent with 2 demonstration examples. For DDR, CBVLM with Idefics3 and 4 demonstrations proves to be the best-performing combination. Overall, the results underscore the effectiveness of CBVLM in enabling arbitrary LVLMs to predict the presence of clinical concepts from an image and use those concepts to ground the final diagnosis, enhancing interpretability and transparency in the model’s responses, all without requiring any training and with just a few annotated examples. Notably, CBVLM outperforms CBM-related approaches across all datasets and even surpasses black-box models when employing ICL. The main drawback of the proposed methodology for generating concept-based explanations with LVLMs lies in the independent prediction of each concept, which is a concern when applied to datasets with a large number of concepts. A similar problem arises with datasets with a large number of classes, as each class is provided as a separate option in the prompt. This can result in excessively long prompts that would require alternative ways of querying the model. Although in medical applications the number of concepts is typically limited, a potential future direction to address concerns regarding the scalability for datasets with numerous concepts could be the adoption of tailored selection policies that prioritize only a small subset of the most informative concepts, as demonstrated in recent works [51] . Additionally, our approach is limited to discrete-valued concepts (e.g., absent/present or, for some concepts of Derm7pt, absent/regular/ irregular), contrasting with traditional CBMs, where each concept is associated with a probability. Nevertheless, this limitation could be addressed by prompting the LVLM to not only answer if a given concept is present in the input image but also to provide a confidence score, as is done in other works [7] . We leave this exploration to future work. Finally, CBVLM is only as good as the LVLM it uses. In a few cases, some of the LVLMs we tested struggled to provide answers to the questions (e.g., instead of answering the question, the LVLM simply described the input image), leading to an increase in unknown responses (as shown in Figs. 3 and 7 ). This phenomenon is particularly common with SkinGPT, which may be due to its pretraining on very specific prompts designed to elicit desired responses [4] . LLava-Med also faced challenges in providing valid responses, especially in few-shot scenarios where n > 1 . This difficulty may stem from the fact that it is not trained with interleaved image-text data; in such models, image data is given at the input in the form of tokens, so as the number of shots increases, so does the number of tokens, making it more difficult for the model to pay attention to the full input sequence [52] . Another relevant concern involves the robustness, security, and inherent biases of LVLMs [53] . While a comprehensive analysis of these aspects is beyond the scope of this work, it remains a critical consideration for future studies aimed at safe and reliable integration of LVLMs into clinical workflows. Collaboration between clinicians and AI researchers is crucial to ensure transparency and explainability of AI models deployed into clinical practice [54] . We propose a simple yet effective methodology, CBVLM , that leverages off-the-shelf LVLMs to produce concept-based explanations and predict disease diagnoses grounded on those explanations, thus offering a more transparent and explainable decision-making process, something that is critical in high-stakes scenarios such as medical use-cases. Through extensive experiments across four medical datasets, and open-source LVLMs, we show that CBVLM outperforms the traditional CBM and even task-specific black-box models across all benchmarks. This is achieved without requiring any training and using just a few annotated examples, thus tackling a very common problem in medical applications, where the annotation process requires a clinician’s expertise. Overall, CBVLM is able to leverage the best of both worlds: (i) its LVLM-based training-free nature presents a major advantage over CBMs, as these models require additional training and are restricted by predefined concepts, and (ii) its two-stage process keeps the interpretability inherent to CBMs but that LVLMs lack. Although CBVLM was tested on medical datasets, it is a general methodology that can be applied in other domains. In the future, we would like to do so, e.g., on the CUB dataset [55] . Given the promising results obtained in this work with open-source LVLMs of around 8 billion parameters, we would also like to experiment with bigger and/or proprietary LVLMs. Cristiano Patrício: Writing – review & editing, Writing – original draft, Validation, Software, Methodology, Conceptualization. CDMT-Unet: a dual-frequency cross-fusion model for skin cancer segmentation In this paper, we propose a novel cross-fusion model, CDMT-Unet, which leverages the MobileNet and Transformer architectures for precise segmentation and diagnosis of skin cancer images. This model integrates the strengths of the Haar wavelet transform, capable of capturing global texture and edge information through multi-scale analysis, with an attention mechanism that focuses on more pertinent information. By combining these methodologies, the model effectively utilizes both high-frequency detail and low-frequency structural information to comprehensively characterize the skin lesion area. Building upon this foundation, the CDMT-Unet model adopts a hybrid architecture encompassing CNN, Transformer, and Unet components. The CNN module is employed to extract local spatial features, while the Transformer module captures global contextual information via a self-attention mechanism. Furthermore, the Unet structure facilitates the fusion and reconstruction of multi-level features through skip connections. Utilizing a dual-frequency cross-fusion strategy, the model adeptly integrates features extracted by the discrete Walsh transform and Haar wavelet transform, thereby enhancing its ability to segment complex skin lesions. Experimental results demonstrate that CDMT-Unet achieves remarkable performance across two public skin cancer datasets (ISIC2017 and ISIC2018). Specifically, on ISIC2017, it achieves mIoU of 80.51%, DSC of 87.88%, ACC of 95.68%, Spe of 96.98%, and Sen of 92.13%; on ISIC2018, it reaches mIoU of 80.31%, DSC of 87.60%, ACC of 95.37%, Spe of 97.93%, and Sen of 89.64%. These results highlight the model’s excellence in accurate segmentation of lesion edges and preservation of small-scale features. This model offers an efficient and reliable solution for the automated diagnosis of skin cancer, demonstrating significant potential for a wide range of clinical applications. CLAV: clustering latent vector aggregation for whole slide image retrieval leveraging foundation models Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) is crucial in cancer diagnosis, assisting pathologists by providing similar image data from previous records for analysis, especially when there is uncertainty in diagnosing a case. This process supports decision-making by providing valuable reference points to guide the diagnostic process. Foundation models have become increasingly important in the medical field due to their ability to generalize across various tasks and datasets, offering valuable support to pathologists by enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of diagnostic processes. In this article, a foundation model pre-trained on histopathology data is leveraged as a feature extractor without the need for task-specific training, in contrast to existing models that require extensive training to learn significant data representations. The proposed method, Clustering Latent Vector Aggregation (CLAV), condenses the significant feature vectors into a unique representative vector for the Whole Slide Image (WSI). Using a unique feature vector offers the advantage of reducing the size of the memory bank, thereby making the process of querying and retrieving similar WSIs more efficient. The experimental results presented in this study demonstrate that the proposed method enhances performance in CBIR tasks. This article highlights the potential of foundation models to achieve superior retrieval metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for CBIR. The experimental results presented in this study demonstrate that the proposed method enhances performance in CBIR tasks. This article highlights the potential of foundation models to achieve superior retrieval metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for CBIR. Methodology Overview . This figure illustrates the framework presented in our study, where the foundation model CONCH is used to extract features from the patches of a WSI. These feature vectors are then clustered using our clustering method to determine the centroids of the clusters. The centroids are subsequently aggregated to form the latent vector that represents the WSI. This process is repeated for all the WSIs in the database to form the memory bank. Finally, given an input query WSI, its unique latent-vector representation is obtained, and the cosine similarity with the entire memory bank is computed, retrieving the top k most similar WSIs. The memory bank stores, for every slide, the aggregated latent vector together with its anatomical-site label and TCGA case ID, enabling each retrieved sample to be traced back to its tissue type and patient. During the query stage we apply a leave-one-out strategy: the latent vector of the query slide–and all vectors belonging to the same patient–are temporarily removed from the bank before the similarity computation, preventing patient-specific bias and data leakage. After retrieval, the memory bank is left unchanged, so no additional online update is required. This process is repeated for each slide in the dataset, treating it as a query in turn. Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) is crucial in cancer diagnosis, assisting pathologists by providing similar image data from previous records for analysis, especially when there is uncertainty in diagnosing a case. This process supports decision-making by providing valuable reference points to guide the diagnostic process. Foundation models have become increasingly important in the medical field due to their ability to generalize across various tasks and datasets, offering valuable support to pathologists by enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of diagnostic processes. In this article, a foundation model pre-trained on histopathology data is leveraged as a feature extractor without the need for task-specific training, in contrast to existing models that require extensive training to learn significant data representations. The proposed method, Clustering Latent Vector Aggregation (CLAV), condenses the significant feature vectors into a unique representative vector for the Whole Slide Image (WSI). Using a unique feature vector offers the advantage of reducing the size of the memory bank, thereby making the process of querying and retrieving similar WSIs more efficient. The experimental results presented in this study demonstrate that the proposed method enhances performance in CBIR tasks. This article highlights the potential of foundation models to achieve superior retrieval metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for CBIR. The dataset used in this work is public under TCGA. Technological advances and digitization have allowed Whole Slide Images (WSIs) to enhance clinical applications and diagnostic pathology in recent years. This discipline, Digital Pathology, enables expert pathologists to examine, annotate, and share cases with other specialists [1] . This digitization enables their analysis through artificial intelligence (AI) models. This process allows large volumes of histological data to be accessed and manipulated efficiently. AI can leverage this digitization to perform complex tasks such as automated pattern recognition [2] , tissue classification [3] , and prediction of clinical outcomes [4] . These capabilities not only enhance the accuracy and speed of diagnosis but also provide additional tools for medical research, enabling the discovery of correlations that may be challenging to identify using traditional methods. The literature documents numerous applications of WSIs in histopathology, including segmentation [5] , classification [6] , anomaly detection [7] , and Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) [8] , among others. These applications demonstrate the versatility and potential of computational pathology (CPath) in revolutionizing traditional pathological practices. Among these, CBIR stands out as a valuable tool for assisting pathologists by retrieving similar cases based on visual patterns, particularly when facing ambiguous or rare diagnostic scenarios. However, most CBIR systems rely on patch-level comparisons or complex indexing of large feature sets, which can be computationally expensive and inefficient. This creates a need for methods that can summarize the information of an entire WSI into a compact and representative form without sacrificing retrieval accuracy. With the evolution of AI, foundation models are now being integrated into computational pathology [9] . These models have proven effective for multiple downstream tasks, thus providing an advantage over task-specific models. For example, in [10] , a model capable of performing tasks such as image zero-shot classification, segmentation, image captioning, cross-modal retrieval in histology has been trained. Some works in the literature, such as [11] , have integrated all these advances to develop a histopathological purpose AI assistant, offering better performance than other established models in the current landscape, such as GPT4V [12] . In the context of CBIR, the use of foundation models offers the opportunity to extract rich and generalizable features without requiring additional training or fine-tuning, making them ideal for scalable and task-agnostic retrieval pipelines. In this work, we propose a clustering method to obtain the unique feature vector representation of a WSI. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first use of a clustering-based method to compress the feature vectors of WSI patches into a unique feature vector using a task-agnostic foundation model (CONtrastive learning from Captions for Histopathology, CONCH [10] ) as the feature extractor. This approach aims to improve the efficiency and scalability of CBIR systems by reducing the memory and computational requirements while maintaining retrieval performance. Additionally, leveraging a task-agnostic foundation model eliminates the need for a training stage, which is typically time-consuming and resource-intensive. Therefore, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • Development of a clustering method for generating a compressed unique feature vector representation of WSIs. • Leveraging a task-agnostic foundation model (CONCH) as a feature extractor for the automated retrieval of WSIs. • Conducting comprehensive experiments and evaluations using Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) metrics, including measures like majority vote. • Integration of robust evaluation methodologies to validate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed clustering approach and feature extraction model. Traditional methods of CBIR in histopathology rely on extracting handcrafted features such as colour, texture, and shape from patches. Examples of these methods include Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [13] and Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) [14] for detecting and describing local features in images. However, these traditional methods often face the issue of a semantic gap, which refers to the disconnect between the low-level features that these algorithms extract and the high-level concepts that expert pathologists perceive and use in their diagnoses [15] . This gap can result in suboptimal retrieval performance, as the hand-crafted features may not fully capture the morphology and complex patterns that expert pathologists recognize. In this sense, deep learning methods offer a solution to this problem by automatically learning hierarchical features from the data to increase confidence in image understanding [15] . Patch retrieval methods have made significant advances in the field of image retrieval. For instance, Tabatabaei et al. [16] proposes a Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) network architecture specifically designed for patch retrieval tasks in prostate and breast cancer studies. This approach utilizes features extracted from the CAE’s bottleneck to perform content-based image retrieval (CBIR) efficiently. Similarly, Hegde et al. [17] introduces SMILY, a method leveraging a deep-ranking network [18] for feature extraction in patch retrieval scenarios. In contrast, Whole Slide Image (WSI) retrieval methods often focus on higher-level image understanding and processing. For example, Kalra et al. [19] employs a DenseNet architecture [20] for feature extraction from image patches without task-specific training, relying instead on a pre-trained model from the ImageNet dataset [21] . The approach includes a novel technique called mosaic generation, which selects the most representative patches from a WSI to accelerate the search for similar WSIs by reducing the number of patches considered. This method utilizes K-means clustering on RGB histograms and spatial coordinates to construct the mosaic, akin to the approach used in SISH [22] . While SISH relies on a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) [23] pre-trained on the TCGA dataset to aid retrieval, such approaches can suffer from suboptimal performance due to domain shifts between natural and histopathological images. Inspired by the concept of mosaic generation, RetCCL [8] introduces a novel method that combines clustering of feature vectors and spatial coordinates for mosaic construction, using a ResNet50 model [24] trained with contrastive learning. However, these methods still rely on handling a large number of patch-level features, which can be resource-intensive. In this context, our work addresses the challenges of managing large-scale feature vectors by proposing a method to obtain a unique feature vector representation for each WSI. By reducing the memory bank to a single feature vector per WSI, we significantly decrease resource consumption and improve efficiency in the retrieval process. Deep-learning based representation learning pretends to extract high-level visual features from the images through different training paradigms. Convolutional neural networks based architectures pre-trained on ImageNet [25] under a fully-supervised learning paradigm have been used in CPath [26,27] . However, this dataset mostly contains natural images which limits the ability of ImageNet pre-trained models to extract discriminative features in images with a large domain shift, such as histopathological images. To address this limitation, extensive in-domain datasets encompassing multiple anatomical sites and conditions have been gathered to pursue in-domain pre-training and improved representation learning. Due to the challenges associated with the time-consuming and expert-dependent annotation of medical images, other pre-training paradigms, such as self- and vision-language supervision, have investigated other forms of supervision beyond fully supervised learning. These foundation models aims to learn discriminative data representation in a task-agnostic approach to later adapt to multiple downstream tasks. Vision-language supervision introduced by Radford et al. [28] has marked a big step in foundation model development by multimodal pre-training using image-captions pairs. In the field of CPath, some works, such as Lu et al. [10] , Huang et al. [29] , retrieved histopathology images and their descriptions in the form of natural text to fit this novel learning paradigm. Meanwhile, self-supervised learning (SSL) does not require any kind of supervision and aims to learn data representations from the images themselves. While CTransPath [30] combined the contrastive learning objectives with transformer architectures, other works, such as Chen et al. [31] , Xu et al. [32] , have used the popular DINO v2 algorithm [33] on large-scale datasets with data scales of tens of millions of patches from WSI of multiple anatomical sites and cancer subtypes. Similarly, RetCCL [8] follows a SSL pre-training scheme carefully designed for content-based WSI retrieval. KEEP [34] , in contrast, adopts a vision-language pretraining paradigm enhanced with structured medical knowledge from disease graphs. Although not designed specifically for CBIR, its strong zero-shot generalization across diagnostic tasks suggests that knowledge-aware models could offer new directions for retrieval tasks as well. We argue that this task-specific pretraining is not required if other foundational models offer great representation learning for diverse tasks such as slide classification, segmentation and image captioning [10] , while they are yet to be explored for CBIR. Our CLAV method is a lightweight, training-free aggregation strategy specifically designed for patch-based encoders, providing an efficient solution for scenarios where training data or computational resources are limited. This study presents a clustering-based method for CBIR of WSIs leveraging an existing task-agnostic feature extractor model, named CONCH. The following sections delve deeper into the theoretical underpinnings of this proposal. In Fig. 1 , a schematic of the framework for memory bank construction and query retrieval is presented. Specifically, the foundation model CONCH extracts the features from the patches that comprise a WSI. Subsequently, our clustering method is applied to obtain the centroids of the clusters, which, after aggregation, form the latent vector representing the WSI. After applying this process to all WSIs in the database, the memory bank is obtained. Finally, for the WSI Query Process, samples most similar to an input WSI query are retrieved from this memory bank. Our framework aims to obtain a unique feature representation for each WSI, enabling the identification of similarities at the slide level. Compressing all information into a unique feature vector significantly reduces memory usage and speeds up the subsequent query process. Formally, we denote x i ∈ X N , with X N representing the set of N patches from a WSI and x i the i -patch of the slide. In this work, we rely on CONCH image encoder to extract patch-level features, and additionally evaluate other patch encoders such as KEEP and RetCCL. We obtain z i , the feature vector corresponding to the x i patch, as follows: z i = F I e ( x i ) where F I e represents the feature extraction performed by the image encoder on patch x i . This work proposes a Clustering and Latent Vector Aggregation (CLAV) to obtain a unique feature vector for each WSI. Specifically, three clustering algorithms, k-means, pc-means, and c-means, have been investigated. These clustering algorithms derive a set of Q centroids aggregated using either Batch Global Average Pooling (BGAP) or Batch Global Max Pooling (BGMP) aggregation methods to conform the WSI latent vector. First, note a clustering method denoted by γ , applied to all z i belonging to the set Z N (let’s denote this set as Z N = { z 1 , z 2 , … , z N } ). Applying the clustering method to all Z N , we obtain Q centroids { C 1 , C 2 , … , C Q } . Next, define an aggregation method denoted by A . Applying A to the Q centroids, we obtain z W S I : z w s i = A ( C 1 , C 2 , … , C Q ) The subsequent paragraphs describe the clustering algorithms employed. K-means++ : K-means is an iterative clustering algorithm that partitions a dataset into K clusters by minimizing the variance within each cluster. It starts by randomly initializing cluster centroids and then iteratively assigns data points to the nearest centroid, updating centroids based on the mean of the assigned points until convergence [35] . K-means++ is an enhanced version of the standard K-means algorithm, specifically designed to improve the initialization of cluster centroids. Unlike the standard K-means, which randomly initializes centroids, K-means++ selects initial centroids so that they are more likely to be spread out across the data. This method randomly chooses the first centroid, and each subsequent centroid is chosen from the remaining data points with a probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing centroid. This careful seeding helps accelerate the algorithm’s convergence and improves the overall quality of the clustering results [36] . C-means (Fuzzy C-means) : C-means is a fuzzy clustering algorithm that assigns membership degrees to data points across multiple clusters based on fuzzy set theory. Unlike k-means, which assigns data points exclusively to one cluster, c-means allows data points to belong to multiple clusters simultaneously based on their membership degrees. It iteratively updates cluster centroids and membership degrees until a convergence criterion is met [37] . PC-means (Possibilistic C-means) : PC-means is a variant of C-means clustering that allows for possibilistic assignments of data points to clusters, rather than strictly probabilistic assignments. Unlike traditional C-means, which assigns membership degrees based on probabilities, PC-means assigns a degree of belongingness to each cluster centroid based on a possibilistic approach, where data points can belong to multiple clusters simultaneously with varying degrees of membership. It iteratively updates cluster centroids and membership degrees until a convergence criterion is met. The formulation of PC-means provides flexibility in handling uncertainties and noise in data clustering tasks, making it suitable for applications where strict probabilistic assignments may not be appropriate [38] . We computed the cosine similarity between the query image and all remaining samples in the memory bank after the leave-one-out strategy. Cosine similarity is formally defined as the cosine of the angle between two vectors in a multidimensional space, providing a measure of similarity that ranges from -1 (dissimilar) to 1 (similar), with 0 indicating orthogonality. Given an input query with its corresponding z wsi , and a memory bank M T consisting of all unique feature vectors from T WSIs, the cosine similarity for each m i ∈ M T is defined as follows: Cosine Similarity ( z w s i , m i ) = z w s i · m i ∥ z w s i ∥ ∥ m i ∥ After computing and sorting all cosine similarities, the k most similar results are retrieved. This study utilised WSIs of gastrointestinal (GAST), pulmonary (PUL), and urinary (URI) anatomic sites. These WSIs were sourced from the TCGA database [39] . All WSIs are divided into patches measuring 1024 × 1024 pixels at 20 × magnification. Annotations specifying cancer subtypes are available at the WSI level. Table 1 displays the number of WSIs for each project, categorized by anatomical site. In this section, we present the experimental setup and detailed analysis of the results obtained from our study. To comprehensively evaluate the performance of different clustering methods, we tested all possible combinations of clustering methods, aggregation methods, and number of clusters. Specifically, the number of clusters Q was set to 10, 20, and 30. The aggregation methods employed were the maximum (max) and the mean (mean). The clustering methods used in the experiments are detailed in the Section 3 . We employed a leave-one-out evaluation method. This method involved systematically excluding one image from the dataset during each evaluation iteration, simulating its retrieval against the remaining images. Furthermore, to ensure robustness in our evaluation, we also excluded any images from the same patient as the query image from the dataset. This approach mitigates biases arising from intra-patient similarities. As an evaluation metric, we employed the majority vote method. This approach assesses whether the most frequent class among the k retrieved instances matches the ground truth class. The majority vote method provides a clear and reliable measure of the clustering method’s performance by determining if the predominant label in the retrieved set corresponds to the actual class. The majority vote is obtained by the following expression: (1) MV@k = 1 P ∑ i = 1 m δ ( y i , MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) ) where y i represents the ground truth label for the i -th instance, P represents the number of query WSIs and MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) denotes the majority vote result from the top k retrieved answers. δ ( ) is a discriminant function used to determine equality, as described earlier. For example, if MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) = y i , then δ ( ) = 1 and 0 otherwise. In this article and following other studies in the literature, the results of this metric are reported for MV@5. In this section, we present the content-based WSI retrieval results obtained for the three clustering methods employed. Table 2 displays the outcomes for K-means, Table 3 showcases those for PCMeans, and Table 4 illustrates the results for CMeans. Specifically, we evaluated three different initializations of centroid numbers and two aggregation methods, mean and maximum. The findings reveal that for the K-means++ algorithm, the optimal configuration consists of Q = 10 clusters with centroid aggregation using the maximum method. For PCMeans, superior results were achieved with Q = 30 clusters and maximum aggregation of centroids. Lastly, CMeans performed optimally with Q = 10 clusters and centroid aggregation using the mean method. Across these methods, employing CONCH as the feature extractor demonstrated that globally, the optimal configuration is to use K-means with Q = 10 clusters and maximum centroid aggregation, as it outperforms the best-performing setups in PCMeans and CMeans. This section presents the results of comparing our proposed CLAV method against two baseline methods. The baseline methods consist of aggregating all the feature vectors of the patches that make up a WSI using either BGAP or BGMP. The results, shown in Table 5 , indicate that our method achieves a higher overall mean compared to these aggregation methods. This demonstrates that our approach is more effective in condensing all the feature vectors from the patches of a WSI into a unique, representative vector. These evaluations were conducted using two different feature extractors: CONCH [29] and KEEP [34] . In both cases, CLAV consistently outperforms the baseline aggregation strategies, further validating the robustness of our method across different representation spaces. Additionally, we include the results of our approach that employs CONCH as the feature extractor in conjunction with our clustering method to obtain the feature vector representing each WSI. The results are summarized in Table 6 . It is important to note that the number of clusters used for the RetCCL + CLAV method is Q = 30 (see Appendix B.1 RetCCL + CLAV), and for the CONCH + CLAV method, it is Q = 10 (see Section 5.3.1 ). The clustering method used for both is kmeans++, as this has been shown in the previous sections to be the optimal configuration for each feature extractor and the optimal number of clusters. The results indicate that the combination of CONCH with our clustering method offers the best results regarding the average performance across the three anatomical sites. Furthermore, it can be observed that the average obtained using the RetCCL feature extractor and our clustering method is superior to that achieved by the authors of RetCCL. This demonstrates that our clustering method enhances the performance of the CBIR task. In addition to improving performance, using a unique latent vector per WSI significantly reduces the size of the database, making our clustering method much more efficient and scalable to a larger amount of data. These results highlight the ability of foundation models to extract rich features even without being trained on these specific data, facilitating the condensation of information from all patches of a WSI into a unique latent vector while preserving the information necessary to differentiate various WSIs for CBIR tasks. This section presents the results obtained for the Yottixel, SISH and RetCCL methods on the dataset used in this study. The number of WSIs utilized in this work is similar to that employed in these methods. Table 7 reflects the results obtained for each method and subtype within each anatomical site. The results indicate that our method, CONCH + CLAV, achieves superior metrics in most cases compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Notable improvements are observed in the pulmonary and gastrointestinal anatomical sites. The enhancements in these metrics underscore the robustness and reliability of our approach. In most cases where our method has shown underperformance compared to existing literature, this is because the methods used for comparison were pre-trained on the same data used to evaluate the metrics, which may have conferred an advantage. Despite this, the macro-average MV@5 metric scores for Yottixel, SISH, RetCCL, and our CONCH + CLAV are 0.6471, 0.7241, 0.7927, and 0.8243, respectively, with our method achieving the highest macro-average score. Moreover, CLAV is fully compatible with any patch-based encoder and can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines. Its ability to produce high-quality WSI-level representations without supervision highlights its practical utility and opens the door to efficient deployment in diverse histopathological tasks. The innovative feature extraction leveraging CONCH and our CLAV is key to our method’s superior performance. This combination allows for a more accurate and meaningful representation of the WSIs. To further illustrate the effectiveness of our CBIR system based on the CLAV representation, we present a set of qualitative retrieval examples in Appendix A. These examples correspond to WSIs retrieved using our system for a variety of input queries across different anatomical sites. In each case, the objective is to retrieve WSIs associated with the same pathology, ideally from the same TCGA project as the query. The visual examples show that our method is able to retrieve a high proportion of relevant slides, indicating that the CLAV-based representation effectively captures the underlying pathological patterns in a compact and semantically meaningful way. This supports the quantitative findings reported in Section 5.3 , and in particular the retrieval metrics discussed in Section 5.3.3 . Notably, retrieval performance varies across anatomical sites. For most tissues, the retrieved sets contain a consistent number of slides with matching pathology and project. However, the GAST (stomach) site exhibits a noticeably higher number of retrieval errors. This is consistent with the lower quantitative performance observed for GAST in Section 5.3.3 , suggesting a higher level of intra-class variability or noise in the corresponding WSI data. Overall, the examples in Appendix A provide further evidence of the capacity of the CLAV method to generate discriminative and compact embeddings for WSIs, enabling reliable retrieval across a diverse set of pathological samples. In conclusion, the CLAV method demonstrates substantial effectiveness in condensing features extracted from WSI patches into a single representative vector. Our results show that this approach improves retrieval performance compared to existing methods in the literature. Specifically, when applied to the RetCCL feature extractor, our method surpasses the retrieval outcomes achieved by its original technique. Similarly, using CONCH as a feature extractor also leads to enhanced performance, underlining that applying foundation models without task-specific training can still produce state-of-the-art results. The performance comparison across different feature extractors and clustering methods reveals that the combination of CLAV with CONCH and the K-means clustering method ( Q = 10 clusters) yields the best retrieval results, outperforming other setups like PCMeans and CMeans. Moreover, when combined with RetCCL and K-means with Q = 30 , our method also outperforms the baseline retrieval results from RetCCL, highlighting the advantage of our approach in improving retrieval accuracy. One of the key advantages of our method is its efficiency, as it eliminates the need for specific task-based training while still achieving competitive retrieval results. This greatly enhances its scalability and potential for integration into larger datasets and diagnostic support systems. Regarding future directions, clinical validation of this method through its application in diagnostic tools for expert pathologists could further validate its practical impact. Additionally, future work could address potential biases by ensuring that the model’s retrievals are based on the morphological and pathological characteristics of the samples, rather than the samples’ origin or color. This could be vital in ensuring the fairness and reliability of the system. Lastly, as foundation models continue to evolve, exploring newer feature extractors may further improve retrieval performance and lead to even more efficient diagnostic support systems. In this work, we introduce CLAV, a training-free strategy that aggregates patch-level features extracted by foundation models into a slide-level embedding representing the entire WSI. CLAV employs a clustering-based aggregation method that does not require any supervised information, making it well-suited for content-based image retrieval (CBIR) as it relies on similarities between slide-level representations. This unsupervised approach offers considerable flexibility, enabling adaptation to various tasks and scenarios without significant challenges. In contrast, weakly supervised models based on multiple instance learning (MIL) have become popular for training classifiers or survival models in computational pathology. MIL-based models are optimized to aggregate features and provide slide-level classifications for specific tasks. Task-specific training of MIL models can be regarded as an upper bound for CBIR performance, since supervised information promotes class discrimination within the aggregated latent space during model optimization. We propose the following strategy to adapt MIL-based classification approaches to a CBIR setting. First, we train an attention-based MIL (ABMIL) model [40] to perform slide-level classification between target classes within a particular anatomical site. The model is trained for 20 epochs using the AdamW optimizer (learning rate = 1E-4) to minimize the categorical cross-entropy loss between slide-level predictions and true labels. Subsequently, patch-level embeddings are forwarded through the MIL model, excluding the classifier head, to obtain slide-level embeddings used for CBIR validation. To assess this approach, we employ a 5-fold cross-validation scheme with patient-level stratification. In each fold, 80% of the embeddings are used to train the MIL model and construct the memory bank, while the remaining 20% serve as input queries for evaluating retrieval performance. The metric reported in Table C.10 is MV@5, which measures the majority-vote accuracy over the top-5 retrieved samples. Our approach demonstrates competitive performance even without specific training is performed for the classification task. Unlike MIL-based methods, which are trained in a task-specific manner and thus optimized for the downstream objective, our aggregation technique is training-free and does not require task-specific supervision. This inherently makes it less tailored to the particular task, which can be observed in cases where MIL slightly outperforms our method. For instance, in the KICH and LUAD subtypes, MIL with KEEP features achieves slightly higher accuracy due to its optimization during training. These methods depend on the availability of labeled data for training, which is often not feasible in real-world scenarios where labeling can be costly, time-consuming, or altogether unavailable. In contrast, our method is label-independent and task-agnostic, making it highly valuable for scenarios involving limited supervision or heterogeneous downstream objectives. Furthermore, CLAV consistently achieves robust performance across multiple subtypes without requiring any retraining or reconfiguration, underscoring its generalizability and potential for broader deployment in clinical and biomedical domains. The ability to operate without labels also reduces the risk of overfitting and supports reproducibility across datasets. In conclusion, while task-trained methods like MIL may outperform in controlled settings with ample labels, our training-free method presents a more versatile and scalable solution for real-world applications where labeled data may be scarce or absent.

Continuous and complete liver vessel segmentation with graph-attention guided diffusion Improving connectivity and completeness are the most challenging aspects of liver vessel segmentation, especially for small vessels. These challenges require both learning the continuous vessel geometry, and focusing on small vessel detection. However, current methods do not explicitly address these two aspects and cannot generalize well when constrained by inconsistent annotations. Here, we take advantage of the generalization of the diffusion model and explicitly integrate connectivity and completeness in our diffusion-based segmentation model. Specifically, we use a graph-attention module that adds knowledge about vessel geometry, and thus adds continuity. Additionally, we perform the graph-attention at multiple-scales, thus focusing on small liver vessels. Our method outperforms eight state-of-the-art medical segmentation methods on two public datasets: 3D-ircadb-01 and LiVS.
