DECODE establishes a new benchmark in AI-driven PAD diagnostics and intervention planning by integrating deep learning-powered segmentation, real-time 3D visualization, and computational modeling within a fully automated, cloud-native ecosystem. By seamlessly bridging the domains of medical imaging, AI-enhanced decision support, and predictive modeling, DECODE delivers a comprehensive digital solution tailored for vascular precision medicine. The primary users of the DECODE platform include clinicians, researchers, and healthcare institutions. Clinicians benefit from enhanced diagnostic accuracy and optimized intervention planning through advanced segmentation and high-fidelity visualization, improving therapeutic outcomes. Researchers utilize DECODE for in-silico simulations, enabling patient-specific modeling for DCB therapy and angioplasty, accelerating drug device development and optimizing therapeutic strategies. Healthcare institutions leverage their secure, scalable cloud infrastructure for multicenter data management and seamless clinical integration, enhancing interoperability and collaboration. DECODE drives innovations in vascular diagnostics, in-silico trials, and personalized treatment planning, revolutionizing PAD management through precision medicine. To align the DECODE Cloud Platform with clinical, research, and industry needs, a user-centered design approach was employed, gathering detailed requirements through a structured questionnaire (provided in Supplementary Material A1) from 16 participants across leading European institutions involved in vascular research, medical imaging, and computational modeling. These included researchers from the University of Ioannina, University of Athens, University of Patras, University of Milan, University of Kragujevac, University of Montpellier, and AGH University of Krakow. The insights provided a multidisciplinary perspective, ensuring DECODE’s integration of AI-driven analytics, real-time visualization, and scalable cloud infrastructure. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (provided in Supplementary Material A2), the platform's development followed eight phases: (1) gathering user requirements; (2) defining key architectural components such as segmentation, 3D visualization, and computational modeling; (3) establishing secure data management and sharing; (4) integrating tools for data conversion, image upscaling, and centerline extraction; (5) implementing deep learning for accurate artery and lumen-intima boundary detection; (6) enabling real-time DICOM rendering and WebGL-based volume visualization; (7) providing predictive simulations for PAD treatment planning; and (8) leveraging open-source cloud infrastructure with RESTful APIs for EHR and telemedicine integration. This structured approach ensures that DECODE meets the demands of modern vascular research and clinical applications. The DECODE Cloud Platform is designed as a modular, cloud-based framework that integrates AI-driven diagnostics, real-time visualization, and computational modeling to optimize the management of PAD. Figure 2 (provided in Supplementary Material A2) presents the package diagram of the platform, detailing its hierarchical structure, interdependencies, and information flow across system modules. The architecture is structured into frontend and backend layers, each of which is responsible for specific functionalities. The frontend, implemented using React.js [ 21 ], leverages its component-based structure and virtual DOM for a highly responsive, interactive user experience. The backend, built with Django [ 22 ], provides a scalable and secure RESTful API-driven environment, facilitating efficient data processing and AI-powered analytics. This architecture ensures a seamless and dynamic workflow, allowing users to interact with medical imaging, computational modeling, and treatment planning in a cloud-based ecosystem. The DECODE Cloud Platform frontend is designed as a progressive web application (PWA) [ 23 ] that integrates AI-driven modules for real-time PAD diagnostics, computational modeling, and 3D visualization. Its modular and scalable architecture, as illustrated in Fig. 3 , ensures a seamless workflow from data acquisition to advanced treatment simulation. The system is structured into interconnected components, facilitating automated medical image processing, deep learning-based segmentation, FEM , and WebGL visualization. This section provides a detailed breakdown of the platform's core modules, their functionalities, and interdependencies, highlighting their impact on PAD diagnosis and intervention planning. The authentication system within DECODE is designed to ensure secure access control. The users’ credential database is managed by an access control module, which authenticates login credentials, assigns user roles, and enforces hierarchical security policies. The authentication mechanism employs a RESTful API-based JWT tokenization system, ensuring that each request is verified against encrypted session tokens before granting access to platform functionalities [ 24 ]. This architecture enables persistent, role-based access management, ensuring data security while maintaining user friendliness. A centralized dataset warehouse functions as the primary storage and retrieval system for medical imaging data, supporting multiple formats, including DICOM [ 25 ] and NIfTI [ 26 ]. The dataset management module facilitates structured metadata indexing, ensuring that uploaded datasets remain traceable and interoperable. Before datasets are processed, they undergo a quality validation step managed by the data quality control engine, which performs format standardization. This automated pipeline ensures that only high-fidelity images proceed to AI-driven segmentation and computational analysis, minimizing errors associated with low-resolution or inconsistent datasets. The workflow manager module is the core orchestration engine of the DECODE Cloud Platform, facilitating automated task execution, data transfer, and AI-powered image processing. This ensures that segmentation, computational modeling, and visualization workflows are executed in a synchronized and scalable manner. The workflow module supports asynchronous execution, allowing multiple computational tasks to run in parallel, thus optimizing processing efficiency [ 27 , 28 ]. Through API-driven task scheduling, the module dynamically allocates computational resources, reducing latency in real-time applications such as image analysis, segmentation, and FEM simulations. (a)Data converters (a)Data converters The data converter module is an automated medical imaging transformation pipeline that facilitates seamless conversion of DICOM and STL data into widely adopted formats, including JPEG, 2D/3D NIfTI [ 26 ], and GLTF for WebXR visualization [ 29 ]. The module ensures a structured information flow, beginning with file acquisition and validation, followed by metadata extraction, spatial calibration, and optimized transformation, culminating in high-fidelity output generation. It integrates DICOM parsing and volumetric consistency checks to preserve anatomical precision, particularly in 3D NIfTI reconstruction, where pixel spacing and slice thickness metadata are leveraged for accurate spatial representation. A notable innovation is the STL-to-GLTF conversion [ 30 ], which optimizes 3D surface geometries for real-time interactive rendering. This transformation extracts vertex coordinates and indexed face sets from binary STL files, efficiently encoding them into the GLTF 2.0 format while minimizing storage overhead by eliminating redundant data. In support of both JSON-based GLTF and binary GLB outputs, the module ensures broad compatibility with WebXR platforms, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR) applications. By embedding visualization tools (Kitware Glance [ 31 ], DECODE-3DViz [ 32 ], WebXR), the data converter enhances accessibility, enabling direct dataset inspection within cloud-based environments. This integration accelerates medical imaging workflows, fosters scalable data exchange, and advances interactive 3D visualization for clinical diagnostics, research applications, and computational modeling. (b)Image upscaling (b)Image upscaling The image upscaling module is an AI-driven super resolution pipeline designed to enhance medical image fidelity by increasing resolution while preserving structural integrity. This module leverages a deep learning-based generative adversarial network (GAN), specifically a ResNet-based generator, to upscale input images by a factor of 4 × [ 33 ]. The pipeline follows a structured information flow, beginning with image acquisition and preprocessing, followed by tensor transformation and normalization, and culminates in high-resolution (HR) image reconstruction. The low-resolution input (LR) undergoes statistical normalization (mean and standard deviation correction) before being processed by the trained GeneratorResNet model [ 34 ], which synthesizes finer anatomical details through learned feature mapping. A key innovation is the GAN-based super resolution technique, which reconstructs high-frequency image details while mitigating artifacts commonly observed in traditional interpolation-based upscaling. The final HR image is denormalized, postprocessed, and stored in a structured output directory for seamless retrieval. By automating deep learning-driven image enhancement, the image upscaling module enables scalable, real-time improvement of medical imaging data, fostering higher diagnostic accuracy, enhanced visualization, and improved dataset quality for downstream computational modeling and clinical applications. (c)Centreline Extraction (c)Centreline Extraction The centerline extraction method enables precise vascular analysis by computing curvature and circularity along a 3D vessel centerline [ 35 ]. Extraction begins with user-defined start and end points within a binary mask, generating a deterministic centerline representation of the vessel ( Fig. 4 a). Circularity computation involves generating cross-sectional slices at each centerline point via a local 2D plane, which is defined by a tangent vector and two perpendicular vectors. Distance transform-based radius estimation ensures full coverage of the vessel’s cross-section ( Fig. 4 b), and increasing the radius further refines the accuracy of the slices ( Fig. 4 c). However, this expansion can capture adjacent vessel structures, introducing artifacts into the extracted cross-sections ( Fig. 4 d). To address this, morphological filtering is applied to eliminate small unwanted artifacts, refining the extracted vessel structure ( Fig. 4 e). In addition, a postprocessing step ensures that the retained vessel area contains the true centerline point, preventing misclassification of adjacent, larger vessel regions ( Fig. 4 f). Circularity is computed as: (1) C = 4 π A P 2 , where A is the cross-sectional area and P is the perimeter. Curvature estimation is derived from finite difference approximations of the first and second derivatives of the centerline points, computed as [ 36 ]: (2) K ( t ) = | r ′ ( t ) × r ″ ( t ) | | r ′ ( t ) | 3 , where r ′ ( t ) and r ″ ( t ) are the first and second derivatives of the centerline curve, respectively. This method ensures high-fidelity of vascular morphology, making it instrumental in hemodynamic simulations, disease progression analysis, and interventional planning in PAD research. (a)Peripheral artery (PA) segmentation (a)Peripheral artery (PA) segmentation Segmentation presents notable challenges due to the intricate vascular structures, close proximity to bony regions, and imaging artifacts introduced by patient motion or limitations in CT acquisition [ 37 ]. To address these challenges, a robust multi-step pipeline was developed that incorporates advanced preprocessing, an AI-driven segmentation model, and postprocessing to ensure accurate and anatomically consistent vessel delineation. Preprocessing: The dataset, consisting of 3D CT angiography (CTA) scans, underwent a standardized preprocessing pipeline to ensure uniformity across all samples and to optimize segmentation accuracy. Initially, the original anisotropic CT volumes were resampled to an isotropic resolution, providing equal voxel spacing across all three dimensions and improving anatomical consistency during model training and inference. A region-of-interest (ROI) clipping step was applied to focus on vascular regions and eliminate irrelevant background information, thereby reducing computational overhead and enhancing the model's focus on arterial structures. Subsequently, percentile normalization was performed to standardize the pixel intensity distributions and enhance contrast, improving the robustness of the neural network to intensity variations. Segmentation and Postprocessing: A convolutional neural network (CNN) was employed to automatically segment the PA structures, achieving high-fidelity vessel extraction. Following segmentation, a postprocessing step transforms the segmented results from isotropic resolution back to the original anisotropic dimensions, preserving clinical relevance and spatial accuracy. This workflow ensures consistent performance across diverse cases and mitigates the challenges posed by imaging noise and anatomical complexity. Dataset and Augmentation: The dataset utilized in this study was provided by Gennimata General Hospital under ethical approval (protocol numbers 9876/28.3.24 and 11,293/9.4.24). Patient selection was based solely on a confirmed diagnosis of PAD, without additional inclusion or exclusion criteria, ensuring diagnostic uniformity while capturing diverse anatomical variations. The 22 3D CTA datasets were split into training (80 %), validation (10 %), and testing (10 %) sets at the patient level to prevent data leakage, with a fixed random seed applied to ensure reproducibility. To address the limited dataset size, data augmentation techniques were applied, including slight rotations of +5° and −5°, effectively increasing variability while maintaining anatomical fidelity. (b)Intima media thickness (IMT) segmentation (b)Intima media thickness (IMT) segmentation IMT segmentation is a crucial step for vascular assessment and disease progression analysis, requiring precise delineation of the lumen and intima boundaries [ 38 ]. Traditional methods, such as Otsu’s thresholding and active contours [ 39 ], were initially employed but exhibited inconsistencies in boundary precision and robustness. To address these limitations, a hybrid segmentation approach was developed that integrates thresholding for lumen detection with active contours to refine the intima border, ensuring geometric center alignment for improved segmentation accuracy. While this method enhanced performance, particularly in Hausdorff distance metrics, it lacked the robustness required for clinical applications. To overcome these challenges, a deep learning-based solution was implemented, leveraging modified U-Net architectures with increased depth (ranging from 24 to 768 feature channels) and enhanced convolutional layer designs [ 40 , 41 ]. Unlike the original U-Net [ 42 ], this adaptation maintains spatial resolution by padding, applies batch normalization before ReLU activation, and optimizes feature extraction for vascular structures with minimal pixel spacing. In addition, state-of-the-art architectures, including DeepLab v3+ [ 43 ] and nnU-Net [ 44 ], were integrated for comparative analysis, further validating the segmentation accuracy and robustness. The dataset comprises 300 IVOCT cross-sectional images of porcine femoral arteries, which are randomly divided into training (80 %), validation (10 %), and test (10 %) subsets. Training and testing were repeated five times via different random splits to ensure the reproducibility and reliability of the results. An early stopping mechanism was employed during training to prevent overfitting, halting training when validation loss plateaued. Finite element (FE) models and numerical simulations were conducted via Abaqus/Explicit 2021 (Dassault Systèmes, SIMULIA Corp., Johnston, RI, USA) to capture highly nonlinear mechanical interactions during balloon angioplasty while maintaining a quasistatic regime. Fig. 5 illustrates the computational pipeline, including the balloon model, artery model, and balloon‒artery interaction analysis. (a) Artery finite element models (a) Artery finite element models Two artery models were constructed to simulate different clinical scenarios. Scenario A represents an idealized healthy artery with a lumen diameter of 4.2 mm and a wall thickness of 1 mm on the basis of porcine femoral artery data [ 45 ]. Scenario B involves subject-specific artery geometry reconstructed from intravascular optical coherence tomography (IVOCT) images, implementing a custom methodology for accurate lumen and wall definition. Both models were meshed via C3D8R linear hexahedral elements, following a mesh sensitivity analysis to ensure computational efficiency and numerical stability [ 46 ]. The arterial wall was modeled as a single-layer isotropic hyperelastic material via a 2nd-order polynomial strain energy function, which effectively captures nonlinear mechanical behavior. The nearly incompressible nature of arterial tissue was accounted for by assigning a Poisson’s ratio of 0.495, ensuring realistic arterial wall deformation under loading [ 47 ]. (b)Balloon Finite Element Models (b)Balloon Finite Element Models To replicate angioplasty procedures, two digital models of semicompliant angioplasty balloons were developed, which serve as substrates for drug-coated balloon (DCB) devices [ 48 ]. A five-folded balloon with a 5 mm nominal diameter was designed for Scenario A, maintaining a balloon-to-vessel diameter ratio (DR) of 1.2, whereas a three-folded balloon with a 3.5 mm nominal diameter was created for Scenario B to match the anatomical artery dimensions [ 46 ]. The balloon membranes were discretized via quadrilateral shell elements (S4R), ensuring accurate deformation behavior during inflation. The material properties were calibrated on the basis of device-specific compliance charts, enabling precise simulation of balloon expansion. These models accurately mimic the mechanical response of real-world angioplasty balloons, capturing the folding, deployment, and inflation processes essential for evaluating their interaction with arterial walls [ 49 ]. (c)Balloon angioplasty simulation (c)Balloon angioplasty simulation The angioplasty procedure was simulated through three sequential steps: folding, positioning, and inflation. Initially, the balloons were folded via a numerical pleating approach, with fivefold-10 pleating jaws for the five-folded balloon and threefold-10 pleating jaws for the three-folded balloon [ 49 ]. A geometrical validation was performed by comparing the simulated cross-sections with real balloon devices, ensuring accurate representation. The folded balloons were then positioned inside the arterial models in an unstressed configuration, ensuring precise alignment within the lumen. During the final step, a uniform internal pressure was progressively applied to the balloon’s inner surface until it reached the nominal inflation value, simulating balloon expansion and arterial wall deformation. To accurately model real-world deployment constraints, the distal end of the balloon was fixed, whereas the proximal end was allowed only longitudinal displacement, preventing excessive deformation at the catheter attachment. A general contact algorithm with a friction coefficient of 0.2 was implemented to model self-contacts and balloon‒artery interactions, ensuring realistic behavior during inflation. To maintain a quasistatic regime, the kinetic-to-internal energy ratio was maintained below 5 %, and a small viscous pressure (1E‒05 MPa) was applied to the balloon and artery surfaces to mitigate artificial dynamic effects. These measures ensured numerically stable simulations, enabling an accurate representation of the angioplasty procedure [ 46 ]. (a) WebXR (eXtended Reality) (a) WebXR (eXtended Reality) The WebXR Viewer module enables real-time, interactive 3D model visualization and AR integration for medical imaging applications. This module is designed to seamlessly render and manipulate GLB-formatted anatomical models directly within a web browser, eliminating the need for specialized software. The workflow begins with file acquisition, allowing users to upload 3D models via drag-and-drop or direct file selection, ensuring an intuitive and accessible interface for medical professionals and researchers. The module uses Google’s Model Viewer API, providing high-fidelity rendering with adjustable shadow intensity, dynamic lighting, and full camera controls to facilitate detailed anatomical inspection [ 50 ]. Once loaded, interactive scene control, such as zooming, rotation, and object manipulation, enhances the ability to examine intricate structures. A key innovation is the integration of WebXR-based AR functionality, enabling users to project and visualize 3D models within real-world environments via AR-supported devices, bridging the gap between digital analysis and physical spatial assessment. (b) DECODE-3DViz: WebGL (b) DECODE-3DViz: WebGL The DECODE-3DViz module [ 32 , 51 ] is a WebGL-powered 3D visualization framework designed for interactive volume rendering of medical imaging datasets, including DICOM and NIfTI formats. This system enables real-time rendering, dynamic parameter control, and high-fidelity volumetric analysis directly in a web environment, eliminating the need for specialized hardware. The visualization pipeline begins with data acquisition, where users can upload single or multiple medical imaging files or fetch them remotely via the URL. The preprocessing stage ensures compatibility by handling anisotropic voxel spacing, intensity normalization, and adaptive resolution adjustments. The core volume rendering engine, built on WebGL [ 52 ] and VTK.js, employs gradient-based opacity mapping and transfer function optimization. Users can dynamically adjust lighting conditions and perform voxel intensity scaling, refining visualization quality for diagnostic precision. In addition, the module integrates interactive clipping planes, real-time cropping, and widget-based selection tools to facilitate focused region analysis. By incorporating customizable rendering presets, multimodal blending, and high-performance GPU acceleration, DECODE-3DViz provides an advanced, browser-based solution for interactive 3D medical visualization, supporting clinical diagnostics, surgical planning, and computational modeling in vascular imaging. The DCB-SimViz module [ 53 ] is a computational modeling and visualization framework designed for simulating DCB deployment, drug concentration dynamics, and vascular response in PA interventions. The system integrates machine learning models and deep neural networks to predict drug absorbance, arterial wall drug diffusion, and pressure‒diameter characteristics under different physiological conditions. The simulation pipeline begins with drug concentration modeling, where pretrained regression models predict free and bound drug concentrations post-DCB application via spatial and temporal variables. The balloon expansion module employs a pressure-dependent radial growth model, leveraging supervised learning algorithms trained on empirical catheterization data to estimate arterial deformation and balloon compliance. A deep learning-driven absorbance prediction model, preloaded with spectroscopic data, is used to evaluate drug absorbance at different wavelengths, ensuring the precise characterization of diffusion kinetics. The visualization layer, implemented via Plotly.js [ 54 ] and the Django REST API, generates interactive 2D and 3D simulations of drug concentration profiles, balloon inflation dynamics, and vascular surface interactions, enhancing real-time interpretability. The simulation results of the balloon folding process demonstrated strong qualitative agreement with experimental balloon cross-sections reported in the literature. Fig. 11 presents the folded configurations of both the five- and three-folded balloons deployed in Scenarios A and B, respectively. The balloon unfolding process was analyzed at two critical stages: the initial interaction between the folded balloon and the arterial wall and the final stage of full inflation. In both scenarios, the unfolding simulations clearly illustrated that the balloon initially interacts with the arterial wall while still in its folded configuration, emphasizing the significance of fold geometry in shaping the balloon‒vessel interaction dynamics. To further analyze the mechanical response, a 2D visualization strategy was developed to assess the distribution of contact pressure and Von Mises stress at the endoluminal surface of the artery. As illustrated in Fig. 12 , the results revealed a heterogeneous interaction pattern, which was primarily dictated by the geometry of the balloon folds. At the onset of inflation, longitudinal stripes of elevated contact pressure—equal in number to the balloon folds—formed at the apex locations of the folds. As inflation progressed, the striped distribution of contact pressure remained prominent, with additional contact zones emerging as the balloon unfolded further. A comparable, although less pronounced, pattern was observed in the von Mises stress distribution, confirming that the stress concentrations followed a similar longitudinally patterned behavior. A notable distinction was observed between Scenario A (idealized artery) and Scenario B (subject-specific artery). In Scenario A, where the balloon-to-vessel diameter ratio (DR) remained constant along the artery length, the distributions of both the contact pressure and Von Mises stress appeared more uniform. Conversely, in Scenario B, which exhibited anatomical irregularities, the interaction patterns varied longitudinally, with localized stress and pressure concentrations occurring in regions where the balloon-to-vessel DR was relatively high. The computed balloon-to-vessel DR along the artery’s longitudinal axis ranged from 1.0 - 1.2, with corresponding fluctuations in mechanical loading. At the final stage of inflation, the results revealed a sudden 9.1 % increase in the balloon-to-vessel DR in response to abrupt lumen narrowing, leading to a 10.4-fold increase in average contact pressure in the affected region compared with adjacent sections. Furthermore, the corresponding von Mises stress values exhibited a 2.8-fold increase, underscoring the direct correlation between geometric irregularities and the mechanical stress distribution. These findings reinforce the importance of accurate anatomical reconstruction and personalized balloon sizing to minimize excessive localized stress, which could contribute to adverse vascular remodeling or mechanical trauma during angioplasty procedures. The DECODE Cloud Platform establishes a transformative approach to PAD management by integrating AI-driven segmentation, computational modeling, and GPU-accelerated visualization within a unified cloud-based framework. As shown in Fig. 14 , DECODE’s architecture uses a modular microservice design to enable efficient medical imaging workflows. The platform is organized into main frontend and sub frontend servers that interact with the main backend and sub backend servers via a centralized API gateway, ensuring secure and efficient data communication. Dataset retrieval is initiated from the DECODE Dataset Repository, which supports structured DICOM and NIfTI formats. The data converter module standardizes the input formats, enhancing the compatibility with deep learning algorithms. The PA segmentation module uses CT imaging to precisely delineate arterial structures with a Dice coefficient 0.91, ensuring high accuracy in vessel extraction. The centerline extraction module computes the vascular centerline, curvature, and circularity, which are essential for computational hemodynamic modeling and predictive simulations. These parameters are processed in the main backend server, with results securely stored in the File Repository and DB server for scalable access. DECODE-3DViz enables real-time volumetric rendering and AR-enabled visualization through GPU-accelerated WebGL, significantly enhancing diagnostic accuracy and procedural planning. The platform supports interactive 3D visualization for comprehensive vascular analysis, enabling personalized treatment planning. While previous mHealth interventions, such as TrackPAD [ 8 ], have improved patient adherence to SET, they lack AI-driven automation and real-time vascular analytics. Furthermore, systematic reviews [ 9 ] have highlighted low adoption rates and the absence of AI-powered monitoring in digital SET programs. As summarized in Table 2 , existing PAD platforms remain limited to narrow functionalities such as exercise tracking or basic data aggregation, without integrating advanced analytics, visualization, or modeling. In contrast, DECODE's cloud-integrated AI framework enables automated segmentation, hemodynamic analysis, and predictive modeling, addressing critical gaps in personalized PAD management. Similarly, advancements in AI-enhanced cloud computing for medical imaging [ 12 ] have improved segmentation accuracy and predictive diagnostics. However, these approaches lack clinical validation for PAD applications and do not incorporate real-time visualization or patient-specific modeling. DECODE surpasses these limitations by integrating deep-learning-powered segmentation, real-time FEM simulations, and WebGL-based 3D visualization, providing clinically actionable insights in a scalable cloud environment. Moreover, DECODE’s IMT segmentation for the IVOCT imaging module represents a substantial advancement over existing vascular assessment methods. CNN-based microchannel detection [ 58 ] achieved a Dice coefficient 0.92, whereas coronary IVOCT segmentation [ 59 ] reported an intraclass correlation 0.97. While these methods are highly accurate, they lack real-time processing, cloud scalability, and multimodal adaptability. DECODE overcomes these limitations with a deep-learning-powered IMT segmentation pipeline, achieving superior spatial accuracy and automation while ensuring cloud-based processing and interoperability for enhanced clinical usability. The DECODE Cloud Platform introduces a groundbreaking cloud-based AI framework that seamlessly integrates deep learning segmentation, computational modeling, and real-time 3D visualization for PAD management. Unlike previous systems that focus on isolated aspects of vascular imaging or exercise therapy, DECODE establishes a fully automated, scalable, and interoperable ecosystem that bridges the gap between AI-driven decision support, in-silico modeling, and interactive visualization. • End-to-End AI-Driven Segmentation: The PA segmentation module achieves a Dice coefficient 0.91, whereas the IMT segmentation module attains Dice coefficients 0.992 for the lumen and 0.988 for the intima, significantly surpassing traditional methods in terms of precision and automation. • Real-Time Cloud-Based Computation: Unlike static image processing workflows, DECODE leverages GPU-accelerated cloud computing for automated segmentation, geometric vascular profiling, and FEM, optimizing PAD treatment planning through patient-specific simulations. • High-Fidelity WebGL Visualization: DECODE-3DViz delivers real-time volumetric rendering and AR-enabled exploration, enabling interactive procedural planning in a fully cloud-integrated environment. • Predictive Modeling for PAD Interventions: The DCB-SimViz module enables DCB therapy optimization, integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and pharmacokinetic simulations to personalize vascular drug delivery strategies. • Seamless Clinical Integration: Through RESTful APIs, DECODE ensures interoperability with PACS, EHRs, and telemedicine platforms, positioning it as a scalable and adaptable solution for precision vascular medicine. By unifying AI-driven vascular analysis, interactive 3D visualization, and predictive modeling, DECODE establishes a new benchmark for digital PAD diagnostics, advancing data-driven and personalized vascular intervention planning. PAD remains widely underdiagnosed owing to limited access to advanced imaging tools. DECODE automates AI-driven segmentation of PAs and the IMT , reducing interobserver variability and enhancing diagnostic confidence. Compared with CTA and MRA, its automated centerline extraction and geometric vascular profiling enable early PAD detection and disease progression monitoring with superior anatomical fidelity, which often misclassifies vascular calcifications. Current PAD treatments lack personalization and rely on generalized protocols. DECODE integrates the FEM to simulate angioplasty and DCB interventions, optimizing vascular response prediction. The DCB-SimViz module enables real-time drug diffusion simulations, shifting treatment planning from empirical data to personalized computational modeling, reducing restenosis risk and improving long-term outcomes. In addition, DECODE supports in-silico clinical trials by virtually testing DCB performance under different anatomical and hemodynamic conditions. It also enables optimized balloon design by simulating drug release kinetics and mechanical interactions with arterial walls. This allows precise adjustments in geometry, material properties, and coatings. The result is improved therapeutic efficacy and personalized treatment. Traditional PAD diagnostic tools often rely on offline processing and can be computationally intensive, limiting real-time clinical decision-making. DECODE eliminates these bottlenecks with a cloud-integrated, RESTful API-based framework, providing instant AI-powered analysis and real-time 3D visualization. Through DECODE-3DViz, clinicians can interactively assess vascular pathologies via WebGL/WebXR-powered volumetric rendering, enabling dynamic exploration, computational flow analysis, and AR-driven visualization for precise procedural planning. Despite its advancements, the DECODE platform still has areas that require further optimization. Future improvements will address both technical and clinical limitations. First, the small and single-source nature of the segmentation datasets poses a risk of overfitting and may limit generalizability. While steps such as ±5° data augmentation and strict patient-level splitting were applied to mitigate this issue, future work will prioritize validation on larger, multi-center datasets and external benchmarks to strengthen the robustness and clinical relevance of PA/IMT segmentation models. From a technical perspective, future enhancements will focus on fully automating centerline detection using graph-based algorithms and topology-aware neural networks to eliminate manual input and improve reproducibility. Expanding DECODE’s segmentation and computational modeling pipeline beyond CT-based imaging will also be a key milestone. This will involve the development of modality-agnostic AI models and adaptive preprocessing pipelines to support multimodal datasets, including ultrasound and MRI data. For visualization, the current WebGL-based DECODE-3DViz module can experience latency with high-resolution datasets, particularly under low-bandwidth cloud conditions. Planned improvements include progressive mesh streaming and WebGPU acceleration to enhance real-time interactivity and scalability. Finally, while DECODE supports RESTful API integration, real-world clinical deployment remains a challenge because of interoperability and regulatory requirements. Future iterations will incorporate FHIR-compliant APIs, encrypted cloud storage, and pilot deployments with clinical PACS/EHR systems to validate the performance in live clinical environments. The DECODE Cloud Platform transforms PAD diagnostics and intervention planning by integrating AI-driven segmentation, computational modeling, and real-time 3D visualization within a scalable, cloud-based framework. The peripheral artery (PA) segmentation module and intima-media thickness (IMT) segmentation module provide automated, high-precision vascular analysis, whereas the centerline extraction module enables detailed geometric profiling for computational hemodynamics. The finite element modeling (FEM) module supports in-silico balloon angioplasty and drug-coated balloon (DCB) simulations, advancing patient-specific treatment planning. DECODE-3DViz, a WebGL/WebXR-powered tool, delivers interactive, high-fidelity 3D visualization, enhancing clinical workflow efficiency. With RESTful API support for PACS/EHR integration, DECODE ensures seamless interoperability and cloud scalability. However, comprehensive clinical validation and large-scale real-world deployment remain forthcoming. The small, single-source datasets used for segmentation may limit generalizability, and further validation on larger, multi-center datasets is needed to confirm robustness and scalability. Future enhancements will focus on automating centerline detection, expanding imaging modality support, and optimizing real-time rendering performance. As an open-source, AI-powered solution, DECODE establishes a new benchmark in precision vascular medicine, bridging the gap between computational intelligence and real-world clinical applications. Deep learning in oncology: Transforming cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a transformative force in oncology, offering unprecedented capabilities in cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis. The integration of DL models with vast and complex datasets, including genomic, transcriptomic, and imaging data, has paved the way for more precise and personalized cancer care. In particular, DL's application in drug efficacy and toxicity prediction is gaining traction, addressing the critical challenge of high drug failure rates in clinical development. By leveraging large datasets and sophisticated algorithms, DL models can predict drug responses and optimize treatment strategies, ultimately improving patient outcomes. Additionally, DL-driven automation in medical imaging processing and report generation is revolutionizing radiology, enhancing diagnostic accuracy and consistency. This review explores the current advancements in DL applications across various aspects of oncology, emphasizing the potential of AI-driven tools to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and personalization of cancer care. Despite the significant progress, challenges such as model validation, ethical considerations, and the need for transparent AI systems remain. Addressing these challenges will be crucial in realizing the full potential of DL in transforming oncology practices. The graphical abstract underscores AI's transformative role in oncology, focusing on three key areas: multiomics integration for personalized cancer treatment, predictive modeling for drug efficacy and toxicity, and enhanced radiologic image interpretation. AI-driven tools facilitate the tailoring of treatments to individual patients by analyzing complex multiomics data, while also optimizing therapeutic strategies through accurate predictions of drug efficacy and potential toxicity. Image, graphical abstract Advancements in deep learning technologies, fueled by innovations such as backpropagation, the availability of extensive datasets from open-source platforms, and the development of powerful computing hardware like graphics processing units, have significantly impacted cancer care ( Chakraborty et al., 2024 Jan 1 , Badwan et al., 2023 Feb 27 , Swanson et al., 2023 Apr 13 ). These technological strides and collaborative efforts between radiologists, clinicians, and technical experts have paved the way for artificial intelligence (AI) to play an increasingly critical role in oncology. By integrating the computational power of computer science, mathematics, and physics, bioinformatics has emerged as a pivotal field ( Brown et al., 2022 Jan 1 , Bajorath, 2023 Dec 1 ), allowing for the sophisticated representation and interpretation of complex biological data. Genomics and proteomics have expanded the capabilities of cancer bioinformatics, particularly in identifying and validating biomarkers for early diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response ( Byju et al., 2024 Sep 1 , Rabi et al., 2024 Apr 15 , Jafari et al., 2023 Sep 1 ). Deep learning, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has shown remarkable promise in image recognition and processing areas ( Tuncer et al., 2024 Sep 1 , Islam et al., 2024 Jun 1 ). CNNs, with their multiple layers, including convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers, have become instrumental in analyzing medical images, contributing to more accurate cancer screening ( Abdelrahman et al., 2021 Apr ), diagnosis ( Bargagna et al., 2023 Dec ), prognosis ( Poirion et al., 2021 Jul 14 ), and treatment planning ( Arends et al., 2022 Jan ). One of AI's most significant potentials in oncology is its ability to enhance patient outcomes through precision medicine ( Bhinder et al., 2021 Apr , He et al., 2023 Jan ). By utilizing deep-learning algorithms, it is possible to predict tumor molecular mutations, assess treatment response, and estimate survival outcomes ( Bera et al., 2022 Feb ), thereby enabling personalized treatment plans to improve patient survival while reducing costs. Additionally, by providing automated decision support based on imaging and clinical data, AI-driven tools can facilitate cancer care in remote areas where access to specialized oncologists may be limited ( Humer and Campling, 2017 Aug , Bakitas et al., 2020 Mar 20 ). Despite the promising advancements, the clinical translation of AI, particularly deep learning, faces several challenges. These include the need for rigorous validation and testing of algorithms, ethical considerations, and the commercialization of AI technologies. This review provides an in-depth examination of the transformative impact of deep learning across various aspects of oncology, including its applications in multiomics, drug efficacy and toxicity prediction, and automated radiology report generation. Additionally, the review highlights the emerging potential of AI-driven tools in enhancing the accuracy, consistency, and personalization of cancer care, offering a comprehensive overview of the current state and prospects of AI in oncology. Deep learning (DL) represents a sophisticated and transformative branch of machine learning (ML), characterized by its ability to process and analyze large volumes of complex data through multi-layered neural network architectures. This technology mimics the human brain's neural networks, enabling the extraction of intricate patterns and relationships within data that traditional ML methods might miss. The iterative nature of deep learning, particularly through techniques such as backpropagation, allows models to refine their predictions by adjusting their internal parameters to minimize errors ( Baldi et al., 2018 Jul 1 , Nápoles et al., 2024 Jul 8 ). This continuous learning process is central to supervised learning, where models improve their performance by aligning their outputs with annotated ground truth data. In the field of oncology, deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for addressing the challenges posed by the vast and complex datasets generated in cancer research and clinical practice. For example, Rehman et al . ( Rehman et al., 2024 Jul 1 ) presented a self-supervised pretraining and hyperparameter tuning for efficient classification of cancer cells belonging to different organs on holographic microscopic images. Cui et al . ( Cui et al., 2023 Sep 22 ) developed a deep learning framework comprising a pretext and downstream task. The pretext task consists in a self-supervised masked graph learning reconstruction task and the downstream consists in a task-specific fine-tuning task, allowing identifying cancer genes associated with the molecular initiation and progression of cancer. The advent of DL has facilitated the development of robust mathematical algorithms capable of translating intricate datasets into actionable insights. This capability is particularly valuable in oncology, where the integration of diverse data types – such as genomic ( Sudlow et al., 2015 Mar ), transcriptomic ( Tomczak et al., 2015 ), epigenetics ( The ENCODE 2004 Oct 22 ), proteomics ( Schmidt et al., 2018 Jan 4 ), and therapeutics ( Gaulton et al., 2017 Jan 4 ) data – is essential for advancing precision medicine ( Srivastava, 2023 Jan ). For instance, Murai et al . ( Murai et al., 2023 Jan 1 ) by using a multiomics-centric approach identified the link between intratumoral steatosis and immune-exhausted immunotherapy-susceptible tumor immune microenvironment. Sun et al . ( Sun et al., 2024 Jan 8 ) generated a multiomic profiling of 257 primary and 176 metastatic regions from 182 hepatocellular carcinoma patients, which allowed to conclude that somatic copy number alterations are events driving metastasis. By multiomics subclone analysis, Poos et al . ( Poos et al., 2023 Nov 9 ) explored how multiomics analysis can be applied to track and characterize distinct multidrug-resistant subclones over time for the identification of molecular targets. Garcia-Recio et al . ( Garcia-Recio et al., 2023 Jan ) by also using multiomics in primary and metastatic breast tumors concluded that DNA hypermethylation and/or focal deletions were identified near HLA-A, being thus associated with reduced expression and lower immune cell infiltrates. In this way, such findings suggest implications for treating individuals with metastatic breast cancer with current immune- and HER2-targeting therapies. Better cancer care is therefore increasingly driven by the need for personalized treatment approaches, which require the analysis of vast and multi-dimensional patient data. DL models excel in this context due to their ability to handle the high dimensionality and complexity of medical data. However, the implementation of deep learning in clinical oncology is not without challenges ( Wainberg et al., 2018 Oct 1 , Zhang and Hong, 2023 Dec ). One of the primary concerns is the need for rigorous validation and testing of these algorithms before they can be safely integrated into clinical workflows. The high stakes involved in medical decision-making necessitate that DL models undergo extensive evaluation using various metrics to ensure their reliability and accuracy. Common evaluation metrics include the accuracy (ACC), F1 score, precision, recall, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R 2 ), predictive relevance (Q2), and geometric mean fold error (GMFE) ( Tran et al., 2023 Jan 17 ). These metrics provide a quantitative assessment of the model's performance, allowing researchers and clinicians to gauge and assess its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Despite these challenges, DL has already begun to revolutionize various stages of cancer care ( Table 1 ). In risk stratification, DL models can analyze patient data to predict the likelihood of developing cancer, enabling early interventions and personalized screening programs ( Jiang et al., 2023 Nov 1 , Uppal et al., 2024 Jun 1 , Zhou et al., 2023 Aug ). In early screening, DL algorithms can process imaging data to detect early signs of cancer, often with greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods ( Dildar et al., 2021 May 20 , Lin et al., 2023 Mar 1 ). For diagnosis, deep learning has been instrumental in interpreting medical images, such as mammograms ( Balkenende et al., 2022 Sep ), CT scans ( Rompianesi et al., 2022 Jan 7 ), and MRIs ( Xia et al., 2024 Mar , Moya-Sáez et al., 2023 ), to identify tumors with high accuracy. Furthermore, DL models are increasingly being used to predict treatment responses, offering insights into which therapies are likely to be most effective for individual patients based on their unique genetic profiles ( Jiang et al., 2023 Aug 15 , Kirelli et al., 2023 Jun 1 ). The integration of deep learning in oncology also extends to prognosis prediction ( Huang et al., 2023 Feb 1 , Huang et al., 2023 Feb 1 ), where models can analyze a combination of clinical, imaging, and genomic data to estimate a patient's survival chances. This information is critical for both patients and clinicians as it guides treatment decisions and helps in managing patient expectations. Moreover, DL's ability to process large datasets allows it to uncover new biomarkers ( Prelaj et al., 2024 Jan 1 ) and therapeutic targets ( Issa et al., 2021 Jan ), paving the way for the development of novel cancer treatments. While the potential of deep learning in oncology is immense, it is important to acknowledge the ethical and practical considerations that accompany its adoption in clinical practice. Issues such as data privacy, the interpretability of models, and the need for human oversight in decision-making are critical factors that must be addressed ( Ching et al., 2018 Apr , Wang and Alexander, 2020 Aug ). The “black box” nature of many DL models, where the decision-making process is not easily interpretable, poses a challenge for clinicians who need to understand the rationale behind a model's predictions. Efforts to enhance the explainability of deep learning models, such as through the development of explainable AI (XAI) techniques ( Combi et al., 2022 Nov 1 , Panagoulias et al., 2024 Aug 15 , Novakovsky et al., 2023 Feb , de Vries et al., 2023 ), are essential for fostering trust and ensuring that these technologies are used responsibly in patient care. In addition to the DL relevance in direct clinical applications, research efforts in better model for predicting drug efficacy and toxicity have also become an essential aspect of modern drug development, particularly in the field of oncology ( Khan et al., 2024 Sep 1 ). AI-based models for drug efficacy prediction also typically involve the integration of various data types, including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and chemical data. Moreover, predicting drug efficacy and toxicity is a major research need since 90 % of drug failures in clinical development are due to lack of efficacy and uncontrolled toxicity ( Tran et al., 2023 Jan 17 ). Thus, the goal is to develop models that can predict the efficacy of a drug in inhibiting or treating a particular cancer type. One common approach is to use supervised learning algorithms, which are trained on large datasets of known drug responses. These models can predict the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) of a drug, which is a key indicator of its efficacy. For instance, Shahzad et al . ( Shahzad et al., 2024 Oct ) proposed a DL algorithm for efficient integration of genomic and compound features in predicting the IC 50 , while using the open-sourced CCLE and GDSC datasets. Joo et al . ( Joo et al., 2019 Dec 12 ) proposed a 1-dimensional convolution neural network to model three drug responsiveness classes, including features such as mutation statuses and various drug molecular fingerprints. The model showed a great cell viability IC 50 prediction accuracy in pan-cancer cell lines (ACC of 0.95), surpassing models as 2D CNN, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Ridge Classifier, and XGBoost (ACCs of 0.82, 0.91, 0.93, and 0.86, respectively). Nonetheless, there are other aspects that affect drug efficacy and toxicity in oncology. For example, drugs targeting oncologic diseases in the central nervous system must penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reach their molecular targets, where several DL models have been suggested to predict the BBB permeability. For example, Wu et al . ( Wu et al., 2021 Mar ) used artificial neural networks in combination with molecular structure and property descriptors, achieving a good performance for prediction with a RMSE of 0.171. Shaker et al . ( Shaker et al., 2021 May 23 ) trained a DL model based on the Light Gradient Boosting Machine algorithm, showcasing an ACC of 89 % for testing BBB permeability. In addition, Singh et al . ( Singh et al., 2020 May ) developed DL-centric BBB classification models using a large curated dataset of 605 compounds, being a pioneer work for early compound screening in drug design projects. Drug efficacy is also linked to a drug's plasma protein binding (PPB) capability, being a major governing factor for drug absorption and distribution ( Di, 2021 Dec ). Recently, an DL model was proposed to predict PPB for 8000 compounds, achieving a balanced ACC of 84 % and an AUC of 92 % ( Venkatraman, 2021 Sep 28 ). Tian et al . ( Tian et al., 2022 Dec 1 ) published a web server for accurate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) for drug-like proprieties, comprising fingerprints and descriptors and a tree-based machine learning model with extreme gradient boosting. Li et al . ( Li et al., 2022 Jan 27 ) developed a DL model taking in consideration molecular descriptors expressing the residue-level local features and circularity of cyclic peptides for PPB rate prediction. The model exhibited excellent performance with a MAE of 4.79 % and R 2 of 0.92 for the public drug dataset. Moreover, due to its importance in a drug's pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic study, predicting its fraction unbound in plasma is also key for proper efficacy and toxicity prediction. The unbound portion of a drug can diffuse into tissues, where it is metabolized or excreted from the body. Essentially, only the unbound fraction can cross membranes and reach sites of action, while the bound portion serves as a reservoir that maintains and extends the drug's effect ( Roberts et al., 2013 Jan ). Esaki et al . ( Foersch et al., 2023 Feb ) built in silico models to predict unbound drug fraction in the brain, showing a solid performance for the task based on 253 measurements from the literature. On the other hand, Mulpuru et al . ( Mulpuru and Mishra, 2021 Mar 16 ) developed a user-friendly DL-based model to predict a drug's unbound fraction in human plasma using chemical fingerprints, reporting a R 2 of 0.85. By testing several DL models, Morales et al . ( Morales et al., 2024 ) reported that the extreme gradient boosting algorithm had an ACC of 0.851 for a curated 157-compound dataset targeting the central nervous system. By leveraging large datasets and sophisticated algorithms, new models provide valuable insights that can guide the development of safer and more effective therapies in cancer care. As the field continues to evolve, the integration of multiple data types and the refinement of predictive models will further enhance the ability of DL to transform drug discovery and improve patient outcomes. In cancer care, the integration with natural language processing (NLP) and natural language generation (NLG), has revolutionized the field of automated radiology report generation ( C Pereira et al., 2024 Mar 1 , Reale-Nosei et al., 2024 Oct 1 , Tang et al., 2024 Mar 1 ). This approach combines the strengths of image analysis ( Nensa et al., 2019 Sep , Bi et al., 2019 Mar , Streiner et al., 2022 Jan ) and language processing ( Bitterman et al., 2021 Jul 1 , Lin et al., 2024 ) to create a powerful tool capable of generating accurate, consistent, and timely reports. Historically, at the core of automated radiology report generation are CNNs and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). CNNs are well-suited for analyzing complex radiological images, extracting detailed features that might be imperceptible to the human eye. These features include patterns, textures, and shapes that are crucial for accurate diagnosis and thus relevant for clinical trials assessment ( Table 2 ). From a research and still development point-of-view, other efforts are pioneer and lead the current state-of-the-art. For example, Mask Reginal-CNN Zhang et al. ( Zhang et al., 2023 Sep 1 ) achieved a 93 % sensitivity for MRI-support breast cancer detection. Naeem et al . ( Naeem and Bin-Salem, 2021 Dec 1 ) proposed a multi-level features extraction-based DL approach for automatic Covid-19 detection, with experimental outcomes indicating an ACC of 98.9 % for the SARS-CoV-2 CT scan dataset and an ACC of 83.0 % accuracy for the SIRM Covid-19 CT scan and chest X-ray dataset. Razali et al . ( Razali et al., 2023 May 1 ) explored a CNN-wavelet scattering textural feature fusion model for classifying breast tissue in mammograms, reaching 98.0 % on 10-fold cross-validation accuracy for tumoral identification. For polyp classification, Zhang et al . ( Zhang et al., 2023 Sep 1 ) tested a Multi-scale and Multi-level based Gray-level Co-occurrence Matrix CNN, reporting a AUC score of 94.0 % with a gain of 1.5 % over current state-of-the-art lesion classification methods. When CNNs and RNNs are integrated ( Banerjee et al., 2019 Jun ), they form a robust framework that can analyze radiological images and convert this analysis into detailed, structured reports. The process begins with the CNN analyzing the input radiology image – whether it's an X-ray, CT scan, MRI, or another modality. The CNN processes the image in layers, each layer identifying and abstracting different levels of features. These features are then used to create a representation of the image, capturing essential diagnostic information. This representation was passed in the past to an RNN, which would interpret the data and generate a narrative report. However, novel CNN-supported developments have boosted medical imaging reporting. For example, Gajbhiye et al . ( Gajbhiye et al., 2022 Jun ) developed an Adaptive Multilevel Multi-Attention (AMLMA) approach offering domain-specific visual-textual knowledge to generate a radiological report for any view of a human chest X-ray image. Aswiga et al . ( Aswiga and Shanthi, 2022 Jun ) proposed a Multi-Level Transfer Learning (MLTL) framework with a Long Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) model, observing an ACC of 96.9 % in radiological findings and reporting. Focusing on rectal cancer magnetic resonance imaging, Liu et al . ( Liu et al., 2024 Feb ) built a rule-based NLP model that could extract 11 key image features of rectal cancer, where such model achieved an ACC of 93.8 %. Kehl et al . ( Kehl et al., 2021 Dec 15 ) trained a NLP model to extract outcomes for participants with solid tumors in a precision oncology study, where the model recapitulated outcome annotation from existent reports, including the presence of cancer, progression/worsening, response/improvement, and metastases, with excellent discrimination (AUC > 0.90). Other authors have explored the NLP usage to accurately extract index lesions and their corresponding imaging features in breast magnetic resonance imaging reports, where such reports were generated in less than 1 s, whereas the manual reviewers averaged 4.47 min and 4.56 min per report ( Liu et al., 2019 Dec 30 ). Therefore, one of the primary benefits of automated radiology report generation is the potential for significantly reducing the time required to produce reports, especially in high-volume centers. Traditional radiology reporting is a time-consuming process that depends heavily on the radiologist's experience and expertise. In busy clinical settings, this can lead to delays in report generation, potentially affecting patient care. Automated systems, however, can generate reports almost instantaneously, allowing for quicker decision-making and improved patient outcomes. This speed is particularly valuable in emergency settings, where timely diagnosis is critical, while also ensuring consistency and accuracy across reports. Deep learning has emerged as a transformative force in oncology, revolutionizing various aspects of cancer care, from diagnosis and treatment planning to prognosis and personalized medicine. Deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable potential in enhancing the accuracy, consistency, and efficiency of oncological practices by harnessing the power of advanced neural networks and integrating them with vast, complex datasets. However, the road to clinical implementation is not without challenges, including the need for rigorous validation, ethical considerations, and ensuring model transparency and interpretability. As research progresses, the continued evolution of deep learning technologies, coupled with efforts to address these challenges, promises to enhance patient outcomes further and redefine the future of cancer care. This manuscript reviews existing literature and does not involve new research with human or animal subjects. Therefore, no ethical approval was required. The manuscript was conducted with respect to the original author's work, and all referenced studies were evaluated to ensure they met the appropriate ethical standards. Deep Learning Segmentation and Quantification of the Left Ventricle from the Parasternal Short-Axis View in Echocardiography Objective Quantitative measurements remain under-used in echocardiography due to measurement variability and time consumption. This study aimed to develop a deep learning (DL) pipeline for the automatic extraction of clinically relevant quantitative measurements from the parasternal short-axis (PSAX) view. Methods We trained an nnU-Net model to segment the left ventricle (LV) lumen and myocardium in PSAX images. Based on end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) frames in the echocardiograms, we calculated the LV lumen area, LV fractional area change, mean wall thickness (MWT) and global circumferential strain. Segmentations and measurements were validated through comparison with two manual observers. Results Compared with manual references, the nnU-Net model achieved a high grade of similarity for the LV lumen and myocardium, with Dice coefficients of 0.93 ± 0.04 and 0.84 ± 0.08 , and 95th percentile Hausdorff distances of 3.2 ± 1.9 mm and 3.4 ± 1.7 mm , respectively. The Dice coefficients and 95th percentile Hausdorff distances were on par or better for the evaluation dataset. DL-based measurements were in line with interobserver precision and variability. Automatic timing of ED and ES frames based on echocardiograms and LV lumen area produced similar results to using manual timing by experts. The subject-level feasibility was 90.4%. Furthermore, DL-based measurement of MWT at ED differentiated subjects with and without hypertension ( p < 0.001 ). Conclusion Our DL-based measurement pipeline for PSAX achieved performance comparable to expert annotators, positioning it as a possible substitute for tedious manual measurements. DL-derived MWT was able to differentiate hypertensive from non-hypertensive subjects, which indicates the potential clinical utility of fully automated PSAX measurements.
