Cardiac imaging is essential for evaluating heart function and diagnosing myocardial disease, and echocardiography is advantageous due to its non-invasive nature, absence of radiation exposure, affordability and broad accessibility. However, interpretation remains time-consuming and is often plagued by substantial observer variability. Deep learning (DL) holds promise for improving the precision and efficiency of analysis. Most DL research to date has focused on B-mode ultrasound images from the apical window, as these views capture comprehensive anatomical regions and are used to derive well-known quantitative measurements such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and global longitudinal strain (GLS) [ 1 ]. GLS is an established marker of LV systolic function, but its acquisition requires three apical planes and subsequent segment-level tracking, which can be time-consuming and variable. In contrast, the parasternal short-axis (PSAX) view captures the entire LV cross-section and all coronary perfusion territories in a single acquisition. This can be beneficial for the assessment of ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction (MI), as it enables simultaneous quantification of radial strain (RS; changes in wall thickness) and circumferential strain (CS; changes in myocardial circumference) throughout the cardiac cycle. Circumferential motion occurs across the myocardial wall but is particularly prominent in the mid-myocardial layers, where fiber orientation is largely circumferential [ 2 ]. This component of myocardial function is not adequately assessed in apical views. Furthermore, concurrent visualization of all myocardial segments allows analysis of contraction synchronicity, such as mechanical dispersion [ 3 ], within a single view. Finally, PSAX can often be obtained in patients where apical views are sub-optimal due to rib or lung interference. Taken together, PSAX provides an underutilized and complementary window to apical imaging that offers unique insight into myocardial mechanics and may enhance quantitative evaluation and patient stratification. Quantitative measurements from the PSAX view are not widely used in clinical practice and have attracted limited attention in research. Previous studies have focused on morphological and functional assessment, mainly using wall thickness (WT) measurements or the magnitude and timing of RS and CS. Alterations in WT are common across various cardiac conditions. In hypertension, concentric hypertrophy or remodeling often leads to increased WT, contributing to systolic or diastolic dysfunction [ 4 ]. Patients are frequently categorized by remodeling pattern [ 4 , 5 ], and while LV hypertrophy is associated with elevated mortality risk, concentric remodeling with increased WT appears to imply an even higher risk [ 6 ]. Conversely, reduced relative WT has been linked to an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmia in heart failure (HF) patients with conduction abnormalities [ 7 ]. Reduced CS, which measures the LV circumferential shortening, has been linked to a higher risk of mortality and hospitalization in HF patients [ 8 ]. Cho et al. [ 9 ] found that CS was predictive of cardiac events and improved prognostic utility when added to LVEF and GLS. RS quantifies the relative increase in WT during the cardiac cycle. Reduced RS has been reported in patients with MI [ 10 , 11 ], and one study suggested that RS may pick up subclinical myocardial dysfunction in muscular dystrophy patients at risk for the development of cardiomyopathy [ 12 ]. In addition to the magnitude of strain, increased dyssynchrony of RS and CS has been linked to adverse remodeling and worse outcomes in MI patients [ 8 , 11 , 13 ]. Reductions in dyssynchrony have been observed following cardiac resynchronization therapy in HF patients [ 14 , 15 ] and after anti-hypertensive treatment in hypertensive patients [ 16 ]. Together, these findings highlight the value of the PSAX view as a complementary window for comprehensive LV assessment. DL has become the dominant approach for automated segmentation and quantification in echocardiography, outperforming traditional methods for LV delineation [ 17 ]. Although few studies have focused on PSAX specifically, reported segmentation accuracy is generally high (mean Dice > 0.8 ) [ 18–22 ]. Cuellar et al. [ 18 ] evaluated multiple DL models trained on PSAX images, showing that U-Net-based architectures outperformed object detection methods such as Detectron2 [ 23 ] and variations of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 24 ] in both accuracy and consistency. In contrast, Hu et al. [ 19 ] proposed a SAM-based architecture for multi-plane segmentation in six different echocardiographic planes, and found it outperformed U-Net-based architectures as well as SAM models. Still, the model performed better on apical views than PSAX, suggesting that view-specific optimization may improve performance. While most studies focus on segmentation alone, Kim et al. [ 20 ] developed a fully automated quantification pipeline for cardiac chamber and function assessment. Their method used both apical and PSAX views to calculate several echocardiographic indices, and found good agreement between the automatic and manual estimates of clinical indices. However, their retrospective study included mainly young subjects with normal clinical characteristics such as body mass index, blood pressure, and LVEF, and excluded patients with cardiovascular diseases, pregnant individuals, and those with abnormal echocardiograms. The results may therefore be biased toward subjects with normal echocardiograms and clinical profiles. Despite recent advances in DL-based segmentation of PSAX images – primarily in healthy cohorts – few studies have translated this into clinical measurements for automated functional and morphological quantification, nor evaluated their clinical relevance. To address these gaps, the aims of our study were to: (i) develop a DL-based method for automatic quantification of the LV using measurements from the PSAX view, (ii) evaluate the method’s performance and compare its results with manual observers, and (iii) assess its ability to classify patients with hypertension based on automatic WT quantification. Datasets from two independent studies acquired at two different sites in Norway were used. The first dataset was composed of 333 volunteers (mean age 62 ± 12 years, 44.0 % female) from the HUNT4 population study [ 25 ], primarily consisting of healthy subjects, with some presenting with mixed cardiac and non-cardiac pathologies. The second dataset was randomly selected from the IMPROVE study (NCT02286908) [ 26 ] and included 98 subjects (mean age 64 ± 12 years, 18.4 % female) with a confirmed MI who had subsequently undergone percutaneous coronary intervention revascularization. Figure 1 illustrates how data from these sources were organized into development and evaluation subsets. The development dataset combined all 333 subjects from HUNT4 with 51 subjects from the IMPROVE study, resulting in a diverse dataset annotated independently by two expert clinicians, with some overlap (79% of subjects) between annotators. This development dataset served as the training set for the segmentation models. The remaining 47 subjects from the IMPROVE dataset formed the evaluation (hold-out) dataset. For this dataset, the annotators segmented identical image frames, allowing direct comparison of segmentation performance and cardiac measurements. The total dataset consisted of PSAX ultrasound images at the papillary muscle and mitral valve levels. The echocardiograms were acquired using a GE Vivid E9 or E95 ultrasound scanner (GE HealthCare, Horten, Norway) equipped with a GE M4S or M5S phased array transducer (2.5 MHz center frequency). The mean imaging depth was 146 ± 15 mm , mean sector width was 149 ± 23 mm , and the average frame rate was 75 ± 9 frames per second (fps). The endocardial border without papillary muscles, and the epicardial border of the LV, were delineated using the open-source annotation tool Annotation Web [ 27 ]. The clinical expert annotators identified end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) by visual inspection as the image frames with the largest and smallest lumen area, respectively. These frames and two additional frames from the same cardiac cycle were annotated. All data were obtained from patient studies approved by the Regional Committee for Medical Research Ethics and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. A DL model was developed to automatically segment the lumen and myocardium from ultrasound images. We utilized the nnU-Net framework [ 28 ] to configure and train the segmentation model, employing a plain 2-D U-Net architecture. The nnU-Net framework automatically determines suitable parameters for data pre-processing, network topology, input size, batch size and post-processing based on dataset characteristics and GPU resources. While other network types have shown promise for segmentation in echocardiography, U-Net-based methods have a proven track record for segmentation in the short axis [ 18–22 ], and nnU-Net has specifically shown strong performance for apical views [ 29–32 ]. We therefore adopted nnU-Net as a robust and well-validated starting point for PSAX segmentation in this study. The input data were normalized using z -score normalization. The median shape of the original input images was 598 × 648 pixels, while the network operated on input patches of size 640 × 768 pixels. The network consisted of eight levels, with the number of feature maps increasing per level with { 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 , 512 , 512 , 512 , 512 } , using 3 × 3 convolution kernels. Spatial downsampling was achieved via strided convolutions and upsampling through transposed convolutions, both with a stride of 2 × 2 . The loss function combined Dice and cross-entropy losses. Consistent with nnU-Net defaults [ 28 ] we used instance normalization, leaky ReLU activation function and deep supervision. Data-augmentation techniques included rotations, scaling, Gaussian noise, Gaussian blur, brightness, contrast, simulation of low resolution, gamma correction and image mirroring. We refer to Isensee et al. [ 28 ] for further details. Tenfold cross-validation with an 80/10/10% split for training, validation and testing was used for training, with data partitioned at the subject level, resulting in ten independent segmentation models. Each split was trained for 1000 epochs using a stochastic gradient descent method with an initial learning rate of 0.01 and a polynomial learning rate scheduler [ 28 ]. During training the best-performing checkpoint on the validation set was saved and subsequently used for evaluation. Each model was evaluated on a unique test set, ensuring that the entire development dataset was covered across folds. Segmentation evaluation. Segmentation performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). The DSC quantifies the spatial overlap between the clinical reference annotations and predicted segmentations and is defined by eqn (1) as: (1) DSC = 2 | A ∩ B | | A | + | B | , where A and B denote the sets of pixels in the ground-truth annotation (from clinician) and the model predictions, respectively. The HD95 measures the maximum distance between the segmentation outlines, while reducing sensitivity to outliers, as eqn (2) : (2) HD 95 ( A , B ) = P 95 ( h ( A , B ) , h ( B , A ) ) , h ( A , B ) = max a → ∈ A min b → ∈ B ∥ a → − b → ∥ , where P 95 is a 95th percentile operator, h ( A , B ) is the directed Hausdorff distance, and ∥ · ∥ denotes the Euclidean distance. Each PSAX recording was divided into individual cardiac cycles using an ECG-based gating algorithm (EchoPAC, GE HealthCare) that triggers on the QRS complex, aligning cycles to start at ED. The segmentation model then delineated the lumen and myocardium in each frame. We calculated the LV lumen area per frame and then applied a moving average filter to identify ES as the frame with the smallest lumen area. Following segmentation, 180 points were evenly distributed every two degrees along the endocardial and epicardial borders to form contours. We derived morphological and functional measurements from these contours and the lumen segmentation across frames. Figure 2 illustrates this process with a summary of the extracted measurements. Ultrasound sequences and ECG signals were manually reviewed for a subset of recordings where manual and DL-based measurements differed the most. Cycles affected by ECG gating errors, e.g., due to extra systoles or premature triggering, were excluded. Detection of unphysiological measurements from a cardiac cycle led to exclusion of the cycle in question, with unphysiological measurements defined as those outside the ranges 0 - 100 c m 2 for ED and ES areas, 0–80% for the LV short-axis fractional area change (LVFAC), 0 . 2 - 2.5 cm for mean wall thickness (MWT) at ED and ES, and -50–10% for global circumferential strain (GCS) ES. After quality control, the measurements were aggregated by calculating first the mean value of each measurement per recording, then per subject. Area-based measurements. LV lumen areas at ED and ES, denoted A ED and A ES , were computed from the lumen segmentation accounting for image spacing. These values were used to derive a functional measure of LV contraction, LVFAC, defined by eqn (3) as: (3) LVFAC = 100 % × A ED − A ES A ED . LVFAC quantifies the relative change in lumen area between ED and ES, analogous to how LVEF reflects changes in volume. W all thickness measurements. We defined WT as the Euclidean distance between corresponding points on the endocardial and epicardial contours. For each frame, the MWT was calculated as the average distance across all 180 point pairs. Circumferential strain. Myocardial centerline points were defined as the midpoints between each pair of endocardial and epicardial points. The length of the circumference, C , was found by summing the distances between consecutive centerline points p as per eqn (4) , (4) C t = ∑ k = 1 180 ∥ p k + 1 − p k ∥ , where ∥ p k + 1 − p k ∥ is the Euclidean distance between neighboring points p k and p k + 1 , and t ∈ { ED , ES } denotes the image frame. GCS at ES was defined as the circumferential shortening of the centerline relative to the ED length, per eqn (5) : (5) GCS ES = 100 % × C ES − C ED C ED . We validated the segmentation-based measurements by comparing them with measurements derived from manually annotated images. Each nnU-Net model from the cross-validation was applied to its respective test set, ensuring that all segmentations and measurements were obtained from unseen data. An ensembled nnU-Net model, created from these ten models, was applied to the evaluation dataset. The DL pipeline computed the ED and ES lumen areas, LVFAC, MWT at ED and ES, and centerline GCS. Analyses included only subjects with complete measurements available from the DL pipeline and both clinicians. We compared the MWT at ED between subjects with and without indications of hypertension using both DL-based measurements and measurements from manual annotations. We defined the hypertensive group as subjects who were either on anti-hypertensive medication at inclusion or who had systolic blood pressure exceeding 160 mmHg at the time of echocardiography. Agreement between measurements (two manual observers and our DL-based algorithm) was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis, reporting the mean bias, variation and 95% limits of agreement, and by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) variant ICC (2,1). For the hypertension discrimination analysis, group differences were assessed using the Student’s t -test for independent samples, and predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. All statistical analyses were performed in Python version 3.11 using the packages pandas, scipy and statsmodels. Segmentation model performance is summarized in Table 1 , which reports the mean and standard deviation of DSC and HD95 across validation and test folds from the tenfold cross-validation, as well as the evaluation dataset. The nnU-Net segmentation model was tested and compared with interobserver variability on the evaluation dataset. The segmentation overlap measured by DSC was slightly higher for nnU-Net versus each observer than for the interobserver comparison, and the difference was larger for the myocardium than for the lumen. HD95 was lower for the DL model than for the interobserver case. The full distributions of metrics, as well as the loss curves from the model training process, are given in Appendix A . Representative segmentation examples for different Dice scores across the evaluation dataset are shown in Figure 3 . We evaluated ED and ES frame timing by calculating differences between automatic and Observer 1 timing (automatic minus Observer 1 frame) on the evaluation dataset. The means and standard deviations of the differences were − 2 ± 35 ms for ED and 3 ± 51 ms for ES frames. Further details are presented in Appendix E . The development dataset included 384 subjects. The automatic measurement pipeline was applied to individual cardiac cycles and results were subsequently aggregated at recording, then subject levels. The pipeline successfully generated measurements from at least one cardiac cycle in 368 subjects (95.8%). Failures were mostly caused by segmentation errors that disrupted the detection of endo- and epicardial borders, and these were most common in noisy or low-quality recordings. Manual inspection revealed occasional errors in ED frame selection due to the ECG-based gating triggering incorrectly on the QRS complex, e.g., due to poor ECG signal. After excluding heart cycles affected by such errors, valid measurements remained for 347 subjects (90.4% of the dataset). Segmentation processing ran at 73.2 ± 4.4 fps (mean ± standard deviation). The frame rate for the generation of measurements for a cardiac cycle was 59.8 ± 3.1 fps, corresponding to approximately 1 second of processing time per cycle, given the average heart rate of the study population of 70 ± 15 beats per minute. The precision of DL-based measurements was evaluated by comparing them with manual reference measurements. Only subjects with measurements from DL and both manual observers were included in the comparative analysis. Summary of measurement values across observers and datasets. Table 2 reports the mean and standard deviation of each measurement on the test folds of the development dataset. Manual references and DL measurements were obtained for 273 subjects. Mean measurements were similar between each observer and DL, except for MWT measurements, which were somewhat smaller for Observer 2 than the others. Table 3 presents corresponding data for the evaluation dataset. DL-based measurements were derived from the ensembled nnU-Net segmentation model using both manual ED and ES timing from Observer 1 and automatic timing. In total, 40 subjects had measurements from all observers. Compared with the others, Observer 2 reported slightly larger ES lumen areas and correspondingly lower values for LVFAC and MWT ES. Notably, in the evaluation dataset the mean lumen area at ED and ES was larger than in the development dataset for all observers, and MWT at ED was slightly higher. MWT at ES remained comparable across datasets. Comparison of manual and DL-based measurements by dataset. Agreement was evaluated by computing pair-wise differences between the two expert observers and between each observer and the DL-based pipeline. Table 4 summarizes the mean, standard deviation and ICC of these differences for the development dataset. Bland-Altman plots are given in Appendix D , Figure D.1 . Each observer selected their own ED and ES frames while the DL pipeline used automatic timing. ICC values were similar for the comparisons of DL-based areas and the interobserver comparisons, and values were generally higher for DL-based comparisons than for interobserver cases. Similarly, results for the evaluation dataset are presented in Table 5 for both expert-defined and automatic timing. ICCs for the evaluation dataset can be found in Appendix B , while Bland-Altman plots are presented in Appendix D , Figures D.2 and D.3 . The absolute biases for area and GCS measurements were similar across comparisons of the different observers and DL. Biases between DL and observers are nearly identical for manual and automatic timing. The measurement reliability measured by ICC was similar for automatic and manual timing across all metrics. We identified significant differences between the mean MWT ED in the hypertensive and non-hypertensive groups for both DL and observers (all p < 0.001 ). Similar differences were found between groups for DL and manual references. The results of the DL-based approach are shown in Figure 4 . The DL-based MWT ED was 0.92 ± 0.13 cm (n = 140) for subjects in the hypertensive group and 0.85 ± 0.14 cm (n = 166) for subjects in the non-hypertensive group. The area under the ROC curve was 0.65 for MWT ED. Additional data with comparisons stratified by sex, as well as metrics and plots from ROC analyses, can be found in Appendix C . Our nnU-Net model demonstrated reliable performance on both development and evaluation datasets, matching manual interobserver agreement. Previous studies that present segmentation performance specifically for PSAX report intersection‑over‑union values of 0.80 for the lumen [ 21 ] and 0.74 for the LV myocardium [ 21 , 22 ], while DSC ranges from 0.91 to 0.95 for LV lumen, and from 0.83 to 0.88 for the LV myocardium [ 19 , 20 ]. This is in line with the presented nnU-Net model. Despite similar DSC values as our method, Hu et al. [ 19 ] report a HD95 of 4.67 mm (mean of lumen and myocardium) for EchoOne, higher than the HD95 of our PSAX-specific nnU-Net method. The qualitative results ( Fig. 3 ) were also convincing. The best- and median-case segmentations showed good agreement (DSC > 0.90 ) between the model and human observers. In lower percentile cases there were some discrepancies between annotations, often due to differences in endocardium delineation between annotators, suggesting challenging delineation of the LV wall in these cases. As expected from training on annotations from both observers, the nnU-Net segmentation tended to fall between the two. As the myocardium segmentations were influenced by the placement of both the endo- and epicardial borders, the HD95s were, as expected, higher than for the lumen. In the worst-case comparison, the nnU-Net model was exposed to a recording where the subject had a pericardial effusion, showing as a bright pericardial line in the inferior wall. This feature is under-represented in the training data and likely caused the nnU-Net model to mistake the pericardial line for the epicardium, which drove the DSC down to 0.60 . The manual annotators had access to the full ultrasound recording during the annotation process and could easily identify this pathology. Incorporating temporal context or multi-frame segmentation strategies, which were beyond the scope of this study, could help prevent such errors in future models. Overall, our results compared favorably to other methods reported in the literature [ 19–22 ], and the 10th percentile DSC of 0.84 and worst-case DSC of 0.60 show that nnU-Net is a robust architecture for segmentation in PSAX ultrasound images. Measurements and measurement variability . Across both datasets, DL-derived measurements closely mirrored those of the experts in magnitude and inter-subject variation. Mean area measurements were higher in the evaluation than in the development dataset, while both the LVFAC and the centerline GCS were reduced in the evaluation dataset. The development dataset mainly consisted of generally healthy subjects, while the subjects in the evaluation cohort had MI. As LVFAC and GCS are functional measures, with LVFAC being analogous to LVEF, the fact that these appeared to differ between groups of mostly healthy subjects and MI patients was expected [ 10 , 11 ]. Agreement analysis ( Table 4 and Appendix D , Fig. D.1 ) showed that the mean biases between DL and manual measurements were small, generally within one standard deviation of a zero mean difference. On the other hand, DL-based MWT measurements aligned more with Observer 1. There was a tendency for Observer 2 to estimate smaller MWTs than both DL and Observer 1, likely caused by differences in endocardial wall delineation, as discussed above. The discrimination between the myocardium and trabeculae of the myocardium in echocardiography is challenging, and differences in training or knowledge of echocardiography may lead to delineation variations of the endocardial border. The thinner wall annotated by Observer 2 also led to slightly higher estimates of the ES area, and to some degree the ED area, for both datasets. The ICC values for DL measurements against manual references exceeded the interobserver comparison for all measurements, indicating that DL found a trade-off between the annotators. In the evaluation dataset ( Table 5 and Appendix D , Figs. D.2 and D.3 ), similar measurement differences were found when comparing automatic timing with manual timing in either dataset. The small differences found between automatic and manual timing suggest that the dominant discrepancy in measurements is due to segmentation differences, despite the good overlaps indicated by high DSC. The measurement reliability of automatic timing was similar to that for manual reference timing, suggesting that automation maintained consistency. Bias between observers was slightly higher in the evaluation compared with the development dataset. The individual timing selection of each observer in the development dataset may have diminished some of the measurement differences that were caused by segmentation variation. In general, DL-based measurements demonstrated measurement reliability on par with human observers, with residual variability largely driven by subtle differences in segmentation border placement. Feasibility. By calculating measurements for each heart cycle, then aggregating per recording and per subject, we enhanced the feasibility of attaining data for each subject and reduced the pipeline’s sensitivity to errors in cycle division (the ECG-based algorithm) or variations in segmentation quality, achieving a high feasibility of 90.4%. Averaging measurements over multiple heart cycles may be a strength that can dampen random variability, but it is also important to retain beat-to-beat variations that may flag subtle signs of pathology or indicate subclinical dysfunction. Because DL-based measurements require far less manual effort than hand-tracing every frame, our approach makes large-scale, multi-cycle analysis practical. As detected by both DL and observer measurements, the MWT at ED was found to be significantly higher in hypertensive versus non-hypertensive subjects. We observed clear sex differences between males and females, with respective mean MWT ED values of 0.92 ± 0.13 cm and 0.82 ± 0.12 cm ( p < 0.001 ) . Values were in line with guideline-defined reference ranges [ 1 ], although in the upper bound. The area under the ROC curve for MWT was higher than for the other measurements. Given that nearly half of the subjects had hypertension or were on anti-hypertensive medication, we would expect some to show early signs of remodeling due to the compensatory effects of elevated afterload. When stratified by sex, hypertension was associated with raised MWT ED in both men and women. Interestingly, female subjects with hypertension had a lower mean MWT ED than non-hypertensive males. These findings highlight the necessity of sex-specific reference ranges, and possibly hypertension-adjusted cutoffs, when interpreting MWT. Single measurements provide limited information, so clinicians should strive to consider all patient characteristics and measured parameters together. DL could play a role in harmonizing available patient data to support personalized clinical decision-making. Although the results indicate that PSAX shows promise for augmenting myocardial function analysis by echocardiography, the method was developed using a combined population of mostly healthy subjects and MI patients, potentially limiting the generalization of results to other populations. While the distribution of WTs falls within reference ranges [ 1 ], potential confounders between WT and hypertension – such as cardiac pathologies, comorbidities or the duration and severity of the hypertensive state – were not evaluated in the present study. Evaluating the method in morphologically and functionally heterogeneous populations such as cardiomyopathies would expose it to a broader spectrum of cardiac phenotypes, helping to identify limitations, refine the algorithm and strengthen its validation for clinical use. Future studies should therefore include thorough documentation and stratification of such potential confounders to establish clinical relevance. The processing time for segmentation is adequate for real-time annotation during image acquisition. As the measurement pipeline runs post-acquisition on segmentations from a full cardiac cycle, it is not necessary that it runs fully in real-time. In practice, segmentation could be displayed live during acquisition, with quantitative measurements updated automatically after each cardiac cycle. The fast processing speed for measurements of almost 60 fps allows for bedside analysis of a cardiac cycle in approximately 1 s, which could facilitate more use of PSAX without increased workload. We have presented a fully automated DL-based pipeline for quantifying LV structure and function from PSAX ultrasound. Leveraging nnU-net to segment the LV lumen and myocardium, the method demonstrated robust and reliable performance when quantifying the LV across two cohorts with varying degrees of pathology. The results matched or exceeded manual interobserver consistency. Furthermore, we showed that the approach was able to distinguish hypertensive from non-hypertensive subjects via MWT at ED. These findings highlight how DL can streamline PSAX analysis and yield reliable morphological and functional LV measurements. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. DFF-U-NET: Deep features fusion u-net for bone marrow cells classification using advanced feature selection techniques U-Net is a widely used tool for precise segmentation in medical image analysis; however, it suffers from high memory usage and feature loss. This study improves U-Net to enhance the stability and efficacy of features for classifying bone marrow cells. First, the standard structure was modified by integrating additional concatenation layers between the encoder and decoder parts to create the Deep Features Fusion U-Net (DFF-U-Net). Dropout regularization and tuned hyperparameters were employed. This boosted the network’s ability to capture higher features from different layers and levels, improving classification accuracy. Finally, a classification head was added with Leaky-ReLU with an alpha value of 0.1 to prevent vanishing gradients. Secondly, three distinct Feature Selection (FS) methods, Univariate Feature Selection (UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV), and Select from Model (SFM), were used to select the most informative features for classification, reducing the memory requirements and accelerating computation. Further, the dataset is balanced using random oversampling. We have compared standard U-Net and DFF-U-Net with other robust EfficientNetV2S classifiers. The results showed that the DFF-U-Net classification models outperformed. In addition, our model achieved a higher performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed DFF-U-Net model was evaluated with higher accuracy, 98.93 %, compared with standard U-Net and EfficientNetV2S, 96.70 % and 94.25 %, respectively. Furthermore, the achieved results of (UFS + DFF-U-Net) are 99.11 %, (SFM + DFF-U-Net) is 99.69 %, and (RFECV + DFF-U-Net) is 99.86 %. The U-Net model is a good choice for overcoming problems in other deep learning techniques, such as limited resources, time constraints, and clinical medical applications. This study improves U-Net to enhance the stability and efficacy of features for classifying bone marrow cells. First, the standard structure was modified by integrating additional concatenation layers between the encoder and decoder parts to create the Deep Features Fusion U-Net (DFF-U-Net). Over more than 100 years old, bone marrow cell sorting still requires professional study to find uncommon essential cells [ 1 ]. In bone marrow (BM), blood cells (BC) are vital for distributing waste products, nutrients, and oxygen throughout the body's tissues. Comprising three primary forms of BC red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes), the BM is a fundamental component of the blood-forming system [ 2 ]. These BC types can lead to various health problems in the human body, including marrow cancer, thalassemia [ 3 ], anemia [ 4 ], sickle cell disease [ 5 ], thyroid disorder [ 6 ], aplastic anemia, etc. The pathologist’s automatic classification of BC using standard methods such as hemocytometer, complete blood count [ 7 ], peripheral blood smear [ 8 ], and blood film preparation in BM test to identify abnormal cells has a vital role in the diagnosis of blood disease [ 9 ]. Although pathological analysis is extensively applied in disease diagnosis, its outcomes are inconsistent. Medical image analysis has been transformed by developments in deep learning, especially CNNs with strong representational learning; these excel in classification [ 10 ], DeepLab [ 11 ], and object detection [ 12 ]. Introduced by Olaf et al. [ 13 ], U-Net provides scalable and accurate solutions and is a fundamental encoder-decoder architecture for biomedical image segmentation. By addressing U-Net's constraints and combining cutting-edge techniques, such as attention mechanisms and iterative refinement, variants such as U-Net++ [ 14 ], Attention U-Net [ 15 ], and GRUU-U-Net [ 16 ] improve segmentation even more. Artificial intelligence development is vital in deep learning problems, as in [ 17–23 ]. Many studies have been done to classify and segment different types of cells using U-Net, a deep learning model [ 24–27 ]. It has demonstrated its effectiveness in various medical imaging [ 28 , 29 ]. Essential for accurate cell, tissue, and organ segmentation in medical uses, including diagnosis and therapy planning, the U-Net architecture is built for semantic segmentation in biomedical imaging. Medical imaging has seen success with U-Net in MRI-based DDC classification [ 30 ], breast cancer diagnosis by tumor segmentation [ 31 ], and advanced variations, including CLIGUNET for soil stratification [ 32 ] and PolSAR image classification [ 33 ]. However, BM cell segmentation still presents difficulties, including differentiating packed cells [ 34 ], maintaining accuracy across modalities, and managing computing requirements. Our work presents the DFF-U-Net, extending U-Net for BM cell classification utilizing sophisticated FS techniques, optimizing efficiency, and reducing computational complexity, and combining improved encoder-decoder connections, random oversampling, and K-means clustering yields exact segmentation and superior precision, thereby providing a dependable, resource-efficient tool for medical imaging in limited conditions. Its architecture consists of an input layer, an encoding path (contracting path) to extract high-level features, a bottleneck, and a decoding path (expanding path) to rebuild the segmentation map. Four convolutional blocks on the encoding path extract hierarchical information: max-pooling lowers spatial dimensions. The decoding method recovers spatial features using four up-sampling blocks with transposed convolutions and skip connections. Predicted masks were thresholded at 0.5 to produce binary masks, which were bitwise AND on original images to retain segmented regions. Pixels with prediction values greater than 0.5 are set to 1 (indicating the object's presence). In contrast, those below or equal to 0.5 are set to 0 (indicating the absence of the object), as shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 . Each image is resized to 128x128 pixels, and brightness/contrast is consistently normalized in our image preprocessing. Using a U-Net model, images are then segmented. The contracting path produces hierarchical feature representations by down-sampling using 2x2 max pooling and extracts features through convolutional layers (64 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation). More complex characteristics are captured in deeper layers—1024 filters. Upsampling (2x2) restores spatial dimensions in the expanding path; skip connections combine low- and high-level information from both paths. After flattening these features into a 1D vector, they pass into a dense layer (256 neurons, ReLU) with a dropout rate of 0.5 for regularization. For class probabilities, the output layer employs SoftMax activation with 21 neurons. Using a batch size of 100 and categorical cross-entropy loss and an Adam optimizer (learning rate: 1e-4), training takes 30 epochs. We overcame the limitations in standard U-Net, as in Fig. 7 (a), by modifying the internal structure based on encoder-decoder parts to enhance feature representation by using extra concatenated layers that fuse features at multiple levels. The model begins by preparing data with preprocessing using the oversampled images, then scaling an input layer of 128 × 128 dimensions. Next, these preprocessed data are fed to the first part of the structure, called the encoder part. The encoder (contracting path) consists of a series of convolutional blocks that gradually reduce the spatial dimensions while increasing the number of filters. Each convolutional block follows this pattern: doable 3x3 convolutional layers with ReLU activation and the same padding. MaxPooling2D layer with a 2 × 2 pool size to down-sample the feature maps to fewer dimensions. In the middle of the structure, a bottleneck block with 1024 filters. It includes double 3 × 3 convolutional layers with ReLU activation. Then, decoder (expanding path): The decoder aims to recover spatial information from the reduced feature maps. Each decoding step consists of UpSampling2D to increase the spatial dimensions, a 2 × 2 Conv2D layer with ReLU activation. Then, a mesh of concatenation features for deep fusion features from different scale layers is used, as described in the architecture in Fig. 7 (b). While many encoder layers are concatenated with each corresponding decoder layer, except for the last decoder block, all blocks are concatenated to help reduce the model's overall complexity and create a good representation feature. This modification produces the desired outcomes, thus improving feature extraction and saving them without losing any information. This method helped to prevent overfitting. Finally, a classification head with Leaky-ReLU and a dense layer (256 neurons) is introduced to stop dead neurons. Dropout (0.5) regularizes the model, and the last dense layer employs SoftMax for class predictions, improving pattern identification and spatial accuracy in image analysis tasks. Extra concatenation in DFF-U-Nets has positive impacts in that it combines low-level features (edges, textures) with high-level semantics (object shapes), thus enhancing representations. Unlike standard skip connections, it keeps the contraction path output's spatial resolution. With K = 16 × 16 and selecting 25 % of the features from every image, UFS finds the most connected features with the target using the K-Best technique. This produces a 128x128 Boolean array in which True marks the chosen features. data.text: Diffusion-based knowledge distillation for effective multi-organ segmentation with reduced computational time Accurate and efficient multi-organ segmentation is crucial for clinical workflows, requiring high accuracy and reduced computational time. In this research, we propose a 3D diffusion-based knowledge distillation framework (3DKD-DiffuseNet) for multi-organ segmentation to achieve higher accuracy with reduced computational time. The core idea is to enhance the training of a lightweight student model by integrating a diffusion mechanism that guides feature learning during knowledge transfer from a high-capacity teacher model. Unlike conventional distillation approaches that rely solely on soft label supervision, our framework incorporates a diffusion consistency loss that encourages the student to learn stable and spatially coherent representations. To further improve computational efficiency, we introduce an organ-specific intensity thresholding strategy, which localizes regions of interest and reduces unnecessary processing without sacrificing critical anatomical detail. The model is validated on both MRI and CT modalities for brain tumor segmentation (BraTS benchmark) and abdominal organ segmentation (RAOS) tasks. On the BraTS benchmark datasets, it achieved outstanding Dice scores for high-grade and low-grade tumors, outperforming the teacher model by 3%–5% across all modalities. On the RAOS dataset, it similarly delivered excellent Dice scores, with improvements of 3%–6% for critical organs compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Experiment shows that the model also achieved a 2–3 × reduction in computational time due to strategic preprocessing. Our diffusion-based student model, supported by strategic preprocessing, offers enhanced segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for clinical applications that require fast and reliable analysis. Accurate and efficient multi-organ segmentation is crucial for clinical workflows, requiring high accuracy and reduced computational time. In this research, we propose a 3D diffusion-based knowledge distillation framework (3DKD-DiffuseNet) for multi-organ segmentation to achieve higher accuracy with reduced computational time. The core idea is to enhance the training of a lightweight student model by integrating a diffusion mechanism that guides feature learning during knowledge transfer from a high-capacity teacher model. Unlike conventional distillation approaches that rely solely on soft label supervision, our framework incorporates a diffusion consistency loss that encourages the student to learn stable and spatially coherent representations. To further improve computational efficiency, we introduce an organ-specific intensity thresholding strategy, which localizes regions of interest and reduces unnecessary processing without sacrificing critical anatomical detail. The model is validated on both MRI and CT modalities for brain tumor segmentation (BraTS benchmark) and abdominal organ segmentation (RAOS) tasks. On the BraTS benchmark datasets, it achieved outstanding Dice scores for high-grade and low-grade tumors, outperforming the teacher model by 3%–5% across all modalities. On the RAOS dataset, it similarly delivered excellent Dice scores, with improvements of 3%–6% for critical organs compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Experiment shows that the model also achieved a 2–3 × reduction in computational time due to strategic preprocessing. Our diffusion-based student model, supported by strategic preprocessing, offers enhanced segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for clinical applications that require fast and reliable analysis. This study utilized two distinct 3D medical segmentation tasks datasets: (1) brain tumor segmentation using BraTS benchmark datasets (BraTS2017-2019), with additional validation on BraTS2020 and BraTS2021 to assess generalizability; and (2) abdominal organ segmentation using the RAOS dataset. The BraTS benchmark datasets are publicly available, and the RAOS dataset is available upon request from the respective dataset owners. ( ). Automated organ segmentation in three-dimensional (3D) medical imaging has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, and disease monitoring [1] . Segmentation of vital organs and precise identification and delineation of structures, such as brain tumors, could aid clinicians in making accurate diagnoses and individualized treatment decisions [2,3] . Manual segmentation, however, is labor-intensive [4] , exhibits significant variability among different observers [5] , and may result in inconsistencies across extensive 3D datasets [6] . These challenges highlight the need for robust, automated segmentation solutions to process high-dimensional data with consistent accuracy. Advanced segmentation methods for 3D medical imaging often involve deep learning models built with 3D convolutional neural networks [7] . The 3D U-Net model, with its encoder–decoder architecture, is a model that is used for this purpose as it efficiently captures details across multiple scales, making it suitable for complex segmentation tasks [8] . A challenge in 3D image segmentation is the computational demand, which escalates with the size and complexity of the datasets [9,10] . Reducing computational time without compromising accuracy is imperative to make these tools practical for real-time clinical applications [11,12] . Enhanced segmentation algorithms that are both faster and more accurate could streamline clinical workflows, enabling expedited diagnosis and facilitating more rapid, data-driven decision-making [13] . Knowledge distillation is a compelling approach to addressing these computational challenges [14] . In this methodology, a smaller, more efficient model (the student) acquires knowledge from a high-performing, complex model (the teacher). This knowledge transfer preserves the teacher model’s accuracy while reducing the complexity of the student model, making it faster and less computationally intensive [14,15] . This is particularly advantageous in medical imaging, where accuracy and efficiency are paramount. Knowledge distillation is a promising technique for tasks such as organ segmentation within large datasets. SOTA studies [16–29] using knowledge distillation methodologies have certain limitations. The models often operate directly on raw 3D medical images without sufficient preprocessing, leading to an unnecessary computational burden. Denoising diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in medical image segmentation due to their powerful nonlinear modeling and superior generalization capabilities [30] . These models iteratively refine noisy predictions toward a target distribution, effectively capturing structural details and mitigating boundary uncertainty. Despite these strengths, diffusion models remain relatively underutilized in the distillation process in the medical imaging domain. Our approach addresses these shortcomings (see Fig. 1 ) by introducing a 3D Knowledge Distillation-based Diffusion Network (3DKD-DiffuseNet). The proposed framework reduces computational overhead while preserving segmentation accuracy. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • We designed an intensity-based thresholding preprocessing and ROI identification step to localize relevant structures and optimize slice selection. This reduces computational demands while preserving critical spatial features. • We introduced a novel teacher–student framework where a lightweight student model is trained using both soft predictions and denoising supervision via a forward-reverse diffusion process to enable robustness to input variability and structural ambiguity. • A novel diffusion consistency loss is formulated that complements standard distillation objectives and enforces spatial fidelity through reconstruction to improve generalization across organs and modalities. • We conduct extensive experiments on both brain and abdominal segmentation tasks across MRI and CT modalities. Our model achieves SOTA segmentation performance while significantly reducing inference time and computational cost. Knowledge distillation-based methods. Recently, knowledge distillation (KD) has gained attention in medical image segmentation as a way to compress large models and improve generalization. For instance, in a work, Hu et al. [31] proposed KD-Net, where a mono-modal student is trained to mimic both the soft predictions and latent space of a multi-modal teacher. The teacher’s weights are frozen, and the student learns to match the teacher’s bottleneck features. On BraTS2018, their T1ce-only student achieved 71.67% Dice for enhancing tumor (ET). Similarly, Rahimpour et al. [22] introduced a cross-modal distillation approach that transfers both soft predictions and intermediate features from a multi-sequence teacher to a single-sequence student. They tested variants with and without feature distillation and found the feature-level variant achieved 77.88% Dice for Whole Tumor using only T1w. In a related direction, Kang et al. [25] proposed MCTSeg, a CNN-Transformer hybrid framework that distills multimodal knowledge into unimodal student encoders. They included modules to transfer features, enhance unimodal signals, and simulate missing modalities during training. On BraTS2020, MCTSeg reached 87.24% Dice for Whole Tumor. On the other hand, Dou et al. [32] addressed unpaired modality distillation between CT and MRI by sharing convolutional weights across modalities and aligning prediction distributions using KL divergence. Without needing registered data, their model improved the MRI segmentation Dice from 83.7% to 89.3% on abdominal organs. In another study, instead of relying on feature similarity, Vadacchino et al. [33] used adversarial knowledge distillation in HAD-Net. In their approach, a student without access to T1ce learns from a full-modality teacher using hierarchical discriminators that align feature maps and outputs. On BraTS2019, HAD-Net achieved 73.3% Dice for enhancing tumor (ET). For weak supervision, Zhai et al. [34] proposed PA-Seg, which first expands sparse point annotations into dense pseudo-labels, then refines them using cross-knowledge distillation between two networks. Their method achieved 0.856 Dice on the brain tumor segmentation task. Unlike teacher–student setups, Yu et al. [35] introduced a self-distillation framework, ACW-SKD, which uses an auxiliary head and a feature reconstruction module to refine class-wise features within a single network. They combined this with a learnable temperature mechanism and achieved 73.74% and 83.18% Dice on Synapse and FLARE2022 datasets, respectively, using a compact ResNet18 backbone. Most existing KD methods focus on transferring knowledge via soft labels or features, often assuming clean input data. While some handle missing modalities or weak labels, they do not explicitly train students to be robust against noisy inputs or structural ambiguity. Diffusion-based models. Diffusion models, originally developed for generative image synthesis, have recently been adapted for medical image segmentation due to their ability to model complex structures and spatial uncertainty. For instance, in a work, Chen et al. [36] proposed HiDiff, a hybrid framework that combines a discriminative segmentor with a generative Bernoulli diffusion model (BBDM). They used an alternate-collaborative training strategy, including a binarized refiner and a cross transformer, and achieved 84.94% Dice on Synapse and 85.80% on BraTS2021. In another study, Chen et al. [37] introduced BerDiff, which employed Bernoulli noise as a discrete diffusion kernel tailored for binary segmentation. Unlike HiDiff, this model emphasized diversity in predictions through stochastic sampling and achieved 89.7% on BraTS2021. Similarly, Wolleb et al. [38] applied diffusion directly to segmentation masks using a DDPM-based approach. They used ground truth masks during training and generated multiple outputs for ensemble prediction, achieving 86.6% (single run) and 88.1% (ensemble) Dice on BraTS2020. Similarly, Xing et al. [39] proposed Diff-UNet, integrating diffusion within a U-Net architecture. They introduced a Denoising module and a Step-Uncertainty Fusion mechanism, reporting 85.35% on BraTS2020 and 73.69% on MSD Liver. Some works used diffusion more indirectly for refinement or enhancement. For example, Li et al. [40] proposed CorrDiff+, a corrective model that refines initial segmentations by addressing systematic errors using a VQ-VAE and multi-fusion attention. It achieved 87.48% Dice on BraTS2019 and 93.02% on the Jun Cheng dataset. In another work, Zhang et al. [41] introduced DiffBoost, which uses diffusion models for data augmentation rather than direct segmentation. By generating synthetic images with text and edge guidance, it achieved 84.56% on Prostate MRI, 94.78% on Spleen CT, and 71.65% on Breast Ultrasound. More recently, Wu et al. proposed MedSegDiff [42] and MedSegDiff-V2 [43] , which incorporate conditioning strategies to guide the diffusion process more effectively. MedSegDiff used Dynamic Conditional Encoding and a frequency parser, while MedSegDiff-V2 introduced spatial and spectral transformers. These models achieved 88.9–89.9% and 90.8% Dice on brain tumor datasets, respectively. Despite notable progress, diffusion-based segmentation models share common limitations. Most models rely on full denoising inference, which is computationally expensive and slow, making real-time deployment difficult. Even with optimizations like binarization or VQ-VAE, these models remain resource-intensive. Corrective models are dependent on the quality of initial segmentations, and augmentation-based methods may introduce bias or lack structural variability. Although few studies [44–47] have attempted to fuse knowledge distillation with diffusion, the implications are notably absent in 3D medical image segmentation tasks. Our work addresses these limitations by introducing a lightweight diffusion-enhanced student model trained within a knowledge distillation framework, where diffusion is used not for generation but to improve robustness and generalization without compromising speed. In this section, we describe the preprocessing steps for segmenting anatomical regions in the datasets, followed by the 3DKD-DiffuseNet model. This model leverages a teacher–student framework with diffusion-based knowledge distillation and attention mechanisms to improve segmentation accuracy. The architecture of our proposed teacher–student model with diffusion, 3DKD-DiffuseNet, is depicted in Fig. 2 . We evaluated our method on two distinct 3D medical image segmentation tasks to demonstrate its broad applicability: (1) brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS2017, BraTS2018, and BraTS2019 datasets [48–50] , with additional generalizability validation on BraTS2020 and BraTS2021; and (2) abdominal organ segmentation using the RAOS dataset [51,52] . BraTS benchmark. The BraTS benchmark datasets include patients diagnosed with high-grade glioblastomas and low-grade glioblastomas. Each patient scan consists of four MRI modalities: T1-weighted, post-contrast T1-weighted (T1ce), T2-weighted, and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR). In the dataset annotations, every voxel is assigned to one of the raw labels: Label 1 corresponds to the necrotic or non-enhancing tumor core (NCR), Label 2 to edema (ED), and Label 4 to enhancing tumor (ET). Following the standard segmentation evaluation metrics, these raw labels are then combined into the three evaluated subregions used in our study: whole tumor (WT = 1 ∪ 2 ∪ 4), tumor core (TC = 1 ∪ 4), and enhancing tumor (ET = 4). Background voxels are labeled separately (Labeled as 0). The results reported in the subsequent sections follow these benchmark guidelines [53] . For the segmentation task, we used the officially designated test sets and evaluated performance using the same offline evaluation methodology applied in the original challenges. RAOS. The RAOS dataset comprises 413 clinical computed tomography (CT) scans and 3,717 magnetic resonance (MR) scans, with nine sequences associated with each case. Annotations cover 19 abdominal organs, each verified by an experienced oncologist. The dataset is split into three subsets to represent different surgical contexts: cases without surgery (Set A, 317), cases after surgery without organ removal (Set B, 22), and cases after surgery with one or more organs missing (Set C, 74). Following the official RAOS study, we used Set A for model development (220 for training and the rest for validation). Since Sets B and C contained fewer samples, we also used them only for testing, as per the official implementation by the authors. This dataset presents challenging cases not covered in other public datasets, such as prostate and seminal vesicles. The preprocessing stage involves isolating key anatomical regions for both the BraTS and the RAOS datasets. Using intensity-based thresholding, brain regions were accurately segmented in 3D MRI volumes for the BraTS benchmark datasets. Similarly, specific abdominal organs (e.g., liver, kidneys, spleen) were isolated in 3D CT volumes for the RAOS dataset by tailoring intensity thresholds to match each organ’s characteristics. To mitigate variability arising from differing acquisition parameters across MRI sequences, voxel intensities were standardized using Eq. (1) : (1) I s t a n d a r d i z e d = I − μ σ where I is the raw voxel intensity, μ is the mean intensity of the sequence, and σ is the standard deviation of the sequence. This transformation ensures that the voxel intensities have a zero mean and a unit variance, improving consistency across samples. In 3D CT volumes for the RAOS dataset, to ensure uniformity across contrast-enhanced and non-contrast CT scans, voxel intensities are normalized to identify suitable intensity thresholds for each organ. Regions of interest (ROIs) were then identified using segmentation masks, rather than fixed cropping, to ensure that only relevant anatomical structures are included while irrelevant areas are discarded. This is defined in Eq. (2) : (2) M ( x , y , z ) = 1 if ( x , y , z ) ∈ ROI 0 otherwise where M denotes the segmentation mask function. This approach preserves critical anatomical features and ensures the model remains anatomy-aware, while reducing computational burden. Following this. the slice range containing relevant data was determined using Eq. (3) : (3) s min = min { s ∣ M ( : , : , s ) ≠ 0 } , s max = max { s ∣ M ( : , : , s ) ≠ 0 } With this step, we reduce unnecessary training overhead without compromising segmentation accuracy by excluding slices that do not contain relevant structures (e.g., no-tumor or no-organ slices). Finally, to manage large data volumes and enable faster training, a custom data generator was implemented to compile 3D volumes into arrays. The compiled batch B consists of n preprocessed 3D volumes, where each volume is denoted by V i , with i ranging from 1 to n . Unlike traditional KD approaches that assume architectural similarity, our framework is agnostic to the internal structure of the student model. As long as the student can produce output logits compatible with the teacher (e.g., same number of classes), the architecture can vary in terms of depth, width, and presence of auxiliary modules. Algorithm 1 provides a brief overview of the proposed methodology. Further architectural details are provided in the following subsections. The teacher model is a 3D attention-based encoder–decoder model built to segment volumetric medical images. The teacher model is visualized in Fig. 3 . The model follows a contraction–expansion path to the downsample and then the upsample of the input. The input volumes enter through layers with a 3 × 3 × 3 convolution, 16 filters, and ReLU activation. Max-pooling reduces the spatial dimensions in each layer, progressively doubling the number of filters (16, 32, 64, 128, 256) until reaching the bottleneck, which captures detailed spatial features. Dropout is applied at increasing rates to promote generalization, especially in the bottleneck layer, where it is set to 0.3. For the 3D convolution operation, the input preprocessed image can be denoted as X ∈ R H × W × D × C , where H , W , and D represent the height, width, and depth of the image, and C is the number of channels. The feature map output at layer i is represented by Eq. (4) : (4) F i = ∑ c = 1 C i − 1 W i c ∗ X i − 1 c + b i where W i c is the 3D convolution kernel applied to the c th channel at layer i , and b i is the bias term. Following this, a 3D convolution is applied to this input, followed by batch normalization (BN) and ReLU activation, σ . A general 3D convolution applied to an input tensor X with a kernel W can be expressed by Eq. (5) : (5) F ( h , w , d , c ) = ∑ h ′ , w ′ , d ′ , c ′ W ( h ′ , w ′ , d ′ , c ′ ) ⋅ X ( h − h ′ , w − w ′ , d − d ′ , c ′ ) where the convolution is computed over the height h , width w , and depth d of the input. The convolutional kernel has dimensions of 3 × 3 × 3, and the number of output channels increases with depth, often doubling after each down-sampling step. For our teacher model, to reduce the spatial dimensions, MaxPooling3D selects the maximum value within non-overlapping windows of size 2 × 2 × 2, to reduce the spatial dimensions. For a feature map F i ∈ R H i × W i × D i × C i , the output feature map after the pooling operation is described by Eq. (6) : (6) F p o , i ( h , w , d , c ) = max ( h ′ , w ′ , d ′ ) ( F i ( h ′ , w ′ , d ′ , c ) ) where h ′ , w ′ , and d ′ are spatial coordinates within each pooling window. The dimensions are reduced, halving H i , W i , and D i . The general formula for representing the MaxPooling is given by Eq. (7) , where h ′ , w ′ , and d ′ represent local positions within the window. (7) F p o ( h , w , d , c ) = max ( h ′ , w ′ , d ′ ) ∈ [ 0 , s ) F ( h + h ′ , w + w ′ , d + d ′ , c ) We have incorporated the attention mechanism to enhance the model’s focus on important regions. An attention map A i is computed using a 3D convolution followed by a sigmoid activation. Here, the A i is an attention mask in the range [0, 1] which highlights important spatial regions in the feature map F i . The output feature map, denoted as F at , i , is then obtained by element-wise multiplication of the attention map with the original feature map, which ensures that relevant features are enhanced while less important ones are suppressed. Following this, the decoder uses 3D transposed convolutions to upsample the feature maps, restoring spatial dimensions. Given the feature map F at , i + 1 from a deeper layer, the upsampled feature map is computed as the transposed convolution operation followed by an activation. We then added skip connections between the corresponding encoder and decoder layers to allow the model to retain spatial details. Following this, upsampled feature maps with their corresponding encoder outputs are concatenated. The final layer of the Teacher model applies the SoftMax function to generate voxel-wise probabilities. For a voxel v and class k , the SoftMax output is given by Eq. (8) : (8) Y T ˆ ( v , k ) = exp ( Z T ( v , k ) ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ( Z T ( v , j ) ) where Z T ( v , k ) is the logit for class k and K is the total number of classes. After obtaining the optimal weight from the teacher model, a student model that distills knowledge from the teacher model is implemented. The student model is a lighter variant of the teacher model, designed with fewer layers, fewer filters, and no attention blocks. It is optimized for reduced computational load while maintaining competitive segmentation performance. The model architecture is shown in Fig. 4 . After training the teacher, the student model is supervised through both the teacher’s soft-label outputs and the original ground truth annotations. Initially, the student model learns to align its predictions with the teacher’s output distribution using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. The softmax outputs of the teacher and student models at voxel v for class k are denoted by Y ˆ T ( v , k ) and Y ˆ S ( v , k ) , respectively. The distillation loss is computed as shown in Eq. (9) : (9) L K = ∑ v ∑ k = 1 K Y ˆ T ( v , k ) log Y ˆ T ( v , k ) Y ˆ S ( v , k ) Additionally, the student is trained using the standard cross-entropy (CE) loss with ground truth labels Y ( v , k ) . We calculate the CE loss L C following Equation (10) : (10) L C = − ∑ v ∑ k = 1 K Y ( v , k ) log Y ˆ S ( v , k ) The KL loss L K (see Eq. (9) ) transfers the teacher’s complex predictive distribution to the student, but it operates only on the final output logits. This provides limited guidance on feature representation formation for noisy inputs. Thus, we introduce a complementary diffusion-based objective, which forces the student’s encoder to learn a fundamental, noise-invariant understanding of the input structure by reconstructing clean volumes from noisy versions. Consequently, the student then more effectively aligns its output with the teacher’s soft labels ( L K ), as its improved features are more capable of capturing the necessary semantics. The diffusion loss (detailed in Section 3.3.3 ) thus works synergistically with L K : one improves feature robustness, while the other refines the final output based on those improved features. Forward and reverse diffusion. Unlike generative diffusion models that perform iterative denoising during inference, we repurpose diffusion as a regularizer to enhance the quality of the student model’s feature representations. To simulate model robustness, we incorporate a forward and reverse diffusion process during training. In the forward diffusion step, Gaussian noise is progressively added to clean inputs according to a noise schedule controlled by variance σ t . This noisy input, denoted as X t , is formulated as shown in Eq. (11) : (11) X t = X + N ( 0 , σ t 2 ) In the reverse diffusion step, the student model’s feature encoder itself acts as the denoising function to estimate the original image from the noisy input. This process teaches the encoder to learn noise-invariant features and iteratively removes noise, guided by the model’s predictions. The denoised output X ˆ 0 is computed as shown in Eq. (12) : (12) X ˆ 0 = f denoise ( X t , Y ˆ S ) Diffusion-augmented knowledge distillation. Standard knowledge distillation transfers the teacher’s knowledge through the alignment of output distributions between the teacher and student. This process is typically realized by minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the softmax predictions of the two networks. However, this formulation supervises only the final prediction layer of the student and does not provide direct constraints on the intermediate feature representations. As a result, the student can reproduce the teacher’s logits but still learn suboptimal or unstable features (see empirical findings in Section 4.3 ), especially around ambiguous tumor boundaries where the teacher itself may be uncertain. In this framework, the student is exposed to noisy inputs during training (via forward diffusion) and learns to reconstruct clean input representations through its own representations through a denoising function (reverse diffusion). This process introduces a novel auxiliary diffusion consistency loss L diff that enforces accurate reconstruction and effectively regularizes the student’s feature extractor. We define the loss in Eq. (13) : (13) L diff = ‖ X ˆ 0 − X ‖ 2 2 This loss complements the standard CE (Eq. (10) ) and KL terms (Eq. (9) ) by guiding the model to produce representations invariant to noise. The entire diffusion process is used only during training and is discarded during inference. Thus, it ensures no computational overhead in the student model. The final loss function for training the student integrates all three components. It is defined in Eq. (14) : (14) L total = α L C + β L K + γ L diff where α , β , and γ are hyperparameters that balance the contribution of the segmentation loss, distillation loss, and diffusion consistency loss, respectively. Our proposed methodology is evaluated using a range of performance metrics. These include Accuracy (Acc), Precision (Prec), Sensitivity (Sen), and Specificity (Spe). Additionally, we used the Dice Score to calculate the overlap between the predicted and true segmentation. It is worth noting that the t/ and s/ suffixes preceding any metrics represent Teacher and Student , respectively, in Tables 7 , 8 , and 9 . For all SOTA comparison results reported in this study, the values were directly sourced either from the respective publications or from the subsequent benchmark studies to avoid implementation bias. All experiments were carried out on a system equipped with an AMD Ryzen 5 5600X 6-core CPU and 16 GB of RAM, along with a ZOTAC GAMING GeForce RTX 3060 Twin Edge OC GPU that has 12 GB of VRAM. Our training configuration involved running the teacher model and the student model, which incorporates diffusion, for 100 epochs (each). For both the teacher and the student models, we used the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001, and the batch size was set to 2. The choice of batch size 2 is due to the high computational cost of training on large 3D volume imaging datasets [54,55] . During training, both models achieved over 99% accuracy, with validation accuracy consistently above 98%. Direct teacher-to-student transfer supervises the student primarily through the alignment of output distributions. While this strategy passes semantic information from the teacher to the student, it does not constrain how the student forms intermediate feature representations. In practice, this can also lead to unstable or noisy features in the student encoder. As a result, the benefit of direct transfer is often limited to small improvements in prediction accuracy. On the other hand, the student model, incorporating diffusion, can potentially outperform the teacher model across imaging types (see Table 1 ). To verify this effect, we trained the teacher and student models for 50 epochs (each) on a subset of the BraTS2019 dataset. Dice scores averaged across four MRI modalities are reported in Table 2 , where we compared (i) direct teacher-to-student transfer without diffusion and (ii) teacher-to-student transfer with diffusion. Although it is observed that direct transfer increases Dice scores, the performance increment is limited to a slight improvement compared to the teacher. However, the student achieves clear improvements across all subregions with the diffusion integration, with an average Dice gain of nearly 4%. These results demonstrate that diffusion provides stronger and more stable supervision than direct teacher-to-student transfer. The following sections report student performances corresponding to the diffusion-augmented variant. As seen in Table 1 , the proposed student model, incorporating diffusion, consistently outperformed the teacher model across all datasets, tumor grades, and imaging types. For high-grade (HG) tumors, the student model achieved Dice scores between 0.942 and 0.947 across T1-weighted, Enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and Flair images, while the teacher model scored between 0.899 and 0.917. Notably, on Flair images of HG tumors, the student model reached a peak Dice score of 0.956, compared to the teacher’s 0.927. Table 3 shows the detailed results for high-grade tumor classification. For low-grade (LG) tumors, the student model’s results were on average 3%–5% higher than the teacher model, with scores ranging from 0.910 to 0.932 across all modalities. It performed best on BraTS2017 HG tumors with an average Dice of 94.27%; and also showed strong stability across all datasets. Flair images generally yielded the highest accuracy for both models. On both HG and LG segmentation tasks, the proposed student model achieved average Dice of 93.50%, 93.11%, and 92.93% on the BraTS2017, 2018, and 2019 datasets, respectively. Fig. 5 illustrates the segmentation output. Our student model demonstrated remarkable performance in classifying high-grade tumors across the BraTS benchmark datasets as well. For instance, on BraTS2017, we achieved an accuracy of 0.985 for enhancing tumors (ET) using T1-weighted images, with a precision of 0.976 and a sensitivity of 0.980. For tumor core (TC), the accuracy was 0.978, and we reached an accuracy of 0.990 for the whole tumor (WT) classification. On the BraTS2018 dataset, our model maintained a high performance, scoring an accuracy of 0.987 for ET in T1-weighted images, 0.981 for Enhanced T1-weighted images, and 0.993 for WT classification. The results were consistent across the tumor grades. Notably, in the high-grade tumors, we achieved average Dice scores of 94.27%, 93.77%, and 93.80% on the BraTS2017, 2018, and 2019 datasets, respectively. Similarly, in the low-grade tumor segmentation tasks, we scored Dice scores of 92.72%, 92.45%, and 92.07% on the respective datasets. The student model demonstrated a strong performance in low-grade tumor evaluations across the BraTS benchmark datasets as well (see Table 4 ). For instance, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.967 for ET in T1-weighted images in BraTS2017. For TC classification, the accuracy increased to 0.972, and for WT, it further improved to 0.978. The preprocessing step (see Section 3.2 ) uses intensity-based ROI localization and slice selection to focus the model on relevant anatomical areas. The preprocessing reduces computational overhead by excluding irrelevant background and non-informative slices that do not contain tumors or organs. It also increases training and inference speed without affecting segmentation accuracy. This reduces the average epoch inference time from 135.4s to 92.8s. Additionally, we also note that knowledge distillation (KD) helps the lightweight student model learn better by mimicking the teacher’s soft outputs. Without KD, the student’s performance drops noticeably. The diffusion consistency loss improves the model’s robustness by encouraging it to handle noisy or uncertain inputs effectively. The detailed results are reported in Table 10 . Weights tuning for loss functions. We evaluated various weighting schemes for the loss components during training of the student model. The total loss combines cross-entropy ( L C ), knowledge distillation via KL divergence ( L K ), and diffusion consistency ( L diff ) terms weighted by α , β , and γ , respectively (see Eq. (14) ). The weights were tuned using a grid search under the constraint that α , β , and γ are constrained such that their total is 1 (except for the baseline). The experiments showed that maintaining a relatively high α was essential, since segmentation loss ( L C ) provides the primary signal for accurate boundary prediction. The distillation weight β was most effective in the range 0.2–0.3, which enabled the student to benefit from teacher guidance without overfitting. On the other hand, the diffusion consistency weight γ was used as a regularizer, with small values (0.1–0.2) improving robustness, while larger values reduced training stability. It is worth noting that, unlike a standard segmentation task where only the cross-entropy loss would typically be prioritized, in our case, all three components were necessary to achieve optimal performance, as reflected in the reported results on BraTS2017 (see Table 11 ). When we trained the student using only cross-entropy, the Dice score was 0.790. Adding knowledge distillation improved it to 0.849. Including the diffusion consistency loss further increased performance, and the best results came with weights [0.5, 0.3, 0.2], reaching a Dice of 0.901. Model’s parameters count. Our method, even with the diffusion module included, maintains a relatively low parameter count, which is substantially fewer than models like MedSegDiff-V2 [43] or SwinUNETR [60] . The student model contains only 21M parameters and is significantly smaller than the teacher (64M) and many SOTA architectures, including SwinUNETR (138M), UNETR (104M), and TransUNet (96M). This is primarily because we decouple the heavy generative nature of traditional diffusion models and instead integrate diffusion as an auxiliary denoising process, rather than modeling the entire data distribution. Additionally, unlike our teacher model (64M), our student model also avoids complex attention mechanisms and deep transformer layers that significantly increase model size in other architectures. Through KD, the student retains high segmentation performance despite the reduction in depth and parameters. In particular, the student network uses a shallow 2-depth architecture guided by diffusion consistency with KD. Although the diffusion module adds a small number of extra parameters (＋3M), the resulting performance gain justifies this tradeoff.
