Medical imaging plays a critical role in modern healthcare by providing essential information for diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. The rapid advancement of imaging technologies and the significant increase in the volume of medical imaging data have led to a growing demand for automated medical image analysis systems. However, these systems often face limitations in robustness and reliability because their performance is highly dependent on the underlying training data distribution [1] . Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and anomaly detection techniques are essential in this context, as they enable the identification of abnormal patterns in medical images that could significantly hamper the performance of deep learning models [2] . OOD detection refers to identifying data that differ from the distribution on which a model was trained, while anomaly detection focuses on detecting samples that deviate from predefined normality, such as lesions or tumors in medical images [2] . Although the applications of the detection principles are different, the methods are often similar, especially for reconstruction-based approaches, which we focus on in this work. Therefore, we use the terms OOD detection and anomaly detection interchangeably throughout this paper. OOD detection in medical imaging is closely tied to the availability of benchmark datasets, which defines what is considered in-distribution (ID) and OOD data. Although this is a significant challenge, our work focuses on addressing three gaps. First, there is a growing trend toward increasingly complex models, yet the potential of simpler models remains underexplored. Second, many current deep learning methods are designed for tasks where training and test data are drawn from the same distribution, but these methods are rarely optimized for OOD detection. Third, the selection of appropriate reconstruction metrics is rarely prioritized, yet it is crucial for improving OOD detection performance. In order to develop and benchmark methods for OOD detection in medical images, the Medical Out-of-Distribution (MOOD) challenge 1 1 . [1] was introduced, first organized in conjunction with MICCAI 2020. The MOOD challenge includes sample-level and pixel-level anomaly detection for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and abdominal computed tomography (CT) datasets. In this context, sample-level anomaly detection refers to identifying whether an entire image (or sample) belongs to the training distribution, while pixel-level anomaly detection focuses on identifying local abnormal regions within the image, such as lesions or tumors. OOD detection methods include reconstruction-based, restoration-based, and generative approaches [3,4] . Reconstruction-based methods rely on encoder–decoder models trained to reconstruct ID inputs, detecting OOD samples through poor reconstruction. Restoration-based methods refine this by modifying the latent space to “heal” anomalies in the reconstructions. Generative approaches model the distribution of ID data and use likelihood for detection. Autoencoders (AEs) are widely used for unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD), leveraging reconstruction errors during training to identify OOD samples at test time [3,5] . However, capturing the healthy distribution and generalizing to unseen anomalies remains challenging [6] . To address these limitations, variations such as scale-space AEs [7] , memory-augmented AEs [8] , reversed AEs [6] , and patch-wise contrastive learning-based AEs [9] have been proposed. Baur et al. [3] found that variational autoencoders (VAEs) generally outperformed traditional AEs in UAD. While VAEs often produced blurrier reconstructions, they exhibited larger differences in reconstruction errors between normal and anomalous pixels [3] . In addition, methods based on generative adversarial networks [3,10,11] and transformers [12–14] have also demonstrated strong performance in OOD detection in medical imaging. More recently, diffusion models have emerged as a powerful alternative, enabling anomaly detection through a partial diffusion process [4,15,16] . Latent diffusion models further improve efficiency [17,18] , while masking and stitching techniques help preserve healthy tissue during the diffusion process [19–21] . Reconstruction-based OOD detection is typically quantified using metrics such as absolute/squared error, structural similarity index measure (SSIM) [22] , and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) [23] . However, Meissen et al. [24] highlighted their limitations, leading to post-processing techniques such as normalization, morphological operations, and body contour masking [3,19] . Standardizing scores based on ID dataset statistics is also a common approach [25] , and Bercea et al. [26] introduced three normative learning-based metrics for robust medical anomaly detection. Some model architectures support combining metric maps over multiple resolutions [7] , modalities [27,28] , latent vectors [14,29] , and reconstructions [18,30,31] . Focusing on SSIM, various ensemble strategies have been explored for OOD detection [32–34] . In this work, we investigated whether a reconstruction-based AE could effectively detect anomalies and artifacts in brain MRI in an unsupervised manner. The decision to use a simple AE was made because it provides a more straightforward and efficient approach compared to the more complex models, while also serving as a foundation for them, thereby effectively addressing the underlying challenges. We first evaluated the trade-off between latent space size and reconstruction capability to determine optimal model configurations. We then examined whether the absolute reconstruction error is sufficient for anomaly detection or whether alternative metrics, such as SSIM, perceptual metrics, or including ensembles of different metrics, provide better performance. These experiments were initially conducted on an OOD dataset with homogeneous circular anomalies to select the optimal configuration. We then performed our analysis on an extended brain MRI dataset containing three types of local artifacts and seven types of global artifacts. Through these experiments, we analyzed deep learning design decisions and proposed refinements to improve OOD detection in medical imaging. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We propose an AE optimized for OOD detection by deviating from standard practices. • We demonstrate that the appropriate selection and combination of models and metrics improves OOD detection. • We conduct an in-depth analysis of artifact severity and its influence on OOD detection. • We provide two OOD brain MRI datasets with controlled local and global artifacts, enabling systematic evaluation and comparison. We propose an AE optimized for OOD detection by deviating from standard practices. We demonstrate that the appropriate selection and combination of models and metrics improves OOD detection. We conduct an in-depth analysis of artifact severity and its influence on OOD detection. We provide two OOD brain MRI datasets with controlled local and global artifacts, enabling systematic evaluation and comparison. An overview of the proposed pipeline is presented in Fig. 1 . To support reproducibility and encourage further research, the code for generating the synthetic OOD datasets, for training and testing the model, including the model weights, is publicly available at . We used the publicly available brain MRI dataset from the MOOD challenge. 2 2 . This dataset contains a brain MRI scan for 800 healthy individuals. The resolution of each scan is 256 × 256 × 256 voxels, and we linearly rescaled the intensities of the 3D volumes to [ 0 , 1 ] . We randomly divided the MOOD dataset into an ID training set (720 cases) and ID validation set (80 cases). For both the training and validation sets, we included the middle 20 axial slices to create a homogeneous dataset for a 2D implementation and evaluation. We call these sets of axial slices MOOD train and MOOD val , respectively. An example of a slice from MOOD val is shown in the upper left corner of Fig. 2 . In addition, we created an OOD validation set with synthetic circular artifacts called MOOD art_circ . This set is based on MOOD val to facilitate direct comparisons between the images in the two sets, and to allow parameter tuning. To generate MOOD art_circ , a homogeneous circle was added to the 1600 axial brain slices in MOOD val . This was done by selecting a non-zero voxel as the center and then randomly selecting a radius r ∼ U ( [ 20 , 40 ] ) and an intensity i ∼ U ( 0 , 1 ) . The added circle inherently provides a ground truth segmentation label for pixel-level evaluation. An example of a slice from MOOD art_circ is shown in the lower left corner of Fig. 2 . An extended set with more types of synthetic artifacts, called MOOD art_ext , was created based on MOOD val to evaluate the performance of the model on more realistic artifacts. Specifically, we introduced three types of local artifacts: circular lesion (similar to MOOD art_circ but smaller circles), black stripe, and patch swap. In addition, we introduced seven types of global artifacts: blurring, noise, elastic deformation, patient motion, MRI bias field, MRI ghosting artifact, and MRI spikes (also known as Herringbone artifact). For each artifact type, artifacts were introduced for the entire validation set, resulting in ten new validation sets of 1600 slices to allow direct comparison with MOOD val . All artifacts were systematically introduced and increased in severity in N steps. The parameters for the creation of these artifacts are summarized in Table 1 and an example for each artifact is shown in Fig. 2 (second to last columns). Note that due to the range of artifact parameter values, some resulting slices may not be distinctly OOD as the severity of the artifact gradually increases. For example, a slice with subtle elastic deformation could be a naturally occurring variation rather than being OOD. A detailed description on the creation of each artifact type can be found in Appendix A and our code is publicly available at . In this work, we use an AE as implemented in the MONAI generative models library [35] for the task of OOD detection. Specifically, the architecture of the Kullback–Leibler (KL)-regularized latent space AE as described in [17,36] was used. However, since our task is not to generate samples, but only to reconstruct, we have removed the latent space sampling and the KL divergence. The network architecture consists of a convolutional cascade using residual blocks [37] followed by down- or up-sampling, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . Furthermore, the model includes a PatchGAN discriminator [38] to allow for adversarial training to improve the image reconstruction. We experimented with four versions of the AE with different latent space sizes: 2 × 2, 4 × 4, 8 × 8, and 16 × 16. Each model achieves its respective latent size by modifying the model depth to include n blocks of the double residual blocks, followed by the down- or up-sampling layer. Note that the last block does not use a down- or up-sampling layer. The number of channels used for the feature representations is described in Table 2 and the number of latent channels is set to c z = 32 unless stated otherwise. The models were trained using a weighted combination of L1 reconstruction loss, perceptual loss [23] (using VGG-16 features [39] ), and least squares adversarial loss, with respective weights of 1, 2e−3 and 5e−3. Each model was trained for 100 epochs with a batch size of 4 using Adam optimizer. The learning rates for the generator and discriminator were set to 1e−4 and 5e−4, respectively. The optimal epoch, i.e. the model with the lowest generator loss for MOOD val , was selected for inference. All models were implemented in Pytorch 2.2.0 with CUDA version 12.1 and trained on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080-Ti 11 GB GPU or an NVIDIA TITAN XP 12 GB GPU. Six different reconstruction metrics were used to assess the reconstruction quality and identify anomalies. Given an input image x and its reconstructed image x ˆ , an error map of the same size as x and x ˆ was calculated for each metric. Absolute error ( E a b s ) was calculated to measure the absolute difference between corresponding pixels in x and x ˆ , defined as (1) E a b s ( x , x ˆ ) = | x − x ˆ | . Structural similarity is based on three components: contrast, luminance, and structure. These components are computed using the mean intensities μ x and μ x ˆ , the standard deviations σ x and σ x ˆ , and the covariance σ x x ˆ between the input image x and the reconstruction x ˆ . Small constants C 1 = 0 . 0001 , C 2 = 0 . 0009 , and C 3 = C 2 / 2 are included for numerical stability. Practically, SSIM is computed over local windows of 7 × 7 pixels to capture local similarity. Additionally, negative values in σ x , σ x ˆ , and σ x x ˆ were clipped to zero to ensure that SSIM scores remain within the [0, 1] range. The three components are evaluated separately and combined as SSIM and are defined as follows: Contrast ( c ) assesses the contrast between the two images, accounting for variations in pixel intensity, defined as (2) c ( x , x ˆ ) = 2 σ x σ x ˆ + C 2 σ x 2 + σ x ˆ 2 + C 2 . Luminance ( l ) measures the brightness of the images, capturing the mean intensity of the pixels in both images, defined as: (3) l ( x , x ˆ ) = 2 μ x μ x ˆ + C 1 μ x 2 + μ x ˆ 2 + C 1 . Structure ( s ) captures the structural information between the two images, reflecting how pixel patterns correlate spatially. It is defined as (4) s ( x , x ˆ ) = σ x x ˆ + C 3 σ x σ x ˆ + C 3 . Structural similarity index measure (SSIM) combines these three components to provide an overall measure of similarity between x and x ˆ , calculated as (5) SSIM ( x , x ˆ ) = c ( x , x ˆ ) ⋅ l ( x , x ˆ ) ⋅ s ( x , x ˆ ) Learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) [23] captures perceptual similarity between x and x ˆ by computing feature-level differences at each spatial location, defined as (6) LPIPS ( x , x ˆ ) = ‖ ϕ ( x ) − ϕ ( x ˆ ) ‖ 2 2 , where ϕ ( . ) represents the features extracted from a pre-trained AlexNet [40] , which is a widely adopted network for extraction of perceptual image features and is in line with previous work on OOD detection [4] . In order to quantitatively evaluate the overall performance of the reconstruction metrics presented in Section 2.4 , the mean of the respective reconstruction map was computed to obtain one prediction score for each slice. To facilitate combinations of reconstruction metrics, the reconstruction error maps must be in the range of 0 (indicating a negative prediction) to 1 (indicating a positive prediction). To ensure that all metrics were consistent with this range, we inverted the SSIM and its components, yielding 1 − SSIM ( x , x ˆ ) , 1 − c ( x , x ˆ ) , 1 − l ( x , x ˆ ) , and 1 − s ( x , x ˆ ) . Then, we averaged multiple (inverted) reconstruction maps to combine metrics, resulting in a final anomaly prediction map A . When evaluating performance per slice, we again took the average of the prediction map A to obtain one score per slice, represented by A ̄ . In cases where local anomalies were present and a ground truth mask was available, the prediction task could be seen as a pixel-level classification problem. This approach enabled the generation of a Precision–Recall curve for any (inverted) prediction map with values ranging from 0 to 1. Finally, we quantified the overall performance using the area under the Precision–Recall curve (AUPRC) as suggested by Baur et al. [3] . We calculated the Precision and Recall at thresholds evenly spaced between 0 and 1, with a step size of 0.02. Furthermore, for subsets consisting of global artifacts, we calculated sample-level AUPRC based on the average score per slice ( A ̄ ). To ensure that both positive and negative samples were represented, each OOD subset was combined with MOOD val . Statistical tests were used to assess the statistical significance of the observed differences in mean prediction maps between the data sets. Specifically, when comparing the results of a validation set with those of the training set, we applied a one-sided Mann–Whitney U test [41] with a significance level of α = 0 . 01 . This non-parametric test, suitable for comparing two independent samples that may not follow a normal distribution, was conducted to assess whether the validation set’s performance is significantly greater than that of the training set. When comparing the performance of one type of artifact in MOOD art_ext with the performance of MOOD val dataset, we used a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test [42] with a significance level of α = 0 . 01 . This test assesses whether the performance of the extended artifact dataset is significantly higher than that of the ID validation set, providing insight into pairwise performance differences between the two sets. We conducted a set of experiments to (1) evaluate general reconstruction capability of the model, (2) analyze the effect training epoch and overfitting, (3) identify the most effective reconstruction metric, (4) assess the feasibility of combining models and/or metrics, and (5) evaluate the effectiveness of our OOD detection model on a more realistic OOD dataset. We analyzed the trade-off between a smaller latent space, which limits the model’s ability to optimally reconstruct ID data, and a larger latent space, which enables the reconstruction of OOD data. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of models with latent space sizes of 2 × 2, 4 × 4, 8 × 8, and 16 × 16. The number of channels in the latent space ( c z ) is set to 32, 64, or 128. We assessed the reconstruction capability on the MOOD train , MOOD val , and MOOD art_circ sets using the mean E a b s (MAE) per slice. Statistical significance is calculated between MOOD val and MOOD train , as well as between MOOD art_circ and MOOD train . To investigate the effect of OOD detection, we analyzed how different training epochs impact the model’s ability to generalize. Overfitting may lead the model to memorize training examples, potentially hindering its performance in detecting OOD data, as we aim for the model to learn the overall training distribution rather than specific instances. However, OOD detection is different from traditional deep learning models, where all sets are assumed to be from the same distribution. Therefore, we examined the effect of selecting the optimal and final epoch for the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models. Again, we analyzed the MAE of the MOOD train , MOOD val , and MOOD art_circ datasets and calculated the statistical significance between MOOD val and MOOD train , and between MOOD art_circ and MOOD train . The MAE is a limited measure of reconstruction quality because it only captures local intensity changes, in a pixel-by-pixel manner, and does not include perceptual, structural, or contrast components. Therefore, in this experiment, we evaluated the usefulness of different reconstruction metrics. The metrics used were all the reconstruction metrics described in Section 2.4 : absolute error, luminance, contrast, structure, SSIM, and LPIPS. Specifically, we visualize the results of all metrics, and then quantitatively select the optimal metric by calculating the AUPRC of the (inverted) metric maps. We present the results of the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models for both the final and optimal epochs. The strengths of different models and metrics can be combined to achieve the best performance. For this experiment, we analyzed the Precision–Recall curve for different combinations of models and/or metrics. Specifically, we examined the reconstruction errors in terms of LPIPS and contrast of the final epoch for the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models. We calculated the final anomaly prediction map A by taking the average of LPIPS and 1 − c ( x , x ˆ ) of both models. To determine the effectiveness of the model in translating to a more nuanced and realistic artifact dataset, we tested the model on MOOD art_ext . Specifically, the final prediction map for each slice ( A ) was calculated as the average of the LPIPS and 1 − c ( x , x ˆ ) maps for both the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models. To obtain a single score per slice, the mean of each final prediction map was taken, which we refer to as A ̄ . For each artifact type we investigated whether each MOOD art_ext sample had a significantly higher score A ̄ compared to its MOOD val counterpart. In addition, for the subsets containing global artifacts, we present sample-level AUPRC values computed from A ̄ . Naturally, evaluating the local artifacts (circular lesion, black stripe, and patch swap) at the global level using A ̄ , yields results that are substantially influenced by the size of the local anomaly. Therefore, for these local anomalies, we also present the pixel-level AUPRC values calculated based on the final prediction maps A . Furthermore, since the extended artifact dataset was systematically constructed based on carefully selected parameter values for each artifact type, we investigated the correlation between parameter values and OOD detection performance. We quantified these correlations by calculating the Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ [43] between the parameter value and the final score A ̄ . This coefficient takes into account the ordinal relationship between the ranks of individual test case performances, providing robustness to variations in the scale and direction of the values. Fig. 4 shows the reconstructions of a random MOOD val input and its MOOD art_circ counterpart for all the different models with a fixed number of latent channels of c z = 32 . We observe that the 2 × 2 model seems to reconstruct a rough average brain image. The 4 × 4 model appears to be more successful in preserving the original anatomy of the brain while roughly inpainting the abnormal region. However, because of the still relatively high absolute error in other parts of the brain, the anomalous region is not standing out in the error map. Furthermore, the less deep models with latent spaces of 8 × 8 and 16 × 16 show that they are not able to “heal” the anomalous region and therefore not able to detect it based on the reconstruction absolute error. Fig. 5 shows that the overall reconstruction error in terms of MAE per axial slice decreases as the depth of the model increases, and thus the size of the latent space decreases. A well-trained OOD detection model would show a low reconstruction error for both the MOOD train and MOOD val datasets, and a high reconstruction error for the MOOD art_circ dataset. However, we observe different patterns for the different model depths. The 2 × 2 model achieves the best distinction between MOOD val and MOOD art_circ , while maintaining consistency between MOOD val and MOOD train . On the other hand, the 4 × 4 model is severely overfitted to the training set since it does not generalize well to MOOD val . The 8 × 8 and 16 × 16 models show less overfitting, but also do not clearly distinguish between MOOD val and MOOD art_circ . Statistical analyses confirm that only for the 2 × 2 model is the reconstruction error for the MOOD val set statistically indistinguishable from that of MOOD train ( p = 0 . 035 ). In contrast, all other reconstruction errors for MOOD val and MOOD art_circ are significantly higher ( p ∼ 0 . 000 ) than for the training set. Based on these observations, the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models were used for further experiments. Furthermore, no large differences in MAE were observed when using a different number of latent channels for the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models (Figure B.1 in Appendix B). However, the models with 32 latent channels showed the highest degree of overlap between MOOD val and MOOD train , and the lowest degree of overlap between MOOD val and MOOD art_circ . Therefore, 32 latent channels were used for further experiments. A general expectation is that when a deep learning model is trained for an extended period, it will overfit to the training data. This was indeed observed by examining the reconstruction errors of our models ( Fig. 6 ). Specifically for the 2 × 2 model, the model shows strong overfitting to the MOOD train set and does not generalize well to the MOOD val set when the last epoch was selected compared to when the epoch with the lowest validation loss was selected. However, when analyzing two examples in Fig. 7 , the reconstruction appears to be of higher quality when the final epoch is selected compared to the optimal epoch. It seems that the anatomy of the brain has changed as a result of the reconstruction based on the final epoch, which also resulted in a large absolute error similar to that of the optimal epoch. In the case of MOOD art_circ , the anomaly is healed in addition to the changed brain anatomy. Thus, at first glance, one would assume that the anomalous region would be detected, but this region is not significantly out of distribution compared to the changed brain structures and therefore not clearly identified when using the absolute error as reconstruction metric. Fig. 8 highlights the impact of metric selection on detecting anomalies in reconstructed images, demonstrating that each metric reveals different reconstruction characteristics. The absolute error for the 2 × 2 model show small deviations across the cortical folds, including both gray and white matter, while the central brain regions show limited errors. In contrast, the absolute error for the 8 × 8 model shows minimal deviations overall, with neither model effectively capturing the abnormality. The contrast component effectively detects the anomaly in both models, although the 2 × 2 model includes more false positive structures throughout the brain. Luminance errors remain generally low for both models, with the 2 × 2 model showing minor errors at the outer brain boundary. The structure component reveals significant reconstruction errors in the cortical folds for the 2 × 2 model. Based on the structure, the reconstruction quality of the 8 × 8 model is relatively low but consistent, which allows better detection of the anomaly. Looking at the SSIM, we observe that the low performance of the structure component overshadows the contrast and luminance components. SSIM again highlights large errors within the cortical folds for the 2 × 2 model, with reduced errors for the 8 × 8 model, where the anomaly is more pronounced. Lastly, LPIPS presents low errors with a smooth appearance, with only slight emphasis on the outer region of the brain in the 2 × 2 model and no effective capture of the brain structure or anomaly. In terms of quantitative analysis ( Fig. 9 ), the contrast metric demonstrated the highest AUPRC of 0.46 for the final epoch of the 8 × 8 model. Furthermore, the LPIPS metric demonstrated a high AUPRC value of 0.42 for the final epochs of both the 2 × 2 model and the 8 × 8 model. These findings suggest that metrics sensitive to perceptual errors, such as LPIPS, and those focusing on contrast variations, such as the contrast metric, may provide more effective anomaly localization. Fig. 10 shows a randomly selected input image alongside its OOD counterpart, along with the reconstructions derived from the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models. The figure includes separate prediction maps for LPIPS and contrast, as well as combined predictions. Notably, the combination of LPIPS and contrast reduces false positive structures in the brain without substantially compromising anomaly detection. The LPIPS metric primarily identifies the anomaly from the 2 × 2 model, while the 8 × 8 model provides a more subtle indication. In contrast, the 8 × 8 model clearly highlights the anomaly with fewer false positive structures compared to the 2 × 2 contrast prediction, which is marked by additional false detections in other brain regions. This observation suggests that combining models and metrics effectively leverages the strengths of both models and metrics, optimizing anomaly detection while reducing false positives. The prediction map that combines both models and both metrics results in a visually coherent and perceptually pleasing representation. This visual observation is further supported by the AUPRC for the individual and combined reconstruction maps ( Fig. 11 ). It can be observed that the combined prediction map resulted in a higher AUPRC than when each model was considered separately. Specifically, for the 2 × 2 model, the combination of LPIPS (AUPRC = 0.41) and contrast (AUPRC = 0.33) resulted in an AUPRC of 0.49. Similarly, for the 8 × 8 model, the combination of LPIPS (AUPRC = 0.41) and contrast (AUPRC = 0.46) resulted in an AUPRC of 0.56. Furthermore, when combining both models per metric, there was an increase in AUPRC when using the LPIPS (AUPRC = 0.49) and contrast (AUPRC = 0.55). Moreover, an even more pronounced improvement in performance was observed when the predictions of both models and both metrics were combined, resulting in an AUPRC of 0.66. All artifact types resulted in a significantly higher A ̄ compared to the A ̄ of MOOD val ( p ∼ 0 . 00 ), indicating that all artifact types resulted in a measurable deviation in OOD detection ( Fig. 12 ). Although the circular lesion and black stripe artifacts had only slightly elevated mean scores of 0.078 and 0.082, respectively, compared to the ID validation mean of 0.070, paired analysis showed that they had consistently higher scores across all paired samples. As mentioned above, the global performance A ̄ for the local artifacts is highly dependent on the size of the anomaly, which is not the case when evaluating at pixel-level. AUPRC values of 0.50, 0.18, and 0.55 were found for the subsets of circular lesions, black stripes, and patch swaps, respectively ( Table 3 ). Contrary to the observations presented in Fig. 12 , the AUPRC indicates that detecting black stripes is more difficult than detecting the circular lesions and patch swaps. For the global artifacts, high sample-level AUPRC values ranging from 0.81 to 1.00 were observed across all subsets ( Table 3 ). High values for A ̄ were found for ghosting, motion, noise, and spikes ( Fig. 12 ). However, for these artifacts, the background pixel intensities were altered due to the design of the artifact generation method. This led to large reconstruction errors in the background regions, resulting in high values for A ̄ (Figure B.2 in Appendix B). In addition, the bias field artifact shows a large spread in A ̄ and was also generally well captured by the model. Nevertheless, a large spread in the values of A ̄ is not unexpected since the datasets were generated by systematically increasing the values of the artifact parameters. The expectation that a higher severity of the artifact would lead to a higher value of A ̄ was confirmed for most artifact types. This is particularly evident for bias field ( Fig. 13 ) and blur ( Fig. 14 ). The standard deviation used for blurring and the coefficients used for the bias field show near-perfect correlations with A ̄ of MOOD art_ext , with Spearman rank correlation coefficients of ρ = 0 . 962 and ρ = 0 . 956 , respectively ( Table 4 ). In contrast, other artifact types showed weaker correlations. For example, for the ghosting artifact there was a strong correlation ( ρ = 0 . 864 ) between the number of ghosts and the score A ̄ of MOOD art_ext , while the intensity showed significantly less impact on the model’s detection capability, with a correlation of only ρ = 0 . 184 . This trend is also reflected in the scatter plots presented in Fig. 15 . A notable observation is the correlation of ρ = − 0 . 123 between the intensity of circular lesions and A ̄ , which stands out as the only negative correlation across all artifact types and the one with the smallest magnitude. A large positive ρ would suggest that brighter circular lesions are better detected, while a large negative ρ would imply that darker lesions are easier to detect. However, the observed weak negative correlation suggests the absence of a strong linear correlation. This could indicate either that there is no relationship or that detection is influenced by non-linear factors, such as the contrast of the lesion relative to the surrounding tissue. One could speculate that circular lesions with extreme intensity values (very dark or very bright) may be better detected because of the higher contrast. Figure B.3 in Appendix B provides further insight into this relationship, showing no strong overall correlation between intensity and A ̄ . Nevertheless, very dark lesions with low intensities appear to stand out slightly, demonstrating marginally better detection compared to other intensity values. Another notable observation, based on Fig. 12 and Table 4 , is that while motion artifact is well detected as anomaly, the correlations between the detected motion and the motion parameters are relatively weak, with values of ρ = 0 . 241 and ρ = 0 . 091 for rotation and translation, respectively. This indicates that the amount of rotation and translation does not substantially affect the detection process. Scatter plots for other artifact types not shown in the main paper can be found in Appendix B, providing a comprehensive overview of these correlations across all artifact parameters. The detection of OOD and anomalies in medical images remains a challenging and unsolved area of research. While numerous pipelines have been developed, many are overly tailored to specific datasets, limiting their generalizability. In addition, we observe a trend to increase model complexity, while the potential of less complex models remains underexplored. Another important research direction is the exploration of deep learning strategies and reconstruction metrics explicitly tailored for OOD detection. In this study, we focused on OOD detection in brain MRI using an reconstruction-based AE, emphasizing the importance of deep learning design choices and metric selection. This study shows that redefining the OOD detection pipeline, specifically the choice of reconstruction metric, in a standard AE can improve performance compared to using a standard OOD detection pipeline with an absolute error reconstruction metric. Our model with the smallest latent space size achieved the best separation between ID and OOD data while maintaining generalizability, whereas models with larger latent spaces reconstructed both ID and OOD data well. These results are consistent with previous research that emphasizes the importance of balancing latent space size and reconstruction capability in OOD detection [3,44] . In addition to selecting an appropriate latent space size, we found that combining multiple models improved performance. While our approach relies on architectural diversity, prior work has demonstrated the benefits of ensembles, specifically ensembles of models trained with different seeds, for OOD detection [45] . Furthermore, our work highlights the critical yet underexplored role of selecting the training epoch and the reconstruction metric in OOD detection. We found that the optimal training epoch for the reconstruction model does not always coincide with the best detection performance, and that metrics sensitive to perceptual errors and those focusing on contrast variations may provide more effective anomaly localization. By selecting a well-converged model and using appropriate metrics, we improved OOD detection performance. Specifically, the AUPRC for the 2 × 2 and 8 × 8 models based on the absolute error was 0.26 and 0.15, respectively, while combining both models and using the LPIPS and contrast metrics resulted in an AUPRC of 0.66. Direct comparisons with existing literature are challenging due to the lack of benchmark data. The closest comparison can be made with the MOOD 2020 challenge [1] , which included a toy brain MRI test set similar to our circular artifact dataset. In this challenge, the median ranked team achieved a pixel-level AUPRC of approximately 0.77 on the toy test set. However, this value reflects the influence of various factors, such as the larger anomaly sizes (up to twice the radius of our maximum radius) and the possibility that teams optimized their models to detect such homogeneous toy-like anomalies, while our model was not specifically tuned for this purpose. These differences prohibit a proper comparison with our AUPRC of 0.66. Among the evaluated metrics, contrast and LPIPS consistently outperformed others in detecting circular artifacts. The strong performance of LPIPS is consistent with previous studies highlighting the usefulness of perceptual metrics in anomaly detection [6] . Other studies have also explored the potential of SSIM ensembles derived from multiple resolutions, features, or implementations [32–34] . However, our study investigates the individual components of SSIM for OOD detection, providing a novel perspective on this widely used metric. We developed our proposed pipeline using a dataset with homogeneous circular artifacts and applied it directly to an extended dataset with more artifact types without any fine-tuning. The results showed variability in performance across artifact types, depending on the nature of the artifact. Local artifacts were significantly more difficult to detect, yielding AUPRC scores ranging from 0.18 to 0.55, compared to an AUPRC of 0.66 on the circular artifact dataset. Although most of the global artifacts were clearly distinguishable from the ID validation set, the severity of some artifacts significantly affected how OOD a sample appeared. This raises a question for OOD detection models in medical imaging: at what point should an image be flagged as OOD, or when might it be better categorized as rare but still ID? Our study has several limitations that may affect the interpretation and generalizability of the results. First, the synthetic nature of our OOD datasets may reduce the applicability to real-world clinical scenarios, where medical anomalies exhibit different characteristics. Additionally, the extended artifact dataset may have caused misleading results due to changes in background intensities in some of the global artifacts caused by data re-normalization and could have been corrected for. These background intensity changes made it challenging to interpret the correlation between artifact parameters and detection performance. Another limitation is our primary focus on pixel-level anomaly detection, leaving binary sample-level assessments unexplored. Because some medical imaging tasks require binary decisions, such as flagging images for downstream analysis, exploring post-processing and thresholding techniques is important. However, we chose not to pursue this, as it requires extensive experiments on large, diverse, and representative OOD datasets, conditions not met by our current synthetic OOD set. Our findings highlight several promising directions for future research. First, a more detailed analysis of model convergence and overfitting for OOD detection is recommended. Such an analysis could, for example, include nearest-neighbor comparisons between test samples and the training set to better understand how overfitting affects the representation of healthy tissue in OOD test samples. Second, validation of the proposed approach on clinical OOD datasets is essential. Such datasets would capture a variety of medical anomalies and/or scanning artifacts, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s performance. In addition, as our setup focused exclusively on brain MRI, future work could explore other imaging modalities or anatomical regions to evaluate the model’s generalizability. The nature of the anomalies (local or global) and the intended application of OOD detection (e.g., anomaly localization or flagging of OOD samples for a downstream task) will determine the need to extend the sample-level prediction pipeline to enhance its utility. A final direction for future work is to investigate how the proposed metric ensemble generalizes to other reconstruction-based approaches, such as (latent) diffusion models for medical OOD detection [15,19,21] . These models have shown strong performance and could benefit from the insights gained through our metric ensemble approach. Our study demonstrates that a straightforward reconstruction-based AE, when combined with perceptually sensitive metrics such as contrast and LPIPS, can effectively improve OOD detection in brain MRI. We highlight the importance of both latent space size and metric selection for accurate detection. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that different deep learning design choices, such as model depth, number of training epochs, and metric selection, must be carefully evaluated for the task of OOD detection, as standard approaches often originate from different objectives and may fail to capture various types of anomalies. Enhancing skin cancer detection through category representation and fusion of pre-trained models The use of pre-trained models in medical image classification has gained significant attention due to their ability to handle complex datasets and improve accuracy. However, challenges such as domain-specific customization, interpretability, and computational efficiency remain critical, especially in high-stakes applications such as skin cancer detection. In this paper, we introduce a novel interpretability-assisted fine-tuning framework that leverages category representation to enhance both model accuracy and transparency. Using the widely known HAM10000 dataset, which includes seven imbalanced categories of skin cancer, we demonstrate that our method improves the classification accuracy by 2.6% compared to standard pre-trained models. In addition to precision, we also achieve significant improvements in interpretability, with our category representation framework providing more understandable insights into the model’s decision-making process. Key metrics, such as precision and recall, show enhanced performance, particularly for underrepresented skin cancer types such as Melanocytic Nevi (F1 score of 0.94) and Actinic Keratosis (F1 score of 0.66). Furthermore, the prediction accuracy of the proposed model of the top-3 reaches 98. 21%, which is highly significant for medical decision making. This observation in interpretability underscores the value of top- n predictions, especially in challenging cases, to support more informed and accurate decisions. The proposed fusion framework not only enhances predictive accuracy, but also offers an interpretable model output that can assist clinicians in making informed decisions. This makes our approach particularly relevant in medical applications, where both accuracy and transparency are crucial. Our results highlight the potential of fusing pretrained models with category representation techniques to bridge the gap between performance and interpretability in AI-driven healthcare solutions. Skin cancer [1] is among the most common types of cancer, marked by abnormal and uncontrolled proliferation of skin cells [2] . It often results from exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun or tanning beds, leading to the formation of malignant tumors. Skin cancer remains a major cause of death worldwide. Dermatologists typically diagnose it through visual examinations, which have an accuracy rate of around 60% [3] . The limitations of dermoscopy and the demand for higher diagnostic accuracy have fueled advances in computer-aided detection methods [4] . These systems generally follow five key steps: image acquisition, pre-processing, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. Medical image processing [5] involves the analysis and interpretation of medical images in 2D and 3D to aid diagnosis, treatment planning, and medical research [6] . Although 3D imaging techniques such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are commonly used to visualize complex internal structures, 2D medical images, such as X-rays or dermoscopic images for the detection of skin cancer, are equally important. Medical image processing is crucial for the identification of diseases, the guide for surgical interventions, and the support of research by providing detailed information on anatomical and pathological conditions. It encompasses a variety of techniques, including image enhancement, segmentation, and analysis, tailored to improve precision in clinical decision-making. The development of medical image processing has evolved significantly, especially with recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), revolutionizing non-invasive diagnostics and making medical imaging an essential component of modern healthcare [7] . AI has enabled more accurate and automated image analysis, improving disease detection, treatment planning, and clinical decision making. However, medical images pose unique challenges compared to other types of images due to their complexity, variability, and the critical need for precision [8] . Medical images often contain subtle features, such as small tumors or abnormalities, that require specialized algorithms for accurate detection to extract the particular ‘subtle’ feature. Furthermore, factors like varying image quality and differences in imaging modalities make it challenging to process medical images with the same techniques used for general images. Addressing these challenges requires AI-driven solutions that can handle the nuances of medical images. There are some very popular and well-known pre-trained models designed for medical data. • CheXNet [9] ( ): A model proposed by Stanford ML Group, trained on chest X-rays images to detect pneumonia, backbone with a 121-layer convolutional neural network. • DeepMind’s RetinaNet [10,11] ( ): A model trained on retinal images to detect diabetic retinopathy, its architecture is based on ResNet CNN backbone. • VNet [12] ( ): A volumetric (3D) extension of the UNet for 3D medical image segmentation, where UNet ( ) is a convolutional network architecture for biomedical image segmentation. • Med3D [13] ( ): A collection of 3D neural network models pre-trained on large-scale medical datasets. • DenseNet121 [14] ( ) pre-trained in CheXpert ( ): A DenseNet model trained on the CheXpert dataset for chest radiograph analysis. • BioBERT [15] ( ): primarily a language model focusing on biomedical text mining that includes entity recognition, relation extraction, question answering, etc., it has been used for various biomedical text tasks, including radiology report analysis. • 3D ResNet [16] ( ): A 3D version of ResNet, used for volumetric medical data. • nnU-Net [17] ( ): A self-adapting framework for biomedical image segmentation that automatically configures itself for different datasets. In clinical applications, neural networks have significantly facilitated the classification of disease categories, particularly with the advent of pre-trained models, ensemble models, and foundation models. These models are especially useful in situations that involve small datasets, enabling them to achieve reasonable results in clinical databases. However, several challenges remain in the skin cancer detection issues. The classification of medical image data faces several critical challenges that require innovative solutions to ensure efficient and effective results. First, many state-of-the-art models used in medical image analysis have complex architectures, making re-training and fine-tuning computationally expensive and storage-intensive. The high number of epochs needed to achieve accurate results significantly increases both computational power and memory requirements. Reducing these costs is essential for broader generalization and practical applications. Second, medical images often contain subtle features that are more difficult to identify compared to general image classification tasks. These features require specialized techniques for detection and classification. Furthermore, medical data sets are frequently imbalanced, with insufficient amounts of data for certain conditions, making it difficult to train models that perform well on minority classes. Addressing this imbalance and developing strategies to improve performance with limited and underrepresented medical data is a significant challenge. Lastly, the interpretability of the model is a crucial factor in medical imaging. Beyond producing accurate predictions, models must provide information that helps healthcare professionals understand the reasoning behind the results. This interpretability helps physicians make informed decisions about further diagnosis and treatment. Managing these challenges can lead to more efficient and accessible medical image processing solutions, ultimately improving patient care and medical outcomes. Summary of Motivation Enhancing pre-trained models is of paramount importance due to their limitations in domain-specific tasks. Although these models are efficient and easy to implement, they often face difficulties with specialized datasets, show potential biases, and lack interpretability, particularly in fields such as medical imaging where understanding the reasoning behind predictions is crucial for diagnosis and treatment. There are several challenges in applying existing interpretability algorithms to medical datasets: 1. Gradient-based interpretability methods , such as SHAP and Captum , use input gradients to provide attribution or highlight important nonlinear activations. However, in skin cancer data, crucial features often contribute equally, resulting in entire images being highlighted with minimal differentiation. This makes it difficult to apply these highlighted regions for accurate cancer identification. 2. Certain interpretability approaches , such as Lime and GradientSHAP, are designed for tabular data, where they assign importance to individual features. However, when applied to image data, these methods face high computational costs due to the need for large candidate datasets, often leading to memory allocation errors. Additionally, small sample support and layer analysis visualization can result in overly complex, all-relevant maps that create biased and inefficient outcomes in medical data. 3. A fundamental limitation of existing classification-based interpretability methods is the lack of a comprehensive analysis. Crucial information, such as the confidence level of the inference, the likelihood of potential errors, and the recommendations of the top- n results, is often absent. Visualizing and interpreting these metrics would be much more useful for medical professionals than simply providing raw numerical output. Summary of Contributions In this paper, we focus on the study of skin cancer data, the most common cancer and one of the leading causes of death worldwide. The standard HAM10000 dataset includes seven imbalanced categories of skin cancer. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose an interpretability-assisted fine-tuning technique to enhance the performance of baseline models. Specifically, we apply category representation derived from sparse representation to identify non-active neurons in pre-trained model, which guide the fine-tune process in low-cost and improve the performance in specific task. Sparse representation involves expressing a signal as a linear combination of a few fundamental components, or “atoms”, from an over-complete dictionary. This concept has diverse applications, including in image processing, machine learning, and medical imaging. The solution of the Sparse representation in the application involves compressed sensing. Meanwhile, sparse representation is also the key Compressed sensing, which is a method that efficiently acquires and reconstructs signals by solving underdetermined linear systems, assuming signals are sparse or can be sparsely represented in a particular domain. By exploiting this sparsity, compressed sensing recovers signals from fewer measurements than typically required. The steps to compute a sparse representation include: • Define the Dictionary: Construct an over-complete dictionary of atoms that exceeds the signal’s dimensionality. • Formulate the Optimization Problem: Set up an optimization problem to represent the signal as a sparse combination of dictionary elements, minimizing nonzero coefficients while maintaining accuracy. • Solve the Optimization Problem: Using algorithms such as Matching Pursuit (MP), Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), Basis Pursuit (BP), or LASSO to iteratively select atoms that best approximate the signal. • Reconstruction: Reconstruct the signal by combining the selected atoms with their corresponding coefficients. The process starts with input images (e.g., skin cancer images) resized to fit the backbone model requirements. The default linear classification layer of the backbone model is replaced with a fully connected layer, customized for the dataset’s number of classes (e.g., seven for the skin cancer dataset). We then extract intermediate feature representations { X s 2 i , … , X s 2 j } from M s 2 using the register hook method, where the user selects the feature layers i and j . Active neurons from these layers are grouped according to their true and correctly predicted class labels, forming the category representation as shown in Fig. 2 . The next step is to verify these representations through validation, constructing a stack of candidate category groups. To identify the worst-performing category group, we evaluated the validation set using sparse representations. The category representations, formed from the training data, serve as a library , while the validation image acts as a query . Sparse coefficient vectors ideally have large values in the regions of the library corresponding to the correct class. The worst category group indicates the region of non-active neurons, leading to a second fine-tuning step where only the non-active neuron regions are updated, resulting in the final model M s 3 . For inference, we combine the decision probabilities from both the backbone model and category representation using a weighted average. The highest probability determines the prediction label. To further evaluate the quality of deep neural networks (DNNs), we utilize WeightWatcher, an open-source diagnostic tool designed to analyze DNNs without requiring access to training or test data. It is grounded in the Theory of Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (SR), which helps determine if and when a specific DNN layer has converged correctly. Unlike traditional tools, WeightWatcher provides unique insights into the performance of individual layers. When running WeightWatcher, the tool generates a results table, with a key metric being the “ alpha ” value, which indicates the quality of the layer’s training. Ideally, alpha values should fall between 2 and 6, signaling that a layer is well-trained. Layers with alpha values outside this range may require further optimization. The proposed category representation not only aids in evaluating and identifying underperforming layers, allowing targeted fine-tuning to enhance the model, but also assists in interpreting feature representations and predicting classification results. The well-trained category representation, later constructed as the Library , can interpret new features derived from test images of unknown types. From a medical standpoint, skin cancer types are rigorously defined according to specialist guidelines on abnormal skin cell behavior. Structurally, different cases of the same skin cancer type share common features aligned with these regulations. Consequently, images of the same type of skin cancer tend to produce homogeneous features when processed through the model pipeline. Various open-source methods have been developed to enhance the interpretability of the model, allowing researchers and developers to easily identify the characteristics that influence the output of a model. In this section, we experiment with Captum (meaning “comprehension” in Latin) , and SHAP (SHapley Additive ExPlanations) , two popular methods for interpreting the results of models M s 3 ResNet and M s 3 EffNet . SHAP is a game-theoretic approach that explains the output of any machine learning model, while Captum, an open-source library built on PyTorch, offers advanced interpretability algorithms such as Integrated Gradients. Due to computational limitations, we specifically employed DeepLIFT and Saliency from the Captum library. DeepLIFT assigns significance to each input pixel by comparing the differences between the output and a reference relative to the differences between the input and the reference. Saliency, a baseline method for input attribution, returns gradients with respect to inputs, providing their absolute values by default. We review the potential trade-offs between interpretability, scalability, and computational overhead as follows. From the deployment point of view, the framework consists of two components: model creation and interpretability. Since only a training and validation dataset are required, retraining and library creation occur in the backend, while medical facilities use a pre-trained model for inference and interpretability analysis. The EfficientNet model (15.8 MB) and category representation library (3.64 MB) are lightweight, with the library available . Computational demands, including UMAP-based visualization, remain feasible for medical facilities. From the scalability point of view, The model requires fine-tuning when new databases become available to ensure unbiased outcomes. As it does not support continuous learning, periodic retraining is necessary for updates. This paper presents an interpretability-assisted framework for improving the performance of pre-trained models, with a specific focus on medical image classification tasks. By incorporating category representation and optimizing computation through fast aggregation techniques, we significantly reduce resource costs while enhancing model generalization and applicability. Additionally, our approach identifies inactive neurons, allowing for targeted model improvements. Experimental results on skin cancer data, along with comparisons with the WeightWatcher tool, demonstrate that our method achieves higher accuracy and better interpretability. These advancements not only improve classification performance but also provide valuable insights for medical decision-making, ultimately contributing to more effective and accessible AI-driven healthcare solutions. In addition, we conducted experiments using the WeightWatcher tool to identify underperforming layers. The results suggest that a more sophisticated strategy may be required to fully leverage WeightWatcher’s analysis for model improvement. In our experiments on skin cancer data, with a few epochs of fine-tuning in active neurons, the model achieved a 2.5% improvement in classification performance in the best case. Furthermore, the projection of category representations aligned well with the classification reports, providing reasonable interpretability. Limitation and Future work Despite the promising results of the proposed methods, there are several limitations related to interpretability and model performance. 1. The category representation technique is designed to be independent of both the baseline model and dataset, as its interpretability focuses on the model’s decisions and confidence in its performance. This flexibility allows the representation to be applied to any baseline model and image dataset. However, in the current framework, the category representation learned from models like ResNet and EfficientNet has shown insufficient feature learning. Furthermore, the framework does not account for metadata, which limits both the performance and the interpretability of medical-related signs and symptom inference. Future work will focus on improving the representation of features and integrating metadata to improve the explanation of critical medical indicators. 2. The interpretability based on category representation provides a general overview of the model’s performance, such as decision confidence, top-n classifications, or potential error sources. However, it lacks specific information on decision-making elements. This approach does not capture critical medical indicators or biomarkers that are essential in medical decision making. For example, in the diagnosis of melanoma, distinguishing signs such as a large brownish spot with darker speckles or a mole that changes in color, size, or texture are crucial to accurate classification. However, such medical signs are not included in the current interpretability framework. In future work, our goal is to focus on identifying and integrating these key medical biomarkers to enhance interpretability and directly inform classification decisions. 3. Additionally, the category representation identifies nonactive neurons in pre-trained models, which helps detect poorly trained layers. However, if each layer performs consistently with only minor variations, the category representation may fail to pinpoint neurons for improvement, and consequently may not enhance model performance. For research goals focused on further increasing the classification accuracy, additional strategies and improvements are required. Enhancing the robustness of CNN-based lung cancer detection models against label-flipping poison attacks using defensive distillation Deep learning has significantly advanced automated medical imaging, particularly in lung cancer detection, yet vulnerability to adversarial manipulation continues to limit clinical reliability. This study investigates the impact of a 30% random-uniform label-flipping poisoning attack on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models trained using the IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset comprising 1190 CT images. A multi-strategy defense pipeline is proposed, integrating defensive distillation, Isolation Forest data sanitization, and a noise-tolerant loss function to enhance robustness against training data corruption. To ensure a valid evaluation framework, Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied only to the clean training subset before any poisoning was introduced, preventing the propagation of corrupted labels and establishing a balanced and uncontaminated foundation for teacher training. A high-accuracy teacher model trained on this clean SMOTE-balanced dataset produces temperature-scaled soft labels that guide the Student model. The Student is then trained on a sanitized dataset filtered to remove anomalous or inconsistent samples, using Symmetric Cross-Entropy loss to reduce sensitivity to mislabeled data. Experimental results show that the pipeline maintains strong performance, achieving 99% accuracy on clean data and 95 to 96% accuracy under poisoning, while preserving stable precision, recall, and confidence calibration across all classes. These findings demonstrate that the proposed strategy effectively mitigates label-flipping poisoning, offering a reproducible path toward secure and trustworthy AI systems for medical imaging applications. Cancer remains one of the leading global health challenges, accounting for nearly 10 million deaths in 2020 and maintaining its position as the second most common cause of death worldwide [1] . The World Health Organization projects that cancer incidence will continue to rise due to aging populations and lifestyle-related factors [2] . Lung cancer is the deadliest, causing approximately 1.8 million deaths annually [3] . The primary reason for this high mortality rate is the late-stage diagnosis of lung cancer, when treatment options are limited and less effective, whereas early detection substantially improves five-year survival rates [4] . Conventional diagnostic methods, including chest radiography, sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, and biopsy, have limitations in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and patient comfort [5] . These procedures are time-intensive, require substantial clinical expertise, and impose financial burdens. Two emerging approaches, liquid biopsy and molecular imaging, have shown promise in improving diagnostic accuracy and reducing invasiveness [6] . Liquid biopsies detect circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood samples [7] , while molecular imaging visualizes biological processes at a cellular level with high precision [8–10] . When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), these tools have the potential to significantly strengthen early detection and augment clinician decision-making. AI, particularly machine learning and deep learning, has transformed medical imaging by enabling the automated recognition of subtle and complex patterns that are beyond human perceptibility [11] . Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), capable of hierarchically learning spatial features [12] , have achieved expert-level accuracy in detecting and classifying lung nodules from CT scans [13,14] . Despite these advancements, clinical deployment of AI models remains hindered by concerns related to data quality, interpretability, and system security. A critical limitation of AI-based diagnostic pipelines is their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. Such attacks manipulate model behavior by introducing imperceptible perturbations or malicious modifications to training data, leading to incorrect predictions that human observers cannot detect [15] . Poison attacks are particularly severe, as attackers compromise the integrity of the training data by introducing or altering samples [16] . Medical imaging datasets are especially vulnerable because they often aggregate data from diverse and inconsistently validated sources [17] . A poisoned lung-cancer detection model could misclassify malignant nodules as benign, delaying treatment with potentially fatal consequences. In realistic clinical environments, a poisoning event could occur if an attacker gains access to the hospital’s PACS ingestion workflow, for example, through unsecured research data import interfaces, compromised external datasets, or manipulated contributions during multi-institutional data aggregation, making large-scale label corruption, such as the 30% random-uniform poisoning simulated in this study, feasible. Although a growing body of research has explored defenses against adversarial and poison attacks, many remain insufficiently validated for medical imaging. Traditional approaches often fail under substantial training data corruption. Standard adversarial training primarily protects against test-time perturbations and is less effective when the attack manipulates the training distribution itself. In medical imaging, label-level corruption can silently propagate through the training pipeline, resulting in high-confidence diagnostic errors without obvious warning signs. This raises legal, ethical, and safety concerns that undermine trust in AI-assisted clinical care [15,18–24] . Therefore, enhancing robustness against label corruption is essential for safe and trustworthy integration of AI systems in healthcare. Defensive distillation, originally proposed for model compression, has emerged as a promising method for improving resilience to adversarial perturbations [25] . The technique trains a secondary student model using softened probability distributions (soft labels) from a primary teacher model , reducing sensitivity to small variations in input data and enhancing robustness [26] . Given the limitations of existing single-stage defenses, this study proposes a structured multi-stage pipeline that integrates data sanitization, soft-label distillation, and noise-tolerant loss functions to counteract label corruption at multiple points in the training workflow. This research aims to: (1) evaluate baseline CNN performance on clean datasets; (2) simulate a 30% random-uniform label-flipping poison attack; (3) measure its impact on diagnostic accuracy and class-wise performance; (4) apply defensive distillation and symmetric cross-entropy to mitigate poisoning; and (5) compare the robustness of baseline and defended models. By addressing these objectives, the study contributes to the development of secure, reliable, and clinically deployable AI systems for lung cancer detection. Over the years, AI has played a significant role in enhancing medical imaging procedures, with CNNs serving as a foundation in the automated detection of diseases. Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of CNN-based models in identifying lung nodules from computed tomography (CT) scans, often achieving or exceeding expert-level diagnostic performance [27–33] . These models leverage hierarchical feature extraction to detect subtle image patterns that may escape human interpretation, thereby enabling early lung cancer detection and improving patient outcomes. Despite these advancements, CNN-based diagnostic systems are not immune to data-related vulnerabilities that can undermine their reliability in clinical image detection domains. Recent research has highlighted a critical vulnerability in AI models, susceptibility to adversarial and poisoning attacks. Adversarial attacks subtly perturb input data to induce misclassification without perceptible changes to human observers [34] . Poisoning attacks, by contrast, target the training phase by injecting malicious or mislabeled samples, thereby corrupting the learned decision boundaries and reducing trustworthiness [35–39] . In medical imaging, such manipulations could result in false negatives that delay treatment or false positives that lead to unnecessary interventions, both of which have serious clinical implications. Furthermore, reliance on pretrained models (e.g., ImageNet-based architectures) to compensate for limited medical datasets increases attack transferability, amplifying the risk of compromised model integrity in clinical use [35] . These findings highlight the urgency of strengthening AI pipelines against data poisoning and adversarial manipulation. To counter these vulnerabilities, several defense mechanisms have been explored, including adversarial training, input preprocessing, feature squeezing, and model regularization. Each approach offers certain advantages but also introduces trade-offs related to computational cost, generalization, and diagnostic performance. Among the more promising methods is defensive distillation , introduced by Papernot et al. [40] . This approach trains a student model on softened probability distributions from a teacher model, effectively reducing sensitivity to small perturbations and improving robustness against certain classes of attacks. However, subsequent studies revealed that adaptive adversaries can still circumvent distilled models, limiting their long-term reliability [41] . Moreover, defensive distillation can impose additional computational overhead, which may hinder its adoption in time-critical clinical settings where efficiency and interpretability are paramount. Despite progress in developing robust AI frameworks, integrating scalable, empirically validated defenses into clinical workflows remains an unresolved challenge. While considerable research has focused on CNN-based medical imaging and general adversarial defenses, few studies have systematically evaluated poison attack resilience within medical imaging pipelines, particularly for lung cancer detection. The existing literature largely emphasizes improvements in diagnostic accuracy rather than security-oriented robustness testing. Defensive distillation, although conceptually suitable for improving resistance to data corruption, has not been rigorously validated in medical imaging processes involving poisoning attacks. Furthermore, prior works rarely consider the balance between robustness and computational feasibility, an essential factor for clinical deployment. Addressing these limitations, the present study evaluates the effectiveness of defensive distillation in mitigating the impacts of poison attacks on AI-driven lung cancer detection models. Specifically, it investigates whether defensive distillation can enhance model robustness without compromising diagnostic accuracy or operational efficiency, thereby contributing to the secure integration of AI into healthcare systems. In this section, we describe the methodology adopted to evaluate and enhance the robustness of our CNN model for lung cancer detection under a 30% random-uniform label-flipping poisoning attack . We developed a structured, multi-stage experimental framework that integrates defensive distillation, data sanitization, and robust loss training to strengthen model reliability against adversarial manipulation. All experiments were conducted using Python ( TensorFlow and Keras ) to ensure reproducibility and transparency. We selected CNNs as the baseline model due to their strong performance in medical imaging tasks requiring hierarchical feature extraction and spatial invariance. Prior research [12,27,28] demonstrates that CNNs achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in CT and MRI analysis, providing interpretability through activation map visualization. Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) and hybrid deep models offer high accuracy on large datasets, their computational demand and data requirements make them less feasible for our dataset size. Given the moderate dataset volume and the need for interpretability in clinical domains, we employed CNNs as the foundation for evaluating adversarial robustness and defense strategies. We developed a four-stage process to assess and improve CNN robustness, as shown in Fig. 1 . The stages include (1) baseline training, (2) poison attack simulation, (3) defensive distillation-based model hardening, and (4) model evaluation and robustness analysis. This structure provides a transparent workflow from data preprocessing to adversarial defense. We used the publicly available IQ-OTH/NCCD Lung Cancer Dataset , containing 1190 CT scan images from 110 patients classified as normal, benign, or malignant. The dataset was collected by the Iraq Oncology Teaching Hospital and the National Center for Cancer Diseases (IQ-OTH/NCCD) in 2019 [42] . All images are anonymized and publicly hosted on Mendeley Data . Since the dataset does not contain personally identifiable information, this research qualifies for exemption from the Institutional Review Board (IRB). We adhered to ethical guidelines for secondary use of medical data, maintaining transparency, data privacy, and non-maleficence. As shown in Fig. 3 , the IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset is moderately imbalanced, with malignant cases representing 51.1% of the samples, normal cases 37.9%, and benign cases only 10.9%. Such an imbalance can bias a CNN toward predicting the majority class and reduce sensitivity to clinically important minority categories, particularly benign nodules. To correct for this, we applied the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) to the clean training split only , before any poisoning was introduced . This sequencing is essential for methodological validity: applying SMOTE after poisoning would artificially replicate corrupted labels and potentially amplify the adversarial signal. By oversampling the clean dataset prior to label flipping, all subsequent experiments, including baseline training, poisoning, teacher-model training, and data sanitization, originate from the same unbiased and balanced feature distribution. SMOTE operates in the feature space by interpolating between minority-class neighbors to generate synthetic samples rather than duplicating existing ones. This helps preserve decision boundaries and improves the robustness of both the teacher and student models during distillation. Because SMOTE was applied after the initial train–validation split , the validation set remained untouched and reflects the natural class distribution of the dataset, ensuring an unbiased evaluation of generalization performance. Our baseline CNN, inspired by the VGG architecture, comprises two convolutional blocks (each with 3 × 3 kernels and 64 filters), followed by max-pooling and dropout. The output is flattened and passed through a dense layer (16 neurons, ReLU) and a softmax layer for classification across three classes. We trained for 50 epochs using the Adam optimizer ( η = 0 . 001 ) and evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score (see Table 1 ). We implemented a defensive distillation pipeline ( Fig. 4 ) combining teacher–student knowledge transfer, data sanitization, and robust loss optimization. The teacher model learns soft distributions from clean data; the student learns from these softened labels even when training data contain corrupted samples. The teacher network was trained exclusively on the clean, SMOTE-balanced dataset prior to any label corruption to ensure unbiased feature learning and reliable soft-label generation. This distinction is critical because using poisoned data for teacher training would propagate corrupted knowledge to the student. This facilitates knowledge transfer by allowing the student network to learn inter-class similarity patterns rather than hard one-hot boundaries, enhancing robustness to label noise. We selected Isolation Forest (IF) algorithm as the data sanitization mechanism in our defense pipeline because its anomaly-based reasoning aligns naturally with how label-flipping poisoning disrupts neural feature representations. When the teacher model is trained on clean data, it produces structured and semantically coherent embeddings for each class. In contrast, samples with corrupted labels retain their true visual characteristics but no longer align with the embedding cluster of their assigned (flipped) class. This feature–label mismatch often pushes poisoned samples toward lower-density or boundary regions of the teacher’s feature space, causing them to behave as representational outliers. IF is particularly effective in this setting because its split-based isolation process identifies points that require fewer partitions to isolate, a behavior expected of samples exhibiting inconsistent embedding patterns. Unlike density-based methods such as LOF or One-Class SVM, IF scales well to high-dimensional CNN features and makes no assumptions about cluster shape, which is advantageous given the complexity of CT-derived lung patterns. Although poisoned samples may not always appear as strong statistical outliers, our observations show that IF reliably detects samples with atypical activation behavior relative to the teacher model’s learned manifold. Removing these anomalous samples before student training reduces the influence of corrupted supervisory signals without additional labels or computational overhead. Thus, IF provides a theoretically grounded, efficient, and lightweight data sanitization step within the broader robustness framework. While visualization techniques, such as t-SNE, could further illustrate the clean versus poisoned separation, the underlying representational principle supports IF as an appropriate choice for mitigating poisoning in clinical AI pipelines. Using an identical architecture enables a controlled evaluation of how defensive distillation improves robustness under label-flipping poisoning without introducing confounding factors related to model compression or representational limitations.
