This section provides a comprehensive evaluation of the model’s robustness under label-based poisoning and demonstrates the effectiveness of the multi-stage defensive distillation framework. We present a detailed progression from the baseline CNN through the poisoned model to the robust student model, using accuracy–loss plots, confidence charts, and classification reports. Each result is contextualized in terms of model behavior, experimental objectives, and comparable findings from prior studies in adversarially robust medical imaging. We first trained our baseline CNN on the clean IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset to establish a reference for evaluating later degradation and recovery. Loss values dropped below 0.02, confirming minimal prediction error and stable optimization. The absence of divergence between training and validation metrics demonstrates that the model generalizes well when labels are correct, establishing a high-fidelity baseline for later comparison. As shown in Fig. 6 , the model predicts Normal and Malignant cases with near-unity confidence ( ≈ 1.00). This level of certainty demonstrates not only high accuracy but also strong calibration, a key requirement in clinical settings where confidence can guide human interpretation. While the perfect metrics for the Benign class should be interpreted with caution due to its smaller support size (30 samples), the results overall demonstrate that, in the absence of poisoning, the CNN learns well-separated and highly discriminative representations for all classes. We next trained the same CNN after randomly flipping 30% of labels. This simulates a realistic data-poisoning attack. The model showed drastic degradation and instability. As seen in Fig. 7 , both training and validation accuracy stagnated around 36%–39%, barely above random guessing for three classes. The loss plateaued near 1.1, reflecting convergence to a trivial constant-class prediction. This phenomenon, known as class collapse , occurs when corrupted supervision prevents the model from forming meaningful boundaries. Fig. 8 shows uniformly low confidences ( ≈ 0.36) across all inputs, with the model defaulting to predict the “Normal” class. This indicates severe uncertainty and loss of calibration, critical evidence of successful poisoning. Table 4 illustrates the severe degradation caused by a 30% label-flipping attack. Both the Benign and Malignant classes exhibit zero Precision, Sensitivity, and F1-Score, indicating that the model fails to identify any samples belonging to these clinically important categories. Instead, it collapses toward predicting the majority of samples as Normal, a failure mode commonly observed when poisoned labels distort class boundaries. Although the Normal class maintains a Sensitivity of 1.00, this comes at the expense of catastrophic misclassification of the other two classes. These results emphasize that overall accuracy alone (38%) masks the extent of the collapse and highlight the necessity of our defense pipeline, particularly to preserve malignant Sensitivity in medical diagnostic settings. We implemented a three-component defense: (1) Defensive distillation using a teacher model with temperature 10.0 and label smoothing 0.1; (2) Data sanitization via Isolation Forest (contamination 0.1); and (3) Symmetric Cross-Entropy (SCE) loss to handle noisy labels. This combination aims to restore accuracy and confidence even under 30% label-flipping (see Tables 5 and 6 ). In evaluating robustness, it is important to distinguish between defenses that target test-time perturbations and those that address corruption within the training process. Adversarial training is designed to counter inference-time attacks and does not correct mislabeled samples or detect inconsistencies introduced through poisoning. Because label-flipping directly alters the supervisory signal, the most informative baseline is a model trained on the poisoned dataset without any defense mechanisms. This baseline exhibited severe degradation, with accuracy falling to 38% and malignant Sensitivity to zero, illustrating the vulnerability of standard CNNs. The defended model’s substantial recovery under the same conditions demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed multi-stage pipeline in mitigating the specific failure mode introduced by label corruption. The teacher model achieved early convergence with validation accuracy of ≈ 99.5%, confirming that it captured robust class features for soft-label generation (see Fig. 9 ). The distilled student model maintained validation accuracy between 98%–100%, despite originating from data once containing 30% flipped labels. The low, stable loss demonstrates that distillation and sanitization together prevent overfitting to noise (see Fig. 10 ). Fig. 11 shows that correct predictions exceed 0.98 confidence, confirming excellent calibration. Even under attack ( Fig. 12 ), the model retains high confidence for correct predictions and reduced confidence for errors, evidence of uncertainty awareness rather than blind overconfidence. Fig. 13 reveals that while training accuracy remains low (due to poisoned labels), validation accuracy stabilizes around 95%, confirming generalization to clean validation data. Under clean validation ( Table 7 ), the robust student model achieved 99% accuracy with near-perfect Precision, Sensitivity (Recall), and F1-Scores across all classes. Importantly, the malignant class preserved a Sensitivity of 1.00, indicating that no malignant cases were missed, a critical requirement in clinical diagnostic settings. Under a 30% label-flipping attack ( Table 8 ), overall accuracy remained high at 95%. Although benign precision dropped to 0.83, the model retained perfect benign Sensitivity (1.00), meaning all true benign cases were correctly identified. Malignant Sensitivity remained strong at 0.95, demonstrating that the defense pipeline maintains reliable detection of cancerous samples even under severe label corruption. The moderation of previously perfect scores reflects a more realistic performance distribution, confirming that the defended model generalizes effectively while preserving clinically essential sensitivity. All experiments were conducted on the Google Colab Pro+ platform equipped with an NVIDIA A100 GPU (40 GB VRAM) and Intel Xeon CPU, providing a high-performance environment suitable for deep learning experimentation. Training the baseline CNN model required approximately 38 min, whereas the complete three-stage defense pipeline, comprising SMOTE preprocessing, Isolation Forest sanitization, and defensive distillation, extended total training time by approximately 2.4 × . The additional overhead is primarily attributed to feature extraction for anomaly detection and the dual forward passes in the teacher–student architecture, which collectively increased memory utilization by about 30% . Despite these computational demands, inference latency remained low at approximately ≈ 42 ms per image, demonstrating the pipeline’s suitability for near real-time clinical decision support. Future optimization efforts will explore quantization, model pruning , and mixed-precision training to further reduce computation and memory requirements for deployment in low-resource healthcare environments. Moreover, given that model training in medical AI workflows is typically performed offline and updated periodically rather than in real-time, this increase in training time is operationally acceptable. The inference speed remains unaffected, ensuring that clinical deployment and real-time decision-support capabilities are not compromised. Although this study evaluates robustness under a 30% label-flipping attack, the model’s performance trends suggest that the defense pipeline remains effective as long as clean samples dominate class structure during teacher training. Prior poisoning studies indicate that distillation-based defenses begin to degrade when poisoning exceeds approximately 40%–50%, at which point corrupted labels overwhelm the feature–label consistency required to form stable class clusters. While higher poisoning rates were not empirically tested here, this range provides a reasonable estimate of the system’s operational safety limits. Establishing the precise breaking point remains an important avenue for future work. Our results parallel previous findings that CNNs are highly sensitive to label corruption yet recover strongly under distillation. Bortsova et al. [35] and Wang et al. [26] reported similar robustness improvements of 50%–60% under defensive distillation. The combined SCE-loss and Isolation-Forest filtering in our pipeline yields a comparable high accuracy recovery while preserving computational efficiency. The progression from 38% (poisoned) to 95% (defended) accuracy validates that knowledge distillation with sanitization meaningfully enhances resilience. The discrepancy between perfect and degraded results across experiments reflects realistic boundary conditions of sample size and attack severity. The defended model exhibits reliable calibration, interpretability, and high diagnostic potential, key prerequisites for trustworthy deployment in clinical AI. While the defensive pipeline significantly enhanced resilience against label-flipping attacks, several limitations remain that motivate future exploration. • Scope of Attack Types: This study focused exclusively on random-uniform label-flipping attacks. However, more sophisticated poisoning strategies exist, including clean-label attacks , where image content is manipulated while labels remain correct, and backdoor or trigger-based attacks , which embed imperceptible patterns that activate targeted misclassification at inference time. Evaluating the proposed pipeline against these emerging threat models represents a critical next step in establishing comprehensive robustness against poisoning. • Ablation Studies: Due to computational constraints, we did not isolate the individual contributions of SMOTE preprocessing, Isolation Forest sanitization, and the Symmetric Cross-Entropy loss. A systematic ablation study will be conducted in future work to quantify the marginal benefit of each defense component. • Dataset Size and External Validation: The IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset is relatively small ( N = 1190 ), and although the model demonstrates strong internal generalization, external validation on multi-institutional or larger-scale CT datasets is necessary to ensure broader clinical applicability and robustness across diverse populations. • Computational Overhead: The combined SMOTE–IF–distillation pipeline increases training time and memory usage compared to a standard CNN. In this research, we proposed a robust defense framework to enhance the reliability of deep learning models for lung cancer detection under label-flipping poison attacks. Recognizing the vulnerability of medical AI systems to adversarially manipulated training data, we designed a multi-strategy defense pipeline that is both interpretable and computationally practical. The framework integrates a teacher–student distillation process, in which a teacher model trained on clean, SMOTE-balanced data generates soft probability targets, followed by Isolation Forest-based data sanitization to filter anomalous or potentially poisoned samples. The student model is subsequently trained using symmetric cross-entropy loss to improve resilience against residual label noise and corrupted supervision. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this defense. The robust student model achieved 99% accuracy on clean validation data and maintained 95% accuracy under a 30% label-flipping attack, with minimal sensitivity loss in clinically critical classes. Confidence-based analysis further showed well-calibrated predictions, characterized by high confidence in correct classifications and reduced confidence in misclassified instances, supporting the framework’s reliability for medical decision support. Looking ahead, future work will extend this defense pipeline to more sophisticated and clinically relevant adversarial threats, including clean-label poisoning attacks and backdoor or trigger-based attacks, which represent the next evolution of poisoning techniques beyond label manipulation. We also plan to evaluate the method on larger and multi-institutional datasets and explore lighter-weight model variants suitable for real-time diagnostic settings. Moreover, the proposed defense pipeline offers a practical, scalable, and effective approach for enhancing the robustness of AI-driven lung cancer detection systems, thereby strengthening their safety and trustworthiness in adversarial and safety-critical clinical environments. Evaluation of liver metastasis volume changes in longitudinal CT images using statistical modeling and adversarial image registration networks Assessing treatment response and disease progression in patients with liver metastases requires accurate quantification of volumetric changes across longitudinal CT scans. Therefore, it is essential to achieve reliable registration of post-treatment volumes to their corresponding pre-treatment scans. This study proposes an adversarial diffeomorphic image registration framework that integrates the Gaussianization transformation for statistical normalization of liver intensities. Because liver CT data often exhibit skewed and heavy-tailed intensity distributions, the Gaussianization transformation maps voxel intensities into an approximately Gaussian distribution, thereby improving conformity with the Gaussian noise assumptions of probabilistic registration models. By incorporating this step within a generative adversarial training pipeline, the model learns to produce accurate and anatomically consistent deformation fields. Experiments on 128 longitudinal CT scans from 64 patients, with external validation on the Liver DIR Landmark dataset, demonstrated that Gaussianization substantially enhanced registration accuracy and convergence stability. The method achieved a mean target registration error of 1.586 ± 0.729 mm, normalized mutual information of 1.229 ± 0.018, and boundary HD95 of 2.756 ± 0.293 voxels (all P < 0.02), while reducing inference time from 120 ± 33 s to 30 ± 9 s per volume (≈75% faster). Application to volumetric analysis showed results consistent with RECIST 1.1 partial response classification. These findings demonstrate that intensity Gaussianization combined with adversarial diffeomorphic registration provides accurate, efficient, and anatomically coherent alignment for quantitative longitudinal liver CT analysis. Volumetric assessment of liver tumors plays a central role in oncologic imaging follow-up, directly informing clinical decisions regarding treatment efficacy and disease progression. Liver tumors may arise as primary malignancies (e.g., hepatocellular carcinoma) or as secondary tumors (metastases) that originate from distant primary sites such as the colon, pancreas, or breast [ 1 ]. In routine clinical practice, patients undergo repeated computed tomography (CT) scans over time to monitor therapeutic response. CT imaging provides essential information about tumor size, shape, and structural alterations. However, direct comparison of pre- and post-treatment scans is often hindered by variability in patient positioning, respiratory motion, and imaging parameters. Accurate comparison of these longitudinal scans is essential to detect subtle changes in tumor burden. Image registration addresses this challenge by aligning pre- and post-treatment scans to a common spatial frame, enabling voxel-level comparison across time points. Misalignment can result in inaccurate estimates of lesion size and morphology, undermining the effectiveness of follow-up evaluation. Automatic image registration techniques, by aligning these images, facilitate precise analysis of metastatic volume changes and contribute to the evaluation of treatment effectiveness. Traditional registration methods use iterative optimization. They extract image features, select a similarity measure and a spatial transformation model, and search for optimal transformation parameters [ 2 ]. The main limitations of this approach are the slow execution speed due to its iterative nature and the susceptibility of most similarity measures to multiple local optima, often leading to premature convergence or stagnation. Recent deep learning–based methods have sought to overcome the limitations of conventional registration by learning complex, nonlinear mappings between fixed and moving images. Many of these approaches utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to directly estimate deformation vector fields or employ encoder–decoder architectures to extract hierarchical spatial features. Among these, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a powerful component within deep learning–based image registration (DLIR) frameworks [ 3 ]. These networks, widely used for image synthesis and translation, consist of two adversarial subnetworks: a generator that produces realistic outputs; and a discriminator that distinguishes real from generated samples [ 4 ]. Through iterative adversarial training, the generator learns to produce anatomically consistent and visually plausible alignments, often achieving strong performance even with relatively small datasets [ 5,6 ]. Accurate registration is particularly critical in longitudinal liver CT analysis, where even small misalignments can lead to substantial errors in estimating treatment-induced volumetric changes. Nevertheless, most existing registration methods, whether classical or deep learning–based, mainly rely on intensity similarity or feature correspondence. In reality, liver intensities vary considerably across patients and scans due to contrast enhancement, scanner differences, and tissue heterogeneity. These factors challenge stable and anatomically consistent alignment. To achieve high-precision alignment, it is important to account for the statistical characteristics of liver CT data rather than relying solely on raw intensity similarities. In this paper, we investigate the role of statistical intensity modeling and Gaussianization transform in improving the performance of deep deformable registration networks for longitudinal liver CT. Our central hypothesis is that transforming CT intensities toward a statistically normalized, Gaussian-like distribution enhances learning stability and leads to more realistic and anatomically faithful deformation fields. To examine this hypothesis, we propose a statistically informed adversarial registration framework that integrates a Gaussianization transform within a GAN-based diffeomorphic model. This design enables the network to learn smooth, physically plausible deformations while preserving local structural details, thereby improving the reliability of volumetric change estimation in metastatic lesions. The proposed method learns non-rigid, diffeomorphic deformations between image pairs by optimizing a GAN-based objective that incorporates both similarity and regularization terms. Notably, integrating Gaussianization into the registration pipeline enhances learning stability and convergence, particularly in anatomically challenging regions such as liver edges. Experimental results show that using Gaussianized inputs improves registration accuracy and anatomical consistency compared to models trained on unnormalized data. The aligned post-treatment volumes were subsequently used for segmentation and longitudinal analysis, enabling reliable quantification of treatment-induced changes in metastasis volume at the patient level. By bridging statistical modeling with deep learning-based registration, our framework provides a clinically applicable solution for monitoring disease progression and evaluating therapeutic response in liver cancer. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: • Longitudinal dataset curation: Collection and annotation of pre- and post-treatment liver CT scans to support research in registration, segmentation, and response evaluation. • End-to-end processing pipeline: Development of a structured workflow encompassing liver segmentation, Gaussianization, deformable registration, metastasis segmentation, and volumetric change analysis. • Statistical normalization: Introduction of a Gaussianization transform to achieve intensity consistency across scans and enhance the accuracy and stability of deformable registration. • Adversarial diffeomorphic registration: Implementation of a GAN-based registration framework that combines a U-Net generator with a PatchGAN discriminator to learn anatomically coherent deformations without ground-truth transformations. • Integrated metastasis analysis: Post-registration segmentation of liver metastases for accurate, automated quantification of treatment-induced volumetric changes. • Empirical validation: Demonstration that statistical Gaussianization improves registration performance and deformation plausibility, leading to more reliable estimation of metastasis volume change over time. Radiological longitudinal follow-up of liver tumors using CT scans is a standard clinical practice for assessing disease progression and evaluating the effectiveness of liver cancer therapies. In such studies, radiologists compare newly acquired CT scans with prior scans to monitor the progression of known tumors, detect new lesions, and quantify tumor size. Clinical practice typically follows RECIST (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors) guidelines, which rely on linear measurements of up to five target lesions to estimate tumor burden and define response categories such as Partial Response, Stable Disease, or Disease Progression [ 7 ]. While volumetric measurements provide more accurate and reliable assessment of tumor size, their use remains limited in clinical workflows [ 8 , 9 ]. Although automated methods have been developed, they are not yet widely adopted for routine longitudinal analysis. To date, only a few studies have specifically focused on the automated analysis of liver lesions in longitudinal CT data in recent years. Vivanti et al. developed an automatic pipeline for longitudinal liver CT analysis that performs deformable registration, detects new tumors, and quantifies volumetric changes in tumor burden. Their method demonstrated high detection accuracy and provided reliable volumetric assessment across serial scans [ 10 ]. Szeskin et al. introduced SimU-Net, a deep learning framework for the simultaneous segmentation and classification of liver metastases in contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scans. Although this approach represents an important step toward enabling longitudinal lesion analysis, its primary focus lies in segmentation. It lacks a dedicated mechanism for anatomically precise and geometrically controlled image registration, which is essential for robust temporal alignment [ 11 ]. In a related effort, Hering et al. proposed an AI-assisted workflow for registration and volumetric segmentation of lymph node and soft tissue metastases in longitudinal CT scans, while the results demonstrated meaningful improvements in reader agreement and reduced evaluation time, the focus of the work remained on enhancing clinical efficiency rather than achieving high precision deformable registration with preservation of anatomical lesion structure [ 12 ]. Cazoulat et al. introduced a vasculature-guided biomechanical DIR method for longitudinal liver CT scans in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma patient post-radiotherapy. By integrating a finite-element biomechanical model constrained by liver surface and vascular centerlines, their approach improved alignment under large deformations but required computationally demanding modeling and accurate vessel segmentation, limiting its automation scalability [ 13 ]. Liu et al. proposed a data-driven framework to analyze and predict liver volume change maps from pre- and post-radiation therapy CT scans. Using voxel-wise Jacobian deformation maps and deep learning–based prediction of local tissue changes, the study demonstrated the potential of learning-based deformation modeling for treatment-induced variations. However, their model was tailored to radiation therapy, where deformations are primarily localized and dose-driven, rather than to the more heterogeneous, treatment-induced changes that occur in chemotherapy-based metastasis monitoring [ 14 ]. In summary, although numerous methods have been proposed for tumor detection and segmentation in CT scans, many have emphasized coarse or superficial alignment rather than achieving high-precision image registration. The primary objective of this paper is to enable accurate analysis of volumetric changes and support reliable treatment evaluation through precise image alignment. Achieving this requires a robust registration framework capable of addressing anatomical variability in longitudinal CT scans and ensuring accurate alignment of liver metastases between follow-up images. Image registration is a fundamental task in medical imaging, enabling the spatial alignment of anatomical structures across scans acquired at different times or under different imaging conditions. Among various techniques, deformable registration methods have garnered considerable attention due to their ability to model complex, non-rigid anatomical deformations. Classical approaches often rely on diffeomorphic transformations, which preserve topology and ensure smooth, invertible mappings. Notable examples include Large Deformation Diffeomorphic Metric Mapping (LDDMM) by Beg et al. and Symmetric Normalization (SyN) by Avants et al., both of which have demonstrated high accuracy in aligning images with large geometric variability [ 15 , 16 ]. While these classical methods are effective, they are computationally intensive and require iterative optimization procedures, which limit their scalability and usability in clinical workflows. To address these limitations, learning-based deformable registration approaches have emerged, leveraging deep neural networks to estimate spatial transformations directly from image pairs. These models offer significant advantages in computational efficiency and modeling flexibility, particularly when trained in unsupervised settings. Early learning-based models primarily employed convolutional neural networks (CNNs). For example, Xiao et al. proposed Quicksilver, a deep learning framework designed to enable fast and efficient image registration, making it well-suited for large-scale applications [ 17 ]. Also, Zhang et al. introduced an unsupervised deformable registration model that eliminates the need for ground truth deformation fields while maintaining high accuracy [ 18 ]. Further, Dalca et al. extended this line of work by integrating probabilistic modeling with diffeomorphic registration in an unsupervised framework, offering improved robustness to anatomical variability [ 19 ]. Extending these advances, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently been adopted for deformable image registration due to their ability to learn more complex transformations through adversarial training [ 20 ]. In GAN-based models, a generator predicts spatial transformations to align images, while a discriminator evaluates the realism of the registered output, encouraging anatomically consistent deformations. Fan et al., introduced a GAN-based registration method applicable to both mono- and multi-modal image pairs, demonstrating improved accuracy through inter-modality similarity learning [ 21 ]. Also, Fu et al. proposed an unsupervised GAN model for 4D CT lung image registration, achieving efficient and precise alignment without labeled data [ 22 ]. Moreover, Hu et al. introduced adversarial deformation regularization, combining supervised training with realistic deformation priors learned from finite element simulations [ 23 ]. Furthermore, Yan et al. presented a GAN-based method tailored for aligning MR and TRUS images, significantly improving multi-modal fusion for prostate cancer diagnosis and intervention planning [ 24 ]. Overall, learning-based registration methods, particularly those based on GANs offer powerful alternatives to traditional approaches by delivering faster, more flexible, and accurate deformable registration, making them well-suited for complex medical imaging tasks and real-time clinical applications. Inspired by these advances, our study employs an unsupervised adversarial registration framework based on GANs. The generator adopts a VoxelMorph-inspired architecture [ 25 ] that estimates dense deformation fields between pre- and post-treatment liver CT scans [ 19 ], while the discriminator learns a similarity metric to guide accurate anatomical alignment [ 26,27 ]. While adversarial training enhances registration capability, its success is heavily influenced by the statistical properties of input image intensities. In medical imaging, CT and MRI scans often exhibit non-Gaussian intensity distributions due to scanner characteristics, anatomical variability, and pathology. These statistical inconsistencies can hinder the performance of models that rely on Gaussian noise assumptions in the likelihood formulation, as seen in probabilistic registration frameworks. To address this, we incorporate statistical modeling and Gaussianization into the registration pipeline. Statistical modeling provides a compact and descriptive representation of intensity distributions, which is essential for robust tasks like segmentation, compression, or denoising [ 28 ]. Previous studies support this approach: for instance, Jorjandi et al. demonstrated the benefits of Gaussianization through histogram matching for OCT images [ 29 ], and others applied similar techniques in a variety of signal and image processing contexts [ 30–33 ]. In parallel, recent advances in prior-driven unsupervised learning have highlighted the potential of integrating implicit or model-based constraints within deep architectures. Li et al. introduced the Model-Informed Multistage Unsupervised Network (MIMUN) for hyperspectral image super-resolution, which incorporates physical degradation priors of hyperspectral imaging into a multi-stage unsupervised process that progressively refines reconstruction through physics-guided constraints and spectral–spatial feature enhancement [ 34 ]. In a subsequent study, Li et al. proposed the Enhanced Deep Image Prior (EDIP) framework which leverages the implicit structural regularization of convolutional networks to reconstruct hyperspectral images from internal image statistics alone [ 35 ]. Both works exemplify the growing trend of prior-driven unsupervised learning in image restoration; however, they remain focused on hyperspectral image reconstruction and do not address deformable registration or longitudinal anatomical correspondence, as required in medical image analysis. While prior studies in deformable image registration have made notable advances through deep learning and adversarial frameworks, they often overlook the statistical properties of medical image intensities that underlie these models. Our work addresses this gap by introducing a principled intensity normalization step using the Gaussianization transformation. This approach reshapes inherently skewed CT intensity distributions into a form more consistent with the Gaussian assumptions embedded in probabilistic registration models. By aligning the data distribution with the underlying likelihood formulation, the transformation enhances both the stability of adversarial training and the anatomical fidelity of the resulting deformations. When integrated into a GAN-based registration framework, this preprocessing not only improves alignment accuracy but also enables precise and reliable quantification of volumetric changes in liver metastases following. This synthesis of statistical modeling and learning-based registration defines the core innovation of our approach. Fig. 1 illustrates the proposed image processing pipeline for quantifying volumetric changes in liver metastases from longitudinal CT scans. The framework consists of five sequential stages. In the first stage, the liver is segmented from both pre- and post-treatment contrast-enhanced CT images. In the second stage, a Gaussianization transformation, specifically the Yeo–Johnson transformation, is applied to reduce skewness in liver voxel intensities and make their distribution more symmetric and Gaussian-like. This improves the compatibility of the input data with the statistical assumptions of the registration network, contributing to more stable and accurate deformation learning. In the third stage, a GAN-based deformable registration network is employed to align the normalized post-treatment liver scan to the pre-treatment reference. The fourth stage involves the segmentation of liver metastases within the registered volumes using a dedicated deep learning model. Finally, in the fifth stage, the volumetric changes in segmented metastases are quantified to support treatment response assessment. The following subsections detail each component of the pipeline, including implementation strategies and design choices. For liver segmentation, we implemented a U-Net-based deep learning architecture. This model has shown strong performance in medical imaging because its encoder–decoder structure with skip connections effectively preserves both spatial and contextual information [ 36 ]. To ensure robustness across varying imaging conditions, the model was trained on a combination of our annotated dataset and the public LiTS17 dataset. A hybrid loss function combining Dice loss and binary cross-entropy (BCE) was employed to simultaneously optimize spatial overlap and pixel-wise classification accuracy [ 31,37 ]. To refine segmentation quality, we applied connected-component analysis as post-processing. The largest connected region was retained as the liver, and smaller components were removed if they were more than eight times smaller or over 200 pixels away from the centroid of the main region, following Pham et al. [ 38 ]. The final segmentation masks were U-Net predictions reviewed and approved by a senior radiologist, ensuring consistent automated processing and clinical accuracy. We began by analyzing the intensity distribution of liver CT images through statistical modeling. Histogram analysis revealed that the data exhibit significant asymmetry and heavy-tailed behavior, deviating substantially from a Gaussian distribution. To accurately represent this structure, we evaluated several candidate models and found that a hybrid mixture of an asymmetric Laplacian and Gaussian distribution most effectively captured the sharp central peak and extended tails present in the data. This model demonstrated superior fit based on both visual inspection and quantitative goodness-of-fit metrics. Based on these findings, we applied a Gaussianization transformation to better align the empirical data distribution with the assumptions of the probabilistic diffeomorphic registration framework. In this framework, the residuals between the fixed image and the warped moving image are assumed to follow an independent and identically distributed Gaussian distribution. When the image intensities deviate from normality, this assumption is violated. By applying GT to both the fixed and moving images prior to training, we normalize the intensity distributions, ensuring compatibility with the Gaussian likelihood model. This alignment improves the statistical consistency of the learning objective and contributes to more accurate and robust deformation estimation. To implement this normalization, we employed a parametric, nonlinear statistical transformation based on the method proposed by Yeo and Johnson, which is specifically designed to reduce skewness and approximate a Gaussian distribution in real-valued data [ 39 ]. The method belongs to the family of power transformations that estimate a parameter λ from the data using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to minimize skewness and excess kurtosis in the intensity distribution. In this paper, λ was estimated independently for each CT volume to adapt to individual intensity characteristics while maintaining consistency across longitudinal scans. This per-volume estimation ensures that the transformation optimally compensates for acquisition-specific bias and patient-specific contrast variations, thereby improving comparability between pre- and post-treatment images. This process produces intensity distributions that more closely approximate a Gaussian form, improving statistical consistency for downstream tasks such as image registration. Following Yeo and Johnson [ 39 ], let x 1 , …, x n be independent and identically distributed random variables and denote the transformed variables by T ( λ , x 1 ) , …, T ( λ , x n ) . they assume that, for some λ , the transformed observations can be treated as normally distributed with some mean μ and variance σ 2 . Under this assumption, the log-likelihood function is: l n ( θ | x ) = − n 2 log ( 2 π ) − n 2 log ( σ 2 ) − 1 2 σ 2 ∑ i = 1 n { T ( λ , x i ) − μ } 2 (1) + ( λ − 1 ) ∑ i = 1 n s g n ( x i ) log ⁡ ( | x i | + 1 ) Where θ = ( λ , μ , σ 2 ) ′ and x = ( x 1 , … , x n ) ′ . They define the power transformation, T ( 0 , 0 ) : R × R → R , where: (2) T ( λ , x ) = { ( x + 1 ) λ − 1 λ ( x ≥ 0 , λ ≠ 0 ) log ( x + 1 ) ( x ≥ 0 , λ = 0 ) − ( − x + 1 ) 2 − λ − 1 2 − λ ( x < 0 , λ ≠ 2 ) − l o g ⁡ ( − x + 1 ) ( x < 0 , λ = 2 ) When λ = 1 , the transformation is nearly linear, leaving the data unchanged; λ = 0 the transformation reduces to a logarithmic function, which is beneficial for highly skewed data; λ < 1 , differences among small values are reduced, making the intensity distribution more uniform. For < 0 , a mirrored power-law function is applied similarly but symmetrically [ 39 ]. The Yeo–Johnson transformation is an extension of the Box–Cox transformation [ 40 ], originally developed as a power transformation for normalizing skewed numerical data. Its applicability has since been extended to medical image data [ 41 ]. In the context of imaging, the transformation is applied by first flattening the 2D or 3D image into a one-dimensional vector of intensity values. The Yeo–Johnson transformation is then applied element-wise across this vector. After transformation, the data are reshaped back to their original image dimensions. In summary, Gaussianization serves as a crucial preprocessing step that aligns the statistical properties of liver CT images with the core assumptions of the probabilistic diffeomorphic registration framework. By transforming skewed and heavy-tailed intensity distributions into a Gaussian-like form, it ensures that the residuals in the likelihood model follow the assumed distribution. This alignment improves the validity of the optimization objective. This statistically consistent input representation enhances the stability, convergence, and accuracy of the registration process, and lays a solid foundation for learning anatomically meaningful deformations in subsequent stages of the pipeline. To enable accurate longitudinal analysis of liver metastases, we apply a GAN-based deformable registration framework to align pre- and post-treatment CT scans. In this approach, the generator network estimates the deformation field, while the discriminator evaluates the alignment quality by distinguishing between well-registered and misaligned images. The discriminator's feedback, in the form of the adversarial loss, encourages the generator toward more accurate registration. The architecture details of these subnetworks are described in the following section. The generator sub-network is implemented using a U-Net-based architecture. It receives a pair of 3D CT volumes, the pre-treatment scan (fixed image) and the post-treatment scan (moving image), and predicts a time-stationary velocity field (z), which defines a diffeomorphic transformation used to warp the moving image to the fixed image [ 19 ]: (3) ∂ Φ ( t ) ∂ t = v ( Φ ( t ) ) , Φ ( 0 ) = I d , Φ ( 1 ) = ϕ z Here, Φ ( t ) denotes the transformation at time t, I d is the identity map and ϕ z denotes the final diffeomorphic deformation field obtained by integrating the SVF over time t ϵ [0 ; 1]. This deformation field is used to warp the moving image (m) into alignment with the fixed image (f) using a differentiable spatial transformer module [ 42 ], enabling end-to-end training of the registration framework. Following the variational probabilistic registration framework, the posterior distribution over transformations p ( z | f , m ) is approximated by a network-parameterized variational distribution q ψ ( z | f , m ) , and the training objective minimizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between them, yielding the evidence lower bound (ELBO) [ 19 ]: (4) L ( ψ ; f , m ) = − E q ψ [ log p ( f | z ; m ) ] + K L [ q ψ ( z | f , m ) ∥ p ( z ) ] Here, the likelihood term p ( f | z ; m ) is modeled as: (5) p ( f | z ; m ) = N ( f ; m ∘ ϕ z , δ 2 I ) which assumes Gaussian residuals between the fixed image and the warped moving image with variance δ 2 . This leads to a mean squared error (MSE) formulation of the negative log-likelihood: (6) − log p ( f | z ; m ) = 1 2 δ 2 ∥ f − m ∘ ϕ z ∥ 2 + c o n s t However, medical image intensities (e.g., from CT scans) often exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics due to scanner artifacts, tissue heterogeneity, or pathology. Such deviations introduce skewness, heavy tails, or multi-modal structures in the intensity distribution, violating the Gaussian residual assumption and potentially degrading model accuracy. To address this mismatch, we use the Yeo–Johnson power transform T λ , applied voxel-wise to both the fixed and moving images: f ′ = T λ ( f ) , m ′ = T λ ( m ) . This transform maps skewed intensity distributions to approximately standard Gaussian ones. As a result, the transformed residuals f ′ ( x ) − m ′ ( ϕ z ( x ) ) better conform to a Gaussian noise model with constant variance. This alignment justifies reformulating the likelihood function as: p ( f ′ | z ; m ) = N ( f ′ ; m ′ ∘ ϕ z , δ 2 I ) . Accordingly, ELBO is updated as: (7) L ( ψ ; f ′ , m ′ ) = 1 2 δ ′ 2 E q ψ [ ∥ f ′ − m ′ ∘ ϕ z ∥ 2 ] + K L [ q ψ ( z | f ′ , m ′ ) ∥ p ( z ) ] + c o n s t This step improves the statistical validity of the likelihood model by aligning the image intensity distributions with the Gaussian noise assumption. It also contributes to more stable optimization by reducing variability in the residuals, makes the estimated uncertainty parameter ( δ ′ 2 ) more meaningful, and helps the model generalize better across variations in image acquisition. By incorporating this transformation into the registration network, the learned deformations become more consistent with both anatomical structure and the underlying probabilistic model. In our framework, the discriminator serves as a learned similarity metric that guides the generator toward anatomically accurate and spatially coherent registrations. To effectively evaluate local alignment between the fixed and warped moving images, we employ a PatchGAN architecture [ 26 ]. Unlike traditional discriminators that operate on entire images, PatchGAN assesses small overlapping patches independently, determining whether each patch appears realistic or synthetically generated. This localized evaluation enhances sensitivity to fine structural details, promoting better preservation of small anatomical features during deformation. Given the limited availability of annotated medical imaging data, discriminator overfitting is a common challenge that can destabilize GAN training. To address this, we incorporate differentiable data augmentation techniques on both the fixed and moving images during training [ 43 , 44 ]. These augmentations enhance the generalization ability of the discriminator and contribute to more stable and reliable adversarial optimization. We adopt a multi-component loss function inspired by Dey et al., which guides the generator toward producing anatomically plausible and accurately aligned deformations [ 45 ]. The total objective combines four key components: image similarity, deformation regularization, adversarial realism, and spatial smoothness. Image similarity loss is computed using Localized Normalized Cross-Correlation (LNCC), a widely used metric in medical image registration due to its robustness to local intensity variations. In our framework, LNCC is applied to the intensity-transformed images f ′ and m ′ ∘ ϕ z , which have been preprocessed using the Yeo–Johnson power transform to better conform to Gaussian assumptions. The LNCC at voxel location x is defined as: (8) C C ( x ) = ∑ i ( ( f ′ ( x i ) − μ f ′ ( x ) ) ( m ′ ( ϕ z ( x i ) ) − μ m ′ ( x ) ) ) 2 ∑ i ( f ′ ( x i ) − μ f ′ ( x ) ) 2 ∑ i ( m ′ ( ϕ z ( x i ) ) − μ m ′ ( x ) ) 2 where x is the center of a local N × N × N neighborhood, x i ​ indexes the voxels in the window, and μ f ′ ( x ) and μ m ′ ( x ) denote the local mean intensities of the transformed fixed and moving images, respectively. Although this computation can be expensive when performed naively, it can be accelerated by precomputing and reusing intermediate terms, as described by Avants et al. [ 46 ]. This loss encourages the warped moving image m ′ ( ϕ z ( x ) ) to be locally correlated with the fixed image f ′ ( x ) improving alignment in anatomically meaningful regions. Deformation regularization is applied to promote both global and local smoothness in the predicted deformation field u, with the regularization loss defined as [ 47 ]: (9) L r e g = λ 1 ∥ u ¯ ∥ 2 2 + λ 2 ∑ P ϵ Ω ∥ ∇ u ( p ) ∥ 2 2 + λ 3 ∑ P ϵ Ω ∥ u ( p ) ∥ 2 2 where u ¯ = 1 n ∑ P ϵ Ω u ( p ) is the mean displacement across all voxels. The first term encourages small average displacements across the dataset, while the second and third promote spatial smoothness and penalize large individual displacements. The adversarial loss is incorporated following the Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) framework, which replaces the standard binary cross-entropy objective with a least-squares loss [ 48 ]. This choice offers two key benefits: improved training stability and higher-quality, more realistic outputs. In our registration context, it encourages the generator to produce deformations that yield anatomically plausible alignments of the moving image with the fixed image. The discriminator receives the transformed fixed image f ′ and either the aligned transformed moving image m ′ ∘ ϕ z ​ or the unaligned moving image m ′ , and learns to distinguish between them. The discriminator loss is defined as: (10) L D = 1 2 E f ′ , m ′ [ ( D ( f ′ , m ′ ) − 1 ) 2 ] + 1 2 E f ′ , m ′ ∘ ϕ z [ ( D ( f ′ , m ′ ∘ ϕ z ) ) 2 ] The generator is optimized to fool the discriminator by minimizing the following adversarial loss: (11) L G A N = E f ′ , m ′ ∘ ϕ z [ ( D ( f ′ , m ′ ∘ ϕ z ) − 1 ) 2 ] This formulation corresponds to minimizing the Pearson divergence between the distributions of real and generated samples. By applying this adversarial constraint to the registered images, the generator is driven to produce deformation fields that align images not only in terms of voxel-wise similarity (e.g., LNCC), but also in terms of global anatomical plausibility. We include L G A N ​ as one of the components in our total loss function (see Equation (13) ), scaled by a weighting factor λ G A N to balance realism with image alignment and deformation regularization. In addition to the similarity, regularization, and adversarial losses, we incorporate a Total Variation (TV) loss to suppress high-frequency noise and promote spatial smoothness in the predicted deformation field. The TV loss is defined as [ 49 ]: (12) L T V = ∑ P ϵ Ω ∑ d = 1 3 | ∇ d u ( p ) | where u ( p ) ϵ R 3 is the displacement vector at voxel, and ∇ d u ( p ) denotes the finite difference along spatial dimension d ϵ { x , y , z } . This regularization term penalizes abrupt spatial changes in the deformation field, encouraging smooth and anatomically plausible transformations across the image domain Ω. All components are combined into the final training objective as follows: (13) L t o t a l = λ s i m L L N C C + λ r e g L r e g + λ G A N L G A N + λ T V L T V + C b a s e Here C b a s e is a constant offset introduced to stabilize the loss during training by preventing numerical instabilities and maintaining balanced gradient flow, particularly in the early training stages. The weighting coefficients were empirically set as: λ s i m = 1 , λ r e g = [ 1 , 1 , 0.01 ] , λ G A N = 0.1 , λ T V = 0.5 . Because a full grid search across multiple hyperparameters is computationally infeasible for 3D medical volumes, the loss weights were tuned through a structured sensitivity analysis rather than arbitrary selection. Starting from the stable configuration reported by Dey et al. [ 45 ], we systematically varied each weight within predefined ranges and evaluated convergence behavior, deformation regularity, and registration accuracy. The final configuration provided the best trade-off between smoothness, stability, and anatomical fidelity. Perturbing individual coefficients by ±20 % caused negligible performance variation, confirming model robustness. Detailed results, including quantitative and qualitative analyses of the Total Variation weight, are provided in Supplementary Material Section 1.1. To achieve accurate and robust segmentation of liver metastases, we implemented and evaluated four state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures: U-Net, U-Net++ [ 50 ], ResUNet [ 51 ], and Attention U-Net [ 52 ]. These models were selected based on their demonstrated success in biomedical image segmentation, particularly in challenging scenarios involving small, heterogeneous, and low-contrast lesions such as liver metastases. All models were trained on cropped liver-region CT slices, obtained by applying liver masks to full abdominal scans. This region-focused strategy was designed to enhance metastatic lesion-to-background contrast and reduce false positives by excluding irrelevant anatomical structures outside the liver. To optimize both boundary precision and overall segmentation performance, we employed a hybrid loss function combining Dice loss and binary cross-entropy (BCE). Standard data augmentation techniques including random horizontal and vertical flipping, rotation, and intensity scaling were applied during training to enhance robustness against variations in metastatic lesion shape, position, and imaging conditions. Our results demonstrate the critical role of architectural design in segmentation performance. Among the evaluated models, ResUNet consistently yielded superior results, highlighting its suitability for the complex task of liver metastasis segmentation when combined with liver-region-focused preprocessing and an appropriate loss function. For metastasis segmentation, a separate post-processing filter based on minimum region size was employed. Unlike liver segmentation, where a single large region dominates, metastatic lesions can be numerous, small, and spatially dispersed. Therefore, we used a fixed size threshold to remove extremely small regions unlikely to correspond to real lesions, helping reduce false positives without compromising sensitivity to true metastases. Following segmentation, volumetric changes in liver metastases between pre- and post-treatment registered scans were quantitatively analyzed and categorized into three clinically meaningful groups: • New metastases, indicative of disease progression; • Persistent metastases, which may increase, shrunk, slightly grew or remain stable in volume reflecting treatment resistance, partial response, or disease stability; • Disappeared metastases, typically associated with favorable treatment response and lesion regression. New metastases, indicative of disease progression; Persistent metastases, which may increase, shrunk, slightly grew or remain stable in volume reflecting treatment resistance, partial response, or disease stability; Disappeared metastases, typically associated with favorable treatment response and lesion regression. For each patient, a comprehensive volumetric profile was generated, including measurements of individual metastasis volumes, total metastasis count, and overall metastatic burden, defined as the cumulative volume of all detected metastases. Changes in these metrics following treatment were assessed to quantify therapeutic impact. By comparing volumetric metrics at both the lesion and patient levels, this analysis enables objective evaluation of treatment response. It supports robust, data-driven clinical decision-making and provides a foundation for longitudinal monitoring of disease progression. All metastasis segmentations and their anatomical presentations were reviewed and approved by a senior radiologist. This work was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Isfahan University of Medical Sciences (IR.MUI.DHMT.REC.1402.054), with informed consent waived. Abdominal contrast-enhanced 3D CT scans were acquired at Al-Zahra Hospital (Isfahan, Iran) from 64 patients (31 females, 33 males; age range, 39–82 years) with pathologically confirmed liver metastases undergoing chemotherapy between August 2022 and January 2025. A total of 128 volumetric scans (50,078 axial slices) were included. In-plane resolution varied across scans, with pixel spacing ranging from 0.5 to 1.0 mm, a fixed slice thickness of 1.2 mm, and 80–1033 axial slices per volume. The dataset exhibits substantial variability in metastasis presentation: the number of metastases per patient ranged from 1 to 16, and individual metastasis volumes varied between 34 mm³ and 1430 mm³. To improve the robustness and generalization of the deep learning models, we additionally incorporated 130 CT volumes (56,713 slices) from the publicly available Liver Tumor Segmentation (LiTS) Challenge dataset. The in-plane resolution for these scans ranges from 0.56 mm to 1.0 mm, with slice thickness ranging from 0.45 mm to 6.0 mm, and axial slices numbering from 42 to 1026. The number of tumors per scan varies between 0 and 12, with volumes ranging from 38 mm³ to 1231 mm³ [ 37 ]. For external validation, we included 20 CT volumes from 10 patients in the publicly available Liver DIR Landmark dataset [ 53 ]. These scans provide paired abdominal CT volumes with expert-annotated anatomical landmarks. The volumes were acquired on various scanners with patient-level variation, but do not necessarily correspond to pre- and post-treatment follow-up scans. A total of 20 test scans from the external dataset were used to evaluate generalizability of the proposed registration framework. All scans were anonymized, converted from DICOM to NIfTI format, and preprocessed using Python (SimpleITK v2.4.1) to ensure consistency across scanners. Each volume was resampled to an isotropic voxel spacing of 1 mm³ using trilinear interpolation for image data and nearest-neighbor interpolation for segmentation masks. Intensities were clipped to the soft-tissue window (–100 to 400 HU) and linearly normalized to the range [0, 1]. Non-relevant regions (thoracic and pelvic slices) were excluded, and only slices containing liver tissue were retained. Background areas were reduced through adaptive cropping, with boundaries adjusted to preserve complete liver anatomy, and zero-padding was applied when necessary to maintain uniform volume dimensions. Liver and metastases were manually segmented in ITK-SNAP [ 54 ], by a radiology resident and an experienced clinician trained in liver imaging. Interobserver agreement prior to consensus was quantified using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) between the binary masks of the two annotators. Mean DSC was 0.97 ± 0.01 for liver segmentation and 0.88 ± 0.05 for metastasis segmentation, indicating excellent baseline agreement. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus discussion between the two annotators, and the final masks were reviewed and approved by a senior board-certified radiologist with over 10 years of experience in hepatic imaging, serving as the reference standard. A combined dataset comprising the in-house scans and the public LiTS17 collection was used for liver segmentation, totaling 258 contrast-enhanced CT scans from distinct patients. This dataset was split at the patient level into a training set of 185 scans, a validation set of 23 scans, and a test set of 50 scans to prevent information leakage. The registration-eligible subset was split at the patient level into a training set of 100 scans from 50 patients, a validation set of 8 scans from 4 patients, and a test set comprising 20 in-house scans from 10 patients and 20 external scans from 10 patients. The segmentation framework was implemented in Python using TensorFlow 2.10.0 and Keras. All experiments were conducted on a high-performance workstation equipped with an Intel Core i9-14,900 K CPU, 128 GB DDR5 RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (24 GB VRAM). Model training was fully GPU-accelerated and optimized using the Adam optimizer, following standard GAN-training conventions. Consistent with TTUR-based GAN optimization [ 56 ], we adopted different learning rates for the two networks (generator: 1 × 10⁻³; discriminator: 3 × 10⁻⁴) and used β₁ = 0 and β₂ = 0.9 to improve training stability by reducing excessive momentum. Segmentation performance of liver and metastasis models was evaluated using standard metrics: • Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) : Assesses spatial overlap between predicted and ground truth segmentations. It is particularly sensitive to both false positives and false negatives, making it a standard metric for medical image segmentation [ 46 ]. • Recall (Sensitivity) : Measures the proportion of true positive metastasis voxels correctly identified by the model. It reflects the model’s ability to detect metastatic lesions, providing insight into the completeness of detection across the dataset [ 57 ]. • Hausdorff Distance (HD95): Measures the 95th percentile of surface distances between corresponding anatomical structures in the fixed and registered images. Unlike the traditional Hausdorff Distance, which captures the single worst-case mismatch, HD95 provides a more robust measure by reducing sensitivity to outliers and noise. It effectively reflects the typical worst-case boundary error in registration [ 58 ]. • Mean Surface Distance (MSD): Provides the average distance between surfaces of the prediction and the ground truth, representing overall boundary smoothness and accuracy. The low median MSD confirms stable surface-level alignment across the cohort [ 59 ]. • Volumetric Similarity (VS): Evaluates the agreement in total predicted versus true liver volumes, with values close to 1 reflecting strong consistency. A mean VS of 0.986 demonstrates reliable volumetric estimation, which is essential for longitudinal monitoring [ 59 ]. • Absolute Volume Difference (AVD): Quantifies the absolute difference in volume (cm³) between predicted and reference segmentations. Liver segmentation was performed using a 2D U-Net architecture trained on a combination of the publicly available LiTS dataset and our in-house annotated dataset of liver metastasis patients. This hybrid training strategy enhanced the model’s robustness to both public benchmark variations and real-world clinical heterogeneity. The combination of heterogeneous intensity distributions and diverse anatomical representations allowed the model to generalize effectively across different scanners, contrast phases, and disease severities. Quantitatively, the model achieved strong and stable performance across the test cohort. The mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) reached 0.879 ± 0.026 (95 % CI: 0.782–0.945), demonstrating close agreement with expert contours. The recall of 0.896 ± 0.041 ensured consistent parenchymal coverage, indicating that the network rarely under-segmented liver boundaries. As shown in Fig. 2 , the predicted liver masks exhibit high spatial correspondence with the ground-truth annotations, confirming accurate boundary delineation and parenchymal coverage across different contrast levels and anatomical variations. Boundary conformity remained high, with HD95 = 7.56 ± 8.26 mm (median = 3.48 mm; 95 % CI: 1.65–13.46 mm) and MSD = 1.27 ± 1.22 mm (median = 0.71 mm), implying that most cases achieved sub-5 mm boundary precision, while a few outliers reflected low-contrast or irregular anatomical regions. Volumetric similarity was also robust (VS = 0.986 ± 0.018; 95 % CI: 0.974–0.996), and absolute volume difference (AVD) = 35.5 ± 42.3 cm³ (median = 16.7 cm³; IQR: 7.1–57.3), confirming reliable volumetric estimation across heterogeneous liver morphologies. These results confirm that training on data from both public and clinical sources helps the network learn features that are independent of scanner type or contrast level. This diversity makes the model more adaptable to intensity variations and leads to better overall generalization and more stable boundary detection. To investigate the statistical distribution of liver intensities, we first computed histograms from the segmented liver volumes. As shown in Fig. 3 , the intensity histogram is distinctly left-skewed and exhibits a heavy-tailed profile. A logarithmic x-axis was used to enhance visualization of the extended left tail. To quantitatively model this distribution, we fitted several candidate probability density functions (PDFs) to the raw intensity histogram: Standard Gaussian distribution, Generalized Gaussian Distribution (GGD), and a Gaussian–Asymmetric Laplace mixture model. The fit quality was evaluated using the Chi-Square ( χ 2 ) statistic, which measures the discrepancy between observed histogram frequencies p i ​ and expected model frequencies q i ​, according to [ 29 ]: (14) χ 2 = ∑ i = 1 B ( q i − p i ) 2 q i where B is the number of histogram bins. Smaller values of χ 2 indicate better fit. The fitting results are visualized in Fig. 4 (left panel), which shows the raw liver intensity histogram overlaid with the fitted candidate models. The standard Gaussian distribution (dashed black line) exhibits the poorest fit, with χ² = 8.35, failing to capture the left-skewed nature of the data. The GGD (orange line) offers only slight improvement (χ² = 9.15), still unable to model the asymmetry effectively. In contrast, the Gaussian–Asymmetric Laplace mixture model (purple line) fits the data most accurately, with χ² = 1.28. It effectively models the sharp central peak and asymmetric tails, confirming its superior descriptive power for the original distribution. Although this hybrid model performs well, its complexity motivates the use of a more efficient method. To this end, we applied the Yeo–Johnson transformation, which reduces skewness while accommodating zero or negative values. The transformation parameter was estimated as λ = 3.68 via maximum likelihood. The right panel of Fig. 4 shows the liver intensity distribution after applying the Yeo–Johnson transformation. The histogram becomes highly symmetric and closely matches the fitted Gaussian model (dashed black line), which now achieves a much lower χ² value of 0.21. This result confirms that the transformation successfully Gaussianizes the liver intensity distribution, simplifying the modeling process and enabling the use of standard Gaussian-based techniques in subsequent analyses. To illustrate the transformation’s visual effect, Fig. 5 presents an axial liver slice before and after the Yeo–Johnson transformation. Although the anatomical structures remain unchanged, the transformed image shows enhanced contrast and more uniform intensity distribution, indicating improved normalization. To further validate the normalization effect, we generated quantile–quantile (QQ) plots of the intensity values before and after transformation, shown in Fig. 6 . The QQ-plot of the original data (left panel) deviates significantly from the theoretical normal line, especially in the tails, confirming non-Gaussian behavior. In contrast, the QQ-plot of the transformed data (right panel) closely follows the diagonal line, indicating that the distribution is now approximately Gaussian. In summary, while complex models like the Gaussian–Asymmetric Laplace mixture can model skewed distributions effectively, the Yeo–Johnson transformation achieves comparable normalization in a simpler and more computationally efficient manner. This makes it a powerful preprocessing tool for standardizing liver intensities in CT data. This normalization is crucial for justifying the use of a Gaussian likelihood function in variational image registration frameworks, where the residuals between fixed and moving images are assumed to follow a normal distribution. Hence, Yeo–Johnson Gaussianization provides both statistical validity and practical robustness for downstream registration and intensity-based modeling. The checkerboard overlays clearly demonstrate that the version of our model with Gaussianization achieves superior boundary alignment, which is essential for precise volumetric analysis of metastases. Improved boundary registration directly enhances the reliability of downstream treatment response assessment, making this preprocessing step a critical component of the pipeline. Local feature matching plays a critical role in evaluating image registration performance, particularly for assessing alignment quality at the level of anatomical landmarks. The process typically involves several stages: detection of salient keypoints, extraction of descriptors, nearest-neighbor matching, outlier rejection, and transformation estimation. Classical approaches such as the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) rely on handcrafted descriptors to establish correspondences between fixed and moving images [ 66 ]. In contrast, modern learning-based methods such as SuperPoint (keypoint detection) and SuperGlue (keypoint matching via graph neural networks) offer enhanced robustness and accuracy by leveraging end-to-end deep feature learning and attention-based matching strategies [ 67 ]. In this paper, we employed SuperPoint for interest point detection and SuperGlue for matching keypoints across fixed and registered liver CT images. To eliminate incorrect matches and estimate the underlying geometric relationships, we further refined the correspondences using the RANSAC algorithm, which improves robustness against spurious alignments caused by local deformations or noise [ 68 , 69 ]. As shown in Fig. 8 , the comparative results demonstrate the spatial quality of keypoint correspondences across four registration scenarios: (a) pre-registration, (b) SyN-ANTs, (c) GAN-based registration, and (d) the proposed method, illustrated both in 2D axial slices and 3D anatomical space. Following the accurate alignment of pre- and post-treatment liver CT images, we performed liver metastasis segmentation and evaluated volume changes over time. To achieve reliable segmentation, we compared four deep learning architectures: U-Net, U-Net++, ResUNet, and Attention U-Net. Each model was trained for 50 epochs using the same data partitions, augmentation strategies, and optimizer configurations to ensure a fair and controlled comparison. Fig. 9 illustrates the training and validation performance of the four models in terms of Dice similarity coefficient and loss values over the training period. All models achieved high segmentation accuracy, highlighting the effectiveness of using liver-focused input crops and consistent preprocessing. Among the models, ResUNet exhibited the most favorable performance, achieving the highest final Dice score and demonstrating both faster convergence and greater training stability. These improvements can be attributed to its residual connections, which enable deeper feature learning and more efficient gradient flow during optimization. U-Net++ and Attention U-Net also delivered competitive results U-Net++ benefited from dense skip connections that facilitated multi-scale feature integration, while Attention U-Net leveraged attention gating to suppress irrelevant activations and enhance focus on metastatic regions. The baseline U-Net, while reliable, lacked the architectural enhancements present in the other models, which limited its final performance. Based on these results, ResUNet demonstrated the best overall accuracy, with Dice = 0.810 ± 0.036 (95 % CI: 0.713–0.876) and Recall = 0.817 ± 0.018 (95 % CI: 0.790–0.832), making it the final choice for volumetric analysis. The HD95 averaged 5.56 ± 4.14 mm, with a median of 3.20 mm (95 % CI: 2.41–8.12 mm; IQR: 2.24–6.20 mm). The MSD was 1.96 ± 0.09 mm, with a median of 1.02 mm (95 % CI: 0.87–2.12 mm; IQR: 1.0–1.5 mm), confirming robust lesion contour conformity across patients. Volumetric reliability was also strong.
