Segmentation of Magnetic Resonance (MR) images is a critical step in the quantitative analysis of skeletal muscle (SM) tissue [1] . Accurate delineation of the different individual muscle groups is needed to precisely extract morphological and functional information from relevant MRI-derived parameters such as volume, cross-sectional area, fat fraction (FF), T2 relaxation time and diffusion MR-related parameters. In particular, FF maps enable the quantification of fat infiltration in muscles, T2 values have been related to edema and inflammation, while mean diffusivity (MD) and fractional anisotropy (FA) are relevant for the assessment of muscle fiber microstructure [1,2] . Extracting these parameters at the level of individual muscle bundles is critical for assessing SM changes in both physiological and pathological conditions. For example, this is particularly important in the context of neuromuscular diseases (NMDs), where disease progression can vary significantly between different muscles [3] . Also, a detailed muscle-specific analysis is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of physical training programs and treatments [4] . SM in healthy individuals typically exhibits well-defined bundles with homogeneous texture and consistent signal intensities in healthy individuals, facilitating segmentation. However, in pathological cases where muscles have undergone fatty infiltration, as in the case of NMDs, the boundaries between muscles and surrounding tissues become less distinct, making segmentation significantly more challenging and prone to errors [3,5] . Automated segmentation methods are crucial for analyzing large cohorts of NMD patients and quantifying biomarkers, as manual segmentation would be too time-consuming. While several multi-atlas-based approaches have been developed for segmenting muscles in healthy individuals, none of these traditional methods have addressed cases of pathological individuals [5] . Advancements in deep learning (DL) have enabled the development of various automated methods for lower limb muscle segmentation, even in subjects with severe fatty infiltration [5–8] . These approaches, often based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) such as U-Net and its variants, have demonstrated significant potential in accurately segmenting individual muscles under challenging conditions. In particular, in the context of medical image segmentation, nnU-Net is a framework considered state-of-the-art (SOTA) when benchmarking different models [9,10] . However, DL models are often regarded as “black boxes” due to their lack of clear decision rules and the difficulty in interpreting the reliability of their predictions [11] . The process of assessing the uncertainty or confidence of a neural network’s predictions, known as Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) [12] , is gaining increasing attention in the context of medical image analysis [13] . In the case of segmentation, ensuring safe and effective use requires a model not only to generate predictions but also to provide a reliable confidence measure, allowing radiologists to assess uncertainty and intervene when necessary [14] . Such trustworthy models are essential for supporting radiologists in complex decision-making scenarios. A critical challenge in the context of UQ is the tendency of DL models to produce overconfident probability estimates, particularly when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) samples or outliers, which can undermine their reliability in clinical applications [15–17] . Therefore, uncertainty estimates must be properly evaluated using quantitative metrics, such as calibration measures, to ensure they accurately reflect the model’s confidence. In the context of muscle segmentation in NMDs, where boundaries are often ambiguous due to significant variability in fatty infiltration, UQ can play a crucial role for identifying cases where segmentation results are less certain and might require further review by radiologists. More recently, there has been growing interest in the use of Foundation Models (FMs) for segmentation tasks, such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [18] and its medical image adaptation MedSAM [19] . These models are pre-trained on vast image datasets and have shown superior generalization capabilities, particularly in handling test samples that exhibit distribution shifts relative to the training data, outperforming classical methods initialized from ImageNet [20] . Additionally, FMs have demonstrated the ability to generate better calibrated uncertainty estimates than CNNs across various segmentation scenarios, further enhancing their potential as reliable decision-support tools for experts [20] . In addition to their generalization capabilities, the strong feature extraction capabilities of these large-scale models have been explored in several studies [21,22] , demonstrating that, with proper fine-tuning, FMs can outperform SOTA specialist models across diverse datasets. However, their effectiveness in terms of both accuracy and UQ estimates for SM segmentation, particularly in heterogeneous datasets where subjects exhibit varying degrees of fatty infiltration, remains unexplored. Given the challenges posed by high anatomical variability and ambiguous muscle boundaries, evaluating and comparing the UQ capabilities of FMs and traditional CNNs in this context is crucial. Following the aforementioned developments and considering the reported open issues, we aim to investigate the potential of FMs to provide both accurate and reliable muscle segmentation from MR images in the challenging clinical scenario represented by patients affected by NMD, many of whom presenting high degrees of fatty infiltration. First, we aim to compare the segmentation accuracies of the renowned FMs for image segmentation, specifically the SAM and its medical adaptation MedSAM, against specialist models based on CNNs including both 2D and 3D versions of nnU-Net. To accomplish this aim, we fine-tune SAM and MedSAM exploring two fine-tuning approaches: adjusting only the decoder and adjusting both the encoder and decoder. Secondly, to complement accuracy with reliability assessment of model predictions, we incorporate UQ for both CNNs and FMs. Specifically, we perform a quantitative analysis of model calibration and sharpness. To this end, we employed Deep Ensembles (DE) to estimate epistemic uncertainty (EU), alongside aleatoric uncertainty (AU), providing a comprehensive evaluation of model confidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic investigation of accuracy and UQ in SAM-like models for multi-class semantic segmentation of NMD muscle MRI. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a summary and analysis of relevant studies. In Section 3 , we introduce the segmentation models used and the UQ estimation techniques. Section 4 presents the segmentation performance, evaluating both accuracy and uncertainty estimates. Finally, Section 5 discusses the findings, and Section 6 concludes the paper. The segmentation of individual lower limb – thigh and leg – muscles in NMDs has been the focus of various DL approaches. The authors in [6] trained a CNN based on V-Net architecture on subjects with mild and severe fatty replacement, reporting good accuracies in these cohorts. This architecture forms the basis of the interactive framework Dafne [15] , which employs federated incremental learning. Similarly, Hostin et al. [4] conducted a performance comparison between U-Net 2D, U-Net 3D, TransUNet, and HRNet, reporting similar results across all models tested. Moreover, they showed that the segmentation maps predicted from the networks could effectively delineate regions of interest and quantify biomarkers. Huysmans et al. [8] employed a U-Net 3D to segment muscles from knee to hip, whereas Rohm et al. [7] compared U-Net 3D, a U-Net with ResNet encoder and DenseNet for the automatic segmentation of lower leg muscles in a heterogeneous database composed by healthy and patients with various NMDs. In this context, the use of nnU-Net [23] (in both its 2D and 3D versions) has not yet been explored. The use of SAM in medical image segmentation has been explored in various ways, particularly in zero-shot settings and through fine-tuning strategies for specific datasets. While SAM has shown promising results in zero-shot applications on certain medical datasets by providing an effective prompt for initial segmentation, its performance has varied significantly, ranging from moderate to poor on others [24,25] , highlighting the challenge of applying SAM to diverse medical imaging tasks without further adaptation. On the other hand, fine-tuning SAM has been shown to improve segmentation performance significantly [26–30] . In the medical domain, Cheng et al. introduced SAM-Med2D, a variant of SAM fine-tuned on a diverse corpus of medical images spanning multiple modalities and 31 anatomical structures [31] . Similarly, Ma et al. introduced MedSAM [19] , which is a fine-tuned version of SAM obtained by training the encoder and the decoder using a dataset of over 1 million medical images comprising 10 different modalities. Fine-tuning is also essential to eliminate the need for manual prompts, which can be a limiting factor in medical contexts involving multiple regions of interest (ROIs), as the original SAM does not support semantic multi-class segmentation. To address this, Zhang and Liu [22] have fine-tuned and adapted SAM for promptless segmentation of the Synapse multi-organ dataset, achieving competitive results compared to specialist models. Gu et al. [21] extensively evaluated 17 medical datasets, comparing various fine-tuning strategies for SAM and MedSAM. Their results demonstrated that a fine-tuned promptless SAM could achieve better segmentation performance than training an nnU-Net 2D from scratch. Despite the importance of incorporating UQ in a critical field such as medical imaging segmentation to quantify the predictive uncertainty of a model [11] , only a few works have addressed this in multi-class segmentation problems. In [32] , the authors compared different Bayesian and non-Bayesian approaches for uncertainty estimation in the four classes of the Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge, whereas in [33] they evaluated the reliability of predictive uncertainty using it as a predictor of misclassification for segmenting the lumen and vessel of carotid arteries in MR images. Regarding UQ in FMs for medical image segmentation, Zhang et al. [34] have exploited uncertainty maps to rectify the SAM segmentation results, while Shen et al. [35] proposed to guide users by specifying which ROIs require additional prompts for improving accuracy. Similarly, Wang et al. [36] proposed U-MedSAM, which integrates a novel uncertainty-aware loss function in the finetuning of MedSAM [36] . Nguyen et al. [20] evaluated the OOD performance of SAM and MedSAM on three medical segmentation tasks, demonstrating that these models exhibited improved OOD performance. They also found that, in these models, predictive uncertainty was closely correlated with OOD performance, with lower uncertainty predictions indicating better OOD performance. However, no studies have quantitatively evaluated the UQ calibration metrics performance in FMs like SAM and MedSAM neither they compared them to CNN-based approaches. To date, the application of fine-tuned versions of SAM and MedSAM for segmenting SM in patients with NMDs has not been systematically explored or compared with SOTA CNNs such as nnU-Net. Furthermore, no quantitative evaluation of UQ calibration metrics has been conducted for this specific task to assess the reliability of segmentation models. Additionally, independent of this task, there has been no quantitative assessment of calibration metrics for FMs like SAM and MedSAM. For this study, a retrospective cohort was selected. Seventy-six volunteers (age 50 ± 21 y/o) with various NMDs were enrolled in this study and underwent thigh MRI investigation from 01/01/2019 to 31/05/2023. The ethical committee, internal to IRCCS Istituto Neurologico Carlo Besta, approved the study under protocol number 46/2017 during the session held on June 7, 2017. All participants provided written informed consent, as the institutional review board approved, following a comprehensive explanation of the procedure. All the participants were positioned supine in the magnet, and their thighs were scanned in cross-sectional planes orthogonal to the body’s long axis using an abdominal RF coil. The MRI images were obtained using 2 points Dixon sequence using a Siemens 1.5T Avanto Fit, with the following acquisition parameters: repetition time (TR) = 11.1 ms, echo times (TEs) = 2.39 and 4.78 ms, slice thickness = 1.1 mm, pixel size = 1 . 13 × 1 . 13 mm . Each volume consisted of approximately 120 slices. The output of the sequence are two volumes, one in which fat and water are in-phase (IP) and the other in which they are out of phase (OP). IP contrast sums the water and the fat signal, while OP subtracts them. The comparison of IP and OP permits the evaluation of the FF. A neuroradiologist with ten years of experience assessed each participant’s fat infiltration severity using the Mercuri grading scale [37] , which is commonly used to assess disease severity and progression in patients with NMDs. This semi-quantitative scale evaluates the extent of fat replacement in muscles by assigning a grade (0, 1, 2a, 2b, 3, or 4) based on the degree of muscle degeneration. The score for each acquired volume was determined by identifying the muscle with the highest level of fat infiltration within that volume. The subjects with Mercuri grading 0 or 1 are referred to as Early, with 2a or 2b as Moderate and 3 or 4 as Severe. Examples of subjects with different infiltration with the corresponding Dixon In-Phase (IP) and Out-of-Phase (OP) contrasts are shown in Fig. 1 . By employing this Mercuri score-based classification, the dataset has 29 subjects classified as Early, 14 as Moderate and 21 as Severe. Two researchers with experience in muscle segmentation labeled the dataset using OP images, which provided better contrast for delineating muscle boundaries. They manually outlined the following muscles in consensus across all volumes acquired : vastus lateralis (VL), vastus medialis (VM), vastus intermedius (VI), rectus femoris (RF), sartorius (SR), gracilis (GC), adductor magnus (AM), semimembranosus (SM), semitendinosus (ST), biceps femoris long (BFL), biceps femoris short (BFS), and adductor longus (AL). The images were segmented considering the terminal portion of RF as the axial upper bound and the terminal portion of SM as the lower bound, resulting in approximately 100 annotated slices for each volume (see Fig. 2 ). The nnU-Net is a SOTA CNN which combines fixed parameters with rule-based adjustments that adapt to the specific characteristics of the training dataset, such as image resolution and size ( Fig. 3 ). This allows to optimize the architecture, preprocessing, and training pipelines without manual tuning, ensuring strong performance across diverse datasets [9] . nnU-Net was used in both 2D and 3D configurations as a benchmark for evaluating the accuracy of fine-tuned SAM and MedSAM. The 2D configuration utilizes a U-Net architecture operating on individual 2D slices, processing each slice independently. In contrast, the 3D configuration employs a 3D U-Net architecture that considers volumetric context by processing entire 3D volumes, capturing spatial dependencies across slices. SAM [18] is a vision transformer-based foundation model which consists of three main components ( Fig. 4 ): 1. Image Encoder: This is a Vision Transformer (ViT) based encoder, pre-trained using a self-supervised Masked Autoencoder (MAE) approach. The encoder takes an image of size 3 × 1024 × 1024 as input and outputs a latent feature representation of size 256 × 64 × 64. The encoder can vary in size and number of parameters, with options such as ViT-Huge (ViT-H), ViT-Large (ViT-L), and ViT-Base (ViT-B) offering different levels of computational efficiency and performance. 2. Prompt Encoder: This processes user-provided prompts, which can be either sparse inputs (such as points or bounding boxes) or dense inputs (such as masks), generating sparse or dense embeddings. The model defaults to automatically generating embeddings if no explicit prompts are provided. 3. Mask Decoder: This is a lightweight transformer-based architecture that generates the final segmentation mask based on the combined embeddings from the image and prompt encoders. MedSAM [19] is a specialized adaptation of SAM, tailored for medical imaging. Unlike the original SAM, which is trained for general-purpose image segmentation, MedSAM is specifically conceived to handle medical images more effectively. This adaptation was achieved by fine-tuning SAM’s encoder and decoder using a dataset of more than one million medical images, such as MRI, CT, and X-rays. MedSAM retains the same functionality as SAM, meaning that it can be used identically for segmentation tasks. The only difference is that users must initialize the model with MedSAM’s fine-tuned checkpoint instead of using the default SAM model weights. First, we had to address how to deploy SAM and MedSAM within multi-class semantic segmentation tasks, since both FMs were not originally designed for such problems. To this end, we implemented the approach proposed within the SAMed model architecture [22] , thus customizing the SAM/MedSAM architecture as follows: 1. We removed user-provided inputs to the prompt encoder (points, boxes, and masks) during both training and inference. When no prompts are given, the prompt encoder outputs two components: a sparse embedding, which is an empty tensor (i.e., contains no prompt tokens); a dense embedding, which is a learned default tensor representing the “no prompt” condition. This embedding is constant across the spatial dimensions and was learned during SAM’s original pretraining. It enables the model to produce segmentation masks without any input guidance. 2. The original segmentation head of SAM outputs three masks to resolve ambiguity arising from prompt usage. Hence, we modified it to accommodate the ROIs for thigh muscle segmentation, which consists of 13 classes (12 muscles plus the background). The 13 logit output masks are then aggregated into the final categorical segmentation mask by applying softmax across the 13 channels, with final outputs given by the standard argmax operator. Using the softmax output from only a single network as uncertainty prediction allows capturing just the aleatoric fraction (inherent to intrinsic noise and random effects within the data), as it considers solely the distribution over the model’s outputs and not the model’s weights. Therefore, to incorporate EU, the DE [39] technique was employed to estimate predictive uncertainty by leveraging multiple models trained with different initializations. DE have achieved competing performance across various application domains [40] . According to [41] , this is supported by their multiple-modes marginalization in the posterior space as opposed to alternative Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) techniques (such as Monte Carlo Dropout) limited to single modes coverage. Specifically, we performed five repetitions of k-fold cross-validation, each with distinct random weight initializations and a unique subset of the training data, resulting in a diverse parameterization. During inference, an ensemble model was created by averaging the output softmax predictions of each individual model. This ensemble approach helps enhance robustness by reducing the variance of predictions and allowing UQ. Specifically, combining multiple models mitigates the risk of overfitting to a particular fold or dataset partition, leading to more stable and reliable predictions [42] . For a given input pixel x n , the ensemble prediction for each class c was computed by a uniform weighting of the individual output probabilities p ( y n = c ∣ x n , ϑ k ) from each of the K = 5 models with weights ϑ k , i.e., p ( y n = c ∣ x n ) = 1 K ∑ k = 1 K p ( y n = c ∣ x n , ϑ k ) . To provide a qualitative assessment of the uncertainty for a particular image of the test set, the pixel-wise uncertainty maps were computed by calculating the variance of the predictions across the five repetitions and then aggregating the values computing the mean variance across all classes to yield a single uncertainty score per pixel. The resulting pixel-wise uncertainty maps were then visualized to highlight regions where the models exhibited high variability, which indicated greater uncertainty. These maps offered a visual assessment of the areas of highest uncertainty and could indicate regions that may require further review by a radiologist. The qualitative insights provided by the uncertainty maps on a slice-by-slice basis were then complemented by the analysis of quantitative metrics evaluated across the entire test set, which offered a more comprehensive understanding of the overall calibration of the different models’ predictions. The dataset was divided into two parts: 64 subjects for training and validation, and 12 subjects for the holdout test set. The test set was created by randomly selecting an equal number of patients with varying levels of infiltration: 4 Early , 4 Moderate , and 4 Severe subjects. Since each scan contained left and right thighs, the volumes were cropped to create separate volumes for the right and left thighs. The left thighs were mirrored along the horizontal axis to standardize all volumes to right-side anatomies. This preprocessing step resulted in a final dataset of 128 volumes for training/validation and 24 for testing (8 volumes for each degree of severity). For fine-tuning SAM, images were normalized following the original SAM protocol, which involves subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the ImageNet dataset. In contrast, fine-tuning MedSAM employed min–max normalization to scale image intensity values to the [ 0 , 1 ] range, as specified in the MedSAM protocol. Both IP and OP images were utilized as inputs. Since the model requires three input channels, the third channel was generated by averaging the IP and OP images. To meet SAM and MedSAM’s input requirements, the input tensor was resized to 3 × 1024 × 1024. The loss function used in all experiments, following [21,22] , was a combined Dice and cross-entropy loss with equal weighting. The model was trained using a learning rate of 1 × 1 0 − 4 , with a warmup period of 200 iterations. AdamW [43] was applied for optimization, with a weight decay of 0.1 after the warmup phase. The batch size was set to 4 when training only the decoder and reduced to 2 when training both the decoder and encoder. Data augmentation techniques were selected to be physically appropriate for MRI lower limb scans. These included: • Random resized cropping with a scale range of 80% to 120% of the image size, • Random affine transformations with rotations of ± 10 ° , • Translations up to 10% of the image size, • Shear transformations within ± 5 ° . Random resized cropping with a scale range of 80% to 120% of the image size, Random affine transformations with rotations of ± 10 ° , Translations up to 10% of the image size, Shear transformations within ± 5 ° . The maximum number of training epochs was set to 200. An early stopping mechanism was employed to terminate training if the highest validation DSC did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs (see Supplementary Table S1 for the specific number of epochs at which training converged via early stopping). Regarding nnU-Net experiments, these were conducted using the default parameters (e.g hyperparameters and data augmentation), except for the training epochs, which were reduced from 1000 to 100 to reduce computation time. This reduction was justified because the training and validation loss plots converged within 100 epochs. The input consisted of two channels using the IP and OP images. All experiments were conducted using the PyTorch framework on an NVIDIA RTX A5000 with 24 GB VRAM. Experiments were conducted five times for each configuration using k -fold cross-validation, partitioning the dataset into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets. The characteristics of each configuration, such as the number of parameters and the virtual memory allocated per sample, are reported in Table S2. The segmentation accuracies and the calibration metrics were assessed for both individual models and the ensemble. Segmentation performance was assessed using three metrics: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD), and the 95th percentile of Hausdorff distance (HD95). The DSC is a widely used metric that quantifies the degree of overlap between the predicted segmentation ( P ) and the ground truth segmentation ( G ). Intuitively, it measures how much the two segmentations agree in terms of shared voxels. Mathematically, the DSC is defined as: (1) DSC = 2 | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | , where | P | and | G | represent the total number of voxels in the predicted and ground truth masks, respectively, and | P ∩ G | is the number of voxels that overlap between them. A DSC value ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates perfect agreement. This metric can be calculated individually for each muscle or, when multiple muscles are present, combined into a single value per volume using the generalized DSC [44] . While DSC focuses on voxel overlap, the ASSD evaluates the accuracy of the predicted boundary relative to the ground truth boundary. Specifically, it measures the average distance from each point on one boundary to the closest point on the other boundary, considering both directions. Formally, ASSD is computed as: (2) ASSD = ∑ x ∈ ∂ G d ( x , ∂ P ) + ∑ y ∈ ∂ P d ( y , ∂ G ) | ∂ G | + | ∂ P | , where ∂ P and ∂ G denote the sets of boundary voxels in the predicted and ground truth segmentations, respectively. The function d ( a , B ) calculates the shortest Euclidean distance from point a to the set B . By averaging distances in both directions, ASSD provides a symmetric measure of boundary agreement, expressed in millimeters. The HD captures the largest discrepancy between two boundaries, identifying the point on one boundary that is farthest from any point on the other. This maximum distance highlights the worst-case segmentation error. It is defined as: (3) HD = max max x ∈ ∂ G d ( x , ∂ P ) , max y ∈ ∂ P d ( y , ∂ G ) . Because the maximum distance can be disproportionately affected by noise or small outliers, we instead report the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95). This metric computes the distance below which 95% of the boundary points lie, providing a more robust estimate of segmentation accuracy. To evaluate the predicted uncertainty we employed common metrics in the literature, namely the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and the Negative Log Likelihood (NLL) [11,16,45] . ECE is a scalar measure derived from reliability diagrams, which visually depict the model’s calibration across different confidence levels for each class. ECE quantifies the difference between the predicted confidence (the probability assigned to the predicted class) and the actual accuracy of predictions across all pixels. ECE is defined as: (4) ECE = ∑ m = 1 M | B m | N | acc ( B m ) − conf ( B m ) | , where: • M is the number of bins (selected as 20), • B m is the set of pixels whose predicted confidence falls into bin m , • | B m | is the number of pixels in bin m , and N is the total number of pixels, • acc ( B m ) is the accuracy in bin m , and conf ( B m ) is the average confidence in that bin. M is the number of bins (selected as 20), B m is the set of pixels whose predicted confidence falls into bin m , | B m | is the number of pixels in bin m , and N is the total number of pixels, acc ( B m ) is the accuracy in bin m , and conf ( B m ) is the average confidence in that bin. ECE is a metric used to evaluate how well the predicted probabilities of a model match the actual likelihood of an event occurring. In the context of multi-class segmentation, this means assessing whether the predicted probability for each class (i.e., the model’s confidence in assigning a pixel to a specific class) aligns with the actual frequency of that class in the ground truth. For example, if a model predicts a pixel with a 0.8 probability of belonging to a certain class, ECE checks whether, empirically, 80% of the time those pixels are actually part of that class. A well-calibrated model would have predicted probabilities that are consistent with the available test observation. A lower ECE indicates a better alignment between the model’s predicted probabilities and empirical observations, suggesting higher reliability of its predictions. In semantic segmentation, NLL quantifies how well the predicted probability distribution aligns with the ground truth labels across all pixels. It evaluates the log-probability assigned by the model to the correct class for each pixel. Formally, for a set of N pixels and C classes, NLL is defined as: (5) NLL = − 1 N ∑ n = 1 N ∑ c = 1 C log p ( y n = c ∣ x n , θ ) ⋅ 1 ( y n = c ) , where: • x n is the input feature at pixel n , • y n is the ground truth class label for pixel n , • θ represents the model parameters • p ( y n = c ∣ x n , θ ) is the predicted probability for class c at pixel n given the model parameters θ , • 1 ( y n = c ) is the indicator function, equal to 1 if the ground truth label is class c , and 0 otherwise. x n is the input feature at pixel n , y n is the ground truth class label for pixel n , θ represents the model parameters p ( y n = c ∣ x n , θ ) is the predicted probability for class c at pixel n given the model parameters θ , 1 ( y n = c ) is the indicator function, equal to 1 if the ground truth label is class c , and 0 otherwise. NLL captures both calibration and sharpness. Sharpness refers to the concentration of the predicted probability distribution and is independent of the ground truth. A sharper distribution implies greater confidence in the predictions. For example, a model predicting probabilities close to 1 for one class and near 0 for others is sharper than a model predicting a more evenly distributed set of probabilities. NLL integrates both properties: a model with low NLL provides sharp, well-calibrated predictions, meaning it is confident and correct in its predictions. ECE and NLL were computed by evaluating the softmax probabilities from each fold and the DE probabilities across all folds. The evaluation was conducted on subjects from the holdout test set, differentiating the metrics according to infiltrated gravity groups to observe how uncertainty metrics varied with increased fatty infiltration. To focus on regions with the highest uncertainty, evaluation was performed as in [45] , using pixels within dilated bounding boxes around the foreground segments. Using bounding boxes removes most of the correct background predictions from the statistics and better highlights the differences among models. Each bounding box was constructed around the foreground ROIs and enlarged by 5 pixels in every direction. To statistically evaluate the significance of performance differences between various approaches (nnU-Net 2D and 3D, SAM Enc/Dec, MedSAM Enc/Dec, SAM Dec, MedSAM Dec), a Friedman test was conducted on the metrics computed for each volume in the test set. This was followed by a post-hoc two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test with a significance level of p = 0 . 05 to assess pairwise differences between configurations. This study aimed to explore the potential of SAM-based FMs in segmenting skeletal muscle MR images, focusing on their potential for multi-class segmentation and investigating their reliability in terms of uncertainty metrics performance. The motivation for studying FMs lies in their training on extremely large and diverse datasets, which enables them to learn rich, transferable features. These features are particularly valuable for heterogeneous datasets like ours, where the model must generalize across varied levels of fatty infiltration in NMD patients. Specifically, we compared the performance of fine-tuned SAM and MedSAM to SOTA CNNs including both 2D and 3D nnU-Net architectures, evaluating them both in terms of segmentation accuracy and UQ metrics such as ECE and NLL. The use of an ensemble of networks for inference significantly improved overall accuracy compared to single-model predictions. For this reason, the following discussion will focus only on the ensemble results. This finding is consistent with [8] , which demonstrated the effectiveness of ensembling in enhancing the accuracy of lower limb muscle segmentation. By combining predictions from multiple networks, the ensemble mitigates the weaknesses and biases inherent in individual models, leading to more robust and precise segmentation outcomes [42] . Considering the segmentation performance in terms of accuracy, we observed, as expected and found in [3,46] , a constant drop in DSC in all the implemented approaches associated with the worsening fatty infiltration. For instance, the DSC performance in the Moderate case shows a decrease ranging from 4.2% to 10%, depending on the network, while in the Severe case, the decrease is more pronounced, ranging from 7.3% to 15.9% when compared to the Early case. More specifically, in the Early set the DSCs are above 0.90 for all models experimented, demonstrating good results that are in line with the accuracies reported in literature for healthy and low infiltrated subjects [3,47,48] . As to the Moderate/Severe cases the accuracies of our best configurations in terms of DSC (0.89 and 0.86) were comparable to those obtained by Agosti et al. [6] , who reported mean DSC values of 0.88 and 0.87 for mild and severe cases, respectively, despite utilizing a larger training set of MRI scans from NMD patients. Hostin [3] achieved a mean DSC of 0.87 in patients with high levels of fatty infiltration (FF > 20%), using a cohort of 67 NMD patients and 14 control subjects for training. Similarly, Huysmans et al. [8] reported a mean DSC of 0.90 and 0.87 in subjects with intermediate and end-stage NMD disease, respectively. However, these results were obtained on a validation set rather than an independent test set, which may impact the generalizability of the reported values. Overall, although these differences were not statistically significant, the fine-tuned SAM Enc/Dec achieved the highest segmentation accuracy across all fat infiltration severity levels, outperforming nnU-Net 3D on Moderate and Severe cases while achieving a comparable DSC on Early cases. It should be noted that the fine-tuned SAM model demonstrated segmentation performance comparable to the nnU-Net 3D model, despite SAM being a 2D model. SAM significantly outperformed its 2D CNN counterpart, nnU-Net 2D, a result consistent with findings from Gu et al. [21] who observed that fine-tuning SAM considering both the decoder and the encoder, led to significant performance gains over nnU-Net 2D across multiple medical imaging datasets. Gu et al. [21] hypothesized that SAM performs particularly well in scenarios involving complex targets, such as those observed in Moderate and Severe cases. However, its differences from nnU-Net are less pronounced when dealing with simpler targets, as seen in our study in the “Early” case. Moreover, we can observe that for a complex multi-class segmentation, as in our case, starting from the MedSAM weights initialization did not allow to achieve superior performance compared to SAM even though MedSAM was originally fine-tuned using images from the medical domain, including MRI [19] . This finding is in line with the experiments conducted by Gu et al. [21] and Li et al. [49] , who also found a decrease in performance when using MedSAM weights as starting point. Li et al. [49] hypothesized that FMs do not require medical pre-training to successfully adapt to downstream medical tasks through fine-tuning. They supported this hypothesis by arguing that the size of medical pre-training datasets is typically too small to provide a significant advantage when adapting to task-specific domains. In the case presented in this study, the gap between SAM and MedSAM initializations is evident in the Severe set for Dec configuration, where MedSAM Dec reached DSC of 0.812 vs. 0.830 of SAM Dec. On the other hand, the MedSAM Enc/Dec configuration reached a DSC of 0.846, while SAM Enc/Dec outperformed it with a DSC of 0.857, although this difference was not statistically significant. Regarding the differences in boundary metrics such as HD95 and ASSD (see Supplementary Tables S3 and S4), the results across the Moderate and Severe test sets were mixed. For instance, in the Moderate set, SAM Enc/Dec achieved slightly better HD95 (3.51 ± 1.05 mm vs. 3.60 ± 1.36 mm), while nnU-Net 3D had marginally better ASSD (1.10 ± 0.29 mm vs. 1.15 ± 0.25 mm). In the Severe set, nnU-Net 3D slightly outperformed SAM Enc/Dec in HD95 (5.33 ± 2.29 mm vs. 5.37 ± 1.64 mm), whereas SAM Enc/Dec showed a slight advantage in ASSD (1.61 ± 0.29 mm vs. 1.66 ± 0.55 mm). These minor variations can be partially attributed to the architectural differences between the models. The 3D nnU-Net exploits volumetric context across slices, leading to more spatially consistent segmentations, which tends to benefit boundary-sensitive metrics like HD95 and ASSD. In contrast, SAM and MedSAM operate on a 2D slice-by-slice basis, lacking inter-slice continuity. This can result in small slice-to-slice inconsistencies, which may negatively impact surface-based metrics, despite the good overlap agreement between predicted and true masks, as indicated by the better DSC scores of SAM Enc/Dec in the Moderate and Severe sets. A central and novel contribution of our work lies in exploring techniques for predicting uncertainty beyond conventional accuracy evaluation. UQ is an area of growing research interest, reflecting the increasing importance of trustworthy AI systems in clinical settings. However, the vast majority of existing studies on NDM segmentation focus solely on point prediction analysis. Performing UQ alongside accuracy evaluation is crucial in segmentation tasks, particularly in clinical applications, as it provides insights into the reliability of the network’s predictions. Relying solely on accuracy metrics may be insufficient for determining the most suitable architecture in high-stakes scenarios, where uncertainty estimation plays a crucial role in decision-making. This is especially valuable when boundaries between individual muscles are unclear, as seen in Severe subjects, where visual assessment alone may not confirm if the segmentation aligns accurately with the underlying image. Beyond the specific task of muscle segmentation, UQ in FMs represents a broader open problem with significant implications across multiple applications, highlighting the need for further research in this area [50,51] . Alongside the qualitative evaluation of sample-wise uncertainty maps, various techniques can be employed in medical image segmentation to assess the quality of uncertainty estimates for the overall test set. These include quantitative assessments using ECE and NLL [11] . In our study we observed distinct differences in calibration performance (measured by ECE) across varying levels of image complexity. The various configurations of FMs, including MedSAM and both decoder-only and encoder–decoder configurations of SAM, demonstrated similarly low ECE values across all severity levels. For example, the lowest ECE in Early was achieved by SAM Dec (2.45%), in Moderate and Severe by MedSAM Dec (2.99% and 2.63%). Focusing on the configurations with the highest segmentation accuracies in terms of DSC – nnU-Net 3D and SAM Enc/Dec – we observe that SAM Enc/Dec maintained consistently lower calibration errors than CNNs despite the increasing complexity of images in the Moderate and Severe sets (e.g., 3.01%, 3.56%, and 3.25%), whereas nnU-Net, both 2D and 3D, exhibited a substantial increase in ECE (e.g., 2.87%, 5.09%, and 7.14% for nnU-Net 3D). This suggests that SAM Enc/Dec provides more reliable predictions in more challenging cases, while CNN-based models tend to become overconfident, as evidenced by their poorer calibration than FMs. The NLL metric provides a complementary view by conveying both calibration and sharpness in the models predictions. In our experiments, nnU-Net 3D exhibited slightly lower NLL values than SAM Enc/Dec in the Early and Moderate cases (0.26 vs. 0.33 and 0.37 vs. 0.41, respectively), while the values were approximately the same for Severe cases (0.48 for SAM Enc/Dec vs. 0.49 for nnU-Net 3D). By combining these observation with the ECE metrics reported above, these values can be related to the sharper patterns typically occurring in over-confident models. In high-stakes scenarios, where reliable predictions are crucial, it is important to target calibration beyond sharpness, as expressed in the general principle of probabilistic forecasting as “maximize the sharpness of the predictive distributions subject to calibration” [52,53] . Hence, the improved calibration, beyond the competitive segmentation accuracy provided by SAM, is a highly desirable property. In our context, this underscores the benefits of fine-tuned SAM for making reliable and accurate predictions, particularly in challenging and limited heterogeneous datasets with varying levels of fatty infiltration. In contrast, these differences between SAM and nnU-Net 3D are not observed in the homogeneous Early dataset, as evidenced by the similar values in DSCs and UQ metrics. This is particularly crucial for fostering the adoption of FMs in clinical practice, thereby leveraging the rich features learned by pre-trained models. The DE technique implemented in this study supports the estimation of both EU and AU, unlike using the softmax output of a single repetition which only provides insight into AU through its categorical distribution output. Although this leads to increased computational costs due to multiple runs, the introduction of techniques to characterize EU becomes increasingly relevant under limited data regimes and potential distribution shifts, as typically occurring in real world SM problems [54] . This technique has been shown in [39] to outperform Monte Carlo Dropout. Moreover, it does not require architectural modification of the network, which makes it suitable for a straight comparison of CNNs and FMs. The introduction of DE techniques proves crucial in improving calibration of the CNN models, especially for the more overconfident nnU-Net 2D. Interestingly, ensembling has led to slight decreases of FM calibration performances in some cases (approximately 1%), mainly observed in Early and Moderate conditions (e.g., in MedSAM Dec). To the best of our knowledge, no previous work in the literature has revealed such issue. Indeed, DE are widely considered as a reference approach for UQ in FMs (see e.g., [51,55] ). A potential explanation for the slight increases in ECE could be related to the lower over-confidence of the backbone FM components compared to CNNs. Indeed, previous studies have reported potential under-confidence issues following aggregation (see e.g., [17,56] and references therein). However, these are initial explanations that warrant further investigation in future extensions of this work, such as exploring additional datasets and ensembling techniques. However, the slight increases in ECE come with sensibly improved segmentation accuracies and lower NLL, which confirms the overall added value of DE deployment. A limitation of the present work is the relatively small dataset, which, although heterogeneous, was acquired from a single center using a consistent protocol. To further validate the capabilities of FMs in this specific task, especially considering their demonstrated reliability in terms of UQ, it would be valuable to test the model on data acquired from different clinics and protocols. This would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s robustness and generalizability. In our work, we focused on SAM and MedSAM, as these models have already been applied to promptless semantic segmentation tasks [21,22] . Other medical adaptations of SAM, such as SAM-Med2D [31] , were not included in our evaluation, as they have not been validated for promptless semantic segmentation. However, based on our earlier discussion regarding the reasons why MedSAM did not outperform SAM, we believe that SAM-Med2D may be subject to similar limitations. Future work could explore alternative UQ techniques, such as Bayesian methods or conformal prediction. Regarding fine-tuning techniques for FMs, the exploration of alternative parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for updating both encoder and decoder weights-such as alternative Adapters beyond LoRA is left for future work. Additionally, to compare the performance of the nnU-Net further in 3D segmentation, it may be valuable to test adaptations of SAM for 3D segmentation. For instance, adaptations like the recent SAM 2 [57] , capable of segmenting video sequences, could be explored, as this approach might generalize well to volumetric segmentation in medical imaging. Additionally, the use of Vision Transformer-based models, which have shown promising results in diseases classification in muscle [58] and other districts [59,60] , could be tested to explore how they contribute to deal with the challenging task of segmentation in fat infiltrated SMs. In this work we developed a comprehensive evaluation framework, applied to both CNNs and FMs, including not only the assessment of accuracy but also a thorough quantitative investigation of uncertainty, addressing both the calibration and sharpness of model predictions in this context. Our findings demonstrate that fine-tuning SAM results in superior performance (considering together accuracy and UQ metrics) compared to the SOTA nnU-Net 3D for muscle segmentation in NMD patients, especially in Moderate and Severe cases. In this challenging scenarios, employing Deep Ensembles to convey EU in addition to the aleatoric counterpart supports more reliable confidence estimates alongside the segmentation masks, thereby assisting radiologists in reviewing regions with high fatty infiltration and ambiguous boundaries. Furthermore, the calibration metrics confirm that fine-tuned SAM delivers more trustworthy predictions, underscoring its potential as a robust tool for clinical applications in high-stakes medical imaging scenarios. Feature analysis for proper intensity scaling and feature distinction in class activation maps Understanding the decisions of deep learning (DL) models is crucial for their acceptance in risk-sensitive applications. Class activation maps (CAMs) are commonly used in image analysis to visualize model reasoning by generating attention maps where signal intensities represent contributions to outputs. However, existing CAM algorithms focus on optimal weight design and salient feature layer selection, neglecting two key limitations in population-level interpretation: (1) lack of an appropriate intensity scale for proper interpretation and quantitative analysis, and (2) inability to identify which features within selected layers predominantly drive model reasoning. These gaps can lead to miscorrelations between CAMs and model outputs, causing erroneous interpretations, while restricting CAMs to case-specific visual inspections. We propose a framework to statistically analyze DL-extracted features at a population level, determinizing feature contributions for global intensity scaling and within-layer feature distinction. The global intensity scale standardizes CAMs, achieving high correlation coefficients (R) with model outputs. Within-layer feature distinction identifies overfitting, confounding factors, outliers, redundancies, and principal features. Applied to eight datasets, including five medical imaging datasets, this framework improved Rs between CAMs and outputs by 10.7–64.2 %, achieving near 100 % consistency. Furthermore, distinguishing principal features (5–25 % in the selected layer) produced CAMs of equal quality while maintaining model output accuracy. This method, relying on minimal assumptions, enhances CAM-model consistency and broadens CAM applications by enabling standardized interpretation and deeper feature-level insights. Validating the reliability of deep learning (DL) models and understanding how these models analyze images are essential requirements before DL models can be deployed in risk-sensitive areas [1–4] . In addition to validation based on large-scale data, it needs to be confirmed that DL models are actually reasoning based on trustworthy evidence and convincing features [5–11] . In image analysis, this confirmation specifically refers to ensuring that the focus of a model on the input images should be spatially and semantically consistent with the focus of expert knowledge. To ensure this consistency, class activation maps (CAMs) and their variants are the most representative methods to reveal the focus of DL models and compare this focus with expert knowledge, since they generate attention maps, in which the signal intensities represent the importance (class specificity or contribution) of a region to the output of the DL model. Especially in image analysis, CAMs became one of the most popular methods due to its high computational efficiency and intuitive ways of displaying, compared to other interpretability methods, such as LIME [12–15] , global interpretation [16–18] and other interpretation methods [19–24] . The family of CAMs shares a similar calculation that is dependent on two main components – features and weights. Features refer to the outputs of certain layer(s) in DL models, which contain spatial information for displaying and activation intensities during reasoning. The weights represent the importance of these features to the output of DL models, similar to the weights for variables in statistical regression models. In Fig. 1 , we summarized the calculation of the most prevailing CAM algorithms and identify certain terms used in the calculation process, including the original CAM [10] , Grad CAM [25] , Grad CAM++ [26] , Layer CAM [27] , xGrad CAM [28] , Score CAM [29] , Smooth Grad CAM++ [30] , SS-CAM [31] , IS-CAM [32] , Eigen CAM [33] , Multi-CAM [34] and Fusion CAM [35] . These algorithms provide an important insight into the decision making process, achieving promising performance in the fields like weakly supervised object detection [37,38] . However, two important issues have not yet been considered when generating CAMs – there is no appropriate intensity scale and they do not give insight into which features within the selected layer(s) substantially contributed to the model’s reasoning. As shown in the formula in the middle of Fig. 1 , five elements are indispensable for CAM calculations: (1) defining weights, (2) selecting layer(s) that contain features, (3) scaling spatially, (4) intensity scaling and (5) selecting features within the selected layer(s). While existing algorithms are designed to optimize the definition of weights and the selection of the layer(s), few investigations were conducted on the remaining three elements as shown in Table 1 . It is generally reasonable to not pay much attention to optimizing spatial scaling [39] - the architecture of mainstream DL models, such as translation equivariance in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and the Transformer encoder’s feature of preserving input dimensionality throughout its layers, help to simplify spatial scaling. However, the remaining two elements, intensity scaling and distinguishing the most important features within the selected layer(s), could have a considerable impact on the accuracy and applicability of CAM algorithms. The lack of appropriate intensity scaling can lead to inconsistencies between CAMs and the DL model, resulting in misinterpretation of CAMs and models. Fig. 2 (a) presents a schematic diagram of the intensity scaling employed in current algorithms and the consequential errors in different image analysis tasks; (b) presents a conceptual solution that builds a global intensity scale to solve the errors. The activation ranges, representing the upper and lower bounds of signal intensities in CAMs given specific inputs, could vary from input to input. Consequently, the individual intensity scaling may cause same activation values projected to different values in the normalized CAMs, and leads to further interpretation problems. Not being able to distinguish the most important (highly-contributing) features within the selected layer(s) limits a CAM’s application to merely a visual inspection tool, as it provides no insight into the features learned over the entire population. Fig. 3 presents a few examples that generate CAMs using all features and randomly chosen 20 % of distinct features from the same selected layer(s). As can be seen, using some subgroups of 20 % features can generate CAMs that are very similar to using all features, indicating the inequivalence among these features, potential model redundancy at the layer(s) and potential relationship between certain image patterns and feature extraction paths. To address the above two issues, we propose a framework, which is essentially a feature analysis on a population level. The framework statistically analyzes DL-extracted features within the selected layer(s) at a population level, determining the contribution of each feature within the selected layer(s) during the reasoning, to achieve a global intensity scale and within-layer feature distinction. Since the framework is data-driven and relying on very few assumptions, it can be applied to CAM algorithms of various weight definitions and layer selections to improve their performance. Furthermore, the framework can provide insights into other characteristics of the model, such as overfitting, confounders, outliers, model redundancies and the most salient features, which are absent in previous algorithms. Furthermore, a challenge in evaluating current CAM algorithms is that, most CAM algorithms conduct evaluations based on the intersection over union (IoU) between the focus of CAMs and the semantic objects in images, which has been proven to be biased [40] . Therefore, in addition to only validating through classical IoU-based metrics, we propose another quantitative approach for evaluating the consistency between CAMs and DL models, by calculating the correlation between the mean activations of a CAM and the corresponding logits from the DL model. We used eight mature datasets from different fields and modalities with accessible and well-trained models to conduct experiments, minimizing the potential errors caused by poorly performing DL models. The experimental results show visually and quantitatively that our framework helps to improve existing CAM algorithms to overcome the errors, which are caused by a lack of a global intensity scale, and to determine features’ importance within the selected layer(s). We summarized the contribution of this paper as follows: • We theoretically analyzed the fundamental issues in existing CAM algorithms, and through this process we successfully explained many erroneous phenomena in applying CAMs in practice. • The proposed feature analysis framework provides an approach to build a global intensity scale for correctly displaying CAMs, and therefore allows correct interpretation of DL models based on these CAMs. • The feature analysis framework also provides an approach to determine the importance of a feature within the selected layers. This ability enables feature-level analysis for DL models and detection of overfitting, confounders, outliers, model redundancies and the most salient features, extending the use of CAMs. • We propose a new quantitative approach for evaluating CAMs by calculating the consistency between CAMs and the DL models’ outputs. This approach brings in an unbiased evaluation without the need for semantic segmentation, ground truth masks or bounding boxes of any objects in images. To address the two limitations, achieving proper intensity scaling and distinguish the difference among features regarding their contribution to the model’s outputs, we propose a framework to analyze the activations of each feature within the selected layer(s) across the dataset used for training. Through this process, the statistical information is recorded for establishing a global intensity scale and an “importance” matrix is generated to determine the contribution of each feature at a population level. Fig. 4 presents a schematic diagram of the framework. The interpretation problems caused by individual intensity scaling are ubiquitous, yet typically ignored due to confirmation biases and lack of proper evaluation methods [40] , especially in CAMs for DL models trained on small datasets. As presented in Fig. 2 , the solution to this issue is simple – establish a global intensity scale. Through the process in Fig. 4 (a), the global intensity scale could be easily established using the maximum and minimum, which are recorded during the pre-CAM calculation phase, across the training set, and then applied to the validation set or new datasets. Furthermore, the activations below zero are also preserved and considered as part the minimum during this process while in current algorithms they were typically discarded. Regarding the scaling method, we choose the hyperbolic tangent function as the intensity scaling projection function, because some outliers with extremely high or low activations in some instances could lead to a considerable dispersion of maximum and minimum. This dispersion may further lead to some displaying and interpretation problems, as some regions could be overly emphasized or underrepresented. The intensity scaling σ ( ) is then defined by: (1) σ P low P high ( x ) = tanh ( α · x − β ) , (2) α = tanh − 1 V high − tanh − 1 V low P high − P low , (3) β = P high · tanh − 1 V high − P low · tanh − 1 V low P high − P low . where α and β are constants, calculated through P h i g h and P l o w . P h i g h and P l o w represent the values of V h i g h th and V l o w th percentiles regarding the activations in CAMs. α controls the steepness or slope of the curve and β shifts the curve horizontally. As shown in Fig. 5 , this function enables a non-linear projection that its domain of definition allows the activations above/below the maximum/minimum of the dataset used for calculate the global intensity scale. This space is reserved for extremely strong signals that only appear in new data, representing new characteristics which should be considered. As the proposed intensity scaling and preservation of negative signals are essentially a functional correction to existing CAM algorithms, we preferred to not call it a new CAM method, but rather an intensity-scaled version of these methods, labeled with subscript “gs” meaning “globally scaled”. For example, for Grad CAM, in the rest of text, “Grad CAM g s ” represents CAMs with a global intensity scale, while “Grad CAM i s ” or “Grad CAM” is used to indicate CAMs with the original intensity scale. Similar to the idea of CAMs where high values represent higher “importance” or more attention, we define the “importance” of a feature (a particular forward path) to a specific class c as the mean activation of this feature k to class c across the entire dataset. By calculating the mean activation within the feature k , the general contribution (the activations of all the pixels/voxels) within feature k is projected into a single value I k , c , n for each input n . Similarly to the C A M g s , which refers to the CAM with a global intensity scale, we use C A M s f (CAM using “selected features”) to refer to CAMs that are generated using selected features in the following context. Evaluation in previous CAM algorithms typically consists of two methods - qualitative evaluation by visual inspection of the CAM and quantitative evaluation by object localization [26] . The visual inspection is performed to ensure that the highlighted regions in the CAMs are consistent with the foci of human knowledge in classifying the inputs. The quantitative evaluation measures how much the confidence is affected by masking the regions in the image that are highlighted in the CAMs, using the so-called “average increase” and “average decrease/drop”. The original image and the image masked by the CAMs (thresholded and normalized) are fed into the model. This produces two output confidence values (one from the original image and one from the masked image).The average increase and decrease are then defined as the difference between the two confidence values. However, these evaluation metrics have some substantial drawbacks: the changes in these metrics can be caused by both the model and the CAM algorithms, but they are only used to evaluate the CAMs, without excluding the impact of model performance and human knowledge involvement. For example, CAMs that always highlighted many regions in an input, because the model was not well-trained and always “looked” everywhere, could also receive consistent average increases and decreases in the quantitative evaluation based on object localization. Furthermore, the evaluation of CAMs by the accuracy of target object localization relies on certain assumptions: (1) a perfect model that has perfect performance and obtains output classes “only” based on the target objects - without any inference from the environment or other objects that might correlate with the output classes. This assumption is so strict that no model has yet been shown to satisfy it. (2) The CAM algorithms must have no prior knowledge that would lead to good object localization without DL models - a randomly initialized model without training could get “convincing” CAMs to pass visual checks by an over-designed CAM algorithm [40] . Derived from the very fundamental idea of CAMs – an input with important information for classification should be more highlighted in the attention maps than those with irrelevant information – we propose a new metric that measures the consistency between CAMs and the model’s logits. This avoids introducing human knowledge of the “meaningful” objects and is therefore independent of the performance of a DL model. The metric in this study, defined as the correlation coefficients Rs between the sum of class activations and the model’s logits, focuses on the relationship between CAMs and the model’s outputs. The use of logits instead of confidences may improve readability, as the activation functions (e.g. the SoftMax function) break the linear relationship between logits and confidences by rescaling according to the logits for other classes, leading to a non-linear relationship between model logits and class activations. Besides the population-level evaluation of the proposed global intensity scaling, we also conducted individual-level evaluation experiments. For more convincing validation, we used the multi-dimensional verification framework, Quantus [41] , to evaluate the performance of the global scaling method before and after application. To assess whether feature distinction effectively differentiates the importance of features within the selected layer(s), we verified whether features identified as important indeed capture the primary information. If these selected features are truly important, then removing the remaining, less important features from the CAM calculation should not undermine the correlation between the model’s outputs and CAMs, or mislead the focus of CAMs. Similarly, removing the less important features from the model should not substantially impact the model’s accuracy. Therefore, we applied the following evaluation to determine: • Whether the correlations between the model’s outputs and CAMs re- main the same after removing the less important features. • Whether the CAM’s ability to localize contributing objects remains unchanged after removing less important features from the CAM calculation, as determined by the feature distinction. • Whether the model’s accuracy is preserved when features of varying importance are blocked. We calculated the correlation between the mean intensity of the original CAMs and the model’s logits, and tested whether this correlation remained when using only 5–25 % most important features (less important features removed) to calculate the CAM. If the correlation does not drop considerably, then these selected features are indeed the most important. Therefore, we generated the CAMs using the 5–25 % most important features and calculated the same correlation-based metrics as the CAMs using all features based on Eq. 5 . Model’s accuracy The model outputs are expected to remain the same, if the most important features are retained and the irrelevant features are filtered out. Since feature masking does not alter the intensity distribution of the inputs, and therefore does not significantly affect the performance of the model, we propose a quantitative evaluation metric based on feature masking. Specifically, we propose to block the forward paths of the unselected features during inference, to obtain the logits based on the selected features only, and then take the accuracy changes as the evaluation metric. Some recent public datasets were excluded mainly due to the lack of high-performance and publicly-available trained models or the high complexity of well-performing models in these datasets (making CAM visualization difficult). The 5–25 % percentages of top features in feature distinction are determined by manually looking at the average activations of each feature in the importance matrices and arbitrarily picking the features whose activation values are substantially higher than the others. There could be some potential approaches to find the optimal percentages, but the definition of “important” features is fuzzy, making it difficult to evaluate the choices. Fig. 7 provides the results of the four basic CAM algorithms, before and after applying global intensity scaling, based on the four different quantitative evaluation aspects in the Quantus framework [41] . In this framework, Faithfulness ( ↑ ) quantifies to what extent explanations (CAMs in this specific case) follow the predictive behavior of the model, asserting that more important features affect model decisions more strongly; Complexity ( ↓ ) captures to what extent CAMs are concise, i.e., that few features are used to explain a model prediction; Randomisation ( ↓ ) tests to what extent CAMs deteriorate when the data labels or the model (e.g. its parameters) are increasingly randomised; Sensitivity (-Robustness ↓ ) measures to what extent explanations are stable when subjected to slight perturbations in the input, assuming that the model output stayed approximately the same. After applying global intensity scaling, the CAMs generally performed substantially better, according to the increase in Faithfulness and decrease in both Complexity and Randomisation in the eight datasets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed global scaling method. The Quantus framework defines Sensitivity as the changes of CAMs after irrelevant input changes have been applied, and the global intensity scaling increased the sensitivity of CAMs. The explanation is that because the global intensity scaling preserves negative activations, it is also more sensitive to irrelevant input changes in these areas. The traditional CAMs, however, simply neglects all negative activations, which makes them insensitive to any changes in these areas but also less explainable. For this reason, we believe that the increase in sensitivity did not undermine the value of the global intensity scaling. Before the visual examples, the difference in the color scale before and after applying the proposed intensity scaling needs to be clarified, as they have a different reference as the lowest-activated objects. In the original intensity scaling, the background activations or zero activation object in the non-normalized CAMs are treated as the reference. Under this setting, the lowest activations represent no contribution. After applying the global intensity scales, all activations are retained, and the lowest activations now represent the negative contribution. This shift in lowest-activation reference from background to the opposite objects results in a green or light blue background in the CAMs after applying the global intensity scale, and reversely highlighted areas (blue instead of red) that represent objects that indicate the other classes. In this paper, we proposed a framework of feature analysis to establish a global intensity scale and distinguish the importance of different features, based on the same premise as the CAM algorithms. It is not a new CAM algorithm or a new definition of weights for CAMs, but a different perspective of using existing weighted features. The intensity scaling and feature selection could be applied to most CAM algorithms without increasing computation time during inference, serving as a useful functional supplement, to minimize the risk of interpretations based on wrong CAMs. The feature distinction succeeds in distinguishing the importance of features within the selected layer(s) and find the most important features for a specific class. In the following subsections, we discuss about the uses of the proposed feature distinction based on the importance matrix, generalizability of the proposed method and the definition of importance. Some other topics (e.g. regression tasks, time costs and evaluation metrics) can be found in the supplementary materials. The importance matrix for feature distinction could provide useful information about both the model and dataset, such as: • Overfitting . The difference in importance matrices between the training and test sets indicates potential overfitting when the class activations of each feature in the training set differ considerably from those in the test set. For example, in the line graphs of Fig. 13 (a), (b), (d), (e), (f) and (g) the importance matrices are shown from both the training and test sets. From the difference between the training and test sets, (a) and (b) indicate more severe overfitting, as they have features that are much more activated in the training sets than in the test sets, while the training and test sets share a very similar pattern in other line graphs. • Principal features . If we select a single column in the importance matrix (thereby selecting a class), each value represents the average class activation level of a specific feature for that selected class. Those features that are more activated (higher class activations) also have a greater influence on this selected model output class in general. Therefore, they can serve as the main features of this study. For example, in the line graphs of Fig. 13 some features are more frequently activated (except for 13.d and 13.h), resulting in a large ratio of total activation values to average importance over the entire dataset. The values of these features indicate the potential of some features to emerge from many others. • Potential confounders . Confounders in deep learning models usually refer to some objects or noise in the background of images or time series that could provide a “shortcut” for a model to be easily trained and make inferences based only on these non-targets. In the importance matrices, confounders could cause extremely high values for some specific features and relatively low values for all other features because they provide the “shortcut”. These potential confounders can therefore be checked by generating CAMs using only the relevant features. As the models are copies of successful models on these public datasets, we did not find any significant signs of confounding in these datasets. In the line graph of Fig. 13 (f) the model may benefit from some potential confounders compared to other datasets, some visual checks on the CAMs are valuable for further investigation. • Special cases and outliers . Special cases or outliers would show very different class activations of the features compared to the importance matrices of their corresponding classes. • Model redundancies . The ratio of highly activated features out of all features in the importance matrices represents the ratio of influential features in the model, as the values are a combination of activation frequency and “amplitude”. Therefore, the rarely activated features in all classes/outputs contribute very little to the model decision in most cases and could be removed by model pruning. For example, in the line graphs of Fig. 13 (b) and (f), compared to other importance matrices, they have more features that are rarely activated across the datasets, while some features are significantly activated. This phenomenon indicates that the models have some “lazy” features that contribute very little and can be pruned. Overfitting . The difference in importance matrices between the training and test sets indicates potential overfitting when the class activations of each feature in the training set differ considerably from those in the test set. For example, in the line graphs of Fig. 13 (a), (b), (d), (e), (f) and (g) the importance matrices are shown from both the training and test sets. From the difference between the training and test sets, (a) and (b) indicate more severe overfitting, as they have features that are much more activated in the training sets than in the test sets, while the training and test sets share a very similar pattern in other line graphs. Principal features . If we select a single column in the importance matrix (thereby selecting a class), each value represents the average class activation level of a specific feature for that selected class. Those features that are more activated (higher class activations) also have a greater influence on this selected model output class in general. Therefore, they can serve as the main features of this study.
