This phenomenon indicates that the models have some “lazy” features that contribute very little and can be pruned. For the definition of “importance” in this paper, we took the average of the sum of class activations over the whole dataset as the “importance” of a feature to a specific class. This originates from the same idea behind CAMs: the more activated features contribute more to the final output and are therefore the more important features. However, the definition of the importance of each feature could be further investigated, as the standard deviation of the average of the weighted features could also be informative. For examples, a rarely activated feature with massive class activation values in only very few cases might obtain high values in the importance matrices based on current definition of “importance”. However, this feature may represent a serious confounder or artifacts that only appear in some cases of a certain class because of unknown reasons. Considering this kind of situation, using average of the weighted features can lead to misunderstanding in some cases. Considering this, it is difficult to find an optimal way of defining the feature importance, delivering simple and clear messages. The definition of feature importance is therefore still an open question, awaiting the exploration through more studies. Some CAM algorithms were not presented in the experiments and results. There are three main reasons: (1) They fell in the scope of the formula in Fig. 1 , and therefore are theoretically the same as the used CAM algorithms. (2) The source code of some CAM algorithms were not accessible. (3) The computational efficiency was an essential issue, especially for perturbation-based CAM algorithms. In most studies, Grad CAM and Grad CAM++ are always the first choice just because of better technical support and high computing efficiency. (4) For multi-layer CAM algorithms, the low-level features have no direct link to the model outputs without going to the high-level features, their information was covered by the high-level features unless there are skip-connections to the output. Moreover, the calculation of weights becomes unreliable because of the increasing non-linearity of models during back-propagation or backward calculation. The advantage of these multi-layer methods is the resolution of CAMs, which is another topic out of the scope of this paper. Metrics such as Dice and IoU with masks of ground truths introduce an assumption that models trained through classification or regression loss functions should naturally focus on the region of interests that is aligned with human knowledge to obtain the output. However, models may predict through confounders, artifacts and even other objects in the foreground that have a high correlation with the targets. Since CAM algorithms are mainly developed to interpret trained models, not to cater to confirmation bias, these metrics based on the assumption were not applied. The framework is generalizable to other datasets, without needing to recalculate the upper and lower limits, provided that they result in similarly distributed class activations. This was accomplished by applying a non-linear projection for the global intensity scaling, that provides some redundant space for displaying extreme values. If a new dataset produces a different distribution of class activations, the framework only needs the inference process to update the upper and lower limit for rescaling all CAMs, without needing to retrain the DL model. Therefore the time cost of the framework is proportional to the DL model’s inference costs, which is considerably less than for training. While the inference process is still the limiting factor of the framework, the following strategies in this study were designed to improve this. Since the goal of global intensity scaling is to make an unbiased comparison between CAMs within the same dataset, inference on the entire training dataset is not always necessary. P h i g h and P l o w could be calculated on the test set, a subgroup of the training set with random sampling or even a subgroup of the test set. This approach has been applied in the experiments on the ILSVRC2012 validation set. If the purpose is to have correct and accurate visualization of only a limited amount of inputs, the P h i g h and P l o w can also be computed on those inputs only. Although the proposed methods are mostly applied to convolutional neural networks, the importance matrix and the common intensity scaling are not limited to these type of networks. They are also feasible for other deep learning models, because the original CAM algorithms are also feasible for different types of models [36] . We had applied the proposed method to the tiny transformer on MNIST to prove its generalizability. However, the integrated feature analysis faced a transition problem that requires further studies on the definition of features in transformers and recurrent neural networks and the spatial reorganization to generate CAMs in these models. The proposed method introduces several hyper-parameters to the original CAM algorithms, including the parameters for color re-scaling and threshold of “top N%” features. These hyper-parameters may significantly influence the visualization and therefore requires proper design. The 5–25 % percentages of top features in our experiments are manually and arbitrarily determined, which may not be optimal. This open question about the approach to define the “principal features” and obtain the “top N%” requires further investigation and may vary from dataset to dataset. The proposed method, incorporating both global intensity scaling and feature distinction, can contribute to two main application areas: visual model improvement and data mining/analysis. Both applications fundamentally depend on the generation of reliable and commensurable saliency maps (as the activation values in these normalized CAMs have the same scale) and the insights they provide into model feature extraction. For visual model improvement, three practical aspects are post-hoc evaluation, architecture optimization, and training guidance: • Post-hoc evaluation of models is intuitive and widely adopted, being one of the earliest applications of saliency maps. By visually or quantitatively inspecting saliency maps, researchers can assess the alignment between model attention and expert knowledge. However, confirmation bias [40] and other influencing factors [41] may lead to misinterpretation, especially when incomparable intensity scaling distorts perception. By introducing global intensity scaling, saliency maps become commensurable, thereby reducing misinterpretation caused by inconsistent intensity scales and enabling more reliable post-hoc evaluation. • Insights into feature importance, as revealed by feature distinction, can aid in analyzing trained models, as discussed in the section Uses of the Feature Distinction. This enables architecture optimization that is not feasible in previous CAM-based methods. For instance, model pruning and distillation can be achieved by progressively removing less-important features from the bottom to the top of the model hierarchy. • Similarly, the ability to analyze models at the feature level also provides guidance for more fine-grained training strategies. In previous studies, samples that were misclassified during training could be oversampled and retrained to improve learning of underfitted features. With saliency maps, one can investigate, which image features contribute to misclassification, allowing for targeted data augmentation (i.e., over- or under-sampling specific features) to guide training. With the proposed method’s more accurate saliency maps and clearer understanding of feature importance, we can more effectively map extracted features to their corresponding input features, and identify which extracted features are under-activated in the dataset ’ determining whether more data is needed to mitigate underfitting. Federated Convolutional Neural Networks (F-CNNs) for privacy-preserving multi-class skin lesion classification Skin lesions include a variety of abnormalities found on the skin. These may be benign (not cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). Every year, the number of cases of skin cancer increases globally, increasing the death rate. Medical data is scarce because people are reluctant to provide their health information due to privacy concerns. In this research, a decentralized machine learning approach, Federated learning, is the primary focus of the discipline to preserve patient data. Using this method, models are trained independently on several dispersed devices without sharing the data. To balance the data and enrich the dataset, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling technique with Edited Nearest Neighbors (SMOTEENN) is used in this study. The HAM10000 dataset was benchmarked using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Seven classes of HAM10000 include vascular skin lesions, benign keratosis, actinic keratosis, melanoma, dermatofibroma, and melanocytic nevi. A centralized method yields an accuracy of 99.39%, and f1-score, precision, and recall of 99.00%. A simulated Federated learning with three clients, ten rounds, and thirty training epochs produced 93.00% precision, 92.00% recall, 92.00% f1-score, and 91.80% accuracy, respectively. At the same time, an increase to four clients and thirty training epochs produced an accuracy, recall, precision, and f1-score of 97.00% with ten rounds. The skin, the largest organ of the body, is fully exposed. Skin lesion refers to the alteration in the skin’s appearance, as represented by Fig. 1 . There are two categories of skin lesions: melanocytic and non-melanocytic [1] . The hierarchy of skin lesions is shown in Fig. 2 . Melanocytic skin lesions can be benign or malignant (melanoma), originating from the melanocytes. Skin lesions that do not originate from melanocytes are classified as Non-melanocytic, and they can be either benign or malignant (malignant - non-melanoma). Skin cancer is emerging worldwide, causing an increase in death rates. Researchers discovered that a further 10% depletion of the ozone layer will raise 4500 melanoma and 300,000 non-melanoma skin cancer cases every year. One out of five Americans is affected by skin cancer [2,3] . Skin cancer remains a significant health concern in the United States, with thousands of individuals affected each year [4] . The best approach to control the fatality rate of skin cancer is to diagnose skin cancer at an early stage [5] . Similarities in lesions make it challenging for dermatologists to detect and diagnose them. It is daunting to notice skin cancer with the naked eye, as it initiates as a small mole [6] . Computer-aided technology for skin cancer diagnosis has not been approved as being very effective due to a lack of data and a focus only on specific tasks, such as dermoscopy. Deep learning models prove to be highly effective in automatically extracting and recognizing features from data. Even with simple computer models, deep learning models can perform tasks efficiently. It led researchers to use deep learning models for classifying images of the diseases [1] . Our objective is to classify skin lesions using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), as they are highly effective in image processing tasks, such as CT scans and MRIs. In this study, seven classes of skin lesions are described and classified, including Actinic Keratoses, Basal Cell Carcinoma, Benign keratosis, Dermatofibroma, Melanocytic nevi, Melanoma, and Vascular skin lesions. With the advancement of technology, privacy issues are emerging [7] . Machine learning models that need to be tested and trained require a dataset in a centralized form. Maintaining the privacy and security of patients’ clinical data is crucial, as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) prohibits the use of patients’ private data in a centralized form. Deep learning models did not perform well when they were not trained on high-scale datasets. To overcome privacy and security issues, the Federated Learning (FL) technique was introduced. Federated Learning is a decentralized approach that allows the training of a shared global model on local clients without revealing confidential data to the server. Clients train the models locally using their private data, and then the updated models are aggregated to create a new global model [2,8–12] . To classify skin lesions accurately and address privacy concerns, our study proposes a Convolutional Neural Network integrated with a Federated Learning approach for classifying skin lesion images using the HAM10000 dataset. The main contributions of our study include: 1. A deep learning-based model called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), with the integration of a Federated Learning approach, is developed for the precise classification of multiple skin lesions while ensuring the privacy of patients. 2. Using SMOTEENN to resolve the issue of an imbalanced dataset, which increases the size of the training dataset and boosts the classification accuracy. 3. Improving the model’s performance by using an activation function, preprocessing the images, optimizing the parameters, and using additional layers like batch normalization layers. 4. The performance of the model is enhanced using a stratified partitioning approach, which ensures that each client participating in a Federated Learning simulation gets the same class distribution as that of the entire dataset. A deep learning-based model called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), with the integration of a Federated Learning approach, is developed for the precise classification of multiple skin lesions while ensuring the privacy of patients. Using SMOTEENN to resolve the issue of an imbalanced dataset, which increases the size of the training dataset and boosts the classification accuracy. Improving the model’s performance by using an activation function, preprocessing the images, optimizing the parameters, and using additional layers like batch normalization layers. The performance of the model is enhanced using a stratified partitioning approach, which ensures that each client participating in a Federated Learning simulation gets the same class distribution as that of the entire dataset. Although federated learning has been applied to skin lesion classification, the present study introduces four significant innovations. First, we employ a stratified partitioning strategy to ensure balanced representation of all lesion classes across FL clients, an aspect largely ignored in prior research. Second, we integrate SMOTEENN as a pre-FL rebalancing method while maintaining privacy, enabling robust learning without exposing client-side data. Third, our multi-layer custom CNN is deeper and more specialized for multi-class skin lesion analysis than prior FL-based models, which typically rely on shallow architectures. Finally, we conduct a detailed comparative analysis of centralized vs. FL performance, demonstrating that our system maintains competitive accuracy (97%) while ensuring privacy preservation, highlighting an accuracy-privacy trade-off rarely discussed in FL-based skin lesion research. The rest of our work is organized in this paper as follows: Section 2 presents an overview of the relevant existing studies, including their methodologies, evaluation metrics, and results. Section 3 discusses the proposed method for privacy-preserving skin lesion multi-classification. Section 4 shows the results we achieved. Section 4.3 presents a discussion about how we achieved the results. Section 5 presents a summary of our research, followed by an outline of future work. This section provides an overview of the related previous research by methodologically organizing the prior studies, which is also illustrated by the gap analysis presented in Table 1 . These studies have focused on the detection and classification of skin lesions using deep-learning-based image processing. Some of these have implemented different deep learning models, including simple CNN models from scratch, transfer learning nets, some have used Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) and analyzed the privacy and security issues that were caused due to Internet of Things (IOT) devices and centralized approach, some have used combined approaches in which one part of model performs the segmentation and detection. In contrast, the other part focuses on classification, while some researchers have explored Federated learning to enhance privacy and security. Their analysis revealed that adding privacy layers decreases accuracy. Some addressed the issues of limited data availability. Jain et al. [13] compared six different transfer-learning nets to analyze their performance for the classification of skin cancer using seven classes of HAM10000. Due to the unbalanced dataset with a significant difference in the number of images for each class, it became difficult to predict the class with fewer images. For this, they used data augmentation and concluded that the replication of images showed better performance than non-replicated images. The Xception net performed better, achieving 90.48% accuracy, 88.76% precision, 89.57% recall, and 89.48% f1-score. Besides the transfer learning nets (VGG-16, InceptionV3, Efficient-B7, and DenseNet201), Islam et al. [4] suggested the IoMT and averaging ensemble classifier (VGG16, InceptionV3, Efficient-B7, and DenseNet-201). Initially, they experimented on the existing dataset of HAM10000 to evaluate the performance. Later, they collected real-time data from patients using an IoMT data-collection device connected to cloud storage. The device sent all the data to the cloud, where it was diagnosed and further assessed by a recommender team using CAD. Furthermore, the team provided medication based on the disease, which was classified using CAD. The outcome of their study was that the ensemble model surpassed other models with the precision, recall, accuracy, and f1-score of 86.72%, 87.22%, 87.22%, and 86.60%, respectively. The studies presented by Srinivasu et al. [14] and Kshirsagar et al. [15] proposed an approach (transfer learning) similar to the previous studies [1,2] that is deep learning based, MobileNetv2, and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) associated with a mobile application, and compared the performance of the proposed model with other state-of-the-art models like CNN, HARIS, FTNN, MobileNetv1, MobileNetv2, and VGG. The outcome of their study showed that MobileNetv2 with LSTM required minimal computational power and effort and enhanced the prediction accuracy and outperformed other models with an accuracy, precision, and recall of 85%–86%, 93.34%, and 89.34%, respectively. Moreover, the mobile application is designed to provide immediate and appropriate results. A two-stage framework was presented by the authors of the study by Adegun et al. [16] , which also demonstrated the value of a deep-learning-based approach. In the first stage, skin lesions were segmented and detected using the ISBI 2017 dataset with a CRF-based encoder–decoder. In the second stage, skin lesions were classified using FCN-based DenseNet and the HAM10000 dataset. According to the authors’ findings, their suggested segmentation and detection method performed best as compared to other cutting-edge segmentation techniques like FrCN and CNN-HRFB, with an accuracy of 95.50%. Their suggested classification method performed best as compared to other cutting-edge models like multilevel DenseNet, Dilated VGG16, and Dilated Inception V3 with 98.00% precision, 98.50% recall, 98.30% accuracy, and 93.00% f1-score, respectively. The study presented by Nigar, Natasha, et al. [1] also highlighted the importance of deep learning. The authors employed the ResNet-18, which is also a transfer learning model, like the ones presented in earlier studies [1–4] . They also introduced the LIME framework, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) system, in addition to this paradigm. After comparing the performance of the two nets, ResNet-18 and Inception-V3, it was revealed that ResNet-18 achieved the highest performance with 94.47% accuracy, 92.00% f1-score, 93.57% precision, and 94.01% recall, respectively, and the incorporation of a LIME framework improved the model’s real-time performance by facilitating user comprehension of the predictions made by the model. Similar to the previously reported findings [1–13] , the authors of this work showed how deep learning may be used to classify skin lesions accurately. Kassem et al. [17] included a transfer learning and a pre-trained GoogleNet model. The author repeated the experiment three times: initially with a dataset of 25,331 images, once using image augmentation (30,079 images), and once by reducing the number of classes to align with the smallest class, which contained 1912 images. The authors concluded that the suggested model performed best when the images were reduced. The results showed that the precision and accuracy were 80.36% and 94.92%, respectively. Additionally, GoogleNet was integrated with multi-class SVM and VGG19 for additional models. However, the performance of GoogleNet with SVM was poor, and GoogleNet with VGG19 required specific hardware specifications. Rather than using pre-trained models, Allugunti et al. [3] constructed a custom CNN model and assessed it using a dataset from the website . The dataset comprised 2475 images representing three distinct melanoma types (malignant melanoma, nodular melanoma, and superficial spreading melanoma). The proposed model was found to be more effective in diagnosing the type of melanoma and outperformed other ML-based algorithms such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Decision Tree with an accuracy of 88.83%, precision of 91.07%, recall of 87.68%, and f1-score of 89.32%, respectively. Chaturvedi et al. [18] addressed that skin cancer is increasing worldwide due to ultraviolet rays. An automated system was proposed to recognize skin cancer using deep learning. Similar to the prior studies, the authors of this study also used a transfer learning network, named MobileNet, which was trained on the HAM10000 dataset to classify skin lesions. The outcome was promising and showed an overall accuracy of 83.1% for the seven classes that were present in the dataset. Deep learning has been increasingly utilized in various medical image modality, such as radiology, ophthalmology, histopathology and dermatology, showing great potential for automatic feature extraction and diagnosis accuracy. Research in the field of chest X-ray pneumonia detection, diabetic retinopathy grading, and histopathological tumor classification demonstrates CNNs are good candidates for automating image pattern learning with minimal human intervention. Together, these developments drive the necessity of privacy-preserving frameworks like FL in order to safely enable the benefits of deep learning to sensitive clinical data. In addition to the transfer learning models (VGG and Inception), Połap et al. [19] presented a Federated Learning approach by simulating the two transfer learning models (VGG and Inception). They simulated 7 hospitals with 7 databases and performed the experiments with 10, 15, 20 rounds, training iterations of 25, 50, 100 and with 1, 7, 14 workers and concluded that by increasing the number of FL iterations, both the accuracy as well as training time increases but by increasing the no. of workers, the accuracy increases from 86.00% to 89.12% and training time reduced by 40% when compared with 7 workers and 56% for 1 worker. After the analysis of the FL approach, they used the Takagi–Sugeno system to test the fuzzy controller for the decision of the degree of risk after the knowledge has been collected from all databases, and found that if the result was below 0.6, it means low risk, if above 0.6, then observation is required, and if above 0.85, then high risk. Hossen et al. [8] proposed a different approach. Instead of using pre-trained nets, they presented a custom CNN model (nine layers). In this study, the model was merged with the FL approach for the classification of skin disease using four classes while preserving data privacy and security. They compared the performance of the proposed model with the benchmark algorithms of VGG16 and AlexNet and concluded that the proposed model surpassed the performance of the other two with the average precision, recall, and f1-score of 47.30%, 46.80%, and 47.05%, respectively. They also concluded that by increasing the number of 29 clients from 1000 to 2500, the accuracy increased from 81.21 to 94.15%. Furthermore, the FedML showed lower accuracy than CNN algorithms. Nam et al. [7] presented an approach similar to that of Hossen et al. [8] , utilizing a custom CNN model (four layers) integrated with the FL approach for skin disease classification, while preserving data privacy and security. They created 10 different clients, each training the CNN model and sharing the local network with the global network. The global network was then distributed to the clients, and this cycle was repeated 100 times. They trained the federated learning system with two different datasets. One with the original unbalanced HAM10000 dataset and the other with the HAM10000 dataset, which was balanced using the SMOTE technique, and concluded that the accuracy achieved by the federated learning system with the balanced dataset was 95%, which was 15% more than that achieved by the unbalanced dataset (79%). Hashmani et al. [9] proposed an adaptive federated machine learning model for skin disease detection, featuring an ensemble convolutional neural network. The architecture, combining local dermoscopy edges and a global server, showed promise in accurately diagnosing skin diseases with continuous improvement. Tested with the ISIC 2019 dataset, it envisioned a federated machine learning-based dermoscopy device for dermatologists for the diagnosis of skin tumors. Yaqoob et al. [20] introduced Async-FL-CNN, a method combining asynchronous federated learning and CNNs to enhance skin lesion diagnosis, while addressing healthcare data privacy concerns. It prioritizes updating shallow layers to minimize communication rounds and incorporates client selection algorithms. Results exhibit superior accuracy and communication efficiency compared to existing methods, indicating promise for advancing skin cancer diagnosis while safeguarding patient data privacy. The presented Async-FLCNN achieved higher performance as compared to existing and baseline models, achieving a remarkable 94.40% accuracy. It allows local clients to train asynchronously, enhancing the model’s efficacy and scalability. Agbley et al. [10] also proposed a Federated Learning approach for the melanoma skin lesion detection, using a transfer learning net called EfficientNet-B6, to ensure privacy and security while accurately detecting skin lesions. They used two modalities: the first modality was the skin lesion images taken from ISIC and from the Society for Imaging Informatics in Medicine (SIIM), and the second was the clinical data, including gender, ID of patients, and a detailed diagnosis of lesions. They performed the experiments with 5 clients and a PyTorch framework, using a federated average (FedAvg) technique to aggregate the parameters of local clients. This approach achieved an accuracy, precision, and recall of 83.01%, 82.14%, and 85.98%, respectively. The study presented by Omran et al. [11] proposed a pre-trained CNN model named VGG16, combined with a centralized Federated Learning framework 33 to categorize skin lesions while ensuring data privacy and security. They employed various strategies, including outlier identification using algorithms, such as One-Class SVM and Isolation Forests. The poisoned data was flagged for further analysis, which identified and addressed the data poisoning attacks. They concluded that the performance achieved by the FL environment was satisfactory, with a minimal difference in the accuracy (93.80%) as compared to the centralized environment (94.50%). The study by Wu et al. [12] explored federated contrastive learning (FCL) for dermatological disease diagnosis on mobile devices, prioritizing data privacy. Utilizing unlabeled data from distributed devices, it employs collaborative pre-training and subsequent fine-tuning. Experiments on diverse skin color datasets, including ISIC 2019, AtlasDerm, Dermnet, and DarkDerm, showcase improved precision and recall with FCL-based methods compared to local fine-tuning. These findings underscore the potential of FCL in enhancing dermatological diagnostics while preserving data privacy. Besides federated learning, several research works have proposed to protect medical images with watermarking and chaotic encryption and frequency-domain authentication. These methods mainly concentrate on the pixel-wise integrity and tamper-resistance, which is unlike the mechanism of privacy preservation at model level considered by federated learning. Although they are not directly comparable with our FL-based framework, such methods provide a more general direction to protect medical images. Further work could integrate watermarking or encryption with federated architectures for more complete end-to-end security. Since the existing approaches presented in the literature review have some limitations, some faced the problem of security and privacy breaches, while others faced data heterogeneity problems. Some models lagged due to poor performance, while others considered a few classes of disease. Additionally, some models required greater computational time and power, as well as fine-tuning to perform better, and some faced the problems of limited data availability. All these problems need to be addressed. Therefore, a better approach is required. Our findings suggest that by merging Federated Learning with a deep learning model, we can address the challenges posed by security and privacy concerns. Although recent FL-based dermatological studies demonstrate promising results, most exhibit key limitations including sensitivity to non-IID data distributions, inadequate class-balancing strategies, and minimal exploration of patient-level heterogeneity. Several works also lack stratified data allocation, contributing to unstable training and inconsistent convergence. Furthermore, federated scalability, communication efficiency, and privacy–utility trade-offs remain under-explored. These gaps reinforce the need for our proposed FL framework, which integrates SMOTEENN, stratified partitioning, and improved CNN optimization to address these limitations. Along with a CNN architecture, we implemented an FL approach, a decentralized method offering numerous benefits. The primary purpose of this approach is to enhance security and privacy for patients who are hesitant to share their medical records due to concerns over privacy and security [20] . Fig. 7 shows the architecture of federated learning, where a global model is distributed among local clients. Furthermore, federated learning will increase the availability of data by ensuring privacy and security [19] . The setup contains a central server and three local devices or clients for the first simulation, and four clients for the second simulation, who downloaded the global model and trained their local data without transmitting it to other devices or the server. FedAvg technique was used to aggregate the updates from the clients and to form a new updated global model [14] . Each client performed training for 3 epochs per round, out of the total 10 rounds, with a batch size of 32. After each round, the global model was updated and sent to all the clients, who kept on training the model for a specified number of rounds. Image 1001 This section illustrates the results we achieved using our proposed methodology of skin lesion multi-classification. To classify multiclass skin lesions, we developed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model, which we trained on the HAM10000 dataset. The dataset was divided into 25% test sets and 75% training sets. First, we conducted experiments in a centralized environment. Initially, the dataset was imbalanced, which prevented us from achieving satisfactory results. Then we balanced our dataset using SMOTEENN, which enabled us to achieve great results. The results of both the imbalanced and balanced datasets are represented by Fig. 9 . To further enhance the performance, additional layers such as batch normalization and activation were added, and we also increased the number of epochs. The training accuracy, validation accuracy, precision, recall, and f1-score of our proposed model (CNN) were 99.99%, 99.39%, 99.00%, 99.00%, and 99.00%, respectively. The validation accuracy and training of the model are too close, indicating good feature generalization. Next, we performed simulations in a decentralized environment, where a stratified partitioning technique is used to partition the dataset among the clients. Fig. 10 illustrates that by using three clients, thirty epochs and ten rounds, the simulation of a Federated Learning approach resulted in 93.00% precision, 92.00% recall, 91.80% accuracy and 92.00% f1-score respectively and Fig. 11 illustrates that by using four clients, thirty epochs and ten rounds, the simulation of a Federated Learning approach gave an accuracy, recall, precision and f1-score of 97.00%. To evaluate generalizability, a subset of 2000 images from the ISIC-2019 dataset [27] was used for external testing. The centralized model trained on HAM10000 achieved 89.4% accuracy, 87.2% precision, 86.5% recall and 86.8% f1-score. These results demonstrate strong generalizability despite variations in dermoscopic imaging devices and clinical settings between datasets, confirming the robustness of our proposed architecture across multiple skin lesion datasets. Table 2 presents a comparative analysis between our proposed method and all the other pre-existing methods that have used the same HAM10000 dataset for the classification of skin lesions. It demonstrates that our proposed CNN model achieved the highest performance of 97.00% accuracy, recall, precision, and f1-score with just four clients and 10 rounds. It concludes that by increasing the number of layers to 22, balancing the dataset, using optimized parameters, and employing effective strategies like the stratified partitioning approach, we were able to enhance the model’s performance and achieve such satisfactory results. The proposed model’s performance particularly the 97% accuracy in FL settings exceeds or matches the results of prior methods listed in Table 2 , including asynchronous FL, multi-layer CNNs, and metaheuristic optimization models. This improvement can be attributed to the combined effects of SMOTEENN balancing, stratified partitioning, and optimized CNN design. These results indicate that the model maintains strong predictive capability even under federated constraints The results obtained demonstrated that by balancing an imbalanced dataset, the size of the training dataset increased, which in turn boosted the classification accuracy. By using an activation function, preprocessing the images, optimizing the parameters, and using additional layers like batch normalization layers, the performance of the model was improved. We analyzed that by increasing the number of rounds and clients, and by using a stratified partitioning approach, which ensures that each client gets the same class distribution as that of the entire In the dataset, the performance of the model was further enhanced. Although the introduced FL framework is very effective, there are still some limitations. The current experiments demonstrate the system’s capabilities using simulated clients and do not investigate the scalability of the framework at higher communication frequencies. Lastly, we only evaluated on one data and cross-dataset generalization remain as future study. Further, we plan to investigate the integration with practical multi-institutional nodes, more sophisticated FL algorithms and hybrid security mechanism such as encryption based client protection. Beyond accuracy, we evaluated our FL setup in terms of communication cost, convergence, and privacy resilience. Each communication round required transmitting approximately 3.2 MB of model parameters per client, resulting in an overall cost of approximately 96 MB for 10 rounds. Compared to heavy transfer-learning models used in skin lesion studies e.g., VGG16, Inception, which require 20–80 MB per round, our architecture is more communication-efficient. The convergence analysis showed that the FL model stabilized after 6 to 7 rounds, consistent with the accuracy trends shown in Figs. 10 and 11 . Although this work does not implement cryptographic enhancements, several privacy-preserving properties naturally arise: no raw skin lesion images or labels are exchanged, and deeper CNN architectures with batch normalization make gradient inversion attacks more difficult. Future work will incorporate differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and homomorphic encryption to further increase security. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed using TensorFlow, the Keras API, batch normalization, convolutional layers, dense layers, and max-pooling layers. The SMOTEENN approach was employed to tackle the issue of class imbalance. To assess the model’s performance, the dataset was divided into training and testing sets. An accuracy of 99. 39%, f1 score, recall and precision of 99.00% were obtained using a centralized Convolutional Neural Network. To preserve patient privacy, we employed Federated learning in a simulated environment comprising three clients and thirty training epochs, resulting in a 92.00% f1-score, 91.80% accuracy, 93.00% precision, and 92.00% recall, after ten rounds, and an accuracy, recall, precision, and f1-score of 97.00% after ten rounds was obtained with a simulation of four clients and thirty training epochs. In the future, other methods for protecting privacy and security can be employed, including Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC), Homomorphic Encryption, and Poisoning Attack Detection. In addition, the system’s performance can be improved by increasing the number of clients and rounds. data.text: Federated learning using quality-based aggregation method for brain tumour segmentation on multimodality medical images Deep learning for medical imaging has shown great potential in improving patient outcomes due to its high accuracy in disease diagnosis. However, a major challenge preventing the widespread adoption of such models in clinical settings is data accessibility, which conflicts with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in a traditional centralised training environment. Hence, to address this issue, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced as a decentralised alternative that enables collaborative model training among data owners without sharing any private data. Despite its significance in healthcare, limited research has explored FL for medical imaging, particularly in multimodal brain tumour segmentation, due to challenges such as data heterogeneity. In this study, we present Federated E-CATBraTS, an advanced federated deep learning model derived from the existing E-CATBraTS framework. This model is designed to segment brain tumours from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) while preserving data privacy. Our framework introduces a novel aggregation method, DaQAvg, which optimally combines model weights based on data size and quality, demonstrating resilience against corrupted medical images. We evaluated the performance of Federated E-CATBraTS using two publicly available datasets: UPenn-GBM and UCSF-PDGM, including a degraded version of the latter to assess the efficacy of our aggregation method. The results indicate a 6% overall improvement over traditional centralised approaches. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive comparison against state-of-the-art FL aggregation algorithms, including FedAVG, FedProx and FedNova. While FedNova demonstrated the highest overall DSC, DaQAvg demonstrated superior robustness to noisy conditions, showcasing its specific advantage in maintaining performance with variable data quality, a critical aspect in medical imaging. However, a major challenge preventing the widespread adoption of such models in clinical settings is data accessibility, which conflicts with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in a traditional centralised training environment. Hence, to address this issue, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced as a decentralised alternative that enables collaborative model training among data owners without sharing any private data. Despite its significance in healthcare, limited research has explored FL for medical imaging, particularly in multimodal brain tumour segmentation, due to challenges such as data heterogeneity. In this study, we present Federated E-CATBraTS, an advanced federated deep learning model derived from the existing E-CATBraTS framework. This model is designed to segment brain tumours from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) while preserving data privacy. Our framework introduces a novel aggregation method, DaQAvg, which optimally combines model weights based on data size and quality, demonstrating resilience against corrupted medical images. We evaluated the performance of Federated E-CATBraTS using two publicly available datasets: UPenn-GBM and UCSF-PDGM, including a degraded version of the latter to assess the efficacy of our aggregation method. The results indicate a 6% overall improvement over traditional centralised approaches. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive comparison against state-of-the-art FL aggregation algorithms, including FedAVG, FedProx and FedNova. These datasets were derived from the following resources available in the public domain: UCSF-PDGM an UPENN-GBM . Confidentiality is a fundamental aspect of protecting sensitive data and fostering trust in healthcare systems. It refers to the set of rules that restrict access to and use of individuals’ information. All healthcare centres and data owners must comply with confidentiality law ( N England, 2013 ). Federated Learning (FL) is one of the latest advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), emphasising the protection of sensitive data, particularly patient information. FL enables the distributed training of AI models on the data owners’ servers, ensuring that data remains confidential and protected from security risks ( Banabilah, Aloqaily, Alsayed, Malik, & Jararweh, 2022 ). This represents a major advancement in integrating deep learning (DL) models into real-world medical imaging applications. By leveraging FL, data owners can contribute to AI model development while maintaining data privacy ( Rieke et al., 2020a ). FL addresses key limitations in centralised DL training, such as restricted access to medical data and privacy concerns. Training high-accuracy models require a large dataset ( Rieke et al., 2020b ). However, acquiring high-quality medical images is often impractical due to the high cost of advanced imaging equipment ( Equipped for the Future: Diagnostics equipment in NHS England – the case for investment, 2024 ). Moreover, in centralised approaches, data must be transmitted over a network to a central server, increasing vulnerability to cyber threats. FL mitigates these risks by eliminating direct data sharing, thereby reducing exposure to security breaches. The application of FL is particularly valuable for complex tasks such as brain tumour segmentation from medical images, where tumours exhibit significant variability and require large, diverse datasets. Furthermore, ensuring data privacy is critical to preventing face reconstruction from MRIs using brain-decoding models ( VanRullen & Reddy, 2019 ). Despite its potential, most research has focused on centralised DL approaches due to challenges in adopting FL, including: (1) data heterogeneity, which requires a generalisable deep learning model capable of segmenting brain tumours across diverse datasets using an efficient and fair aggregation method, (2) the trade-off between model accuracy and data confidentiality, where ensuring privacy may come at the cost of model performance. A review of the literature highlights a critical limitation: existing frameworks often rely on homogeneous datasets that fail to capture the diverse nature of medical data, raising concerns about their generalisability in real-world applications ( Manthe, Duffner, & Lartizien, 2024 ). Furthermore, balancing model accuracy with data confidentiality remains a significant challenge, underscoring the need for a more robust and adaptable approach in FL model development. Given these challenges, this study aims to advance the field by introducing Federated E-CATBraTS, a novel FL framework designed to enhance the accuracy of brain tumour segmentation while rigorously protecting medical data. E-CATBraTS is a hybrid deep learning model that integrates Vision transformers (ViT) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to perform 3-dimensional (3D) segmentation of brain tumours on MRI scans. Its strong generalisation capabilities make it well-suited for handling diverse medical datasets, addressing the limitations of existing approaches ( El Badaoui, Bonmati Coll, Psarrou, Asaturyan, & Villarini, 2025 ). To further improve FL performance, we propose a novel aggregation method, Data Quality Averaging (DaQAvg), which optimally balances data quantity and quality from each participating client. We rigorously evaluate our framework on two distinct datasets using established metrics, including the DSC and Intersection over Union (IoU). We evaluate DaQAvg against prominent state-of-the-art FL algorithms, namely FedAVG, FedProx and FedNova, to provide a comprehensive assessment of its effectiveness, relative performance, and robustness in improving segmentation accuracy to validate its effectiveness in improving segmentation accuracy while maintaining patient confidentiality across varying conditions. The full code is available at The main contributions of this study are: • Presenting a generalisable FL framework for brain tumour segmentation using E-CATBraTS, effectively improving segmentation accuracy without exposing medical data. • Proposing a novel weighted aggregation method (DaQAvg) that optimally integrates both data quality and size. • Demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed FL model on brain tumour segmentation tasks. • Evaluating the proposed FL framework on two distinct brain tumour datasets, contributing to the understanding of its real-world applicability. Demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed FL model on brain tumour segmentation tasks. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: The next section reviews state-of-the-art approaches in Federated Learning and traditional deep learning models. Section 3 describes the methodology, datasets, and experimental setup, and Section 4 provides theoretical analysis and convergence guarantee of our proposed aggregation method. Section 5 presents our experimental findings, while Section 6 provides a critical analysis of the results and discusses the limitations of our proposed framework. Finally, Section 7 summarises our key findings and conclusions. Federated learning is a collaborative machine learning approach to train AI models on decentralised data without putting users’ data at risk. This approach enhances the security of the healthcare system by protecting patients’ data from potential attacks associated with traditional centralised AI models. Therefore, several studies have been published on the integration of federated learning in healthcare. This section reviews recent research in this area and addresses its current limitations. Federated learning is a technology introduced by Google in February 2016 ( McMahan, Moore, Ramage, Hampson, & y. Arcas, 2017 ) to enhance the user experience on modern mobile devices by leveraging decentralised training. While the concept initially promised significant enhancements, their proposed weighting algorithm, Federated Averaging (FedAvg), assumes uniform data distribution and quality across clients, which is often not the case in real-world applications where data heterogeneity is a major challenge. FL has since been adopted across various sectors, including banking and transportation ( Nguyen et al., 2021; Shingi, 2020 ). Additionally, the implementation of federated learning is widely adopted in smart homes due to the significant increase in smart (IoT) devices. A study from 2020 ( Zhao, Zhao, Jiang, Tan, Niyato, Li, Lyu, & Liu, 2021 ) suggests that federated learning can empower manufacturers to analyse consumer behaviour by training models on client data. Furthermore, the study incorporates differential privacy (DP) and Laplacian noise during training to prevent sensitive data leakage and protect against attackers obtaining the actual information. However, this approach can sometimes affect model accuracy, highlighting the trade-off between privacy and performance, which is particularly critical in high-accuracy domains like medical imaging. Beyond cross-device FL, where models are trained on personal devices, cross-silo FL has emerged as a valuable alternative for settings involving a small number of reliable institutions, such as hospitals, universities, and industry partners ( Huang, Tang, Ma, Huang, & Liu, 2024 ). This paradigm allows organisations to collaborate on training robust models while keeping their data decentralised and private. One example is FL in the agri-food sector, where a study ( Durrant et al., 2022 ) enabled data sharing across supply chains, aiming to optimise production through soybean yield prediction. The FL approach improved crop yield prediction by 1.32% using satellite images compared to the centralised models. This study employs a distributed machine learning approach, facilitating individual participants to train models using their local data silos and then share those models for ensemble predictions. Similar to the previous study, the authors explored DP to mitigate attacks on the data. However, challenges remained, including limited performance due to small data silos and a lack of scalability assessment, as the study tested FL with only 9 to 11 silos. Despite these limitations, the findings demonstrated the potential of FL in optimising production across distributed networks. In the past decade, there has been a growing interest in using DL for brain tumour segmentation. In a recent study ( B.R.A., Patro, Allam, Jamjoom, & Samee, 2023 ), researchers proposed a modified DL model based on the well-known U-Net network. This modified U-Net was trained and evaluated using two datasets, BraTS 2018 and BraTS 2017, to segment brain tumours from 3D MRI scans. The encoder of the modified model utilises a pre-trained ResNet34, and the decoder is made up of four U-Net blocks. The results showed improved accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods, including SegNet and U-Net, with a DSC of 0.93. Although the results demonstrate a significant improvement in accuracy, future research should focus on enhancing the model’s generalisability, its robustness against variations in imaging protocols, and ensuring the privacy of patient data. Researchers from NVIDIA ( Li et al., 2019 ) implemented the first federated learning framework for medical image processing, specifically for brain tumour segmentation. The privacy-preserving framework uses a deep neural network (DNN) with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for gradient optimisation. A single dataset was used, the BraTS 2018 dataset, which contains 285 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans for cases with brain tumours. The dataset includes four MRI modalities for each case, including T1-weighted, T1-weighted CE (contrast enhancement), T2-weighted, and T-Flair. The images were collected from thirteen different medical centres and distributed to thirteen clients based on the source of the images. By training the model on data that has already been cleaned and pre-processed following the same techniques, the study undermines the essence of true FL, which seeks to utilise diverse data from various datasets in a decentralised environment. The federated training starts by sending the global model parameter to all clients, and then the clients train the model on their local data for a fixed number of epochs (two epochs). After all the clients finish the training phase, they send the weights back to the server to aggregate them. The whole training process runs for 300 federated rounds. The FL framework results were compared to the data-centralised approach, showing a trade-off between protecting the patients’ sensitive data and the DL model’s segmentation performance. While the effort to create a FL framework for medical imaging is noteworthy, the study’s limitations and methodological shortcomings raise concerns about the realism of the federated setup, despite claims. In another major study, an enhanced variant of the U-Net architecture, SU-Net, was proposed to advance brain tumour segmentation through federated learning ( Yi et al., 2020 ). SU-Net integrates an inception module ( Szegedy et al., 2015 ) and dense block ( Huang, Liu, Van Der Maaten, & Weinberger, 2017 ) for adding width and depth to the network. The network was assessed using both Federated learning and centralised approaches on a single dataset containing a total of 3,929 low-grade glioma (LGG) images from 110 patients, which may limit the generalisability of the results as the size and diversity of the dataset are crucial for developing robust models. SU-Net demonstrated superior performance compared to all other networks. With the federated learning setup, SU-Net demonstrated a slight improvement over the non-federated approach, ultimately outperforming the other networks. For the federated framework, the research utilised Google’s open-source federated learning framework, TensorFlow Federated (TFF), and distributed the data across five clients. While the results suggest promising applications for federated learning, significant challenges remain, including data privacy and model convergence across heterogeneous environments, which is vital for clinical applicability. Ullah et al. (2023) proposed a FL framework for brain tumour segmentation that utilises the U-Net architecture on the high-quality BraTS 2019 dataset. However, the model’s performance may degrade when clients provide biased or low-quality data. To aggregate the weights returned from the clients, the authors employed the widely used FedAvg aggregation method, which does not fairly account for the clients’ contributions. Factors such as variability, data quality, and labelling quality collectively influence the dataset’s effectiveness. In addition, several techniques for model compression and sparsification were applied to minimise communication costs, although this was acknowledged to increase the computational cost of the aggregation process. Despite the high accuracy of deep learning models in brain tumour segmentation and the privacy and confidentiality offered by FL, both the centralised and the decentralised approaches have notable limitations. These limitations contribute to uncertainty among medical clinicians regarding the adoption of these methods. When it comes to deep learning approaches, there are several current challenges to consider: (I) Insufficient datasets: The performance of deep learning models relies on the size and quality of the datasets used for training and validation. Smaller medical centres may lack access to high-quality datasets, which can result in suboptimal model performance ( Ng, Lan, Yao, Chan, & Feng, 2021 ). (II) Breach of confidentiality laws: Healthcare centres are required to comply with confidentiality regulations when handling patient data. Transmitting data over the network to a central server for training can expose patient information to potential breaches and malicious attacks ( Aich et al., 2022; Finlayson et al., 2019 ). While the FL framework addresses certain privacy concerns, several challenges and unresolved issues remain. One significant challenge is data heterogeneity, where collaborating clients collect and label their data differently, potentially leading to a decline in the model’s performance ( Babar, Qureshi, & Koubaa, 2024; Karani, Chaitanya, Baumgartner, & Konukoglu, 2018 ). Another major concern is the efficient aggregation of model weights, which is an essential component in FL. Each site-specific model’s contribution should be accurately weighted based on factors such as labelling quality and the quality of data at each client. This paper primarily focuses on enhancing privacy in deep learning models and effectively segmenting brain tumours from multimodal 3D MRI scans while ensuring the protection of patients’ data even in noisy conditions. The study aims to evaluate the performance of federated learning compared to centralised machine learning for brain tumour segmentation. We present a federated approach that uses an existing generalisable neural network (NN), Enhanced E-CATBraTS, explained in 3.1 . The proposed approach enables distributed training of E-CATBraTS on two distinct datasets containing MRI images acquired from various clinics, detailed in 3.4 . Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed federated framework. We adopt the Flower ( Beutel et al., 2022 ) framework with E-CATBraTS to enable collaborative DL model training while ensuring the privacy and security of patient data. Within this framework, the E-CATBraTS model is trained locally on each client’s server, utilising their unique datasets. The federated framework consists of a single central server and multiple clients. Initially, each Flower client is prepared with its own local copy of the model and its unique dataset for training. On the server side, the system orchestrates the entire federated learning process by sending and receiving model parameters, as well as training configurations and hyperparameters. Within the central server, the aggregation function and the overall federated learning strategy are configured. A commonly used weighted average algorithm is employed as the aggregation function and is compared to our proposed aggregation method based on the quality of the medical images, which will be explained in greater detail in the following section. In our method, we define key parameters, including the aggregation technique, the minimum number of training rounds and evaluations, and the process for updating and saving the global model on the central server. Several federated learning frameworks have been proposed for brain tumour segmentation. These frameworks utilise deep neural networks based on the broader concept of CNNs or, specifically, U-Net. Choosing the right DL model for federated learning is a crucial step that has a significant impact on the quality of the federated segmentation, especially when dealing with Non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) datasets, which is often the case in federated environments. Hence, the chosen DL model should possess high accuracy, good generalisability and effective convergence. Therefore, in this study, we utilise a generalisable model, E-CATBraTS ( El Badaoui et al., 2025 ). E-CATBraTS performs volumetric semantic segmentation of brain tumours on multi-modality MRI scans, and we use it as the base model for the federated clients to train on their local data within the federated learning environment. Notably, E-CATBraTS is a novel model that demonstrates high generalisability, surpassing the current state-of-the-art on several datasets for brain tumour segmentation on multi-modal MRIs. The model takes four volumetric MRI sequences as input, namely T1-weighted CE, T1-weighted, T2, and T-Flair. As part of the ViT architecture, the input is divided into patches, flattened and embedded with positional information before being fed into Swin-T. Following the ViT phase, a channel shuffling block is applied to each ViT patch to enhance information transfer between channels. In this way, the information flow and interaction between the feature channels are improved, which optimises the generalisability and accuracy of the model. It also helps mitigate overfitting by encouraging the model to learn more robust features that are less specific to the training data. Subsequently, the shuffled blocks are processed using advanced channel-attention down-sampling blocks that incorporate a channel shuffling module. The encoding blocks comprise a single 3 × 3 × 3 convolutional layer followed by 3D batch normalisation, a channel attention layer, and a LeakyReLU function. Finally, the weights are up-sampled using decoding blocks to compute the segmentation features. Through various training scenarios, E-CATBraTS has demonstrated better stability and higher accuracy, making it a compelling choice for federated brain tumour segmentation across different datasets. After the Flower clients train the model locally, they send the updated parameters to the server. The server then aggregates the weights once it has received updates from all the participating clients. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is one of the most widely used aggregation algorithms in federated Learning. FedAvg is a simple aggregating function that calculates the average parameters from all participating clients, taking into account the size of each client’s dataset. The FedAvg formula for the new global model w t + 1 is: w t + 1 = ∑ k = 1 K n k w k t N where K represents the number of participating clients, n k the data samples on client k , N the total number of data sample across all clients and w k t + 1 is the local update from client k at communication round t . Data Quality Averaging (DAQAVG) In this paper, we introduce a novel weight-averaging technique called Data Quality Averaging (DaQAvg), designed to enhance the training of models by incorporating the quality of medical scans. This method aims to efficiently reflect the contributions of individual clients, taking into account both the size and quality of the datasets they provide. DaQAvg can be mathematically defined as follows: w t + 1 = ∑ k = 1 K ( n k + q k ) w k t N + Q where Q represents image quality metric values at all clients and q k is the quality metric value for client k . To identify the most appropriate quality metric for our analysis, we have explored several cutting-edge metrics for image quality. These include the Perception-based Image Quality Evaluator (PIQE) ( V.N.P.D, Bh, Channappayya, & Medasani, 2015 ), the Natural Image Quality Evaluator (NIQE) ( Mittal, Soundararajan, & Bovik, 2013 ), and the concept of entropy. Both PIQE and NIQE are significant metrics for assessing the quality of natural images without the need for reference images. PIQE mimics human visual perception by identifying distortions in images. It has been applied in medical imaging contexts, including the evaluation of MRI image quality following the application of an anisotropic diffusion filter for denoising and enhancing MRI images ( Kumar, Kumar, & Srivastava, 2020 ). Additionally, it has been utilised to assess the performance of the super-resolution (SR) DL model in enhancing the visibility of microcalcifications in mammography ( Honjo et al., 2022 ). In another study, PIQE, NIQE, and entropy were employed as metrics to evaluate various techniques aimed at improving MRI image quality ( Abin, Thakare, Fasate, Suryawanshi, & Surdas, 2024 ). PIQE can be computed using: P I Q E = ∑ k = 1 N b D s k + C 1 ( N b + C 1 ) Where N b , is the number of distorted blocks in an image, C 1 is a positive constant number, and D s k is the local distortion measure. On the other hand, NIQE measures deviations from expected natural statistical properties by analysing features such as brightness variations, colour distribution, and pixel relationships. This metric has also been leveraged in medical imaging to assess the quality of brain MRIs generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) ( Treder, Codrai, & Tsvetanov, 2022 ). Furthermore, it has been tested on simulated X-ray images, underscoring its applicability to clinical imaging ( Buytaert, Taeymans, De Wolf, & Bacher, 2021 ). NIQE can be computed using: N I Q E = ( μ 1 − μ 2 ) T ( Σ 1 + Σ 2 2 ) − 1 ( μ 1 − μ 2 ) Where μ 1 and Σ 1 are the mean and covariance matrix of the natural image multivariate Gaussian model. While μ 2 and Σ 2 are the mean and covariance matrix of the test image’s multivariate Gaussian model. Lastly, we also consider the image entropy, which quantifies the amount of information or uncertainty present in an image based on the distribution of pixel values. The entropy H with L discrete intensity levels can be computed using: H = − ∑ i = 0 L p i log 2 ( p i + ϵ ) Where p i is probability of intensity level i . ϵ is an arbitary number 2 . 2 × 1 0 − 16 . By integrating and evaluating these diverse image quality metrics, we aim to further improve the accuracy and reliability of the DaQAvg method, establishing it as an effective aggregation technique for merging the weights returned by participating clients. A pseudocode algorithm outlining this approach is provided in Algorithm 1. Considering the associated communication cost, the total number of trainable parameters is 113,399,301, resulting in an estimated model size of 432.58 MB. With a maximum of 50 communication rounds, 432.58 MB will be transmitted by each client and the server. To provide a comprehensive evaluation of DaQAvg, our study includes a rigorous comparison against the baseline FedAVG in addition to FedProx ( Li et al., 2020 ) and FedNova ( Wang, Liu, Liang, Joshi, & Poor, 2021 ). FedProx is designed to mitigate client drift in heterogeneous settings by adding a proximal term to the local loss function, ensuring local models remain close to the global model. FedNova, on the other hand, normalises local updates by their effective local sample sizes, which addresses the issue of varying local training times and data distributions, leading to more stable and accurate convergence. The experiment was carried out using two distinct workstations, Workstation A and Workstation B. Workstation A is equipped with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 graphics processing unit (GPU) that boasts a graphics memory capacity of 10 GB. It also features a powerful Intel Core i9 processor and is supported by 32 GB of RAM. In contrast, Workstation B utilises an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 GPU, which offers a graphics memory capacity of up to 12 GB. This workstation is powered by an Intel Core i7 processor from the 13th generation and is equipped with 16 GB of RAM. The programming language Python was employed throughout the experiment to facilitate the necessary computations and model training processes. Due to constraints in available resources, we limited the experiment to two clients for the federated learning processes. Notably, both the central server and the participating clients were connected to the same local network, ensuring seamless communication and data exchange. We undertook multiple experiments with a variety of configurations, adjusting the number of training rounds and local epochs to assess their impact on performance. The details of these configurations and the results obtained will be elaborated in the subsequent section. For optimising the model parameters during training, we employed the AdamW stochastic optimisation method. We initialised the learning rate at 5 × 1 0 − 5 , and it simultaneously decays over the training process using a CosineAnnealingLR scheduler. This scheduler adjusts the learning rate following a cosine curve, which helps in fine-tuning the model during training and can contribute to achieving better convergence. To rigorously assess the statistical significance of the observed performance differences between the proposed DaQAvg method and FedAvg, we employed the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test statistical validation technique. Two datasets were used for this study, which are The University of Pennsylvania glioblastoma (UPenn-GBM) ( Bakas et al., 2022 ) and the University of California San Francisco Preoperative Diffuse Glioma MRI (UCSF-PDGM) ( Calabrese et al., 2022 ) datasets with a total of 630 scans and 500 scans, respectively. Both datasets contain multi-modal MRI volumes of the brain for patients with brain tumours. Only cases with the following MRI sequences were included: (i) T1-weighted (T1), (ii) T1-weighted with contrast enhancement (T1-Gd), (iii) T2-weighted (T2), and (iv) T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR). The tumour segmentation annotation is provided for each subject and is labelled into three subregions, namely enhancing tumour (ET), whole tumour (WT), and tumour core (TC). ET surrounds the necrotic cells of the TC, while WT surrounds all abnormal cells. Additionally, we added a third dataset, which is a noisy version of UCSF-PDGM. This modification was essential given the high quality of the original datasets, as it allowed us to examine the model’s efficacy under noisy and noise-free conditions, which otherwise could lead to overly optimistic performance metrics. We aimed to simulate real-world scenarios when testing the aggregation algorithm with combinations of UPENN and UCSF and UPENN alongside the noisy UCSF. Fig. 2 , shows an example image before and after applying the noise. The noise added was carefully selected to reflect common artefacts and disturbances typically encountered in MRI images. Our analysis emphasises the relationship between data quantity and quality, especially in heterogeneous (non-IID) environments. Consider K clients, each with local dataset D k of size n k and quality metric q k ≥ 0 . The global objective is: min w F ( w ) = ∑ k = 1 K α k F k ( w ) , where α k = n k + λ q k N + λ Q , N = ∑ k = 1 K n k , (1) Q = ∑ k = 1 K q k Here F k ( w ) is the local loss for client k , and λ ≥ 0 controls the quality-quantity trade-off. DaQAvg’s aggregation weights clients by both data quantity and quality to prioritise reliable updates.
