In this section, our focus is on three critical areas: attention mechanisms, multi-scale contextual feature fusion techniques, and uncertainty awareness for the segmentation of breast lesions in ultrasound images. Prior research on this task is increasingly dependent upon these methods. Recent advancements in attention mechanisms have significantly boosted the performance of CNN-based models, particularly in the segmentation of breast lesions in ultrasound images. Techniques such as squeeze-and-excitation network (SE-Net) [42] , efficient channel attention (ECA) [43] , convolutional block attention module (CBAM) [44] , and triplet attention [45] have been instrumental in enhancing segmentation precision by focusing computational resources on the most relevant portions of the image. An example of this advancement is ESKNet [46] , which features an enhanced encoder–decoder architecture. ESKNet incorporates the enhanced selective kernel module that combines channel and spatial attention mechanisms. This integration within a U-Net framework, supported by deep supervision, enables the network to effectively manage the complex and variable characteristics of breast tumors. However, it is computationally intensive and has a higher inference time. EMCAD [47] significantly reduces computational complexity of Transformer-based encoders and CNN-based decoders through multi-scale grouped attention and hierarchical spatial refinement. It employs channel and spatial attention for feature recalibration, preserving fine details in early decoder stages. While EMCAD indirectly leverages global context through pre-trained encoders, it lacks explicit global self-attention within the decoder, potentially limiting direct modeling of long-range spatial dependencies. TaiChiNet [48] introduces a dual U-Net with negative-positive cross-attention to enhance lesion and background feature representation. It employs cross-attention for bidirectional information exchange and a complementary head with MLPs for shallow feature refinement, reinforced by a complementary loss function. Nevertheless, the complementary supervision mechanism requires careful tuning to avoid redundant feature interactions. Ma et al. [49] propose ATFE-Net for breast mass segmentation, leveraging an axial transformer for self-attention along spatial axes. This design connects shallow and deep features while reducing computational complexity. However, its fixed spatial attention and lack of uncertainty modeling can limit adaptability to lesion variations. Zhao et al. [50] integrate a focal self-attention block into the U-Net architecture to capture fine-grained local features for better boundary detection of breast lesions and coarse-grained global context to reduce noise. However, the model has slow inference speed due to focal self-attention. MaS-TransUNet [51] incorporates edge attention to refine boundary delineation, channel attention (CA) for feature relevance prioritization, and feedback attention for iterative refinement using previous predictions. Nevertheless, its reliance on iterative refinement through feedback attention can potentially lead to increased computational complexity during both training and inference. AMS-PAN [52] integrates spatial and channel attention (SCA) with multi-scale feature extraction. They use depthwise separable convolutions (DSConv) in the encoder and an SCA module in the decoder to enhance edge details and refine features with a global attention upsampling module for feature fusion. However, it demonstrates limited effectiveness when dealing with variable lesions that have ambiguous boundaries. Over the past few years, breast lesion segmentation in ultrasound images has witnessed significant improvements, thanks largely to deep learning-based methods that integrate multi-scale feature extraction and contextual fusion. More recently, researchers have begun to incorporate Transformer-based architectures — renowned for their ability to model long-range dependencies — into these workflows. The result is a new generation of hybrid networks that combine CNNs, Transformers, and attention mechanisms to improve segmentation accuracy and robustness. Zhang et al. [31] propose FET-UNet, a hybrid CNN-Transformer model that integrates ResNet34 and Swin Transformer branches for multi-scale local–global feature extraction in breast ultrasound segmentation, where features are fused via an advanced feature aggregation module combining spatial self-attention and channel recalibration. Liu et al. [53] present MFAR-Net, another CNN-Transformer hybrid network that employs ResNet34 and a Pyramid Pooling Transformer as parallel encoder branches, complemented by a Multi-level Feature Interaction module and a Dual-Dimension Adaptive Reinforcement module to improve feature representation and correct lesion predictions. Although both architectures [31,53] adopt dual-branch encoders, the fusion of CNN and Transformer features may not always fully preserve complementary information, potentially leading to suboptimal representation learning, especially when feature distributions across branches differ significantly. Feng et al. [54] propose HTBE-Net, a hybrid CNN-Transformer model for breast ultrasound segmentation. It employs a dual-branch encoder for local and global features, a boundary-guided module, and selective feature enhancement. While improving boundary preservation, HTBE-Net struggles with scattering noise and overfitting due to its fixed boundary enhancement strategy. He et al. [55] propose HCT-Net, a hybrid model combining CNNs and Transformers. It uses Transformer blocks for global context in the encoder and spatial-wise cross-attention in the decoder. However, its high computational cost, memory inefficiency, and rigid feature extraction can limit adaptability. DAU-Net [56] integrates Positional CBAM for local spatial attention and shifted window attention in the bottleneck for global context. Nevertheless, its fixed feature aggregation lacks multi-scale refinement. Roy et al. [57] propose EU 2 Net which fine-tunes the U2-Net architecture [58] by replacing standard convolutions with separable convolutions to reduce parameter overhead. Their attention-aided triple feature fusion module integrates multi-scale features using similarity-based attention to highlight pixel-wise correlations, SE-Net-based attention for adaptive feature re-calibration, and Sobel-filter-based edge features to ensure precise boundary information; nonetheless, the method relies on pre-defined network depths that potentially can limit adaptability to varying lesion complexities. Iqbal et al. [32] propose MDA-Net, integrating a multi-scale fusion block and dual attention (channel and lesion) for improved feature representation. However, its lack of global context aggregation and manual feature weighting limits adaptability to varying lesion structures. [59] take a different path with a rolling-Unet network that employs a rolling multilayer perceptron (R-MLP) to capture linear dependencies across image dimensions. The design extends this idea with orthogonal-MLP and double orthogonal-MLP modules for multi-directional dependency modeling, all integrated within a long-local block to efficiently merge global and local feature information. Regardless, the method is less robust for low-contrast lesion segmentation. Wang et al. [34] introduce MF-Net, a multiple-feature extraction network integrating a Transformer-based auxiliary bi-encoder that combines a Transformer branch for global context with a CNN branch for local detail extraction. The multiple-feature extraction module enhances feature representation using multi-scale local features and frequency domain information, while the global feature enhancement module strengthens high-level semantic features for robust segmentation. However, the reliance on frequency domain transformation adds computational complexity, and the direct fusion of CNN and Transformer features may introduce feature inconsistency. Feng et al. [5] propose GBE-Net, which integrates a GBE block within UX-Net [60] for fine-grained spatial features and a dual-branch encoder combining spatial and boundary cues via edge detection. A boundary enhancement module and loss function refine segmentation. Nonetheless, GBE-Net suffers from boundary misalignment due to fixed edge detection, and possible redundant computations from its dual-encoder design. Zhu et al. [61] in their proposed architecture SECA-Net, modify the U-Net structure with a ResNet-based encoder and introduce two key modules. SECA-Net employs squeeze and excitation (SE)-based multi-scale atrous convolution for feature extraction and a Spatial-Channel Attention module for refinement. A Feature Fusion block integrates encoder–decoder context, although its fixed feature weighting and lack of global feature integration limit adaptability to lesion variations. Chen et al. [62] introduce RRCNet, extending SegNet [63] with deep supervision for coarse saliency maps and residual networks to correct missed and false detections using dilated convolutions. However, its sequential refinement lacks a global feedback loop, potentially propagating early segmentation errors. Uncertainty estimation plays a crucial role in medical image analysis, particularly in the MIS domain, serving as an essential tool for robust feature modeling and model regularization. Some researchers have improved lesion segmentation in BUS images by addressing uncertainty due to boundary ambiguity and inter-patient variability in medical images. Zhou et al. [37] propose UHA-Net, which enhances segmentation accuracy through hierarchical feature fusion, uncertainty-induced cross-level integration, and multi-scale feature aggregation; however, it does not explicitly refine uncertain features at the spatial level. Similarly, Tang et al.’s [38] UG-Net utilizes coarse segmentation, uncertainty-guided learning, and feature refinement to directly incorporate uncertainty into the segmentation process, improving the handling of boundary ambiguities. Kuang et al. [41] introduce a cross-task supervised framework that generates pseudo-labels from lower-cost annotations and employs uncertainty-aware corrective training to enhance annotation efficiency while maintaining high segmentation performance. Furthermore, Qu et al. [4] present the EH-Former, which uses region-wise curriculum learning and a two-stage transformer architecture to tackle the challenges of low contrast and ambiguous boundaries in BUS images. By dynamically integrating easy and hard regions through uncertainty maps and adaptive feature fusion, EH-Former addresses complex segmentation scenarios. However, despite uncertainty modeling, its high computational cost and binary distinction between easy/hard regions may oversimplify nuanced uncertainty variations, potentially neglecting subtle spatial uncertainties. Mehrtash et al. [64] emphasize confidence calibration via model ensembling, highlighting the need for reliable uncertainty estimation in robust segmentation, particularly for challenging lesions. The EUGIS paradigm [65] introduces an interactive segmentation framework leveraging evidential uncertainty estimation based on Dempster–Shafer theory and Subjective Logic. It prioritizes high-uncertainty regions for interaction, reducing the number of prompts needed for accurate segmentation while employing a trainable calibration mechanism to refine uncertainty estimation. The model’s performance depends on the accuracy of uncertainty maps; miscalibrated estimates can cause misplaced prompts that can negatively affect segmentation accuracy. Additionally, U-Net variants such as UM-Net [39] employ probabilistic modeling with variance rectification for uncertainty estimation; nevertheless, they lack structured integration of multi-scale spatial feature modeling explicitly within uncertainty estimation. Moreover, variance-based rectification may not adequately capture spatial nuances of uncertainty. Similarly, UCTNet [40] refines uncertain regions using a hybrid CNN-Transformer guided by uncertainty maps; however, its heavy reliance on uncertainty maps risks amplifying noise and obscuring ambiguous boundaries. D-DDPM [35] employs a denoising diffusion probabilistic framework coupled with a U-Net architecture enhanced by Residual U-blocks, progressively adding and removing noise to improve lesion segmentation. However, uncertainty estimation is primarily applied during the mask generation phase rather than being incorporated early within the encoder, limiting its influence on high-level semantic feature learning and feature refinement. Zhang et al. [66] propose SFRecSAM, a Segment Anything Model (SAM) [67] -based model that improvises SAM with a Spatial-Frequency Feature Fusion module and a Dual False Corrector to improve boundary detail and correct prediction errors. However, as also noted by the authors, in cases where lesions closely resemble artifacts, the SFF may fail to recover clear structural information, and the DFC may introduce errors by misclassifying artifact regions, ultimately limiting segmentation performance. Table 1 presents a comparative summary of the discussed architectures for lesion segmentation in BUS images. While these methods highlight notable advancements in combining attention mechanisms and multi-scale feature fusion for contextual learning, we observed a gap in approaches that also integrate fuzzy uncertainty estimation within the model pipeline. Relying solely on multi-scale fusion and conventional channel-spatial attention may overlook subtle contextual dependencies. This can lead to redundant feature representations and hinder precise delineation of fine lesion boundaries amid ultrasound noise. Our proposed FusionSegNet addresses these limitations by unifying hierarchical multi-scale feature fusion, hierarchical feature refinement with multi-axis attention, and fuzzy learning-based uncertainty-aware learning into a cohesive framework. By incorporating fuzzy membership-based uncertainty estimation and hierarchical feature integration between encoder and decoder, FusionSegNet offers a robust and noise-resilient solution tailored for the MIS task. MIS frequently encounters inconsistencies such as under-segmentation, over-segmentation, and blurred or poorly defined boundaries [68] . These challenges complicate the accurate identification of anatomical structures, which is crucial for reliable diagnosis and effective treatment planning. To mitigate this, we propose FusionSegNet, a U-shaped architecture based on the encoder and decoder. In this section, the overall structure of the proposed FusionSegNet is introduced in detail. As presented in Fig. 1 , the FusionSegNet architecture is a multi-stage breast lesion segmentation model that combines advanced feature extraction and fusion by exploring multi-scale features from varying perspectives and a newly designed attention mechanism. It comprises a four-stage fuzzy multi-scale attention network (FMSAN) encoder to capture multi-scale features, followed by a weighted multiplicative fusion module (WMFM) to integrate these features to the same shape as the final encoder output. WMFM fuses the information from all stages of the encoder into a single feature map, capturing multi-scale information from each stage of the encoder. The fused output is re-calibrated through a hierarchical multi-axis attention (HMAA) mechanism, which combines local and global attention mechanisms and refines the features at multiple axes, such as height (block) and width (grid). This output is further processed by the gated multi-scale feature aggregation module (GMFAM) to learn long-range dependencies through a gated attention mechanism. At the bottleneck, an atrous attention fusion module (AAFM) is applied to capture contextual information at varying scales. The convolutional decoder stages then reconstruct the segmentation map by performing an upsample operation, convolution, and refining the features using a gated multi-scale fusion block (GMSFB) and HMAA mechanism. The final output is resized to match the original input dimensions, ensuring precise segmentation. The network architecture employs 64, 128, 256, and 512 channels (C) in the first through fourth encoder stages and 512, 256, 128, and 64 channels in the corresponding decoder stages. The overall workflow is detailed in Fig. 1 , and the step-by-step operations are summarized in Algorithm 1. The proposed FMSAN encoder, as shown in Fig. 2 , employs a hierarchical, stage-wise feature extraction strategy with integrated uncertainty awareness, drawing inspiration from both Transformer-based architectures (e.g., ViT [69] , SegNeXT [70] ) and CNN-based multi-stage encoders. Unlike pure Transformers that rely solely on self-attention for feature aggregation, FMSAN incorporates multi-scale convolutional attention and structured feature refinement to enhance the representation quality in BUS images. It has been observed by recent studies [71,72] that, despite the widespread availability and convenience offered by pre-trained backbones such as ResNet [73] , MobileNet [74] , EfficientNet [75] , or MaxViT [76] , their application to specialized downstream tasks like breast ultrasound lesion segmentation is not always beneficial, primarily due to the presence of unique challenges often encountered with BUS imaging, such as high uncertainty, ambiguous lesion boundaries, significant speckle noise, and subtle textural variations. Moreover, these models are typically trained on large-scale natural image datasets (i.e., ImageNet [77] ), which do not reflect the statistical characteristics or diagnostic patterns of medical imaging data. In fact, transferring knowledge from less relevant sources can degrade performance due to domain discrepancies and lack of alignment with medical-specific patterns [72,78] . In contrast, the proposed FMSAN encoder is explicitly designed to address these challenges, offering enhanced feature extraction capabilities tailored for BUS images and medical imaging tasks in general. Each FMSAN encoder stage is structured to progressively refine input features to capture increasingly abstract and discriminative representations necessary for precise segmentation. At the start of each stage, a feed-forward network (FFN) block processes the input tensor X ∈ R H × W × C . The FFN employs a 1 × 1 pointwise convolution (PConv) to align channel dimensions and facilitate efficient feature transformation. A subsequent layer normalization (LN) and ReLU activation stabilize training, followed by a 3 × 3 convolution with another LN. The original input tensor is then added back to the transformed features, establishing a residual connection that fosters information reuse and gradient flow stability. After the FFN, we incorporate the Multi-Scale Contextual Attention Unit (MCAU), which employs depthwise separable strip convolutions with elongated kernels ( 3 × 1 , 5 × 1 , 11 × 1 ) and their transposed counterparts ( 1 × 3 , 1 × 5 , 1 × 11 ) . These depthwise separable convolutions combine depthwise filtering and 1 × 1 PConv, effectively capturing directional lesion boundaries in BUS images while enhancing multi-scale contextual representation. Each branch undergoes layer normalization (LN) after the PConv for stability. We then aggregate the outputs from the multi-scale branches via element-wise addition to produce a consolidated representation. An efficient channel attention (ECA) mechanism [43] is then applied to this aggregated representation. The ECA module adaptively enhances channel importance without the computational overhead of full spatial attention. Element-wise multiplication of the input features with the attention-modulated output refines salient features for further processing. The final component of each FMSAN stage is the proposed Fuzzy Learning Module (FLM), designed to address the inherent uncertainty in ultrasound images, including noise, ambiguous lesion boundaries, and variations in imaging conditions. Conventional probabilistic [79,80] or ensemble-based uncertainty estimation techniques [64,81] , which rely on multiple forward passes [82] , Bayesian approximations, averaging multiple model outputs, or treating all features similarly across multiple model evaluations [83] . Unlike those methods, FLM explicitly models uncertainty at the feature level during training by using fuzzy membership functions (FMFs). This approach enables a more adaptive and fine-grained representation of uncertainty distributions. Each feature element X i j k is assigned a Gaussian-like fuzzy membership value parameterized by a learnable mean μ n and a standard deviation σ n , enabling adaptive uncertainty modeling. Here, i , j , and k denote the spatial height (row), width (column), and channel (feature map) indices, respectively. The module not only estimates uncertainty but also facilitates uncertainty-aware feature separation to effectively distinguish between high-confidence and ambiguous regions. These membership values are computed as (1) f i j k n = exp − ( X i j k − μ n ) 2 2 σ n 2 where n indexes the N membership functions (e.g. N = 5 in our setup). To represent the overall uncertainty, the fuzzy values across all membership functions are aggregated using a product operation, producing a fuzzy representation that encodes the degree of belonging for each feature element as F i j k = ∏ n = 1 N f i j k n , allowing the model to incorporate uncertainty directly into its representations. We refine these fuzzy features by employing a 1 × 1 PConv, which learns efficient linear combinations of the aggregated membership values as F i j k ′ = PConv 1 × 1 ( F i j k ) . Subsequently, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout [82] is applied to F i j k ′ during training, introducing stochasticity into the feature activations. The model estimates pixel-wise uncertainty by computing the variance of these activations across the batch, reflecting variability induced by the dropout mechanism. This strategy was adopted to allow the network to learn confidence estimates and differentiate between high-certainty and ambiguous regions. During inference, the model utilizes the learned uncertainty representations to refine segmentation predictions by adaptively weighting feature importance. We then compute the pixel-wise variance to generate an uncertainty map u i j k . This map is activated using a sigmoid activation function and can be expressed as u i j k = σ variance ( F i j k ′ ) . The uncertainty map partitions the input features into high-confidence ( 1 − u i j k ) X i j k and low-confidence u i j k X i j k components, enabling targeted processing for each feature type. The low-confidence features, which typically arise from ambiguous regions, are processed using a (5 × 5) depthwise convolution (DConv) followed by a (1 × 1) PConv, stabilized with batch normalization (BN). These features are then further refined with another (3 × 3) DConv and (1 × 1) PConv to improve contextual dependencies and representation quality. The process can be formulated as (2) low_context i j k = DConv 5 × 5 u i j k X i j k , low_fused i j k = PConv 1 × 1 low_context i j k , low_fused_bn i j k = BN low_fused i j k , low_refine_context i j k = DConv 3 × 3 low_fused_bn i j k , low_refined i j k = PConv 1 × 1 low_refine_context i j k . For high-confidence features, we apply a 1 × 1 PConv followed by a 3 × 3 DConv and a subsequent 1 × 1 PConv, so that confident predictions remain stable while enhancing feature representation. This can be formulated as (3) high_context i j k = PConv 1 × 1 ( 1 − u i j k ) X i j k , high_refined_context i j k = DConv 3 × 3 high_context i j k , high_refined i j k = PConv 1 × 1 high_refined_context i j k . The low-confidence and high-confidence features are then concatenated and further refined using an additional 3 × 3 DConv layer, followed by a 1 × 1 PConv and BN. A residual connection is added back to the original input. This process can be summarized as (4) y i j k = BN concat ( high_refined , low_refined ) ⊕ BN X i j k Our goal for this design choice is to allow the FLM to effectively handle uncertainty within both global and localized information and progressively refine them in each stage. Finally, a residual connection merges the uncertainty-aware features from the FLM with the output of FFN. To progress through the encoder hierarchy, each stage concludes with a 3 × 3 convolution at stride 2, performing spatial down-sampling, formulated as H s + 1 = H s 2 , W s + 1 = W s 2 , while the number of filters doubles at each stage as C s + 1 = 2 C s . Here, H s , W s , and C s represent the height, width, and number of channels at stage s , and each subsequent stage s + 1 progressively increases the abstraction level by reducing spatial dimensions while expanding feature channels. In medical image segmentation (MIS), accurately focusing on target regions, especially small lesions or anatomical landmarks, is challenging due to the progressive downsampling in the encoder, which causes deep feature maps to lose boundary details. For smaller target areas, the boundary details in deep feature maps can be reduced to just a few pixels or even disappear entirely, which significantly impacts segmentation accuracy [68] . One straightforward solution is to use larger input images to generate larger feature maps, thereby preserving more information about the lesion areas. However, this approach demands considerable computational resources. Another strategy is to fuse shallow and deep features, with shallow feature maps providing detailed boundary information. Two common feature fusion methods are addition and concatenation, which involve simply merging shallow and deep features. However, these approaches can overlook the correlation between multi-scale features [33] . In addition, shallow feature maps also contain noise, and most fusion methods inadvertently introduce irrelevant information during the process, leading to a final fused image that includes a certain amount of noise. This noise can degrade the segmentation results, highlighting the need for more sophisticated fusion techniques that can effectively combine useful information while minimizing the introduction of noise. Moreover, improper modeling of feature representations can lead to duplicate data utilization throughout the architecture [47] . To address the abovementioned issues, inspired by [33] , we propose a weighted multiplicative fusion module (WMFM) that effectively fuses features from encoder stages and suppresses the impact of irrelevant information. In Algorithm 2, we describe the weighted multiplicative approach of the WMFM. Through WMFM, we fuse feature maps from different encoder stages through element-wise multiplication, denoted as ⊙ . This operation is designed to amplify meaningful patterns while diminishing noise. We begin by transforming each feature map F i into F i ′ using a 1 × 1 convolution and resizing them to a consistent spatial resolution ( target_shape ), ensuring that all features are properly aligned for the fusion process. Next, we introduce learnable weights W = [ w 1 , w 2 , … , w n ] , which are normalized using a softmax function, resulting in W normalized . These trainable weights allow the proposed architecture to learn the relative importance of each feature map output by the encoder stages, emphasizing the contextually relevant features for the segmentation task while downplaying the less critical ones. By normalizing the weights, the model can prevent any single feature from dominating the fusion process. We then apply these normalized weights w i to each corresponding transformed feature F i ′ to produce the weighted feature maps F i W = w i ⊙ F i ′ . The fusion itself is carried out by element-wise multiplication of these weighted features. We start with the first weighted feature map and sequentially multiply it with each subsequent one: F F = F W [ 0 ] ⊙ F W [ 1 ] ⊙ … ⊙ F W [ n ] . This multiplicative fusion approach allows us to enhance the consistency across features, reducing the impact of noise since inconsistent noise signals tend to be minimized during this process. Moreover, the multiplicative fusion influences gradient dynamics, making the network’s gradients dependent on the interdependent product of multiple feature maps [33] . Thus, the WMFM enhances robustness by correlating multi-scale features. In contrast to existing channel attention, spatial attention, and self-attention mechanisms [42–44,69,84,85] , and inspired by [76] , we propose a hierarchical multi-axis attention (HMAA) mechanism that amplifies the model’s ability to focus on localized anatomical details, complex morphological features, and subtle variations, improving the accuracy of delineating small or complex tissue structures. Unlike standard CBAM [44] or SE-Net [42] , HMAA combines coarse-to-fine spatial patterns with channel cues using a hierarchically gated structure which enables richer and more adaptive feature refinement. While most prior works fuse spatial and channel attention sequentially, HMAA achieves a more integrated and synergistic representation. Height-wise (block) and width-wise (grid) attention offer significant advantages over traditional spatial attention, which may dilute focus by operating on the entire feature map. Medical images often contain intricate patterns and fine details, such as small lesions or organ boundaries, crucial for accurate segmentation. By applying attention within smaller, partitioned regions, the model can better highlight these critical features, leading to improved delineation of structures. We process attention at hierarchical levels, beginning with channel attention, followed by spatial attention across height and width dimensions. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , we first compute local attention using global average pooling and global attention using global max pooling, both of which are processed through shared dense layers that reduce the channel dimensions by a reduction ratio r , set to 16, before being passed through a sigmoid activation and combined into a unified channel attention map. This channel attention is then element-wise multiplied by the input feature map, resulting in a channel-refined output. After the computation of channel-refined output, we then adopt height-wise attention by reshaping the channel-refined feature map into a tensor of shape ( b , h / / bs , bs , w , c ) , where b is the batch size, h is the height of the feature map, w is the width, and ‘bs‘ is the block size, set to 7, following SwinUNet [26] . This reshaping segments the height into smaller, non-overlapping blocks. The tensor is then transposed to ( b , h / / bs , w , bs , c ) , aligning the block dimension (formerly height) with the width, allowing the attention mechanism to focus on vertical regions. The tensor is reshaped such that each row corresponds to a block, with all its channels grouped together, allowing for efficient processing of the blocks while maintaining the structure of the channel dimensions, followed by LN and attention weight computation. These weights, computed via a dense layer, are multiplied by the block features to produce the height-attended feature map. Afterwards, we adopt a similar process for width-wise attention, where the feature map is reshaped into a tensor of shape ( b , h , w / / gs , gs , c ) , transposed to ( b , w / / gs , h , gs , c ) , where ‘gs‘ is the grid size, also set to 7, and then reorganized so that each grid segment is grouped together along the channel dimension. The tensor is then normalized and processed to generate grid-specific attention weights, resulting in the width-attended feature map. The grid-based operation applies global attention across a broader, sparsely defined grid structure. It operates globally on the feature map, but instead of focusing on every pixel, attention is performed to the uniformly spaced grid points or sparsely sampled regions. These height and width-attended feature maps are then added together and passed through a sigmoid activation, and GAP and GMP operations are performed and later concatenated along the channel dimension and processed through a 7 × 7 convolutional layer with another sigmoid activation, creating a unified spatial attention map. This spatial attention map is element-wise multiplied by the previous feature map combining height and width attention, effectively refining both local and global feature representations. The output feature map of the HMAA is produced by performing another element-wise multiplication with the channel-refined feature map. In MIS, the challenge often lies in accurately distinguishing between tissues that have ambiguities in the boundaries and are affected by noise artifacts. These challenges become worse in cases where the anatomical structures of tissues vary significantly in size and appearance. To address these issues, it is essential to extract and utilize features at multiple scales within the network. Features from the shallower layers of the network often capture detailed spatial structures and well-defined edges, while those from the deeper layers provide more abstract, semantic information [86] . However, simply merging these features without any form of selection can lead to information overload, where irrelevant or conflicting data may weaken the model’s ability to differentiate between different regions effectively. To truly capitalize on the strengths of multi-scale features, the implemented method must selectively fuse the most relevant features at each scale. This approach ensures that only the most informative aspects are integrated, leading to improved segmentation accuracy and consistency across varying tissue types. Inspired by [86] , we propose a gated multi-scale feature aggregation module (GMFAM) that incorporates a gating mechanism that allows the model to emphasize specific features that are more relevant for capturing high-level semantics. In the context of MIS, by learning to selectively gate features, the model can suppress noisy or irrelevant information that could otherwise confuse the high-level semantic understanding and, therefore, adapt to the context. In the GMFAM, as demonstrated in Fig. 4 , we first resize the feature map from the second-to-last encoder stage F 3 and the feature map generated by the HMAA module F HMAA to match the resolution of the last encoder stage F 4 , which has the lowest spatial resolution. This resizing ensures that all features have the same spatial dimensions. The resizing results in the feature maps F 3 ′ and F HMAA ′ . Subsequently, the F 3 ′ and F HMAA ′ feature maps are concatenated with F 4 to create the combined feature map F concat . We do not include F 1 and F 2 encoder layer features to avoid fusing shallow features lacking proper context, as F 3 and F 4 contain essential high-level global context. The F concat is then processed through shared depthwise separable convolutions (SDSConv) with kernel sizes of 1 × 1 , 3 × 3 , and 5 × 5 , generating multi-scale features S 1 , S 3 , and S 5 . Each of these multi-scale features will have the same spatial dimensions with reduced channels. The SDSConv applies a depthwise convolution (DConv) followed by a PConv to the F concat feature map. These features are concatenated to form F multi . The F multi feature map is further refined through a DConv, denoted as M , followed by BN. This convolution produces a feature map with an additional 3 channels reserved for spatial gating. Later, we split M into four distinct parts: N (global features) and three spatial gating features a 3 , a 4 , and a HMAA , each with the same dimensions and representing a distinct subset of features. This partitioning allows the model for independent processing of these feature subsets, enabling targeted attention or refinement mechanisms. These spatial gating features are matched to the channels of F 4 , F 3 ′ , and F HMAA ′ via 1 × 1 convolutions with sigmoid activation, resulting in a 4 ′ , a 3 ′ , and a HMAA ′ , respectively. Subsequently, these gated features a 4 ′ , a 3 ′ , and a HMAA ′ are multiplied element-wise with their corresponding feature maps to generate the gated features F 4 _gated , F 3 _gated , F HMAA_gated . These gated features and the global features, N are then fused through concatenation to form F gated_concate , which is passed through a final 1 × 1 convolution to obtain the final output feature map. Through GMFAM, both local and global information of channel dimension and spatial attention across height and width dimensions is effectively integrated into the feature representation used for subsequent processing to capture both small, localized features and larger, more global patterns from both coarse and fine-level details. As features of interest can appear at various scales, it is pivotal to ensure that the model is capable of distinguishing subtle and varying features across different scales. In MIS, deep convolutional layers excel at feature extraction but often lose information from target regions of varying sizes due to pooling and down-sampling, which can lead to the loss or incorrect representation of rich spatial and semantic information. While integrating multi-scale feature processing and fuzzy logic in the encoder can enhance segmentation performance by addressing uncertainty and imprecision, this alone is not enough. Without specific mechanisms in the decoder to refine boundaries and reconstruct details, the benefits of improved feature extraction in the encoder may be diminished, resulting in blurred or inaccurate boundaries. Multi-scale learning has proven effective in capturing scale variations, significantly improving segmentation accuracy [68,87] . To address this, we propose an atrous attention fusion module (AAFM), which fuses high-level semantic features from multiple scales using different dilation rates. As illustrated in Fig. 5 , the generated features from the GMFAM module are passed to the atrous attention fusion module (AAFM) as input. The AAFM applies a series of DSConv with progressively increasing dilation rates (1, 2, 4, and 6) to the input feature map ( F ). In each stage, a DSConv block is applied. In each DSConv, a DConv is first applied with a specified dilation rate to capture spatial features from different receptive fields, followed by BN and ReLU activation. After this, a PConv-BN-ReLU operation is applied to combine the depthwise features across channels. By varying the dilation rates, the module effectively captures contextual information at multiple scales, ensuring that both fine and coarse details are integrated into the feature representation. As each atrous convolution is performed, the resulting feature maps ( F 1 , F 2 , F 3 ) and ( F 4 ) are progressively summed with their preceding outputs ( F 1 _ sum , F 2 _ sum , F 3 _ sum ) which ensures that multi-scale information is integrated coherently. These features are then summed and concatenated to create a unified multi-scale representation. To emphasize the most informative channels, we apply an ECA mechanism [43] . The ECA mechanism performs a GAP operation on the concatenated feature map, resulting in a global context vector that represents the channel-wise global information. This vector is then processed through a 1D convolution operation to capture cross-channel dependencies. The output of this convolution is passed through a sigmoid activation function ( σ ) which produces the channel-wise attention weights. These weights modulate the original concatenated feature map through element-wise multiplication, resulting in the refined feature map. This refinement assists the network in maintaining subtle or small lesion details across multiple scales, while also capturing the surrounding tissue context. The decoder refines the input tensor through a series of stages that involve up-sampling, convolution, and feature fusion. In each stage, up-sampling is performed first to increase the spatial resolution, followed by 3 × 3 convolution and BN to process the feature maps. The gated multi-scale fusion block (GMSFB) then merges features from the corresponding encoder stage with the decoder stage, ensuring the integration of both high-resolution details and contextual information. Next, HMAA further refines the features by focusing on critical information across different scales. The output of each decoder stage is recursively fed into the next, which can progressively improve the accuracy of the segmentation maps. Skip connections in segmentation networks combine features from shallow and deep layers to reduce the semantic gap between the encoder and decoder. However, using raw skip connections or simple concatenation, especially when there are significant scale differences between the feature maps, may introduce redundant information that can lead to suboptimal feature representation and result in a loss of semantic information. To address this, we propose a gated multi-scale fusion block (GMSFB), which fuses the local spatial information from shallow layers of the FMSAN encoder with the high-level semantic and contextual information from deeper layers in the decoder. As shown in Fig. 6 , the GMSFB integrates feature fusion between the encoder and decoder stages through a gated attention mechanism and multi-scale feature processing. First, we align encoder features with decoder feature dimensions using bilinear interpolation. Then, a gating mechanism is applied, where decoder features are passed through a 1 × 1 convolution with a sigmoid activation to create an attention map. This attention map modulates the encoder features so that relevant information gets emphasized. We then process the modulated features through three DSConv with dilation rates of 1, 2, and 4 to capture multi-scale contextual information. The resulting features are concatenated and fused with a 1 × 1 convolution, and a residual connection is added to fuse the features back to the attention-modulated features, producing the final output of the block. To verify the validity of our proposed FusionSegNet, we conducted a series of experiments on two benchmark breast ultrasound image datasets, BUSI dataset [88] , and UDIAT [89] . The summary of the utilized datasets in this study is shown in Table 2 . The BUSI dataset comprises 780 BUS images collected from 600 female patients aged between 25 and 75 years at Baheya Hospital in Cairo, Egypt. The images, provided in PNG format with an average resolution of 500 × 500 pixels, include 437 cases of benign tumors, 210 cases of malignant tumors, and 133 images of normal breast tissue. For training and testing the proposed segmentation model, we have utilized the images of benign and malignant tumors along with their corresponding masks, which serve as the ground truth annotations. The UDIAT dataset, obtained from the UDIAT Diagnostic Center at the Parc Tauli Corporation in Sabadell, Spain, using a Siemens ACUSON Sequoia C512 system, includes 163 breast ultrasound images — 110 benign and 53 malignant — each accompanied by a corresponding ground truth mask. The ultrasound images and masks have an average resolution of 760 × 570 pixels. We performed a 5-fold cross-validation to evaluate the segmentation performance of all methods. To quantitatively evaluate the segmentation performance of the proposed method, we followed the previous works [46,68] and selected the following metrics: Intersection Over Union (IoU) = Jaccard Index (JI) = TP TP + FP + FN , Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) = 2 × TP 2 × TP + FP + FN , Precision = TP TP + FP , Recall (Sensitivity) = TP TP + FN , where TP, FP, TN, and FN indicate the numbers of pixels corresponding to true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives, respectively. We implemented the proposed method using TensorFlow 2.10.0 and conducted all experiments on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU with 48 GB of RAM. We employed Nadam (Adam with Nesterov momentum) as the optimization algorithm, setting the initial learning rate to 0.0001 and reducing it by a factor of 0.1 after 10 epochs when validation loss plateaued. To prevent overfitting, we applied EarlyStopping with a patience of 15 epochs, restoring the best-performing weights. Moreover, we designed a hybrid loss function combining focal Tversky loss [90] and binary cross-entropy Dice loss. The focal Tversky loss prioritized hard-to-segment regions, while the binary cross-entropy Dice loss enhanced boundary adherence and overall segmentation accuracy. For consistency, we resized all images to 224 × 224 pixels before processing. Both datasets were split into training (80%), validation (10%), and testing (10%) using stratification. To evaluate generalizability, we also conducted cross-dataset testing, training and validating on BUSI while testing on UDIAT, and vice versa. In the training process, we employed data augmentation methods, increasing the dataset size by a factor of ten. To track training performance, we employed ModelCheckpoint, saving weights based on validation loss. After training, we evaluated the model on the test subset to ensure robust segmentation performance. In addition, the hyperparameter search space included learning rates (1e-5, 1e-4, 1e-3), optimizers (Adam, AdamW, Nadam), and batch sizes (4, 8, 16). We systematically tested these hyperparameters and the final configuration, as shown in Table 3 was selected based on validation performance. Several contemporary state-of-the-art (SOTA) segmentation models have been selected for comparison, encompassing both CNN and transformer-based approaches. CNN-based methods include UNet [18] , UNet++ [21] , Attention-UNet [22] , DeepLabV3+ [91] , EU 2 Net [57] , PVT-Emcad [47] , ESKNet [46] , RRCNet [62] , and Transformer-based models include SwinUNet [26] , UNetR [24] , and Transfuse-S [29] . To ensure a fair comparison, each model is trained under identical conditions, with consistent hyperparameter settings and data augmentation techniques applied throughout. The quantitative results for UDIAT and BUSI datasets are presented in Table 4 and Table 5 , respectively. We observed that FusionSegNet achieved the highest overall performance in breast lesion segmentation on the UDIAT dataset, outperforming traditional benchmarks, including UNet, UNet++, Attention-UNet, and DeepLabV3+. FusionSegNet particularly excelled in critical evaluation metrics such as the mDSC of 93.22% and mIoU of 88.05%. While it was seen that RRCNet and UNetR achieved a strong precision of 93.24% and 92.83%, respectively, FusionSegNet demonstrated a more balanced performance across all metrics, with a higher precision of 94.72% and recall of 90.28%. FusionSegNet surpasses ESKNet by 5.21% and PVT-Emcad by 5.36% in the mIoU and outperforms Transfuse-S and UNetR by 4.37% and 5.22%, respectively, in the mDSC metric. In terms of EU 2 Net, though it obtained a commendable precision and recall of 93.44% and 89.03%, respectively, it did not overcome FusionSegNet in terms of critical mDSC and mIoU metrics, pointing to its inadequacy in precise localization of lesion shapes and edges. We found UNet to be consistently ranked lowest across multiple metrics, particularly in recall and mIoU, indicating comparatively less reliable segmentation performance on the UDIAT dataset. Overall, it was observed that FusionSegNet outperformed other models while delivering the most reliable and accurate segmentation results on the UDIAT dataset. On the BUSI dataset, FusionSegNet also demonstrated superior performance, achieving the highest mDSC (87.52%) and mIoU (80.10%), outperforming traditional models such as UNet, UNet++, Attention-UNet, and DeepLabV3+. These metrics, along with precision and recall values, indicate that FusionSegNet provided superior segmentation accuracy and overlap quality, effectively capturing the intricate details of breast lesions. Compared to other models, RRCNet and ESKNet delivered competitive performance; however, they fell short in mDSC and mIoU metrics. For instance, while ESKNet demonstrated a strong performance in the recall metric, its mDSC and mIoU were lower, highlighting a gap in overall segmentation reliability. SwinUNet, on the other hand, exhibited the lowest mIoU at 69.68%, reflecting limitations in capturing lesion boundaries as accurately as FusionSegNet. FusionSegNet outpaced RRCNet, PVT-Emcad, and ESKNet in mDSC by 7.79%, 3.69%, and 4.74%, respectively, and outperformed UNetR and SwinUNet in mIoU by 6.64% and 13.00%, respectively, highlighting its precision in accurately delineating lesion boundaries. However, it is important to note that our proposed FusionSegNet model shows a slightly lower recall value compared to some of these models, suggesting a potential trade-off between precision and recall. FusionSegNet effectively balances efficiency and segmentation accuracy, as evidenced by its strong performance on both the BUSI and UDIAT datasets. On the BUSI dataset, it maintains a moderate model size of 316 MB, smaller than RRCNet and ESKNet, while outperforming them in key segmentation metrics such as mDSC and mIoU. Its inference time of 25.85 ms is competitive, striking a balance between speed and accuracy compared to computationally heavier models like UNetR, RRCNet, and ESKNet. Moreover, FusionSegNet demonstrates efficiency with just 29.27M parameters, significantly fewer than UNetR, SwinUNet, RRCNet, and ESKNet, while achieving top-tier results, including 94.72% precision and 93.22% mDSC on the UDIAT dataset. Even in terms of computational cost, its 78.15 GFLOPS remains reasonable, ensuring that the model retains a strong balance between complexity and effectiveness. While models like ESKNet, RRCNet, and UNetR have higher GFLOPS, FusionSegNet surpasses them in segmentation quality in terms of object shape and boundary delineation, thereby making it a practical yet high-performing solution for lesion segmentation. We chose the mDSC metric for this evaluation. For a fair comparison, both ultrasound datasets were chosen, as they originate from different sources, which makes achieving optimal performance more challenging. For the first instance, we used the BUSI dataset during training and validation and the UDIAT dataset for testing. We do the vice versa in the second instance. Through this cross-dataset study, we demonstrate the better generalization capability of the FusionSegNet method compared to other competitor methods. Furthermore, while these results provide strong evidence of FusionSegNet’s ability to generalize across different datasets, we acknowledge the importance of evaluating its performance on entirely unseen clinical datasets. As part of our future work, we plan to extend this study by testing the model on additional datasets with diverse imaging protocols, equipment variations, and patient populations to further validate its robustness and real-world applicability. As shown in Fig. 7 , for the BUSI dataset, we observed that the proposed FusionSegNet demonstrates superior performance in both boundary accuracy and shape preservation, particularly in the segmentation of larger breast lesions, where it closely aligns with the ground truth (GT), showing minimal smoothing. True positives (TP) are well-represented in purple, indicating that FusionSegNet captures most of the lesions with high accuracy and also captures the true negatives (TN) very well, represented in black. While we observed that FusionSegNet faces slight challenges in capturing finer boundary details for smaller lesions, reflected by a few false positives (FP) in blue and false negatives (FN) in red, it consistently outperforms the other models in this regard. Similarly, Transfuse performs well, especially with larger lesions, but introduces more boundary inaccuracies compared to FusionSegNet, with more visible FP and FN regions, particularly in complex boundaries. In contrast, ESKNet and RRCNet exhibit significant over-segmentation, particularly with smaller lesions, leading to an increase in FP and noticeable shape distortion, compromising their clinical reliability. We also observed that UNet and UNetR manage the overall lesion shape reasonably well for larger lesions, but overly smooth boundaries result in a loss of critical details, especially for smaller lesions, where boundary irregularities are crucial for diagnosis, often reflected in an increase of FN. UNet++ offers slightly improved boundary delineation over UNet; however, it still struggles with subtle lesion contours, occasionally leading to smoothing artifacts. PVT-Emcad effectively preserves lesion shape and minimizes FP in large lesions. Nonetheless, it was observed that it under-segments small or complex lesions, leading to increased FN near boundaries. SwinUNet performs moderately, showing better results with larger lesions but still exhibiting boundary inconsistencies and smoothing issues with smaller ones, leading to more FP and FN regions, thus containing a lot of noise. Ultimately, we found that FusionSegNet excels in preserving both lesion boundaries and shapes, making it particularly effective for larger lesions while still demonstrating reliable performance on smaller lesions, with fewer FP and FN regions compared to the other models. For the UDIAT dataset (as shown in Fig. 7 ), we found that FusionSegNet consistently performs well, closely aligning with the GT and accurately preserving the shape of larger, irregular lesions with only minor boundary deviations. TPs are well-represented in purple, indicating accurate segmentation. Transfuse also performs reasonably, though it introduces slightly more boundary inaccuracies, particularly in complex regions, with some FP and FN. In contrast, ESKNet and RRCNet exhibit significant over-segmentation, leading to more FPs around the lesion edges, which compromises shape accuracy. UNet, UNet++, UNetR, and SwinUNet tend to over-smooth boundaries, which results in the loss of finer details, increasing false negatives in some areas. PVT-Emcad performs consistently well in preserving the shape of large lesions with minimal FP; however, we observed that it misses small peripheral structures, leading to localized FN errors. Overall, FusionSegNet remains the most reliable in maintaining lesion boundaries and shape, especially for complex lesions with fewer FP and FN regions compared to other models. This extensive evaluation confirms that each proposed component uniquely and synergistically improves lesion segmentation performance in BUS images. Furthermore, their modular design allows seamless integration into other computer vision and medical image analysis tasks, making them adaptable as plug-and-play components for effective feature learning in various architectures. The visualization of stage-wise feature representations from the UDIAT and BUSI datasets at different layers of the proposed model is shown in Fig. 8 , and Fig. 9 , respectively. We calculate the average activation across all channels and generate heatmaps using OpenCV-Python. In both of these visualizations, we can see that the encoder layers of the proposed FusionSegNet model capture broad, contextual features, progressively narrowing the focus as depth increases. By the bottleneck, features become highly concentrated on the region of interest, filtering out irrelevant information. As the features propagate through the decoder, the segmentation becomes increasingly refined, with spatial details reconstructed and lesion boundaries precisely localized in the final layer—closely aligning with ground truth. This stage-wise refinement not only enhances segmentation accuracy but also provides a transparent view into how the model identifies and emphasizes important features at each step. Consequently, these visualizations contribute to improving the model’s interpretability, offering clinicians clearer insights into the decision-making process behind the segmentation results. The quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate the superiority and effectiveness of the proposed FusionSegNet model in lesion segmentation from breast ultrasound images. However, our FusionSegNet struggles to accurately segment lesions in certain challenging scenarios, such as large lesions and ambiguous backgrounds. From the first row in Fig. 10 , we can observe that our model can segment the main regions of large lesions while lacking finer edge details where the boundary of the lesion is ambiguous. In the second row of Fig. 10 , it is evident that the model still has considerable room for improvement in handling cases where low contrast and a similar background make it difficult to distinguish the lesion. These challenging conditions lead to reduced segmentation accuracy, as the model struggles to differentiate between the lesion and surrounding tissue. In future work, we aim to enhance boundary refinement techniques and integrate advanced semantic consistency learning to improve feature representation and segmentation accuracy, particularly in challenging cases involving large lesions and ambiguous backgrounds. This paper proposes FusionSegNet, a lesion segmentation model for BUS images that effectively handles noise and ambiguous boundaries through multi-scale contextual feature extraction, uncertainty-aware fuzzy feature decomposition, and hierarchical attention-guided refinement to improve feature representation and segmentation precision. A key innovation of our approach is the FMSAN method, which strengthens the encoder’s ability to capture diverse lesion characteristics by leveraging multi-scale convolutions and fuzzy learning. Additionally, the HMAA mechanism refines feature integration by simultaneously processing spatial and channel-wise information, ensuring that fine-grained lesion boundaries and structural details are preserved. To further enhance the model’s robustness, our model employs WMFM, which selectively emphasizes informative features by suppressing irrelevant details through element-wise multiplication. Further, the GMFAM strengthens lesion boundary delineation by combining high-resolution spatial and global contextual features while filtering out unnecessary information. On the decoder side, the AAFM utilizes dilated convolutions to effectively capture multi-scale contextual features, allowing for precise segmentation of lesions with varying shapes and textures. Additionally, the GMSFB is integrated to ensure a seamless fusion of encoder and decoder features, thereby improving spatial coherence and lesion localization. Extensive experiments on the BUSI and UDIAT datasets confirm that FusionSegNet consistently outperforms existing SOTA MIS methods. Our newly developed portable modules bridge the semantic gap between the encoder and decoder stages, leading to substantial gains on both datasets. Although FusionSegNet has demonstrated strong performance on the BUSI and UDIAT datasets, further validation on diverse clinical datasets is necessary to evaluate its robustness across different imaging protocols, equipment, and patient populations. Moving forward, enhancements will focus on deploying the model in real-world clinical settings to assess its generalizability, reliability, inference speed, and practical usability in assisting radiologists with breast lesion diagnosis. Future research could further enhance segmentation robustness by integrating dynamically adaptive uncertainty-aware attention mechanisms, responsive to spatial ambiguity and structural variability, and leveraging self-supervised learning to reduce dependency on labeled data. We also aim to make the model more lightweight by integrating optimized pre-trained encoders for efficient deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings. Additionally, explainable artificial intelligence strategies could advance clinical interpretability and adoption; in particular, we plan to explore rule-based interpretations of the fuzzy logic module to further enhance transparency by linking segmentation outcomes to human-interpretable decision conditions. GloW-VSNet: A scribble-based weakly supervised framework for global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation Vitiligo lesion identification is essential for quantifying disease severity, monitoring disease progression and assessing treatment response, particularly for objective quantification. However, segmenting vitiligo lesions from clinical images is challenging due to indistinct borders, complex backgrounds, and image artifacts. The difficulty increases when handling small and sparse lesions in global-view photographs. Fully supervised segmentation models require extensively annotated datasets, making the labelling process time-consuming and costly. To address these challenges, we propose GloW-VSNet, a scribble-guided weakly supervised segmentation method for global-view vitiligo detection. Our approach integrates differentiable feature clustering with a spatial attention mechanism based on physician-provided scribble annotations, enabling the model to focus on relevant spatial features and improve segmentation accuracy despite background noise and artifacts. Additionally, we introduce spatial continuity optimization to preserve the natural distribution of vitiligo, enhancing segmentation consistency while reducing computational demands. Extensive experiments on two public vitiligo datasets and two private datasets demonstrate that GloW-VSNet achieves state-of-the-art performance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore weakly supervised global-view vitiligo segmentation, addressing a critical research gap. Our method enhances the assessment of disease severity and monitoring of treatment response through an objective assessment for real-world applications. Vitiligo is a common dermatological condition characterized by localized or widespread depigmentation resulting from the destruction of melanocytes, often imposing a substantial psychosocial burden on affected individuals. Those with vitiligo frequently experience significant psychological distress, particularly in social settings where heightened self-consciousness about their appearance is common. The clinical severity of vitiligo is typically quantified by the percentage of body surface area affected by depigmentation. Unlike other dermatological conditions such as psoriasis or eczema, vitiligo is notable for the absence of prominent inflammatory or morphological skin changes, thereby making clinical photography a reliable and objective method for assessing disease severity ( Boniface et al., 2018; Dahir and Thomsen, 2018; Picardo and Taïeb, 2019; Frisoli et al., 2020 ). Accurate assessment of vitiligo poses significant challenges, primarily due to the diverse characteristics exhibited by the lesions. These include variability in number, size, location, morphology, and topographical patterns of depigmentation. Currently, clinical evaluation relies heavily on semi-objective validated tools or clinical scales, such as the Vitiligo European Task Force assessment (VETFa) and the Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (VASI), which may introduce subjective bias if not conducted in a standardized manner ( Taïeb et al., 2007; Komen et al., 2015 ). To address this limitation, objective methods such as automated image segmentation and quantification have started to gain increasing attention in vitiligo assessment. Accurate segmentation of skin images to identify depigmented regions enables subsequent quantification of lesion extent, offering a more consistent and reproducible evaluation of disease severity. However, segmenting vitiligo lesions in clinical color images presents several obstacles, including variations in lighting, heterogeneous lesion shapes and sizes, blurred lesion borders, the presence of coexisting hair, and halo effects. Additionally, unlike a Wood’s lamp, which enhances depigmentation for improved visualization in clinical practice, standard color images provide lower contrast, further complicating lesion identification. Moreover, due to the large and unpredictable area covered by vitiligo lesions, it is often necessary to capture as much of the body as possible when acquiring images and inevitably introduce complex background content in the periphery. These broad-field images, referred to as global-view images, provide a more realistic representation of lesion distribution and are useful for assessing overall disease burden. However, the increased anatomical coverage and surrounding visual clutter make segmentation more difficult. In contrast, local-view images capture smaller, focused regions with minimal background, improving segmentation accuracy but limiting clinical relevance due to the lack of contextual information. This distinction is illustrated in Fig. 1 . In the early stages of related research, traditional machine learning methods were employed in identifying vitiligo lesions ( Nugroho et al., 2013; Das Gupta et al., 2015; Anthal et al., 2017 ). These methods utilized techniques such as principal component analysis, image enhancement, and multi-color channel combination. Although they enhanced the distinction between vitiligo and normal skin, they faced challenges including confusion with complex backgrounds and low detection accuracy. In the past decade, with the advent of deep learning, significant advancements have been made in medical imaging, which has promoted progress in vitiligo detection. Contemporary studies have started integrating early research experiences with the representative visual features learned by deep learning models, in order to further enhance detection performance ( Low et al., 2020; Yanling et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023b; Lei et al., 2023; Hillmer et al., 2024 ). However, deep learning models require large datasets for training. Like much medical data, vitiligo is constrained by a limited number of patient cases. In addition, annotation of vitiligo lesions is particularly time-consuming and labour-intensive due to its convoluted shape and extended size that could cover a large body area. To address the issue of data scarcity, two primary data preparation strategies have been adopted in existing research. The first involves annotating entire regions of visually apparent lesions, while the second employs an image-slicing approach to increase the number of training samples. Although both strategies can improve model performance to some extent, they commonly rely on pre-cropped local-view patches with limited background context. This reliance significantly restricts their practical applicability, as such patches omit anatomical information and prevent realistic assessment of lesion distribution. In terms of algorithmic development, semi-supervised methods based on partially annotated datasets have also been increasingly explored. However, these methods often depend on specific data formats, such as Wood’s lamp images ( Dyer and Foy, 2022 ), and still require accurate ground truth annotations, which limits their generalizability in varied clinical scenarios. Weakly supervised learning has emerged as a promising approach in scenarios where detailed annotations are limited or unavailable ( Zhou, 2018; Li et al., 2023a; Yang et al., 2024 ). By relying on less precise and potentially incomplete labels, these methods enable the development of models that are resilient to imperfect supervision. This characteristic makes them particularly advantageous in clinical workflows, where annotation is time-consuming and resource-intensive. However, the use of weakly supervised methods for global-view lesion detection in vitiligo remains rare, with most existing studies primarily focused on local-view lesions ( Bian et al., 2019; Shih et al., 2022; Tanvir et al., 2024 ). In light of the aforementioned research status and key challenges, this study introduces an end-to-end weakly supervised detection method for vitiligo lesions in a global view. The objective is to enable accurate segmentation of vitiligo lesions using easily accessible prompts and standard color images. The proposed method incorporates a spatial attention learning mechanism tailored to scribble annotations, effectively capturing the sparsely distributed vitiligo lesion information across the global field of view. Additionally, the optimization process integrates feature similarity and spatial continuity. The feature similarity ensures the strengthening of intra-class relationships and weakening of inter-class relationships during semantic segmentation, while the spatial continuity enhances training efficiency and reduces computational costs. The main contributions of this study can be summarized as follows: • We propose GloW-VSNet, a novel weakly supervised method for segmenting vitiligo lesions with minimal input prompts. By incorporating initial medical assessments into a spatial attention framework using scribble annotations, the model effectively focuses on critical areas while ensuring comprehensive coverage of both detailed and sparse lesions. To our knowledge, this is the first approach leveraging scribble annotations for global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation. • We introduce a dual-constraint learning system to vitiligo segmentation, incorporating feature similarity and spatial continuity, to optimize segmentation performance. Feature similarity enhances inter-class separation (lesions vs. normal skin/background) and intra-class consistency (across distant lesions), while spatial continuity improves computational efficiency and reduces training complexity. • The model supports task-specific segmentation, providing flexibility for either lesion/other segmentation or lesion/human body/background segmentation. The latter enables seamless integration with existing clinical evaluation methods, facilitating precise quantification for condition analysis. • Our method has been extensively validated on both public and private datasets, demonstrating consistent superiority in accuracy, robustness, and generalization compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. These results confirm its effectiveness and reliability in real-world clinical applications. We propose GloW-VSNet, a novel weakly supervised method for segmenting vitiligo lesions with minimal input prompts. By incorporating initial medical assessments into a spatial attention framework using scribble annotations, the model effectively focuses on critical areas while ensuring comprehensive coverage of both detailed and sparse lesions. To our knowledge, this is the first approach leveraging scribble annotations for global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation. We introduce a dual-constraint learning system to vitiligo segmentation, incorporating feature similarity and spatial continuity, to optimize segmentation performance. Feature similarity enhances inter-class separation (lesions vs. normal skin/background) and intra-class consistency (across distant lesions), while spatial continuity improves computational efficiency and reduces training complexity. The model supports task-specific segmentation, providing flexibility for either lesion/other segmentation or lesion/human body/background segmentation. The latter enables seamless integration with existing clinical evaluation methods, facilitating precise quantification for condition analysis. Our method has been extensively validated on both public and private datasets, demonstrating consistent superiority in accuracy, robustness, and generalization compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. These results confirm its effectiveness and reliability in real-world clinical applications.
