Vitiligo segmentation has evolved significantly over the past decades, driven by the need for precise assessment of disease severity and the development of detection technologies. Early approaches predominantly relied on traditional machine learning techniques to distinguish vitiligo lesions from healthy skin. Nugroho et al. ( Nugroho et al., 2013 ) employed Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to generate melanin-based images to segment vitiligo lesions from normal skin. The training strategy employed a region-growing approach. Das et al. ( Das Gupta et al., 2015 ) presented a method for segmenting vitiligo regions with varying depigmentation levels using symmetric Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-based clustering and superpixel aggregation with augmented albedo and shading features. Anthal et al. ( Anthal et al., 2017 ) proposed a method using vector quantization neural networks to detect and classify visible vitiligo-affected areas in dark-skinned persons. Bian et al. ( Bian et al., 2019 ) introduced a weakly supervised framework for high-quality segmenting vitiligo regions using pre-trained classification networks, activation maps, and saliency propagation on superpixel graphs. Additionally, they presented the first large private vitiligo image dataset Vit2019. These traditional methods, restricted by the capacity of the extracted features, are invariably constrained in their field of application to a localized view or the cropping of large areas of very distinct vitiligo lesions. With the rapid advancement and widespread adoption of deep learning, research integrating vitiligo analysis with deep learning models has emerged, leveraging the strong visual feature extraction capabilities of these models. Early work by Khatibi et al. ( Khatibi et al., 2021 ) proposed an ensemble framework combining deep learning and K-means clustering for patch-wise vitiligo lesion segmentation, demonstrating improved accuracy. To address the challenge of limited annotated data, Li et al. ( Yanling et al., 2021 ) utilized synthetic vitiligo face images for effective segmentation of facial lesions. Several studies have explored deep learning methods using global-view images to enhance clinical relevance. Shih et al. ( Shih et al., 2022 ) developed a weakly supervised system based on Wood’s lamp images, integrating activation maps, limited expert annotations, and face recognition techniques across three stages to improve lesion localization and area estimation. Luo et al. ( Luo et al., 2023 ) employed Cycle-GAN to enhance vitiligo classification using both clinical and Wood’s lamp images, achieving a 9 % improvement in accuracy over ResNet50 in a whole-face vitiligo lesion segmentation task. Li et al. ( Li et al., 2023b ) further contributed by introducing a confidence score refinement module that links deep learning-based segmentation with clinical scores using whole-body images of the same individual. More recent studies, although incorporating more advanced feature extraction techniques, remain limited to local-view patched lesion images. For example, Zhong et al. ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) applied a stacked CNN and Transformer architecture with class activation maps for vitiligo classification, while Hillmer et al. ( Hillmer et al., 2024 ) integrated deep learning models with clinical criteria to assess the severity of facial vitiligo using standardized HSV images. Medical image segmentation is a cornerstone of medical image analysis, enabling clinicians to assess the severity of the lesion and perform tasks such as disease classification. Segmentation methods can be broadly classified into supervised, semi-supervised, weakly supervised, and unsupervised approaches, based on the type and amount of labeled data they require ( Tajbakhsh et al., 2020 ). Supervised deep learning segmentation methods achieve high accuracy by leveraging fully annotated datasets, complex architectures, and robust feature extraction capabilities. Ciresan et al. ( Ciresan et al., 2012 ) were pioneers in applying deep neural networks to medical image segmentation, introducing a convolutional encoder to extract latent representations, followed by fully connected layers for pixel-level predictions. Subsequently, Long et al. ( Long et al., 2015 ) proposed fully convolutional networks (FCNs), which employed a successive up-sampling process through convolutional blocks in the decoding path. This approach gradually increased spatial resolution, enabling fine-grained segmentation and improved performance. Building on FCNs and encoder-decoder architectures, Ronneberger et al. ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) introduced the Unet model, a landmark development in biomedical image segmentation that has since become one of the most widely used methods in various modalities ( Zhou et al., 2018; Ibtehaz and Rahman, 2020; Waiker et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Ruan and Xiang, 2024 ). Despite the success of supervised methods, creating high-quality annotated datasets for medical imaging is time-consuming and requires specialized expertise, limiting the availability of large-scale datasets. In contrast, unsupervised and self-supervised methods provide viable alternatives in scenarios with limited annotations, as they do not rely on labeled data. These approaches typically employ deep learning for feature extraction, combined with clustering algorithms guided by domain knowledge ( Hansen et al., 2021; Holilah et al., 2021 ), contrastive learning techniques ( Tian et al., 2023; Xing et al., 2023 ), or knowledge transfer from related data modalities ( Perone et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023; Xian et al., 2023; Ji and Chung, 2023 ). In healthcare contexts where highly precise results are not critical, these methods can alleviate workload demands and support downstream tasks. However, their performance is often limited by the absence of labeled guidance. Semi-supervised and weakly supervised methods significantly reduce the dependency on extensive pixel-level annotations by adopting more efficient labeling approaches. Semi-supervised methods leverage a combination of a small set of fully labeled data with a larger pool of unlabeled data ( Chen et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022 ). In contrast, weakly supervised methods rely on less detailed annotations, such as image-level tags, bounding boxes, or sparse scribbles, minimizing the need for precise pixel-level labeling ( Felfeliyan et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2025 ). Among weakly supervised techniques, scribble-based segmentation has gained prominence because it requires only sparse annotations in the form of scribbles over regions of interest. This method drastically reduces annotation time and yet effectively guides models toward accurate segmentation ( Kim et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b ). In medical imaging, where fully annotated datasets are often challenging to obtain, scribble-based approaches offer a cost-effective and efficient solution by leveraging expert knowledge embedded in scribble annotations. This unique balance of reduced annotation burden and reliable segmentation quality makes scribble-based segmentation an invaluable tool in medical image analysis, bridging the gap between unsupervised and fully supervised methods ( Can et al., 2018; Ji et al., 2019; Zhang and Zhuang, 2022 ). Recently, Li et al. ( Li et al., 2024 ) proposed a novel scribble-supervised framework, Scribformer, which combines Transformer and CNN architectures, achieving impressive performance on three open-access datasets. However, despite the success of scribble-based segmentation techniques in medical imaging, studies that have explored their application for the segmentation of lesions in vitiligo remain scarce. Fig. 2 illustrates the overall schematic workflow of our proposed GloW-VSNet architecture. The lightweight segmentation framework relies on two attention residual blocks (ARB) as essential elements of the feature extraction process. The framework starts and ends with convolutional blocks. The eventual segmentation outcome is achieved by refining the extracted features via a multi-angle constrained loss function, followed by batch normalization and an argmax operation. In the remainder of this section, we provide a detailed exposition of the essential modules and the proposed loss function. As shown in (A) of Fig. 2 , this study utilizes a dataset consisting of paired images, where each pair comprises an original image x and its corresponding scribble annotation s as: (1) D = { ( x , s ) n } n = 1 N where N is the total number of pixels in an image, and n indexes each pixel. The input feature x n is first processed through a convolution block followed by a residual convolution block, resulting in the transformed feature x n ′ . All convolutional and residual blocks in this study adopt a bottleneck structure, designed to reduce feature dimensionality, extract compact features, and minimize computational complexity. To effectively utilize the scribble annotations enriched with expert knowledge, the transformed feature x n ′ is fed into two-layer ARBs for spatial attention feature learning and extraction. Each ARB incorporates directional attention maps a n , learned using a Direction Weighted Module (DWM) applied on top of a residual block. The ARB’s output is formulated as: (2) f ARB = ReLU ( Conv ( BatchNorm ( x n ′ ⊙ a n ) ) + x n ′ ) where x n ′ is the ARB input, ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and a n is the directional attention map generated by the DWM, as shown in (C) of Fig. 2 . The DWM, inspired by spatial attentive mechanism ( Wang et al., 2019 ), employs Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) with ReLU activation and covariance matrix initialization (IRNN) to learn gradient weights in four distinct directions: top-to-bottom ( a n ,tb ), bottom-to-top ( a n ,bt ), left-to-right ( a n ,lr ), and right-to-left ( a n ,rl ). For a given input feature map x n ′ , the directional feature maps f dir, d for each direction d ∈ {tb, bt, lr, rl} are computed using dilated convolution blocks: (3) f dir , d = DilatedConv ( x n ′ ) where the dilation rate expands the receptive field without increasing computational cost. Directional attention maps are obtained by weighting these directional features with learned direction-specific weights w d : (4) a d = f dir , d · w d where w d is a direction-specific scalar weight optimized during training. Note that ⊙ in Eq. 2 denotes element-wise multiplication over spatial dimensions, whereas · represents scalar multiplication applied to each directional feature map. The resulting weighted attention maps are then concatenated along the channel dimension: (5) a n = Concat ( [ a tb , a bt , a lr , a rl ] ) This results in a comprehensive attention map a n , which is used in the ARB. To ensure compatibility with the input feature map x n ′ , a 1 × 1 convolution is applied to a n after concatenation to restore the original channel dimensionality. After the ARB, f ARB undergoes batch normalization to scale and shift the features, improving convergence and stability: (6) f ^ ARB ( x ) = BatchNorm ( f ARB ( x ) ) Next, the output is passed through an argmax layer to perform clustering on the pixel-wise class scores, producing the semantic segmentation result y n : (7) y n ( i , j ) = argmax k ∈ { 1 , ⋯ , q } f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j , k where q denotes the number of classes, and f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j , k represents the predicted score for class k at pixel ( i, j ). In this study, q is set to either 2 or 3 depending on the task requirements. When q = 2 , the segmentation separates the lesion from the rest of the image. When q = 3 , the segmentation distinguishes among the lesion, the region of interest (ROI), which generally refers to the human body, and the background. To better leverage the information from the image itself and the corresponding scribble labels, we incorporate several constrained loss functions from different perspectives, including feature similarity, spatial continuity, scribble guidance, and attention graph orientation. These constraints enable the proposed method to achieve more accurate segmentation of vitiligo lesions. The specific details are provided below. As described in Eq. 7 , the predicted values are obtained by classifying the features f ^ ARB ( x ) after processing through the ARB layers and batch normalization, using the argmax operation. The optimization objective is to ensure a compact distribution within each class. Specifically, after clustering image pixels based on their features, the feature vectors within the same class should exhibit high similarity, while those from different classes should remain distinct. To enforce this, we calculate the cross-entropy loss between f ^ ARB ( x ) and y n , constraining both inter-class and intra-class feature similarity. The classified labels y n are further used as pseudo targets to guide the optimization process. This loss is expressed as: (8) L sim = ∑ n = 1 N ∑ m = 1 q − δ ( m − y n ) ln f ^ ARB ( x ) n , m where N is the total number of pixels in the image and q is the number of categories as defined in Eq. 1 and Eq. 7 , respectively. The function δ ( g ) is defined to impose a condition within the loss formulation: (9) δ ( g ) = { 1 , if g = 0 0 , otherwise In addition to considering the similarity of pixel features and grouping similar features into a single class, we account for the regional depigmentation characteristic of vitiligo lesions. This introduces an additional constraint: neighboring pixels are more likely to be classified into the same class. To implement this, we consider each pixel along with its neighboring pixels in both horizontal and vertical directions, applying an L1-norm as the restriction. This process can be mathematically expressed as: (10) L con = ∑ i = 1 W − 1 ∑ j = 1 H − 1 ( ∥ f ^ ARB ( x ) i + 1 , j − f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j ∥ 1 + ∥ f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j + 1 − f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j ∥ 1 ) where H and W represent the width and height of the input image, and f ^ ARB ( x ) i , j represent the pixel value at ( i, j ) in the normalized feature map f ^ ARB ( x ) . In addition to aligning with the distributional characteristics of vitiligo lesions, this restriction helps prevent an excessive number of initial categories in Eq. 8 caused by the complex visual features of the images, thereby significantly improving computational efficiency. This approach is particularly well-suited for the real clinical images utilized in this study. In this study, scribbles serve as crucial expert guidance, providing valuable information to help prevent misaligned segmentation caused by overfitting during model optimization. Similar to the computation of L sim , we employ partial cross-entropy for attentive loss calculation. However, unlike L sim , the class information used for this computation is derived from s n , as expressed by: (11) L scr = ∑ n = 1 N ∑ m = 1 q − u n δ ( m − s n ) ln f ^ ARB ( x ) n , m Here, s n represents the scribble label for each pixel and should follow the same category indexing as the predefined ground truth label y n . The binary indicator u n ∈ {0, 1} is defined as: (12) u n = { 1 , if pixel n is annotated with a scribble 0 , otherwise which ensures that only scribble-annotated pixels contribute to the loss, effectively guiding the model with sparse but reliable supervision. As previously introduced, DWM and ARB based spatial attention play an important role in efficiently processing global vitiligo images with low computational cost in this study. To enhance the quality of the attention map, the loss function incorporates a strategy similar to Eq. 8 , where the predicted value y n serves as a pseudo label. The L2-norm is then applied between y n and the attention map a n for the loss computation, which can be expressed as: (13) L att = ∥ a n − y n ∥ 2 2 Combining the detailed loss calculations described above, the total loss function can be expressed as: (14) L total = L sim + α L con + β L scr + γ L att where α, β , and γ are weight parameters used to balance the different constraints and ensure that all terms are at the same value scale. In this study, we demonstrated the applicability of the proposed method to vitiligo lesion segment under global-view using two publicly available datasets, Kaggle ( Kaggle, 2023 ) and the Global Skin Atlas (GSA) ( Atlas, 2019 ), along with two private datasets, UBC-EEM-Vitiligo (UEV) and UBC-VIT, used for additional validation. Representative examples from these datasets, illustrating the diversity in lesion morphology, skin tones, and anatomical locations, are shown in Fig. 3 . Kaggle contains 32 images from 17 patients, with 6 patients used for testing and images having a resolution of 300×225 pixels. GSA contains 34 images from 14 patients, 7 patients were selected for testing, and all images have a standard resolution of 768×1024 pixels. UEV includes 64 images from 49 patients, with 10 patients for testing, and all the images also have a standard resolution of 768x1024 pixels. In contrast, the UBC-VIT dataset does not have a uniform resolution, with vertical resolutions ranging from 1779 to 3570 pixels and horizontal resolutions from 1529 to 5728 pixels. This dataset, collected by our research team at UBC Dermatology, adheres to international standards for vitiligo image collection and includes 115 images from 7 patients, and 3 patients were used for testing. All the test images were carefully screened by a dermatologist (HL) based on criteria such as the inclusion of diverse diagnostic features, the patient’s original skin color, and the severity of vitiligo. The two publicly available datasets (Kaggle and GSA) and one private dataset (UEV) were utilized for comparisons with other methods, self-ablation experiments, and quantitative pixel-level evaluations using common evaluation metrics. Meanwhile, the UBC-VIT dataset was employed to assess clinical scores, as it provides comprehensive images from the same patients, including multiple perspectives and full-body parts, enabling the validation of the proposed method’s practical clinical utility. All annotations, including semantic masks and scribble maps, were prepared and approved by two dermatologists (HL and SK) within our research group. Our proposed method supports processing customized input sizes. For the GSA, Kaggle and UEV datasets, the original image resolutions were retained to preserve data fidelity. For the training set, we applied general data augmentation techniques, including rotation, inversion, and center cropping, to ensure better adaptability across all methods. In the case of the UBC-VIT dataset, images were resized to 1024×1024 pixels to balance training efficiency and segmentation performance. The training process utilized the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimizer, with an initial learning rate of 0.01 and a momentum of 0.9. To enhance training efficiency and prevent overfitting, an early-stopping strategy was applied. The stopping criterion was defined as generating predictive labels up to a predefined threshold ( Section 3.1 ), set to two for binary segmentation and three for three-class segmentation. The weight parameters used in the loss constraints in Eq. 14 are set as α = 0.1 , β = 1 , and γ = 0.5 . All experiments were conducted on a NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU card (32 GB memory). In this study, we selected three widely used evaluation metrics in semantic segmentation tasks: Dice coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), and Accuracy, to enable comprehensive comparisons with related research. • Dice Coefficient (Dice): The Dice coefficient measures the overlap between the predicted segmentation ( P ) and the ground truth ( G ), expressed as: (15) Dice = 2 | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | where | P ∩ G | is the number of pixels common to both the predicted and ground truth masks, and | P | and | G | are the total number of pixels in the predicted and ground truth masks, respectively. Dice ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better overlap. • Intersection over Union (IoU): IoU quantifies the agreement between the predicted and ground truth masks by dividing the area of their intersection by the area of their union: (16) IoU = | P ∩ G | | P ∪ G | Higher IoU values represent greater alignment between prediction and ground truth. • Accuracy (Acc): Accuracy evaluates the proportion of correctly classified pixels across the entire image: (17) Acc = Number of correctly classified pixels Total number of pixels . It provides a general measure of segmentation performance but may be influenced by class imbalances. Dice Coefficient (Dice): The Dice coefficient measures the overlap between the predicted segmentation ( P ) and the ground truth ( G ), expressed as: (15) Dice = 2 | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | where | P ∩ G | is the number of pixels common to both the predicted and ground truth masks, and | P | and | G | are the total number of pixels in the predicted and ground truth masks, respectively. Dice ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better overlap. Intersection over Union (IoU): IoU quantifies the agreement between the predicted and ground truth masks by dividing the area of their intersection by the area of their union: (16) IoU = | P ∩ G | | P ∪ G | Higher IoU values represent greater alignment between prediction and ground truth. Accuracy (Acc): Accuracy evaluates the proportion of correctly classified pixels across the entire image: (17) Acc = Number of correctly classified pixels Total number of pixels . It provides a general measure of segmentation performance but may be influenced by class imbalances. In addition, for the UBC-VIT dataset, we propose an evaluation method that aligns more closely with clinical practice. Specifically, the patient’s condition is assessed based on the ratio of the vitiligo lesion area to the total body area, denoted as R , which is calculated using the following equation: (18) R = A lesion A total , where: • A lesion is the total area of the vitiligo lesions, and • A total is the total body surface area. A lesion is the total area of the vitiligo lesions, and A total is the total body surface area. Since an image contains certain body parts, which needs to be further standardized according to the percentage of total body surface area. Specifically, the adjustment factor P region is defined according to the established clinical practice used for VASI ( Hamzavi et al., 2004; Komen et al., 2015 ) as: (19) P region = { 0.05 , Hands , 0.20 , Upper extremities , 0.30 , Trunk , 0.40 , Lower extremities , 0.05 , Head and neck . To calculate the total lesion ratio R , we consider the proportion of each region affected by vitiligo, denoted as P lesion , which represents the percentage of the region’s surface area affected. The total lesion ratio R is computed as the weighted sum of P lesion , with P region serving as the weights: (20) R = ∑ region R region = ∑ region ( P region × P lesion ) , This formulation ensures that regions with larger surface areas contribute proportionally to the overall lesion percentage, preventing the overrepresentation of smaller regions. To prepare the ground truth label for R , we used the clinical estimate that a patient’s palm represents approximately 1 % of the total body surface area. This reference, provided by our dermatologists (HL and SK), served as a guideline to normalize the global lesion ratio R across different anatomical sites and imaging conditions. Then, to evaluate the accuracy of our segmentation method, we compare the predicted total lesion ratio R pred and the ground truth R GT as two sets of paired observations. The Bland-Altman analysis assesses the agreement between these two measures by analyzing the distribution of their differences relative to their means. For each sample t , the difference between the predicted and ground truth lesion ratios is computed as: (21) D t = R pred , t − R GT , t , where R pred, t represents the lesion ratio predicted by the proposed method, and R GT, t denotes the corresponding ground truth ratio. The mean of the predicted and ground truth lesion ratios for each sample is given by: (22) M t = R pred , t + R GT , t 2 . The overall bias (mean difference) across all samples is then calculated as: (23) D ¯ = 1 T ∑ t = 1 T D t . To determine the expected range of agreement, we compute the limits of agreement (LOA), which define the interval within which most differences lie: (24) LOA = D ¯ ± 1.96 × S D D , where SD D is the standard deviation of the differences D t . The LOA provides insight into the variability of the differences and helps determine whether the segmentation method’s predictions align with expert annotations. Once all the values are calculated, we can build a Bland-Altman plot, where each sample is plotted with its mean value M t on the x-axis and its difference D t on the y-axis. The bias is represented as a central dashed line at D ¯ , while the upper and lower LOA are indicated by boundary lines. A narrow LOA range and a bias close to zero indicate strong agreement between the predicted and ground truth segmentation results. By applying this method, we systematically evaluate the reliability of our proposed segmentation approach in approximating expert annotations, ensuring its robustness for clinical applications. In this section, we present a comprehensive comparison with related studies. The comparison is divided into two parts. The first part involves fully supervised learning methods trained using complete masks as ground truth, including Unet ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ), Unet++ ( Zhou et al., 2018 ), and Medsam ( Lei et al., 2023 ), which is widely recognized benchmarks for semantic segmentation, as well as ISD-CSR ( Li et al., 2023b ) and HSV-PAT ( Hillmer et al., 2024 ), both specifically applied to vitiligo segmentation. The results are visually illustrated in Fig. 4 (GSA), Fig. 5 (Kaggle), and Fig. 6 (UEV) while the quantitative analysis is summarized in Table 1 (GSA), Table 2 (Kaggle), and Table 3 (UEV). The second part focuses on weakly or semi-supervised segmentation methods that use scribble annotations or partial masks for training. These include the semi-supervised BVLS ( Wang et al., 2023a ), scribble-based Medsam ( Lei et al., 2023 ), DFC ( Kim et al., 2020 ), and Scribformer ( Li et al., 2024 ). Here, BVLS is included as one of the few works addressing global-viewed vitiligo segmentation, even though it employs a semi-supervised training approach, differing from the other methods in this category. The results are visually illustrated in Fig. 7 (GSA), Fig. 8 (Kaggle), and Fig. 9 (UEV) while the quantitative analysis is also summarized in Table 1 (GSA) and Table 2 (Kaggle), and Table 3 (UEV). Across the above mentioned figures, the samples are grouped into three levels of diagnostic difficulty, including simple, medium, and difficult, as determined by expert dermatologists. These difficulty levels reflect the visual discernibility of the lesion, with higher contrast and clearer boundaries indicating simple cases, whereas lower contrast, color similarity, boundary ambiguity, or confounding artifacts correspond to difficult cases. All experiments were conducted on the same dataset, and each method strictly adhered to its original code or paper description to ensure fair and reliable comparisons. Overall, our proposed method achieves the highest Dice (0.87 for GSA, 0.82 for Kaggle, 0.89 for UEV), IoU (0.78 for GSA, 0.70 for Kaggle, 0.81 for UEV), and Accuracy (0.96 for GSA, 0.93 for Kaggle, 0.96 for UEV) among all compared methods, including SOTA fully supervised approaches such as Medsam and HSV-PAT, which rely on pixel-level annotations. Our approach demonstrates an improvement of up to 14 % in Dice and 19 % in IoU, underscoring its effectiveness. Furthermore, our method also surpasses other weakly supervised approaches, including Scribformer and Medsam (Scribble), highlighting its superior ability to leverage limited supervision. While fully supervised approaches such as Unet, Unet++, and Medsam perform competitively, their dependence on extensive pixel-level annotations limits their scalability. In contrast, our method achieves comparable or superior results with significantly reduced annotation effort, making it a more practical choice for large-scale applications. Notably, supervised learning methods exhibit strong performance on simpler vitiligo lesion cases, as observed in Fig. 4, Fig. 5 , and Fig. 6 , but struggle with more complex cases. In contrast, our method maintains consistent performance across all levels of difficulty, indicating better generalizability with a limited number of training images. Another key observation is that segmentation results from traditional supervised methods are highly susceptible to variations in background and lighting conditions, which can negatively impact performance. Our scribble-based framework, however, effectively mitigates these issues, demonstrating greater robustness to imaging variations compared to traditional local-viewed lesion-normal skin image segmentation methods. These findings further validate the advantages of our weakly supervised approach in global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation. Since our proposed method integrates multiple loss constraints, we conducted ablation experiments to assess the contributions of different loss functions, particularly the scribble-based supervision and attention mechanism. As shown in Table 4 , we evaluated the GSA and Kaggle datasets by incrementally adding L scr and L att to the baseline, which consists of L sim and L con as the backbone. The results across three datasets exhibit a consistent trend. Incorporating L att into the baseline led to a 10–13 % increase in Dice and a 7–12 % improvement in IoU, demonstrating the attention mechanism’s effectiveness in enhancing feature representation and segmentation accuracy. Similarly, adding L scr to the baseline resulted in performance gains, with Dice increasing by 11–18 % and IoU improving by 8–18 %, underscoring the role of weak supervision in refining segmentation boundaries. These results confirm the complementary effects of L att and L scr . The attention mechanism enhances feature localization, while scribble-based supervision improves segmentation reliability. The combination of all loss terms achieves the most robust performance, validating their necessity in our framework. To evaluate the effectiveness of the attention components in our architecture, we conducted ablation experiments on the GSA and Kaggle datasets by incrementally adding the ARB and the DWM to the CNN backbone ( Kim et al., 2020 ), as summarized in Table 5 . Here, ARB represents a standard spatial attention mechanism, while DWM introduces directional spatial attention to better capture local anisotropy in vitiligo progression. On the GSA dataset, adding ARB led to a 7 % improvement in Dice and a 7 % gain in IoU, confirming its effectiveness in enhancing feature representation. Incorporating DWM further boosted Dice by 4 % and IoU by 6 %, highlighting the benefit of directional spatial modeling. Accuracy also improved steadily, reaching 0.96 in the full model. Similarly, on the Kaggle UEV dataset, ARB improved Dice and IoU by 6–7 % for Kaggle and 4–5 % for UEV, and the addition of DWM brought another 3–4 % improvement for Kaggle and 6–9 % for UEV. These results demonstrate the necessity of directional spatial attention in our framework. In addition, to further elucidate the role of DWM, we compared the heatmap visualizations between the non-directional spatial attention ( Belton et al., 2021 ) and the proposed DWM, as shown in Fig. 10 . The results show that DWM produces more coherent and lesion-focused activations, effectively suppressing irrelevant background structures and artifacts. The multi-directional aggregation mechanism in DWM enables each pixel to integrate contextual responses from multiple orientations, leading to a more comprehensive delineation of lesion boundaries and subtle depigmented extensions. In contrast, the conventional spatial attention module (first column) is more susceptible to uneven illumination and texture interference, resulting in less stable lesion emphasis. Quantitatively, incorporating DWM increased the mean Dice coefficient by 2.3 % and IoU by 4.3 % compared with the non-directional spatial attention baseline on the GSA dataset, confirming that the direction-weighted design enhances segmentation accuracy while preserving lesion-specific focus and robustness against artifacts. To examine the potential influence of threshold selection on segmentation performance, we conducted a segmentation threshold analysis on the GSA, Kaggle, and UEV datasets using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the corresponding area under the curve (AUC) metrics, as shown in Fig. 11 . Same as the previous validations, for each dataset, we evaluated three diagnostic difficulty levels (Simple, Medium, and Difficult) and each level has two samples. In this evaluation, a sigmoid activation was applied before the argmax step to produce continuous-valued probability maps during inference, enabling computation of ROC curves and AUC values without altering the trained model parameters. The results show consistently high AUC values across all difficulty levels. Even for the most challenging subsets, the AUC remained above 0.92, indicating strong discriminative capability over a wide range of thresholds. These findings confirm that the proposed method is robust to threshold variation, reinforcing its reliability in diverse and complex clinical scenarios. Scribble annotations play a crucial role in our proposed method, and analyzing the impact of their quality on segmentation results is essential. To investigate this, we prepared different levels of scribble annotations and categorized them into three grades: fine, moderate , and coarse . The comparative results are presented in Fig. 12 , with the corresponding quantitative analysis shown in Fig. 13 . As illustrated in Fig. 13 , the segmentation performance consistently improves with finer scribble annotations across all evaluation metrics, including Dice, Acc, and IoU. Specifically, fine scribbles achieve the highest Dice coefficient (0.87), Acc (0.96), and IoU (0.78), whereas moderate scribbles exhibit slightly lower values (0.73 for Dice, 0.93 for Acc, and 0.60 for IoU). The performance degradation is more evident with coarse annotations, where Dice, Acc, and IoU drop to 0.63, 0.90, and 0.51, respectively. These results highlight the importance of precise scribble annotations in achieving accurate segmentation. While moderate annotations still provide reasonable performance, coarse annotations significantly reduce segmentation quality, emphasizing the necessity of high-quality supervision for optimal results. The percentage of total body surface area affected by vitiligo serves as a crucial metric for assessing disease severity and monitoring treatment efficacy over time. In this study, we leverage the UBC-VIT dataset to simulate real-world clinical diagnostic scenarios. Following international standards, we employ Eq. 20 and Bland-Altman analysis to evaluate the consistency between automated predictions and expert dermatologist assessments. Fig. 14 illustrates a representative patient sample comprising 15 images captured from different angles, providing a comprehensive view of vitiligo distribution across the body. Our segmentation approach classifies each image into three categories: background, body, and vitiligo lesions. Based on these segmentations, we compute the affected area percentage and compare the results against ground truth annotations. Fig. 15 presents the Bland-Altman analysis for our predictions on all test images, illustrating the agreement between the automated method and expert evaluations. The bias, represented by the blue dashed line, indicates the mean difference between predicted and ground truth values. The upper and lower limits of agreement (LOA), marked by red and green dashed lines respectively, define the range within which most differences lie. The analysis suggests that our method maintains a high level of agreement with expert assessments, with minimal bias and an acceptably narrow LOA range, supporting its potential for clinical applications in vitiligo monitoring. In this study, we present a novel approach for global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation using physician-provided scribble annotations, thereby eliminating the need for labor-intensive and costly pixel-level labels. In contrast to conventional methods that rely on complete masks, our framework demonstrates the feasibility of leveraging sparse expert input while maintaining clinically meaningful performance. This section provides an in-depth discussion of key experimental findings, shedding light on the advantages, challenges, and potential extensions of the proposed method. One critical but often overlooked factor in weakly or semi-supervised segmentation is the quality of the guiding supervision. While scribble-based learning has gained popularity for medical image segmentation, few studies have systematically evaluated the influence of scribble quality on model performance. Our investigation fills this gap by comparing segmentation results under varying scribble annotation conditions. The results suggest that although pixel-level precision is not required, the effectiveness of scribbles strongly depends on their clarity and coverage of relevant lesion areas. Inadequate or poorly placed scribbles diminish the model’s ability to capture lesion boundaries, highlighting the necessity of medical expertise in preparing high-quality, informative annotations. To facilitate the preparation of higher-quality scribble annotations, we have developed comprehensive guidelines based on in-depth discussions with experienced dermatologists and aligned with the design of our proposed loss function. These are provided in the Appendix as supplementary material to support future related research. The proposed framework also prioritizes model efficiency, featuring a lightweight architecture with only 0.25M parameters. This compact design is enabled by shallow bottleneck residual convolutional layers and a directional attention mechanism optimized for sparse supervision. Compared to existing SOTA methods such as Scribformer (50.42M) and MedSam (93.70M), our approach significantly reduces computational overhead, making it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings. A promising future direction is to automate the scribble annotation and segmentation process within a unified pipeline, further improving usability and minimizing dependence on manual preprocessing. Although we conducted experiments using datasets from four different sources, this study still has a limitation in terms of data volume. For example, the largest dataset, UEV, includes only 64 images from 49 patients. Given the high variability of vitiligo across different skin types and body regions, such sample sizes may not fully capture the diversity required for broad generalization. This limitation highlights the need for further validation to assess the extensibility of our method. In future work, we plan to address this challenge by integrating the proposed method with simple user-provided scribbles to generate initial ground truth labels, which can then be refined under dermatological supervision. This strategy allows the model to provide feedback during the annotation process, thereby facilitating large-scale dataset creation and broadening the potential application scenarios of the method. For real-world clinical applicability, expanding the framework to incorporate multimodal data is essential. While this study is limited to standard RGB images, additional modalities such as Wood’s lamp imaging and patient-specific meta information, including skin tone variations, may substantially influence segmentation accuracy. These modalities can potentially offer complementary information that could inform both the attention mechanism and the training workflow. Future research should investigate strategies for effectively integrating multimodal inputs and adapting the model architecture accordingly, ultimately moving toward more robust and generalizable vitiligo segmentation solutions. In this study, we introduce GloW-VSNet, to the best of our knowledge, the first lightweight global-view vitiligo lesion segmentation method based on scribble annotations. By leveraging a physician-guided attention mechanism and optimizing multiple loss functions within a logistic-type feature learning framework, our approach effectively segments vitiligo lesions even in complex imaging scenarios with limited data. We conducted extensive analysis to evaluate annotation quality, and overall performance across multiple datasets. The results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves accurate and reliable segmentation, highlighting its potential for practical assessment of skin disease severity using clinical photography. To ensure annotation consistency and compatibility with our weakly supervised learning framework, we outline the following annotation standards based on clinical rationale and model design. 1. Annotation categories. Based on the task setting, which may involve binary segmentation (lesion vs. non-lesion) or three-class segmentation (lesion, non-lesion, and background), scribbles should clearly distinguish among the following semantic categories: • Lesion: Regions exhibiting depigmentation or visible skin abnormalities. • Non-lesion (Normal skin): Unaffected skin areas within the region of interest (ROI). • Background: Non-skin or irrelevant regions (e.g., clothing, walls). 2. Annotation density levels. We define three levels of scribble annotation density to represent different degrees of supervision. Unlike boundary annotations, scribbles highlight representative regions of target structures and prevents the need to outline precise borders. The density levels are determined by the spatial distribution and compactness of scribbles, as illustrated in Fig. 12 . Lesion: Regions exhibiting depigmentation or visible skin abnormalities. Non-lesion (Normal skin): Unaffected skin areas within the region of interest (ROI). Background: Non-skin or irrelevant regions (e.g., clothing, walls). Scribble density definition. Let S = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N denote the set of pixels belonging to the scribble. We first compute the tight axis-aligned bounding box that encloses all scribble pixels: (A.1) x min = min i x i , x max = max i x i , y min = min i y i , y max = max i y i . The area of this box is defined as: (A.2) A box = ( x max − x min + 1 ) ( y max − y min + 1 ) . The scribble density is then defined as: (A.3) ρ = | S | A box , where | S | denotes the number of pixels forming the scribble. This measure reflects how densely the scribbles are distributed within their enclosing region and can be computed directly from the scribble map without requiring a ground-truth mask. Density thresholds. According to our annotation protocol, scribble annotations were grouped into three density levels based on the proportion of annotated pixels ρ : • Fine-level: ρ ≥ 0.10. This level corresponds to high annotation density, where a substantial fraction of pixels are annotated. • Moderate-level: 0.05 ≤ ρ < 0.10. This level reflects medium annotation density, with a moderate fraction of pixels annotated. • Coarse-level: ρ < 0.05. This level indicates low annotation density, characterized by a minimal fraction of annotated pixels. These thresholds were empirically determined through pilot annotation sessions with dermatology experts and can be slightly adjusted depending on image resolution or annotator variability. Although the density measure ρ offers a quantitative approximation of scribble complexity, it does not fully characterize the spatial properties that differentiate the three levels. Scribble categorization therefore cannot rely on ρ alone. In practice, classification follows our annotation protocol, which jointly considers both the numerical density and the qualitative spatial distribution of strokes. Specifically, Fine-level scribbles not only exhibit high density but also tend to be spatially extensive, covering both central and peripheral lesion regions and providing abundant pixel-level cues. Moderate-level scribbles, while having medium density, generally distribute across representative lesion structures and capture the main morphological patterns with reduced annotation effort. Coarse-level scribbles, despite their low density, typically appear as sparse strokes placed at key diagnostic locations, often near salient lesion areas, providing minimal yet essential supervisory signals. Thus, the ρ thresholds serve as an auxiliary guideline for classification, whereas the descriptive spatial criteria remain essential for distinguishing Fine-, Moderate-, and Coarse-level annotations. Fine-level: ρ ≥ 0.10. This level corresponds to high annotation density, where a substantial fraction of pixels are annotated. Moderate-level: 0.05 ≤ ρ < 0.10. This level reflects medium annotation density, with a moderate fraction of pixels annotated. Coarse-level: ρ < 0.05. This level indicates low annotation density, characterized by a minimal fraction of annotated pixels. 3. Annotation structure and location. To ensure spatial coverage and representation consistency, the following principles should be followed: • Directionality: Scribbles should reflect the internal texture or directional pattern of the lesion rather than outlining its border. • Contextual coverage: Both central and peripheral regions of each semantic category should be annotated to capture variation in appearance (e.g., smaller lesions, shadowed areas). • Global-view images: In whole-body or large-area images, scribbles should be distributed across different anatomical regions to improve spatial diversity and generalization. 4. Prohibited annotation practices. Directionality: Scribbles should reflect the internal texture or directional pattern of the lesion rather than outlining its border. Contextual coverage: Both central and peripheral regions of each semantic category should be annotated to capture variation in appearance (e.g., smaller lesions, shadowed areas). Global-view images: In whole-body or large-area images, scribbles should be distributed across different anatomical regions to improve spatial diversity and generalization. To avoid contradictions with loss designs (e.g., similarity loss, continuity loss) and to maintain label reliability, the following practices must be avoided: • Cross-class scribbles: A single scribble must not span across different semantic categories (e.g., from lesion to normal skin). • Disjointed or scattered scribbles: Avoid disconnected scribbles unless the lesion itself is inherently scattered. • Overly dense or overlapping scribbles: Excessive scribbling in a small region can bias the model and reduce its generalizability. 5. Consistency and annotator training recommendations. Cross-class scribbles: A single scribble must not span across different semantic categories (e.g., from lesion to normal skin). Disjointed or scattered scribbles: Avoid disconnected scribbles unless the lesion itself is inherently scattered. Overly dense or overlapping scribbles: Excessive scribbling in a small region can bias the model and reduce its generalizability. To maintain consistency across annotators and datasets, the following steps are recommended: • All annotators should strictly follow this protocol. • A brief training session with visual examples should be conducted before annotation begins. • All annotations should undergo quality control to identify and revise inconsistent or substandard scribbles. data.text: HarmonicEchoNet: Leveraging harmonic convolutions for automated standard plane detection in fetal heart ultrasound videos Fetal echocardiography offers non-invasive and real-time imaging acquisition of fetal heart images to identify congenital heart conditions. Manual acquisition of standard heart views is time-consuming, whereas automated detection remains challenging due to high spatial similarity across anatomical views with subtle local image appearance variations. To address these challenges, we introduce a very lightweight frequency-guided deep learning-based model named HarmonicEchoNet that can automatically detect heart standard views in a transverse sweep or freehand ultrasound scan of the fetal heart. HarmonicEchoNet uses harmonic convolution blocks (HCBs) and a harmonic spatial and channel squeeze-and-excitation (hscSE) module. The HCBs apply a Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT)-based harmonic decomposition to input features, which are then combined using learned weights. The hscSE module identifies significant regions in the spatial domain to improve feature extraction of the fetal heart anatomical structures, capturing both spatial and channel-wise dependencies in an ultrasound image. The combination of these modules improves model performance relative to recent CNN-based, transformer-based, and CNN+transformer-based image classification models. We use four datasets from two private studies, PULSE (Perception Ultrasound by Learning Sonographic Experience) and CAIFE (Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Fetal Echocardiography), to develop and evaluate HarmonicEchoNet models. Experimental results show that HarmonicEchoNet is 10–15 times faster than ConvNeXt, DeiT, and VOLO, with an inference time of just 3.9 ms. It also achieves 2%–7% accuracy improvement in classifying fetal heart standard planes compared to these baselines. Furthermore, with just 19.9 million parameters compared to ConvNeXt’s 196.24 million, HarmonicEchoNet is nearly ten times more parameter-efficient. Fetal echocardiography offers non-invasive and real-time imaging acquisition of fetal heart images to identify congenital heart conditions. Manual acquisition of standard heart views is time-consuming, whereas automated detection remains challenging due to high spatial similarity across anatomical views with subtle local image appearance variations. To address these challenges, we introduce a very lightweight frequency-guided deep learning-based model named HarmonicEchoNet that can automatically detect heart standard views in a transverse sweep or freehand ultrasound scan of the fetal heart. HarmonicEchoNet uses harmonic convolution blocks (HCBs) and a harmonic spatial and channel squeeze-and-excitation (hscSE) module. The HCBs apply a Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT)-based harmonic decomposition to input features, which are then combined using learned weights. The hscSE module identifies significant regions in the spatial domain to improve feature extraction of the fetal heart anatomical structures, capturing both spatial and channel-wise dependencies in an ultrasound image. The combination of these modules improves model performance relative to recent CNN-based, transformer-based, and CNN+transformer-based image classification models. We use four datasets from two private studies, PULSE (Perception Ultrasound by Learning Sonographic Experience) and CAIFE (Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Fetal Echocardiography), to develop and evaluate HarmonicEchoNet models. Experimental results show that HarmonicEchoNet is 10–15 times faster than ConvNeXt, DeiT, and VOLO, with an inference time of just 3.9 ms. It also achieves 2%–7% accuracy improvement in classifying fetal heart standard planes compared to these baselines. Furthermore, with just 19.9 million parameters compared to ConvNeXt’s 196.24 million, HarmonicEchoNet is nearly ten times more parameter-efficient. In most economically developed countries, assessment of the fetal heart as part of routine screening typically takes place at 20 weeks of gestation ( Carvalho et al., 2023b; Moncrieff et al., 2021 ). It is important to note the health inequality present where some other countries might not be in a position to offer such fetal heart assessments at 20 weeks of gestation as part of routine screening. During these routine ultrasound scans, the fetal heart anatomy is assessed by acquiring standard echocardiographic plane still frames. These frames contain all anatomical landmarks in the correct spatial orientation and position, as defined by clinical guidelines (e.g., ISUOG). For the fetal heart, frames are captured for the following standard views: the four-chamber view (4CHV), the left ventricular outflow tract view (LVOT), the three-vessel view (3VV), and the three-vessel trachea view (3VTV) ( Carvalho et al., 2023b ). Recognizing fetal heart standard planes is a time-consuming and highly specialized task, that relies heavily on sonographer skill. To illustrate this point, two experienced sonographers were asked to annotate the same set of 10 transverse sweeps videos of the fetal heart with frame-level labels to identify whether the frames comprise a standard plane for that particular anatomy or not. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the average agreement between sonographers is 66%, highlighting the inherent difficulty of the task. Notable variability in both inter- and intra-observer acquisition has also been reported in other studies ( Sarris et al., 2012; Dudley and Chapman, 2002 ). In a typical fetal ultrasound scan, clinicians use a freehand approach to capture various views of the fetus, including both short-axis and long-axis views of the fetal heart. This manual process requires precise transducer positioning and frequent adjustments to capture the necessary images. It can be time-consuming, and sonographers often face the challenges of maintaining accuracy and managing fatigue due to continuous adjustments and repositioning. The transverse sweep protocol, introduced by Yagel et al. (2001) and further refined by Yang et al. (2016) , simplifies fetal heart ultrasound acquisition by providing a structured approach to acquire five specific short-axis views: the upper part of the abdomen (SITUS), the four-chamber view (4CHV), the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) view, the three-vessel view (3VV), and the three-vessel trachea view (3VTV). This acquisition protocol reduces the need for extensive manual probe adjustments, potentially decreasing both scanning time and patient discomfort while easing the workload for sonographers. However, automatically detecting these standard frames in transverse sweep video data poses significant challenges. The frames preceding and following the standard frames often have small appearance differences, with only subtle variations in anatomical landmarks. This high level of global structural similarity with minor local changes complicates the task of accurately detecting anatomical temporal boundaries. Additionally, the fetal heart is in constant motion (beating) and undergoing deformations, further complicating the automatic detection of standard frames. These factors make it challenging to develop effective automated systems for identifying and analyzing standard frames in transverse sweep videos. To tackle the challenges of standard plane detection in transverse video sweeps and utilize the sweeps for detailed analysis of different views of the fetal heart we introduce HarmonicEchoNet. Our contributions are summarized next: • We present HarmonicEchoNet, a novel architecture for modeling standard frame detection in transverse sweep and freehand fetal heart ultrasound (US) videos that makes use of harmonic convolutions (HC). This approach combines learned kernels with pre-defined spectral filters (DCT filters), enhancing feature learning while reducing model overfitting and computational complexity with the use of DCT filters. The model also incorporates HC within squeeze and excitation (scSE) blocks, allowing it to focus on the most informative regions or pixels in US images, thus optimizing computational efficiency (see Fig. 2 ). • HarmonicEchoNet’s DCT-based harmonic convolution is designed to be less sensitive to changes in pixel intensities than standard convolution. This makes it more effective in modeling feature extraction and classification tasks, even in the presence of varying pixel intensity levels. • Extensive experiments on four fetal heart US datasets demonstrate that HarmonicEchoNet models achieve superior standard plane detection performance when compared to models that do not make use of DCT-based harmonic convolution. We are the first to analyze and validate an approach on fetal heart ultrasound transverse sweeps, showcasing the suitability of HarmonicEchoNet models for locating heart sub-anatomy regions in sweeps as a pre-processing step for congenital heart condition detection. This makes it more effective in modeling feature extraction and classification tasks, even in the presence of varying pixel intensity levels. Standard plane detection for the freehand ultrasound case is well-studied in the literature. An example of early work on standard plane (SP) detection, Rahmatullah et al. (2011) , employed an AdaBoost-based classifier to detect key anatomical structures that defined a biometry plane, achieving a recall rate of 91.29% for automatic standard plane acquisition. Yaqub et al. (2015) investigated using random forests for SP classification, achieving 75% accuracy for six-plane categorization. Automation of SP acquisition in 2D fetal ultrasound videos has since made significant strides with the application of deep learning-based architectures. Chen et al. (2014) utilized deep convolutional neural networks with transfer learning, attaining over 90% classification accuracy on fetal abdominal videos. Their subsequent work ( Chen et al., 2015 ) integrated a deep hierarchical visual feature extractor with a time-series learning model, specifically a knowledge transfer recurrent neural network (T-RNN) to better leverage and explore spatiotemporal features in fetal heart videos. Baumgartner et al. (2016) applied a variant of the VGGNet to detect 12 standard planes defined by the UK Fetal Anomaly Screening Program (FASP), achieving 69% average recognition accuracy and an 80% recall rate. This approach was subsequently refined through weak supervision via image-level labeling, and extended to the detection of 13 standard planes ( Baumgartner et al., 2017 ). Other studies report the use of a multiscale architecture and Multiscale Dense Network (MSDNet) to achieve a 98.15% mean average precision (mAP) ( Kong et al., 2018 ), and a method for identifying standard fetal face planes with Fisher vectors, achieving 99.19% mAP on the reported dataset ( Lei et al., 2015 ). Another notable approach ( Cai et al., 2018 ) introduced Multi-task SonoEyeNet (M-SEN), a multi-task convolutional neural network that generates clinically relevant visual attention maps from sonographer gaze tracking data to detect abdominal circumference (AC) standard planes. This method, featuring an adversarial training scheme, achieved Precision of 96.8%, Recall of 96.2%, and an F-1 score of 96.5%, removing the need for gaze tracking data during inference. Recent studies have also explored the temporal dimension in ultrasound videos, with Zhao et al. (2022, 2023) leveraging temporal data to detect clinically significant video clips based on reconstruction error, although not specifically locating SP frames. Most recently, Men et al. (2023) trained spatio-temporal generative models to guide a sonographer to a standard plane when they are close it, by synthesizing the SP or automatically selecting standard plane images from video clips. Specific to fetal echocardiography analysis, several notable studies have utilized advanced machine learning techniques for the detection and analysis of standard plane frames. Huang et al. (2017) presented Temporal HeartNet, a spatio-temporal CNN-based architecture to predict the visibility, standard plane, location and orientation of the heart at frame level. Li et al. (2024) introduces a deep learning-based approach “FHUSP-NET” that simultaneously recognizes five fetal heart ultrasound standard planes (FHUSPs) and detects ten key anatomical structures in freehand fetal ultrasound video, achieving a mAP@0.5 of 0.955, precision of 0.958, recall of 0.931 and an accuracy of 0.964 at a processing speed per frame of 13.6 ms. The aforementioned approaches have significantly contributed to advancing the fetal ultrasound SP detection literature. However, these methods are designed for analysis of freehand ultrasound video and all use conventional convolutional kernels. In contrast, our work is the first to address the analysis of fetal heart transverse sweeps (t-sweep), where a sonographer scans continuously over the anatomies without pausing. This results in high spatial similarity between video frames at the frame (or global) level, with frequently only minor, subtle local appearance variations. Further, and unlike for the freehand ultrasound case, the object of interest (the fetal heart) is in motion and deforms both spatially and temporally, further complicating the standard plane detection task. A key requirement is to distinguish between these subtle local variations. We introduce harmonic spatial convolution Squeeze Excitation (hscSE) blocks to do this. In addition to using convolutional kernels, these blocks incorporate Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) filters. DCT filters capture spatial frequency information alongside spatial details, enabling our model to detect subtle changes that are often missed by traditional convolution-based approaches. As we show later in Section 5 , this leads to a significant improvement in standard plane detection performance. The proposed framework for the classification of fetal heart standard views, HarmonicEchoNet, is detailed in the schematic in Fig. 3 . The core layers in the HarmonicEchoNet architecture design are harmonic convolutional neural networks (HCNN) based on the discrete cosine transform (DCT) ( Ulicny et al., 2022 ). In a HCNN, the DCT filters are used instead of standard convolution filters to compute harmonic features. While a standard convolution filter captures the local patterns in the spatial (image) domain, DCT filters capture spatial frequency information. Specifically, we replace standard convolution layers in the original scSE ( Roy et al., 2018 ) blocks with harmonic convolution (HC)-based spatial and channel “Squeeze & Excitation” (hscSE) blocks. In HarmonicEchoNet, we used five HC and five hscSE blocks with one average pool (AP) and one fully-connected (FC) layer. Each HC block consists of two harmonic convolutions followed by two batch normalizations (BN), two activation functions (ReLUs), and a Max-Pooling layer. The feature map of each HC block, denoted as F H C B is defined as; (1) F H C B = M a x P o o l ( F H C ( F H C ) ) , where F H C = ReLU(BN(HC)) , and HC and BN denote the harmonic convolution and batch normalization, respectively. The HC block operates by processing the data in two steps. First, a harmonic decomposition is performed on the input features via a DCT. The transformed signals are then combined using weights that are learned during training. The hscSE consists of one harmonic spatial and one harmonic channel squeeze & excitation (SE) attention module. The harmonic spatial SE (hsSE) module focuses on the spatial dimensions of the input features to identify important regions. The feature map of the hsSE module, represented as F h s S E , is defined as; (2) F h s S E = S i g m o i d ( H C ( R e L U ( H C ( A P ) ) ) ) , where HC and AP denote the harmonic convolution and adaptive average pooling, respectively. On the other hand, the harmonic channel SE (hcSE) attention module focuses on the channel dimensions to determine the most relevant features. The feature map of the hcSE module, represented as F h c S E , is defined as: (3) F h c S E = S i g m o i d ( H C ) , Thus, the proposed hscSE is the combination of these two attention modules that allow the hscSE model to capture both spatial and channel-wise dependencies in the US image. The feature map of the hcSE module, represented as F h c S E , is defined as the sum of Eqs. (2) and (3) : (4) F h s c S E = F h s S E + F h c S E The final feature maps are pooled in an average pool layer to calculate the average value for each patch on the feature map. The pooled feature map is then integrated into the fully connected (FC) layer to produce an output prediction. We initially resize the original input video frames to dimensions 224 × 224 × 3 pixels. We input the resized image into the initial HC block, employing a 3 × 3 kernel with padding set to 1. The output feature maps from this block are of size 112 × 112 × 32. Following this, the output feature maps are forwarded to the initial harmonic spatial and channel squeeze-and-excitation (hscSE) block. This block utilizes a 1 × 1 kernel, with a channel reduction size of 2 for the harmonic channel-wise spatial excitation (hcSE) component and 0 (zero, i.e. no reduction) for the harmonic spatial-wise spatial excitation (hsSE) component. Consequently, the feature maps remain unchanged in size. This process is performed four times, giving feature maps of sizes 56 × 56 × 64, 28 × 28 × 256, 14 × 14 × 512, and 7 × 7 × 1024. The final feature maps of size 7 × 7 × 1024 are fed to the average pooling layer, resulting in a tensor of size 1 × 1 × 1024. The feature maps are flattened into a vector of size 1024 and input to the FC layer, producing prediction scores for a set of 5 classes, each representing one of the heart views (SITUS, 4CHV, LVOT, 3VV, 3VTV). In this section, we first introduce our video frame definitions and then describe the datasets used in the research. Finally we provide implementation details related to model training. As noted previously, fetal echocardiography standard plane frame detection in video sweeps is challenging due to the high spatial similarity between frames and views. In particular, transverse sweeps (t-sweeps) capture a video of the moving heart. Depending on the use case of the video, the goal may be to detect traditional standard plane frames, or a video clip of the beating heart close to a standard plane, say to assess heart kinematics or to check anatomical structures that move over the cardiac cycle, such as valves. We therefore chose to introduce three frame-level label types — standard, para-standard, and transitional frames — as defined next, and as illustrated for freehand scanning and t-sweeps in Fig. 4 . A standard frame is an ultrasound image displaying the heart structures according to the ISUOG Practice Guidelines ( Carvalho et al., 2023a; Donofrio et al., 2014 ). A para-standard frame is an ultrasound image acquired before or after standard frames where most of the heart structures defining a standard plane are visible but it is considered sub-optimal when compared to the standard plane. A transitional frame is an ultrasound image containing heart anatomy captured during the transition between successive para-standard video segments belonging to two different heart views. The datasets used in the experiments come from two research studies: PULSE (Perception Ultrasound by Learning Sonographer Experience) ( Drukker et al., 2021 ), and CAIFE (Development of Clinical Artificial Intelligence Models in Fetal Echocardiography for the Detection of Congenital Heart Defects). Ethics approval for the CAIFE study was granted by the West of Scotland Research Ethics Service, UK Research Ethics Committee (Reference 18/WS/0051). Ethics approval for the PULSE study was granted by the East Midlands, Leicester Central Research Ethics Committee (Reference 23/EM/0023). For the CAIFE study, women aged > 18 years old in their second trimester of pregnancy ( > 16 weeks) were recruited. Imaging was performed by a team of two experts: a fetal cardiologist and a sonographer using a standard curvilinear probe (C2-9-D or C1-6-D), and GE Voluson ultrasound machines (General Electric Healthcare) models E8 or E10. US machine settings were adjusted to meet operator preference in relation to patient BMI in order to acquire the best anatomy visualization for the video sweep. Video sweeps were acquired in a transverse trajectory with cephalad movement of the transducer from the fetal abdomen towards the fetal chest, allowing visualization of five heart views ( Carvalho et al., 2023b ) in its trajectory in the following sequence: situs, four chambers (4CHV), left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), three vessels (3VV), and three-vessel trachea (3VTV) ( Fig. 5 ). The sweep takes approximately 10 s to complete and captures approximately 200 frames per video. We selected a subset of 90 t-sweep (19 participants) from the CAIFE study based on the following criteria: (i) recognizable anatomy of the heart and (ii) visibility of the five heart views in the transverse sweep. The selected videos were manually annotated at the frame level, where individual frames received one of five heart view labels, giving a total of 31,530 annotated frames (avg. 1659 frames per video). The frames were manually annotated by a fetal cardiologist with 14 yr of experience((O.P.). We also selected heart video clips around a standard plane from 400 freehand videos (200 participants) and a total of 1121 images from the CAIFE study based on the following criteria: (i) visible heart anatomy, and (ii) includes sonographer annotation indicating one of five heart views. The sonographer annotation was extracted using optical character recognition and used as the ground truth label. For the PULSE study, data acquisition protocol details are described in Drukker et al. (2021) Briefly, participants included women aged > 18 years old in their second trimester of their pregnancy (gestational age of approximately 20 weeks). Video clips were obtained using a General Electric (GE) Healthcare Voluson ultrasound machine model E8 or E10 equipped with a curvilinear (C2-9-D or C1-6-D or C1-5-D) probe. We selected a subset of 357 freehand videos (151,467 images) from the PULSE dataset based on the following criteria: (i) visible heart anatomy, and (ii) includes sonographer annotation indicating one of five heart views. The sonographer annotation was extracted using optical character recognition and used as the ground truth label. The fourth column in Table 1 corresponds to freehand video clips retrieved from the PULSE dataset (PULSE freehand standard). The PULSE pre-training dataset described in Table 2 consists of 3 s videos (approximately 100 frames) taken before the standard plane selection. The assumption is that the probe undergoes minor movement during the three seconds and hence you are observing the beating heart in the standard plane in this video. In turn, this ensures that the pre-trained model learns from different phases of the beating heart. Our experiments were conducted on four distinct private datasets, captured using different protocols to assess the model across a range of real-world clinical scenarios. These datasets consist of real-world patient data from the UK’s NHS, which cannot be shared publicly due to privacy restrictions on sharing sensitive data. However, the data was acquired to according well-established clinical acquisition protocols used worldwide and hence others can reproduce the data acquisition process. We have reported details of the PULSE study protocol ( Drukker et al., 2021 ) earlier in this section. The CAIFE study protocol is as of yet unpublished but a protocol paper is under review. However, the details of the CAIFE study pertaining to the data acquisition have also been mentioned earlier in this section. The HarmonicEchoNet architecture was implemented using PyTorch v1.7.1+cu110. Two distinct model training strategies were compared: training from scratch and using pre-trained models. For the training from scratch strategy, a learning rate of 1 e − 2 , a batch size of 16, and 500 epochs were used. Early stopping was applied to prevent overfitting, with loss as the monitoring metric and patience of 10 epochs. This approach validated the architecture design and assessed model performance without pre-trained weights. For the pre-trained training strategy, we compared CNN-based, transformer-based, and CNN+transformer-based models using ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) pre-trained weights. HarmonicEchoNet was initially pre-trained exclusively on the PULSE pre-training dataset and then fine-tuned with one of the other datasets. This strategy employed a learning rate of 1 e − 3 , a batch size of 16, and 100 epochs, with the same early stopping settings as the scratch strategy. Data augmentation techniques, including horizontal and vertical flipping, random rotation (up to 90 degrees), and shift-scale-rotate (shift limit of 0.0625, scale limit of 0.2, rotate limit of 45 degrees), were applied to the input images. During training, model weights with the highest classification accuracy on the validation set were saved. The final model was trained on 224 × 224 images using the Focal Loss function. Classification results were evaluated using four performance metrics: accuracy (AC), precision (PR), recall (RE), and F1 score (F1). To ensure a fair comparison among the models with different architectures, we fine-tuned three baseline models pre-trained on ImageNet: ConvNeXt ( Liu et al., 2022 ), DeiT ( Touvron et al., 2021 ), and VOLO ( Yuan et al., 2022 ). In this section, we evaluate HarmonicEchoNet by comparing it with established CNN, transformer, and CNN+transformer-based models that have been pre-trained on ImageNet. Our baseline models include ConvNeXt ( Liu et al., 2022 ), DeIT ( Touvron et al., 2021 ), and VOLO ( Yuan et al., 2022 ). We assess model performance for the task of detecting standard or para-standard planes of the fetal heart for the 4 different datasets/use cases. Quantitative results comparing HarmonicEchoNet models with baseline models are shown in Table 3 . For each model architecture, four models are built, each trained with a different dataset (PULSE freehand standard, CAIFE freehand standard, CAIFE t-sweep standard, or CAIFE t-sweep para-standard datasets). This allows us to evaluate how a model with our proposed architecture performs compared to other models of different architectures across different datasets. Models that have been trained on the same dataset are compared with each other as Table 3 shows. These results focus on detecting standard and para-standard frames in fetal heart ultrasound videos. For models built with the freehand ultrasound datasets (PULSE and CAIFE) for standard plane detection, HarmonicEchoNet models outperform the best-performing baseline by 4.95% in accuracy (AC), 5.13% in precision (PR), 4.54% in recall (RE) and 4.73% in F1 score. For standard plane detection in t-sweep, the HarmonicEchoNet model performs best, surpassing the ConvNeXt model by 3.11% in accuracy. A comparison of the three CAIFE models is also interesting, although care needs to be taken in interpreting findings as data from a different number of subjects is used to build each model. However, the data was acquired with the same ultrasound machine and sonographers with some overlap in imaging subject. We note that the CAIFE freehand standard model has the highest performance for all metrics. Lower performance is expected for t-sweep models, given that freehand frames are of the highest quality, have less variability in appearance, and are more carefully acquired. However, t-sweep model performance is good (77% for standard plane images), and the HarmonicEchoNet model results are superior to equivalent models built with CNN-based architectures. The confusion matrix for fetal heart standard plane classification is reported in Fig. 6 for the PULSE-Freehand standard dataset. According to the experimental findings, the HarmonicEchoNet model demonstrates a superior ability to classify standard planes correctly. In approximately 24% of the 3VV cases, the model misclassified images with the most common misclassification being with 3VTV. This result is not surprising as the 3VV and 3VTV are anatomically similar in appearance. A fetal cardiologist specialist reviewed the images that had been misclassified by a HarmonicEchoNet model trained on the CAIFE t-sweep para-standard dataset. Examples of misclassified images are shown in Fig. 7 . Table 4 provides a comprehensive comparison of the computational complexity of HarmonicEchoNet, ConvNeXt, DeiT, and VOLO models built using the CAIFE t-sweep para-standard dataset. The HarmonicEchoNet model significantly outperforms the other models for all reported metrics. It has 19.9 million parameters, which is approximately 10 times fewer than the ConvNeXt model and 15 times fewer than both the DeiT and VOLO models. In terms of FLOPS, the HarmonicEchoNet model is highly efficient, requiring just 18.16 GFLOPS. This is over 7 times fewer than for the ConvNeXt and VOLO models, and more than 13 times fewer than the DeiT model. The efficiency extends to MACs, with the HarmonicEchoNet model GMACs being 9.06 which is roughly 7.5 times fewer than ConvNeXt, 13 times fewer than DeiT, and 30 times fewer than VOLO. These performance metric values underscore the HarmonicEchoNet model superior computational efficiency, making it an ideal potential choice for medical imaging settings where minimal resource usage and rapid, reliable processing are critical for real-time diagnostics. The baseline CNN architecture without hscSE blocks achieves an accuracy of 86.19% with 18.51 million parameters, serving as a starting point for our analysis. In contrast, the baseline Harmonic Convolution (HC) model, which maintains the same parameter count as the baseline CNN (18.51 million), outperforms the latter with an accuracy of 90.31%. This improvement highlights the effectiveness of the HC architecture in enhancing model accuracy without adding complexity.
