Besides, we also consider fusing the relative positional embeddings into the attention weight calculation process [23,31] . Relative Position Encoding. The relative position is encoded across three dimensions: height, width, and time frames. Let E H ∈ R C × 1 × H × 1 , E W ∈ R C × 1 × 1 × W , and E F ∈ R C × L × 1 × 1 represent the height, width, and frame position encodings, respectively. The overall relative position encoding is finally obtained as: (5) E = E H + E W + E F , where each E ∗ is a learnable tensor that varies only along its dedicated axis. Both the frame-wise and spatial relative-position matrices are initialized with N ( 0 , 0 . 02 ) and updated end-to-end during training. Transformation for Multi-Head Attention. The encoded tensor E is reshaped to facilitate multi-head attention, forming a new tensor M , which is in shape of ( F , H × W , C n h e a d ) where F , H , W , and n h e a d denote the number of frames, height, width, and the number of attention heads, respectively. Multi-Head Self-Attention. The self-attention mechanism for each head is computed as follows. Let Q i , K j , and V j denote the query, key, and value vectors. The attention scores e i j between each query Q i and key K j , modified by the relative position matrix M j , are calculated by: (6) e i j = Q i ⋅ ( K j T + M j ) d , where d is the scaling factor, typically the dimensionality of the key vectors. The attention weights a i j are then obtained using the softmax function: (7) a i j = e x p ( e i j ) ∑ j = 1 N e x p ( e i j ) . Subsequently, the output vector Y i for each query is derived by aggregating over all values V j , weighted by the computed attention weights: (8) Y i = ∑ j = 1 N a i j V j , where N is the total number of keys and values. Output Reshaping and Final Adjustment. The resulting attention outputs are reshaped back to the original dimensions and combined with the original position encodings: o u t p u t = Y + E , where Y ∈ R C × F × H × W represents the output of the attention mechanism, and the addition operation integrates the learned attention with the original relative position encodings. To ascertain whether the effectiveness of DEP-MHSA stems from its medically-inspired logic rather than from an increased parameter size, we evaluate its performance across permutations with similar logic but different sequence in generating matrices Query, Key, and Value, as depicted in Fig. 2 . We rigorously tested variants named DEP-MHSA-B, DEP-MHSA-C, and DEP-MHSA-D. Specifically, DEP-MHSA-B alternates the convolution settings for generating Query and Key, and reverses the convolution sequence in Value generation. DEP-MHSA-C solely reverses the convolution sequence in Value generation, while DEP-MHSA-D exclusively swaps the convolution settings between Query and Key. The self-collected dataset 1 1 Ethical approval (L2024018) was obtained from the hospital ethical committees. consists of 747 subjects diagnosed with May-Thurner syndrome, mainly sourced from patients with chronic lower extremity venous insufficiency (varicose veins and edema) attending our hospital’s vascular surgery department. Some patients also have coexisting Cockett syndrome. Each subject comprises 10 to 12 frames. Notably, 366 of these subjects possess both CT scan images and their corresponding Enhanced-CT scan images. MTS-CT has a balanced gender distribution, comprising 396 males and 351 females, with an average patient age of 62.4 yr, and a higher prevalence in younger adults. All patients gave consent for CT and venous ascending phlebography, and the study was approved by the hospital’s ethics committee. This is a single-center observational study. Furthermore, the MTS-CT Dataset provides essential 3D spatial information for MTS diagnosis, complementing the limitations of ultrasound and IVUS. Its large-scale contrast-enhanced CT scans enable reliable detection of iliac vein compression patterns, supporting both clinical practice and AI model development. The CT images were obtained using the United Imaging uCT 960+ system, which features a 320-slice, 640-detector array with 16 cm coverage and a spatial resolution of 30 lines/cm. It supports high-precision anatomical display, with standard reconstruction layer thickness ≤ 5 mm and multi-planar reconstruction (MPR) ≤ 1 mm. Contrast agent was administered at 80–100 mL (1.0–1.2 mL/kg body weight) with a flow rate of 2.5–4 mL/s, followed by saline. Scan timing was based on arterial and venous phases: arterial phase 30–35 s after injection, and venous phase 50 s later. The dataset is categorized into light-to-moderate (see Fig. 3 ) and moderate-to-severe (see Fig. 4 ) stenosis groups based on the area stenosis rate, calculated by comparing the diameters of the narrowest and widest iliac vein segments. A stenosis rate ≤ 50% is labeled as negative (light-to-moderate), while > 50% is labeled as positive (moderate-to-severe). The surgeons who participated in the data evaluation and classification were those who had been engaged in vascular surgery for more than 10 yr and had extensive experience in reading and analyzing CT images. The grading standard for the degree of stenosis was to use the diameter ratio of the narrowest part to the widest part of the iliac vein on the cross-sectional CT and then square it to estimate the area stenosis rate of the iliac vein stenosis. The data was then retested and verified by another expert at a sampling ratio of 1 in 10 cases to ensure its controllability (see Figs. 3 and 4 ). Preprocessing. Each CT scan image is originally saved in DICOM format at a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels. The patient-specific information is anonymized and de-identified to comply with regulations regarding the sharing of medical images. Each image undergoes a transformation using a gray-scale mapping function, also known as a windowing function, with a window center of 50 and a width of 200. This transformation maps Hounsfield units (HU) to standardized pixel value from 0 to 255 . Since medical experts primarily concentrate on the lumbar vertebrae, adjacent arteries, and veins in the central region of CT scans to diagnose MTS, we therefore apply a center crop to the image, as illustrated in Fig. 5 . Metrics. In this work, we use the following metrics to evaluate our proposed method. Specifically, we employ accuracy, F1-Score and area under curve (AUC) for MTS classification of 3D CT scans under various settings. We also calculate the size of parameters to discuss the trade-off between model size and performance. We have chosen 100 subjects for our test set, ensuring a balanced positive-negative ratio of 50 : 50. The remaining data were utilized as training and validation set for various tasks. When integrating the DEP-MHSA attention mechanism into the network, it was only applied to the final two layers, i.e., Layer 3 and Layer 4. The earlier stages remain identical to ResNet-18: Layer 1 and Layer 2 each contain two BasicBlocks; Layer 1 keeps the spatial resolution and 64 channels, whereas the first block of Layer 2 employs a 2 × 2 spatial stride (temporal stride 1) to halve the resolution while expanding the width to 128 channels. This implementation was selected by considering the balance between augmenting the network’s capability for feature extraction and maintaining computational efficiency. After Layer 4, global spatio-temporal average pooling produces a 512-dimensional feature vector that is passed to a fully connected layer Linear for the final binary classification. MTS-Net was implemented in PyTorch and trained through an NVIDIA RTX 4090 24 GB GPU with a mini-batch size of 32. An initial learning rate of 5 × 1 0 − 4 was selected because rates of 3 × 1 0 − 4 or 8 × 1 0 − 4 each lowered the test accuracy by roughly 3 percentage points, indicating under- and over-aggressive updates, respectively. Likewise, we retained the 512-dimensional projection before the classifier because compressing it to 256 dimensions or expanding it to 1024 dimensions degraded the average accuracy by about 5 percentage points, which demonstrates, respectively, that the smaller bottleneck diminishes discriminative capacity whereas the larger one exacerbates over-fitting. A step decay with factor g = 0.2 was applied every 25 epochs until convergence over 100 epochs. We run each configuration 10 times and report the results on the test set with the average and standard deviation of three evaluation metrics. We established the architectural frameworks of ResNet-18 with both 3D and ( 2 + 1 )D convolutions as baselines, with distinctions summarized as follows. ResNet-18 (2+1)D . This design decomposes 3D convolutions into separate spatial and temporal components, as detailed in Section 3.1 . In the stem layer, the spatial convolution uses a 1 × 7 × 7 kernel, while the temporal convolutions employs a 3 × 1 × 1 kernel. For the remaining network layers, kernel sizes are adjusted to 1 × 3 × 3 for spatial and 3 × 1 × 1 for temporal convolutions, except for those specified in the attention modules at Layer 3 and Layer 4. ResNet-18 (3D) . The stem layer in this design employs a convolution kernel of size 3 × 7 × 7 in its Conv-BN-ReLU sequence. Subsequent convolutions throughout the network consistently apply a 3 × 3 × 3 kernel except for those specified in the attention modules at Layer 3 and Layer 4. In addition to the DEP-MHSA module, we have also implemented other attention mechanisms for comparison purpose in Table 1 . Except where specifically noted, all convolution kernels in these self-attention modules follow a 1 × 1 × 1 configuration. Note that the configurations regarding different attention mechanisms and 3D convolutions are stated in Section 4.2 . 3D Self-Attention . This mechanism was implemented in a manner akin to the multi-head self-attention (MHSA) methods outlined in [23,31] . It utilizes 3D relative positional encodings integrated into the Key matrix. In its multi-head architecture, the intermediate representation’s channels are segmented by the number of heads, and the final two dimensions of R L × C × H × W are flattened to generate the Query, Key, and Value matrices. (2+1)D Self-Attention . In line with approaches described in [22,29] , this two-step mechanism first applies MHSA on the H × W spatial dimensions and then on the temporal (frames) dimension. Channel-wise Vanilla Attention . The implementation of channel-wise attention module follows the design presented in [32] , utilizing a Conv-ReLU-Conv- σ ( x ) sequence to derive attention weights. The first Conv of the sequence is a convolution with a kernel size of 1 × 3 × 3 and the second convolution uses a kernel size of 3 × 1 × 1. The σ ( x ) is a sigmoid function which maps outputs to the range of ( 0 , 1 ) . The output undergoes an adaptive average pooling across channels before being channel-wise multiplied with the input x . (2+1)D Vanilla Attention . The design of this module is similar to the channel-wise attention framework. Distinctively, it comprises two Conv-ReLU-Conv- σ ( x ) sequences. The first sequence, all convolution operation utilize 1 × 3 × 3 kernels for spatial emphasis on the H × W dimensions. In contrast, the second sequence employs 3 × 1 × 1 kernels, focusing on temporal features. In this study, we utilize a variety of models for comprehensive benchmarking, encompassing both classic and cutting-edge deep learning approaches for the classification of May-Thurner Syndrome (MTS) using 3D CT scans. Considering the dataset size, we establish our baseline using a vanilla 3D ResNet-18 [33,34] . We further analyze the impact of employing a larger model or fine-tuning with a pre-trained model [35] . Additionally, we conduct comparative experiments with models utilizing ( 2 + 1 )D convolutions [11] , as well as those equipped with attention mechanisms. Specifically, we explore various attention mechanisms for this task such as multi-head self attention [23] , spatial–temporal attention, and channel-wise attention [36] . We adopted 3D self-attention implementation from [23] , and ( 2 + 1 )D self-attention implementation from [29] . For DenseNet-BC( k = 32 , depth = 201), we adopt the implementation from [37,38] . All models are trained under consistent settings. We engaged five radiologists, each with approximately ten years of experience, to interpret CT images for the 100 patients. They achieved an average diagnostic accuracy of 78.4%. The F1-Score is not reported and the AUC score is not applicable in this case. Evaluation and Analysis. Table 1 shows quantitative comparisons between (a) proposed method: MTS-Net and (b) baseline methods: ResNet-18 ( 2 + 1 )D [11] , ResNet-18 (3D) [11] . We discover that without any attention mechanisms, the spatial–temporal structure of ResNet-18 ( 2 + 1 )D has better performance than ResNet-18 (3D). Our baseline analysis also reveals that the integration of attention modules into neural networks does not consistently lead to enhanced performance. The most optimal outcome in our study is achieved through the implementation of the proposed method. Utilizing the spatial–temporal architecture of ResNet-18, our novel dual-enhanced positional multi-head self-attention (DEP-MHSA) mechanism attains highest average score in all metrics. Additionally, training from scratch for models with larger capacity such as ResNet-50, ResNeXt-50 [39] and DenseNet-BC [37] does not guarantee performance enhancement. However, fine-tuning with the pre-trained ResNet-50 [35] can achieve better results. In summary, models with similar depth as ResNet-18 have sufficient capability for the scope and scale of our MTS-CT dataset. This suggests that models with more layers may not necessarily yield better performance in this specific context. We conduct an ablation study to understand the effectiveness of MTS-Net with respect to the DEP-MHSA module. Table 2 underscores the enhanced performance achieved through the DEP-MHSA module, which employs meticulously chosen strategies to generate Q , K , V matrices and augments position information using dual-enhanced positional embeddings in self-attention. The backbone network used is ResNet-18 ( 2 + 1 )D with variation in its attention module and position embedding. The MHSA(3D) refers to the multi-head self-attention module mentioned in [23] , and the MHSA( 2 + 1 )D denotes the self-attention module with proposed method in generating Q , K and V . The DEP-Embedding indicates the dual-enhanced position embedding in the attention block. Further, Table 3 shows another ablation study which validates the effectiveness of various configurations for generating the Query, Key, and Value matrices, i.e., DEP-MHSA, DEP-MHSA-B, DEP-MHSA-C and DEP-MHSA-D. Our proposed DEP-MHSA consistently outperforms other configurations, underscoring the superiority of our meticulously designed structure, which mirrors the diagnostic logic of medical experts. CT vs. Enhanced-CT. Our study focuses on May-Thurner Syndrome classification by proposing a novel self-attention module that demonstrates superior performance using 3D CT scans. In this section, we further conduct the performance comparison between CT scans and Enhanced-CT scans through the proposed method (see Fig. 6 ). Enhanced-CT technique has been shown to assist medical experts in improving accuracy in diagnosing May-Thurner Syndrome compared to CT scans. Therefore, we perform another in-depth analysis aiming to determine whether deep learning approaches can achieve similar benefits from the Enhanced-CT technique. As seen in Table 4 , the training set and validation set are in size of 263 in total, which is significantly less than the experiments which are exclusively carried only CT scans in Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 . With the limited training dataset, a significant performance gap is observed between the two types of data, indicating that enhanced CT scans enable better diagnostic performance with fewer training samples. Dataset Size. The dataset used in this study, despite having a small number of frames for each subject, includes a relatively large number of subjects (747 subjects) compared to other popular CT scan image datasets [40–43] . To our knowledge, this is the first publicly available CT scan dataset for May-Thurner Syndrome. Its significance is highlighted by the fact that around 20% of the population are likely to have this anatomical variant [2,44,45] , laying the groundwork for further studies. Parameter Size. Table 2 shows that our MHSA( 2 + 1 )D approach significantly increases the model’s parameters, nearly doubling those of the standard ResNet-18( 2 + 1 )D. Performance variance is observed with and without DEP-Embedding, attributed to the disruption of relative positional information arising from distinct strategies for generating Q , K and V matrices. While these strategies enrich the model’s intermediate representations, they complicate the alignment across dimensions in subsequent computations. In contrast, a uniform approach to generating Q , K and V maintains this crucial alignment. Thus, the introduction of dual-enhanced position embedding becomes necessary, making it easier to restore the lost relative positional information and enhancing performance in our MHSA( 2 + 1 )D module. We have developed MTS-Net, a novel 3D deep learning framework that significantly advances the automated diagnosis of May-Thurner Syndrome from CT scans. By integrating our specially designed Dual-Enhanced Positional Multi-Head Self-Attention (DEP-MHSA) module with a 3D ResNet-18 architecture, the system effectively captures subtle venous compression patterns through innovative multi-scale convolution and enhanced positional embeddings, closely replicating clinical diagnostic processes. We also determine the best practices of DEP-MHSA through rigorous experimental analysis on the convolution sequence in generating Query, Key and Value. To enable this research and support future studies, we have created and released the first public MTS-CT dataset, containing carefully curated scans from 747 gender-balanced subjects. Rigorous testing shows MTS-Net’s strong performance with 0.79 accuracy, 0.84 AUC, and 0.78 F1-score, surpassing existing 3D CNN models including BabyNet and DenseNet implementations by 6%, further validating the effectiveness of the proposed DEP-MHSA. Beyond its technical innovation in vascular compression analysis, this work makes important practical contributions through its high-quality benchmark dataset and demonstration of deep learning’s clinical potential for MTS diagnosis. Looking ahead, the framework shows promise for extension to other vascular compression syndromes, with future work planned for multicenter validation. We are making both the dataset and code publicly available to support continued progress in automated vascular disorder detection. Multi-cancer framework with cancer-aware attention and adversarial mutual-information minimization for whole slide image classification Whole Slide Images (WSIs) are crucial in modern pathology, offering high-resolution data for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and research. Deep learning methods have recently been proposed to harness this data by extracting and interpreting complex patterns. However, these approaches often focus on specific tumor types, limiting their generalizability across diverse pathological conditions and restricting scalability. This relatively narrow focus ultimately stems from the inherent heterogeneity in histopathology and the diverse morphological and molecular characteristics of different tumors. To this end, we propose a novel approach for multi-cancer WSI analysis, designed to leverage the diversity of different tumor types. We introduce a Cancer-Aware Attention module that models both shared patterns across cancers and cancer-specific variations to address heterogeneity and enhance cross-tumor generalization. Furthermore, we construct an adversarial cancer regularization mechanism to minimize cancer-specific biases through mutual information minimization. Additionally, we develop a hierarchical sample balancing strategy to mitigate data imbalances and promote unbiased learning. Together, these form a cohesive framework for unbiased multi-cancer WSI analysis. Extensive experiments on a uniquely constructed multi-cancer dataset demonstrate significant improvements in generalization, providing a scalable solution for WSI classification across diverse cancer types. However, these approaches often focus on specific tumor types, limiting their generalizability across diverse pathological conditions and restricting scalability. Whole Slide Images (WSIs) are high-resolution digital scans of tissue biospecimens, designed to capture detailed cellular and morphological patterns for histological examination ( Ghaznavi et al., 2013; Dimitriou et al., 2019 ). WSIs play a key role in clinical diagnosis and prognosis and are often regarded as ground truth in medical practice ( Kumar et al., 2020; Hanna et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020; Mariani et al., 2018 ). In cancer research, in particular, WSIs are instrumental in determining disease severity ( Hanna et al., 2020 ), evaluating treatment outcomes ( Kumar et al., 2020; Mariani et al., 2018 ), and identifying critical biomarkers ( Liu et al., 2018a; De Smedt et al., 2015; Jachimowicz et al., 2021; Hamilton et al., 2014 ). Given this central role, pathologists are increasingly overwhelmed, creating a strong motivation for computational pathology methods that can not only alleviate workload but also enhance diagnostic accuracy by providing more objective and sensitive analyses of features that may elude the human eye. This, in turn, paves the way for more scalable and expedited patient care ( Kumar et al., 2020 ). Building on this motivation, recent years have seen a tremendous amount of work dedicated to applying deep learning to WSIs ( Javed et al., 2024; Zamanitajeddin et al., 2024; Banerji and Mitra, 2022; Srinidhi et al., 2021; Abdel-Nabi et al., 2023; Bilal et al., 2021; Chan et al., 2023; Godson et al., 2024 ), with growing evidence of its potential impact on clinical pathology workflows ( Wu et al., 2022 ). However, due to the immense size of WSIs, most approaches rely on the decomposition of slides into smaller, processable patches ( Bilal et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Kather et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020 ). Since annotations are typically provided at the slide level rather than for individual patches, histopathological image analysis is commonly formulated as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) task ( Zhang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Bontempo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Tourniaire et al., 2023 ), where each slide is treated as a collection of instances. Despite these advances, the majority of existing deep learning studies on WSIs focus on individual tumor types ( Wang et al., 2025; Tourniaire et al., 2023; Bilal et al., 2021; Kather et al., 2019 ). Such datasets are typically small, often composed of only a few hundred training samples, making models more prone to overfitting. In this regime, each slide can contain a wide variety of morphological patterns, resulting in a high-dimensional feature space relative to the limited number of slides. This imbalance increases the risk of learning spurious correlations and reduces the robustness to unseen data. Combining multiple cohorts could, in principle, mitigate data scarcity; however, naïve multi-cohort training has been shown to degrade performance ( Noorbakhsh et al., 2020 ). Previous work ( Park et al., 2021; Noorbakhsh et al., 2020 ) demonstrates that carefully structured multi-cohort strategies can yield substantial gains, motivating the need for principled frameworks that capture this potential while avoiding known pitfalls. Furthermore, from a deployment perspective, single-tumor training requires maintaining separate models for each type of cancer, increasing computational, maintenance, and regulatory burdens. A unified multi-cancer framework offers a more scalable alternative by providing a single point of model management. Incorporating multiple types of cancer into a unified learning framework presents a promising direction. By exposing models to a wider spectrum of pathological patterns, such an approach can enable the learning of richer representations, improve generalization, and potentially reveal shared and cancer-specific biomarkers. Moreover, simplifying model maintenance and deployment can increase clinical confidence and facilitate real-world adoption ( Park et al., 2021 ). Fig. 1 illustrates this motivation by contrasting the standard joint training paradigm, which struggles to establish a single classification boundary due to misalignment across cancers, with our proposed framework, which mitigates cancer-specific biases and learns universal representations aligned with the task. Nevertheless, integrating multiple types of cancer also introduces new challenges that arise from the inherent heterogeneity of histopathology and the diverse phenotypes observed in tumors. In particular, aligning pathological features across cancer types complicates both training and evaluation. Additionally, aggregating data from multiple sources can exacerbate class and cohort imbalances, potentially skewing the learning process and leading to biased predictions and reduced performance. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework for multi-cancer WSI analysis that explicitly leverages tumor diversity while controlling for bias. Our approach introduces a Cancer-Aware Attention Encoder designed to extract tumor-specific features while simultaneously synthesizing shared pathological patterns across cancers. This dual capability improves generalization while ensuring that both commonalities and cancer-specific nuances are effectively captured during training. We further incorporate an adversarial regularizer that minimizes the mutual information (MI) between MIL representations and cancer type, thereby reducing reliance on cancer identity as a spurious shortcut in imbalanced multi-cancer datasets and encouraging convergence toward universally meaningful, task-relevant features. In addition, we propose a novel hierarchical sample balancing strategy to address the layered imbalances inherent in multi-cancer data, ensuring that optimization remains aligned with the downstream task. Together, these components form a cohesive and robust framework for unbiased multi-cancer WSI analysis. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1. Cross-tumor learning framework : We propose a novel framework that integrates multiple types of cancer, significantly improving generalization over existing state-of-the-art methods by enabling the discovery of both shared and tumor-specific pathological patterns. 2. Cancer-Aware VisionTransformer (CAViT) : We introduce CAViT as our tile encoder, enabling the capture of cancer-specific features while synthesizing shared pathological patterns across cancers. 3. Adversarial regularization : We implement an adversarial regularizer that minimizes mutual information between MIL representations and cancer types, guiding the model toward universally meaningful features. 4. Hierarchical sample balancing : We present a novel hierarchical sample balancing strategy to address multi-cancer data imbalances, ensuring unbiased learning aligned with the downstream task. 5. Cross-tumor benchmark dataset : We establish a benchmark dataset that integrates multiple cancer types, providing a foundation for evaluating multi-cancer learning strategies in digital pathology. Multi-cancer analysis in histopathology While cross-tumor analyses, such as pan-cancer studies ( Kather et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2020 ), have been conducted, these efforts primarily focus on identifying common mutations and genomic variations rather than integrating distinct cancer types into a cohesive learning framework for histopathology. As a result, the exploration of multi-cancer learning in histopathological image analysis remains relatively limited. Early efforts in this direction include the work of Noorbakhsh et al. (2020) , who showed that although “universal” models tend to underperform relative to tumor-specific models, identifying cancer types with similar morphological characteristics can lead to notable performance improvements. Building on this observation, Park et al. (2021) proposed forming super-cohorts , i.e., groups of cancer types whose joint training improves model performance. Although these approaches demonstrate the potential benefits of combining multiple cancer types, their reliance on heuristic-based grouping limits adaptability across datasets. Consequently, a more data-driven framework that can dynamically leverage tumor diversity remains a critical open problem. Data scarcity in WSI analysis Data scarcity is a persistent challenge in WSI analysis, motivating recent efforts toward foundation histopathology patch encoders ( Xu et al., 2024; Vorontsov et al., 2023; Dippel et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2023 ). These models are trained on large-scale WSI datasets spanning multiple organs and cancer types and have demonstrated strong general-purpose representations that transfer effectively to a wide range of downstream tasks. In line with this direction, we likewise leverage the diversity inherent in multi-cancer data, but with a complementary focus. Rather than relying solely on general-purpose transfer, we explicitly enrich learned representations with cancer-aware context. To this end, we introduce a cancer-aware attention module that augments general-purpose features by modeling both cancer-specific variations and shared pathological patterns, enabling more precise and context-aware downstream analysis. Multi-dataset in deep learning Beyond histopathology, significant progress has been made in applying deep learning to multi-dataset (MD) learning scenarios ( Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Hu and Singh, 2021 ). Much of this work has focused on multi-dataset multi-task (MD-MT) learning, which aims to solve multiple tasks simultaneously using shared inputs ( Hu and Singh, 2021; Xu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023 ). These approaches emphasize interactions between tasks, leveraging correlations among related objectives to improve overall performance. In contrast, studies that focus on interactions across datasets typically combine losses ( Chen et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2022; Hu and Singh, 2021 ) or fuse label spaces ( Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023 ) to facilitate cross-dataset learning. However, existing MD and MD-MT approaches generally assume access to very large datasets, often consisting of millions of samples, in order to effectively learn a joint dataset space ( Hu and Singh, 2021; Xu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023 ). In this work, we directly model interactions between datasets during joint training, enabling effective learning even in regimes where datasets are small and composed of only a few hundred WSIs. Cross-attention Self-attention, originally introduced in Vaswani et al. (2017) , has since been extensively adapted to facilitate interactions between multiple entities ( Hassanin et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2019 ). One prominent adaptation is co-attention ( Lu et al., 2019 ), which enables interactions between different entities by using the query matrix to mediate cross-entity information exchange. This observation, that the query matrix can induce cross interactions, has been widely explored in a variety of contexts ( Xu et al., 2023; Lee, 2022; Lopes et al., 2023; Hu and Singh, 2021; Bhattacharjee et al., 2022 ). Such cross-attention mechanisms are typically applied in settings with explicit multiple entities, such as multi-modal learning ( Lu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2023; Mercea et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2020 ) or multi-task learning ( Xu et al., 2023; Lee, 2022; Lopes et al., 2023; Hu and Singh, 2021 ). However, direct cross-attention is not readily applicable in unimodal multi-cancer datasets, where inherent entity interactions are absent. To overcome this limitation, our Cancer-Aware approach introduces a novel attention mechanism based on a learnable Query-Attention (QA) component. By enabling token-wise attention to dynamically integrate dataset-wide and cancer-specific queries, each token can attend to either global patterns or cancer-specific features based on contextual relevance, thereby improving generalization across cancer types. Hierarchical imbalance Class imbalance is a well-studied problem, and traditional balancing techniques ( Johnson and Khoshgoftaar, 2019; Wang et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Reshma et al., 2021; Khened et al., 2021 ) have been widely adopted. However, these methods often fall short in multi-dataset settings with hierarchical structures, such as multi-cancer WSI analysis. To address this, prior work has proposed class-aware or hierarchical sampling strategies ( Zhou et al., 2022; Hu and Singh, 2021; Chen et al., 2024 ). While effective in many large-scale settings, our experiments indicate that sampling-based approaches can be unstable when applied to small datasets, frequently resulting in skewed batches and suboptimal convergence. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel hierarchical sample weighting strategy that adapts to multiple levels of data granularity in multi-cancer WSI analysis. By enforcing a balanced loss formulation, our approach promotes more robust and unbiased learning across datasets with significant disparities. Adversarial learning Adversarial learning, originally introduced through Generative Adversarial Networks, has since been widely adopted across a range of representation learning problems. In domain adaptation, adversarial losses have proven effective for aligning feature distributions across domains ( Tzeng et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020; Tang and Jia, 2020 ). Similarly, within multi-task learning frameworks, adversarial strategies have been used to disentangle and refine task-specific representations ( Liu et al., 2017; 2018b; Zhou et al., 2020 ). In this work, we incorporate an adversarial regularizer that explicitly controls the mutual information between MIL representations and cancer types during training. This mechanism aligns pathological representations across cancers while mitigating cancer-specific biases, enabling the model to focus on universally meaningful, task-relevant features. Let S = { s 1 , s 2 , ⋯ , s N } represent a set of WSIs, where each slide s i is associated with a cancer type c i ∈ { 1 , 2 , ⋯ , k } and a label y i ∈ { 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m } . Each slide s i is divided into a set of tiles T s i = { t i 1 , t i 2 , ⋯ , t i n i } , where t i j ∈ R h × w × 3 , and n i is the number of tiles for slide s i . Each tile t ij is passed through a pretrained tile encoder E ( · ), resulting in a feature representation f i j ∈ R d , where d is the dimensionality of the encoded features. The slide s i is then represented as a collection { f i j } j = 1 n i of encoded tile features. These collections are passed through a MIL model M ( · ), which aggregates the tile-level features to a final prediction y ^ i for the slide. In this paper, we present a novel Cancer-Aware Attention (CAA) module designed to address the challenges of multi-cancer WSI analysis. This module is capable of capturing cancer-specific variations and commonalities, thereby enabling efficient cross-tumor learning and enhancing model performance across the entire dataset. While the CAA module can be applied in various ways, in this work, we deploy it within a VisionTransformer (ViT) ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ), creating a Cancer-Aware VisionTransformer as our tile encoder. Fig. 2 , depicts the structure of the cancer-aware attention module and its integration within the VisionTransformer block. The key innovation of the CAA module lies in its ability to facilitate interactions between different cancer types during a joint training. Unlike conventional cross-attention, typically applied in multi-modal or multi-task setups with naturally interacting entities, our approach tackles the challenge of a multi-cancer, uni-modal dataset where direct cross-attention is not feasible. The CAA module enables cross-cancer interactions by engaging different components of the self-attention mechanism during training, capturing both shared and cancer-specific patterns. Given an input matrix X ∈ R n × d , where n denotes the length of the patch sequence and d represents the feature dimension, along with a cancer identifier c ∈ { 1 , 2 , ⋯ , k } , the CAA employs distinct projection matrices for cancer-specific queries W Q c ∈ R d × d k and a shared dataset-wide query matrix W Q d ∈ R d × d k , while utilizing common key and value matrices W K , W V ∈ R d × d k across all cancers. The queries, keys, and values are computed as: (1) Q d = X W Q d , Q c = X W Q c , (2) K = X W K , V = X W V The cancer-aware query Q ca is then constructed by dynamically integrating the dataset-wide query Q d with the cancer-specific query Q c . This integration is facilitated by a learnable Query-Attention (QA) component, which dynamically maps each individual token query q i ∈ R 1 × d k (where q i is the i -th query vector from the query matrix) to its corresponding attention weights: (3) α d = QA ( Q d ) , α c = QA ( Q c ) where α d , α c ∈ R n × 1 is the attention weights for the dataset query and cancer query of each token, respectively. The QA component is implemented as a non-linear fully-connected network, which can be viewed as a form of non-linear projection that maps each query token q i d or q i c to its corresponding weight. While this differs from the canonical query-key attention used in Transformers, we adopt the term “attention” in the broader sense, as it adaptively assigns context-dependent importance weights to competing information sources. In our case, the QA module modulates the contribution of dataset-wide and cancer-specific queries for each token, enabling selective emphasis on the most relevant representation. The cancer-aware query Q ca is then obtained as the element-wise product of the attention weights with their respective queries: (4) Q c a = α d ⊙ Q d + α c ⊙ Q c The CAA weights are computed using Scaled Dot-Product Attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017; Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ) as follows: (5) Attention ( Q c a , K , V ) = softmax ( Q c a K T d k ) V The Q ca matrix adapts dynamically, allowing inputs to attend to either global patterns via Q d or cancer-specific features via Q c , depending on the contextual importance. In our design, each cancer-specific projection matrix W Q c is used exclusively for samples originating from cancer type c , ensuring that its updates are based solely on gradients from that cohort. In practice, for each batch, every sample is first mapped to its corresponding W Q c according to its cancer origin. The forward pass computes cancer-specific queries using the assigned W Q c , while the dataset-wide projection remains shared across all samples. During backpropagation, the computational graph naturally restricts parameter updates to only those W Q c matrices that were used in that batch. This design guarantees that each W Q c is precisely tuned to the distinct characteristics of its respective cohort. Notably, distinct projection matrices are used for cancer-specific queries, i.e., a separate learnable W Q c is maintained for each cancer type. The added cost is negligible since these are lightweight linear projections and, during a forward pass, only the projection corresponding to the sample’s cancer type is applied. As a result, the FLOPs remain constant with respect to the number of cancer types, and the only overhead is the memory required to store W Q c , which is modest. This design therefore remains scalable in practice. To create our CAViT tile encoder, we modified the standard VisionTransformer ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ) by replacing the Multihead Self-Attention (MHA) module ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) with our Multihead Cancer-Aware Attention (MCAA) module. The parameters are initialized from a pretrained ViT ( Kang et al., 2023 ): the dataset-wide matrices W Q , W K , W V are directly inherited, and the cancer-specific queries W Q c are also initialized from the pretrained W Q . Thus, at initialization, the dataset-wide and cancer-specific queries produce identical outputs, ensuring no bias toward any parameter group, while during training each evolves according to the data it is applied on. In this architecture, the MCAA block processes both the input image x and cancer identifier c to generate attention scores that are attuned to cancer-specific characteristics while simultaneously learning global features. The output of the MCAA layer is then passed through a residual connection and layer normalization (Add & Norm). This is followed by a fully-connected layer and an additional Add & Norm layer. The result is then propagated to the subsequent block in the CAViT architecture, as illustrated in Fig. 2 . In multi-cancer WSI analysis, a critical challenge arises from misaligned tile representations. During self-supervised training, tile representations are designed to capture diverse and nuanced features, ideally including cancer-specific subtleties. While this ability can enrich and enhance representation learning, it may inadvertently pose challenges when combining multiple cancers for downstream tasks such as WSI classification. Our observation, based on preliminary experiments (see B.1 ), is that MIL representations in multi-cancer settings often retain sufficient information to accurately predict cancer type using a simple linear classifier. While cancer-specific information can sometimes aid generalization, in imbalanced multi-cancer datasets it may also serve as a spurious shortcut, with the model exploiting cancer type as a proxy for the target label. This can produce biased predictions misaligned with task-relevant features, motivating our debiasing strategy. We demonstrate this in B.1 , where removing this bias improves generalization. Motivated by this, we propose to minimize the mutual information (MI) between MIL representations and cancer-type associations, thereby encouraging unbiased, pathology-aligned representations. Direct computation of MI for continuous high-dimensional random variables is intractable. In our framework, we address this by using the Smoothed Mutual Information “Lower Bound” Estimator (SMILE) ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ), which reduces variance and improves upon the popular MINE algorithm ( Belghazi et al., 2018 ). To clearly separate the components within the MIL model, we denote the MIL aggregator function as A ( · ), which aggregates the tile-level features into a slide-level representation: (6) z i = A ( { f i j } j = 1 n i ) The slide-level representation z i is then passed through the MIL head H ( · ), to generate the final prediction: (7) y ^ i = H ( z i ) Our adversarial network leverages the I SMILE estimator ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ) to estimate the mutual information (MI) between the MIL representations z i ∈ Z and the one-hot cancer-type association vectors c i ∈ C during training. I SMILE estimator utilizes a score network T θ ( Belghazi et al., 2018; Song and Ermon, 2019 ) which designed to estimate the log-density ratio between the joint distribution P Z,C ( z, c ) and the product of the marginal distributions P Z ( z ) P C ( c ). Our T θ consists of three non-linear transformations. First, the slide-level representation z i and the cancer association c i are independently mapped to hidden representations h z i , h c i ∈ R h , respectively. These hidden representations are then concatenated and further processed by a final transformation to produce the score T θ ( z i , c i ). Given an input batch { z i } i = 1 B and { c i } i = 1 B , positive pairs ( z i , c i ) and negative pairs ( z i , c j ) i ≠ j are constructed. The adversarial network is trained to maximize the I SMILE ( T θ , τ ) estimator: (8) E P Z , C [ T θ ( z , c ) ] − log E P Z P C [ clip ( e T θ ( z , c ) , e − τ , e τ ) ] where clip ( v , l , u ) = max ( min ( v , u ) , l ) , and τ is a hyperparameter. The procedure is outlined in Algorithm 1 and can be summarized as follows. For a batch of tile embeddings { x i } i = 1 B , the slide-level representations z i are generated using the aggregator A ( · ) as defined in Eq. (6) . Positive and negative pairs are constructed from { z i } i = 1 B and { c i } i = 1 B , and a backward pass is performed to update the adversarial network I SMILE , as outlined in Eq. (8) . Following this, an MI estimation loss − I SMILE ( { z i } i = 1 B , { c i } i = 1 B ) is calculated with the adversarial network now updated and frozen. The MIL head H ( · ) then generates the final prediction scores, as shown in Eq. (7) . The overall training objective is defined as: L = L MIL + λ L MI where L MIL is the original MIL loss, L MI is the mutual information loss, and λ is a hyperparameter. This adversarial framework compels the MIL model to produce unbiased MIL representations, thus promoting the learning of more generalizable features across different cancers. Aggregating data from multiple cancer types increases training diversity but it may introduce imbalances at class, slide, or tile levels. If not properly addressed, these imbalances can skew the learning process. Existing methods, which often rely on sampling techniques ( Zhou et al., 2022; Hu and Singh, 2021; Chen et al., 2024 ), struggle to effectively mitigate these imbalances in smaller datasets, where sampling can skew the composition of training batches, leading to suboptimal model performance. To this end, we propose a new hierarchical balancing strategy that ensures equitable representation across multiple levels of data granularity inherent in a multi-cancer WSI analysis. Fig. 3 illustrates our hierarchical balancing strategy. In the pretraining phase, we balance weights across cancer types, slides, and tiles, ensuring equal contribution at each hierarchical level. During MIL training, we balance cancer-class combinations and distribute weights equally among slides within each combination, preventing any single cancer or class from dominating training. WSI cohorts often display significant disparities in tile counts or class distributions, which may cause certain samples to be disproportionately weighted. Therefore, we clip sample weights within two standard deviations of the mean and apply batch normalization during training. This approach not only minimizes over- or under-representation but also acts as a regularization technique, dynamically adjusting sample weights based on batch composition during training. TCGA multi-cancer subtyping dataset (MCSD) benchmark: We utilized three cohorts from the Cancer Genome Atlas 2 2 (TCGA) project ( Weinstein et al., 2013 ): CRC (colorectal adenocarcinoma), STAD (stomach adenocarcinoma), and UCEC (endometrial carcinoma). All slides are H&E stained diagnostic slides, which are the reference standard for diagnostic medicine ( Evans et al., 2018 ). Slides counts are detailed in Table 1 . The TCGA-MCSD dataset is structured to facilitate two crucial cancer subtyping tasks: Microsatellite Stable (MSS) versus Microsatellite Instability (MSI), and Genomic Stability (GS) versus Chromosomal Instability (CIN). We selected these tasks due to their significant importance across various forms of cancer ( De La Chapelle and Hampel, 2010; Amato et al., 2022; Vishwakarma and McManus, 2020; Zhao et al., 2019 ). Labels for GS/CIN were sourced from cBioPortal; 3 3 labels for MSS/MSI were derived from the auxiliary materials provided by TCGA. The TCGA-MCSD dataset provides a unique benchmark for cross-tumor WSI studies through its carefully construction, which integrates multiple cancer types and classification tasks, thus laying the foundation for the evaluation of multi-cancer learning strategies. Preprocessing. Tissue regions were segmented using the Otsu method ( Otsu et al., 1975 ) and tessellate into 512x512 pixel patches (tiles) at a field of view (FoV) of 20x (0.5µm/px). Slides with less than 100 tissue tiles were considered curropt and were excluded from the analysis. Unlike previous subtyping studies ( Bilal et al., 2021; Kather et al., 2019; Hezi et al., 2024; Echle et al., 2021; Schirris et al., 2022 ), which manually filter for tumor regions, our approach utilizes the entire slide for prediction. Although deep learning methods have achieved high accuracy in detecting tumor regions for the CRC cancer ( Bilal et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2022 ), the availability of labeled datasets for other cancer types remains limited, making it impractical for multi-cancer studies. Training details. To ensure robustness, we obtained results using nested 5-fold cross-validation, repeated three times with different seeds. Importantly, splits were conducted on a patient basis to prevent any leakage, and were stratified by class label and cohort association to ensure representativeness. Due to dataset differences, the results for all other methods were carefully reproduced using the official code under the same settings. We portion 10% of the training data for validation. During training, models were validate after each epoch, and the three best models (selected based on overall patient AUC) were bagged. To further ensure robustness of the results, a few tuning steps were performed for each model, with the best result reported. In total, 16 Nvidia A100 GPUs were used. Evaluation metrics. In line with previous studies, we assess model performance primarily using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) metric, with Balanced Accuracy as a secondary measure. Unless specified otherwise, a ViT-small backbone ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ) was used as tile encoder. For our approach, a Cancer-Aware ViT-small backbone was employed, as describe in Section 3.2 . Both encoders were pretrained under similar settings. For additional details on implementation and stability analysis, please refer to the supplementary materials. To demonstrate the benefits of our multi-cancer WSI analysis framework, we compared it against two other training approaches: Independent Training, where each cancer type is analyzed separately, and Joint Training, where all cancers are naively combined during training. We utilized the DTFD-MIL ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) model for this comparison, with additional analysis using the MHA-MIL ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) model provided in the supplementary material. The results for MSS/MSI and GS/CIN tasks using the DTFD-MIL model are shown in Tables 2 and 3 , respectively. For the MSS/MSI task, joint training resulted in a performance drop across all cohorts, indicating that naive joint training can be counterproductive. For example, the AUC for UCEC declined notably, from 66.62 with independent training to 63.53, demonstrating the challenges of combining cohorts without a tailored strategy. Similarly, CRC and STAD also saw drops in performance with joint training. In contrast, our multi-cancer approach achieved significant improvements across all cohorts, with a standout AUC of 87.94 for CRC, outperforming both independent and joint training methods by a clear margin. In the GS/CIN task, joint training showed some improvement for CRC, where the AUC increased from 73.86 (Independent Training) to 81.97, suggesting some potential in certain cases. However, joint training was less effective for UCEC, where the AUC dropped from 91.80 to 89.47, and offered only marginal gains for STAD. By contrast, our multi-cancer approach demonstrated superior generalization across all cohorts, achieving the highest AUC values: 82.13 for CRC, 81.09 for STAD, and 92.28 for UCEC, further highlighting its effectiveness in balancing cancer-specific nuances while maintaining robust performance. These results demonstrate the added value of our multi-cancer framework, which effectively balances cancer-specific nuances while enhancing overall generalization and performance. This motivates the adoption of multi-cancer strategies in WSI analysis. We compared our approach with several popular existing MIL models: conventional instance-level MIL methods, including Mean-Pooling and Max-Pooling; GNN-based MIL (GCN-MIL) ( Zhao et al., 2020 ); convolution-based MIL (SparseConvMIL) ( Lerousseau et al., 2021 ); and attention-based MIL models, such as the classic AB-MIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ), TransMIL ( Shao et al., 2021 ), DTFD-MIL ( Zhang et al., 2022 ), and MHA-MIL ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ). For our multi-cancer approach, we selected DTFD-MIL ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) and MHA-MIL ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) as representative models due to their consistent strong performance in our experiments. The results for MSS/MSI and GS/CIN are provided in Tables 4 and 5 , respectively. For the MSS/MSI task, our approach shows significant improvements, especially in the CRC cohort, where our DTFD-MIL variant achieved the highest AUC of 87.94%, a notable increase over baselines. In the UCEC cohort, although our approach led in both AUC and B-Acc, the overall performance was degraded. We attribute this to the frequent overlap with the POLE subtype in UCEC cases ( Yao et al., 2024 ), which complicates the learning process due to its distinct characteristics. For the GS/CIN task, our method also delivers superior performance. Both the DTFD-MIL and MHA-MIL variants of our model lead in overall AUC and B-Acc, with the DTFD-MIL variant achieving the best results on the CRC cohort (AUC 82.13%) and UCEC cohort (AUC 92.28%). In both tasks, our approach consistently performs well across all cohorts, while baseline models tend to excel in one cohort but degrade in others. This stability across cohorts highlights the effectiveness of our multi-cancer strategy in balancing cancer-specific nuances, ultimately leading to enhanced generalization and overall model performance. For more extensive stability analysis, please refer to the supplementary materials. We systematically evaluate each component of our framework, highlighting its incremental contribution to overall performance. In this section, we focus on TCGA-MCSD dataset and evaluate the model using the AUC metric. As before, we selected DTFD-MIL ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) and MHA-MIL ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) as representative models. To isolate the contribution of our cancer-specific training paradigm, we compared our CAViT encoder against an otherwise identical ViT-small encoder trained without cancer-specific weights. Both encoders were initialized using the Lunit ( Kang et al., 2023 ) pretrained backbone and further tuned with DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ) on the TCGA-MCSD dataset using our hierarchical balancing strategy for pretraining. Downstream MIL models (DTFD-MIL and MHA-MIL) were trained with identical hyperparameters. As summarized in Table 6 , CAViT consistently outperformed the non-cancer-aware ViT-small across both MSS/MSI and GS/CIN tasks. For example, with MHA-MIL, AUC improved from 76.19 (ViT-small) to 80.60 (CAViT) on MSS/MSI, and from 84.44 to 85.95 on GS/CIN. These consistent gains demonstrate the benefits of our cancer-aware representations. To further evaluate the quality of our encoder, we compared CAViT with recently proposed histopathology foundation models, including: GigaPath ( Xu et al., 2024 ), Virchow ( Vorontsov et al., 2023 ), and Lunit ( Kang et al., 2023 ). All encoders were used as frozen feature extractors, and downstream MIL models (DTFD-MIL and MHA-MIL) were trained with identical hyperparameters to ensure comparability. A key difference between the encoders lies in their embedding dimensionality: GigaPath (1536), Virchow (1280), and Lunit/CAViT (384). Since embedding size serves as a bottleneck between the tile representations and the MIL model, larger dimensionalities generally offer greater representational capacity and are expected to provide an advantage. The results, presented in Fig. 4 , indicate that CAViT achieves competitive or superior performance despite operating at a substantially smaller embedding size (384). When compared to Lunit, which shares the same embedding dimensionality, CAViT showed a clear performance advantage across both classification tasks. GigaPath, with the largest embedding size (1536), produced consistently strong results, while Virchow (1280) was less competitive, particularly on the MSS/MSI task. These findings suggest that while large-scale foundation models provide strong baselines, our cancer-aware encoder remains highly competitive, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a more compact and nuanced representation. Our approach utilizes the SMILE algorithm ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ) as an adversarial estimator of mutual information (MI) between cancer associations and MIL representations. This MI estimation is incorporated as a regularization term for the main network, controlled by λ hyperparameter. Fig. 5 presents the impact of the λ values on the model performance. Higher λ values generally led to improved performance in both tasks, where the optimal λ was 1 for the MSS/MSI task and 0.5 for GS/CIN. We evaluate our hierarchical balancing technique (H.Balancing) against other established methods: standard class balancing (Class), hierarchical weighted sampling (H.Sampling), which samples according to the hierarchical weights of samples, and when no balancing is applied (Null). Fig. 6 compares the different balancing strategies. Our H.Balancing technique consistently achieved the best performance across all models and tasks. For the MSS/MSI task, our approach demonstrated a notable improvement, whereas H.Sampling underperformed when used with the DTFD-MIL model. Our study has several limitations that suggest directions for future work. First, while our ablation studies confirm that each component of the framework provides complementary benefits, hierarchical balancing emerged as a particularly strong driver of performance. This highlights opportunities to design more advanced weighting strategies. For example, balancing schemes that explicitly account for similarities between cancer types could ensure that morphological diversity is more effectively represented during training. Such refinements may also help mitigate per-cancer performance disparities, which is critical for clinical adoption. Second, our evaluation was limited to TCGA-based cohorts, as no comparable multi-cancer public datasets are currently available. Although we addressed this by constructing a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple cancers and subtyping tasks, extending validation to external cohorts will be essential for assessing generalizability in broader clinical contexts. Additionally, quantitative analysis and interpretable visualization of cohort-aware attention mechanisms represent an important direction for future work. Comparing cancer-aware and universal representations and examining how attention patterns vary across pretrained backbones could provide deeper insight into how shared and cancer-specific features are emphasized, supporting interpretability and strengthening trust in clinical pathology settings. Finally, the modular design of our framework naturally supports extension to additional cancer types and raises interesting directions for incremental and data-efficient learning. In particular, leveraging universal representations or selectively adapting cancer-specific components may be beneficial for small or under-represented cancer cohorts, a common scenario in clinical practice. Together, these considerations highlight promising directions for advancing multi-cohort learning, including further refinement of balancing strategies and deeper validation of cancer-aware representations across diverse patient populations. Despite the availability of larger WSI datasets, combining cancers remains essential due to the diversity and rarity of many tumor types, necessitating a multi-cancer approach. In this paper, we introduced a cancer-aware attention module integrated into a VisionTransformer for tile encoding, along with adversarial training to ensure unbiased slide representations. To address multi-cancer data imbalances, we implemented a hierarchical sample balancing strategy, enabling more balanced learning. Importantly, the modular design of our framework naturally supports extension to additional cancer cohorts and provides a foundation for exploring more flexible and scalable multi-cancer learning scenarios. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our approach, reinforcing the benefits of multi-cancer WSI analysis and encouraging further research into the integration of distinct cancer types, a critical step for advancing digital pathology. To further demonstrate the heterogeneity and diverse phenotypes across different tumors, we provide a grid of representative tissue tiles from each cancer type and each molecular subtype in Fig. A.1 . This visualization highlights the distinct morphological characteristics observed across various tumor types, underscoring the challenges discussed in the main paper. As shown in the grid, the differences in cellular structures emphasize the complexity of aligning pathological patterns across cancers. These variations illustrate the inherent imbalance and heterogeneity that complicate model training and evaluation in multi-cancer settings. By showcasing the phenotypic diversity, Fig. A.1 offers a visual reference to the challenges of integrating multi-source data for comprehensive and unbiased learning. In addition to the methods discussed in the main text, we provide an extension of our hierarchical balancing strategy, specifically designed for tile-based tasks. Fig. A.2 illustrates how this approach can be applied to ensure a more equitable distribution of weights across cancer type-class combinations, slides, and tiles, addressing the potential imbalances inherent in multi-cancer datasets. As described in the main paper, our balancing strategy operates at multiple levels of data granularity, ensuring that each cancer type, slide, and tile contributes proportionally to the learning process. Extending this strategy to tile-based tasks involves an additional layer of balancing within each slide. First, we balance across cancer type-class combinations to ensure that no cancer type or class dominates the training process. Within each combination, we balance the weights among the slides, and finally, within each slide, we equally distribute weights across all tiles. This layered approach ensures that all tiles, regardless of their cancer type or class, are fairly represented in the training batches. By balancing weights at the cancer type, slide, and tile levels, this method mitigates the risk of over-representation by any particular tile or slide, promoting a more stable and effective learning process across the entire dataset. Furthermore, this extension highlights the versatility of our hierarchical balancing strategy in handling complex multi-cancer datasets with varying tile counts and class distributions, ensuring that both inter- and intra-slide variations are accounted for, resulting in a more robust and unbiased model. We conducted a preliminary analysis to assess the extent to which MIL representations retain cancer-type information in a multi-cancer setting, and to examine whether such retention can act as a shortcut in imbalanced datasets. This motivated our use of mutual information (MI) minimization for debiasing. We focused on the MSS/MSI classification task using two representative MIL models: DTFD-MIL and MHA-MIL. For each model, we first trained it on the downstream task. The resulting MIL representations were then frozen and used as fixed features for a simple linear classifier to predict cancer type (cancer label). The cancer-type classifier was trained using cross-entropy loss. Data splits were stratified by both cancer label and target label to prevent leakage. The experiment was conducted in two settings: (1) without debiasing, and (2) with MI minimization applied during the original downstream training. The results in Table B.1 show that without debiasing, cancer type can be predicted with high accuracy from the MIL representations, confirming strong retention of cancer-specific features. All models were implemented using their official codebases to ensure consistency across experiments. For models lacking explicit sample balancing strategies, class balancing ( Johnson and Khoshgoftaar, 2019; Wang et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016 ) was applied to the training data. Our hierarchical balancing approach was used specifically for our method. All models were trained using a batch size of 8, with the Adam optimizer ( Diederik, 2014 ) and Cross-Entropy (CE) loss ( Mao et al., 2023 ) for prediction tasks. A nested 5-fold cross-validation scheme was employed. Importantly, the splits were stratified by class label and cohort association to avoid any leakage and maintain representativeness. We allocated 10% of the training data for validation, and models were validated after each epoch. For robustness, the three best models (based on overall patient AUC) were bagged. To prevent overfitting, a warm-up period consisting of 10% of the total training time was used at the start of training, where the learning rate (LR) was set to a lower value of 1 × 10 − 6 . Similarly, a cooldown phase with the same learning rate was applied during the final 10% of training. Pretraining All tile encoders discussed in the paper were pretrained using all tiles from all three cohorts under similar training settings. Specifically, the pretraining was conducted using DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ) with a batch size of 80 per GPU and an output dimension of 32,768. The momentum for the teacher network was set to 0.999, with a learning rate initialized at 5 × 10 − 4 and a minimum learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 . A warmup phase was applied for the first 5 epochs, where the teacher temperature increased from 0.01 to 0.05. The global crop scale ranged from 0.25 to 1.0, while the local crop scale ranged from 0.05 to 0.25. A drop path rate of 0.1 was used, and the last layer was frozen for 1 epoch. We used directly the code provided by Caron et al. (2021) , such that for our Cancer-Aware VisionTransofmer (CAViT) we deployed our hierarchical sample balancing strategy during pretraining. During pretraining, tiles were filtered using the Otsu method and augmented with RandStainNA ( Shen et al., 2022 ), which introduces diverse staining variations to the tiles. Additionally, the NCT-CRC-HE-100K dataset ( Kather et al., 2018 ) was employed to differentiate tumor tissues from normal tissues. Slides containing fewer than 10 tumor tiles were excluded from further analysis. Adversarial training For our mutual-information (MI) estimator we utilize the Smoothed Mutual Information ”Lower Bound” Estimator (SMILE) ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ). The τ clipping hyperparameter was set to 1. Tuning Each model underwent a few tuning steps for hyperparameter optimization to ensure the robustness of the results. We tested various epoch settings (15, 30, and 100) and found that all models performed optimally with fewer epochs, with 15 or 30 epochs yielding the best results. Learning rate scheduling followed a linear decay after each step, to ensure a slow and stable decaying. Tuning performed for LR values of 1 × 10 − 4 , 5 × 10 − 5 , and 1 × 10 − 5 . Weight decay was treated similarly to LR, with tuning of 1 × 10 − 4 or 1 × 10 − 5 . Model-specific settings. For attention-based models, including AB-MIL, DTFD-MIL, MHA-MIL, and TransMIL, the attention dimension was uniformly set to 128 to ensure a fair comparison across methods. MHA-MIL used a single-head architecture, while DTFD-MIL performed best with 6 pseudo-bags. SparseConvMIL yielded optimal results with a sparse map downsample factor of 4. Our approach incorporated Cancer-Aware ViT (CAViT) embeddings with DTFD-MIL and MHA-MIL architectures. CAViT and ViT embeddings had a dimension of 384, while ResNet50 embeddings had a dimension of 1024. The lambda regularization parameter for each task and model was tuned, as shown in Table 4 , where the optimal lambda values were selected for each case. Computational resources. Multi-Modal masked autoencoder and parallel Mamba for 3D brain tumor segmentation Accurate segmentation of brain tumors from multimodal MRI is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, most existing approaches can only process single type of data modality, without exploiting the complementary information across different modalities. To overcome this limitation, a novel framework called MFMamba which integrates modality-aware masked autoencoder pretraining, a gated fusion strategy, and a Mamba-based backbone for efficient long-range modeling is proposed. In this design, one modality is fully masked while others are partially masked, forcing the network to reconstruct missing data through cross-modal learning. The gated fusion module then selectively incorporates generative priors into task-specific features, enhancing multimodal representations. Experimental results on the BraTS 2023 dataset show that MFMamba achieves Dice score of 93.77% for Whole Tumor and 92.69% for Tumor Core, corresponding to 1.6–2.1% improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The gains are statistically significant ( p < 0 . 05 ), indicating the framework’s ability to deliver more precise tumor boundary delineation. Overall, the results suggest that modality-aware fusion can enhance segmentation quality while maintaining computational efficiency, underscoring its potential application for clinical image analysis.
