Accurate segmentation of brain tumors in three-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis evaluation. Multimodal MRI, including T1, T1-Gd, T2, and FLAIR sequences, provides complementary information that enables precise delineation of tumor subregions. The integration of these modalities, however, remains challenging due to variations in acquisition protocols, missing sequences, and heterogeneous tumor appearances. Traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) such as U-Net [1] , V-Net [2] have shown strong ability to capture local structures, yet their limited receptive fields hinder the modeling of irregular and global tumor boundaries. Transformer-based methods extend the receptive field through self-attention but incur high computational costs, restricting scalability to 3D volumes. Recently, state space models (SSMs), particularly Mamba and its segmentation-oriented variant SegMamba [3] , have demonstrated efficient long-range modeling with linear-time complexity, making them promising backbones for volumetric medical imaging. However, existing SSM-based methods generally stack multimodal inputs without explicitly modeling modality-specific interactions, limiting their capacity to fully leverage complementary information. In parallel, masked autoencoders (MAEs) [4] have emerged as powerful self-supervised learners. By reconstructing missing regions, MAEs capture semantic priors that are transferable to downstream tasks. In the medical domain, M3AE [5] has shown the potential of MAEs for handling missing-modality scenarios in brain tumor segmentation. Yet, the integration of modality-aware generative priors into end-to-end segmentation pipelines is still underexplored. Beyond the field of neuroimaging, cross-domain studies provide additional evidence for the importance of multimodal fusion and efficient architectures. For example, semantic segmentation has been applied to microbial alterations using SegFormer backbones [6] , while YOLO-based segmentation frameworks have been deployed for livestock monitoring [7] and crop disease detection [8] . Attention-enhanced deep vision models have improved food quality assessment [9] , and blockchain-integrated deep learning frameworks have enabled secure medical classification in lung and colon cancer [10] . Further, machine learning has been used for hepatocellular carcinoma prediction [11] , mental health monitoring [12] , and other cross-domain applications such as super-resolution [13] and entropy-based edge detection [14] . Although these works target different problems, they collectively demonstrate that explicitly modeling cross-modal interactions and incorporating robust priors can lead to more reliable and generalizable systems. To address above-mentioned challenges, we propose MFMamba , a modality-aware framework that integrates masked autoencoder pretraining with efficient SSM-based segmentation. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce a modality-aware masking technique for generative pretraining, in which one modality is fully masked while others are partially masked. The design enables the network to reconstruct the missing modality, thus enhancing cross-modal representation learning. • We design a gated fusion module that selectively merges generative priors with task-driven features, enabling more effective and reliable multimodal integration. • We implement a Mamba-based segmentation backbone with modality-aware fusion, which achieves a balance between computational efficiency and segmentation accuracy for 3D brain tumor analysis. We introduce a modality-aware masking technique for generative pretraining, in which one modality is fully masked while others are partially masked. The design enables the network to reconstruct the missing modality, thus enhancing cross-modal representation learning. We design a gated fusion module that selectively merges generative priors with task-driven features, enabling more effective and reliable multimodal integration. We implement a Mamba-based segmentation backbone with modality-aware fusion, which achieves a balance between computational efficiency and segmentation accuracy for 3D brain tumor analysis. Extensive experiments on the BraTS 2023 dataset demonstrate that the proposed MFMamba framework achieves consistent improvements over strong baselines, underscoring the value of modality-aware generative priors for robust multimodal MRI segmentation. Brain Tumor Segmentation. Deep learning has advanced brain tumor segmentation from multimodal MRI. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), such as U-Net [1] , V-Net [2] , and 3D U-Net [15] , have demonstrated strong performance in capturing local structures but remain constrained by their limited receptive fields, reducing their effectiveness in modeling complex tumor boundaries. To overcome this, Transformer-based architectures have been proposed, including UNETR [16] and Swin-UNETR [17] , which employ global self-attention to extend receptive fields. However, the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms substantially increases computational costs, limiting their scalability to high-resolution volumetric data. Recent developments in state space models (SSMs), such as Mamba [18] and SegMamba [3] , have emerged as efficient alternatives for long-range dependency modeling. These methods achieve linear-time sequence modeling while preserving representational power, making them a more computationally feasible solution. Nonetheless, existing SSM-based approaches often process multimodal MRI inputs through simple stacking, without explicitly capturing modality-specific interactions. In parallel, CAD systems for brain tumors have been developed to combine multimodal MRI with robust classification pipelines, further illustrating the importance of integrating modality-aware strategies [19] . Masked Autoencoders and Representation Learning. Masked autoencoders (MAEs) [4] have emerged as powerful self-supervised learning tools by reconstructing missing parts of the input data. They have been widely applied in medical imaging, where incomplete acquisitions are common. M3AE [5] extends this concept to the challenge of missing modalities in brain tumor segmentation, showcasing the ability of MAEs to handle heterogeneous inputs. More recently, multimodal MAEs [20] have been proposed to improve cross-modal alignment and consistency, further enhancing the utility of generative pretraining. These studies highlight the potential of modality-aware reconstruction for robust representation learning. Despite these advances, the integration of such generative priors into end-to-end segmentation frameworks is still limited. Medical and Multimodal Applications. Multimodal and feature-driven methods have also been explored in diverse biomedical tasks, including brain lesion boundary refinement, multimodal diagnostic modeling, and the design of efficient architectures for medical image segmentation [21–23] . Beyond healthcare, related approaches have been applied to areas such as cancer prediction, microbial analysis, face recognition, and classical computer vision problems including super-resolution, edge detection, and content filtering [24–27] . Although these studies differ from brain tumor segmentation, they collectively highlight the broad applicability of multimodal learning strategies. In summary, prior research reveals three persistent gaps: (i) CNN and Transformer-based methods either lack efficient long-range modeling or face high computational demands; (ii) while SSM-based methods such as SegMamba improve scalability, they typically ignore modality-aware fusion; and (iii) MAE-based approaches have demonstrated strong potential for cross-modal representation learning but remain underexplored in end-to-end multimodal segmentation pipelines. The framework proposed in this study, MFMamba, addresses these gaps by combining modality-aware MAE pretraining, a gated fusion mechanism, and an efficient Mamba-based backbone. We propose MFMamba, a novel framework for multimodal brain tumor segmentation that integrates generative pretraining with long-range dependency modeling. An overview of the MFMamba architecture is shown in Fig. 1 . MFMamba consists of two components: a modality-aware masked autoencoder (MAE) and a Mamba-based segmentation network with a Gated Fusion Feature (GFF) module. During pretraining (upper part of Fig. 1 ), the MAE masks one modality completely and partially masks the others, driving the model to reconstruct the fully masked modality using the remaining modalities. This cross-modal reconstruction helps the network learn shared representations that capture complementary information. After pretraining, the segmentation phase begins (lower part of Fig. 1 ). The GFF module fuses the features from the masked modalities with the learned priors. The unmasked modalities are processed normally, while the masked ones benefit from the prior information, enriching their feature representations. These features are then passed through the Mamba-based segmentation network, which models long-range dependencies across depth, height, and width, enabling accurate tumor segmentation. The model is jointly optimized with both the MAE reconstruction loss and segmentation loss, ensuring the priors contribute to the segmentation task. Brain tumor segmentation with multimodal MRI is a voxel-level multi-class problem. Given input volumes X = { X 1 , … , X M } from modalities such as T1, T1-Gd, T2, and FLAIR, the goal is to predict a label map Y ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , C − 1 } H × W × D covering whole tumor (WT), tumor core (TC), and enhancing tumor (ET). Each modality provides complementary cues (e.g., T1 for anatomy, T1-Gd for enhancement, T2 for edema, FLAIR for fluid-suppressed lesions). The segmentation network learns (1) f θ : X → Y , with parameters θ optimized by a supervised segmentation loss L seg over labeled data. The MAE architecture used in MFMamba follows a typical encoder–decoder structure designed for 3D medical image segmentation. The encoder consists of four convolutional blocks, each containing three 3D convolutional layers, progressively downsampling the input while increasing the number of channels from 16 to 128. The decoder, similarly, consists of three upsampling and convolutional layers that restore the spatial resolution of the image and use skip connections to combine features from the encoder. This structure enables the model to effectively capture both global and local features, facilitating accurate modality reconstruction and improving the model’s cross-modal inference capabilities, especially when handling missing modalities during segmentation [4] . To exploit cross-modal dependencies, we adopt a modality-aware masking strategy: in each iteration, one modality is fully masked while the others are partially masked with ratio ρ = 0 . 75 . Formally, (2) X ̃ = { M 1 ( X m ′ ) , M ρ ( X m ) , m ≠ m ′ } , where M 1 removes all patches and M ρ randomly masks a fraction ρ of patches. The pretraining objective is to reconstruct each modality from X ̃ : (3) L MAE = 1 M ∑ m = 1 M ‖ X m − X ˆ m ( X ̃ ) ‖ 2 2 . This design compels the model to infer a fully missing modality from the remaining ones while denoising partially masked inputs, yielding stronger generative priors for downstream segmentation. To integrate generative priors into segmentation, we propose a Gated Fusion Feature (GFF) module that adaptively merges the features of masked modalities with MAE-generated guidance. For a masked modality m , its feature X m and the corresponding prior X MAE are concatenated and passed through a lightweight gating network: (4) G = σ W 2 ∗ ReLU ( W 1 ∗ [ X m ; X MAE ] ) , where W 1 and W 2 are 1 × 1 × 1 convolutions and σ ( ⋅ ) is the sigmoid function. The fused representation is then computed as: (5) F m = G ⊙ X m + ( 1 − G ) ⊙ X MAE . Unmasked modalities remain unchanged, and the final multimodal representation is obtained by concatenating all feature maps. This mechanism enables masked modalities to benefit from generative priors without distorting unmasked features, improving multimodal integration and segmentation accuracy. Our segmentation backbone builds upon SegMamba [3] , which employs a tri-orientated Mamba (ToM) module to capture long-range dependencies along depth, height, and width, and a Gated Spatial Convolution (GSC) module for local refinement. While effective, SegMamba processes all modalities uniformly, neglecting their distinct and complementary characteristics. To address this, we introduce a modality-aware extension. Each modality first passes through a GSC layer. For masked modalities, their features are further enriched using the Gated Fusion Feature (GFF) module, which incorporates generative priors from MAE pretraining: (6) Z m = GFF ( GSC ( X m ) , X MAE ) , if m masked GSC ( X m ) , otherwise . The fused representations are then processed by Mamba modules for global dependency modeling across spatial axes: (7) Z out = ∑ a ∈ { d , h , w } Mamba ( Z a ) . Finally, outputs from all modalities are aggregated into a unified representation for segmentation. This design ensures that masked modalities benefit from generative priors while unmasked ones retain their original structure, enabling the model to fully exploit cross-modal complementarities. To ensure that generative priors learned during pretraining contribute meaningfully to the segmentation task, we adopt a joint training objective. This combines the loss from the segmentation network with the reconstruction loss from the MAE phase. The total loss function is defined as: (8) L total = λ seg L seg + λ MAE L MAE where L seg is the segmentation loss, L MAE is the MAE reconstruction loss, and λ seg , λ MAE are weighting coefficients. Through this combined objective, the segmentation network is encouraged to incorporate knowledge from generative pretraining, leading to improved performance. In this section, we present experimental evaluation of the proposed MFMamba framework for brain tumor segmentation using 3D MRI. We used the BraTS 2023 dataset [28] which includes four MRI modalities per case: T1, T1-Gd, T2, and FLAIR. The dataset contains 1,251 cases, 875 of which are annotated with segmentation labels for training and validation, and 376 are reserved for testing with hidden ground truth. We split the labeled dataset into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% internal testing (See Table 2 ). All scans are skull-stripped, aligned to a standard anatomical template, and resampled to a 1 mm isotropic resolution. The four modalities are stacked as input channels for the segmentation network. In addition, standard data augmentation techniques such as random flipping, rotation, and intensity normalization were applied during training to enhance model generalization. The proposed method was implemented based on the PyTorch framework and executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (24 GB). Training was performed on randomly sampled 3D patches of size 12 8 3 , with a batch size of 2 for both the segmentation and MAE networks. One epoch is defined as 250 iterations (mini-batches), following the patch-based sampling strategy commonly used in BraTS segmentation tasks, rather than a full pass over the training set. This ensures balanced coverage of foreground and background regions through oversampling. We used stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for optimization. To train the segmentation network, we used an initial learning rate of 1 × 1 0 − 2 with momentum of 0.99 and Nesterov acceleration, and the MAE pretraining network was optimized with a learning rate of 3 × 1 0 − 4 , weight decay of 1 × 1 0 − 5 , and the same momentum and Nesterov parameters. Training was scheduled for up to 1000 epochs (250k iterations), although convergence is typically observed around epoch 150. A hybrid Dice + cross-entropy loss was applied to segmentation, whereas mean squared error (MSE) was used for MAE reconstruction. As for the model details, the specific parameters for the MAE pretraining model and the Mamba-based segmentation model are provided in Tables 4 and 5 , respectively. In the Mamba-based segmentation model, the Encoder and MambaEncoder modules were trained alternately. The MambaEncoder includes the Gated Fusion Feature (GFF) module, which is crucial for modality fusion during processing. We evaluate the segmentation quality using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) on the tumor subregions: whole tumor (WT), tumor core (TC), and enhancing tumor (ET). Higher Dice and lower HD95 values indicate better performance. Statistical significance of improvements is assessed using paired t-tests with p < 0 . 05 . We compare our proposed MFMamba against several leading methods in 3D medical image segmentation, including SegResNet [29] , UX-Net [30] , MedNeXt [31] , UNETR [16] , SwinUNETR [32] , SwinUNETR-V2 [17] , and SegMamba [3] . Table 1 shows both the segmentation performance (Dice and HD95) and model complexity (Params and FLOPs) of different methods. MFMamba outperforms existing models on WT and TC, achieving a Dice score of 93.77% and 92.69%, respectively, with significant improvements over SegMamba and Mamba-based models. Specifically, the improvements over the best-performing baseline (i.e., the SegMamba) are statistically significant ( p < 0.05) on WT and TC tumors. Examples of tumor subregion segmentation by MFMamba are shown in Fig. 2 . To examine the contribution of each component in MFMamba, we perform ablation studies on the BraTS 2023 test set. We isolate the effects of the modality-aware masking (A), joint loss strategy (B), and gated fusion module (C). Table 3 summarizes the results. Removing any of the components causes performance to decline. Without modalityaware masking (A), cross-modal dependencies are underutilized, reducing segmentation accuracy. Excluding the joint optimization (B) or gated fusion (C) also leads to lower Dice scores and higher HD95 values. The full model, with all components enabled, performs best. The proposed MFMamba framework achieves reasonably good performance on the BraTS 2023 dataset, demonstrating clear improvements in Whole Tumor (WT) and Tumor Core (TC) segmentation compared to baseline methods. With Dice scores of 93.77% for WT and 92.69% for TC. The framework has been shown to be highly effective, even under conditions where one modality is missing. The proposed MFMamba maintains robust segmentation quality despite modality loss, suggesting its resilience and adaptability. The success of MFMamba can be attributed to the integration of modality-aware masked autoencoder (MAE) pretraining and gated fusion. The MAE pretraining enables the model to reconstruct missing modalities through cross-modal learning, strengthening its ability to capture complementary features from the remaining modalities. The gated fusion module further refines the task-specific features by selectively incorporating the learned generative priors, enhancing the model’s overall segmentation accuracy. Despite these promising results, some limitations remain. The performance on Enhancing Tumor (ET) segmentation is slightly lower compared to WT and TC. A possible explanation is that during the MAE pretraining, fine-grained discriminative information may be lost, particularly for complex tumor regions. These imperfect reconstructions could lead to amplified errors when fused, causing a decrease in performance. Furthermore, failure cases emphasize this issue. In cases where tumors present heterogeneous appearances or weak contrast between modalities, the MAE occasionally generates suboptimal reconstructions, affecting the fused representations. This often results in mis-segmentation, especially along irregular tumor boundaries or in small enhancing tumor regions. These observations suggest that, while generative priors provide useful guidance, they may also propagate uncertainty in more challenging cases, indicating a need for more reliable and consistent structural priors across modalities. Another important aspect to consider is the computational efficiency of MFMamba. While our approach introduces a modest increase in model parameters and FLOPs compared to existing methods, the added complexity may not always justify the performance gain in clinical contexts where speed and simplicity are essential. However, we show that the model is feasible for both training and inference on high-end GPUs, with training memory consumption around 16–17 GB and inference taking approximately 2–3 min for a full validation epoch of 175 cases. Although this trade-off is acceptable for research and clinical workflows focused on accuracy, future work will explore lightweight adaptations to enhance computational efficiency for broader deployment. Future work will focus on the extension of the method to improve fusion strategies and cross-domain generalization. In particular, we will investigate efficient self-attention mechanisms to enhance long-range interactions across modalities without incurring prohibitive memory costs. Another promising direction is to evaluate the framework under domain shifts, such as data from different hospitals or scanner types, to ensure robustness and applicability in diverse clinical settings. Finally, the generalization of MFMamba to handle missing or completely unseen modalities is a critical consideration. Unlike many baseline methods that require all modalities to be available, MFMamba leverages modality-aware MAE pretraining to handle missing modalities during inference. This makes it particularly relevant in clinical practice, where incomplete acquisitions are common. However, extending the framework to entirely new modalities or tasks outside the brain domain presents an open challenge. Future research will focus on exploring attention-based fusion strategies to improve modality interaction. Although current 3D self-attention designs are memory-intensive, efficient variants may offer a promising path to more scalable multimodal integration. We developed MFMamba, a multimodal brain tumor segmentation framework that combines modality-aware generative pretraining with an efficient Mamba-based segmentation backbone. On the BraTS 2023 benchmark, MFMamba achieved Dice scores of 93.77% for Whole Tumor (WT) and 92.69% for Tumor Core (TC), representing improvements of up to 2.1% over competitive baselines. These gains are statistically significant ( p < 0 . 05 ) and demonstrate the benefit of integrating generative priors into downstream segmentation tasks. The method is potentially useful for enhancing delineation consistency across challenging tumor subregions for clinical diagnosis. Our method achieves a balance between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. While our framework introduces a moderate increase in parameters and FLOPs compared to conventional baselines, it remains computationally feasible on a single high-end GPU, with acceptable training and inference costs. More importantly, the modality-aware design naturally equips the framework to handle missing inputs, a common issue in clinical practice. Multimodal framework for TACE treatment response prediction in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is a first-line treatment for intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that can cause side effects. An accurate prediction of TACE response is important to improve clinical outcomes and avoid unnecessary toxicity. This study pursues a dual objective: to propose a standardized evaluation pipeline that enables reproducible benchmarking of state-of-the-art approaches on publicly available datasets, including both internal and external validation with public dataset, and to introduce a novel multimodal framework that integrates clinical variables, radiomic and deep features extracted from CT scans using the Vision Transformer MedViT to predict treatment response. Experiments were conducted using two publicly available datasets, the HCC-TACE-Seg, used as training and internal validation sets, and the WAW-TACE cohort, used as external validation set. The results demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches. Independent validation on the external WAW-TACE dataset achieved promising results, confirming the robustness of the model and its potential to support treatment planning. The data used in this work are part of publicly available datasets. Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE) is a minimally invasive procedure used to treat hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). According to the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), TACE is recommended for patients with intermediate-stage HCC with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage B that is characterized by small multinodular tumours, preserved liver function, absence of vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread and with normal liver activity ( Galle et al., 2018 ). This treatment aims to provide local control of tumour growth by intra-arterial administration of chemotherapeutic agents, often mixed with an embolising medium to occlude the blood vessels feeding the tumour ( Farasati Far et al., 2023 ). TACE has potential adverse effects, including enzyme abnormalities, organ failure and even death. Furthermore, studies have shown that many patients with HCC who underwent TACE do not benefit from the procedure, despite the number of sessions, which results in a burden on the patient’s health ( Llovet et al., 2002; Garwood et al., 2013 ). Early identification of non-responders can help avoid unnecessary procedures, reduce complications, and guide timely transitions to alternative systemic therapies, ultimately improving patient outcomes and optimizing healthcare resources. However, despite extensive studies, the factors that predict treatment response are still unclear and further research is warranted ( Piscaglia and Ogasawara, 2018 ). Over time, many criteria for establishing response to TACE treatment have been developed and investigated, ranging from purely anatomical assessments to methodologies that take into account tumour viability and, more recently, integrate others quantitative approaches ( Raoul et al., 2019 ). Clinical guidelines point to the BCLC staging system as a key criterion to guide therapeutic decisions in HCC patients, clearly identifying patients with intermediate-stage cancer (BCLC Stage-B) as those most suitable for treatment ( Bolondi et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015 ). More complex predictive models have been developed, integrating not only clinical staging but also histological tumour markers such as vascular endothelial growth factor, biological markers such as alpha-fetoprotein or a multimodal combination of clinical, radiological and molecular features, to improve personalization of treatment and prediction of therapeutic response ( Pugh et al., 1973; Hiraoka et al., 2017; Kadalayil et al., 2013; Sieghart et al., 2013; Kamath et al., 2001; Lanza et al., 2025 ). In the 2000s, the Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumours (RECIST) ( Therasse et al., 2000 ) and the modified RECIST (mRECIST) ( Lencioni and Llovet, 2010 ), have been assumed to guide therapeutic strategies for HCC patients. The early response assessed by mRECIST within 4–8 weeks after the first TACE can be used not only as a prognostic measure, but also to decide whether to continue with repeated TACE, to discontinue treatment or to diverse treatment strategies. In addition, mRECIST criteria have been integrated into decision-making models to identify patients most likely to respond to TACE, thus improving treatment customization and risk stratification ( Morshid et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015 ). All these methods which rely on clinical parameters, offer a first-level stratification of patients based on their suitability for this treatment but have limitations, as they do not adequately account for factors such as tumour burden, liver function, and the underlying cause of liver disease. Moreover, response criteria that rely solely on the strict presence or absence of imaging evidence and on a limited number of clinical parameters may be too simplistic to accurately assess tumour response, particularly in the context of advanced therapies ( Barman and Su, 2016 ). To address these limitations, in recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques has enabled the development of frameworks that seek to improve the prediction of treatment with promising results. It is possible to leverage the large amount of information extractable from computed tomography (CT) images, which are routinely used in the diagnostic and therapeutic workflow of HCC. Indeed, radiomics, a technique that extracts a large number of quantitative features, such as shape, statistic, and texture, from medical images, has emerged as a powerful tool for characterizing tissue heterogeneity and tumour phenotype in a non-invasive fashion ( Lambin et al., 2012; Zaccaria et al., 2024 ). Radiomics has been increasingly applied in a wide range of pathologies for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response prediction either independently or in combination with clinical, laboratory, or genomic variables ( Avanzo et al., 2020; Bera et al., 2022 ). Later, deep learning (DL) algorithms have been applied to CT scans to automatically learn discriminative features to predict the treatment response ( Cui et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2025; Romm and Tsigelny, 2020 ). However, despite the promising results achieved so far, several limitations still affect the effectiveness and clinical applicability of these models. Firstly, a limited number of studies adopt robust cross-validation strategies to ensure the robustness of their prediction method. In addition, there is substantial heterogeneity in image pre-processing protocols, feature extraction methods, and response labeling criteria, which complicates comparison across studies. A major limitation lies in the widespread use of private, non-public datasets, which prevents direct comparison between studies and hinders reproducibility and benchmarking of proposed approaches. Furthermore, existing studies vary in their prediction target for classifying individual CT slices, while other ones aim to classify the response to treatment at the patient level. This heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of results and limits the ability to assess clinical applicability in real-world decision-making settings. Furthermore, only a very limited number of studies performed external validation, and none of the reviewed papers evaluated their models on a publicly available dataset collected at an independent center not allowing reproducibility, losing generalizability and not comparing with the rest of the works present in the SoA. Finally, incorporating explainability techniques into predictive models can help obtain a small set of features very important for the model. In the presented context, this article has a twofold objective: (1) to introduce a standardized evaluation pipeline that enables reproducible benchmarking of state-of-the-art approaches designed to predict the response to TACE treatment, and (2) to propose a novel multimodal predictive framework that integrates clinical, radiomic, and deep learning-based features extracted from HCC patient data to predict the response to TACE treatment. Specifically, the proposed framework uses a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based model to extract deep features from CT images and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) based feature selection to keep the most predictive features. The main contributions of this paper are summarized below: • proposal of a standardized evaluation pipeline enabling reproducible benchmarking of state-of-the-art approaches on public datasets, including both internal and external validation; • development of a multimodal framework integrating clinical and imaging data to predict TACE response, leveraging a transformer-based architecture for global and local feature extraction from CT scans, and incorporating a SHAP-driven feature selection strategy to identify and retain the most relevant predictors. proposal of a standardized evaluation pipeline enabling reproducible benchmarking of state-of-the-art approaches on public datasets, including both internal and external validation; development of a multimodal framework integrating clinical and imaging data to predict TACE response, leveraging a transformer-based architecture for global and local feature extraction from CT scans, and incorporating a SHAP-driven feature selection strategy to identify and retain the most relevant predictors. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides an overview of the state-of-the-art methods. Then, Section 3 describes the dataset, preprocessing steps, and the design of the proposed multimodal framework. Section 4 details the experimental setup, including training procedures, evaluation protocols, and the methods used for comparison. Section 5 presents and discusses the performance of the proposed framework, including a comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art methods and independent validation. Finally, Section 6 reports the conclusion of the work. Traditional clinical models for predicting TACE response are often limited in their ability to capture the full complexity of tumour behavior and patient heterogeneity ( Barman and Su, 2016 ). To address this gap, recent studies have increasingly turned to machine learning (ML) and DL methods, which offer the potential to uncover hidden patterns in imaging and clinical data ( Cho et al., 2025; Soni et al., 2025 ). This section briefly presents a systematic review of the data-driven machine and DL based strategies for TACE response prediction. To identify relevant studies, a systematic literature search was conducted. A query was formulated to target studies specifically focused on the use of AI techniques for predicting clinical outcomes of TACE treatment from CT imaging analysis. The search was performed across titles, abstracts, and keywords, and included studies that referred to TACE, either through its acronym or full term. It also considered research involving methods from the field of AI, specifically approaches based on ML and DL. To capture studies focused on outcome prediction, the search included any word variations related to prediction tasks. The search was conducted in both Scopus and Google Scholar, targeting papers that included in their title, abstract, or keywords terms matching the following rule: (‘‘TACE’’ OR ‘‘transarterial chemoembolization’’) AND (‘‘machine learning’’ OR ‘‘deep learning’’ OR ‘‘artificial intelligence’’) AND (predict*) AND NOT combined . Only studies consistent with the objectives of the present work were included. As a result, Scopus and Google Scholar databases yielded 39 scientific studies published both in conference proceedings and journals. Following a thorough screening process, 21 articles were ultimately selected for analysis. Relevant studies are summarized in Table 1 , which highlights key aspects such as imaging type, data size, modeling approach, data-types (clinical, radiomic, or DL), and the cut-off time at which the post-treatment CT scan was evaluated to assess the response to the first TACE procedure, when reported in the study. The analysis of the selected studies showed that the scientific works could be classified into a few categories, where each category is characterized by a shared computational pipeline. Generally, the process begins with feature extraction, followed by a selection phase, and ends with the application of ML for classification. When clinical data are included, statistical tests, such as univariate or multivariate, are typically used for feature reduction. In contrast, when the input consists of imaging data, feature extraction can be performed either through radiomic techniques or by employing DL models as feature extractors, i.e. pre-trained models on large datasets that serve to capture the intrinsic characteristics of the image. As an alternative approach, imaging data can be directly used as input to DL models that function as end-to-end classifiers. These models may be used as feature extractors, or trained from scratch or fine-tuned starting from pre-trained weights values. Traditional ML models only encompassing clinical features have been largely used in the prediction of TACE response. These models use patient-specific factors, such as tumour size, alpha-fetoprotein levels, liver function tests, and BCLC stage, which are critical indicators of how a patient might respond to treatment ( Ma et al., 2023 ). Radiomics has been already involved in studies focused on TACE response prediction to therapy ( Wang et al., 2024 ). A study by Zhang et al. employed a Random Forest (RF) model to predict TACE response using arterial and portal venous CT phases ( Zhang et al., 2024a ). This study integrated clinical data, including alpha-fetoprotein levels and tumour size, with radiomic features. This integration significantly improved the accuracy of the prediction model, demonstrating that clinical and radiomic data are complementary in predicting treatment outcomes. Additionally, the use of radiomic features in combination with ML models led to the development of predictive scores specifically designed for TACE response prediction ( Morshid et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Bai et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024a; İnce et al., 2023 ). These scores are linear combinations of the most relevant features selected during the feature selection process often based on Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) selection method: each score assigns a weight to the chosen features, and the weighted sum is used to stratify patients according to their likelihood of responding to treatment. While these models improved interpretability and offered a practical tool for clinical application, their performance strongly depends on the robustness of feature extraction and the stability of feature selection procedures. In addition to techniques based on radiomic feature extraction, a growing number of studies have explored the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), often pre-trained on large-scale generic datasets, to extract informative representations from CT images, enabling a data-driven characterization of imaging patterns. Many studies employed the Residual Neural Network, known as ResNet ( He et al., 2016 ), architectures that showed impressive results in the field of image classification, to extract deep feature from different phases of CT and, combining the latter with others type of features, classify with good results the response to TACE ( Sun et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2025 ). DL models can also be employed as end-to-end classifiers rather than feature extractors. Some studies employed DL models to directly classify CT images to predict TACE response in HCC patients ( Fateema et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2021; Pino et al., 2021 ). These works typically rely on CNNs that have been pre-trained on large datasets or employ customized architectures to learn discriminative patterns from arterial or venous phase CT scans. In parallel, hybrid approaches have also emerged, aimed to integrate DL with additional data modalities or task-specific structures ( Li et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Ren et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024 ). These frameworks typically combine segmentation and classification tasks, or fuse deep features with clinical variables. Ren et al. studied benchmark multiple feature extractors and classifiers in ensemble settings ( Ren et al., 2022 ). Finally, it is worth noting that the definition of responders was not uniform across the included studies, as the cut-off depended on the timing of the follow-up imaging assessment. Table 1 summarizes the different cut-off values, that is, the time points at which post-treatment CT scans were evaluated to assess the response to the first TACE procedure. Despite the analyzed studies reports promising results, several limitations persist in current classification-based approaches: few models have been subjected to a cross-validation strategy; only two out of 21 studies use a publicly available dataset thus complicating direct comparison of the various approaches; studies that propose new methodologies rarely compare their results with previously published models, making it challenging to assess whether these innovations truly represent an advance in predictive accuracy; some studies focus on classifying individual images instead of classifying patients as responders or non-responders, which is ultimately more relevant from a clinical perspective. Such lack of standardization and direct benchmarking highlights the need for more unified evaluation. To address the current fragmentation and lack of comparability among existing studies, the primary objective of this work is to reproduce and benchmark representative models from the literature within a unified pipeline, applying them to the same preprocessed dataset and evaluating their performance using consistent metrics. This comparative analysis serves as a solid foundation for identifying the true potential and limitations of existing methods. Following the comparative analysis, an innovative predictive framework was introduced to classify treatment response at the patient level. The design leverages recent deep learning advances by incorporating ViT-based models, which have demonstrated superior performance in medical imaging tasks. ViT pretrained model for features extraction enhance the complementarity between imaging, radiomic, and clinical features compared to conventional CNN-based representations. Recent studies have shown that transformer-based representation outperforms CNNs in multimodal medical imaging classification tasks, achieving higher predictive accuracy and generalization when integrating radiomic and clinical information and proving that the mechanism of combination of different feature’ set enable transformers model to learn an informative global representation of the domanin ( Bi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025 ). Moreover, the proposed model uses a multi-slice approach since it allow to consider assess micro variations in regions that are crucial for the analysis of volumetric data ( Yu et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024 ). This section presents the dataset used in this study, the proposed multimodal classification framework (See Fig. 1 ), the comparative methods, and the experimental setup. It outlines the preprocessing strategies applied to analyze clinical and imaging data, the evaluated ML models, and the metrics used for the performance assessment. The analysis included the publicly-available HCC-TACE-Seg dataset 2 2 . ( Moawad et al., 2023 ). This dataset was collected by Morshid et al. at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and includes data from 105 single HCC focus-diagnosed patients, spanning from 2002 to 2012, featuring pre- and post-treatment multi-phase enhanced CT images taken within 1 to 12 weeks before initial TACE treatment. It includes portal venous CT scans segmentations of the liver, primary liver tumours, intra-hepatic vessels and the abdominal aorta. Each CT scan size was 512 × 512 pixels. For each scan, a windowing operation was applied to better visualize both hepatic parenchyma and tumour, using a window width of 150 Hounsfield Unit and a window level of 50 Hounsfield Unit ( Mayo-Smith et al., 1999; Okimoto et al., 2024 ). The dataset includes a comprehensive set of clinical variables, such as demographic characteristics (e.g., age, sex), laboratory test results (e.g., alpha-fetoprotein, albumin, bilirubin), and established clinical scoring systems such as the Child-Pugh score and the BCLC stage. The dataset also includes treatment response before and after treatment assessments according to RECIST, EASL and mRECIST criteria. The analysis considered only the following pre-treatment features: the values of the radiological criteria assessed in the baseline CT, the pre-treatment CT acquired in portal venous phase and the associated liver tumour segmentation. Patients were grouped into TACE-sensitive and TACE-refractory according to the time-to-progression (TTP) as described in Morshid et al. (2019) and Moawad et al. (2023) . TTP was defined as the number of weeks from the treatment TACE to the date of radiological evidence of progression according to mRECIST criteria. In this case, a cut-off of 14 weeks was used to divide patients in two groups. This cut-off was based on the expected date for repeat chemoembolization which was around 14 weeks on average after the first TACE session in the patient cohort ( Morshid et al., 2019 ). A list of features is reported in Supplementary Table S1. This section presents the proposed approach for predicting individual patient response to TACE treatment. The methodology involves data preparation, multimodal feature extraction from CT images and clinical data, and models training using a cross-validation strategy. A representative scheme of the proposed workflow is depicted in Fig. 1 . The workflow is summarized as follows: 1. Data Preparation . Among all clinical variables contained in the dataset (see Section 3.1 ), all features measured and collected after treatment were excluded. 2. Processing . Radiomic and deep features have been extracted from CT scans and selected using a correlation analysis: (a) Radiomic features , including shape, first-order statistics, and texture descriptors, are computed using the PyRadiomics library, enabling a quantitative characterization of tumour heterogeneity. (b) Deep features are extracted using a Vision Trasformer Model called MedViT ( Manzari et al., 2023 ) pre-trained on ImageNet, which leverages self-attention mechanisms to model global spatial dependencies within the image. 3. Classification models . For each patient, clinical, selected radiomic and deep features were concatenated to form a comprehensive feature representation used as input to various classification models. The following machine learning classifiers were trained and evaluated: Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). The hyperparameter set of each model was optimized using a grid search strategy. 4. SHAP based feature selection . SHAP values were computed to select a reduced subset of features and retrain all the considered classification models. Specifically, for each training set and for each model, retraining and testing were performed using only the features with a non-zero SHAP value. This SHAP-based feature selection method is favored for several methodological advantages it presents over traditional approaches ( Casalicchio et al., 2019; Freijeiro-González et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2012 ). For example, LASSO, in making linear assumptions, may miss nonlinear and complex relationships that multimodal data tend to exhibit, where clinical, radiomic, and deep features may all interact. Similarly, while Mutual Information operates in a non-parametric manner and serves as a global measure of feature relevance useful for an overall ranking of features, it does not consider redundancy or some higher-order feature interactions and cannot give explanations for individual predictions, thereby posing some restrictions to its applicability in the clinical decision-support context. As a first step, tumour size was excluded from the analysis, as nearly 50% of patients had missing values for this feature. Subsequently, if the same clinical information is encoded both as a continuous and as a categorical variable, the categorical one is retained to improve model interpretability and reduce sensitivity to outliers ( Pasta, 2009; Dougherty et al., 1995; Maslove et al., 2013; Zaidi et al., 2017 ). As a result, 97 patients were included in the analysis (see Table 2 ) : 38 patients were classified as non-responders to TACE while the remaining 59 were classified as responders. This section presents the procedure that has been adopted to extract both radiomic and deep features, along with the feature selection methodology that has been independently executed on the two feature types. For each patient, 1743 radiomic features were globally extracted from the entire portal venous phase CT scan using PyRadiomics, based on the 3D liver tumour reconstruction obtained from the segmentations. All images were resampled to an isotropic voxel spacing of 1 × 1 × 1 mm 3 using B-spline interpolation. Multiple image types were considered, including original, wavelet, Laplacian of Gaussian with parameter sigma from 1.0 to 5.0 with a unitary step, and other intensity-based transforms i.e. square, square root filter, gradient, exponential and logarithm. Features extracted included shape descriptors, first-order statistics, and texture features from various type of matrix built by the original images. Table 3 reports the number of features extracted for every filtered image. Deep features have been extracted using a Vision Transformer model called MedViT. The decision to use a ViT instead of a conventional CNN was motivated by growing evidence from medical imaging studies showing that ViTs often deliver higher accuracy, more stable training, and stronger robustness. Unlike CNNs, ViTs can capture long-range spatial dependencies and subtle intensity variations across the whole image, enabling the model to preserve a global understanding of liver anatomy and tumour distribution. This broader contextual awareness is particularly important for representing the heterogeneous enhancement patterns, vascular involvement, and spatial relationships between lesions and the surrounding hepatic structures seen in liver CT scans. As a result, ViTs can provide a more accurate characterization of tumour heterogeneity, a key factor in predicting the TACE response ( Maurício et al., 2023 ). ViTs leverage partitioning input images into patches, applying positional encoding to retain spatial information, and leveraging self-attention to capture global context more effectively than traditional convolutional networks. They have shown great predictive capacity in various medical and non-medical tasks ( Manzari et al., 2023; Maurício et al., 2023; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2024 ). MedViT integrates efficient convolutional and transformer blocks to capture both short- and long-range dependencies. Compared to other ViT, MedViT combine two special modules, i.e. Efficient Convolution Block (ECB) and Local Transformer Block (LTB), to address this aim. ECB extracts fine-grained local information by applying multiple convolutional filters in parallel and passing the resulting patch-level features through a locally feed-forward module. LTB fuses this information with global context by combining Efficient Self-Attention (ESA) and Multi-Head Convolutional Attention (MHCA). ESA captures long-range spatial dependencies with reduced computational cost, while MHCA focuses on short-range relations between adjacent regions. Together, these modules act as a multi-frequency feature mixer that enhances the latent representation of complex medical images. This design allows the model to simultaneously capture known diagnostic imaging features like tumour micro-heterogeneity, such as tubular microstructures that reflect aggressiveness, as well as macro-level tumour characteristics ( Vietti Violi et al., 2019; Manzari et al., 2023 ). Since MedViT relies on a 3-channel input, a 2.5D approach was adopted. For each patient, the MedViT’s input was constructed through the following steps: • Identification of the axial CT slice containing the tumour with the largest area; • Extraction of a fixed-size patch of dimensions 3 × 224 × 224 pixels, centered at the centroid of the tumour mask within the slice selected in the previous step. • All input images were normalized using the mean and standard deviation values of the ImageNet dataset. Identification of the axial CT slice containing the tumour with the largest area; Extraction of a fixed-size patch of dimensions 3 × 224 × 224 pixels, centered at the centroid of the tumour mask within the slice selected in the previous step. All input images were normalized using the mean and standard deviation values of the ImageNet dataset. It is worth reporting that the procedure described above was successfully applied to the considered dataset. No cases were encountered in which the tumour mask bounding box exceeded 224 × 224 pixels in size or the extracted patch extended beyond the boundaries of the CT scan. Thus, for each patient, a single 3-channel image was processed through the MedViT encoder. The resulting feature vectors from the penultimate layer were aggregated using average pooling to obtain a single patient-level embedding, as illustrated in Fig. 2 , thus producing a 1024 element vector representing the deep imaging characteristics of each patient. A correlation-based feature selection procedure was carried out independently for radiomic and deep features by employing a threshold for the Pearson correlation coefficient. When a pair of characteristics exhibited a correlation coefficient higher than the selected threshold, the one with lower variance was removed, i.e. less variability between patients and therefore potentially less informative for discrimination. According to previous studies dealing with similar data and tasks ( Dai et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022; Morshid et al., 2019 ), a correlation threshold of 0.85 was commonly applied to radiomic features. In SoA approaches, the same threshold has typically been used for both radiomic and deep features. However, those methods are based on CNNs, which may produce highly correlated features. In contrast, the authors’ approach employs a Transformer-based model, which is known to generate more diverse and less correlated feature representations due to its self-attention mechanism ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Raghu et al., 2022; Arslanoglu et al., 2025; Scabini et al., 2024 ). Therefore, a lower threshold of 0.6 was adopted in this study. As will be discussed in more detail in Section 4 , in this work feature selection is performed exclusively and independently on the training sets. Once the features are selected, the same subset is extracted from test set to evaluate the trained models. The selected clinical, radiomic, and deep features were concatenated to create a comprehensive multimodal representation for each patient to train and test machine learning models. Ordinal features were first encoded using ordinal encoding and then, like the continuous features, transformed using z-score. In contrast, categorical features were encoded using one-hot encoding. The following paragraphs provide a brief description of each classifier and the specific hyperparameters tuned during optimization. The optimized values of parameters can be found in Supplementary Table S2. • LR . Logistic Regression is a simple and interpretable model that estimates class probabilities by applying the sigmoid function to a weighted sum of input features. The inverse regularization strength C , the parameter that balances model complexity and fits accuracy, was optimized to control the L2 penalty and reduce overfitting in high-dimensional feature spaces. • RF . Random Forest is an ensemble method based on bagging, which combines predictions from multiple decision trees trained on bootstrap samples and random subsets of features. This approach reduces variance and improves generalization. Key hyperparameters included the number of trees (estimators), the maximum depth of each tree, and the minimum number of samples required to split a node—parameters that control model complexity and help prevent overfitting. • SVM . Support Vector Machines construct a decision boundary that maximizes the margin between classes in a transformed feature space. For non-linearly separable data, a Radial Basis Function kernel was used to map inputs into a higher-dimensional space where linear separation is possible. Key hyperparameters included the regularization parameter C , which balances margin size and classification error, and the kernel coefficient γ , which determines how much influence each training sample has in the feature space. • XGB . Extreme Gradient Boosting is a boosting algorithm that constructs an additive model using weak decision trees. It applies regularized gradient descent in function space to improve both generalization and training efficiency. Key hyperparameters included the learning rate η , which controls the contribution of each tree, the maximum tree depth and minimum child weight, which influence tree complexity, the subsample ratio, which helps prevent overfitting, and L1/L2 regularization terms, which penalize overly complex models. Unlike RF, which builds trees independently in parallel, XGB builds trees sequentially, where each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones, typically resulting in higher predictive performance at the cost of increased training complexity. • MLP . The Multi-Layer Perceptron is a fully connected feedforward neural network designed to model non-linear relationships through hierarchical transformations of input features. The architecture included two hidden layers with Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activations and batch normalization to stabilize training. Dropout layers were incorporated to reduce overfitting by preventing the co-adaptation of neurons. This section outlines the experimental setting used to train and test the proposed pipeline, and compare it with different approaches selected from the SoA. All experiments were carried out in a controlled software environment, summarized in Table 4 . To evaluate the performance of the proposed framework, it was systematically compared with state-of-the-art approaches previously reported in the literature for TACE response prediction. Following a thorough review of state-of-the-art approaches, five representative pipelines were selected, capturing the key design patterns recurring across the literature: • Approach I : This approach represents all the studied pipelines that feed radiomic features and clinical variables as input to traditional machine learning models ( Zhang et al., 2024b,a; Wang et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023; Bernatz et al., 2023; An et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Niu and He, 2021; Guo et al., 2021; Morshid et al., 2019 ). Clinical variables are filtered through univariate analysis and selected via multivariate analysis. Radiomic features undergo correlation filtering followed by LASSO regression for dimensionality reduction. • Approach II : This method considers end-to-end classifiers based on pre-trained CNN, e.g. ResNet, that take as input a stack of three CT slices ( Peng et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025 ). • Approach III : This pipeline employs ResNet to extract deep features from normalized CT images ( Ren et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2022 ). Feature selection is performed using Mutual Information Maximization and selected features are classified using a K-nearest neighbors model, where the optimal number of neighbors is determined through grid search. • Approach IV : This approach is a multimodal pipeline that jointly uses clinical variables, radiomic features, deep features extracted via a ResNet18 pre-trained on ImageNet ( Sun et al., 2024 ). The final prediction is made using multivariate logistic regression combining all three types of features. • Approach V : This approach performs slice-level classification using all CT slices containing the tumour from each patient, leveraging an EfficientNetV2 model pre-trained on ImageNet ( Chang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Fateema et al., 2024; Tan and Le, 2021 ). Patient-wise predictions are then derived using a majority voting scheme. The following paragraphs describe the compared approaches more in detail. The first approach represents the majority of the reviewed studies ( Zhang et al., 2021, 2024a; Wang et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023; Bernatz et al., 2023; An et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Niu and He, 2021; Guo et al., 2021; Morshid et al., 2019 ), that consider traditional machine learning models fed with clinical variables and radiomic features. These pipelines exemplify conventional approaches widely adopted in early investigations for predicting response to TACE treatment. Feature selection is typically performed independently for each data type. Clinical variables are initially filtered through univariate logistic regression, retaining only those with a p -value less than 0.1, in order to avoid prematurely excluding potentially relevant predictors. Variables that pass this initial screening step are subsequently analyzed with a multivariate logistic regression model to maintain only the significant features using a p -value lower than 0.1. Radiomic features are computed as described in paragraph “Radiomic Features Extraction” within Section 3.2.2 and undergo a two-step dimensionality selection process. First, pairwise Pearson correlation analysis is employed to identify and eliminate redundant features, with a threshold of 0.85 applied to exclude highly collinear descriptors. Then the remaining radiomic features are selected using LASSO, with the regularization parameter α optimized via five-fold cross-validation. In addition, using the weights computed by LASSO might be used to extract a composite radiomic score, i.e. Rad-Score, as a weighted linear combination of the selected features: (1) Rad-Score = Q + ∑ i = 1 N c i ∗ F i . where Q is the intercept term adjusting the baseline of the score, which is not penalized by the LASSO regularization, N is the number of radiomic features selected by LASSO (i.e., those with non-zero coefficients), F i denotes the i th selected radiomic feature and c i is the coefficient associated with feature F i , as determined by the LASSO model. Subsequently, the classifiers listed in Section 3.2.3 are trained using the radiomic and clinical feature sets, either individually or in combination. Combinations including both the raw radiomic features and the Rad-Score are excluded, as the Rad-Score already encapsulates a linear combination of the radiomic descriptors. The second approach considers the studies that use pre-trained convolutional neural networks as end-to-end binary classifiers. A ResNet50 model ( He et al., 2016 ), originally trained on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, is adapted to the target task. Typically, the initial convolutional layers are frozen to retain generic feature representations, while the final fully connected layers are retrained to map to the task-specific output space. To ensure compatibility with the pre-trained model’s learned weights, input images are built as described in paragraph “Deep Features Extraction” within Section 3.2.2 . The third approach follows a high-throughput benchmarking design, in which deep features extracted from multiple pre-trained CNN architectures are combined with traditional machine learning models. The best pipeline presented within the analyzed study by Ren et al. (2022) has been selected and replicated as Approach III. This setup involves extracting deep features using a ResNet model pre-trained on ImageNet. Input images were processed in the same manner as described in paragraph “Deep Features Extraction” within Section 3.2.2 . For feature selection, the Mutual Information Maximization method was employed, which identifies the most relevant and non-redundant features by maximizing the mutual information between each feature and the class labels. As a classifier, a K nearest neighbors model was used, with the optimal number of neighbors k determined by grid search optimization. The fourth approach follows the only work in the literature to adopt a comprehensive pipeline integrating radiomic features, deep features extracted via transfer learning, and clinical variables for TACE response prediction ( Sun et al., 2024 ). Radiomic Features were extracted using CT scan and deep features were extracted using a ResNet18 architecture pre-trained on ImageNet. In this case, the input was made by stacking three times a 256 × 256 patch centered at the center of the tumour. Feature selection was performed through correlation analysis followed by LASSO regression to eliminate redundancy and retain the most predictive features. The final classification was carried out using multivariate logistic regression, combining all three modalities into a single predictive model. This method is drawn from studies that perform prediction at the slice level ( Chang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022; Fateema et al., 2024 ). Patient-wise predictions are then derived using a majority voting scheme. In particular, a fine-tuned EfficientNetV2 ( Tan and Le, 2021 ) pretrained on ImageNet is used as end-to-end classifier. Each CT slice containing a tumour is used to generate a network input as follows: • Extraction of a fixed-size patch of dimensions 224 × 224 pixels, centered at the centroid of the tumour mask. • Generation of the input with a size 3 × 224 × 224 by stacking three identical copies of the patch extracted at the previous step. • All input 3-channels images were normalized using the mean and standard deviation values of the ImageNet dataset. Extraction of a fixed-size patch of dimensions 224 × 224 pixels, centered at the centroid of the tumour mask. Generation of the input with a size 3 × 224 × 224 by stacking three identical copies of the patch extracted at the previous step. All input 3-channels images were normalized using the mean and standard deviation values of the ImageNet dataset. The experimental strategy began with a comparison between the proposed pipeline and state-of-the-art approaches, using HCC-TACE-Seg dataset and a stratified 5-fold cross-validation scheme. Furthermore, the best model according the first analysis has been trained on the HCC-TACE-Seg dataset and tested on an external dataset. It is important to note that, for each method, the training pipeline was executed exclusively on the training data, without utilizing the test data for any preprocessing or processing steps. The dataset assumed as validation set is the WAW-TACE dataset 3 3 . ( Bartnik et al., 2024 ). This dataset includes abdominal pretreatment CT images from 233 treatment-naive patients with HCC treated with TACE and includes handcrafted liver tumour masks and clinical features. In reference to the HCC-TACE-Seg dataset, the WAW-TACE dataset differs for: • The number of lesions. The HCC-TACE-Seg dataset includes only patients with a single tumour lesion, whereas the WAW-TACE dataset also contains patients with multiple lesions; • A subset of clinical features. The WAW-TACE dataset provides a more limited subset of variables than HCC-TACE-Seg dataset. • The TACE technique. The HCC-TACE-Seg dataset involves both DEB-TACE and c-TACE whereas the WAW-TACE dataset comprises only patients treated with c-TACE; • The minimum time between the first TACE session and the possible second session after a progression event differs between the two protocols: 14 weeks for HCC-TACE-Seg and 4–6 weeks for WAW-TACE.
