Taking into account the proposed procedure specifications, all patients with more than one lesion were excluded for external validation. Data preparation and encoding of the features shared with the HCC-TACE-Seg dataset were carried out as in Section 3 . In the WAW-TACE dataset, the response was assessed on LI-RADS treatment response that divide lesions in nonviable, equivocal or viable after 4 weeks from the initial TACE. In order to classify the patients as responders or non-responders consistently as described in the HCC-TACE-Seg dataset, this study used the following steps: • if tumour was assessed as viable, this patient was considered as non-responder, as a tumour assessed as viable at week 4 would also have been indicated as viable at week 14, thereby indicating a lack of response to treatment. • Patients with non-viable tumour featuring a progression time or a follow-up without progression higher than 14 weeks were labeled as responder. All other non-viable cases were excluded in order to ensure consistency with the first dataset, where treatment response was assessed strictly at 14 weeks. • Patients with equivocal tumour were excluded. if tumour was assessed as viable, this patient was considered as non-responder, as a tumour assessed as viable at week 4 would also have been indicated as viable at week 14, thereby indicating a lack of response to treatment. Patients with non-viable tumour featuring a progression time or a follow-up without progression higher than 14 weeks were labeled as responder. All other non-viable cases were excluded in order to ensure consistency with the first dataset, where treatment response was assessed strictly at 14 weeks. Patients with equivocal tumour were excluded. Thus, the final subset encompassed 49 responders and 77 non-responders. A list of features of this dataset is reported in Supplementary Table S3. To conduct the validation on the independent dataset, the best model among the models considered within the proposed approach trained on HCC-TACE-Seg dataset, has been tested using 5-fold cross-validation. Since there is no complete overlap between the clinical feature set of the two datasets, as a first step, the proposed approach was trained using the features selected with SHAP, excluding those not available in the WAW-TACE dataset. Then such a model was tested on the two datasets. The performance of all methods were assessed using the following metrics: the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) and the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC). To evaluate whether the performance differences between the best proposed approach and the best-performing models among the compared methods were statistically significant, pairwise comparisons were conducted using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with a significance level set at α = 0 . 05 . All statistical tests were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), version 21.0.0.0. In this section, the evaluation metrics of all the conducted experiments are reported and compared. First, the comparison among the models trained using the proposed approach is described. Next, the performance of the best proposed model is compared to that of the SoA methods. Finally, the performance of the models trained using the features selected based on SHAP values is presented. The multimodal framework introduced in this study, which integrates imaging features extracted from MedViT, radiomics and clinical features, achieved high performance across all the evaluated classifiers. Among all them, Random Forest achieved the highest average AUROC of 0.87 with minimal inter-fold variability, as well as the highest AUPRC value of 0.90. Table 5 reports the mean and standard deviation of AUROC and AUPRC achieved for each classifier among the folds. From a clinical perspective, an AUROC of 0.86 demonstrates good discriminative ability in distinguishing between responders and non-responders. AUPRC is particularly relevant in this case, achieving a significant value of 0.90 that indicates that the model could identify most true responders with minimal errors. A slightly higher AUPRC compared to AUROC portrays a model that also provides emphasis on precision and recall, mainly in the positive class. In clinical terms, this indicates that fewer patients would be misclassified as responders, averting the dangerous scenario of offering TACE to individuals who would not benefit. Taking everything into account, these metrics confirm the model’s utility in assisting tailored treatment strategies, enhancing patient healthcare, and improving resource distribution in clinical settings. The results of the compared SoA approaches are presented here. Table 6 shows the average metric values across folds achieved by Approach I. It is worth noting that Approach I used the same classifiers as the proposed pipeline, along with different combinations of input feature sets. When comparing all models and feature set combinations, it merges that the best model is the RF that takes as input the combination of clinical and radiomic features. This model achieves a mean AUROC of 0.63 and a mean AUPRC of 0.69, with low standard deviation values, indicating limited predictive capability. The other classification models reach slightly lower metric values. It is worth noting that, as shown in Table 6 , Random Forest was the only state-of-the-art method to perform slightly better when combining clinical and radiomic features, whereas all the other algorithms performed better with clinical features alone. The authors hypothesize that this finding is related to the greater complexity of the models mentioned above, which in the context of the small sample size are more prone to overfitting, especially when noise is introduced by radiomic features. Random Forest, simpler, was more robust to this effect and yielded more stable results. The best model identified within Approach I was compared with the other four approaches, which consist of a single model trained on a single feature set, unlike Approach I that includes multiple model and feature set combinations,. Table 7 presents this comparison. As reported, the RF model trained according to the pipeline of Approach I outperforms the others. Approaches II and V perform only slightly worse. Table 8 provides a direct comparison between the SoA approaches and the best model from the proposed method. Pairwise comparisons of AUROC and AUPRC scores between the proposed model and the compared methods clearly highlight a statistically significant difference, indicating that the proposed model outperforms the SoA approaches, with relative improvements shown in Table 9 . To provide a more visual comparison of model performance, box plots illustrating the distribution of AUROC and AUPRC across folds are shown in Figs. 3 and 4 , respectively. The boxplot in Fig. 3 reports the AUROC distributions for six different methods, including the proposed approach. While most baseline methods yield AUROC scores centered around 0.6, the proposed method clearly surpasses them, achieving the highest median values. Similarly, in Fig. 4 all baseline methods tend to cluster around an average AUPRC of 0.6, whereas the proposed method consistently achieves higher values. Statistical tests were conducted to assess whether the observed differences in performance between models were statistically significant. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that the pairwise differences between the best model of the proposed approach and the best model among the compared methods were statistically significant, with p -values less than 0.05. In this section, the comparison between models trained using the full feature set and those trained with the feature set selected through the SHAP value-based approach is presented. SHAP can support both feature selection and the identification of the most suitable models across various tasks ( Berloco et al., 2024; Kraev et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022a ). For the proposed pipeline, each model was retrained using only the new reduced features set. Table 10 provides a direct comparison and shows that all classifiers benefit from SHAP-based feature selection. Confirming the discussions reported in Section 5.1 , the best-performing model remains the random forest, featuring an average AUROC of 0.92 and an average AUPRC of 0.95, with an average improvement of 0.03 in AUROC and 0.04 in AUPRC across folds. Fig. 5 shows the importance of the top 30 features for the best-performing model (RF, see Table 10 ), computed by averaging, for each feature, the mean absolute SHAP value obtained across the five folds. The results indicate that deep features are the most numerous and this indicates that automatically learned representations from CT images provide a relevant predictive contribution. Radiomic texture features also contribute meaningfully. In fact, several descriptors computed on Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrices (glcm) and Gray Level Run Length Matrices (glrlm) after Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) or wavelet (w) filtering have high importance. These features quantify texture uniformity, local intensity transitions, and run-length entropy related to all tissue structures that may contribute to the model’s decision process. Within the top 30 features from the aggregated SHAP analysis, hepatitis as an etiology factor emerged as an important variable. This finding might confirm the potential interaction between etiological factors, such as viral hepatitis, the therapeutic response to TACE, as previously discussed in literature ( Yoshitomi et al., 2024; Cun, 2021; Jin et al., 2021; Brito et al., 2025 ). Such analysis confirms that the complementary multimodal information is important for predicting the response to TACE. As reported in Table 10 , the best model is the RF trained following the proposed procedure considering the features set selected with SHAP. Hence, such model has been used to perform the independent validation of the WAW-TACE dataset. Firstly, using the same folds as in the previous analyses, the impact on the HCC-TACE-Seg test set was evaluated when employing the set of features selected by SHAP, after excluding those not shared with the WAW-TACE dataset. A decrease in performance metrics was observed, with AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.74 ± 0.05 and 0.78 ± 0.02, respectively. This decrease can be reasonably attributed to the removal of informative clinical features that were not available in the WAW-TACE dataset. The exclusion of these features likely reduced the model’s ability to capture relevant patterns in the original data. On the other hand, when the same model, trained on the HCC-TACE-Seg dataset, was evaluated on the entire WAW-TACE dataset, it achieved an AUROC of 0.66 ± 0.05 and an AUPRC of 0.69 ± 0.02. This comparatively limited reduction in performance suggests that the model retained a reasonable level of generalizability when applied to an external cohort. In addition to the differences in clinical features between the two datasets, it is also important to consider that they differ in terms of treatment protocols. Specifically, the HCC-TACE-Seg cohort includes both DEB-TACE and c-TACE procedures, whereas the WAW-TACE dataset only contains patients treated with c-TACE. Although current guidelines and several studies reported no major differences between these techniques, their clinical application remains heterogeneous and not yet standardized across centers ( Galle et al., 2018; Elshaarawy et al., 2019; Lanza et al., 2025 ). These differences may affect treatment response prediction, and future works should specifically investigate the role of different TACE procedures once appropriate datasets become available. The authors are also aware that the limited dataset size might lead to overfitting; however, several measures were adopted to mitigate this risk, including the use of 5-fold stratified cross-validation, feature selection to reduce the impact of noise, and validation on an entirely independent external dataset. Despite the differences in therapeutic regimen and evaluation criteria, the models maintained comparable performances, with only a moderate decrease of approximately 10% in predictive metrics, thus bearing witness to the validity and generalizability of our approach. In this work, we address two main goals: first, to establish a standardized evaluation framework that ensures reproducible benchmarking of state-of-the-art methods for predicting Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) treatment response; and second, to develop a novel multimodal predictive model that combines clinical, radiomic, and deep features extracted from hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patient data to estimate treatment outcomes. Several set of experiments were conducted using two publicy available datasets, training and internal validation dataset HCC-TACE-Seg and an external validation cohort from the WAW-TACE dataset. The framework proposed in this work provided robust predictive performance reaching 0.92 AUROC value and 0.95 AUPRC values and outperformed representative state-of-the-art approaches on a public dataset. The proposed approach yields a relative improvement over the selected baseline methods, ranging from 30% to 88%. This study, thanks to the obtained results, emphasizes also the effectiveness of integrating SHAP feature selection to guide the feature selection process and improve the accuracy of the model. Despite the exclusion of not common among datasets features, the model trained on the HCC-TACE-Seg achieved solid performance on the external WAW-TACE dataset, with an AUROC of 0.66 ± 0.05 and an AUPRC of 0.69 ± 0.02. These results demonstrate a good level of generalizability. Future work will investigate more sophisticated model either for feature extraction or end-to-end classifier like 3D Vision Transformers or hybrid CNN-Transformer networks that could capture the volumetric nature of medical images. Additionally, it should consider how to adapt the approach to patients with multiple lesions, possibly by integrating methods that support lesion-level or multi-lesion analysis. Performance enhancement of visual transformer models via dual-module collaboration for skin tumor classification This study develops and evaluates an artificial intelligence-based method for classifying skin tumors using clinical and dermoscopic images across seven benign and malignant types. Building on this dataset, we propose an optimized Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture incorporating two key modules: a data preprocessing module, CrossNorm and SelfNorm (CNSN), and a feature adaptation module, Multi-cognitive Visual Adapter (MONA), to enhance model performance and generalization. Comparative and ablation experiments were conducted, with rigorous evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the curve (AUC). Results demonstrate that the improved ViT achieves a classification accuracy of 92.14%, surpassing other neural network models by 0.13–18.75 percentage points, with precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC of 88.27%, 84.80%, 86.41%, and 99.38%, respectively. Ablation studies show that integrating CNSN and MONA increases accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC by 1.12, 1.63, 3.48, 2.71, and 0.03 percentage points compared with the baseline ViT. The proposed model effectively supports physicians in diagnosis, offering more precise and efficient decision-making and holds significant potential for advancing skin tumor diagnostic technologies. Skin tumors are among the most common cancers worldwide and continue to show a rising incidence, posing a major global health burden [ 1 , 2 ]. Their development results from the interplay of multiple factors. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is the predominant environmental cause, inducing DNA damage and immunosuppression [ 3 ]. Additional contributors include genetic susceptibility, chronic inflammation, environmental pollutants, immune dysfunction, and epigenetic alterations [ 4 , 5 ]. Clinically, skin tumors are classified as benign or malignant, and misdiagnosis between the two carries serious consequences. Misclassifying benign tumors as malignant can expose patients to unnecessary surgical procedures, psychological stress, and increased medical costs. Conversely, misidentifying malignant tumors as benign ones can delay timely intervention, significantly increasing the risk of disease progression and mortality. Hence, early and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective treatment planning and favorable patient outcomes [ 6 ]. For example, in cutaneous melanoma, failure to achieve timely and accurate diagnosis at an early stage often leads to distant metastasis, substantially compromising patients’ survival and quality of life [ 7 ]. In recent years, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have advanced rapidly in cancer detection and are now widely applied in the diagnosis of malignant tumors [ 8 ]. Among these approaches, convolutional neural networks (CNNs)—a class of DL models tailored for grid-structured data—have been extensively used in skin tumor image analysis due to their ability to automatically extract features for tasks such as classification and detection [ 9 ]. Nasr-Esfahani et al. were the first to develop a CNN-based melanoma detection system, training on 6,120 clinical images of melanomas and benign nevi, and reporting a sensitivity of 81 % and specificity of 80 % [ 10 ]. In another study, the GoogLeNet Inception model was pretrained on 1.28 million images and fine-tuned with 129,450 dermatoscopic images, achieving 72.1 % accuracy with an area under the curve (AUC) above 0.91 [ 11 ]. Similarly, a study using 2,200 dermoscopic melanoma images applied DL algorithms for segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. Compared to traditional ML methods, the Inception V3 model achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 93.74 % [ 12 ]. Despite these successes, CNNs face limitations in complex tumor analysis, particularly in capturing complete feature representations and leveraging broader contextual information. The Transformer architecture, with its self-attention mechanism, marks a major breakthrough in DL. Its adaptation to computer vision, the Vision Transformer (ViT), introduced a novel paradigm by partitioning images into patches and employing Transformer encoders with self-attention to capture global contextual information [ 13 , 14 ]. Unlike conventional approaches, ViT can automatically extract deep, highly discriminative features from large-scale datasets, effectively overcoming the limitations of traditional CNN-based methods in feature extraction. This capability has opened new possibilities for addressing the challenges of skin tumor classification. Building on this foundation, the present study seeks to optimize and extend the ViT architecture for skin tumor classification. Specifically, it aims to evaluate the applicability, effectiveness, and advantages of the enhanced model in this domain. The ultimate goal is to provide an innovative computational approach that improves diagnostic accuracy and supports clinical decision-making in dermatology. The dataset used in this study was compiled from two primary sources: 1) the publicly available International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2018 dataset and 2) clinical images collected from outpatients and inpatients at the Department of Dermatology, Second Hospital of Jilin University, between 2021 and 2024. It includes seven histopathologically confirmed tumor categories: melanoma (MM), melanocytic nevus (NV), basal cell carcinoma (BCC), benign keratosis (BK), actinic keratosis (AK), dermatofibroma (DF), and vascular lesions (VL). All images underwent hybrid preprocessing before being randomly divided into training and validation sets at an 8:2 ratio. The two sets were kept strictly independent to prevent data leakage. The training set was used for model parameter learning, while the validation set served as an independent dataset for performance evaluation. The distribution of cases across disease categories is summarized in Table 1 , and representative examples are shown in Fig. 1 . All clinical cases were confirmed via a rigorous pathological diagnostic protocol to ensure data accuracy and reliability, providing a solid foundation for subsequent analyses. During data collection, patient identifiers were anonymized, and clinical images retained only diagnostically relevant features. Data were stored in encrypted systems with strict access controls, accessible solely to authorized and certified professionals, ensuring the protection of patient privacy. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Hospital of Jilin University (Approval No. 2025165). The ViT architecture is based on the following key components [ 15 , 16 ]: • Image Patching: The input image is divided into non-overlapping patches. For example, a 224 × 224 image can be partitioned into 16 × 16 patches, each acting as a fundamental processing unit. These patches are then flattened and arranged into a sequential format, where the sequence length equals the number of patches. • Patch Embedding and Positional Encoding: Each patch undergoes a linear projection into a lower-dimensional vector space to generate its embedded representation. To preserve spatial relationships, a learnable positional encoding is added to each embedding, enabling the model to capture the relative positions of patches within the original image. • Class Token Introduction: A trainable classification token (Class Token) is prepended to the patch sequence. The final representation of this token is used for downstream classification tasks. • Multi-head Self-attention (MSA): A core component of the Transformer, MSA employs multiple parallel attention heads, each learning relationships between patches in different subspaces. This enables the model to capture complex dependencies among sequence elements. Stacking MSA layers allows hierarchical feature extraction and richer contextual representation. • Classification Output: The final representation of the Class Token is passed through a fully connected layer to produce class probability predictions. Key mathematical formulations of the ViT processing pipeline are presented below: Image Patching: N = H × W P 2 . An input image of size H × W × C (height × width × channels) is divided into N non-overlapping patches, each of size P × P × C , where P denotes the patch edge length. Linear Embedding: X emb = Reshape ( Linear ( I patch )). Each patch I patch undergoes a linear projection into a lower-dimensional feature space via a learnable weight matrix. The resulting embedding vector X emb is obtained after reshaping. Attention Score Calculation: Attention ( Q , K , V ) = S o f t m a x ( Q K T D K ) V. The similarity between the query Q and key K is computed, scaled by D K , and normalized using Softmax to obtain attention weights. These weights are then multiplied by the value V to produce the weighted output. MSA Calculation: MSA ( Z ) = Concat [ Attention 1 ； ··· ； Attention H ] W O . In multi-head attention, outputs from H parallel attention heads are concatenated and linearly transformed using the weight matrix W O . This enhances the model’s capacity to capture complex visual relationships, yielding a richer and more comprehensive feature representation. Layer Normalization: LayerNorm ( X ) = γ x - μ σ 2 + ∈ + β. Here, X is the input tensor, μ and σ 2 denote the mean and variance along the feature dimension, and ε is a small positive constant to prevent division by zero. γ and β are learnable scaling and bias parameters, respectively, applied to adjust the normalized output. The resulting tensor is passed to subsequent layers of the network. In this study, the baseline ViT architecture was optimized by targeting two key aspects: data preprocessing and feature refinement. Dedicated modules were introduced to enhance both model performance and generalization. Normalization techniques standardize data to improve training efficiency and model generalization. In this framework, two complementary approaches were employed. CrossNorm (Cross Normalization) method generates augmented data with diverse styles by exchanging normalization statistics (μ, σ) across samples or channels. By reducing the model’s reliance on specific data styles, CrossNorm improves robustness to distribution shifts. SelfNorm (Self Normalization) approach dynamically adjusts the statistics of individual samples via an attention mechanism, mitigating dependence on fixed training data styles. During testing, SelfNorm calibrates input styles to reduce the gap between training and test distributions. CrossNorm Formula: σ B A - μ A σ A + μ B , σ A B - μ B σ B + μ A . Here, A and B represent distinct feature maps; μ A and μ B denote the channel-wise means, while σ A and σ B denote the channel-wise variances of feature maps A and B . This operation exchanges the statistical properties (mean and variance) between channels of different feature maps, effectively expanding the training data distribution and enhancing both model training and generalization performance. SelfNorm Formula: σ ′ A A - μ A σ A + μ ′ A . Here, A is the feature map, μ A and σ A are its original channel-wise mean and variance, and μ’ A and σ’ A are the recalibrated mean and variance obtained via an attention mechanism. By dynamically adjusting the feature statistics, SelfNorm reduces the distribution gap between training and test data, thereby improving model generalization and robustness. The combination of CrossNorm and SelfNorm, termed CNSN [ 17 ], was incorporated into our model before the input data enter the core Transformer blocks. This module performs advanced preprocessing to optimize feature distributions, standardizing and enhancing fundamental image characteristics such as color, contrast, and texture. By improving data quality and compatibility with the model, CNSN enables the Transformer blocks to process inputs more efficiently, providing a robust foundation for subsequent feature extraction and analysis. The Multi-cognitive Visual Adapter (MONA) is a novel fine-tuning approach [ 18 ] that enhances adapter design by incorporating multi-cognitive convolutional filters and scaled normalization layers. MONA improves model performance while reducing computational and storage costs. It has demonstrated significant gains in complex visual tasks, offering a promising strategy for efficient and effective fine-tuning in advanced vision applications. The second enhancement in this study involves integrating the MONA module after each stage of the Transformer block. As the Transformer extracts and transforms features, MONA performs targeted adjustments, exploring inter-feature relationships and reinforcing the representation of critical features. In image classification, it amplifies discriminative features, suppresses irrelevant information such as background noise, and thereby improves overall model accuracy. MONA Input Optimization Formula: X norm = S 1 · | X 0 | LN + S 2 · X 0. Here, X 0 is the original input, |·| LN denotes the layer normalization operation, and S 1 ​ and S 2 are learnable weights. This formula combines the normalized and raw inputs, weighted respectively, to adjust the input distribution and optimize feature representation for subsequent processing. The overall MONA formula is as follows: X = X 0 + U ι σ (f pw (f dw (D ι (X norm ))). Here X 0 is the original input, and X norm is the normalized input after MONA’s input optimization. D ι and U ι denote the down-projection and up-projection operations of the ι-th adapter layer, respectively, and σ represents the GeLU activation function. The computation proceeds as follows: X norm is first down-projected via D ι , then processed through depth-wise separable convolution f dw and pointwise convolution f pw . A nonlinear transformation is applied using GeLU, followed by up-projection via U ι . Finally, the result is added to the original input X 0 to yield the output X. By strategically integrating the CNSN and MONA modules, this study proposes the ViTwithCNSNMONA model. Optimizations are applied both at the data input stage and throughout the feature processing pipeline, enhancing the model’s ability to capture complex features in skin tumor classification. This architecture improves classification accuracy and diagnostic reliability. The experimental model’s architecture is illustrated in Fig. 2 and Fig. 2.1 . All models were pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned using a standardized approach. Implemented in Python with the PyTorch framework, fine-tuning employed the stochastic gradient descent optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001, momentum of 0.9, and weight decay of 5e − 5. Training was performed on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (24 GB) and a 16-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8358P CPU (2.60 GHz), using a batch size of 16 over 50 epochs. The model’s performance was assessed using accuracy (Acc), precision (Pre), recall (Rec), F1 score, and AUC. The corresponding evaluation metrics are defined as follows: A c c u r a c y = TP + T N TP + T N + F P + F N . P r e c i s i o n = TP TP + F P . R e c a l l = TP TP + F N . F 1 = 2 × P r e c i s i o n × R e c a l l P r e c i s i o n + R e c a l l . Accuracy represents the proportion of correctly predicted samples among the total number of samples. Precision measures the proportion of correctly predicted positive samples out of all predicted positives. Recall, also referred to as sensitivity or the true positive rate, is the proportion of correctly predicted positives relative to all actual positives; a higher recall indicates a lower likelihood of missed diagnoses. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced assessment of the model’s classification performance. In the formulae above, TP (True Positive) denotes the number of samples correctly predicted as positive, TN (True Negative) denotes the number of samples correctly predicted as negative, FP (False Positive) denotes the number of samples incorrectly predicted as positive, and FN (False Negative) denotes the number of samples incorrectly predicted as negative. The AUC quantifies the overall performance of a classification model by measuring the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plotted against the false positive rate. Typically, AUC values range from 0.5 to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating higher diagnostic accuracy and better classification performance. Confusion matrix diagrams were also generated for each model. A confusion matrix provides a detailed assessment of classification performance by showing the relationship between predicted and actual classes, including TP, FP, TN, and FN. It enables a class-wise analysis of model performance, facilitating a deeper understanding of the model’s strengths and weaknesses. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is a widely used visualization technique for interpreting CNN decisions, generating heatmaps that highlight the image regions the model focuses on during prediction [ 19 , 20 ]. The method calculates the gradients of the target class with respect to the convolutional feature maps and performs a weighted summation to produce a heatmap, reflecting the contribution of different image regions to the class prediction. In image classification tasks, Grad-CAM allows researchers to identify the critical regions influencing the model’s decisions and provides an intuitive understanding of the features associated with specific classes [ 21 ]. To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the ViTwithCNSNMONA model, 11 representative network architectures were selected as baseline comparisons: MobileNet, EfficientNetV2, SwinTransformer, ConvNeXt, ShuffleNetV2, VGG19, ResNet50, Data-efficient Image Transformers (DeiT), Leaked ViT (LeViT), Single-head ViT (SHViT), and Naflex ViT (NaflexViT). MobileNet and ShuffleNetV2 are lightweight models widely used in resource-constrained scenarios, reducing computational complexity through techniques such as depth-wise separable convolutions [ 22 , 23 ]. EfficientNetV2 employs a compound scaling strategy to balance model efficiency and accuracy [ 24 ]. SwinTransformer introduces a sliding window mechanism, extending the Transformer architecture to visual tasks and effectively modeling long-range dependencies [ 25 ]. ConvNeXt, a CNN-based model, rethinks and optimizes traditional convolutional layers by incorporating Transformer-inspired design concepts [ 26 ]. The classic VGG19 provides a foundational framework in image recognition with its simple and regular architecture [ 27 ], while ResNet50 uses residual connections to mitigate gradient vanishing in deep networks, facilitating the development of deeper neural architectures [ 28 ]. DeiT is an efficient image classification algorithm based on the ViT architecture, addressing small-sample medical scenarios through improved training strategies and knowledge distillation [ 29 ]. LeViT is a hybrid visual Transformer that reduces computational complexity by combining CNN-based local feature extraction with the global modeling capabilities of Transformers [ 30 ]. SHViT, a ViT variant, balances efficiency and performance through lightweight architecture design, channel dimension optimization, partitioning strategies, and hierarchical feature fusion [ 31 ]. Similarly, NaflexViT supports multi-sequence length inputs while preserving the original image aspect ratio, leveraging flexible partitioning, dynamic sequence complementation, and phased training strategies to achieve a balance between computational efficiency and feature representation. The ViTwithCNSNMONA model was compared against these diverse architectures to comprehensively and objectively evaluate its performance across multiple technical approaches and perspectives. Similarly, ViTwithCNSNMONA outperformed others in Rec and F1 score, with values of 84.80 % and 86.41 %, respectively, confirming its high sensitivity, balance, and overall reliability. Among the comparison models, EfficientNetV2 and DeiT showed strong performance across multiple metrics, closely approaching ViTwithCNSNMONA and reflecting a favorable balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. In contrast, LeViT and SHViT exhibited lower scores on several evaluation metrics, highlighting limitations in classification performance and indicating room for improvement in recognition accuracy and robustness. In the ROC curve analysis, ViTwithCNSNMONA clearly outperforms the other models, reflecting its superior classification ability and strong generalization. Overall, across all performance metrics and ROC evaluations, ViTwithCNSNMONA demonstrates significant advantages, establishing it as the top-performing model in this study. These results provide a valuable reference for model selection and optimization strategies in future research and practical applications. They also highlight the importance of prioritizing architectures with robust multi-dimensional performance, such as ViTwithCNSNMONA, to further enhance model effectiveness. Consequently, the model demonstrates a recognition capability that surpasses the average performance level of dermatologists. However, some misclassifications still occur, as illustrated in Fig. 12 . Case-level analysis suggests several contributing factors. First, lesion morphology can interfere with diagnosis: early-stage features of MM and BCC may closely resemble NV, while some benign tumors exhibit malignant-like characteristics such as uneven pigmentation or blurred boundaries, confusing the model. Second, deviations in key regions can mislead the model; for example, clinical diagnosis of malignant tumors often relies on atypical pigment networks and abnormal vasculature in the lesion center, but the model may focus on peripheral normal skin, missing the critical diagnostic regions. Finally, subtle clinical manifestations or dermoscopic features resembling normal skin can cause misclassification of healthy tissue or minor lesions. The skin, as the body’s outermost tissue, is continuously exposed to ultraviolet radiation, heat, light, dust, and other environmental stressors. Skin tumors have emerged as a major public health concern, with their incidence steadily increasing [ 32 , 33 ]. These tumors are classified as benign or malignant, with malignant tumors being invasive, metastatic, and potentially life-threatening. For example, malignant melanoma accounts for approximately 55,000 deaths annually [ 34 ]. Non-melanoma malignant tumors, such as BCC and squamous cell carcinoma, not only pose serious health risks but also occur more frequently than melanoma [ 35 , 36 ]. Due to overlapping characteristics between benign and malignant lesions, accurate diagnosis requires comprehensive evaluation of lesion morphology, dermoscopic findings, pathological results, and clinical information. While DL has achieved notable success in medical image analysis, most prior studies have relied on single-modal model architectures. Consequently, substantial challenges remain in the intelligent recognition of skin tumor images. Clinical and dermoscopic images provide complementary information due to their inherent differences, offering a more comprehensive perspective for disease assessment. Accordingly, we developed an intelligent skin tumor classification model integrating both modalities. Based on the ViT architecture, the model innovatively incorporates the CNSN and MONA modules, achieving substantial performance improvements in skin tumor image classification. The CNSN module emphasizes in-depth data preprocessing through the combination of two normalization strategies: CrossNorm and SelfNorm. CrossNorm enhances data diversity by exchanging channel-wise statistics of feature maps during training, while SelfNorm dynamically calibrates statistics via an attention mechanism to bridge the distribution gap between training and testing data. The two methods are complementary, markedly enhancing robustness under synthetic and natural distribution shifts. This design strengthens the model’s ability to jointly capture subtle texture details and global morphological structures, particularly in lesions with blurred boundaries or variable morphology. Compared with conventional normalization techniques, CNSN demonstrates distinct advantages across multiple dimensions, as detailed below. CNSN differs from conventional normalization techniques in several key aspects. First, in normalization logic and dependency: traditional methods such as Batch Normalization (BN) and Layer Normalization (LN) rely on batch- or layer-level statistics, limiting performance based on data size and batch characteristics [ 37 , 38 ]. In contrast, CrossNorm performs cross-distribution fusion by exchanging statistics between samples or channels, while SelfNorm dynamically predicts sample-specific parameters via a lightweight sub-network, eliminating dependence on batch statistics. Second, in adaptability to distribution shifts: conventional methods assume stable data distributions and are prone to fluctuations under small-batch training, non-stationary distributions, or domain shifts [ 39 ]. CNSN addresses this by enabling CrossNorm to promote generalized feature learning through mixed distributions, while SelfNorm ensures stable operation at the sample level. Third, in scenario specificity: conventional methods are optimized for stable-distribution, fixed-batch tasks (e.g., large-scale classification) with a focus on accelerating convergence [ 40 ]. In contrast, CNSN is optimized for distribution shift scenarios: CrossNorm improves domain adaptation by exchanging cross-domain feature statistics, and SelfNorm enhances stability in few-shot learning and reinforcement learning through dynamic statistical calibration. Moreover, their synergistic interaction allows precise capture of sample-specific variations in fine-grained tasks. The MONA module enhances the model’s multi-level cognitive ability for visual signals via multi-scale deep convolutional filters and learnable feature normalization layers. When integrated into Transformer blocks, MONA efficiently extracts local spatial features through multi-scale depth-wise separable convolutions and feature distribution adjustment. Compared with standard visual adapters, MONA offers several advantages. First, it provides superior feature processing: standard adapters typically rely on static linear or convolutional layers with fixed weights, lacking the capacity to adapt based on input content [ 41 ], whereas MONA performs modality-aware dynamic normalization using input-dependent generated parameters, enabling automatic adaptation to feature distributions across diverse modalities or varying inputs, thereby achieving more flexible and superior processing capability. Second, it optimizes input feature distributions more effectively: standard adapters often pass features directly or use fixed normalization, which may not suit downstream task requirements [ 42 ]; MONA’s distribution adaptation layer dynamically scales and shifts features to align with downstream needs. Third, in terms of training efficiency, MONA’s optimized filter and structure design reduces additional parameters significantly and accelerates convergence compared to standard visual adapters, enabling efficient training. In contrast, standard visual adapters need more parameters for comparable performance, increasing storage costs and computational overhead [ 43 ]. This study also conducted comparative experiments between the ViTwithCNSNMONA model and current mainstream neural network architectures. The results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior performance across multiple key metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC, reflecting its strong classification ability and robust generalization. Ablation experiments further validate the architectural innovations of the model: compared with the baseline ViT, the integration of CNSN and MONA modules significantly enhances the model’s capacity to extract and fuse features, confirming their scientific rationale and practical value. Additionally, Grad-CAM visualization reveals that the model produces highly localized response regions with clear clinical relevance in feature activation maps, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the ViTwithCNSNMONA architecture in skin tumor image analysis. Notably, this innovative architecture still has room for optimization. The CNSN module improves generalization under distribution shifts by exchanging feature statistics and performing attention-based calibration, but it relies on low-order statistics and is sensitive to hyperparameters, limiting its performance in complex style or cross-domain tasks. The MONA module, while enhancing feature adaptation, introduces increased computational cost due to its multi-branch convolution mechanism and complex architecture; additionally, its structural hyperparameters, such as intermediate dimensions, require task-specific tuning, which can constrain practical deployment efficiency. Furthermore, the clinical image data in this study originate from a single institution and, compared with dermoscopic data, are relatively limited in scale, posing a potential risk of overfitting. Although the model’s generalization has been partially validated through multi-modal datasets and independent validation sets, future work should expand sample size and disease coverage via multi-center collaboration. Techniques such as data augmentation and transfer learning could further mitigate overfitting. In clinical practice, integrating model outputs with existing diagnostic workflows requires verification. Key challenges include enabling clinicians without technical backgrounds to interpret and trust the model’s decisions, and managing misclassifications to minimize medical risk. While this study qualitatively demonstrates the clinical relevance of Grad-CAM through case comparisons, showing general consistency with expert-focused lesion features, limitations remain in complex or atypical cases. Future research should incorporate quantitative metrics, such as overlap with pathological annotations, and conduct detailed analyses of misclassified cases to enhance the clinical utility and interpretability of the model. Despite these limitations, the module integration strategy proposed in this study offers a novel technical approach for intelligent skin tumor image diagnosis, and its design principles and validation methods provide valuable guidance for improving models in similar visual tasks. This study presents an optimized ViT-based model integrating a data preprocessing module (CNSN) and a feature adaptation module (MONA). CNSN enhances input data by optimizing feature distribution, while MONA refines processed features to strengthen the representation of key information. The resulting ViTwithCNSNMONA model demonstrates superior performance in classifying both clinical and dermoscopic images of skin tumors, achieving optimal results across multiple evaluation metrics. These findings provide valuable insights and practical reference for the development of intelligent, computer-aided diagnostic tools for skin tumor assessment. Pixel-level annotations of context region for trustworthy diagnosis of Breast Lymph Node Metastasis from Histopathological WSI There is a dearth of annotated images in digital pathology, and annotations are pivotal for supervised automated diagnosis. This work aims to create a set of data on breast lymph node metastatic whole slide images (WSI) that is truly valuable as it is annotated by the domain experts in a very precise and intensive manner. The annotations provided here are of rare kind that has pixel-level labels divided into three categories; first is based on the diagnostically significant tissue regions, second is background tissue and the third is artefacts present in breast lymph node metastatic WSI. High level annotations, as is provided in this work, for areas apart from the metastatic region is crucial for diagnosis as this is the context region which is critical for cancer diagnosis. Breast lymph node metastasis is a severe medical condition that requires significant efforts by pathologists to examine cancer under microscope using glass slides. Automated cancer diagnosis using WSI, the digitized versions of glass slides, needs to be trustworthy and responsible, which is ensured by involving domain experts in the process that begins with identifying diagnostically significant regions on a WSI. In this dataset, a two-stage high-value pixel-level annotation protocol is designed where selected 73 training images of Camelyon16 dataset are annotated by doctors and verified by pathologists for their accuracy. These annotations would help researchers to reliably prepare patches for further processing that can be used as training samples for extracting more such significant regions for data preparation from WSI for diagnosing metastasis. These reliable and trustworthy annotations would help to take it to the clinic from the research lab much quickly. Breast cancer is the second most common cancers among woman all over the world [ 1 ]. H&E stained histopathology is the gold standard for breast cancer diagnosis [ 2 ]. Recently, digital pathology has been becoming increasingly popular for automating the diagnosis process. Cancer diagnosis is done by identifying abnormal tissue regions and on these abnormal regions the deep learning diagnostic models are predominantly trained. Models are either trained for binary classification where images are divided into normal and abnormal classes, or multiclass where image regions are divided into multiple classes based on cancer stage or type. There is dearth of annotated data in which the context region which plays a significant role in validating the presence and severity of cancers is labelled at pixel-level. In breast lymph node histopathology, for a single whole slide image, the tissue region, apart from the main lymph node which is also termed as background tissue region holds invaluable information about the cancer its history and possible proliferation [ 3 ]. Thus, the context region is extremely important for making a trustworthy and reliable diagnostic model. The classification models built on context along with the abnormal tissues bear more weightage than the models trained solely on abnormal classes. The original Camelyon16 is an H&E stained histopathological WSI dataset of breast lymph node metastasis. From this dataset the training set of abnormal class are downloaded, which is available on GigaScience Database [ 4 ]. Out of the total images 73 images are selected from the dataset. The original WSI from the dataset are not included because of the ethical issues. However, link to the original dataset is provided in reference section [ 4 ]. The annotations for three categories, namely tissue, background tissue and artefacts are stored as separate .xml files in their respective folders, the number of xml files generated for each of the categories is mentioned in Table 1 . The annotation along with the masks when combined together can be used to generate patches for three different classes in addition to annotations provided in Camelyon16 dataset as shown in Fig. 1 . These patches can be used to train supervised learning model for further analysis. Tissue region is the portion of the slide that includes the cellular mass, lymphoid tissue and tumour cells. This region also contains small amounts of adipose or other connective tissue, which is present within the lymphoid tissue mass. All other types of tissue visible on the slide, mainly connective tissues like blood, blood vessels, adipose tissue, etc. are marked as 'background tissue'. White background of the WSI is not annotated and is excluded. Various blemishes in slide preparation, such as dirt, hair, crushed tissue, staining artefacts which appear as dark spots or dots or lines, folds in tissue, defocused tissue either due to folds in the tissue or improper focusing while capturing WSI are annotated as “artefact”. An example of annotation is shown in Fig. 2 . A few .tiff files of the binary masks generated using .xml files are provided for reference. The python code, adapted from Camelyon16 dataset, is used for generating this binary mask is also provided in this dataset. The annotations in the form of .xml files are obtained my providing domain experts with 73 original Camelyon16 WSI. ASAP which is a WSI viewer cum annotation tool was used, the whole experiment design is visually represented in Fig. 3 . Medical doctors, trained to identify various tissue types, used polygon annotation tool in the ASAP software to mark regions in three categories; tissue, background tissue, and artefacts. This step is crucial to delineate precise boundaries around specific regions of the slides. A trained pathologist verified all the annotations done by doctors using same ASAP software. This verification ensures the data is reliable as pathologist have thorough understanding of objects present on the slides. Pathologist also ensures the errors present in the primary annotation stage are minimized to make the annotations more accurate and robust for downstream processing. In some images the tissue region lies totally inside the background tissue region. To extract masks for only background tissue region image subtraction is needed. This exhaustive annotation was done only on 73 WSI of abnormal class of training set. Only abnormal class is annotated because its background contains most of the context for classification. Artefacts for the WSI is not available because of the absence or negligible presence on the slides. The data size is small, this number maybe insufficient in dealing with various biases possibly present in the WSIs. Annotation subjectivity could be an issue because of inter-observer variability although minimised using standard protocols and terminologies. Large number of data points in annotation file take tremendous amount of time for mask generation. Users need to install python based multiresolutionImageInterface library for using the code provided in the repository. Although users can implement the same using open source libraries like openslide for the same. We utilized a public dataset and added new annotations. PLUME-OCT: A quality control tool to enhance statistical power in the analysis of biomarkers from 3D biomedical datasets of OCT images High-dimensional imaging data are central to biomedical research, enabling extraction of quantitative biomarkers for disease modeling and association studies. While quality control (QC) often targets individual 2D slices, many applications rely on the integrity of full 3D volumes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), used here as a representative modality, illustrates the need for automated QC methods assessing volumetric coherence to support reliable biomarker extraction. We developed Phase-Level Unified Metric Evaluation (PLUME-OCT), a preprocessing tool that quantifies inter-slice misalignments in 3D biomedical image volumes using a Discrete Fourier Transform-based approach. The method was validated against 73,920 pairwise comparisons annotated by four human graders across 40 OCT volumes from the OphthalmoLaus cohort. As a large-scale case study, PLUME-OCT was applied for QC of 88,247 OCT scans from the UK Biobank prior to 3D biomarker extraction and genome-wide association analysis. PLUME-OCT effectively ranked OCT scans by quality, detecting misalignments between OCT B-scans in agreement with human annotators. In large datasets, its use enhanced the detection of statistically significant signals in 3D retinal biomarkers analysis, increasing significant genetic associations by 21.1 % (p = 1.6 × 10−7) and heritability estimates by 19.1 % (p = 5.0 × 10−12) across 30 genome-wide association studies. PLUME-OCT is an open-source, lightweight, and scalable QA tool that enhances statistical power in 3D biomarkers analysis from biomedical imaging datasets. Although demonstrated on retinal OCT, the method applies broadly to other volumetric imaging modalities and can be seamlessly integrated into biomedical informatics workflows for high-quality, large-scale data preprocessing. Quality control (QC) in medical imaging is crucial for extracting robust biomarkers, as high data quality directly impacts the reliability of analyses and the clinical and research utility of the resulting biomarkers [ 1 ]. By ensuring that only reliable data are included, QC maximises statistical power and minimises errors. This is especially important in large-scale studies, where even subtle imaging artefacts can produce false associations, ultimately compromising the accuracy and impact of research findings. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), widely used in ophthalmology [ 2 , 3 ], exemplifies high-resolution 3D imaging by providing detailed visualisation of ocular microstructures. Much like other 3D imaging modalities such as CT, PET, MRI, and X-rays, OCT images can be compromised by artefacts resulting from eye movements, head motions, and media opacity [ 4 ]. OCT technology not only contributes significantly to the understanding of retinal anatomy [ 5 ], but it also enhances the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of various retinal pathologies [ 6 ]. Existing research has employed mathematical models and machine learning to enhance parameter extraction and quality control in OCT imaging [ 7,8 ]. Many current approaches rely on device-reported signal-level metrics such as Signal Strength (SS) and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), which, despite their widespread use, remain insensitive to motion artefacts and cannot ensure diagnostic reliability [ 9 ]. To improve objectivity, the Quality Index (QI) was introduced as a quantitative, histogram-based parameter that provides reproducible discrimination between excellent and poor-quality images and aligns closely with expert grading [ 10 ]. Subsequent work demonstrated that signal variability and image uniformity metrics correlate with human graders and can be applied across different OCT systems [ 11 ]. In parallel, several non-AI, physics-based approaches have focused on improving volumetric coherence in 3D OCT datasets. Retrospective motion-correction and registration strategies have been proposed to reduce artefacts between adjacent B-scans, including per-A-scan motion correction and merging of orthogonal volumes [ 12 , 13 ], rigid stack alignment for volumetric registration [ 14 ], and radial–linear compounding to enhance spatial consistency [ 15 ]. Reviews of such methods [ 16 ] confirm their effectiveness in restoring 3D coherence but also highlight the lack of standardised, quantitative metrics that can objectively score volumetric misalignment. More recently, deep-learning frameworks have achieved high accuracy in automatic OCT quality assessment, providing real-time, grader-independent classification of individual B-scans or en-face images [ 17–19 ]. These models outperform traditional signal-based indices for 2D quality assessment but depend on large annotated datasets and remain focused on slice-level artefacts, without evaluating volumetric coherence across the cube. A concise summary and benchmarking of these approaches, including their scope, principle, and computational characteristics, is presented in Table S1 . For clarity, a condensed subset of volumetric methods is also reported in Table 1 , highlighting that none of the existing 3D approaches provide a fast, reference-free quantitative QC score for large-scale OCT datasets. Despite these advancements, a critical gap remains in current QC approaches for OCT biomedical datasets: most methods evaluate the signal quality of individual 2D OCT scans (B-scans) but overlook the volumetric coherence of full OCT cubes (C-scans). Misalignment of individual 2D slices in 3D medical imaging datasets can significantly affect the accuracy of 3D biomarkers [ 20–23 ]. Misalignments between adjacent slices—commonly caused by subtle eye or head movements—disrupt anatomical continuity, degrade the accuracy of 3D biomarker extraction, and introduce errors in structural modeling. These distortions also impair the performance of deep learning models by reducing spatial consistency, leading to unreliable segmentation and classification outcomes. This highlights the need for QC methods that can automatically assess volumetric alignment and distinguish between well-aligned and poorly aligned scans at the 3D volume level. To contextualize PLUME-OCT within existing volumetric OCT alignment and correction approaches, we provide a concise comparison of representative 3D methods ( Tables 1 and 1 ). This overview highlights that current approaches either require reference scans, aim to correct motion retrospectively, or rely on computationally intensive registration steps, whereas none provide a fast, reference-free volumetric QC measure tailored for large-scale datasets. In this work, we propose Phase-Level Unified Metric Evaluation (PLUME-OCT), a lightweight and automated preprocessing method for evaluating the quality and volumetric coherence of 3D OCT datasets. The method quantifies inter-slice misalignment without relying on reference images and operates with minimal computational overhead. PLUME-OCT was validated against 98,720 human annotations across four independent graders. While demonstrated on retinal OCT, the approach is modality-agnostic and, in principle, applicable to a broad range of 3D biomedical imaging datasets. By improving the reliability of input data, PLUME-OCT enhances the statistical power and sensitivity of downstream analyses, offering a robust solution for large-scale biomarker studies. We extracted data from two distinct cohort studies. The first cohort, the UK Biobank, is a comprehensive biomedical database that aggregates health, imaging, and genetic information to advance medical research and enhance healthcare outcomes. We utilised 88,247 OCT C-Scans from as many participants. The second cohort, OphtalmoLaus, a sub-study of the Cohorte Lausannoise (CoLaus), focuses on cardiovascular risk factors and metabolic syndrome [ 24 ]. For this study, we analysed 1458 OCT C-Scans from as many individuals. Data engineering for both cohorts was conducted using the Cohort Builder tool [ 25 ]. In the UK Biobank cohort, Spectral Domain OCT (SD-OCT) imaging was performed using the Topcon 3D OCT-1000 Mark II device. The imaging protocol involved measuring visual acuity, autorefraction, and intraocular pressure (IOP) in a dark room without pupil dilation. The 3-dimensional macular volume scan mode, covering 6 × 6 mm 2 , was employed to capture 512 A-scans per B-scan, with 128 horizontal B-scans arranged in a raster pattern. In the second cohort, OphtalmoLaus, SD-OCT imaging was conducted using the Topcon DRI OCT Triton device. Measurements for visual acuity, autorefraction, and IOP were taken prior to imaging in a dark room without pupil dilation. The 3-dimensional macular volume scan mode (6 × 6 mm 2 ) was used, with three different acquisition modes capturing 128, 256, or 320 B-scans, respectively. We collected a total of 73,920 manual annotations from 12,320 B-scans from the OphtalmoLaus cohort to evaluate misalignment in individual scans. The annotation process involved four graders who first worked individually to annotate the scans, followed by pair-based consensus sessions, resulting in six annotations per B-scan ( Fig. 1 a and b). The six annotations per B-scan correspond to the six possible annotator pairs (Annotator 1–2, 1–3, 1–4, 2–3, 2–4, 3–4), rather than six different annotation types. The dataset included 20 OCT cubes containing 360 B-scans and 20 OCT cubes containing 256 B-scans, resulting in (20 × 360 + 20 × 256) = 12,320 × 6 = 73,920 annotations. Each grader compared consecutive B-scans, identifying rotational or translational misalignments (horizontal, vertical, or a combination). B-scans that were entirely dark or uninterpretable were also marked as misaligned. Accordingly, each B-scan pair could be assigned to one of six annotation types: (1) horizontal shift, (2) vertical shift, (3) combined horizontal–vertical shift, (4) rotational misalignment, (5) no detectable misalignment, or (6) fully dark or uninterpretable B-scan. Annotation accuracy was ensured by performing pairwise consensus sessions between graders and by computing inter-annotator F1 scores across displacement magnitude categories ( Fig. 7 ). To further quantify inter-annotator agreement, we computed additional statistics (precision, recall and Cohen's κ) across all annotated B-scans of the consensensus sessions. These complementary metrics, together with corresponding confusion matrix, are reported in Supplementary Table S2 and Supplementary Fig. S1 . We recorded the average computation time for processing an OCT with PLUME-OCT, and calculated the total time for processing all images. To improve signal clarity and contrast, and to reveal noise in lower-quality images, we individually normalised each A-scan [ 26 ]. This normalisation involved linearly scaling the pixel intensities to a range of 0–1. Specifically, each A-scan was divided by its peak-to-peak value after subtracting its minimum intensity. To evaluate misalignment between consecutive B-scans within an OCT C-Scan, we employed the Phase-Only Correlation (POC) method [ 27 ]. This technique, widely used in image registration, leverages a 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) to measure phase similarity between a reference image and a target image, thereby providing pixel-wise offset information. To evaluate the phase similarity between consecutive B-scans, we constructed the POC Matrix. For this, each nth B-scan was designated as the reference image and compared to the (n+1) th B-scan as the target image. This process involved several steps: First, both reference and target B-scans were subjected to Hanning windowing (using the numpy.hanning function). Next, we applied a 2D DFT (using the scipy.fftpack.fft2 function) to each windowed image. The cross-phase spectrum was then calculated and a low-pass filter was applied to mitigate aliasing and noise. Finally, the inverse DFT of the cross-phase spectrum was computed, resulting in the POC Matrix, which reflects the phase similarity between consecutive B-scans. We defined the misalignment between consecutive B-scans as: (Eq. 1) m i s a l i g n m e n t B s c a n = | δ x | + | δ y | , Where δ x and δ y are the horizontal and vertical misalignments, respectively, obtained by identifying the peak location within the POC matrix and calculating the corresponding pixel displacement in each direction. This approach was preferred over calculating the Euclidean distance to provide a straightforward measure of cumulative displacement, capturing total misalignment along both axes and simplifying downstream correction calculations. We assessed the quality of an OCT cube (C-Scan) by calculating the cumulative misalignment of its constituent B-scans, which we defined as the total displacement score of the C-Scan. This score was derived by integrating the misalignment landscape, a curve where peaks represent misalignments between individual B-scans (as illustrated in Fig. 3 ): (Eq. 2) t o t a l d i s p l a c e m e n t m m = x f a c t o r · y f a c t o r m m 2 / p x 2 z f a c t o r s m m / p x · ∑ m i s a l i g n m e n t p e a k s p x , Here, x f a c t o r and y f a c t o r convert pixel displacement in the horizontal and vertical directions into millimetres, while z f a c t o r s converts the B-scan index spacing into millimetres, ensuring that the cumulative displacement integrates misalignment across the full 3D volume. Additionally, we provided an option to adjust the misalignment score for each B-scan by weighing it with a Gaussian function centred on the middle of the C-Scan: (Eq. 3) s p a t i a l l y w e i g h t e d d i s p l a c e m e n t = ∑ m i s a l i g n m e n t p e a k s · g a u s s i a n . This weighting approach accounted for the increased medical and biological importance of the central region of the retina, particularly the fovea, which is essential for sharp central vision compared to peripheral areas. The parameters of the Gaussian function were adjusted to emphasise this central weighting. The current scoring system is specific to this use case and can be adjusted if needed: PLUME-OCT is open source, allowing users to develop customised displacement scores tailored to their specific needs (see Discussion). Based on these definitions, a high-quality OCT scan was characterised by low displacement scores, while a low-quality OCT scan exhibited high displacement scores. We estimated the SNR in decibels (dB) using a “two-region” approach [ 28 , 29 ] as: (Eq. 4) S N R [ d B ] = k · log 10 ( m e a n ( S i g n a l R e g i o n ) s t d ( N o i s e R e g i o n ) ) , where the S i g n a l R e g i o n defines the area of the image with the 20 % of horizontal lines with highest pixel intensity, which consistently corresponds to the highly reflective photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) layers in OCT scans [ 26 ]. he N o i s e R e g i o n is denoted by the 20 % of horizontal lines with lowest intensity, typically representing the vitreous cavity or background, which contains minimal tissue reflectivity and is dominated by system noise (as shown in Fig. 2 ). k is a scaling factor set to 20 for imaging applications to convert the amplitude ratio of pixel intensity into dB, following standard practice for root-power quantities. To obtain a single SNR value per OCT C-Scan, we averaged the SNRs of all individual B-scans. To generate a 2D en-face visualisation of the information contained within an OCT cube (C-Scan), we performed an en-face reconstruction by projecting each B-scan. This was achieved by averaging pixel intensities along the axial dimension of each image and normalising the result to match the shape of the acquisition, typically a square. In the study datasets, high-quality OCTs were expected to display discernible retinal vessels. To qualitatively evaluate the performance of PLUME-OCT in assessing misalignment between B-scans, we displayed the misalignment landscape alongside the en-face reconstruction (as shown in Fig. 3 ). Unlike anatomical en-face projections used for retinal layer or choroidal analysis, this projection was not intended to delineate specific tissue interfaces (e.g., retinal-choroidal boundary). Instead, it served only to qualitatively illustrate discontinuities caused by B-scan misalignment—visible as breaks in vascular structures or bands (see Fig. 3 ). Although more sophisticated slab-based reconstructions can enhance structural detail, this approach provides sufficient contrast to visually convey inter-slice incoherence, which was its sole purpose in this study. We validated the metrics generated by PLUME-OCT by comparing its displacement scores with human annotations of B-scan alignment. Specifically, we assessed the correspondence between alignment assessments made by human annotators, who classified each B-scan as either aligned or misaligned, and the displacement scores produced by PLUME-OCT. To quantify agreement, we used the F1 score, which evaluates consistency in binary classifications of B-scan alignment. B-scan misalignments were categorised into four groups based on misalignment magnitude: small (<5 pixels), medium (5–10 pixels), medium-large (10–25 pixels), and large (>25 pixels). We calculated the F1 scores for each displacement category, reporting the means and standard deviations. In addition, to assess the complementary value of PLUME-OCT's metrics, we compared the total displacement score with the classical SNR by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient between these two metrics. To demonstrate the ability of PLUME-OCT QC to enhance statistical power in the analysis of biomarkers from 3D biomedical datasets we leveraged genome-wide association studies (GWAS) as a downstream application sensitive to data quality. GWAS provides a powerful framework for assessing whether improved QC leads to enhanced statistical power because lower-quality OCT scans introduce noise into 3D biomarker measurements, which can obscure genetic signals: if QC effectively filters out low-quality data, the resulting biomarkers should yield stronger statistically significant associations with genetic variants, characterised by smaller p-values. To evaluate the impact of PLUME-OCT QC, we used genomic analysis as a case study. We assessed the impact of PLUME-OCT's QC on the statistical significance of signals derived from genomic analysis of 3D retinal biomarkers by comparing results with and without PLUME-OCT QC. The QC process was applied to the UK Biobank dataset (88,247 OCT scans), using a total displacement threshold of 1 mm and an SNR threshold of 10 dB. On average, PLUME-OCT required 6.3 s to process each C-scan, running on a computational node of the Swiss Ophthalmic Imaging Network [ 30 ] with 96 GB of RAM and 16 CPU cores. This computation time included image loading, calculation of total and spatially weighted displacement scores, SNR computation, and storage of the result. With parallelized implementation, processing the full dataset took 11 h and 7 min. Through the PLUME-OCT QC process, we excluded 5.1 % of the OCT scans. For the remaining scans, we extracted the thickness of six retinal layers [ 25 ] measured using the Discovery® software by RetinAI [ 31 ] and averaged the values across five distinct regions that we defined based on the ETDRS grid: the central region (i.e., the fovea), superior, inferior, nasal, and temporal regions. The rationale for averaging thicknesses across these regions lies in the distinct morphology and function of the retina in different areas. For example, retinal layers are naturally thinner in the central region, where photoreceptors are densely concentrated to support sharp central vision, compared to the thicker layers in more peripheral regions. Additionally, anatomical features such as the optic nerve head, which connects the retina to the brain, introduce asymmetries between the nasal and temporal regions. This process resulted in five biomarkers for each of the six retinal layers, calculated individually, leading to a total of 30 Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to examine the relationships between ocular biomarkers and common genetic variations, known as Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs), following methodologies established in previews large scale studies [ 32 , 33 ]. Given that GWAS analyses are highly sensitive to noise and artefacts, they served as a critical validation measure for the effectiveness of our QC method. To evaluate the impact of PLUME-OCT QC, we conducted statistical analyses by comparing the distribution of SNP p-values from GWAS performed with and without PLUME-OCT QC. A one-tailed paired t -test was used to assess differences, and Cohen's d was calculated to quantify the effect size. Furthermore, SNP-level statistics were aggregated to identify gene associations [ 34 ] and estimate total heritability [ 35 ]. A one-tailed paired t -test was again employed to determine whether PLUME-OCT QC significantly increased the number of statistically significant gene associations and the total heritability of the analysed traits.
