In this section, we compare the quality and robustness of the learned representations for various pre-training paradigms. First, standard SimCLR. Secondly, SimCLR + , where we train a model using classic SimCLR on a training set enriched with domain counterfactuals. Finally, CF-SimCLR combines SimCLR with our proposed counterfactual contrastive pair generation framework. We then repeat the same analysis for models pre-trained with the DINO objective, comparing DINO, CF-DINO and DINO + . Note that in SimCLR + (resp. DINO + ), counterfactuals and real images are not paired during the contrastive learning step; they are all considered as independent training samples. As such, SimCLR + /DINO + represent the common paradigm of simply enriching the training set with synthetic examples. In CF-SimCLR/CF-DINO, on the other hand, we systematically pair real images with their corresponding counterfactual for positive pair creation ( Fig. 1 ). We compare the effect of these three pretraining strategies on chest X-rays and mammograms. For chest X-rays, we evaluate the quality of the learned representations by assessing downstream performance on pneumonia detection. For mammography, we focus on the task of breast density prediction (important for risk modelling). Pre-training strategies are evaluated with linear probing (i.e. classifiers trained on top of frozen encoders) as well as full model finetuning (unfrozen encoders). Linear probes are best representative of the quality of learned representation during pre-training, as representations are unchanged during downstream training. However we also include the comparison with full model finetuning, as this is often the training paradigm of choice in practical scenarios. All models are finetuned with real data only, using a weighted cross-entropy loss. We evaluate the pre-trained encoders in two settings. First, we test the encoders on ID datasets, i.e. using the same data for pre-training, finetuning and testing. Secondly, encoders are evaluated on OOD datasets, i.e. where the model is finetuned/linear-probed and tested on data external to the pre-training data. Evaluation on external datasets is crucial to assess how counterfactual contrastive pretraining performs on unseen domains (outside of scanner distribution used for training the causal inference model). All encoders are pretrained on the full, unlabelled, PadChest and EMBED datasets. However, the main motivation for self-supervised pretraining is to increase robustness when only a limited amount of labelled data is available ( Azizi et al., 2023 ). Hence, we evaluate the encoders for varying amounts of annotated data. Specifically, we finetune (or linear-probe) the encoder using a pre-defined amount of labelled samples, and then evaluate the resulting classifier on a fixed test set. We repeat this process several times, varying the amount of labelled samples to assess the effect of pre-training in function of number of labelled samples available for training the downstream classifier, e.g. for PadChest, the number of labelled training samples varies from 3249 to 64,989. All our code is publicly available at . For each task, we compare downstream performance across various pretraining strategies, for each scanner, for both SimCLR ( Figs. 5 and 7 ) and DINO ( Figs. 9 and 11 ) objectives. Moreover, to help visualise performance differences across encoders, we report the performance differences between the proposed encoders and the baseline in Figs. 6, 8, 10 and 12 . First, we focus on comparing counterfactual contrastive strategies (CF-SimCLR, CF-DINO) versus standard contrastive learning (SimCLR, DINO) to assess whether our cross-domain contrastive pair improve downstream performance across various domains. First, we focus on comparing counterfactual contrastive strategies (CF-SimCLR, CF-DINO) versus standard contrastive learning (SimCLR, DINO) to assess whether our cross-domain contrastive pair improve downstream performance across various domains (i.e. orange versus blue in Figs. 5 and 7 and orange bars in Figs. 6 and 8 ). We will compare CF-SimCLR with SimCLR + in the next section. Results on pneumonia detection, in Fig. 5 , show that CF-SimCLR outperforms the SimCLR baseline (orange versus blue), across datasets, irrespective of the amount of labels, with improvements particularly striking for linear probing. Gains can be best observed on the performance difference plots in Fig. 6 , where we observe that in all settings the performance difference compared to the SimCLR baseline is positive, i.e. CF-SimCLR performs better than SimCLR. For example, for linear probing, on PadChest, when using 3249 training samples for training the Pneumonia classifier, the performance improves by 2.5% on the Imaging scanner from PadChest and 0.6% ROC-AUC on the Phillips scanner. On CheXpert, performance gains vary between 1% and 2% compared to the baseline with linear probing. Mammography results in Fig. 8 show that CF-SimCLR consistently outperforms the SimCLR baseline across most ID scanners for both linear probing and finetuning, particularly when the amount of labelled data is limited ( < 20k). On the external VinDR dataset, CF-SimCLR beats both baselines on both scanners in the low data regime. CF-SimCLR pretraining mainly benefits scanners under-represented in the training set (all except Selenia Dimensions for EMBED and PlanMed Nuance for VinDr), regardless of the amount of labelled data. For example, in linear probing, for EMBED, with 2230 labelled samples, performance increases by 3% on Clearview CSM, 0.7% on Lorad Selenia, 1.3% on Pristina when comparing CF-SimCLR with SimCLR. Importantly, CF-SimCLR benefits the OOD scanners as well, in particular VinDR, where improvements range between 4%–6% ROCAUC compared to SimCLR when using 560–1121 labelled samples. For higher levels of labels, the differences between encoders slowly vanish, particularly in finetuning settings. This is expected as starting representations matter less if many labels are available for training the classifier, during which learned representations may be substantially updated (in full model finetuning). For both modalities, the improvement on external datasets is particularly worth highlighting, given that the encoder was not exposed to these external domains during pretraining (nor during counterfactual generation). Crucially, performance improvements and increased robustness to acquisition shift equally hold for encoders trained with the DINO-v2 objective, demonstrating the versatility of the proposed method. In Figs. 9 and 10 , we can see that CF-DINO outperforms DINO for all EMBED scanners, across all levels of labels, for both linear probing and full model finetuning. Interestingly, on this dataset, we note that, for most scanners, the performance improvements between CF-DINO and DINO are even larger than between CF-SimCLR and SimCLR. Again, the gains mostly affect scanners under-represented during training with CF-DINO closing the performance gap between the majority scanner (Selenia Dimensions) and the other scanners ( Fig. 9 ). For linear probes, in Fig. 10 , we note that the improvement for low levels of labels ( < 20k) are substantial for some under-represented scanners on EMBED: on Senograph 2000D (resp. Clearview CSm) we see a 4% (resp. 2.8%) improvement with 2223 labelled samples and 2% (resp. 1%) with 11,154 labels. On Lorad Selenia, improvements vary between 1% and 1.5% when training with up to 55k samples, whereas on Senographe Pristina, we observe 1% improvements with 2223 labelled samples and 2% improvements for all other levels of labels. For VinDR, as for CF-SimCLR, performance improvements are mostly noticeable for the minority scanner PlanMed nuance, where performance gains are 5% for 560 labels, 6% for 1121 labels and 2% for 2803 labels, with gains vanishing for 11,212 labels (where all encoders perform equally). For finetuning, performance gains are mostly observed for low levels of labels and under-represented scanners (bottom two rows in Fig. 10 ). For chest X-rays, in Figs. 11 and 12 , we can see that training with CF-DINO closes the performance gap between both PadChest scanners for both linear probing evaluation and finetuning. Indeed, without CF-DINO, there is a substantial performance drop from Phillips images to Imaging images, whereas this gap is much smaller with performance improving substantially with CF-DINO across all levels of labels for images from Imaging ( Fig. 11 ). Similarly, in Fig. 12 , we observed that CF-DINO outperforms DINO on the external RSNA Pneumonia dataset by a substantial margin 2% with 863 labelled samples, 3.5% with 2158 labels and 1.1% with the full training set with linear probe, and improvements varying from 1 to 2% in finetuning as well. For CheXpert, CF-DINO outperforms DINO in model finetuning (and linear probing with 10% of labels). However, it slightly underperforms on the 25% and 100% for linear probing. Note that results on the CheXpert dataset are to be interpreted with some caution as labels are NLP sourced and, in general, of rather low quality ( Irvin et al., 2019 ), which may explain the consequent drop of performance for all models between CheXpert and the expert-labelled RSNA Pneumonia dataset. We have shown that the models trained with counterfactual contrastive learning outperform models trained with standard contrastive pairs. However, it is important to note that models trained with CF-SimCLR (resp. CF-DINO), are exposed to additional (synthetic) data during training. Hence, in this section, to isolate the effect of the ‘smart pair creation’ proposed in this work, we compare it to another baseline, SimCLR + (resp. DINO + ), where we use the same extended training set but where generated samples are considered as independent samples and are not paired with real images during training, details can be found in Section 3.2 . Differences between CF-SimCLR and SimCLR + are best observed in Figs. 6 and 8 (resp. Figs. 10 and 12 for CF-DINO versus DINO + ). Overall, CF-SimCLR outperformed SimCLR + consistently across all experimental settings ( Figs. 8 and 10 ), with similar results for CF-DINO. On mammography, CF-SimCLR/ outperformed SimCLR/DINO + across all EMBED datasets. CF-SimCLR consistently also outperforms SimCLR + on VinDr, while CF-DINO/DINO + perform similarly on VinDR. On chest X-rays, in Fig. 6 , CF-SimCLR consistently outperforms SimCLR + across all settings. In Fig. 12 , CF-DINO outperformed DINO + by a large margin on PadChest and RSNA Pneumonia for linear probing, and both performed similarly for model finetuning. We especially noticed that the performance gains of SimCLR + (resp. DINO + ) over SimCLR were not very stable, improving for some domains while performing on par with standard SimCLR (resp. DINO) for others. In general, the counterfactual contrastive approaches offered much more consistent performance improvements. The starkest differences were observed on scanners under-represented during training (see Fig. 8 ). These experimental results align with the theoretical benefits of counterfactual contrastive learning: by explicitly creating realistic cross-domain positive pairs during training, we directly encourage the network to create domain-agnostic image representations. The more domain-agnostic image representations are, the bigger the expected improvement in terms of robustness to acquisition shift. Such an increase in robustness leads to higher performance on devices under-represented during training, even more so in limited data settings. The increase in domain alignment is directly visible in the t-SNE plots of feature embeddings in Fig. 13 , where embeddings of mammography models trained with SimCLR and SimCLR + exhibit clear domain clustering, whereas the model trained with CF-SimCLR generate embeddings where domains are less separated. To further assess the domain separability of the features from those encoders, we train a scanner classifier on the features from each classifier. To reduce scanner-imbalance during training of the scanner classifier, we randomly select 1000 images from the test set for each scanner (except for Senographe Pristina where we only had 101 test images), and extract corresponding features with each encoder. We then run 5-fold cross-validation, classifying scanners from the features of each pretrained model, using PCA (with 16 components) followed by logistic regression. Our results show that SimCLR and SimCLR+ achieve the same domain classification performance of 85% and 87% balanced accuracy, on the contrary CF-SimCLR only achieves 68% balanced accuracy, confirming that CF-SimCLR significantly reduces scanner separability in feature space. To implement counterfactual contrastive learning, we need to train an additional causal image generation model, this raises the question of computational overhead. Fortunately, the HVAE used here to generate image counterfactuals is relatively lightweight (as opposed to alternative generative approaches such as diffusion models). This HVAE not only trains relatively fast (e.g. only 20 epochs needed for EMBED, about 250k steps), it is also relatively frugal in terms of VRAM requirements (20 GB of GPU VRAM were sufficient), which has the advantage of low hardware requirements. In terms of generation speed, we were able to generate over 1 million 224 × 224 mammography images in under 7 h (on an NVIDIA RTX-3090 GPU). These computational requirements need to be put in perspective compared to the requirements of the contrastive pretraining step. Contrastive pretraining is resource intensive both in terms of VRAM (large batch sizes) and in terms of training time. Each SimCLR model was trained for 450 epochs for EMBED (resp. 1000 epochs for PadChest), and required 2 × 46 GB VRAM. For DINO, memory requirements were even higher (6 × 46 GB VRAM for a batch size of 300). The overhead of the counterfactual generation part is negligible, and its benefits clearly outweigh the added computational costs. In this section, we aim to assess the effect of the counterfactual image generation model quality on the downstream performance of the proposed counterfactual contrastive objective. To this end, we here compare three counterfactual image generation models, trained on EMBED: • HVAE - : an HVAE-based counterfactual image generation as per Ribeiro et al. (2023) trained for one epoch only (13k steps). • HVAE : the HVAE used in the experiment so far, trained for 20 epochs, without counterfactual finetuning. • HVAE + FT : where we additionally add the counterfactual finetuning step, as proposed by Ribeiro et al. (2023) , to the HVAE model. This step allows for improved effectiveness by further finetuning the counterfactual generation models using guidance from external classifiers. HVAE - : an HVAE-based counterfactual image generation as per Ribeiro et al. (2023) trained for one epoch only (13k steps). HVAE : the HVAE used in the experiment so far, trained for 20 epochs, without counterfactual finetuning. HVAE + FT : where we additionally add the counterfactual finetuning step, as proposed by Ribeiro et al. (2023) , to the HVAE model. This step allows for improved effectiveness by further finetuning the counterfactual generation models using guidance from external classifiers. First, we assess counterfactual quality for all three models using the metrics proposed in Monteiro et al. (2022) . Results in Fig. 14 show that effectiveness varies strongly across models, especially for scanners under-represented in the training set (e.g. Senographe Pristina). Moreover, results in Table 2 show that while effectiveness varies strongly across the compared models, reversibility and composition are strong for all models, indicating that all models preserve identity well. This can also be seen in the qualitative examples in Fig. 15 . Strong semantic identity preservation is key for creating meaningful contrastive pairs, as the network will consider any changes across views in a positive pair as non-semantic information to disregard. Besides computational considerations, this further motivates the use of the HVAE counterfactual approach in this study, over, for example, diffusion-based counterfactual generation approaches as diffusion models have been shown to not always preserve identity well ( Preechakul et al., 2022; Mokady et al., 2023 ). In Fig. 16 , we compare the downstream performance of the three CF-SimCLR encoders trained using generated counterfactuals from the three counterfactual generation models analysed above: HVAE - , HVAE and HVAE + FT. The graphs depict differences in ROC performance compared to the SimCLR baseline (i.e. no counterfactuals) across several levels on labels and scanners. These results first show that even when using a model with relatively low effectiveness, CF-SimCLR with HVAE - is either on par with or outperforms the baseline (positive performance differences), especially on under-represented scanners and for lower levels of labels. However, as effectiveness increases, the downstream performance for under-represented scanners tends to increase. We can see that the effectiveness of the HVAE model is substantially better compared to the HVAE - model for generating Lorad Selenia (＋30%) and Senographe Pristina (＋70%) counterfactuals. Further improving effectiveness with counterfactual finetuning (i.e. HVAE + FT) leads to striking improvements in the most under-represented scanner Senograph Pristina (where effectiveness increases by 60% between HVAE and HVAE + FT). On this scanner, we see improvements of 4%, 2%, 0.5% and 1.8% ROC-AUC between CF-SimCLR with HVAE and CF-SimCLR with HVAE + FT across the various levels of labels, while also observing noticeable improvements on ID Lorad Selenia and the OOD VinDr Mammomat scanner. However, we also do notice somewhat diminishing returns of effectiveness improvements, where performance on ClearviewCSM, for example, is not substantially changing between CF-SimCLR with HVAE - , HVAEand HVAE + FT despite effectiveness improving from 85% to 97%, with similar results observed on Senograph 2000D where increase in effectiveness did not help to improve downstream performance. Results indicate that a scanner effectiveness above 80% is satisfactory for CF-SimCLR. The main focus of this work is to improve robustness to acquisition shift. However, by simply changing the types of generated counterfactuals, the counterfactual contrastive pair generation framework can be easily extended to other distribution shifts. For example, we may use the same framework to increase robustness to population shift, improving the performance of under-performing subgroups. We illustrate this on chest radiography in Fig. 17 , where we generate sex counterfactuals instead of domain counterfactuals in the positive pair creation step, aiming to reduce performance disparities between the ‘male’ and ‘female’ subgroups. We can see that the baseline approach (SimCLR) performs sub-optimally on female patients for pneumonia detection across all datasets (top row in Fig. 17 ). Using cross-subgroup counterfactuals positive pairs by intervening on biological sex, we observe performance improvements across subgroups in all datasets and for most levels of training labels. For example, on PadChest we observe an improvement of 2% ROC-AUC with 3249 labelled samples for females compared to the SimCLR baseline (resp. 1% with 16 247 labels). On CheXpert, we also get + 5% ROC-AUC with 1381 labelled samples, and + 3% with 3452 labels. For PadChest and CheXpert, we even observe small performance improvements on the male subgroup. On RSNA however, while Sex-CFSimCLR successfully reduces the performance gap across both groups (bottom row), this here comes at the cost of a slight performance reduction in the male subgroup (top row), a phenomenon commonly known as the ‘levelling down’ effect in the fairness literature ( Zietlow et al., 2022 ). Overall, analysing performance differences across subgroups (bottom row in Fig. 17 ), we notice that Sex-SimCLR yields a consistent reduction in performance disparities across all datasets. Like in previous experiments, we notice that performance improvements are most notable in settings where it is most beneficial to have aligned representations across subgroups: in limited label settings and for the underperforming subgroups. In this work, we present counterfactual contrastive learning , a novel contrastive pair generation framework enhancing the robustness of contrastively-learned image representations to domain shifts. Evaluating across five datasets, two modalities and two clinically-relevant classification tasks, we show that the proposed counterfactual contrastive pretraining approach yields higher downstream performance than standard contrastive pretraining, improvements which are particularly noticeable for domains less represented in the training set. Moreover, the proposed counterfactual pair generation method is agnostic to the choice of the contrastive objective, as demonstrated by our experiments showing that counterfactual positive pair generation improves results for models using SimCLR as well as DINO-v2 objectives. Importantly, we show that CF-SimCLR (resp. CF-DINO) also improves performance on external domains, which are not included in the pretraining set compared to SimCLR (resp. DINO). Our experiment on subgroup counterfactual contrastive learning demonstrates its broader applicability beyond acquisition shifts. In general, improvements arising from counterfactual contrastive learning are most visible in settings where learning domain-aligned representations presents a strong advantage over having domain-clustered representations (as learned in standard SimCLR). This is notably the case for scanners under-represented during finetuning, and in settings with limited label availability, where insufficient data is present to learn a ‘scanner-wise’ decision boundary. Conversely, when a large amount of labels is available for model finetuning (e.g. up to 223k labelled samples on EMBED and 65k on PadChest), all pre-training strategies often converge to similar performance. This is explained by the fact that, with high amounts of labels, the benefit of domain-aligned representations is reduced as enough data is present at finetuning time to learn meaningful decision boundaries for each scanner, even if representations are clustered per domain. Moreover, it is important to highlight that, in the case of full model finetuning, representations may change substantially over the pre-trained representations, further explaining why downstream performance differences are often more visible in linear probing experiments. However, it is important to highlight that the counterfactual contrastive objective performs consistently either better or, depending on the number of labels, on par with existing baselines. Naturally, gains arising from counterfactual contrastive learning are bounded by the ability to generate realistic domain changes. Generated counterfactuals must be of sufficient quality to capture the variation relevant for pre-training faithfully. Our results demonstrate that current counterfactual image generation models can already produce images of sufficient quality to significantly improve learned representation over the baseline approaches. Importantly, results in our ablation study in Section 5.4 show that even when the effectiveness of the counterfactual image generation model is moderate, CF-SimCLR remains on par with, or still outperforms the SimCLR baseline. However, as effectiveness increases, the performance on particularly under-represented scanners can substantially increase (e.g. CF-SimCLR with HVAE + FT on the Pristina scanner). As image synthesis models continue to improve, we may expect further improvements with counterfactual contrastive learning in future works. Importantly, the choice of the intervention variable in the counterfactual image generation step depends on which types of shifts downstream models should be robust against. In the main experiments (Section 5.1 ), where the goal was to achieve scanner robustness, we intervened on the scanner variable. In the experiment in Section 5.5 , the goal was to be robust against gender shift. Hence, we generated sex counterfactuals. A combination of multiple variables could also be considered in future work. In practice, we can summarise the process to determine which variables to intervene on, as follows: 1. First, an in-depth data analysis should be performed to determine likely causes of biases and subgroup disparities, and to determine which variable the downstream representations should be robust to, i.e. should ignore. 2. The set of identified variables in step 1, should then be discussed with domain experts to decide which variables downstream models should be robust against, and whether any interactions between these variables should be considered in the causal graph used to generate the counterfactuals. 3. Train the counterfactual generation model with the previously identified causal graph. 4. Use the generated counterfactuals to create cross-domain pairs in the counterfactual contrastive framework, with interventions randomly sampled among all possible values when sampling positive pairs. First, an in-depth data analysis should be performed to determine likely causes of biases and subgroup disparities, and to determine which variable the downstream representations should be robust to, i.e. should ignore. The set of identified variables in step 1, should then be discussed with domain experts to decide which variables downstream models should be robust against, and whether any interactions between these variables should be considered in the causal graph used to generate the counterfactuals. Train the counterfactual generation model with the previously identified causal graph. Use the generated counterfactuals to create cross-domain pairs in the counterfactual contrastive framework, with interventions randomly sampled among all possible values when sampling positive pairs. Note that our proposed approach is compatible with other generative-based augmentation methods, such as generating additional images for under-represented classes or subgroups ( Ktena et al., 2023; Khosravi et al., 2024 ), as we can also apply the counterfactual generation to synthetic images. Our experiments comparing SimCLR + with CF-SimCLR show that the proposed approach has benefits beyond complementing the training set with synthetic data and that the proposed counterfactual pair generation framework fundamentally changes the organisation of the embedding space ( Fig. 13 ), as such it may complement other approaches to enhance training set diversity. data.text: Scalable Clinical Annotation with Location Evidence (SCALE) Deep learning can mitigate the global radiologist shortage but its development requires large-scale annotated datasets. This study introduces SCALE (Scalable Clinical Annotation with Location Evidence), a fully automated method for generating voxel-level annotations. It uses location priors that are automatically extracted from medical reports, tracked biopsy coordinates, or provided anatomical sectors. We annotated a large-scale dataset comprising 17 896 cases from 16 562 patients across 24 hospitals in 10 countries and 2 continents, using both SCALE and a count-based weakly semisupervised learning (CWSSL) method. An optimized algorithm was developed and trained on these datasets. Evaluation with 1561 cases from 1561 patients across 19 hospitals in 3 countries and 1 continent showed the superiority of the model trained on the dataset with SCALE annotations, achieving a case-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.856. This is ＋0.012 compared to supervised learning ( p = 0 . 02 ), ＋0.007 compared to training with CWSSL ( p = 0 . 12 ), and ＋0.006 compared to the Prostate Imaging: Cancer AI (PI-CAI) Ensemble AI System. These results demonstrate that automated, location-guided annotation enables scalable development of AI for clinically significant prostate cancer detection on MRI, surpassing previous methods, and paving the way for broader clinical deployment. It uses location priors that are automatically extracted from medical reports, tracked biopsy coordinates, or provided anatomical sectors. We annotated a large-scale dataset comprising 17 896 cases from 16 562 patients across 24 hospitals in 10 countries and 2 continents, using both SCALE and a count-based weakly semisupervised learning (CWSSL) method. Evaluation with 1561 cases from 1561 patients across 19 hospitals in 3 countries and 1 continent showed the superiority of the model trained on the dataset with SCALE annotations, achieving a case-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.856. This is ＋0.012 compared to supervised learning ( p = 0 . 02 ), ＋0.007 compared to training with CWSSL ( p = 0 . 12 ), and ＋0.006 compared to the Prostate Imaging: Cancer AI (PI-CAI) Ensemble AI System. Expert-level artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have significant potential to enhance healthcare quality and reduce clinical workloads [1–3] . This capability is particularly valuable in response to the increasing global demand for medical imaging [4,5] . Developing AI models that perform at an expert level requires extensive, high-quality annotated datasets [6–8] . In applications such as cancer detection, localized annotations within the medical scan are critical, substantially raising the annotation burden. Weakly semisupervised learning methods offer a cost-effective solution by inferring voxel-level labels from coarser, case-level annotations [9–13] . For detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) using MRI, previous research has employed the count of radiologically suspected csPCa lesions as case-level guidance [9] . The recent PI-CAI (Prostate Imaging—Cancer Artificial Intelligence) challenge provided AI-derived annotations guided by the number of histopathologically confirmed csPCa lesions, an approach adopted by each of the top five teams participating in the challenge [14] . Incorporating location information has been shown to enhance AI-derived annotation accuracy for radiologically suspected lesions [15] , but its utility for histopathologically confirmed lesions has yet to be investigated. Radiologically suspicious csPCa lesions typically undergo biopsy for histopathological confirmation of cancer aggressiveness. A recent large-scale reader study involving 62 radiologists reported an average precision (positive predictive value) of 53.2% when using the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) version 2.1 ≥ 3 threshold [16] . This means that almost half of the cases deemed suspicious by the radiology read do not harbor csPCa, underscoring the importance of integrating histopathological confirmation into the annotations process. This study investigates whether incorporating location information can improve AI-derived annotations for histopathologically confirmed csPCa lesions. Histopathological evaluations typically present location information either using anatomical descriptors (e.g., left/right, anterior/posterior) or by referencing specific radiological findings (e.g., “the PI-RADS 5 lesion”). Manually extracting precise lesion locations from clinical reports – which often involves correlating pathology with radiology findings – is labor-intensive and requires domain knowledge. To automate this process, we developed a pipeline utilizing large language models (LLMs) to extract lesion location information directly from clinical reports. We then incorporated this extracted information into a novel framework designed to generate AI-based annotations with location priors. Additionally, to facilitate generalizable location-guided annotation generation, our method also supports annotations derived from manually extracted anatomical sectors or tracked biopsy coordinates. This study retrospectively utilized axial biparametric MRI scans of the prostate (T2-weighted, high b-value diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI, b ≥ 1000 s/mm 2 ], and apparent diffusion coefficient [ADC] map) for prostate cancer detection. For development, 17 896 cases (16 562 patients) from 23 European sites and 1 United States site (10 countries, 2 continents) were included. These cases originate from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Dataset [14] , ProstateNet [17] , Antoni van Leeuwenhoek (AvL) Hospital, and University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) [18] . Informed consent was waived, given the retrospective scientific use of deidentified patient data. For evaluation, 1561 cases (1561 patients) from 19 European sites (3 countries) were included, of which 758 cases (758 patients) from 12 European sites (2 countries) were external to the development set. These cases originate from the PI-CAI Testing Dataset [14] and the PROMIS Dataset [19] . An overview of the hospitals included in these datasets is provided in Table 1 . To characterize acquisition heterogeneity, we provide Supplementary Note 8, detailing vendor and scanner distributions, field strength (74% at 3 T), and broad variability in T2-weighted, ADC, and high-b DWI parameters (Tables 8–10; Figures 24–44). For each dataset, the reference standard for positive cases was set by histopathology, with csPCa defined as ISUP 2–5 (intermediate to very high risk) [20] , later also referred to as ‘malignant’. For development, the reference standard of negative cases was set by either negative histopathology (ISUP ≤ 1) or negative MRI (PI-RADS ≤ 2). For evaluation, the reference standard of negative cases was set by at least 3 years of negative follow-up for 1000 cases [14] , or by a negative template mapping biopsy (a core every 5 mm) outcome for the remaining 561 cases [19] . Manual voxel-level annotations were performed for 1166 malignant cases (1164 patients) out of the 2055 malignant cases (2052 patients) from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set. Additionally, all 1000 cases (1000 patients) from the PI-CAI Testing Set were manually annotated. Annotations were done in 3D in the MRI scans, based on the diagnostic radiology and pathology reports. ITK-SNAP v3.80 was used for lesion delineation, and manual rigid registration (six degrees of freedom) was performed for cases with significant inter-sequence misalignment. Annotations were created by one of ten trained investigators or one radiology resident, supervised by one of three expert radiologists from Radboudumc, Prostaat Centrum Noord Nederland, and St. Olavs Hospital. Standardized imaging protocols were used to reduce variability, ensuring high-quality annotations. Patient characteristics are provided in Table 2 . Inclusion and exclusion STARD diagrams are shown in Supplementary Note 6. We developed Scalable Clinical Annotation with Location Evidence (SCALE), a fully automated method to generate voxel-level annotations for csPCa detection on MRI, guided by histopathological location priors. SCALE utilizes three types of location evidence: (1) anatomical descriptors automatically extracted from radiology and pathology reports using a cascade of LLM steps, (2) prostate map sectors manually derived from the radiology and pathology reports with the option to consult the imaging, and (3) tracked biopsy coordinates. The automatic extraction of anatomical descriptors is described in Section 2.7 . For each histopathologically confirmed csPCa lesion, a voxel-level location prior was created based on the available evidence. Location information from radiology and pathology reports included anatomical descriptors such as left/right, apex/mid/base, and peripheral/transition zone. These descriptors were translated into voxel-level priors using an automated procedure involving a zonal segmentation of the prostate gland. Specifically, the prostate segmentation was divided into anatomical sectors according to standardized definitions: left/right was defined by the median sagittal plane, anterior/posterior by the median coronal plane, apex/mid/base by dividing the prostate into equal thirds along the axial plane, and lateral/medial by dividing the gland into central and peripheral sections. Clock-face direction (e.g., location as 9 o’clock) was incorporated by further subdividing the voxel-based prior into 12 wedge-shaped regions, each spanning 30 degrees. Tracked biopsy coordinates were used to generate precise priors for the UCLA dataset. Each biopsy trajectory was converted into a cylindrical region with a 10 mm radius, extended by 10 mm at both ends beyond the start and end points. Following the creation of voxel-level priors, SCALE automatically matches each prior to the most likely lesion candidate within the MRI scan ( Fig. 1 ). Lesion candidates were generated by the fully supervised algorithm. To identify the optimal match among multiple potential candidates, we defined an evidence score calculated as the product of lesion probability (confidence) and the number of overlapping voxels within the location prior. The lesion candidate with the highest evidence score is selected, and the entire lesion is annotated, including any portions extending beyond the prior region’s boundaries. If there is no overlap between a location prior and any lesion candidates, either (1) the entire case is excluded in the strict version of SCALE, or (2) the location prior is disregarded (with no annotation applied) in the full version of SCALE, and the user is notified accordingly. The efficacy of the AI-derived annotations was evaluated by generating annotations for the manually annotated subset of the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set [14] , and by training csPCa detection models using datasets in which the unlabeled cases were annotated with the AI-derived labels. Annotations generated by SCALE incorporated location priors derived from three sources. Automatic extraction from reports was performed for datasets where the reports were available at the central coordinating center of this study, which was the case for cases from Radboudumc, Ziekenhuisgroep Twente and AvL. For the ProstateNet dataset [17] , only the anatomical sectors manually extracted by trained annotators were available. For the dataset from UCLA [18] , tracked biopsy coordinates were available, which provide precise and objective location priors directly from the biopsy procedures. To ensure comparability, all experimental conditions employed the same deep learning architecture, training pipeline, and hyperparameter settings. The training algorithm is detailed in Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Note 2, and Supplementary Note 3. Independent models were trained separately for each annotation condition. Model performance was evaluated on the predefined independent evaluation dataset comprising 1561 cases, including 758 external evaluation cases. All evaluations were performed using manual annotations as the reference standard, no AI-derived annotations were used for evaluation. The primary performance metric was case-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Additional metrics, including sensitivity and specificity at clinically-relevant operating points, were computed to comprehensively assess model performance. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed SCALE method, we compared an algorithm trained with SCALE annotations against three baselines: a fully supervised algorithm, an algorithm trained using the previous state-of-the-art weakly semisupervised learning method incorporating pathology outcomes [9,14] , and the PI-CAI-1 algorithm, previously published as the PI-CAI ensemble AI system [14] . We did not adapt pathology-oriented location/registration-guided weak-supervision methods [10–13] , as fair comparison on 3D MRI would require non-trivial redesign beyond this paper’s scope. The fully supervised algorithm was trained using 8192 cases (7206 patients) with manual voxel-level annotations from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set. The count-based weakly semisupervised learning (CWSSL) method leverages the number of clinically significant lesions ( n sig ) to guide AI-derived label generation [9] . Lesion count information directly guides AI-derived label generation by iteratively selecting the n sig most likely lesion candidates from the predicted cancer detection map. The detection maps were generated by the fully supervised algorithm. If fewer than n sig lesion candidates are available, then either (1) the entire case is excluded in the strict version, or (2) all available lesion candidates are used in the full version, with the user notified accordingly. For the PI-CAI dataset, lesion counts were manually extracted from radiology and pathology reports with optional imaging consultation by trained annotators under expert supervision. For the AvL dataset, counts were automatically extracted using cascaded LLM steps described in Section 2.7 . In the UCLA dataset, counts were set to zero for negative cases, to one for cases with a single positive biopsy (ISUP ≥ 2), and cases with multiple positive biopsies were excluded. Cases with multiple positive biopsies were excluded because the number of positive lesions is then ambiguous, as biopsies can stem from the same or multiple lesions. Subsequently, this algorithm was trained with manual annotations from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set where available and the CWSSL annotations for the other cases. The PI-CAI-1 AI system is the ensemble of the top 5 submissions to the PI-CAI challenge. Each member algorithm was trained using the 9107 cases (8029 patients) from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set [14] . We used an optimized variant of the PI-CAI-1 AI system, referred to as the PI-CAI-2A algorithm, which builds upon the top-performing submission to the PI-CAI challenge (DataScientX, Guerbet Research, France) [14] . Several adaptations were introduced to improve efficiency, robustness, and compatibility with our larger, more heterogeneous dataset. These included cross-sequence registration, instance-wise ADC normalization, and the removal of components that offered limited diagnostic value. A full description of the algorithm and preprocessing steps is provided in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Note 2. T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted sequences are typically acquired in succession in 15–30 min, but patient movement and processes like bladder filling can lead to misalignment of the prostate between sequences [21] . To align these sequences, we developed a task-specific adaptation of the convexAdam deformable registration algorithm [22–24] . Using the standard convexAdam deformable registration output, we calculated the average displacement vector within the prostate gland and rounded this to full voxels in each direction. This integer-voxel translation registration preserves slice geometry and avoids interpolation artifacts, ensuring compatibility with csPCa detection models. Additional details are provided in Supplementary Note 3. To extract anatomical descriptors for ISUP ≥ 2 lesions, we employed a structured cascade of LLM steps using the LLM Extractinator Python module [25] . This module utilizes Ollama to locally host open-source LLMs and employs LangChain to build prompts and ensure consistent, structured outputs across diverse radiology and pathology reports. Lesion location descriptors were often embedded in pathology conclusions or referenced indirectly via radiological findings. Therefore, lesion-level information was extracted through cross-referencing reports, involving (1) Gleason scoring and anatomical descriptors from pathology, (2) PI-RADS scoring and location from radiology, and (3) linking of corresponding findings. The extracted descriptors were translated to English and mapped to standardized anatomical descriptors for integration into the SCALE pipeline. This multilingual, structured parsing approach enabled robust and scalable extraction of clinically relevant lesion information across institutions. By automating this step, we significantly reduced manual annotation workload, making the annotation process more scalable and applicable to hospitals regardless of local expertise or language. Model performance was compared across annotation strategies using a hierarchical statistical analysis plan, designed to control the family-wise type I error rate. Three algorithms were trained: (1) a fully supervised model using manual annotations only, (2) a semisupervised model using count-based AI-derived annotations, and (3) a semisupervised model using location-based SCALE AI-derived annotations. These were evaluated against each other and against the PI-CAI-1 AI system on multiple test sets, including the PI-CAI Hidden Testing Set [14] and the PROMIS trial [18] . The primary outcome was case-level diagnostic performance measured by AUROC. Statistical significance was assessed using permutation tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple comparisons. Further details are provided in the preregistered Statistical Analysis Plan, which was approved by an expert biostatistician [26] . A total of 17 896 development MRI examinations (16 562 patients) from 24 hospitals were included for development. Manual voxel-level annotations for csPCa were available for 1166 malignant cases. Automatic parsing of the radiology and pathology reports from the AvL hospital assigned 1184 cases to be benign, resulting in 11 901 benign cases (10 793 patients) in the development dataset. The remaining 4829 unannotated malignant cases (4808 patients) were used for voxel-level AI-derived annotation. SCALE and CWSSL automatic label generation can be performed for all cases, or with strict settings which excludes a case when the generated annotation is incomplete. The full generation was able to create an annotation for 4827/4829 (99.96%) cases for SCALE, and 4829/4829 (100%) cases for CWSSL. The strict generation created an annotation for 3764/4829 (77.95%) cases for SCALE, and 3860/4829 (79.93%) cases for CWSSL. STARD diagrams showing the number of generated or excluded cases per annotation method are provided in Supplementary Note 7. A breakdown of the number of lesions per case generated by the automatic annotation methods is provided in Supplementary Table 7. The strict versions of SCALE and CWSSL excluded 22.1% and 20.1% of malignant cases, respectively, resulting in over 16 000 examinations available for model training. Of the excluded cases, 447 were flagged by both methods, and 1253 were excluded by either, indicating a 35.67% overlap. Notably, 46.1% of cases excluded by CWSSL were also excluded by SCALE. If the exclusions had occurred independently, only 214 cases would be expected to overlap, suggesting that both methods tend to flag similar sources of uncertainty. The performance of the SCALE and CWSSL annotation methods was assessed using the manually annotated malignant cases from the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Set [14] . The lesion candidates for this evaluation were generated with the fully supervised algorithm using cross-validation. The results are shown in Table 3 . Multiple models were trained to compare the full and strict versions of the SCALE and CWSSL annotation methods and to identify the optimal nnU-Net configuration. As detailed in Supplementary Note 2, this process selected the algorithm trained with strict SCALE annotations and the one trained with full CWSSL annotations for further evaluation. An independent testing cohort of 1561 cases (1561 patients) from 19 hospitals was used for model testing. On the combined PI-CAI and PROMIS testing cohort, the SCALE model achieved the highest case-level AUROC of 0.856, and outperformed the fully supervised algorithm with statistical significance ( p = 0 . 024 ). The performance difference between the SCALE and CWSSL algorithms was not statistically significant ( p = 0 . 121 ), so no further statistical testing was performed, in concordance with the statistical analysis plan [26] . The performance of each algorithm on each testing dataset is shown in Table 4 . The assessment including lesion-level performance of each algorithm on the PI-CAI Test Set is provided in Table 5 . The receiver operating characteristic curves are shown in Fig. 2 . The performance of prostate radiologists was assessed by comparing diagnostic reads conducted during multidisciplinary practice to the strongest available reference standards. Positive cases were validated histopathologically, while negative cases were confirmed by either a minimum of 3 years of negative clinical follow-up (for 1000 cases [14] ) or negative outcomes from template mapping biopsies (for the remaining 561 cases [19] ). Using a threshold of PI-RADS ≥ 3 , these radiology reads demonstrated a sensitivity of 90.9% (95% CI 88.6%–93.1%) at a specificity of 62.2% (95% CI 59.1%–65.4%) on the combined PROMIS & PI-CAI test cohort. At the same sensitivity, the SCALE algorithm achieved a lower specificity of 51.4% (95% CI 39.0%–59.7%). As part of the PI-CAI study, a reader study involving a subset of 400 cases from the PI-CAI test set was conducted, in which 62 radiologists independently reviewed 100 cases each. At the PI-RADS 3 threshold, the radiologists achieved an average sensitivity of 89.4% (95% CI: 85.3%–92.9%) with a specificity of 57.7% (95% CI: 51.6%–63.3%). At matched sensitivity, the SCALE algorithm achieved a higher specificity of 74.6% (95% CI: 69.3%–79.8%) on this subset. Lesion-specific information was manually extracted from the radiology and pathology reports for all cases in the PI-CAI Public and Private Training Sets. For these cases the LLM extraction pipeline achieved ≥ 99 % accuracy in determining case positivity, had 97.0% concordance in the extracted PI-RADS scores, as evaluated on 3835 cases (3665 patients). A random 300-case audit of the Gleason score extraction predictions, yielded 98.7% (296/300) cases with correct lesion-level predictions. The four clinically meaningful errors were missed ISUP ≥ 2 lesions. A detailed performance breakdown is provided in Supplementary Note 4. An overview of how often each location descriptor was extracted for each of the datasets in this study is provided in Supplementary Note 5. Introducing the integer-voxel translation registration increased AUROC of the PI-CAI-1 algorithm from 0.792 to 0.802 (＋1.0%) on the PROMIS cohort, with four of five constituent models improving by 0.5 to 1.2% (Supplementary Table 3). Computational efficiency was substantially better for the PI-CAI-2A pipeline, reducing inference time by a factor of five (from 30.5 to 5.9 min per case on typical cloud computing hardware) and lowering GPU training requirements by an order of magnitude compared to the PI-CAI-1 pipeline. Additional details are provided in Supplementary Note 1. This study introduced SCALE, a fully automated method to generate voxel-level annotations for csPCa detection using MRI, guided by histopathologically-confirmed location priors. These priors, automatically extracted from radiology and pathology reports via advanced LLM parsing, tracked biopsy coordinates, or manually specified anatomical sectors, enabled substantial expansion of effectively annotated training data. The algorithm trained with SCALE annotations achieved superior diagnostic performance compared to traditional supervised training, and achieved higher performance compared to prostate radiologists in an independent reader study. Notably, substantial performance gains were observed on the heterogeneous PROMIS dataset, highlighting the enhanced generalizability achieved by training on the extended dataset with SCALE annotations. Algorithms were trained on multi-center data and tested across 19 sites. Together with Supplementary Note 8 documenting scanner and protocol variability, these results indicate improved robustness to distribution shifts in hardware and acquisition when training on the extended development dataset with SCALE annotations. Design choices such as integer-voxel translation registration and instance-wise ADC normalization addressed sequence misalignment and protocol scaling, supporting generalization without site-specific tuning. On PROMIS, training with SCALE increased AUROC by 2.0 to 2.6 percentage points versus alternatives. The AUROC equals the probability that a randomly selected csPCa case is ranked above a non-csPCa case, so the PROMIS gain corresponds to 2.0 to 2.6% more correctly ordered case–control pairs, i.e., improved ranking. Improved ranking can translate to fewer missed csPCa or fewer unnecessary biopsies, depending on threshold and use case. On PI-CAI, the change was − 0 . 4 to + 1 . 0 points. Notably, 81.3% of PI-CAI test cases originate from centers represented in PI-CAI-1 training, consistent with in-domain evaluation. The larger external gain on PROMIS indicates improved cross-site generalization, which is the relevant setting for deployment. Translating these improvements to patient outcomes depends on the deployment mode (e.g., triage, lesion proposals, second opinion, etc.) and requires a prospective study in which the AI output influences patient care, which is beyond this study’s scope. Related pathology studies report similar gains from weakly semisupervised learning. Automated Gleason grading with semi-automatic, report-derived labels [10] , registration-enhanced multiple-instance learning [11] , sparse patch annotation with teacher–student consistency [12] , and global-attention graph neural networks with collaborative pseudo-labels [13] convert weak spatial cues into fine-grained targets and improve accuracy with far less manual labeling. These results in whole slide imaging support SCALE’s central claim that location-guided auto-annotation is effective. The LLM-based report parsing demonstrated high reliability, achieving ≥ 99 % accuracy for identifying case positivity and ≥ 83 % accuracy for lesion-level score extraction. The relatively lower lesion-level accuracy can be partly attributed to ambiguities in lesion counting. For example, when systematic and targeted biopsies are close together they can be reported as a single lesion’s result or reported separately. Importantly, the SCALE annotation pipeline effectively mitigated these inconsistencies, ensuring stable and precise annotations. Using annotations that contain bias or errors can affect algorithm reliability. To validate whether SCALE annotations compromise the algorithm’s reliability, the csPCa detection models trained with these AI-derived annotations were evaluated on independent datasets with manual labels. This evaluation revealed improved performance, demonstrating that model performance was not compromised and the annotations were reliable. Moreover, SCALE inherently reduces bias by using histopathologically confirmed location priors, and potential bias in the lesion candidates is mitigated by integrating independent information sources (anatomical descriptors, prostate map sectors, or tracked biopsy coordinates) during annotation generation. Computational efficiency was improved by a factor of five for the PI-CAI-2A pipeline, compared to the PI-CAI-1 pipeline. These advancements substantially reduce environmental impact and resource demands, making expert-level diagnostic AI more accessible to small and mid-sized healthcare centers. Additionally, the newly developed integer-voxel translation registration method preserved voxel integrity by preventing interpolation artifacts, which boosted diagnostic performance. Addressing residual deformable misalignments represents a promising area for future enhancement, likely benefiting a minority subset of cases. Despite these achievements, our study has notable limitations. First, the impact of the manually annotated dataset size was not explicitly assessed. Prior literature demonstrated greater performance gains from automated annotations with smaller manually annotated datasets [9] , but this dynamic remains unexplored for SCALE. Second, lesion candidate generation relied on a supervised detection model, potentially limiting the accuracy compared to dedicated delineation approaches. This also requires an initial set of manual voxel-level annotations before AI-derived annotations can be generated for new cases. Third, both PI-CAI and PROMIS employ strict reference standard protocols: positives are histopathologically confirmed, while negatives require either ≥ 3 years of follow-up (PI-CAI) or dense template mapping biopsies (PROMIS). These reduce the risk of noisy labels, though some uncertainty from biopsy sampling and spatial registration may persist, likely leading to slight underestimation of model performance. Fourth, a quantitative ablation of the contribution of each location evidence type (LLM-parsed location descriptors, anatomical sectors, and biopsy coordinates) could not be performed. Each dataset provides only one form of location evidence, meaning that including or excluding a specific evidence type would inherently coincide with including or excluding a particular dataset. As a result, the observed performance differences cannot be attributed solely to the evidence type. Beyond generating annotations for new cases, SCALE has additional promising applications. Existing manual annotations can be refined using SCALE by using the manual annotations as location priors. Furthermore, SCALE is suitable for post-market surveillance by automatically tracking algorithm performance over time. This can be achieved by parsing the radiology and pathology reports to match the histopathology outcomes against the model predictions. Finally, the inherent adaptability of the SCALE methodology suggests considerable potential for broader clinical applications. Other diseases described using structured anatomical locations, such as liver segments or lung lobes, could benefit similarly from automated annotation workflows. In summary, SCALE offers a scalable, precise, and practical method for generating high-quality annotations, significantly advancing AI-driven diagnostics in medical imaging, and facilitating widespread deployment of expert-level AI capabilities. This study demonstrates that large-scale, fully automated, location-guided annotation is both feasible and improves downstream diagnostic performance for MRI-based detection of csPCa. When these labels were used to train an optimized, lightweight variant of the PI-CAI algorithm, the resulting model achieved a case-level AUROC of 0.856 on an independent, multi-center test cohort, outperforming a strong fully-supervised model trained on manual delineations (＋0.012, p = 0.02), and achieving higher performance compared to using the best prior weakly-supervised approach that ignored spatial information (＋0.007, p = 0.12), and the PI-CAI-1 AI System (＋0.006). The gains were most pronounced on the heterogeneous PROMIS trial, highlighting the ability of the model trained with SCALE annotations to generalize beyond the centers used for development. Joeran S. Signal-aware synthesis of tissue polarization uniformity from OCT images guided by an SNR-based heuristic Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is a powerful imaging modality that captures both structural and polarization-related tissue features, offering significant diagnostic value. Among these, the degree of polarization uniformity (DOPU) is critical for characterizing tissue microstructure. However, obtaining DOPU images typically requires specialized hardware and complex system configurations. To address this limitation, we propose a knowledge-guided deep generative framework, signal attention GAN (SA-GAN), to synthesize DOPU images directly from standard OCT intensity scans. SA-GAN integrates a signal-guided attention mechanism inspired by signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) principles, enabling selective focus on regions with meaningful polarization patterns while suppressing noise-dominated areas. This design allows for the generation of accurate, high-fidelity DOPU images without additional imaging hardware. We validated SA-GAN on three independent datasets: SKIN-PSOCT, CARTILAGE-PSOCT, and the public Retinal-OCT2017 dataset. On SKIN-PSOCT, SA-GAN achieved a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 97.8 % and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 28.6 dB. On CARTILAGE-PSOCT, it reached an SSIM of 93.9 % and a PSNR of 24.8 dB in cross-dataset testing. Applied to the Retinal-OCT2017 dataset, SA-GAN achieved state-of-the-art performance in a four-class retinal disease classification task. These results demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of our method. SA-GAN provides a cost-effective and practical solution to extend PS-OCT capabilities, supporting the development of intelligent imaging systems for biomedical diagnostics and digital medicine. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is a powerful imaging modality that captures both structural and polarization-related tissue features, offering significant diagnostic value. Among these, the degree of polarization uniformity (DOPU) is critical for characterizing tissue microstructure. However, obtaining DOPU images typically requires specialized hardware and complex system configurations. To address this limitation, we propose a knowledge-guided deep generative framework, signal attention GAN (SA-GAN), to synthesize DOPU images directly from standard OCT intensity scans. SA-GAN integrates a signal-guided attention mechanism inspired by signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) principles, enabling selective focus on regions with meaningful polarization patterns while suppressing noise-dominated areas. This design allows for the generation of accurate, high-fidelity DOPU images without additional imaging hardware. We validated SA-GAN on three independent datasets: SKIN-PSOCT, CARTILAGE-PSOCT, and the public Retinal-OCT2017 dataset. On SKIN-PSOCT, SA-GAN achieved a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 97.8 % and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 28.6 dB. On CARTILAGE-PSOCT, it reached an SSIM of 93.9 % and a PSNR of 24.8 dB in cross-dataset testing. Applied to the Retinal-OCT2017 dataset, SA-GAN achieved state-of-the-art performance in a four-class retinal disease classification task. These results demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of our method. SA-GAN provides a cost-effective and practical solution to extend PS-OCT capabilities, supporting the development of intelligent imaging systems for biomedical diagnostics and digital medicine.
