Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a widely used imaging technique valued for its non-invasive, high-resolution, and depth-resolved visualization of microstructures ( Bouma et al., 2022; Israelsen et al., 2019; Podoleanu, 2005 ). Its applications span multiple domains, including ophthalmology, cardiology, dermatology, and material science ( Lu et al., 2024; Minakaran, de Carvalho, Petzold, & Wong, 2021; Xia, Umezu, Scully, Wang, & Larina, 2023 ). Polarization-sensitive OCT (PS-OCT) extends conventional OCT by capturing polarization-resolved information, enabling additional contrast mechanisms beyond intensity ( Tang et al., 2021 ). These polarization features are especially useful for revealing structural and mechanical differences in tissue composition that are not discernible with intensity-based imaging alone. A key metric in PS-OCT is the degree of polarization uniformity (DOPU), which quantifies the consistency of polarization states across neighboring tissue regions. In biomedical imaging, DOPU is widely used as an indicator of tissue uniformity, with low values often corresponding to structural disorganization or heterogeneity. By providing additional functional contrast, DOPU has shown strong potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy in various clinical settings ( Baumann et al., 2012; Makita, Hong, Miura, & Yasuno, 2014 ). However, the broader adoption of DOPU imaging has been limited by the hardware and computational complexity associated with PS-OCT systems. In fields such as dermatology, where non-invasive and cost-effective imaging is essential for diagnosing and monitoring skin conditions, generating DOPU from standard OCT data could greatly expand the utility and accessibility of polarization-based analysis without increasing system complexity. Efforts to simplify PS-OCT and DOPU acquisition systems often involve trade-offs in imaging performance or require complex nonreciprocal optical operations that are sensitive to the direction of light propagation ( Moon, Miao, & Chen, 2019; Rivet, Marques, Bradu, & Podoleanu, 2017; Wang, Al-Qaisi, & Akkin, 2010 ). Recently, data-driven methods have shown promise in synthesizing DOPU images directly from conventional intensity-based OCT data ( Le et al., 2024; Makita, Miura, Azuma, Mino, & Yasuno, 2023; Sun, Wang, Shi, & Boppart, 2021 ). However, most existing approaches treat the problem as a generic image translation task and overlook the underlying principles. As a result, they are prone to learning spurious correlations and may fail to capture critical features, such as the nonlinear influence of signal to noise ratio (SNR) on DOPU formation ( Makita et al., 2014 ). Incorporating domain knowledge into model design offers a promising direction to improve both the accuracy and interpretability of synthetic PS-OCT imaging. Recent advances in optical and medical imaging have increasingly emphasized the integration of domain knowledge to improve model interpretability and generalization ( Hippalgaonkar et al., 2023; Nourani, King, & Ragan, 2020; Wang, Cai, Louie, Wang, & Lee, 2021; Zhou, Yang, Qiao, & Xiang, 2021a ). Incorporating expert priors into deep learning frameworks has been shown to enhance diagnostic reliability and clinical trust ( Goceri, 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024 ). Meanwhile, attention mechanisms have become a key component in neural architecture design, enabling selective focus on task relevant features while suppressing irrelevant information ( Chefer, Alaluf, Vinker, Wolf, & Cohen-Or, 2023; Zheng, Dong, Hu, Chen, & Wang, 2023; Zheng et al., 2024 ). In this study, we propose a lightweight, knowledge-guided deep generative framework for synthesizing PS-OCT DOPU images from conventional OCT intensity inputs. Our model, signal attention generative adversarial network (SA-GAN), incorporates an attention mechanism guided by a SNR-based heuristic, which dynamically reweights image regions based on signal strength. This design enhances image fidelity while suppressing non-informative areas, enabling accurate DOPU synthesis without the need for specialized polarization-sensitive hardware. By leveraging a system-specific SNR threshold as a practical, physics-informed heuristic, SA-GAN improves accessibility, reduces cost, and enhances robustness under suboptimal imaging conditions. • We propose SA-GAN, a deep generative model that synthesizes DOPU images directly from conventional OCT intensity scans without requiring specific PS-OCT hardware modules. • We introduce a signal-aware attention mechanism guided by a system-specific SNR heuristic, which emphasizes signal-reliable and structurally meaningful regions based on the nonlinear relationship between SNR and DOPU. • The proposed framework is computationally lightweight and generalizable across multiple tissue types, supporting broad applicability in both clinical and research contexts. • Comprehensive experiments on two private PS-OCT datasets and one publicly available OCT dataset validate the effectiveness of SA-GAN in generating accurate and interpretable DOPU images, consistently outperforming existing baseline methods. We propose SA-GAN, a deep generative model that synthesizes DOPU images directly from conventional OCT intensity scans without requiring specific PS-OCT hardware modules. We introduce a signal-aware attention mechanism guided by a system-specific SNR heuristic, which emphasizes signal-reliable and structurally meaningful regions based on the nonlinear relationship between SNR and DOPU. The proposed framework is computationally lightweight and generalizable across multiple tissue types, supporting broad applicability in both clinical and research contexts. Comprehensive experiments on two private PS-OCT datasets and one publicly available OCT dataset validate the effectiveness of SA-GAN in generating accurate and interpretable DOPU images, consistently outperforming existing baseline methods. PS-OCT is an advanced extension of conventional OCT, enabling assessment of birefringence, depolarization, and optic axis orientation beyond standard intensity contrast. These polarization-resolved contrasts have demonstrated clinical value in diverse applications such as melanoma staging, scar tissue characterization, retinal nerve fiber mapping, and cartilage degeneration analysis. Hariri et al. (2019) utilized PS-OCT birefringence to differentiate tumor from fibrosis in lung nodules, enabling biopsy site selection guided by collagen content. Motschi et al. (2021) proposed an algorithm to detect and quantify fibrotic lesions in retinal OCT volumes, achieving high accuracy by compensating for anterior tissue birefringence. Goodwin, Klufts, Workman, Thambyah, & Vanholsbeeck (2022) applied PS-OCT to detect early-stage cartilage and subchondral bone degeneration, revealing microstructural changes noninvasively. In dermatology, Chang ( Chang, 2025 ) introduced a method to enhance polarization contrast in PS-OCT images by integrating multiple polarization parameters, improving skin tissue visualization at depth. These studies highlight the diagnostic potential of PS-OCT and underscore the need for robust, automated analysis methods capable of handling complex, multidimensional polarization data. Early PS-OCT analysis methods primarily relied on handcrafted features combined with classical machine learning techniques. These methods leveraged metrics such as birefringence strength in combination with classifiers like support vector machines or random forests ( Basu, Agarwal, & Srivastava, 2024; Dubey, Srivastava, & Dalal, 2018; Kansal, Bhattacharya, & Srivastava, 2020 ). While interpretable and grounded in domain knowledge, they often lacked scalability and struggled to generalize across heterogeneous tissues or acquisition conditions ( Varghese, Varghese, & Preethi, 2024 ). With the rise of deep learning, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become widely used for PS-OCT tasks such as tissue classification, segmentation, and polarization denoising ( Makita et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024 ), demonstrating improved performance through data-driven feature learning. Despite these advances, most studies rely on directly measured PS-OCT outputs. In contrast, synthesizing polarization-derived parameters such as DOPU from conventional OCT remains underexplored. Traditional DOPU estimation requires additional hardware and tightly controlled acquisition environments. To overcome these limitations, recent work has explored data-driven methods for generating DOPU from OCT intensity images. For instance, Sun et al. (2021) employed a Pix2pix GAN with SSIM loss to generate DOPU images, achieving an SSIM of 0.85. Makita et al. (2023) used a U-Net to synthesize retinal DOPU maps, supporting ocular disease detection. Le et al. (2024) introduced a contrastive unpaired translation (CUT) model that learned to generate PS-OCT images without paired training data, outperforming Pix2pix and Cycle GAN and achieving over 90 % accuracy in downstream classification tasks. These methods demonstrate the feasibility of PS-OCT synthesis but remain limited in interpretability and integration of optical priors, which are essential for clinical trust and generalizability. In parallel, knowledge-guided learning has gained traction in the broader field of medical image analysis. By integrating domain expertise or physics-based priors, such approaches improve model interpretability and diagnostic robustness. Yuan, Wu, Wu, Liu, & Huang (2018) proposed a domain attention model for sentiment classification that uses domain representations to guide feature extraction. Xu, Zhao, Li, & Li (2024) introduced VAMNet, which incorporates vessel structure and granularity cues for cataract classification. Niu et al. (2024) proposed EHR-KnowGen, a generative model that integrates external knowledge with multimodal clinical data to improve diagnosis. Xia, Zhan, Shen, & Yang (2024) developed EIDiffuSeg, a diffusion-based segmentation framework that incorporates both explicit and implicit priors. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of embedding domain knowledge into AI models, though such strategies have yet to be widely explored in the context of PS-OCT image synthesis. Image to image translation has become a foundational technique in medical imaging, enabling the synthesis of one imaging modality from another. This approach is especially valuable when direct acquisition is costly, invasive, or requires specialized equipment. By learning mappings between image domains, image translation supports tasks such as modality conversion, enhancement, and harmonization ( Chen, Chen, Wee, Dekker, & Bermejo, 2023; Pang, Lin, Qin, & Chen, 2021 ). Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have played a central role in advancing this field. Models such as Pix2pix ( Isola, Zhu, Zhou, & Efros, 2017 ) and Cycle GAN ( Zhu, Park, Isola, & Efros, 2017 ) have proven effective for translating between paired and unpaired datasets, respectively. These models have been applied to a wide range of medical tasks, including synthesizing CT from MRI ( Liu et al., 2021 ), generating pseudo-CT for PET attenuation correction ( Singh et al., 2023 ), and translating between histopathology stain styles ( Zingman, Frayle, Tankoyeu, Sukhanov, & Heinemann, 2024 ). The flexibility of GANs in capturing complex structural mappings makes them especially valuable when paired datasets are limited or unavailable. To further improve performance, recent efforts have explored more adaptive and domain guided architectures. Platscher, Zopes, & Federau (2022) combined multiple image translation models to synthesize stroke lesion MRIs from semantic maps, significantly enhancing segmentation accuracy. Wang et al. (2022) used multi network translation to generate synthetic LGE-CMR from bSSFP-CMR, enabling unsupervised segmentation without labeled data. Kassab et al. (2024) introduced FFPE++, an unpaired translation framework based on contrastive learning, to reduce artifacts in histopathology slides. Despite these advances, conventional GAN-based models often lack domain specific constraints, which can result in visually realistic but clinically unreliable outputs. To address this, recent studies have integrated anatomical priors, physics based loss functions, and attention mechanisms into the training process ( Chen et al., 2023; Goceri, 2023 ). These strategies improve both performance and interpretability, guiding models to learn medically meaningful transformations. The images used in this study were acquired using a custom-built, Jones matrix based PS-OCT system ( Ju et al., 2013 ). A schematic of the system is shown in Fig. 1 . The setup is constructed around a swept-source laser (Axsun Technology Inc., MA) with a center wavelength of 1.06µm, a full width at half maximum (FWHM) bandwidth of 110nm, and a scanning rate of 100kHz. The light from the laser is split using a single mode fiber coupler, with 90 % of the power directed to a passive polarization delay unit and 10 % to the reference arm. In the sample arm, the polarization delay unit separates the light into two orthogonal polarization states with a temporal delay. These are then directed to the sample. Backscattered light from the sample and light from the reference arm are combined and detected by a polarization diversity (PD) detection unit. Polarization-resolved features are extracted using a Jones matrix reconstruction method ( Hyle Park, Pierce, Cense, & de Boer, 2004; Ju et al., 2013 ). The system delivers an average power of approximately 1.8mW to the sample. The measured system sensitivity is 92 dB. The axial and lateral resolutions are approximately 7.2 µm and 19.2 µm, respectively. The horizontal scanning range is adjustable between 2mm and 12mm. Although the theoretical depth detection range is around 2.8mm (in air), the practical penetration depth in our experiments ranges from 0.8mm to 1.2 mm, depending on tissue properties. Actual tissue penetration depth is computed by accounting for the refractive index. Following system acquisition and preprocessing, pixel resolved Jones matrix data are obtained. These are further processed to compute DOPU maps using standard procedures described in ( Zhou et al., 2021b ). The SKIN-PSOCT dataset comprises 32,528 valid pairs of OCT and PS-OCT images collected from eleven healthy volunteers between December 2021 and June 2022. The study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Board at the University of British Columbia (H19-02887). Imaging was performed in vivo at five standardized body sites: the medial palm, finger knuckle, ventral forearm, forehead, and lateral eye corner. In select participants, melanocytic lesions were also imaged to introduce additional variability. The CARTILAGE-PSOCT dataset consists of 15,022 valid OCT and PS-OCT image pairs acquired from nine arthritis patients undergoing total hip joint replacement. Informed consent was obtained, and the study was approved by the University of British Columbia Clinical Research Ethics Board (H14-03050). Six patients were diagnosed with primary osteoarthritis (OA) based on clinical and radiographic criteria, while three presented with non-OA conditions such as intracapsular femoral neck fractures. This dataset has previously been used in studies validating OA diagnosis against histological grading, underscoring its pathological diversity ( Zhou, Ju, Huang, & Tang, 2019 ). Cartilage-bone specimens were harvested from five anatomically distinct regions of the hip joint, including superior (S), posterior (P), anterior (A), superior anterior (SA), and superior posterior medial (SPM), to ensure consistent topographic representation. Cylindrical blocks (18 mm diameter) were extracted using a drill and stored at − 20 ∘ C. Prior to imaging, specimens were thawed and equilibrated in saline for up to two hours. PS-OCT imaging was performed with perpendicular laser incidence, and surface curvature was adjusted to approximate central symmetry. The Retinal-OCT2017 dataset was introduced by Kermany et al. (2018) and is publicly available via the Kaggle official website ( Kaggle, 2018 ). It contains 83,844 high-quality retinal OCT images acquired from 4657 patients, covering four diagnostic categories: choroidal neovascularization (CNV), diabetic macular edema (DME), drusen, and normal. Each image is a horizontal foveal slice obtained using a Heidelberg Spectralis OCT system as part of routine clinical care at multiple centers, including the Shiley Eye Institute and collaborating hospitals. Labels were assigned based on a multi-tiered image grading protocol involving trained graders, board-certified ophthalmologists, and senior retinal specialists, ensuring high labeling accuracy and clinical relevance. All image filenames follow the convention [label]-[patient ID]-[slice ID], ensuring that all slices from the same patient are consistently grouped during analysis. This organization prevents any potential information leakage. The dataset has been widely used for benchmarking AI models in retinal disease classification and represents a diverse and large-scale resource for evaluating generalizability. In this work, we used the Retinal-OCT2017 dataset exclusively for external validation of the synthesized DOPU images. While the dataset contains only standard OCT images and lacks corresponding PS-OCT DOPU ground truth, it offers substantial pathological diversity and clinical relevance. Therefore, direct image-level comparisons are not possible. Instead, we evaluated the effectiveness of the synthesized DOPU in a downstream disease classification task. This approach allows us to assess the generalizability and utility of the generated DOPU representations in a domain not seen during model training. Each 3D PS-OCT volume consisted of 255 cross-sectional B-scans. For each B-scan, an OCT intensity image and the corresponding ground-truth DOPU image were recorded. Raw image dimensions were 250 pixels (vertical) by 500 pixels (horizontal); the vertical axis was cropped to retain the relevant tissue region. To prevent data leakage during training and evaluation, a leave-one-out strategy was applied (see Section 3.6 for details). Typically, each measurement site yielded 510 paired images. For SKIN-PSOCT, a total of 60 measurement sites from 11 subjects produced 32,528 valid image pairs. For CARTILAGE-PSOCT, 122 sites from nine subjects yielded 15,022 valid image pairs. All scans covered a 4.5 mm × 4.5 mm lateral field of view. The lateral and axial pixel resolutions were approximately 9.1 µm and 5.1 µm (optical path length), respectively, with an inter-scan spacing of approximately 18.2 µm between adjacent B-scans. Hardware and software-based dispersion compensation was applied following established methods ( Zhou et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019 ). A foundational assumption of this work is that generative transformation across imaging modalities can reflect underlying physical relationships. In the context of polarization-sensitive imaging, this assumption is particularly nuanced. For example, polarization behavior cannot be inferred from intensity images of isotropic samples like pure glass retarders, where identical intensity profiles may correspond to distinct polarization states. Prior studies have hypothesized a link between polarization randomness and OCT speckle patterns ( Makita et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2021 ), both of which are influenced by complex scattering processes. This observation motivates the design of a signal-attention network that highlights speckled regions rich in structural variation while suppressing non-informative noise. The DOPU signal comprises stochastic components arising from both additive Gaussian noise and optically induced speckle. The detected horizontal and vertical polarization signals can be modeled as: (1) [ g H g V ] = [ E H + n H E V + n V ] , where E p denotes the true electric field in each polarization channel, and n p represents additive noise. The corresponding Stokes vector is perturbed by a zero-mean noise component ϵ, yielding: (2) S measured = S true + ϵ . While additive noise can be treated stochastically, speckle patterns often reflect underlying biological structures such as birefringence or collagen alignment and therefore cannot be modeled purely as noise. Traditional PS-OCT methods mitigate these effects through spatial averaging of Jones matrices and SNR masking via calibration phantoms ( Zhou et al., 2021b ). However, these approaches risk discarding diagnostically meaningful variations. To address this, we incorporate the nonlinear relationship between DOPU and SNR into the network via a physics-guided attention mechanism. This is realized through an adaptive modulation term: (3) δ = F ˜ ( SNR ) , where δ dynamically modulates the attention weights based on the estimated SNR (see Appendix A for implementation details). This mechanism enables the model to enhance structurally and biologically informative regions, such as those reflecting collagen disorganization or pigmentation heterogeneity, while attenuating areas dominated by acquisition noise, improving both interpretability and generative fidelity. The overall architecture of SA-GAN is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Feature extraction begins with a convolutional layer followed by a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU). To mitigate information loss during deep feature extraction, the generator replaces standard convolutional layers with residual blocks, each consisting of two convolutional layers, two ReLU activations, and a skip connection, as shown in Fig. 2 (b). At the core of the generator is a guided learning module composed of four stacked signal attentive blocks (SABs) ( Fig. 2 (c)). Each SAB contains a dilated signal attentive module (DSAM) that generates multi-scale attention maps via dilated convolutions, and a signal attentive residual block (SARB) that integrates these maps into the feature stream ( Fig. 2 (d-e)). For each input OCT image, a binary mask is generated using an SNR threshold derived from prior calibration. This mask serves as a region-of-interest (ROI) input and is used to supervise the learning of attention maps. A structural similarity-based loss function is employed to align the attention distribution with the ROI mask, promoting accurate and signal-aware feature learning. The discriminator consists of five convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. It evaluates the realism of the generated images using dynamically learned thresholds and provides feedback to iteratively refine the generator. This adversarial training loop ensures faithful and robust DOPU synthesis across diverse imaging conditions. The objective of the proposed framework is to synthesize high-fidelity DOPU images from conventional OCT images without requiring specialized polarization-sensitive hardware. To this end, we formulate the task as a paired image-to-image translation problem and construct a multi-component loss function that integrates both adversarial learning and signal-informed priors to improve reconstruction fidelity, perceptual quality, and structural coherence. At the core of the framework lies a conditional GAN ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ), where a generator G synthesizes DOPU images from input OCT images, and a discriminator D learns to distinguish between real and synthetic DOPU images. This adversarial mechanism encourages the generator to produce visually plausible outputs that align with the empirical distribution of ground-truth DOPU data. As described in Section 3.2 , the original OCT intensity images have a resolution of 250 × 500 pixels for the two private datasets and 512 × 496 pixels for the Retinal-OCT2017 dataset. To satisfy the square input requirement of the deep learning models used in this study, including the proposed SA-GAN, the private dataset images were centrally cropped to 250 × 250 pixels, while the Retinal-OCT2017 images were resized to 250 × 250 pixels. Cropping was chosen for the private datasets to preserve structural integrity and avoid resizing artifacts, whereas for Retinal-OCT2017 we adhered to the preprocessing protocol of the original study ( Kermany et al., 2018 ). To ensure fair comparison across models, each method was trained to its optimal performance on the dataset without bias. An early-stopping mechanism was applied, with a maximum of 200 training epochs. After each epoch, the loss was evaluated, and the model was saved if the loss decreased. A patience of 20 epochs was used, halting training if no improvement was observed for 20 consecutive epochs. For the SKIN-PSOCT dataset, 32,528 images from 11 volunteers were used. Given the small number of subjects, we employed a subject-based leave-one-out cross-validation strategy, ensuring fair subject-wise separation to avoid data leakage. For both the CARTILAGE-PSOCT and Retinal-OCT2017, all 15,022 and 83,844 images, respectively, were used exclusively for testing purposes. Model training was conducted using the Adam optimizer ( Kingma & Ba, 2014 ) with a batch size of 16 and four data loading threads. The initial learning rate was set to 0.0001 and decayed progressively for fine-tuning. To balance the weights within the loss functions, the parameters were set as follows: λ from Eq. (8) was set to 10, while α and β from Eq. (13) were set to 10 and 1, respectively, ensuring that all values remained within the same magnitude without introducing training bias. All deep learning experiments were implemented in the PyTorch framework ( Paszke et al., 2019 ). Preliminary training and preprocessing were performed on a local NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB memory, while final model training was conducted on UBC’s ARC Sockeye high-performance computing platform using an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU with 32GB memory. We employed structural similarity index measure (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and mean squared error (MSE) as the primary quantitative metrics to evaluate the fidelity of the synthesized DOPU images. In addition, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) was used to visualize feature-level differences between healthy and diseased samples. For the downstream classification tasks, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were used to provide a comprehensive evaluation. Definitions and formulations of all evaluation metrics are provided below. SSIM evaluates perceptual similarity between two images by comparing luminance, contrast, and structure. The SSIM score ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater similarity. (14) SSIM ( x , y ) = ( 2 μ x μ y + C 1 ) ( 2 σ x y + C 2 ) ( μ x 2 + μ y 2 + C 1 ) ( σ x 2 + σ y 2 + C 2 ) Here, μ x and μ y denote the mean intensities, σ x 2 and σ y 2 the variances, and σ xy the covariance of images x and y . Constants are defined as: (15) C 1 = ( K 1 L ) 2 , C 2 = ( K 2 L ) 2 where L is the dynamic pixel range, K 1 = 0.01 , and K 2 = 0.03 . PSNR quantifies image quality by measuring the ratio between the maximum signal and the noise introduced by reconstruction. It is given by: (16) PSNR = 10 · log 10 ( I max 2 MSE ) where I max is the maximum possible pixel value and MSE is defined below. MSE computes the average squared difference between the corresponding pixels of two images: (17) MSE = 1 m n ∑ i = 1 m ∑ j = 1 n [ x ( i , j ) − y ( i , j ) ] 2 where x and y are two images of size m × n . Lower MSE values indicate better reconstruction accuracy. Accuracy measures the overall proportion of correctly classified samples: (18) Accuracy = T P + T N T P + T N + F P + F N Here, TP, TN, FP , and FN represent true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively. Higher accuracy indicates better overall classification performance. Sensitivity, also known as recall, evaluates the model’s ability to correctly identify positive cases: (19) Sensitivity = T P T P + F N A higher sensitivity indicates fewer false negatives, which is particularly important in clinical diagnosis. Specificity quantifies the model’s ability to correctly identify negative cases: (20) Specificity = T N T N + F P High specificity reflects fewer false positives, contributing to the reliability of negative predictions. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, offering a balanced measure of classification performance, particularly under class imbalance: (21) F1 score = 2 · T P 2 · T P + F P + F N Here, a high F1 score indicates that the model achieves both high precision (low false positive rate) and high recall (low false negative rate), which is critical for reliable clinical decision-making. AUC measures the model’s ability to distinguish between classes across all decision thresholds. It is calculated as the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. AUC values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better discriminative performance. An AUC close to 1.0 reflects excellent classification capability, while an AUC near 0.5 suggests random performance. To explore feature-level differences, we applied t-SNE on 1000 randomly selected images (600 from healthy subjects and 400 from patients). A pretrained ResNet-18 model ( Deng et al., 2009 ) was used to extract feature vectors, which were then projected into a two-dimensional space using t-SNE implemented via sklearn ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ). We set perplexity to 50, learning rate to 200, and initialized the algorithm with PCA and a fixed random seed of 41 for reproducibility. The resulting 2D visualization provided intuitive insights into clustering and group separability. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using the SKIN-PSOCT dataset from three perspectives: (i) image level , i.e., per-image comparison; (ii) subject level , i.e., per-volunteer aggregation; and (iii) group level , i.e., all test images collectively. At the image level , we compute horizontal DOPU distribution profiles via A-scan averaging (column-wise mean) to compare synthetic and real DOPU images. At the subject level , we average the DOPU values across B-scans for each individual and use paired t -tests with Bonferroni correction ( Weisstein, 2004 ) to assess statistical differences. At the group level , we report SSIM, PSNR, and MSE across the test set. For comparison, we evaluated three representative models, Pix2pix GAN ( Sun et al., 2021 ), Cycle GAN ( Zhu et al., 2017 ), and Transformer GAN ( Jiang, Chang, & Wang, 2021; Yang, Zhou, Cao, & Guo, 2022 ), as well as two recent state-of-the-art methods in this field, CUT GAN ( Le et al., 2024 ) and XDL GAN ( Park et al., 2025 ), under identical experimental settings. In addition to the adversarial generative network architecture, we also considered the paired generative architecture based on UNet ( Makita et al., 2023 ) and employed the same loss function. Ablation studies on the loss functions were conducted to fairly evaluate the contribution of each component within the workflow. Additionally, to evaluate generalization, we used the CARTILAGE-PSOCT dataset as an external test set without fine-tuning. Metrics were computed in the same manner, and t-SNE ( Van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008 ) was employed to visualize feature distributions between synthetic and real DOPU images across different diagnostic categories. To further assess the clinical utility of the generated DOPU images, we introduced an additional downstream disease classification task on both CARTILAGE-PSOCT and Retinal-OCT2017 using ResNet-18 ( Deng et al., 2009 ), followed by a comprehensive evaluation of classification performance. As shown in Fig. 3 , results from various body sites across different patients, including the eye corner, forehead, hand, knuckle, and palm edge, are compared. The first and second columns show the input OCT intensity images and their corresponding binary masks generated based on SNR threshold as defined in Eq. (6) . The third column presents the attention heatmaps learned by our model. The fourth and fifth columns display the ground truth DOPU images and the synthetic images produced by our method, respectively. The results demonstrate that our method accurately identifies relevant attention regions and effectively guides the generative process. To assess visual and structural fidelity, we compare horizontal A-scan average DOPU profiles across multiple methods ( Figs. 4 and 5 ). Our approach demonstrates closer alignment to the real DOPU profiles than other models. The generated profiles (blue) follow the ground truth (red) with minimal deviation, capturing detailed hierarchical signal variations and layer-specific characteristics. As mentioned earlier, we collected OCT image data from multiple body sites for each individual. We assume that the distribution of skin information across different body regions within the same individual reflects person-specific characteristics. Based on this assumption, we evaluate whether the generated DOPU images exhibit individual distinctiveness and representativeness by statistically comparing the distributions of DOPU values between real and synthetic images at the individual level. To this end, we analyzed the DOPU values per subject by averaging across all B-scans. For each generation method, we compared the distributions of synthetic and real DOPU values using paired t -tests with Bonferroni correction. Fig. 6 presents the results from three representative individuals. Our method consistently produced mean DOPU values that were statistically indistinguishable from the ground truth ( p > .0125), whereas other methods, such as Pix2pix, showed significant differences. These findings suggest that our approach not only reconstructs local polarization features but also preserves individual-specific optical properties. In order to better compare with existing methods, quantitative results for SSIM, PSNR, and MSE across all test images are presented in Fig. 7 . Our method achieved the highest SSIM (97.8 %), outperforming Pix2pix (81.7 %), Cycle GAN (86.4 %), UNet (82.5 %), Transformer GAN (80.2 %), XDL GAN (84.6 %), and CUT GAN (84.7 %). This demonstrates enhanced preservation of polarimetric microstructures. In terms of PSNR, our model achieved 28.6 dB, compared to 18.3 dB (Pix2pix), 18.8 dB (Cycle GAN), 16.6 dB (UNet), 17.2 dB (Transformer GAN), 18.9 dB (XDL GAN), and 18.2 dB (CUT GAN), indicating lower noise and finer polarization detail retention. For MSE, our method attained the lowest value (0.05), confirming its superior pixel-level accuracy and robustness across diverse test scenarios. To evaluate the role of each loss component, we performed an ablation study on both the SKIN-PSOCT and CARTILAGE-PSOCT datasets using SSIM, PSNR, and MSE as evaluation metrics ( Table 1 ). Four configurations were compared: the baseline with adversarial loss L a d v only, L a d v + L L 1 , L a d v + L a t t , and the full model with all three terms. On the SKIN-PSOCT dataset, the baseline achieved an SSIM of 0.79 and PSNR of 16.45 dB. Adding L L 1 improved SSIM to 0.82 and PSNR to 18.32 dB, while introducing L a t t yielded larger gains, with SSIM reaching 0.88 and PSNR 22.25 dB. The full model achieved the best performance, with SSIM of 0.98 and PSNR of 28.60 dB, corresponding to a 24 % improvement in SSIM and a 12.15 dB increase in PSNR compared to the baseline. MSE decreased consistently from 0.13 to 0.05. A similar trend was observed on the CARTILAGE-PSOCT dataset. The baseline achieved SSIM of 0.74 and PSNR of 16.12 dB. With L L 1 , SSIM increased to 0.78 and PSNR to 17.74 dB. The attention loss further boosted SSIM to 0.87 and PSNR to 20.98 dB. The full model achieved SSIM of 0.94 and PSNR of 24.80 dB, representing a 27 % gain in SSIM and an 8.68 dB increase in PSNR relative to the baseline. MSE dropped from 0.14 to 0.04. These results demonstrate that L L 1 primarily enhances pixel-wise fidelity, L a t t substantially improves structural similarity and noise suppression, and the combination of all three produces the most significant overall gains. This confirms that the attention-guided loss plays a critical role in model performance and validates the choice of loss weighting in the final design. To evaluate the generalizability of the proposed SKIN-PSOCT-trained model beyond the training domain, we conducted two external validation experiments on datasets with distinct anatomical and imaging characteristics: the CARTILAGE-PSOCT dataset and the Retinal-OCT2017 dataset. In both experiments, the model was trained exclusively on the SKIN-PSOCT dataset and tested directly on the external datasets without any fine-tuning or subject overlap. In the first experiment, the model was evaluated on the CARTILAGE-PSOCT dataset, which features tissue structures different from those in the skin dataset but shares the same PS-OCT imaging modality. As shown in Figs. 8 and 9 , comparisons of A-scan-averaged DOPU profiles for three representative samples demonstrate that the synthetic DOPU distributions remain highly consistent with the corresponding ground truth, despite substantial differences in tissue morphology. Quantitative reconstruction metrics computed across all 15,232 images yielded an SSIM of 93.9 %, a PSNR of 24.80 dB, and an MSE of 0.04, closely matching the model’s performance on the SKIN-PSOCT dataset. These results suggest that the model does not rely on dataset-specific characteristics and generalizes well to unseen anatomical domains. To further examine whether diagnostic integrity is preserved in the synthetic outputs, we conducted a downstream binary classification task to distinguish healthy versus diseased cartilage samples. As shown in Table 2 , models trained on synthetic DOPUs achieved comparable classification performance to those trained on real DOPUs, with an accuracy of 0.90 ± 0.02, F1 score of 0.87 ± 0.02, and AUC of 0.96 ± 0.01, confirming the reliability of the generated representations. Specifically, when using OCT as the baseline for comparison, it can be observed that on the identical task, both the real DOPU and the synthetic DOPU outperform OCT, yielding a 7 % higher AUC. Additionally, deep features extracted using a pretrained ResNet-18 from 1000 randomly selected samples were visualized using t-SNE, as illustrated in Fig. 10 , the synthetic DOPUs produced well-separated class clusters that closely mirrored the ground truth distribution, further supporting the diagnostic validity of the generated images. In the second validation experiment, we applied the trained model to the publicly available Retinal-OCT2017 dataset, which contains only conventional OCT images without PS-OCT ground truth. This dataset represents a more challenging setting due to the complete domain shift in both tissue type and imaging characteristics. Despite these differences, the model successfully generated DOPU representations, as shown in Fig. 11 , capturing disease-specific structural information across four retinal conditions: Normal, CNV, DME, and Drusen. Downstream classification based on the synthetic DOPUs achieved good performance for all categories (see Table 3 ), with AUC values higher than 0.988 across all disease types and mean accuracy exceeding 97 %, highlighting the robustness of the learned representations even in biologically and technically unrelated domains. It should be noted that the results for this classification task appear exceptionally high, primarily because OCT imaging itself has already reached the upper limit of detection capability for this specific problem, as reported in prior study ( Kermany et al., 2018 ). Therefore, the primary objective of our external validation experiment is not to pursue further performance improvement, but to evaluate the model’s generalizability beyond our custom imaging hardware and to rule out potential mode collapse under strictly separated data conditions. The converted retinal images remain fully isolated from skin data and continue to support accurate retinal disease classification, which explains the high accuracy achieved under leakage-free settings. To better interpret the model’s probabilistic outputs, we conducted an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) analysis ( Nixon, Dusenberry, Zhang, Jerfel, & Tran, 2019 ). The model exhibited good calibration, with class-wise ECE values ranging from 0.046 to 0.117. Lower ECE values indicate closer agreement between predicted confidence and true accuracy, suggesting reliable probability estimates. The CNV class achieved the best calibration (ECE = 0.046), whereas the Normal class showed mild overconfidence (ECE = 0.117). The detailed confusion matrices for the 5-fold cross-validation are also provided in Fig. 12 . These results collectively demonstrate that the SKIN-PSOCT-trained model exhibits strong cross-domain generalizability, preserves essential diagnostic features, and supports high-fidelity image synthesis and classification across diverse anatomical regions and imaging modalities. To ensure practical applicability in clinical scenarios, it is essential to evaluate not only the performance but also the computational efficiency of deep learning models. Therefore, we compared the number of trainable parameters and the average training time across representative GAN architectures, as summarized in Table 4 . Unlike conventional models such as Pix2pix GAN and Cycle GAN, which rely on paired supervision and cycle-consistency, respectively, more recent approaches adopt advanced learning strategies, including contrastive learning (CUT GAN) and saliency-masking (XDL GAN). Our proposed method employs a signal-attention mechanism that achieves both parameter efficiency and fast convergence. The generator of our model contains only 2.1 million parameters, substantially fewer than Pix2pix GAN (54.4M), Cycle GAN (22.8M), UNet (7.8M), CUT GAN (22.8M), Transformer GAN (21.3M), and XDL GAN (45.6M). In addition, our model requires the shortest average training time (5.5 h), compared with 9.8-22.3 h for other GAN models. We have also incorporated additional evaluation metrics, including FLOPs, memory usage, latency, and throughput, into Table 4 . These metrics further demonstrate that our method achieves lower training cost and higher computational efficiency. And the overall results confirm the lightweight and computationally efficient nature of the proposed framework. In one of the earliest attempts at synthetic PS-OCT, Sun et al. (2021) suggested that polarization information could be inferred from OCT intensity images, attributing this to reflectance as the primary polarimetrically active mechanism. While the underlying physical interpretation requires further investigation, the strong visual and quantitative similarity between SA-GAN-generated and ground-truth DOPU images supports a meaningful correlation between OCT intensity features and polarization properties. As shown in Fig. 13 , we present a close-up comparison from sample Cartilage 1 in Fig. 8 . Despite being trained exclusively on the SKIN-PSOCT dataset, SA-GAN produces DOPU maps for cartilage samples with high visual fidelity. Appendix A further demonstrates the highly nonlinear relationship between DOPU and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which justifies the incorporation of SNR as a system-specific heuristic in the design of SA-GAN’s attention mechanism. Importantly, this approach is not intended as a broadly applicable optical principle but rather as a practical, data-informed strategy tailored to our PS-OCT system. Notably, Fig. 13 also reveals a performance gap in high-DOPU regions (depicted in dark red), where the synthetic images show less accurate correspondence. This limitation is largely attributed to the insufficient representation of high-DOPU values in the SKIN-PSOCT training data, as illustrated in Fig. 14 . By incorporating the cross-datasets training strategy, this imbalance is effectively alleviated, and the model achieves more accurate generation of high-DOPU regions, as further demonstrated by the comparison in Fig. 13 . The proposed signal-attention mechanism, originally developed for synthesizing DOPU images in PS-OCT, shows strong potential for generalization beyond this specific application. In our framework, the attention mechanism is guided by the SNR, which functions as a system-specific indicator of information reliability. This design enables the model to emphasize informative regions while suppressing noise-dominated areas, thereby improving the quality and interpretability of the synthesized images. This concept is not limited to PS-OCT. The core idea of using domain-specific indicators to guide attention can be applied to a wide range of computer vision tasks. For example, in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), signal intensity or tissue contrast metrics could be used to focus the model’s attention on diagnostically relevant regions. In digital pathology, cellular density or staining intensity may serve as guidance cues to prioritize histologically significant areas. These domain-adapted attention mechanisms allow the model to learn from features that are meaningful within each specific context. Such adaptability highlights the flexibility of our design and its potential for broader impact. With appropriate domain-specific criteria, the proposed method could be extended to other applications. These possibilities suggest that the signal-attention mechanism offers a generalizable approach for enhancing the performance and interpretability of deep learning models across diverse imaging domains. We proposed SA-GAN, a lightweight, knowledge-guided generative framework for synthesizing DOPU images directly from conventional OCT intensity data. By incorporating an attention mechanism informed by the nonlinear DOPU-SNR relationship, SA-GAN effectively emphasizes signal-reliable and structurally meaningful regions, thereby improving both fidelity and robustness. Unlike conventional approaches, it achieves accurate DOPU synthesis without requiring PS-OCT hardware, enhancing accessibility while reducing system cost. Extensive experiments on three PS-OCT datasets demonstrate that SA-GAN achieves competitive performance in terms of accuracy, generalizability, and parameter efficiency, maintaining robust results across tissue types while requiring substantially fewer parameters and reduced training time. These findings underscore the value of integrating signal-aware priors into deep learning architectures for biomedical imaging. Further refinement of high-DOPU region modeling and exploration of clinical applications will help translate this approach into practical diagnostic tools with a tangible impact in clinical settings. data.text: SkinDisNet: A comprehensive dataset of clinical images and metadata for skin disease detection and classification Skin diseases are considered among the most important health problems worldwide, affecting millions of people. Early diagnosis can prevent complications and therefore improve the outcomes for patients. However, accurate diagnosis can be challenging due to the visual similarity of different conditions, variability in symptoms, and the shortage of region-specific annotated datasets for developing robust machine learning models. To bridge the gap, this paper presents a new dataset that aims to further the field of skin disease detection through machine learning and computer vision techniques. There are 1710 clinical images of skin diseases, captured using smartphones cameras from hospitals in Bangladesh. The images are organized into six classes of skin diseases—Atopic Dermatitis, Contact Dermatitis, Eczema, Scabies, Seborrheic Dermatitis, and Tinea Corporis. Each image is uniquely identified and stored in categorized folders, with all entries reviewed to ensure accurate classification. Moreover, this paper includes metadata that has been curated meticulously to provide essential clinical and demographic details, enabling precise analysis and reproducible research. Our dataset is intended to facilitate research and advancement in skin disease detection and classification using machine learning and computer vision techniques. SPARSE data, rich results: Few-shot semi-supervised learning via class-conditioned image translation Deep learning has revolutionized medical imaging, but its effectiveness is severely limited by insufficient labeled training data. This paper introduces a novel GAN-based semi-supervised learning framework specifically designed for low labeled-data regimes, evaluated across settings with 5 to 50 labeled samples per class. Our approach integrates three specialized neural networks: a generator for class-conditioned image translation, a discriminator for authenticity assessment and classification, and a dedicated classifier, within a three-phase training framework. The method alternates between supervised training on limited labeled data and unsupervised learning that leverages abundant unlabeled images through image-to-image translation rather than generation from noise. We employ ensemble-based pseudo-labeling that combines confidence-weighted predictions from the discriminator and classifier with temporal consistency through exponential moving averaging, enabling reliable label estimation for unlabeled data. Comprehensive evaluation across eleven MedMNIST datasets demonstrates that our approach achieves statistically significant improvements over six state-of-the-art GAN-based semi-supervised methods, with particularly strong performance in the extreme 5-shot setting where the scarcity of labeled data is most challenging. The framework maintains its superiority across all evaluated settings (5, 10, 20, and 50 shots per class). Our approach offers a practical solution for medical imaging applications where annotation costs are prohibitive, enabling robust classification performance even with minimal labeled data. Deep learning has demonstrated remarkable potential in revolutionizing medical imaging ( Chen et al., 2022 ). However, insufficient labeled data for model training is one of the main challenges hindering its effectiveness that arises from several constraints such as: the stringent privacy regulations and ethical guidelines governing patient data access and distribution ( Chiruvella and Guddati, 2021 ), and the necessity of specialized medical expertise for data annotation, a resource limited by healthcare professionals’ primary commitment to patient care ( Bull et al., 2015 ). These constraints often result in what is known as the low-data regime, i.e., a situation where the number of labeled medical images falls below the threshold needed for reliable convergence of deep networks, typically ranging from dozens to a few hundred samples depending on the complexity of the task and model architecture. To address this issue, researchers have explored unsupervised, supervised and semi-supervised learning. The approaches in the first category tackle the low-data regime through unsupervised learning, which exploits the abundant unlabeled medical images to learn meaningful representations. Models are trained to capture underlying data patterns through tasks like image reconstruction, anomaly detection, or feature learning. This approach is particularly valuable in medical imaging where unlabeled data is available, but a fundamental challenge remains: without sufficient labeled validation data, it is difficult to ensure that the extracted features are clinically relevant rather than merely statistically significant in the data distribution. In the second case of supervised learning, researchers have explored various strategies to mitigate the limited availability of labeled samples, such as transfer learning, data augmentation and synthetic data generation. Transfer learning leverages models pre-trained on large datasets by fine-tuning them for specific tasks with limited data ( Ruffini et al., 2025 ), but its effectiveness diminishes when the target domain differs significantly from the source domain Bau et al. (2017) . Data augmentation techniques artificially expand training datasets through various transformations ( Chen et al., 2023 ), but cannot introduce new information. Synthetic data generation through simulation or generative models has emerged as another strategy ( Sariyildiz et al., 2023; Azizi et al., 2023 ), though generating fully synthetic datasets that realistically capture real-world data distributions remains challenging ( Geng et al., 2025; Salmè et al., 2025 ). The third approach is semi-supervised learning (SSL) that simultaneously leverages labeled and unlabeled data. Traditional SSL methods relied on machine learning techniques such as self-training and co-training. However, recent advances in generative models, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) based methods, have improved SSL performance, not by generating completely synthetic data but by learning to extract meaningful features from the real unlabeled data distribution to enhance the learning process ( Sajun and Zualkernan, 2022 ). Despite these advances, existing SSL methods often struggle in low-data regimes as it happens in medical imaging. In this paper we tackle this issue and we introduce the following contributions: • A novel GAN-based semi-supervised learning method specifically designed for medical image classification in low labeled-data regimes. • A dynamic training schedule that alternates between supervised phases and unsupervised phases to optimize learning efficiency. • An image-to-image translation mechanism employed as a secondary task that, unlike purely generative approaches that create images de novo from noise vectors, modifies existing real unlabeled images to preserve authentic anatomical features while enriching feature representations beyond what traditional generative approaches provide. • A confidence-weighted temporal ensemble technique that combines predictions from multiple model components and previous training iterations, significantly improving pseudo-labeling reliability in low-data scenarios. • A comprehensive empirical evaluation demonstrating competitive performance against six state-of-the-art SSL methods across eleven benchmark datasets for medical image classification tasks. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the related works in the field, providing context for our research contributions. Section 3 details our proposed method. Section 4 describes the experimental configuration, including datasets, parameters, and evaluation metrics. Section 5 presents our results and provides comprehensive analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper with a summary of our findings and suggestions for future research directions. Semi-supervised learning methods aim to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. A recent survey ( van Engelen and Hoos, 2020 ) has established a clear taxonomy of SSL approaches, distinguishing between two main classes: inductive methods, which construct classifiers that can generate predictions for any input, and transductive methods, which optimize directly over predictions for a given set of unlabeled data points. Inductive methods can be further subdivided into three categories based on how they incorporate unlabeled data: (1) wrapper methods, which iteratively train classifiers on labeled data and use their predictions to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled samples; (2) unsupervised preprocessing methods, which extract features or determine initial parameters from unlabeled data before supervised training; and (3) intrinsically semi-supervised methods, which directly incorporate unlabeled data into the objective function or optimization procedure. Since our proposed approach falls within this third category, and it exploits GANs, the remainder of this section reviews the GAN-based SSL methods across various domains, focusing on approaches that have introduced key architectural innovations, while the interested readers can refer to Sajun and Zualkernan (2022) for a comprehensive review of approaches within this category. Semi-supervised learning is built on the fundamental assumption that the data distribution in the input space contains substantial information about label distribution in the output space. Within this context, GANs are particularly suitable candidates for SSL applications, given their inherent ability to model underlying data distributions and reveal patterns in the input space. The first significant work in this context introduced the SGAN model ( Odena, 2016 ), which expands the traditional GAN architecture by augmenting the discriminator to perform dual functions that distinguish between real and synthetic samples while simultaneously predicting class labels for input data. This dual-purpose approach represented an important extension of the framework through pseudo-labeling, where the discriminator/classifier is trained on both labeled data and generated samples with known class labels. SGAN exemplifies what is known as a two-player model in GAN-based SSL, where the traditional generator-discriminator architecture is maintained but the discriminator is extended to perform both adversarial discrimination and classification tasks simultaneously. Building on these foundations, MatchGAN ( Sun et al., 2020 ) introduced an innovative approach that leveraged the Wasserstein distance and conditional generation. As a semi-supervised conditional GAN, MatchGAN utilizes the label space in the target domain along with unlabeled samples to generate additional labeled training data. The framework assigns labels from the pool of labeled samples to unlabeled samples, then passes these through the generator to create synthetic versions of images based on the target labels. This work also introduces a match loss term that compares the generated images to the original labeled images from which the target labels are sampled. A breakthrough in GAN-based SSL came with the introduction of TripleGAN ( Li et al., 2022 ), which addressed the difficulty of simultaneously optimizing both generator and discriminator performance. TripleGAN pioneered the three-player model architecture by incorporating an additional classifier that works independently from the discriminator, creating a tripartite interaction between generator, discriminator, and classifier. In this three-player setup, the classifier works in conjunction with the generator to characterize conditional distributions between images while limiting the discriminator’s role to identifying fake image-label pairs. This separation of concerns allows each component to specialize in its primary task, potentially leading to improved overall performance compared to two-player models where the discriminator must balance competing objectives. Recent developments have significantly expanded upon the TripleGAN framework ( Haque, 2021; Zhen et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023 ). EC-GAN ( Haque, 2021 ) proposed a mechanism where generated images are immediately processed by a classifier to produce pseudo-labels. This classifier-generator interaction is regulated through a hyperparameter-weighted loss function that precisely controls the influence of generated samples on classifier training. SEC-CGAN ( Zhen et al., 2023 ) introduced a co-supervised learning paradigm where a conditional GAN is trained alongside the classifier, providing semantics-conditioned, confidence-aware synthesized examples during training. CISSL-GAN ( Xie et al., 2023 ) then extended the Triple-GAN framework to address semi-supervised learning with class-imbalanced data through a dynamic class-rebalancing sampler that strategically selects pseudo-labeled samples from unlabeled data. Beyond GAN-based approaches, recent efforts in semi-supervised learning have focused on medical image segmentation tasks, introducing several innovative paradigms that offer valuable insights for SSL methodologies. VerSemi ( Zeng et al., 2025a ) proposes a versatile framework that unifies multiple SSL segmentation tasks within a single model using dynamic task prompts and CutMix-based synthetic task generation, demonstrating that learning across diverse tasks improves model generalization. In a complementary direction, PICK ( Zeng et al., 2025b ) employs masked image modeling as a pretext task, masking pseudo-label-guided attentive regions and reconstructing them to learn robust representations while mitigating the impact of erroneous pseudo-labels. Building on the theme of leveraging model discrepancies, the consistency-guided differential decoding approach (LeFeD) ( Zeng et al., 2025c ), exploits feature-level differences between multiple decoders to enhance representation learning, showing that differential features naturally emerge when decoders pursue consistent predictions. From a different perspective focused on classification, PEFAT ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) introduces loss distribution modeling for pseudo-label quality assessment, using Gaussian Mixture Models to distinguish high-quality pseudo-labels from noisy ones while employing feature-level adversarial training to leverage low-confidence samples. These advances in segmentation demonstrate the value of ensemble mechanisms, multi-task learning, and sophisticated pseudo-labeling strategies, i.e., principles that resonate with our approach, though applied here to the distinct challenge of classification in extremely low labeled-data regimes. The analysis of the literature reported so far shows that several open issues still exist in current GAN-based SSL approaches: • None of the existing methods specifically addresses the challenges of extremely low labeled data regimes, such as the case where only 5–10 labeled samples per class are available. • Current approaches like SGAN ( Odena, 2016 ), TripleGAN ( Li et al., 2022 ), and EC-GAN ( Haque, 2021 ) primarily rely on generation-based paradigms for unsupervised learning, lacking effective mechanisms to integrate supervised and unsupervised signals. • Existing methods rely on a single discriminator or on a single classifier, while none has investigated possible advantages given by the use of an ensemble of models that, in other domains, has proven to provide complementary outputs that enhance model robustness ( Cao et al., 2020; Guarrasi et al., 2022 ). We propose a novel semi-supervised learning strategy called SPARSE ( S emi-supervised P seudo-labeling via A dversarial R epresentation tran S lation E nhancement), designed to achieve robust classification performance in extremely low labeled-data regimes. Our approach integrates three specialized neural networks: a generator ( G ) that performs class-conditioned image translation, a discriminator ( D ) that assesses image authenticity while providing classification signals, and a dedicated classifier ( C ) that focuses exclusively on the classification task. Our approach consists of three main phases: 1. Supervised training phase ( Fig. 1 a): it jointly trains the three aforementioned networks, G , D and C . Each model is trained with a supervised dataset D s u p = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N , where N is the number of few-shot samples, x i is the input sample, e.g., an image in our experiments, and y i is the corresponding one-hot encoded ground truth vector, with y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } K × 1 where K is the total number of classes. This initial phase is crucial for maintaining classification accuracy and preventing drift in the unsupervised learning process, represented in panel b of the same figure, by providing supervised signals from the limited labeled data. 2. Self-supervised pre-training phase ( Fig. 1 b), which consists of two components. The first is an ensemble-based pseudo-labeling block that combines the confidence-weighted scores provided by D and C given a set D u n s = { x ˆ i } i = 1 M of M unsupervised samples, with M ≫ N . This ensemble outputs the pseudo-labels { y ˆ i } i = 1 M , with y ˆ i ∈ { 0 , 1 } K × 1 , assigned to each sample in D u n s . The second component of the self-supervised pretraining phase introduces a class-conditioned image translation task that uses randomly sampled class conditions { z i } i = 1 M , with z i ∈ { 0 , 1 } K × 1 . Hence, this phase leverages the abundant unlabeled data to improve feature representations and model generalization capabilities through image-to-image translation tasks. 3. Synthetic data enhancement phase ( Fig. 1 c): it receives as input D u n s paired with one-hot encoded class vectors { z i } i = 1 P randomly sampled from a uniform distribution, which are processed by the generator G to create synthetic training samples D s y n = { s i } i = 1 P , with P ≫ N . Subsequently, D s y n is used to train the classifier C with these same class vectors { z ˆ i } i = 1 P serving as supervision signals. This final phase aims to expand the effective training set by creating synthetic samples that augment the limited labeled data.
