Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with a global socioeconomic burden and is predicted by the World Health Organization to be the third leading cause of death by 2030 [ 1 ]. Its pathophysiology involves airway disease [ 2 ], emphysema [ 3 ], vascular lesions, and various comorbidities induced by systemic inflammation. These factors jointly impair the quality of life and activities of daily living (ADLs) of patients. However, COPD symptoms vary among patients and may not correlate with the severity of airflow limitation. These usually cause the underdiagnosis of COPD and delay interventions such as the use of bronchodilators, physical therapy, and nutritional care, reducing healthy life expectancy. Thus, a novel approach is required to ensure timely diagnosis [ 4 ]. Insights into the functional trajectory of the lung based on a simple and easily implementable methodology may improve the management of patients with COPD. Deep learning-based imaging is common in the medical field. Deep learning techniques enable the efficient processing of large datasets, yielding novel results that are not readily achieved in conventional methodologies. For example, deep learning benefits automatic classification [ 5–7 ] and decision-making assistance. In addition, deep learning is particularly helpful for image classification tasks involving highly complex anatomical differences. The utility of deep learning has been extended to the early diagnosis of disorders with high accuracy, as the technology improves object detection [ 8 , 9 ], segmentation [ 10 ], and image reconstruction [ 11–14 ] performances. Recent studies have demonstrated the usefulness of deep learning algorithms for diagnoses based on computed tomography (CT), the determination of disease progression, and the selection of regular therapies, such as the use of bronchodilators, in COPD. The assessment of airflow limitation (forced expiratory volume in 1 s [FEV 1 ]/forced vital capacity [FVC] and percentage predicted value of FEV 1 [%FEV 1 ]) is required for the diagnosis and spirometric classification of COPD and the application of disease management techniques [ 15 , 16 ]. Deep learning improves numerical predictions based on images [ 17–19 ], particularly when combined with regression methods. For example, an FEV 1 prediction model based on a combination of spirometric data with sex, age, height, weight, smoking history, and CT images was used to categorize %FEV 1 (>80 or <80), FEV 1 /FVC (>70 or <70), and %FVC (>80 or <80) exhibited a high accuracy in a recent study [ 20 ]. Advancements in the numerical prediction of %FEV 1 using CT imaging may help identify COPD subtypes with a high risk of accelerating lung function decline. This could help optimize the management of smokers with or without airflow limitation by maintaining ADLs and reducing healthcare costs. To achieve this goal, we validated a CT data pre-processing method to improve the classification of COPD Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease stages by extracting image features from CT imaging data. The prediction of definite spirometry values may substantially benefit clinical settings. We primarily aimed to evaluate and compare the performances of two deep learning-based prediction models (two-dimensional [2D]-central neural network (CNN) study specifically focused on comparing the effectiveness of 2D slice-based analysis and three-dimensional [3D] volumetric analysis) in determining COPD severity from CT images. We used the data of patients with COPD from the Hokkaido COPD cohort [ 21 , 22 ], a multicenter observational prospective study with a 10-year follow-up. All participants were current or former smokers with a smoking history of at least 10 pack-years. We excluded those who a respirologist diagnosed with asthma or bronchiectasis, active tuberculosis, or a history of lung cancer, lung resection, cystic fibrosis, allergic alveolitis, or pulmonary fibrosis. Participants underwent CT and pulmonary function tests according to the manufacturer's protocol. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Hokkaido University Hospital (reference: med 02-001: December 2002, 018–0392 : 20th of February 2019, 025–0143 : 12th of August 2025)) and performed per the amended Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained according to the Hokkaido COPD Cohort Protocol. The study protocol was issued online, and participants could opt out voluntarily. Spirometry, lung volume, the carbon monoxide diffusion capacity of the lungs, and alveolar volume were measured using a Chestac-33 spirometer (Chest M.I., Tokyo, Japan). The CT data of 20 patients with COPD with %FEV 1 matching that of the internal data were selected from the Kyoto University cohort [ 3 , 23 ] for external validation. Participants in the Kyoto University cohort underwent chest inspiratory CT and pulmonary function tests using a Chestac-65V instrument (Chest M.I. Inc., Tokyo, Japan). The characteristics of the patients with COPD in the two cohorts are described in Table 1 . CT images were captured using a Siemens CT system (SOMATOM plus Volume Zoom; Siemens AG, Berlin, Germany) with the following parameters: tube voltage, 140 kVp; tube current, 150 mA; tube rotation speed, 0.5/s; slice thickness, 1.25 mm; and image reconstruction function B60f (lung-field segment image reconstruction function). Images for external validation were acquired using a CT system (Aquilion; Canon Medical Systems, Otawara, Japan) under the following conditions: tube voltage, 120 kVp; tube current, 260 mA; tube rotation speed, 0.5/s; and slice thickness, 0.5 mm. The FC56 (edge-enhancing convolution kernel) image reconstruction function was used. Data were stored in the DICOM format and saved on a personal computer for analysis. Only the cross-sectional images of the lung fields in the captured images were imported into MATLAB (MATLAB 2024b; MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) and converted into coronal sections. Twenty images of the anterior and posterior sections centered on the tracheal bifurcation in the coronal section were the target sections, and the images were adjusted to fit the display conditions (window width [WW] = 1,400, window level [WL] = −700) on the DICOM image. Subsequently, the images were resized to 512 × 512 pixels and saved in JPEG format in a separate folder, with each folder labeled with the corresponding %FEV 1 of the patient. For data augmentation, rotation processing was applied to the images, with angles ranging from −15° to +15° in 3° increments. The augmented data were used to train a regression CNN based on the ResNet-18 architecture ( Fig. 1 ). During data pre-processing, we ensured no missing data points. All CT images and corresponding spirometry values were available for each participant, enabling a comprehensive analysis without the imputation or exclusion of cases owing to missing data. For the 3D-CNN analysis, all cross-sectional DICOM images were adjusted to fit the display conditions (WW = 1,400, WL = −700), ensuring consistency with the 2D-CNN pre-processing pipeline. The adjusted images were combined into a 3D matrix and resized to the dimensions of 224 × 224 × 224. These processed images were saved as NIfTI files in separate folders, with each folder labeled with the corresponding %FEV 1 of the patients. For data augmentation, the 3D matrices were rotated in axial and coronal planes, with angles ranging from −15° to +15° in 3° increments. The processed images were converted to uint8 format before being saved as NIfTI files to ensure consistency with the bit-depth processing used in the 2D analysis ( Fig. 1 ). During pre-processing, we ensured that no data points were missing. All CT images and corresponding spirometry values were completed for each participant, enabling a comprehensive analysis without imputing or excluding cases. The CT examination data of 200 patients (%FEV 1 ) were arranged in a 40-row, 5-column matrix. The %FEV 1 values were first sorted in ascending order and distributed vertically to create five subsets (labeled A–E), with each subset (column) containing 40 % FEV 1 values. The values were arranged sequentially from top to bottom in each column when filling the matrix, indicating that the smallest %FEV 1 values were placed at the top of each column, and the largest values were placed at the bottom. This column-wise arrangement ensured that each subset contained a similar %FEV 1 distribution because the sorted values were evenly distributed across the five subsets. These five subsets were used to perform five-fold cross-validation. During each fold of the cross-validation, one (40 patients) and four (160 patients) subsets served as the test and training data, respectively. This process was repeated five times, with each subset serving as test data exactly once. This systematic approach to data organization ensured that the training and test datasets maintained similar distributions of %FEV 1 values in the cross-validation process, minimizing potential bias and improving the reliability of the model evaluation. We implemented two CNN architectures to predict %FEV 1 . The 2D-CNN was based on ResNet-18 and adapted for regression by replacing the final classification layers with regression layers. For each participant, 20 images from the top to the bottom of the lungs were used for the prediction. The 3D-CNN architecture was based on 3D-ResNet-18, modified for a 224 × 224 × 224 volumetric input, and the 3D convolutions and pooling operations were adapted for %FEV 1 prediction. Training was performed in MATLAB on a workstation equipped with two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. The parameters were as follows: learning rate drop period = 10, drop factor = 0.1, and L2 regularization = 0.0001. Model predictions were plotted against ground-truth test values. Linear regression was performed to determine the correlation coefficient (r), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and the coefficient using the following linear regression equation: (Eq. 1) Y = aX + b The RMSE was calculated using the following formula: (Eq.2) M A E = ∑ i | f i − x i | n R M S E = ∑ i ( f i − x i ) 2 n ( E q . 3 ) where f i is the %FEV 1 , as predicted with the regression model, and x i is the known %FEV 1 . The Bland–Altman method was used to assess agreement between true and predicted values by calculating mean differences and constructing limits of agreement (mean ± 1.96 Standard Deviation: SD). The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Cronbach's alpha coefficient (threshold: 0.70) were used to evaluate the reliability. Data analysis was performed using the SPSS software (version 29.0; Chicago, Armonk, NY, USA). After five-fold cross-validation, an overall regression model was created using the entire training dataset of 200 patients. External validation data were used to obtain the coefficient in Y = aX + b. We concatenated the test cases from the five folds into a single evaluation set (n = 200) and computed Pearson's correlation coefficient (r). Two-sided P-values were obtained, and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Fisher's z-transformation. To compare correlations from the two models on the same subjects, we used Steiger's test for dependent correlations (df = 195). For the concatenated internal test (n = 200) and external validation (n = 20) sets, we computed RMSE. We defined ΔRMSE as RMSE_3D − RMSE_2D and the relative reduction as 1 − (RMSE_3D/RMSE_2D). We estimated 95 % CIs via subject-level paired bootstrapping (B = 10,000) and assessed statistical significance with a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-subject squared-error differences ( di = ( yi −ŷ 3 D , i ) 2 − ( yi −ŷ 2 D , i ) 2 ). As practical thresholds, we considered a ≥10 % relative RMSE reduction as a primary improvement criterion and ΔRMSE ≥ +5 %FEV 1 as a clinically meaningful deterioration. For external validation, non-inferiority was judged informally by verifying that the upper bound of the 95 % CI for ΔRMSE was < +5. The correlation coefficient r, MAE, RMSE, and coefficients in the linear regression equation Y = aX + b were obtained by inputting the external validation data into the overall regression model. The model was trained using the entire dataset of 200 patients, as described in the “Model training and evaluation” section. The analysis was conducted using the Bland–Altman method, as discussed in the “Model training and evaluation” section. We quantified the ratio of wall area to airway dimension (%WA) at the segmental bronchi of B1 and B8 in the right lungs and the percentage of low-attenuation volume (%LAV, defined as lung volume with attenuation values < -950 Hounsfield unit [HU]) using A-VIEW software (Coreline Soft Inc., Seoul, South Korea) [ 24 ]. A prediction equation was constructed using the regression analysis based on the averaged values of %WA at two sites and %LAV. The details of the Commercial Software Analysis are described in an online supplementary material. In addition, a five-fold cross-validation was adopted, as described in the CNN models. As a phenotype-stratified subanalysis, we defined airway-dominant (AD) and emphysema-dominant (ED) subgroups using imaging markers that are independent of the functional outcome (%FEV 1 ), following the CT-based phenotype classification used in our previous report [ 25 ]. Percentage wall area (%WA) and percentage low-attenuation volume (%LAV; <-950 HU) were standardized within site/vendor (z-scores). Cases were classified as AD when standardized %WA exceeded a prespecified threshold, while standardized %LA was below the same threshold. However, cases were ED when standardized %LAV exceeded the threshold, while standardized %WA was below the threshold. Cases with both indices simultaneously high or low (no single predominance), or with missing indices or failure to meet quality-control criteria, were labeled indeterminate and excluded. Consequently, 22 and 72 of 200 cases were classified as AD and ED, respectively, in the internal cohort. The remaining cases were indeterminate and excluded from this subgroup analysis. Analyses within each phenotype were performed, as described in Section 2.4 . Briefly, we used the concatenated out-of-fold predictions, computed RMSE for each model, and summarized the difference (ΔRMSE = RMSE_3D − RMSE_2D) and the relative reduction (1 − RMSE_3D/RMSE_2D) with 95 % CIs using subject-level paired bootstrapping. Statistical significance was assessed with a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-subject squared-error differences. In addition, Pearson's correlation coefficients (with Fisher 95 % CIs) were computed, and correlations were compared between models using Steiger's test for dependent correlations. When a minor row mismatch existed between the 2D and 3D files in a subgroup, predictions were aligned by matching ground-truth %FEV 1 values within a small tolerance, and only the matched common subjects were analyzed. The 2D model achieved r = 0.606 (95 % CI: 0.509–0.687, P < 0.05), while the 3D model achieved r = 0.717 (95 % CI: 0.641–0.778, P < 0.05). The signed-rank test was significant (P < 0.05), favoring the 3D model. Externally (n = 20), RMSE_2D and RMSE_3D were 12.382 and 11.480, respectively, yielding a ΔRMSE of −0.902 (95 % CI: −4.299, 3.324) and a 7.3 % relative reduction (95 % CI: −40.8–28.2 %). Although not statistically significant (P = 0.9108), the point estimate favored the 3D model, the direction matched the internal analysis, and absolute RMSEs did not deteriorate. Notably, the upper bound of the 95 % CI for ΔRMSE was +3.324 (below the +5 %FEV 1 margin), suggesting non-inferiority and robust generalization. Using the phenotype definitions and matching procedure described in Section 2.7 , we evaluated performance within the AD and ED subgroups based on the matched common subjects. In AD (n = 22), the 3D-CNN substantially outperformed the 2D-CNN: RMSE was 6.488 vs. 13.102, yielding a ΔRMSE (3D−2D) of −6.613 (95 % CI: −9.269, −3.693) and a 50.5 % relative reduction (95 % CI: 36.3–62.8 %). The paired signed-rank test on per-subject squared-error differences was significant (P = 0.01424). Correlations were r_2D = 0.080 (95 % CI: −0.353–0.485; P = 0.723) and r_3D = 0.784 (95 % CI: 0.542–0.906; P = 1.55 × 10 −5 ), with Steiger's test confirming a significantly higher correlation for 3D (t = −5.050; df = 19; P = 7.11 × 10 −5 ). In addition, 3D showed superior accuracy in ED (n = 72): RMSE was 10.739 vs. 14.366, with a ΔRMSE of −3.628 (95 % CI: −6.525, −0.440) and a 25.3 % relative reduction (95 % CI: 3.2–42.7 %); the signed-rank test was significant (P = 6.72 × 10 −4 ). Correlations were r_2D = 0.691 (95 % CI: 0.547–0.795; P = 1.87 × 10 −11 ) and r_3D = 0.850 (95 % CI: 0.770–0.904; P = 3.76 × 10 −21 ), and Steiger's test favored 3D (t = −6.121; df = 69; P = 4.99 × 10 −8 ). Overall, these subgroup analyses indicate that the advantage of the 3D-CNN is not driven by phenotype imbalance. It rather holds within AD and ED, with a particularly large effect in AD and a consistent, statistically significant improvement in ED. The proposed 2D-CNN and 3D-CNN models performed differently for patients with COPD. The 3D-CNN model demonstrated superior performance, with an average correlation coefficient of 0.88 and RMSE of 10.73. The 2D-CNN model showed a correlation coefficient of 0.66 and RMSE of 16.76. The improvement in accuracy with the 3D-CNN approach suggests that volumetric analysis sufficiently captures the complex structural features of COPD on CT images. For external validation, both models maintained reasonable performance; however, certain degradation was observed. The 3D-CNN model showed slightly better results (correlation coefficient of 0.59 and RMSE of 11.48) than did the 2D-CNN model (correlation coefficient of 0.47 and RMSE of 12.38). These results suggest that both models, particularly 3D-CNN, are resilient against variations in CT acquisition parameters or CT vendors. In addition, 3D-CNN maintained better generalizability. To compare the relative performance of the CNN-based proposed models with that of an alternative method, we conducted prediction using a commercial software, which showed no inferiority in predicting the %FEV 1 compared with the performance of the CNN-based models. We used %WA as an index of airway disease and %LAV as an index of parenchymal disease, which are representative indices of airflow limitation in COPD [ 26 , 27 ]. This prediction does not reflect the maximum performance of a commercial software because certain other indices correlate with %FEV 1 . In some cases, commercial software analysis requires manual modifications for lobe segmentation or airway assessment. Regression prediction using the software was based on the entire Hokkaido COPD cohort dataset. Thus, the cases used for internal validation were included to construct the prediction model, which is presumed to increase the accuracy of the software for %FEV 1 . In contrast, both deep learning-based models were validated using cases that were excluded during testing. The RMSE values for both deep learning-based models were better than that of the commercial software (RMSE 23.18); 3D-CNN had a particularly strong performance. The radiological features recognized by deep learning models and software may differ. Thus, an ensemble of deep learning- and software-based models may offer complementary insights and improve %FEV 1 prediction. Regarding inferences, our internal analysis demonstrated a statistically higher correlation between predicted and observed %FEV 1 for the 3D-CNN than for the 2D-CNN. In the concatenated out-of-fold test set (n = 200), the 2D model achieved an r of 0.606 (95 % CI: 0.509–0.687; P < 0.05), and the 3D model had r = 0.717 (95 % CI: 0.641–0.778; P < 0.05). Steiger's test for dependent correlations confirmed that the 3D correlation was significantly higher (t = −3.368; df = 195; P < 0.05). These results support the interpretation that volumetric representation improves the strength of association with a functional outcome. Error-based comparisons were concordant. In the internal test, RMSE was lower for 3D than for 2D (14.830 vs. 16.858, respectively), with ΔRMSE = −2.029 (95 % CI: −4.963–0.727) and a significant paired test on per-subject squared-error differences (P < 0.05), corresponding to a 12.0 % relative reduction (95 % CI: −4.3–30.0 %). Externally (n = 20), absolute RMSEs did not deteriorate, and the point estimate favored 3D in the same direction, as that in the internal test (11.480 vs. 12.382; ΔRMSE = −0.902, 95 % CI: −4.299–3.324; P = 0.9108). While the external comparison was not statistically significant, the upper bound of the 95 % CI for ΔRMSE (+3.324) remained below a pragmatic +5 %FEV 1 margin for clinically meaningful deterioration and thus supports non-inferiority and robust generalization. This margin was not pre-specified, and the external sample size was limited; however, the consistency in direction and the absence of deterioration across datasets validate 3D-CNN as a more reliable estimator of %FEV 1 . In phenotype-stratified analyses (Section 2.7 ), the 3D-CNN outperformed the 2D-CNN within AD and ED subgroups, indicating that the advantage of the 3D approach is not driven by phenotype imbalance but holds within each phenotype. In AD (n = 22), the 3D-CNN roughly halved the error in 2D (RMSE = 6.488 vs. 13.102), with ΔRMSE (3D–2D) = −6.613 (95 % CI: −9.269, −3.693) and a 50.5 % relative reduction (95 % CI: 36.3–62.8 %); the paired signed-rank test on per-subject squared-error differences was significant (P = 0.01424). In addition, correlations favored 3D (r = 0.784, 95 % CI: 0.542–0.906; P = 1.55 × 10 −5 ) over 2D (r = 0.080, 95 % CI: −0.353–0.485; P = 0.723), with Steiger's test confirming a significantly higher correlation for 3D (t = −5.050; df = 19; P = 7.11 × 10 −5 ). In ED (n = 72), error was also significantly lower for 3D than for 2D (RMSE = 10.739 vs. 14.366; ΔRMSE = −3.628, 95 % CI: −6.525, −0.440; relative reduction 25.3 %, 95 % CI: 3.2–42.7 %), and correlation was higher in the former (r = 0.850, 95 % CI: 0.770–0.904; P = 3.76 × 10 −21 vs. r = 0.691, 95 % CI: 0.547–0.795; P = 1.87 × 10 −11 ; Steiger P = 4.99 × 10 −8 ). Taken together with the external analysis, these subgroup results support phenotype-agnostic generalization of the 3D-CNN, with a particularly large gain in AD and a consistent, statistically significant improvement in ED. The vendor and reconstruction functions significantly affected the quality of the lung-field images in the CT data. In this study, the CT images were captured at 140 kV, whereas the external validation data were captured at 120 kV. Given the small sample size used for the external validation, both proposed models should be validated using larger datasets from multiple centers to address potential variations in the acquisition parameters. The filtering conditions in the image files depend on the vendor in the DICOM format, which is standard in medical practice. Standardization of CT scanning, together with advancements in data processing, may reduce variations in image quality. In addition, it may allow the establishment of feasible settings for research and medical practice. This proposed model was constructed using the data of patients with COPD. Thus, application to cases beyond COPD requires validation. Prediction for clinical course is another possibility for deep learning-based prediction models. A survival prediction model using deep learning based on chest radiographs and the COPD assessment test [ 28 ] performed better than did other established prognostic indicators. Notably, a 3D–CNN–based prediction model for subtyping patients with poor prognosis may play a complementary role to other tools in a clinical setting. This study has some limitations. First, both models accurately predicted %FEV 1 regardless of age, sex, or body size; however, they should be further validated using CT data from female patients because the participants in the current study were predominantly male Japanese patients with COPD. Second, the Bland–Altman analysis revealed systematic errors, which are attributable to the relatively limited nature of the training data. Third, we did not evaluate the predictive models in terms of interpretability. Therefore, the consistency of the rationale for deriving the predicted values with a focus on actual clinical practice should be examined. The true and predicted %FEV 1 values had significant positive correlations, particularly for the 3D-CNN model. Training with a larger variety of supervised data may have lowered the error in this study. Both models were based on cross-sectional data, necessitating validation using longitudinal datasets. Deep-learning-based prediction models for %FEV 1 demonstrated promising results, with the 3D-CNN model showing superior performance over the 2D-CNN model. Both models outperformed commercial software analysis, suggesting their potential as effective tools for estimating the spirometric severity of COPD. SupReMix: Supervised contrastive learning for medical imaging regression with mixup In medical image analysis, regression plays a critical role in computer-aided diagnosis. It enables quantitative measurements such as age prediction from structural imaging, cardiac function quantification, and molecular measurement from PET scans. While deep learning has shown promise for these tasks, most approaches focus solely on optimizing regression loss or model architecture, neglecting the quality of learned feature representations which are crucial for robust clinical predictions. Directly applying representation learning techniques designed for classification to regression often results in fragmented representations in the latent space, yielding sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we argue that the potential of contrastive learning for medical image regression has been overshadowed due to the neglect of two crucial aspects: ordinality-awareness and hardness. To address these challenges, we propose Supervised Contrastive Learning for Medical Imaging Regression with Mixup (SupReMix). It takes anchor-inclusive mixtures (mixup of the anchor and a distinct negative sample) as hard negative pairs and anchor-exclusive mixtures (mixup of two distinct negative samples) as hard positive pairs at the embedding level. This strategy formulates harder contrastive pairs by integrating richer ordinal information. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on six datasets spanning MRI, X-ray, ultrasound, and PET modalities, we demonstrate that SupReMix fosters continuous ordered representations, significantly improving regression performance. In medical image analysis, regression plays a critical role in computer-aided diagnosis. It enables quantitative measurements such as age prediction from structural imaging, cardiac function quantification, and molecular measurement from PET scans. While deep learning has shown promise for these tasks, most approaches focus solely on optimizing regression loss or model architecture, neglecting the quality of learned feature representations which are crucial for robust clinical predictions. Directly applying representation learning techniques designed for classification to regression often results in fragmented representations in the latent space, yielding sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we argue that the potential of contrastive learning for medical image regression has been overshadowed due to the neglect of two crucial aspects: ordinality-awareness and hardness . To address these challenges, we propose Sup ervised Contrastive Learning for Medical Imaging Re gression with Mi xup ( SupReMix ). It takes anchor-inclusive mixtures (mixup of the anchor and a distinct negative sample) as hard negative pairs and anchor-exclusive mixtures (mixup of two distinct negative samples) as hard positive pairs at the embedding level. This strategy formulates harder contrastive pairs by integrating richer ordinal information. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on six datasets spanning MRI, X-ray, ultrasound, and PET modalities, we demonstrate that SupReMix fosters continuous ordered representations, significantly improving regression performance. Regression problems aim to predict continuous values based on given input data. They encompass a broad range of medical imaging applications such as predicting brain age using MRI ( Peng et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2024 ), assessing pediatric development through bone age prediction from hand X-rays ( Halabi et al., 2019; Escobar et al., 2019 ), analyzing cardiac function by measuring left-ventricular ejection fraction (LEVF) from echocardiograms ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ), and evaluating amyloid accumulation in brain PET scans by prediction of standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR) ( Pemberton et al., 2022 ). The accuracy and reliability of these quantitative predictions are paramount, as they directly influence clinical diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Recent works on medical image regression often use neural networks to learn mappings from complex medical images to continuous targets. For example, Peng et al. (2021) proposed an efficient VGG-like 3D CNN for structural MRI brain-age prediction, and Hara et al. (2018) ; He et al. (2021a,b) explored transformer backbones. For rs-fMRI brain age, Hong et al. (2020) employed a 1D-ResNet, and Caro et al. (2023) used a vision transformer to predict the target from ROI-by-time representations. In cardiac function regression, Ouyang et al. (2020) used an R(2+1)D encoder to predict LVEF (%) from echocardiogram videos, while Mokhtari et al. (2022) ; Muhtaseb and Yaqub (2022) proposed graph and transformer variants under the same objective. For amyloid-PET SUVR, Pemberton et al. (2022) proposed a lightweight 3D CNN that predicts global or regional SUVR for longitudinal tracking. Across these examples, a recurring template emerges: a modality-matched encoder f ( x ) and a lightweight regressor p ( · ) trained end-to-end with a single, task-appropriate loss-that is, vanilla deep regression.Vanilla deep regression refers to the approach of training a deep model to estimate the target value, with the distance ( e.g. , L1 distance Hsieh et al., 2021 ) between the prediction and ground-truth defined as the loss function. The core limitation of vanilla deep regression lies in its singular focus on minimizing prediction error, while neglecting the quality of the learned feature representations themselves. In other words, it learns What to predict, but ignores How (i.e., the underlying latent space). A standard regression loss provides no explicit instructions on how to organize samples within the high-dimensional latent space. This can lead to twisted representations that fail to capture the inherent continuity and ordinality of the regression task ( Fig. 7 provides the quantitative evidence, showing that the poorer ordered continuity of the representations from vanilla regression directly correlates with its suboptimal performance). Such poorly-structured representations can compromise model robustness and generalization, especially in challenging clinical scenarios with limited data ( Fig. 9 demonstrates the enhanced robustness of ordered and continuous representations in low-data regimes). Contrastive learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm of learning representations. It aims to learn a structured feature space by pulling representations of “positive” pairs (an “anchor” and a similar sample) together, while simultaneously pushing representations of “negative” pairs (the anchor and a dissimilar sample) apart (A.13) ( Chen et al., 2020a ). In the realm of classification, techniques such as supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) extend this framework to the fully-supervised setting, enabling effective leverage of rich label information. However, there has been limited research dedicated to developing representation learning methods specifically tailored for regression tasks. Learning robust feature representations, beyond just optimizing regression loss, ensures reliable generalization across different clinical scenarios ( Chen et al., 2019 ). One might consider directly adapting SupCon for regression tasks. However, such direct application of SupCon tends to neglect the inherent ordinal nature of regression, i.e. , lack of ordinality-awareness ( Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, prior work in classification underscores the significance of hard contrastive pairs in contrastive learning ( Ho and Nvasconcelos, 2020; Robinson et al., 2020; Kalantidis et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, they mainly focused on hard negatives with hard positives underexplored, and the hardness of contrastive pairs in contrastive learning for regression remains inadequately examined ( Fig. 4 ). Data mixing techniques ( Zhang et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2022 ) have been used to create hard samples in previous contrastive learning methods for classification ( Kalantidis et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023 ). However, these methods do not leverage the label distance to differentiate the hardness among hard negative mixtures. There have been some notable attempts to address regression problems with constrastive learning. Rank-N-Contrast (RNC) proposes a ranking-based contrastive learning method for regression tasks ( Zha et al., 2023 ) (D.17) . Adaptive Contrast for Image Regression (AdaCon) introduces an adaptive loss function to preserve label relationships in the latent of medical imaging ( Dai et al., 2021a ). However, these methods are limited by their reliance on data augmentation, making them not applicable to domains without well-established augmentation techniques, such as time series data. In neuroimaging, for example, it is standard practice to analyze functional MRI (fMRI) as parcellated time series ( Dong et al., 2024; Caro et al., 2023 ). For this important data modality, the lack of well-established augmentation techniques therefore limits the applicability of prior methods that fundamentally rely on them. In this paper, we propose Sup ervised Contrastive Learning for Medical Imaging Re gression with Mix up ( SupReMix ), a novel framework for regression representation learning. Our aim is to better leverage the inherent ordinal relationships among various inputs and foster the generation of “harder” contrastive pairs. Instead of relying on real samples in conventional contrastive learning, the proposed SupReMix approach constructs new contrastive pairs at the embedding level in an anchor-inclusive and anchor-exclusive manner. We take anchor-inclusive mixtures as hard negatives: mixing the anchor with a distinct negative sample, thus pulling the negatives closer to the convex hull between the anchor and negatives in order to encourage continuity. On the other hand, we take anchor-exclusive mixtures as hard positives: merging two negative samples, the convex combination of whose labels equals to that of the anchor, to encourage local linearity. Moreover, we assign weights to the negative pairs to incorporate label distance information. Our theoretical analysis offers a robust foundation, demonstrating that SupReMix is capable of formulating continuous ordered representations. For the remainder of the paper, we will refer to our hard negatives and hard positives as “Mix-neg” and “Mix-pos”, respectively. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on six medical imaging datasets spanning diverse modalities ( Fig. 1 ): brain age prediction from both structural and functional MRI, bone age assessment from X-rays, cardiac function estimation from echocardiograms, and amyloid burden quantification from PET scans. By comparing with other representation learning methods, we demonstrate that SupReMix consistently outperforms existing approaches across all modalities. For example, on the RSNA bone age dataset ( Halabi et al., 2019 ), SupReMix achieves state-of-the-art performance with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 4.08 months, significantly improving upon the baseline’s 6.79 months. Through both qualitative and quantitative analysis, we validate that SupReMix learns continuous, ordered representations that better capture the inherent structure of regression tasks, leading to more robust and accurate predictions in medical imaging analysis. Furthermore, we show that SupReMix exhibits strong generalization capabilities when handling challenging scenarios such as missing targets and few-shot cases, and can serve as an effective pre-training strategy to enhance existing task-specific architectures. Most modern representation learning structures embeddings by pulling together semantically similar samples while pushing apart dissimilar ones ( Chen et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b ). In the supervised setting, SupCon generalizes triplet and N-pair losses by contrasting each example against all same-class positives and different-class negatives ( Khosla et al., 2020; Weinberger and Saul, 2009; Sohn, 2016 ). Within the domain of medical imaging , recent progress has been driven by domain-tailored pretraining at scale: (i) foundation models trained via self-supervision on millions of images (e.g., RETFound for retinal imaging) deliver strong label efficiency and transfer ( Zhou et al., 2023b ); (ii) vision–language pretraining aligns images with radiology text to enable zero-shot and few-shot recognition (e.g., CheXzero, MedCLIP, and knowledge-enhanced VLP on chest X-rays) ( Tiu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ); and (iii) masked image modeling has been adapted to clinical data with radiology-report-guided masking that targets semantically informative regions ( Xie et al., 2024 ). Recent surveys synthesize these trends and document consistent gains on classification/segmentation/detection benchmarks under limited annotation ( Huang et al., 2023; Haghighi et al., 2024 ). By contrast, regression-oriented representation learning in medical imaging remains comparatively underexplored. Beyond earlier adaptive-contrast ideas ( Dai et al., 2021b ), newer works begin to encode label distances or ordinality directly for quantitative prediction (e.g., brain age and diffusion MRI tractometry), reporting improved generalization across sites and noise conditions ( Barbano et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2024 ). However, these methods target specific domains rather than general regression in medical imaging. Furthermore, they fail to model the overall morphology of latent representations while lacking control over contrastive pair hardness. Our method continues in this direction by designing a supervised contrastive objective that encodes (i) ordinality and (ii) hardness through mixup-based pair construction, yielding globally ordered and locally smooth embeddings for medical regression . Prior research in classification emphasizes the crucial role of hard contrastive pairs in contrastive learning. It generally falls into two categories: hard sample mining and hard sample generation. The former aims to identify the most challenging samples from existing ones, with notable work by Robinson et al. (2020) devising an importance-based sampling strategy for mining hard negatives without computational overhead. In the realm of hard sample generation, Ho and Nvasconcelos (2020) utilized adversarial attacks to augment the training dataset, incorporating pixel-level disturbances into clean samples. Kalantidis et al. (2020) proposed hard negative mixing strategies at the feature level. Wu et al. (2023) developed a data generation framework enhancing contrastive learning through combined hard sample creation and contrastive learning. These approaches markedly diverge from ours, mainly as they revolve around self-supervised contrastive learning without utilizing label information, and target classification rather than regression. Previous contrastive learning methods for classification have utilized data mixing techniques ( Zhang et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2022 ) to generate hard samples ( Kalantidis et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023 ). However, these methods are unable to use label distance to differentiate hardness among hard negative mixtures in regression. C-Mixup ( Yao et al., 2022 ) selects samples in regression for mixup based on the label distance. Anchor data augmentation (ADA) Schneider et al. (2023) proposes a data augmentation method in nonlinear over-parameterized regression. However, these methods lack a clear definition of the relationship between outcomes (positive or negative) which makes it difficult to define contrastive pairs and explicitly integrate label distance information into the contrastive learning process. Medical image regression has emerged as a critical tool in quantitative healthcare, enabling precise measurements across diverse clinical applications. Brain age prediction from structural MRI serves as a biomarker for neurological health, helping identify accelerated aging patterns that may indicate early disease onset ( Cole and Franke, 2017; Smith et al., 2019; Franke and Gaser, 2019 ). In pediatrics, bone age assessment from hand radiographs aids in evaluating developmental disorders and growth abnormalities ( Halabi et al., 2019; Escobar et al., 2019 ). Cardiac function quantification through metrics like ejection fraction from echocardiograms provides essential diagnostic information for heart conditions ( Ouyang et al., 2020; Muhtaseb and Yaqub, 2022; Mokhtari et al., 2022 ). In neurology, amyloid PET quantification through standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR) enables early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression ( Pemberton et al., 2022 ). Despite sharing fundamental challenges as regression tasks, these applications have traditionally been approached in isolation, with methods developed specifically for each task separately. For instance, brain age prediction methods often focus on brain-specific architectures ( Peng et al., 2021 ), while cardiac function estimation employs specialized temporal modeling ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ). This fragmented approach overlooks the common underlying challenge of learning meaningful representations from medical images for regression tasks. Through extensive experiments across six medical regression tasks, we demonstrate the potential benefits of improving representation learning in medical image regression generally. In a regression task, our goal is to train a neural network that consists of two main components: an encoder f ( · ): X ↦ z ∈ R d e which encodes inputs to embeddings, and a predictor p ( · ): z ∈ R d e ↦ m ∈ R which outputs the target value m ∈ R . Given one mini-batch, hard contrastive pairs are first created utilizing the mixup technique. Following this, we calculate our supervised contrastive regression loss, denoted as L SupReMix , based on both the real and our hard contrastive pairs. To predict the target value, f ( · ) is followed by p ( · ), trained by a regression loss ( e.g. , L1 loss). In this section, we outline our approach to supervised contrastive regression. We begin in Section 3.1 with an explanation of our mixup strategy for generating hard negative and positive pairs. This is followed by Section 3.2 , which is about our weights defined for contrastive pairs. This introduces distance magnifying (DM) , a behavior that is greatly advantageous in supervised contrastive regression, differentiating it from classification. In Section 3.3 , we bring together the preceding elements to formulate our supervised contrastive regression loss, L SupReMix . In Section 3.4 , we present a theoretical analysis of the distance magnifying property of our weights for negative pairs, as well as the ordinality-awareness of L SupReMix . Notations. Let I : the set of embeddings from real samples with N ≔ | I | (i.e. mini-batch size), M ⊂ R : the set of all initial labels (bounded by m max and m min , the maximum and minimum of regression label respectively.), ρ : I ↦ M : the function mapping an embedding to its label. Order I such that ρ is monotone. I m ⊂ I : the set of embeddings with ρ = m and k m ≔ | I m |, which we take to be 0, if m ∉ M . We give an order for elements in I m , ( m, i ), meaning the i th embeddings in I m . Anchor-inclusive mixtures are hard negatives. Given an anchor, a “mixed” negative-created through the convex combination of the anchor itself and a real negative-can be more challenging to differentiate compared to a real negative. This occurs in the latent space where the mixed negative is pulled closer to the anchor, thereby diminishing the discernible differences between the anchor and the hard negative. Given an anchor z m,i ∈ I m , we generate a set of Mix-neg z m , i − defined by: (1) z m , i − = λ 1 · z m , i + ( 1 − λ 1 ) · z ′ (2) k m , i − : = N − k m where z ′ ∈ I \ I m , λ 1 ∼ Beta( α, β ), and m ‾ = λ 1 · m + ( 1 − λ 1 ) · m ′ . k m , i − is the number of Mix-neg generated for the anchor z m,i , m ‾ is the label of Mix-neg, which is the convex combination of anchor’s label m and a distinct negative’s label m ′. Different from vanilla mixup ( Zhang et al., 2018 ), we use λ 1 as a “control” of hardness in our Mix-neg, modulating it through the adjustment of α and β parameters that shape the Beta distribution from which λ 1 is sampled ( Fig. 2 ). If we choose α and β to produce a skewed distribution where a majority of the values cluster close to one, the anchor z m,i will almost surely predominate over the real negative z ′, thereby generating a harder negative. Conversely, if we choose α and β so that λ 1 is drawn from a distribution that leans heavily towards zero, the anchor z m,i has a relatively smaller share in the mixup, resulting in a reduction of the mixup hardness. Anchor-exclusive mixtures are hard positives. In contrastive learning, a common practice is to create positive pairs by augmenting an anchor to generate different views ( Chen et al., 2020a ); despite their visual differences, these augmented input retain their core identity, as they originate from a single input. However, relying solely on this method can limit the richness of the learned representations, as it overlooks the potential value of incorporating other similar objects that offer additional valuable perspectives ( Wu et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, it is not applicable for domains with no appropriate data augmentation methods such as time series. Finally, this approach does not take into account the underlying ordinal relationships among inputs and labels, which is particularly important in regression tasks. To address these limitations, we mix two negative embeddings - one with a label value greater than the anchor’s label and one with a label value less than the anchor’s label - serve as hard positives ( Fig. 2 ). This strategy not only preserves the natural order of the data but also expands the diversity of the positive pairs, creating a more stringent constraint that guides the learning process to a locally linear embedding space. Given an anchor z m,i , and a window size γ ∈ Z + , we create Mix-pos z m , i + : (3) z m , i + = λ 2 · z m ′ , i ′ + ( 1 − λ 2 ) · z m ″ , i ″ (4) k m , i + : = ∑ j = 1 γ k i − j · ∑ l = 1 γ k i + l where i ′ < i < i ″ , i − i ′ , i ″ − i ≤ γ , and λ 2 · m ′ + ( 1 − λ 2 ) · m ″ = m . k m , i + is the number of Mix-pos for the anchor z m,i . 0 < λ 2 < 1 is deterministic for each Mix-pos. Local linearity means that, in a small neighborhood, embeddings for intermediate labels lie close to the line between their two bracketing neighbors in label order. Geometrically, Mix-pos “stitch” embeddings from adjacent label neighborhoods together, preventing the representation from fragmenting into disconnected islands or purely class-like clusters. In the loss function derived from contrastive pairs, we incorporate a vital parameter - the label distance information for each negative pair (including both real and mixup instances). Leveraging label distance as a metric facilitates a more fundamental approach to handling negative pairs. For each negative pair z m and z m ‾ ( m ≠ m ‾ ), we define a weight w m , m ‾ as: (5) w m , m ‾ = 1 + | m − m ‾ | m max − m min where m max and m min are the maximum and minimum of regression label respectively. (Note that in the implementation, all contrastive pairs will be multiplied by w in the loss calculation. Adding 1 to the numerator ensures that w remains non-zero and the same for all positive pairs). In our loss function ( Section 3.3 ), the logit corresponding to each contrastive pair is modulated by multiplication with w . To examine SupReMix’s effectiveness across different imaging modalities and regression tasks, we conducted experiments on six different medical imaging datasets spanning brain age prediction (UK Biobank Miller et al., 2016 , HCP-Lifespan Tisdall et al., 2012 ), bone age assessment (RSNA-BAA Halabi et al., 2019 , RHPE-BAA Escobar et al., 2019 ), cardiac function estimation (Echo-Net Ouyang et al., 2020 ), and amyloid burden quantification (A4 Sapra and Kim, 2009 ). These datasets represent a broad spectrum of medical imaging modalities including structural and functional MRI, X-rays, echocardiogram videos, and PET scans (B.14) . The key characteristics of each dataset are summarized in Table 1 , and we describe each dataset in details below. Additional details about the datasets, including preprocessing steps, are provided in Appendix B.1 . UK Biobank ( Miller et al., 2016 ) is a large-scale biomedical database and research resource containing in-depth genetic and health information from half a million UK participants. From this rich database, we utilize the T1-weighted structural MRI scans collected from 24,371 participants (aged 42–82 years) to evaluate brain age prediction. The original non-skull-stripped T1-weighted images with 1×1×1 mm³ resolution were resampled to 2×2×2 mm³ and center cropped into 100 x 100 x 100 to reduce computational overhead. Detailed preprocessing steps are described in ALF (2018) . Human Connectome Project (HCP) Lifespan ( Tisdall et al., 2012 ) dataset is part of a comprehensive initiative to map human brain connectivity across the adult lifespan, collecting data from participants aged 36–100 years. From this dataset, we utilize resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from 656 participants, acquired using the standard HCP protocol at 2mm isotropic resolution. The fMRI data were preprocessed following the pipeline described in Li et al. (2019) , which includes global signal regression to enhance behavioral associations, and parcellated using the Schaefer-400 atlas ( Schaefer et al., 2018 ). Consequently, our input data is in the shape of [400 (# parcells), 478 (# time frames)]. For bone age assessment, we utilize two X-ray datasets: the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) Bone Age Challenge dataset ( Halabi et al., 2019 ) and the Radiological Hand Posture Estimation (RHPE) dataset ( Escobar et al., 2019 ). The RSNA dataset contains 12,811 hand radiographs with ages ranging from 1 to 228 months. All radiographs were preprocessed and resized to 520×400 voxels to maintain consistent input dimensions. The RHPE dataset comprises 6292 hand radiographs annotated with bone ages ranging from 10 to 242 months. For RHPE preprocessing, since each image contains both left and right hands, we first isolated the left hand by taking the left half of each image. Following Escobar et al. (2019) , we then applied the ground truth bounding boxes to crop the hand region. The cropped images were subsequently resized to 520×400 pixels to maintain consistency with the RSNA dataset preprocessing pipeline. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is a critical cardiac function metric that measures the percentage of blood leaving the heart with each contraction, serving as a key indicator for diagnosing various heart conditions ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ). The Echo-Net dataset ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ) consists of 10,030 apical-4-chamber echocardiogram videos acquired from Stanford University Hospital using various ultrasound machines including iE33, Sonos, Acuson SC2000, Epiq 5G, and Epiq 7C. Each video contains 32 frames and is annotated with LVEF values ranging from 6.91 to 96.96. The dataset has been preprocessed to remove extraneous text information, and all frames were rescaled to 112×112 pixels. During training, frame jitter was applied as an augmentation technique to enhance model robustness. The Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s (A4) study ( Sapra and Kim, 2009 ) is a prevention trial in clinically normal older individuals to test whether an anti-amyloid antibody can slow memory loss caused by AD. The dataset consists of 4448 minimally processed, native-space amyloid PET scans acquired using [18F]-Florbetapir (FBP). Each PET acquisition comprises four five-minute frames collected between 50–70 mins post-injection, with only these frames included to ensure an adequate signal-to-noise ratio. Each PET scan was generated by averaging co-registered frames. The scans remained in native space without spatial normalization or structural MRI-based processing. Standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) were calculated using the whole cerebellum as the reference region across six cortical regions: medial orbital frontal, temporal, parietal, anterior cingulate, posterior cingulate, and precuneus, with values ranging from 0.45 to 2.58. Amyloid positivity (A β +) was determined based on a predefined SUVR cutoff of > 1.15, following established criteria for amyloid burden classification. We performed quality checks and center-cropped each volume to 128 x 128 x 128. We conducted comprehensive comparisons against both representation learning methods and task-specific approaches. For representation learning baselines, we compared SupReMix with classification-based methods including SimCLR ( Chen et al., 2019 ) and SupCon ( Khosla et al., 2020 ), as well as regression-based approaches including AdaCon ( Dai et al., 2021a ) and RNC ( Zha et al., 2023 ). Data augmentation strategies for baselines were modality-specific: for 2D images (bone age estimation), we employed standard techniques including color distortion and cropping ( Chen et al., 2020a ); for 3D volumetric data (amyloid SUVR and structural MRI), we utilized rotation, flipping, zooming, and color distortion following ( Taleb et al., 2020 ). For modalities without well-established augmentation methods (fMRI time series), we omitted augmentation during training. Detailed augmentation protocols and a comparison with discretization alternatives are provided in Appendices B.1 and D.5 , respectively. Furthermore, we compared SupReMix with state-of-the-art task-specific methods across different medical imaging domains. For brain age prediction with UK Biobank, we included ResNet-18 ( Hara et al., 2018 ), ViT-B ( He et al., 2021b ), Global-Local Transformer ( He et al., 2021a ), and the fully convolutional SFCN ( Peng et al., 2021 ). The HCP-Lifespan time-series analysis incorporated 1D-ResNet ( Hong et al., 2020 ), Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) ( Lea et al., 2017 ), and ViT ( Caro et al., 2023 ). Cardiac function estimation on Echo-Net was evaluated against EchoNet ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ), graph neural network-based EchoGNN ( Mokhtari et al., 2022 ), and transformer-based EchoCotr ( Muhtaseb and Yaqub, 2022 ). For bone age assessment (RSNA-BAA and RHPE-BAA), we compared with BoNet ( Escobar et al., 2019 ), PEAR-Net ( Liu et al., 2020 ), Doctor Imitator (DI) ( Chen et al., 2021 ), SIMBA ( González et al., 2020 ), and multi-scale MMANet ( Yang et al., 2023 ). For Amyloid PET quantification (A4), we evaluated against SFCN ( Peng et al., 2021 ), 3D DenseNet ( Huang et al., 2017 ), and attention-based FiA-Net ( He et al., 2021b ). All methods were implemented following their original training protocols. For RSNA and RHPE datasets (X-ray, 2D image), we adopted a ResNet-50 ( He et al., 2016 ) as the backbone network. For UK Biobank and A4 (T1/PET MRI, 3D volumetric images), we adopted a 3D-ResNet-18 ( Hara et al., 2018 ) as the backbone network. For Echo-Net (Echocardiogram, video), we used a r2plus1d-18 network as the backbone ( Tran et al., 2018 ). For HCP-Lifespan, we adopt an 18-layer 1D-ResNet ( Hong et al., 2020 ) as the backbone network to process time-series data. Across all experiments, we utilized Adam optimizer ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) with an initial learning rate of 10 − 3 . For representation learning frameworks, all methods were pretrained for 200 epochs for a fair comparison, followed by linear probing for 100 epochs. Temperature parameter ( τ ) selections are dataset-dependent, with values of 0.5 for UK Biobank and HCP-Lifespan and 1.0 for RSNA, RHPE, Echo-Net and A4 (C.15) . When applying a vanilla regression approach, our implementation follows the guidelines established in previous studies ( Yang et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2023 ). Complete implementation details are in Appendix C.1 . We use common metrics for regression ( Yang et al., 2021 ) to evaluate the performance, including Mean-Absolute-Error (MAE), Mean-Square-Error (MSE), Geometric Mean (GM) error, and Pearson correlation coefficient ( ρ ). In regression tasks, a well-constructed model should learn representations where the ordering of data points in the latent space reflects the ordering of their corresponding labels ( Zha et al., 2023 ). To evaluate this property, we performed a label permutation experiment on RSNA X-rays ( Halabi et al., 2019 ) for bone age prediction. Our label permutation protocol randomly reassigns a new value to each bone age group in the dataset. For example, all X-rays originally labeled as 12 months would be reassigned to the same new value ( e.g. , 48 months), while X-rays from a different age group would be collectively reassigned to another value ( e.g. , 12 months). While this permutation preserves the equivalence relationships within each bone age group, it deliberately disrupts the natural ordering between groups. A model that truly captures the ordinal nature of regression data should exhibit markedly different behavior when trained with permuted versus groud truth. Shown in Fig. 3 , when trained with groud truth, SupReMix produces embeddings that form a continuous, ordered structure reflecting the natural progression of bone age (left panel-A). However, this structure is significantly disrupted with permuted labels (left panel-B), indicating SupReMix’s sensitivity to label relationships. Conversely, SupCon treats different bone ages as discrete classes, producing clustered embeddings that remain largely unchanged between genuine and permuted labels (right panel). This reveals a fundamental limitation of applying classification-based contrastive learning to regression tasks – such approaches fail to leverage the ordinal information inherent in regression labels. Previous studies on contrastive learning have demonstrated that as the training process advances, a diminishing number of hard negative samples make contributions to the overall loss function ( Kalantidis et al., 2020 ). Our observations confirm this phenomenon and extend it to positive samples as well, particularly when applied to regression problems. In Fig. 4 , we utilized the RSNA bone age dataset to examine the average of logit values ( i.e. , the inner product of two embeddings with norm of 1) representing the similarity between two embeddings over the training process. We monitor all positive pairs and the top 1k most challenging negative pairs. We note that, in SupCon, the logit values for positive pairs saturate swiftly, approaching 1 after around 100 training epochs. This indicates a reduced reliance on these pairs in later learning stages as they contribute less to the loss function. Similarly, fewer negative pairs contribute to the loss function over time. In contrast, SupReMix continued to improve its performance throughout 100 epochs, due to its more challenging contrastive pairs. We compare SupReMix against both classification-based (SimCLR Chen et al., 2019 , SupCon Khosla et al., 2020 ) and regression-based (AdaCon Dai et al., 2021a , RnC Zha et al., 2023 ) representation learning methods across six medical imaging regression datasets spanning different modalities (MRI, X-ray, ultrasound, and PET). As shown in Fig. 5 , SupReMix consistently achieves lower MAE than all baseline methods. Taking bone age prediction on RSNA as an example, SupReMix reduces the MAE to 4.08 months compared to the classification-based method SupCon (6.79 months). The performance gains are particularly notable in challenging tasks such as cardiac function estimation, where SupReMix achieves an MAE of 4.02 compared to SupCon’s 5.88. Moreover, we observe that SupReMix consistently outperforms vanilla regression (shown in dashed line). Additional performance metrics including Mean Squared Error (MSE), correlation coefficient ( ρ ), and Geometric Mean (GM) error are provided in Tables 2–7 . To better understand the relationship between prediction performance and distribution of learned latent representations, we analyze different methods through both scatter plots (showing prediction accuracy) and t-SNE ( Van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008 ) visualizations in two tasks: brain age prediction from UK Biobank MRI ( Fig. 6 , shown in blue) and amyloid burden (SUVR) prediction from A4 PET scans ( Fig. 6 , shown in red). As illustrated in Fig. 6 , the visualization reveals distinct characteristics and limitations of existing approaches. SimCLR, Van der Maaten and Hinton (2008) while maintaining reasonable prediction accuracy, produces scattered representations that lack a clear ordinal structure in the latent space. Classification-based methods such as SupCon tend to form discrete clusters, which is suboptimal for continuous regression tasks, as evidenced by the disconnected groups in its t-SNE plot. RnC shows improved ordinal awareness but still struggles to fully capture the continuous nature of the underlying data, particularly at the extremes of the value range. In contrast, SupReMix demonstrates superior representation learning performance by preserving both local smoothness and global ordering, as shown by the more coherent progression in the t-SNE space and tighter alignment along the perfect prediction line in the scatter plots. The visualization aligns with the quantitative improvements observed in our empirical evaluation. We have qualitatively observed the continuity of representations through t-SNE plot in Fig. 6 . For each medical imaging regression task, researchers have proposed various specialized architectures and loss functions to address task/modality-specific challenges. For instance, in brain age prediction, SFCN ( Peng et al., 2021 ) introduces a fully convolutional architecture with careful kernel size selection to capture age-related brain patterns, while Global-Local Transformer ( He et al., 2021a ) leverages both local anatomical features and global brain structure through a dual-branch design. To understand whether SupReMix pretraining can improve on top of these task-specific methods, we compare two configurations for each architecture ( Fig. 8 ): direct training with task-specific methods (blue bars) and training combined with SupReMix pretraining (orange bars), with SupReMix serving as a plug-and-play solution that requires no modifications to the core architecture designs. As shown in the Fig. 8 , for brain age prediction on UK Biobank, we evaluate four methods including the widely-used ResNet-18 ( Hara et al., 2018 ), the vision transformer ViT-B ( He et al., 2021b ), the Global-Local Transformer ( He et al., 2021a ) designed for capturing multi-scale features, and SFCN ( Peng et al., 2021 ) specialized for brain age estimation. Across all these methods, SupReMix pretraining improves the MAE by 4.5%-17.3% compared to training from scratch. Similarly, for HCP-Lifespan, we examine three architectures including 1D-ResNet ( Hong et al., 2020 ), temporal convolutional network (TCN) ( Lea et al., 2017 ), and ViT ( Caro et al., 2023 ) for sequential feature extraction, where SupReMix leads to consistent improvements of 4.3%-7.1% . In Echo-Net, where we evaluate methods for echocardiography analysis, we compare architectures including EchoNet ( Ouyang et al., 2020 ), EchoGNN for graph-based architecture ( Mokhtari et al., 2022 ), and EchoCotr ( Muhtaseb and Yaqub, 2022 ) with a CNN-transformer architecture, observing MAE reductions of 0.7%-14.2% . For RSNA-BAA and RHPE-BAA (bone age assessment), we examine specialized architectures such as BoNet ( Escobar et al., 2019 ), PEAR-Net ( Liu et al., 2020 ), DI ( Chen et al., 2021 ), SIMBA ( González et al., 2020 ), and MMANet ( Yang et al., 2023 ), achieving improvements up to 7.4% and 27.6% , respectively. In Amyloid-PET analysis, we evaluate SFCN ( Peng et al., 2021 ), 3D DenseNet ( Huang et al., 2017 ), and FiA-Net ( He et al., 2021b ), with improvements ranging from 2.4% to 10.6% . These systematic comparisons demonstrate that SupReMix pretraining can consistently achieve performance improvements across a diverse range of medical imaging regression tasks regardless of modalities and underlying architectures (CNNs, transformers, or graph neural networks) and their task-specific optimizations. While modern deep learning has achieved remarkable success through large-scale training datasets, obtaining extensive labeled medical images with precise continuous annotations ( e.g. , age, disease scores, organ measurements) remains a significant challenge. This challenge stems from the high cost of expert annotations and time-intensive clinical assessments. This is particularly true for regression tasks in medical imaging, where acquiring accurate numerical labels often requires specialized expertise and complex clinical measurements ( Zhou et al., 2023a ). To address this limitation, developing methods that can perform robustly under limited training data scenarios is crucial for practical medical image analysis applications. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive analysis to investigate how SupReMix influences model performance under different data availability scenarios across five medical imaging datasets. As shown in Fig. 9 , we evaluate the performance by varying the training set sizes. Our experiments span diverse datasets with different scales: UK Biobank (2,500-20,000 samples), A4 Amyloid-PET (500-3,500 samples), RSNA-BAA (2,000-12,000 samples), RHPE-BAA (1,000-5,000 samples), and EchoNet (1,000-7,000 samples). For each dataset and sample size configuration, we compare two settings while keeping all other training parameters consistent: vanilla training (blue solid lines) and SupReMix (orange dashed lines). The results demonstrate SupReMix’s significant advantages, particularly in low-data regimes. This is evidenced by consistent performance gains across all three metrics (MAE, R, and MSE) when training data is limited. In the extreme low-data scenario of UK Biobank (2,500 samples), SupReMix achieves an MAE of 3.8 years compared to 4.7 years for vanilla training - a 19% reduction in error. The performance advantage is even more pronounced in the A4 dataset, where SupReMix maintains R > 0.7 with just 500 samples, while vanilla training requires approximately 2000 samples (4x more data) to achieve comparable performance. Similar patterns emerge in RSNA-BAA, where SupReMix achieves R = 0.62 with 2000 samples, matching vanilla training performance at 6000 samples. We evaluate the transferability of representations learned by SupReMix across different bone age assessment datasets. Our evaluation focuses on two transfer learning scenarios: (1) from RSNA (source, 12K samples) to RHPE (target, 2K subsampled samples), and (2) from RHPE (source, 6K samples) to RSNA (target, 2K subsampled samples). For each scenario, we assess two transfer learning strategies: linear probing, where we train only a linear layer while keeping the pre-trained encoder frozen, and fine-tuning, where we update the entire network on the target dataset. As shown in Table 8 , SupReMix consistently outperforms all baseline methods across both transferring scenarios and different strategies. In the RSNA → RHPE transferring, SupReMix achieves MAEs of 9.58 and 7.85 for linear probing and fine-tuning, respectively, representing substantial improvements of 19.2% and 16.7% over SimCLR. The performance advantage persists in the RHPE → RSNA direction, where SupReMix attains MAEs of 10.12 (linear probing) and 8.04 (fine-tuning). In addition, the strong correlation coefficients achieved by SupReMix in all settings further validate its ability to learn robust and transferable representations for bone age assessment tasks. These results demonstrate that SupReMix not only excels in single-dataset scenarios but also facilitates effective knowledge transferring across different bone age assessment datasets. Another key characteristic of SupReMix is its ability to preserve important biological factors when forming contrastive pairs. In the RSNA dataset, our approach generates hard-negative and hard-positive pairs exclusively within the same gender groups, which directly contributes to the gender-aware representations shown in Fig. 10 . The visualization reveals distinct continuous trajectories for male and female subjects, both following clear age progression patterns. By constraining mixup operations within gender boundaries, SupReMix effectively models the natural gender differences in bone maturation-where females typically mature earlier than males of the same chronological age. This approach highlights the importance of biologically informed representation learning in medical imaging regression tasks. We conduct ablation studies on RSNA-BAA dataset to investigate each component in SupReMix. As shown in Table 9 , each component contributes to performance improvement, with the complete SupReMix framework achieving the best results. We also examine the impact of window size γ for Mix-pos pair generation. Table 10 shows that moderate window sizes ( γ = 5 for RSNA, γ = 1.0 for UK Biobank) achieve optimal performance, while too small or too large windows lead to degraded results. Finally, we study three beta distributions for sampling the mixing ratio λ 1 in Mix-neg generation, each representing different sampling strategies relative to the anchor point. The Beta(2,8) distribution represents a “close-to-negative” sampling strategy, where the generated mix-neg samples are biased towards the negative samples, creating more moderate hard negative pairs. In contrast, the Beta(8,2) distribution represents a “close-to-anchor” strategy where mix-neg samples are closer to the anchor, resulting in more aggressive hard negatives. The Beta(5,5) distribution provides a symmetric sampling strategy with no bias towards either anchor or negative samples. As shown in Table 11 , the “close-to-negative” strategy (Beta(2,8)) consistently outperforms other configurations across all six datasets, with notable improvements on UK Biobank (MAE/GM: 2.98/14.37) and Echo-Net (4.88/6.30). This suggests that generating mix-neg samples closer to the negative examples, rather than the anchor, leads to more effective training by avoiding overly aggressive hard negative pairs that could potentially destabilize representation learning. In this work, we targeted medical image regression tasks, which often receive less attention compared to classification problems. When examining learned representations in regression tasks like bone age estimation, we identified two key challenges: (1) ordinality-awareness in the representation space (Section 5.1.1) and dummyTXdummy-((2) hardness of contrastive pairs (Section 5.1.2). To address these limitations, we developed SupReMix, a supervised contrastive learning framework specifically designed for regression tasks that incorporates mixup techniques at the embedding level. SupReMix addresses the regression representation challenge through two components. First, it implements anchor-inclusive mixtures as hard negatives and anchor-exclusive mixtures as hard positives, enhancing the continuity and local linearity of the learned representations. Second, it incorporates label distance information through distance magnifying weights, explicitly capturing the ordinal relationships inherent in regression tasks. Moreover, the theoretical analysis shows that SupReMix promotes globally ordered and locally linear representations, which align with the continuous nature of regression problems. Experiments across six diverse medical imaging datasets (Section 4.1) confirm SupReMix’s effectiveness, consistently outperforming both classification-based methods (SimCLR, SupCon) and regression-specific approaches (AdaCon, RNC) as shown in Section 5.2 . On the RSNA bone age dataset, SupReMix achieved an MAE of 4.08 months compared to SupCon’s 6.79 months-a 39.9% improvement. Our analysis of representation continuity through Normalized Lipschitz Factor Distribution (Section 5.3) provides quantitative evidence that SupReMix learns smoother representations that better preserve ordinal relationships, with t-SNE visualizations confirming more coherent, ordered embeddings compared to classification-based methods. The performance improvements demonstrated by SupReMix directly translate to enhanced clinical diagnostics across medical domains. For instance, the reduced error in bone age assessment enables more precise growth disorder diagnosis, while improved brain age prediction and cardiac function estimation support earlier neurological intervention and more accurate heart failure management, respectively. More importantly, SupReMix offers strong generalizability for cross-site deployment, a critical advantage in healthcare where model adaptation between different hospitals and imaging equipment often degrades performance. Our transfer learning experiments (Section 5.6) suggest that models pretrained with SupReMix maintain reliability when adapting across institutions with different imaging protocols and patient demographics. Additionally, SupReMix’s effectiveness in low-resource settings (Section 5.5) addresses a fundamental challenge in clinical implementation, where smaller hospitals may have access to limited labeled cases but could still benefit from AI-assisted diagnostics for specialized tasks like brain age estimation or cardiac function assessment. While SupReMix demonstrates significant advantages in the scenarios above, it is important to acknowledge areas where further develepment could be beneficial. The application of SupReMix faces limitations in its adaptability to higher-dimensional regression labels. This challenge stems from a fundamental issue: while ordinality is crucial in regression tasks, it is undefined for vectors in dimensions greater than one, as the topology on R n does not form an order topology. In Mix-pos, obtaining a weights vector (whose dimension matches that of the label) by solving a linear system is theoretically feasible. However, this solution is not always assured due to potential linear independence between selected samples and the anchor. Moreover, the approach’s scalability is hindered as the dimensionality of the regression label increases, posing significant practical challenges. Future research could focus on exploring methods to preserve ordinality in regression representations when dealing with higher-dimensional labels. To conclude, in this paper, we propose Supervised Contrastive Learning for Medical Imaging Regression with Mixup (SupReMix) , a novel framework that generates hard negatives and hard positives for supervised contrastive regression. Supported by theoretical analysis, SupReMix leads to continuous ordered representations for regression. Extensive experiments on six different medical imaging datasets have shown that SupReMix consistently improves over baselines, including vanilla deep regression, previous contrastive learning frameworks, and task-specific methods, across datasets, tasks, and input modalities. Beyond its core performance, SupReMix shows robust generalization when handling challenging scenarios like missing targets and few-shot cases, while also proving valuable as a pre-training strategy for existing architectures. In this section, we analyze the generalization bound from SupReMix following Zha et al. (2023) . Given a regression task with training set S = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N , let H 1 be the hypothesis set containing all possible mapping functions from x i to y i , f be an encoder mapping x i to z i , g ( z i ) = y i . An embedding set is called “ ϵ − ordered ” if, for any label value m , there exists embedding z m such that any x i with y i = m , we have | z i − z m | < ϵ , and for any x i , x j with y i ≠ y j we have | z i T · z j | < 1 − ϵ . With SupReMix, f is guaranteed to map x to ϵ − ordered set. We denote the class of all possible h with f that could lead to ϵ − ordered set by H 2 . Both H 1 and H 2 contain the optimal hypothesis h * such that for any x, y , h * ( x ) = y . Denote u i as the upper bound of the loss from ( x i , y i ), the set of loss from the training set as A k for each hypothesis in a hypothesis set H k , with Rademacher Complexity ( Bartlett and Mendelson, 2002 ) R ( A k ). The gap between training error and test error is upper bounded by 2 R ( A i ) + 4 u i 2 ln ( 4 / δ ) / N , with probability 1 − δ . Since H 2 ⊂ H 1 , we have A 2 ⊂ A 1 and u 2 ≤ u 1 . By the monotonicity of Rademacher Complexity we have R ( A 2 ) ≤ R ( A 1 ). Table A2 Definitions and examples of key contrastive learning terms used in this paper. Table A2 Term Definition and Example Anchor The reference sample used in contrastive learning to compare against other samples. For example, in an image-based regression task, an MRI scan from a specific subject is the anchor. Positive Sample A sample semantically similar to the anchor, which should be pulled closer in the embedding space. Example: another scan from the same subject, or the same underlying label (e.g., similar age in brain age prediction). Negative Sample A sample semantically different from the anchor, which should be pushed farther in the embedding space. Example: a scan from a different subject with a very different target value. Contrastive Pair A tuple consisting of the anchor and one other sample (positive or negative), used to measure similarity or dissimilarity in the loss function. Augmented View A transformed version of the original sample produced via data augmentation (e.g., random cropping, rotation, or intensity shift in MRI). Multiple augmented views of the same image can form positive pairs. Embedding Space The latent feature space learned by the encoder network, where samples with similar semantics are placed closer together. Temperature A scaling factor in the contrastive loss (e.g., InfoNCE) that controls the concentration level of similarity distribution, affecting how sharply the model separates positives from negatives.
