Ablation studies further demonstrated that our proposed TGM and DECA modules markedly improved performance, particularly on dose levels not seen during training. Clinical evaluation through SUV analysis further demonstrates the model’s ability to preserve quantitative accuracy across different regions. Our experiments demonstrate that conditioning on a timestep enables TiDE-Net to generalize across unseen noise levels, achieving consistent denoising performance across different noise conditions. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a functional imaging technique that uses positron-emitting radiotracers to produce three- dimensional maps of metabolic and physiological processes, enabling the study of biological function in the human body [1] . PET imaging is widely used in clinical practices and monitoring treatment [2] . In clinical PET imaging, however, noise arises from various sources, including the stochastic nature of radioactive decay, dose-dependent radiotracer statistics, photon attenuation, scanner hardware limitations, and patient-specific attributes such as body size and physiological conditions. These factors collectively degrade image quality and challenge quantitative analysis. Further, a typical PET scan delivers a substantial amount of radiation, and repeated scans can lead to significantly higher cumulative exposure [3,4] , prompting the adoption of low-dose or shorter scan time protocols, where applicable, to reduce potential health risks and associated costs [5,6] . However, dose reduction reduces signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and may compromise diagnostic imaging quality. Hence, a key objective in low dose PET imaging is to accurately denoise images acquired under reduced radiotracer protocols, such that the output closely approximates the quality and quantitative accuracy of standard-dose PET scans. Motivated by these challenges, prior studies have explored the potential of using low-dose (typically acquired at 10%–50% of standard radiotracer doses) PET (ldPET) or ultra-low dose (less than 10% of the standard dose) PET (uldPET) images with deep learning techniques for denoising to produce image quality that better resembles standard-dose PET (stndPET), which represents 100% dose protocols. Earlier approaches focused on using pixel-wise prediction models used for segmentation, like U-Net [7] and 3D U-Net [8] , which preserve spatial details through their encoder–decoder structure with skip connections. Variants such as 2.5D multi-slice input U-Net [9] , 3D U-Net with shuffle/unshuffle layers [10] , and residual learning [11] improved spatial representation and training stability. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have also been adopted for PET denoising by leveraging a generator–discriminator framework to synthesize realistic images through adversarial training. Wang et al. [12] proposed a 3D Conditional GAN (3D c-GAN) with a U-Net-like generator for high-quality stndPET synthesis. Subsequent works introduced enhancements such as CycleGANs with supervised loss [13,14] , AR-GAN with spectral regularization [15] , hybrid 2D/3D convolutions [16] , classification-guided recovery [17] , and SS-AEGAN [18] , which incorporates self-supervised pretraining to enhance PET image quality. However, the performance of these methods is heavily reliant on the availability of varying noise levels in the training dataset. In practice, it is challenging to cover all possible noise or dose levels during training, especially given the variability introduced by patient characteristics, underlying conditions and acquisition protocols. Recently, Transformer-based methods have been increasingly explored for PET denoising to overcome the identified limitations of CNN and GAN methods [19–21] . Transformers use a self-attention mechanism [22] to capture global context, such that it minimizes the restriction of limited receptive fields. Luo et al. [23] and Zeng et al. [24] combined Transformer with CNN or GAN methods, respectively, to leverage the Transformer’s long-range dependency together with CNN’s local spatial feature learning for PET denoising. However, the spatial-wise attention in Transformer models is computationally and memory-intensive, limiting their application to lower image resolutions and restricting detailed textural representation at full image resolution. To improve computational efficiency, channel-wise self-attention mechanisms have been introduced to capture informative features with lower computational cost [25–27] . Channel-wise attention modules [26,28,29] are particularly effective in highlighting informative features across channels, thereby improving contextual understanding [30] . In parallel, spatial-wise attention [22,31,32] functions as an adaptive mechanism that helps the model focus on critical image regions [30] . Jang et al. [27] combined both spatial and channel-wise attention in SPACH to balance global context and local detail to improve the denoising performance in PET images. Recently, diffusion models such as Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [33] have shown strong performance in PET denoising by iteratively reversing a noise process to achieve high-quality PET images, including on whole-body PET reconstruction [34] and ultra-low-dose brain imaging [35] . Diffusion has also been combined with Transformers to enhance spatial learning [36–38] . However, despite their effectiveness, the high computational cost of iterative denoising, in both training and inference, limits their practicality [39] . Additionally, the training of the diffusion model is complex, and early denoising steps often struggle to capture or preserve fine structural details. Although numerous deep learning models have been proposed for PET image denoising, they are typically trained and evaluated on fixed noise levels. This assumes that all the patient images exhibit similar administered dose; however, with PET imaging protocols that adopt low-lose or shorter scan time, it potentially results in patient-specific dose levels and unseen noise levels. This mismatch between fixed training settings and patient-specific variability limits model generalizability. Consequently, there is a growing need for PET denoising approaches that can adapt to varying noise levels without relying on multi-noise training datasets, which have not been explored. Recent studies have explored domain adaptation techniques to improve generalizability in medical image denoising, particularly under domain shift conditions such as with different scanners or acquisition protocols. Diffusion-based methods, i.e., the Iterative Partial Diffusion Model [40] and the CoreDiff [41] , leverage iterative generation to improve robustness. In another study, the DANRF model [42] , they used domain transfer learning to improve the generalizability of supervised training approaches. While these approaches explicitly tackled domain shifts, our method focuses on achieving strong generalization across noise levels without requiring domain adaptation during training. To address the challenge of generalizing PET denoising across varying noise levels, we propose TiDE-Net, a time-guided dual-encoder ResUNet designed to handle a range of noise conditions, despite being trained on a single, fixed noise level. Our main contributions are as follows: • Simulating varying noise levels via a time-guided Poisson noise generator for augmenting the training dataset. Unlike Gaussian noise commonly used in diffusion models’ forward processes, we employed a count-scaled Poisson model, which more closely reflects the photon statistics of clinical PET imaging. This approach allows to associate each timestep value with a corresponding noise pattern, and therefore removes the reliance on using PET images with fixed noise levels at the training and inference stages. Here, scalar t is used to control the amount of noise added to the ground-truth PET image, thereby simulating varying noise levels. By conditioning on t , the denoising process becomes adaptive and generalized to a wide range of noise levels that are absent/unseen in the training dataset. • Using a dual-encoder architecture with complementary attention (DECA) mechanism to capture both global contextual information and local structural features for PET denoising. We purposely designed two synergistic encoding pathways, where one encoder focuses on capturing global contextual information via channel-wise attention, while the other specializes in preserving local structure using ResNet blocks coupled with spatial attention. By fusing these complementary features, DECA enriches the extracted features and enables more robust representation learning, particularly in denoising challenging studies. Our preliminary study on PET low-to-high was published as a conference proceeding [43] . In this new study, we introduced the following new contributions: (1) our TiDE-Net integrates a time-guided mechanism that enables the model to learn noise characteristics across different noise levels, whilst our prior work relied on using PET images with fixed noise levels; (2) our TiDE-Net introduces a dual-encoder architecture, one utilizing channel-wise attention and the other combining spatial attention for joint denoising, compared to a single branch design used previously and, (3) we conducted more comprehensive experiments using an additional uEXPLORER dataset to evaluate the generalizability of the proposed TiDE-Net with ablation study demonstrating the performance improvement compared to [43] , (4) we provide a region-based SUV analysis between the denoised ldPET images and stndPET image to evaluate the model from a clinical perspective. Our proposed TiDE-Net is a 3D ResUNet with a dual-encoder design and a Time-Guided Mechanism (TGM) for effective PET image denoising. The TGM combines two components: Noise-Guided Target Corruption (NGTC), which simulates varying noise levels through corrupted supervision, and Noise-Aware Conditioning via Timestep (NACT), which conditions the network on a scalar noise-level input. This design enables the model to generalize to a wide range of unseen noise levels using only single-noise-level training data. The architecture is shown in Fig. 1 . To support noise-adaptive learning from single-noise data, we introduce a Time-Guided Mechanism (TGM) composed of two parts: Noise-Guided Target Corruption (NGTC) for simulating noise variation in supervision, and Noise-Aware Timestep Conditioning (NACT) for guiding the network with a noise-level input. To enable supervision across varying PET noise levels using a single fixed-noise input, we simulate diverse noise conditions on the PET image I t from the stndPET image I S by (i) projecting to sinogram space, (ii) injecting Poisson noise, and (iii) reconstructing back to image space. In PET, detected events are photon counts. The variance equals the mean, so higher counts (dose or time) imply lower relative noise. In the Noise-Guided Target Corruption (NGTC), the noise intensity is controlled by the timestep t , where longer t equates to higher count statistics and therefore less noise. This follows a diffusion-style scheduling of noise levels [34–36] . However, unlike common diffusion setups that inject Gaussian noise, we use Poisson corruption because PET measurements arise from photon counting and are well approximated by a Poisson process [44] . We used count-scaled Poisson noise applied to sinogram space, followed by the same reconstruction protocol as used for the full-dose data. We associate each diffusion timestep t with an expected count (dose) level, and conditioned TiDE-Net on t , so that the denoiser adapts to a continuum of noise/dose regimes, including levels absent during training. This design grounds the study’s rationale in the realistic count statistics of clinical PET while preserving the time-guided training paradigm that enables generalization across varying noise conditions. This is formulated as follows: Let R Θ be the Radon transform at view angles Θ , and let R Θ , F B P − 1 be its filtered backprojection (FBP). Then we can get the sinogram (1) s = R Θ ( I S ) . We then generate a t-step noisy sinogram through a count-scaling schedule κ ( t ) > 0 (higher κ ⇒ higher counts, lower noise): (2) y t ∼ Poisson ( κ ( t ) , s ) , s ̃ t = y t κ ( t ) . Finally, we map the sinogram back to image space to obtain the t-step noisy PET image: (3) I t = R Θ , F B P − 1 ( s ̃ t ) . The noisy PET image I t serves as an intermediate reference to estimate the discrepancy between simulated and real low-dose PET (ldPET) images I L , which is minimized through a loss function. The model takes two inputs: the ldPET image I L , which the network aims to map to its high-quality counterpart, and the timestep t , which conditions the model on the expected noise level. To incorporate this conditioning, we apply a sinusoidal embedding function inspired by Ho et al. [33] , which maps the scalar t into a continuous, high-dimensional embedding τ ( t ) ∈ R d embed : (4) τ ( t ) = cos t M 2 i d embed , sin t M 2 i d embed i = 0 d embed / 2 , where M is a frequency scaling constant, and i is an index for the embedding dimension. This sinusoidal embedding is then passed through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to project it into the model’s feature space: (5) τ ′ ( t ) = SiLU ( Linear ( τ ( t ) , d embed ) ) , (6) τ ′ ′ ( t ) = Linear ( τ ′ ( t ) , d embed ) , where Linear ( x , d ) denotes a fully connected layer projecting x to dimension d , and SiLU ( x ) is the Sigmoid Linear Unit activation function. The embedding dimension d embed is defined as: (7) d embed = 4 × d channels , where d channels corresponds to the number of feature channels in the first layer of the model. The final encoded timestep τ ′ ′ ( t ) is injected into each ResNet block in the encoder and decoder via conditional residual pathways. This process is illustrated in the right of Fig. 1 , showing how the timestep conditions each stage of the network. By conditioning on the timestep t , the network learns a noise-aware representation to dynamically adjust its feature extraction and reconstruction process according to the input’s dose level. Our proposed Dual-Encoder Architecture with Complementary Attention (DECA) is designed to capture both global contextual information and local structural details. It employs two parallel encoder branches to process the input in complementary ways before merging their features for decoding. The first encoder branch, referred to as the channel encoder, incorporates transformer-based modules to extract global semantic features across channels. This path is particularly effective for capturing long-range dependencies and contextual patterns, which are essential for differentiating true signals from noise in highly degraded inputs. The second encoder branch, known as the spatial-resunet encoder, is built on residual convolutional blocks and focuses on preserving spatial precision and fine-grained textures. Spatial attention is applied in the last layers of this path to emphasize key anatomical regions within the image, which is critical for preserving the image quality in PET scans. The outputs from both encoders are fused and passed through downsampling blocks with optional attention and timestep embeddings, enabling the model to jointly capture global context via channel-wise attention and preserve local structure through spatial-wise attention. The decoder mirrors the encoder hierarchy, using skip connections and residual-attention blocks to integrate features across scales, resulting in accurate and robust PET image denoising. Compared to single-encoder architectures, the dual-encoder design in DECA offers complementary feature extraction: the channel encoder excels at capturing global context, while the spatial encoder preserves localized structural information. This separation allows the network to more effectively handle diverse noise patterns, improve feature representation, and enhance denoising performance, especially in low signal-to-noise conditions where single-path encoders may fail to retain both context and detail. The structure of the attention mechanism in the dual-encoder is shown in Fig. 2 . We used a composite loss function for training the TiDE-Net, where our loss function combines an image reconstruction loss and a noise consistency loss. These losses are designed to enforce accurate PET denoising and consistency with the simulated noise conditions derived from the timestep-based degradation process. Let I S denote the ground-truth standard-dose PET (stndPET) image and I L denote the corresponding low-dose PET (ldPET) input. Given a randomly sampled timestep t ∈ { 0 , … , T − 1 } , where T = 1000 is the total number of timesteps, the noisy image I t is generated according to Eq. (3) . The model receives I L and timestep t as inputs and produces the predicted standard-dose PET image I ˆ S = F ( I L , t ) . The total loss function used for training is: (8) L total = L recon + L noise , where L recon is an L1 loss measuring the pixel-wise reconstruction error: (9) L recon = ‖ I ˆ S − I S ‖ 1 , and L noise is an MSE loss enforcing consistency between the simulated noisy image I t and the real ldPET image I L : (10) L noise = ‖ I t − I L ‖ 2 2 . This dual-loss design encourages the model to generate PET outputs that are not only close to the target stndPET images but also consistent with the noise levels implied by the dose-aware timestep t . By learning from this continuous noise spectrum, the model gains robustness and generalization ability across a wide range of dose levels, including those unseen during training. We used Ultra-low Dose PET Imaging Challenge [45] data. The challenge consists of two datasets: 377 patient cases using Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra scanner and 1060 patient cases using United Imaging uEXPLORER scanner. To assess the generalizability across varying dose levels, we used patient data with complete multi-dose PET scans. All 377 patients in the Quadra dataset contain PET images at six distinct dose levels. From the uEXPLORER dataset, we selected a subset of 287 patients that included all six dose levels. All these patients were imaged using the FDG tracer. In addition, to further evaluate the model’s generalizability, we also did the cross-scanner and cross-tracer experiments. For the cross-tracer test, we included uEXPLORER scans from 6 patients imaged with the Ga-68 tracer and 15 patients imaged with the DOTA tracer. All images were reconstructed with OSEM. Quadra scans were reconstructed to be 440 × 440 × 644 voxels at a voxel spacing of 1 . 65 mm 3 . uEXPLORER scans were reconstructed to be 360 × 360 × 673 voxels at a voxel spacing of 1 . 67 mm × 1 . 67 mm × 2 . 89 mm . Before training, we converted all PET images to SUV units. To facilitate efficient data loading and training, all 3D total body PET images were preprocessed and converted into HDF5 format with the shape of 32 × 256 × 256 (slices × height × width). For the Quadra dataset, 50 patients were allocated for testing and 50 for validation, with the remaining used for training. Similarly, for the uEXPLORER dataset, 45 cases were used for testing and 45 for validation, and the rest were used as the training set. All acquired data were in ’list mode’, which can be used to reconfigure the acquisition duration to simulate various low-dose scenarios. Each low-dose PET was characterized by a dose reduction factor (DRF) derived from reconstructed counts over a reduced acquisition time frame centered around the midpoint of the original acquisition duration. The generation of low-dose images employed DRFs of 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, and 100, in conjunction with a corresponding full-dose image, to span a wide range of dose levels. All experiments were conducted using PyTorch, using an i7-14700K CPU and a 24 GB NVIDIA RTX A3090 GPU. The model contained 14.4 million trainable parameters and approximately 576.8 GFLOPs per 3D patch inference. The average inference time was 280.93 ms per patch volume. Optimization was carried out using the Adam optimizer [46] . In our training, the learning rate was initially set to 2 × 1 0 − 4 and then decreased by a factor of 0.5 every 15 epochs. For regularization, we set a weight decay about 1 × 10 − 4 The model was trained for over 300,000 iterations (40 epochs) with a batch size of 1. The proposed TiDE-Net was evaluated against several state-of-the-art PET denoising methods, including the traditional 3D U-Net [8] ; SS-AEGAN [18] ; two Transformer-based architectures: Restormer [26] and SPACH-Transformer [27] ; and our previous work, Full-TrSUN [43] . To maintain comparable computational cost among the transformer-based methods, the feature dimensions were set to 6 for Restormer, 10 for SPACH-Transformer, and 16 for Full-TrSUN. For consistency with our previous work, TiDE-Net was also configured with a feature dimension of 16. Ablation experiments were conducted to investigate how training on different dose levels impacts model generalization to unseen noise conditions. We used DRF100 (as in the comparison experiments), DRF20, and DRF2 as training inputs, representing high-, medium-, and low-noise data, respectively. This setup aimed to identify the most effective training dose level for achieving robust performance across a range of noise conditions. We also conducted an ablation study to evaluate the individual contributions of the key components within TiDE-Net. Specifically, we evaluated the impact of the dual-encoder architecture, the inclusion of spatial-wise attention, and the TGM which incorporates NGTC and NACT. These experiments were designed to validate the robustness, adaptability, and design rationale of the proposed framework. We evaluated the performance of our method using both standard image-level quality metrics and clinically relevant quantitative measurements. The denoised PET images were evaluated using four standard metrics: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE), and Mean Square Error (MSE). We followed the existing literature and used a weighted scoring scheme [18] defined as: (11) SCORE weighted = λ 1 ⋅ score DRF100 + λ 2 ⋅ score DRF50 + λ 3 ⋅ score DRF20 + λ 4 ⋅ score DRF10 + λ 5 ⋅ score DRF4 + λ 6 ⋅ score DRF2 , where score refers to any of the evaluation metrics mentioned above. We assign weights as follows: λ 1 = 20 % , λ 2 = 15 % , λ 3 = 15 % , λ 4 = 15 % , λ 5 = 15 % , and λ 6 = 20 % . The DRF100 score evaluates the model under matched conditions, as it reflects the same high-noise level used during training. In contrast, DRF2 represents the lowest noise level scenario, with the largest noise gap from training data, thus assessing the model’s generalization ability. By assigning higher weights to DRF100 and DRF2, we emphasize the model’s performance at both extreme consistency on known noise and adaptability to unseen, low-noise conditions while maintaining balanced evaluation across intermediate levels. To evaluate the clinical relevance of the denoised images, we conducted a quantitative SUV analysis based on the PERCIST [47] guideline. Specifically, a 3 cm spherical region of interest (ROI) was placed in the right lobe of the liver for each test patient. We then calculated SUV mean , SUV max and SUV min within this ROI. For each dataset (Quadra and uEXPLORER), we report the average and standard deviation of the SUV metrics across all test patients in different noise levels. Left side of Table 1 presents the quantitative results of all comparison models on the Quadra dataset. Our TiDE-Net outperformed all baseline and state-of-the-art methods across all evaluation metrics from DRF100 to DRF2, with the exception of NRMSE at DRF100 and DRF2, where Restormer was slightly better. Compared to SS-AEGAN and the traditional 3D U-Net, TiDE-Net delivered substantial improvements across all metrics. In terms of weighted score, TiDE-Net outperformed SS-AEGAN by 4.37% in PSNR, 0.41% in SSIM, 37.47% in MSE, and 21.16% in NRMSE. While transformer-based methods outperformed traditional approaches, TiDE-Net achieved the highest performance across all noise levels. Notably, TiDE-Net achieved a 0.254 dB (0.4%) improvement in PSNR over the strongest baseline, Restormer. It also achieves lower error values, with MSE reduced by 8.2% and NRMSE decreased by 2.6% compared to the Restormer. Results of the uEXPLORER dataset are presented on the right side of Table 1 . Similarly, our TiDE-Net outperformed all comparison methods across most of the evaluation metrics from DRF100 to DRF2, except for NRMSE and PSNR at DRF100. Also, the weighted score of TiDE-Net remained the highest among all methods. Compared to SS-AEGAN, TiDE-Net performed better than 4.69% in PSNR, 1.00% in SSIM, 42.87% in MSE and 21.07% in NRMSE based on the weighted score. When compared to the transformer-based methods, TiDE-Net outperformed Full-TrSUN with a 0.304 dB gain in PSNR and a 2.061% reduction in NRMSE. The results of the ablation study using different training noise levels are summarized in Table 2 . The model trained on DRF20 achieved the best overall performance in terms of weighted score with a PSNR of 56.296 dB, SSIM of 0.995 and MSE of 0.016, showing strong generalizability to all the noise levels. Training on DRF100 yielded the lowest overall MSE (0.016), the same with DRF20, and also performed well on higher noise level data (DRF100 and DRF50). However, it was slightly less effective than DRF20 when tested on higher-noise levels. In contrast, the model trained on DRF2 showed excellent performance on low-noise test sets (e.g., DRF2: PSNR 61.196 dB, SSIM 0.999), but failed to generalize well to higher-noise inputs (e.g., DRF100: PSNR 44.726 dB, NRMSE 0.705%). This highlights the limitation of low-noise training data in handling high-noise scenarios. These results confirm that training on medium noise levels (DRF20) provides a balanced representation, enabling better robustness across a range of PET noise conditions. To evaluate the contribution of each major component in our framework, we conducted an ablation study using four model configurations: (1) the baseline Full-TrSUN model; (2) TiDE-Net with a dual-encoder structure but without spatial-wise attention (SA) in the second encoder; (3) TiDE-Net incorporating the full Dual-Encoder Architecture with Complementary Attention (DECA); and (4) the complete TiDE-Net integrating both DECA and the Time-Guided Mechanism (TGM), which includes Noise-Aware Conditioning via Timestep (NACT) and Noise-Guided Target Corruption (NGTC). The results are summarized in Table 3 . The baseline Full-TrSUN model uses a single encoder that contains a channel-wise attention module. Then we replaced the single encoder with a dual-encoder design but excluded spatial-wise attention from the second encoder. On the Quadra dataset, this variant slightly underperformed Full-TrSUN at DRF100 and DRF50 but outperformed it across higher dose levels (DRF20, DRF10, DRF4, and DRF2), resulting in a higher overall weighted score. However, on the uEXPLORER dataset, this configuration did not outperform Full-TrSUN until the lowest noise level image input (DRF2). To further enhance performance, we introduce the full Dual-Encoder Architecture with Complementary Attention (DECA), by adding spatial-wise attention to the final layer of the second encoder and the first layer of the decoder. This addition led to performance improvements across all DRF levels and a higher weighted score on the Quadra dataset. On the uEXPLORER dataset, although the model still underperformed at DRF100 and DRF50 compared with Full-TrSUN, it achieved better results at higher dose levels (DRF20 to DRF2). Additionally, it outperformed the variant without the spatial attention module across most evaluation metrics. Finally, the complete TiDE-Net, integrating DECA along with the Time-Guided Mechanism (TGM) which consists Noise-Guided Target Corruption (NGTC) and Noise-Aware Conditioning via Timestep (NACT), achieved the highest overall performance across all evaluation metrics on both datasets except DRF100. The weighted score further demonstrates that the inclusion of TGM improves the model’s generalizability. To further demonstrate the generalizability of our TiDE-Net, we conducted cross-domain experiments by testing the model on both cross-scanner and cross-tracer datasets. The results are shown in Table 4 . Here, we only show the weighted score to evaluate the model’s overall performance on multiple noise levels. The detailed performance on each level is provided in Appendix Table B.6 . In the cross-scanner validation, we trained TiDE-Net with the uEXPLORER dataset and tested the model on the Quadra dataset. The result achieved 52.25 dB PSNR and 0.988 SSIM, while the reverse transfer (trained on Quadrau dataset and tested on EXPLORER dataset) reached 53.12 dB and 0.990 SSIM, both with low NRMSE (0.281% and 0.273%) and MSE (0.031 and 0.025). Notably, the cross-scanner validation from Quadra to uEXPLORER slightly exceeded the uEXPLORER in-domain baseline, indicating robust scanner generalization. For cross-tracer transfer (single-tracer training on FDG), the model preserved image quality on DOTA (51.278 dB, SSIM 0.989, NRMSE 0.341% and MSE 0.026) and performed even better on GA-68 (54.398 dB, SSIM 0.989, NRMSE 0.220% and MSE 0.052). Overall, the degradation relative to in-domain evaluation was modest (typically about 1–2 dB PSNR), with SSIM consistently above 0.988, demonstrating that TiDE-Net generalizes effectively across both scanner and radiotracer distributions. These results demonstrate that TiDE-Net not only improves perceptual image quality but also maintains clinically relevant uptake metrics across scanners. As shown in Fig. D.8 in appendix, the close alignment between the Standard and Predicted PET distributions suggests that TiDE-Net effectively preserves quantitative accuracy. In this study, we introduced TiDE-Net, a PET denoising framework that combines a Time-Guided Mechanism (TGM) with a Dual-Encoder Architecture with Complementary Attention (DECA). TiDE-Net outperformed all methods across different noise levels on the Quadra dataset and produced strong performances on the uEXPLORER dataset, particularly under lower-noise conditions (DRF50–DRF2). These findings demonstrates our model’s strong generalization capability, especially in challenging, unseen low-dose conditions, making it a robust and practical solution for real-world PET imaging scenarios. Our experimental results ( Table 1 ) show that TiDE-Net consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple dose levels and datasets. On the Quadra dataset, it achieved the best performance across nearly all metrics and dose levels. On the uEXPLORER dataset, although TiDE-Net showed slightly lower performance than Full-TrSUN at DRF100, it surpassed all other methods at lower-noise levels (DRF50–DRF2) at most of the evaluation metrics, where the gap from the training noise level was larger. The slightly reduced performance at higher noise levels may be due to TiDE-Net’s focus on broad generalization, which trades off some high-noise specificity to better handle unseen moderate and low-noise inputs. These differences may be influenced by dataset-specific factors such as reconstruction protocols, image resolution, or the range of visual noise present at different dose levels. TiDE-Net consistently demonstrated effective denoising and robustness across a wide range of dose conditions, particularly under lower-noise constraints (e.g., DRF50 to DRF2), highlighting its capacity to generalize beyond the specific noise level used during training. The results also show that transformer-based methods perform more robustly across varying noise levels during testing. Through the transformer-based method, our TiDE-Net demonstrates strong generalization to unseen noise levels not present during training. These results, despite minor dataset variations, highlight the model’s strong generalization and robustness across different noise levels. TiDE-Net’s performance is primarily driven by the TGM. NGTC simulates noise in clean targets using a timestep variable, enabling the model to learn noise patterns without multi-dose training data. NACT conditions the network on this timestep input, guiding it to adaptively denoise across a range of unseen noise levels. The strength of TGM lies in its ability to train the model using only one noise level, while still performing well on data with different noise levels: the model learns from a single, fixed-noise dataset (DRF100) and generalizes across a continuum of dose levels. At the same time, DECA enhances denoising by combining global context extraction via channel-wise attention with local detail preservation through residual convolution and spatial attention, improving stability, convergence, and fine-detail recovery. Generalization in PET image denoising is crucial for clinical applications, as patient-specific factors and varying acquisition protocols often result in unpredictable noise levels. Existing methods trained on fixed or multiple dose levels either suffer from poor generalization or require curated dose-varied datasets, which are often impractical to collect. In contrast, TiDE-Net remains efficient, scalable, and robust. The qualitative results further support the performance of our TiDE-Net, which consistently produced higher-quality denoised PET images across a range of noise levels compared to its counterparts. Notably, the denoised outputs preserve lesion visibility and structural boundaries even under challenging noise conditions, as illustrated by the cropped regions and error maps in Fig. 3 , aligning with the design of TiDE-Net to integrate both global and local features through its dual-encoder architecture. While some oversmoothing is observed in all models, particularly when compared to the ground truth, this also results in a loss of signal and fine structural detail. This may be partly due to training the models exclusively on high-noise data (DRF100), limiting their ability to retain finer features when tested on cleaner, low-noise inputs. Additionally, the limited photon counts in uldPET inputs may also be a reason. The box plot ( Fig. 4 ) results further confirm TiDE-Net’s strong generalization and stability across varying noise levels. Its consistent performance on the Quadra dataset, especially in PSNR, indicates robustness across patients. The observed improvement with lower-noise inputs also validates the effectiveness of the time-guided mechanism in adapting to varying noise intensities. The ablation study on training data with different noise levels revealed that using a moderate-noise input (DRF20) resulted in the best generalization across all dose conditions. This outcome suggests that DRF20 provides a balanced representation which contains enough noise to train the model to handle high-noise inputs and sufficient signal to preserve fine details. In contrast, models trained solely on low-noise data (DRF2) lacked exposure to severe noise, making them less effective when tested on high-noise inputs. Conversely, models trained on high-noise data (DRF100) learned to suppress noise but tended to oversmooth structural details, especially when applied to cleaner inputs. These findings highlight the critical role of training data selection in optimizing generalization and demonstrate that moderate-noise training offers the best trade-off. Moreover, they reinforce the utility of timestep-guided conditioning as a mechanism to bridge the gap across a wide range of noise levels. The ablation studies further validated the individual contributions of each core component in TiDE-Net. First, introducing the dual-encoder structure (DECA) improved performance, especially on moderate and high-noise test data, by capturing complementary global and local features. Second, spatial-wise attention in the ResNet encoder and decoder contributed to structural detail preservation, as reflected in SSIM improvements. Finally, incorporating TGM (comprising NGTC and NACT) significantly boosted denoising performance, particularly at unseen noise levels, by allowing the model to learn noise-conditioned transformations via the timestep variable. Notably, while the TiDE-Net exhibited strong generalizability and robustness across a wide range of noise levels, a slight reduction in SSIM was observed. This drop may be attributed to the model’s focus on denoising and pixel-level reconstruction, which could result in mild smoothing of fine structural textures—features to which SSIM is particularly sensitive. Nevertheless, the consistent gains in PSNR, NRMSE, and MSE validate the effectiveness of the proposed architectural enhancements and demonstrate the model’s capacity to denoise ldPET images under diverse noise conditions. Our experiments demonstrated that TiDE-Net generalized effectively across a variety of clinically relevant scenarios, including scanner type, tracer type, and patient-specific noise variability. In the cross-scanner setting, the model trained on uEXPLORER data generalized well to the Quadra dataset, despite differences in reconstruction protocols, voxel spacing, and scanner geometry. This suggests that TiDE-Net is robust to domain shifts commonly encountered in clinical deployments. In the cross-tracer evaluation, we tested a model trained solely on FDG data against Ga-68 and DOTA PET scans from the uEXPLORER scanner. The model maintained strong denoising performance down to DRF10 for both tracers, showing its ability to adapt to variations in radiotracer distribution without retraining or fine-tuning. To further assess clinical reliability, we conducted a quantitative SUV analysis following the PERCIST guideline, using a 3 cm spherical ROI in the liver. TiDE-Net preserved SUV max , SUV mean and SUV min values across all dose levels and datasets, with minimal deviation from standard full-dose PET. These findings indicate that the model not only enhances perceptual image quality but also maintains essential quantitative features needed for diagnostic accuracy, highlighting its potential for real-world clinical integration. Complementing these clinical findings, TiDE-Net’s computational profile aligns with routine workflow demands as mentioned in Section 3.2 . At this latency, the effective throughput is about 3.6 patches per second, yielding 15 s to 1–2 min denoising for typical whole-body studies, depending on patch tiling and overlap. While TiDE-Net demonstrated strong performance across varying noise levels under multiple evaluation settings, several limitations remain. In some cases, the model exhibited over-smoothing, particularly in low-contrast or homogeneous regions. While this effectively suppressed noise, it also obscured fine anatomical or pathological details. Future work will explore the use of perceptual or texture-aware loss functions [49] to mitigate this effect and better preserve subtle structures. The dataset used in our study contains multi-dose PET images but does not provide paired CT or lesion annotations, which preclude lesion-level assessment and reader studies. In future work, once PET datasets with paired CT and lesion masks are available, we plan to conduct lesion-focused evaluation and reader studies in real patient imaging workflows to further validate the clinical impact of TiDE-Net and support its potential clinical deployment. Our method, TiDE-Net, demonstrated strong denoising performance across a range of noise levels, including unseen dose conditions, using only single noise level training data. Experiments on two clinical PET datasets demonstrated that our method consistently outperformed baseline and SOTA methods, particularly in denoising PET image quality at lower-noise dose levels. Beyond standard image quality metrics, TiDE-Net also showed robust generalization across scanners and tracers, maintaining denoising performance even when applied to unseen domains without retraining. Additionally, clinical SUV analysis confirmed that the model effectively preserved quantitative uptake values across both datasets. These results highlight the effectiveness of our time-guided training strategy and dual-encoder architecture in enabling robust generalization. Future work will focus on further improving structural detail preservation, optimizing inference efficiency, and validating the model’s diagnostic impact in real-world clinical PET workflows. Unified ARP-ViT-CNN system: Hybrid deep learning approach for segmenting and classifying multiple skin cancer lesions Skin cancer continues to be one of the most difficult conditions to diagnose accurately, as different lesion types can look very similar, and the images used for diagnosis often contain noise and large variations. Many existing deep learning models, such as traditional Neural Networks and Transformer-based models, often struggle to capture both the fine-grained local details and the broader context of the image. To address these challenges, we developed a hybrid ARP-ViT-CNN model that employs a three-stream feature extraction process, where Angular Radial Partitioning (ARP) extracts geometric and structural patterns, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) extract subtle local features, and exploits Vision Transformers (ViT) to code long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms. Then, use this feature representation to develop a more advanced classification model that can differentiate several forms of skin malignancies. The Proposed model integrates a comprehensive Pre-processing pipeline, including balancing and enhancing the dataset, to address the problem of underrepresented classes and image variability. We evaluated our model on the publicly available HAM10000 dataset for multi-class skin cancer classification and segmentation. As anticipated, the ARP-ViT-CNN model beat the conventional CNN-only and Transformer-only models on the dataset, achieving an overall accuracy of 98.2% with a precision of 0.94, a recall of 0.96, and a macro-F1 score of 0.95. The ARP-ViT-CNN segmentation module for outlining lesion boundaries performed well, and was especially reliable in providing accurate boundary delineation in the presence of the complicated lesions in the test data. The overall results indicate that our ARP-ViT-CNN framework is effective, and with the ViT being suitable for global contextual learning, ARP being the mechanism by which we were making the model invariant to rotation and scale features, and this is likely contributing to the model’s tolerance to complex dermatological expressions. The ARP-ViT-CNN model has established itself as a modern approach to fully automated skin cancer imaging for automated diagnosis and a basis for future AI-powered medical imaging. Skin cancer represents an acute public health menace because it leads to extensive patient death rates and increased mortality throughout the international community. Millions of new healthcare cases are diagnosed each year by the World Health Organization (WHO) which classifies both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer as severe health threats. Incidence rates increase because of long-term exposure to Ultra Violet (UV) radiation and environmental factors as well as hereditary risk factors. Healthcare systems encounter substantial expenses for treating skin cancer that demands refined diagnostic techniques for prompt detection to reduce both death rates and treatment expenses. The requirements for an automatic skin cancer classification system that operates efficiently [1] became essential because existing diagnostic techniques show clear disadvantages. The dermatologist-based diagnosis procedure with its biopsy verification step uses time-intensive and expensive methods that suffer from human error. The rapid technological development has led to the adoption of Machine Learning(ML) and Deep Learning(DL) techniques [2] which enhance diagnostic precision and accelerate diagnostic processes. The current techniques experience several obstacles including overfitting issues and inadequate characteristic extraction as well as performance limitations during type identification of skin malignancies. The main types of skin cancer comprise both melanoma together with non-melanoma skin cancer. The most dangerous form of skin cancer exists as melanoma because of its aggressive behavior which leads to high rates of metastasis. Non-melanoma skin cancers consist primarily of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) along with Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) that occur frequently yet do not prove fatal to patients [3] . Early diagnosis and thorough classifications of skin diseases greatly influence the right course of treatment. Since fine-grained details of skin lesions show several different traits, a diagnostic model with improved capability is required to detect them. Many well-known programs and tools that help dermatologists help to diagnose skin cancer. Mobile skin lesion analysis applications through AI algorithms exist within the market alongside cloud platforms [4] using Artificial Intelligence(AI) solutions for diagnostics including IBM Watson Health. Room for improvement exists in these platforms because their traditional CNN architecture fails to capture extensive dependencies and complex components within the data. A framework combining multiple feature extraction methods should be developed to boost dermatological classifications’ accuracy. From early 2000 to the present day, the assessment of skin cancer classification models has experienced substantial advancements. During the early years of the 2000s researchers predominantly used thresholding and edge detection as their primary image processing methods as given in Fig. 1 . Support Vector Machines (SVM) alongside Random Forests (RF) started to become popular [5] within the period extending from 2010 to 2015. A breakthrough occurred between 2016 and 2020 when CNNs took over as the top technique for achieving superior results in this field. Adopting ViTs and hybrid models after 2020 has increased classification effectiveness by using self-attention mechanisms that perform notably well in medical imaging analysis. The initial activity in skin cancer classification involves acquiring data for processing by first extracting features and performing segmentation. Medical images serving dermatological purposes can be obtained from free research datasets [6] including The International Skin Imaging Collaboration(ISIC) and Dermatalogy Information System(DermIS). The application of pre-processing methods including contrast enhancement noise reduction and normalization works to enhance picture quality. The combination of U-Net and threshold-based segmentation procedures allows complete separation of skin lesions for accurate feature extraction which results in improved classification results. Studies have widely investigated the application of ML and DL approaches for the classification of skin cancer. The implementation of traditional ML algorithms k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Decision Trees (DT), and Support Vector Machines (SVM) utilizes human-made features [7] . This new generation of models named CNNs surpassed previous systems through their capacity to build inclusive feature representations at different levels automatically. The advanced ResNet, EfficientNet and DenseNet architectures show superior performance alongside Transformers that improve feature extraction using self-attention technology [8] . The creation of most classification models with deep learning foundations uses CNNs as their key component. The architecture of these convolutional networks contains different component layers which begin with convolutional filters to extract features, followed by pooling operations for dimension reduction, and conclusion through fully connected layers for classification. The model performance improves when using deeper architectures namely ResNet-50 and EfficientNet-B7 because they master elaborate feature recognition patterns. There are many widely used optimization techniques including Adam, RMSprop, and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Each of these optimization techniques provides either fast convergence or good generalization [9] . In addition, meta heuristic techniques such as Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) have been used to optimize model hyperparameters. However, conventional optimization techniques often fail to classify images accurately, and they cannot model the complex characteristics of skin lesions; thus, more sophisticated techniques are needed. Transformers [10] have emerged as the new state-of-the-art in medical image analysis and have demonstrated superior performance when compared to conventional optimization methods. While traditional CNNs use local receptive fields, transformers use self-attention mechanisms to capture global dependencies, resulting in superior extraction and classification accuracy. The fact that Vision Transformers (ViTs) can process and classify the entire image at once without considering spatial locality will make ViTs highly successful for skin cancer classification, as ConvNets suffer from optimization difficulty when classifying skin lesions. Effective data partitioning and segmentation are very important for analyzing complex data, searching for patterns, and making better decisions. These techniques are widely used in machine learning and image processing to search for meaningful data structures. However, traditional clustering techniques fail to produce desirable partitions on high-dimensional, scale-varying, or dynamic data. The data partitioning and segmenting methods include k-means, hierarchy, spectrum, and mean-shift clustering algorithms, each with its own strengths and weaknesses for adapting to high-dimensional, complex, or scale-variant data. Among them, k-means can easily cluster the data but is sensitive to the initial centroids and non-standard shapes. Hierarchical clustering requires immense computational power. Spectral clustering can separate non-linearly separable clusters, but is very time and memory-consuming. Mean-shift clustering has excellent identification capabilities over clusters without many limitations regarding the number of clusters to be identified, which creates a problem in high-dimensional data or cases of density variations. There exists a common limitation, namely that they are scale-sensitive, meaning that they do not function well under dynamic conditions. The Angular Radial Partitioning (ARP) model utilizes scale-invariant feature extraction based on angular and radial transformation, allowing its performance to be unaffected by input variations. This offers ARP the means to secure better dividing efficiency and robustness compared to traditional clustering techniques. In practice, clinicians commonly misclassify lesions that are visually ambiguous (e.g., melanoma and benign nevi) because color and texture models can be similar between lesions. In the example above, it can be seen that existing models often misclassify ambiguous lesion cases by including examples of true negatives. The ARP-ViT-CNN framework that we present in Fig. 2 addresses this lurking limitation by incorporating ARP, CNN, and ViT, which helps to capture independent complementary local (CNN), global (ViT), and structural (ARP) features. As such, the unified ARP-ViT-CNN (AVC)system improves the reverse probability classification decision-making process and can correctly distinguish cases of melanoma compared with benign nevi, even when the lesions appear visually similar. The proposed hybrid ARP-ViT-CNN framework provides the following novelty: (i) The geometric and structural information of ARP, global context dependencies of ViT and hierarchical local information of CNN together contribute a multi-scale representation for skin lesion and leading to an improvement in diagnostic accuracy and generalization. (ii) It surpasses binary or reduced-class approaches, distinguishing eight skin cancer classes through a fusion of spatial and non-spatial features using in-class feature classifiers to improve diagnostic accuracy. (iii) The complete workflow, from image acquisition to pre- processing, presents a step-by-step approach for optimizing the diagnosis process, including normalization, noise reduction, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. (iv) The architecture combines bilateral filtering and data augmentation to address issues specifically noise, imbalanced classes, as well as lesion variability, making it a clinic-implementable system. Further, ViT captures long-range contextual relationships while CNN captures local patterns; hence successful lesion discrimination will be possible. Feature Extraction block, is a key component of the overall architecture, meant to extract diverse and combine various feature representations from skin lesion images. This stage has three parallel pipelines: Angular Radial Partitioning (ARP), CNN, and Vision Transformers (ViT). Each pipeline provides its distinct feature set to the overall representation. Specifically, the ARP pipeline has been constructed to extract spatial features, in other words, geometrical features, shapes, and scale-invariant properties of the lesions. The ViT pipeline, on the other hand, produces non-spatial, global feature representation by learning contextual relations in the whole image through the self-attention mechanism. The CNN-based attention model extracts deep hierarchical features based on the local patterns and textures by utilizing the multiple layers of CNNs. Although these three pipelines process each image independently, they operate in parallel for maximum feature extraction. The result from ARP, CNN, and ViT is then concatenated to get a combined feature representation that is ready for the next stage in the process of the model. At this stage, the process begin by defining the parameters for ARP feature extraction. This means that the input image is dissected into radial and angular segments, bearing in mind the localized features. The first set of partitions to open the radial partition (M), which in principle divides the image into concentric circular bands with a common point towards the center of the image. These radial bands are proportional to the dimensions of the image, physically the radius being designated as the lowest of the two dimensions; this will ensure that each radial partition fits fully within the image. Each radial band contains features at a certain distance from the center, allowing for model-led extractions of a pattern varying on the grown radial position, such as variations in lesion spread, texture, etc are shown in Fig. 9 . At the same time, the angular partitions (N) are defined by dividing the image into equal angular slices that radiate outward from the center. The Vision Transformer (ViT) is a state-of-the-art deep learning architecture for image processing, rather than treating the entire images as grids, ViT treats fixed-size patches of the images as tokens. These patches are flattened into a sequence, then linearly mapped onto a higher-dimensional space, and appended with positional encodings to provide spatial context. The transformer encoder with multi-head self-attention and feed-forward layers processes patch embeddings to extract both local and global image features. As shown in Fig. 10 it enables the ViT to capture complex interactions between varying areas of an image, moving towards a rich representation of the input. From there, the final output is a global feature vector regularized for downstream tasks for instance classification, segmentation, or object detection, having provided state-of-the-art results in computer vision applications. Convolutional Neural Networks have as Input Layer images labeled with a size of (Cin, H, W). Here Cin is equal to the number of channels present in the image (for instance RGB images have Cin = 3) while H and W denote height and width, respectively. The learning process of CNNs is initiated by feeding pre-processed images into the algorithm. Preprocessing, in general, includes normalization and possible augmentation intended for better robustness and generalization of the model. The flattened feature vector enters the connected (FC) layers in Fig. 11 where trainable weights and biases create high-level links between extracted features and predicted classes. The first FC layer grasps global context and boosts classification accuracy. The last FC layer uses the SoftMax activation function, which turns activations into a probability distribution across K classes. This enables understanding through confidence scores given to each class, and the predicted class will be the one with the highest probability. The central part of CNN is the Feature Extraction Module, which is made of several convolutional layers, and each is designed to detect increasingly complicated features. Starting with the low-level features such as edges, lines, and textures in the initial layers, while in deeper layers, the high-level abstractions such as the object’s shapes and the relationships between these objects in space were learned. The convolution layer would perform each operation on a set of filters whose sizes are in increasing order across layers (say 32 → 64 → 128 → Hidden dim ). This progressive transformation allows the network to analyze multiple layers combining finer details and broader patterns. To increase the training efficiency and stability, this approach applies Batch Normalization after the convolutional operations which normalizes the activations reduces internal covariate shifts, and ensures faster convergence. The non-linear nature allowed by the ReLU activation functions encourages the models to learn more complex patterns. In between the convolutional layers, Max Pooling layers are included in the architecture to reduce the number of feature maps to an extent while retaining the most significant information possible to prevent overfitting. Pooling does keep the computational efficiency of the model and the performance from degenerate concerning meaningful pattern extraction. Such feature maps contain information containing the most representative features responsive to the input data, making them favorably placed for later tasks such as classifications and object detection. The integration of ARP, CNN, and ViT in the proposed framework is done by combining the merits of each to overcome their shortcomings. CNNs are well known in the community for capturing local spatial features such as texture and shape patterns which are useful in skin lesion classification. However, CNNs are known for being constrained in capturing long-range dependencies as they consider only the localized receptive fields. Hence it is difficult for the same model to capture the complex structure of the skin lesions. On the other hand, ViTs have recently emerged and shown their superior capabilities in capturing global contextual information by employing self-attention. Further, unlike CNNs, ViTs process an entire image as a sequence of patches which makes it possible to model non-local dependencies. In addition, it can maintain classification accuracy even for challenging cases with subtle boundaries and patterns within the lesion. Again, due to patch-wise processing, ViTs suffer from the loss of spatial information. Further, ViTs require large data sets for effective training, and it is computationally expensive for training. To overcome these limitations, ARP is applied as a complementary module. ARP enhances the scale-invariant feature extraction by partitioning the image into angular and radial segments, thus, preserving the geometric and edge information. Unlike the traditional segmentation process, ARP does not depend on the spatial positioning of the lesion, rather it extracts the structural patterns that are invariant to the lesion size, shape, and orientation. The ability of ARP to preserve the structural patterns comes in handy in differentiating the skin cancer subtypes, as lesions often possess high intra-class variation and inter-class similarity. In this regard, by using CNN for local spatial features, ViT for global contextual patterns, and ARP for structural patterns, the proposed hybrid model can represent skin lesions more comprehensively and robustly. In this way, the proposed framework is capable of outperforming the CNN-based model by capturing the fine details while addressing the long-range dependencies. Further, using the three methodologies collectively for classification and segmentation tasks resulted in a clinically feasible and computation-friendly method for the automatic detection of skin cancer. The unified ARP-ViT-CNN Table 1 encapsulates a compact, computationally lightweight and methodologically different design that is appropriate for real-world dermatology workflows. At its highest level, the architecture integrates three streams together: (i) an Angular Radial Partitioning (ARP) encoder, which transforms a 256 × 256 dermoscopic image into a 3 × 16 grid of rotation- and scale-invariant edge features; (ii) a lightweight CNN hierarchy ( ≈ 1 M parameters), which extracts fine-grained local textures via seven convolutional layers with alternate batch-normalization, ReLU activations, max-pooling, and dropout; and (iii) a narrow Vision Transformer (hidden dim = 16, 12 encoder layers, eight heads) which takes the ARP tokens and learns long-range semantic dependencies. By concatenating the 48-channel CNN feature map, the 48-token ViT output, and the raw ARP vector, the model incorporates structural geometry, the local appearance and the global context prior to making a final soft-max classifier prediction. This stream fusion is rare in skin-lesion literature, and CNN-ViT hybrids were rarely built with a Fourier-based geometric module especially ARP, and they have rarely been deliberately constructed to run with a million trainable weights two to three order(s) of magnitude smaller than a vanilla ViT-Base. The ARP-ViT-CNN model incorporates a Vision Transformer branch with a low hidden dimension (16) and relatively short set of 48 input tokens from the ARP module as opposed to inputs that were raw image patches. This is intentional, since the ARP partitions provide semantically meaningful, rotation- and scale-invariant structural descriptions with encapsulated higher-order spatial information. Consequently, the vision transformer is not used in the usual dense patch-wise embedding feature, but as a lightweight encoder aimed exclusively at capturing dependencies across structured lesion partitions that reduce computation and risk of overfitting and potential for overfitting on a moderate dataset. The CNN component employs seven convolutional blocks with ascending depths of filter counts, batch normalization, ReLU activations, and dropout but does not include deep bottleneck layers or residual connections typical of ResNet or DenseNet architectures; The sequential blocks produce a total of 224 feature maps. This shallow model is consistent with the overall hybrid model where the CNN extracts texture information locally which is then added to the ViT global attention and the ARP structural encoding. The gains in performance on classification and segmentation tasks when adding the CNN to the other branches supports the utility of this compact CNN. In order to fuse the outputs, it was simply concatenated as from the CNN, ViT, and ARP modules for feature fusion meaning that we get to keep everything that we learned (structural, local, and global) and the computational overhead or inference time did not add additional complexity. An option is to explore higher dimensional fusion methods such as attention-based weighting or gated fusion to optimize model performance; however, this could lead to a larger computational burden and remain outside of the intended real-time deployment of the monitoring system. In the experimental evaluation, we have already demonstrated that even the simple concatenation was very beneficial, and it received the largest model evaluation dividends in this evaluation. Classification is the final and very important stage, wherein the extracted features of the ARP, CNN, and ViT pipelines are fused to categorize the input image into a set class. This stage is a bridge between the raw feature representations and the semantically rich class predictions, which guarantee that the model will perform efficiently and reliably in any multi-class classification task. After extracting features from ARP, the CNN features, and the ViT, these maps are concatenated into a unified feature vector as shown in Fig. 14 . Combining the ancillary features into one which forms a very rich and holistic feature space that improves its ability to distinguish from subtle differences between classes in skin lesion classification. This unified feature representation is then passed to the classifier for further processing. This involves multiple kinds of fully connected (dense) layers which efficiently reduce the dimensionality of the fused feature vector while substantially preserving relevant information. In brief, these layers play a very important role as feature selector layers focusing on the high-level patterns and relationships that assist in a particular classification task. Each of the dense layers is typically followed by another activation layer, which is usually ReLU or GeLU, thus providing the model with nonlinearities to learn discriminative decision boundaries better. Dropout latent functions are useful in classifiers because they lower overfitting and improve generalization. They randomly set a specified percentage of neurons to zero during training. As a result, the model is forced to learn some diversity in different feature pathways. In training, batch normalization is used to stabilize training and maintain the feature distribution across the layers. The last layer of the classifying mechanism is commonly the soft-max layer, which gives probabilities per class or the model’s confidence concerning the assignment of a certain class to an input image. During training, states run optimally, reducing a loss function, for instance categorical cross-entropy, to produce the best possible predictions from the model. The weights of the dense layers are updated through backpropagation by updating the weights using the value of the loss to allow the model to effectively discriminate among the classes. In a multi-class classification task, the last layer receives a neuron for each class, and the neuron whose probability is highest predicts a class. It is built upon a solid feature extraction framework. In a bid to further enrich model performance, which would probably cut down on overfitting, dropout regularization is patched throughout with probabilities set at 0.3 and 0.35. These dropout layers randomly put down a percentage of the neurons during training, making the network learn more resilient features, not dependent on any single activation. In the segmentation refinement module, skip connections are used in some strategic spots, particularly in transformer layers 3, 6, 9, and 12. This allows information to be passed in a direct route from early information-holding layers to the later layers thus ensuring that important spatial information stays intact, such that the information from both sides of the skip connection is blended nicely at the decoder. Such an architectural approach will surely make the segmentation task more stable and accurate. In summary, the classification part of the model acts as a decision component translating the rich, fused feature representations into worthy class labels. The developed stage achieves robust, high-performance classification on different kinds of datasets, with advanced regularization and optimization techniques that leverage the complementary strengths of the ARP, CNN, and ViT features. The ARP-ViT-CNN framework is efficient in the segmentation and classification of skin lesion. The CNN and ViTs are combined to leverage both of their strengths. The segmentation results indicate the model captures the lesion boundary effectively and classifies the healthy skin region accurately, with efficient background noise suppression. Angular radial partitioning helps the model capture complicated morphological structures, texture variations and complex lesion patterns. In this way, fine textural features of the lesion types are well captured. The ARP-ViT-CNN framework makes sure the subtle textural differences between the lesion types are well captured and as a result overall segmentation performance improves as shown in the Figures illustrated of different cases of in 15 (a to h). The segmentation based on transformers is able to successfully utilize skip connections to preserve the spatial details of the model at multiple layers. This prevents the loss of fine-grained features, thereby ensuring that the regions segmented correspond to the actual lesion boundary. This analysis demonstrates that while CNN-based models excel in capturing fine-grained local texture features, they are prone to misclassify visually similar lesions due to lack of capability to model long-range dependencies. On the contrary, ViT-based models learn global contextual relationships effectively, but struggle to capture subtle local features and require large datasets for robust training. Existing hybrid CNN-ViT models alleviate these issues to some extent but still suffer from structural invariance, thereby rendering them vulnerable to variations in lesion shape, scale, and orientation. Our proposed ARP-ViT-CNN framework addresses these combined limitations by leveraging the complementary strengths of ARP, CNNs and Vision Transformers. ARP helps to capture rotation and scale, invariant structural features, CNNs assist in capturing fine-grained local information, and ViTs capture the global contextual learning, thus creating a robust and discriminative unified representation. This combination allows the model to classify more ambiguous lesions such as melanoma vs. benign nevi, which the baseline models fail to do. The comprehensive evaluation shows that our proposed ARP-ViT-CNN consistently outperforms all the baselines on important metrics, thereby proving its generalizability and clinical reliability for multi-class skin lesion classification task. The framework is highly adaptable to the shape, size, and contrast of skin lesions. Clinically, the model can capture vascular patterns in BCC and VASC and pigmentation asymmetry in the melanoma, two important characteristics in the diagnosis of skin cancer. The ablation studies will help to isolate the effect of each component so the synergistic impact of structural, local and global feature representation on classification and segmentation may be understood. There are still some practical limitations. First, while using a variety of geometric and color augmentations to expand our 700-image corpus into 4900 samples, we have not tested specifically for our robustness to additive noise, image artefacts (e.g., motion blur or illumination flickering), or skin tone variation that is out of distribution. For this reason, and just as with the performance of any deep learning model, we may experience a performance drop when making predictions on real-world dermoscopic images which contain perturbations. Future work has the potential to incorporate explicit noise perturbations and domain-adaptation techniques to better characterize and perhaps even eliminate this type of sensitivity. Second, the training procedure we employed used 200 epochs, for 123 batches, with a single CUDA-compliant GPU under the Device = ‘cuda’ instruction. The value for EPOCHS = 200 was applied before exiting the loop to develop a single experiment. Therefore, all on the GPU, it merely took a few hours of total run-time for each experiment run. Because of the training intensity of our work, getting repetition of these results for the groups that do not have CUDA-enabled compute or time for large hyperparameter sweeps may be unlikely. Finally, the dual-branch ViT + CNN architecture we employed patchifies each image (1–64 patches) and creates two streams of representation learning (one for segmentation and another for classification). This leads to large memory and compute usage. Extending this approach to higher resolution images or a significantly larger dataset, in most cases, we expect would require model parallelism or a distributed training framework. Our next step is to remedy these shortcomings through noise robust augmentation, utilizing more efficient training practices. The ARP-ViT-CNN model proposes a novel hybrid method for skin cancer classification and segmentation which outperforms both the state-of-the-art CNN models and the Transformer-based methods. The combination of ViTs and CNNs makes the features extracted more comprehensive, which helps the model perform better. The scale-invariant spatial patterns extracted by the ARP model can further improve the segmentation accuracy. Unified graph-based framework for visual explainability in convolutional neural networks In deep learning, understanding the decision-making processes of complex models is essential for advancing interpretability and trust in artificial intelligence systems. We introduce Causal Relational Attribution Graph (C-RAG), designed to deliver comprehensive, multi-perspective explanations of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) via a graph representation. C-RAG integrates gradient-based local attribution with global feature importance by constructing a graph-based representation that captures hierarchical feature inter-dependencies. In this framework, feature clusters are represented as graph nodes, and their interactions are quantified through combined localized and global attribution metrics, ensuring interpretable insights into model behavior. We evaluate C-RAG across diverse benchmark datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-10, MNIST) and CNN architectures (ResNet18, VGG19, DenseNet201, LeNet), demonstrating significant advancements over state-of-the-art explainability methods in faithfulness, robustness, and computational efficiency. The proposed approach facilitates accurate spatial feature localization, robust dependency mapping, and efficient explanation generation, making it a valuable tool for critical applications such as medical imaging and autonomous systems. We provide a novel graph-based explainability framework, which bridges the gap between local and global interpretability, C-RAG addresses key limitations in existing methods, establishing a robust foundation for explainable AI in computer vision.
