This section evaluates the probabilistic outputs and calibration performance of all models across the validation, internal, and external datasets. We employ Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to visualize how closely the predicted probability distributions match the ground truth (GT) class distributions, offering insight into class-wise prediction confidence. Additionally, Reliability Diagrams are used to assess the alignment between predicted confidence scores and actual classification accuracy. These plots provide a quantitative and visual assessment of model calibration, highlighting the generalization capability and identifying potential overconfidence issues that may arise under distribution shifts. KDE plots ( Fig. 10 ) visualize the distribution of predicted classification probabilities for correct and misplaced placement cases across the validation, internal, and external datasets. Gray histograms indicate the ground truth (GT) class distributions for comparison. Dashed vertical lines denote classification thresholds determined from the validation dataset. The Wang 2-Stage model exhibits well-separated peaks for correct placement and misplaced placement near 0 and 1 in the validation dataset, with class proportions closely aligning with the GT distribution. In the internal dataset, although the peaks remain well-separated, the proportion of correct placement predictions appears slightly underestimated, indicating potential difficulty in maintaining accurate class proportions. In the external dataset, the alignment with the GT class ratio further deteriorates, with the misplaced placement peak being overly emphasized and indicating a deviation from the expected class distribution (approximately 11:1). These observations suggest that, although the Wang 2-Stage model achieves strong performance on familiar data, it struggles to maintain robustness when faced with unseen or shifted data distributions. The Unified Baseline, Unified Focal, and Unified Smoothing models also show highly concentrated peaks near 0 and 1 in the validation and internal datasets, reflecting overconfident predictions. Although Unified Focal and Unified Smoothing models slightly alleviate this overconfidence by producing less concentrated peaks, their distributions still fail to capture the correct GT ratio when applied to the external dataset. This suggests that standard regularization methods such as Focal Loss and Label Smoothing are insufficient for maintaining calibration under domain shift. In contrast, Unified Entropy and Proposed models exhibit notably different probabilistic behaviors. Both models produce smoother, less sharply peaked distributions, often centered around moderate probabilities (e.g., 0.25 and 0.75), indicating reduced overconfidence. Importantly, their predicted probability distributions closely reflect the GT class ratios across all datasets, including the external dataset with its domain shift and severe imbalance. This behavior demonstrates the effectiveness of entropy-based regularization in promoting calibrated confidence outputs in achieving calibrated confidence distributions without sacrificing class discrimination. The Proposed model showed the most consistent and well-calibrated probability distributions across all datasets. This suggests that introducing stochasticity into the entropy-based regularization discourages overconfident predictions, leading to more reliable behavior under distribution shifts. These results confirm that the proposed penalty entropy-based regularization, especially when combined with random scaling, effectively mitigates overconfidence, improves calibration, and enhances generalization across internal and external datasets. This property makes the proposed approach especially suitable for clinical deployment, where calibrated and cautious predictions are critical for patient safety. We used reliability diagrams to evaluate calibration performance by comparing predicted confidence levels with actual accuracies across prediction bins. A well-calibrated model produces a reliability curve that closely follows the diagonal, indicating that predicted probabilities correspond well with observed accuracies. Fig. 11 presents the reliability diagrams across the validation, internal, and external datasets, alongside quantitative calibration metrics, as well as two quantitative calibration metrics: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Maximum Calibration Error (MCE). The Wang 2-Stage model exhibited inconsistent calibration across datasets. Although the model achieved a low ECE (0.072) on the validation set, its high MCE (0.467) and a notable drop in accuracy at high-confidence bins indicated miscalibration. Calibration further deteriorated on the internal dataset (ECE: 0.087, MCE: 0.779) and significantly worsened on the external dataset (ECE: 0.374, MCE: 0.959), where the reliability curve showed severe deviations, highlighting its limited adaptability to unseen or heterogeneous data distributions. The Unified Baseline model exhibited near-perfect calibration on the validation and internal datasets in both the validation (ECE: 0.006, MCE: 0.083) and internal datasets (ECE: 0.010, MCE: 0.115). However, under external conditions, calibration degraded sharply (ECE: 0.373, MCE: 0.900), suggesting overfitting to the training distribution and reduced confidence reliability under domain shift. The Unified Focal model exhibited improved calibration compared to the baseline. Its ECE and MCE were consistently low in both validation (ECE: 0.020, MCE: 0.065) and internal (ECE: 0.020, MCE: 0.069) evaluations. Notably, it achieved the lowest ECE (0.245) among all models on the external dataset. However, its relatively high MCE (0.656) and fluctuation in high-confidence regions suggested local miscalibrations. The reliability curve exhibited fluctuations—particularly declines in accuracy at high confidence levels—suggesting instability in confidence estimates when the distribution shifts. These findings indicate that while Focal Loss contributes to improved average calibration, it remains vulnerable to localized miscalibrations in high-confidence regions when applied to unseen data. The Unified Smoothing model exhibited similar trends to the baseline, with marginally higher ECE and MCE values across validation and internal datasets. Its degraded performance on the external dataset (ECE: 0.373, MCE: 0.934) indicates that label smoothing alone is insufficient to improve calibration robustness under distribution shifts. The Unified Entropy and Proposed models exhibited distinct calibration. In in-distribution settings (validation and internal datasets), both models showed slightly higher ECE and MCE values than the baseline, reflecting the inherent trade-off of promoting generalization and reducing overconfidence. However, under domain shift, both models demonstrated improved calibration, with the Proposed model achieving the best overall performance. The Proposed model achieved the second-lowest ECE (0.274) and the lowest MCE (0.429) among all models. Its reliability curve displayed a smooth, gradual alignment with increasing confidence levels, avoiding the sharp deviations observed in other models. These findings suggest that although the proposed model shows slightly higher calibration errors in in-distribution data in in-distribution settings, this behavior stems from its conservative probabilistic predictions aimed at reducing overconfidence. As a result, they produce more cautious and calibrated predictions under distribution shifts, which is particularly important in clinical applications where cautious decision-making is critical. We applied TS to all models. A single temperature was fitted per model on the internal validation set and then kept fixed for the internal and external evaluations. TS modestly reduced average miscalibration (ECE) without altering case ranking. Crucially, the relative calibration patterns observed pre-TS were preserved post-TS ( Fig. 12 ). Thus, our main conclusions remain robust to post-hoc adjustments. To further validate the proposed Random Penalty Entropy (RPE) loss, we conducted a sensitivity analysis over the penalty coefficient λ t sampling range. In addition to the fixed setting (Fixed, λ = 1 . 0 ) and our proposed configuration (Proposed, λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 5 , 1 . 2 ] ), we trained two additional variants with a narrower range (Narrow, λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 8 , 1 . 0 ] ) and a wider range (Wide, λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 2 , 1 . 5 ] ), while keeping all other training settings identical. Fig. 13 summarizes AUROC and ECE on both the internal and external test sets. Overall, Fig. 13 suggests that introducing stochasticity in λ t can be beneficial. Still, its effect depends strongly on the range of λ t . On the internal test set, sampling λ t across a range consistently improves both AUROC and ECE relative to the fixed- λ baseline. However, in an external test, the behavior becomes non-monotonic. The narrow range (Narrow, λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 8 , 1 . 0 ] ) leads to inferior external performance relative to Fixed, which is consistent with insufficient diversity in regularization strength: the variability is too small to expose the model to diverse training regimes, yet it can still introduce optimization noise that does not translate to improved generalization. In contrast, the wide range (Wide, λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 2 , 1 . 5 ] ) provides substantial regime diversity. It yields a slight improvement over Fixed on the external test set. Nevertheless, excessively large variability in λ t may introduce excessive stochasticity into training, limiting additional gains under distribution shift. Taken together, these results indicate that an appropriately chosen λ t range is critical for achieving robust performance and calibration across institutions; in our experiments, the proposed range ( λ t ∼ U [ 0 . 5 , 1 . 2 ] ) provides the most favorable and consistent behavior on both internal and external test sets. In this study, we proposed a unified deep-learning model capable of performing NG tube placement classification and segmentation simultaneously. The architecture enables end-to-end optimization of both tasks, allowing the classification branch to leverage spatial cues from shared encoder features directly. This integrated design reduces error propagation between tasks and improves learning efficiency. To further enhance robustness, we introduced a novel regularization strategy—Random Penalty Entropy Loss—where entropy-based regularization is dynamically scaled during training to mitigate overconfidence and promote better generalization. The proposed unified framework outperformed the state-of-the-art Wang 2-Stage model in classification performance on the internal dataset, validating the advantage of joint modeling. While models employing Focal Loss or Label Smoothing showed slightly improved calibration on internal data, their performance degraded significantly on the external dataset, suggesting overfitting to familiar distributions. In contrast, the proposed model with Random Penalty Entropy Loss consistently maintained both high classification accuracy and reliable calibration across all datasets. On the external test set, it achieved the best balance between performance and reliability, surpassing other unified variants in both the F1 score and maximum calibration error. The use of random scaling further reduced overconfidence, especially in ambiguous or low-quality cases. Several directions remain for future work that will address the current limitations of this study and broaden its clinical scope. First, the relatively small number of misplaced NG tube cases limited the granularity of our sensitivity analyses. We plan to expand the dataset to include more misplacement data and a broader range of countries, which is expected further to improve the robustness and stability of the model. Second, from a clinical standpoint, ideal NG tube placement requires not only that the tip lie within the stomach but also that all side holes lie within the stomach. However, the longitudinal positions of side holes differ across NG tube products, leading to device-specific definitions of a normal placement range. We therefore plan to extend our framework to incorporate device type or product specifications, enabling the model to learn product-specific criteria for correct placement. Third, we plan to move beyond tube-only analysis by explicitly modeling the position of the NG tube relative to surrounding organs (e.g., lungs, diaphragm, and stomach) through additional anatomical segmentation or landmark detection. Jointly reasoning about the tube trajectory and nearby structures may enable more precise characterization of malposition patterns and better support clinically meaningful risk stratification. At the point of care, particularly in emergency and intensive care units, the model could be deployed on bedside or portable CXR systems to provide immediate feedback on NG tube placement, enabling earlier detection of high-risk misplacements even during off-hours. In such a deployment, the AI output would be used as a decision-support tool rather than as a stand-alone reader: When the model’s prediction and the interpreting clinician’s assessment are concordant, the analysis results are immediately utilized. Whereas discordant cases would be reviewed for additional expert or multidisciplinary discussion before nutrition or medication is administered, establishing a structured safety net around uncertain cases. Together with the model’s consistently robust performance and reliable calibration across internal and external datasets, and its ability to generalize under distribution shifts while producing cautious yet accurate predictions, this workflow highlights its strong potential for safe real-world clinical deployment, where safety and reliability are paramount. Unsupervised contrastive analysis for anomaly detection in brain MRIs via conditional diffusion models Contrastive Analysis (CA) detects anomalies by contrasting patterns unique to a target group (e.g., unhealthy subjects) from those in a background group (e.g., healthy subjects). In the context of brain MRIs, existing CA approaches rely on supervised contrastive learning or variational autoencoders (VAEs) using both healthy and unhealthy data, but such reliance on target samples is challenging in clinical settings. Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (UAD) learns a reference representation of healthy anatomy, eliminating the need for target samples. Deviations from this reference distribution can indicate potential anomalies. In this context, diffusion models have been increasingly adopted in UAD due to their superior performance in image generation compared to VAEs. Nonetheless, precisely reconstructing the anatomy of the brain remains a challenge. In this work, we bridge CA and UAD by reformulating contrastive analysis principles for the unsupervised setting. We propose an unsupervised framework to improve the reconstruction quality by training a self-supervised contrastive encoder on healthy images to extract meaningful anatomical features. These features are used to condition a diffusion model to reconstruct the healthy appearance of a given image, enabling interpretable anomaly localization via pixel-wise comparison. We validate our approach through a proof-of-concept on a facial image dataset and further demonstrate its effectiveness on four brain MRI datasets, outperforming baseline methods in anomaly localization on the NOVA benchmark. Despite substantial progress in image classification models, they still face two significant challenges: (i) dependence on extensive amounts of labeled data; and (ii) limited interpretability. These challenges are particularly critical in sectors such as healthcare, where explaining the decision process is essential for clinicians to trust the model outcome, and unhealthy samples are scarce and hard to obtain [1] . Contrastive Analysis (CA) represents a promising solution to this problem [2–4] by learning the fundamental generative factors that distinguish a target (TG) dataset from a background (BG) dataset (referred to as anomalous patterns) and are shared across both datasets (referred to as common patterns). However, state-of-the-art CA methodologies have several limitations: (i) they often result in blurred images when utilizing Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) or are susceptible to mode collapse and unstable training when using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [5,6] ; (ii) they depend on the availability of healthy (BG) and unhealthy (TG) samples during training; (iii) they struggle to preserve common patterns of the original image during the reconstruction process. On the other hand, UAD has emerged as an established approach for modeling the distribution of healthy anatomy and identifying deviations from this distribution as potential anomalies, thus removing the dependence on annotated unhealthy (TG) samples. While Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [7] are commonly adopted as generative models in UAD, their training process lacks explicit constraints to preserve common patterns during reconstruction, hindering the fidelity of normal (healthy) reconstructions. Throughout this paper, we use the terms CA and UAD interchangeably to denote the task of detecting anomalous patterns in images. This choice is motivated by their shared objective: identifying deviations from a background (healthy) distribution. The key distinction lies in the data assumptions. While CA requires access to both background and target samples, UAD relies solely on background data. Our work bridges this gap by reformulating contrastive analysis principles for the unsupervised setting, thereby combining the interpretability of CA with the practicality of UAD. In this work, we propose an unsupervised methodology for the task of anomaly detection in brain MRIs. Specifically, we build upon a contrastive-guided conditional diffusion model ( Fig. 1 ) to reconstruct a healthy version of the input image while preserving its common anatomical patterns. This is achieved by conditioning the denoising diffusion process on a target-invariant latent feature. To this end, we employ a self-supervised contrastive encoder (referred to as target-invariant encoder) trained exclusively on samples from the healthy (BG) dataset. To approximate potential anomalous variation factors, we apply data augmentation techniques such as random cutout and Gaussian noise, which simulate features like tumor presence in brain MRIs. By relying exclusively on healthy (BG) samples during training, our approach reflects the clinical scenarios where annotated pathological brain MRI scans are scarce. During inference, the diffusion model processes unseen samples belonging to the healthy (BG) or unhealthy (TG) distributions by reconstructing the input image such that the anomalous patterns are replaced with learned common (healthy) patterns. By computing pixel-wise differences between the original image and its generated counterpart, high-intensity values can be used to (i) classify the input image as background (normal) or target (anomalous), based on the magnitude of the reconstruction error; and (ii) localize potential anomalies, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (bottom-right), which can aid radiologists in localizing potential tumor regions. Recent studies [8,9] indicate that combining AI with clinical expertise not only enhances diagnostic accuracy but can also reduce interpretation time by up to 23% [8] . These findings underscore the importance of developing AI-driven approaches to support radiologists and alleviate their workload. Proof-of-concept validation on facial imagery data demonstrates the utility of our method. Additionally, an extensive comparative analysis against state-of-the-art methods for UAD on four brain MRI benchmarks highlights the effectiveness of our approach, achieving top performance on the recent and challenging evaluation-only NOVA benchmark [10] . Our major contributions are as follows: • We propose a methodology for learning common features between background (healthy) and target (unhealthy) distributions, enabling the generation of a healthy (normal) counterpart of the input image by encoding only common information; • We introduce a target-invariant encoder that learns representations which are both class-invariant and instance-aligned, facilitating common features preservation during the generative process; • We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of our approach on a facial images and four brain MRI datasets, encompassing both healthy (background) and tumor (target) images, to validate the generalization of our approach. Early work in contrastive analysis (CA) relied on the use of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [11–13] . A recent method proposed by [13] , SepVAE, aims to distinguish common (healthy) from class-specific (unhealthy) patterns in image data. They utilized VAEs with regularization to encourage disentanglement between common and salient representations, along with a classification loss to separate target and background salient factors. However, the resulting reconstructions were often blurry, limiting their interpretability and utility. Alternative approaches [5,6,14] leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been explored, but they suffer from issues like mode collapse and unstable training. More recently, Diffusion Denoising Probabilistic Models [15–17] (DDPMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for high-quality image generation, addressing the drawbacks of both GANs and VAEs. Our work aligns closely with the setting of CA and UAD. In the context of brain MRI, several works have been proposed [18–20] . For example, [18] introduced a patch-based diffusion model for UAD in brain MRIs. They divide the input image into predefined patches and apply noise to each patch individually in the forward pass. In the backward pass, the partly noised image is utilized to recover the noised patch. One drawback of their work is the extensive duration required for inference. More recently, [20] proposed to conditioning a DDPM to better capture intensity characteristics and domain shifts in brain MRIs during reconstruction, thereby improving segmentation performance. In contrast, our method incorporates contrastive learning during encoder training to explicitly enforce a target-invariant embedding space. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models [7] work by corrupting a training image x 0 ∼ q ( x 0 ) with a predefined multi-step scheduled noise process to transform it into a sample from a Gaussian distribution. Then, a DNN is trained to revert the process, i.e., starting with a sample from a Gaussian distribution to generate a sample from the data distribution q ( x ) through a sequence of T sampling steps. Given a training image x 0 , the noising process consists of gradually noise-corrupting the image x 0 by adding Gaussian noise according to some variance schedule given by β t : (1) q ( x t | x t − 1 ) = N ( x t ; 1 − β t x t − 1 , β t I ) . Contrastive Learning (CL) approaches aim at pulling positive samples’ representations (e.g. of the same class) closer together while repelling representations of negative ones (e.g. different classes) apart from each other. Contrasting positive pairs against negative ones is an idea that dates back to previous research [23–25] and has seen various applications in different tasks, such as face recognition [26] . Let x ∈ X be an anchor sample, x + a positive sample (wrt the anchor), and x − a negative sample. CL methods look for a parametric mapping function f : X → S d − 1 that maps semantically similar samples close together in the representation space (i.e. a hypersphere) and dissimilar samples far away from each other. Once pre-trained, f is fixed, and its representation is evaluated on a downstream task, such as classification, through linear evaluation on a test set. Depending on how positive and negative samples are defined, CL can be employed in self-supervised [27] or supervised [28] settings. Our method employs a target-invariant encoder to extract a latent representation capturing common features of the input image. A diffusion-based model is then conditioned on this latent representation to reconstruct a normal (healthy) counterpart of the input. The absolute difference between the reconstructed and original images reveals potential anomalies, where brighter areas indicate abnormalities. This encoder has the goal of learning an input representation which is invariant to the target variable (e.g. presence of eyeglasses in facial images or tumor in brain MRIs) but retains the common information of the input sample. The rationale of this approach is that an invariant representation can allow us to correctly reconstruct a realistic normal version of the input image, as it only encodes its common (healthy) information. The above definitions provide the theoretical support of the contrastive learning approach used for training the target-invariant encoder. Considering that the learning process of the encoder is based on a contrastive learning strategy that is instance-aligned and class-invariant, our encoder is expected to produce features which preserve common information of the input image, regardless of whether the image belongs to the background or target set. Our conditional diffusion decoder p θ ( x t − 1 | x t , z b g ) takes as input the noisy sample x t and the common feature z b g ∈ R 1 × d = f θ ( x 0 ) , a non-spatial vector of dimension d that encodes common patterns observed in the input sample, derived from the properties of the target-invariant encoder f θ (Section 4.1 ). Our primary objective is to reconstruct the background version of the input image, preserving its common information. Hence, we deviate from the step-wise sampling process in Eq. (3) , which is typically employed to generate new images from noise p θ ( x T : 1 ) , x T ∼ N ( 0 , I ) . Instead, we directly estimate the input image x 0 ˆ ∼ p θ ( x 0 | x t , z b g ) given the noisy sample x t . This is achieved by revising Eq. (2) , following [15] , allowing prediction of the denoised observation, which is an estimation of x 0 given x t : (8) g θ ( x t , t , z b g ) ≔ ( x t − 1 − α t ⋅ ϵ θ ( x t , t , z b g ) ) / α t The model is then trained by minimizing the following objective function [17] , which is a modified version of the MSE objective in Eq. (5) : (9) L d i f f = ∑ t = 1 T E x 0 , ϵ t ‖ ϵ θ ( x t , t , z b g ) − ϵ t ‖ 2 2 We condition the U-Net by incorporating timestep and conditioning embeddings into each residual block through scaling and shifting of the normalized activations. Additional details are provided in the Supplementary Material. We first conduct proof-of-concept experiments on CelebA [31] dataset, containing 202,599 facial images with diverse attributes. We create a subset focusing on subjects wearing eyeglasses and those without accessories, resulting in 15,353 images divided into two distinct classes: (1) Eyeglasses (EG) : Images with the ‘Eyeglasses’ attribute and no other accessory-related attributes, used solely for evaluation as target images; (2) No Eyeglasses (NEG) : Images without the ‘Eyeglasses’ attribute or any accessory-related attributes, used for training as background images. Our target task with this dataset is to remove glasses from input images while preserving subject-common information. Facial images are chosen due to their ease of visual interpretation, as identity preservation can be readily assessed during reconstruction. More details on dataset partitions and preprocessing are provided in the supplementary material. We evaluate our approach in brain MRIs for the task of tumor detection and localization. For a comprehensive comparison, we utilize the IXI 2 2 . dataset as a background (healthy) reference for training, as in previous studies [18,20] . Evaluation is conducted in the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2021 (BraTS21) [32–34] and the multiple sclerosis dataset (MSLUB) [35] , featuring tumor and Multiple Sclerosis (MS) samples, respectively. Furthermore, we evaluate our model on the recently evaluation-only NOVA [10] dataset, comprising 906 brain MRI scans spanning 281 rare and diagnostically diverse pathologies. Following [18] , we utilized T2-weighted images from all datasets across our experiments, as well as performed some pre-processing steps involving brain registration, skull stripping and downsampling. Further details on data pre-processing partitioning are provided in the supplementary material. As target-invariant encoder, we use a ResNet-50 backbone with a fully connected layer and a 128-dimensional output. For brain MRI experiments, we adapt the Spark2D [36] framework to incorporate the ϵ -InfoNCE loss. Notably, the encoder is pre-trained in the healthy training set. At the inference phase, we fine-tune it along with the denoising network. For the diffusion model, structured simplex noise [37] is applied. During training, timesteps t ∈ [ 1 , 1000 ] are sampled uniformly, while inference uses a fixed value of t = 500 . The denoising network follows a U-Net architecture. Brain MRI volumes are processed on a slice-wise fashion, with slices uniformly sampled with replacement during training and all slices iterated over at test time to reconstruct the full volume. Training runs for up to 1600 epochs on NVIDIA A40 GPUs with Adam optimizer (learning rate of 1e-4, and a batch size of 32). To assess statistical significance, we conduct hypothesis testing using the scipy.stats library. We used a t -test with a significance level of α = 0 . 05 to verify the null hypothesis that two related methods share the same average metrics. Code is publicly available at . We begin by validating the effectiveness of our method on the CelebA dataset. Subsequently, we evaluated its performance in anomaly detection and localization tasks, comparing it with established state-of-the-art UAD methods. Table 1 presents the reconstruction quality results of our method against baseline models [13,17,38] . These models were trained in the CelebA dataset using only background samples (NEG) and evaluated in both background (NEG) and target (EG) images. Evaluation metrics include SSIM ( ↑ ), LPIPS ( ↓ ), and MSE ( ↓ ). Our method (w/ RE) achieves the highest SSIM (0.9763) and the lowest MSE (0.0003) and LPIPS (0.0059) when reconstructing background examples (NEG). Although our method (w/o RE) and DDIM produce similar results, they fail to capture common information and high-level details compared to our method (w/ RE), as visually demonstrated in Fig. 2 . Furthermore, the supplementary material includes ablation studies analyzing reconstruction quality for different corruption timesteps t ∈ [ 1 , 1000 ] and various values of ϵ in ϵ -InfoNCE. Tab. 1 provides metrics for distinguishing between the two classes (NEG vs. EG), with the magnitude | Δ | = | N E G − E G | indicating distinctiveness (histogram plots shown in Fig. 3 ). Diff-AE and SepVAE exhibit overlapping distributions across metrics, while our method demonstrates well-separated distributions, yielding the highest ROC AUC score (see Fig. C.3 in the supplementary material). Varying the margin ϵ in Eq. (7) can influence identification accuracy by affecting the separation of different classes within the latent space. We conduct an ablation study on ϵ to observe its impact on identification accuracy using a k -NN classifier with k = 3 . Results depicted in Fig. 4 (right) show that the highest accuracy is achieved when ϵ is chosen from the ranges [ 0 . 5 , 2 . 5 ] with the random erasing (RE) transformation and [ 0 . 15 , 1 . 0 ] without it. We conduct a linear probing analysis to assess the encoder’s class-invariance ( Definition 4.2 ). The objective is to evaluate the encoder’s capability to distinguish between EG and NEG samples. Subsequently, a logistic regression classifier was trained on the extracted image latent features. Results in Fig. 4 (left) show lower target accuracy with RE, suggesting stronger common information preservation. However, instance classification performs worse with RE, possibly due to built-in augmentations in contrastive learning. Table 2 compares different UAD methods on three brain MRI datasets using evaluation metrics such as DICE score, AUPRC, and ℓ 1 reconstruction error (calculated only on healthy IXI dataset). We reproduce results for DDPM [37] , pDDPM [18] , and cDDPM [20] , while results for other methods are taken from [18] . To assess overall reconstruction quality, we use the held-out test set from the healthy IXI dataset and report the ℓ 1 -error, calculated as the average absolute difference between the reconstructed images and their corresponding inputs. As shown in Table 2 , our approach achieves competitive performance with cDDPM and significantly outperforms all other baselines ( p < 0 . 05 ). These results suggest that our model effectively preserves healthy anatomy from the input image during reconstruction. This can be attributed to the influence of the ϵ -InfoNCE regularization (Eq. (7) ) within the target-invariant encoder, which improves the representation space with regard to the anatomy. Ablating the target-invariant constraint from our encoder leads to suboptimal reconstruction quality, with the average l 1 error increasing from 9.75 to 11.56 on IXI, as shown in Table 2 (last two rows). Furthermore, Fig. 5 illustrates the anomaly maps obtained with and without the target-invariant constraint. To evaluate segmentation performance in the context of UAD, we use all unhealthy test sets and report two metrics: (i) Dice score and (ii) Area Under Precision–Recall Curve (AUPRC). As shown in Table 2 , our method achieves performance comparable to the top baseline (cDDPM) and significantly outperforms all other baselines ( p < 0 . 05 ), except pDDPM in MSLUB. We achieve the best results with ϵ = 0 . 5 (Eq. (7) ). Additional results with other ϵ values are available in the supplementary material. Analogous to the experimental findings on the CelebA dataset, this model can be used to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy MRIs by analyzing the generated saliency maps, as shown in Fig. 1 (bottom-right). For instance, if the difference between a reconstructed brain MRI and its original counterpart shows high-intensity values across large regions, this may indicate presence of tumor and can be flagged for further review by a radiologist. This strategy can be seen as a form of clinical triage, while also contributing to the model’s explainability by providing a rationale for its decisions. Examples of reconstructions and corresponding tumor segmentation (anomaly maps) are shown in Fig. 6 . Anomaly localization involves identifying and detect abnormal regions within brain MRIs. This task holds significant clinical importance, as many medical errors arise from failing to detect a pathology altogether. The objective is to predict one or more bounding boxes per image that correspond to abnormal regions, using annotations provided by radiologists as ground truth. As shown in Table 3 , our method outperforms cDDPM and pDDPM with statistical significance ( p < 0 . 05 ), except for DDPM, where the improvements are marginal. Specifically, we achieve these results by considering only T2-weighted images and selecting the top- 5 predicted largest bounding-boxes. When considering more than the top- 5 bounding-boxes the performance tends to saturate while the number of false positives increases (1492 to 2348). We empirically found that including all modalities available in the NOVA dataset degrades performance, which is expected, as the models were pre-trained only on T2-weighted images from IXI. Compared to pDDPM and cDDPM, our pre-training strategy, which is based on contrastive learning, appears to be more robust than simply using data augmentation. As illustrated in Fig. 7 , our model is capable of detecting larger and more accurately localized anomalies, while baseline methods tend to produce smaller and more fragmented predictions. For example, pDDPM underestimates lesion size, likely due to its patching strategy, which may rely on suboptimal patch sizes. Notably, considering the top- 3 largest bounding boxes our method reduces the number of false negatives by nearly 40%, suggesting that future work could explore post-processing strategies to remove isolated or implausible detections, thus improving trust in clinical workflows. These results highlight the effectiveness of our methodology, particularly given that NOVA is considered a challenging and realistic evaluation-only benchmark dataset. In this work, we proposed an unsupervised framework for anomaly detection in brain MRIs that integrates contrastive learning with conditional diffusion models. Our method reconstructs a healthy version of input images while preserving common patterns, enabling both accurate classification and precise and interpretable localization of anomalies. By relying exclusively on healthy data, our approach mitigates the reliance on scarce or poorly annotated unhealthy samples. Moreover, the use of saliency maps derived from reconstruction errors provides intuitive visual evidence that enhances model interpretability, addressing key challenges in clinical adoption. Providing clinicians with reconstructed healthy images for comparison could help reduce diagnostic errors by enhancing visualization of abnormalities and supporting the differential diagnosis process. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which achieves competitive performance compared to existing UAD methods and ranks first in anomaly localization on the challenging NOVA benchmark. Nevertheless, our work has limitations and open challenges that are important to acknowledge. The exclusive use of 2D T2-weighted images during training may limit generalization to other structural modalities. In addition, proper clinical validation is needed to assess the potential of our approach to reduce radiologists’ workload and to facilitate early and fast diagnosis. Future work could explore integrating multimodal imaging data and investigate the model’s robustness across diverse pathological conditions. In addition, ethical aspects regarding potential misdiagnosis and privacy concerns remain crucial for safe adoption in practice. Vulnerabilities of feature clustering in EIT radiomics Background We aimed to determine whether unsupervised machine learning was able to discover latent and possibly clinically-relevant clusters, hidden in dynamic electrical impedance tomography (EIT) images within a population of mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients. Dynamic EIT images visualize the distribution of electrical impedance within the patient's lungs, and is clinically used for the optimization of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) when supporting patients with mechanical ventilation helping them to overcome their critical disease. The task selected here was to use unsupervised learning on 2D radiomics features extracted from clinical time-varying EIT images. The hypothesis was that we could find clusters of patients with similarly-appearing pathophysiology according to dynamic EIT. We were motivated to learn on which image-characteristics the resulting clusters were based and whether radiomic features confounded the results. Methods The setting of our study was an intensive care unit of a large tertiary academic hospital in the Netherlands. We used an unsupervised learning workflow that extracted 108 radiomics features and used principal components analysis, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding, and k-means to find latent clusters of similar dynamic lung impedance during the EIT-guided trials optimizing PEEP. Latent clusters were described by patient characteristics, and ventilation variables. We examined image acquisition parameters to control for confounding of radiomic features. Findings We included mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients subjected to a clinical EIT measurement from March 2020 until September 2021, totalling 172 patients with 528 unique EIT-guided PEEP trials. We analyzed approximately 250,000 EIT images. Five latent clusters were identified each consisting of similar EIT-guided PEEP trials, which differed regarding patient characteristics, ventilation variables, chosen PEEP level, and clinical outcomes. Analysis showed that these clusters contained artifacts that encoded information about image acquisition process (the number of PEEP steps examined during an EIT-guided PEEP trial) rather than patient- or clinical characteristics. Interpretation Despite the clinically significant differences observed in the clusters identified by unsupervised machine learning, our analysis showed that the clusters were ultimately confounded by the number of PEEP steps set by our ventilation practitioners at the bedside during the data acquisition process. To overcome this confounder effect, we possibly need more standardized acquisition of EIT-guided PEEP trials or a larger dataset than we currently have. Nevertheless, this clustering may still hold clinical relevance, as it shows that the EIT-guided PEEP trial is applied differently across patients, and these differences are associated with distinct clinical outcomes. This, in turn, implies that the ventilation practitioner—consciously or unconsciously—makes decisions during the process that ultimately have a strong association with patient outcomes. Image 1 Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) is a valuable bedside tool for optimizing positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during mechanical ventilation [ 1–6 ]. Dynamic EIT images visualize the distribution of electrical impedance within the patient's lungs and contain a wealth of information, offering opportunities for quantitative analysis using machine learning Unsupervised clustering methods can be used to identify latent and clinically relevant patterns in large amounts of data. Such approaches may reveal groups of patients with similar pathophysiological characteristics as captured by dynamic EIT. These techniques can be applied on imaging data by employing radiomics techniques, that involve extracting and analyzing a large number of quantitative features from images [ 7–9 ]. Radiomics has shown promise in identifying predictive and prognostic factors [ 10–16 ] and has successfully been used in unsupervised learning tasks [ 17–19 ]. However, a known limitation in supervised learning is the risk of confounding, where observed associations between the medical images and disease outcomes may be confounded by underlying radiomic features [ 20 ]. Similarly, unsupervised algorithms used to cluster medical images may be susceptible to confounding by underlying radiomic features. Accordingly, we formulate two primary research questions. First, can unsupervised clustering of radiomic features extracted from dynamic EIT images reveal clinically relevant patient groups? Second, to what extent are the resulting clusters driven by specific image characteristics and do radiomic features introduce confounding effects into the clustering results? To explore these questions, we apply unsupervised clustering techniques to EIT-guided PEEP trials (EPTs) and examine the role of image characteristics in shaping the identified clusters. The data used in the present study are part of the prospective Maastricht Intensive Care Covid (MaastrICCht) cohort on mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients at a tertiary teaching hospital in the Netherlands, ongoing since March 2020 [ 2 , 21–25 ]. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (as revised in 2013), approved by the local medical ethics review committee (METC MUMC+: 2020–1565), and registered in the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (NL8613) with the public title Serial measurements in COVID-19-induced acute respiratory disease to unravel heterogeneity of the disease course: design of the Maastricht Intensive Care COVID cohort: MaastrICCht . The patient characteristics, data collection, and protocol for serial EIT measurements have been described extensively [ 2 , 21 , 26 , 27 ]. We included patients from the MaastrICCht cohort from March 2020 until September 2021 who had a COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CO-RADS) score of 4 or 5 (high or very high level of suspicion SARS-CoV-2 infection based on CT scans scored by a radiologist), and/or a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test proven SARS-CoV-2 infection [ 28 ]. Patients mechanically ventilated by controlled mechanical ventilation (i.e., pressure-controlled ventilation) and subjected to a clinical EIT measurement were considered eligible in our study. Several clinical contra-indications for the EIT measurements were specified and applied as exclusion criteria ( Supplementary Material - S1 ). Both patients in the prone and supine positions were investigated at the moment of measurement. All included participants received multiple EPTs during their stay in the intensive care unit (ICU). For a detailed comparison of the patient population included in this study versus excluded patients from the MaastrICCht cohort (without EIT), please refer to Supplementary Materials S9. Significant differences were observed, including higher APACHE II scores in the included patients, greater use of prone positioning, lower prevalence of chronic lung disease, lower PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio (arterial oxygen partial pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen ratio - a measure of how well oxygen passes from the lungs into the blood), longer ICU length of stay, and higher ICU mortality. On admission to the ICU, comprehensive clinical baseline characteristics and risk scores, including Acute Physiology And Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE-II) scores, were collected [ 21 , 29 ]. The APACHE II score is a severity-of-disease classification system that quantifies the degree of physiological derangement in critically ill patients. Higher scores indicate greater disease severity and an increased risk of mortality. In addition, ventilator settings and arterial blood gas analyses were collected before and after each EPT. An EIT belt was placed around the patients' chest at the fourth or fifth intercostal space at the parasternal line and connected to an EIT monitor (Pulmovista 500, Dräger Medical GmbH, Lübeck, Germany). To obtain accurate serial measurements, the position of the electrode belt was marked on the patients’ skin to ensure that each subsequent measurement was performed at the same position. The band remained in place during the EPT. The number of steps performed during the EPT varied between patients and measurements based on the condition of the patient. Performing of EPTs and the process of deciding on a clinically-guided PEEP and an EIT-guided PEEP is described in S2 [ 30 ]. We report the PEEP upper limit and PEEP lower limit of each EPT since these vary between patients and trials due to the patient's clinical status at the moment of measurement. We also report the resulting number of PEEP steps between the upper limit and the lower limit and the mean number of images recorded per PEEP step. The ventilation practitioner assessed the quality of EIT images [ 2 ][S3]. Only EPTs with good or intermediate quality EIT images were included. We report the percentage of good-quality EIT images. Last, we report whether the patient was prone or supine during the EPT. All EPT were performed using the same device used by one of our two ventilation practitioners (not reported). The data pre-processing has been described in S4. To explore the potential value of EIT radiomics in COVID-19-related respiratory failure, we aim to investigate whether using radiomics enables us to reveal latent, clinically relevant information from the EIT images. We use unsupervised machine learning clustering techniques for this purpose and describe the revealed clusters in terms of patient characteristics at admission, clinical parameters before and after the EPT, and imaging acquisition parameters. First, we clustered each EPT based on the radiomic features obtained from the EIT images. Each unique EPT functioned as a single case characterized by the related radiomic features. In other words, we aimed to find distinct latent patterns in the dynamical changes of impedance that were recorded during the EPTs. For this purpose, we used principal components analysis (PCA), followed by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) and k-means (see S8 for more information). This approach was chosen because of the high dimensional character of the data. PCA enabled us to find linear components representing the highest variability in the high-dimensional data, reducing dimensionality. We used the default option for PCA to maintain consistent with commonly used settings and to ensure transparency by showing results based on a standard, widely accepted approach. T-SNE enabled us to map the still high-dimensional data to a 2D representation while preserving the structure of the data. The x- and y-coordinates of the resulting scatterplot are the final coordinates of the data points in this 2D representation. K-means enabled us to assign cluster membership to each single EPT. The process of parameter tuning during the clustering process (e.g., the number of clusters) was semi-automated (S8). We examined different clustering strategies on subsets of the data to better understand the findings and eliminate associated artifacts. Second, we examined the relation between the revealed clusters and patient characteristics at admission, clinical measurements before and after the EPT, and image acquisition characteristics to gain an understanding of the meaning of these clusters. We described the continuous variables by mean (standard deviation) or median (first and third quartile), where appropriate, and the categorical variables by number (percentage). To examine the patient admission characteristics, we filtered the clusters on the first EPT of each patient and compared the values between the clusters using analysis of variance (ANOVA), the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or Pearson's chi-squared test, where appropriate. We compared the values between the clusters through a multilevel linear regression model with a random effect for individual patients (i.e., a random intercept) for both the dynamic clinical measurements and dynamic image acquisition characteristics. We took account of the dependency between multiple trials per patient using a continuous autocorrelation structure of order 1. A logistic multilevel regression was used for categorical variables. All multilevel regression models were reported as a fixed-effect estimate (standard error) or odds ratio (standard error) per cluster, compared to the reference cluster (cluster 1). Data pre-processing was performed in Python version 3.7, the list with required packages can be found in S10. Dimensionality reduction, clustering, and multilevel regression models were performed in R version 4.1.2 using the R-package Rtsne [ 31 ], stats [ 32 ], nlme [ 33 , 34 ], and lme4 [ 35 ]. All further data descriptions and statistical tests were performed in IBM SPSS 25. From March 2020 to September 2021, 324 COVID-19 patients were included in the MaastrICCht cohort. EIT was performed in 173 patients, resulting in 554 EPTs. After excluding trials with an erroneous connection between the EIT device and ventilator device and trials for which the set PEEP level was unknown, 538 EPTs from 172 patients were included in the analyses ( Fig. 1 ). In total, we analyzed 257,637 EIT images. The sample of patients who underwent EIT was not similar to our sample of patients of the MaastrICCht cohort who did not undergo EIT. Of the 172 patients that underwent an EPT, the percentage of male patients was 1.27 times higher, the percentage of prone patients positioned was 1.70 times higher, ICU length of stay was 1.88 times longer, and ICU mortality was 1.47 times more frequent, all statistically significantly different. In addition, compared to 152 patients that did not underwent an EPT, the prevalence of chronic lung disease was 0.66 times lower, the APACHE II score was 1.14 times higher, the highest FiO 2 was 1.15 times higher, the lowest respiratory rate was 1.06 times higher, and the PaO 2 /FiO 2 -ratio was 0.79 times lower (S9). We found 5 well-separated clusters of EPTs based on the radiomics features of the lung impedance data during these EPTs (S11 for parameterization process and outcomes) ( Fig. 2 ). Patient characteristics of the five clusters were described by admission and outcome variables ( Table 1 ). Clusters were statistically significantly different regarding their average BMI, pre-ICU length-of-stay, and ICU mortality rate. To describe the clinical characteristics of the five clusters, we examined the dynamic clinical data per EPT (S12). Clusters were statistically significantly different in terms of FiO 2 and PEEP levels prior to the PEEP trial. After the PEEP trial, the clusters represented statistically significant differences in inspiratory pressure and PEEP level. In addition, we have examined the differences between the clusters in terms of trial- and EIT data characteristics ( Table 2 ). We found that the clusters differed in PEEP upper limit and PEEP lower limit, the number of images per PEEP step (i.e., length of breathing cycle), and the number of PEEP steps in the EPT. These are all variables that were set by the highly trained ventilation practitioner, and thus, at least some variation in bedside decisions by human interaction is possible. In particular, the number of PEEP steps during the trial was a significant predictor for cluster membership ( Tables 2 and 3 ). Therefore, we named the clusters according to the number of PEEP steps chosen for the majority of the EPTs in each cluster. When we clustered on only the data of every patient's first EPT (i.e., included each patient only once), no well-defined clusters were detected (S10 for parameterization process and outcomes). To investigate clustering independent of the dominant effect of PEEP steps, we clustered again only with the data of the largest cluster (PEEP_7) and examined whether latent clusters emerged. In this analysis, no well-separated clusters were detected (S11 for parameterization process and outcomes). As another investigation to find clusters independent of the dominant effect of PEEP steps, we have clustered again with only the EIT data recorded during the PEEP level that was ultimately chosen as optimal PEEP. Because the number of images per breath cycle varied per trial, we binned the EIT data into 30 bins. Again, no well-separated clusters were found in this analysis (S11 for parameterization process and outcomes). Altogether, no well-defined or well-separated clusters emerged, supporting the robustness of our main findings and highlighting the influence of PEEP-steps on cluster formation. In this study, we investigated whether dynamic imaging information derived from EIT measurements enables us to reveal latent, clinically relevant clusters in mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients in ICU. In particular, we aimed to investigate whether such clusters depend on pathophysiology as seen on the dynamic images or were confounded by underlying radiomic features. This study has two main findings. First, EIT radiomics clustering was possible, and five well-separated clusters were identified. These clusters were statistically significantly different regarding the chosen optimal PEEP level and showed different patient characteristics (such as BMI and pre-ICU length-of-stay), oxygenation variables (such as the PaO 2 /FiO 2 - ratio), and clinical outcomes (such as mortality). Second, the clusters were strongly based on the number of PEEP steps during an EPT between the PEEP upper limit and PEEP lower limit. Despite extensive preprocessing and transformation of the large EPT dataset, the unsupervised learning workflow primarily revealed differences in the number of PEEP steps between the upper and lower limits. Moreover, alternative clustering strategies within the same workflow revealed no other patterns in the data. This suggests that the underlying radiomic features mainly reflected the number of PEEP steps, indicating a potential confounding effect driven by these features. These findings align closely with the work of Welch et al. who highlight that radiomic features are susceptible to underlying dependencies [ 20 ]. This means that certain radiomic features may not be entirely independent but are influenced by external factors such as the number of PEEP steps. Welch et al. emphasize the importance of testing radiomic features to determine whether they provide additional prognostic and predictive value beyond established clinical factors. If the number of PEEP steps influences radiomic features, it suggests that the features are not solely capturing biological information from the dynamic EIT images but also incorporate technical artifacts, which can undermine its reliability and lead to misleading conclusions. One of the safeguards proposed by Welch et al. to mitigate such issues is the use of rigorous testing methodologies to identify dependencies within radiomic models. This safeguard is best done with clinical engagement according to Welch et al. We can firmly agree to that as we found the underlying confounder in our study also only by a strong cooperation with the clinicians. While the study of Welch et al. primarily employs supervised learning, we demonstrate that similar issues persist within unsupervised learning frameworks. The vulnerabilities associated with radiomic signature development are not exclusive to supervised learning models. Our findings highlight that acquisition-related biases, such as the number of PEEP steps influencing radiomic features, can also permeate unsupervised approaches, underscoring the need for methodological safeguards across different learning paradigms. This reinforces the broader implication that radiomic models, irrespective of their learning approach, require rigorous validation to ensure that extracted features genuinely contribute to prognostic or predictive accuracy rather than reflecting technical artifacts. Our results underscore the necessity of critically assessing the presence of artifacts and acquisition-related confounders in radiomic data. Even robust unsupervised clustering methods may identify patterns driven by such confounders rather than true biological or clinical features. Therefore, ongoing vigilance is required to distinguish meaningful signals from artifacts, particularly in retrospective datasets, to ensure reliable and clinically valid machine learning applications. The findings of this study are, most likely, not specific to COVID-19 ARDS, as the identified clusters were primarily influenced by data acquisition characteristics, rather than underlying disease features. Therefore, similar data acquisition effects may be expected in other cohorts where unsupervised clustering is applied to radiomics data from EPTs. A strong relationship was observed between the number of PEEP steps and patient characteristics, oxygenation variables, and clinical outcomes. This demonstrates that the highly skilled ventilation practitioners, alongside the use of our EPT protocol, were able to distinguish various clinical phenotypes and adjust the EPT accordingly. This suggests that the clinical interpretation and adaptation of an EPT by the expert at the bedside holds information related to patient outcomes. Therefore, the number of PEEP steps selected by the ventilation practitioner may offer diagnostic feedback on their decision-making process. The present study had several strengths. First, using a large cohort of EPTs enabled us to examine latent patterns in the data. Second, we could analyze the high dimensional data of EPTs using extensive data pre-processing and dimensionality reduction techniques. Third, our approach became transparent and repeatable by creating a semi-automated algorithm for parameter tuning during clustering. Fourth, previous research has summarized the various challenges of using radiomics in predominantly static imaging techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and CT images in terms of image acquisition, reconstruction, segmentation, post-processing, and feature extraction [ 7–9 ]. We, therefore, examined the influence of image acquisition characteristics and revealed similar challenges in using radiomics in EIT. As a solution, van Timmeren et al. [ 8 ] suggest standardizing imaging protocols and acquisition. However, this is often not feasible due to the retrospective nature of radiomic studies. If considering a prospective design for EIT-guided PEEP trials, there remain inherent limitations to protocol standardization in the clinical setting. Each patient has a unique respiratory cycle length as well as individualized minimum and maximum PEEP levels, making it impossible to mandate a fixed number of images per PEEP step across all patients. Consequently, the data are collected primarily for clinical decision-making rather than research purposes, which introduces unavoidable variability. This highlights the continued importance of the practitioner's expertise and decision-making during EIT acquisition and emphasizes the relevance of combined clinical and radiomic knowledge to draw valid conclusions. Our study also had several limitations. First, not all patients in the MaastrICCht cohort underwent an EPT. When we compared the patients who underwent EIT-guided PEEP titration to patients on mechanical ventilation who did not undergo EIT-guided PEEP titration, we observed that patients included in our study were more likely men without a history of pulmonary diseases who had a lower PaO 2 /FiO 2 at admission, a higher APACHE II score at admission, a longer ICU stay and higher mortality. The lower PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio might have led to redirecting scarce EIT resources to more critically ill patients. A similar mechanism might have led to select patients without a history of chronic pulmonary disease, as EIT-guided PEEP titration might be perceived as riskier in those patients. With regard to disease severity, the difference in the APACHE II score was small in absolute terms. Overall, these analyses suggest that EIT-guided PEEP titration was done in patients most severely affected due to COVID-19 pulmonary disease. Second, patients in both prone and supine positions were deliberately included in the analyses. The EIT images of prone-positioned patients are flipped compared to supine-positioned patients, and different gravitational influences on lung mechanics play a role. Somewhat unexpectedly, these differences were not picked up by the clustering method. Third, we only explored one unsupervised learning workflow to detect patterns in the data. We acknowledge that alternative methods might uncover different patterns, which may or may not be more clinically relevant. Therefore, we do not rule out the possibility that clinically relevant clusters can be identified in dynamic EIT data. Future research should explore whether other techniques, such as convolutional neural networks, are able to reveal other patterns in the data [ 36 ]. Fourth, the research is only based on a specific dataset for analysis and conclusion derivation. In general, it is essential to verify findings with additional datasets, especially prior to use in a clinical setting. As this study represents an initial exploration with the primary aim to share knowledge and to contribute to collaborative learning about unsupervised clustering in dynamic EIT data, extern validation was out of scope of our research. In conclusion, our study demonstrated that unsupervised clustering of radiomic features extracted from dynamic EIT images can reveal clinically relevant patient groups. Additionally, we found that the resulting clusters were influenced by specific image characteristics, with radiomic features potentially confounding the clustering results. These findings underscore the importance of considering both the technical and clinical factors when clustering dynamic EIT data, as the radiomic features themselves may introduce confounding effects in the analysis. A Comprehensive Deep Learning Approach for Dermoscopic Image Enhancement Image enhancement plays a pivotal role in improving image quality within the field of image processing. In the context of dermoscopic imaging, it serves as a critical and challenging pre-processing step, essential for facilitating accurate automated diagnosis. However, current techniques often struggle to address the diverse range of degradations encountered in real-world scenarios. The primary objective of this study is to propose a robust deep learning approach capable of restoring high-quality images from a wide range of realistic degradation scenarios. To achieve this, we introduce two key contributions: first, EnhanceNet-U, a U-Net architecture modified with a simplified bottleneck and an enhanced decoder path for improved feature restoration; and second, a comprehensive synthetic dataset simulating common dermoscopic degradations, including Gaussian noise, variations in brightness and contrast, and blur. Extensive experiments were conducted, evaluating our proposed method against several established baseline models and analyzing the impact of various loss functions and optimizers to determine the optimal configuration. The results show that EnhanceNet-U consistently outperformed all competing models, demonstrating a peak improvement of 15.75% in SSIM and 15% in PSNR when compared to the lowest-performing DnCNN model. The combination of perceptual loss and MSE emerged as the most effective loss function for balancing quantitative accuracy with perceptual quality. These findings validate our proposed method, proving its capability to restore high-quality images under realistic degradation scenarios and highlighting its potential as a robust solution for the complexities of dermoscopic image enhancement. Data will be available upon reasonable request. Malignant melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, is one of the fastest-growing cancers globally. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual incidence of invasive melanoma increased by 27% [1] . Early detection is critical, as melanoma can often be treated effectively with a simple surgical excision when identified in its early stages [2] . Dermoscopy, a non-invasive imaging technique, has become a vital tool for diagnosing melanoma and other pigmented skin lesions. By utilizing optical magnification, it provides enhanced visibility of subsurface skin structures, offering significant advantages over standard clinical images [3] . Despite its importance, dermoscopic imaging is often affected by challenges such as noise, low contrast, and artifacts, which can hinder accurate diagnosis. Enhancing these images [4] is essential for better visualization of skin lesions and for improving segmentation quality, ultimately leading to more reliable diagnostic outcomes. Various methods have been developed to address these challenges. To tackle the issue of low contrast in dermoscopic images, a multi-scale morphological technique based on top-hat reconstruction [5] has been proposed. This method extracts and adjusts local bright and dark features, significantly enhancing image clarity and proving highly beneficial for medical diagnosis. Additionally, medical imaging often encounters complications such as overlapping objects and closely related pixel values, which further complicate the diagnostic process. To enhance the quality of such images, another approach employing morphological transforms [6] has been introduced, which progressively applies a Top-Hat transform with increasing mask sizes. The final enhanced image is then selected based on the Contrast Improvement Ratio (CIR). In the broader field of medical imaging, low contrast remains a significant challenge. An exposure-based contrast-limited bi-histogram equalization method has been proposed to enhance visual quality [7] . This method divides the input histogram into two sub-histograms based on exposure thresholds, preserving mean brightness while enhancing fine details. Clipping is applied to control contrast amplification, followed by individual equalization of each sub-histogram. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques regarding contrast, brightness preservation, and computational efficiency. Additionally, comparative analyses of contrast enhancement techniques – such as neighborhood operations, bilateral retinex, and sigmoid functions – have been conducted using metrics like peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and mean square error (MSE) to identify effective approaches for medical images [8] . In the existing literature, various image enhancement techniques using deep learning models have been explored. For instance, the work described in [9] addresses challenges caused by wavelength-dependent light absorption and scattering in underwater images. To mitigate these degradation issues, a method called MLLE is proposed, which enhances image quality by minimizing color loss and locally adapting contrast to improve visual clarity. Another CNN-based method for underwater image enhancement, explored in [10] , utilizes both RGB and HSV color spaces. First, a pixel-level block in the RGB color space handles basic enhancement tasks like color cast removal and denoising. Then, a global-adjust block in the HSV color space is employed to refine overall image properties such as luminance and saturation. Similarly, [11] introduced a CNN-based network named LE-net to enhance low-light images. LE-net’s robust nonlinear mapping capability allows it to effectively model the relationships between image pairs under different lighting conditions, thus improving the model’s generalization performance. In medical imaging, fundus image enhancement [12] is highlighted as essential for accurate ocular disorder diagnosis. Previous methods focused on rare distortions like Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, limiting their practicality. To address common issues, five frequent distortions—macula and border uneven illumination, brightness, darkness, and haze—were identified, and synthetic images were generated for each. A new RDC-UNet architecture, integrating residual dense connections, was proposed and trained on these distortions. It improved visual quality by 8% over existing methods and performed effectively in blood vessel segmentation. In [13] , a low-light image enhancement technique is proposed through the LLIE learning framework, which is specifically designed for edge devices. The framework integrates a lightweight deep learning model and a deployment strategy optimized for edge environments. This optimization also contributes to improved performance in various generic vision tasks. Medical image degradation is often more complex than artificial simulations, which leads to reduced performance when the degradation does not match initial assumptions. Many CNN-based methods treat all channels equally, underutilizing important information and resulting in super-resolution (SR) images with insufficient texture detail. To address this issue, [14] introduces a blind image super-resolution technique that combines edge reconstruction with a feature enhancement module. This approach produces high-resolution images with enriched texture and performs better than current state-of-the-art methods when applied to both natural and medical image datasets. The existing literature reveals several critical research gaps that this paper aims to address. Firstly, while deep learning has transformed tasks like dermoscopic image segmentation and classification [15] , its specific application to image enhancement remains significantly underdeveloped. Many current diagnostic systems still rely on traditional pre-processing techniques or include enhancement as only a minor, non-specialized step. This leaves an opportunity for dedicated deep learning models designed specifically to improve the foundational quality of the images themselves. Furthermore, this gap is particularly impactful because dermoscopic images present a unique and complex set of challenges that existing methods handle poorly. Artifacts such as poor contrast, blur, and obscuring hairs often occur simultaneously. Traditional methods, which typically address these issues in isolation, are often insufficient, as they can fail to correct all degradations or may even introduce new distortions [16,17] . A robust solution must be able to tackle this variety of co-occurring artifacts at once while carefully preserving the subtle textural and color details that are vital for an accurate diagnosis. Finally, progress in this area is fundamentally hampered by a lack of specialized datasets suitable for training supervised deep learning models. Developing these models requires large collections of degraded images paired with their corresponding high-quality, artifact-free ground truth versions. Since creating such datasets from real-world clinical images is often impractical, there is a pressing need for well-curated synthetic datasets. Such datasets, by realistically simulating common degradations, are essential for effectively training and validating new, more powerful enhancement models. To address these research gaps, this paper introduces a comprehensive framework for enhancing dermoscopic images. The key contributions of this work are: • A modified U-Net architecture is proposed to enhance dermoscopic image quality by effectively removing noise and artifacts while preserving critical diagnostic features. • To facilitate robust training and evaluation, we have created a synthetic dataset that emulates real-world conditions by incorporating common degradation factors, including Gaussian noise, brightness and contrast variations, and Gaussian blur. • Comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the impact of various loss functions and optimizers on model performance. Results demonstrate that the proposed EnhanceNet-U significantly outperforms existing CNN-based models – such as DnCNN, DSRN, FSRCNN, EDSR, VDSR, RDC-UNet, and the original U-Net – in enhancing dermoscopic image quality.
