Melanoma is among the most dangerous forms of skin cancer, underscoring the urgent need for early and accurate diagnosis to improve patient survival rates. Due to its visual similarity to benign skin lesions, such as nevi, as shown in Fig. 1 , melanoma is often challenging to distinguish, emphasizing the role of automated diagnostic tools in early detection [18] . Dermoscopy images reveal a range of skin diseases that can be broadly categorized into melanocytic and nonmelanocytic groups. Melanocytic diseases include melanoma and melanocytic nevi, while nonmelanocytic conditions encompass basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), vascular lesions (VASC), benign keratosis lesions (BKL), and dermatofibroma (DF). Among these, melanoma stands out as particularly dangerous and potentially lethal, becoming incurable at advanced stages, making it one of the most prevalent and serious cancers worldwide [19] . Diagnostic methods for melanoma include dermoscopy, computed tomography (CT) scans, and ultrasounds, though advanced imaging tests are generally unnecessary for early-stage melanomas. Dermoscopy, in particular, is the most widely used technique for the early detection of skin cancer, especially for differentiating melanomas from nevi [20] . Despite the effectiveness of dermoscopy, it still requires expert dermatologists to interpret the images, and human error remains a risk. Misdiagnosing atypical melanoma can have severe, potentially fatal consequences [21] . Early detection of atypical melanoma (AM) remains particularly challenging due to the close visual resemblance between malignant tumors and benign moles, posing difficulties even for experienced dermatologists. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques have shown great potential in automating the diagnostic process for non-invasive dermatologic imaging. However, the success of these techniques relies heavily on the quality and diversity of the datasets used for training. High-quality machine learning algorithms can enhance diagnostic speed and accuracy, but inconsistencies in image quality and algorithm development can lead to variability in results [22] . Skin disease diagnosis is often complicated by variations in skin color, image artifacts, and overlapping features between conditions. These challenges are further exacerbated in developing countries by insufficient medical resources and high treatment costs, delaying early detection and adversely impacting social and health outcomes [23] . In dermoscopic image processing, variability in image quality and the lack of standardized datasets pose significant obstacles, limiting the diagnostic accuracy of AI models and hindering their generalizability. Addressing these challenges requires advancements in image diversity and consistent standards to facilitate better AI integration into clinical practice [24] . The accuracy of automated skin cancer detection can be significantly improved through the enhancement of dermoscopic images. By enhancing image quality and diversity, current limitations can be addressed, and dermatological care can be revolutionized, ensuring early and precise diagnosis. The workflow of our experimental procedure, as illustrated in Fig. 2 , begins with data acquisition, followed by the application of controlled degradations. The dataset is then preprocessed and split into training, validation, and test sets. The training phase encompasses the selection of the model, loss function, and optimizer, followed by iterative evaluation on the validation set to refine the configuration. Finally, the optimized model is assessed on the test set and further evaluated across different degradation types. The images used in this study were sourced from the Task 1 dataset of the ISIC 2018 challenge [25,26] . This task focused on skin lesion segmentation [27,28] , providing a robust set of dermoscopic images specifically curated for analyzing and segmenting skin lesions. The dataset encompasses a diverse range of lesion types, making it ideal for evaluating image enhancement techniques aimed at improving medical image quality. Sample images are presented in Fig. 3 . To simulate real-world imaging challenges, four degradation parameters were selected: 1. Gaussian Noise : Gaussian noise [29,30] is a type of statistical noise that has a probability density function (PDF) equal to that of the normal distribution, often referred to as Gaussian distribution. In image processing, Gaussian noise manifests as random variations in pixel values, where each pixel’s intensity is altered by a small, normally distributed amount. This noise simulates electronic noise from imaging sensors, commonly encountered in real-world medical imaging scenarios. Different levels of Gaussian noise were introduced by varying the standard deviation ( σ ) to test the robustness of the enhancement model across diverse noise conditions. 2. Brightness Variation : Brightness variation, controlled by the parameter β , refers to changes in the overall lightness or darkness of an image. This type of variation is commonly used to replicate conditions of overexposure or underexposure that can occur due to uneven lighting during image capture. 3. Contrast Variation : Contrast variation, controlled by the parameter γ , alters the difference between the lightest and darkest parts of an image. This adjustment affects how distinct the details in an image appear, with increased contrast making details more pronounced and decreased contrast making them more subdued [31] . By simulating contrast changes, the study assesses how well the enhancement model can handle images where lesion visibility is compromised due to contrast issues. 4. Gaussian Blur : Gaussian blur [32] is applied to reduce image detail and smooth out edges by convolving the image with a Gaussian filter of radius r . The filter uses a weighted average around each pixel, with weights following a Gaussian distribution. By varying r , the blur simulates out-of-focus or motion-blurred images, common in clinical settings. These parameters were combined in five distinct ways to replicate various real-world scenarios encountered in dermoscopic imaging, as detailed in Table 1 . The application of these degradation combinations followed a structured process, outlined in Algorithm 1. The dataset was divided into three subsets: Train, Test, and Validation, as summarized in Table 2 . The training set comprised 3500 images, while both the test and validation sets contained 500 images each. All subsets were equally degraded using the five combinations of degradation parameters. This balanced distribution allows for a thorough assessment of model performance under various degradation scenarios. The degradations were applied before any other preprocessing steps to ensure that the input images reflected challenging imaging conditions. After applying the simulated degradations, all images were resized [33] to a fixed dimension of 256 × 256 pixels. Resizing was necessary to maintain uniformity across the dataset and to meet the input size requirements of the CNN architectures used in this study. The selected resolution balances the need to retain sufficient detail while being computationally efficient for model training. The pixel intensity values of the resized and degraded images were normalized to a range of [0, 1] by dividing each pixel value by 255. Normalization helps stabilize the training process by ensuring that the input values are within a consistent range, which is important for preventing issues related to gradient instability during training. In this study, we introduce a novel convolutional neural network architecture specifically designed for image enhancement. This architecture, named EnhanceNet-U, is built upon the widely recognized U-Net model [34] , which has become a cornerstone in the field of biomedical image analysis due to its impressive capabilities in image segmentation tasks. Originally developed for the segmentation of biomedical images, U-Net features a symmetric architecture characterized by a contracting path that captures context and a symmetric expansive path. This design allows U-Net to effectively learn hierarchical features at multiple scales, making it particularly adept at distinguishing fine details within complex structures, such as skin lesions in dermoscopic images. Our modifications to the original U-Net aim to optimize the network for image enhancement, specifically targeting various types of image degradation that are often prevalent in medical imaging applications. These degradations include noise, blurriness, low light, and contrast variation, which can hinder diagnostic accuracy in clinical settings. By enhancing its performance in super-resolution and denoising tasks, EnhanceNet-U addresses these challenges head-on, providing clearer and more detailed images crucial for accurate analysis and diagnosis. The following section provides a thorough overview of the EnhanceNet-U architecture, highlighting the significant modifications made to the original U-Net and the rationale behind these changes. The modifications introduced to U-Net in EnhanceNet-U, as illustrated in Fig. 4 , include the integration of dropout layers, a modified bottleneck layer, additional convolutional layers in the expansive path, and enhanced connections between the encoder and decoder. The rationale for each of these architectural changes is as follows: 1. Dropout Layers : Dropout layers were integrated into each block of the contracting path (with a rate of 0.1) and the bottleneck layer (with a rate of 0.2) to mitigate overfitting during training. By randomly dropping a fraction of the neurons, the model becomes more robust and generalizes better to unseen data. This is particularly beneficial for medical images, where variability and noise are common. 2. Bottleneck Layer Modification : In the original U-Net architecture, the bottleneck layer consists of two consecutive convolutional layers that process the compressed features of the input before passing them to the expansive path. In EnhanceNet-U, one of the convolutional layers was removed, leaving a single convolutional layer followed by a dropout layer (with a rate of 0.2). This adjustment was made to simplify the model and mitigate overfitting, particularly when working with smaller datasets like those in dermoscopic imaging. 3. Enhanced Feature Processing in the Expansive Path : Unlike the original U-Net, where upsampled features are immediately concatenated with those from the contracting path, EnhanceNet-U introduces an additional convolutional layer before concatenation. This allows the network to refine the contextual information from the deeper layers before it is merged with the spatial details from the skip connection. By processing the features both before and after they are merged, the model achieves a more precise reconstruction. In addition to these modifications, the network employs a standard filter progression strategy to effectively learn hierarchical features. The number of filters doubles at each block in the contracting path, from 64 to 1024 at the bottleneck, allowing the model to capture increasingly complex features. This process is mirrored in the expansive path, where the filter count is halved at each upsampling stage. The architecture concludes with a final 1 × 1 convolutional layer with a linear activation function, a standard choice for image regression tasks that produces a continuous-valued output suitable for image enhancement. The performance of our model was evaluated using various loss functions, each designed to capture different aspects of image quality. The loss functions used in this study are described below: The Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss measures the average squared difference between the predicted ( y ˆ i ) and true ( y i ) pixel values across all pixels in an image, with N representing the total number of pixels. This loss function is widely used for its simplicity and effectiveness in penalizing large errors, ensuring that the overall difference between the original and reconstructed images is minimized. (1) L MSE = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N y i − y ˆ i 2 The Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [35] loss function measures the structural similarity between two images. SSIM values range from −1 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect structural similarity. SSIM emphasizes structural information in images, making it well-suited for capturing perceptual similarity rather than just pixel-level accuracy. (2) L SSIM = 1 − SSIM ( y i , y ˆ i ) This combined loss function leverages both MSE and SSIM [36] , balancing pixel-wise accuracy with perceptual quality. The weight parameter α allows control over the relative importance of each component, providing flexibility in optimizing the model for different image enhancement goals. This combination helps the model focus on both quantitative accuracy and perceptual realism. (3) L MSE+SSIM = ( 1 − α ) ⋅ L M S E ( y i , y ˆ i ) + α ⋅ L S S I M ( y i , y ˆ i ) The VGG Perceptual Loss [14] uses a pre-trained VGG16 model to compare high-level features of the true ( y i ) and predicted ( y ˆ i ) images. By first extracting feature maps ( ϕ ( y i ) ) and ( ϕ ( y ˆ i ) ) from the pre-trained VGG16 model for both images, this loss function calculates the Mean Squared Error between these feature maps. Unlike pixel-based losses such as MSE, which primarily focus on raw pixel values and may lead to blurry results, the VGG Perceptual Loss captures high-level structures and textures. This approach encourages the predicted image to match the perceptual features of the true image, resulting in visually sharper and more accurate reconstructions. Consequently, the VGG Perceptual Loss is particularly suitable for tasks such as image super-resolution, style transfer, and image synthesis. (4) L VGG = MSE ( ϕ ( y i ) , ϕ ( y ˆ i ) ) This loss function combines the benefits of both MSE and VGG Perceptual Loss [37] , aiming to produce images that are both quantitatively accurate and perceptually pleasing. By adjusting the weight parameter, the model can be fine-tuned to prioritize either pixel-level fidelity or perceptual quality, depending on the specific requirements of the task. This flexibility makes the combined loss function versatile for a variety of image enhancement applications. The model was trained in mini-batches with a batch size of 32 for 50 epochs. The initial learning rate was set to 1 × 1 0 − 4 and decayed by a factor of 0.75 every 15 epochs. During training, model performance was assessed on the validation set using PSNR, SSIM, MSE, and MAE. Through ablation studies, the combination of the Nadam optimizer and the MSE + VGG loss function was identified as the optimal configuration. This optimized setup was subsequently used to train all models for the final comparative analysis. Training was conducted on an Nvidia Tesla T4 GPU (via Google Colab) utilizing the TensorFlow 2.15 deep learning framework, with each model requiring approximately 5 h to complete the 50 epochs. In this section, the proposed image-enhancement deep learning model, “EnhanceNet-U” has been evaluated using various criteria, including comparisons with different models, analysis of the impact of loss functions, assessment of the effect of optimizers, and performance analysis across different types of degradation. Several deep learning models, including DnCNN [39] , DSRN [40] , FSRCNN [41] , VDSR [42] , EDSR [43] , RDC-UNet [12] , U-Net, and proposed EnhanceNet-U, were evaluated for the task. These models were trained and tested on the same datasets using the Nadam [44] optimizer and the MSE + VGG loss function. This comparison was conducted using two main evaluation methods: (a) Visual Assessment and (b) Quantitative Analysis. Based on the visual examination, as shown in Fig. 5 , it is clear that the EnhanceNet-U produces the highest quality reconstructions, with predictions that closely match the reference/ground truth. This model excels in preserving both structural details and color accuracy across all images, a fact further validated by its consistently high PSNR and SSIM scores. The standard U-Net and RDC-UNet also performs well, providing visually appealing predictions that are close to the ground truth, albeit with minor differences in some details. EDSR and VDSR deliver reasonably good results, although they occasionally introduce slight artifacts and color deviations. In contrast, FSRCNN and DSRN show limitations in their ability to accurately restore degraded images. The DSRN model often introduces a reddish hue that diverges from the ground truth, negatively affecting both the visual quality and quantitative scores. While FSRCNN performs relatively well in maintaining sharpness, it introduces noticeable bluish or pinkish hues that diverge from the ground truth. These color distortions compromise the model’s ability to achieve accurate fidelity, a strength observed in the top-performing models. The DnCNN model consistently provides the least accurate predictions, with significant blurring and poor color preservation. Its low PSNR and SSIM scores reflect its inability to effectively restore images, making it the weakest performer in this comparison. The visual comparisons and corresponding PSNR/SSIM scores demonstrate that EnhanceNet-U excels in enhancing medical image quality, with superior visual clarity and quantitative metrics highlighting its effectiveness for this task. The metrics presented in Table 3 strongly corroborate the visual evaluation in Fig. 5 . EnhanceNet-U emerges as the top performer, achieving the highest PSNR of 26.90 dB and SSIM of 0.8426. To provide rigorous statistical validation for this observation, we conducted paired t-tests comparing EnhanceNet-U against each baseline model. The results, detailed in the final columns of Table 3 , show that the observed performance gap is highly statistically significant ( p < 0 . 001 for all PSNR and SSIM comparisons). This low p -value indicates that the probability of observing such a performance difference due to random chance is exceedingly low, providing strong statistical evidence that the architectural improvements in EnhanceNet-U are genuinely effective. U-Net follows closely with a PSNR of 26.24 dB and SSIM of 0.8220, offering solid performance but slightly lagging behind EnhanceNet-U in both metrics. Notably, RDC-UNet achieves a higher SSIM score of 0.8374 compared to U-Net, indicating its superior perceptual quality in the reconstructed images. However, it falls slightly short in PSNR, with a value of 26.17 dB, which corresponds to higher MSE and MAE values. This suggests that RDC-UNet sacrifices some image fidelity for improved perceptual similarity. EDSR and VDSR show decent performance, achieving SSIM values of 0.8058 and 0.7842, respectively, and PSNR values of 25.57 dB and 24.52 dB. While not surpassing U-Net, RDC-UNet, or EnhanceNet-U, these models perform reasonably well and demonstrate moderate reconstruction quality, as corroborated by the visual comparison. The remaining models, including DnCNN, DSRN, and FSRCNN, exhibit less competitive results, suggesting they are less effective at producing high-quality reconstructions The PSNR and SSIM trends of the models over iterations, as depicted in Fig. 6 , reinforce the metrics in Table 3 . EnhanceNet-U stands out not only for achieving the highest scores but also for its rapid convergence, reaching peak performance within 40 epochs. Similarly, U-Net and RDC-UNet show steady and competitive trends, with RDC-UNet maintaining its superior SSIM but lagging slightly in PSNR. EDSR and VDSR exhibit gradual improvements, aligning with their moderate performance in Table 3 . Conversely, the slower convergence and lower overall performance of DnCNN, DSRN, and FSRCNN mirror their less competitive results, further affirming the effectiveness of the top-performing models. The selection of an appropriate loss function is critical for balancing quantitative accuracy and perceptual quality in image reconstruction tasks. The combined MSE + VGG loss function was found to be the most effective in our study, a result that can be attributed to the complementary nature of its two components. The Mean Squared Error (MSE) component ensures high pixel-level fidelity by penalizing the average squared difference between predicted and true pixel values. However, a known limitation of MSE is its tendency to produce overly smooth or blurry images, as it does not adequately capture the high-frequency details and textures essential for human perception. To address this, the VGG perceptual loss component operates not on pixels but on a deep feature space, comparing high-level feature maps extracted from a pre-trained VGG network. This encourages the model to generate images that are structurally and perceptually aligned with the ground truth, preserving sharp details and realistic textures. By combining these two functions, we create a synergistic objective where MSE grounds the model in quantitative accuracy while VGG guides it toward perceptually superior solutions. This rationale is empirically validated by the results presented in Table 4 , which demonstrate that the MSE + VGG loss function outperforms other loss functions across nearly all metrics, achieving the highest PSNR of 26.90 and SSIM of 0.8426 on the test set. In comparison, the MSE loss function alone achieved a high PSNR (26.42) but fell short in perceptual quality. Conversely, the VGG loss, which prioritizes perceptual features, exhibited the weakest performance in terms of quantitative metrics (PSNR of 22.65), underscoring the necessity of a balanced approach. Other functions, such as SSIM and MSE + SSIM, showed moderate performance but did not surpass the comprehensive benefits of the MSE + VGG combination. The PSNR and SSIM trends over 50 epochs, depicted in Fig. 7 , further validate these findings. In addition to experimenting with different loss functions, we evaluated the performance of various optimizers in our EnhanceNet-U model. The optimizers evaluated include Adam [45] , Adamax [44] , RMSProp [44] , and Nadam [44] , as summarized in Table 5 . The objective was to identify the optimizer that best enhances image quality. The results indicate that the Nadam optimizer consistently outperforms the others, achieving the highest PSNR of 26.90 and SSIM of 0.8426 on the test set. The Adam optimizer follows closely, with a PSNR of 25.90 and SSIM of 0.8287, reflecting robust performance in maintaining pixel accuracy but falling short of Nadam in perceptual quality. In contrast, RMSProp and Adamax exhibited comparatively lower performance, underscoring their limitations in balancing these aspects effectively. The PSNR and SSIM trends over 50 epochs, depicted in Fig. 8 , align with these observations. Overall, Nadam emerges as the most effective optimizer, making it the optimal choice for our image enhancement task. This section provides an in-depth evaluation of our model’s performance across various types of image degradations, as illustrated in Fig. 9 , which showcases input images with different degradation types alongside the corresponding enhanced outputs generated by the proposed model. By comparing the PSNR and SSIM values of EnhanceNet-U with those of other models, we aim to assess its effectiveness in restoring images affected by different noise and distortion parameters. Figs. 10–14 visually illustrate the performance comparisons across five distinct degradation types. EnhanceNet-U achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM scores in D1, outperforming the next best model, U-Net, by approximately 4.2% in PSNR (25.52 vs. 24.50) and 2.7% in SSIM (0.858 vs. 0.835). In D2 and D3, EnhanceNet-U continues to excel, with RDC U-Net achieving a comparable SSIM score in D2 (0.812 vs. 0.813), though it lags behind U-Net in PSNR in D3 (30.31 vs. 30.49). EDSR also performs decently in D3, with a PSNR of 29.85, about 4.6% lower than EnhanceNet-U’s score. In D4, U-Net delivers competitive results, with a PSNR of 23.50, just 1.4% higher than EnhanceNet-U’s score (23.17). Finally, in D5, while EDSR, U-Net, and RDC U-Net show solid performance, EnhanceNet-U outperforms all of them, achieving an SSIM of 0.886, around 1.4% higher than RDC U-Net’s score (0.874) and 1.95% higher than U-Net’s score (0.869). To observe the impact of each architectural modification, an ablation study was conducted. This involved systematically adding each of the three key modifications – dropout layers, the modified bottleneck, and the enhanced expansive path – to the baseline U-Net architecture. Each resulting model variant was then trained and evaluated under identical conditions to ensure a fair comparison. The results of this study are presented in Table 6 and reveal a synergistic relationship between the proposed modifications. U-Net + Dropout Layers: The primary goal of integrating dropout layers was to mitigate overfitting and improve generalization. The observed slight decrease in performance metrics is a well-known and often acceptable trade-off for this benefit, as regularization can prevent the model from fitting too closely to the specific noise patterns, which is critical for real-world performance. U-Net + Modified Bottleneck: This modification was intended to simplify the model and further mitigate overfitting. While this simplification, when applied in isolation, leads to a loss of some feature information as suggested by the results in Table 6 , it was a strategic choice. Its purpose was to create a more efficient architecture that allows the enhanced expansive path in the final model to perform its more detailed feature reconstruction without being prone to overfitting. U-Net + Enhanced Expansive Path: This modification was designed to achieve a more precise reconstruction by refining contextual information. The results in Table 6 validate this approach, showing a notable increase in the SSIM score when this modification is applied in isolation. This confirms its inherent strength in enhancing the model’s ability to capture perceptual quality, a potential that is fully realized in the final, balanced EnhanceNet-U architecture. EnhanceNet-U (All Modifications): The performance of the final architecture validates the synergistic design of its components. The dropout layers provide essential regularization, creating a stable training environment that prevents overfitting. The simplified bottleneck, while leading to a loss of some feature information in isolation, creates a more efficient and salient feature representation. This streamlined information flow is then capitalized on by the enhanced expansive path, which leverages its increased representational capacity to perform a more detailed and precise feature reconstruction, effectively compensating for the bottleneck’s simplification. The final model’s superior performance is enabled by a carefully balanced interplay of regularization, efficiency, and enhanced reconstruction power, allowing it to achieve a superior synthesis of pixel-level accuracy (PSNR) and perceptual quality (SSIM). While the findings of this study are robust within its experimental design, it is important to acknowledge certain limitations that define the scope of our work. The primary limitation is that our analysis was conducted on a relatively small dataset with a specific, predefined set of synthetic degradations. This approach was essential for ensuring a controlled and reproducible comparison between models. However, it also means that the model’s performance has been validated on a particular subset of lesion types and image artifacts, highlighting the need for future studies to further explore its generalizability across larger datasets and more real-world scenarios. In this study, we introduced EnhanceNet-U, a modified U-Net architecture, and a corresponding synthetic dataset to address the challenge of enhancing dermoscopic images. Our experimental results demonstrated that the proposed model consistently outperformed a suite of established baseline models, achieving a final PSNR of 26.90 and an SSIM of 0.8426—representing an improvement of approximately 2.5% in SSIM and 2.5% in PSNR compared to the original U-Net. Furthermore, our analysis identified the optimal training configuration, finding that a combined MSE + VGG loss function and the Nadam optimizer were critical for achieving these top results. The primary practical implication of this work is the potential for our proposed approach to serve as a robust pre-processing step in automated diagnostic pipelines. By improving the quality and clarity of input images, this method can enhance the reliability of downstream tasks such as lesion segmentation and classification, ultimately aiding dermatologists in making more accurate and timely diagnoses. While the current study establishes a strong foundation, future work should aim to build upon these results to develop even more robust enhancement models. A critical direction is the use of large-scale, multi-center clinical datasets with naturally occurring degradations, which would enable the training of models with superior real-world applicability. Furthermore, the exploration of more advanced network architectures, specifically designed to handle the unique complexities of dermoscopic images, presents another promising avenue for pushing the boundaries of enhancement performance. data.text: A hybrid architecture with separable convolutions and attention for lung and colon cancer detection Early and accurate detection of lung and colon cancer is critical for improving patient survival rates. However, conventional classification techniques often struggle with the complexity of medical imaging data. In this study, we propose a novel hybrid architecture, the Separable Convolution and Attention Mechanism (SCA-mechanism), to enhance the accuracy of cancer classification. The proposed model integrates separable convolutions with residual connections to facilitate efficient feature extraction while incorporating attention mechanisms to emphasize key regions indicative of malignancy. We evaluated the performance of the SCA-mechanism model against state-of-the-art deep learning techniques using a benchmark dataset of lung and colon cancer images. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves superior classification performance, outperforming conventional deep learning methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. These findings highlight the potential of the SCA-mechanism as a promising tool for automated cancer diagnosis, offering significant advancements in computationally efficient medical applications and clinical decision making. Lung and Colon Cancer Histopathological Image Dataset (LC25000) Available at . Lung and colon cancers are two of the most prevalent and life-threatening malignancies globally, accounting for more than two million deaths annually [1] . Early and accurate diagnosis plays a crucial role in improving patient prognosis, as the five-year survival rate can exceed 90% when detected at an early stage, in stark contrast to less than 20% for late-stage diagnoses [2] . This critical disparity has catalyzed the development of automated and scalable diagnostic solutions that can assist clinicians in high-throughput, high-stakes decision-making environments. Histopathological image analysis remains the gold standard for confirming cancer diagnoses. These high-resolution microscopy images contain intricate tissue structures and cellular details that are indispensable for detecting malignancies. However, the analysis process is often hindered by domain-specific challenges such as staining variability, high inter-class similarity, intra-class heterogeneity, and subtle morphological variations. Manual interpretation by expert pathologists is time-consuming, subject to fatigue and variability, and difficult to scale. While traditional machine learning methods have attempted to assist in diagnostic interpretation, their dependency on handcrafted features and shallow representation learning often limits their ability to generalize across datasets and cancer types [3] . Deep learning–especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs)–has revolutionized medical image analysis by enabling end-to-end feature extraction and classification from raw pixel data [4] . Nevertheless, most conventional CNN architectures are computationally intensive and require substantial resources for training and inference, especially when dealing with ultra-high-resolution histopathological images. Moreover, CNNs pretrained on natural image datasets may fail to capture domain-specific patterns that are critical in differentiating benign from malignant tissues. These limitations constrain the deployment of deep learning models in computationally efficient or resource-constrained clinical settings. To address these challenges, we propose the SCA-mechanism—a hybrid and computationally efficient deep learning architecture tailored for histopathological cancer classification. The model combines three key innovations: (1) Separable Convolutions , which decouple spatial and channel-wise processing to significantly reduce parameter count and training cost; (2) Residual Connections , which mitigate vanishing gradient issues and enable stable training of deeper networks; and (3) Attention Mechanisms , which dynamically prioritize clinically relevant features such as abnormal nuclei or glandular structures. Together, these components allow the SCA-mechanism to capture fine-grained visual cues while maintaining a lightweight and interpretable design. We validate the model on the publicly available LC25000 dataset, which contains 25,000 histopathological images evenly distributed across five classes, including both benign and malignant lung and colon tissue categories. The proposed architecture achieves a classification accuracy of 98.82%, surpassing several state-of-the-art CNN models in both predictive performance and computational efficiency. Notably, our model reduces average training time per epoch by nearly half compared to widely adopted architectures such as VGG16, ResNet50, and EfficientNetB7. This performance advantage positions the SCA-mechanism as a practical candidate for integration into edge computing devices or computationally efficient clinical diagnostic pipelines. The major contributions of this study are summarized as follows: 1. We introduce a novel hybrid architecture (SCA-mechanism) that integrates separable convolutions, residual learning, and attention mechanisms to enhance classification accuracy and interpretability in histopathological cancer detection. 2. The model achieves 98.82% classification accuracy on the LC25000 dataset while reducing training time significantly compared to conventional deep learning architectures. 3. The design supports computationally efficient deployment and efficient inference, making it suitable for computationally efficient diagnostic systems and resource-limited clinical environments. We introduce a novel hybrid architecture (SCA-mechanism) that integrates separable convolutions, residual learning, and attention mechanisms to enhance classification accuracy and interpretability in histopathological cancer detection. The model achieves 98.82% classification accuracy on the LC25000 dataset while reducing training time significantly compared to conventional deep learning architectures. The design supports computationally efficient deployment and efficient inference, making it suitable for computationally efficient diagnostic systems and resource-limited clinical environments. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly influenced the field of cancer detection, particularly in the classification of histopathological images for colon and lung cancer. However, a number of technical and clinical challenges persist, including limited generalization, computational inefficiency, and lack of interpretability, all of which impact the feasibility of computationally efficient deployment in healthcare settings. This section reviews recent works in two major application areas–colon cancer and lung cancer detection–and outlines their limitations in contrast to the design motivations of the proposed SCA-mechanism. In colon cancer detection, Khan et al. [5] introduced a Swin Transformer-based model using the LC25000 dataset, which achieved high binary classification accuracy. However, the model’s performance dropped notably under multiclass conditions due to its reliance on local attention windows, which limited its ability to capture global contextual features. Alsubai et al. [6] combined Inception-ResNetV2 with Local Binary Pattern (LBP) features to leverage texture descriptors, but the handcrafted LBP component rendered the model sensitive to noise and resolution inconsistencies often present in real-world histopathological images. Sobur et al. [7] employed image augmentation techniques on a CNN model to boost diversity [8,9] yet such transformations risk distorting structural tissue features and may inadvertently hinder interpretability or generalization. Mohamed et al. [10] applied a Fisher Mantis Optimizer to fine-tune CNN weights, achieving competitive accuracy but at the expense of training complexity and scalability, particularly for time-constrained clinical environments [11] . Karthikeyan et al. [12] proposed a CNN pipeline with a ranking module trained on a very small dataset (284 training samples), which severely limited the model’s generalizability to larger or more diverse populations. Across these approaches, common limitations include overreliance on handcrafted components, poor scalability to multiclass classification tasks, and sensitivity to dataset quality—particularly in terms of class balance and image variation. These shortcomings motivate a need for end-to-end learnable, computationally efficient architectures that remain robust across variable imaging conditions and can be deployed in resource-constrained environments. In the domain of lung cancer detection, Yao et al. [13] implemented a nnU-Net framework incorporating a segmentation-classification pipeline based on contrast-enhanced CT images. Although effective, the model required complex pre- and post-processing, making it less suitable for rapid or scalable deployment. Sangeetha et al. [14] proposed a multimodal fusion deep neural network (MFDNN) that achieved high accuracy by combining multiple imaging modalities, yet its dependency on synchronized multimodal data complicates generalization and reduces feasibility for hospitals lacking such infrastructure. Wani et al. [15] developed DeepXplainer–a two-stage CNN-XGBoost hybrid that enhanced interpretability–but this came at the cost of increased inference time, which is critical in clinical workflows requiring computationally efficient decision support [16] . Gayap and Akhloufi [17] surveyed major CNN and ViT-based frameworks, identifying significant issues in model reproducibility due to dataset overfitting and lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. Deshpande et al. [18] proposed a hybrid system combining handcrafted radiomic features and deep learning for lung nodule classification, improving performance on specific datasets like LIDC-IDRI. However, their approach necessitated domain-specific feature engineering, limiting its adaptability across institutions with varying imaging standards. These studies highlight persistent issues such as architectural complexity, interpretability-efficiency trade-offs, dependence on handcrafted or modality-specific features, and poor real-world adaptability—especially when imaging artifacts, resolution inconsistencies, or limited resources are involved. Despite promising results in research environments, many of the models reviewed face critical challenges in real-world deployment. Deep networks such as Swin Transformer [19] often incur significant latency, making them impractical for computationally efficient clinical use, especially in screening workflows or resource-limited hospitals. Moreover, image quality variations–stemming from different scanning devices, staining protocols, and sample preparation–pose significant risks to models trained on highly curated datasets. Handcrafted features (e.g., LBP or radiomics) are often dataset-specific and non-transferable across institutions [20] . Most notably, interpretability is often treated as an afterthought; either absent altogether or appended post hoc, limiting transparency and clinician trust [21] . The lack of integrated attention or explanation modules reduces the utility of AI systems in high-stakes decisions where visual rationale is crucial. Finally, dataset-related challenges such as class imbalance, small sample sizes, or homogeneous imaging sources exacerbate performance variance and weaken model generalization—issues that are rarely addressed systematically across studies. Across the literature, there remains a clear need for a unified, lightweight architecture that overcomes the combined challenges of interpretability, efficiency, and robustness under real-world imaging variability. Existing approaches either focus on accuracy at the expense of scalability (e.g., complex transformer models), or on handcrafted feature enrichment without addressing deployment bottlenecks. In contrast, the proposed SCA-mechanism responds directly to these research gaps by integrating Separable Convolutions for computational efficiency, Residual Connections for gradient stability and generalization, and Attention Mechanisms for built-in interpretability. For this study, we utilized the Lung and Colon Cancer Histopathological Image Dataset (LC25000), a well-structured and widely used benchmark dataset for cancer classification tasks. The dataset consists of 25,000 high-resolution histopathology images, each with a resolution of 768 × 768 pixels in JPEG format. It is systematically categorized into five distinct classes, with 5000 images per class, representing both malignant and benign tissue samples. The five classes include: • Lung adenocarcinoma (lung_aca)—Malignant lung tissue. • Lung squamous cell carcinoma (lung_scc)—A subtype of malignant lung tissue. • Benign lung tissue (lung_n)—Normal lung tissue. • Colon adenocarcinoma (colon_aca)—Malignant colon tissue. • Benign colonic tissue (colon_n)—Normal colon tissue. This dataset serves as a valuable resource for training and evaluating machine learning models for cancer detection, given its high-quality annotations and balanced distribution of classes. We made a few pragmatic choices in preprocessing to keep the pipeline fast, reproducible, and fair to all baselines, while still respecting the fine detail in histopathology images. Below we explain each step and the trade-offs we considered. • Image resizing: All images are resized to 224 × 224 to match the network input. We are aware that downscaling can soften very small textures (e.g., nuclear chromatin). To mitigate this, we use anti-aliased bilinear interpolation and avoid aggressive cropping so that nuclei and gland boundaries remain visible. This size strikes a practical balance between detail and throughput; in future work, a simple extension is to add a multi-scale pathway (e.g., larger inputs or image pyramids) to further protect fine-grained cues. • Normalization: Our default is per-pixel min–max scaling to [ 0 , 1 ] (divide by 255), which is simple and stable across models. An equally reasonable alternative is per-channel standardization (mean subtraction and standard-deviation scaling) computed only on the training split to avoid leakage. We keep min–max as the default for comparability, and note that switching to z-score normalization does not change the rest of the pipeline. • Data splitting: We explicitly use three stratified splits to aid model tuning and guard against overfitting: – Training (80%) —used to learn parameters, – Validation (10%) —used for hyperparameter selection, early stopping, and learning-rate scheduling, – Test (10%) —held out once for the final report. The validation set provides a clean signal for stopping before overfitting and choosing sensible training settings. • Data augmentation: We apply light, morphology-preserving transforms on the fly: – Random rotations within ± 15 ° —a conservative range that captures typical slide orientation changes without bending tissue structures, – Horizontal and vertical flips—to reflect lateral and axial variability. – Bounded zoom ( [ 0 . 9 , 1 . 1 ] ) or small random resized crops (area [ 0 . 9 , 1 . 0 ] ) was enabled to add scale invariance when needed, while keeping distortions controlled. These choices increase diversity without introducing artifacts that could mislead the model. • Shuffling and class balance: To avoid order effects and maintain stable gradients, we shuffle samples every epoch within each class and construct mini-batches that respect class proportions (i.e., batches remain approximately balanced). This prevents any class from dominating updates, especially early in training. All random operations are seeded for reproducibility. This section presents the design and implementation of the Hybrid Architecture Combining Separable Convolutions and Attention Mechanisms (SCA-mechanism), developed for the automated diagnosis of lung and colon cancer. Our approach integrates advanced convolutional techniques with attention mechanisms to enhance feature extraction and emphasize clinically significant regions in medical images. The architectural design prioritizes both high classification accuracy and computational efficiency, ensuring its suitability for computationally efficient diagnostic applications. To effectively process and analyze medical images for lung and colon cancer detection, we developed the SCA-mechanism model. The proposed SCA-mechanism combines depthwise–separable convolutions (for low-cost spatial filtering), pointwise projections (for channel mixing), residual connections (for stable optimization), and lightweight channel attention (for feature recalibration). Compared with conventional backbones (e.g., VGG/ResNet/EfficientNet), SCA targets a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off suitable for histopathology tiles: separable convolutions reduce parameters and FLOPs, residual links preserve gradient flow and mitigate degradation, and attention emphasizes diagnostically salient responses (e.g., nuclei and gland boundaries) without incurring heavy computational overhead. In ablation study, we quantify the contribution of each component and compare against alternative design choices (dilated convolution, pooling variants, optimizers, and regularization levels). Separable convolutions decompose standard convolution operations into depthwise and pointwise convolutions, significantly reducing the number of parameters and computational overhead while preserving feature extraction capabilities. This makes them particularly advantageous for processing high-resolution histopathological images in computationally efficient diagnostic applications. A conventional convolution operation is mathematically expressed as follows [22] : (1) Y= I⋅K + b where I represents the input image, K denotes the convolutional kernel, b is the bias term, and ( ⋅ ) signifies the convolution operation. In contrast, a depthwise separable convolution divides this operation into two sequential steps: 1. Depthwise Convolution: This step applies individual convolutional filters to each input channel separately, capturing spatial features independently. Given an input with C channels, depthwise convolution [23] applies C distinct kernels K c , producing intermediate feature maps D c : (2) D c = I c ⋅ K c, ∀ c ∈ { 1 , 2 , … , C } 2. Pointwise Convolution: This step employs 1 × 1 convolutions to integrate the depthwise convolution outputs across channels, yielding the final feature maps Y [24] : (3) Y = ∑ c=1 C D c ⋅ W c where W c represents the pointwise convolutional weights. To support practical deployment and broad accessibility, the trained SCA mechanism was converted into a TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) model for lightweight on device inference. The mobile application was developed in Android Studio using Kotlin and XML to ensure a seamless and responsive user interface. The application allows users to capture new histopathological images or upload existing ones from their device. Once an image is provided, the model performs local inference without requiring an internet connection, thereby preserving data privacy and ensuring low latency predictions. This offline and self-contained design makes the system particularly suitable for use in resource-limited or remote healthcare settings where stable network connectivity may be unavailable. An illustration of the application interface is shown in Fig. 7 . Validation on unseen histopathological images of lung and colon cancer tissues demonstrated that the mobile application consistently produced accurate and high-confidence predictions. Overall, integrating the SCA model into a mobile environment bridges the gap between computational pathology research and practical diagnostic support. The results of this study highlight the strong potential of the SCA-mechanism as an effective and computationally efficient approach for lung and colon cancer classification. Across all evaluation metrics, the model demonstrates high accuracy, stable generalization, and reliable discrimination of malignant and benign tissue patterns. The combination of separable convolutions, residual connections, and channel attention contributes to consistent performance gains, confirming the value of integrating lightweight feature extraction with adaptive feature prioritization. The ablation study further reinforces the robustness of the architecture, showing that the full SCA configuration offers a favorable balance between predictive power, model size, and inference speed. The explainability analysis with LIME and Grad-CAM also shows that the model consistently focuses on clinically meaningful regions, strengthening confidence in its decision-making process. Moreover, the successful conversion to a TensorFlow Lite format and deployment within a mobile application illustrate the practical feasibility of using the model in real world scenarios, particularly where local inference and data privacy are essential. Although the findings are highly encouraging, certain considerations remain for future development. The model has been trained and evaluated on the LC25000 dataset, which provides high quality and balanced samples but does not encompass the full range of variability encountered in diverse clinical settings. Additional validation on multi institutional datasets and different imaging conditions would help reinforce the model’s general applicability. Similarly, the use of 224 × 224 resized images, while beneficial for computational efficiency, may limit the capture of extremely fine morphological details. Incorporating multi scale feature extraction techniques could further enhance performance. Finally, while the current work focuses on image level classification, extending the framework to region level or slide level analysis may broaden its clinical utility. Overall, the SCA mechanism delivers strong and consistent performance, efficient computation, and promising interpretability, positioning it as a viable candidate for real world computational pathology applications and future clinical integration. This study introduced the SCA-mechanism model, a novel hybrid architecture integrating separable convolutions and attention mechanisms for lung and colon cancer classification. By enhancing feature extraction and prioritizing critical image regions, the model significantly improved classification accuracy, and computational efficiency. The SCA-mechanism model outperformed traditional deep learning models, surpassing DenseNet121, EfficientNetB7, ResNet50, and others, achieving a 98.82% accuracy. This hybrid architecture represents a step forward in AI-driven cancer detection, with the potential to enhance clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. While the SCA-mechanism model demonstrates strong performance, there are areas for further improvement. Currently, it has been trained on the LC25000 dataset, and additional testing on diverse datasets, including other imaging modalities like radiographic or endoscopic images, would enhance its generalizability. A lightweight and extensible cell segmentation and classification model for H&E-stained cancer whole slide images Developing clinically useful cell-level analysis tools for cancer digital pathology in H&E-stained whole slide images remains challenging due to limitations in dataset granularity, inconsistent annotations, high computational demands, and difficulties in integrating new technologies into clinical workflows. To address these issues, we propose a solution that enables finer-grained cell labels at inference, improves model performance, and enhances usability by creating a lightweight, extensible cell segmentation and classification model. First, we update data labels through cross-relabeling to refine annotations of PanNuke and MoNuSAC, producing a unified dataset with seven distinct cell types relevant to tumor pathology. Second, we leverage the H-optimus-0 foundation model as a fixed encoder to improve feature representation for simultaneous segmentation and classification tasks. Third, to address foundation models’ computational demands, we distill knowledge to reduce model size and complexity while maintaining comparable performance. Finally, we integrate the distilled model into QuPath, a widely used open-source digital pathology platform. Results demonstrate improved segmentation and classification performance using a model built on H-optimus-0 compared to a CNN-based model. Specifically, average R 2 improved from 0.575 to 0.871, and average P Q score improved from 0.450 to 0.492, indicating better alignment with actual cell counts and enhanced segmentation quality. The distilled model maintains comparable performance while reducing parameter count by a factor of 48. By reducing computational complexity and integrating into workflows, this approach may significantly impact diagnostics, reduce pathologist workload, and improve outcomes. Although the method shows promise, the present evaluation is restricted to H&E-stained patches from PanNuke and MoNuSAC. Extending the approach to additional cell types and tissues will require further fine-tuning and validation. In cancer digital pathology, and particularly in immuno-oncology, accurate segmentation and classification of cells are crucial for diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive analyses [1–4] . Nowadays, developments in computational pathology offer multiple solutions [5,6] to utilize cell-level datasets to train machine learning models that solve these problems. The quality and specificity of training datasets are critical for robust and accurate models. Adhering to the principle of “garbage in, garbage out”, it is essential to ensure that these datasets are extensively and accurately labeled with distinct classes that reflect the diverse biological characteristics of different cell types. Unfortunately, the number of open-source datasets comprising such high-quality annotations is limited. Existing cell segmentation datasets [7–9] may offer extensive annotations for certain cell types while providing more general labels for others. For example, in PanNuke, which is one of the largest open-source datasets comprising labeled cells, various types of morphologically and functionally different inflammatory cells like macrophages and lymphocytes are clustered in a broad “inflammatory” class. Consequently, these classes are frequently omitted from analyses or aggregated into broader meta-classes [10] and likely interfere with other cell classes included in the dataset. This and similar inconsistencies in annotation granularity limit the ability of machine learning models to learn the comprehensive and nuanced features necessary for accurate cell segmentation and classification. To address these challenges, methods for refining and standardizing dataset annotations are essential to enhance the quality of training data. A complementary approach to mitigate the absence of high-quality training data is the use of foundation models. Foundation models as encoders are defined as large-scale, versatile networks pre-trained on vast, diverse datasets using self-supervised learning, contrasting with convolutional neural network (CNN) pre-trained encoders that rely on supervised learning with labeled data. In practice, foundation models leverage enormous amounts of weakly or unlabeled data from millions of whole slide images (WSIs) and employ self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies and global context [11–14] . As a consequence, foundation models are able to produce transferable feature representations across different cell types and tissue environments. The feature representations can be leveraged by decoder networks to produce segmentation masks and pixel-level classifications. Because foundation models have comprehensive feature representations, they can be effectively fine-tuned using much smaller amounts of cell-level data compared to the large datasets needed to train models from scratch. Furthermore, foundation models incorporate adversarial training elements or contrastive learning [11,14] , enhancing their resilience and adaptability by exposing them to challenging and varied scenarios during training. This may result in more generalizable models, often making them well-suited for diverse and complex tasks in digital pathology. Despite the inherent advantages of foundation models, their deployment for practical use faces its own obstacles. In particular, they require substantial computational power, financial investments and rigorous testing to ensure reliability and efficacy for a given task [15–18] . Moreover, while foundation models enhance feature representation and performance, they depend on the quality of available annotations for decoder fine-tuning and, like any other model, cannot resolve existing inconsistencies or ambiguities in data labels. Therefore, there remains a critical need for solutions that address both data quality and practical deployment considerations. Further, integrating new technologies into existing clinical workflows often encounters resistance, as it necessitates adjustments to established diagnostic processes. So, there is a need to develop solutions that could be integrated into current practices, minimizing the burden on medical professionals to adopt new tools [19] . Additionally, organized community challenges that evaluate and push state-of-the-art methods for nuclear and cell detection and classification [20] have catalyzed rapid progress on benchmark datasets. However, they typically focus on narrowly defined tasks with fixed nuclei classes within a single tissue type, and rarely address deployment considerations such as inference speed, model compression, or integration into routine pathology software. Existing solutions for cell detection in H&E WSIs [21–23] , while addressing some aspects of these challenges, fall short of providing a comprehensive approach that covers integration with computational pathology tools, inference speed, quality and usability across multiple cancers and cell types, and the ability to fine-tune to specific use cases. To address these data quality and clinical deployment issues, we propose a multi-faceted solution that encompasses data refinement, model optimization, and integration with existing pathology tools ( Fig. 1 ). The outcome is a lightweight cell segmentation and classification model that can be integrated into digital pathology workflows for practical clinical use. While the model and workflow we propose is generally applicable to cell segmentation and classification in H&E-stained WSIs, it may be specifically useful for detection and subtyping of immune cells in cancer, as the composition and spatial organization of the tumor immune microenvironment are established biomarkers of prognosis and treatment response across multiple tumor types, including lung, breast, and colorectal cancers [24,25] . Our approach begins with preparing the data for the fine-tuning and training of the machine learning models. We create a refined dataset, acquired via cross-relabeling two cell-level datasets, enhancing annotation specificity and consistency of the labeled data. Subsequently, we create a cell segmentation and classification model based on the foundation model. We leverage the foundation model as a fixed encoder and fine-tune a decoder using the refined dataset to improve generalization across diverse tissue- and cell types. To ensure that the model remains lightweight and deployable in a possibly resource-constrained environment, we employ knowledge distillation to approximate the functionality of the foundation model. Finally, to facilitate the practical application of our model in digital pathology workflows, we integrate it with the QuPath [26] application. Each methodological component contributes to the overarching goal of enhancing model performance, generalizability, and usability in clinical settings. The primary contributions of this paper are: 1. Data labels refinement through cross-relabeling: We propose a new method for refining labels of cell-level datasets through cross-relabeling. This method employs classification models to re-label broad and ambiguous instances, resulting in a more diverse dataset. Our evaluation demonstrates that these classification models achieve high accuracy on test subsets, indicating the reliability of the method for label refinement. 2. Enhanced model performance via foundation models: We employ a foundation model as a feature extractor for the cell segmentation and classification task. In comparison with training a CNN model from scratch, the foundation model backbone only needs fine-tuning, which significantly reduces training time, computational resources and data requirements. We show that using a foundation model encoder leads to better performance in cell segmentation and classification networks than using a CNN-based encoder. This improvement may enable the model to generalize more effectively across various tissue types and imaging methods. 3. Model optimization through knowledge distillation: We show that a smaller student model trained using knowledge distillation on the refined dataset obtained via our cross-relabeling approach from a foundation model achieves comparable performance in cell segmentation and quantification tasks. As a result, this model is more suitable for deployment in environments without high-performance computing resources. 4. Integration with QuPath: We integrate the distilled cell segmentation and classification model into QuPath, a widely used open-source digital pathology platform, to accelerate clinical adaptation by enabling pathologists to more easily incorporate advanced computational tools into their existing workflows.
