Through these methodological steps, we aim to bridge the gap between advanced machine learning techniques and practical clinical applications, making accurate and efficient digital pathology accessible in a broader range of healthcare settings. To address the limitations of sparse and ambiguous labeling of cell-level datasets, we propose a generalizable cross-relabeling strategy that can be applied to any dataset containing broadly categorized or imprecisely labeled cell types. This approach involves training and subsequently leveraging classification models to refine broad categories into more specific or biologically relevant classes. When applied to cell-level data, the methodology includes extracting individual cell images from the dataset patches, preprocessing these images to standardize the size and accommodate partial cells, and then training deep learning classifiers capable of distinguishing between the finer cell subtypes within the coarser categories. To illustrate our approach, we focus on the PanNuke [7,10] and MoNuSAC [9] datasets that we have used to train models for cell quantification for oncology-related tasks in our previous works [27,28] . We find that for better cell differentiation we have to introduce more granular labels. PanNuke includes a broad classification of “inflammatory” cells, encompassing lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils. Each cell type differs significantly in structure, function, and clinical relevance. Conversely, MoNuSAC uses the label “epithelial” for a class that comprises both benign epithelial cells and malignant neoplastic cells. This practice makes it challenging to differentiate between benign and malignant epithelial cells in the dataset, which is a critical distinction when identifying tumor areas within tissue samples. To address these issues, we implement a cross-relabeling strategy as shown in Fig. 2 . The key components are two classification models: one is trained on singular cell images from PanNuke data to classify the epithelial meta-class into epithelial and neoplastic classes. The other is trained on MoNuSAC to refine the inflammatory class into lymphocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages. The refining approach consists of three consecutive steps. The first is the preprocessing step, in which we extract individual cells from both datasets ( Fig. 3 ). The specifics of PanNuke and MoNuSAC patch preparation before cell preprocessing are provided in Appendix A1. During preprocessing, we extract cell type maps from the ground truth label mask and calculate bounding boxes around each cell instance. To accommodate partial cells at patch borders, a common issue in cropped patch images, we employ mirror padding and extend the field of view of the cell label by 15 pixels to capture adjacent cells. We then crop and resize the identified regions to 64 × 64 pixels using bicubic interpolation. The preprocessed PanNuke dataset comprises 68,031 neoplastic and 23,207 epithelial cell images, while MoNuSAC comprises 33,104 lymphocytes, 1252 neutrophils, and 1695 macrophages, which we subsequently use in training cell classification models and classifying cell image data (Appendix Figure A2 (1)). The next step is to train two distinct ResNet50-based classifiers tailored to address the specific labeling challenges inherent in each dataset. We use ResNet50 for classification models due to its proven effectiveness for image classification tasks in histopathology [29] , and its compatibility with small images. For the PanNuke dataset, we design the classifier, trained on MoNuSAC data, to disaggregate the heterogeneous “inflammatory” cell category into distinct subtypes: lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils. Similarly, for the MoNuSAC dataset, the classifier is trained on PanNuke data and distinguishes between benign and malignant epithelial cells within the overarching “epithelial” label. By applying these targeted classifiers to their respective datasets, we assign more specific labels to individual cell instances, thus enabling us to create a unified dataset. The objective of this step is to improve label granularity within patch-level scope for downstream training and fine-tuning of supervised cell segmentation and classification models. To ensure a balanced representation of classes, we train both models on datasets that had been equalized to match the size of the least represented class. Thus, we obtain datasets comprising 23,207 samples per class for PanNuke and 1252 samples per class for MoNuSAC data. Next, we partition both of them into training (70%), validation (20%), and testing (10%) subsets. To mitigate the risk of overfitting, we use a single dropout layer with a rate of p = 0.5 in both models and data augmentation using randomized color perturbations, rotation, and horizontal and vertical flipping. We employ AdamW [30] optimizer and the cross-entropy loss function for the training criterion. To evaluate the two trained models, we measure the classification accuracy on the respective test subsets. The accuracies on the test subset for both classifiers are presented in Table 1 . The PanNuke model achieves an average accuracy of 93.57%, with higher accuracy for neoplastic cells (96.06%) compared to epithelial cells (86.26%). The confusion matrix in Appendix Figure A3.1 shows that the model predominantly distinguishes accurately between epithelial and neoplastic tissues, with a substantial number of correct classifications and relatively few misclassifications. The MoNuSAC model demonstrates an average accuracy of 98.92%, excelling in classifying lymphocytes (99.67%) and macrophages (94.12%), with lower performance for neutrophils (85.71%). The confusion matrix in Appendix Figure A3.2 shows that the model identifies lymphocytes and performs reasonably well with macrophages and neutrophils. Finally, during the last step, we use the model trained on PanNuke data for epithelial cells in MoNuSAC and the model trained on MoNuSAC for the inflammatory cells class in PanNuke. Specifically, we use classifier models to relabel epithelial cells in MoNuSAC and inflammatory cells in PanNuke data. Then we combine cells with refined labels and the rest of the cells in both datasets to create a refined dataset (Appendix Figure A2 (2)). The process of relabeling cells and visualizing them on a patch is shown in Fig. 4 . The cell counts in the refined dataset are provided in Appendix Table A4. Relabeling and combining datasets have been explored in a prior study [31] , where consecutive fine-tuning on multiple datasets was employed to account for hierarchical class label structures. While the method presented in [31] is intuitive, it often lacks consistency and requires multiple fine-tuning runs, which can be cumbersome and time-consuming. In contrast, cross-relabeling simplifies this process by using specialized classification models tailored to each dataset’s specific labeling challenges. This approach provides better transparency and produces a unified dataset encompassing seven distinct cell types across multiple tissue samples, enhancing data diversity for further model training or fine-tuning. Despite these improvements, cross-relabeling does not entirely resolve issues related to poor labeling quality or the amount of labeled data. Specifically, our results show lower accuracies persist for underrepresented classes, such as macrophages, which may stem from a limited sample availability and intrinsic challenges in distinguishing these cells based solely on H&E staining. Furthermore, while our method enhances label specificity, it still depends on the initial quality of the broad labels, so any inaccuracies in the original annotations can propagate through the relabeling process. A rigorous evaluation of the approach, ideally supported by additional independent cell-level datasets or complementary immunohistochemistry, is needed to quantify any introduced bias and to improve the robustness of subsequently trained models. Although the reported performance metrics are obtained from evaluations on the native test sets of each dataset, it is important to note that the primary application of these classifiers is to perform cross-relabeling, where a model trained on one dataset (e.g., PanNuke) is applied to another (e.g., MoNuSAC) and vice versa. We acknowledge that a more systematic evaluation of cross-dataset generalization is needed and could be performed in future work. Overall, the refined dataset produced by our approach can enhance the supervised training or fine-tuning of cell segmentation and classification models, especially those that utilize pre-trained foundation models to improve feature extraction robustness. In addition, these models can detect nuanced classes that enable researchers to conduct more detailed analyses of biological processes in computational pathology. Accurate cell segmentation and classification in cancer digital pathology are hindered by limited labeled data and the fact that conventional CNNs are unable to capture global contextual information due to their local receptive field constraints [32,33] . Traditional approaches in cell quantification have predominantly relied on CNN encoders, such as ResNet50, given their proven effectiveness in semantic segmentation tasks [8,34–36] . However, approaches that include fine-tuning of pretrained CNNs, data augmentation, and stain normalization to partially increase data variability and address staining differences often fail to achieve the necessary generalization and robustness across diverse tissue types and staining conditions [37–39] . To overcome these challenges, we leverage an encoder–decoder network that uses a foundation model as the encoder and a CNN-based upsampling decoder ( Fig. 5 ) for simultaneous cell segmentation and classification in 2D patches extracted from WSIs. Foundation models with transformer-based architectures are viable alternatives to CNN-based encoders [40,41] . They enable the creation of more advanced architectures that can decode or transform learned features more effectively [42–44] . Recent studies in computational pathology demonstrate that self-supervised foundation encoders trained on large unlabeled H&E datasets can be fine-tuned and used for patch-level image retrieval, region-of-interest detection, WSI-level classification, and instance-level detection and segmentation, often achieving state-of-the-art performance with limited annotations [45–47] . Acknowledging these applications in digital pathology, we adopt a transformer-based foundation encoder within a UNETR-like architecture for simultaneous cell segmentation and classification. By utilizing a transformer-based encoder, we incorporate global contextual information into the feature extraction process, which is a key advantage of such architectures [48] . The self-attention mechanism in transformer encoders models relations among patch tokens across the entire image rather than being restricted to local receptive fields. In the proposed UNETR-like model, skip connections from non-adjacent transformer blocks deliver globally contextualized features to the decoder, which can improve instance separation in crowded regions and support context-aware assignment of cell labels. This encoder integration facilitates accurate pixel-wise segmentation and classification without extensive encoder training, potentially improving generalization across varied cellular structures and tissue types. In our implementation, we employ a modified UNETR [49] architecture that combines a vision transformer (ViT) [50] encoder with a CNN-based decoder. The encoder utilizes the pretrained H-optimus-0 foundation model, which contains approximately 1.1 billion parameters and is trained on more than 500,000 H&E-stained WSIs [12] . We selected H-optimus-0 as the encoder because it is pretrained on a large and diverse set of H&E WSIs, provides wide range of ViT features at multiple encoder depth suitable for patch-level cell instance segmentation, exposes intermediate transformer block activations that can be integrated as residual connections in a UNETR-style decoder, and offers publicly available checkpoints for reproducibility. We extract outputs from four evenly spaced transformer blocks Z i , where i ∈ [ 1 , 14 , 26 , 38 ] , to serve as residual connections for the CNN decoder. This selection was identified through testing of multiple block combinations, where using non-adjacent, evenly spaced blocks yielded the best validation performance. The CNN decoder upsamples the feature representations, acquired from the transformer blocks, to generate an intermediate vector that is handled by two task-specific layers that generate cell segmentation and classification masks. The first task-specific layer is the ‘Cellpose head’, which is used to delineate cell instances. The layer generates horizontal and vertical gradient maps to form vector fields that are refined through gradient tracking in a post-processing step using the Cellpose algorithm [36] , known for its efficacy in cell segmentation tasks and generalizability across multiple domains [51,52] . The second task-specific layer is the “Cell type head”, which assigns labels to individual pixels. In the post-processing step, we determine the output classification label of each segmented cell instance by majority voting over the labeled pixels that comprise the cell in the segmentation map. The overall model design is encoder-agnostic and can be adapted to other transformer-based encoders, which produces feature representation vectors for embedded patches. To evaluate model performance and measure the impact of adding a foundation model as backbone, we compare it to a ResNet50-based model. ResNet50 is a widely used solution for encoders in segmentation architectures in the medical domain [8,34–36] . For the model built on H-optimus-0, we utilize frozen weights for the encoder and only fine-tune the decoder to take advantage of the extensive pre-training of the foundation model. For the ResNet50-based model we start with ImageNet [53] weights and train both encoder and decoder parts. Hyperparameters for the training step are set to be identical, where possible, for comparable evaluation. For this evaluation, we deliberately use the PanNuke dataset to provide a standardized and controlled comparison between the H-optimus-0 and ResNet50-based models (Appendix Figure A2 (3)). Specifically, we use two of the default PanNuke dataset splits (66%) for training and validation, and reserve the third split (33%) for testing. To address the challenge of cell class imbalance in the PanNuke dataset, which is a common characteristic in most cell-level H&E patch datasets, both models’ training processes employ a weighted loss function comprising cross-entropy and focal loss [54] . The focal loss component is adjusted with coefficients derived from each cell class’ instance frequency, emphasizing learning from underrepresented classes and enhancing the model’s sensitivity to rare but significant cellular patterns. The cross-entropy loss is augmented with spectral decoupling regularization [55,56] and spatially varying label smoothing [57] , which potentially stabilizes training and improves generalization in case of complex tissue morphologies. For optimization, we employ the AdamW [30] to counter unbalanced class scenarios, with cosine annealing learning rate scheduler. We utilize the scikit-learn library [58] and HoVer-Net [8] implementations of R 2 (the coefficient of determination) and P Q (panoptic quality) to evaluate our experiments. Complete mathematical formulations and detailed explanations of these metrics are provided in Appendix A5. To compute confidence intervals, we use nonparametric bootstrapping, where after calculating the metric on the full sample, we generated 1000 bootstrap replicates by resampling with replacement and then determined the 95% confidence intervals as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting empirical distribution. The model comparisons are summarized in Table 2 . The model based on H-optimus-0 achieves higher R 2 across all cell classes compared to the ResNet50-based model, which means that its predictions are more closely aligned with the PanNuke cell counts, indicating a stronger correlation with the observed data. Substantial improvements in R 2 for dead, epithelial, and neoplastic cells may indicate that the transformer encoder captures long-range context and enables better differentiation of context-dependent cell types. In terms of segmentation and classification quality combined, measured by the PQ score, the model based on H-optimus-0 demonstrates notable improvements across most cell classes. Overall, the average R 2 improved from 0.575 to 0.871, while the average P Q score improved from 0.450 to 0.492, demonstrating better performance of the model built on H-optimus-0. Our results show that integrating the H-optimus-0 foundation model within the UNETR architecture enhances the model’s ability to segment and classify cells across diverse tissues from PanNuke data. The pretrained transformer encoder provides robust feature representations, resulting in higher average R 2 and P Q scores compared to the CNN-based model. This leads to more reliable cell quantification and more accurate downstream analysis. Additionally, the streamlined fine-tuning process reduces computational overhead and training time, making the model more adaptable for new data. Despite these advancements, the foundation model-based approach does not fully resolve all challenges related to cell segmentation and classification. We observe lower metric scores for underrepresented classes in the training data. Furthermore, foundation models typically encompass billions of parameters, resulting in substantial computational and memory requirements. It therefore poses challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments, limiting their practical applicability in certain clinical and research settings. To address the limitations posed by the extensive size of foundation models, we implement knowledge distillation — a model compression technique that leverages the teacher–student paradigm [59] . By training a smaller, more efficient student model to replicate the output of a larger, pre-trained teacher model, we retain performance while significantly reducing the model’s complexity and resource requirements ( Fig. 6 ). We employ knowledge distillation to compress the teacher model based on H-optimus-0 into a more efficient student model. The teacher model is the modified UNETR architecture with the H-optimus-0 foundation model described in the previous chapter. The student model is based on a U-Net architecture augmented with residual connections and incorporates a smaller ViT encoder with 9 million parameters [60,61] . First, we fine-tune the teacher model using the refined dataset from the cross-relabeling procedure (Section 2 ). Initially we train the decoder of the teacher model while keeping the encoder weights frozen. We split the refined dataset into train (70%), validation (20%) and test (10%) subsets (Appendix Figure A2 (4)). During fine-tuning, we use the train and validation subsets, while leaving the test subset for model evaluation. We set the training procedure and model hyperparameters to be identical to those that were used to demonstrate the utility of foundation models for the simultaneous cell segmentation and classification task. Next, we perform knowledge distillation from teacher to student using the refined dataset used to fine-tune the teacher model. The student model is trained to replicate the teacher model’s outputs. We utilize a specialized loss function that aligns the student’s predicted probability distribution with the teacher’s, incorporating the teacher’s class probability distribution derived from the output. Following the methodology of Hinton et al. [59] , we experiment with various hyperparameter settings for the temperature ( T ) and the balancing coefficients ( α and β ) in the loss function. We vary T from 1 to 20 and adjust α and β to balance the distillation and student losses. Through iterative tuning and evaluation, we identify that setting T = 14 , α = 0 . 3 , and β = 0 . 7 yields a configuration that converges and closely approximates the teacher model’s performance during training. Finally, we assess the performance of both models using the R 2 and P Q (defined in Appendix A5) on the test set of the refined dataset ( Table 3 ). We observe that the 95% confidence intervals overlap for most cell types, so we cannot claim statistically significant performance differences between the teacher and student models. One exception appears in the neoplastic class. The teacher model produces an R 2 of 0.919, while the student model shows an R 2 of 0.852. In addition, the student model achieves higher P Q values for the neoplastic and connective classes, though the confidence intervals show overlap. We further decompose the P Q metric into its S Q and D Q components (Appendix Table A6). Both models produce nearly identical S Q values, which indicates that they predict instance boundaries with similar precision. Although the student model shows some improvement in D Q scores for certain classes, the confidence intervals overlap and do not confirm a statistically significant difference. To assess feasibility for scientific use beyond PanNuke and MoNuSAC datasets and inspect model performance qualitatively, we applied the distilled student model, without additional fine-tuning, to representative H&E-stained regions from a lung cancer WSI and adjacent normal tissue and rendered the outputs, shown on Fig. 7 and Fig. 8 . First shows predominant neoplastic cells labeled within malignant epithelium and epithelial cells in normal epithelium, with stromal nuclei and lymphocytes mapped in surrounding compartments. Second illustrates cell labeling in connective tissue, lymphocyte aggregates, and macrophage-rich areas. Macrophage misclassifications were more frequent than for other classes, consistent with lower quantitative performance for macrophages. We observe that the student and teacher models yield comparable detection performance despite the student model using a much smaller and simpler architecture. A model with fewer parameters reduces the risk of overfitting when training data are scarce relative to the model’s complexity [62] . The knowledge distillation process also encourages the student model to focus on the most generalizable detection features learned from the teacher. These factors enable the student model to achieve similar detection performance across different cell types. Additionally, considering the model sizes reported in Table 4 , the distilled model achieves a significant reduction compared to the teacher model, with a 48-fold decrease in parameter count and a 5.5-fold reduction in on-disk size. In inference mode, the teacher model requires 16 GB of VRAM for a batch size of 32, while the distilled model only needs 3 GB of VRAM for the same batch size. These reductions make the distilled model significantly more practical for fine-tuning and deployment in resource-constrained environments. With recent advancements in complex network architectures and the use of pretrained encoders to achieve state-of-the-art performance [22,63] in cell segmentation and classification tasks, model size, computational complexity, and processing times have increased. This limits the scalability and accessibility of these models. As we demonstrate, this may be mitigated using knowledge distillation. Studies in the field of natural language processing have demonstrated the efficacy of knowledge distillation in retaining the capabilities of the teacher model while achieving significant reductions in size and complexity [64,65] . We demonstrate the feasibility of knowledge distillation in digital pathology, specifically for cell segmentation and classification tasks. Moreover, we achieve this performance while also significantly reducing the parameter count. In addressing the challenge of knowledge transfer, we found that distillation from a transformer-based model to a smaller transformer is more straightforward than attempting to map transformer features to CNN blocks. In our experiments, using a CNN-based network as a student results in worse cell quantification performance due to the structural constraints of CNN feature space dimensions. Although our primary approach relies on a transformer-based student model that performs well, it can be further optimized to incorporate advantages from CNN architectures. For example, employing alternative techniques such as using ViT adapters [42] or 1 × 1 convolutions to adjust feature map sizes may be beneficial for harnessing CNN advantages like enhanced local feature extraction. Moreover, if additional performance improvements are desired, the process can be further enhanced by applying supplementary knowledge distillation techniques, such as self-distillation [66] or online distillation [67] . Beyond cell quantification, the proposed model can support bio-marker prediction and prognostic modeling. Per-class instance maps enable interpretable features such as cell-type densities and ratios, necrosis burden, and spatial statistics including immune cell proximity to tumor and stromal composition, while the lightweight distilled model facilitates large-scale extraction of these features across cohorts. These features can be incorporated as inputs or auxiliary modalities in patient-level survival models that fuse image features and clinical data [68] , or complement WSI-only risk score inference and stratification models pretrained with self-supervised learning [69] . Although the use proposed distilled model is not evaluated for prognostic endpoints, this approach may offer explainable signals that may improve risk stratification and should be validated prospectively across cohorts. Despite these promising results, further validation on independent datasets is necessary to fully understand the model’s limitations. Underrepresented classes may pose challenges when addressing complex cases. Pathologists need to validate these models before adopting them in clinical settings. The distilled models are smaller and more deployable but a technological gap persists since pathologists traditionally rely on established methods for inspecting WSIs and diagnosing diseases. It is essential to address the complexities of deploying models for inference and support pathologists in adopting new tools to integrate these models into clinical workflows. Digital pathology tools with graphical user interfaces are essential for visualizing and analyzing WSIs. To make our student model useful in pathology workflows, it needs to be integrated into a tool that enables inspecting regions, creating annotations, and providing quantitative analyses of biomarkers. Therefore, we integrate the trained student model from the previous chapter into the QuPath open-source platform [26] . QuPath provides the required annotation, visualization, and analysis tools to interpret complex histological data, including workflows for cell segmentation, classification, and quantification ( Fig. 9 ). To identify the regions in a WSI critical for prognosticating tumor development, such as specific tumor areas or border regions without overlapping healthy tissue, the pathologist uses QuPath to outline these regions. Then, the pathologist initiates a cell segmentation and classification script through the QuPath interface for the selected regions. The resulting annotations and quantified cell information are then directly overlaid onto the WSI in the QuPath interface. Additional design and implementation details are in Appendix A7. Two common approaches for integrating deep learning models into QuPath are Java-based native QuPath extensions [21] and the execution of RESTful API requests to a model server coupled with handling the response via an extension, as demonstrated in the application of cell segmentation models applied to immunofluorescence images [70] . While the community is actively working on these integration strategies, there is currently no universal solution that fully addresses all integration and performance requirements. Extensions may offer better integration with QuPath, allowing slightly improved performance and more widespread usage of the built-in QuPath models, but they lack the flexibility to customize models and modify their behavior. For example, the newest version of QuPath includes models such as StarDist [23] and InstanSeg [21] that can perform cell segmentation. Both models pose limitations when applied to simultaneous cell segmentation and classification. StarDist performs well only on convex, round shapes by design, whereas some neoplastic, inflammatory, and connective cells exhibit complex and non-convex shapes. InstanSeg provides only semantic segmentation without assigning classes to the segmented cells. In contrast, our approach offers an alternative integration strategy. It utilizes the paquo library to directly interact with QuPath’s internal application programming interface from within Python. This enables data exchange and processing without the need for intermediate conversion steps and provides greater control over model customization, retraining, and the incorporation of custom processing steps. The integration of our custom model with QuPath underscores its potential to significantly enhance the diagnostic process by reducing the time burden on pathologists and enabling them to focus on more complex interpretative tasks using familiar software. Leveraging a tool that is already well-established among pathologists increases the likelihood of its adoption into daily clinical workflows. The quantitative data generated through the automated workflow is critical for both clinical decision-making and research, facilitating more accurate biomarker analysis, enabling robust statistical evaluations, and supporting hypothesis generation and testing. Additionally, by streamlining cell segmentation and classification, the tool enhances the scalability and reproducibility of pathological assessments, ultimately contributing to improved diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes. In this study, we address critical challenges in cancer digital pathology and tackle the usability and deployment issues of the developed models in standard computing environments without the need for high-performance computing systems. Our multi-faceted approach encompasses data refinement through cross-relabeling, leveraging foundation models for robust cell segmentation and classification, optimizing model performance via knowledge distillation, and integrating the optimized model into the QuPath software for practical applications. This approach is used to construct a capable, versatile, and adjustable model for cell segmentation and classification, with enhanced performance and usability. While our approach shows potential in the field of computational pathology, certain limitations persist. The PanNuke and MoNuSAC annotations used for models training are obtained from H&E images without using immunohistochemical markers. Thus, they represent a pragmatic ground truth rather than a definitive biological ground truth, and some label ambiguity and noise may persist. Also, our model currently exhibits lower performance in detecting macrophages. This serves as an instance of the broader challenge of accurately identifying complex cell types. Given the marked morphological variability of macrophages in H&E [71] , their annotations and statistical performance estimates should be interpreted with particular caution compared to cell populations with less variability. Potential strategies to mitigate this limitation include incorporating additional independent datasets to better capture macrophage heterogeneity, evaluating alternative modeling approaches, and integrating complementary modalities such as immunohistochemical staining, which may improve detection and classification accuracy. Moreover, although the distilled model reduces computational demands, integrating advanced deep learning models into clinical practice requires addressing technological gaps and potential resistance to adopting new tools within established diagnostic processes. Overall, in its current form, the approach serves primarily as a proof-of-concept for scientific use that lays the groundwork for future advancements and validation rather than as a complete solution ready for clinical deployment. Future work could focus on several key areas to refine the proposed approach, strengthen validation in research settings, and facilitate adoption in clinical environments. Enhancing the cell-relabeling process with additional datasets [72] could improve the representation of underrepresented cell types and enhance overall model performance. Future studies should also validate the accuracy of the relabeled subclasses and trained models on independent whole-slide cohorts, incorporating pathologist review and WSI-level performance metrics to establish reliability. Additionally, incorporating additional data sources, such as multi-modal imaging or complementary staining methods, may address limitations related to cell type differentiation and class imbalance. Exploring other foundation models [13,73] for feature representation or introducing additional modalities [74,75] may provide alternative architecture configurations better suited to specific tasks or offer improved efficiency. Implementing more complex knowledge distillation techniques [66,67] could further optimize the model’s performance and adaptability. Additionally, deeper integration with QuPath or other digital pathology software could provide pathologists more control over cell quantification analysis directly within the QuPath interface, thereby increasing accessibility and usability. Such enhancements would not only refine model performance but also ensure greater adaptability and scalability within various clinical environments. Finally, extensive validation of the model by pathologists and benchmarking on independent datasets are essential to establish reliability for scientific use and to inform potential clinical utility. data.text: A novel explainable AI framework for medical image classification integrating statistical, visual, and rule-based methods Artificial intelligence and deep learning are powerful tools for extracting knowledge from large datasets, particularly in healthcare. However, their black-box nature raises interpretability concerns, especially in high-stakes applications. Existing eXplainable Artificial Intelligence methods often focus solely on visualization or rule-based explanations, limiting interpretability’s depth and clarity. This work proposes a novel explainable AI method specifically designed for medical image analysis, integrating statistical, visual, and rule-based explanations to improve transparency in deep learning models. Statistical features are derived from deep features extracted using a custom Mobilenetv2 model. A two-step feature selection method – zero-based filtering with mutual importance selection – ranks and refines these features. Decision tree and RuleFit models are employed to classify data and extract human-readable rules. Additionally, a novel statistical feature map overlay visualization generates heatmap-like representations of three key statistical measures (mean, skewness, and entropy), providing both localized and quantifiable visual explanations of model decisions. The proposed method has been validated on five medical imaging datasets – COVID-19 radiography, ultrasound breast cancer, brain tumor magnetic resonance imaging, lung and colon cancer histopathological, and glaucoma images – with results confirmed by medical experts, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing interpretability for medical image classification tasks. Existing eXplainable Artificial Intelligence methods often focus solely on visualization or rule-based explanations, limiting interpretability’s depth and clarity. This work proposes a novel explainable AI method specifically designed for medical image analysis, integrating statistical, visual, and rule-based explanations to improve transparency in deep learning models. Statistical features are derived from deep features extracted using a custom Mobilenetv2 model. A two-step feature selection method – zero-based filtering with mutual importance selection – ranks and refines these features. Decision tree and RuleFit models are employed to classify data and extract human-readable rules. Additionally, a novel statistical feature map overlay visualization generates heatmap-like representations of three key statistical measures (mean, skewness, and entropy), providing both localized and quantifiable visual explanations of model decisions. All data used in the experiments are freely available. In the paper, all databases have been referenced. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) have revolutionized domains requiring high predictive accuracy, particularly in high-stakes applications like healthcare, criminal justice, and beyond ( Aamir et al., 2021 ) in recent years. In healthcare, DL models have significantly improved diagnostic accuracy across various imaging modalities, including Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), chest radiographs, histopathology, and ultrasounds ( Qayyum et al., 2024; Ullah et al., 2023 ). Despite their success, these models face criticism for their lack of transparency and interpretability, raising trust and ethical concerns, especially in critical fields like healthcare ( Rudin, 2019; Poon and Sung, 2021 ). To address these challenges, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Interpretable Artificial Intelligence (IAI) have emerged as solutions ( Ullah et al., 2024a ). XAI techniques explain the decision-making logic of DL models, enhancing transparency and trust without sacrificing accuracy. Post hoc XAI methods, such as feature importance rankings ( Wojtas and Chen, 2020 ), saliency maps ( Gomez et al., 2022 ), and gradient-based visualizations ( Selvaraju et al., 2017 ), aim to provide insights into black-box models. In contrast, IAI develops inherently transparent models, such as decision trees or rule-based systems, to present decision-making processes in a human-readable format ( Reyes et al., 2020; De Falco et al., 2023 ). However, some key limitations persist. While effective for classification, deep features extracted from convolutional layers are abstract and lack semantic interoperability for experts, making it difficult to understand how specific features influence decisions. Additionally, most visualization methods, like saliency maps, only highlight general input regions relevant to predictions but fail to provide detailed feature-level explanations. Rule-based approaches often lack integration with visual interpretations, leading to fragmented insights. This disjointedness is particularly problematic in healthcare, where transparent and precise explanations are crucial for trust and decision-making. To address these issues, this work proposes statistical, visual, and rule-based explainable (SVIS-RULEX). This new framework integrates statistical, visual, and rule-based explanations to explain how DL-based models make decisions when applied to medical images. Unlike traditional methods, this framework transforms deep features into interpretable statistical attributes, enabling traceable and quantifiable predictions. Moreover, a novel method called Statistical Feature Map Overlay Visualization (SFMOV) is introduced. SFMOV enhances visualization by overlaying statistical measures (e.g., mean, skewness, entropy) onto feature maps, providing localized and feature-specific insights. By merging statistical, visual, and rule-based explanations, this approach ensures greater transparency and interpretability, which is crucial for healthcare applications. To validate its robustness and generalizability, the SVIS-RULEX framework is evaluated on five diverse medical imaging datasets from Kaggle, covering chest radiographs, breast ultrasounds, brain MRI, histopathological and retinal fundus images. This broad evaluation demonstrates the framework’s adaptability and effectiveness across various imaging modalities and medical conditions. The major contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. A dual-path approach integrating visual and rule-based explanations for enhanced interpretability while maintaining classification performance. 2. Deep feature extraction using a custom MobileNetv2 model, capturing high-dimensional representations from diverse medical imaging modalities. 3. Introduction of a novel statistical feature engineering approach, generating 26 human-readable attributes (e.g., mean, variance, skewness, entropy) from deep features for improved interpretability. 4. Development of the novel Zero-based Filtering with Mutual Importance Selection (ZFMIS) strategy for feature ranking and selection, ensuring compact and informative feature sets. 5. Rule-based interpretation using Decision Tree (DT) and RuleFit, providing human-understandable insights into the model’s decision-making process. 6. Proposal of the novel SFMOV technique to visualize statistical overlays (mean, skewness, entropy) of convolutional features, weighted by dense-layer properties, for deeper interpretability. 7. Clinical validation of the SFMOV visualizations with radiologists, confirming their diagnostic relevance and practical significance. A dual-path approach integrating visual and rule-based explanations for enhanced interpretability while maintaining classification performance. Deep feature extraction using a custom MobileNetv2 model, capturing high-dimensional representations from diverse medical imaging modalities. Introduction of a novel statistical feature engineering approach, generating 26 human-readable attributes (e.g., mean, variance, skewness, entropy) from deep features for improved interpretability. Development of the novel Zero-based Filtering with Mutual Importance Selection (ZFMIS) strategy for feature ranking and selection, ensuring compact and informative feature sets. Rule-based interpretation using Decision Tree (DT) and RuleFit, providing human-understandable insights into the model’s decision-making process. Proposal of the novel SFMOV technique to visualize statistical overlays (mean, skewness, entropy) of convolutional features, weighted by dense-layer properties, for deeper interpretability. Clinical validation of the SFMOV visualizations with radiologists, confirming their diagnostic relevance and practical significance. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details the proposed methodology. Section 4 presents and discusses the results, while Section 5 concludes the paper. Recently, AI has proved extremely useful in the healthcare domain, specifically in medical image analysis ( Van der Velden et al., 2022; Bevilacqua et al., 2024 ). In literature, DL models are largely used for image classification tasks in the healthcare domain because of their high classification performance. This high classification performance has often been achieved through increased model complexity. These complex models are usually called back box systems because their decisions are hard to understand and interpret. Hence, these models are difficult to be trusted, which restricts the use of these models in critical sectors, such as healthcare. However, XAI has emerged to address the need for transparency in complex black box classification models. In the literature, the two main methods for achieving explainability in Machine Learning (ML) are post-hoc explainability and ante-hoc explainability. The kind of insights that these approaches may provide, as well as how and when interpretability is provided, vary widely. Post-hoc XAI techniques are applied to analyze the model after training the model whereas in the case of ante-hoc the models are intrinsically explainable ( Retzlaff et al., 2024 ). Traditional ML models, such as DT, linear or logistic regression ( Tripepi et al., 2008 ), Bayesian models ( Wang et al., 2017 ), rule-based ( Nauck, 2003 ), and k-nearest neighbor models ( Papernot and McDaniel, 2018 ) are inherently interpretable (glass-box models) whereas DL models are not. These models are more transparent and explainable from the start and incorporate interpretability directly into the model ( Sarkar et al., 2022 ). Linear interpretable models offer direct insight into feature importance through their coefficients, allowing users to understand feature influence and interaction in a straightforward, step-by-step manner. DTs are also the most prominent interpretable ML models. DTs split the data multiple times to produce separate subsets of the dataset or features based on certain threshold values in the features, with each instance belonging to one subset ( Safavian and Landgrebe, 1991 ). The tree structure of these models starting from the root node to the successive nodes and edges until you arrive at the output (leaf node) makes these models interpretable. Each path from the root node to the leaf can be represented as a hierarchical structure of if-then-else-rules that are straightforward for humans to grasp and comprehend ( Christoph, 2020 ). Although in-model XAI methods promote transparency, it often comes at the expense of model performance and complexity. This is because interpretable models such as DTs or linear models struggle to capture complex patterns in high-dimensional data. Whereas DL models capture more complex patterns, but they are black boxes and lack interpretability. To address this, DT have been widely employed as surrogate models in a post hoc manner, providing an interpretable approximation of the decision boundaries of black boxes. In Confalonieri et al. (2021) , Trepan Reloaded was developed based Trepan algorithm that extracts surrogate decision trees from black-box models, incorporating ontologies to improve the comprehensibility of the explanations. In this paper, the focus is on adding explainability post hoc to existing DL models. Post-hoc XAI techniques interpret, analyze, and increase the interpretability of trained black box models providing insights into how the model makes specific predictions. The advantages of the post hoc XAI approaches include providing explanations without modifying the architecture and applicability to various black box models. In the medical image analysis domain, post hoc explainability methods are most widely used nowadays. In post-hoc explainability, a white box surrogate model is constructed for the trained black box model ( Adadi and Berrada, 2018 ). Post-hoc techniques transfer the learned knowledge from a complex black-box model into a simple white-box or surrogate model ( Confalonieri et al., 2021 ). These are independent of models and are applied once the trained model has made the prediction. These techniques provide an approximate explanation of what the black-box model is doing, but not exactly how or why it arrived at a prediction. This approximate explanation provides a close and useful understanding of the black-box model’s internal logic and does not negatively impact the underlying model’s predictive accuracy ( Burkart and Huber, 2021 ). Post-hoc explainability techniques traditionally generate two types of interpretability i.e., global and local interpretability ( Stiglic et al., 2020 ). Global interpretability explains the overall logic and behavior behind all possible outcomes of a black box model ( Nian et al., 2024 ). This helps to identify the most important rules and patterns learned during model training and display them through the model’s structure and parameters. The coefficients of a linear regression model and the rules formed along the paths from root nodes to leaf nodes of a decision tree are examples of global interpretability ( Stiglic et al., 2020 ). On the other hand, local interpretability explains a single prediction and the impact of each feature on a specific outcome. This granular approach is often more accurate than global interpretability because instead of explaining the entire model and its overall logic, it examines every aspect of the model’s decision-making process. The two most widely used techniques for local interpretability in ML are SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) ( Lundberg, 2017 ) and Locally Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) ( Ribeiro et al., 2016a ). SHAP is based on cooperative game theory, specifically Shapley values, which assign an importance value to each feature in a prediction. This method provides a correct and detailed explanation of the influence of each feature on the model’s output in a given instance. In contrast, LIME generates a simple surrogate model, such as linear regression, to replicate the behavior of the difficult model in the local neighborhood of the instance under examination. Both LIME and SHAP focus on explaining individual predictions rather than overall model behavior, making them suited for applications requiring instance-level insights. Post-hoc explainability can be applied in two ways i.e., model-specific and model-agnostic interpretability. The model-specific interpretability techniques provide explanations about the internal representation or learning process of a particular model. Therefore, these techniques are inherently tailored for every model and cannot be used to explain any other model. Whereas model-agnostic explanations approximate the underlying behavior of models and generate end-user explanations independent of the internal logic of models ( Ribeiro et al., 2016b ). Model-agnostic methods have the potential to be applied to any black box model because they do not consider the internal components of a model, such as weights or structural information, and are not model-specific explainers. Therefore, they have wide-scale applications. Post-hoc model-agnostic explanations fall into the broader category of explaining by removing ( Covert et al., 2021 ). To identify feature importance these methods remove input features and examine their impact on the prediction. Features are considered important only if their removal significant impact on prediction ( Troncoso-García et al., 2023a ). Kim et al. (2018) proposed Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV), a post-hoc explainability method that interprets model predictions in terms of human-interpretable concepts rather than low-level features. Unlike saliency maps that report feature importance at the pixel or input level, TCAV estimates a model’s dependency on high-level, user-specified concepts by computing directional derivatives along concept vectors in neural network activations. This technique provides an overall numerical measure of a concept’s salience to the decision of a model and is, therefore, particularly useful in situations where model thinking is critical, such as healthcare. The avoidance of the requirement for retraining the model provided by TCAV renders it an excellent tool to use in understanding biases and dependencies on features for deep learning models. Given our research focus on integrating statistical, rule-based, and visual explanations, TCAV can be regarded as a complementary perspective that emphasizes concept-level interpretability. Furthermore, post-hoc methods can be categorized into several key types based on the way they convey interpretability to the user, such as rule-based interpretability, visualization-based techniques, feature importance analysis, and example-based methods. These approaches aim to shed light on complex, “black-box” models while preserving their predictive accuracy. Rule-based methods provide human-readable explanations by extracting logical statements or interpretable rules. These approaches are mainly used for structured problems with tabular data. DTs and rule extraction algorithms such as TREPAN ( Confalonieri et al., 2021 ) are examples of rule-based interpretability ( Troncoso-García et al., 2023b ). These methods explain the behavior of complex models using a simpler surrogate model, such as a DT, that represents decision boundaries in terms of “if-then-else” rules. The explanations in the form of rules help non-technical stakeholders to understand the reasoning behind predictions. Visualization techniques are the most commonly used post-hoc explainability methods. These methods use visual explanations to highlight the contribution of input features to a model’s predictions. Recently, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) ( Selvaraju et al., 2017 ) is most commonly used in image-based tasks to identify the most important regions of an image that influence a particular prediction. This method overlays the heatmaps generated using gradient information from the trained model on the input image to highlight significant areas. In the case of textual data, attention maps or saliency visualizations help users understand which words contributed to a decision. Visualization methods are particularly effective in domains like medical imaging and computer vision, where they enable domain experts to validate model decisions intuitively. Feature importance approaches are model-agnostic techniques that measure the contribution of each input feature to a model’s prediction. Methods like SHAP and LIME explain individual predictions by perturbing the input features and assessing the changes in model output. These approaches produce global feature rankings or local explanations, allowing users to determine the most relevant aspects for a single prediction or overall model behavior. Example-based interpretability is founded on case-based reasoning, in which explanations are offered by referring to specific examples from the training dataset ( Poché et al., 2023 ). This is consistent with the psychological mechanics of human thinking, making example-based explanations natural and easy for consumers to grasp. Indeed, people learn and reason by creating mental models of concepts based on instances. This category includes techniques, such as counterfactual explanations ( Verma et al., 2020 ), that reveal the minimal adjustments to the input features required to modify the prediction outcome, providing consumers with actionable insights. Another example is prototype-based ( Casalino et al., 2024 ) approaches that choose representative instances from the training data that are comparable to the input instance, allowing users to better understand model behavior through analogous scenarios. Evaluating explainability approaches is a subjective and challenging task since interpretability often depends on the specific application domain and the target audience’s degree of knowledge. While ante-hoc techniques include interpretability directly into the model’s structure, post-hoc approaches rely on additional tools to extract insights from complex models. The effectiveness of these tactics depends on end users’ capacity to comprehend the reasoning behind predictions and confidently act upon them. Initiatives like user-centered validation and standardized evaluation frameworks are essential for assessing the suitability of XAI approaches across a range of domains as research advances. The effectiveness of an explainable model ultimately depends on its ability to bridge the gap between the complex technicalities of black box models and the real-world needs of its users, encouraging trust and informed decision-making. Existing explainability methods for black-box models face several limitations. Post-hoc explainability approaches in the literature focus solely on one aspect, visualization, rule-based explanation, or statistical analysis, without integrating them to provide a holistic understanding of model behavior. DTs are used for rule-based interpretability but are not integrated with other explainability techniques (e.g., statistical and visual methods). Additionally, post-hoc methods, mostly rely on gradient-based attributions or raw feature importance and often overlook the potential of statistical transformations derived from deep features, which can offer richer insights into data patterns. Techniques such as TCAV provide concept-based explanations but require predefined human-interpretable concepts, limiting their applicability in scenarios where defining such concepts is challenging. Furthermore, visual explanation techniques, neglect the visualization of statistical features critical for classification and focus only on activation or feature attribution maps. Given the existing gaps in the literature, such as the lack of integrated statistical, visual, and rule-based approaches for explainability, and the limitations of conventional visualization methods like generic saliency maps, this work proposes the SVIS-RULEX approach. This novel method addresses these issues by combining statistical, visual, and rule-based explainability techniques for a more comprehensive post hoc interpretation of deep learning models. Moreover, the proposed SFMOV goes beyond traditional heatmaps by providing localized and quantifiable insights into model decisions, using key statistical measures (mean, skewness, and entropy) to enhance transparency and interpretability. This work integrates rule-based modeling and visualizations with statistical feature engineering and DL-based feature extraction to produce human-understandable explanations. This method bridges the gap between interpretable techniques’ transparency and black-box DL models’ predictive power. Fig. 1 shows an overview of the proposed method. First, some existing techniques are used in preprocessing, like data augmentations, image resizing, and region of interest cropping. The resultant dataset is then fed into the custom MobileNetv2 DL model for feature extraction to capture complex visual patterns and get more discriminative and informative deep features, which are crucial for accurate classification. These extracted features are then used for statistical transformation to compute interpretable, summary-level insights. Next, a novel ZFMIS technique ranks and filters features based on their interpretive value. The filtered and selected features are then used to train the decision tree and RuleFit interpretable rule-based models. Finally, Grad-CAM-inspired heatmaps (SFMOV) are generated to visualize the most important statistical features and highlight spatial regions of the images that contribute significantly to the model’s decision-making process. Visual overlays enhance statistical interpretation by illustrating how specific patterns affect categorization judgments, providing stakeholders with an intuitive understanding of the prediction model’s behavior, a model-agnostic visual explanation technique. DL models, including custom and pre-trained architectures, have been extensively used for feature extraction, enabling hierarchical pattern recognition in applications like COVID-19 detection, skin cancer classification, and brain tumor diagnosis ( Ullah and Javed, 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024; Raza et al., 2024; Verde et al., 2023; Ullah et al., 2024b; Verde et al., 2021 ). Since this work proposes a general methodology, any DL model can be used for deep feature extraction. However, MobileNetV2 is used for its lightweight architecture, memory efficiency, and suitability for mobile and resource-constrained environments. MobileNetV2 employs depth-wise separable convolutions, inverted residuals, and linear bottleneck structures to reduce computational complexity while maintaining high representational power. Furthermore, the selection of MobileNetV2 is based on its superior classification performance compared to other DL models including DenseNet201 ( Huang et al., 2017 ) and ResNet18 ( He et al., 2016 ) on the studied dataset. This flexibility allows the proposed methodology to be adapted to other datasets and DL models, ensuring broad applicability across diverse domains such as chest radiographs, CT scans, MRI images, etc. To adapt the MobileNetV2 model to this specific medical imaging task in this study, the original classification head is removed and replaced by a custom classification head. Before classification, the high-dimensional feature maps of the convolutional layers must be converted to a compact fixed-size feature vector. For this purpose, Global Average Pooling (GAP) is employed. GAP reduces each feature map’s spatial dimensions by averaging all of its spatial values, essentially condensing each map into one representative value. This technique not only reduces the number of parameters and minimizes the risk of overfitting but also retains the most valuable global information from each feature map. The resulting fixed-size feature vector holds the pertinent features of the input image and is fed into both the deep statistical feature extraction and the custom classification head. To enhance model adaption, a fine-tuning strategy is utilized: all layers in MobileNetV2 are frozen except the last 50, which are modified during training to learn target dataset-specific patterns while maintaining general knowledge from the pre-trained model. Furthermore, a custom classification head with three dense (with ReLU activation functions), two batch normalization, and two dropout layers is used to classify the new data. The ReLU activation function is used to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem, batch normalization is applied to stabilize the learning process, and dropout layers are used to reduce overfitting. Finally, the softmax activation function is used to produce class probabilities. The features are extracted from the fourth-last layer (second dense layer) of the custom MobileNetv2 model. The dense layer is chosen because it contains a high-dimensional feature map and retains both spatial information and an abstract representation of the images. Before feature extraction, the input images are processed and organized into training, validation, and test datasets. The data generator is used to supply a batch of input images to the model and extract a single feature vector with a corresponding label for each image ( F e a t u r e s = M o b i l e N e t V 2 ( I m a g e ) ). The extracted features are saved in a format (pickle file) so that they can be retrieved and used in the future for classification and rule extraction. Statistical features are considered as a consistent pattern of information or structure in raw data. In literature, various methods are used to extract statistical features including transform-based, statistical, and structural approaches. In Latif et al. (2018) , statistical-based feature extraction methods were employed to extract first-order statistical features (entropy, kurtosis, variance, mean, skewness, and energy) and second-order statistical features (maximum probability, absolute value, angular second-moment energy, inertia, correlation, inverse difference, entropy) from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images. Such statistical features have proven valuable for enhancing medical image classification tasks, where ensemble approaches that combine deep spatial features with handmade statistical features have been widely used ( Iqbal et al., 2024; Lai and Deng, 2018 ). Building on this idea, statistical feature engineering complements DL by transforming the abstract, highdimensional representations extracted from DL models – such as MobileNetV2 – into interpretable statistical measures. Although deep features capture complex patterns and abstract representations, they often lack the semantic interpretability required for practical applications. However, statistical features, on the other hand, may not be inherently interpretable in isolation; they serve as structured and quantifiable descriptors of activation patterns, allowing for a structured understanding of feature distributions and help to bridge the gap between raw deep features and human-interpretable insights. Such statistical summaries provide a more tangible interpretation of how the network processes input data, making them useful for analyzing and explaining model decisions. To address the limitation of deep features (lack of the interpretability required for practical applications), a comprehensive set of 26 statistical metrics is employed to provide a deeper analysis of the feature space. These metrics, including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape, provide a systematic way to highlight feature distributions within activation maps, thereby enhancing transparency in model decision-making. Additionally, statistical feature extraction allows for dimensionality reduction while preserving key characteristics, facilitating the training of interpretable models such as decision trees and RuleFit, which provide human-readable rules. Feature selection plays a crucial role in identifying the most relevant features while reducing noise, overfitting, and training times ( Hira and Gillies, 2015 ). Recently, hybrid multi-stage selection strategies have also been explored, as demonstrated in Uysal (2018) for text classification. In this study, the ZFMIS a two-stage feature selection approach is developed to remove less important or irrelevant statistical features and select only informative ones. The first stage of the ZFMIS feature selection approach is zero-based filtering, which eliminates features with a high proportion of zero values (sparse data) which can introduce noise into the learning process. This key step refines the statistical features by removing features with limited relevance or minimal variability. Discarding uninformative and sparse features reduces the dimensionality of the dataset while enhancing the computational efficiency. This study applies two rule-based models, i.e., Decision Trees ( Vasilev et al., 2020 ) and RuleFit ( Friedman and Popescu, 2008 ) for the classification of final statistical features. These models generate human-understandable rules to enhance interpretability and show how features contribute to predictions. The rules are explicit “if-then” conditions that capture the relationship between features and the target classes. A DT is a model that recursively splits data (statistical features) into subsets based on its values in a hierarchical manner, resulting in a tree-like structure. The nodes represent the conditions used for feature classification, whereas branches represent the outcomes of those conditions. The final nodes, also called leaf nodes, represent the predicted classes. By default, DT uses the Gini impurity measure ( Tangirala, 2020 ) for feature splitting at the nodes. DTs directly map the decision path from the root node to the leaf nodes (specific prediction), forming interpretable rules. RuleFit is a rule-based ensemble model that combines the strengths of rule-based learning and linear modeling, capturing both linear and complex interactions within data. It uses DTs and linear regression to identify non-linearities and linear links. The DTs generate decision rules, and the regression model optimizes performance and prevents overfitting. RuleFit balances expressive power and interpretability, making it ideal for applications requiring clear model insights. The model generates a set of rules from the dataset’s features, evaluates each rule’s performance, selects the most relevant rules, and then applies the most appropriate rules to predict or classify new samples based on their features. RuleFit generates rules with the default gradient boosted trees ensemble model. The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) linear regressor is used to identify the most important rules for predictions by assigning weights to the extracted rules. This study uses the Grid Search technique for hyperparameter optimization to evaluate various combinations of hyperparameters systematically. The Grid search selects optimal hyperparameter values based on the highest validation accuracy achieved during model training, enhancing the performance of the custom MobilNetV2 model, DT, and RuleFit models. This study uses a novel Grad-CAM-inspired statistical feature map overlay visualization (SFMOV) technique to generate heat maps and enhance transparency. The SFMOV pseudocode is presented in Algorithm 3. SFMOV does not use activations like traditional approaches, including Grad-CAM, but uses statistical measures, i.e., mean, skewness, entropy, and a combination of these measures to visualize the most important regions for classification within medical images. The statistical feature maps are computed per pixel x , y for each color channel. Specifically, the mean map M c x , y represents the mean pixel intensity at location x , y across all channels (c), providing a brightness-based interpretation of the image. The skewness map S c x , y captures asymmetry in pixel distributions, while the entropy map E c x , y emphasizes texture complexity. To provide a more comprehensive visualization, a combined heatmap H ( x , y ) is constructed as: (8) H ( x , y ) = w 1 M c ( x , y ) + w 2 S c ( x , y ) + w 3 E c ( x , y ) where w 1 , w 2 , and w 3 are the dense values corresponding to mean, skewness, and entropy, respectively. This integrated heatmap leverages multiple statistical indicators to highlight diagnostically relevant regions more effectively than any individual map alone. While the mean heatmap primarily reflects overall intensity, the combined heatmap incorporates asymmetry and texture complexity, ensuring that subtle but clinically significant structural variations are captured. Eq. (8) provides a structured integration of multiple statistical measures, allowing for a more robust and informative visualization. The selection of mean, skewness, and entropy as the key statistical features in the proposed SFMOV method is because they have the ability to represent the inherent characteristics of medical image regions in a comprehensible and effective manner. Specifically, the mean characterizes the overall brightness or intensity distribution and indicates the overall tissue density; skewness is a quantitative measure of asymmetry in pixel intensity distributions and can be employed to reveal abnormal or aberrant structures; and entropy defines texture complexity and indicates regions with heterogeneous patterns typically associated with pathological alteration. This combination provides a complementary and integral knowledge of global and local image characteristics, allowing for finer visualization of diagnostically relevant regions. By integrating these three descriptors, the method enhances interpretability, allowing clear differentiation between critical regions without relying on complex statistical metrics. On the other hand, other measures such as harmonic mean or autocorrelation, as logically valid as they are, often fail to allow intuitive visual interpretation, thus becoming less accessible to clinicians or researchers to directly correlate with anatomical or pathological significance. Therefore, focusing on mean, skewness, and entropy ensures that the resulting visual explanations are not only meaningful but also accessible and practically useful for understanding model decisions. This approach has two stages as shown in Fig. 2 . In the first stage, it calculates the statistical properties (mean, skewness, and entropy) from each channel in the convolutional layer of the custom MobileNetV2 model. In the second stage, the dense layer statistical properties (mean, skewness, and entropy) are used as weights for the convolutional maps. Finally, this method overlays these statistical measures onto the original image using a jet color scheme, where red represents the most critical and highly activated regions, and blue signifies less significant or inactive areas. The jet color scheme effectively highlights the crucial regions for enhanced interpretability. This study uses five publicly available Kaggle datasets with various medical imaging modalities to assess the proposed approach’s generalizability and robustness across distinct medical conditions. The five datasets are well-known datasets, and each covers diverse diseases, imaging techniques, and anatomical regions. The summary of the datasets is given in Table 3 whereas the representative samples from these datasets are given in Fig. 3 . The first dataset used in this study is the “COVID-19 Radiography Database” ( Rahman et al., 2022 ), a multiclass dataset consisting of 21,165 chest radiograph images. The dataset is created by a team of researchers from different countries including Pakistan, Qatar, Bangladesh, and Malaysia. The dataset contains images of four classes with their corresponding masks. The recent version of the dataset consists of 10,192 normal, 3616 COVID-19, 1345 viral pneumonia, and 6012 lung opacity chest radiograph images. The second dataset used in this study is “Ultrasound Breast Images for Breast Cancer” ( Sairam, 2024 ). This dataset used rotation and sharpening augmentation techniques and contains 9016 ultrasound images after augmentations with 4574 benign and 4442 malignant breast cancer images.
