This study further explored rule extraction using DT and RuleFit after achieving satisfactory classification results on a diverse medical image dataset using these models to enhance interpretability and transparency. This transparency is necessary, especially for medical imaging data to ensure that the decisions made by these classifiers are understandable and can be validated by users or domain experts. Rule extraction in this study aims to extract simple, human-understandable, and interpretable conditions that explain the relationship between specific feature values and classification outcomes. In this study, a comprehensive set of 26 statistical features is used for all datasets, so using and evaluating them all at once in rules might result in complicated rules that could be harder to comprehend. On the other hand, using only the top three selected features after the hierarchical feature selection approach provides more understandable rules while yet maintaining satisfactory classification performance. Therefore, to balance classification performance and interpretability, this work focuses on rule extraction utilizing three statistical features. Furthermore, the rules generated from the DT and RuleFit models are simplified to reduce redundancy and improve interpretability. The strictest bounds are retained for each feature, ensuring minimal overlap between conditions. For example, if a feature has conditions like “ G M > 2 ” and “ G M > 3 ”, the less restrictive condition is discarded, and only “ G M > 3 ” is retained. This approach eliminates logical redundancies and maintains only the most restrictive thresholds for each feature. The rules, presented in a simplified “If-Then” format and prioritized by significance scores, make it easier to identify the model’s most important decision-making processes. The simplification process is widely recognized in the field of rule-based machine learning and follows standard practices for enhancing rule interpretability. In this study, to enhance simplicity and clarity, rules for two representative datasets on which more than 90% classification accuracy is achieved are presented instead of all five datasets. The selected datasets (Brain MRI Images for Brain Tumor Detection and Lung and Colon Cancer Histopathological Images) are representative of the model’s ability to generalize across diverse medical imaging data while maintaining high classification accuracy. Furthermore, thousands of potential rules are produced by both the DT and RuleFit models after the execution of our approach on each medical imaging dataset. Therefore, to ensure relevance and clarity in the results, careful consideration is applied to select the most interpretable and impactful rules for presentation. Therefore, rules from both DT and RuleFit are selected based on their importance scores, which quantify the contribution of each rule to the model’s predictions. Rules with greater importance scores demonstrate stronger and more persistent connections between features and the target class, making them valuable for understanding model behavior and identifying decision-making patterns. The importance score is calculated as the product of the absolute value of the rule’s coefficient and support values. The importance of each rule r is calculated as: (9) importance r = | coef r | × support r where coef r is the absolute value of the rule’s coefficient, indicating its predictive power, and support r is the fraction of samples where the rule holds true, reflecting its relevance. Higher importance scores indicate rules with greater predictive strength and applicability in the dataset. To provide a balanced representation, the rules for each class are selected based on their importance scores. The two most significant rules are chosen for each class. This method provides interpretable information on the key feature patterns affecting every class’s predictions. Furthermore, it is important to note that the obtained rules are based on statistical measures such as corr, CV, and SNR. These features capture patterns in image texture and intensity that could be related to tumor characteristics. However, these features are not directly interpretable from a clinical perspective, they provide quantitative measures that may help distinguish between tumor types. As an example, SNR is a common measure of image quality, with higher values representing potentially higher quality images with lower noise, which could be used to discriminate between tumor features and background noise. Correlation as a texture feature detects patterns in the relationship between pixel intensity and can be reflective of tissue homogeneity. Variations in correlation could be a reflection of differences in tissue structure that may distinguish benign from malignant tumors, but such correlations must be confirmed by clinical experience. The entropy, skewness, and mean enhance the ability to highlight important areas and have distinct visual effects on image regions. Entropy distinctly brings out complex textures, skewness shows asymmetric structures, and mean illustrates the general brightness or density in an area. Using a combination of these three features provides a comprehensive and more differentiated visualization. Furthermore, more complex features such as harmonic mean or autocorrelation, are harder to interpret visually, as their impact on an image may not clearly distinguish crucial areas. Hence, visualizing the most impactful features will highlight the key regions truly influential for the model. Decision trees produce hierarchical, straightforward, and interpretable rules based on split data using feature thresholds. The initial rules obtained from DT are complex and less readable, containing redundant conditions, and the same features are repeated multiple times with slightly varying thresholds. Therefore, the raw rules extracted from the trained DT model are simplified to enhance the interpretability of DT rules and reduce the complexity of rules without compromising the model’s predictive accuracy. Table 12 represents the top two rules based on importance extracted using DT for each class for the two top datasets based on the classification performance. RuleFit generates rules using a mixture of linear regression and tree-based methods. It selects the most important rules from a large number of candidate rules produced using DTs based on regularization. These rules are more compact and effective and incorporate linear terms for improved performance. These rules add depth by incorporating combinations of features, capturing more detailed relationships that may not be explicitly represented in DT splits alone. Similar to DT, the rules from the RuleFit are also simplified to generate more concise and interpretable rules. This simplification preserves prediction accuracy while ensuring that the rules are clear and concise. This approach improves the rules’ interpretability and usefulness, making them suitable for both practical and research uses. Table 13 represents the two top rules extracted using DT for each class for the two top datasets based on the classification performance. However, the relatively low importance scores in RuleFit ( Table 13 ) are the result of its operational mechanism. RuleFit generates a compact set of rules from weak decision trees and assigns coefficients to them using a sparse linear model with L1 regularization. Therefore, the rules have small coefficients, and when multiplied by their respective support values, the total importance scores are reduced. In addition, RuleFit rules are generally more specific and cover fewer samples, which reduces their support and, therefore, their importance scores. Despite the lower importance measures, the rules derived are still applicable to feature interactions and model decisions since RuleFit can capture fine-grained patterns through an additive effect of multiple low-impact rules. The rules extracted from both models highlight different aspects of the data and comprehensively explain the patterns found in a simplified and human-readable way. This approach helps bridge the gap between complex black-box models and interpretable ML, allowing for a clearer understanding of the key factors driving classification outcomes. To evaluate the explainability of the proposed model and highlight the regions most influential to the model’s predictions, the study employed the SFMOV technique, which overlays statistical features (mean, skewness, and entropy) onto the input images. The results are assessed across five datasets, and for each dataset, the visualization for two representative images is presented. Each color intensity in the SFMOV is equivalent to the magnitude of the statistical measures, the warm colors (red) represents high values (more important regions) and cold colors (blue) represents low values (less important regions), providing a quantitative description of the attention areas of the DL model. The resulting visualizations using SFMOV are analyzed and validated by a radiologist, confirming their clinical relevance and highlighting their potential for diagnostic decision-making. However, it is known that prior knowledge of the predicted class by the model can induce a reading bias in radiologists’ reading of the overlays. Therefore, a blind reading process is advised, where the statistical overlays are read without looking at the predicted class first, in order to provide an unbiased assessment of the explainability of the model. This expert validation emphasizes the practical importance of the proposed visualization technique, particularly for medical imaging tasks requiring chest radiographs, Histopathological Images, MRIs, Ultrasound images, and retinal fundus images. This study proposed SVIS-RULEX as an innovative framework to enhance the interpretability of deep learning models, particularly for critical applications in healthcare. By combining statistical feature engineering, rule-based modeling, and visual overlays, the methodology addresses key limitations of existing XAI approaches, offering a holistic solution for interpreting black-box models in medical diagnostics. The framework demonstrated the ability to provide transparent, interpretable insights without compromising predictive performance. By integrating statistical metrics such as mean, skewness, and entropy, the method enriched the interpretive capacity of deep learning models, while ZFMIS effectively reduced dimensionality, preserving only the most critical features. This approach facilitated the development of interpretable and high-performing models, offering valuable insights into the underlying patterns and decision-making processes of the model. Visual overlays generated by SFMOV provided meaningful heatmaps, highlighting diagnostically relevant areas and demonstrating the model’s focus on critical regions within medical images. These visualizations supported clinical trust in the decision-making process, ensuring that the results were interpretable and actionable. The versatility of the framework was evident in its ability to perform consistently across a variety of medical imaging modalities, including radiographs, ultrasounds, and histopathological images. This scalability emphasizes its potential for broad application in diagnostics, making it particularly valuable in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Importantly, the rule-based explanations offered by decision trees and RuleFit models bridged the gap between computational predictions and human understanding, enabling a clearer interpretation of the model’s decision-making process. The study not only highlights the proposed framework’s interpretability and transparency but also establishes its relevance for improving trust and adoption in real-world clinical settings. Despite its promising contributions, the proposed SVIS-RULEX framework has certain limitations. While the rule-based explanations provide clarity, they might oversimplify the underlying decision-making process of deep learning models, potentially missing nuanced patterns that contribute to predictions. The reliance on visual heatmaps for interpretability also assumes that the highlighted regions fully capture diagnostically relevant features, which may not always align with domain experts’ expectations. Furthermore, the framework’s evaluation focused on specific imaging modalities and datasets, raising the need for extensive validation across broader, more heterogeneous datasets to ensure its generalizability. It is worth noting that SFMOV does not necessarily coincide exactly with clinically marked tumor or consolidation areas. While these regions often overlap with areas typically examined by human experts during diagnosis, it is important to note that XAI methods, such as SFMOV, are not designed to exactly replicate expert attention. Instead, they may capture subtle, discriminative patterns that inform the model’s decisions but do not always align with clinically defined tumor or consolidation boundaries. The current SFMOV approach employs statistical feature maps (mean, skewness, entropy), computed directly from the original activation maps of the final convolutional layer without applying additional learned or domain-specific weights. This deliberate choice preserves the direct interpretability of the features of the learned model and avoids introducing external bias, ensuring that the visualizations remain faithful to the representations of the inherent features of the network. Although this method is computationally efficient and effectively highlights regions of model attention, the absence of learned weighting may result in broader, less localized feature activations. However, integrating the learned weights could improve visualization clarity while preserving the integrity of the model. Furthermore, another limitation of the proposed method is that, for some data sets, the SFMOV combined heatmaps are visually very close to the mean heatmap. This closeness means that the effect of the mean feature can dominate the visualization and could undermine the contribution of skewness and entropy under such scenarios. Future work will focus on addressing this limitation by enhancing the weighting of statistical features in a way that makes the discrimination higher in combined heatmaps. Finally, the computational overhead introduced by combining statistical, rule-based, and visual methods may pose challenges for real-time deployment in resource-constrained settings. Addressing these limitations in future work will be essential to further enhance the framework’s robustness and applicability in diverse and practical clinical environments. A self-supervised framework for improved generalisability in ultrasound B-mode image segmentation Ultrasound (US) imaging is clinically invaluable due to its non-invasive and safe nature. However, interpreting US images is challenging, requires significant expertise, and time, and is often prone to errors. Deep learning offers assistive solutions such as segmentation. Supervised methods rely on large, high-quality, and consistently labelled datasets, which are challenging to curate. Moreover, these methods tend to underperform on out-of-distribution data, limiting their clinical utility. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising alternative, leveraging unlabelled data to enhance model performance and generalisability. We introduce a contrastive SSL approach tailored for B-mode US images, incorporating a novel Relation Contrastive Loss (RCL). RCL encourages learning of distinct features by differentiating positive and negative sample pairs through a learnable metric. Additionally, we propose spatial and frequency-based augmentation strategies for the representation learning on US images. Our approach significantly outperforms traditional supervised segmentation methods across three public breast US datasets, particularly in data-limited scenarios. Notable improvements on the Dice similarity metric include a 4% increase on 20% and 50% of the BUSI dataset, nearly 6% and 9% improvements on 20% and 50% of the BrEaST dataset, and 6.4% and 3.7% improvements on 20% and 50% of the UDIAT dataset, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate superior generalisability on the out-of-distribution UDIAT dataset with performance boosts of 20.6% and 13.6% compared to the supervised baseline using 20% and 50% of the BUSI and BrEaST training data, respectively. Our research highlights that domain-inspired SSL can improve US segmentation, especially under data-limited conditions. US imaging provides a non-invasive, portable and low-cost imaging solution for clinicians compared to alternative imaging modalities, such as CT and MRI. US is a popular and widely used imaging tool within clinical practice for imaging various organs, such as cardiac, breast and abdominal examination [1] . US images are often noisy, have poor contrast, and are affected by artefacts such as reverberation, mirror imaging, acoustic enhancement and acoustic shadowing. Several examples are shown in Fig. 1 . These issues are largely unique to US due to its reliance on sound wave propagation and reflection [2] . Image quality varies with patient-related factors (e.g. subcutaneous fat [3] ) and clinician-dependent factors (e.g. focal depth, gain, and probe positioning [4] ), all of which influence how reflected signals are captured and interpreted. Consequently, US is a highly operator-dependent modality [5] , with data acquisition and interpretation requiring considerable skill and prone to error. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer support by identifying key anatomical features, reducing human error, and minimising inter-operator variability. Deep learning (DL) approaches for US image segmentation have been extensively researched in many clinical domains. State-of-the-art supervised learning approaches have been developed using both recent transformers and convolutional neural network (CNN) based architectures [6–8] . Furthermore, memory banks have been used in supervised learning to store image features [8] or class features [9] , providing additional information to enhance image segmentation through cross-image feature aggregation [8,9] . However, supervised learning methods are dependent on large data samples to perform effectively. These datasets are difficult to curate in the US domain with significant expertise required to acquire, anonymise, and annotate the data. Even with improvements in model development, many supervised approaches result in a steep drop in performance on unseen out-of-distribution data [10] . Models applied to data from alternative centres and under different imaging protocols can hinder performance [11] . Furthermore, most development is focused on a single clinical domain. We recognise that US B-mode image data is commonly used across many clinical domains but with unique challenges. We hypothesise that a generalisable framework can be applied to a range of public US B-mode image datasets without a significant drop in performance on out-of-distribution data. To overcome issues with limited annotated training data for effective supervised learning, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods are becoming increasingly popular in medical image analysis [12,13] . SSL pretext learning methods learn semantically meaningful feature representations from unlabelled data. The trained model is then fine-tuned for downstream tasks, such as segmentation, using available labelled data. SSL approaches improve model performance in the downstream task with limited labelled data as well as improved generalisability to out-of-distribution datasets [14,15] . Several SSL approaches have been applied to US imaging, however, these are often tailored to specific clinical domain challenges, with limited generalisability assessment (e.g., wrist US [16] and thyroid US [17] ). The contrastive learning approach has demonstrated improved performance for downstream tasks like segmentation [18] in an SSL setting. All SOTA contrastive SSL approaches rely on a transformed image to support representation learning [19] . Transformations often include image rotation, flipping, colour jittering or more complex augmentation approaches [20] . Combining transformations has also been shown to benefit representation learning in SSL [19,21] . However, we hypothesise that learnt representations depend on a domain-specific data-engineering technique and hence we can improve US B-mode image segmentation using domain understanding. Inspired by pretext-invariant representation learning (PIRL) [19] strategy, we propose a novel self-supervised pretext learning approach consisting of spatial and frequency-based augmentations for US B-mode images. In addition, we develop a novel loss function that aims to minimise the feature-level discrepancy and logit-level contrastive discrepancy. AI techniques in US B-mode imaging are typically centred around DL model development within a supervised learning framework, often tailored to a specific clinical application. SOTA approaches for segmentation in US imaging have developed from pure convolutional approaches using CNNs. CNN-based approaches often use variants of U-Net [22] . Shareef et al. [23] introduced the ESTAN network aimed at improving small breast tumour segmentation. ESTAN uses two encoder branches with different kernel shapes and sizes and three skip connections to improve multi-scale contextual information. Banerjee et al. [24] proposed SIU-Net for segmenting lumbar and thoracic bony features using their proposed inception block. This block uses multiple filter sizes with improved computational efficiency through combined 1 × 1 and 3 × 3 convolutions. They also combined features of multiple scales through dense skip connections. Meshram et al. [25] improved carotid plaque segmentation using dilated convolutional layers in a U-Net model and Qiao et al. [26] used dilated convolution and squeeze excitation blocks on skip connections to improve fetal skull segmentation. With advancements in transformer-based architectures, the latest SOTA approaches for US segmentation combine transformer and convolutional methods leveraging complementary global and local feature information, respectively. Zhang et al. [7] used a CNN-Transformer combination in a U-Net framework. The authors used a ResNet backbone and a novel local–global transformer block nested into skip connections to capture long-range feature information efficiently for breast US segmentation. Jiang et al. [6] also explored a CNN-Transformer U-Net model to improve US segmentation of the breast, thyroid and left ventricle. The authors used a coordinate residual block to extract local feature information with absolute position information and enhanced channel self-attention blocks to extract global features. Wu et al. [8] introduced a BUSSeg model for breast US segmentation by using a parallel bi-encoder in a U-Net style architecture consisting of a transformer and CNN blocks. In addition, the authors use a cross-image dependency module to capture cross-image long-range dependencies utilising feature memory banks. These supervised learning models have demonstrated promising segmentation results across various US clinical domains. However, due to the limited availability of US data, self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a more robust approach, enabling high segmentation performance while minimising performance degradation when applied to out-of-distribution data. Also, combined transformer and convolutional approaches [6–8] often require higher computational training and inference time that hinders clinical translation, whereas SSL techniques are independent of the model choice and can boost performance significantly. Self-supervised learning often follows a two-stage training strategy. Firstly, pretext learning is focused on learning representations from unlabelled data. Secondly, these learnt weights are then used in the fine-tuning downstream supervised learning tasks, such as segmentation. The objective is to learn semantically meaningful feature representations without requiring labels, thereby improving the performance of a downstream task on limited labelled datasets. Since the labels are not required during the pretext task, a large number of available unlabelled samples can be used which makes the SSL approach more generalisable to out-of-distribution samples. The pretext learning task is critical for developing meaningful representations of the target domain in SSL [15] . Often a combination of image augmentation benefits contrastive SSL pretext learning, with this unsupervised learning stage also benefiting from stronger augmentation than supervised learning [21] . For example, geometric rotation transformation was applied to an image in [27] while the Jigsaw pretext task with a set of shuffled patches within an image was used in [20] . The Jigsaw approach provides a strong geometric transformation to an image, a common strategy used in contrastive SSL [14,28,29] . The traditional Jigsaw approach learns a representation that is covariant to the perturbation, the pretext-invariant representation learning (PIRL) [19] approach adopts the Jigsaw task in an invariant learning strategy. Several SSL approaches have been established involving generative, contrastive and generative–contrastive techniques applied to medical image analysis [18] . The pretext learning strategy differs for each approach with a generative task focused on reconstruction, for example, recovering masked areas of an image [30] . However, the contrastive approach aims to discriminate similar and dissimilar samples [19] . Contrastive approaches are often preferred to generative approaches for downstream discriminative applications [18] . By avoiding low-level abstraction objectives, such as pixel-level reconstruction, contrastive learning tends to be more lightweight, as it does not require a decoder during pretext learning [18] . Widely known contrastive learning approaches include SimCLR [21] , MoCo [31] , PIRL [19] and BYOL [32] . SimCLR introduced a contrastive learning framework using strong augmentations, a projection head, and large batch sizes to learn visual representations [21] . MoCo addressed the batch size limitation by using a momentum encoder and a dynamic dictionary of negative samples [31] . MoCoV2 added stronger augmentations and a multi-layer perceptron projection head [33] , while MoCo v3 adapted the framework for vision transformers [34] . BYOL was introduced using two interacting neural networks to learn from each other. The online network predicts the target network representation, both using the same image, but under different augmented views [32] . PIRL introduced a method to learn invariant representations rather than covariant representations to the pretext task used [19] . These approaches demonstrate improved performance in self-supervised learning and continue to be widely adopted both as baselines [17,35,36] and as primary SSL frameworks [37,38] in recent research. Subsequent work has built upon the MoCo framework. Liu et al. [35] proposed a learnable adaptive patch embedding module, referred to as CDOA, which facilitates rich representation learning without relying on handcrafted pretext tasks. This module is attached to the momentum encoder within the MoCo framework. Chin et al. [36] introduced a saliency guided mask augmentation (we refer to as SGMA) for contrastive SSL using CNNs as the backbone encoder. Their approach was evaluated using both SimCLR and MoCoV2, achieving best segmentation performance with MoCoV2. Metric learning aims to learn a function to effectively compare similarities between data samples. Siamese networks [39] was used to learn a similarity function to map input pairs into a shared embedding space. The network was trained to bring similar pairs together and push dissimilar pairs apart using a linear distance metric, e.g., Euclidean distance. Prototypical networks [40] learn an embedding that is a non-linear transformation of the input data, mapping it into an embedding space where the nearest neighbour classification is effective. The classification is based on the proximity of query instances to class prototypes in this learned embedding space. Relation Networks [41] use an embedding module to obtain sample feature embeddings and a relation module to compute sample pair similarity. Unlike [39,40] , the addition of the relation modules enables learning of similarity metrics in a data-driven way. Our work focuses on contrastive learning because it excels in discriminative downstream applications, is more lightweight during pretext learning, and favours high-level abstract feature learning compared to generative approaches [18] . With contrastive learning dependent upon data transformations in the pretext learning task, we utilise a combination of data-specific augmentations, shown to improve SSL feature learning [21] . In this work, we explore novel combined spatial and frequency-based augmentation strategies aimed at US images to improve representation learning in US data. Furthermore, inspired by relation networks [41] as a metric learning technique, we utilise relation networks and propose a novel relation contrastive loss (RCL) in a contrastive learning setting. To further guide representation learning, we propose to combine RCL with perceptual loss to weight feature learning with high-level features tackling high noise and poor contrast of US images. We propose a novel self-supervised framework that explores the impact of a domain-inspired pretext task for US B-mode image data along with a novel integration of relation networks for contrastive self-supervised learning (see Fig. 3 ). We also explore the impact of perceptual loss on its ability to focus on model understanding of high-level abstract features. Given the high noise and low contrast often present in ultrasound images, perceptual loss guides representation learning towards higher-level features extracted from deeper encoder layers. This helps the network become more robust to misleading low-level signals and encourages attention to semantically meaningful structures, such as lesion boundaries and tissue textures. Our pretext task explores a novel data engineering Cross-patch Jigsaw strategy aimed at providing US B-mode image data-specific augmentation to support distinctive and meaningful representation learning during the pretext task. In addition, we apply frequency augmentations to enhance the model’s ability to distinguish lesion patterns in low-contrast US images. We propose using Relation Networks in contrastive SSL. Commonly, contrastive loss approaches, for example Noise Contrastive Estimation loss use a fixed metric like cosine similarity to assess similarity between samples. These methods depend on the encoder to learn both meaningful and linearly separable representations. In contrast, we use Relation Networks to learn similarity in a data-driven manner. This allows for modelling non-linear interactions between feature embeddings, moving beyond linear measures like cosine similarity. Our proposed Relation Contrastive Loss (RCL) supports the encoder in learning semantically rich representations, while the Relation Network — comprising two fully connected layers — learns a more flexible, robust similarity function. This separation of representation learning and similarity modelling allows the encoder to focus on capturing meaningful patterns in ultrasound images, while the Relation Network captures higher-order relational structure. See Section 3.3 for more details. Our pretext tasks combine spatial and frequency-based transformations, applied at each training iteration. US image quality depends on the frequency content of reflected sound waves. In the frequency domain, high-frequency components capture fine texture, while low-frequency components represent broader tissue deformation. This frequency content can be distorted by imaging depth, tissue interactions, beam geometry, hardware limitations, and artefacts [4] . To improve model robustness to variable image clarity and artefacts, we apply frequency-based augmentation using band-stop and X-shaped filtering. Our spatial transformation builds upon the Jigsaw task used in the PIRL approach [19] , which applies a strong transformation and has shown improved performance in self-supervised learning [19] . However, since US images exhibit a characteristic layer-wise anatomical structure, shuffling all patches may disrupt important spatial context. Our spatial transformation is designed to balance global spatial continuity with localised patch-level variation, supporting effective contrastive learning with improved feature representations. To improve model robustness to image variations e.g. reverberation artefacts speckle noise, and harmonic distortions, we utilise band stop filtering in the frequency domain. The frequency domain of a US image can be obtained by computing the 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT): (1) F ( u , v ) = ∑ x = 0 M − 1 ∑ y = 0 N − 1 f ( x , y ) ⋅ e − j 2 π u x H + v y W F ( u , v ) denotes the frequency domain value at coordinates ( u , v ) , while f ( x , y ) denotes the spatial domain value at coordinates ( x , y ) . Here, H and W are the height and width of pixels of the image, respectively. According to Euler’s formula ( e i θ = cos θ + i sin θ ) Eq. (1) can be written in the form: (2) F ( u , v ) = ∑ x = 0 H − 1 ∑ y = 0 W − 1 U ( x , y ) [ cos 2 π u x H + v y W − i sin 2 π u x H + v y W ] In Eq. (2) , real F r (cosine term) and imaginary part F i (sine term) can be written as F ( u , v ) = F r ( u , v ) + i F i ( u , v ) . The amplitude and phase can be obtained from: (3) | F ( u , v ) | = F r ( u , v ) 2 + F i ( u , v ) 2 ∠ F ( u , v ) = arctan F i ( u , v ) F r ( u , v ) The amplitude and phase indicate the strength and position of frequency components in the US image. We experiment with filtering frequency components within a random cropped section of the US image to distort textual information, whilst maintaining critical low-frequency components related to structures in the image. Fig. 4 indicates several example augmentations applied in the frequency spectrum of a cropped US image. As shown these filters impact the overall image smoothness and become more blurred from left to right. This filter visually distorts structures within the image. Visually similar effects may happen during data acquisition using sub-optimal acquisition settings or poor coupling. The inner circular band stop filter has random thickness stopping frequencies within a range from radius 10 to radius 100. A minimum inner region of radius 10 is preserved for critical low-frequency information. Furthermore, we include an X-shaped band stop filter from the edge of the circular filter to apply further smoothing to the image, along the diagonal axes. We randomise the thickness of this filter from 0 to 10 and apply this filter in cases where the outer diameter of the circular filter is over 20. This threshold prevents the X-shaped filter from distorting critical visual details, ensuring meaningful image variability. Consider an ultrasound B-mode image dataset U D consisting of N image samples in the training data, U D = { I 1 , I 2 , I 3 , … , I N } and a set of image transformations, t ∈ T . Original images ( I ∈ U D ) undergo simple geometric and photometric transformations, referred to as t 1 . These include random horizontal flipping, vertical flipping and colour jitter (brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue set to 0.4). I t 1 denotes transformation t 1 applied to original images I . Patch-level transformed images ( I p ) undergo our data-engineered strategy. The strategy includes random frequency-based filtering for a random cropped region of each image in U D and then obtaining patch-level augmented images by flipping and shuffling focal and non-focal patches (see Section 3.1.2 ). I p also undergoes an additional transformation ( t 2 ) that includes random colour jitter for each patch (brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue set to 0.4) denoted by I t 2 p . A CNN with parameters θ (in our case ResNet50 [43] ) is used to encode image- and patch-level representations denoted as Φ θ ( I t 1 ) and Φ θ ( I t 2 p ) , respectively. At the patch level, we concatenate features from each patch, resulting in a feature vector ϕ θ ( C ( I t 2 p ) ) . These image and patch-level representations are projected onto a 128-dimensional vector using a fully connected linear layer f ( . ) and g ( . ) , respectively. These are then normalised with the l 2 - norm resulting in final feature representations at image- ( v t 1 ) and patch-level ( v t 2 p ). The memory bank M is implemented as described in [19] . The t 1 transformed original image I t 1 0 are encoded and normalised like the original images to form v t 1 0 and stored in M . The pre-computation at each epoch enables us to utilise negative and positive sample representations in the memory bank without needing to increase the batch size to build a large sample of negative samples. These representations are updated through an exponential moving average of v t 1 0 computed in previous epochs with weight ( m w = 0 . 5 ). We adopt a relation network (RN) [41] with network parameters β ( Fig. 3 ) for pretext learning. Here, we proposed to compute relation scores in a contrastive learning fashion and refer to this as “Relation Contrastive Loss (RCL)”. Consider a normalised positive sample representation of an image instance as v t 1 and a normalised target feature embedding from our moving average memory bank M , be v t 1 + . Similarly, let v t 1 − denote a normalised negative image sample representation from M . We form positive ( z + ) and negative ( z − ) relation pairs through the element-wise product ( z + = v t 1 ⊗ v t 1 + , and z − = v t 1 ⊗ v t 1 − ). Three publicly available breast ultrasound datasets have been used in this study: BUSI [45] , BrEaST [46] and UDIAT [47] . BUSI was collected from 600 women aged 25 – 75 years old from Baheya Hospital, Egypt. BUSI contains 780 anonymised images with 487 benign, 210 malignant, and 133 normal cases. Images were acquired using a LOGIQ E9 Agile US system using a 1 – 5 MHz ML6-15-D linear probe. Ground truth mask annotations for all images were reviewed and adjusted by expert radiologists at Baheya Hospital. BrEaST dataset contains 256 anonymised breast ultrasound images from 256 patients ( 18 – 87 years old) collected in medical centres in Poland in 2019 − 2022 . Benign ( 154 images), malignant ( 98 images), and normal ( 4 images) cases were collected. Four different US systems and transducers were used in the acquisition. UDIAT dataset B contains 163 anonymised Breast Ultrasound images collected and labelled at the UDIAT-Centre Diagnostic, Corporacio Parc Taul, Sabadell, Spain. Benign ( 110 images) and malignant ( 53 images) breast cases were acquired using a Siemens ACUSON Sequoia C512 US system with 17L5 HD linear array probe (8.5 MHz). A summary of all datasets with samples for training (train), validation (val) and test are outlined in Table 1 . All methods were implemented using Pytorch and performed on a Tesla V100 GPU. A summary of the settings for the pretext learning task and the segmentation task is provided in Table 1 . We adjusted the batch size ( B ) for experiments with different datasets, due to variations in dataset sizes. To ensure experimental reproducibility, all experiments were conducted using a random seed of 42. For pretext learning we trained for 2000 epochs, using the last checkpoint for downstream task training. An SGD optimiser is used with a learning rate optimised for each method, (see Table 2 ). All input images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels and the ResNet50 model was pre-trained on ImageNet before pretext learning. For all downstream tasks, a polynomial l r scheduler was used with initial and final learning rates of 1 e − 3 and 1 e − 6 , respectively, with a learning rate decay of 0.9. An Adam optimiser and cross-entropy loss were used for all downstream tasks. Downstream training was run for 500 epochs with convergence occurring below 200 epochs. The metrics we used to evaluate segmentation performance include: Dice score (DSC = 2 ⋅ | y pred ∩ y true | | y pred | + | y true | ), Jaccard Coefficient (JC = | y pred ∩ y true | | y pred ∪ y true | ), Hausdorff distance (HD = max sup a ∈ y pred inf b ∈ y true d ( a , b ) , sup b ∈ y true inf a ∈ y pred d ( b , a ) ), precision (PPV = | y pred ∩ y true | | y pred | ) and recall (Rec. = | y pred ∩ y true | | y true | ). y pred and y true represent the predicted segmentation mask and ground truth segmentation masks, respectively. The distance function d ( . ) used is Euclidean distance for the computation of Hausdorff distance. Supervised learning models have shown promising improvements in US image segmentation [6–8] . However, performance is significantly affected when training samples are limited [15] . Our results in all datasets demonstrate that the supervised baseline is consistently among the lowest performing methods when either 50% or 20% training samples are used. This finding suggests that our SSL approaches can effectively learn meaningful representations for US data during pretext learning that supports the downstream segmentation task ( Tables 4–7 ). Furthermore, supervised model generalisability is significantly impacted when training samples are limited. This is evident in our generalisability study (see Table 7 ). The baseline supervised method shows a significant 23.6% drop in DSC and a 76% increase in HD when training data is reduced from 100% to 20%. This highlights the benefits of SSL in improving segmentation performance on out-of-distribution data, particularly when downstream data is limited. Therefore, incorporating SSL techniques into US model development can enhance clinical applicability. Improving performance on data acquired using different hardware systems, patient populations, and clinical operators relative to training data improves model robustness and real-world method adoption. To enhance the performance of contrastive SSL for segmentation of US images, we first introduced a data-engineered, domain-inspired pretext task aimed at US B-mode image data. Our results demonstrate that our frequency augmentation in pretext learning benefits the downstream segmentation task performance in US images. This addition occurs in the top two approaches across all datasets explored, including our generalisability study and in all training proportions of 100%, 50% and 20%. Our frequency augmentation improves feature learning by exposing the model to a broader range of image degradations. This is reflective of real-world clinical settings, where image quality can vary significantly across different hardware, users and patients. Our proposed Cross-patch Jigsaw spatial transformation performed comparably well to the Jigsaw pretext task. It occurred within the top two approaches (often with frequency augmentation included) when 50% of the training data is used across all datasets explored, including the generalisability study. This is encouraging, as this transformation was designed to preserve partial layer-wise structural information within the ultrasound image. In more complex imaging domains, such as abdominal ultrasound, which involve additional structures and more detailed layer-wise information, this approach could offer an improved alternative. In addition to our novel data engineered pretext task, we proposed a combined loss function, which includes RCL and perceptual loss. From our results perceptual loss benefits both PIRL and RCL, with perceptual loss occurring in the top two performing methods across all training data proportions and datasets explored, occurring in 11 of 12 cases. This loss component was added to focus representation learning on higher level more abstract features from deep within the encoder network (in our case layer 40 from ResNet50). Our results indicate that the use of perceptual loss is beneficial for feature representation learning in ultrasound for downstream segmentation tasks, particularly in combination with our relation contrastive loss (RCL). RCL consistently ranks among the top two performers in each data set, demonstrating notable benefits in limited data scenarios. Specifically, RCL achieves top-two segmentation performance using 50% and 20% of training samples in the BUSI, BrEaST and UDIAT datasets. This shows that by combining encoder-learned features with a relation network, we can enhance learned feature representations by improving the differentiation between positive and negative samples during pretext learning. Furthermore, our qualitative results demonstrate focussed attention to tumour areas using RCL. As shown in Fig. 7 , this approach exhibits reduced attention to auxiliary regions compared to the baseline and other SSL methods explored. This suggests greater robustness to noise and artefacts. Adding perceptual loss complements the attention profile with increased attention to the whole tumour area whilst minimising attention to surrounding areas of the tumour. Lastly, Fig. 6 shows our approach, RCL with perceptual loss, along with our proposed spatial and frequency pretext tasks, can improve the segmentation of irregular tumours. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive exploration of domain-inspired data-engineered pretext tasks for US image analysis within a contrastive self-supervised learning framework. We introduced the novel Relation Contrastive Loss (RCL) combined with perceptual loss, a unique and previously unexplored approach. This method demonstrated improved downstream segmentation performance, particularly in limited data scenarios. Furthermore, combining contrastive loss with perceptual loss consistently improves segmentation performance and generalisability in noisy US image data. Additionally, we showed that frequency-based band-stop filtering as an augmentation technique in contrastive self-supervised learning improves the learning of generalisable features. Our novel Cross-Patch Jigsaw approach delivered comparable performance to the traditional Jigsaw task, and combining our spatial and frequency-based pretext tasks with RCL and perceptual loss further improved segmentation of irregular tumour areas. In our future work, we aim to apply and extend this method to US images in more challenging clinical domains, such as abdominal ultrasound for bowel and gall bladder segmentation. Advanced Dual-Branch U-Net Decoder for Precise and Robust Surgical Instrument and Organ Segmentation The accurate segmentation of surgical instruments and organs is crucial for improving the safety, precision, and efficiency of laparoscopic and robot-assisted surgeries, where real-time guidance and error reduction are paramount. Surgical environments present significant challenges, such as image noise, organ deformation, and tool occlusion, making precise segmentation difficult. This paper presents a surgical image segmentation approach based on a modified U-Net model. The encoder of the neural network used residual blocks, and the decoder architecture is based on a dual-branch model to improve the segmentation performance. One branch focuses on segmenting surgical instruments, while the other on the intervened organ. This design ensures the detection of specific features from the surgical instruments and organs, improving segmentation accuracy. Experimental results evaluate the performance of the proposed neural network model using real surgical datasets. The proposed method achieved superior results, with a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 92% for surgical instruments segmentation and 96% for organ segmentation. These findings demonstrate the robustness of the proposed model in challenging surgical environments. Minimally invasive surgery has significantly improved surgical procedures by reducing incision size, minimizing damage to healthy tissues, and consequently leading to smaller wounds and shorter postoperative recovery times. For this reason, the use of semi-automated surgical systems has increased significantly in recent years, replacing many traditional procedures that require large incisions to access the internal structures of the patient. However, these surgeries present significant challenges to surgeons due to reduced tactile and visual feedback from the surgical instruments and the patient’s anatomy [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those based on computer vision, have been implemented to address these challenges. These technologies are fundamental in the development of semi-automated surgical robots that assist surgeons during procedures by accurately identifying surgical instruments and anatomical structures [ 4 ]. Unlike traditional methods, which have problems with object detection and segmentation in the presence of noise, lighting variations, or other distortions inherent to surgical environments, neural networks have demonstrated greater robustness in such conditions [ 5 ]. Neural networks learn generalizable image features from large datasets and identify relevant structures in real-time surgical scenarios. This paper presents a method for segmenting surgical instruments and anatomical structures during surgical procedures using a modified U-Net neural network. The encoder incorporates residual blocks to enhance feature learning and improve the detection accuracy of surgical instruments and operated anatomical structures. The decoder employed a dual-branch architecture: one branch is dedicated to detecting and segmenting surgical instruments, while the other focuses on the operated anatomical structure. This separation allows each branch to extract task-specific features, resulting in more precise and detailed segmentation. The main contributions of the proposed method are as follows: A dual-branch decoder is introduced to enhance multitask image segmentation, where one branch specializes in segmenting surgical instruments and the other in segmenting operated anatomical structures. This separation enhances segmentation accuracy, enabling the model to perform reliably in complex scenarios. The decoder architecture improves segmentation performance under image distortions. Each branch focuses on features relevant from instruments or anatomical structures, ensuring more robust and precise segmentation. The proposed neural network is adaptable to different surgical contexts, including robotic-assisted and laparoscopic procedures. The following section presents a literature review of prior work related to the segmentation of surgical tools and anatomical structures. The segmentation of surgical instruments in medical images provides surgeons with essential visual information, enhancing the precision of surgical procedures. In this context, neural networks achieve accurate recognition of surgical instruments, even in the presence of image distortions. Furthermore, neural networks identify surgical instruments in different environments without requiring algorithm modifications. Several studies have explored different neural network architectures to improve surgical tool segmentation. Ovi et al. [ 7 ] proposed a convolutional block attention module to capture the relationships between RGB feature channels. Their neural network encoder architecture is based on the Res2Net model, which enhances feature extraction by utilizing multi-scale representations. Similarly, Lou et al. [ 8 ] introduced Min-Max Similarity (MMS), a contrastive learning approach that applies contrastive loss for surgical tool segmentation by comparing the decoder output with the original ground truth. Other approaches use generative adversarial networks (GANs) to enhance segmentation performance. Zhang et al. [ 9 ] used a GAN-based unpaired method that generates images belonging to either the ground truth or surgical tools. This method is based on the U-Net model as a generator but removes the skip connections between the encoder and decoder. The model identifies image features to generate new images specifically for surgical tool segmentation. Likewise, Colleoni and Stoyanov [ 10 ] developed a method for generating synthetic data using a GAN encoder based on the ResNet model. This approach utilizes the ground truth of surgical instruments to create new data, which is subsequently used to segment the surgical tool within the original image. Other studies focus on enhancing image preprocessing and feature extraction. Attia et al. [ 11 ] segmented the background, surgical tool shaft, and surgical tool manipulator using a recurrent neural network (RNN). Their proposed architecture incorporates a convolutional autoencoder to extract pixel-level features, combined with an RNN utilizing LSTM layers to capture spatial dependencies between patches of deep features. Huang et al. [ 12 ] improved segmentation accuracy with a polar transformation. The segmented output is then transformed into the original image, and a U-Net model is trained using both coordinate systems with data augmentation techniques to mitigate overfitting. Mishra et al. [ 13 ] applied adversarial transfer learning for surgical tool segmentation, using a generator to create accurate masks. On the other hand, a discriminator was applied to match the ground truth. Finally, Ayobi et al. [ 14 ] employed Mask2Former for region classification and a Multi-Scale Vision Transformer to enhance segmentation accuracy. The segmentation of surgical instruments has several challenges due to the surgical environment, such as illumination conditions, noise adding, and overlapping of instruments. These challenges require the development of a robust architecture to adapt the neural network to dynamic surgical environments. In addition, most of the studies focus on segmenting surgical instruments. In contrast, organ segmentation together with the surgical instrument is necessary to enhance surgical precision and patient safety. Therefore, the proposed approach performs organ and surgical tool segmentation, providing valuable visual information to the surgeon and supporting the development of technologies for semi-automating surgeries. This section presents a method for segmenting surgical instruments and anatomical structures using a modified U-Net model. U-Net architecture is used for identifying critical features in complex structures, such as surgical tools and patient anatomy. For this reason, accurate segmentation is essential to minimize errors, locate the instruments and anatomical structures in the image, and reduce complications during surgeries. This is particularly crucial in semi-automated and robot-assisted surgical procedures, where segmentation errors can compromise surgical outcomes and patient safety. While other segmentation models, such as SegNet and Fully Convolutional Neural Networks (FCNNs), may offer faster training times, these methods sacrifice segmentation accuracy. This inconvenience can create significant challenges in surgical procedures, where high precision is required to ensure patient safety. The proposed modified U-Net model addresses the limitations of traditional U-Net architectures in the simultaneous segmentation of surgical instruments and anatomical structures. The traditional U-Net neural network realized an accurate segmentation in general tasks, but the accuracy decreases in segmenting overlapping regions [ 15 , 16 ]. This limitation of the U-Net model tends to generalize the features related to the target classes. The decoder processes redundant and irrelevant patterns associated with surgical instruments and anatomical structures. This process reduces efficiency in distinguishing overlapping regions from anatomical complex structures. The proposed modified U-Net model improved the segmentation efficiency by incorporating residual blocks in the encoder and dual-branch architecture in the decoder. The residual blocks learn robust features and capture complex structures in the images without generating redundancies. For this reason, residual blocks enhance feature extraction from distorted images, thereby improving segmentation accuracy. Additionally, this element accelerates the training process by vanishing gradient problem [ 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Fig. 1 depicts the structure of the residual block. On the other hand, the dual-branch decoder design improves image segmentation. Each branch learns different patterns related to its respective task, optimizing segmentation accuracy for both surgical tools and organs [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. The proposed architecture of the decoder ensures a precise segmentation of surgical instruments and organs. The first branch B si identifies and segments the organ under surgical intervention, producing the output y 1 (2). This branch is trained to learn unique patterns and structures associated with surgical tools. The second branch B o , segments surgical instruments, resulting in the output y 2 (3). These blocks enable the learning of more robust features. This design enhances feature extraction, ensuring an efficient performance for organ and surgical tool segmentation. The proposed segmentation framework incorporates a dual-decoder architecture in which a shared encoder extracts common features from the input image, and two independent decoders process these features separately. Each decoder generates different segmentation maps, surgical instruments, and anatomical structures, allowing the network to specialize in distinct tasks simultaneously. This architectural separation enables each decoder to focus on learning the most relevant from the target outputs. The encoder captures visual information, while the decoder identifies the region of interest for each task. Unlike Siamese neural networks, the decoder branches in this design do not share weights or parameters, ensuring independent learning and reducing the risk of negative transfer between tasks. As a result, the dual-decoder approach improves segmentation performance by minimizing feature interference and segmenting different regions of interest. Advanced hybrid UNet architectures for retinal vessel segmentation Retinal blood vessel segmentation is a critical step in the early detection and diagnosis of various vision-threatening diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, hypertension, and glaucoma. Manual segmentation by medical professionals is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to variability, highlighting the need for robust automated solutions. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown significant promise in addressing these challenges by enabling accurate and efficient segmentation of retinal blood vessels from fundus images. In this paper, we propose three advanced deep learning architectures for retinal blood vessel segmentation: VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet. These models combine the strengths of pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the U-Net architecture, leveraging transfer learning to enhance feature extraction and segmentation performance. We evaluate the proposed models on a publicly available retinal image dataset, achieving Dice coefficients of 79%, 79% and 80% for VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet, respectively. Our results demonstrate that the ResNet50-UNet model outperforms the other two variants and surpasses several state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness. This study underscores the potential of deep learning-based approaches for improving the automation and reliability of retinal blood vessel segmentation, paving the way for more efficient and accurate diagnostic tools in ophthalmology.
