The retina, a complex structure of the eye, comprises multiple layers of neural tissue, including photoreceptors such as rods and cones. These photoreceptors are responsible for detecting light and converting it into electrical signals, which are then transmitted to the brain, enabling vision [1] . Any abnormalities or anomalies in the retina can disrupt its function, potentially leading to vision impairment or blindness. Therefore, early detection and appropriate treatment of retinal disorders are crucial to preserving vision. However, identifying issues within the retinal vessels remains challenging due to the retina’s delicate and intricate nature [2] . Accurate diagnosis and effective treatment planning by medical professionals are essential to address these conditions. One of the primary diagnostic tools for retinal examination is ophthalmoscopy (or funduscopy), a procedure that involves visualizing the back of the eye using a light source and a specialized magnifying lens. This technique generates a fundus image, which captures detailed structures of the retina, optic disc, choroid, and ocular blood vessels. Fundus imaging plays a vital role in diagnosing and monitoring various retinal and systemic conditions, making it an indispensable tool in ophthalmology. Various diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy (DR), cardiovascular conditions, and glaucoma, can be identified through the analysis of retinal blood vessels. Automated segmentation of these vessels from retinal images has become a key area of research, as it has the potential to address the limited availability of ophthalmologists in underserved and remote regions. The structural characteristics of retinal blood vessels provide essential information for disease diagnosis and treatment, making accurate segmentation a fundamental step in medical image analysis. Deep learning-based approaches have significantly improved the detection and classification of retinal diseases, particularly in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, where CNN models such as VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet152-V2 have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in identifying and categorizing DR stages [3] . These advancements highlight the effectiveness of deep feature extraction techniques in fundus image analysis. Retinal blood vessel segmentation has been a focal point of research over the past decade due to its significant role in the early detection of diabetic retinopathy (DR) and related diseases. Even minor changes in vascular structures can lead to various abnormalities, making precise segmentation essential. While abnormal retinal images are crucial for diagnosis, comparative analysis also requires healthy vessel images [4] . The extraction of blood vessels from fundus images is a fundamental step in DR diagnosis, yet it presents several challenges, particularly in distinguishing diseased vessels from other pathological features. Retinal images often contain additional disease-related structures, such as microaneurysms and retinal detachments, further complicating segmentation. Manual extraction is not only labor-intensive but also requires expert intervention. Moreover, effective object detection relies on accurate foreground–background separation, while variations in illumination conditions can introduce additional segmentation errors [5] . To address these challenges, image preprocessing techniques, including illumination normalization and contrast enhancement, have been proposed to improve image quality and assist in deep learning-based segmentation tasks [6] . Traditional retinal vessel segmentation methods include approaches based on vessel tracking, matched filtering, and mathematical morphology processing [7] . These methods are computationally efficient and easy to implement, as they do not require iterative training or labeled segmentation data, making them suitable for unsupervised applications. Wang et al. [8] proposed a segmentation method that integrates morphological techniques with filtering, employing the vector field divergence approach to improve vessel connectivity and reduce missegmentation. However, traditional methods face limitations in accurately segmenting complex vascular structures, as filtering and morphological processing steps may introduce noise, thereby affecting segmentation performance. Khuram et al. [9] improved segmentation accuracy by applying an ES-BM3D filter to reduce noise and enhance contrast in retinal images. UNet [10] , a supervised encoder–decoder network, has demonstrated notable success in medical image processing. However, in retinal vessel segmentation, its convolution-based feature extraction is limited to local contextual information, restricting its ability to capture long-range dependencies. This limitation can lead to incorrect semantic interpretation in continuous vessel segmentation tasks. Moreover, UNet processes all information equally, which may introduce redundant data and affect segmentation accuracy. To overcome these challenges, attention mechanisms have been incorporated to enhance model performance. SENet [11] utilizes 2D global pooling to compute channel attention, achieving significant performance improvements with minimal computational cost. However, it only captures inter-channel relationships and disregards spatial information, which is essential for accurately modeling vessel structures. BAM [12] and CBAM [13] address spatial attention through convolution, yet their reliance on local feature extraction limits their ability to model long-range dependencies, which are critical for precise segmentation. Several recent studies have proposed modifications to improve segmentation performance. Yicheng Wu et al. [14] developed Vessel-Net, integrating UNet with a residual network for retinal vessel segmentation. Bo Wang et al. [15] introduced a dual-encoding UNet to enhance vascular feature extraction. Cage Li et al. [16] introduced FANet, which employs a bi-directional attention block to address intra-class imbalance and replaces conventional convolution blocks with SK modules to extract multi-scale features effectively. Shihao Zhang et al. [17] proposed AG-Net, incorporating an attention-guided filter to recover spatial details, merge structural information at different resolutions, and suppress noise in complex backgrounds. Despite considerable advances in segmentation methods based on both traditional and deep learning approaches, challenges persist. Conventional UNet architectures predominantly utilize convolutional operations that focus on local features, which limits their ability to capture long-range spatial dependencies essential for the precise segmentation of thin and intricate retinal vessels. Consequently, this limitation often leads to segmentation discontinuities, misclassification of pathological regions, and elevated false positive rates. While attention-based techniques have been proposed to address these issues, they often introduce significant computational complexity, which can hinder their practical application in clinical settings. To overcome these challenges, this study presents three hybrid architectures VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet that integrate robust pre-trained CNN encoders into the UNet framework. These models are specifically designed to enhance feature extraction and segmentation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Compared to existing traditional UNet models and attention-based variants, our approach eliminates the need for additional complex modules by leveraging transfer learning with established CNNs. This enables more effective segmentation of fine vascular structures and improved generalization across diverse retinal imaging conditions, making our models well-suited for real-time clinical applications. The proposed architectures leverage the strengths of pre-trained convolutional neural networks, known for their efficacy in medical image analysis tasks such as diabetic retinopathy classification [18] . VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet exploit deep hierarchical features with small receptive fields to refine fine vessel delineation, while ResNet50-UNet employs residual connections to facilitate gradient flow and improve feature propagation in deeper layers. The main contributions of this study are as follows: – We propose three enhanced UNet-based architectures by integrating powerful deep encoders: VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50 to improve retinal vessel segmentation performance. These architectures leverage the strengths of pretrained convolutional networks to extract rich and discriminative features. – We demonstrate that these models capture more informative and contextually relevant features from retinal images, resulting in better vessel connectivity and continuity. This leads to a significant reduction in false positives compared to traditional UNet and shallow CNN-based segmentation methods. – We show that the use of residual learning in the ResNet50-UNet architecture effectively alleviates the vanishing gradient problem, facilitating deeper feature learning and more stable training. This contributes to more robust and accurate segmentation, especially in complex and low-contrast vascular regions. We propose three enhanced UNet-based architectures by integrating powerful deep encoders: VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50 to improve retinal vessel segmentation performance. These architectures leverage the strengths of pretrained convolutional networks to extract rich and discriminative features. We demonstrate that these models capture more informative and contextually relevant features from retinal images, resulting in better vessel connectivity and continuity. This leads to a significant reduction in false positives compared to traditional UNet and shallow CNN-based segmentation methods. We show that the use of residual learning in the ResNet50-UNet architecture effectively alleviates the vanishing gradient problem, facilitating deeper feature learning and more stable training. This contributes to more robust and accurate segmentation, especially in complex and low-contrast vascular regions. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of existing literature on blood vessel segmentation methodologies proposed by various researchers. Section 3 presents the proposed models for retinal blood vessel segmentation. In Section 4 , a detailed analysis of the experimental results is conducted, accompanied by a discussion of the findings. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper. Several research studies employing deep learning techniques have explored the challenge of segmenting retinal vessels. In [19] , the authors introduced the Residual SimAM Pyramid-Spatial Attention UNet (RSP-SA UNet), an enhanced UNet architecture designed to improve blood vessel segmentation. This model incorporates key modifications to the encoding, decoding, and upsampling layers. Specifically, the proposed RSP structure integrates a residual framework with SimAM and Pyramid Segmentation Attention (PSA), enabling the extraction of multi-scale spatial information and essential features across dimensions with greater accuracy. Additionally, spatial attention (SA) is incorporated into the upsampling layer to perform multi-attention mapping on the input feature map, enhancing the segmentation of small and low-contrast blood vessels. The effectiveness of RSP-SA UNet was validated on the CHASE_DB1, DRIVE, and STARE datasets, achieving segmentation accuracy (ACC) scores of 0.9763, 0.9704, and 0.9724, respectively. Furthermore, the area under the ROC curve (AUC) reached 0.9896, 0.9858, and 0.9906, demonstrating the model’s high precision and robustness in retinal vessel segmentation. In [20] , the authors proposed an improved U-Net-based model for retinal vessel segmentation, incorporating multi-scale feature extraction and fusion techniques. The conventional convolutional layers of U-Net were replaced with an enhanced dilated residual module, which, combined with a dual attention mechanism and varying dilation rates, facilitates more effective extraction of multi-scale vascular features. Additionally, an adaptive feature fusion module was introduced in the skip connections to improve vessel connectivity. To further optimize network training, a hybrid loss function was employed to address the class imbalance between blood vessels and the background. Experimental evaluations on the DRIVE and CHASE_DB1 datasets demonstrated the model’s effectiveness, achieving accuracy scores of 96.27% and 96.96%, sensitivity of 81.32% and 82.59%, and AUC values of 98.34% and 98.70%, respectively. These results underscore the model’s superior segmentation performance. Deep learning-based models have also been successfully applied to diabetic retinopathy detection, an area closely related to retinal vessel segmentation. CNN architectures such as VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet152-V2 have demonstrated high accuracy in DR classification, highlighting the effectiveness of deep feature extraction techniques in medical image analysis [18] . These models leverage pretrained deep networks to enhance feature representation, a strategy that is also beneficial for vessel segmentation. More recent advancements have explored feature attention mechanisms and spatial refinement techniques to improve segmentation performance, as demonstrated in the CCS-UNet and SE-UNet models [21,22] . These architectures incorporate channel and spatial attention mechanisms to enhance vessel feature extraction, mitigating the challenges posed by scale variations and background noise. In [23] , the authors proposed a hybrid approach that combines pre-processing, data augmentation, and a deep learning model for retinal vessel segmentation. The pre-processing step was implemented to address irregular illumination issues and enhance the contrast between the background and retinal blood vessels. Following this, a convolutional neural network (CNN) was designed and trained for vessel extraction. To improve training performance, data augmentation was applied during the training phase. The CNN model was trained and evaluated on the DRIVE dataset, a widely used benchmark for retinal vessel segmentation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed system achieved a sensitivity of 77.78%, specificity of 97.84%, precision of 84.17%, and accuracy of 95.27%, highlighting its effectiveness in extracting retinal blood vessels. A similar illumination normalization strategy was employed in diabetic retinopathy detection studies, demonstrating improvements in image quality and aiding CNN-based analysis [6] . Such preprocessing techniques are particularly useful for enhancing segmentation accuracy. In [24] , the authors proposed a U-Net-based architecture for segmenting retinal blood vessels from fundus images. To further enhance the performance of the proposed method, three pre-processing algorithms were introduced. Experimental evaluation on the publicly available DRIVE dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach, achieving an average accuracy of 95.77%, sensitivity of 74.36%, specificity of 98.38%, and an F1 score of 79.31%. Beyond CNN-based approaches, optimization techniques such as the Barnacles Mating Optimizer (BMO) have been explored in other biomedical imaging applications, improving classification accuracy in malaria detection through deep transfer learning strategies [25] . These optimization-based deep learning models could be adapted to vessel segmentation to enhance convergence and model efficiency. More recent works have focused on enhancing UNet-based models with advanced attention mechanisms, such as squeeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks and cross-channel spatial attention (CCSA) modules. SE-UNet, an improved UNet-based framework, integrates adaptive feature selection via SE blocks, improving feature suppression in nonvascular regions and strengthening vessel-specific feature extraction [21] . Similarly, CCS-UNet incorporates ResNeSt blocks and soft attention mechanisms to improve information flow across channels, leading to better vascular segmentation results [22] . These strategies have been validated on multiple datasets, demonstrating superior segmentation performance compared to traditional UNet-based architectures. In [26] , a novel retinal vessel segmentation approach based on deep learning is introduced. The proposed method enhances segmentation performance by increasing the convolutional kernel size, allowing for more effective feature extraction by covering vessel pixels and their neighboring regions. The primary contribution involves determining the optimal kernel size in relation to retinal image resolution through an experimental approach. Based on these findings, an extended U-Net architecture is developed, integrating convolutional layers with the identified kernel sizes. The method is evaluated on two public datasets, DRIVE and HRF, which have different resolutions. The results demonstrate superior segmentation performance, with optimal kernel sizes of 5 × 5 for DRIVE and 7 × 7 for HRF. The model achieves an average accuracy of 97.85% and sensitivity of 84.74% on DRIVE, while attaining 96.40% accuracy and 80.30% sensitivity on HRF, outperforming the standard U-Net. In [27] , the authors introduced automated segmentation models for retinal vessel segmentation utilizing convolutional neural networks. To mitigate noise introduced by interpolating small retinal patches to high resolutions, the study incorporates additional convolutional layers into standard deep architectures, enhancing adaptability to varying resolutions. The proposed models include LeNet, Modified AlexNet (M-AlexNet), Modified ZF-Net (M-ZF-Net), Modified VGG (M-VGG), and Deformable-ConvNet, with the latter being applied to retinal vessel segmentation for the first time. The models were trained from scratch and evaluated on the DRIVE and STARE datasets. The best-performing model achieved an accuracy of 0.9628/0.9690, a loss of 0.1045/0.0968, and an AUC of 0.9764/0.9844 on DRIVE/STARE. A comparative analysis with other segmentation methods demonstrated the superior performance of CNN-based approaches. Other studies have proposed hybrid UNet-based architectures that incorporate multi-scale attention, domain adaptation, and multi-branch feature fusion techniques. LadderNet [28] combines multiple parallel paths for feature extraction, enabling improved vascular segmentation in retinal imaging tasks. IterNet [29] , another refined U-Net model, exploits structural redundancy in vessel networks, demonstrating superior segmentation performance compared to conventional models. Additionally, multi-level attention mechanisms, such as attention gates [30] and NFN+ cascaded U-Net structures [31] , have been introduced to improve retinal vessel segmentation accuracy by optimizing spatial and semantic feature fusion. In [32] , the authors introduce a novel deep learning-based model for retinal vessel segmentation, termed Multichannel U-Net (M-UNet), which incorporates multi-scale equalization sampling to enhance vessel extraction. This technique generates new image data by splicing patches, while the M-UNet architecture is utilized to train the segmentation model. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on grayscale images, the proposed model processes three-channel images as input. The performance of M-UNet is evaluated on the DRIVE and STARE datasets. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing vessel networks, particularly in extracting peripheral vascular structures. The method achieves an average accuracy of 0.9716, a sensitivity of 0.8168, a specificity of 0.9860, and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.9843 on the DRIVE dataset. In [33] , five advanced deep learning models: U-Net, DenseU-Net, LadderNet, R2U-Net, and ATTU-Net along with an enhanced customized R2-ATT U-Net, were employed for retinal blood vessel segmentation. The segmentation process utilized a patch extraction approach, generating 10,000 patches per image, with 8,000 allocated for training and 2,000 for testing on the publicly available STARE dataset. Each model underwent training and evaluation, with a comprehensive analysis including test logs, ROC curves, precision–recall curves, confusion matrices, and key performance metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, precision, and AUC. Comparative analysis demonstrated that LadderNet achieved the highest accuracy of 0.971, highlighting its competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the enhanced R2-ATT U-Net exhibited strong performance, closely approaching that of LadderNet. In [34] , the authors proposed MSTP-Net, a Multi-Scale Three-Path Network for retinal vessel segmentation. The architecture consisted of a backbone and three output paths: the Local Path, Global Path, and Fusion Path. The backbone transformed the input image into high-level feature representations. The Local Path captured fine-grained vascular details, the Global Path extracted the overall vessel structure, and the Fusion Path combined local and global features to generate fusion features. Finally, the local, global, and fusion features were integrated to produce the final segmentation output. The method was evaluated on four public retinal datasets (DRIVE, STARE, CHASE_DB1, and HRF), and the results showed that MSTP-Net achieved competitive performance in retinal vessel segmentation. In [35] , the authors introduced a retinal vessel segmentation network based on U2Net, enhanced with feature channel attention and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). They integrated channel and spatial attention into the RSU blocks to better highlight important regions and reduce noise. Dilated convolutions were also used to enlarge the receptive field and improve contextual understanding. Evaluated on multiple clinical datasets, the model achieved high accuracy (98.71%), demonstrating strong segmentation performance. The network was deemed generalizable to other medical image segmentation tasks involving complex structures and scale variations. In [36] , a novel segmentation network named SMFDNet, which combines spatial and multi-frequency domain features, was proposed specifically for vessel segmentation in OCTA fundus images. This network enhances segmentation accuracy by effectively integrating these complementary features. The method was evaluated on three public datasets: Retinal Vessels Images in OCTA (REVIO), Retinal OCT-Angiography Vessel Segmentation (ROSE), and Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography-500 (OCTA-500). Experimental results demonstrate that SMFDNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially in handling low-contrast regions and complex vascular structures. In [37] , the authors introduced the RetinaDA dataset for retinal vessel segmentation, which consolidates images from six publicly available datasets. By incorporating diverse fundus images, RetinaDA facilitates benchmarking of domain adaptation models designed to generalize effectively across different retinal vessel domains. Despite significant advancements in deep learning-based retinal vessel segmentation, existing models still face several challenges that hinder their effectiveness in real-world applications. Traditional UNet-based architectures have demonstrated strong performance in medical image segmentation; however, their reliance on convolutional operations limits their ability to capture long-range dependencies, which is crucial for segmenting complex and fine vascular structures. This limitation leads to segmentation inaccuracies, particularly in distinguishing vessels from other pathological features such as microaneurysms and hemorrhages. While modifications like residual learning and attention mechanisms have been proposed to mitigate these challenges, many existing models require additional computational resources, making them less suitable for real-time clinical applications. Recent studies have explored integrating attention modules such as SE blocks and cross-channel spatial attention (CCSA) to refine feature selection and improve segmentation accuracy [21,22] . Although these methods have yielded improved Dice coefficients, they introduce additional architectural complexity and computational overhead, making them challenging to deploy in practical settings. Furthermore, existing models often struggle with generalization across different datasets, as performance varies significantly when transitioning from one dataset (e.g., DRIVE) to another (e.g., CHASE DB1 or STARE). This variation suggests that models optimized on a single dataset may not be robust enough to handle diverse retinal imaging conditions. Another critical limitation in current segmentation approaches is the lack of effective multi-scale feature fusion. Many deep learning models extract features at different hierarchical levels but fail to efficiently integrate spatial and contextual information. This can lead to fragmented vessel structures and discontinuities in segmentation outputs, particularly in areas with low contrast or overlapping anatomical structures. Although some architectures incorporate multi-scale processing, they often require additional training time and parameter tuning, which reduces their efficiency in real-time applications. Moreover, while deep learning models have achieved high accuracy, explainability and interpretability remain significant challenges in medical AI. Many segmentation models function as black-box systems, providing limited insights into their decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses a barrier to clinical adoption, as medical practitioners require trustworthy and interpretable AI-assisted tools. Methods such as Grad-CAM and SHAP have been proposed to enhance explainability, but their integration into vessel segmentation models remains an underexplored area. To address these gaps, this study introduces VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet, leveraging the strengths of deep feature extraction and spatial reconstruction while maintaining computational efficiency. Unlike attention-enhanced architectures that increase model complexity, the proposed models integrate well-established deep learning frameworks within the UNet structure, achieving competitive segmentation accuracy without requiring additional computational overhead. The incorporation of VGG-based architectures provides deep hierarchical feature extraction, while ResNet50-UNet benefits from residual learning, improving gradient flow and feature propagation. By optimizing feature extraction and spatial reconstruction, the proposed models aim to enhance vessel connectivity, minimize segmentation errors, and improve generalization across datasets. Additionally, this study sets the groundwork for future improvements by identifying areas where attention mechanisms, multi-scale feature fusion, and explainability-driven AI can be further integrated to enhance segmentation accuracy and robustness. The proposed models serve as an efficient and scalable solution for retinal vessel segmentation, making them suitable for real-time clinical applications and large-scale screening programs for diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. Given these limitations, particularly the difficulty in capturing long-range spatial dependencies, the high false positive rates, and the computational cost of complex attention mechanisms, there is a clear need for an alternative segmentation approach that balances accuracy with efficiency. This motivates the development of our proposed hybrid models — VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet — which incorporate pre-trained encoders into the UNet framework to improve feature extraction and vessel continuity while minimizing architectural complexity. The Vessel Segmentation Dataset from Kaggle [38] is designed for vessel segmentation tasks and comprises 40 training images and 20 test images, each accompanied by corresponding ground truth masks. The images are primarily grayscale, while the segmentation masks are binary, differentiating vessel structures from the background. This dataset was utilized to train and evaluate deep learning-based segmentation models, particularly for retinal vessel analysis and medical image processing. It enables the development of automated vessel extraction techniques, which are essential for applications such as ophthalmic disease diagnosis and vascular structure analysis. The VGG16-UNet model is a hybrid architecture that combines the VGG16 network, a pre-trained image classification model on ImageNet, with the UNet structure, designed for semantic segmentation. This combination leverages the powerful feature extraction capabilities of VGG16 while integrating an efficient spatial reconstruction mechanism through the UNet decoder. The VGG19-UNet model is a deep learning architecture designed for image segmentation, leveraging the VGG19 network as an encoder and incorporating a U-Net-style decoder. The model consists of three primary components: the encoder, which extracts hierarchical features from the input image; the center block, which further refines the deepest feature representations; and the decoder, which reconstructs the segmentation map by progressively upsampling and merging features. The encoder is based on the VGG19 architecture, a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) with 19 layers, originally designed for image classification. Given an input image x , the encoder extracts feature maps through a series of convolutional layers: (10) E ( x ) = { f 1 ( x ) , f 2 ( x ) , … , f n ( x ) } where f i ( x ) represents the output feature maps at different depths of the network. Each convolutional layer applies the following transformation: (11) f i ( x ) = σ ( W i ∗ x + b i ) where, W i and b i are the learned weights and biases, ∗ denotes the convolution operation, and σ is the activation function (ReLU in this case). The encoder outputs a set of feature maps at different resolutions, which are used in both the center block and the decoder. The center block refines the deepest feature representation using additional convolutional layers: (12) c ( x ) = σ ( W c 2 ∗ σ ( W c 1 ∗ x + b c 1 ) + b c 2 ) where W c 1 and W c 2 are convolutional filters with corresponding biases b c 1 and b c 2 . This stage helps capture high-level contextual information before upsampling in the decoder. The decoder reconstructs the segmentation map by progressively upsampling and concatenating the encoder’s feature maps. Each decoder block includes an upsampling operation followed by a sequence of convolutional layers: (13) d i ( x ) = σ ( W d 2 ∗ σ ( W d 1 ∗ Upsample ( x ) + b d 1 ) + b d 2 ) where W d 1 and W d 2 are convolutional filters, and the upsampling function increases the spatial resolution of feature maps by a factor of 2. The decoder also employs skip connections by concatenating encoder features at corresponding levels: (14) d i ( x ) = Concat ( Upsample ( x ) , f n − i ( x ) ) This skip connection mechanism helps retain spatial information lost during downsampling. The proposed models VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet were trained using a batch size of 4 and an initial learning rate of 0.001 over 80 epochs. These architectures were selected due to their strong performance in image segmentation tasks. The VGG-based models leverage deep hierarchical features for precise localization, while ResNet50-UNet benefits from residual connections, which facilitate gradient flow and improve training stability in deeper networks. The batch size of 4 was chosen to accommodate the high-resolution input images and the memory limitations of the available hardware. Smaller batch sizes are often beneficial in medical imaging applications, as they allow the model to process detailed spatial features without compromising training stability. Additionally, small batches can introduce useful stochasticity into the optimization process, potentially enhancing generalization. The learning rate of 0.001 was selected as a standard initialization for the Adam optimizer, which is widely used for its adaptive learning rate capabilities and efficiency in converging toward optimal solutions. This value provides a good balance between convergence speed and stability, particularly when training deep neural networks. The training process employed the Adam optimizer in conjunction with the Cross Entropy Loss function, which is appropriate for multi-class semantic segmentation tasks. Overall, the selected training configuration was designed to balance computational efficiency with model performance, enabling stable convergence while preserving fine-grained details in the segmentation outputs. To evaluate the performance of the proposed models (VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet), two key metrics were employed: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Loss Function. These metrics assess both the segmentation accuracy and the optimization process of the models. The Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) is a widely used metric for image segmentation, measuring the overlap between the predicted segmentation ( P ) and the ground truth ( G ). It is defined as: (24) DSC = 2 | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | In terms of pixel-wise values, the formula can be rewritten as: (25) DSC = 2 ∑ i = 1 N P i G i ∑ i = 1 N P i + ∑ i = 1 N G i where: • P i represents the predicted binary segmentation map at pixel i , • G i represents the ground truth segmentation at pixel i , • N is the total number of pixels in the image. P i represents the predicted binary segmentation map at pixel i , G i represents the ground truth segmentation at pixel i , N is the total number of pixels in the image. The numerator calculates the number of correctly segmented pixels (true positives) multiplied by 2. The denominator is the sum of all pixels in the predicted and ground truth masks. For segmentation tasks such as VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet, the Cross-Entropy Loss is applied pixel-wise, meaning that each pixel in the image is treated as a separate classification problem. The loss function is computed as: (26) L Seg = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N ∑ c = 1 C G i , c log ( P i , c ) where: • N is the total number of pixels in the image, • C is the number of segmentation classes, • G i , c is a binary indicator (0 or 1) if class label c is the correct classification for pixel i , • P i , c is the predicted probability that pixel i belongs to class c . N is the total number of pixels in the image, C is the number of segmentation classes, G i , c is a binary indicator (0 or 1) if class label c is the correct classification for pixel i , P i , c is the predicted probability that pixel i belongs to class c . Fig. 5 compares the performance of three UNet-based architectures VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet for retinal vessel segmentation. The figure includes the original retinal image, the ground truth segmentation, and the outputs of the three models. This analysis evaluates the effectiveness of each model in segmenting retinal vessels, a task critical for diagnosing and monitoring eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma. The original retinal image serves as the input to the segmentation models. Retinal images are characterized by complex structures, including blood vessels, the optic disc, and the macula. The quality of the original image, including factors such as contrast, noise, and resolution, significantly influences the segmentation task. The ground truth, which is a manually annotated binary mask of the retinal vessels, provides the benchmark for evaluating the models. It ideally captures all vessel structures, including thin and low-contrast vessels, which are often challenging to segment accurately. The VGG16-UNet model, which uses the VGG16 architecture as its encoder, is relatively simple and shallow compared to the other models. While it may perform reasonably well in segmenting thicker vessels, it often struggles with thin or low-contrast vessels due to its limited ability to capture fine details. Additionally, it may produce false positives in noisy regions, reducing its overall accuracy. The VGG19-UNet model, which employs a deeper VGG19 encoder, shows slight improvements over VGG16-UNet. The additional layers in VGG19 allow it to capture more complex features, resulting in better segmentation of thicker vessels. However, like VGG16-UNet, it may still struggle with thin or low-contrast vessels and noisy regions. In contrast, the ResNet50-UNet model, which utilizes the ResNet50 encoder, demonstrates superior performance. The residual connections in ResNet50 enable better gradient flow and feature extraction, allowing the model to capture both high-level and low-level features effectively. This makes ResNet50-UNet particularly well-suited for segmenting thin and low-contrast vessels, as well as handling complex structures such as vessel branching and crossings. The segmentation output of ResNet50-UNet is expected to be closest to the ground truth, with fewer missed vessels and false positives compared to the VGG-based models. The challenges in retinal vessel segmentation are evident in the figure. Thin vessels, which are often difficult to segment due to their low contrast and small size, are better captured by ResNet50-UNet. Noise and artifacts in retinal images, such as uneven illumination, can also affect segmentation performance. ResNet50-UNet’s robustness to noise gives it an advantage in producing accurate segmentations in such conditions. Additionally, the complex structures of vessel branching and crossings require precise segmentation, which ResNet50-UNet achieves through its multi-scale feature extraction capabilities. To complement the visual comparison, quantitative metrics such as Intersection over Union (IoU), Dice coefficient, sensitivity, and specificity should be reported. These metrics provide an objective assessment of model performance and are expected to show higher scores for ResNet50-UNet compared to the VGG-based models. The clinical relevance of accurate retinal vessel segmentation cannot be overstated, as it is crucial for diagnosing and monitoring eye diseases. ResNet50-UNet’s superior performance makes it a promising tool for clinical applications, although its computational cost should be considered, especially for real-time applications or large-scale screening programs. ResNet50-UNet outperforms VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet due to its ability to capture fine details and handle complex structures. However, the choice of model should consider the specific requirements of the task, including computational resources and the need for precision. Future work could explore advanced techniques, such as attention mechanisms or hybrid architectures, to further improve segmentation accuracy and robustness. It is essential to emphasize the trade-offs between model complexity and computational efficiency, particularly in the context of real-time applications. Although ResNet50-UNet delivers superior segmentation performance due to its deeper architecture and the incorporation of residual connections, it demands significantly higher computational resources. This increased complexity may hinder its deployment in time-sensitive or resource-constrained environments. In comparison, VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet provide a more practical balance, offering competitive segmentation accuracy while reducing inference time and memory consumption. These characteristics make them more suitable for real-time applications, such as embedded systems or clinical scenarios requiring fast and efficient processing. Table 1 presents the performance evaluation of UNet models with different backbone architectures, specifically VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50. The evaluation metrics include Loss and Dice Coefficient (Dice_Coef), which are commonly used in segmentation tasks to assess model performance. The results indicate that ResNet50-UNet achieves the best performance, with the lowest loss value of 0.09 and the highest Dice coefficient of 0.80. A lower loss suggests that the model’s predictions are closer to the ground truth, while a higher Dice coefficient reflects better segmentation accuracy. Both VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet exhibit similar performance, with a Dice coefficient of 0.79. However, VGG19-UNet achieves a slightly lower loss (0.10) compared to VGG16-UNet (0.11), suggesting a minor improvement in optimization. Despite the overall strong quantitative performance, the models exhibit specific challenges that warrant further examination. One notable difficulty lies in segmenting thin retinal vessels, which are characterized by low contrast and small spatial dimensions. Both VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet tend to miss some of these finer vessel structures or produce false positives in noisy regions, likely due to their limited depth and feature representation capacity. In contrast, ResNet50-UNet demonstrates improved sensitivity to these thin vessels, attributable to its residual connections and deeper architecture, which enable better feature extraction across multiple scales. Additionally, noisy regions caused by uneven illumination or image artifacts remain a challenge for all models, although ResNet50-UNet shows greater robustness in such conditions. These findings highlight the importance of model architecture in handling subtle and complex image features and suggest that future work could focus on integrating advanced noise reduction techniques or attention mechanisms to further improve segmentation accuracy in difficult regions. Overall, these findings suggest that incorporating ResNet50 as a backbone in the UNet architecture enhances segmentation performance compared to VGG-based architectures. This improvement can be attributed to ResNet50’s deeper architecture and the residual connections that help mitigate vanishing gradient issues, enabling better feature extraction. The proposed models demonstrate significant advantages over traditional U-Net variants, achieving comparable or superior performance with fewer architectural modifications and lower computational costs. Both VGG16-UNet and VGG19-UNet attain a Dice coefficient of 0.79, matching the performance of state-of-the-art U-Net extensions. However, ResNet50-UNet outperforms all other models in our dataset, achieving a Dice coefficient of 0.80, highlighting the effectiveness of residual learning in vessel segmentation. Unlike attention-based architectures such as SE-UNet [21] and CCS-UNet [22] , which incorporate complex attention mechanisms and feature recalibration modules, our models achieve comparable accuracy with a more efficient framework. The efficiency of our approach makes it particularly advantageous for real-time clinical applications, where computational cost and inference speed are critical factors. While attention-enhanced architectures may offer marginal improvements in Dice coefficient, they often require higher computational resources and longer training times, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments. The efficiency of our models is particularly relevant in clinical practice, where real-time inference is crucial. Unlike SE-UNet and CCS-UNet, which require additional attention modules and complex feature recalibration, our models achieve high accuracy using only pre-trained feature extractors. This design ensures faster inference and lower computational overhead, making our models more practical for deployment in medical imaging systems. The integration of VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50 within the U-Net framework allows for deep hierarchical feature extraction without the need for additional attention modules. ResNet50-UNet, in particular, benefits from deep residual connections that enhance feature propagation while maintaining efficiency. While SE-UNet and CCS-UNet show slightly higher Dice scores, the difference remains incremental ( ∼ 0.02–0.03 points), which may not be clinically significant. However, the simplicity and efficiency of our approach make it more feasible for deployment in medical imaging applications, where model interpretability and real-time processing are essential. Despite the strong performance of our models, further improvements could be explored to enhance segmentation accuracy and generalizability. One promising direction for future research is the integration of attention mechanisms such as Transformer-based self-attention modules or SE blocks to improve spatial feature refinement. The incorporation of spatial and channel attention mechanisms could further improve vessel segmentation accuracy by selectively enhancing relevant vascular structures while suppressing background noise. Multi-scale feature fusion techniques could also be explored to capture contextual information at different spatial resolutions, allowing for better vessel delineation. Inspired by CCS-UNet [22] , cross-channel spatial attention and hierarchical feature fusion could be integrated into our models to capture fine and coarse vessel details more effectively. By aggregating information across multiple scales, segmentation precision could be further improved without excessive computational costs. Another critical aspect for future exploration is the generalization of our models across multiple datasets. While our models have demonstrated strong performance on the Vessel Segmentation Dataset, additional evaluations on DRIVE, CHASE DB1, and STARE would provide further insights into their robustness. Domain adaptation techniques could be employed to enhance model generalizability across different imaging conditions, ensuring consistent performance across datasets. Improving cross-dataset generalization is essential for making segmentation models more robust to variations in image quality, noise, and lighting conditions, which are common challenges in real-world clinical applications. Future work will also focus on integrating explainability-driven AI techniques to enhance trust and interpretability in clinical applications. The use of visualization methods such as Grad-CAM and SHAP could provide insights into the decision-making process of our models, allowing clinicians to better understand why specific vessel structures are segmented in a particular way. Explainability is particularly important in medical AI, as it can help build confidence among practitioners and ensure that segmentation results align with expert interpretations. By improving transparency in AI-assisted segmentation, our models could facilitate wider adoption in clinical workflows. The comparative analysis demonstrates that our proposed models, particularly ResNet50-UNet, outperform traditional U-Net-based architectures while maintaining high computational efficiency. While SE-UNet and CCS-UNet exhibit slightly higher Dice coefficients, they introduce additional complexity that may not always be justified in real-world clinical settings. By balancing high segmentation accuracy, computational efficiency, and clinical feasibility, our models provide a scalable and deployable solution for medical imaging applications. Future research will focus on further architectural optimizations, dataset generalization techniques, and explainability improvements to refine segmentation performance and advance real-world applicability in ophthalmology and beyond. This study evaluated the performance of various UNet-based architectures for vessel segmentation, comparing VGG16-UNet, VGG19-UNet, and ResNet50-UNet with state-of-the-art models. The results demonstrated that ResNet50-UNet achieved the highest Dice coefficient of 0.80, outperforming traditional U-Net variants and other competing segmentation approaches. This improvement highlights the effectiveness of deep residual learning, which enhances feature extraction and gradient propagation, leading to more accurate vessel delineation. Despite these promising results, achieving higher segmentation accuracy remains a challenge in medical image analysis. Future research will focus on incorporating advanced attention mechanisms, multi-scale feature fusion, and domain adaptation techniques to further refine segmentation performance. The findings of this study emphasize the potential of deep learning-based methods in automating vessel segmentation, contributing to improved diagnostic accuracy and better patient outcomes. AI-clinic fusion: Multimodal deep learning redefines IBD diagnostics via synergistic CT-clinical feature integration Background Traditional methods like endoscopy and imaging are important for IBD management, which are limited by operator dependency, complexity, and high costs, making standardization and routine monitoring difficult. Methods In this study, seven machine learning algorithms were applied to the UK Biobank database to optimize the selection of clinical features and identify key variables associated with IBD. The nnUNetv2 model was then used for CT gut segmentation and validated by a local dataset. Next, the YOLOv10 algorithm was employed to accurately detect IBD lesion regions in the intestine. Finally, an IBD diagnostic model was developed by integrating the selected clinical features with the YOLOv10 identification results, thereby demonstrating the advantages of multimodal data integration. Results A machine learning-driven feature selection identified chronic abdominal pain, LDL-C, gender, TC, RDW, WBC, ALB, HDL-C, and neutrophil counts as clinical predictors. The nnUNetv2 model achieved high-precision intestinal segmentation, while YOLOv10 demonstrated robust lesion detection. A multimodal nomogram combining clinical features with YOLOv10-derived imaging biomarkers significantly enhanced IBD diagnosis, achieving an AUC of 0.967 that surpassed the clinical-only model (AUC = 0.730). This improvement highlights the synergistic value of deep learning-augmented diagnostics for classification accuracy. Conclusion Integrating clinical features with AI-driven image analysis improves IBD diagnostic precision, enabling better clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. Novelty To our knowledge, this is the first multimodal nomogram that combines the predictive clinical features of the UK Biobank scale with CT-based YOLOv10 lesion detection for IBD diagnosis. Different from prior models that solely rely on clinical data or radiomics, our approach achieves integration of population-level epidemiology and deep learning-based imaging, and was validated through external datasets. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of chronic inflammatory bowel disorders with unknown etiology, primarily encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). In recent years, the global incidence of IBD has increased markedly, emerging as a major public health challenge worldwide [ 1 ]. According to analyses from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) database, the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) of IBD in China significantly increased from 0.74 (95% CI: 0.64–0.90) per 100,000 population in 1990 to 1.40 (1.21–1.68) in 2021 [ 2 ]. The chronic progressive course, relapsing-remitting nature, and complications (e.g., intestinal fistulas, strictures, and malignant transformation) of IBD not only severely impair patients' quality of life but also impose a substantial healthcare burden [ 3 ]. While conventional diagnostic modalities (e.g., endoscopy and imaging examinations) remain indispensable in IBD management, their subjective reliance on operator expertise, procedural complexity, and high costs hinder the standardization of diagnosis and widespread adoption of longitudinal monitoring. Early diagnosis and timely therapeutic intervention constitute the cornerstone for improving clinical outcomes and optimizing long-term health preservation [ 4 ]. Computed tomography (CT) imaging plays a central role in the diagnosis and evaluation of IBD, providing high-resolution anatomical information of the intestinal tract and enabling precise identification of pathological regions and associated complications [ 5 ]. CT imaging is widely utilized in IBD for assessing diverse clinical manifestations, including bowel wall thickening, luminal stenosis, fistula formation, and extraintestinal complications such as abscesses and intestinal obstruction [ 6 ]. Additionally, CT enterography (CTE), as a non-invasive diagnostic modality, has become an essential tool for diagnosing Crohn's disease and evaluating disease activity [ 7 , 8 ]. However, conventional CT image analysis faces multiple challenges: First, the complex anatomy of the intestinal tract and the time-consuming nature of lesion segmentation and recognition—often influenced by subjective interpretation-hinder standardized implementation in clinical practice [ 9 ]; Second, inadequate integration of multimodal data (e.g., clinical features and imaging biomarkers) may lead to the oversight of potential correlations, compromising diagnostic comprehensiveness and accuracy [ 10 ]; Finally, the heavy reliance on specialized radiologists for CT image analysis limits its feasibility for large-scale screening and dynamic monitoring [ 11 ]. These limitations underscore the urgent need to develop efficient and automated analytical tools. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has provided novel approaches to overcoming the aforementioned challenges. In the realm of medical imaging, artificial intelligence has showcased remarkable advancements in automated analytical capabilities. Specifically, nnUNet achieves state-of-the-art organ segmentation. Meanwhile, the YOLO family demonstrates exceptional lesion detection accuracy [ 12–14 ]. These technological innovations not only streamline diagnostic workflows but also enable objective, quantitative assessments that enhance clinical decision-making by providing granular insights into pathological manifestations. The synergy between high-resolution imaging and AI-driven analysis creates transformative opportunities for standardized interpretation and longitudinal monitoring of complex conditions, underscoring their pivotal role in modern radiology practice. Recent studies have shown that AI can construct predictive models through the integration of multimodal data (e.g. combining genomics, clinical indicators and imaging features), significantly improving the accuracy of IBD disease activity scoring and treatment response prediction [ 15 , 16 ]. For example, deep learning models have achieved over 90% accuracy in assessing mucosal healing during endoscopy [ 17 , 18 ]. These advancements highlight the pivotal role of AI in enabling precision diagnosis and treatment of IBD, while also laying the technical foundation for the development of efficient and scalable automated diagnostic tools. Unlike prior IBD models that have leveraged clinical data, radiomics, or convolutional networks in isolation, this study pioneers the synergistic integration of UK Biobank-scale clinical features with YOLOv10-based CT lesion detection—a combination not previously attempted for IBD diagnosis. The research objectives were four-fold: (1) to refine clinical feature selection through multi-algorithm machine learning optimization leveraging the UK Biobank dataset; (2) to perform high-precision CT-based intestinal segmentation using the nnUNetv2 framework, with cross-validation of model generalizability on a localized imaging cohort; (3) to implement the YOLOv10 architecture for automated, high-sensitivity detection of IBD-specific intestinal lesions; and (4) to construct a multimodal nomogram integrating both clinical and imaging biomarkers to quantitatively demonstrate the diagnostic superiority of combined feature analysis. Combining multi-modal data with deep learning creates a novel IBD diagnostic workflow. This approach improves precision diagnosis and enables longitudinal monitoring beyond conventional methods. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (Approval No. K2023-295). The requirement for informed consent was waived by the Ethics Review Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University due to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of anonymized data. This study developed an intelligent analysis model for intestinal lesions by integrating multi-source heterogeneous data, with the workflow detailed as follows: First, we identified IBD patients from the UK Biobank cohort using International Organization for the Study of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IOIBD) diagnostic criteria. Second, to enhance model robustness, we pre-trained an intestinal segmentation model using the publicly available Whole-Organ Radiomics Dataset (WORD), comprising 30,495 high-resolution abdominal CT images from 150 subjects. This dataset fully captures intestinal anatomy and surrounding tissues, with standardized preprocessing to eliminate scanner-related variations and ensure cross-institutional generalizability. Finally, A prospective validation cohort was established by recruiting 82 IBD patients (4 patients were excluded due to missing data. Missing rate: 4/86 = 4.65%) and 110 healthy controls (16 patients were excluded due to missing data. Missing rate: 16/126 = 12.70%) from the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University between January 2019 and December 2024. Strict inclusion criteria followed IOIBD diagnostic standards, while exclusion criteria encompassed: the inclusion criteria were: patients definitively diagnosed with IBD according to the diagnostic standards recommended by the IOIBD. The exclusion criteria were: (i) a history of intestinal resection; (ii) definitive treatment including anti-tuberculosis drugs, immunosuppressive drugs, and chemotherapy drugs prior to referral to the hospital; (iii) under 15 years of age; (iv) incomplete clinical data, including clinical manifestations, laboratory tests, endoscopic findings, radiological and histopathological features, due to various reasons; and (v) uncertain diagnosis or a shift from IBD to another disease during follow-up. All enrolled patients underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans focusing on typical IBD lesions (ulcers, strictures, fistulas). Lesion annotations ("lesion" labels) were independently performed by two senior radiologists using LabelImg, with inter-rater agreement confirmed by Kappa testing (κ > 0.85). Fig. 1 illustrates the overall study design and data flow, demonstrating an innovative framework integrating population-level phenomics with radiomics for developing interpretable IBD diagnostic models. To ensure the generalizability of the selected clinical features in the local dataset, we extracted the following clinical features from the UK Biobank: demographic information (age, gender), lifestyle factors (smoking status), symptom profiles (abdominal/stomach pain 3+ months), and laboratory test results (C-reactive protein, lipid profile, complete blood count, and blood biochemistry indicators). To ensure data quality, we preprocessed the raw data, including the removal of outliers based on the 3-standard deviation rule and the standardization of continuous variables using Z-score normalization. To identify the most predictive clinical features, we employed seven widely used machine learning algorithms for model construction and comparison. These included Logistic Regression (LR), Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), LightGBM, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Random Forest (RF). All models were trained using 5-fold cross-validation to mitigate the risk of overfitting and ensure the robustness of model performance. After model training, the optimal model was selected based on its performance on the internal validation set, specifically by comparing the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC). Subsequently, we performed variable importance ranking based on this optimal model and selected the top 10 most important clinical features. Additionally, we further validated these selected features in the local dataset to ensure the reliability of the clinical feature selection. This study adopted the nnUNetv2 framework, a state-of-the-art deep learning architecture renowned for its computational efficiency and robust performance in medical image segmentation tasks. Specifically, we employed the 2D U-Net architecture under the nnUNetv2 framework for model training. The 2D U-Net consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder extracts image features through convolutional and downsampling layers, while the decoder gradually restores image resolution and generates segmentation masks through upsampling and convolutional layers. We used the Cross-Entropy Loss as the optimization objective and the Adam optimizer (initial learning rate of 3 × 10 −4 ) for model training. To enhance convergence stability, we incorporated an adaptive learning rate scheduling mechanism (ReduceLROnPlateau), wherein the learning rate was reduced by a factor of 0.1 if validation loss plateaued for three consecutive epochs without improvement. All training procedures were executed on the high-performance computing cluster at Chongqing Medical University, employing a batch size of 16 and a total of 1000 training epochs. Prior to model training, rigorous preprocessing protocols were applied to standardize the CT imagery. Raw DICOM data underwent resampling to a uniform isotropic resolution of 1 mm 3 , followed by grayscale normalization that scaled Hounsfield Unit (HU) values to the [0,1] range. To focus model attention on clinically relevant regions, images were center-cropped to retain the intestinal anatomy while excluding extraneous tissues. Furthermore, a comprehensive data augmentation strategy was implemented to improve model generalization, including: (1) random rotation (±15°), (2) isotropic scaling (0.9–1.1 × ), and (3) bidirectional flipping (horizontal/vertical axes). These transformations were dynamically applied during training to simulate anatomical variability and imaging artifacts, thereby enhancing the model's robustness across heterogeneous clinical datasets. To evaluate the model's performance, we divided the WORD dataset (Number of slices = 30,495) into training, validation, and test sets with ratios of 70%, 15%, and 15% (Number of slices = 21347, 4574, and 4574, respectively), respectively. During training, we monitored the model's performance on the validation set in real-time and selected the model with the highest Dice coefficient on the validation set as the final model. On the test set, we comprehensively evaluated the model's performance using multiple metrics, including the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Intersection over Union (IoU). After completing model training and validation, we applied the trained 2D U-Net model to the local dataset to generate intestinal segmentation results. The local dataset included abdominal CT images from multiple IBD patients, with imaging parameters consistent with those of the WORD dataset. To ensure the accuracy of the segmentation results, we preprocessed the local data using the same methods as the training data. Ultimately, we obtained segmentation masks for each patient, providing foundational data for subsequent IBD lesion region identification. In summary, the function of the nnUNetv2 model is to segment and trim the intestinal area from a full abdominal CT scan and then pass it on to YOLOv10 for lesion detection. The local dataset (Number of lesion slices = 4298; Number of normal slices = 5624) was used for the identification of intestinal IBD lesion regions. The dataset was divided into training and validation sets in a 7:3 ratio, with the training set used for model training and the validation set for performance evaluation. You Only Look Once version 10 (YOLOv10) is a single-stage object detection deep learning model widely recognized for its efficiency and accuracy in the field of object detection. We adopted the default configuration of YOLOv10 for model training, including the use of CSPDarknet53 as the backbone network, PANet as the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN), and the Complete Intersection over Union Loss (CIoU Loss) as the optimization objective. During training, we employed the AdamW optimizer (initial learning rate of 1 × 10 −3 ) and utilized the Cosine Annealing Learning Rate Scheduler to dynamically adjust the learning rate. All training was conducted on the supercomputing platform of Chongqing Medical University, with a batch size of 16 and a total of 300 epochs. To evaluate the model's performance, we comprehensively tested the trained YOLOv10 model on the validation set. The primary evaluation metrics included Average Precision (AP), Mean Average Precision (mAP), Recall, and F1 Score. Since each patient had multiple CT imaging slices, our processing strategy was as follows: (1) compare the bounding boxes identified by YOLOv10 with the lesion boxes annotated by radiologists and calculate the overlapping area (IoU); (2) if the IoU ≥0.50, consider the YOLOv10 identification as correct; (3) for all correctly identified boxes of a patient, calculate the average recognition confidence to determine the final recognition confidence of YOLOv10 for that patient. Based on the local dataset, we constructed two nomogram models for predicting IBD risk: (1) a model using the important features selected from the UK Biobank database, and (2) a model combining the selected important features with the recognition confidence scores from YOLOv10. To evaluate the predictive performance of the nomogram models, we employed a series of evaluation metrics, including the AUC-ROC, calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). The AUC-ROC was used to assess the model's discriminative ability, the calibration curve to evaluate the consistency between predicted probabilities and actual risks, and the DCA to assess the model's utility in clinical decision-making. Based on these metrics, we compared the two nomogram prediction models to evaluate the added value of incorporating YOLOv10. The gut segmentation model and IBD lesion identification model were constructed using phython 3.9.4. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of the statistical results, all statistical analysis of data was performed using SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.1. For data description, quantitative data following a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, and intergroup differences were compared using the t -test. For data with a skewed distribution, the median (interquartile range) was used, and intergroup differences were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as counts (percentages), and intergroup differences were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The local dataset included a total of 192 participants (82 IBD patients and 110 normal individuals). Table 1 presented the clinical characteristics of the two groups. As shown, IBD patients had significantly higher levels of C-reactive protein (CRP, P = 0.036), neutrophils (N, P = 0.028), and red cell distribution width (RDW, P < 0.001), as well as significantly lower levels of albumin (ALB, P = 0.004) and lymphocytes (L, P = 0.019) compared to normal individuals. Additionally, a majority of IBD patients had a history of smoking (59.76%, P = 0.002) and exhibited symptoms of abdominal/stomach pain 3+ months (74.39%, P = 0.007). After excluding participants with missing values, a total of 31,534 participants were ultimately selected from the UK Biobank. Their clinical characteristics were presented in Table 2 . Fig. 2 A indicated that LR was the optimal model (AUC = 0.700). Based on the variable importance ranking from the optimal model, the top 10 variables were abdominal/stomach pain 3+ months, L, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), gender, total cholesterol (TC), RDW, WBC, ALB, HDL-C, and N ( Fig. 2 B). Using these variables, we validated the model in the local dataset. Fig. 2 C showed that LR remained the optimal model and demonstrated good predictive performance (AUC = 0.840). The training process based on the WORD dataset was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1A–E . The results demonstrated that the CT intestinal segmentation model based on the 2D U-Net architecture performed exceptionally well on the WORD test set, achieving an average Dice coefficient of 0.976 and an average IoU of 0.953, indicating the model's ability to accurately segment intestinal structures. The application of the model on the local dataset further validated its generalization capability, with segmentation results highly consistent with manual annotations by radiologists. Specific results were shown in Fig. 3A2-A3 and B2-B3. Across the 9922 slices, 6672 suspected lesion regions were identified by YOLOv10. The results of this study demonstrated that the YOLOv10-based model for intestinal IBD lesion region recognition performed well on the validation set, achieving a mAP50 of 0.7829, a recall rate of 0.714, and a mAP50-95 of 0.399 ( Fig. 4 ). These results indicated that the model could accurately detect and localize intestinal lesion regions. Fig. 3A4 and B4 illustrated examples of IBD lesion regions identified by radiologists, while Fig. 3A5 and B5 showed examples of IBD lesion regions recognized by YOLOv10. Figs. 5 and 6 presented our findings. For the model constructed using only the selected important features, the AUC was 0.730 ( Fig. 5 A and B). The calibration curve showed a high consistency between the model's predicted probabilities and actual risks ( Fig. 5 C). DCA indicated that the nomogram prediction model demonstrated net benefits within a risk threshold range of 0.12–0.68 ( Fig. 5 D). After incorporating the recognition confidence scores from YOLOv10 as an additional variable, the constructed nomogram model performed exceptionally well (AUC = 0.967, Fig. 6 A and B), demonstrating its ability to effectively distinguish IBD patients from non-IBD patients. The calibration curve indicated improved consistency between predicted probabilities and actual risks ( Fig. 6 C). DCA further confirmed that the model provided high clinical net benefits across a wide range of threshold probabilities ( Fig. 6 D). This study introduces an innovative multimodal diagnostic paradigm for IBD, seamlessly integrating clinical biomarkers with cutting-edge AI-driven endoscopic image analysis. By synergistically combining optimized clinical predictors with lesion detection confidence scores from a YOLOv10-based system, we achieved a robust diagnostic performance (AUC-ROC = 0.967). Complementing this, a nnUNetv2-powered intestinal segmentation model provided anatomical precision (Dice = 0.976), while YOLOv10 demonstrated precise lesion localization (mAP50 = 0.783). These findings highlight the transformative potential of fusing clinical phenotyping with deep learning-enhanced endoscopy to elevate IBD diagnosis, offering a paradigm shift toward data-driven precision gastroenterology [ 19 , 20 ]. The diagnostic process of IBD is complicated by the diversity of its clinical manifestations and the nonspecificity of its symptoms in relation to those of other digestive disorders. Because of the lack of specificity in its clinical manifestations (e.g. abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, etc.), IBD can be easily confused with a wide range of diseases, such as chronic bacillary dysentery, amebic enterocolitis, and intestinal tuberculosis, which can lead to misdiagnosis or delayed treatment [ 21 ]. In addition, the etiologic mechanism of IBD is still unclear, involving genetic, environmental and immune factors, which makes its early diagnosis relatively difficult. Among the diagnostic tests, colonoscopy and imaging are indispensable in the diagnosis of IBD. Small colonoscopy is able to directly observe the intestinal mucosa and assess the degree of inflammation and lesion characteristics, but it is invasive and costly, thus limiting its application in mass screening [ 22 ]. Imaging provides high-resolution anatomical information, but there are still limitations in lesion identification and grading, especially in the context of complex intestinal anatomy, and differences in subjective interpretation may lead to inconsistent diagnostic results [ 7 ]. In addition, traditional screening methods often rely on the experience of specialists and lack a standardized process, resulting in impaired diagnostic accuracy and consistency, limitations that highlight the urgency of developing efficient and automated diagnostic tools. Currently available AI-assisted diagnostic methods mostly focus on lesion identification by colonoscopy [ 23 ], whereas in the early stages of IBD, the intestinal mucosa may only have mild inflammation or no obvious ulcer formation, and at this time colonoscopy may not be able to accurately capture these subtle lesions, leading to missed diagnosis. Second, enteroscopy mainly observes the colon and rectum, and may not be able to directly observe lesions in the small intestine, whereas IBD, especially Crohn's disease, may involve the small intestine, which limits the ability of enteroscopy in comprehensively evaluating the extent of IBD lesions. Third, the enteroscopic manifestations of IBD may be similar to other intestinal disorders, such as infectious enteritis and ischemic bowel disease, making it difficult to accurately differentiate between IBD and other intestinal disorders based solely on enteroscopy [ 24 ]. CT examination techniques such as CT or CT contrast of the small intestine (CTE) are able to assess small bowel lesions non-invasively and rapidly, and have a higher diagnostic value for types of IBD that may involve the small bowel, such as Crohn's disease. In particular, CTE can clearly outline the intestinal wall, lumen, and extraintestinal lesions, providing a comprehensive image of the bowel and surrounding tissues, and helping to evaluate extraintestinal complications of IBD, such as enlarged abdominal lymph nodes and mesenteric vasculopathy [ 25 ]. Our AI-driven approach aligns with recent advancements in medical imaging analysis. Deep learning models like nnUNet have been widely validated for organ segmentation tasks, achieving good performance in gastrointestinal imaging [ 26 , 27 ]. Similarly, YOLO-based frameworks have shown promise in detecting mucosal lesions in endoscopy [ 28 , 29 ]. However, prior studies predominantly focused on unimodal data (e.g. imaging or clinical features alone) [ 30 , 31 ], whereas our integration of both modalities addresses a critical gap in comprehensive IBD assessment. The superior AUC of the combined nomogram model (0.967 vs. 0.730 for clinical-only) highlights the additive value of AI-processed imaging biomarkers, corroborating emerging evidence that hybrid models outperform single-modality approaches in chronic disease diagnosis. The clinical implications of our findings are twofold. First, the automated segmentation and lesion detection framework could standardize CT image interpretation, reducing inter-observer variability inherent to conventional radiological assessments. Second, the integration of routine laboratory markers (e.g., CRP, albumin) with AI-derived imaging features enables dynamic monitoring of disease activity. This aligns with recent calls for personalized IBD management, where quantitative biomarkers guide therapeutic adjustments. For instance, the YOLOv10-derived confidence scores may serve as objective surrogates for mucosal healing, complementing invasive endoscopic evaluations. Such advancements could streamline clinical workflows and reduce reliance on subjective evaluations. Our study has several limitations. First, the validation of clinical features was conducted solely against healthy controls, without evaluating their discriminative power against disease comparators, which limits the assessment of specificity. Second, the limited sample size (n = 192) precluded stratified analyses by disease activity or severity. Third, while we validated the model using the WORD dataset, additional external validation with large multicenter cohorts is necessary to ensure generalizability. In conclusion, this AI framework integrates clinical phenotyping with imaging analytics to improve IBD diagnosis and enable personalized management. Future studies should validate the model across institutions, longitudinal datasets, and real-world settings. Combining quantitative imaging with clinical decision-making enhances triage, prognostic stratification, and patient outcomes. AI to protect AI: A modular pipeline for detecting label-flipping poisoning attacks Modern machine learning models are vulnerable to data poisoning attacks that compromise the integrity of their training data, with label flipping being a particularly insidious variant. In a label flipping attack, an adversary maliciously alters a fraction of the training labels to mislead the model, which can significantly degrade performance or cause targeted misclassifications while often evading simple detection. In this work, we address this threat by introducing a modular, attack-agnostic detection framework (“AI to Protect AI”) that monitors model behaviour for poisoning indicators without requiring internal access or changes to the target model. A Behaviour Monitoring Module (BMM) continuously observes the model’s outputs, extracting telltale features such as prediction probabilities, entropy, and margins for each input. These features are analysed by an ensemble of detector models, including supervised classifiers and unsupervised anomaly detectors, that collaboratively flag suspicious training samples indicative of label tampering. The proposed framework is dataset-agnostic and model-agnostic, as demonstrated across diverse image classification tasks using the MNIST (handwritten digits), CIFAR-10 (natural images), and ChestXray14 (medical X-rays) datasets. Experimental results indicate that the system reliably detects poisoned data with high accuracy (e.g., an area under the ROC curve exceeding 0.95 on MNIST, above 0.90 on CIFAR-10, and up to 0.85 on ChestXray14), while maintaining low false alarm rates. This work highlights a novel “AI to protect AI” approach, leveraging multiple lightweight detectors in concert to safeguard learning processes across different domains and thereby enhance the security and trustworthiness of AI systems.
