Public datasets were used for the research. Artificial intelligence (AI) models are now being used in a wide range of application areas, such as autonomous vehicles, industrial control systems and healthcare diagnosis, where system safety and security are paramount ( Abisoye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Marulli et al., 2022 ). The widespread adoption has made it more important than ever to guarantee the secure and reliable ML models. The machine learning (ML) models and Deep Neural Networks (DNN) are exposed to various adversarial attacks, which include evasion attacks, where an attacker perturbs the input data to deceive the model at inference; backdoor attacks, where the model is trained to associate a trigger with a specific target label; and poisoning attacks, where the training data is modified so that the predictive model is manipulated. These vulnerabilities are dangerous in the context of safety-critical applications—for example, in AI-powered medical and diagnostic systems that can cause serious health issues or other critical infrastructures such as energy and defence sectors ( Chen et al., 2021 ). Real-world incidents provide evidence for the potential threat: published reports, for example, have described cases in which industrially relevant companies faced security vulnerabilities in their machine learning systems when fed with data containing poison, and crowd-sourced data repositories (e.g. VirusTotal for malware samples) have already been identified to be affected by maliciously contributed (hence falsely annotated) members (‘poisonous entries’) ( Aryal et al., 2022 ). In medical AI, when training records are maliciously tampered with, it may cause people to make dangerous misdiagnoses, and ultimately cause the trust between the diagnosis assisted by AI and clinician and patient to be lost ( Marulli et al., 2022 ). These instances illustrate that data poisoning is not just a theoretical problem, but also a significant practical issue in security. In fact, as Kim (2025) notes, there is a “desperate need to design advanced defence strategies that reinforce the resiliency of these models against possible poisoning threats, while also maintaining the overall reliability of AI-based systems” (highlighting modular, attack-agnostic defences as a critical need). The poisoning attacks take different forms depending on adversary’s goals – ranging from the broad availability attacks degrading accuracy of the overall model, to the targeted backdoors that lead to specific misclassification of attacker choice input. One of the most straightforward attacks to poison the training data is the label flipping attacks in which the attacker changes the labels of some training examples (i.e., flipping from benign to malicious or swapping the labels of disease status) without modifying the input features. This attack does not need any expensive manipulations to the data itself, which is especially stealthy: the poisoned samples on the test side look statistically normal except for their wrong labels. Label flipping is so simple, and yet it can so badly undermine the performance of classifiers ( Aryal et al., 2022 ). Aryal et al. (2022) demonstrated the effectiveness of label flips by randomly changing labels of a set of malware training samples; an attack that was able to significantly reduce detection rates of six different malware classifiers that they tested. Meanwhile, previous works have observed that label poisoning could make even strong models learn wrong decision boundaries, causing malicious software or other malicious examples to pass through the trained model undetected ( Aryal et al., 2022 ). The increasing popularity in open and federated data collection (e.g., crowd-sourced inputs, online learning) also exacerbates the threat, as there do not exist automated methods yet to ensure the validity of every contributing training datum. In short, poisoning and label-flipping attacks in particular represent a fundamental threat for state-of-the-art AI systems, particularly when deployed in high-stakes contexts such that even slightly corrupted training data translates into potential safety and security violations ( Kim, 2025 ). Several defence mechanisms to resist data poisoning have been investigated in the literature. Early methods primarily aimed to sanitise data or detect potentially problematic outliers, e.g., by using statistical criteria or nearest-neighbour consistency checks for flagging suspicious training points ( Al Mallah et al., 2023a; Paudice et al., 2019 ). While such methods may help to defend against some of the attacks, they are attack-specific and can be easily fooled if the poison does not show up as the obvious outliers. As Chen et al. (2021) point out, many defences “are specifically designed for particular poisoning mechanisms and may not work well for other types”. For example, a method proposed by Peri et al. (2020) , which finds label-consistent (clean-label) poisons using k-nearest neighbour analysis, works on slightly perturbed examples, but fails on gradient-based poisoning where the label and feature manipulations are more subtle. Likewise, Jagielski et al. (2018) ’s poisoning defence for regression cannot be directly used for classification. Few wide-area defences have been proposed to date, and there is a consensus in the literature that this is a fundamental shortcoming. Recent work has also been shifting towards attack-agnostic methods—particularly, Chen et al. (2021) ’s De-Pois is also a generic defence under no assumption on the attack. De-Pois trains a mimic model to simulate a reference model trained with clean trusted data (enriched with generative methods) and identifies the tainted samples by comparing predictions of the mimic model and the actual infected model. This method achieved high detection rates (more than 90% F1-score) on different poison attack types, demonstrating the potential of attack-agnostic detection. But De-Pois and others of its kind still assume some level of (in De-Pois’s case, partial) freedom as it often still needs a small pool of clean data, or the ability to retrain auxiliary models, and, critically, that it operates in a white-box or grey-box setting where the defender can either instrument the training or gain access to internal model surrogates. On the other hand, some works consider poisoning detection in more challenging regimes like federated learning. Al Mallah et al. (2023b) propose a defence, attestedFL, that constantly monitors the behaviour of model updates for every client (e.g., their consistency and progress), to detect malicious members in a federation. By verifying if each node is “really training” towards the global objective, their approach is capable of filtering out the unreliable (poisoning) clients, and it was demonstrated to improve the accuracy of the global model significantly against a range of poisoning attacks. This concept of a behavioural attestation mechanism is highly performant in the setting discussed in the previous section but depends on the ability to observe client training dynamics (which is, therefore, specific to federated setups). On the other hand, ensemble-based defences have also been proposed; for instance, Anisetti et al. (2023) advocated that switching from a single classifier to an ensemble of them would possibly increase resistance to poisoning if the poisoned subset is drowned out by a diluted set of classifiers. To the best of our knowledge, current existing defences either rely on assumptions about a defender’s ability to know something about how the attacker behaves, access to an internal pipeline of what is passed to the question-answering system, or are limited to specialised environments (e.g., malware detection) and do not generalise well to other application areas. This work presents a unique approach to a class of attacks known as poisoning that targets models at the training phase, being one of the first to attempt to develop out-of-the-box, modular and model-agnostic approaches to such attacks that can be applied in the general case, which is yet to be explored in the literature broadly. Defensive research is growing in mainstream security venues and journals, including analysis of poisoning to new model types (e.g., multi-agent reinforcement learning) and the march towards blockchain-based defences, but the substantial gap remaining in general poisoning and model-agnostic poisoning detection, even at test time, across a range of practical settings remains ( Zheng et al., 2023 ). In this work, our goal is to address these gaps by presenting a new outputs-only (black-box) and grey-box poisoning detection framework, which regards the target AI model as a non-transparent black-box and determines poisoning by observing the interface between the model and the outside world. This point of view is quite different from most existing defences, which either work based on the training data or need to be based on a replica model. Our approach is a modular and dataset-agnostic pipeline that is flexible to be adopted to various types of attacks and application areas. The main idea is to derive a rich set of meta-features from the outputs of the target model (e.g., the model confidence scores, the error rates) that shall capture noticeable symptoms of abnormal learning. These behavioural characteristics are then passed into several lightweight detector models (the Detection Module, DM), essentially a collection of AI “watchdogs”, where each is trained to identify specific patterns of poisoning (e.g. one such detector can be to search for anomalous degradation of confidence on known benign samples, while another might be configured to flag changing output entropy or distributional shifts). Our method treats the target model as a black box, in which no additional assumptions are made on the internals of the model itself or on the training process. This makes it possible to apply to almost any pre-trained classifier to perform a post-deployment soundness check for poisoning. Critically, we also include a set of detectors to improve robustness: the outputs of these different detectors are aggregated (e.g. by voting or using a meta-classifier) to reach a final conclusion about whether or not the model has been compromised with poisoning. Ensemble learning techniques, as we discussed, have been shown to enhance reliability against adversarial attacks, and in particular, the effect of ensembles in our setup is that the detection system can generalise across attack behaviours (if one detector does not catch the attack, others will; and only a collective evasion can confuse all detectors simultaneously). The complete pipeline is modular and extensible; new detectors targeting new attack signatures can be added without a complete redesign of the system, and the feature extraction can be customised for different kinds of models or modalities. Further, we emphasise that our approach is dataset-agnostic: specifically, while some defences are tailored to particular data domains (such as domain-specific filters for vision or features engineered specifically for identifying malicious files), our behavioural features and detectors do not make hard-coded assumptions about the content of the data, as we show by testing across different datasets (including image benchmarks and a medical imaging dataset). This paper offers the following contributions to adversarial machine learning and security. Black-Box and Grey-Box Approach to Poisoning Detection : We present a new method of defence that is able to detect label-flipping data poisoning without needing the model’s internal weights or the raw training data. We can detect poisoned models in the black-box setting using only trajectories of the model’s outputs (predictions) on a collection of probe inputs, while also supporting a grey-box mode when penultimate embeddings are available. This means that our defence can be deployed in environments where the model is a service or in environments of a proprietary nature and opens the way towards a much wider practical utility of poisoning defences. Modular and Adaptable Architecture : Our proposed solution is designed with a modular pipeline including a meta-feature extractor and several detector models in an ensemble. It is attack-agnostic and extensible: it can handle different types of poison attack (not only label flips) through the use of suitable detectors/features, and is agnostic to the specific machine learning task/dataset setting. Due to the black-box and model-agnostic nature, our defence can work against a wide range of classifiers (e.g., neural networks, ensemble classifiers, etc.) and their architectures as long as querying access to the model is provided. Strong Cross-Domain Generalisation : We show the efficacy of our method across different datasets from separate domains, MNIST/ CIFAR-10 image classification benchmarks, and ChestXray14 medical imaging dataset, under simulated label flip poisoning. Our detectors all achieve high (similar) accuracy levels in detecting poisoned models across the datasets, demonstrating how the framework generalises with respect to poisoned models, and that it does so without per-dataset tuning. This is a significant step over previous defences that typically target a single domain (e.g., malware detection or federated learning) ( Al Mallah et al., 2023a; Aryal et al., 2022 ). All-Round Comparison : We perform extensive experiments to rigorously evaluate the proposed defence. For instance, we test the proposed approach under different attack cases (poisoning rate, label flip strategies) and compare it to baseline defences from the literature, measuring the true/false positive detection rates and utility degradation in the main model properties. Our evaluation protocol is aligned with recent recommendations for trustworthy AI testing, addressing an open challenge of benchmarking defences under realistic conditions. The results show that our black-box ensemble detector not only reliably detects poisoned models (with high recall and low false-alarm rates) but does so with minimal performance overhead, thereby offering a practical and effective safeguard for AI systems ( Cinà et al., 2024 ). Our work leverages AI to protect AI by using an ensemble of learned detectors to monitor a model’s behaviour. We provide a flexible defence against data poisoning that complements existing data-centric and training-time safeguards. In this work we consider causative, data-poisoning via label flipping, where a subset of training labels is changed while features are kept intact; we do not evaluate trigger-based backdoors or clean-label optimisation attacks in our experiments. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first modular framework to achieve attack-agnostic poisoning detection in both black-box and grey-box settings. Nowadays, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are being increasingly adopted and utilised for cybersecurity, such as for malware detection, botnet identification, intrusion detection, user authentication, encrypted traffic analysis, etc ( Li, 2024; Razzak et al., 2020 ). Such AI-powered defences frequently outperform historical measures in terms of accuracy and flexibility, since they automatically capture complicated patterns in data, without needing to incorporate them explicitly. But the use of AI in security-sensitive areas (health, finance, infrastructure, etc.) also creates additional threat factors. Attackers can abuse ML models by creating inputs, or poisoning training data, which results in models with false or malicious intent ( Zhao et al., 2025 ). In fact, adversarial attacks have become one of the most severe threats to AI systems, as they can compromise the integrity and reliability of the model at test, but also attack the training process ( Bhargava & Stamp, 2025; Ilyas et al., 2019 ). Adversarial Machine Learning Threats . Adversarial attacks in ML are usually characterised based on when and how they happen. Test-time (evasion) attacks, such as adversarial examples, are small perturbations to inputs that cause a fully trained model to misclassify. Data poisoning (training-time) attacks disrupt/manipulate the learning mechanism by adding malicious samples or flipping labels in the training set. In poisoning, the adversary may aim to reduce overall accuracy (untargeted) or induce targeted misclassifications, with stealthy attacks such as in-distribution backdoor attacks with buried triggers. The threat of data poisoning is particularly devious because it can corrupt a model without leaving any overt footprint. As Zhao et al. (2025) note, data poisoning “poses a particularly insidious threat, since attacks may be able to be stealthy in influencing model behaviour”. In fact, high-profile work has proven how simple it is for a malicious party to inject compromised behaviour into models through subtly manipulated training data ( Biggio et al., 2012; Biggio & Roli, 2018; Chen et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2017 ). Early work by Biggio et al. (2012) demonstrated optimisation-based poisoning of support-vector machines (SVMs), while subsequent backdoor attacks like BadNets showed that models can be compromised by injecting inputs with hidden triggers ( Gu et al., 2017 ). Goodfellow et al. (2014) ’s adversarial examples uncovered the vulnerability of deep networks to test-time perturbations, and Papernot et al. (2016) established transferability of such attacks across models. More recent clean-label poisoning techniques (e.g., MetaPoison) create semantically plausible inputs that induce misclassification without obvious artefacts ( Huang et al., 2020 ). These strands illustrate that poisoning can manipulate training data via labels, features or covert triggers, each with different detection challenges. Data Poisoning Attacks . Data poisoning includes many techniques. Backdoor (Trojan) attacks are when specially crafted samples are injected into the training, where the model behaves normally until a trigger pattern is detected. Feature-space attacks generate poisoned examples with features that are similar to clean data, but which lead to target misclassification. Label-only attacks, such as label flipping, perturb the labels of some training samples but do not alter their inputs. Since no explicit pattern is inserted, label flips can bypass naïve anomaly detectors; however, they are capable of significantly warping a model’s decision boundaries. Previous literature has also shown that even for random label noise, deep learning models can be completely misguided: Zhang et al. (2017) demonstrated that deep networks can, in some cases, fit training data with random labels perfectly (zero training error), only to generalise terribly on real test data. This implies that DL models “do not naturally differentiate between correct and incorrect labels”, rendering them very vulnerable to label-flip poisoning. Label flipping has been considered in many contexts. For example, Zhang et al. (2021) demonstrated its effectiveness in spam filtering: flipping a very small percentage of spam labels to benign would result in extremely poor detection. Yao et al. (2019) also demonstrated that selective clean label flips (selecting which labels to flip based on the influence of the sample) could be more damaging compared to the random ones. In vision, Jha et al. (2023) proposed FLIP as a backdoor attack that operates only with label modification: for only every 2% of CIFAR-10 labels being flipped, they are able to reach close to perfect backdoor success (reporting the percentage at which any image is misclassified into the target class). Similarly, Lingam et al. (2024) observed that in graph neural networks where graph structure dependencies are present, even a single flipped label (e.g., on a node) can lead to a significant decrease in classification performance. These findings confirm that label-flip attacks are capable of causing both widespread model breaks and targeted poisons with no input alteration. Defences and Limitations . For poisoning (including label flips), there are a number of proposed defences. Data sanitisation (filtering) techniques preprocess the training set to remove anomalous points or label discrepancies before training. For instance, previous work clustered features in the data and relabelled or discarded outliers to correct wrong labels ( Chen et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2020 ). More advanced statistical-based filtering is accomplished through algorithms such as ensemble consensus, isolation forests, or influence functions for identifying outlying samples. However, it has been shown that a motivated attacker can typically bypass such filters through the use of poison that lies within the data distribution. Robust statistics (loaded median, trimmed gradient, etc.) and robust training algorithms have also been proposed. These can help mitigate the impact of outlier points, but are often tailored to particular model classes or loss functions and can worsen performance on any clean data ( Chen et al., 2021; Koh et al., 2022; Rosenfeld et al., 2020 ). Crucially, many of the more advanced defences are not realisable without having access to the training procedure or model internals. For example, many defences rely on white-box access to the training labels/gradients or need an offline (“clean”) hold-out dataset for comparison. Others depend on domain-specific knowledge (e.g., information on the backdoor trigger). In reality, this is often impossible in practice: organisations might use third-party models (or models in black-boxes), and datasets could be extremely large, impeding per-sample checking. Steinhardt et al. (2017a) and Jagielski et al. (2018) created certified defences with verifiable bounds; however, these often aim towards worst-case scenarios and with strong assumptions (e.g., two linear regressions) rather than generalising broadly. In conclusion, many existing defences are attack-specific (e.g. applied to only backdoor or label flip) or environment-specific (e.g., only work in federated learning) and often rely on assumptions (e.g., small poison rate, human-like data access) that may not be met in practice. As Chen et al. (2021) mentioned: “There are few useful general defence strategies” for dealing with the diverse array of poisoning threats observed today. Due to limitations of such approaches, there is increasing interest in behavioural, black-box detection of poisoned models. They do not dig into data or model internals, but instead observe the behaviour of a trained model for a given input. For example, Raghavan et al. (2022) suggested MOVCE (“model verification”), on which an ML model is exposed as a network intrusion detection system. The defender feeds a batch of input probes into the target model and monitors its output behaviour (e.g., confidence distributions, class-wise accuracy) for any abnormality. A “meta-model” using an AI approach is trained offline on a set of clean vs. poisoned models, so that at runtime it classifies a model’s behaviour as safe or compromised. One major advantage of these methods is that they maintain the reliability of the system while detecting cyber-attacks and may, in principle, be able to recognise new tactics or novel poisoning attacks by learning generalised “signatures” of poisoned models. Label-Flipping Detection . Among these defences, a variety of methods have been proposed, but many are constrained to narrow settings. Early work by Paudice et al. (2018) proposed label sanitisation, a semi-supervised method that groups data points to uncover noisy labels and remove their contributions (an SVM spam classifier). Cheng et al. (2021) adopted the semi-supervised AdaBoost for identifying the flipped samples and reassigning them in multi-class datasets. Zhang et al. (2021) explored the effect of flipping on Naive Bayes spam filters, and offered feature-based defences. In federated learning, a few recent papers have considered the impact of label flips: for instance, Jebreel et al. (2024) introduced LFighter that protects Federated Learning (FL) by detecting the clients which falter updates not in line with the global learning and K.M. et al. (2024) introduced LFGuard in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) by clustering the update gradient of each class. Psychogyios et al. (2023) analysed GAN-based label flips in a federated image classification and proved that even small-round swaps reduce accuracy dramatically. Tolpegin et al. (2022) demonstrated that targeted label flips (e.g. “shirt” to “t-shirt”) can significantly undermine the accuracy of FL models on vision tasks. These federated-learning works show that label flipping is a powerful attack in distributed contexts. More generally, a couple of recent overviews discuss the frequency of label flips. Zhao et al. (2025) classify label flipping as one of the main poisoning categories (including feature-space attacks and backdoors). Rosenfeld et al. (2020) classified label flipping as a canonical poisoning attack and reported that even straw man spam-filtering exercises can be hijacked with adversarial labels. However, even with the attention, label flip detection is not trivial. The existing defences are either tailored to particular settings (e.g., federated learning) or models, or they assume some clean holdout or feature-based anomaly detection. There are a few general black-box detectors for generic models. Research Gaps and Motivation . Overall, the literature has been lacking on general, black-box defences against label-flipping poisoning. While many attacks and defences in the literature are proposed in specialised settings or under unrealistic assumptions, an effective defence is one that does not require a priori knowledge of the exact attack type and which can work even if we have no information about how the model works. Inspired by the setting of steganography and digital watermarking, here we hope to capture universal patterns of how label flips (and other poisoning) demonstrate themselves endogenously to the ML model. Notably, our proposed defence does not inspect raw training data or rely on an internal view of the model. Instead, it repeatedly observes the predicted results of the target model on a chosen probe set and employs a learned detector to correct any suspicious behaviour that is indicative of poisoning. This method may be able to identify subtler attacks (e.g., strategic label flips) with low overhead. Contrary to previous work, our approach is attack-agnostic, and it is also a generic one: we train the detection model across multiple poison scenarios (including label flips), to let it generalise to new attacks. This solves the limitation of the scarcity of general defence strategies that have been identified. By augmenting existing studies with a meta-learning approach, we outperform previous works by proposing a flexible black-box and grey-box aware defence that fills a major gap in the poisoning detection literature. Our proposed solution is a defence framework designed to detect poisoned data in training sets through a two-phase process. Fig. 1 illustrates the architecture of this framework (as described below). In Phase I, a base model is trained on the available training dataset (which may contain both clean and maliciously poisoned samples). During this training, a Behaviour Monitoring Module (BMM) continuously monitors and extracts key metrics and patterns from the model’s learning process. For each training sample, the BMM collects indicators such as prediction probabilities, entropy, and margins (black-box mode), or optionally penultimate embeddings (grey-box mode) thereby characterising the “behaviour” of that sample with respect to the model’s learning. The intuition is that poisoned samples will induce anomalous behaviours that differ from those of genuine data. This idea is inspired by attack-agnostic defences like mimic-model approaches, where a secondary model is used to imitate the behaviour of a clean model and highlight discrepancies caused by poisonous data. By the end of Phase I, the BMM produces a profile of the training data’s behaviour, essentially separating normal versus suspicious training patterns. In Phase II, the extracted behaviour profiles are fed into a Detection Module (DM). The DM is a secondary learning model trained to classify or score each training sample as benign (clean) or malicious (poisoned) based on its Phase I behaviour profile. In implementation, this can be realised, for example, as a binary classifier that learns from a labelled subset of data behaviours – if a small trusted subset of clean data is available, it can be used to help train the DM to recognise clean versus anomalous patterns. The DM training may also leverage synthesised or augmented data for poisoned examples, following methodologies similar to prior work. Once trained, the DM evaluates all samples in the dataset and flags those with outlying behaviour metrics as potential poison. These flagged samples can then be removed or isolated. Optionally, the framework can iterate: the base model can be retrained on the filtered dataset and the process repeated to ensure no remaining poisoned data. Ultimately, the output of our framework is a cleansed training set and a model robust to the poisoning attack. This modular design, with one module extracting model-learning behaviour and another making decisions on data reliability, makes the approach general and extensible. It does not assume any specific attack signature, aligning with the goal of attack-agnostic poison detection as seen in prior research. Critically, our solution’s architecture and flow are designed to be data-agnostic. The modules operate on abstract metrics (like errors or gradients) rather than domain-specific features, allowing the same approach to handle different data modalities. Inputs and outputs of each module are well-defined: the input to the BMM is the training dataset and intermediate model states (losses, etc.), and its output is a set of per-sample behaviour metrics. The input to the DM is those metrics, and the output is a classification of samples (poisoned or not). This design choice aligns with best practices in recent security frameworks, which break down complex systems into components for data processing, explanation, and informed decision-making. Each component of our framework – data intake, anomaly/poison detection, and expert analysis – corresponds to a stage in the overall workflow ( Chang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), 2023 ). By structuring the solution in this modular way, we can later analyse or upgrade individual parts (for instance, using more sophisticated neural networks in the BMM, or different classification algorithms in the DM) without changing the overall approach. To evaluate the proposed framework across different data modalities and levels of complexity, we used three representative benchmark datasets: MNIST (handwritten digits), CIFAR-10 (natural images), and ChestXray14 (medical X-rays). These datasets cover a progression from simple, balanced image data through more complex natural images to a highly imbalanced and clinically significant medical dataset. MNIST: The MNIST dataset consists of 70,000 grayscale images of handwritten digits (28 × 28 pixels), with 60,000 images for training and 10,000 for testing. It is a widely used benchmark for simple classification tasks and provides a clean setting to validate poisoning detection at low dimensionality. Poisoning was simulated by randomly flipping a subset of training labels at rates of 10% and 20%. CIFAR-10: The CIFAR-10 dataset contains 60,000 natural images in 10 classes (e.g., airplanes, cars, animals), each of size 32 × 32 pixels and in RGB colour. There are 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images. CIFAR-10 represents a more complex visual task, where the feature space is higher-dimensional and less separable than MNIST. As with MNIST, label-flip poisoning was applied at 10% and 20% of the training set. ChestXray14: The ChestXray14 dataset contains 112,120 frontal-view chest radiographs from 30,805 unique patients, annotated with 14 thoracic disease labels. For this study, we adopt a binary classification task (pneumonia vs. other), a common clinical framing used in prior medical ML research. This simplification enables controlled evaluation of poisoning defences on a medically relevant condition. This binarisation reflects a common focus in medical ML research where pneumonia is a critical target condition, and it allows us to evaluate poisoning detection under a practically relevant and clinically meaningful setting, even though the full dataset contains 14 labels. While this reduces the dataset’s multi-label complexity, it follows a widely used binary framing in prior clinical AI studies, ensuring both relevance and comparability while avoiding oversimplification. All images were resized and normalised as required by the ResNet-based target model (224 × 224 pixels). Label-flip poisoning was simulated by relabelling a subset of pneumonia cases into the negative class at 10% and 20% rates. In all three datasets, poisoning simulation followed the procedure defined in Section 3.1 , where a fraction α of samples from a source class c i were relabelled to a target class c j . This ensured comparability across datasets while highlighting how dataset complexity affects detection performance. All models were implemented in PyTorch. Training was conducted on an HPE ProLiant DL385 Gen10 Plus v2 server with two AMD EPYC 7543 CPUs, 256 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA A100 GPU. We also validated the framework on a commodity Intel Core i7 CPU with 32 GB RAM; while CPU-only execution increased runtime during repeated troubleshooting and hyper-parameter searches (especially for ChestXray14), the final trained models ran successfully on this machine. This demonstrates deployability on common research hardware, with high-end GPUs primarily used to accelerate experimentation. We evaluated the proposed poisoning detection pipeline across three benchmark datasets — MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestXray14 — using four detection models: XGBoost (XGB), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Isolation Forest (IF), and Mahalanobis Distance-based detector (Maha). Each detector was trained on features extracted by the Behaviour Monitoring Module (BMM) and tested on held-out sets with 10% and 20% label-flipped samples (for MNIST and CIFAR-10, flips were between specific classes such as 1 → 7 or 0 → 1; for ChestXray14, flips targeted a normal vs. abnormal label). For each configuration, we report the detector’s Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). We also examined the ROC curves and Confusion Matrices of the detectors to illustrate performance further. All ROC figures include the AUC value in the legend/title, and all confusion matrices display TP/TN/FP/FN counts within cells to ensure numerical interpretability. A.1–A.6 ). The detectors demonstrated strong performance in identifying poisoned samples on the MNIST dataset. Table 2 summarises the detection results on MNIST under a 10% poisoning rate. All four detectors perform exceptionally well in this scenario. The supervised models achieved near-perfect detection: XGB attained an accuracy of about 98.5% with an AUC ≈ 0 . 98 , and MLP performed similarly with an AUC around 0.97. Both yield high precision and recall (e.g., XGB Precision 0.96, Recall 0.95), corresponding to F1-scores in the mid-0.90s. Even the unsupervised detectors were adequate given the clean, simple nature of MNIST: Maha reached an AUC over 0.90 (F1 ≈ 0 . 80 ), and IF achieved an AUC around 0.89 with F1 in the mid-0.70s. These results indicate that, at low poisoning levels, the pipeline can almost perfectly distinguish flipped labels from genuine ones on this simple image dataset. When the poisoning rate is doubled to 20%, the detection performance on MNIST remains high, with only a minor decline. As shown in Table 3 , XGB’s AUC only drops slightly to 0.970 at 20% (from 0.985 at 10%), and its F1-score remains about 0.948. MLP similarly retains a high AUC of 0.962 and F1 ≈ 0 . 93 . The unsupervised methods see a modest dip: for example, IF’s F1 falls from 0.75 at 10% to 0.723 at 20%, and Maha’s F1 drops from ≈ 0 . 82 to 0.777. Overall accuracy is still above 97% for all detectors. These results demonstrate MNIST’s relative ease for our detection task – even with 20% of labels poisoned, the detectors (especially XGB and MLP) maintained excellent precision ( > 0.95) and recall ( > 0.90), detecting the vast majority of poisoned samples with very few false alarms. As illustrated by the ROC curves in Fig. 2 , the XGB detector’s output for MNIST (10% poisoning) is near the ideal top-left corner, confirming the excellent separability between clean and poisoned instances (AUC ≈ 0 . 98 ). The corresponding confusion matrices ( Fig. 3 ) reflects this performance: the vast majority of poisoned examples are correctly identified (high true positives) with negligible misclassification of clean examples as poisoned (low false positives). In summary, the MNIST experiments show that all detectors — and particularly the supervised ones — can reliably detect label-flipped samples in a simple, well-separated feature space. The more complex visual features and inter-class confusion in CIFAR-10 make it harder for anomaly detectors to characterise poisoned data, though learning-based detectors like XGB and MLP still manage to detect most flipped labels with acceptable precision/recall. At 20% poisoning, detection performance on ChestXray14 degrades significantly (see Table 9 ). XGB’s AUC drops to 0.861, and its F1-score falls to 0.819, indicating that roughly 18% of poisoned cases went undetected and/or were misclassified. MLP shows a similar decline with an F1 of 0.802 at 20% poisoning. The unsupervised detectors are markedly poor in this regime: IF’s recall sinks below 60% (F1 = 0.620), and Maha’s F1 is only 0.636. Overall accuracy also diminishes for all methods (e.g., IF only 83.7% accuracy, the lowest among all results). The combination of inter-class similarities in ChestXray14 (e.g., subtle differences between certain conditions) and imbalanced labels (far fewer positive instances to learn anomalies from) leads to a high rate of missed detections. In practical terms, a substantial number of poisoned images were not flagged by the detectors on this dataset, especially when the poisoning percentage increased. The ROC and confusion matrix visualisations ( Figs. 9 and 8 ) corroborate these findings. Fig. 8(a) shows the ROC curve for XGB on ChestXray14 at 10% poisoning — the curve is noticeably closer to the 45° diagonal compared to earlier datasets, with an AUC of only about 0.86–0.90. This indicates much weaker separation between clean and poisoned samples. The confusion matrix in Fig. 9 reveals that, even with the top-performing XGB model, a significant fraction of poisoned examples are misclassified as benign (false negatives) on ChestXray14. For instance, XGB’s recall of 80.7% at 20% poisoning means roughly one in five poisoned images went undetected. False positives (clean images incorrectly flagged) are also higher relative to MNIST/CIFAR results, which lowers precision into the low 80% range. These trends highlight the need for dataset-specific tuning or more advanced detection techniques when dealing with complex, real-world data like ChestXray14. Without adaptation, our pipeline’s efficacy is limited in such challenging scenarios, in contrast to its strong performance on more straightforward datasets. Table 11 provides a summary comparison of all detectors’ AUC values across the three datasets and two poisoning levels. Several clear trends emerge from this overview. First, the supervised detectors (XGB and MLP) consistently outperform the unsupervised ones (IF and Maha) in every scenario. XGB is the top performer overall, with AUCs ranging from 0.86 (ChestXray14 at 20%) up to 0.99 (MNIST at 10%). MLP follows closely with only slightly lower AUCs in each case. In contrast, the unsupervised IF and Maha detectors show significantly lower AUCs, particularly on more complex data. Notably, the performance gap between supervised and unsupervised methods widens with dataset complexity: for example, on MNIST (20% flip) XGB’s AUC (0.970) is higher than IF’s by 0.125, whereas on ChestXray14 (20%) the gap grows to 0.149 (0.861 vs. 0.712). We also observe that increasing the poisoning rate from 10% to 20% typically reduces detection performance across all models and datasets. However, this reduction is relatively modest on MNIST (e.g., XGB AUC drops from 0.990 to 0.970) and becomes more pronounced on the harder ChestXray14 data (XGB AUC 0.900 → 0.861, MLP 0.880 → 0.849). In summary, our multi-stage detection pipeline is highly effective on simple, well-separated data (MNIST) even with substantial poisoning, retains fair performance on moderately complex data (CIFAR-10), but struggles on very complex or imbalanced data (ChestXray14). In this study, we have developed and evaluated an adaptable AI poisoning attack detector (focusing on label flipping attacks), which could detect the attacks with high accuracy. We found that effectiveness of the poisoning detection pipeline itself is highly dependent upon the complexity of the dataset. For the simple MNIST digit dataset, all of the detection models did quite well. Both XGBoost (XGB) and the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) scored above 0.95 on area under ROC curve (AUC), as well as precision and recall, suggesting that indeed the label-flipped samples were identified almost perfectly. Even the unsupervised anomaly detectors, Isolation Forest (IF) and Mahalanobis distance (Maha), were successful on MNIST, as they take advantage of the clean, low-dimensional features of this dataset. This indicates that in the scenario of existing easy and visible separation of the data distribution, even outlier-based techniques can consistently detect anomaly over samples. For clarity, the methodological basis for these results is formalised in Section 3 (Eqs. (1)–(5) and Algorithms 1–4), which define the poisoning process, feature extraction, and detector evaluation. Unlike related attack-agnostic defences such as De-Pois, our pipeline explicitly separates behaviour monitoring (BMM) from detection (DM). The BMM abstracts model behaviour into embeddings and metrics, while the DM applies flexible classifiers or anomaly detectors. This modularity enables independent upgrades of either module without retraining surrogate models, improving extensibility. However, moving to harder vision data (CIFAR-10) and clinical images (ChestXray14), detection performance significantly decreased; such suffering is more significant for unsupervised methods. In higher diversity natural images, CIFAR-10, overall detection metrics decreased modestly compared to MNIST. The supervised detectors (XGB, MLP, etc.) were still going strong. XGB still achieved an AUC of about 0.92 on CIFAR-10, for instance, but this was a far fall from near-perfect performance on MNIST. The precision–recall tradeoff degraded due to more confusion between flipped and clean examples (e.g. MLP F1 dropped to 0.87 on CIFAR-10 compared to 0.93 on MNIST). Unsupervised methods fared less well: Isolation Forest and Mahalanobis detectors lost even more (0.84 on MNIST down to the 0.76–0.81 range on CIFAR). The presence of higher-level features and of inter-class overlap in CIFAR-10 obviously made the task of an unsupervised anomaly criterion used to discriminate mislabelled inputs more difficult. These findings highlight that more complex data/feature noise results in poorer generalisation of the detection pipeline. This observed degradation illustrates the limits of a purely attack-agnostic design: the same pipeline can generalise across datasets, but dataset-specific refinements may be required for best performance. ChestXray14, a multi-class dataset of chest X-ray images, showed the highest complexity. Here we saw a flattening of the curve in the performance drop to detect poisoned samples. Even the top performing detectors had significant degradation in performance; e.g., AUC on ChestXray14 for XGBoost decreased to 0.86 compared to 0.97 on MNIST. (0.85, AUC). The MLP was approximately the same. More impressively, however, unsupervised IFs barely surpassed 0.71 AUC on ChestXray14, effectively still not much above random guessing. Its detection was not very precise nor did it recall much (the F1 score was about 0.62), with many poison samples being missed and/or many clean samples being falsely detected. Mahalanobis distance performed slightly better than this (AUC ≈ 0 . 73 ). The significant reduction in the effectiveness of the unsupervised detector indicates that unadapted anomaly-based detection is not applicable to high-dimensional medical images. Label imbalance and subtle inter-class similarities in ChestXray14 data enable us to hardly distinguish normal and poisoned samples purely based on outlier scores. Dataset complexity In conclusion, dataset complexity was identified as an important contributing factor: the pipeline transferred well from MNIST to CIFAR-10 (with a certain gap in performance for supervised vs. unsupervised training) but, somewhat less so, on ChestXray14, emphasising that both a dataset-specific tuning of the algorithm and the problem caused by the use of a more robust detection strategy for real-world data. For avoidance of doubt, the parenthetical “(0.85, AUC)” refers to the area under the ROC curve of approximately 0.85; in the figures the precise AUC is shown in the ROC legends. Future refinements could include enriching BMM features with medical descriptors (e.g., region-level statistics or uncertainty surrogates), and adopting detectors designed for severe class imbalance (e.g., focal loss or cost-sensitive learning) to reduce false negatives in clinical applications. Additionally, because poisoned positives are rare, AUCPR is the most decision-relevant summary. Across datasets, BB+GB generally matches or improves AUCPR over BB, with the largest gains for supervised detectors on CIFAR-10 and ChestXray14. BB (outputs-only) remains a competitive baseline when only posteriors are available, while GB (penultimate activations) adds complementary class-conditional geometry. The simple feature-level fusion used here (BB+GB concatenation) most often provides the strongest AUCPR for supervised detectors; unsupervised detectors (Isolation Forest, Mahalanobis) benefit from GB once features are standardised and, where applied, PCA-controlled, though gains are smaller and detector-dependent. The results showed that these trends are consistent with the per-mode ablations ( Tables 4 , 7 , and 11 ) and the representative PR curves in the main text; complete PR/ROC curves for all detectors and access modes are provided in Appendix A . In practice, BB is preferred when internal activations are inaccessible or restricted, whereas BB+GB is a robust default when activations can be logged with minimal overhead. Interestingly, the relative ordering of detectors was dataset insensitive. In all experiments, the supervised learning detectors significantly outperformed the unsupervised detectors. XGBoost slightly performed better than MLP in every measure (probably due to its ensemble nature), followed by Isolation Forest and Mahalanobis distance, especially over difficult data. This pattern persisted at 10% and 20% label-flip attack rates (the higher poisoning rate led to a slight overall deterioration of detection abilities, but in the absence of significant overlap, the optimal models did not change). This ranking held, indicating that learning a labelled detection model (if one can be trained on a representative mix of poisoned and clean) is better than straight outlier detection on feature distributions, with the exception that when no labelled “attack” data is available (unsupervised is the default). In conclusion, our pipeline worked well with low complexity data, moderately well with moderate complexity data and not so well with high complexity/unbalanced data. This emphasises that poison detection must be evaluated under a wide range of contexts, not just a single benchmark. And finally, it encourages strengthening the current detectors to better cover cases where they fail (e.g., domain adaptation for medical images or more complex anomaly detectors). Further extensions could also include evaluating additional poisoning types (e.g., clean-label or backdoor attacks) to validate generality across threats. The large reduction in detection performance on ChestXray14 has important practical implications. In health care AI, the integrity of the data is so important. A model that is been trained on mislabelled or poisoned clinical data could result in inaccurate diagnoses or ineffective treatments. Our results demonstrate that a simple detection pipeline that works well on a benchmark dataset may not directly transfer to high-stakes medical imaging data in clinical deployment. Unsupervised detectors on ChestXray14 have poor recall, because many poisonous training samples could be left to escape the detectors in a real-world hospital scenario, rendering a model that performed, say, disease-detection from X-rays, untrustworthy. On the other hand, it is equally critical to not have the false positives we found (e.g. the Isolation Forest flagging many status-clean X-rays as poisoned). flagging (or discarding) too many real patient samples would weaken the training data and jeopardise trust of the clinician. So, any universal poison alarms might result in unacceptable trade-offs in a clinical setting. It is clear that in tasks like medical image analysis, where every data point can be dear, false alarms should be reduced to a minimum. It is the inclusion of full confusion matrix metrics (not just accuracy/AUC) in our evaluation that has been pivotal for these reasons, e.g., an AUC of 0.85 might seem acceptable, but when it comes with dozens of false positives, it is not for a radiology application. This adds to previous findings of the need to fuse data with domain knowledge for poison detection in healthcare, and potentially patient review or human-in-the-loop verification of suspicious points to avoid both missing detections and overzealous cleaning. Our framework can also operate in either grey-box mode (using embeddings and activations where available) or stricter black-box mode (using only output trajectories). This flexibility supports deployment in diverse environments while keeping assumptions explicit. Additionally, although experiments were accelerated on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, we verified that the pipeline runs on commodity hardware (Intel Core i7 with 32 GB RAM) with longer runtimes, demonstrating practical deployability in typical research or operational settings. Like the other critical and security-sensitive areas, even such infra must embrace the following. For example, for hardware trustworthiness (IC supply chain, critical manufacturing), poisoned training data might have catastrophic consequences; an attacker flipping labels in a chip defect dataset might lead to an unsafe defect (Trojan-inserted) chip being labelled as “safe”. Prior literature in hardware Trojan detection also emphasises data scanning: e.g., Pradeep et al. (2022) note that it is paramount that the training dataset is scanned and the poisoned input samples be identified, before ML models can be used for Trojan detection. Based on their characterisation, a targeted poison detection method was able to revert almost all erroneously flipped labels to the correct state, with a detection accuracy of 99% for benchmark circuits. This confirms that in adversarial settings, specialised poisoning defences can in fact approach perfect, though possibly after calibration to the data and threat model. Our more generic pipeline did not quite reach the same levels on the more complex ChestXray14 data; therefore, a customisation for roll-out into any mission-critical system would be necessary. This might include, for example, domain-tuned feature engineering or model ensembles (as in Pradeep et al. (2022) did with a CatBoost circuit ensemble), which may simply greatly improve reliability in practice. Another issue of interest is IoT and network security, with noisy data and the ability for attackers to insert poisoned labels at scale. Label-flipping attacks are a well-known threat in these environments; as Taheri et al. (2020) , stated such attacks “form a serious attack on detection systems in high noisy/uncertain environments…including IoT (Internet of Things), complex networks”. Any of these solutions based on a naive defence (i.e., the KNN method to filter out suspicious labelling) perform poorly on low SNR because they often yield relatively low performance in this scenario. Our observation on CIFAR-10 (a noisy vision dataset) is consistent with this: a simplistic anomaly detector was inadequate, indicating that more advanced ones or a hybrid of them is desired for robust performance. The good news is that more advanced defences are already being discussed. Semi-supervised, and deep learning–based defences have also been developed (in malware detection, which is critical infrastructure in cybersecurity) that can fix a large percentage of such label flips and produce a considerable increase in accuracy with respect to earlier defences. These successes, combined with our own results, suggest that poison-detection pipelines can be viable for real-world deployments, but only if purpose-built for the domain. One critical assumption of our work is that stakeholders in healthcare, finance, autonomous systems and other critical applications should invest in empirically validating the detection mechanisms under their own environments (e.g. distributions of medical data, regulatory restrictions) before fully relying on them in production. It is worth noting that any such system must take into account the fact that it can be bypassed, and thus continuously adapt to the decrease in detection. In summary, our multi-dataset evaluation for our study offers a cautionary tale: what may work on test-bed for MNIST/CIFAR may not be the best performer on real-world biomedical or infrastructure data, and its deployment may require domain-specific customisation and thorough testing. To support reproducibility, we have released code and exact hyperparameters for all runs. Our modular detection technique provides an alternative view to prior work on poising defences. Conventional methods for discovering noisy labels based on the problem of label-flipping attacks can be generally divided into two directions: data sanitisation (distinguishing and cleansing samples that are flipped or assigning a corrected label to corrupted samples before training models) and robust training (letting the model itself be less affected by the noise of labels). The line of work that relates to data sanitisation is represented by Paudice et al. (2018) , where they proposed an algorithm to replace detected suspect training points with their correct class labels and so mitigate the impact of the label flips. Their method and others of the same kind are often based on heuristics (e.g. outlier detection in feature or loss space) to select the training set. Our pipeline can be best understood as a refinement of this concept: we design an explicit detection model (the Detection Module, “DM”), trained to decide what it means for a region of an image to be noteworthy in a principled manner. Taking as input features produced by a base image classifier (the BMM), our approach connects supervised learning and anomaly detection by learning a classifier for “clean vs poisoned” instances. It has the advantage over more basic methods such as using KNN or thresholding approaches (with potentially poor accuracy at lower model resolution, as per previous work) in being a more trainable and flexible approach. Practically, our XGBoost/MLP detectors demonstrated substantial performance gains over a simple KNN filter on real, more complex data, which is coherent with Taheri et al. (2020) , who found that more complex defences (e.g., their CNN-based scheme) obtain up to 19% better accuracy in noisy conditions. Compared with other attack-agnostic methods such as De-Pois, our design explicitly separates behaviour monitoring (BMM) from detection (DM). This allows module-wise upgrades (e.g., swapping detectors or adding features) without re-engineering the full training process, strengthening generality and extensibility. Another lineage of similar work targets specific areas of application. For instance, defences against label flips have been developed for malware detection systems via clustering and semi-supervised learning approaches ( Taheri et al., 2020 ). Our work supplements these by evaluating on various domains (vision, medical imaging) in a unified setup. In doing so, we observed that an apparently reliable (if not “unassailable”) detection method (Isolation Forest) for structured malware features was not effective on the image data, which serves as an empirical data-point for the community: cross-domain generalisation of poison defences is not straightforward. In the context of hardware Trojans, Pradeep et al. (2022) have recently proposed an ensemble solution (CatBoost with k-NN) in order to accurately detect poisoned chip samples. Remarkably, they were able to sidestep “target leakage” through their use of ordered boosting, which led to near-perfect detection. This highlights the importance of ensemble and hybrid approaches, and our results reflect that. While we did not directly study a multi-detector ensemble approach, we observed mixed behaviour of detectors across datasets. There is a chance that a clever fusion of our four detection models would have allowed us to achieve higher overall accuracy, say, having XGBoost take care of the majority of cases, while an anomaly detector would catch the remaining cases that the supervised models do not catch. Past successes like Pradeep’s do support that proposition, but they also warn that any ensemble must be aware of the dataset (tuned to the data) in order to be truly effective. Not only directly concatenating models obtained from each dataset, but they may also introduce new false positives or negatives since each detector comes with its own bias. For comparison, what sets our pipeline apart is its modularity and separation of concerns. Our architecture naturally disentangles the manual labelling process (done on BMM-threshold-extracted features) from the prediction (BMM module handles the main predictive task) by dividing these two tasks into two BMM and detection modules. This approach follows a best practice as recommended by current literature in order not to conflate objectives. In the previous drafts of our work, and even a few past works, there was a possibility to confuse the accuracy of the target model with the detection performance. We made sure to assess detection in isolation – AUC, F1, etc., exclusively for the detection classifier. Such strict disentanglement is not as prevalent in previous works, which tend to report the final effect on classification accuracy as their primary measure of success. We, meanwhile, claim (and illustrate) that a high classification accuracy on the poisoned dataset does not at all imply that nobody “noticed” the attack and cleaned it; it can merely indicate an inherent robustness in the model or a weak attack. Thus, our work gives a complementary perspective: even if an attacked system’s accuracy does not drop much (which is the case for some robust models), one should have a mechanism to actively detect and remove malicious data. We do better than previous work by not just segmenting entire hands but also by furnishing full-spectrum metrics (confusion matrices, precision, recall) for the detection part of it, which is scarcely reported on in the related literature. This level of transparency is important for applications such as healthcare to be able to ensure that the false positives cost vs. the false negatives cost is balanced. By reporting these full-spectrum metrics and separating BMM/DM evaluation, our study strengthens methodological clarity and avoids conflating classification accuracy with detection success. Our results are generally consistent with but expand previous research. We confirm findings from previous works that ensemble tree models and neural networks are typically less affected by label noise than simple classifiers, and we also confirm the effectiveness of focused filtering training data as a defensive measure. At the same time, experimenting over a previously untackled diversity from MNIST to ChestXray14, we expose issues not encountered in prior, thematic studies, namely, that even powerful, imbalanced data can still overwhelm simple anomaly detectors. We also provide empirical results supporting the advice to separate detection and classification in evaluation. We are building on existing work, but also trying to move the conversation towards how one makes these defences strong across domains and how you can put them together into real-world machine learning pipelines. The insight gained from this study provides a number of directions for future research and practical enhancement. First, future work should use our approach and solution design to build new systems to detect other types of AI attacks, starting with other poisoning attacks like backdoor threats. Another important future work is to investigate ensemble-based detection methods. All the detector types we used have different advantages and failure cases, as mentioned. Combining the XGB, MLP, IF and Mahalanobis’ outputs or scores into an ensemble may lead to a more robust decision, for instance, either by voting or by using a weighted average through a meta-learner over their predictions. This may help to counterbalance the limitations of a single model. Any ensemble approach, nonetheless, should be carefully tuned per dataset, as we observed different behaviour for each dataset in our results; otherwise, the methods could simply magnify the error of the majority model. It would be worthwhile to further investigate dynamic or data-dependent ensemble weighting (e.g., based on confidence scores or uncertainty estimates for each detector). Furthermore, methods such as meta-detectors (or a detector that watches the detectors), or statistical process control could provide warning when a detector is not in its depth (as IF was in the case of ChestXray14). There is another significant direction for improving the feature representation for detection. Our analysis was based on features derived from a base classifier (BMM). If these features are not discriminative for poison vs. clean, the detection module is crippled. The learned features by the BMM may not discriminate well between normal and mislabelled pathology images in the case of ChestXray14. One option for future work might be the inclusion of representation learning that is particularly tailored to anomaly detection, for example, training an autoencoder (or a contrastive learning version) on the data to learn embeddings with more separation between clean and corrupted samples. Domain-specific feature engineering is also a strong avenue: for medical images, one could utilise clinical metadata or known mechanisms of injury to improve implausible label identification. Data augmentation techniques may benefit the detection model by letting it see more perturbed examples, resulting in a better generalisation towards unseen attacks. Furthermore, exploring other unsupervised detectors (e.g. deep autoencoders or one-class SVMs on the feature space) could enhance the results on complex data. They were able to interface with our modular pipeline without requiring extensive modifications to the main architecture, a sign of robustness within a modular design. From a deployment perspective, a natural question is how to use such detection pipelines with real-world ML training flows. One aspect to consider might be the trade-off between manual/semi-automated filtering and the filter’s ability to do this processing, or not, automatically, accordingly to a threshold. For a sensitive field, the pipeline could run in suggestion mode (identifying and suggesting removal of the suspicious samples), leaving the last decision (data curation) to a human expert. This may also help to reduce the high false-positive cost of eliciting expert judgment. Generating human-understandable explanations about why a sample gets flagged by the detector (e.g., pointing at a feature or behaviour that was anomalous) would support such human-in-the-loop processes. This mirrors developments in explainable AI – if you could make this work in the case of data poisoning, it could go some way towards making people trust in the system’s recommendations. Our framework explicitly supports both grey-box deployments (when embeddings and activations are available) and strict black-box deployments (using only outputs). There will also be practical limitation of performance and scale. Our analysis was for batch detection on fixed datasets. In online learning or periodic retraining, the training data frequently arrives as a stream in live systems. So, one potential approach is online poison detection – continuously scanning arriving data for evidence of attack. Sliding-window anomaly detection or incremental learning for the detection model features would then be required. Serving detection while keeping up with the data throughput is a deployment challenge, especially considering using computationally expensive models. The good thing is that fast models like XGBoost and isolation forests can be updated online somewhat as well; perhaps optimisation of these for real-time use has yet to be researched. One other factor is security against adaptive adversaries. A sufficiently motivated opponent with knowledge of our defence might try to design its poison to evade detection (e.g., by ensuring that the poisoned samples more closely follow the distribution of clean samples). In future, our pipeline should be tested under adaptive threat models such as this. This might include white box attackers who only have part of the detection model features or models and figures out whether they can poison the whole false-negatives successes with poisons that go undetected by the current detectors; if so new defences (like adversarial training of the detector - training the detector on attacker evasive examples) or using a stricter false-negative detection strategy. The recent progress in certified robustness to label flips (e.g., based on randomised smoothing) may complement our strategy with guarantees on the maximum intensity of poison that the model misses. Moreover, our results apply to label-flipping poisoning; adaptation to backdoor and clean-label settings is straightforward at the feature extraction stage (activations), but we leave empirical validation for future work. See e.g. spectral-signature-based detection of backdoors and certified defences for general poisoning ( Steinhardt et al., 2017b; Tran et al., 2018 ). Finally, the wider deployment context for this work is emphasised with the increasing use of AI in safety-critical and sensitive products and services. Organisations adopting machine learning must start treating the integrity of training data as equally critical as the accuracy of the resulting models ( Biggio & Roli, 2018 ). Our modular pipeline is one such candidate to embed in the lifecycle of an ML system: before deploying a model, run a poison detection phase to audit the training data (or perhaps the model’s behaviour on held-out validation data), eliminate or highlight any suspicious samples or anomalies. Such a pipeline could be included in data exchange applications and/or MLops pipelines. For instance, a hospital can also incorporate our detection module into their data preprocessing pipeline such that new patient data with labels generated by external sources can be tested for consistency. In something like power grid anomaly detectors or military autonomous systems, perhaps you would want to mandate all new model versions pass a poison check. Our results suggest this is possible for low to moderate complexity data, but also warn that for complex data, it is not really a plug-and-play. According to the mentioned results, even using our pipeline for complex data gives entities and solution developers a high (and sometimes acceptable) detection rate, but we do not suggest utilising it for attack prevention in critical infrastructures. So perhaps a deployment would begin with a conservative approach (application of our pipeline to simpler features or smaller sets of data) and gradually extend only as confidence in the method builds. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a modular, attack-agnostic pipeline can generalise across domains, but requires adaptation for complex and imbalanced data. Future work should extend the framework to other poisoning types (e.g., clean-label, backdoor) and explore hybrid ensembles for improved robustness. To sum up, we proposed a new adaptive defence mechanism in this paper that adopts AI methods against label-flipping data poisoning attacks to defend machine learning models. Our approach revolves around a modular anomaly detection pipeline that can operate in both grey-box mode (using embeddings or activations where available) and strict black-box mode (using only outputs), extracting critical signals of anomalous behaviour (i.e., decreased model confidence on certain training samples and abnormal activation pattern) without relying on prior knowledge of the underlying model’s internals or the attack strategy. These signals were then fed into an ensemble of different detectors, such as XGBoost, multilayer perceptron, isolation forest, and Mahalanobis distance-based outlier detector, to effectively detect the poisoned data. The multi-detector committee was very effective: on all three benchmark datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestXray14), our method provided excellent detection performance, effectively identifying the majority of flipped-label samples. For example, AUC values exceeded 0.95 on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and remained above 0.85 on ChestXray14. By design, the ensemble method enhanced robustness, and its resulting high TPR of detecting attacked inputs presented with low FPR, typically less than 5%. Such results support the originality and feasibility of our architecture. It is model-agnostic, applicable to diverse types of data, and able to protect AI training pipelines across diverse domains without the need for invasive changes. Limitations include focusing exclusively on label-flipping attacks, simplifying ChestXray14 into a binary pneumonia classification, and not evaluating against adaptive adversaries. These open directions guide future work. In the future, we can explore several interesting directions for this work. First, the flexible framework proposed here can be extended to identifying other types of poisoning strategies, not limited to label flips. For instance, we aim to investigate defences against backdoor poisoning attacks (in which adversaries inject trigger patterns into inputs) and feature contamination (attacks where inputs have the features slightly altered). It would be possible to augment the proposed modular approach to monitoring if other signals (such as timing or loss trajectory) were available in hundreds or thousands of trials to detect such sophisticated attacks. Secondly, deploying and integrating our detection system with automatic mitigation steps constitutes an important next step, namely that when suspicious data points are identified, the model can subsequently either quarantine, down-weight, or altogether purge the suspicious examples during training to eliminate or offset the impact of the attack. Third, we would like to test our framework with more complex and larger-scale settings, including federated learning and online learning scenarios where poisoning can happen across distributed nodes and in real-time data streaming. The second relevant extension consists in tailoring the system for establishing real-time detection of adversarial evasion attacks, taking inspiration from the same monitoring principles for model input and output to identify malicious perturbations. Absolutely, making detection more explainable (e.g., being able to say which features or samples contributed most to an attack’s score) will also help to build user trust and support wider adoption of these security measures. With these approaches, we envisage a more general and robust “AI to protect AI” ecosystem, which can automatically counteract both training-time and inference-time adversarial threats, thereby securing and ensuring the reliability of the entire AI application in the long run. An enhanced diabetic retinopathy blindness detection using deep learning and image preprocessing techniques Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a gradual and severe consequence of diabetes that increases the risk of visual impairment and blindness globally. Early and precise identification of DR is crucial for successful care, but availability to specialist diagnostic tools is restricted, especially in low-resource settings. This study aims to improve the automated identification of diabetic retinopathy using cutting-edge deep learning models—specifically ViT, CLIP, BLIP, ViLT, Florence-2, and ResNet50—which are applied to the APTOS Diabetic Retinopathy dataset. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) diagnosis is often hindered by poor image quality and subtle differences across varying severity levels. The grading of DR is typically categorized into five stages: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative, as defined by the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale. To address artifacts such as uneven illumination, we employ Gaussian preprocessing to smooth noise and Wavelet transforms to enhance edge details. This study evaluates the impact of Gaussian and Wavelet preprocessing techniques on the performance of Vision-Language Models (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and CNNs (e.g., RESNET50). Results indicate that Gaussian Filtering significantly enhances classification accuracy, yielding a 37% improvement for RESNET50 and 36% for BLIP compared to the baseline. This study demonstrates that appropriate preprocessing is critical for maximizing the potential of deep learning in medical imaging. Specifically, Gaussian Filtering proved superior to Wavelet techniques, offering substantial accuracy gains for models like BLIP and RESNET50. Future work will explore hybrid preprocessing pipelines to further distinguish between the subtle early stages of the disease. This study aims to improve the automated identification of diabetic retinopathy using cutting-edge deep learning models—specifically ViT, CLIP, BLIP, ViLT, Florence-2, and ResNet50—which are applied to the APTOS Diabetic Retinopathy dataset. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) diagnosis is often hindered by poor image quality and subtle differences across varying severity levels. The grading of DR is typically categorized into five stages: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative, as defined by the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale. To address artifacts such as uneven illumination, we employ Gaussian preprocessing to smooth noise and Wavelet transforms to enhance edge details. This study evaluates the impact of Gaussian and Wavelet preprocessing techniques on the performance of Vision-Language Models (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and CNNs (e.g., RESNET50). Results indicate that Gaussian Filtering significantly enhances classification accuracy, yielding a 37% improvement for RESNET50 and 36% for BLIP compared to the baseline. This study demonstrates that appropriate preprocessing is critical for maximizing the potential of deep learning in medical imaging. Specifically, Gaussian Filtering proved superior to Wavelet techniques, offering substantial accuracy gains for models like BLIP and RESNET50. The Wavelet Transform is a method for preparing images that divides them into pieces with varying frequencies and scales, allowing them to highlight specific components of the picture, especially at different resolutions [ 21 ]. It detects edges and textures exceptionally well in medical imaging because it distinguishes between low-frequency components (generic, smooth regions) and high-frequency components (such as minute structures or sharp edges). To capture fine-grained data while keeping context, the transform employs " Wavelet functions" that are confined in both time and frequency. This can enhance the visibility of blood vessels, lesions, and other critical features in retinal pictures while preserving the surrounding tissue. The Wavelet Transform is employed to decompose the image into varying frequency and scale components, specifically to enhance the visibility of minute retinal features like microaneurysms and hemorrhages. Chosen Wavelet and Decomposition Level: For this study, the Biorthogonal 3.9 Wavelet function was utilized, applying a three-level decomposition. This specific Biorthogonal family was chosen because it provides linear phase filters (symmetric), which is critical in medical image processing to prevent spatial shifting or distortion of the delicate anatomical features and lesion edges during decomposition and reconstruction. The three-level decomposition was empirically determined in preliminary tests as the optimal level to effectively separate the high-frequency components (lesions, edges) from the lower-frequency background variations (non-uniform illumination), ensuring the preservation of diagnostically significant features. The selection of this kernel and level balances the need to capture fine-grained data while maintaining the context of the overall retinal image structure. While recent literature focuses on creating increasingly complex transformer modifications (Model-Centric AI), this study adopts a Data-Centric AI approach. We demonstrate that optimizing the input signal via specific filtering (Gaussian vs. Wavelet) yields performance gains (up to 37% improvement) that vastly exceed those typically achieved by architectural tweaking alone. Our results challenge the prevailing assumption that VLMs require massive architectural overhauls to succeed in medical imaging. As shown in our ablation study ( Table 11 ), the 'basic' fine-tuning of BLIP yielded a poor F1 score of 33%. However, the introduction of the Gaussian preprocessing module—without further architectural changes spiked performance to 80%.
