Additionally, the field is moving toward more complex fusion and hybrid frameworks. While Han et al. (2025) [ 19 ] demonstrated advanced multi-source mapping in environmental science, the underlying strategies for fusing complex spatial data are highly applicable to multimodal retinal imaging (e.g., combining fundus photos with OCT). Finally, the emergence of large language models offers new avenues for interpretability; Yang et al. (2025) [ 33 ] proposed hybrid frameworks combining LLMs with autoencoders, which could pave the way for next-generation Vision-Language models capable of generating descriptive diagnostic reports alongside DR classification. A notable limitation of this study is that the APTOS 2019 dataset predominantly contains high-quality, well-centered retinal fundus images, and the preprocessing pipeline further excludes samples with severe blur, illumination imbalance, or poor focus. While this ensures consistent input for model training, it may restrict the generalizability of the proposed approach to real-world clinical environments, where image quality is often variable and influenced by differences in camera hardware, operator expertise, and patient movement. To address this limitation, future work will incorporate strategies aimed at improving robustness to low-quality or degraded images. First, the model can be exposed to artificially degraded samples through augmentations such as motion blur, Gaussian blur, brightness reduction, uneven illumination, and noise injection, thereby enabling it to learn more resilient representations. Second, integrating heterogeneous datasets such as EyePACS, Messidor, or IDRiD, which contain a wider spectrum of image quality—can reduce overfitting to competition-grade images and enhance cross-domain performance. Third, a quality-aware diagnostic pipeline may be adopted, in which an image-quality assessment (IQA) module automatically evaluates the input and either restores low-quality images using enhancement techniques (e.g., CLAHE, illumination normalization, or advanced denoising) or routes them to a specialized model trained on degraded data. Finally, model architectures with strong attention mechanisms (e.g., ViT-based or hybrid CNN-Transformer networks) may be further explored to ensure reliable lesion localization even when global image clarity is suboptimal. This study examines how appropriate deep learning models identify and classify diabetic retinopathy from APTOS images and examine the importance of the latest and most recent learning models. We showed the substantial influence of preprocessing and model architecture on classification performance by methodically training and assessing six models: CLIP, ViT, FLORENCE-2, BLIP, VILT, and RESNET50 on datasets treated with original, Gaussian-filtered, and Wavelet-transformed imagery. When trained on Gaussian-filtered data, RESNET50 achieved the best accuracy (99%) across all measures, indicating that image enhancement methods such as Gaussian filters significantly increase model performance across metrics. Wavelet transformation, on the other hand, produced less noticeable performance gains, indicating that its applicability can vary depending on certain model designs and underlying data properties. Although they show encouraging promise, transformer-based models like FLORENCE-2, VILT and BLIP needed computationally demanding training configurations in order to provide competitive results, especially on improved datasets. While this study establishes the baseline robustness of foundation models like CLIP, ViT, and ViLT on fundus imagery, several avenues remain for translating these findings into clinical practice. Since models like CLIP and BLIP are pre-trained on vast image-text pairs, they are uniquely positioned to process multimodal clinical data. Future work will extend our framework to fuse retinal fundus images with patient clinical history from Electronic Health Records (EHR). This integration aims to improve diagnostic accuracy by contextualizing visual biomarkers with systemic health indicators (e.g., diabetic history, hypertension levels). The heavy computational load of Transformer-based models (e.g., ViT, BLIP) can hinder deployment in low-resource clinics. We propose investigating model compression techniques, such as knowledge distillation and quantization, to develop lightweight versions of these robust models. This would enable real-time, offline screening on edge devices without compromising the robustness benefits observed in our Gaussian and Wavelet noise experiments. To facilitate clinical trust, future iterations will incorporate Explainable AI methods. We plan to generate saliency maps and visualize attention weights (e.g., using Attention Rollout for ViT) to explicitly show which regions of the fundus image drive the model's predictions. Analysis of major segmentation models for intracranial artery time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography images Intracranial arterial stenosis (ICAS) is a leading cause of cerebrovascular accidents, and accurate morphological assessment of intracranial arteries is critical for diagnosis and treatment planning. Complex vascular structures, imaging noise, and variability in time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) images are challenging issues for the manual delineation that motivates the use of deep learning (DL) for automatic segmentation of the intracranial arteries. DL based automatic segmentation offers a promising solution by providing consistent and noise-reduced vessel delineation. However, selecting an optimal segmentation architecture remains challenging due to the diversity of network designs and encoder backbones. Therefore, this study presents a systematic benchmarking of five widely used DL segmentation architectures, UNet, LinkNet, Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN), Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), and DeepLabV3+, each combined with nine backbone networks, yielding 45 model variants, including previously unexplored configurations for intracranial artery segmentation in TOF-MRA. Models were trained and cross-validated on four datasets: in-house, CereVessMRA, IXI and ADAM, and evaluated on held-out independent test set. Performance metrics included Intersection over Union (IoU), Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), and a Stability Score, combining the coefficient of variation of IoU and DSC to quantify segmentation consistency and reproducibility. Experimental results demonstrated highest DSC score was achieved with UNet–SE-ResNeXt50, LinkNet-SE-ResNeXt50, FPN-DenseNet169, FPN-SENet154. The most stable configurations were LinkNet–EfficientNetB6, LinkNet–SENet154, UNet–DenseNet169, and UNet–EfficientNetB6. Conversely, DeepLabV3+ and PSPNet variants consistently underperformed. These findings provide actionable guidance for selecting backbone–segmentation pairs and highlight trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, and reproducibility for complex intracranial artery TOF-MRA segmentation tasks. Intracranial atherosclerosis (ICAS), also referred to as intracranial arterial stenosis, is a major contributor to ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack, accounting for approximately 9%–33% of global ischemic stroke cases ( Shi et al., 2020 ). Accurate morphological assessment of intracranial arteries is therefore critical for diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment planning. Automated segmentation of intracranial arteries (IA) from medical imaging has emerged as a key enabling step for visualization, extraction, and measurement of stenotic regions, which can subsequently serve as computational biomarkers for disease severity, treatment efficacy, and risk prediction. Several imaging modalities are used for intracranial vascular assessment, including digital subtraction angiography (DSA), computed tomography angiography (CTA), and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). While DSA and CTA provide high spatial resolution, their invasive nature, radiation exposure, and contrast dependency limit routine and longitudinal use ( Tian et al., 2020 ). In contrast, time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) enables non-invasive visualization of intracranial vasculature without contrast agents, making it particularly suitable for screening and follow-up examinations. The modality also offers high spatial resolution, three-dimensional coverage, and fast acquisition, facilitating the mapping of both major arteries and smaller perforating branches ( Ge et al., 2019; Min et al., 2024 ). However, TOF-MRA presents unique segmentation challenges due to flow-related signal variability, intensity inhomogeneity, vessel overlap, and limited boundary contrast, especially in maximum intensity projection (MIP) representations. Despite these advantages, accurate segmentation of intracranial arteries in TOF-MRA remains an open challenge. Several intrinsic imaging characteristics complicate the task. First, intensity inhomogeneity, arising from variable blood flow velocity, slice orientation, and scanner parameter discrepancies, produces inconsistent contrast levels between and within slices ( Deshpande et al., 2021 ). For instance, in Fig. 1(a) , slice B appears substantially brighter than slice A due to localized flow acceleration. Second, signal similarities between vascular and parenchymal tissues (e.g., between small vessels and adjacent white matter) often lead to segmentation ambiguity. Third, shadow-like distortions induced by gray–white matter boundaries, as shown in Fig. 1(b) , can obscure true vessel contours, complicating boundary extraction. Fourth, the presence of numerous fine, overlapping arteries, can mask or fragment the primary arterial trunk ( Fu et al., 2020 ). Fifth, orientation-dependent morphological variability, for example, the tortuosity of the ICA across axial slices, Fig. 1(c) , poses additional difficulties for segmentation algorithms. Finally, flow-related artifacts and motion-induced noise can mimic stenoses or occlusions, leading to diagnostic misinterpretations. Manual annotation under these imaging conditions is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and highly operator-dependent, limiting its practicality in both clinical and research settings. Consequently, there is a growing imperative to develop robust, automated IA segmentation algorithms capable of handling these confounding factors while maintaining clinical-grade accuracy. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have significantly improved vascular segmentation performance across modalities. Numerous architectures have been proposed for vessel and aneurysm segmentation, including nnUNet-based frameworks ( Nageler et al., 2023 ), attention-driven networks, e.g., ARU-Net ( Mu et al., 2023 ), artery-aware pipelines, e.g., AASeg ( Yao et al., 2024 ), and multi-scale learning models, e.g., MGLIA-Net ( Hou et al., 2025 ). While these approaches demonstrate strong task-specific performance, most studies focus on proposing new architectures or optimizing a single model on a specific dataset. As a result, existing literature offers limited insight into how different segmentation architectures interact with encoder backbones, particularly for ICAS-specific TOF-MRA, and how such design choices affect robustness and reproducibility. In particular, DL-based encoder–decoder architectures such as U-Net ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ), LinkNet ( Chaurasia & Culurciello, 2017 ), Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) ( Martinsson & Mogren, 2019 ), Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet) ( Zhao et al., 2017 ), and DeepLabV3+ ( Chen, Papandreou, Schroff, & Adam, 2017 ) have significantly improved segmentation performance. The effectiveness of these models critically depends on the ability of their encoders to extract meaningful features. While these architectures include their own encoders, replacing them with pre-trained classification models, such as VGG ( Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014 ), Residual Networks (ResNet) ( He et al., 2016 ), DenseNet ( Huang et al., 2017 ), and EfficientNet ( Tan & Le, 2019 ), has been shown to further enhance segmentation accuracy ( Abdelrahman & Viriri, 2023b; Hussain et al., 2025; Li & Xie, 2025; Sharma et al., 2023; Sulaiman et al., 2024 ). Pre-trained backbones efficiently capture hierarchical features, accelerate convergence, and improve accuracy, particularly in medical imaging tasks with limited training data ( Abdelrahman & Viriri, 2023a; Rayed et al., 2024 ). Although such backbones have demonstrated strong performance across various segmentation tasks ( Bhatti et al., 2025; Chen, Papandreou, Kokkinos, et al., 2017; Long et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2025 ), their relative effectiveness is highly task and data-dependent, and systematic comparisons of backbone–segmentation combinations for IA segmentation in TOF-MRA remain scarce. Moreover, most prior studies emphasize peak performance metrics such as Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) or Intersection over Union (IoU), while largely overlooking performance stability and reproducibility. In clinical settings, segmentation models must exhibit consistent behavior across patients, acquisition conditions, and validation folds. Models that achieve high average accuracy but exhibit high variability may produce unreliable segmentations, limiting their translational potential. Despite its importance, stability-aware benchmarking has received little attention in IA segmentation research. To address this gap, the present study systematically evaluates nine widely used classification architectures, VGG Net, ResNet, SE-ResNet, Residual Networks with Cardinality (ResNeXt), Squeeze-and-Excitation Residual Networks with Cardinality (SE-ResNeXt) ( Hu et al., 2018 ), Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks (SENet) ( Hu et al., 2018 ), DenseNet, Inception Net ( Szegedy et al., 2015 ), EfficientNet ( Tan & Le, 2019 ), as encoder backbones within five encoder–decoder based segmentation networks, UNet, LinkNet, FPN, PSPNet, and DeepLabV3+, resulting in 45 model variants. Each segmentation model was chosen to represent distinct architectural strategies: UNet for its symmetric skip connections that preserve fine-grained spatial information, LinkNet for residual connections enabling efficient encoder–decoder feature transfer, FPN for top-down multiscale feature fusion that captures vessels of varying sizes, and PSPNet for pyramid pooling to integrate global contextual information. Furthermore, the evaluation of these 45 combinations are conducted across four heterogeneous TOF-MRA datasets, including an in-house clinical dataset and three public datasets (CereVessMRA ( Guo et al., 2024 ), IXI (Information eXtraction from Images) ( I.X.I. Project, 2025 ), and ADAM (Aneurysm Detection and Segmentation Challenge ( Timmins et al., 2020 )), enabling a multi-domain assessment of generalizability. In addition to conventional accuracy metrics, we introduce a coefficient-of-variation–based stability score to quantify segmentation consistency across cross-validation folds and test cohorts. By jointly analyzing accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency, this work provides practical guidance for selecting reliable backbone–segmentation model pairs for ICAS-oriented TOF-MRA segmentation. A systematic and controlled evaluation of 45 previously unexplored encoder–decoder combinations is conducted for IA segmentation in TOF-MRA. To the best of current knowledge, no prior study has jointly benchmarked segmentation architectures and backbone networks for this task. 2. A comprehensive benchmark is performed across segmentation accuracy, IoU, DSC, computational complexity, trainable parameters, and runtime efficiency, median inference time, enabling a precise characterization of performance–efficiency trade-offs among models. 3. The evaluation spans four datasets, an in-house TOF-MRA dataset and three public datasets (CereVessMRA, ADAM, IXI), providing a multi-domain assessment of generalizability across scanners, populations, and annotation protocols. 4. A Coefficient-of-Variation–based stability metric is introduced to quantify cross-fold and cross-subject variability in IoU and DSC, facilitating the identification of model configurations that exhibit both high accuracy and statistical robustness. The in-house TOF-MRA slices exhibited noticeable intensity inhomogeneity due to variations in acquisition parameters, motivating the need for preprocessing to achieve consistent contrast throughout the dataset. Intensity enhancement was therefore applied to improve vessel–background separation and support downstream segmentation. Several commonly used enhancement methods were evaluated, including contrast stretching (CS), min–max scaling (MMS), max-absolute scaling (MAS), histogram equalization (HEq), gamma transformation (GT), and logarithmic transformation (LT). For quantitative comparison of enhancement approaches, the original unprocessed slice I ( x , y ) was used as the reference image when computing similarity-based measures, such as, mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and structural similarity index (SSIM) ( Sara et al., 2019 ). These metrics were not used as indicators of diagnostic improvement; rather, they were used to ensure that enhancement did not alter or distort arterial morphology. Thus, lower MSE and higher PSNR/SSIM were interpreted as evidence of structural fidelity with respect to the original anatomy. Because similarity metrics alone do not directly quantify diagnostic relevance, qualitative assessment of vessel conspicuity was also conducted. Representative slices were visually examined to assess clarity of major intracranial arteries (ICA, MCA, ACA, PCA, BA, VA) with attention to lumen definition, contrast uniformity, and background suppression. This combined quantitative–qualitative evaluation ensured that the selected enhancement method preserved anatomical structure while improving visibility of vascular features. Each enhancement technique was applied to all slices, and performance was assessed using MSE, PSNR, and SSIM. As summarized in Table 1 , GT with γ = 0 . 9 yielded the best results, achieving the lowest MSE of 28.658, highest PSNR of 34.673, and highest SSIM of 0.9906, indicating optimal brightness and contrast. GT enhances each pixel of the normalized input image I ( x , y ) on a pixel-by-pixel basis using a power-law transformation: (1) I ˆ ( x , y ) = α ⋅ I ( x , y ) γ Here, I ˆ ( x , y ) is the enhanced output, α controls brightness, and γ adjusts contrast. In this study, α was set to 1, and γ < 1 was chosen to produce brighter images, as values γ > 1 tend to darken the output ( Pedregosa et al., 2011; Rahman et al., 2016 ). As illustrated in Fig. 5 , varying γ produces markedly different visual characteristics: • γ = 0 . 1 to 0.3: excessive brightening, loss of vessel boundaries, background washout. • γ = 0 . 4 to 0.6: moderate enhancement but inconsistent contrast across thin vessels. • γ = 0 . 7 to 0.8: improved arterial visibility but occasional over-sharpening and lumen non-uniformity. • γ = 0 . 9 : optimal balance; clear delineation of intracranial arteries, improved vessel–background separation, and excellent preservation of morphology γ = 0 . 1 to 0.3: excessive brightening, loss of vessel boundaries, background washout. γ = 0 . 4 to 0.6: moderate enhancement but inconsistent contrast across thin vessels. γ = 0 . 7 to 0.8: improved arterial visibility but occasional over-sharpening and lumen non-uniformity. γ = 0 . 9 : optimal balance; clear delineation of intracranial arteries, improved vessel–background separation, and excellent preservation of morphology Quantitatively, γ = 0 . 9 produced the lowest MSE of 14.96 and highest PSNR of 36.38 among all tested values, indicating minimal structural distortion. Visual inspection further confirmed consistent enhancement of both large and small arterial segments without amplifying background noise. The automated ROI generation pipeline was developed to isolate clinically relevant intracranial arterial regions while suppressing non-informative background structures. This process, applied exclusively to the in-house dataset, consists of two sequential steps: (1) radiologist-guided polygonal cropping, followed by (2) automated bounding-box–based normalization. The full workflow is illustrated in Fig. 6 . Initial arterial demarcation was performed using polygonal cropping on the enhanced TOF-MRA image I ˆ ( x , y ) obtained from Section 2.2 . Two board-certified neuroradiologists, each with more than 8 years of experience, independently delineated polygonal regions encompassing the major ICAS-relevant arteries (ICA, MCA–M1, ACA–A1, PCA–P1, BA, and VA–V4), following anatomical criteria described in Sartoretti et al. (2020) . All polygon masks were created using the open-source polygon-crop 0.0.3 tool ( Chiang, 2020 ). A slice-wise annotation strategy was adopted to ensure that subtle morphological variations across axial slices were accurately captured. To maintain consistency, a three-expert consensus protocol was implemented. Initially, two neuroradiologists independently annotated a subset of cases, and any discrepancies were resolved through joint discussion with a third senior neuroradiologist. Following this calibration phase, the remaining slices were annotated collaboratively by two raters, with every annotation subsequently reviewed and verified by the third rater for quality control. The resulting polygon-cropped image I ˆ p c ( x , y ) preserved the original spatial dimensions of I ˆ ( x , y ) while setting all non-ROI regions to zero intensity. While this step effectively isolates vessel-rich regions, the resulting images often contained large zero-valued background areas. This introduced foreground–background imbalance which could negatively affect subsequent model training, motivating the second stage of automated normalization. To reduce redundant background while preserving all vascular structures, an automated cropping stage was implemented using OpenCV 4.2.0. For every polygon-cropped slice, the software identified the smallest bounding box containing all nonzero pixels. These per-slice bounding boxes were collected across all patients and aggregated to determine the union bounding region that consistently enclosed ICAS-relevant arterial segments for the entire in-house dataset. By analyzing the union of all bounding boxes across 1003 slices, we empirically observed that all polygon-defined arterial regions fell within a stable spatial zone. This led to the determination of fixed cropping coordinates: (100:350) along the y -axis and (150:350) along the x -axis. These coordinates represent the minimal rectangular region that fully contained the anatomical ROIs for all subjects in our in-house cohort during visual and quantitative verification. Applying this global crop resulted in the final ROI-normalized image, I ˆ A c ( x , y ) , ensuring uniform input dimensions and facilitating efficient batch processing during model training. However, it is important to note that these coordinates are in-house dataset-specific and may not generalize to other TOF-MRA acquisitions, scanner geometries, or head orientations. Column 1 shows the enhanced image I ˆ ( x , y ) obtained after gamma transformation ( γ = 0 . 9 ), Column 2 depicts the polygonally cropped output I p c ˆ ( x , y ) , and Column 3 displays the final automatically cropped ROI I A c ˆ ( x , y ) used for mask generation and model training. For IA segmentation, the task is binary: distinguishing the ROI from the background. Accordingly, binary masks were generated where class 0 represents the background and class 1 corresponds to the ROI ( Fig. 4 ). The process of generating these masks is a crucial step, as they serve as ground truth labels for model training, validation, and quantitative evaluation of segmentation accuracy. To achieve consistent and anatomically accurate annotations, the Medical Image Processing, Analysis, and Visualization (MIPAV) software (version 10.0.0) was employed. MIPAV provides robust semi-automated segmentation tools with pixel-level precision, allowing radiologists and imaging experts to refine the ROI boundaries interactively while maintaining reproducibility across samples. This semi-automated approach reduces manual bias, enhances efficiency, and ensures uniformity in labeling across all TOF-MRA slices. Each binary mask, denoted as B I A c ˆ ( x , y ) , corresponds directly to the automatically cropped input image I A c ˆ ( x , y ) obtained from Section 2.3 . The generated masks delineate only the arterial structures, with all non-ROI regions assigned zero intensity values. These curated masks form the foundational dataset for evaluating segmentation model performance through overlap-based metrics such as Dice coefficient, IoU, and pixel-wise accuracy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have consistently demonstrated superior performance across a wide range of computer vision tasks, including vascular segmentation. Numerous segmentation architectures have been proposed, each tailored to specific applications and data characteristics, which makes the selection of an appropriate model for IA segmentation non-trivial. To systematically evaluate their suitability, a comparative analysis was conducted using several widely adopted deep learning-based encoder–decoder semantic segmentation architectures, including UNet, PSPNet, LinkNet, FPN, and DeepLabV3+. Segmentation performance is strongly influenced by the choice of encoder, as modern decoders commonly benefit from feature representations learned by encoders pre-trained on large-scale classification datasets. Consequently, examining a diverse set of encoder architectures becomes essential. General representation of encoder families and the corresponding decoder structures are schematically expressed in Fig. 8 . In typical hierarchical CNN design, the spatial resolution of feature maps is progressively reduced by factors of 1 / 2 , 1 / 4 , 1 / 8 , 1 / 16 , 1 / 32 across five stages, which are denoted as Stage 1 through Stage 5, while the feature dimensionality increases accordingly. All TOF-MRA slices are single-channel images. To ensure compatibility with ImageNet-pretrained encoders, each slice is replicated across three channels (1 to 3), followed by backbone-specific preprocessing, mean-subtraction and scaling, using the g e t _ p r e p r o c e s s i n g _ f n function from the s e g m e n t a t i o n _ m o d e l s ( Yakubovskiy, 2019 ) framework. This ensures consistent input normalization and preserves the integrity of pretrained feature statistics. Besides, batch-normalization layers included in the pretrained encoders remain trainable for all experiments. This configuration allows the normalization statistics to adapt to the target medical domain while maintaining stable initialization. Decoder blocks also retain batch-normalization layers as implemented in the standard architectures within the library. Backbone networks serve as the primary feature extractors within modern segmentation architectures. These networks are typically pre-trained on large-scale image datasets, enabling segmentation models to leverage well-established low- and mid-level representations through transfer learning. Such initialization is particularly advantageous in medical image segmentation, where annotated datasets are often limited, as it accelerates convergence and improves overall representational quality. Each backbone architecture embodies distinct design choices, including depth, connectivity patterns, scaling strategies, and computational efficiency, that directly influence segmentation performance (see Table 2 ). For instance, VGG16 ( vgg16 ) provides a classical sequential baseline, characterized by stacked 3 X 3 convolutional layer. Two successive 3 X 3 convolutions achieve a receptive field comparable to a single 5 X 5 convolution while requiring fewer parameters, making the architecture computationally efficient despite its simplicity. Residual networks such as ResNet-50 ( resnet50 ) introduce identity skip connections that alleviate the vanishing-gradient problem and facilitate feature reuse across layers. ResNeXt-50 ( resnext50 ) extends this design by incorporating grouped convolutions; the use of cardinality (i.e., multiple parallel transformation paths) enhances representational capacity without proportional increases in complexity. The integration of squeeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks further augments feature discrimination by applying channel-wise recalibration through learned nonlinear interactions. This mechanism underpins architectures such as SEResNet-50 ( seresnet50 ), SEResNeXt-50 ( seresnext50 ), and the deeper SE-enhanced variant SENet-154 ( senet154 ). DenseNet-169 ( densenet169 ) adopts dense connectivity wherein each layer receives feature maps from all preceding layers via channel-wise concatenation. This facilitates feature reuse, strengthens gradient propagation, and provides a highly parameter-efficient architecture. InceptionResNet-V2 ( irv2 ) combines the multi-scale feature extraction capabilities of Inception modules, using parallel convolutional branches of varying kernel sizes, with residual connections that stabilize gradient flow. This hybrid design supports the training of very deep networks while maintaining strong multi-scale contextual encoding. Finally, EfficientNet-B6 ( efficientnetb6 ) employs compound scaling, uniformly adjusting network depth, width, and input resolution based on a principled scaling coefficient. Combined with mobile inverted bottleneck convolution (MBConv) blocks, this architecture achieves a favorable balance between accuracy, computational cost, and memory efficiency, making it suitable for high-resolution medical imaging tasks. The decoder component of a semantic segmentation network is responsible for progressively reconstructing a high-resolution output from the compressed feature representations generated by the encoder. Its primary role is to recover spatial detail, refine object boundaries, and integrate multi-scale contextual cues to enable accurate pixel-wise classification. Typical decoder designs employ a combination of upsampling operations, convolutional refinement, and feature fusion strategies, often incorporating skip connections—to effectively restore fine-grained structural information while preserving the semantic richness learned at deeper layers (see Table 3 ). For instance, the most popular medical image segmentation architecture, UNet, reconstructs high-resolution segmentation maps through a sequence of upsampling stages which involves bilinear upsampling or transposed convolution to double spatial resolution, followed by concatenation with encoder skip features, and two successive 3 × 3 convolutions + ReLU. This design preserves fine-grained anatomical boundaries and enables precise localization. LinkNet, on the other hand, employs a lightweight, efficient decoder designed around residual blocks. For every encoder stage, the decoder applies 1 × 1 convolution for channel reduction,followed by bilinear upsampling, and residual refinement block. Different from UNet, here skip connections from encoded are additive in nature rather than concatenative as seen in case of Unet, reducing computational load and memory usage while maintaining spatial detail. FPN introduces a top-down pathway merged with lateral connections. High-level, semantically strong features are progressively upsampled and summed with spatially detailed lower-level features. Each pyramid level undergoes 1 × 1 lateral convolution, followed by upsampling, and 3 × 3 smoothing convolution. This produces a multi-scale feature pyramid effective for segmenting structures of varying sizes. PSPNet uses a pyramid pooling module (PPM) to aggregate global contextual information. The decoder pools features at multiple spatial scales (e.g., 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 6 × 6 bins), applies 1 × 1 convolutions, upsamples each branch to the original size, and concatenates them. A final 3 × 3 convolution refines fused features. This allows the model to capture long-range dependencies and contextual relationships. DeepLabV3+ integrates atrous (dilated) convolutions inside an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module, followed by a lightweight decoder. The decoder upsamples ASPP output by 4×, concatenates it with low-level encoder features (after 1 × 1 convolution to reduce channels), followed by application of two 3 × 3 convolutions and final upsampling. The combination of atrous convolution and multi-scale context yields robust segmentation in complex anatomical structures. Unlike UNet, LinkNet, DeepLabV3+ does not employ skip connections from all encoder stages, providing a computationally efficient yet effective decoder for complex anatomical structures. During the training phase, data augmentation technique was implemented using Tensorflows’ ImageDataGenerator with the rotations ranging from 10°to 40°in the axial plane, zooming by 0.05, width and height shifts of 0.05, shearing by 0.05, and both horizontal and vertical flipping set to True. All augmentations were applied stochastically. For each batch, the generator randomly samples whether to apply each transformation and with what magnitude, resulting in a unique augmented realization of every training image. The same augmentation pipeline and training setup were applied uniformly across all backbone architectures and segmentation models to ensure fair comparison. Augmentation hyperparameters were selected during an initial tuning stage and subsequently fixed for all experiments. This consistent design avoids model-specific bias and stabilizes the evaluation of robustness and segmentation performance across architectures. The performance of the segmentation models across various backbone was evaluated both quantitatively and statistically to ensure comprehensive assessment. Statistical evaluation was performed through cross-validation-based stability analysis. Quantitative evaluation employed IoU, DSC, as primary metric, and secondary metric involved MCC, Precision, and Recall. DSC, equivalent to the F1-score for binary segmentation, reflects the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall. Precision and Recall, measure the accuracy of positive predictions and the completeness of detected positives, respectively. IoU assesses the overlap between predicted and ground truth segmentations. MCC is crucial due to class imbalance, as it incorporates all confusion matrix elements and remains robust when background dominates. Metrics like pixel accuracy and specificity were excluded due to their sensitivity to class imbalance, as noted in Jun et al. (2020) . In this binary segmentation task, artery pixels were classified as the positive class and background pixels as the negative class. True positives (TP) were correctly predicted artery pixels, while false positives (FP) were incorrectly predicted ones. False negatives (FN) were background mistaken for artery, and true negatives (TN) were correctly predicted background pixels. While metrics such as IoU and DSC assess segmentation accuracy, they do not capture the consistency of model performance across folds. A model may achieve high average scores yet exhibit substantial variability, which can compromise reliability and reproducibility, key considerations for clinical deployment. Although standard deviation (S.D) quantifies variability, it does not account for differences in mean performance; two models with similar S.Ds may have very different relative stability depending on their average IoU or DSC. To address this, the coefficient of variation (CV) ( Everitt & Skrondal, 2010 ) was calculated for IoU and DSC across 10-fold cross-validation. CV normalizes the S.D by the mean, providing a relative measure of dispersion that allows fair comparison across models with differing average performance levels. To summarize overall consistency in a single metric, a composite stability score was defined as: (3) Stability Score = I o U C V + D S C C V 2 where I o U C V and D S C C V are the CV for the IoU and DSC, respectively. Lower stability scores indicate more consistent and reproducible segmentation, which is crucial for reliable clinical applications. While high mean IoU and DSC reflect segmentation accuracy, the stability score provides a normalized and comprehensive measure of model robustness across different data splits, ensuring confidence in deployment for critical medical tasks. This study presents a systematic and large-scale evaluation of five DL-based segmentation architectures, LinkNet, FPN, PSPNet, UNet, and DeepLabV3+, across four distinct TOF-MRA datasets, highlighting how backbone selection, model complexity, and dataset characteristics jointly influence segmentation performance and robustness. By benchmarking 45 model–backbone combinations across four heterogeneous datasets, the analysis extends beyond peak segmentation accuracy to examine performance stability and robustness, which are critical yet often underexplored aspects in clinical image segmentation. A consistent observation across all experiments is that segmentation performance is strongly dataset-dependent. The in-house dataset, derived from clinical MIP-based TOF-MRA, differs substantially from public whole-slice datasets in terms of contrast distribution, spatial context, and vessel continuity. These differences directly influenced how segmentation architectures leveraged contextual and multi-scale information. On the in-house dataset, UNet with seresnext50 achieved the highest segmentation accuracy, whereas LinkNet with efficientnetb6 demonstrated superior stability, indicating more predictable and reproducible behavior across folds and test data. In contrast, for whole-slice-derived datasets (CereVessMRA, IXI, and ADAM), FPN-based configurations frequently achieved the highest cross-validation DSC values; however, these gains were often accompanied by increased variability on held-out test sets. Conversely, LinkNet and UNet variants exhibited more consistent generalization behavior, despite occasionally lower peak accuracy. These findings highlight that segmentation models optimized for one dataset or acquisition protocol may not generalize reliably to others, emphasizing the importance of cross-dataset benchmarking when assessing clinical suitability. Table 10 summarizes the backbone–architecture combinations that consistently achieved either the highest accuracy or the best stability across datasets. The comparatively weaker performance of PSPNet across all datasets, and the reduced robustness observed for DeepLabV3+, can be attributed to architectural design choices in relation to the characteristics of TOF-MRA data. While global context aggregation and atrous convolution strategies are effective for natural scene understanding, they appear less effective at consistently preserving fine-scale boundary information that is critical for accurate vascular delineation. In particular, PSPNet showed limited ability to segment thin and elongated vessel structures, resulting in lower overlap-based accuracy across datasets. DeepLabV3+, although capable of achieving moderate-to-high segmentation accuracy on several datasets, exhibited higher variability and reduced generalization to held-out test data compared to UNet- and LinkNet-based configurations. In addition, the relatively lightweight decoder designs of these architectures may constrain their capacity to reliably reconstruct small-caliber vessels from 2D MIP-based TOF-MRA images, where contrast between vascular and surrounding brain tissue is limited. Overall, these findings suggest that segmentation architectures originally designed for natural image understanding may require task-specific architectural adaptation to achieve both accurate and robust IA segmentation. By incorporating stability-aware evaluation alongside conventional accuracy metrics, this study provides a more nuanced framework for benchmarking segmentation models. In clinical applications, reproducibility and predictable behavior across patients and acquisition conditions are essential for building trust in automated systems. Models that exhibit high variability across cross-validation folds or test cohorts may yield inconsistent segmentations despite achieving high average performance, thereby limiting their translational potential. While hyperparameter optimization and fine-tuning can improve peak segmentation accuracy, such improvements do not necessarily translate into enhanced robustness or reproducibility. The current findings indicate that model-backbone combinations exhibiting low intrinsic stability tend to retain higher variability even when accuracy is optimized, underscoring the importance of evaluating stability as a complementary criterion during model selection. The stability analysis enables the identification of model-backbone configurations that achieve a favorable balance between segmentation accuracy and consistency, offering practical guidance for deployment in real-world and resource-constrained clinical settings. This stability-aware perspective aligns with emerging trends in medical image analysis that emphasize robustness, reliability, and uncertainty awareness alongside conventional performance metrics. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, all experiments were conducted on 2D MIP projections, which simplify inherently three-dimensional vascular anatomy and may obscure depth-related information. This choice may disadvantage architectures optimized for volumetric learning, such as nnUNet, and limits direct comparison with 3D segmentation approaches. Second, the in-house dataset originates from a single institution and scanner, which may introduce residual domain-specific bias despite the inclusion of three public datasets. However, the individual results on public comparatively larger dataset provide valuable guidance on segmentation-backbone selection on whole-slice TOF-MRA. Third, fixed cropping strategies, although empirically validated for the in-house cohort, may not generalize to atypical vascular anatomy or alternative acquisition protocols. Fourth, the in-house dataset primarily focuses on main trunk arteries, where TOF-MRA is more reliable, but future work will extend segmentation to include small-flow arteries alongside the main trunks. However, the three public dataset are derived from whole-slice TOF-MRA, and thus they capture a more complete representation of the cerebrovasculature, including both large and small vessels. Finally, although multiple datasets were included, domain adaptation and cross-institutional generalization were not explicitly addressed. Future research will focus on extending this benchmarking framework to 3D volumetric TOF-MRA, integrating adaptive region-of-interest extraction, and incorporating domain adaptation strategies to improve cross-institutional robustness. Additional, task-specific contrast metrics such as Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) will be explored in future work. Therefore, exploring hybrid architectures that jointly optimize accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency will further enhance the clinical applicability of IA segmentation models. This study presents a large-scale, systematic benchmarking of DL encoder–decoder architectures for IA segmentation from TOF-MRA across heterogeneous datasets. Evaluation of 45 architecture-backbone combinations on both in-house and public datasets (CereVessMRA, IXI, ADAM) demonstrates that segmentation performance is governed by a complex interplay between architectural design, backbone capacity, and dataset characteristics. Importantly, high overlap-based metrics alone are shown to be insufficient for identifying clinically reliable models. Architectures achieving the highest Dice or IoU scores frequently exhibited substantial variability across cross-validation and independent test cohorts, limiting reproducibility. In contrast, LinkNet configurations with backbones such as efficientnetb6 , densenet169 , and senet154 consistently demonstrated greater stability, whereas UNet with seresnext50 , densenet169 and FPN with senet154 and densenet169 often achieved higher peak DSC values at the cost of increased variability. PSPNet variants underperformed consistently, and DeepLabV3+ exhibited reduced robustness despite competitive accuracy, highlighting stability and generalization as key challenges in this task. However, the analysis was restricted to 2D MIP representations, which simplify the inherently three-dimensional vascular anatomy and may obscure depth-related information, particularly in complex or overlapping vessel structures. The in-house dataset was acquired from a single institution and scanner, potentially introducing domain-specific bias. In addition, fixed cropping strategies, while effective for the studied in-house cohort, may not generalize to atypical anatomy or alternative acquisition protocols. Future research should extend this benchmarking framework to fully 3D volumetric TOF-MRA, incorporate adaptive ROI extraction, and integrate domain-adaptive and uncertainty-aware learning strategies to improve cross-institutional robustness. The development of hybrid architectures that jointly optimize segmentation accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency is expected to play a critical role in enabling reliable clinical translation of automated IA segmentation. Automated segmentation of peripheral arteries in 3D CT data based on a Single-Depth vascular network Peripheral artery disease (PAD), if left untreated, can lead to cardiovascular mortality. The diagnosis of PAD typically requires complex and costly procedures, such as computed tomography (CT), followed by extensive examinations. In addition, segmenting peripheral arteries through deep networks still remains challenging due to their small and complex structure, motion artifacts, class imbalance, and variations in field of view in different datasets. Furthermore, handling large-scale whole-body scans efficiently complicates the segmentation process. To address these limitations, this study employs three-dimensional CT scans to segment peripheral arteries. Firstly, a YOLOv8 network is developed to extract the region of interest (ROI) from whole-body scans. This approach optimizes processing by focusing on ROI while reducing memory usage and processing time. Afterwards, ROI is fed into a novel Single-Depth Vascular Network for peripheral artery segmentation. The Single-Depth Vascular Network encapsulates an encoder–decoder architecture with a skip connection to improve the accuracy and precision of segmentation. Through this approach, the network achieves an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.91, a Hausdorff distance of 12.60 mm, and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance of 1.12 mm against unseen data. This approach provides a tool for medical professionals to diagnose and treat PAD with greater precision. Peripheral artery disease (PAD), if left untreated, can lead to cardiovascular mortality. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is a prevalent circulatory condition characterized by narrowed or blocked arteries, leading to reduced blood flow to the limbs and potentially serious complications [1] . Common symptoms of PAD include discomfort, spasms, and, in severe instances, tissue damage or gangrene [2] . In extreme cases, PAD can result in cardiac death [3] . Recently, there is a rise in PAD cases, closely linked to cardiovascular diseases that contribute to increased mortality and morbidity [4] . In the human body, the aorta serves as the largest artery [5] , supplying oxygenated blood as the primary route to systemic circulation. It consists of three main sections: the ascending aorta, the aortic arch, and the descending aorta, which further branches into the common iliac arteries [5,6] . These iliac arteries continue into the femoral arteries, which, along with their branches, form the peripheral arterial system [7] . These peripheral arteries (PAs) are crucial for delivering oxygenated blood to the lower limbs, thereby ensuring their health. The diagnosis of the PAD can be time-consuming and a complex process. Identifying PAs through medical imaging techniques is the initial step. Commonly utilized imaging methods encompass computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasonography (USG). CT scans are one of the most commonly used imaging techniques for the examination of PAs. Since MRA has a higher sensitivity to motion, which affects the image quality, especially for smaller blood vessels [8] . A CT scanner employs a contrast agent to generate images of blood vessels. This technique effectively displays the arterial system, including the abdomen, pelvis, and lower extremities [9] . CT scans produce high-quality images that help doctors see the arteries in detail. In addition, CT scans can provide a complete evaluation of the arterial system in one scan, making them an important tool for the diagnosis of PAD [10] . The interpretation of medical images is subjective, leading to diagnostic variability among practitioners. Healthcare professionals face multiple challenges when analyzing medical images, making the task both complex and demanding [8] . These variations may lead to incorrect diagnoses or postponements in treatment, adversely affecting patient outcomes. In addition, the complexity of medical images is increased by issues such as noise, low resolution, and artifacts, which obstruct accurate analysis. The large volume of medical images also adds to the workload, which requires significant time and effort from medical experts (e.g. CT data with a resolution of 512 × 512 × 2311). These challenges underscore the need for automated systems to support practitioners, ensuring more consistent, accurate, and efficient analysis [11] . The literature has proposed multiple approaches to identify and segment arteries from the rest of the body, considering their structure and nature. Early methods for artery segmentation relied heavily on edge detection and region-growing algorithms. These methods often struggled with the noise and artifacts present in medical images [12] . Techniques such as active contour models (snakes) and level-set methods have been used to improve segmentation accuracy. These methods use prior knowledge about the shape and appearance of the arteries to guide the segmentation process [8] . Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have significantly improved segmentation performance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and U-Net architectures are among the applications. These models can learn complex features from large datasets, making them highly effective for medical image segmentation [13] . Combining traditional image processing with machine learning techniques has also shown promise. These hybrid methods leverage the strengths of both approaches to achieve better segmentation results [14] . Flores et al. presented the use of machine learning and AI in the detection of advanced and undiagnosed PAD, the refinement of disease characterization, the personalization of medical decision-making, the improvement of risk stratification, the automaton of image analysis and the direction of vascular surgical care [15] . Dima et al. presented a novel method for segmenting 3D peripancreatic arteries from single annotated 2D projections with depth supervision, demonstrating effective capture of depth information from 2D projections [16] . Guo et al. addressed the challenge of annotating vessels in 3D space by using maximum intensity projection (MIP) to reduce the dimensionality of 3D volumes to 2D images for efficient annotation. The 2D labels guide the training of a 3D vessel segmentation model, which is further refined using confidence learning and uncertainty estimation [17] . In contrast, Chen et al. proposed a novel 3D shape-guided local discrimination model for 3D vascular segmentation, leveraging limited guidance from public 2D vessel annotations. The model uses a 3D region discrimination loss to learn voxel-wise similarities and a Crop-and-Overlap strategy to generate reference masks from 2D annotations [18] . However, in case of segmentation of PAs, Hu et al. presented the association between the lower extremity muscle characteristics of CTA and the severity of PAD using digital subtraction angiography (DSA) as a reference standard [19] . In addition, Westenberg et al. focused on developing and validating methods for accurately measuring vessel diameters, crucial for diagnosing and treating PAD using gadolinium contrast-enhanced three-dimensional MRA [20] . Despite these advancements, there is still no dedicated solution for CT-based segmentation of PAs. The intricate branching structures and varied diameters of the PAs require models to account for high variability in arterial morphology, particularly in regions with bifurcations and overlapping vessels, which can confuse segmentation algorithms [21] . Furthermore, in CT scans, PAs often appear with low contrast against surrounding tissues such as muscles and bones, making it difficult to clearly distinguish arterial boundaries. Image artifacts caused by patient motion, metal implants, or limitations of the scanner further obscure PAs, complicating segmentation efforts. Identification of smaller vessels in the legs represents specific challenges. These arteries are thin and often consist of few pixels with scan, leading to difficult detection and segmentation. In case of lower image resolution, this task becomes more complicated [22] . The use of deep neural networks for large amounts of 3D medical imaging datasets requires substantial memory and processing resources. Accurate segmentation on these volumes in a reasonable time span requires significant computational resources and effective algorithms to prevent bottlenecks [23] . Class imbalance is another challenge, as the arteries occupy a relatively small portion of the image volume compared to surrounding tissues, such as muscles or bones. In addition, patient-specific factors such as age, body habit, and the presence of comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, obesity) influence the appearance of the arteries on scans, complicating the development of generalized models that can accurately segment PAs in a diverse population of patients [24] . In addition, indicating the region of interest (ROI) in medical imaging is challenging because scans often include structures that do not contain PAs, making it harder to isolate and accurately segment relevant regions. Non-relevant structures such as the lungs, heart, and major thoracic vessels (e.g. the aorta, subclavian, and carotid arteries) can dominate the scan, leading to the unnecessary inclusion of non-target anatomy. Moreover, medical imaging often captures a wide field of view, and precisely segmenting the relevant region while excluding the upper body without losing crucial lower-body information requires accurate localization. To address these challenges, an advanced methodology for detecting ROI and a model for segmenting PAs is necessary. This study presents a novel approach that integrates advanced techniques to improve the precision and efficiency of PAs segmentation. This work presents a You-Only-Look-Once version 8 (YOLOv8) based method for ROI extraction integrated with cumulative intensity projection (CIP). This integration significantly detects key regions on CT scan. In addition, the study develops and presents a novel Single-Depth vascular network (SDVN) for PA segmentation considering the limitations. SDVN consists of a single encoder–decoder and skip connection to optimize the segmentation process. The SDVN captures more contextual information while maintaining computational efficiency. The simplicity of the single encoder–decoder structure reduces complexity while still providing robust performance in segmenting PAs. This approach advances medical image segmentation by integrating the advanced ROI detection capabilities of YOLOv8 with the SDVN architecture. This integration improves segmentation accuracy and efficiency, which are essential for the diagnosis and evaluation of PAD. The dataset consists of multiple samples, each containing regions of the body not related to PAs. Including these additional regions in the training data can lead to class imbalance, which complicates the training process. This imbalance may reduce the model’s performance by causing it to focus on irrelevant body parts, which affects its ability to effectively segment the PAs. To address this issue, an automated method using You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) is proposed to accurately identify ROI, specifically the PAs structure, which helps to reduce this imbalance. YOLOv8 [27] , developed by Ultralytics, is designed for real-time object detection, image classification, instance segmentation, and pose estimation. YOLOv8 was chosen for the extraction of the ROI due to its integrated pose estimation and keypoint detection capabilities, which offer more precise anatomical localization compared to traditional object detection methods that rely solely on bounding boxes. This advanced functionality is crucial for accurately identifying specific anatomical landmarks, thereby streamlining and improving the ROI extraction process. In particular, the YOLOv8 pose estimation feature significantly improves PAs detection and analysis on CT by identifying key points that correspond to critical anatomical structures. By providing both keypoints and bounding boxes, YOLOv8 enables highly accurate localization within the ROI — an essential advantage in medical imaging, where precise spatial relationships between anatomical features are vital. Moreover, benchmarking studies, such as Jegham et al. [28] , have shown that YOLOv8 outperforms the available YOLO versions by delivering superior inference speed while maintaining competitive precision, in complex datasets. This combination of speed, accuracy, and built-in keypoint detection makes YOLOv8 particularly well suited for medical imaging workflows. In this study, YOLOv8 identifies key points, particularly points of bifurcation of the arteries. By accurately marking these keypoints, the model focuses on essential aspects of arterial anatomy, improving its ability to learn and generalize from the data. This targeted approach improves overall performance, allowing the model to focus on the most informative examples and minimize the influence of irrelevant data that could weaken its training efficacy. This precise localization of vascular features supports downstream segmentation tasks. After the detection of ROI, grid samplers were utilized to improve the model training process. Grid samplers are used to extract patches from extensive volumetric data, thereby substantially decreasing computational expenses. Furthermore, grid samplers play a vital role in choosing a representative subset of spatial data points, ensuring that the model is trained on a variety of important features [29] . The Single-Depth Vascular Network (SDVN) is a convolutional neural network, precisely developed for the segmentation of PAs from three-dimensional volumetric imaging data. The SDVN architecture is designed to preserve high spatial resolution across the processing pipeline, starting with a primary convolutional layer that emphasizes the extraction of essential features from the input data. This preliminary phase is crucial to the network’s effectiveness, as it lays the groundwork for a more accurate and streamlined encoding procedure. The following key features highlight the SDVN architecture: • SDVN employs a single encoder–decoder pathway with one skip connection, significantly reducing architectural complexity compared to traditional multi-depth or multi-branch networks. • Prior to each downsampling step, the network utilizes a residual convolutional block that preserves critical spatial information and enhances feature representation stability, ensuring essential details are maintained despite the reduction in spatial resolution. • This streamlined design reduces the number of trainable parameters, enabling faster training and inference. • The single skip connection — from the highest encoder level to the decoder — effectively preserves high-resolution spatial details, ensuring precise and detailed vessel segmentation. SDVN employs a single encoder–decoder pathway with one skip connection, significantly reducing architectural complexity compared to traditional multi-depth or multi-branch networks. Prior to each downsampling step, the network utilizes a residual convolutional block that preserves critical spatial information and enhances feature representation stability, ensuring essential details are maintained despite the reduction in spatial resolution. This streamlined design reduces the number of trainable parameters, enabling faster training and inference. The single skip connection — from the highest encoder level to the decoder — effectively preserves high-resolution spatial details, ensuring precise and detailed vessel segmentation. Moreover, SDVN addresses sensitivity to small sensor variations and noise through its targeted skip connection and residual convolutional block. These components preserve high-resolution spatial details and critical features early in the network pipeline, enhancing robustness against minor variations and noise in imaging data. A schematic of the SDVN architecture is shown in Fig. 3 , which illustrates the interaction between the different components of the network, highlighting its structural flow and functional integration. The encoder is built with multiple convolutional layers using ( 3 × 3 × 3 ) kernels and operates with a stride of 2, which not only extracts intricate patterns but also reduces the spatial dimensions of the input data. To introduce controlled non-linearity and prevent the issue of dead neurons, Leaky ReLU (LReLU) activations follow each convolutional layer. As the encoder processes the data, it uses these down-sampling layers (with a stride of 2) to progressively build deeper and more abstract feature representations. The transition between the encoder and decoder is facilitated by bridge layers, which act as intermediaries that effectively transfer and prepare the high-dimensional features from the encoder for the decoder. These bridge layers ensure that feature maps retain crucial information needed for accurate spatial reconstruction in the later stages. A critical component of the SDVN is the single skip connection. This skip connection transfers information specifically from the highest feature level of the encoder directly to the corresponding layer in the decoder. This allows the decoder to access essential high-resolution features that are necessary for detailed and precise segmentation of the PAs. By leveraging this single skip connection, the network ensures that critical spatial details are integrated without over-complicating the architecture. The decoder restores the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, ensuring that the final segmentation map aligns with the resolution of the original input image, which is essential for accurately reconstructing the detailed structures of the PAs. To optimize network performance, group normalization is applied throughout, normalizing the inputs at each layer to accelerate training and improve overall efficiency. In summary, the SDVN architecture features a single encoder and decoder connected via strategic bridge layers and a single, precisely positioned skip connection. Using down-sampling and up-sampling layers with strides of 2, the network effectively balances precision. This streamlined design minimizes computational complexity, making it a suitable solution for clinical applications that require advanced image analysis techniques. This study uses a loss function that integrates various elements to improve segmentation accuracy, avg_loss . The avg_loss function includes three main loss terms: Binary Cross Entropy (BCE), soft Dice loss, and soft clDice loss. Each component serves a distinct purpose in improving segmentation precision, especially for tubular structures such as the PAs. The BCE loss is frequently employed in binary classification tasks at the pixel level to measure the deviation between the predicted probability and the ground truth for each pixel [30] . The BCE loss is defined as: (3) BCE = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N y i log ( p i ) + ( 1 − y i ) log ( 1 − p i ) where y i is the ground truth label, p i is the predicted probability, and N is the number of pixels. Although BCE effectively ensures class distinction, it falls short in accounting for spatial coherence and structural preservation. Therefore, additional loss functions are often incorporated to mitigate these limitations [31] . Soft Dice Loss aims to enhance the alignment between the predicted segmentation and the ground truth. It is designed to address class imbalance and improve volumetric overlap. The Dice_loss is defined as: (4) Dice_loss = 1 − 2 ∑ i = 1 N p i y i ∑ i = 1 N p i + ∑ i = 1 N y i where p i is the predicted probability and y i is the ground truth label. This loss function is effective in improving segmentation in medical imaging by ensuring that predicted and actual volumes are closely aligned [32] . The clDice loss [33] includes topological information to improve the traditional clDice loss. Assesses where the morphological skeletons of the predicted and actual segments intersect. The clDice_loss metric can be defined as follows: (5) clDice_loss = 1 − 2 ⋅ | S ∩ G | | S | + | G | where S is the set of skeletonized pixels of the predicted segmentation and G is the set of skeletonized pixels of the ground truth segmentation. Soft clDice prioritizes the central paths of tubular structures to maintain connectivity of segmented vessels, crucial for vascular segmentation tasks. The avg_loss is computed as the average of these three components. (6) avg_loss = BCE + Dice_loss + clDice_loss 3 This approach ensures a balanced contribution from each loss function, thereby improving overall segmentation quality. The BCE loss maintains the accuracy of the pixel level, the Dice_loss enhances the volumetric overlap, and the clDice_loss preserves the vascular structure. These components collectively form an effective loss function for PAs segmentation, improving structural accuracy. Grid aggregators are utilized after network operation to merge segmented results into a unified image. This integration combines segments to preserve the continuity of the vascular system, resulting in an accurate segmentation map that represents the intricate PAs anatomy. Grid aggregators demonstrate the network’s ability to efficiently process substantial data volumes. During the post-processing phase, false positives are removed by detecting and keeping only connected regions, ensuring the validity of the final results. Furthermore, the segmented data are converted back to their anisotropic resolution to align with the initial dimensions, thereby maintaining anatomical precision. This section outlines the dataset division and the training processes of YOLOv8 and SDVN for segmentation. The datasets RIDER , KiTS , Dongyang , Gennimatas_1 , and Gennimatas_2 are partitioned into three segments: 80% is allocated for training purposes, 10% is used for validation, and the remaining 10% is utilized for testing. This division was selected to ensure sufficient training data while retaining representative subsets, in line with standard practices in medical image analysis [34–37] . The RIDER , KiTS , and Dongyang datasets are publicly accessible, while Gennimatas_1 and Gennimatas_2 are private. YOLOv8 is developed to recognize and distinguish PAs, with a particular emphasis on determining the bifurcation point. The training procedure encompasses following steps to precisely identify these points. The intensity clipping process is applied to the 3D CT dataset. Intensity clipping limits intensity values to a specific range, removing unnecessary details and improving the visibility of PAs in the images. A two-dimensional cumulative intensity projection (CIP) is created. This technique maps a three-dimensional image volume onto a two-dimensional plane by combining intensity values along the anatomical axis. Anatomically, this process involves projecting intensity values along the axis that aligns with the natural orientation of the body, which can include the coronal, sagittal, or axial planes, depending on the orientation of the imaging data. This method simplifies the visualization of complex three-dimensional structures in a two-dimensional format, preserving important intensity data for further analysis while reducing the dimensionality. The standard equation that regulates this procedure is as follows: (7) C I P ( x , y ) = ∑ z = 1 N I ( x , y , z ) Where: • C I P ( x , y ) represents the 2D cumulative intensity projection located at the coordinates of the plane ( x , y ) . • I ( x , y , z ) indicates the intensity value at the coordinates ( x , y , z ) in the 3D volume. • z denotes index along the projection axis (depth or third dimension). • N represents the total number of slices or layers along the projection axis. The CIP enhances the visibility of PAs blood vessels by compiling intensity values across their depth, resulting in a clearer projection. Data normalization is conducted within the range [0, 1], which helps to reduce variability and contributes to a more stable and effective training process. The procedure utilizes the equation below: (8) I norm = I − I min I max − I min where: • I norm denotes the normalized intensity value. • I is the initial intensity value. • I min indicates the minimal intensity value. • I max indicates the maximum intensity value. In each sample, expert radiologists annotate a keypoint at the bifurcation of the PAs using Label Studio [38] , where the vessel splits into two branches. These keypoints are essential for guiding the model during training. Additionally, the model uses spatial context by placing a bounding box around the bifurcation area, which is the ROI. The processed dataset, identical to the training set used for the SDVN model, is employed to train YOLOv8 with annotated keypoints and bounding boxes. This enables precise predictions for the specific anatomical area. This method improves the efficiency and speed of detecting arterial structures in medical imaging, particularly to identify ROI. After identifying ROI, the samples are used to train the SDVN network to segment PAs. This procedure involves several steps necessary for precise segmentation of the artery within the specified ROI. In the preprocessing stage, CT scan images are clipped on the basis of the intensity values at the 0.5 and 99.5 percentiles. This method minimizes the influence of extreme outliers (e.g. implants, ECG electrodes), thus enhancing image quality. Percentile-based clipping is chosen instead of fixed threshold values because the dataset comprises scans from multiple centers, each with varying acquisition settings and intensity distributions. This ensures a more adaptive and consistent preprocessing across diverse data. After clipping the intensity values, the next step involves normalizing them to a standard range of [0, 1] using Eq. (8) . The model undergoes training for 250 epochs with a learning rate of 0.001 to identify patterns in the dataset. The training environment for SDVN comprises an AMD Ryzen Threadripper Pro 3995WX CPU, which operates at a clock speed of 2.7 GHz and possesses a 256 MB cache. The system also features 64 GB of Micron DDR4 RAM, organized into 8 x 8 GB modules operating at 3200 MHz. This section outlines and analyzes the performance of the proposed approach. Initially, YOLOv8 is used in test samples to detect key points that indicate ROI, specifically the arterial bifurcation point. Upon identifying these critical points, SDVN is employed to segment the arteries based on the specified locations. The trained YOLOv8 model was tested on a multicenter dataset with various artery shapes and varying intensity distributions, ensuring robustness in anatomical and imaging variations. The model accurately identified bifurcation points that aligned with the intended anatomical structures. BCE loss delivers comparable overlap performance while being better suited to recovering weak or thin vessel segments. Although soft clDice loss yields lower Dice scores and higher Hausdorff distances, it excels at preserving the continuity of elongated and branching structures, which makes it particularly beneficial for vascular segmentation. Among the publicly available segmentation tools trained in diverse large-scale medical imaging datasets, SAM-Med3D and TotalSegmentator have emerged as two of the most widely adopted for the delineation of anatomical structures. SAM-Med is recognized for its strong performance in segmenting medical structures using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) within medical imaging contexts. Adapted to the anatomical variability and imaging characteristics of CT scans, it benefits from training on a wide range of annotated medical datasets. However, SAM-Med requires manual interaction in the form of point selection to initiate the segmentation process, which limits its applicability in fully automated clinical workflows. This reliance on user input makes it less practical for large-scale or time-sensitive applications where automation and consistency are critical. In terms of performance, SAM-Med achieved moderate results with Dice scores ranging from 0.67 to 0.81, it was unable to accurately follow the course of the internal iliac artery, leading to inconsistent segmentation in complex vascular regions. Furthermore, TotalSegmentator is well-known for effectively segmenting over 100 anatomical structures in CT and MRI images, supporting 117 CT classes and 56 MRI classes. It is trained on a diverse dataset from various scanners and institutions, built on the nnU-Net [45] framework. The proposed method and TotalSegmentator are compared using DSC, HD, and HD95, as shown in Table 4 . The proposed method achieved mean values of 0.91 for DSC, 12.60 mm for HD, and 1.12 mm for HD95, whereas TotalSegmentator recorded mean values of 0.71 for DSC, 63.82 mm for HD, and 38.95 mm for HD95. The proposed method is accurate and reliable in detecting the PA system in CT data, allowing detailed tracking of vascular structures, crucial for surgical planning, disease monitoring, and interventions. In contrast, TotalSegmentator exhibits significant limitations in both scope and consistency. Its segmentation is largely limited to the common iliac artery, with reduced performance in detecting distal or smaller vascular structures. The common iliac artery, originating from the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta, is a critical vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the pelvis and lower limbs. Subsequently, it divides into the internal iliac artery, which supplies the pelvic organs, and the external iliac artery, which continues towards the lower extremities. TotalSegmentator fails to provide a complete representation of the PA system, making it less suitable for comprehensive vascular analysis. Fig. 8 presents a comparison between the proposed methodology and the existing segmentation tool, TotalSegmentator. TotalSegmentator segments the common iliac artery but is limited to this proximal region, not capturing the entire PAs. In contrast, the proposed method is designed to segment the entire PAs network, which includes both the common iliac artery and its distal branches. The ability of the proposed method to segment the entire arterial tree improves diagnostic insight and supports more effective surgical planning, especially in complex vascular cases where distal artery involvement is critical. Additionally, Table 6 provides a quantitative comparison of the proposed methodology and TotalSegmentator for segmenting only the common iliac artery across five centers. The proposed method achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.92, a Hausdorff Distance (HD) of 4.77 mm, and a HD95 of 1.08 mm. In contrast, TotalSegmentator obtained a DSC of 0.836, an HD of 8.92 mm, and a HD95 of 1.85 mm. These results highlight the improved accuracy and consistency of the proposed approach. Despite the promising results, some limitations remain. In particular, the model was not trained on cases involving highly tortuous or occluded arteries. The absence of fully or partially occluded arteries in the training data further restricts the model’s ability to accurately detect or segment vessels affected by severe stenosis or blockage. These gaps limit the applicability of the method for patients with advanced vascular disease. To address this, future work will explore transfer learning to improve model generalization, particularly for cases with limited annotated data or complex pathological variations [46,47] . Using pre-trained models and fine-tuning them in domain-specific data sets, the robustness and applicability of the method in various vascular anatomies are expected to improve. In addition, efforts will focus on ensuring that the segmentation output is compatible with widely used hemodynamic simulation platforms such as ANSYS and SimVascular. This integration will facilitate the application of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analyses, which are increasingly used in clinical settings for the evaluation and treatment planning of vascular diseases. Segmentation of PAs is a challenging task due to factors such as variable vessel diameters, low image resolutions, and significant anatomical differences, which traditional techniques often struggle to resolve. The suggested method addresses these issues by using diverse datasets, thereby improving segmentation reliability in a range of imaging circumstances. A key advancement of this method is the integration of an improved YOLOv8 model to precisely detect ROI before segmentation, reducing computational complexity and increasing segmentation accuracy. Additionally, the SDVN network, single encoder–decoder architecture preserves high-resolution features, enabling segmentation of both large and small vessels, including those crucial for the early diagnosis of PAs disease. Pre-processing techniques improve image quality, while post-processing refinements eliminate false positives and maintain vessel continuity. These improvements contribute to more precise and reliable segmentations, which are essential for clinical decision-making in vascular assessment. Future work will focus on further improving performance by incorporating adaptive learning strategies and multimodal imaging data to improve segmentation across diverse clinical settings.
