Automatic discovery of robust risk groups from limited survival data across biomedical modalities Survival prediction from medical data is often constrained by scarce labels, limiting the effectiveness of fully supervised models. In addition, most existing approaches produce deterministic risk scores without conveying reliability, which hinders interpretability and clinical trustworthiness. To address these challenges, we introduce T-SURE, a transductive survival ranking and risk-stratification framework that learns jointly from labeled and unlabeled patients to reduce dependence on large annotated cohorts. It also estimates a rejection score that identifies high-uncertainty cases, enabling selective abstention when confidence is low. T-SURE generates a single risk score that enables (1) patient ranking based on survival risk, (2) automatic assignment to risk groups, and (3) optional rejection of uncertain predictions. We extensively evaluated the model on pan-cancer datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using gene expression profiles, whole slide images, pathology reports, and clinical information. The model outperformed existing approaches in both ranking and risk stratification, especially in the limited labeled data regimen. It also showed consistent improvements in performance as uncertain samples were rejected, while maintaining statistically significant stratification across datasets. T-SURE integrates as a reliable component within computational pathology pipelines by guiding risk-specific therapeutic and monitoring decisions and flagging ambiguous or rare cases via a high rejection score for further investigation. Predicting patient survival is a fundamental task in clinical research and practice, playing a key role in understanding disease progression, evaluating treatment efficacy, assessing patient risk, and guiding therapeutic decisions. To support this goal, large-scale clinical datasets have been increasingly collected across diverse modalities, including whole slide images (WSIs), gene expression profiles, pathology reports, and structured clinical variables. Such data can provide a rich foundation for developing predictive models that inform personalized care ( Alzaid, Pergola, Evans, Snead, & Minhas, 2024b; Archetti, Ieva, & Matteucci, 2023; Parekh, Shaikh, Simran, Manan, & Hasibuzzaman, 2023; Sinha et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2023 ). A wide range of machine learning methods have been developed for survival prediction, from classical approaches such as Cox proportional hazards regression to deep learning architectures, with increasing application in computational pathology. However, these methods often fail to address critical limitations that undermine their robustness, generalizability, and clinical reliability as discussed below. First, most models require fully labeled training data, where each patient is annotated with a survival time and censoring status. In practice, obtaining these labels is challenging due to the need for long-term follow-up and expert annotation, making large-scale labeled datasets difficult to curate. Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) models ( Cox, 1972 ) and neural network-based approaches such as DeepSurv ( Katzman, Shaham, Cloninger, Bates, Jiang et al., 2018 ) and MTLR ( Fotso, 2018 ) are widely used for survival prediction, but they depend heavily on fully labeled datasets for supervised learning. Recent advances, including transformer-based models ( Wang et al., 2023; Wang & Sun, 2022 ), Swarm intelligence models ( Al-Tashi et al., 2023 ), and graph neural networks ( Mackenzie, Dawood, Graham, Eastwood, & ul Amir Afsar Minhas; Wang et al., 2024 ), have shown promise in modeling complex data, yet they also assume access to substantial labeled training data, which is often infeasible in real-world clinical settings. A second limitation lies in the underutilization of unlabeled data. In clinical settings, especially within large-scale cohorts where survival labels are often censored or missing, such data are typically abundant. However, most existing survival models are trained solely on labeled data, ignoring the broader distribution of available samples. This restriction limits the model’s ability to generalize, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or biased. Only limited work has explored leveraging unlabeled data in survival analysis. Some recent efforts have begun to address this gap ( Chen & Wei, 2022; Nateghi Haredasht & Vens, 2022 ), but the field remains largely dominated by fully supervised approaches. Another common limitation is that most models perform risk stratification after training by applying dataset-specific thresholds to separate patients into high- and low-risk groups. This strategy introduces sensitivity to the underlying cohort distribution and often requires recalibration when models are applied to new datasets, limiting their clinical utility. For example, in Yang et al. (2022) , patients are stratified based on the median risk score output by DeepSurv, and the MultiSurv framework ( Vale-Silva & Rohr, 2021 ) uses a similar approach for multimodal survival prediction. These methods typically involve post hoc threshold selection tailored to each cohort, which limits their generalizability and requires manual tuning for deployment across datasets. Finally, survival models rarely provide estimates of predictive uncertainty. Without measures of confidence, it is difficult to assess when predictions are unreliable, which can reduce clinical trust and hinder safe deployment in decision support settings. In broader machine learning, considerable attention has been given to uncertainty quantification using methods such as Bayesian neural networks ( Lin et al., 2023 ), stochastic computing architectures ( Hess, Aich, Pan, & Boers, 2025 ), and uncertainty-guided training frameworks ( Peiris, Hayat, Chen, Egan, & Harandi, 2023 ). However, this focus has only recently begun to extend into survival analysis, where the need for reliable uncertainty estimates is equally critical. Recent work has introduced Bayesian approaches and deep ensembles to estimate uncertainty in survival models ( Lillelund, Magris, & Pedersen, 2023; Tang et al., 2025; Yan, Lv, Yang, Lin, Zheng et al., 2024 ). However, such techniques tend to be computationally expensive and are rarely integrated into practical workflows. Consequently, most survival models produce deterministic outputs without indicating whether a prediction should be trusted. An additional motivation for incorporating uncertainty estimation is that risk stratification forces every sample into either a high or low-risk group, even when the evidence is ambiguous. If uncertainty were quantified, models could identify such borderline cases and abstain from making unreliable predictions, ultimately improving clinical safety and decision-making. To address these limitations, we propose a Transductive Survival ranking with Uncertainty-based Rejection (T-SURE) a model that incorporates both labeled and unlabeled data during training. Its transductive nature enables data-driven separation of risk groups by incorporating unlabeled samples to guide the decision boundary away from high-density regions. It produces a single risk score that supports automatic stratification using a fixed threshold of zero, avoiding the need for post hoc tuning. Furthermore, the model quantifies predictive uncertainty directly from the score distribution, enabling principled rejection of high-uncertainty cases. While T-SURE builds upon the Transductive Survival Ranker (TSR) ( Alzaid, Dawood, & Minhas, 2024a ), it extends it by modeling prediction uncertainty near the decision boundary and introducing a selective rejection mechanism, enabling reliable and confidence-aware survival prediction. By integrating transductive learning with uncertainty-aware rejection, T-SURE provides a unified framework that addresses label scarcity, improves generalization, and enhances the reliability of survival predictions in real-world clinical applications. In this section, we describe the T-SURE predictive pipeline and present key results. We first introduce model architecture and datasets, then evaluate T-SURE’s performance on survival ranking and automatic risk stratification. We also discuss the model’s label efficiency, robustness of the rejection method, and the systematic nature of its uncertainty estimates. We consider datasets that contain both labeled and unlabeled patient samples. Labeled samples include observed survival times and event indicators, while unlabeled samples lack this outcome information. Each patient is represented by a single feature vector derived from one of several modalities, such as whole slide images (WSI), gene expression profiles, clinical variables, or pathology reports. T-SURE processes this data to perform three key tasks: it ranks patients based on predicted risk, divides them into high and low-risk groups using a fixed threshold on the risk score, and assigns a rejection score that reflects the model’s confidence, enabling the exclusion of uncertain predictions. This transductive formulation allows T-SURE to learn from the structure of both labeled and unlabeled data, improving generalization and stratification without requiring additional supervision. T-SURE is trained using a joint objective that combines a pairwise ranking loss (to ensure correct survival ordering) with a transductive loss (to enforce separation between risk groups). This setup leads to automatic stratification using a fixed threshold of zero on the model’s output score, applied uniformly across datasets without any need for retraining or cohort-specific tuning. Uncertainty is quantified directly from the model’s score distribution (see Methods), enabling the rejection of high-uncertainty predictions and improving performance on retained, high-confidence samples. An overview of the pipeline is shown in Fig. 1 . As the model operates on a feature vector that can be derived from any data modality, it allowed us to evaluate its robustness and generalizability across an extensive set of datasets. We applied T-SURE to 10 cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) ( Liu et al., 2018 ), a comprehensive public repository of multi-modal cancer data. To ensure statistical reliability and meaningful evaluation, we selected 10 cancer types of cohorts with more than 200 samples and an event rate above 7.5% for Disease-Specific Survival (DSS). Refer to the Methods section for more information about the datasets and how features where encoded. To assess the effectiveness of T-SURE, we first evaluate its ranking performance against a diverse set of established survival models. Fig. 2 summarizes the results across all datasets and data modalities, reporting the mean concordance index (C-index) of 5-fold cross validation, standard deviation, and combined log-rank p -value for stratification (see Methods for details on evaluation metrics). We can observe that T-SURE either matches or outperforms all baseline models in nearly all settings. Notably, RSF emerged as the most competitive baseline, particularly in structured data modalities like gene expressions and clinical variables. This may be attributed to its ensemble-based robustness and ability to handle noisy tabular data. T-SURE achieved its highest C-index of 0.95 on the KIRP gene expression dataset, demonstrating strong ranking performance in well-structured feature spaces. In some cases, the performance gap is especially pronounced. For instance, in the LUAD cohort using WSI embeddings, T-SURE achieved a mean C-index of 0.65, compared to just 0.61 for the next best model. Similarly, across the pathology report datasets, T-SURE demonstrated substantial improvements in BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, and UCEC, suggesting that text-derived embeddings may pose challenges for traditional models but are effectively leveraged by T-SURE’s transductive learning framework. Deep neural models like DeepSurv showed no consistent ranking advantage, and in several datasets (e.g., BRCA and COAD gene expressions), performance dropped close to 0.5, indicating near-random ranking. These results highlight the effectiveness of our minimalist architecture, which avoids unnecessary depth while benefiting from the transductive signal. Moreover, T-SURE exhibits low standard deviation across folds, reflecting stable ranking behavior and reliable generalization. To better understand how the transductive loss shapes the model’s predictions, we analyzed the distribution of T-SURE’s risk scores ( Fig. 3 , left panels). In both WSI and gene expression datasets, we observe that the model avoids placing samples near the decision threshold (score = 0), resulting in a clear margin of low-density scores. This behavior is directly induced by the transductive loss and reflects the model’s ability to learn from the overall data structure, including unlabeled samples. While the previous section focused on overall ranking performance, here we assessed each model’s ability to stratify patients into distinct risk groups and determine whether these groups exhibit statistically significant differences in survival outcomes. As shown in Fig. 2 , asterisks above each bar indicate whether a model achieved significant stratification ( p < 0 . 05 ). Notably, T-SURE achieved statistically significant stratification in all cancer types and across all data modalities, using a fixed threshold of zero on the risk score. This threshold was applied uniformly without retraining or post hoc adjustment. In contrast, no other baseline model achieved significance across all settings, even in cases where their ranking performance (C-index) was relatively high. This highlights an important distinction where a good ranking model does not necessarily produce risk scores that are well-calibrated for threshold-based stratification. For example, in the LIHC cohort using WSI embeddings, several models (CoxPH, DeepSurv, GBM, and RSF) achieved C-index scores close to T-SURE’s, yet failed to produce statistically significant separation between risk groups. The superior stratification performance of T-SURE can be attributed to its use of transductive loss, which encourages clearer separation between low and high-risk groups by leveraging structure in the unlabeled data. This results in a wider margin around the decision boundary, making stratification more reliable without the need for data-specific threshold tuning. To statistically validate the improved stratification significance of T-SURE across folds and cancer types, we compared its stratification p -values with those of all models using both the paired t -test ( Student, 1908 ) and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test ( Wilcoxon, 1945 ). Both tests yielded highly significant results ( p = 1 0 − 105 and p = 1 0 − 102 , respectively), confirming that T-SURE consistently achieves more significant risk group separation than existing methods. To visually confirm the stratification results, Fig. 3 illustrates how the separation induced by the transductive loss leads to significant survival differences between automatically stratified risk groups. The Kaplan–Meier curves show clear divergence in both WSI and gene expression datasets, demonstrating that the model produces clinically meaningful groupings without requiring threshold tuning. To evaluate generalization beyond the training cohorts, we assessed all models on an independent external dataset from the Australian Breast Cancer Tissue Bank (ABCTB) ( Carpenter & Clarke, 2014 ) (see Methods). Each baseline model was trained on the full TCGA-BRCA cohort using the hyperparameters selected during cross-validation, and predictions were then computed on the external cohort without any additional fine-tuning. For T-SURE, the TCGA-BRCA cohort served as the labeled set, while the external dataset was incorporated as the unlabeled set to compute the transductive loss term during training. Importantly, no hyperparameter tuning was performed for T-SURE in this setting (the same fixed configuration was used across all experiments). The results are summarized in Table 1 . T-SURE achieved the highest concordance on the external dataset (C-index = 0.74) and the most significant risk stratification ( p = 7 . 8 × 1 0 − 32 ), outperforming both conventional and deep survival baselines. While CoxPH retained moderate ranking performance, its stratification significance was considerably lower, and deep models such as DeepSurv and MTLR exhibited poor generalization to unseen data. For some baselines (GBM and DeepSurv), the log-rank test was undefined due to flat or overlapping risk distributions, reported as N/A in Table 1 . These findings highlight that incorporating the transductive objective term improves robustness and facilitates reliable, well-separated risk predictions across independent patient cohorts. A critical challenge in clinical survival modeling is the scarcity of labeled data, as obtaining reliable survival labels is time-consuming, costly, and often infeasible at scale ( Archetti et al., 2023 ). To evaluate whether transductive learning with unlabeled samples can reduce dependence on labeled data, we compared T-SURE against three representative baselines: CoxPH as a classical linear model, RSF as an ensemble method, and DeepSurv as a deep neural network across varying levels of labeled data availability. For a rigorous comparison, we evaluated their performance across 20 different training set sizes: 1% to 10% (in 1% increments) and 10% to 90% (in 10% increments) of the full dataset, while reserving the remaining samples for testing and, in the case of T-SURE, for use as unlabeled data in the transductive setting. For each setting, we conducted 100 bootstrap runs using the same train-test splits across models. We recorded the C-index to evaluate predictive performance and used the log-rank test to compute stratification p -values, which were then aggregated using Fisher’s method. We chose the KIRC cohort with WSI embeddings for this analysis due to its high event rate (22%) and consistent high baseline performance across models, which is particularly important for stability and statistical power in small training set experiments. The resulting plots for ranking and stratification performance across different labeling sizes are illustrated in Fig. 4 . For ranking performance, T-SURE showed a consistent upward trend in C-index as the number of labeled samples increases. While CoxPH initially performs well with very few labels, its performance plateaued early and started dropping with the availability of more labels. DeepSurv showed higher variance and instability across training sizes, and RSF fails to rise above random performance (C-index ≈ 0 . 5 ) until at least 10% of the labeled data was available. In contrast, T-SURE continues to improve as more labeled data was introduced, without significant fluctuations. In terms of risk stratification, T-SURE achieves statistically significant separation between high and low-risk groups with as few as 5 labeled samples. While previously showing high performance, RSF required substantially more labeled data to reach significance. The significance gap between models is especially large, with highly significant p-values of as small as 10 −12 . These results highlight the label efficiency of T-SURE, showing that exposure to unlabeled data during training enables the model to produce well-separated risk scores and achieve reliable stratification, even with limited labeled samples. To evaluate the contribution of the transductive loss term, we conducted an ablation study on the WSI datasets comparing the full T-SURE model against a baseline trained with the ranking and regularization objectives only. The comparison was performed in terms of patient stratification performance (log-rank p -value) as reported in Table 2 . In the baseline setting, stratification required computing a cohort-specific threshold, defined as the median of the prediction scores in the training set. Without the transductive loss, the model was unable to achieve statistically significant stratification ( p > 0 . 05 ) in the CESC dataset. For the remaining cohorts, while the baseline model achieved significant stratification, T-SURE consistently produced lower p-values, indicating stronger separation between high and low-risk groups. Moreover, the inclusion of the transductive loss removed the need for data-dependent threshold selection by introducing a fixed, model-inherent decision boundary. We examined how model performance changes as more samples are rejected by performing 1000 bootstrap resampling iterations with replacement to validate the effectiveness of the rejection score R (see Methods) in identifying uncertain samples. Since uncertainty is derived directly from the ranking score magnitude rather than probabilistic outputs, standard calibration metrics are not applicable in this context. Due to space limitations, we report results from five representative cancer types in the main text, with additional results included in the Supplementary Figure S1. Fig. 5 shows the percentage of rejected samples plotted against the median C-index for the DSS endpoint across different modalities and cancer type subsets. It is important to note that the model is not exposed to the actual labels to perform rejection. Across all settings, the rejection curves demonstrate a consistent, monotonic increase in C-index as a greater percentage of high-uncertainty samples are removed. This trend indicates that the rejection score R effectively identifies uncertain samples that negatively affect model performance. Statistical analysis confirms this effect, with paired t-tests showing highly significant differences ( p ≪ 0 . 001 ) between baseline performance (no rejection) and post-rejection performance at each rejection level. In contrast, random rejection (shown as dashed lines) led to constant performance. While the overall trend is consistent, certain cancer-modality combinations demonstrated especially pronounced gains. For example, in the LIHC cohort using WSI embeddings, rejecting the top 50% most uncertain samples improved the C-index from 0.70 to 0.78. This substantial gain may be attributed to LIHC’s high intratumor heterogeneity ( Wu et al., 2025 ), which leads to variability in histopathological features. Similarly, in the LUAD dataset with gene expression data, despite the inherent difficulty in survival prediction for this cancer type ( Wen et al., 2023 ), the rejection strategy led to a 0.09 increase in C-index, reaching a final performance of 0.74. In contrast, the performance gains in KIRC and LIHC using clinical data were less pronounced, likely due to the limited diversity and lower resolution of the available clinical features compared to molecular or imaging-based modalities. Importantly, T-SURE’s ability to distinguish between risk groups was preserved across all rejection thresholds, with stratification remaining statistically significant even as samples were excluded. This demonstrates that the rejection mechanism enhances ranking performance without compromising automatic stratification. Moreover, we verified that the model’s rejection decisions are systematic by training a classifier to predict whether T-SURE will reject or accept a sample based on its features. The classifier achieved an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve of 0.98, confirming that uncertainty aligns with meaningful structure in the data. As expected, at high rejection rates (60%–80%), performance variability increased due to smaller sample sizes, highlighting the importance of balancing the benefits of rejecting uncertain samples with the potential drawbacks of excessive sample exclusion. To further explore the biological relevance of T-SURE’s predictions, we examined the expression of highly prognostic genes in high, low, and uncertain groups. For each dataset, we selected 20 patients with the highest risk scores (i.e., scores closest to − 1 ), 20 patients with the lowest risk scores (closest to + 1 ), and the 20 most uncertain patients based on the highest rejection scores. The heatmaps in Fig. 6 display gene expression profiles for selected cancer types, using predefined gene sets associated with unfavorable (top rows) and favorable (bottom rows) prognosis according to the Human Protein Atlas ( Uhlen et al., 2019 ). Patients are grouped by predicted risk category: high-risk, rejected, and low-risk. As expected, unfavorable genes tend to be highly expressed (red) in the high-risk group, while favorable genes show elevated expression in the low-risk group. Rejected samples typically exhibit mixed or intermediate expression patterns, reflecting the model’s uncertainty in confidently assigning them to either category. In the BRCA cohort, PTGES3 (Prostaglandin E Synthase 3) shows elevated expression in the high-risk group, consistent with its reported role as a tumor promoter and poor prognostic marker in breast cancer ( Adekeye, Agarwal, & Nayak, 2022; Yin et al., 2024 ). Conversely, SOCS3 (Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling 3) is more highly expressed in the low-risk group, aligning with its known tumor-suppressive functions and association with favorable outcomes ( Mahony, Ahmed, & Diskin, 2016; Sun et al., 2021 ). Additionally, we observed the high expression of S100A16 in the high-risk group of LUAD cases. This observation aligns with its role in driving malignancy in lung adenocarcinoma, particularly through ITGA3-mediated ECM–receptor interaction pathways ( Basnet, Vallenari, Maharjan, Sharma, Schreurs et al., 2023; Yang, Shen, Wang, & Zheng, 2024 ). In contrast, CLIC6 shows higher expression in the low-risk group as it holds favorable prognostic signatures associated with improved survival outcomes in LUAD ( Al-Dherasi et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023 ). To further assess the molecular basis of uncertainty, we performed gene-level differential expression (DGE) tests on BRCA by comparing gene expression values between rejected samples and both low and high-risk groups using Mann–Whitney U test ( Mann & Whitney, 1947 ). Several unfavorable genes differed significantly between rejected and high-risk samples, including PTGES3, which we previously reported as a tumor promoter and poor prognostic marker, and PCMT1, which is also a prognostic marker in BRCA ( Rogaczewski, Janiak, Borowczak, & Szylberg, 2025 ). Conversely, multiple favorable genes differed significantly between rejected and low-risk samples, such as KYAT3 and DEF6, where both are linked to favorable prognosis and better survival outcomes ( Girithar et al., 2024; Yuan, Zhong, Hu, Zhang, & Wang, 2023 ). These opposing patterns indicate that rejected samples diverge from both risk groups, consistent with their biologically ambiguous status. These patterns suggest that T-SURE captures biologically meaningful distinctions between risk groups, with high-risk and low-risk stratification aligning with known prognostic markers, while the intermediate expression profiles observed in the rejected group reflect genuine biological ambiguity, justifying their exclusion from confident predictions. We introduced T-SURE, a transductive survival ranking model that simultaneously enables ranking, automatic risk stratification, and uncertainty-aware rejection. The model is simple, interpretable, and uses a single risk score for all tasks. A key innovation of T-SURE is its ability to leverage unlabeled samples during training through transductive learning, reducing the dependence on large labeled datasets while improving robustness and generalization. T-SURE achieves competitive or superior ranking performance compared to multiple baseline models across 40 datasets spanning 10 cancer types and four data modalities. It enables statistically significant risk stratification using a fixed threshold, without the need for dataset-specific tuning. Leveraging unlabeled data through transductive learning, the model performs well even with minimal labeled samples, achieving significance trained with as few as five labeled samples. Its uncertainty-aware rejection mechanism further improves ranking by removing unreliable predictions while maintaining stratification. Finally, the model enables biologically grounded interpretation by aligning its risk groupings with known prognostic markers and expression patterns. Its ability to generate transparent, evidence-supported predictions, while identifying and excluding uncertain cases, offers a practical safeguard against overconfident or unreliable decision-making. These qualities improve trustworthiness and may facilitate integration into real-world clinical workflows, where reliability, simplicity, and clarity are essential. Recent survival analysis research has highlighted key challenges, many of which are explicitly addressed by T-SURE. One such challenge is domain shift, as discussed in StableCox ( Fan, Xu, Dong, He, Chang et al., 2024 ), A model that improves generalization by identifying stable covariates across cohorts using fully labeled data. In contrast, T-SURE incorporates unlabeled test samples through a transductive loss, allowing it to exploit target distribution structure and improve robustness without requiring extensive annotation. Similarly, T-SURE responds to the challenges outlined in the PUQ-AI framework ( Chakraborti et al., 2025 ), which calls for individualized uncertainty estimates to improve interpretability and trust. While PUQ-AI outlines desirable directions for uncertainty-aware AI, T-SURE implements a concrete mechanism by quantifying per-sample uncertainty and enabling rejection of unreliable predictions. This aligns with broader efforts in trustworthy healthcare AI, such as fairness-aware and interpretable modeling frameworks like FAIM ( Liu et al., 2024 ), which emphasize transparency and reliability in clinical decision support. To the best of our knowledge, no existing model in survival analysis offers this combination of ranking, stratification, and uncertainty estimation within a single unified framework. In contrast to recent semi-supervised survival models based on pseudo-labeling ( Salmanpour et al., 2025 ) or additional partial supervision ( Haredasht & Vens, 2022 ), which typically address only one or two objectives (e.g., ranking and calibration), T-SURE jointly achieves three complementary tasks; ranking, automatic stratification, and uncertainty estimation, within a single, minimal framework. This integration allows T-SURE to simultaneously provide accurate, interpretable, and reliable predictions, distinguishing it conceptually and functionally from existing semi-supervised approaches. To continue developing solutions to address such challenges, future work will aim to expand the flexibility and clinical applicability of T-SURE. We plan to explore alternative formulations of transductive learning to further improve robustness under distribution shift. Another direction is to extend the model’s stratification capability beyond binary risk groups, enabling finer-grained patient subtyping. Evaluating performance on more external or prospective clinical datasets will also be critical to assess generalizability. In addition, we are interested in explicitly modeling uncertainty through dedicated training objectives and investigating how rejection scores can be leveraged to drive active learning and optimize label acquisition. The proposed model is designed to take in input vectors of labeled and unlabeled samples and generate a single prediction score for the unlabeled samples that is used for survival ranking, automatic risk stratification, and rejecting uncertain samples. Let D = { ( x i , t i , δ i ) } i = 1 N be a dataset of N samples. Each sample i has a feature vector x i ∈ R d capturing d predictors (e.g., clinical information, gene expressions, etc.). It also includes an observed time t i representing either the event occurrence time or the last follow-up time if the event has not occurred. The censoring indicator δ i can be either δ i = 1 indicating the event was observed at t i , or δ i = 0 meaning the event was not observed by t i . The aim of the survival model is to learn a ranking function f ( ⋅ ) mapping each feature vector x i to a prediction score f ( x i ) ∈ R . A key intuition behind T-SURE is that the model should avoid assigning similar risk scores to samples that are densely clustered in feature space. When risk scores are concentrated near the stratification threshold (zero), small variations can lead to unstable or ambiguous group assignments. To promote clearer separation between low and high-risk groups, T-SURE pushes unlabeled samples away from the threshold, creating a margin of low prediction density around it. This is achieved through a transductive loss term that penalizes risk scores near zero, aligning the model’s output structure with the underlying structure of the data. T-SURE builds the Transductive Survival Ranking (TSR) model ( Alzaid et al., 2024a ), which we adopted as the baseline survival framework in this study. TSR incorporates both labeled and unlabeled samples during training through a composite loss function that combines three components: an ℓ 2 -regularization term ( L w ), a pairwise ranking loss ( L rank ), and a transductive loss ( L T ). The complete objective is defined as: (1) L w ( w ) = ‖ w ‖ 2 (2) L rank ( w ; D ) = 1 | P ( D ) | ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ P ( D ) max 0 , 1 − ( f ( x i ; w ) − f ( x j ; w ) ) (3) L T ( w ; D ′ ) = ∑ k ∈ D ′ exp ( − 3 f ( x k ; w ) 2 ) Combined objective: (4) L = L rank + λ u L T + λ w ‖ θ ‖ 2 2 In L rank , D is the labeled set (patients with observed survival times and event indicators), and D ′ is the unlabeled set. P ( D ) represents all comparable patient pairs from the labeled set where one patient experienced the event before the other. The model prediction for a sample x using model parameters w is denoted by f ( x ; w ) , and λ w , λ u are hyperparameters controlling the contributions of the regularization and transductive terms, respectively. The regularization term helps prevent overfitting while the pairwise ranking loss encourages correct survival ordering among labeled pairs. The transductive term penalizes prediction scores near zero, effectively pushing the model to place unlabeled samples away from the decision boundary. This encourages separation of low and high-risk groups in regions of low data density, a principle similar to that used in large-margin classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) ( Cortes & Vapnik, 1995 ). There, the margin avoids densely populated regions, reducing uncertainty near decision boundaries. The current implementation of the prediction function f ( x ; w ) is a shallow neural network consisting of a linear transformation followed by dropout and a TanH activation. While deeper and nonlinear networks could be used, this architecture preserves transparency and stability, which are critical for clinical applications. T-SURE extends TSR by introducing an uncertainty-aware rejection mechanism, allowing the model to not only rank and stratify patients but also reject high-uncertainty predictions to improve reliability and performance in low-label settings. The transductive loss inherently creates a margin of uncertainty around prediction scores near zero, as such values are penalized. We observed that rejecting these samples in a controlled manner improved the overall performance of the model, as they are more likely to result in incorrect rankings. We defined the rejection score R for each sample i as: (5) R i = 1 − | f ( x i ; w ) | where f ( x i ; w ) is the prediction score for sample i generated by the model using x i features. The prediction scores f ( x ) are constrained to the range [ − 1 , 1 ] (by using TanH activation), and a fixed stratification threshold of 0 is used to separate risk groups. Samples with f ( x ) ≤ 0 are classified as high risk, while samples with f ( x ) > 0 are classified as low risk. Higher values of R indicate a greater likelihood of an unreliable prediction. It is important to note that during the calculation of the transductive loss and training in general, the model is not exposed to the actual survival labels of the unlabeled test samples. Consequently, the decision to reject a test sample is not influenced by its label in any way. WSI analysis has traditionally relied on patch-based methods, where large WSIs are divided into smaller regions for feature extraction. However, an alternative approach that has gained interest among researchers is the development of single-slide representations, which aim to encode the entire WSI into a compact and meaningful embedding vector. Such representations enable efficient downstream analysis while reducing computational complexity ( Shaikovski et al., 2024 ). TITAN ( Ding et al., 2024 ) is a recently developed pretrained model designed for generating WSI-level embeddings. The authors had released TCGA-UT-8K dataset which consists of 8 K × 8 K pixels tumor Regions of Interest (ROIs) for over 9 K WSIs from TCGA ( Liu et al., 2018 ). Each WSI in this set is represented by a 768-dimensional embedding vector. It is important to note that there was no patient-overlap between the labeled and unlabeled samples to avoid information leakage. For the external cohort ABCTB ( Carpenter & Clarke, 2014 ), we extracted WSI embeddings from randomly sampled ROIs using the same pretrained TITAN model. This cohort is comprised of approximately 2700 breast cancer cases with disease-specific survival. The TCGA dataset contains gene expression profiles for multiple cancer types. Each sample is represented by a set of gene expressions selected based on their prognostic relevance ( Uhlen et al., 2019 ). Since prognostic genes vary across cancer types due to differences in molecular pathways, tumor biology, and microenvironment interactions, we used distinct sets of prognostic genes for each cancer type. The number of selected genes varies depending on the cancer type, ranging from 300 to 5000 genes per sample in each subset (more details in the Supplementary Table S1). Pathology reports contain valuable clinical observations, including tumor characteristics and morphological details, making them a rich source of prognostic information. We generated text embeddings of reports from TCGA ( Kefeli & Tatonetti, 2024 ) to test the model on an additional modality. To generate the embeddings, we used OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small ( OpenAI, Achiam, Adler et al., 2024 ) which is designed to transform textual data into high-dimensional numerical representations that capture semantic meaning and contextual information. A recent study has demonstrated that such embeddings can effectively encode prognostic signals from pathology reports, making them valuable for survival prediction tasks ( Alzaid et al., 2024b ). This dataset offers a complementary evaluation setting by incorporating clinically relevant features rather than molecular-level predictors. For each dataset, we applied the following preprocessing steps: categorical variables were converted to one-hot encoded representations; features with very low variance (threshold < 0.05) were removed to reduce noise and redundancy; and any columns directly indicative of survival time (such as progression-free survival) were excluded to avoid label leakage. Features per cancer type are provided in the Supplementary Table S1. For each dataset, we performed 5-folds Cross Validation to assess the performance of the survival model in ranking samples. The primary evaluation metric used was the Concordance Index (C-index) ( Harrell, Califf, Pryor, Lee, & Rosati, 1982 ), which was calculated for each fold. The C-index is a widely used metric in survival analysis that measures the model’s ability to correctly rank survival times. Given a pair of samples ( x i , t i ) and ( x j , t j ) where t i > t j (i.e., sample i survives longer than sample j ), the C-index calculates the proportion of such pairs for which the predicted risk scores maintain the correct ranking, i.e., f ( x i ) > f ( x j ) . A C-index of 1.0 indicates perfect ranking, while a value of 0.5 suggests that the model’s predictions are no better than random chance. Additionally, we evaluated the statistical significance of the stratification results by computing the p -value to measure the distinction between the two risk groups. The stratification was performed using a fixed threshold of 0, where samples with f ( x ) < 0 were assigned to the high-risk group and those with f ( x ) > = 0 to the low-risk group. For comparison models, we have used the median of training predictions as the stratification threshold following a common practice in survival analysis ( Chen, Kodell, Cheng, & Chen, 2012 ). The p -value was obtained using the log-rank test ( Bland & Altman, 2004 ), which assesses whether the survival distributions of the two groups are significantly different. A lower p -value indicates stronger statistical evidence that the model effectively differentiates between high risk and low risk samples. A combined p -value of all folds is calculated by Fisher’s method ( Fisher ) to assess overall statistical significance. Kaplan–Meier (KM) ( Kaplan & Meier, 1958 ) curves were used to visualize the survival distributions of the stratified risk groups. By plotting the estimated survival probabilities over time, KM curves provide an intuitive representation of the difference in survival between high and low-risk groups. To estimate the impact of rejecting uncertain samples, we performed an iterative rejection procedure by progressively removing samples with the highest rejection scores and re-evaluating the model performance. This evaluation method was introduced in the literature as the Accuracy-Reject Curve (ARC) ( Nadeem, Zucker, & Hanczar, 2009 ). In each iteration, the top 10% of test samples with the highest rejection scores were identified and removed. The C-index was then recomputed using the remaining samples to quantify the effect of excluding uncertain predictions. This procedure was repeated iteratively, with an additional 10% of the remaining samples being rejected in each step, allowing us to observe the trend in model performance as progressively more uncertain samples were removed. We further examined the statistical significance of these changes in C-index by performing a paired t-test ( Student, 1908 ) at each rejection step. Specifically, we compared the baseline C-index (computed with all test samples) against the C-index obtained after each rejection iteration. The corresponding p -value was computed to assess whether the improvement in C-index was statistically significant. We optimize T-SURE with a joint objective in which both the ranking loss L rank and the transductive term L T are active at every epoch. We fix the loss weights to λ w = 0 . 5 and λ u = 0 . 5 , apply dropout of 0.1, and train for 2000 epochs using Adam optimizer with a constant learning rate of LR = 1 0 − 4 . We use full-batch training as feature matrices fit in GPU memory. A small sensitivity sweep (varying each loss weight by ± 0 . 25 ) showed limited sensitivity to modest changes, whereas increasing λ u to ≳ 1 . 5 partially degraded ranking (lower C-index), suggesting over-emphasis of unlabeled samples can dominate the ranking signal. In addition, we evaluated runtime and memory on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 using 768-dimensional WSI embeddings (full-batch training). For T-SURE, mean wall-clock training time was 1.77 s per fold and inference latency was 0.005 ms/sample. The corresponding baseline variant without the transductive term trained in 1.34 s and achieved 0.005 ms/sample at inference. Thus, including the unlabeled-data term increased training time by 32% while leaving inference unchanged. Because inference cost does not depend on unlabeled data, the transductive component primarily affects training time, not deployment feasibility. For memory consumption, T-SURE used 2 . 6 × 1 0 − 3 GB GPU VRAM and 2.64 GB RAM, while the baseline variant used 2 . 3 × 1 0 − 3 GB VRAM and 2.64 GB RAM (averaged across folds), indicating a negligible VRAM footprint. To benchmark the performance of T-SURE, we implemented a range of widely used survival analysis models across different libraries. The CoxPH model was implemented using the lifelines library ( Davidson-Pilon, 2019 ). For deep learning-based baselines, we used the pycox package ( Kvamme, Borgan, & Scheel, 2019 ) to train DeepSurv and MTLR models. Additionally, we employed the sksurv ( Pölsterl, 2020 ) library to implement GBSM, RSF, and SVM for survival ranking. All baseline models were initially trained using their default hyperparameters as provided by the original implementations. To ensure fairness, we additionally performed hyperparameter tuning for the baseline models during both internal and external validation to assess whether optimized settings would improve generalization; however, the tuned parameters did not lead to notable performance gains. Benchmarking foundation models and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for prognosis prediction in medical imaging Background and Objectives: Despite the significant potential of Foundation Models (FMs) in medical imaging, their application to prognosis prediction remains challenging due to data scarcity, class imbalance, and task complexity, limiting their clinical adoption. This study introduces the first structured benchmark to assess the robustness and efficiency of transfer learning strategies for FMs compared with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in predicting COVID-19 patient outcomes from chest X-rays. The goal is to systematically compare fine-tuning strategies, classical and parameter-efficient, under realistic clinical constraints related to data scarcity and class imbalance, offering empirical guidance for AI deployment in clinical workflows. Methods: Four publicly available COVID-19 chest X-ray datasets were used, covering mortality, severity, and ICU admission, with varying sample sizes and class imbalances. CNNs pretrained on ImageNet and FMs pretrained on general or biomedical datasets were adapted using full fine-tuning, linear probing, and parameter-efficient methods. Models were evaluated under full-data and few-shot regimes using Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and Precision–Recall AUC (PR-AUC) with cross-validation and class-weighted losses. Results: CNNs with full fine-tuning performed robustly on small, imbalanced datasets, while FMs with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), particularly LoRA and BitFit, achieved competitive results on larger datasets. Severe class imbalance degraded PEFT performance, whereas balanced data mitigated this effect. In few-shot settings, FMs showed limited generalization, with linear probing yielding the most stable results. Conclusions: No single fine-tuning strategy proved universally optimal. CNNs remain dependable for low-resource scenarios, whereas FMs benefit from parameter-efficient methods when data are sufficient. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a transformative wave in medical imaging, widely adopted across specialties such as radiology, oncology, and pathology [1,2] . Its effectiveness in disease detection, cancer subtype classification, and early screening [3–5] was exceptionally evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the development of AI-based diagnostic models for radiology were essential to address the crisis [6–8] , underling the pivotal role of AI in managing large-scale health emergencies [8] . In a complementary direction, prognostic models have made significant advancements, incorporating sophisticated AI-based approaches to estimate and anticipate clinical outcomes, as the progression of pathology and mortality risk [9,10] . However, prognosis tasks remain more complex and less explored than diagnostic tasks, primarily due to data-related challenges such as the inherent temporal structure of the data and the limited availability of high-quality annotations or adequately large cohorts to effectively harness the full potential of AI-driven models [11,12] . Among these models, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been central to medical imaging, particularly for diagnostic tasks. They demonstrate strong performance when first trained in a supervised manner on large-scale natural image datasets (e.g., ImageNet [13] ) and subsequently fine-tuned on clinical data [14] . Thanks to their inductive biases and computational efficiency, CNNs are particularly well-suited to medium-sized radiological datasets publicly available for diagnostic tasks. However, their effectiveness diminishes in prognostic settings, where datasets are typically smaller and the modeling of temporal dependencies is essential. The need for full fine-tuning, combined with their limited capacity to capture temporal structure, reduces their suitability for tasks involving complex prediction objectives or constrained sample availability [15,16] . As an alternative to supervised pre-training, which requires huge labeling effort to acquire the datasets needed during training, Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has emerged as a scalable paradigm that reduces or eliminates the need for manual annotations [17,18] . Models like DINO [19] or CLIP [20] symbolize this shift, leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data to learn rich visual representations through contrastive or knowledge distillation objectives. SSL-pretrained models demonstrated remarkable transferability to unseen downstream tasks and strong robustness in high-variance clinical settings [21,22] . Building on these advances, FMs emerged, based on the adoption of large transformer-based architectures pretrained on massive unlabeled datasets, extending the principles of self-supervised learning to a broader and more generalist perspective of AI. In healthcare, FMs have been extensively developed to align with domain-specific diagnostic and classification tasks [23–25] . However, the application of FMs to prognosis prediction remains largely underexplored, despite their presumed generalist adaptability and the expectation that they could transfer effectively across diverse clinical settings. The limited deployment of FMs in this domain is mainly due to the inherent challenges of adapting large-scale models to the noisy, heterogeneous, and temporally structured nature of prognostic data, conditions that exacerbate the weaknesses of conventional adaptation methods [26,27] . To address these issues, more effective adaptation strategies are required. Fine-tuning remains the most widely adopted approach; however, its performance is often constrained by domain shifts, limited supervision, and suboptimal representation learning in small target datasets. Despite these drawbacks, it continues to serve as a practical baseline due to its simplicity and demonstrated effectiveness across various clinical prediction tasks. Yet, given the massive scale and complexity of FMs, the growing need for more efficient and intelligent approaches to adapt them to new domains. Rather than updating all model parameters, PEFT methods modify only a small subset of task-specific components, such as bias terms [28] , low-rank adapters [29] , or scaling vectors [30] , while keeping the backbone frozen. These approaches drastically reduces the computational and memory demands typically associated with full fine-tuning, mitigates overfitting, and enables more flexible adaptation across tasks with limited data availability. Despite their growing success in diverse domains, the use of PEFT techniques in prognostic modeling remains remarkably underexplored, leaving a significant gap in understanding how such methods perform in temporally structured and highly heterogeneous clinical settings. Moving in a similar direction, Few-Shot Learning (FSL) has emerged as a complementary paradigm particularly suited to prognosis prediction, where annotated cohorts are often small and imbalanced. FSL methods aim to learn transferable representations from only a handful of labeled examples [31,32] , leveraging prior knowledge from pretrained models through meta-learning or prototype-based strategies. Their ability to generalize from minimal supervision is especially appealing for rare disease scenarios, where data scarcity is intrinsic. In this context, the integration of PEFT within FSL frameworks represents a compelling avenue, combining the efficiency of parameter-sparse adaptation with the data economy of few-shot learning to advance real-world prognostic modeling [33] . This work fills a critical gap in the application of FMs in prognosis prediction tasks, by introducing the first large-scale benchmark of fine-tuning, encompassing Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), Linear Probing (LP), and multiple Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods. We systematically assess how dataset size, class imbalance, and model architecture influence adaptability, robustness, and efficiency across both CNNs and FMs. Our benchmark evaluates fine-tuning methods on a diverse set of pretrained models, including general-purpose architectures (e.g., ResNet, CLIP) and biomedical-specific ones (e.g., MedCLIP, BioMedCLIP), covering both CNN and transformer-based FMs. We focus on COVID-19 chest X-ray (CXR) prognosis as a clinically meaningful use case, leveraging public datasets with heterogeneous outcome types, sample sizes, and imbalance levels. In detail, our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • Comprehensive Benchmark of CNNs and FMs. We present the first systematic comparison of PEFT techniques against classical fine-tuning strategies (FFT and LP) across CNNs and FMs pretrained on both general and biomedical domains. The benchmark identifies which combinations of model architecture and fine-tuning method remain most resilient to data scarcity and class imbalance, two central challenges in clinical prognosis modeling. • PEFT for Prognostic Foundation Models. While CNNs have been widely explored, the application of FMs to prognosis remains largely untested. We perform an extensive evaluation of PEFT, LP, and FFT strategies on FMs, quantifying the trade-off between predictive performance, computational efficiency, and model complexity, thereby establishing the first systematic assessment of PEFT effectiveness in medical prognosis tasks. • Few-Shot Learning under Clinical Constraints. Lastly, we simulate few-shot learning scenarios to evaluate the ability of PEFT-adapted Foundation Models to generalize effectively under extreme data scarcity. This analysis mirrors real-world conditions such as rare disease modeling, emerging outbreak response, and underrepresented patient cohorts, demonstrating the practical feasibility of PEFT-based fine-tuning for rapid clinical deployment. Comprehensive Benchmark of CNNs and FMs. We present the first systematic comparison of PEFT techniques against classical fine-tuning strategies (FFT and LP) across CNNs and FMs pretrained on both general and biomedical domains. The benchmark identifies which combinations of model architecture and fine-tuning method remain most resilient to data scarcity and class imbalance, two central challenges in clinical prognosis modeling. PEFT for Prognostic Foundation Models. While CNNs have been widely explored, the application of FMs to prognosis remains largely untested. We perform an extensive evaluation of PEFT, LP, and FFT strategies on FMs, quantifying the trade-off between predictive performance, computational efficiency, and model complexity, thereby establishing the first systematic assessment of PEFT effectiveness in medical prognosis tasks. Few-Shot Learning under Clinical Constraints. Lastly, we simulate few-shot learning scenarios to evaluate the ability of PEFT-adapted Foundation Models to generalize effectively under extreme data scarcity. This analysis mirrors real-world conditions such as rare disease modeling, emerging outbreak response, and underrepresented patient cohorts, demonstrating the practical feasibility of PEFT-based fine-tuning for rapid clinical deployment. By addressing these questions, this study establishes a methodological foundation for adapting FMs to prognostic prediction, providing actionable insights for building robust, efficient, and generalizable AI systems in real-world medical environments. Moreover, it contributes to the broader field of radiomics by advancing the integration of deep foundation models within quantitative imaging workflows, promoting a shift from handcrafted feature engineering toward data-driven, transferable representations for prognostic analysis. The remainder of this work is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related efforts on FMs and PEFT in medical imaging, emphasizing the lack of systematic studies on prognosis. Section 3 describes the datasets, methodological framework, model selection criteria, fine-tuning strategies, and experimental setup. Finally, Section 4 presents the results and discussion, structured around the three central research questions introduced above. To contextualize this benchmark, we review prior research on (i) the use of FMs in medical imaging and (ii) PEFT as an emerging strategy for adapting large pretrained models to medical tasks. Despite rapid progress in both fields, structured analyses of fine-tuning and PEFT for prognostic prediction remain largely absent, particularly under clinically realistic constraints such as limited data and severe class imbalance. FMs have redefined medical imaging by transferring large-scale SSL paradigms into clinical domains [25] . Trained on massive unlabeled datasets, these models enable general-purpose representation learning and have led to biomedical adaptations such as MedCLIP [34] , BioMedCLIP [35] , and CheXagent [36] , developed for radiological interpretation and multimodal reasoning. In segmentation and 3D imaging, extensions like MedSAM [37] and time-to-event pretraining [38] demonstrate the versatility of large vision-language architectures in capturing anatomical or temporal features. However, most works focus on diagnostic and segmentation tasks, emphasizing classification or localization rather than patient-level outcome prediction. Prognostic modeling introduces additional challenges, small sample sizes, class imbalance, and temporal dependency structures, that remain poorly addressed by current FM adaptation strategies [39] . While isolated attempts, such as BEPH [40] , explore survival prediction, no large-scale benchmark currently evaluates FMs or PEFT approaches in prognosis-oriented tasks. PEFT has emerged as a lightweight alternative to full fine-tuning, allowing large pretrained models to adapt to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters [41,42] . Approaches such as BitFit [28] , LoRA [29] , and VeRA [43] have proven effective in reducing computational cost while maintaining strong predictive performance. Medical applications have largely focused on diagnostic or segmentation tasks, as demonstrated by FairMedFM [44] , FairTune [45] , and Med-SA [46] , which show that PEFT can improve model fairness and generalization under low-resource conditions. In parallel, FSL has emerged as a complementary paradigm for extreme data scarcity [31,32] . Integrating PEFT into FSL frameworks further enhances efficiency and transferability, as demonstrated in MetaAdapters [33] . While prior research has established the utility of FMs and PEFT in diagnostic and segmentation applications, several key limitations persist: 1. Lack of structured benchmarks assessing fine-tuning and PEFT performance under prognostic conditions; 2. Limited focus on data imbalance and temporal dynamics, which are intrinsic to clinical outcome prediction; 3. Insufficient evaluation of biomedical-specific versus general-purpose, leaving unclear which pretraining strategies best generalize to prognosis; 4. Absence of unified methodological frameworks that compare full fine-tuning, linear probing, and PEFT under controlled, clinically realistic settings. Lack of structured benchmarks assessing fine-tuning and PEFT performance under prognostic conditions; Limited focus on data imbalance and temporal dynamics, which are intrinsic to clinical outcome prediction; Insufficient evaluation of biomedical-specific versus general-purpose, leaving unclear which pretraining strategies best generalize to prognosis; Absence of unified methodological frameworks that compare full fine-tuning, linear probing, and PEFT under controlled, clinically realistic settings. Our work directly addresses these gaps by introducing the first systematic benchmark of fine-tuning strategies across CNNs and FMs for prognosis prediction, explicitly designed to analyze the interplay between dataset size, class balance, and model architecture. This framework provides a standardized foundation for evaluating FM adaptability in data-limited and high-impact medical applications. Our experimental pipeline, illustrated in Fig. 1 , defines the key methodological framework adopted in this benchmark. It is structured into five main stages, ensuring a systematic and reproducible evaluation of fine-tuning strategies and model transferability for clinical prognosis prediction using medical imaging data. Each stage has been carefully designed to simulate real-world clinical conditions, balancing methodological rigor with practical applicability. Dataset Selection. We employ four publicly available COVID-19 CXR datasets annotated with a variety of prognostic outcomes, including mortality, severity, and ICU admission. These datasets cover a wide range of clinical scenarios and data challenges, including varying degrees of class imbalance, outcome heterogeneity, and differences in sample size, ranging from highly underrepresented cases to larger, more balanced datasets. This diversity reflects the complexities typical in prognosis prediction and enables a robust evaluation of model adaptability under different data regimes [47,48] . Further details of the datasets are provided in Section 3.1 . Model Categorization. We systematically evaluate models grouped into two main architectural families. The first group composed of three CNNs pretrained on ImageNet using supervised learning, as a strong baselines in medical imaging. The second group composed entirely by FMs, pretrained through self-supervised or contrastive learning, either on large-scale general image-text datasets or specialized medical datasets. These two group allow us to explore the interplay between architectural design, pretraining paradigms, and domain specificity in prognosis prediction tasks. Further details of the models are provided in Section 3.2 . Fine-Tuning Strategies. Each model undergoes adaptation to the target prognostic tasks using one of several fine-tuning strategies. These include FFT as a performance upper bound; LP to evaluate the quality of frozen representations; and multiple PEFT techniques, which are designed to minimize computational overhead and improve adaptation efficiency. The full range of supported configurations and their applicability to specific architectures are detailed in Section 3 . Training Regimes. To assess the generalization capabilities of models under realistic constraints, we benchmark each configuration under two training regimes. In the full-data regime, where models are trained using all available labeled samples. And the FSL regime, where we limit the training to few samples per class, simulating extreme data scarcity common in rare disease contexts or emerging health crises. This dual evaluation framework enables a comprehensive analysis of model robustness and the effectiveness of fine-tuning strategies across a spectrum of data availability scenarios. Inference & Evaluation. We evaluate model performance primarily using the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), a metric known for its robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is a prevalent issue in prognostic datasets. This ensures a fair assessment of model predictions across both majority and minority classes. An Additional evaluation metric, Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), is employed to provide a broader understanding of the models’ behavior. We employ four publicly available COVID-19 CXR datasets annotated with a variety of prognostic outcomes, including mortality, severity, and ICU admission. These datasets cover a wide range of clinical scenarios and data challenges, including varying degrees of class imbalance, outcome heterogeneity, and differences in sample size, ranging from highly underrepresented cases to larger, more balanced datasets. This diversity reflects the complexities typical in prognosis prediction and enables a robust evaluation of model adaptability under different data regimes [47,48] . Further details of the datasets are provided in Section 3.1 . We systematically evaluate models grouped into two main architectural families. The first group composed of three CNNs pretrained on ImageNet using supervised learning, as a strong baselines in medical imaging. The second group composed entirely by FMs, pretrained through self-supervised or contrastive learning, either on large-scale general image-text datasets or specialized medical datasets. These two group allow us to explore the interplay between architectural design, pretraining paradigms, and domain specificity in prognosis prediction tasks. Further details of the models are provided in Section 3.2 . Each model undergoes adaptation to the target prognostic tasks using one of several fine-tuning strategies. These include FFT as a performance upper bound; LP to evaluate the quality of frozen representations; and multiple PEFT techniques, which are designed to minimize computational overhead and improve adaptation efficiency.
