While lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, breast cancer stands as a primary cause of cancer death among women [ 1 ]. According to the latest estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), there were approximately 2.3 million new breast cancer cases and 670,000 deaths recorded in 2022, underscoring the urgent need for improved diagnostic strategies to enhance patient outcomes [ 1 , 2 ]. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for enabling timely interventions, such as surgical resection, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy, which significantly improve survival rates [ 3 ]. Medical imaging modalities, including ultrasound (e.g., BUSI dataset) and histological analysis (e.g., BACH dataset), are indispensable for breast cancer detection and classification. Critically, the clinical task is not merely to identify malignancy, but to accurately differentiate malignant lesions from benign findings and normal tissue, thereby guiding patient management and avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures. For this reason, our study addresses the complete diagnostic challenge by classifying these key categories. Ultrasound imaging, valued for its non-invasive, cost-effective, and radiation-free nature, facilitates the differentiation of benign, malignant, and normal tissues. Histological images, derived from biopsy samples, provide detailed cellular insights, enabling the identification of carcinoma subtypes, such as invasive, in situ, benign, and normal. Ultrasound imaging, valued for its non-invasive, cost-effective, and radiation-free nature, facilitates the differentiation of benign, malignant, and normal tissues [ 4 ]. Histological images, derived from biopsy samples, provide detailed cellular insights, enabling the identification of carcinoma subtypes, such as invasive, in situ, benign, and normal [ 5 ]. Despite the diagnostic value of these imaging techniques, manual interpretation by radiologists and pathologists is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and subject to inter-observer variability. Subtle differences in tissue texture, shape, and boundary definition can lead to misclassification, particularly when distinguishing malignant tumors in ultrasound or differentiating invasive and in situ lesions in histology [ 6 ]. These challenges and limitations necessitate the development of automated, robust, and accurate classification systems to support clinicians in computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems, thereby improving diagnostic consistency and efficiency [ 1 ]. Deep learning has revolutionized medical image analysis by enabling automated feature extraction and achieving high classification accuracy, surpassing traditional machine learning approaches reliant on hand-crafted features [ 7 ]. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been the dominant paradigm due to their ability to capture hierarchical spatial features through convolutional operations [ 8–10 ]. Architectures like ResNet [ 11 ], which introduces residual connections to mitigate vanishing gradients, and EfficientNet [ 12 ], which optimizes network scaling across depth, width, and resolution, have achieved state-of-the-art performance on large-scale natural image datasets like ImageNet. These models have been successfully adapted to medical imaging tasks. For example, Zhantao et al. [ 13 ] applied a custom CNN to the BUSI dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.89 for classifying ultrasound images into benign, malignant, and normal categories. Similarly, Filipczuk et al. [ 14 ] utilized a ResNet-based model on the BACH dataset, reporting an accuracy of 0.90 for four-class histological classification. Despite their success, CNNs often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies in complex medical images, such as varied tissue textures in ultrasound or intricate cellular structures in histology, which can limit their performance on datasets with high variability [ 15 ]. Vision Transformers (ViTs), introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. [ 16 ], offer a promising alternative by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to model global dependencies across image patches. ViTs divide images into fixed-size patches (e.g., 16 × 16 or 32 × 32 pixels), embed them into vectors, and process them through transformer layers, enabling the capture of long-range relationships critical for medical images with complex patterns [ 17–19 ]. In medical imaging, Ali et al. [ 20 ] applied ViT-Base to the BUSI dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.87, while Hong-Yu et al. [ 21 ] used BeiT, a self-supervised ViT, on the BACH dataset, reporting an accuracy of 0.85. However, ViTs face significant challenges, including high computational costs (e.g., 86 M parameters for ViT-Base) and reliance on large-scale pre-training datasets like ImageNet, which may introduce domain mismatch when applied to smaller, domain-specific datasets like BUSI (780 images) and BACH (400 images) [ 22 ]. Lightweight ViT variants, such as MobileViT [ 23 ] and MobileViTv2 [ 24 ], reduce parameters (e.g., 4.94 M for MobileViT) but may compromise accuracy, necessitate careful fine-tuning and preprocessing to achieve optimal performance. Hybrid approaches combining CNNs and ViTs have emerged to leverage the complementary strengths of both architectures: CNNs excel at extracting local, spatially invariant features, while ViTs capture global context through attention mechanisms [ 25–27 ]. Yueyang et al. [ 28 ] proposed a hybrid CNN-Transformer model for medical image segmentation, integrating ResNet’s convolutional features with ViT’s attention layers to improve performance. Jaouad et al. [ 29 ] combined EfficientNet and Swin Transformer [ 30 ] for breast cancer ultrasound classification, achieving an accuracy of 0.91 on a private dataset. Ensemble methods, as explored by Breiman [ 31 ], further enhance robustness by combining predictions from multiple models using weighted voting. Dina A et al. [ 32 ] applied an ensemble of CNNs to the BUSI dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.88. However, these approaches are often evaluated on non-standardized or private datasets, limiting comparability, and rarely address computational efficiency for clinical deployment in resource-constrained settings, such as rural clinics or mobile health units. Challenges in breast cancer image classification persist, including class imbalance (e.g., 56 % benign in BUSI), domain mismatch between pre-training and medical data, and the need for computationally efficient models suitable for real-world deployment. Data augmentation techniques, such as random rotations, and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), have been critical for mitigating overfitting and enhancing model generalization [ 33 ]. Domain mismatch, arising from pre-training on natural images (e.g., ImageNet) versus application to medical imaging data. Transfer learning, using pre-trained weights from ImageNet, accelerates convergence on small medical datasets but requires fine-tuning to adapt to medical image characteristics [ 34 ]. Computational efficiency, especially for deployment in resource-constrained environments such as rural clinics or mobile health units. Moreover, the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and benchmarks for datasets like BUSI and BACH hinders direct comparisons across studies, underscoring the need for rigorous, transparent methodologies [ 35 ]. Significant progress has been made in applying deep learning models, particularly CNNs and ViTs, to breast cancer image classification [ 36 ]. However, most existing studies focus on a limited number of architectures or a single imaging modality. A large-scale, systematic comparison that evaluates a wide range of modern architectures under identical conditions is still lacking [ 37 ]. Furthermore, there is a need for a clearer understanding of how the architectural choice relates to the specific characteristics of different imaging types, such as ultrasound versus histology, and how performance balances with the computational efficiency required for practical clinical deployment. Our study is designed to fill these critical gaps and provide a robust empirical foundation for future research in the field. Our study addresses the existing gaps by making the following key contributions. • Presents a broad, systematic benchmark of nearly 30 state-of-the-art CNN and ViT architectures. All models are evaluated under identical conditions using a robust methodology that includes transfer learning and advanced data augmentation techniques to ensure a fair and direct comparison. • Provides critical, modality-specific insights into model performance, demonstrating that CNN-based architectures are generally more effective for ultrasound images (BUSI dataset), while ViT-based models tend to achieve superior results on histological images (BACH dataset). This offers clear guidance to researchers on selecting appropriate architectures for different imaging tasks in breast cancer analysis. • Conducts a thorough analysis of the trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency by evaluating both high-parameter and lightweight models. This highlights practical and efficient solutions suitable for deployment in resource-constrained clinical environments where computational power may be limited. • Establishes a transparent and highly reproducible framework for breast cancer classification. This is achieved by using standardized public datasets, well-documented open-source models, and including Grad-CAM visualizations to enhance model interpretability and build clinical trust. This comprehensive approach allows other researchers to build upon and verify our findings. 2: 2 Related works The application of deep learning to breast cancer image classification has transformed medical diagnostics, driven by advancements in CNNs, ViTs, and hybrid architectures. This section provides a comprehensive review of prior work on these techniques, focusing on their application to the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset, and the Breast Cancer Histology (BACH) dataset. We discuss CNN-based methods, ViT-based approaches, hybrid learning, data augmentation, and emerging trends, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and our contributions. 2.1: 2.1 Convolutional neural networks for breast cancer classification Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been a cornerstone of medical image analysis due to their ability to extract detailed spatial features, such as edges and textures, from images [ 39 ]. He et al. [ 11 ] introduced ResNet, a deep architecture with residual connections that prevent performance degradation in deeper networks, achieving strong results on large-scale natural image datasets. On the ImageNet dataset, ResNet50 achieved a top-1 accuracy of 0.76, making it a popular choice for transfer learning in medical imaging. In breast cancer classification, Al-Dhabyani et al. [ 5 ] applied a custom CNN to the BUSI dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.89 for classifying benign, malignant, and normal ultrasound images. They employed data augmentation techniques, such as random rotations within a 10-degree range and horizontal flips with a 50 % probability, to address the dataset’s class imbalance. However, their model’s shallow architecture limited its ability to capture complex patterns, resulting in lower performance compared to deeper or more advanced models. Huang et al. [ 38 ] developed DenseNet, which enhances feature reuse by connecting each layer to all preceding layers, improving efficiency and performance. Filipczuk et al. [ 14 ] utilized a ResNet-based model on the BACH dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.90 for four-class classification. Their approach leveraged pre-trained weights from ImageNet and fine-tuning on histological images, demonstrating the effectiveness of transfer learning for small datasets. However, high-parameter models like VGG [ 34 ], with over 128 M parameters, often overfit on small datasets like BUSI (780 images) or BACH (400 images), making them impractical for resource-constrained clinical settings. Simonyan and Zisserman [ 34 ] demonstrated VGG’s effectiveness on natural images, but its application to medical datasets is limited by overfitting on small datasets like BUSI. Recent lightweight CNNs, such as MobileNetV3 [ 40 ] with 4.21 M parameters, RepGhostNet [ 41 ], and EfficientNetV2 [ 12 ], which optimizes network scaling across depth, width, and resolution, offer competitive performance with reduced computational demands. Our study evaluates a range of CNNs, including EfficientNetV2-Small (0.9052 accuracy on BUSI) and MobileNetV3-Large-100 (0.9167 on BACH), as shown in Table 3 , prioritizing both high performance and computational efficiency for real-world deployment. 2.2: 2.2 Vision transformers in medical imaging Vision Transformers (ViTs), introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. [ 16 ], offer an alternative to CNNs by modeling global relationships across image regions, which is particularly valuable for complex medical images with varied textures and structures. ViTs divide images into fixed-size patches (e.g., 16 × 16 pixels), embed them into vectors, and process them through transformer layers to capture long-range dependencies. Liu et al. [ 30 ] proposed the Swin Transformer, a hierarchical ViT that uses shifted windows to extract multi-scale features, improving performance on histological datasets like BACH. Feng et al. [ 42 ] applied ViT-Base to the BUSI dataset, reporting an accuracy of 0.87, but highlighted challenges with high computational costs (86 M parameters) and sensitivity to patch size, which affects performance on small datasets. Similarly, Fatemeh et al. [ 43 ] used BeiT, a self-supervised ViT, on the BACH dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.85. Their results were limited by domain mismatch, as models pre-trained on natural images like ImageNet struggle to adapt to medical imaging characteristics, such as grayscale ultrasound or detailed cellular structures in histology. To address computational constraints, lightweight ViT variants have emerged. Mehta and Rastegari [ 23 ] introduced MobileViT, which combines CNN and transformer modules, achieving an accuracy of 0.84 on BUSI with only 4.94 M parameters. Similarly, MViTv2 [ 24 ] incorporates multi-scale attention, improving efficiency. These models reduce resource demands but require careful fine-tuning to match the performance of heavier ViTs. Our study evaluates a broad range of ViTs, including MViTv2-Base (0.9167 accuracy on BACH) and MobileViTv2–100 (0.8966 on BUSI), as shown in Table 4 . We mitigate domain mismatch through fine-tuning and advanced preprocessing ( Section 3.3 ), achieving higher accuracies (e.g., 0.8966 for ViT-Base-Patch32 on BUSI) than prior work. 2.3: 2.3 Hybrid and ensemble approaches Hybrid approaches combining CNNs and ViTs leverage their complementary strengths: CNNs excel at capturing local feature extraction like edges and textures, while ViTs model global context, such as tissue patterns across an image. Huijuan et al. [ 44 ] proposed a hybrid CNN-Transformer model for medical image segmentation, integrating ResNet’s convolutional features with ViT’s attention mechanisms to improve performance. In breast cancer classification, Mohsin Furkh et al. [ 45 ] combined EfficientNet and Swin Transformer for ultrasound image analysis, achieving an accuracy of 0.91 on a private dataset. Their approach used a fusion layer to combine features but lacked evaluation on standardized datasets like BUSI or BACH, limiting comparability. Ensemble methods further enhance robustness by combining predictions from multiple models. Breiman [ 31 ] introduced ensemble techniques, where model predictions are aggregated using weighted voting based on performance metrics like F1-scores. P. Manju et al. [ 32 ] applied an ensemble of CNNs to the BUSI dataset, achieving an accuracy of 0.88, but their approach did not incorporate ViTs, limiting its ability to capture global dependencies. Recent studies have explored hybrid and ensemble methods for breast cancer classification. Al-Dhabyani et al. [ 4 ] applied a custom CNN to BUSI, achieving an accuracy of 0.89, but their shallow architecture limited performance on complex cases. Similarly, Aresta et al. [ 5 ] evaluated CNN-based approaches on BACH, contributing to robust histological classification but without lightweight model integration. Our hybrid approach ( Section 3.5 ) integrates EfficientNetV2-Small, MViTv2-Base, and DenseNet169 through weighted ensemble voting, achieving superior performance (0.9224 accuracy on BUSI, 0.9333 on BACH), as shown in Section 4.5. By prioritizing lightweight models and advanced preprocessing, our framework outperforms prior methods while ensuring clinical applicability 2.4: 2.4 Recent advances and emerging trends Recent studies have explored multi-modal learning, combining ultrasound and histological data to provide unified diagnostic frameworks [ 46 ]. Others have investigated federated learning for privacy-preserving training across hospitals [ 47 ] and model compression techniques (e.g., quantization, pruning) for deployment in low-resource settings [ 48 ]. Explainable AI (XAI) is another growing area, with methods like Grad-CAM [ 49 ] and attention visualization helping clinicians understand model decisions. Integrating explainability into future CAD systems will be crucial for gaining trust in clinical environments. 3: 3 Materials and methods This section presents the datasets, preprocessing techniques, model architectures, training strategies, and the proposed hybrid CNN–ViT framework used in this study. The goal is to provide a reproducible, transparent, and scalable methodology for breast cancer classification using ultrasound and histological images 3.1: 3.1 Datasets This study's empirical foundation is built upon two publicly available, well-established benchmark datasets that represent distinct and clinically vital imaging modalities: breast ultrasound and histology. The choice of these specific datasets, Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) and Breast Cancer Histology (BACH), was driven by their widespread use in the research community, which ensures the comparability and reproducibility of our findings. It is critical to clarify that this study evaluates deep learning models on these two separate imaging modalities independently. The datasets originate from different patient cohorts, and there are no paired images between them. Consequently, this work does not involve multi-modal data fusion. Instead, we conduct two parallel and distinct evaluation tracks: one for classifying ultrasound images and a second for classifying histological images, with the objective of benchmarking architectural performance on each modality. 3.1.1: 3.1.1 BUSI breast cancer dataset The Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset is a publicly available collection of grayscale ultrasound images, created by Al-Dhabyani et al. It contains a total of 780 images, captured from 600 female patients using a LOGIQ E9 ultrasound system. The images are in PNG format with an average resolution of 500 × 500 pixels. The dataset is categorized into three classes: benign, malignant, and normal. Sample images from the BUSI dataset, illustrating the visual characteristics of each class, are presented in Fig. 1 . For our experiments, the dataset was partitioned into predefined training, validation, and testing sets to ensure robust and consistent model evaluation. The training set consists of 546 images (306 benign, 147 malignant, 93 normal). The validation set contains 118 images (66 benign, 32 malignant, 20 normal), and the testing set includes 116 images (65 benign, 31 malignant, 20 normal). This distribution reflects a real-world clinical scenario with a significant class imbalance, which poses a key challenge for model training. This distribution ensures a balanced representation of classes, with approximately 56 % benign, 27 % malignant, and 17 % normal images in the training set. Sample images for each class are presented in Fig. 1 , highlighting visual differences in tissue characteristics. The dataset partitioning can be formally expressed as: (1) N total = N train + N test + N val where N train = 546 , N test = 116 , and N val = 118 . Class-wise proportions are given by: (2) P c = N c N total , c ∈ { benign , malignant , normal } . 3.1.2: 3.1.2 BACH breast cancer dataset The Breast Cancer Histology (BACH) dataset was introduced as part of the ICIAR 2018 Grand Challenge on Breast Cancer Histology Images [ 5 ]. This dataset consists of 400 high-resolution, RGB color histological images derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained breast tissue slides. The images represent four distinct classes: benign, in situ carcinoma, invasive carcinoma, and normal. Representative histological patterns for each of these four classes are displayed in Fig. 2 . Crucially, these images are derived from biopsy samples, aligning the dataset with standard clinical diagnostic workflows. A key characteristic of this dataset is its perfect class balance, with exactly 100 images per class. This balance minimizes the risk of class-related bias during model training and evaluation. Following the challenge's protocol, the dataset is partitioned into a training set of 280 images (70 per class), a validation set of 60 images (15 per class), and a testing set of 60 images (15 per class). By leveraging the complementary strengths of these architectures, we propose a novel hybrid ensemble model that integrates CNNs and ViTs through weighted ensemble voting based on F1-scores. This approach aims to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness while prioritizing computational efficiency for clinical deployment in resource-constrained environments, such as rural clinics or mobile health units. The evaluation includes both heavyweight models, like ResNet50 and ViT-Base, and lightweight architectures, such as EfficientNetV2-Small and MobileViTv2–100, to balance performance with practical applicability. Our methodology incorporates transfer learning from ImageNet, advanced data augmentation, and fine-tuning tailored to the unique characteristics of medical images, addressing challenges like class imbalance in BUSI and domain mismatch between natural and medical imaging datasets. 3.2.1: 3.2.1 Convolutional neural networks Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were selected for their robust ability to extract hierarchical spatial features from medical images, making them highly effective for breast cancer classification tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , a typical CNN architecture consists of convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers. Convolutional layers apply learnable filters to detect features such as edges, textures, or shapes in images, producing feature maps that capture spatial patterns critical for distinguishing benign, malignant, or normal tissues in ultrasound (BUSI dataset) and cellular structures in histological slides (BACH dataset). Pooling layers, such as max-pooling, reduce spatial dimensions to enhance computational efficiency and prevent overfitting by retaining the most prominent features. Fully connected layers at the end of the network combine these features to produce classification outputs, mapping to the three classes in BUSI (benign, malignant, normal) or four classes in BACH (benign, invasive, in situ, normal). The output feature map for a convolutional layer is given by: (5) F out = σ ( W * I + b ) where ( I ) is the input image, ( W ) is the filter kernel, ( * ) denotes the convolution operation, ( b ) is the bias, and ( σ ) is the activation function, typically ReLU, defined as: (6) σ ( x ) = max ( 0 , x ) The ReLU activation introduces non-linearity, enabling the network to learn complex patterns by setting negative values to zero while preserving positive values. Pooling layers, such as max-pooling, operate on feature maps to select the maximum value within a defined window, reducing spatial dimensions while maintaining essential information. The CNN models evaluated in this study span a diverse range of architectures to balance performance and computational efficiency, ensuring applicability in clinical settings. ResNet50 [ 11 ]: A deep network with 25.6 M parameters, featuring residual connections that mitigate vanishing gradient issues by adding shortcut paths, enabling effective training of deep architectures. It excels at capturing complex features in medical images, such as tumor boundaries in BUSI ultrasound images. VGG13 [ 34 ]: A 13-layer architecture with 128.96 M parameters, known for its simplicity but prone to overfitting on small datasets like BUSI or BACH due to its high parameter count. It is effective for feature extraction but less suitable for resource-constrained environments. DenseNet169 [ 38 ]: A network with 14.1 M parameters that enhances feature reuse through dense connectivity, where each layer receives inputs from all preceding layers, improving efficiency and performance for histological analysis in BACH. EfficientNetV2-Small [ 12 ]: A lightweight model with approximately 20 M parameters, optimized through compound scaling of depth, width, and resolution. It achieved an accuracy of 0.9052 on BUSI, as shown in Table 3 , demonstrating strong performance with reduced computational demands suitable for clinical deployment. ConvNeXt-Base: A modern CNN incorporating transformer-like design principles, such as patch-based processing, with around 88 M parameters, offering robust feature extraction for both BUSI and BACH datasets. RepGhostNet-130: An ultra-lightweight model with only 4.2 M parameters, designed for resource-constrained environments, making it ideal for deployment on portable devices in rural clinics or mobile health units. MobileNetV3-Large-100 [ 40 ]: A lightweight model with 4.21 M parameters, leveraging depth-wise separable convolutions to achieve an accuracy of 0.9167 on BACH ( Table 3 ), balancing high performance with computational efficiency. These models were fine-tuned on the BUSI [ 4 ] and BACH [ 5 ] datasets to optimize performance for breast cancer classification. Fine-tuning involved modifying the final classification layer to match the dataset-specific class counts (three for BUSI, four for BACH) and applying transfer learning using pre-trained weights from ImageNet. Transfer learning accelerates convergence on small datasets by initializing models with features learned from large-scale natural image datasets, though fine-tuning is critical to adapt to medical image characteristics, such as the grayscale nature of ultrasound images or the intricate cellular patterns in histological slides. 3.2.2: 3.2.2 Vision transformers (ViTs) Vision Transformers (ViTs) were employed to leverage their self-attention mechanisms for modeling long-range dependencies in medical images [ 50 ], which is particularly valuable for capturing global contextual relationships in complex patterns, such as tissue interactions in ultrasound images (BUSI) and cellular structures in histological slides (BACH). Unlike CNNs, which focus on local spatial features like edges or textures, ViTs excel at understanding global relationships across an entire image, making them well-suited for tasks requiring comprehensive context, such as distinguishing subtle differences in tumor characteristics or cellular arrangements in breast cancer classification. As depicted in Fig. 4 , the ViT architecture divides an input image into fixed-size patches (e.g., 16 × 16 or 32 × 32 pixels), which are flattened and embedded into a sequence of vectors using a learnable linear projection. These patch embeddings are augmented with positional encodings to retain spatial information and processed through a series of transformer encoder layers. Each encoder layer applies a self-attention mechanism followed by a feed-forward neural network, enabling the model to weigh the importance of different image regions dynamically. The self-attention mechanism is defined as: (7) Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ( Q K T d k ) V where (Q), (K), and (V) are query, key, and value matrices derived from the input embeddings, and ( d k ) is the dimension of the keys used to scale the dot-product to prevent large values that could destabilize training. The softmax operation normalizes the attention scores, determining how much focus each patch receives relative to others, enabling the model to capture long-range dependencies critical for medical images. The output of the transformer encoder is passed through a multilayer perceptron (MLP) head to produce classification outputs, mapping to three classes for BUSI (benign, malignant, normal) or four classes for BACH (benign, invasive, in situ, normal). The ViT models evaluated in this study were selected to balance performance and computational efficiency, ensuring applicability in clinical settings. ViT-Base-Patch16 [ 16 ]: A standard ViT model with 86 M parameters, processing 16 × 16 patches. It achieved an accuracy of 0.8966 on BUSI ( Table 4 ), but its high parameter count makes it less suitable for resource-constrained environments. Swin-Base [ 30 ]: A hierarchical ViT that uses shifted windows to capture multi-scale features, with approximately 88 M parameters. It is effective for histological images in BACH due to its ability to model complex cellular patterns, achieving strong performance in prior studies. BeiT-Base [ 43 ]: A self-supervised ViT model with 86 M parameters, leveraging masked image modeling to improve feature learning. It achieved an accuracy of 0.85 on BACH in prior work [ 43 ], limited by domain mismatch between ImageNet pre-training and histological data. MobileViTv2–100 [ 24 ]: A lightweight ViT variant with only 4.39 M parameters, combining convolutional and transformer modules for efficiency. It achieved an accuracy of 0.8966 on BUSI ( Table 4 ), making it ideal for deployment on portable devices in rural clinics or mobile health units. MViTv2-Base [ 24 ]: An enhanced lightweight ViT with approximately 25 M parameters, incorporating multi-scale attention to improve performance. It achieved an accuracy of 0.9167 on BACH ( Table 4 ), demonstrating robust performance with reduced computational demands. MaxViT-Base: A ViT variant with 118.7 M parameters, designed for high performance but computationally intensive, suitable for research settings but less practical for low-resource clinical deployment. These models were fine-tuned on the BUSI [ 4 ] and BACH [ 5 ] datasets to optimize performance for breast cancer classification. Fine-tuning involved adjusting the MLP head to match the dataset-specific class counts (three for BUSI, four for BACH) and applying transfer learning using pre-trained weights from ImageNet to leverage features learned from large-scale natural image datasets. However, domain mismatch between ImageNet’s RGB images and medical imaging data (e.g., grayscale ultrasound or histological slides) necessitated extensive fine-tuning, including layer-wise learning rate adjustments and unfreezing specific transformer layers to adapt to medical image characteristics. The inclusion of both heavyweight ViTs (e.g., ViT-Base, MaxViT-Base) and lightweight variants (e.g., MobileViTv2–100, MViTv2-Base) ensures a comprehensive evaluation, addressing the trade-off between high accuracy and computational efficiency. Lightweight ViTs are particularly critical for clinical deployment in resource-constrained settings, such as rural healthcare facilities or mobile diagnostic units, where computational resources may be limited. For instance, MobileViTv2–100′s low parameter count (4.39 M) enables deployment on portable ultrasound machines, while MViTv2-Base’s strong performance (0.9167 on BACH) supports accurate histological analysis in low-power environments. By combining these models with CNNs in a hybrid ensemble (Section 3.5), our approach leverages ViTs’ global context modeling to enhance diagnostic accuracy, outperforming prior studies (e.g., 0.85 accuracy for BeiT on BACH [ 30 ]) while maintaining clinical applicability. 3.3: 3.3 Data augmentation and preprocessing To enhance model generalization and mitigate overfitting on the small-scale Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset and Breast Cancer Histology (BACH) dataset, a comprehensive set of data augmentation and preprocessing techniques was applied. These strategies address critical challenges in medical image analysis, including class imbalance (e.g., BUSI’s skewed distribution with 56 % benign cases), domain mismatch between pre-trained models (e.g., ImageNet) and medical imaging data, and variability in imaging conditions, such as differences in ultrasound probe angles or histological staining. By augmenting the training data and tailoring preprocessing to the unique characteristics of ultrasound and histological images, we improve model robustness, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and ensure applicability in clinical settings, such as rural healthcare facilities or mobile diagnostic units. Data augmentation artificially expands the training dataset by applying transformations that simulate real-world variations, thereby improving model generalization and reducing overfitting, particularly for small datasets like BUSI and BACH. To improve model generalization and prevent overfitting, several data augmentation techniques were applied, including random rotations (( θ ∈ [ − 15 ∘ , 15 ∘ ] )), horizontal and vertical flips (probability ( p = 0.5 )), scaling (zoom range ( [ 0.8 , 1.2 ] )), and color jittering (brightness, contrast, and saturation adjustments by factors of 0.2 ) [ 23 ]. Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels for CNNs and 256 × 256 pixels for ViTs, with pixel values normalized to ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) using: (8) I norm = I − I min I max − I min Z-score normalization was applied using dataset-specific mean ( μ ) and standard deviation ( σ ) ): (9) I z − score = I − μ σ For the BUSI dataset, ultrasound-specific preprocessing included Gaussian noise reduction ( σ = 1.0 ) to enhance image contrast. These augmentation techniques were carefully selected to reflect realistic variations in clinical imaging, ensuring that models like EfficientNetV2-Small, MobileNetV3, and MViTv2-Base generalize well to unseen data. For instance, rotations and flips address the positional variability in BUSI ultrasound images, while color jittering mitigates inconsistencies in BACH histological staining, improving performance on minority classes (e.g., malignant cases in BUSI, 27 %). These strategies were specifically chosen to address key challenges. To counteract the class imbalance in the BUSI dataset, our augmentation pipeline ensures that transformations are applied to all images, artificially increasing the sample size and diversity, particularly for the under-represented malignant and normal classes. This prevents the model from developing a bias towards the majority benign class. Furthermore, the use of macro-averaged metrics for evaluation ensures that performance on each class is weighted equally, providing a fair assessment of the model's ability to identify minority classes. 3.4: 3.4 Transfer learning Transfer learning was employed to initialize models with pre-trained weights from ImageNet, reducing training time and improving performance on smaller medical datasets [ 34 ]. This approach significantly reduces training time and mitigates overfitting, a critical challenge when working with limited medical imaging data. By leveraging pre-trained features, such as edges, textures, and shapes learned from ImageNet, models can adapt these general representations to the specific characteristics of ultrasound and histological images, addressing the domain mismatch between natural RGB images and medical images, such as grayscale ultrasound or stained histological slides. Transfer learning was applied to both CNNs and ViTs, including ResNet50, VGG13, DenseNet169, EfficientNetV2-Small, ViT-Base-Patch16, Swin-Base, and MobileViTv2–100. Models were initialized with ImageNet pre-trained weights to provide a strong foundation for feature extraction. Fine-tuning was performed to adapt these models to the BUSI and BACH datasets by unfreezing the top layers while keeping earlier layers fixed, preserving low-level feature representations like edges and textures that are broadly applicable across domains. For CNNs, the final fully connected layer was replaced with a new classification head tailored to the dataset-specific class counts (three classes for BUSI: benign, malignant, normal; four classes for BACH: benign, invasive, in situ, normal). For ViTs, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) head was similarly modified to align with the target classes. The top layers of each model were unfrozen to allow fine-tuning, while earlier layers remained fixed to preserve low-level feature representations. The loss function used was categorical cross-entropy: (10) L = − ∑ i = 1 C y i log ( y ^ i ) where ( y i ) is the true label, ( y ^ i ) is the predicted probability, and ( C ) is the number of classes. Learning rates were set to ( 1 × 10 − 4 ) for CNNs and ( 5 × 10 − 5 ) for ViTs, using the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimizer for training, with a momentum parameter of 0.9 to accelerate convergence by accumulating past gradients, smoothing updates in the optimization process. The SGD update rule is: (11) θ t + 1 = θ t − η t ∇ L ( θ t ) + m ( θ t − θ t − 1 ) where ( θ t ) represents the model parameters at iteration ( t ), ( η t ) is the learning rate, ( ∇ L ( θ t ) ) is the gradient of the loss function, and ( m = 0.9) is the momentum term that stabilizes updates. 3.5: 3.5 Overall approach The proposed approach integrates CNN and ViT architectures to achieve robust and accurate classification of breast cancer on the BUSI and BACH datasets. By combining CNNs’ strength in extracting localized spatial features, such as tumor boundaries in ultrasound images or cellular textures in histological slides, with ViTs’ ability to model global contextual relationships across image regions, we develop a hybrid ensemble model that leverages the complementary capabilities of these architectures. The hybrid architecture, illustrated in Fig. 5 , employs an ensemble strategy where predictions from multiple models are combined via weighted voting [ 31 ]: (12) P ensemble = ∑ m = 1 M w m P m , ∑ m = 1 M w m = 1 where ( P m ) is the prediction from model ( m ), and ( w m ) is the weight based on model performance (e.g., F1-score). The model was trained for 50 epochs with a batch size of 32, using cross-entropy loss and early stopping to prevent overfitting. Data augmentation and preprocessing were applied consistently across models to ensure fair comparison. The hybrid model combines a diverse set of CNNs (e.g., ResNet50, EfficientNetV2-Small, DenseNet169, MobileNetV3-Large-100) and ViTs (e.g., ViT-Base-Patch16, Swin-Base, MViTv2-Base, MobileViTv2–100) to capitalize on their complementary strengths. CNNs excel at capturing hierarchical spatial features, such as edges and textures, which are critical for identifying tumor boundaries in BUSI ultrasound images or cellular patterns in BACH histological slides. ViTs, by contrast, leverage self-attention mechanisms to model long-range dependencies, enabling them to understand global tissue interactions or cellular arrangements that may span across an image. The hybrid model integrates these architectures through an ensemble strategy, where predictions from individual models are combined via weighted voting based on their performance metrics, ensuring that more accurate models contribute more significantly to the final prediction. 4: 4 Results This section presents the experimental results of our proposed hybrid CNN–ViT framework for breast cancer classification using the BUSI and BACH datasets. We evaluate individual CNNs, ViTs, and the proposed hybrid model, reporting performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The figures included provide visual insights into model performance, including confusion matrices, AUC curves, prediction outcomes, and Grad-CAM visualizations, which highlight the models’ decision-making processes. 4.1: 4.1 Experimental setup The computational experiments for this research were conducted on a high-performance workstation running the Ubuntu 24.04 LTS operating system. The hardware configuration featured an Intel Core i9 14th-generation multi-core processor, delivering exceptional parallel processing performance for computationally demanding tasks. This was paired with 64 GB of high-speed DDR5 RAM, ensuring efficient handling of large datasets and memory-intensive operations. GPU computations were optimized using the CUDA Toolkit 12.4 alongside the compatible cuDNN library, ensuring maximum performance, stability, and compatibility for the implemented experimental workflows. 4.2: 4.2 Evaluation metrics Model performance was assessed using several key metrics. For multi-class classification tasks like ours, a prediction is assigned to the class with the highest probability score from the model's output layer (i.e., the argmax of the softmax output). This standard approach does not use a manually set probability cutoff (e.g., 0.5) for making decisions. The confusion matrices and all subsequent metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score) were calculated based on these highest-probability predictions. Model performance was assessed using four key metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, defined as: (13) Accuracy = TP + TN TP + TN + FP + FN (14) Precision = TP TP + FP (15) Recall = TP TP + FN (16) F 1 − score = 2 · Precision · Recall Precision + Recall where TP (true positives), TN (true negatives), FP (false positives), and FN (false negatives) were computed per class. Macro-averaging was applied to account for class imbalance, particularly in the BUSI dataset. For the BACH dataset, with its balanced class distribution, macro-averaging ensured equitable metric computation across benign, invasive, in situ, and normal classes. Additionally, confusion matrices were generated to analyze misclassification patterns, and the number of parameters (in millions) was reported to evaluate model efficiency. 4.3: 4.3 Empirical evaluation of CNN-based This section presents a rigorous empirical evaluation of diverse CNN architectures on the BUSI (ultrasound) and BACH (histology) datasets. For instance, EfficientNetV2-Small, which demonstrated superior efficacy on the BUSI ultrasound dataset, exhibited a marked performance decline on the BACH histology dataset, achieving an accuracy of only 0.8000. Furthermore, the statistical parity observed between the top-performing models on the BACH dataset (e.g., DenseNet169 and MobileNetV3-Large-100) indicates that their relative advantages could be further elucidated through more extensive validation, such as k-fold cross-validation or evaluation on larger, more diverse histological datasets. This is often due to subtle differences and overlapping features in their overall tissue architecture, reinforcing the quantitative findings from the confusion matrix. 4.4.3: 4.4.3 Comparative analysis A comparative analysis of the ViT models across both datasets reveals a strong architectural affinity for specific imaging modalities, a critical finding of this study. For example, ViT-Base-Patch32 exhibited superior performance on the BUSI dataset but was markedly less effective on the BACH dataset, with its accuracy dropping to 0.8333. This suggests its larger patch size is well-suited for capturing the global features of distinct tumor boundaries in ultrasound images but is suboptimal for resolving the fine-grained cellular details required in histology. Conversely, MViTv2-Base, the top performer on BACH, yielded only moderate performance on BUSI. Its multi-scale attention mechanism, ideal for the complex patterns in histology, appears less advantageous for the ultrasound classification task. This demonstrates that there is no single ViT architecture that is universally optimal; instead, the design must be matched to the specific characteristics of the imaging data. While these findings are insightful, the evaluation is subject to several limitations that also inform future research directions. The constrained size of both the BUSI and BACH datasets increases the risk of overfitting, particularly for heavyweight models with high parameter counts, such as MaxViT-Base (118.7 M parameters) and GcViT-Base (89.3 M parameters). Additionally, the significant computational overhead of these large models limits their practical utility in resource-limited clinical settings, emphasizing the value of the efficient lightweight alternatives identified in this study. A key modeling challenge was highlighted by the poor performance of BeiT-Base on the BACH dataset, which achieved an accuracy of only 0.7500. This underscores the significant difficulty of domain adaptation when transferring self-supervised models pre-trained on natural images to highly specialized medical imaging domains, indicating a need for more extensive, domain-specific fine-tuning or pre-training on medical data. Finally, the lack of a statistically significant performance difference between top-performing models like MViTv2-Base and Swin-Base on the BACH dataset suggests that their relative advantages could be further clarified through more rigorous validation methods, such as k-fold cross-validation or testing on larger, multi-institutional datasets. 5: 5 Discussion This study's large-scale comparative analysis provides critical insights into the performance of modern deep learning architectures for breast cancer classification. Our central finding is that architectural suitability is highly modality-dependent. Rather than merely reiterating our results, this section aims to contextualize these findings within the existing state-of-the-art literature, critically evaluate the clinical implications while acknowledging our study's limitations, and justify our methodological framework. 5.1: 5.1 Contextualizing performance within the State-of-the-Art 5.1.1: 5.1.1 Analysis of CNN architectures The empirical evaluation of CNN architectures revealed a strong, modality-dependent performance hierarchy. On the BUSI ultrasound dataset, EfficientNetV2-Small demonstrated the highest efficacy, achieving a top accuracy of 0.9052 (±0.012) and an F1-score of 0.8976 (±0.010). Its success can be attributed to its compound scaling strategy, which optimizes the balance between network depth, width, and resolution, enabling robust feature extraction from tumor margins with a moderate parameter count (20.18 M). This model also achieved a high recall for malignant cases, a critical factor for minimizing false negatives in clinical screening. In contrast, while heavyweight models like VGG13 (128.96 M parameters) achieved respectable accuracy, their significant computational overhead limits their practical utility. The viability of clinical deployment for low-resource settings was underscored by the performance of lightweight models like RepGhostNet-130, which delivered a competitive F1-score of 0.8580 with only 4.2 M parameters. On the BACH histology dataset, a different set of architectures excelled. DenseNet169 and the highly efficient MobileNetV3-Large-100 jointly achieved the highest accuracy of 0.9167. DenseNet169’s architecture, which facilitates feature reuse across layers, proved highly effective for capturing the complex cellular patterns in histological slides, yielding the highest precision (0.9227). Concurrently, MobileNetV3-Large-100 delivered this top-tier performance with a minimal parameter count (4.21 M), leveraging depth-wise separable convolutions to provide an optimal balance of accuracy and efficiency suitable for pathology labs. Conversely, the lower performance of models like RegNet-120 suggests their architectures were less suited for distinguishing the subtle differences between invasive and in situ carcinomas. 5.1.2: 5.1.2 Analysis of vit architectures The evaluation of ViT based models also demonstrated distinct, modality-specific strengths. On the BUSI dataset, high-parameter models proved most effective, with ViT-Base-Patch32 and BeiT-Base attaining the highest accuracy of 0.8966. The success of these models highlights the aptitude of the self-attention mechanism for capturing the long-range dependencies and global contextual information inherent in ultrasound tissue patterns. However, their large size (≈86 M parameters) presents significant computational demands, limiting their deployment feasibility. While some lightweight ViT variants like MobileViTv2–100 offered greater efficiency, their reduced architectural complexity led to a comparative decrease in accuracy on this specific task. On the BACH histology dataset, the architectural requirements shifted. Here, MViTv2-Base emerged as the clear top performer, achieving the highest accuracy (0.9167) and F1-score (0.9159). Its multi-scale transformer architecture is uniquely suited to histology, enabling it to capture both local cellular details and the broader global tissue context simultaneously. This evaluation also highlighted a key challenge in domain adaptation; the significant underperformance of BeiT-Base (0.7500 accuracy) suggests that its self-supervised pre-training on natural images did not transfer effectively to the specialized domain of histopathology. Encouragingly, lightweight models like MobileViTv2–100 performed well on this dataset (0.8833 accuracy), demonstrating their suitability and potential for resource-limited pathology settings. 5.2: 5.2 Clinical implications and future pathways While our findings are promising, they must be interpreted as a foundational benchmark rather than a definitive clinical directive. The results suggest that certain models are promising candidates for integration into Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems, but their real-world efficacy is contingent upon further validation. For instance, EfficientNetV2-Small's strong performance on ultrasound images indicates its potential to assist radiologists by reducing inter-observer variability, though this must be confirmed in large-scale, prospective clinical trials, as noted in our limitations. Similarly, for histopathology, the high accuracy of models like MViTv2-Base and MobileNetV3-Large-100 demonstrates significant potential for use in pathology labs to triage cases or highlight regions of interest. The success of a lightweight model like MobileNetV3-Large-100 is particularly relevant, as it underscores the possibility of deploying accurate diagnostic tools in resource-constrained settings. However, it is crucial to recognize that the transition of these models from a research setting to clinical practice requires overcoming the challenges of data heterogeneity and domain shift. Therefore, these results should not be seen as confirming immediate deployability, but rather as establishing a strong empirical basis that warrants further investigation and development toward clinical translation. 5.3: 5.3 Justification of methodological choices The reliability of the clinical implications discussed above is predicated on the rigor of our experimental design. This study addressed several inherent challenges in medical image analysis through deliberate methodological choices aimed at ensuring a fair, robust, and reproducible comparison. To counteract the challenges of small dataset sizes (780 images in BUSI, 400 in BACH) and significant class imbalance in the BUSI dataset, we employed a dual strategy of extensive data augmentation and transfer learning. We opted for a transfer learning approach with ImageNet pre-training for several strategic reasons. Firstly, this paradigm provides a powerful and validated starting point, equipping models with a robust understanding of generalizable low-level features like edges and textures that are highly transferable to medical imaging. Secondly, the widespread availability of these pre-trained models enhances the reproducibility of our work. This foundational step was complemented by a meticulous fine-tuning process to actively bridge the domain gap and adapt the models to the specific characteristics of ultrasound and histological images. Furthermore, the foundation of this work is its commitment to reproducibility and transparency. The use of standardized, publicly available datasets (BUSI and BACH) allows other researchers to verify our findings and build upon this work. By evaluating all architectures under identical training and testing protocols, we provide a reliable benchmark for the field. The inclusion of model interpretability through Grad-CAM visualizations further enhances the transparency of our framework, providing insight into the models' decision-making processes, which is a critical step for clinical validation and adoption. In addition, we opted for a transfer learning approach with ImageNet pre-training based on a deliberate methodological rationale. The primary objective of this study was to establish a fair, reproducible, and unbiased benchmark of architectural performance. A foundational prerequisite for such a comparative analysis is to maintain a uniform baseline, a methodological control essential for isolating the architectural design as the primary independent variable. We selected the ubiquitous ImageNet pre-trained weights as the gold-standard baseline to provide this single, standardized starting point for all models. While we recognize the immense potential of emerging medical foundation models, the current landscape does not yet offer a standardized set of pre-trained weights across the vast architectural spectrum we investigated. Many such models are proprietary, modality-specific, or not generalizable in a way that would support the reproducibility and fairness of our benchmark. Furthermore, the universal availability of ImageNet weights enhances the reproducibility of our work, a core tenet of our study. 6: 6 Limitations and future directions While this study provides a significant contribution by systematically benchmarking a wide array of deep learning architectures across two distinct imaging modalities for breast cancer classification, a critical appraisal of its boundaries is essential for guiding future scientific progress. This section outlines the primary limitations stemming from the nature of the datasets, the methodological choices made, and the pathway to clinical translation, while also proposing a forward-looking vision for subsequent research. 6.1: 6.1 Data scope and generalizability constraints The primary limitation of this work stems from its reliance on public datasets (BUSI and BACH) that, while standardized, are relatively small and homogeneous. The limited sample size heightens the risk of overfitting, particularly for the high-parameter models such as VGG13 and MaxViT-Base. More importantly, these datasets may not fully capture the "real-world" data heterogeneity that arises from diverse patient demographics, different imaging hardware, and varying clinical protocols. This raises questions regarding the extent to which the high performance achieved in our study can be generalized to more diverse and noisy data encountered in a different clinical setting. The pronounced class imbalance within the BUSI dataset also remains a challenge that can impact model performance on minority classes. To overcome these constraints, future work must focus on validating the top-performing architectures on larger, multi-institutional, and heterogeneous datasets, such as those from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Furthermore, advanced synthetic data generation techniques, like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or diffusion models, should be explored as a powerful means to augment data diversity and mitigate class imbalance. 6.2: 6.2 Methodological and model-centric limitations Methodologically, this study employed a fixed train-validation-test split to ensure direct comparability with existing literature. However, we acknowledge that this approach may not estimate generalization performance as robustly as k-fold cross-validation, especially given the size of the datasets used. Future benchmarking studies should therefore consider adopting cross-validation schemes to provide more reliable performance estimates. On the model front, our research highlights the challenges of domain adaptation when using models pre-trained on ImageNet. The suboptimal performance of the BeiT-Base model on the histology dataset, for example, underscores the significance of the "domain gap" between natural and highly specialized medical images. To address this, future research should move beyond a sole reliance on ImageNet pre-training and investigate more advanced strategies, such as self-supervised learning on large, unlabeled medical corpora or the fine-tuning of emerging medical foundation models. 6.3: 6.3 Expanding the scope for clinical translation The scope of this study addresses each modality independently, whereas a definitive clinical diagnosis often results from the synthesis of multiple information sources. A truly transformative next step would be to develop a multi-modal fusion model that integrates paired ultrasound and histological data from the same patients, which has the potential to yield a more holistic and accurate diagnostic framework. Furthermore, computational efficiency is a critical factor for the deployment of these models in clinical settings, especially in resource-constrained environments. Future work should explore model compression techniques, such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, to create lightweight yet powerful versions of the top-performing architectures. Finally, transparency is indispensable for fostering clinical trust in AI systems. The integration of advanced Explainable AI (XAI) techniques beyond Grad-CAM is necessary to provide deeper, human-interpretable insights into the models' decision-making processes. To overcome data privacy and access barriers, federated learning paradigms, which enable model training across multiple institutions without centralizing sensitive patient data, will pave the way for more scalable and ethically responsible AI in healthcare. 7: 7 Conclusion This study conducted a broad, systematic comparison of state-of-the-art CNN and ViT architectures for breast cancer classification across two distinct medical imaging modalities: ultrasound (BUSI) and histology (BACH). The central conclusion from our findings is that architectural suitability appears to be highly modality-dependent, as our results strongly suggest that no single model is universally superior. We found that CNNs, exemplified by EfficientNetV2-Small, are particularly effective for ultrasound image analysis, whereas a combination of advanced multi-scale ViTs like MViTv2-Base and efficient CNNs such as MobileNetV3-Large-100 excel at histological classification. The primary contributions of this work are threefold. First, it contributes a publicly verifiable performance benchmark for a wide range of modern deep learning models under a unified protocol, which can guide future research. Second, it provides clear, evidence-based guidance for selecting appropriate architectures tailored to specific clinical imaging tasks. Third, and perhaps most critically for clinical translation, it identifies several computationally efficient models that achieve top-tier accuracy, underscoring the feasibility of deploying advanced diagnostic tools in resource-constrained environments. While persistent challenges such as the need for larger datasets and improved domain adaptation strategies remain, this study represents a rigorous step toward the clinical application of AI in oncology. By providing a transparent and comprehensive evaluation, this work contributes to the ongoing development of more accurate, accessible, and clinically viable computer-aided diagnosis systems, with the goal of assisting radiologists and pathologists to improve patient outcomes.

Title: A computation-efficient network with feature aggregation for cancer subtype classification on histopathological images Abstract: Histopathology whole-slide images (WSI) capture detailed structural and morphological features of tumor tissue, offering rich histological and molecular information. Deep learning (DL) methods have emerged to assist in automatically examining histopathology WSIs and supporting tumor classification. Traditional DL approaches for WSI images face challenges due to the intrinsic complexity of tumor tissue characteristics and the extremely large image size. Multiple instance learning (MIL) methods have been proposed to address these issues by splitting the WSI images into small non-overlapping tiles and aggregating predictions from selected informative tiles for the final classification outcome. However, MIL methods still face challenges such as the need for accurate pseudo-labels, the risk of losing local information, or the failure to learn explicit class-relevant information. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that uses a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN)-based tile encoder (CTE) to extract local tile features and a Transformer-based feature aggregator (TFA) to fuse local features into a representative global feature for WSI classification. Three key contributions of our framework are as follows. Firstly, we design a two-stage training strategy that decouples a lightweight CTE pre-training (using sparsely sampled tiles for efficiency) and TFA fine-tuning (using all tiles for accuracy). It significantly reduces computational costs compared to existing MIL methods while alleviating local information loss. Secondly, dynamic self-attention-based aggregation is designed in TFA, leveraging the Transformer’s self-attention to weigh all local tile features without accurate pseudo-labels. It ensures comprehensive integration of local information from both tumor and ambiguous non-tumor regions to enrich global representations from input WSIs, which benefits the final classification performance. Finally, interpretable saliency maps are generated from TFA attention scores, highlighting histopathologically relevant regions to align model decisions with clinical reasoning. Comprehensive experiments on three cancer subtype datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method over existing MIL approaches. We also conduct further investigations into the impacts of various factors on model performance, gaining in-depth insights into our method. Our framework achieves higher classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency, making it a promising tool for histopathology image analysis.
