Graphical abstract 1: 1 Introduction Cancer is a complex disease characterized by its diverse subtypes, each exhibiting distinct responses to standard treatments such as chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, and targeted therapies ( Kuijjer et al., 2018; Agostinetto et al., 2022; Escudier et al., 2019 ). Accurate diagnosis of tumor origin and histologic subtype is crucial for determining the optimal therapeutic strategy. Traditionally, cancer diagnosis has been performed by pathologists examining hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained tissue on glass slides via a microscope. Recently, digital whole-slide imaging has become a promising tool in assisting the diagnosis process by enabling the scanning of tissue glass slides into high-resolution images, which preserve detailed morphologic information about the structural and cellular characteristics of tumor tissue ( Gurcan et al., 2009 ). With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), computer-aided analysis using AI-driven methods has emerged as a powerful tool for classifying histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) ( Van der Laak et al., 2021 ). These methods alleviate the need for time-consuming manual inspections by pathologists. However, employing deep learning (DL) models for histopathological image classification remains challenging due to the intrinsic complexity of tumor tissue characteristics and the extremely large size of WSIs, which can contain up to 10 billion pixels. The most common solution is to split the WSIs into a large number of non-overlapping small tiles for further processing. Traditional supervised DL approaches rely on extensive labeled data, which is expensive and practically infeasible to obtain for all tiles in a WSI ( Cheng et al., 2021; Gadermayr and Tschuchnig, 2024 ). To avoid the need for precise tile-level WSI annotations, weakly supervised learning methods based on multiple instance learning (MIL) have become mainstream. MIL methods treat the input WSI as a “bag” of tiles, where only the bag-level label (i.e., the WSI label) is known and the labels for individual tiles are unknown. These MIL methods typically train a model to identify discriminative tiles that correlate with the WSI label and then aggregate their features or predictions to infer the overall WSI classification. Most MIL approaches for WSI classification can be categorized into three types: pseudo-labeling (PL)-based methods ( Campanella et al., 2019; Bergner et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022b; Cui et al., 2023 ), self-supervised learning (SSL)-based methods ( Chen et al., 2022; Tellez et al., 2019; Dehaene et al., 2020; Schirris et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023 ), and attention-based methods ( Shao et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2021b; Ilse et al., 2018 ). While MIL methods have shown promise, they face several limitations. PL-based MIL methods ( Sandarenu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Tellez et al., 2019; Dehaene et al., 2020 ) assign pseudo-labels to tiles based on model predictions, but these pseudo-labels can be noisy and unreliable, especially in regions where tumor and non-tumor tissues are intermixed. SSL-based MIL methods ( Sandarenu et al., 2022; Dehaene et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022 ) learn useful representations from tiles without relying on accurate tile class labels. However, the unsupervised encoder training process focuses on distinguishing all tiles based on their unique features. They may fail to capture explicit class-related information, leading to suboptimal performance in downstream classification tasks. Attention-based MIL methods ( Shao et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2021b; Ilse et al., 2018 ) dynamically weight tiles via learned attention scores to focus on diagnostically relevant regions, avoiding the need for pseudo-labels and retaining all tiles. However, these methods often suffer from quadratic computational complexity due to pairwise tile interactions, making them impractical for gigapixel WSIs. In this study, we propose a novel WSI classification network to address the limitations above. Our method, named CETA , leverages a lightweight C NN-based Tile E ncoder to extract local features from tiles and a T ransformer-based Feature A ggregator to aggregate a comprehensive global feature for WSI classification. A decouple training strategy is developed for model training, including CTE pre-training with sparsely sampled tiles and TFA fine-tuning with all tiles. It enables the model to capture local information without requiring accurate tile annotations and mitigates the risk of local information loss by using all tiles. The main contributions of this study are as follows. • Decoupled two-stage training strategy for hybrid CNN- Transformer model architecture. Unlike existing MIL methods that rely on resource-intensive end-to-end training or pseudo-label refinement, we introduce a sequential training paradigm that decouples local feature learning (CTE pre-training) and global aggregation (TFA fine-tuning). During CTE pre-training, sparse tile sampling is designed to train the model with a small number of local tiles at each training iteration, reducing computational costs while ensuring robust local feature extraction. During TFA fine-tuning, the frozen CTE allows full utilization of all local tiles, minimizing local information loss while maintaining computational efficiency. In both training stages, WSI class labels are explicitly utilized to supervise the training procedure. It enables the model to learn class-related information and avoid the necessity for accurate pseudo labels for individual tiles. These unique designs address the computational bottleneck of gigapixel WSIs without sacrificing classification performance. • Dynamic self-attention-based feature aggregation. Unlike existing Transformer-based MIL methods that process fixed subsets of tiles or rely on pseudo-labels, our hybrid CNN-Transformer model is optimized for gigapixel WSIs with various input image sizes. Particularly, TFA leverages the Transformer’s inherent self-attention mechanism to fully utilize and dynamically weigh local features from all tiles with varying tile numbers during fine-tuning. This design eliminates the need for error-prone pseudo-labels and ensures that both tumor and ambiguous non-tumor regions contribute to the global representation, thus preventing critical information loss and ensuring model scalability and performance in WSI classification. • Interpretable saliency maps for clinical relevance. Beyond classification, our framework generates attention-based saliency maps that highlight the potential regions of interest (ROIs) that may influence model decisions. These saliency maps indicate the most informative regions and provide visual explanations aligned with histopathological patterns. Our approach can assist clinicians in making decisions and bridge the gap between AI-driven predictions and human interpretation. Comprehensive experiments on three cancer subtype datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art approaches, including pseudo-labeling (PL), self-supervised learning (SSL), and attention-based MIL methods. Our framework achieves higher classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency, making it a promising tool for histopathology image analysis. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 3 describes the network architecture and training strategy. The experiments and results are shown in Section 4.4 , and the discussion and conclusion are described in Sections 5 and 6 , respectively. 2: 2 Related work 2.1: 2.1 Multiple instance learning for WSI classification Multiple instance learning is a widely used weakly supervised learning method in WSI classification ( Campanella et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021a; Shao et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2023; Sandarenu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Tellez et al., 2019; Dehaene et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022b, 2024b ). MIL methods predict WSI labels by identifying and aggregating informative local tile-level features from training data, even when accurate individual tile labels are unavailable. Previous MIL approaches for WSI classification often relied on max-pooling aggregation ( Coudray et al., 2018 ), where the slide-level prediction is determined solely by the tile with the highest predicted score, assuming that a single discriminative tile defines the WSI label. While computationally efficient, this method suffers from significant limitations: (1) it ignores complementary information from other tiles, leading to information loss in heterogeneous tumors; and (2) it is highly sensitive to noisy tiles, as a single incorrect prediction can dominate the final result. Current MIL methods can be roughly grouped into three categories as follows. 2.1.1: 2.1.1 Pseudo labeling-based multiple instance learning PL-based MIL methods leverage unlabeled data to train the model alongside available labeled data to improve model performance. These methods initially train a model on available labeled bags and then use the partially trained model to predict labels for unlabeled bags (tiles). Only bags with high-confidence predictions are used to assign pseudo-labels, and the model is re-trained on a mix of originally labeled data and pseudo-labeled data. This training process can be iterated multiple times to refine the model performance further. For example, Shao et al. proposed a MIL framework that minimizes false positives in the noisy pseudo-labels using a super-patch-based method ( Shao et al., 2023 ). Gao et al. proposed a semi-supervised MTL framework for cancer classification, which consists of a backbone feature extractor, two task-specific classifiers, and a weight control mechanism ( Gao et al., 2023 ). Campanella et al. designed tile filtering modules to select discriminative tiles with pseudo labels inherited from the WSI-level label, and only top-ranked tiles were employed to train the model ( Campanella et al., 2019 ). However, the predicted pseudo-label accuracy heavily depends on the initial model’s performance, and poor initial predictions can exacerbate errors in subsequent training iterations. Selecting only top-ranked discriminative tiles might further lead to critical local information loss in the aggregated feature (e.g., missing tumor tissue regions), degrading model performance. 2.1.2: 2.1.2 Self-supervised learning-based multiple instance learning SSL-based MIL integrates SSL with the MIL framework, enabling learning from data with sparse explicit labels. SSL-based MIL methods leverage pretext tasks such as tile reconstruction or contrastive learning to pre-train a feature encoder on unlabeled tiles, extracting generalizable representations without relying on explicit annotations ( Li et al., 2021b; Xie et al., 2022 ). These pre-trained features are then aggregated via MIL to predict WSI labels. For instance, Tellez et al. proposed neural image compression to retain high-level information from WSIs in an unsupervised manner ( Tellez et al., 2019 ). Li et al. utilized self-supervised contrastive learning to extract tile representations ( Li et al., 2021b ). Tang et al. proposed a self-supervised representation distribution learning framework for patch-level representation learning with an online representation sampling strategy for patch feature extraction and WSI-level data augmentation ( Tang et al., 2024 ). Wang et al. proposed a multi-resolution SSL framework that effectively learns complementary information from multiple WSI resolutions during the pre-training stage, which can lead to improved performance in the subsequent tasks ( Wang et al., 2024 ). However, the pretext tasks often focus on low-level or instance-specific patterns (e.g., tile rotation prediction), which may not align with the histopathological patterns critical for cancer subtype classification, resulting in suboptimal discriminative power for downstream classification tasks. 2.1.3: 2.1.3 Attention-based multiple instance learning Attention-based MIL methods address the limitations of static aggregation strategies like max-pooling by dynamically weighting tiles based on their relevance to WSI labels. These methods employ attention mechanisms to assign importance scores to tiles, enabling the model to focus on critical regions while suppressing noise from non-informative tiles. For example, Ilse et al. proposed an attention-based MIL framework that learns to weigh tiles via a gated attention module to improve feature aggregation ( Ilse et al., 2018 ). Lu et al. introduced DSMIL, which combines instance-level and bag-level attention to enhance feature representation ( Lu et al., 2021 ). While attention-based MIL methods reduce reliance on pseudo-labels, they still face two key challenges. Xiang et al. proposed a novel end-to-end interpretable deep MIL framework for WSI analysis, by using a two-branch network and a multi-scale representation attention mechanism to directly extract features from all patches of each WSI ( Xiang et al., 2023 ). Liu et al. proposed a prototype attention-based MIL method to merge prototype learning with attention mechanisms, enabling the model to quantify the similarity between prototypes and instances, thereby improving the model’s reasoning interpretability without compromising its classification performance at the WSI level ( Liu et al., 2024 ). Traditional attention mechanisms require pairwise interactions between tiles, leading to quadratic complexity with respect to the number of tiles, which is impractical for large WSIs with numerous tiles. These methods typically process fixed subsets of tiles that limit their ability to adaptively scale to gigapixel WSIs with varying image sizes. 2.2: 2.2 Vision transformer in WSI classification Vision Transformers (ViTs) ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) have emerged as a powerful alternative to CNNs in medical image analysis ( Shamshad et al., 2023 ), offering superior global context modeling through self-attention mechanisms. ViT processes images by dividing them into small non-overlapping patches, each flattened into a one-dimensional embedding. The self-attention mechanism in ViT allows the model to weigh the importance of each patch relative to others, capturing long-distance dependencies and enhancing the representativeness of the learned embedding. In WSI classification, ViTs are typically applied in two paradigms: (1) hierarchical processing, where multi-scale patches are encoded and aggregated ( Chen et al., 2022 ), or (2) instance-based aggregation, where tile-level features are fused into a slide-level representation ( Li et al., 2021b; Shao et al., 2021 ). For example, Li et al. employed a pre-trained ViT to encode tiles and a transformer-based aggregator for slide-level classification ( Li et al., 2023 ). However, directly applying vanilla ViTs to gigapixel WSIs remains computationally prohibitive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention over thousands of tiles. In contrast, the proposed CETA utilizes pre-training with sparse sampling and decoupled two-stage training to avoid ViT’s computational bottlenecks on gigapixel WSIs. More differences between CETA and ViT are further highlighted in Appendix A.1 . 3: 3 Methods 3.1: 3.1 Model architecture of CETA The proposed classification framework is shown in Fig. 1 . It consists of a WSI tile sampling module, a CTE, a projection layer, a TFA, and a classifier. Given WSIs as input, the tile sampling module splits the input slide images into small non-overlapping tiles. It also performs initial filtering to discard bland and non-informative tiles and selects a subgroup of tiles along with their corresponding positional embeddings for further processing. The CTE extracts informative local features from the selected tiles. The computational burden for training CTE is reduced with limited but informative tiles. The projection layer reduces the dimensionality of the tile features to match the input feature dimensions required by the subsequent TFA. The positional embeddings corresponding to the selected tiles are fused with the extracted local features via element-wise addition to maintain the spatial context. Following the ViT design ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ), TFA accepts a sequence of tile features and a classification (CLS) token as inputs. The CLS token attends to all the tile features in each attention layer, aggregating global information across the entire image. The TFA outputs the CLS token as an attentive global feature, which is further used by the classifier for tumor subtype classification. This design makes the model capture a rich representation that integrates local and global semantic information, improving classification performance and alleviating the demand for computational resources. 3.1.1: 3.1.1 WSI tile sampling module Considering the impractical computational burden of directly processing the gigapixel WSIs, the tiling module splits the input WSI into non-overlapping square tiles similar to traditional MIL methods ( Gadermayr and Tschuchnig, 2024; Cheng et al., 2021 ). Given a 2-dimensional WSI X ∈ R W × H , this process can produce a large volume of small tiles with M × M pixels. M ≪ W a n d H and is set as M = 384 in this study. However, a significant proportion of these tiles (approximately 20%–60%) contain no tissue area or only a small percentage of tissue area. To improve computational efficiency, the module employs the Otsu filtering algorithm ( Otsu, 1979 ) to exclude non-tissue tiles. This algorithm analyzes the histogram of the tile’s grayscale pixel intensities and calculates an optimal threshold that maximizes the variance between the tissue and background classes. After applying the Otsu threshold to create a binary mask of the tissue, we quantify the percentage of the tile covered by tissue. We define a non-informative tile as one where the tissue area constitutes less than 5% of the total tile area. All the non-informative tiles will be discarded. After Otsu filtering, a subset of K tissue tiles is retained as input for the following processing stage. Even with background tile filtering, the number of remaining tissue tiles might still be large. Training an encoder on all these tiles is infeasible due to the heavy computational demands. The tile sampling module mitigates this issue by selectively capturing useful features across the WSI without losing essential information. This module randomly samples J tiles as input for the subsequent encoder, where J is adjusted according to different training stages. This dynamic adjustment allows for optimal computational efficiency while capturing a representative set of features from the WSI. 3.1.2: 3.1.2 CNN-based tile encoder (CTE) A CTE is designed to extract features from the selected tiles. It aims to capture useful local representations with essential morphological and textural information. To optimize the balance between computational efficiency and effective representation learning, lightweight CNN networks are employed as the encoder rather than computationally intensive transformer networks. We used ResNet ( He et al., 2016 ) in this study due to its relatively low computation demand and robust representation learning capability. Given the sampled WSI tiles, the CTE extracts corresponding one-dimensional feature vectors. A projection layer is applied to align the dimensions of the CTE-extracted tile features with the input requirements of the TFA. It includes a fully connected layer with D = 768 neurons, matching the default input dimension used in the ViT architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ). 3.1.3: 3.1.3 Transformer-based feature aggregator (TFA) The TFA serves as a decoder to aggregate the local representations of all sampled tiles to obtain a comprehensive global representation of the input WSI. In this study, the TFA is designed as a lightweight transformer architecture with multiple transformer decoder layers ( Vaswani et al., 2017; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ), as shown in Fig. 2 . The TFA contains two transformer decoder layers to manage computational efficiency. Following the ViT paradigm, the positional embeddings generated during the tile sampling process are fused to the corresponding learned tile features via element-wise addition. These positional embeddings help maintain the positional context of each tile, providing extra spatial knowledge, which is crucial for accurate feature aggregation. In particular, sinusoidal positional encoding is used to define these embeddings ( Vaswani et al., 2017; He et al., 2022 ). The processed tile features and the CLS token are concatenated into a sequence and fed into the 2-layer transformer decoder, outputting the corresponding attentive features and CLS token. The output CLS token, with the same dimension D = 768 of tile features, is treated as an attentive WSI global feature. It captures comprehensive global features with essential spatial correlations between different tiles. This TFA design yields three major advantages. First, the inherent self-attention mechanism allows it to flexibly manage varying numbers of input tile features, accommodating the input WSIs with variable sizes. Second, the self-attention mechanism dynamically calculates the correlation between all input local tile features and the CLS token. The CLS token is randomly initialized and specifically introduced as a dedicated learnable parameter to aggregate global information from the entire sequence of tile features. Third, the learned model weights of the inherent self-attention mechanism can be decoded to generate saliency maps. These saliency maps highlight regions of interest within the WSI, offering insights into the model’s decision-making process and enhancing the interpretability of the model’s prediction. 3.1.4: 3.1.4 Classifier Once the global feature is extracted by the TFA, the classifier predicts the probability of the input WSI belonging to each of the cancer subtypes. It comprises a fully-connected layer with N neurons, where N equals the number of cancer subtypes to be differentiated. In this study, N was set to 2. 3.2: 3.2 Decoupled two-stage training strategy Fig. 3 shows the decoupled two-stage training strategy designed to improve the model’s classification performance and alleviate the computational burden. The detailed training process is described in Appendix A.2 . In the first stage, both the CTE and TFA are pre-trained using a subgroup of J tiles selected through tile sampling from the total of K tissue tiles from an individual WSI. The small number of sampled J tiles ( J ≪ K ) can reduce the heavy computational load and allow more practical training at this stage. To mitigate the risk of losing local information due to tile omission, the pre-training involves a substantial number of training epochs. The random seed is reset every epoch to ensure different tile subsets are sampled across epochs and the model does not overfit to specific regions. It ensures that the CTE can encounter a distinct subset of tiles from each slide, improving its exposure to diverse morphological patterns. By pre-training on sparse but diverse samples, the CTE learns discriminative local features to prioritize specific areas. Over multiple epochs, the model encounters diverse regions of the WSI, approximating full-tile coverage. This way, our model can alleviate the computation costs and mitigate the risk of missing critical regions with sparse sampling. The model is trained using WSI-level labels in a fully supervised learning manner, and cross-entropy was employed as the loss function. In the second stage, only the TFA and classifier are fine-tuned while the CTE is frozen, serving solely to extract tile features without further updating via back-propagation. It enables the inclusion of all filtered tiles of an individual input WSI for training in a fully-supervised manner, ensuring that all class-related knowledge is preserved in the learned features. Given the complete set of local tile features from the input WSI, TFA is trained to fuse the local information to formulate a representative global feature. Stage 2’s objective is not to improve the CTE, but solely to teach the TFA how to optimize the interpretation and aggregation of local features from the fixed CTE. Such comprehensive global features potentially prevent the loss of crucial local information loss and improve overall classification accuracy. Additionally, the decoupled training strategy in a fully-supervised manner can alleviate the potential issue of feature mismatch between the CTE and TFA. First, the pre-training in Stage 1 ensures that the TFA is initially trained on the exact feature distribution from the CTE, allowing it to adapt to the CTE’s feature space. Stage 2 allows the TFA to refine local feature aggregation using a much larger set of these same task-relevant features. Second, the training process in both stages is supervised by the WSI-level classification label. This forces the CTE to learn features that are explicitly relevant and discriminative for the final classification task. The cross-entropy loss function is also employed during this stage. 4: 4 Experiments and results 4.1: 4.1 Datasets The proposed method was evaluated on three H&E-stained histopathological image datasets from the Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA) database ( Heath et al., 2021 ). 2 2 TCGA data portal homepage: . The first dataset is the invasive breast carcinoma (BRCA) dataset, which includes two cancer subtypes, Invasive Ductal (IDC) and Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC). The second dataset is the non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) dataset, which includes lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC). The last dataset is the renal cell carcinomas (RCC) dataset, which includes kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma (KIRP). Each dataset contains an equal number of slides per subtype to ensure class balance. The detailed number of training, validation, and test sets of each tumor type is shown in Table 1 . 4.2: 4.2 Performance evaluation The framework was trained on the training set for 800 epochs in the pre-training stage and 100 epochs in the fine-tuning stage. Detailed training information is provided in Appendix B . After each epoch, the trained model was evaluated on the validation set. The model weights with the best validation performance were further assessed on the test set. Model performance was evaluated with metrics including accuracy (ACC), precision (Prec), recall (Rec), F 1 -score, and area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (AUC). The number of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations was calculated to assess the model’s computational costs. 4.3: 4.3 Compared baselines The proposed method has been compared with max-pooling aggregation, four PL-based MIL methods, three SSL-based MIL methods, and four attention-based MIL methods. The max-pooling method used an Inception-v3 network as the tile encoder and max pooling to aggregate the outcome ( Coudray et al., 2018 ). The four PL-based methods include MIL-RNN ( Campanella et al., 2019 ), IPS ( Bergner et al., 2023 ), DTFD-MIL ( Zhang et al., 2022b ) and Bayes-MIL ( Cui et al., 2023 ). The three SSL-based methods include DeepMIL ( Dehaene et al., 2020 ), DeepSMILE ( Schirris et al., 2022 ), and PMIL ( Yu et al., 2023 ). The four attention-based methods include CLAM ( Lu et al., 2021 ), ACMIL ( Zhang et al., 2024b ), DSMIL ( Li et al., 2021b ), and ABMIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ). 4.4: 4.4 Experiment results and ablation studies 4.4.1: 4.4.1 Cancer subtype classification performance Table 2 demonstrates the superior classification performance of the proposed method compared to 12 other methods across three different datasets. Compared to the max-pooling method, our method achieved 8.5%, 7.4%, and 1.8% increase in AUC on all three datasets, respectively. It indicates that our method can explicitly learn class-related information to improve classification performance without relying on accurate tile labels, a critical advantage over max-pooling that heavily depends on such labels. Our method also outperforms the comparative PL-based MIL methods (MIL-RNN, IPS, and DTFD-MIL), which only process top-ranked discriminative tiles to train the classification model and neglect a large portion of local tiles. These approaches often result in losing critical tumor tissue-related information, which our method retains by aggregating all local tile features for final classification. Compared to the attention-based MIL methods (CLAM, ACMIL, DSMIL, and ABMIL), the proposed method can adaptively scale to gigapixel WSIs with a varying number of local tiles, capturing more representative global features and achieving better performance. Furthermore, the SSL-based MIL methods (DeepMIL, DeepSMILE, and PMIL) show relatively lower performance. This implies that the tile encoder trained via an unsupervised method might fail to capture essential class-related information explicitly and lead to suboptimal model performance. 4.4.2: 4.4.2 Ablation study: impact of TFA fine-tuning on model performance An ablation experiment was conducted to assess the impact of FTA fine-tuning on classification performance. The ablated model was only pre-trained without the TFA fine-tuning. In this case, TFA was only exposed to the sparsely sampled local tiles selected during pre-training. Fig. 4 demonstrates the model performance with and without the fine-tuning stage, utilizing ResNet50 or ResNet18 as the CTE. The results highlight that fine-tuning the TFA with all available tiles significantly enhances the model’s ability to capture comprehensive information from all local tiles, thereby improving overall classification accuracy. Without fine-tuning, essential class-related local information embedded in tiles that are neglected during pre-training might be lost, leading to suboptimal performance. These results underscore the necessity of fine-tuning stage design in the training strategy to ensure optimal model performance. 4.4.3: 4.4.3 Ablation study: impact of using transfer learning for CTE training on model performance Transfer learning (TL) is a widely used technique that leverages pre-trained model parameters to enhance model performance, especially in scenarios involving small datasets ( Shorten and Khoshgoftaar, 2019 ). In WSI classification, using model weights pre-trained on the extensive ImageNet is a prevalent transfer learning approach ( Deng et al., 2009 ). We conducted experiments to understand the impacts of using TL on the CTE on model performance. The CTE was initialized with two different strategies for comparison: one using model weights pre-trained on ImageNet and another using random initialization. As shown in Fig. 5 , our method using ResNet50 as the CTE significantly improves model performance when applying the TL strategy. This result demonstrates that transfer learning is critical in improving model classification performance. Similar results are observed when employing other CTE architects (ResNet18 or ResNet101). Across these models, transfer learning consistently enhances performance, demonstrating its universal advantage regardless of the specific CTE used. 4.4.4: 4.4.4 Impact of CTE architecture on model performance The impact of various CTE architectures on model performance was investigated. Five widely employed CNN networks and one transformer-based network were employed as alternatives for the CTE. The CNN networks include ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ResNet-101 ( He et al., 2016 ), EfficientNet-B0 ( Tan and Le, 2019 ), and Inception-v3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ), while the transformer-based network is the data-efficient image transformer (DeiT)-B ( Touvron et al., 2021 ). All other experimental settings are the same as described in Section 3.2 . The performance for each encoder architecture are shown in Table 3 . Using ResNet-50 as the CTE yields superior performance across all the evaluated architectures. This result suggests that using deeper tile encoders with more trainable parameters does not guarantee better model performance. Compared to traditional MIL methods (e.g., MIL-RNN), our method significantly outperforms them across all tested CTE architectures. It underscores the general effectiveness of our method in WSI classification. Performance variations exist, depending on the specific capabilities of different CTEs in capturing local tile features. 4.4.5: 4.4.5 Impact of selected tile numbers during pre-training on model performance During the pre-training stage, only a small number of tiles were selected for model training to reduce computational burden while maintaining the model performance. The impact of varying numbers of tiles was investigated with experiments conducted using 1,5, 10, 20, and 50 tiles. Fig. 6 shows the model performance across these tile number configurations, using either ResNet50 or ResNet18 as the CTE. We observed that aggregating multiple tiles significantly improves model performance compared to using one single tile. This demonstrates the efficacy of feature aggregation from multiple local tiles in boosting model performance. Interestingly, increasing tile numbers did not consistently enhance classification performance across different datasets. This suggests that there might be an optimal number of tiles beyond which additional tiles could not further support WSI classification. Further analysis was conducted to quantify the computational burden under different tile selection settings using multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations. MAC estimates the computational intensity of training process and the time it takes for a trained model to make final predictions. As shown in Fig. 6 , increasing the selected tile number leads to a linearly increased computational burden. Selecting ten tiles offered an optimal balance between model performance and computational efficiency in this study, highlighting a potentially efficient configuration for training in resource-constrained scenarios. 4.4.6: 4.4.6 Impact of the number of attention layers in TFA on model performance The number of transformer decoder layers in TFA can potentially influence the model’s representation learning capability, affecting the quality of aggregated global features and overall classification performance. To explore this, we experimented with varying the number of transformer decoder layers, testing configurations with 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 12 layers. As shown in Fig. 7(a) , our method with ResNet50 as the CTE achieves superior performance by using two transformer decoder layers across all datasets. It suggests that a lightweight TFA with a shallow-layered transformer architecture might be sufficient to aggregate local tile features into a representative global feature. When increasing the number of decoder layers, the model performance decreases. The possible explanations for this phenomenon include (1) the higher risk of overfitting due to increased model complexity; (2) limited datasets for training deeper transformer architecture; (3) the increased risk of redundant feature interactions. As shown in Fig. 7(b) , when using ResNet18 as the CTE, the shallow-layered transformer decoder continues to outperform those with deeper layers (e.g., 8 and 12). However, the number of decoder layers required for optimal performance varies. This suggests that different CTEs may have distinct capabilities in extracting useful features, necessitating TFAs with varying decoding capacities to achieve the best results. Given that all tiles are processed in the fine-tuning stage, increasing the number of transformer decoder layers can lead to a linear increase in model complexity, potentially making the training infeasible. For example, our method using a TFA with 12 transformer decoder layers needs 403G MAC during the fine-tuning stage if the input WSI contains 2000 tiles. Reducing the number of decoder layers to two reduced the computation demand to just 29G MAC. It is critical to determine a suitable number of decoder layers to balance the model performance and computational burden. 4.4.7: 4.4.7 Visualization of WSI attention maps for model interpretability The self-attention mechanism within the trained transformer offers a powerful tool for model interpretability by enabling the visualization of discriminative regions that influence decision-making. Specifically, the attention weights of trained TFA can be decoded via averaged interpolation ( Cordonnier et al., 2020 ), producing a saliency map that manifests as pixel-wise heatmaps indicating regions of importance. To confirm that the learned attention scores of TFA network reflect the importance of specific local regions, saliency maps of several sample images across different tumor categories were visualized, as shown in Fig. 8 . The local regions highlighted by the learned attention weights correspond closely to the ground-truth tumor tissue area annotated by an expert pathologist. This result demonstrates that our method can automatically assist the extraction of discriminative local features and attentive fusion of global features, even without explicit annotated tumor contours. Such capability underscores the efficacy of our method in elucidating the internal mechanism and providing insights into the model’s decision-making process. Similar phenomena are observed in more attention maps of each cancer subtype, as detailed in Appendix C.1 . 4.4.8: 4.4.8 Tile pathological patterns To validate the clinical relevance of our method, we analyzed tiles with varying attention scores across different tumor subtypes, linking model focus to histopathological patterns. The differences in model performance across the BRCA, NSCLC, and RCC datasets ( Table 2 ) can be attributed to several intrinsic factors related to the unique characteristics of each tumor type. Breast tumor : IDC tiles ( Fig. 8(c) ) with high attention scores typically originate from tumor regions. They exhibit critical morphological patterns of tumor cells, such as high cellular density, abnormal cell morphology, increased mitotic activity, and distinct staining effects. Conversely, the IDC tiles with low attention scores generally come from non-tumor areas, displaying low cellular density, absent significant abnormal cells, no tissue degeneration, and a lack of specific tissue staining. The patterns match the fact that these tiles are from the non-tumor areas. Notably, both IDC and ILC subtypes ( Fig. 8(d) ) share these discriminative patterns. They might contain heterogeneous tumor–stroma interactions like inflammatory infiltrates that increase intra-class variability. These histopathological characteristics pose challenges to the model in aggregating spatially dispersed features, probably causing slightly lower classification performance compared to other datasets. Lung tumor : For LUAD ( Fig. 9(c) ), high-attention tiles highlight glandular formations and mucin production, while low-attention tiles often contain inflammatory infiltrates or fibrotic stroma. In LUSC ( Fig. 9(d) ), high-attention regions reveal keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, whereas low-attention areas show necrosis or normal bronchial epithelium. These distinct patterns align with known histopathological criteria for lung adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma. Lung tumor slides may include mixed patterns like lepidic or micropapillary growth in both subtypes, but the dominant subtype-specific features remain distinguishable. These differences enable the classification model to achieve strong performance. Kidney tumor : In KIRP ( Fig. 9(e) ), high-attention tiles emphasize papillary structures and foamy macrophages, whereas low-attention regions display normal glomeruli or tubules. For KIRC ( Fig. 9(f) ), high-attention areas exhibit nuclear atypia (enlarged, irregular nuclei) and prominent vasculature, while low-attention tiles correspond to hyalinized stroma or non-neoplastic parenchyma. These unique distinctions simplify tile filtering and feature extraction from kidney tumor WSIs, thus contributing to the highest observed classification performance. These visualizations demonstrate that our method’s attention scores correlate strongly with histopathologically validated tumor regions, even in morphologically heterogeneous subtypes. By highlighting diagnostically critical features (e.g., mitotic figures in IDC, glandular structures in LUAD), the model provides interpretable insights that align with pathologists’ diagnostic workflows. 5: 5 Discussion 5.1: 5.1 Advantages of the proposed method In this study, we introduced a computationally efficient framework for cancer subtype classification of histopathology WSIs, leveraging efficient local feature extraction and global feature aggregation. The proposed approach directly aggregates the local features from all split tiles into a comprehensive global WSI feature using a transformer architecture for further classification. Our method eliminates the need to determine each tile’s potentially noisy pseudo-label, thereby avoiding the risk of losing essential local details. A decoupled two-stage training strategy is designed to train this framework to significantly reduce computational demands while enabling explicit learning of class-related information. This way, our method can enrich the informativeness of the aggregated feature and benefit the classification performance. Furthermore, the intrinsic self-attention mechanism of the transformer architecture can be facilitated to highlight possible ROIs in the input data, thus improving the interpretability of the prediction process. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three different cancer subtype datasets demonstrated the superiority of our method in improving WSI classification performance compared to five traditional WSI classification methods. An ablation study further validated the importance of the fine-tuning stage in our training strategy, showing it is critical for achieving optimal model performance. In-depth exploration was implemented to analyze the potential impacts of various model-related factors on model performance. These factors include the CTE architecture, usage of transfer learning on the CTE, the number of selected tiles of the tile sampling module, and the number of self-attention layers in the TFA network. 5.2: 5.2 Limitations While the proposed model shows promising performance, there are still several potential limitations worth discussing. First, sampling bias in tile selection might exist. Random tile sampling may fail to capture sufficient tumor regions in WSIs with sparse lesions. For example, in the BRCA dataset, about 15% of WSIs exhibited tumor coverage < 5 % , leading to potential bias during pre-training. Second, our experiments show the performance degradation with increased decoder layers ( Fig. 7 ). One potential reason is that additional layers add trainable parameters and increase the risk of overfitting. Also, deeper layers in transformer architecture may learn redundant or noisy correlations between tiles. In histopathology, tumor subtype classification often relies on localized morphological patterns, such as nuclear texture and glandular structures. Using more layers may over-smooth these critical fine-grained local details through excessive cross-tile correlations, degrading subtype classification accuracy. Training deeper transformer models usually requires large-scale datasets for good generalization capabilities, while the current datasets are still limited. Third, SSL-based MIL methods underperformed in our study, even lower than the traditional max-pooling method. Such a large performance gap might be caused by several challenges. SSL-based methods usually need large amounts of training data to ensure the generalization of learned features when applied to unseen data. However, small-sized WSI datasets (250 WSIs per cancer type) were used for model training, the over-fitting issues might reduce the performance more than other methods. Also, SSL-based MIL methods pre-train encoders using pretext tasks (e.g., contrastive learning, tile reconstruction) that do not explicitly optimize for subtype discrimination. For instance, contrastive learning focuses on instance discrimination, maximizing similarity between augmented views of the same tile while pushing apart all others, rather than task-specific histopathological patterns. One other reason is that SSL pretext tasks often learn generic, low-level features that are not specific to cancer subtypes. The extremely high similarity between tumor-tissue and non-tumor-tissue tiles in WSIs impedes the model from capturing robust representations during SSL. Prior work highlights similar limitations of SSL in medical imaging ( Raghu et al., 2019 ). 5.3: 5.3 Future work To investigate the potential sampling bias and improve training efficiency, we will explore more advanced adaptive sampling strategies like diversity-driven sampling ( Shao et al., 2021 ) to dynamically sample highly diverse tiles to reduce bias and improve consistent feature representation learning across different image scales. We also plan to explore the bottleneck of SSL-based methods by utilizing larger annotated WSI datasets with more discriminative tumor and non-tumor tissues. We will compare distributions of SSL- and CETA-extracted features by t-SNE ( Van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008 ), and assess class separability. We will quantify the overlap between the SSL-highlighted areas and pathologist annotations to evaluate clinical relevance. To alleviate potential performance degradation with increased decoder layers, larger datasets will be employed to pre-train the TFA architectures. Dynamic depth adaption technique will be explored to properly adjust TFA layers to achieve an optimal model architecture based on the complexities of distinct WSI datasets. Also, more diverse pathological datasets will be investigated to evaluate the model’s robustness and the effect of the pathological complexity of different cancer types. Furthermore, more lightweight and efficient CNN architectures, such as RegNet ( Radosavovic et al., 2020 ) and EfficientNet ( Tan and Le, 2019 ), will be explored as the tile encoder to enhance model performance and reduce computational burdens. We will explore the potential of the integration of advanced learning strategies, such as variance-constrained modeling ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) and collaborative learning ( Zhang et al., 2022a ), into TFA to improve the robustness of learned global representations, especially from ambiguous regions. The flexibility of the TFA design allows our method to accommodate input features from other data modalities, such as genomic or clinical data (e.g., radiologic imaging data and mutation profiles) that contain complementary information for subtype classification. We will extend our method to incorporate multi-modal input data to provide more comprehensive information for patient diagnostic support, such as tumor grading and survival analysis after treatment. 6: 6 Conclusions A computationally efficient WSI classification network is proposed for the cancer subtype classification in histopathological images. A decoupled two-stage training strategy is designed to separate lightweight CTE pre-training from TFA fine-tuning, significantly reducing computational costs while retaining critical local and global information. Dynamic self-attention aggregation via TFA eliminates reliance on pseudo-labels by adaptively weighting all tile features to construct comprehensive slide-level representations and improve classification performance. Interpretable saliency maps can be derived from transformer attention scores, which highlight histopathologically relevant regions and align model decisions with clinical reasoning. Extensive experiments conducted on three TCGA WSI image datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method. The framework’s efficiency and interpretability make it a practical tool for clinical deployment. A.1: A.1 CETA vs. ViT Compared to the standard ViT model, our proposed model has four key differences, as shown in Table A.4 . A.2: A.2 Algorithm for decoupled two-stage model training The detailed training process of the two-stage sequential training of the proposed framework is shown in Algorithm 1. B.1: B.1 Preparation of TCGA datasets For each cancer subtype, 250 WSIs were selected from the public TCGA database. The detailed selection criteria are shown below. • Source and availability: All slides were sourced from the TCGA public repository, which provides histopathological WSIs with confirmed diagnostic and molecular annotations. Slides were included only if they had a pathologist-validated diagnosis of each cancer subtype (e.g., IDC/ILC for BRCA). • WSI quality: We selected only high-quality H&E-stained slides and excluded slides with significant artifacts (e.g., folds, tears, air bubbles) or poor staining quality (e.g., faded H&E, uneven dye distribution) guided by an experienced pathologist. Slides with < 5 % tissue area after automated Otsu filtering are excluded to avoid non-informative samples. We use the “threshold_otsu” function in the scikit-image package to achieve this goal. • Class balance: We selected the same number of slides for each cancer subtype to ensure a balanced representation. Subtype labels were directly inherited from TCGA’s clinical annotations. No patient contributed more than one slide to avoid data leakage. B.2: B.2 Model specification B.2.1: B.2.1 CTE (CNN backbone) • Architectures tested: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ResNet-101. • Pre-trained Weights: Downloaded from Torchvision ( torchvision.models.resnet* ) with ImageNet normalization (mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]) ( Deng et al., 2009 ). • Modification: Removed the final fully connected layer; used the last convolutional block’s output (feature dimension D = 2048 for ResNet-50/101 and D = 512 for ResNet-18). B.2.2: B.2.2 TFA (Transformer Aggregator) • Architecture: two transformer blocks with embed_dim = 768 , num_heads = 12 , mlp_ratio = 4 , and dropout = 0.1. • Positional Embeddings: Sinusoidal positional encoding ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) with max_seq_len = 10,000. For a WSI divided into a grid of non-overlapping tiles, each tile’s position is represented as a 2D coordinate ( x , y ) , where x ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , W − 1 } denotes the column index; y ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , H − 1 } denotes the row index; and W and H are the total number of columns and rows in the WSI grid, respectively. The embeddings are fixed to reduce model complexity and avoid overfitting to slide-specific positional biases. Next, we normalize tile coordinates by scaling x and y to the range [ 0 , 1 ] : x norm = x W , y norm = y H For each normalized coordinate p ∈ { x norm , y norm } , compute a D / 2 -dimensional vector using sinusoidal functions of varying frequencies: PE ( p , 2 i ) = sin p ⋅ 1 1000 0 2 i / D , PE ( p , 2 i + 1 ) = cos p ⋅ 1 1000 0 2 i / D where D is the embedding dimension (768 in this study), and i indexes the dimension. The final positional embedding for a tile at ( x , y ) is the concatenation of its x and y embeddings: PE ( x , y ) = PE ( x norm ) , PE ( y norm ) ∈ R D After extracting tile features f i ∈ R D using the CNN encoder (CTE), positional embeddings are fused via element-wise addition: f ̃ i = f i + PE ( x i , y i ) These enriched features f ̃ i are then fed into the transformer aggregator (TFA). • Initialization: Xavier uniform for all linear layers ( Glorot and Bengio, 2010 ); LayerNorm with eps = 1e−6. B.2.3: B.2.3 Classifier • Structure: Single fully connected layer (768 → N, where N = 2 for binary classification in this study). • Activation: Softmax for probability prediction. B.3: B.3 Hyperparameters specification We used fixed hyperparameters across all tested models. B.3.1: B.3.1 Tile processing • Tile Size: 384 × 384 pixels (extracted at level 0 from WSI slide .svs files). • Sampling: J = 10 tiles randomly selected during pre-training; all tiles used during fine-tuning. • Otsu Filtering: Discarded tiles with tissue area < 5 % . B.3.2: B.3.2 Optimization • Weight Decay: 0.05 (AdamW optimizer ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 )). • Gradient Clipping: Global norm clipped at 1.0. B.4: B.4 Training protocol B.4.1: B.4.1 Data augmentation • Random Resized Crop: Scale = [0.8, 1.25], ratio = [0.5, 2], interpolation = bicubic. • Spatial Augmentations: Horizontal/vertical flip (p = 0.5), 90°rotation (p = 0.5). • Color Augmentations: None (to preserve H&E stain patterns). B.4.2: B.4.2 Learning rate schedule We implemented a hybrid learning rate schedule that combines linear warmup with cosine annealing to stabilize early training and enable refined convergence ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ). • Warmup: Linear increase from 0 to 1e−5 over 50 epochs. • Decay: Cosine annealing to 0 over 50 epochs. B.4.3: B.4.3 Training Training epochs: 100, and batch size: 1. We processed one WSI slide at each iteration because most WSIs have different image sizes. B.4.4: B.4.4 Software version PyTorch = 2.0.1, CUDA = 11.7, Torchvision = 0.15.2. B.4.5: B.4.5 Compute resource specification Models were trained on four NVIDIA A40 GPUs. Since the model design significantly reduces the computational cost, the model inference and evaluation can be executed on devices with limited resources, e.g., one NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU. These heatmaps indicate that the high attention scores learned by the TFA network show the important specific local regions during classification. However, if the lesion occupies the majority of the tissue, the model might misallocate attention to non-tumor regions or much smaller lesion areas, as illustrated in Figs. C.10(b) and C.12(b) . The possible explanation for this phenomenon is that the attention mechanism may get diluted across the entire region when the lesion occupies a large portion of the tissue. It is difficult for the model to pinpoint the most critical parts of the lesion. As a result, the model might end up focusing on smaller, less representative regions or even misallocating attention to irrelevant areas.

Title: A distributed deep learning approach for blood sample-based early detection of dementia Abstract: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), the prevailing form of dementia, is a neurological condition that significantly impacts individuals globally, leading to devastating effects. The early detection of AD is of paramount importance in mitigating its impact. Numerous methodologies have been suggested for diagnosing AD through medical imaging techniques such as positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Nevertheless, it is anticipated that utilizing blood biomarkers would enhance the identification of individuals with AD and cognitive impairments. This paper introduces an innovative distributed deep-learning methodology for the early identification of AD through the analysis of blood samples. This study aims to investigate the application of federated learning (FL) in the analysis of blood samples to predict the likelihood of getting AD. Our study employed a dataset of many blood samples characterized by various features. A generative adversarial network (GAN) has been applied to regenerate data from original data to improve model generalization, increase diversity, and reduce overfitting. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach maintains high accuracy and provides better privacy. The accuracy, recall, specificity, and F1 score achieved were 85.1%, 75.5%, 93.8%, and 84.9% for original data and 89.8%, 87.8%, 91.3%, and 89.9% for regenerated data.
