One illustrative instance of such a pathological condition is dementia [13,14] . The challenge of overcoming dementia is a substantial public health concern in contemporary society. According to several sources [15,16] , the global prevalence of this particular disease is estimated to be approximately 55 million individuals. With advancements in medicine and the consequent increase in life expectancy, it is anticipated that the prevalence of dementia will rise, particularly within the elderly population. The incidence of dementia is expected to increase further due to the factors above and declining birth rates. Despite the allocation of substantial financial resources towards research aimed at discovering a cure for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the prevailing form of dementia, there is currently a lack of commercially accessible medicines capable of halting the progression of the disease [17] . An estimated 7.2 million Americans age 65 and older are living with AD in 2025 [18] . 74% are age 75 or older. About 1 in 9 people age 65 and older has AD. Almost two-thirds of Americans with AD are women. The lifetime risk for AD at age 45 is 1 in 5 for women and 1 in 10 for men. Neurodegenerative disease is currently the sixth leading cause of death in the United States. One out of every three seniors dies from AD or related dementia. It claims the lives of more individuals than breast and prostate cancer combined. Only 4 in 10 Americans would immediately seek medical attention if they were suffering from early memory or cognitive loss. If early AD detection might lead to earlier treatment, 4 in 5 Americans would want to know. Nearly 12 million Americans provide unpaid care for people with AD or other dementia [18] . Implementing preventive measures is the sole reliable approach to mitigating the consequences of a public health catastrophe of such magnitude [19] . Dementia significantly impacts an individual’s daily life and routines. Dementia frequently correlates with behavioral changes, personality issues, and many clinical complications. Dementia is identified by a decline in cognitive function and a reduced ability to carry out everyday activities. The behavioral and psychological symptoms associated with Dementia include neuropsychiatric issues such as delusions, hallucinations, apathy, anxiety, depression, and disinhibition. There is no single known cause for these symptoms. Instead, the biopsychosocial model suggests they arise from the interplay between a person’s biological makeup, life history, and current environment. These symptoms are also linked to imbalances in several neurotransmitter systems, including cholinergic, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic, and glutamatergic pathways [20] . Hip fractures are just one example; urinary incontinence is also a significant factor in the need for long-term care [21] . Considerable advancements have been achieved in comprehending the multifaceted origin of Dementia, thereby facilitating the exploration of diverse therapeutic interventions for this debilitating condition [22] . Despite the challenging nature of degenerative Dementia in terms of curability, early detection, and intervention can effectively alleviate symptoms and decelerate the condition’s advancement. Moreover, research suggests that approximately 23% of dementia cases can be reversed if detected in the early stages. The majority of the early symptoms of Dementia are a loss of ability to communicate or think critically [23] . At the time of writing, identifying AD was a complex and time-consuming task that required a brain imaging report and human expertise. Needless to say, this old way of diagnosing Alzheimer’s is costly and often wrong. This paper investigates an alternative, quicker, less costly, and more trustworthy technique. In order to diagnose AD, it is necessary to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s medical history, behavioral evaluation, cognitive testing, brain imaging, and blood collection. The comprehensive examination of the patient’s medical background and assessing their behavioral patterns are crucial components of the evidentiary basis for a clinical diagnosis. Nevertheless, acquiring medical histories and conducting behavioral examinations necessitate multiple consultations with expert doctors over a prolonged duration. It is essential to propose a robust diagnostic methodology. Advanced medical imaging technologies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) [24] have enhanced capabilities to provide compelling diagnostic information for AD. Researchers have made significant advancements in medical imaging by developing a range of practical algorithms that effectively diagnose AD across different data types [25] . PET and lumbar puncture have been employed as methods for acquiring cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples in order to quantify the biomarkers tau and amyloid beta ( A β ) [26] . The aforementioned pathological pillars have emerged as valuable markers in assessing diagnostic criteria for AD, contributing to a better understanding of the illness’s biological definition. These biomarkers can now be measured in vivo [27,28] . Due to the considerable expenses associated with PET imaging and the invasive procedure involved in acquiring CSF through lumbar puncture, these approaches are deemed unsuitable for extensive utilization in research or primary care settings, which are the main areas for conducting dementia diagnostics. According to current predictions, the utilization of blood biomarkers is expected to yield substantial advancements in the timely detection of individuals with early-onset dementia and cognitive symptoms [29] . The utilization of plasma biomarkers can facilitate the understanding of illness mechanisms, hence enhancing the development of more effective symptom management strategies and ultimately improving the overall quality of patient care. Recent studies have indicated a correlation between blood levels and the deposition of A β [30,31] , astrogliosis [32] , and neurodegeneration [33,34] . One of AD’s most noteworthy blood biomarkers is Tau phosphorylated at threonine181. Multiple investigations conducted on separate cohorts have demonstrated the elevated specificity of the test for AD, strong correlations with Tau PET and A β , and remarkable accuracy in predicting the progress of AD dementia [35] . Using machine learning (ML) to analyze blood samples makes it easier to diagnose dementia and find early warning signs years before significant symptoms show up. Our approach in this paper is based on creating a model for processing blood samples that can predict the risk of developing dementia. Training a classification algorithm on the levels of tau and A β protein in a blood sample can help differentiate between a healthy individual and one with a cognitive disorder (such as mild cognitive impairment (MCI) [36] or dementia). Using a dataset available on Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) [37] , we build a model to detect AD early based on blood sample parameters [38] . Because the AI model can look at a lot of data and still classify it correctly, this technology could improve the overall accuracy of screening for dementia. Dementia-related blood samples were used for model training and validation. The data set shows people of varying ages separated into two groups: those in good health and those with the disease. The dataset includes data from subjects of varying ages, genders, and degrees of illness. Federated learning (FL) [39] is a decentralized ML approach wherein numerous devices, including edge devices, collaborate to collectively train a common model while ensuring that their raw data remains undisclosed to a central server. FL demonstrates a high level of compatibility with early-stage AD due to its ability to effectively preserve patient information privacy, resulting in superior outcomes compared to alternative classes. The FL can utilize data at a local level to construct a model. Distributed FL aims to train ML models without exchanging raw data across several local systems. In FL, data remains decentralized on individual devices or nodes, such as smartphones, IoT devices, or edge servers. Instead of transferring private data to a central server, each device trains a local copy of a model using its data and then shares only the model updates (e.g., gradients or weights) with a central aggregator. This central server aggregates the updates, typically using techniques like Federated Averaging, into a global model and redistributes it back to the devices for further training. By avoiding the centralization of sensitive raw data, FL inherently enhances privacy and security. Additional privacy-preserving mechanisms, such as differential privacy and secure multiparty computation, can be incorporated to further protect against potential leakage from model updates. This decentralized training paradigm is well-suited for applications involving sensitive or regulated data, such as healthcare, finance, and personalized services. A 622-sample dataset from the ADNI, which comprises persons who have AD symptoms or are healthy, has to be expanded, and the context highlights the necessity for data regeneration to do this. The goal is to build a more varied dataset for ML models. Oversampling [40] , augmentation [41] , and generative adversarial networks (GANs) [42] are three key techniques for producing new tabular data. Since the dataset is not skewed, oversampling is inappropriate here. The work focuses on using augmentation and GAN-based regeneration techniques, which increase diversity in the data while maintaining its fundamental properties and patterns. A bigger and more varied dataset is required to implement the FL model, in addition to the methods for data regeneration that have already been mentioned. It is critical to obtain enough data from several local systems or segments to prove the robustness and generalizability of the model and demonstrate the FL model’s efficacy. In situations where data privacy and decentralization are primary considerations, data regeneration becomes crucial for enhancing individual models’ performance and establishing FL’s viability and advantages. Effective hyperparameter tuning in FL is essential as it directly affects the main benefits of this strategy, including data privacy protection and the ability to facilitate collaborative training. Achieving the right balance between overfitting and underfitting, well-tuned hyperparameters ensure that models can adapt to the various data distributions found throughout local systems. The performance and generalization ability of the FL model may be jeopardized by models that fail to capture crucial insights from separate datasets due to inaccurate hyperparameter choices. Therefore, careful hyperparameter adjustment is essential to fully utilizing FL in distributed and heterogeneous data contexts. The contribution of the paper can be summarized as follows: • Data regeneration for the ADNI dataset is done using the GAN technique. • A novel distributed FL-based method is introduced for early diagnosis of AD. • Hyperparameter tuning is done for each client, and then aggregation is done to discover the best hyperparameter for the whole model. • The results are evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. The remaining sections of our paper are organized as follows: In Section 2 , we briefly review other existing schemes. In Section 3 , we explain our proposed scheme. Next, we delve into the details of our proposed scheme’s performance evaluation, followed by a detailed discussion in Section 4 . This paper then concludes, and future work is explained in Section 5 . 2: 2 Related work Several studies have applied ML and deep learning (DL) models to predict dementia at early stages. Islam et al. [43] demonstrated high accuracy (98%) using SVM and KNN. Similarly, Kabir et al. [44] developed an ML-based approach in Bangladesh with 96% accuracy, offering significant potential for early diagnosis in low-resource settings. Singh and Upadhyay [45] identified essential imaging and clinical features using statistical inference for dementia classification, achieving an accuracy of 89.30%. Jayashree et al. [46] achieved 98.75% using Random Forest, highlighting the robustness of personalized ML models. Zheng et al. [47] leveraged facial mesh features with CNN and LSTM, reaching 76% accuracy. Balamurali et al. [48] and Kshirsagar et al. [49] applied DL for stage-wise prediction. Sen et al. [50] combined intrinsic time-scale decomposition with CNNs for EEG-based detection, outperforming baseline methods. Gonzalez [51] used general type-2 fuzzy reasoning to model modifiable risk factors, enabling robust interpretation of patient data. Ibrahim et al. [52] explored one-class classification to handle imbalanced data. HifsaN et al. [53] incorporated eye movement analysis into a classification based on ML, suggesting novel noninvasive diagnostic possibilities. Additionally, the authors of [54] presented a novel system designed to predict dementia by tracking the physical activity of older individuals. The principal component analysis (PCA) algorithm is employed to extract the primary features from data obtained by infrared sensors. A deep neural network is utilized to classify the extracted features and make predictions on the probability of dementia. The methodology above was employed in a study involving 18 individuals who exhibited diverse daily living circumstances. The proposed methodology demonstrates a prediction accuracy of 63.38%. A novel strategy for detecting dementia using MRI was proposed in the study conducted in [55] . The integration of MRI images with deep convolutional GAN is utilized in diagnosing and categorizing different types of dementia. The accuracy of the proposed approach is 74%. Arifoglu et al. [56] employed convolutional neural networks (CNN) to ascertain if individuals with dementia exhibit behavior that has consequential outcomes. Synthetic data is created to depict the behavioral difficulties experienced by individuals affected by dementia. The CNN is employed to generate labeled activity sequence patterns. Furthermore, it acquires the ability to identify atypical behavior resulting from dementia by observing deviations from regular patterns. In [57] , the authors propose a sandpiper-based recurrent neural system method for early detection of AD using electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. This method is used to categorize the severity of AD into low, medium, and high classes. The effectiveness score of the methods is calculated using key metrics such as accuracy, precision, specificity, recall, and misclassification score. The method is implemented on MATLAB, and the results show that the classification accuracy is 99.8% and the sensitivity is 99.9%. In [58] , the authors propose a recurrent neural network-based long-short-term memory (LSTM) network to improve AD detection using MRI evaluation. The LSTM method is tested using an MRI dataset and works efficiently on sequential patterns captured in MRI scans, and the result shows the method achieves an accuracy of 98.62%. Other recent studies presented an FL framework for AD diagnosis based on multimodal data such as MRI, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, and neuropsychological testing. The research analyzed multimodal data using a hybrid CNN–RNN architecture and found that the FL technique obtained greater classification accuracy than the centralized learning strategy [59,60] . Speech analysis plays a crucial role in identifying cognitive decline. Tao et al. [61] presented the PROCESS challenge using spontaneous speech, while Pan et al. [62] introduced a novel path signature technique using wav2vec2.0. Soleimani et al. [63] incorporated text pause encoding in LLM, significantly improving model performance. Zafar et al. [64] utilized acoustic features for multi-class classification with high validation performance. Hanai et al. [65] introduced a technique for categorizing dementia. This technique relies on the examination of spontaneous speech. To ascertain the presence of dementia, the methodology utilizes casual discourse as part of a clinical interview. The methodology was used for 136 participants aged 45 to 84 to incorporate AD and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). The results yielded a classification accuracy of 77%. Innovative sensor technologies have been proposed for the remote monitoring of dementia. Anwar et al. [66] designed a wearable RF-based system for detecting vascular dementia. Bijlani et al. [67] proposed a self-supervised contrastive learning model using home sensors, achieving a recall of 86% Izutsu et al. [68] introduced a life-logging app for behavioral and voice monitoring in older adults. Huang and Ishibashi [69] explored haptic and olfactory games for dementia detection, providing an engaging sensory-based evaluation framework. Utsunomiya and Banno [70] used Twitter data with BERT to automatically classify four types of dementia. Routray et al. [71] proposed an LLM-powered chatbot that demonstrated high sensitivity (85%) and specificity (88%) in detecting early dementia signals through conversational analysis. Detecting AD has several limitations and challenges. Small sample sizes and a lack of participant diversity plague many studies, making it difficult for the results to be applied to larger groups. Furthermore, the reproducibility of some methods is questioned due to the lack of validation on independent datasets. Early identification of AD is also challenging due to the lack of reliable biomarkers, and the disease’s variable symptoms and frequent co-morbidity with other illnesses make it even more challenging to distinguish AD from different diseases. It is imperative to address these limitations to develop more precise and reliable approaches to the early detection of AD, which can potentially affect patient outcomes and the efficacy of therapies. Compared with the previous schemes, our innovative approach to diagnosing AD solves numerous significant shortcomings of existing techniques. Our strategy reduces the problem caused by the lack of biomarkers of specific diseases by adding appropriate biomarkers, resulting in a more accurate and reliable diagnostic tool. Additionally, we use FL, which helps us overcome the limitation of the lack of variety among research participants by enabling us to access and analyze data from multiple populations while maintaining privacy and data security. Additionally, our method’s performance is optimized through hyperparameter tweaking, increasing its accuracy and generalizability even with smaller sample sets. By offering a more inclusive, precise, and scalable solution, our method has the potential to overcome these restrictions, improve early AD detection, and perhaps change the environment of Alzheimer’s diagnosis. 3: 3 The proposed method Our proposed model’s purpose is to preserve the privacy of patients’ data by using FL techniques and simultaneously provide reliable classification results. The flow diagram of the proposed method has been depicted in Fig. 1 . The dataset is the first step in the suggested process, and it can either be the original data or a regenerated version that aims to increase diversity and size. After that, the data is preprocessed to prepare for ML tasks. An ML model is then trained using the preprocessed data. To enhance the model’s performance, its hyperparameters are adjusted. The chosen best-performing model then becomes the core of the FL. Hyperparameter tweaking is explicitly done for the FL scenario to adapt the model to several local systems. The final model is generated when FL and hyperparameter tweaking are successful. Our proposed method section is composed of several parts. First, we explained the FL technique in Section 3.1 . Second, the ADNI dataset used in our model was introduced [37] , in Section 3.2 . Third, the preprocessing step of the original and regenerated datasets is explained in Section 3.3 . Fourth, methods for data regeneration were addressed in Sections 3.4 , 3.5 , and 3.6 . Finally, our FL model with hyperparameter tuning is represented in Section 3.7 . 3.1: 3.1 Federated learning FL is a methodology that facilitates collaborative training of a model on several devices while ensuring that data remains decentralized and not shared directly between devices [39] . The data is distributed among multiple devices, and the model is trained on each device individually. Subsequently, a central server consolidates and integrates the local models into a global model. The global model is then transferred back to the individual devices for additional training. The methodology above is pursued until the model attains convergence. One of the primary advantages of FL is its ability to mitigate the need to transfer large quantities of data to a central server. This process may sometimes be time-consuming and costly, particularly in cases where the data being transferred is of a sensitive or confidential nature. In contrast, FL adopts a practice of storing data on local devices, mitigating the risk of data breaches and enhancing data privacy. Furthermore, since it divides the computing task among numerous devices that might be placed in various geographical areas, FL enables more efficient resource consumption and scalability. This makes FL ideal for cases involving many devices and low network capacity. However, there are certain obstacles to FL, such as preserving consistency across local models and handling communication and synchronization concerns between devices. FL exhibits notable distinctions compared to traditional ML regarding data ownership, privacy, scalability, and robustness. In FL, the data resides on the participants’ devices while the central server performs the training process without directly accessing the data. Moreover, it is worth noting that the system’s distributed architecture allows the central model to remain operational and continue running even when specific local devices become inaccessible. Furthermore, FL is applicable when data is distributed across multiple devices, and privacy preservation is a prominent consideration. Using FL has made it feasible to achieve real-time monitoring while ensuring the confidentiality and privacy of personal data [72] . Furthermore, FL can potentially decrease the expenses related to communication and latency arising from transferring data to a central server. FL is a subject of ongoing research to enhance its efficiency, application, and scalability. Researchers in the field of edge computing are now engaged in endeavors to train models utilizing data sourced from edge devices. This approach aims to mitigate communication expenses and preserve privacy by ensuring the data remains localized on the edge devices themselves [73] . Various research papers have explored the application of FL in the domains of security and privacy. These studies encompass topics such as differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, secure aggregation, and others [74] . Integrating FL with natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as language modeling and sentiment analysis, can enhance privacy when dealing with sensitive data, such as financial or healthcare information. Furthermore, the utilization of FL has been observed to effectively tackle scalability and privacy issues in the context of deep reinforcement learning, particularly in domains like robotics and gaming [75] . Various aspects of drug discovery, including assessing the effectiveness and safety of a novel drug, can be investigated by utilizing data from diverse origins while maintaining data confidentiality using the FL. Although FL offers the advantage of preserving privacy by allowing aggregation of ML models from remote devices, it has challenges and limitations. The distributed devices within a network can exhibit heterogeneity, manifesting in variations in storage capacity, computational capabilities, and communication functionalities. The efficiency of coordination is crucial for the optimal functioning of the central server. Statistical heterogeneity by device can pose an additional concern, as the presence of identically distributed data across multiple devices has the potential to induce misinterpretation. Furthermore, while solely providing model parameters represents a positive stride in preserving data privacy, it is essential to acknowledge that sending model updates can potentially disclose sensitive information. The pursuit of privacy improvement has led to the emergence of secure multi-party computation and differential privacy techniques. However, it should be noted that these approaches are not without drawbacks, as they have been found to exhibit deterioration in efficiency and performance in many models [74] . 3.2: 3.2 Dataset description The original dataset used in this study was acquired from the mass spectrometry dataset, a subset of the ADNI [37] data inventory. The ADNI mass spectrometry dataset was created to identify biomarkers using proteomics to diagnose AD. To identify these biomarkers, mass spectrometry [36] was used using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples and plasma samples collected from the participants, which calculated the peak intensities for proteins and peptides. The expression of proteins that behave differently for AD than healthy controls is separated for study in our dataset; 622 samples were used from data collected from 2010 to 2013. Proteome data from 52 CSF and plasma samples obtained from ADNI study participants and processed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) are included in the ADNI mass spectrometry dataset 2010. The samples were from a subset of patients who had MRIs and PET scans in 2005 and 2006. The proteome data in the ADNI 2011 mass spectrometry dataset were derived from 185 CSF and plasma samples taken from ADNI research participants using LC–MS/MS techniques. The collection includes information on the concentrations of 190 proteins in each CSF and plasma sample as well as demographic and clinical data on the participants. The proteome data from 145 CSF and plasma samples and 77 CSF and plasma samples acquired from ADNI study participants using LC–MS/MS techniques are included in the ADNI 2012 and 2013 mass spectrometry datasets, respectively. The total number of features in the dataset is 73, which includes peak intensity corresponding to a particular protein or peptide fragment. The “peak” represents an ion with a specific mass-to-charge ratio detected by the mass spectrometer. The height and area of the peak are proportional to the presence or abundance of the ion in the sample, so the peak intensity can be used to measure how much that specific protein or peptide in the CSF and plasma samples collected from ADNI participants can be used to diagnose AD is available in the model. In Fig. 2 , the distribution of the class variables according to the exam year is shown. According to [38] , plasma A β 42/A β 40 can be used to screen cognitively normal people for brain amyloidosis and is an accurate diagnostic tool for the disease, particularly when paired with age and APOE e4 status. People who have a positive plasma A β 42/A β 40 and a negative amyloid PET scan are more likely to become amyloid PET-positive. In preventative trials, plasma A β 42/A β 40 could be used to screen for those who are at risk for AD dementia and are likely to be amyloid PET-positive. The ADNI dataset is one of the most widely used and comprehensive datasets for AD research. It includes a wide range of clinical, imaging, genetic, and biomarker data collected longitudinally from participants at different stages of cognitive health. Here is a summary of the key feature categories in the ADNI dataset. 1. Clinical and Demographic Data: Age, gender, education, ethnicity, diagnosis (e.g., CN, MCI, AD), and APOE genotype. 2. Cognitive Assessments: Standardized test scores such as MMSE, ADAS-Cog, CDRSB, and RAVLT are used to evaluate memory and cognitive function. 3. Biomarkers cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) markers: A β 42, tau, p-tau; blood-based biomarkers. 4. Neuroimaging Data Structural MRI: brain region volumes (e.g., hippocampus, ventricles). PET imaging: amyloid (AV45), glucose metabolism (FDG), and tau PET. 5. Genetic Data: Genotypes, including APOE and SNP data (if available). 6. Longitudinal Information: Follow-up data over months/years with progression of diagnosis and biomarker changes. Our work focuses on biomarkers, especially blood-based biomarkers. Four out of the 73 columns from the obtained dataset were used due to their high correlation with dementia in our algorithm [76] . The four columns included the peak areas of N-14 and N-15 isotopes of α β 40 and α β 42 plasma biomarkers. The experiment used two different mass spectrometer instruments developed by Thermo Fisher Scientific: Altis and Lomus [77] . Altis is part of triple quadrupole mass spectrometers, known for their high performance in chemical analyses. Lumos is a part of the Orbitrap series of mass spectrometers, highly regarded for their high-resolution capabilities and precision. It is crucial to remember that the participant pool could not accurately reflect the general population’s diversity, even though the dataset used in this study — the ADNI mass spectrometry subset — offers high-quality proteome data from CSF and plasma samples across several years. Specific individuals and groups might be underrepresented. 3.3: 3.3 Data preprocessing The preprocessing phase is a crucial component that guarantees the completion of appropriate data cleaning, transformation, and reduction procedures [78] . Data cleaning involves identifying and removing or correcting erroneous, incomplete, or inconsistent data, enhancing overall data quality. In the context of data integration, it is imperative to have a comprehensive strategy to combine or consolidate data originating from diverse sources effectively. During the data transformation phase, it is necessary to modify the data to conform to a statistical model’s underlying assumptions, hence facilitating the training process of ML models. Various transformation techniques commonly used include standardization, scaling, normalization, etc. Data reduction and feature selection are two crucial steps in data preprocessing. These steps aim to address the challenges posed by large datasets. In the data reduction step, techniques such as sampling or dimensionality reduction are employed to reduce the size of the dataset. On the other hand, the feature selection step involves selecting relevant features while eliminating redundant ones using various methods. The procedures necessary are contingent on the nature of the dataset, the intended goal, and the expected input format for training and evaluating the model. The dataset was initially examined for the presence of duplicate or missing data. The number representation of the data column reflects whether the participant in the sample has been diagnosed with AD or not. To facilitate categorization, the target variable in this study was transformed from a numerical variable to a categorical variable with two distinct categories: positive and negative. Subsequently, an examination was conducted to assess the features’ interrelationships to determine their relevance. Furthermore, any data point deviating significantly from the expected pattern or exhibiting an unexpected value increase was thoroughly analyzed. The model performance, convergence speed, and avoidance of overfitting are improved by normalizing the data. The data scale became independent by the normalization to avoid particular features dominating by relying on a larger amplitude, so a bias is presented. This process is significant for sensitive algorithms due to the input values’ scale. Regarding outliers, the data normalization makes those values closer to the mean, reducing their influence. This paper uses the ‘MinMaxScaler’ function to normalize the selected features from the dataset and to make the range of numerical data from 0 to 1 [79] . This process is based on subtracting the minimum value of some specific features from each data point from the same column, and the result is divided by the original data’s range of the same column. The original dataset contains 73 columns of information, including procedural and biomarker data. Based on an earlier study [37] , plasma A β 40 and A β 42 showed high correspondence with amyloid PET status. Individuals with a negative amyloid PET scan at baseline and a positive A β 42/A β 40 had a 15 times higher risk of probable conversion to amyloid PET-positive than negative plasma A β 42/A β 40 [37] . Based on those discoveries, four features were chosen for ML algorithms to detect Alzheimer’s. Those features are the ratio of A β 42 and A β 40, the peak area of A β 40 with N14 and N15, and also A β 42 with N14 and N15. In data analysis and statistics, pairwise distribution and correlation analysis are crucial methods that reveal hidden patterns and relationships between variables in a dataset. These analytical methods are crucial because they offer insightful information about the relationships between variables, assist us in understanding how they affect one another, and ultimately direct data-driven decision-making. Fig. 3 shows the pairwise distribution of the chosen features, and Fig. 4 is the correlation heatmap. The patterns from both Figs. 3 and 4 clearly indicate a strong relationship between the selected elements. After finalizing the four selected features, those column data were normalized to avoid the impact of values from different parts in different scales. Also, normalizing the ML model’s convergence will be faster than non-normalized data and help avoid overfitting. 3.4: 3.4 Data regeneration In this context, data regeneration refers to producing additional data from an existing dataset to increase the overall size of the dataset. The main objective is to create a sufficiently large dataset with enough variety to train models for ML algorithms properly and also to maintain the data balancing [80] . The current dataset from ADNI, which has been used here, consists of 622 data samples where the participants either have symptoms of Alzheimer’s or are healthy. A more extensive dataset must be regenerated based on the original ADNI dataset to make the outcome of the ML model’s performance more credible and consistent. The regenerated data should follow the underlying pattern and characteristics of the original data. For example, a standard method of data regeneration of an image is to fold, flip, rotate, or adjust the brightness or other image parameters to regenerate more pictures from the original one. Since this study involves tabular data, the discussion will only be restricted to the regeneration method suitable for tabular data. For tabular data, there are three main types of regeneration methods: oversampling, augmentation, and GAN. In the oversampling process, new training samples are regenerated based on existing data; the typical scenario for oversampling is when datasets are imbalanced. So, oversampling can be used for minority classes to even out the distribution of class variables. Since the existing dataset from ADNI is not imbalanced, this method was not implemented for data regeneration. The augmentation technique involves generating new data by applying transformations to the current data; the typical use for this technique is to include more variation while preventing overfitting. In this method, noises are added to add variation, so the data is realistic but, at the same time, not identical to the original dataset. GAN [42] has two networks: the generative network and the discriminator. Those work together to produce new samples after the generator becomes proficient enough to bypass the ability of the discriminator to detect derivative data. GAN is an excellent choice when there is limited availability of original data and the training model requires additional data. In the coming subsections, the two primary data regeneration techniques, augmented data generation and GAN-based data regeneration, are implemented, and the rationale behind the choice used in this study is discussed. 3.5: 3.5 Data regeneration based on augmentation In ML, data augmentation is a common technique for increasing training data where the original data is limited in numbers and procuring additional original data is difficult. The process involves modifying or transforming the existing data to create additional data. The objective is to achieve a more generalized model and risk a lesser chance of overfitting. Different implementation types are available for augmentation-based data regeneration, such as autoencoder-based, feature scaling, random feature selection, synthetic data generation, and data perturbation. The autoencoder [81] is a neural network that compresses the input data and reconstructs the original data in the decoding phase. The autoencoder is trained on the initial training data in the context of data augmentation and regeneration, and the encoded representations of the input data are then used to produce new, augmented data. This is achieved by decoding encoded representations back into the original data space after randomly using complex perturbing of the representations. The training set can then be expanded regarding data type and volume by including improved data. In feature scaling and engineering, the input features are modified, such as scaling the numeric features using the original data. In random feature selection, a random subset of the original data is chosen to reduce the dimensionality of the data. Compared to both, the autoencoder technique can generate new data by randomly perturbing the encoded presentation of original data (input) and works over the whole input data (no subset). Synthetic-based data augmentation techniques are less effective when the data distribution is complex, and data perturbation involves introducing random noise to the original data. Still, in encoder-based augmentation, the perturbation is not limited to only random noise and can be complex. Also, perturbation occurs over encoded representations of the original data. After regenerated data using the augmented technique, the pairwise distribution is shown in Fig. 5 , and the correlation matrix is depicted in Fig. 6 . The process for implementing the autoencoder-based data augmentation to regenerate data, which was followed in this study, is as follows: Step 1: The input data is passed through an encoder to obtain mean and log variance vectors to sample a latent vector. Step 2: The latent vector is then passed through a decoder to get reconstructed data to calculate loss compared with the original input. Step 3: Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence loss [82] is calculated from mean and log variance vectors, and the sum of reconstruction loss with KL divergence makes the total loss. Step 4: The autoencoder is optimized by minimizing the total loss using Adam with a learning rate of 0.01. 3.6: 3.6 GAN based data regeneration In this process, the GAN, a DL-based architecture, has regenerated data based on the original input data. The generator network is trained using an original dataset, and the discriminator network is trained to discriminate between the input and the generated output from the generator. Once the discriminator network fails to identify the generated input from the generator as fake, the output becomes realistic. Figs. 7 , 8 , and 9 depict the generator loss vs. the batch size, epochs, and generator learning rate, respectively. The GAN, which was implemented for this study, followed the subsequent steps: Step 1: This step defines the generator model of the GAN, which takes random noise as input and generates non-original or fake data. The generator network consists of four dense layers, batch normalization, ReLU, and the sigmoid activation function to keep the output within the [0,1] range. Step 2: The discriminator network has been defined to distinguish between original data and generated data from the generator network. It consists of three dense layers with ReLU activation and a sigmoid activation function to generate a probability value as output. Step 3: This step defines the loss function of the GAN based on the binary cross-entropy loss to minimize the difference between the generator network and the original data. Step 4: Next, the training loop takes the actual data, generator, discriminator, and optimizer as input. The training loop computes the gradient, applies those to the optimizers, and updates the weights of the generator and discriminator networks. Step 5: Finally, a grid search was executed to find the best hyperparameters for the training model, including batch size, learning rate, and number of epochs. A popular loss function in GANs is binary cross-entropy (BCE), which accurately quantifies the discrepancy between actual binary labels and projected probability. In this instance, it directs the Generator to provide more realistic outputs while assisting the Discriminator in differentiating between generated and actual data. The Generator attempts to deceive the Discriminator by minimizing this loss, while the Discriminator learns to assign a high probability to genuine data and a low one to produced data. Because BCE loss is straightforward, stable, and has been shown to function well in common GAN frameworks, we decided to use it. During training, it offers comprehensible, transparent feedback, enabling both networks to advance effectively. BCE is a good fit for our application because it does not require additional tweaking or architecture adjustments, unlike more complicated solutions. In early training stages, when generated data is far from realistic, it also manages uneven training distributions well. All things considered, BCE loss provides a good trade-off between performance and simplicity of use, which makes it a reasonable and appropriate option for our GAN model. In Fig. 10 , the generator losses and discriminator losses were graphed based on different hyperparameter combinations. After getting the regenerated data using the optimized hyperparameters for the GAN network, the pairwise data distribution was found, as shown in Fig. 11 . Also, the correlation matrix using the newly regenerated data using GAN [83] is depicted in Fig. 12 . Comparing the pairwise data distribution and the correlation matrices from the augmented data regeneration technique and GAN-based regeneration techniques, it is evident that the GAN-based technique performed better, and the statistical behavior fits closer to the original data. Based on the implemented outcome, the data regenerated by the GAN-based technique was chosen for the study. 3.7: 3.7 Model description The proposed FL model is described in Algorithm 1, which comprises a server and several clients. The objective of the method is to train a global model by combining individual updates from the clients [83] . The FL model is partitioned into the server and client components. The procedure starts with the server initializing the global model W 0 . During each training iteration, the server randomly chooses a subset of clients, represented as S r , to engage in the training procedure. Concurrently, every client c within the set S r does a local update operation, indicated as LocalUpdate( c , W r ), utilizing the existing global model W t . The local update is executed iteratively for a specified number of local epochs, denoted as E p . During each local epoch, the client processes its local data in batches of a specific size, referred to as B . After processing each batch of data, the client performs model updates on its local model, utilizing the learning rate α and the gradient ∇ ( w , b ) computed from the respective batch. After the local epochs are completed, the client returns its revised model w to the server. On the server side, the algorithm aggregates the models obtained from the clients by calculating a weighted average, determined by the number of samples N c each client possesses. The number of clients utilized in each round is defined by the variable m r , which is calculated as the maximum value between M ⋅ | C | and 1, where M represents a constant. The produced aggregated model is subsequently employed as the global model for the subsequent round of training. The algorithm iteratively performs this procedure for numerous iterations, progressively enhancing the overall model by integrating localized updates from various clients. The objective is to utilize the variety of data from clients while upholding privacy and reducing communication expenses. In this study, a thorough hyperparameter tweaking method was carried out to improve various ML classifiers’ performance. For example, when optimizing logistic regression (LR), a thorough investigation of the hyperparameters was conducted, including regularization strength (C) in the range of [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0], penalty types [“l1”, “l2”, “elasticnet”, and “none”, as well as solver methods [“newton-cg”, “lbfgs”, “liblinear”, “sag”, and “saga”]. Similar to this, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) underwent adjustment by altering the number of neighbors (n-neighbors) between [3, 5, 7, 9], experimenting with weighting schemes (weights) like “distance” and “uniform”, and taking into account various distance metrics (such as “euclidean” and “manhattan”). Support vector machines (SVM) were included in the process, and evaluations were performed using kernel types (’linear’, ‘poly’, and ‘rbf’), C values [0.1, 1, 10], and gamma values [0.01, 0.1, 1]. Researchers improved decision trees (DTs), random forests (RFs), and gradient boosting (GB) by repeatedly modifying hyperparameters while accounting for variables like tree depth (max-depth), minimum samples for splitting (min-samples-split), and minimum samples per leaf (min-samples-leaf). The most efficient hyperparameter configurations were found using grid searches and cross-validation, which improved the performance of the classifiers and provided important insights into how they behaved in the study context. This methodical approach ensured that the classifiers were optimized to the fullest extent possible, leading to better results for the tasks under examination. Using the ADNI dataset, Algorithm 2 acts as a systematic method for improving the performance of an ML model. It begins by dividing the dataset into two sections: a 30% segment for performance evaluation and a 70% segment for training the model. Defining a “configuration space” encompassing a range of hyperparameters, which are significant factors influencing the model’s behavior, is crucial. The method employs the hyperparameter optimization (HPO) [84] technique to adjust specific hyperparameters, namely α and E p , in an attempt to optimize a performance measure. This optimization procedure iterates across several time steps, investigating various hyperparameter combinations each time. The hyperparameters for different models are listed in Table 1 . 4: 4 Performance analysis 4.1: 4.1 Evaluation metrics There are seven ML algorithms used in the paper, starting from SVM, NB, GB, DT, LR, RF, and KNN [85–92] . To assess the performance of various ML models, we allocated 70% of each class’s dataset to the training set and 30% to the test set in our trials. The training set is used to optimize and train the ML models, whereas the test set assesses the generated models. All of the lengthy trials were analyzed using a variety of metrics to determine the efficacy of ML approaches. The confusion matrix and the accuracy, recall, precision, specificity, and F1 score metrics are presented below. Every assessment metric Eq. (1) – (5) was computed using the work published in [59,83] . The data is partitioned into four quadrants, with each quadrant corresponding to a projection for true positives ( T P ), true negatives ( T N ), false positives ( F P ), and false negatives ( F N ). The proportion of properly categorized cases is called accuracy, which is given by Eq. (1) . (1) A c c u r a c y = ( T P + T N ) / ( T P + F P + F N + T N ) The use of a confusion matrix proves to be a valuable instrument in evaluating the efficacy of a model, as it facilitates a comparison between the algorithm’s predictions on a designated test data set and the verifiable ground truth labels. When evaluating model performance, sensitivity is often compared to specificity. The fraction of real negatives detected adequately by the model is measured as specificity. A high specificity indicates that the model correctly identifies most negative findings, while a low specificity indicates that the model incorrectly labels many negative results as positive. Specificity may be determined mathematically through Eq. (2) . (2) S p e c i f i c i t y = ( T N + F P ) / ( T N + F P ) Precision is defined as the percentage of projected positive cases that were really positive, as given by Eq. (3) . (3) P r e c i s i o n = ( T P ) / ( T P + F P ) The percentage of accurately classified positive cases is called recall, which is given by Eq. (4) . (4) R e c a l l = ( T P ) / ( T P + F N ) The harmonic mean of accuracy and recall is the F1 score, which is calculated by Eq. (5) . (5) F 1 s c o r e = 2 ∗ ( ( P r e c i s i o n ∗ R e c a l l ) / ( P r e c i s i o n + R e c a l l ) ) 4.2: 4.2 Choosing FL model LR is a strong option for FL when comparing the performance data of several ML models, such as SVM, NB, GB, DT, RF, and KNN, as shown in Fig. 13 . Although LR is frequently used for regression tasks, its effectiveness in binary classification tasks, as shown in this dataset, is noteworthy. In FL, where global model accuracy is critical, LR earns the greatest accuracy-test score of 87.3016% among all the models. It also has a high accuracy-train score of 83.89%, demonstrating its capacity to make accurate predictions. A balanced performance between sensitivity and specificity is also seen by LR, which has a sensitivity score of 94.1176% and a specificity score of 79.3103%. This balance is crucial in FL, especially in sensitive data or unbalanced classes. The FL process is more reliable because the model can handle positive and negative cases well. Additionally, LR is well-suited for environments where model decisions must be clear and accessible to participants because of its simplicity and interpretability. The transparency of the model, which has distinct coefficients for each input feature, promotes cooperation and confidence among stakeholders. Additionally, FL setups benefit from LR’s computational effectiveness and implementation simplicity, which makes adoption by participating parties easier. Furthermore, LR’s capacity to accommodate non-linear patterns through tools like polynomial features or interaction terms expands the range of data sources it can handle, a crucial aspect in FL contexts. The other models are not as suitable as linear regression for the best place in FL. This is mainly because LR outperformed them with an accuracy-test score of 87.3016%. Furthermore, several of these models — like KNN and DT — display computationally costly behavior, which makes them less effective in FL setups. Additionally, there are worries regarding DT and RF overfitting, particularly in settings with little data and noisy surroundings. Additionally, GB’s lack of interpretability can hinder transparency and trust among FL participants, which is a crucial component of collaborative model training. 4.3: 4.3 Experimental results Three separate models (Model 1, Model 2, and Model 3) were created with separate data where no data were being shared either with each other or with a central location. Using the coefficients from the three models, the central model was created. All the performances from the combined model and those three models were evaluated using standard metrics. Several significant insights are revealed while analyzing the performance of the four models using original data, as shown in Fig. 14 , which comprises a “Model combined” produced through FL and three separate local models. First, “Model combined” is the best performer in accuracy, obtaining an accuracy of 85.11%. This shows that FL, a collaborative method of incorporating information from several separate models, considerably improves overall forecast accuracy. With an accuracy percentage of 84.04%, “Model 3” is the second-best performer among the individual models. The accuracy of “Model 1” and “Model 2” are only slightly better, at 82.98% and 77.66%, respectively. This suggests that significant improvements in prediction accuracy can result from the synergistic benefits of model cooperation. Second, focusing on recall, we find that “Model combined” and “Model 3” demonstrate high recall scores of 75.56% and 71.11%, respectively. Recall assesses the models’ ability to identify positive cases correctly. This demonstrates their skill in precisely identifying affirmative situations. At 71.11% and 80.00%, respectively, “Model 1” and “Model 2” had somewhat lower recall ratings. This shows that the collaborative method improves the models’ capacity to find pertinent positive occurrences and overall accuracy. Thirdly, we observe that “Model combined” and “Model 1” both display high specificity scores of 93.88%, indicating their efficacy in correctly identifying negative situations. Specificity is a metric that gauges the models’ capacity to identify negative occurrences correctly. With a specificity score of 75.51%, “Model 2” falls short in this area, indicating a comparatively larger probability of false positives. With a score of 95.92%, “Model 3” excels in specificity, demonstrating an extraordinary ability to categorize negative situations. Considering the F1 score, which balances precision and recall, we see that the “Model combined” earns an exceptional F1 score of 84.94%, demonstrating its capacity to do so. “Model 3” also performs well, scoring 83.74% on the F1 scale. F1 scores for “Model 1” and “Model 2” are 82.70% and 77.67%, respectively. The “Model combined” emerges as the top performer regarding accuracy and F1 score while retaining competitive recall and specificity values. Using the regenerated data sample from GAN, logistic regression, which was found to work best with the original dataset, was chosen for the FL algorithm. In Fig. 15 , the confusion matrices from all the models were given, and in Fig. 16 , the accuracy, recall, specificity, and F1 score were compared. With an excellent accuracy rating of 89.85%, “Model combined” emerges as the leader in terms of reliability. This demonstrates how FL, a cooperative strategy that combines information from several isolated models, effectively increases overall predicting accuracy. The second-best performance among the individual models, “Model 3” follows closely with an accuracy of 88.00%. We now turn our attention to recall, where we find that “Model combined” and “Model 3” both have impressive recall scores of 87.80% and 87.31%, respectively. Recall measures how well the models can recognize positive situations and assesses how well they can identify positive cases. Even though “Model 1” and “Model 2” had somewhat lower recall rates, 85.20% and 87.31%, respectively, this highlights the collaborative approach’s potential to strengthen the models’ capability to recognize pertinent positive events and increase overall accuracy. Furthermore, it is clear from the specificity analysis that “Model combined” and “Model 1” both receive remarkable specificity ratings of 91.30%, demonstrating their accuracy in recognizing unfavorable scenarios. The models’ performance is highlighted by specificity, which measures how well they can identify unfavorable events. With a specificity score of 88.33%, “Model 2” falls short in this area and suggests a somewhat larger risk of false positives. Looking at the F1 score, which strikes a compromise between precision and recall, we see that the “Model combined” performs admirably, receiving an exceptional F1 score of 89.85%, confirming its robustness. Additionally, “Model 3” puts in a solid performance, earning an F1 rating of 87.31%. For “Model 1” and “Model 2”, the corresponding F1 scores are 85.20% and 88.27%. Overall, the “Model combined” comes out on top, scoring highly in F1 score and accuracy while still having a respectable recall and specificity value. 5: 5 Conclusion AD is a neurological disorder that profoundly affects persons worldwide, resulting in severe consequences. AD is difficult to cure once diagnosed and affects sufferers for the rest of their lives. The number of people affected by AD has lately risen. Early AD identification is crucial for decreasing the illness’s development. Various strategies have been proposed for diagnosing AD using medical imaging techniques, including positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). It is expected that utilizing blood biomarkers would improve the detection of patients with AD and cognitive impairments. The proposed method successfully demonstrates a privacy-preserving and performance-driven approach to medical data classification using FL, integrating data pre-processing, regeneration, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning within an FL framework. The goal was to make sure sensitive patient data remains decentralized while contributing to a robust and global model. This paper analyzes blood samples to develop a novel model for diagnosing AD using the FL technique. Our study utilized the ADNI dataset comprising numerous blood samples characterized by diverse characteristics. GAN has been utilized to regenerate data from the original dataset to enhance model generalization, enhance variety, mitigate limitations due to small or imbalanced datasets, and mitigate overfitting. Using the ADNI and regenerated datasets, the proposed model is evaluated, and the results are compared to various standard approaches. Three models are built, and the combined model is used as a distributed FL model. Hyperparameter tuning is done for each client, and then aggregation is done to discover the best hyperparameter for the whole model. The results are compared to the popular seven classifiers in ML, and our results show the supremacy of the distributed FL over the existing ones. The accuracy, recall, specificity, and F1 score achieved from the combined model using FL were 85.1%, 75.5%, 93.8%, and 84.9% for original data and 89.8%, 87.8%, 91.3%, and 89.9% for regenerated data. Our proposed method offers a practical and scalable solution for privacy-aware and accurate medical data analysis to detect dementia early, which is well suited for deployment in real-world, privacy-sensitive healthcare environments.

Title: A dynamic Bi-CSAM-Net for brain tumor segmentation Abstract: The accurate segmentation of brain tumors from MRI scans is a critical task in medical image analysis and is essential for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. Despite advancements, many existing segmentation methods focus primarily on extracting global semantic features from 3D volumetric data, often neglecting finer voxel-specific details, inter-layer connections, and subtle anatomical variations. To address these limitations, we propose a novel deep learning architecture, Bi-CSAM-Net, that integrates advanced data preprocessing techniques, attention mechanism, and the CNN model as a benchmark for segmentation tasks. The preprocessing techniques use dynamic contrast enhancement, multi-resolution data integration, and patient-specific normalization (DCA-TR) to focus on the finer voxel-specific features to enhance model performance. The attention mechanism called the BiC-AM employs a Bi-LSTM to enhance the Channel Attention Mechanism within a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) framework to capture spatial and sequential MRI data dependencies better. Our extensive evaluation of two benchmark datasets; ASNR-MICCAI-BraTs 2021 and BraTs Adult-Giloma 2023, reveals that the proposed model achieves a high segmentation Dice score for all the modalities, consistently outperforming existing methods, specifically the whole tumor (WT) and tumor core (TC) for the BraTs 2021 and 2023 datasets. The results also demonstrate significant improvements in sensitivity and specificity across various tumor sub-regions, underscoring the model’s robustness. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of our proposed modules, highlighting their effectiveness in enhancing segmentation performance. These findings underscore the potential clinical applicability of Deep Bi-CSAM-Net for accurate and reliable brain tumor segmentation.

Title: A learnable transformer decoder for blurred near-infrared blood vessel segmentation using domain adaptation with limited data Abstract: Transillumination imaging using near-infrared (NIR) light is an effective method for visualizing subcutaneous blood vessels. However, as the vessel depth increases, images become severely blurred due to strong light scattering in body tissue. Although deep learning has shown great promise in clear vessel segmentation, many models face challenges achieving accurate segmentation on blurred NIR blood vessels, due to limited training data and the non-learnability of bilinear upsampling. To address these challenges, in this study, a new decoder model named the DeMerge Transformer (DMTrans) is introduced. This model uses a new learnable upsampling approach that can adaptively enlarge useful information from the encoder pretrained in related fields, maintaining accurate results with limited data during fine-tuning. The DMTrans model includes both a DeMerging (DM) operation and a channel transformer mechanism. The DM operation also leverages channel information, which becomes more sufficient as the model layers deepen, to initialize spatial features. The transformer reconstructs the DM features to fuse global information and long-range dependencies, facilitating a dense, learnable upsampling process. The proposed method was evaluated on five blood vessel datasets (DRIVE, STARE, CHUAC, CHASE_DB1, and HRF) and an NIR transillumination image dataset (HV_NIR). The proposed method achieved an average 1.89% improvement in the Dice score across these benchmarks. The results demonstrate that the DMTrans model not only offers stronger capabilities for transferring prior knowledge but also proves to be an effective approach for datasets that are small in scale but require high precision.
