For example, observing and analyzing the patterns of subcutaneous blood vessels is necessary in cancer diagnosis and various surgical procedures [1,2] . Traditionally, X-ray contrast or fluorescent media have been used in medical facilities. However, due to potential side effects, repeated imaging within a short period is not recommended. To address this issue, imaging with near-infrared (NIR) light has become a promising solution, offering a safe and convenient method for visualizing subcutaneous blood vessels. This method is suitable for use at the patient’s bedside [3,4] and helps in visualizing brain function through transillumination imaging [5] . However, as the vessel depth increases, images can become increasingly blurred due to strong light scattering in body tissues, posing a major challenge for accurate blood vessel segmentation [6] . Recent advances have shown that deep learning-based approaches surpass traditional methods in vessel segmentation tasks, providing highly accurate results and reducing the reliance on expert analysis [7–11] . However, two primary challenges remain in applying these models to the task of blurred vessel segmentation. The first challenge stems from a lack of data. Unlike the retinas, which are composed of densely populated and intricately branched blood vessels, near-infrared (NIR) transillumination imaging often targets the hands and wrists, making it difficult to collect a large amount of blood vessel images due to the prevalence of scattering blur. This lack of available data has limited the development of a highly accurate end-to-end model for blurred vessel segmentation. To overcome this challenge, utilizing existing clear retinal vessel datasets is necessary for providing prior knowledge to the model. For example, blur simulation algorithms can preprocess clear retinal vessel datasets, such as DRIVE [12] and STARE [13] , to generate additional blurred training data. In this way, large amounts of data can be used for model pretraining, to enhance the ability to distinguish between blurred and clear information. Finally, pretrained models can be fine-tuned on NIR transillumination blurred vessel datasets. This process, which involves pretraining on a source domain and fine-tuning on a target domain, is known as domain adaptation (DA) [14,15] . While DA has proven to be effective for medical image processing with limited data [16–18] , many existing models are constructed under the assumption that training data (from the source domain) and test data (from the target domain) share the same data distribution [19] . In the case of blurred vessel segmentation, blurring represents a global loss, leading to significant differences between the source and target domains. Furthermore, models designed with an assumption of identical distributions rely on prior knowledge learned during pretraining. In reality, this knowledge is only partially effective and performing uniform amplification of all information through non-learnable upsampling can negatively impact model generalizability. For example, blurring in images can make it difficult to distinguish between dark areas and branching vessels (see Section 4.6 ). Therefore, this assumption restricts the ability of these models to be generalized to NIR blood vessel image segmentation tasks. The second challenge is the non-learnability of the upsampling process, which makes it difficult to achieve accurate vessel segmentation through DA. Upsampling is a technique that expands spatial features into dense formats. This approach, which is essential for image segmentation, involves dense pixel prediction since features processed by encoders become smaller in the spatial scale. Therefore, we need an upsampling method in the decoder to progressively restore the spatial information layer by layer, converting abstract semantic information into dense spatial information. A common upsampling method is bilinear interpolation, which calculates the values of new elements by linearly interpolating between the four nearest pixel values. While this method is efficient for clear images, it tends to indiscriminately receive all information, including both clear and blurred information. This issue becomes particularly pronounced when an encoder is pretrained on a related domain, as not all features extracted by the encoder are helpful for downstream tasks. The non-learnability of the upsampling process can be detrimental, especially if irrelevant information is not sufficiently suppressed in the decoder. This problem explains why networks, even when fully pretrained on large datasets, struggle to achieve satisfactory results with limited target domain data. Therefore, an end-to-end network solution is necessary for high-precision segmentation of blurred NIR images with limited data, particularly by incorporating a learnable upsampling method for handling blurred input images. This study focuses on the segmentation of blurred NIR images through DA and introduces a novel model named the DeMerge Transformer (DMTrans). The main aim is to redesign the upsampling path, making it learnable and more suitable for cases where the source and target domains differ significantly. Upsampling plays a critical role in image segmentation as it restores abstract semantic information to detailed pixel-level representations. During this resolution enhancement process, traditional non-learnable upsampling methods compute missing information based on surrounding pixels. This characteristic prevents the model from learning this missing information through backpropagation and simultaneously amplifies all prior knowledge. Such an approach is feasible when sufficient training data are available, as the presence of adequate information during fine-tuning can gradually eliminate noise from prior knowledge. However, this becomes problematic when only a small amount of data are available. In such cases, the simultaneous amplification of features may prevent the model from effectively filtering out noise from pretraining priors (see Appendix C.1 ). Learnable upsampling becomes particularly important under these conditions, as its adaptability allows the model to selectively amplify useful information while avoiding the amplification of noise. One key strategy in our approach is the integration of self-attention mechanisms into the upsampling process, which effectively suppresses interference from blurring and adaptively amplifies relevant information during the restoration of detailed features. As a result, this framework can achieve accurate fine-tuning without being affected by irrelevant knowledge learned during pretraining, even with limited data. To achieve this goal, we introduce a new operation named DeMerge, which serves as the reverse of the patch merging (PM) technique used in the Swin Transformer [20] . PM flattens neighboring pixels along the channel dimension to reduce resolution. In contrast, DeMerge converts the channel dimension features into broader spatial information. This process effectively doubles the height (H) and width (W) of the features, achieving the desired resolution restoration for upsampling. The challenge in this DM operation is the disruption of channel information. Since we use channel information from the same locations for spatial conversion, the channel dimension becomes disrupted and inconsistent. To overcome these problems, a transformer is utilized to reconstruct the channel information from upsampled features. Inspired by the query object method in the detection transformer (DETR) [21] , we introduce a query token generator (QTG) module to create queries for each channel in the dense output feature map. Then, by utilizing self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms, the channel relationships between the demerged features and the original features are reestablished. This approach allows for the adaptive enhancement or suppression of prior knowledge acquired during pretraining, with attention scores identifying the most useful features to improve segmentation accuracy. Specifically, the query (Q) and key (K) matrices are redesigned to capture abstract semantic information from high-level features and learn global dependency information through upper layer connections (see 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 ). Next, the attention map calculated between Q and K is then used to reconstruct demerged features to obtain the optimal output. The effectiveness of the proposed technique was validated on six different datasets, including four retinal vessel benchmark datasets, one coronary angiography dataset, and one real NIR blurred dataset. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies and validation experiments performed with variants further demonstrated that our approach achieved optimal performance when pretrained on extensive data from multiple domains and fine-tuned on smaller target datasets. The primary contributions of this study can be summarized as follows: • A transformer-based decoder (DMTrans) is introduced, which is specifically designed to improve the segmentation accuracy of limited blurred near-infrared (NIR) vessel images under DA conditions. To our knowledge, this problem has not been addressed previously. • A DeMerging (DM) operation is developed to enhance spatial information along the upsampling path. The benefits of this operation are maximized by introducing a new learnable transformer to rearrange channel relationships. This technique also introduces a learnable upsampling method that can efficiently select beneficial components from pretrained encoders. • Extensive experiments conducted with simulated blurred vessel datasets, retinal vessel benchmarks, and real NIR transillumination datasets presented an average Dice score improvement of 1.89% across these benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed technique in transferring features learned by the encoder across different domains. 2: 2 Related works 2.1: 2.1 Domain adaptation Domain adaptation (DA) has become a pivotal strategy for overcoming data limitations in medical image processing. In recent years, an increasing number of studies have investigated advanced strategies for improving domain generalization in medical image segmentation tasks. These techniques include shared convolutional structures, contrastive training schemes, generative models that synthesize intermediate or style-mixed domains, and disentangled representation learning. Each of these methods aims to better capture domain-invariant features while mitigating distributional gaps across modalities. For instance, Gu et al. [22] introduced a domain specific batch normalization segmentation network with shared convolutional kernels. This network learned from labeled source and target data to provide supervision and resolve cross-anatomy gaps. In this process, prior knowledge was learned through joint training of teacher–student networks and learnable weights were then shared with the student network to produce results. Gong et al. [23] utilized a diffusion model to generate high-quality image-mask pairs with target domain characteristics and diverse structures, which were then used to augment target domain data and enhance training outcomes. Similarly, Wen et al. [24] proposed a coupled structure-preserved diffusion model to synthesize intermediate images in multiple steps, making intermediate image distributions more accessible. Cai et al. [25] introduced a disentangled style mix-up strategy in feature space and combined pixel-wise consistency with dual-level contrastive and adversarial learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance for cardiac and brain segmentation tasks. Unlike these methods, which require reconstructing the decoder, pretraining with pseudo-labels, joint training with multiple subnetworks, or generating additional similar training images, our proposed technique facilitates domain adaptation through fine-tuning of the same network, thereby avoiding the introduction of noise and the training overhead caused by additional operations. We also focus on blurred NIR transillumination images, for which large quantities of accessible training data are unavailable. By simulating blurring in retinal blood vessel images, our approach can overcome the different distributions between simulation and reality, eliminating the need for external pseudo-label generation. In such cases, our method is capable of addressing DA tasks effectively, even when there is a considerable domain gap. 2.2: 2.2 Transformers in computer vision The integration of transformers into image processing has led to significant advancements and highly accurate model architectures. The Vision Transformer (ViT) [26] is a foundational work that applies transformers directly to image patches for classification tasks. In other encoder structures, such as the Swin Transformer [20] , shifted windows are introduced into the transformer to improve the efficiency, by limiting self-attention computations to non-overlapping local windows. Recent advances in vision transformers have focused on enhancing token interaction modeling, improving frequency-aware feature extraction, and reducing computational complexity through hybrid architectures. For example, SpectFormer [27] introduced a hybrid vision transformer architecture that combines spectral layers for capturing high-frequency information with deeper multi-head attention layers for use in modeling token interactions. Similarly, VcaNet [28] integrated a vision transformer with 3D enhanced convolutions and a CBAM-based decoder to improve brain tumor segmentation by effectively capturing both local and global features. Furthermore, G2ViT [29] employs a multi-scale edge feature attention module leverages dilated convolutions with varying dilation rates. A novel graph-structured representation was then established for graph reasoning, using high-level features extracted by CNNs. These efforts primarily focused on architectural improvements for general visual tasks, while this study further extends transformer-based decoding into the domain adaptation setting using blurred medical images and limited training data. By combining transformers with DA, our approach amplifies learned priors within the domain while suppressing noise interference through the learnable self-attention mechanism. This enables high-quality transfer learning, even in scenarios with limited data. 2.3: 2.3 Query features in image segmentation DETR [21] employs an efficient and learnable architecture that has achieved promising results by using query features to guide outputs. BPT [30] has extended the use of query features to boundary-enhanced patch-merging transformers that dynamically allocate tokens to informative regions, thereby enriching fine details. MaskFormer [31] was the first to integrate mask predictions into query features. This method directly predicts a set of binary masks, each associated with a single global class label prediction. Mask2Former [32] further improved this technique by extracting localized features through cross-attention constrained within predicted mask regions, using query features to produce the final outputs. Spike2Former [33] implemented architecture-aware modifications and normalized integer spiking neurons to enhance training stability. In addition, the model employed learnable object query features to initialize each pixel in a segmentation map, achieving significant mIoU gains. These studies have focused on the direct application of query features to masks or pixels, leveraging self-attention mechanisms in transformers to enable learnable feature processing for detection or segmentation tasks. In contrast, our method applies query features to the upsampling process. Through appropriate global initialization and generation modules, more comprehensive upsampled features can be output. 2.4: 2.4 Medical image segmentation tasks In recent years, considerable progress has been made toward the development of advanced encoder–decoder frameworks for use in medical image segmentation tasks, particularly through the integration of transformers and Mamba architectures. These state-of-the-art models [8,11,29,34–36] aim to improve global contextual representations, enhance fine vessel detail preservation, and optimize computational efficiency. Specifically, CNN- and Transformer-based techniques primarily focus on the establishment of attention mechanisms, allowing the model to adaptively adjust the importance of different feature maps during the learning process. Similarly, TransUnet [7] applied a ViT [26] structure to features extracted by a Unet. Self-attention was then utilized to reorganize model features and ultimately improve performance. FRUnet [37] expanded both horizontally and vertically through a multiresolution convolution interactive mechanism while preserving full image resolution. TPUnet [38] incorporated a detail enhancement and denoising block to improve the segmentation precision for thin vessels, replacing the simple skip connections in the original Unet. MCDAUnet [34] introduced cascade dilated spatial pyramid pooling to improve recognition capabilities for low-contrast and fine vessels. GSCADE [8] progressively refined multistage feature maps generated by hierarchical transformer encoders using an efficient graph convolution block. C2MUnet [10] introduced a dual global coordinate attention module to encode long-range dependencies and coordinate information in both the horizontal and vertical directions. RRWNet [11] utilized a base subnetwork to generate initial segmentation maps from input images and a recursive refinement subnetwork to iteratively and recursively improve the resulting maps. Additionally, Mamba-based techniques expand on this approach by introducing a state space model (SSM) that effectively captures long-range dependencies while maintaining linear computational complexity. This strategy provides new opportunities for deploying medical segmentation models in low-power devices. Specifically, UMamba [35] enhanced the representation modeling capabilities of SSMs by introducing large-window Mamba blocks used to capture long-range dependencies. This approach utilizes a hierarchical and bidirectional large-window block design, thereby improving the modeling of global contextual information. SwinUMamba [39] employed a shift window-based encoder to integrate the capabilities of pretrained vision models with a well-designed decoder. VMUnet [36] is a purely SSM-based U-shaped architecture designed to capture extensive contextual information. This framework introduced visual state space (VSS) blocks within both the encoder and decoder and employs an asymmetric encoder–decoder structure. While the methods discussed above have achieved excellent results in several medical segmentation tasks, they generally lack generalizability to small datasets and often struggle to effectively fine-tune the network when available data is limited. This is because these models are built on the assumption that training and testing data share the same distribution. However, when the training and testing data exhibit varying degrees of interference (e.g., different levels of blur, as in our task), these models tend to perform poorly and fail to leverage knowledge transferred from related domains. Unlike these methods, our approach enables the model to automatically suppress blur information learned from the domain, while amplifying only clear vessel features. By pretraining on related domains and leveraging DMTrans to enhance effective components, our technique can achieve accurate results for blurred vessel segmentation tasks, even with smaller datasets. 3: 3 Methodology Fig. 1 illustrates the overall structure of the proposed DMTrans for blurred NIR image segmentation using DA. The encoder is a Swin Transformer [20] to ensure consistency between the encoder and decoder features. To ensure simplicity and flexibility, the proposed DMTrans only affects the original upsampling modules. Similar to other decoders, convolution or transformer operations can be inserted between two successive DMTrans blocks, providing more comprehensive representations of the decoder features. However, in our model, we avoid additional operations between the blocks to emphasize the effectiveness of the proposed pure transformer decoder. Generally, the model employs a structure composed of L layers, while the encoder produces outputs given by F = [ f 1 , f 2 , … , f L ] , where each f i ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i . Here, B denotes the batch size, ( H i , W i ) represents the spatial resolution of the feature map at the i t h layer, and C i is the number of channels. The overall workflow of the proposed method can be better described by defining decoder features in the i t h layer as X i ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i , which also serves as the input to the demerge transformer. Since this method operates in an upsampling manner, the output at the i t h layer is used as input to the ( i − 1 ) t h layer. Thus, we have X i − 1 ∈ R B × ( 2 H i ) × ( 2 W i ) × C i − 1 . For the deepest layer, X L = f L , since no upsampling is required at this stage. To maintain consistency with other Unet-based methods [36,40,41] , we also set L = 5 . Section 3.1 introduces the DeMerge operation and Section 3.2 discusses the utilization of the transformer for remodeling channel information. 3.1: 3.1 DeMerging for resolution expansion Patch merging (PM) is a crucial process in transformer encoders [20] . The PM module performs a downsampling process using linear operations to avoid domain mismatch issues caused by convolution operations. In the PM module, to generate hierarchical feature maps, the features from each group of 2 × 2 neighboring patches are concatenated. Then, a linear layer is applied to reduce the number of output channels. This operation ensures the consistency of the transformer-based encoder, preventing information loss caused by convolution or pooling [42] . Similarly, we aimed to extend this operation in the decoder by reversing this process through a demerging (DM) operation. As shown in Fig. 2 , this operation transfers channel information to the spatial dimension. To prevent a rapid decrease in the number of channels, a linear layer is first applied to double the channel numbers. Then, each set of pixels is grouped into four channels. Finally, the original feature channel H i × W i × 4 C is flattened to obtain a 2 H i × 2 W i × C feature map. The DM operation transfers channel information back into the spatial dimension, ensuring that upsampled feature maps maintain similar local features and do not corrupt the final segmentation results. In this manner, channel information is transferred strictly from corresponding spatial locations (as illustrated in Fig. 2 ), thereby maintaining spatial coherence of the expanded information at its initial position. Furthermore, the included DM operation transforms inherent channel information (already present in the feature map) into spatial information, without requiring any explicit initialization of the channel. For example, in a typical ResNet50 [43] encoder with an input size of 224 × 224 × 3, feature maps evolve through stages such as 112 × 112 × 64, 56 × 56 × 128, 28 × 28 × 256, and 14 × 14 × 512. The spatial resolution then progressively decreases from 224 to 14, while the number of channels increases significantly, from 3 to 512. The DM operation leverages this trade-off by converting redundant channel capacity back into spatial features, thereby facilitating resolution expansion. Additionally, since the linear layer smoothly expands the channel dimension, the distribution of pixels does not change abruptly after the DM operation, ensuring more stable training. Furthermore, we introduce a 1 × 1 convolution layer to perform channel alignment for generalization, since the inter-layer channel numbers in many decoders no longer adhere to a simple twofold amplification pattern [20,44,45] . This process can be formulated as follows: (1) Z value i = conv 1 × 1 ( Demerge ( linear ( C i , 2 C i ) ( X i ) ) ) ∈ R B × 2 H i × 2 W i × C i − 1 where i is the layer index, X i ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i denotes decoder features at the i t h layer, and linear ( C in , C out ) ( ∗ ) refers to a linear layer operation that takes a C in -dimensional tensor as input and generates a C out -dimensional tensor as output. Demerge denotes the proposed DM operation and conv 1 × 1 is the convolution operation used to adjust channel numbers to match the feature size of the previous layer. The output Z value i represents the matrix output by a DM process in the i t h layer and is used as a value token in the attention process. Notably, the DeMerge operation transfers linearly extended channel information to the spatial dimension. Due to the invariance of relative spatial positions, this operation ensures the continuity of the spatial scale in the 2 × resolution feature maps. However, as illustrated in Fig. 2 , the channel number in Step (1) and (4) changes from 2 C to C . This means half of the input channels are entirely lost after flattening, producing incomplete channel information. Previous studies [46,47] have shown that maintaining a correct channel sequence is important for generating accurate segmentation result. Therefore, a single DeMerge operation alone is insufficient to produce comprehensive upsampled features. To overcome this limitation, we propose a transformer decoder to help rebuild the relationship between the demerged and original features. The core of this transformer is the self-attention mechanism, used to indicate which parts of the input sequence pay attention to each other. Similarly, channel information was reconstructed by adapting self-attention into channel cross-attention, by setting input features as keys and upper layer connections as queries. By establishing a channel attention mechanism across multiple layers, this transformer decoder can avoid performance degradation caused by broken channel sequences. In Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 , we introduce two learnable token generators: key tokens and query tokens. 3.1.1: 3.1.1 Key tokens from deeper layers A multilayer perceptron (MLP) [48] is integral to transformer neural networks. Transformers usually use MLPs at the final stage to refine the outputs from multi-head self-attention (MSA). An MLP consists of input, output, and hidden layers. The input layer receives the initial signal, while the output layer is responsible for task-specific output generation, such as channel alignment. The core of an MLP comprises an arbitrary number of hidden layers bridging the input and output. The size of these hidden layers is then controlled by an MLP ratio hyperparameter, which was set to 4 in this study to align with common ViT practices [26] . In other words, the intermediate MLP layer expands the number of feature channels to four times that of the original input. This choice, determined through ablation experiments (see Appendix C.2 ), achieves a good balance between computational efficiency and expressive capacity. In addition, a GELU activation function was employed to avoid common activation issues and maintain consistency with the majority of vision transformers, as is standard practice in other transformer-based models. In our model, this process is used to handle semantic features from deeper layers and align channel information with the target channel number. Therefore, features from the bottom layers pass through an MLP to unify the channel dimensions. The entire computation is defined as: (2) Z key i = MLP ( LN ( X i ) ) ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i − 1 where X i ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i represents decoder features in the i t h layer, LN ( ∗ ) denotes layer normalization [49] for stable training and faster convergence, and MLP ( ∗ ) is the multilayer perceptron used to adjust the number of channels. The output Z key i represents the matrix used as the key token for the attention process at the i t h layer. 3.1.2: 3.1.2 Query tokens from upper layers To establish global dependencies among multiscale features, we introduce the query token generator (QTG) module, which is designed to aggregate features from upper layers. As shown in Fig. 3 , first, feature scaling is unified through adaptive average pooling (AAP), which allows the self-attention mechanism to remain responsive to all tokens, rather than disproportionately focusing on those with the largest values. Since query tokens are used for calculating attention maps, filtering out small features is unsuitable. In other words, the transformer should adaptively minimize irrelevant features instead of solely responding to the most prominent feature values. A convolution operation is then used to aggregate features from all upper layers and the resulting query tokens are initialized based on these aggregated features, where each pixel corresponds to a learnable feature vector used for upsampling.
