Taking the deepest layer of DMTrans as an example, the corresponding encoder output feature map exhibits a size of ( B × 9 × 9 × 768 ) . In this case, the target size of the AAP is 9 × 9 , the output dimension for the linear layer is 768, and the input dimensions correspond to the number of channels in the feature maps of each upper encoder layer. This means all upper layer features are equal to the number of channels produced by the linear operation. After applying both linear and AAP to each f l yields f ˆ l ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i − 1 . We can then define F ˆ = [ f ˆ 1 , … , f ˆ i − 1 ] , which concatenates processed features from all upper layers along the channel dimension. Consequently, F ˆ ∈ R B × H i × W i × ( ( i − 1 ) C i − 1 ) . The conv 1 × 1 operator is then employed to adjust the concatenated feature channels back to C i − 1 , ensuring consistency for attention calculations. The output Z query i represents the matrix used as the query token for the attention process in the i t h layer. In this design, the features from the first layer remain connected to the channel information reconstruction, even in the deepest layer. This step is critical for building complete channel information. In traditional methods, complete channel information is usually obtained through convolution operations, where each kernel is responsible for extracting specific features. However, in the case of processing poor quality images, these approaches cannot fully capture the global context within the image. To address this issue, many methods have employed channel attention [47] . These methods emphasize important features and suppress unimportant ones by assigning different weights to different channels. Our method goes further by using the query feature approach to generate complete channel attention. By combining the methods discussed in Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 , the DeMerge transformer can handle features across all layers. For example, the MLP provides semantic features from the bottom layers, while the QTG module provides localization features from the upper layers. In this process, the transformer acts as a bridge between multiple layers, guiding the direction of model upsampling to minimize blur loss. Overall, this design ensures that the model can effectively use comprehensive semantic information from different scales and layers, enhancing its ability to understand and process the input data with a fine-grained approach. 3.2: 3.2 Introducing the transformer for channel remodeling Before computing attention using Q, K, and V tokens, we adopt the approach discussed in [20,51,52] by including a relative channel position bias B bias i ∈ R C i−1 × C i−1 , to account for the original channel order before generating the attention map. Transformers are insensitive to location, and the proposed DeMerge operation disrupts the previous channel order to expand the image size. Therefore, it is necessary to add a relative channel position bias in the design of DMTrans to consider the original channel order. Furthermore, prior to implementing K and Q during cross channel attention, query tokens were enhanced by integrating a self-attention module (a basic transformer block [53] ) to refine query features. After adding the self-attention and relative channel position bias, the DeMerge transformer block consists of a sequence of blocks, each containing cross-attention with a feedforward network (FFN). The FFN comprises a two-layer MLP and a Gaussian linear error unit (GELU) for introducing nonlinearity after the initial linear transformation. Layer normalization (LN) is performed before each block, and residual shortcuts are added after each block. As shown in Fig. 1 (b), our DMTrans transfers rich channel features to the spatial scale. Consequently, our transformer formula is based on the channel space. This approach allows channel attention to be used in evaluating the significance of different channel features at specific locations, thereby enhancing relevant components while suppressing the impact of blurred information. This calculation process can be represented as follows: (6) Z CA i = softmax Z key i ⊺ Z query i d k + B bias i Z value i ∈ R B × 2 H i × 2 W i × C i − 1 where softmax ( ∗ ) denotes the softmax function, d k is the scaling factor for normalization, B bias i is the relative channel position bias, and Z CA i represents the DMTrans outputs at the i t h layer. The DM operation generates the V token, resulting in a feature map twice as large as that of the K and Q tokens. Channel attention is obtained by performing matrix multiplication of the transposed K and Q tokens. The size of the channel attention map is R C i−1 × C i−1 . Consequently, the output size of the DeMerge transformer block is the same as that of the V token. Reshaping the output from a 1D sequence into 2D images yields a resolution twice that of the input features, achieving upsampling through channel information remodeling. Subsequently, as shown below, an MLP and residual shortcuts are added following the design of other transformers: (7) X i − 1 = MLP ( LN ( Z CA i ) ) + Z CA i where X i − 1 ∈ R B × 2 H i × 2 W i × C i − 1 represents the DMTrans output ready for the ( i − 1 ) t h layer. Through this process, we establish a complete workflow that transforms the i t h layer decoder feature X i ∈ R B × H i × W i × C i into the upsampled feature X i − 1 . 3.3: 3.3 Demerge transformer decoder The DMTrans model, as depicted in Fig. 1 , incorporates the DeMerging operation, MLP rectification, and QTG module to effectively process inputs. The Q token comprises all upper layers, while the K token captures deeper, abstract semantic features refined by the MLP. These tokens are subjected to dot attention to compute the channel attention weights, which are subsequently applied to the output of the DM operation to produce the final segmented output. By applying the described attention mechanism, broken channels can be reconstructed to suit the newly upsampled features. In summary, DMTrans is a learnable transformer-based decoder that enhances the segmentation of blurred vessel images using DA methods with limited data. The attention capabilities of transformers enable the model to adaptively amplify the main components in the decoder, which is particularly suitable for DA methods. Since the prior knowledge learned from another domain is only partially effective, it can be challenging for the model to eliminate the influence of ineffective components during the fine-tuning process if the target domain data are limited. However, our proposed DMTrans allows the model to establish connections from both global attention and multiscale perspectives, ensuring that the upsampling process can learn from long-range dependencies and provide more accurate outputs. Although learnable upsampling processes can also be implemented through methods such as dilated convolution [54] or deconvolution [55] , these methods differ fundamentally from DMTrans. Convolutions are based on a sliding window, which achieves upsampling by focusing on local features from the same layer feature map. In contrast, blurring is a global phenomenon that requires considering the common features across all layers for more accurate dense feature generation. The ablation experiments in Section 4.5 further prove the superiority of DMTrans compared to other learnable upsampling methods. 4: 4 Experiments 4.1: 4.1 Datasets 4.1.1: 4.1.1 Blood vessel datasets The DRIVE [12] dataset consists of 40 retinal images with segmentation annotations, each captured at a resolution of 565 × 584 pixels, with eight bits per color plane. Similarly, CHASE_DB1 [56] is a retinal vessel segmentation dataset containing 28 images with a resolution of 999 × 960 pixels. Following previous studies [41,57,58] , the first 20 images were used for training, while the remaining eight images were used for testing. STARE [13] comprises 20 retinal fundus images with a resolution of 700 × 605 pixels. CHUAC [59] contains 30 coronary angiography images with an image resolution of 189 × 189 pixels and a ground truth with 512 × 512 pixel resolution. Following [37] , the original images were enlarged to 512 × 512 pixels through image interpolation to align with the ground truth. The HRF [60] database consists of 45 high-quality visual retinal images with a resolution of 3504 × 2336. Notably, these datasets exhibit varying resolutions, which poses a challenge for the DA method. To address this issue, overlapping image patches [58] with a 16-pixel overlap and a patch size of 144 × 144 pixels were used, allowing all data to be aligned to the same size while ensuring sufficient representation of small and thin branches. During the evaluation process, overlapping image patches were averaged back to their original locations to obtain the same resolution as that of the ground truth. 4.1.2: 4.1.2 Blurring simulation This study focuses on blurred NIR vessel segmentation tasks, but all images in the blood vessel benchmarks were clear. Thus, to simulate the blurring of subcutaneous blood vessels, we convolved the clear images with the point spread function (PSF), which represents the blurring of a point caused by light scattering in body tissue. The PSF was theoretically derived, and its effectiveness and applicability were confirmed in experiments [61] . This PSF was defined as a function of the blood vessel depth below the skin surface. The clear images were considered at a depth of d = 0 mm . The blur simulation process can be formulated as follows: (8) f simulation ( x , y ; d ) = f clear ( x , y ) ∗ h PSF ( x , y ; d ) where f simulation is the simulated blurred image, f clear is the clear image, h PSF is the point spread function of the whole optical system, which is essentially the above theoretical PSF modified with an imaging system function if necessary, and d is the depth of the blood vessel in the body. In this paper, the term “depth” refers to this vessel depth from the skin surface or the retinal surface. For our simulated data, Eq. (8) was used to generate blurred images with depths ranging from 1 mm to 6 mm. Minor data augmentation, such as random rotation and horizontal and vertical flipping, was performed to simulate natural imaging conditions. The training method was based on DA, requiring the training and test domains to be separated. Thus, these datasets were manually combined, as listed in Table 1 , with randomly setting 80% and 20% of the images used for training and validation, respectively. Fig. 4 shows the intermediate images obtained after each preprocessing step of the simulation dataset. Additionally, since there are many factors contributing to vessel blur, beyond the aforementioned PSF scattering blur, we also compared the effects of Gaussian blur and motion blur on the DA method in Section 4.5.5 . This comparison further validates the stability and generalizability of the model on blurred images. 4.1.3: 4.1.3 Hand vessel NIR dataset In addition to using the simulated data mentioned above, the domain adaptation capabilities of the DMTrans model were further tested using real blurred NIR images. Specifically, we investigated whether training with simulated blurred retinal vessel data could yield better results for real blurred NIR images, compared to training without DA. We used a 16-bit charged-coupled device (CCD) camera in a dark room illuminated by a 750 nm wavelength light source and captured 30 images of the human palm and wrist areas with a resolution of 1344 × 1024 pixels. The resolution and background inhomogeneity of the images were reduced by cropping areas of 320 × 240 pixels containing blood vessels. The resulting dataset consists of 100 images with 320 × 240 pixels each. We used 80 of these images for training and the remainder for testing. To enhance the HV_NIR dataset, we applied several augmentation techniques, including Gaussian noise, elastic transformer [62] , contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) [63] , grid distortion, and random flipping. This process generated a total of 560 augmented images, 20% of which were randomly selected for validation. 4.2: 4.2 Evaluation metrics To make a comparison with other models, we included evaluation metrics that have been widely used in recent years. In the following tables, we report the metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) [64] curve (AUC), Dice similarity coefficient (Dice), sensitivity (Sen), specificity (Spe), accuracy (Acc), intersection over union (IoU) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) [65] . The calculation formula of each metric is shown in Table 2 . In the table, true positive (TP) and true negative (TN) refer to blood vessel and background pixels in the ground truth images, respectively. Moreover, false positive (FP) and false negative (FN) represent the pixels that are incorrectly classified as blood vessels and background pixels, respectively, among the remaining pixels. All metrics indicate that higher values represent superior performance. To ensure a fair comparison, we also evaluated our method against some of the latest advanced methods from three different target domains below. 1. Comparison of DA-simulated datasets (DA_DRIVE and DA_CHASE) : This experiment was designed to compare each model’s ability to adaptively suppress blurring from simulated sources. Importantly, the training and testing source data were completely independent, and the reported models were reimplemented based on the open-source codes provided in the literature. 2. Comparison with several benchmarks (FT_CHASE, FT_CHUAC, FT_HRF) : This experiment demonstrated that our method excels in determining clear details, even when it is pretrained on blurred vessel images. This experiment highlights the learnability of extracting clear vessel details from the pretrained encoder, reducing the negative impacts of blurring. Notably, the results of other models were reported directly from published works, meaning that these results were not influenced by blurry pretraining. 3. Comparison of real NIR-blurred transillumination images (HV_NIR) : This experiment demonstrated our method’s ability to effectively leverage simulated blurred image pretraining and fine-tuning on real datasets. Through these three evaluations across different scenarios, we showed that our approach can learn useful knowledge from related domains, leading to improved performance in blurred vessel segmentation tasks. 4.3: 4.3 Implementation details The DMTrans model was implemented using PyTorch and trained using an NVIDIA Titan RTX GPU. The Swin-S [20] architecture was used as the backbone to extract features in the encoder. Rectified adaptive moment estimation (RAdam) [67] was employed as the optimization algorithm with a weight decay of 1 e − 4 and an initial learning rate of 1 e − 3 . Cosine annealing [68] with five warm-up epochs was used for the learning rate scheduler. The dropout rate for the transformers was set to 0.2. The proposed model was trained for 60 epochs using the DA_DRIVE and DA_CHASE datasets and for 40 epochs using the FT_CHUAC, FT_CHASE, FT_HRF and HV_NIR datasets. Batch sizes of 128 and 4 were used for the DA and other datasets, respectively. 4.4: 4.4 Comparisons with other models 4.4.1: 4.4.1 Results from domain adaptation datasets Model capabilities were verified in domain adaptation scenarios by first comparing training results in related domains and then fine-tuning in the target domain. In cases where data were subjected to simulated blurring, superior performance is indicated by fully learning prior knowledge in related domains during pretraining with simulated blur. All these models were trained using two DA datasets: DA_DRIVE, which includes models trained on the simulated STARE and CHASE datasets and tested on the simulated DRIVE test dataset; and DA_CHASE, which consists of models trained on the simulated STARE and DRIVE datasets and tested on the simulated CHASE test dataset. Comparison methods were categorized into three major groups: CNN-based, transformer-based, and Mamba-based techniques. We selected the state-of-the-art (SOTA) studies from recent years and reimplemented comparison models using available open-source code obtained from corresponding papers, ensuring identical setup conditions for all models. Table 3 shows a comparison of our model with several advanced methods. The best results are highlighted in red and the second-best results are in blue. As shown, DMTrans consistently outperformed other methods across all simulated blood vessel depths, achieving higher Dice and IoU scores. The table demonstrates that the proposed model achieved the highest average Dice score of 73.70%. Compared to CNN-based models, DMTrans exhibited an average improvement of 2.06%. Compared to Mask2Former, a transformer-based segmentation model with a query feature, our model achieved a 2.14% higher Dice score. Our model also outperformed TransUnet, a hybrid model that combines convolution and transformer techniques for medical image segmentation, by 1.84%. Compared to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) Mamba-based VMUnet model [36] , which employs a state space block to capture extensive contextual information, our model achieved an average improvement of 1.28% in Dice scores across six simulated depths in two DA datasets. In addition to this quantitative analysis, intuitive visual results are provided in Section 4.6 . The figures in this visualization section clearly illustrate how DMTrans outperformed other algorithms across different datasets, highlighting the specific aspects in which the proposed model demonstrated superior performance. These results indicate that under simulated blur conditions, the proposed DMTrans algorithm can adaptively suppress feature blur components, enabling the model to overcome domain gaps and achieve improved performance. 4.4.2: 4.4.2 Benchmark results The generalizability of our model was evaluated using the CHASE_DB1, CHUAC, and HRF datasets. This experiment specifically aimed to demonstrate the proposed method’s capability to obtain learnable attention maps during the upsampling process, applying them to differentiate between blurred and clear information. Better results prove that the model can adaptively enhance useful information. Since few studies include all three datasets, we reported the results of each dataset separately. Importantly, we reported the performance metrics directly from their respective publications to make fair comparisons. In addition, unlike other models pretrained on ImageNet or clear retinal vessel datasets, we first pretrained our model on DA datasets and then transferred the model to a target dataset. This design introduces greater challenges for achieving high performance, as the model must contend with the added complexity of blur interference during pretraining. Despite these challenges, Table 4 shows that our transformer decoder design yielded highly competitive results. The top two results are highlighted in red and blue, and ’-’ indicates that the experimental data were not provided in the original literature. Specifically, the DMTrans model achieved the highest Spe, Acc, and MCC metrics, with scores of 98.94%, 98.03%, and 81.02% for the CHASE_DB1 dataset, respectively. DMTrans also surpassed other SOTA models applied to the CHUAC dataset, with improvements of 0.76% (Acc of 98.87%) and 2.13% (Dice of 78.25%), respectively. The model also maintained strong performance with the HRF dataset, achieving Acc, AUC, Dice, and MCC scores of 97.27%, 98.73%, 82.14%, and 80.25%, exceeding SOTA models by 0.67%, 0.16%, 1.11%, and 1.16%, respectively. Although some metrics were not optimal with the proposed model, it still provided highly competitive performance, particularly in the presence of challenging pretraining interference. This finding shows that our DMTrans model can not only produce accurate results but also learn to differentiate various elements within pretrained encoders from related domains. These improvements validate the ability of DMTrans to dynamically extract and refine clear vessel information from a pretrained encoder, utilizing an attention mechanism for learnable upsampling, thus confirming its effectiveness. 4.4.3: 4.4.3 Results from the HV_NIR dataset The performance of the proposed DMTrans model in segmenting real, blurred vessel images using the DA method was compared with that of other existing methods applied to the HV_NIR dataset under two conditions. (1) With pretraining, all models were trained and fine-tuned using the DA_DRIVE and HV_NIR datasets, respectively; (2) without pretraining, all models were trained on the HV_NIR dataset and weights were initialized from ImageNet, due to the small size of HV_NIR. Table 5 shows corresponding experimental results, indicating that DMTrans outperformed other models across most metrics after pretraining on the simulated blurred image domain. The top two results for each metric are highlighted in red and blue. Compared to the second-best model, DMTrans achieved improvements of 0.52%, 0.48%, 1.69%, 1.32%, and 1.22% in sensitivity, accuracy, MCC, AUC, and Dice score, respectively. Notably, the most significant increases were observed in MCC and AUC, reaching 85.86% and 98.63%, respectively. We also observed that only a few networks benefited substantially from pretraining. For example, FRUnet showed an average improvement of 0.18% across six reported metrics after pretraining on DA_DRIVE. Similarly, TpUnet achieved an average improvement of 0.40%. This limited benefit resulted from these models struggling to extract clear information from blurred pretraining data, resulting in minimal gains using the DA approach. These findings suggest that incorporating global information and long-range dependencies is critical for addressing blur degradation. In contrast, transformer and Mamba-based models exhibited relatively higher gains after pretraining. For instance, TransUnet, which corrects features extracted by Unet using self-attention, achieved an average improvement of 0.98% across six metrics. VMUnet, which processes image features linearly using a state space block, achieved an average improvement of 1.06%, doubling the gains of TpUnet. Our proposed DMTrans adaptively processes prior knowledge in the decoder through a learnable upsampling method and utilizes transformer technology to reconstruct channel attention. This produced average improvements of 1.93% among the six reported metrics. Additionally, transformer-based methods generally performed worse than convolution-based methods without pretraining. This indicates that the transformer structure is very sensitive to data quantities and the volume of related domain data significantly affects the training results. 4.4.4: 4.4.4 Analysis of computational complexity This experiment evaluated the computational costs and efficiency of the proposed DMTrans model, compared to recent works on blood vessel segmentation tasks. Consistency with the results reported for SwinMam [39] were ensured by resizing the input image resolution to 320 × 320 when calculating FLOPs. A fair comparison was also established by directly presenting the reported results for models with available data in their respective papers. Models without reported results were retrained using the hyperparameters specified in Section 4.3 . The FT_CHASE dataset includes results obtained by pretraining on a simulated blurred dataset and fine-tuning on clear retinal vessel images. Similarly, the HV_NIR dataset provides results achieved by pretraining on a simulated blurred dataset and fine-tuning on blurred NIR vessel images. This DA strategy is critical as it assists the model in learning prior knowledge from a large number of synthetic images, ultimately enabling high performance on a limited number of target images. Table 6 provides a comprehensive comparison of computational complexity for various models. As in previous studies involving TransUnet [7] , VMUnet [36] , and GCASCADE [8] , we report both Params and FLOPs as efficiency metrics, providing a direct comparison of computational complexity across different models. DMTrans was less efficient than the SOTA Mamba-based VMUnet [36] , as measured by the number of parameters and FLOPs. However, DMTrans achieved better results on both datasets, with an average Dice score improvement of 0.94%. Additionally, DMTrans achieved reasonable results compared to other transformer- and CNN-based models. For example, while DMTrans produced a Dice score decrease of 0.72%, compared to GCASCADE [8] applied to the FT_CHASE dataset, it required only half the FLOPs. DMTrans also outperformed TransUnet by an average Dice score margin of 0.96% with fewer parameters and FLOPs. This performance gain can be attributed to the design of the DMTrans decoder, which integrates learnable processes directly into the upsampling phase. This design avoids the need for additional convolutional layers or transformer modules for processing features after bilinear interpolation. This architectural innovation enables DMTrans to achieve a balance between computational efficiency and precision, making it a highly effective solution for vessel segmentation tasks. VMUnet [36] , one of the latest Mamba-based models, has achieved significant breakthroughs in computational efficiency. A detailed comparison with DMTrans suggested that VMUnet reduced the required number of parameters and FLOPs by 39.40% and 92.49%, respectively. Similarly, compared to other reported models, VMUnet achieved reductions of 44.27% (parameters) and 93.84% (FLOPs). This efficiency is primarily attributable to a novel architectural design that leverages several Mamba-based operations to achieve inherent linear complexity through state space models, effectively eliminating the overhead introduced by multi-head self-attention mechanisms, as in traditional Transformers. In addition, VMUnet retains the simplicity of a basic Unet architecture by omitting extra fusion or refinement steps. However, it is worth noting that VMUnet experiences a significant decrease in performance when applied to complex multi-dataset segmentation tasks (see Appendix B.2 ). As described in the appendix, a limited model capacity (resulting from a small number of parameters) makes it difficult to accommodate all learned knowledge when multiple segmentation tasks are involved, potentially leading to substantial performance degradation. As such, the integration of Mamba-based architectures with large-scale medical vision models requires further in-depth investigation [73,74] . In contrast, DMTrans introduces a carefully designed Transformer-based decoder that incorporates learnable upsampling operations, allowing the model to directly optimize spatial recovery without relying on additional convolutional or post-processing attention layers. In addition, DMTrans achieved an average Dice score improvement of 0.94% compared with VMUnet. As such, we suggest that by maintaining consistency with existing large-scale model architectures, DMTrans is more adaptable to future developments in large medical vision foundation models. These four experiments demonstrate the superiority of our model for selectively extracting blurred and clear information. By introducing learnability during the upsampling process and transformer in the DM operation, the decoder effectively utilizes information from the pretrained encoder. Although improvements in computational costs and efficiency may have been modest compared to current SOTA Mamba-based models, these experimental results confirm the learnable demerge transformer design significantly improves accuracy in domain adaptation tasks. Furthermore, as this method is founded on a transformer architecture, it is well-suited for the development and application of future large-scale medical image segmentation models. 4.5: 4.5 Ablation study 4.5.1: 4.5.1 The effect of different decoder designs using the same encoder In this experiment, the performance of the DMTrans decoder is compared with that of several widely used decoder designs, including bilinear interpolation in Unet, feature fusion convolution in Upernet [75] , and a lightweight all-MLP decoder in SegFormer [44] . Each of these decoders was slightly adjusted, specifically using a convolution with a 1 × 1 kernel size to align the channel numbers with the output sizes from the Swin-S encoder. These baseline methods and the proposed method were trained under the same conditions described in Section 4.3 . Fig. 5 presents the performance of the different decoder designs on handling blurred images. The following observations can be made: (1) Blur negatively affects all models, highlighting the need for a decoder that can accurately enhance details and reduce blur; and (2) while the feature fusion approach showed a slight improvement over bilinear interpolation, the DMTrans decoder significantly surpassed the others. The proposed method surpassed the compared methods at every simulated depth. Upon examining the average Dice scores across all simulated depths, DMTrans outperformed Upernet, Unet, and the Segformer decoder by 1.4%, 1.9%, and 3.2%, respectively, achieving an average score of 73.89%. This finding indicates that the DMTrans approach could effectively replace traditional decoders to achieve better segmentation accuracy. 4.5.2: 4.5.2 The influence of the relative channel position bias As mentioned previously, the original channel order from previous features could not be directly transferred to the DMTrans. To address this, a relative channel position bias was introduced, ensuring that this information was accurately maintained in the upsampled features. The ablation study shown in Fig. 6 examines the impact of this channel position bias across different datasets, focusing on the DA_DRIVE, DA_CHASE and HV_NIR datasets. It can be observed that introducing a relative channel position bias improved the Dice scores of DMTrans applied to DA_DRIVE, DA_CHASE, and HV_NIR by 0.97%, 0.56%, and 1.8%, respectively. This result shows that adding the channel position bias effectively improves the accuracy of the model, as indicated by better Dice scores across various DA datasets. 4.5.3: 4.5.3 The effects of various encoder backbones In this experiment, we tested the adaptability of DMTrans to different encoders. All the previous experiments were conducted using Swin-S as the encoder. Unlike other fixed encoder–decoder models, the DMTrans design allows the use of different encoders. To demonstrate the portability of DMTrans, the encoder was switched among ResNet50, SegFormerB2 [44] , PVTv2 [76] , and TransUnet [7] . All models were trained using the same framework. Notably, these selected models represent three main types of encoder designs: ResNet50, which is based on convolution operations; SegFormerB2 and PVTv2, which are based on a pure multiscale transformer design; and TransUnet, which combines convolution and transformer features. Fig. 7 provides Dice score comparisons for these decoder settings across four datasets. Subfigures (a) and (b) present the performance on the DA datasets. Since these datasets are generated by simulating different vessel depths, violin plots are used to illustrate the distribution of metrics corresponding to various simulated depths for different encoder designs. Subfigures (c) and (d) depict the performance on the FT datasets. To facilitate direct comparison with previous works, bar charts are used to display the specific metrics for different encoders. The violin and bar plots indicate that most configurations using a DMTrans decoder exhibited narrower interquartile ranges and higher Dice scores. The orange color in the figure represents Dice scores achieved using the DMTrans decoder across all simulation depths for the DA_DRIVE and DA_CHASE datasets, as well as fine-tuned results from the FT_HRF and HV_NIR datasets. The blue color represents scores acquired using the original decoder structure. As shown, the proposed method not only achieved higher mean values and narrower interquartile ranges, but also produced larger performance improvements across most metrics when applied to finetuned datasets (compared to the original method), demonstrating its consistency and reliability. It is worth noting that no performance improvements were observed for the ResNet50 architecture on the DA_DRIVE and HV_NIR datasets, likely because CNN-extracted features struggled to fully adapt to a transformer-based architecture. However, in the case of transformer-based or hybrid architectures, the DMTrans decoder effectively adapted to features from various encoders, further enhancing performance using this DA approach. These findings suggest that DMTrans helps maintain accuracy even with images that are severely blurred. In conclusion, DMTrans with different encoder backbones can improve the segmentation results compared to its original designs for different DA datasets. This highlights the potential of DMTrans to overcome data limitations in medical imaging tasks, since improvements were achieved by merely replacing the decoder without retraining the entire encoder from scratch. 4.5.4: 4.5.4 Comparisons with other learnable upsampling methods In addition to common methods for upsampling (e.g., interpolation), there are methods based on convolution, such as dilated convolution [54] and deconvolution [55] , that can also achieve learnable upsampling. Dilated convolution was first used in the DeepLab series [54] to increase the receptive field of convolutional layers. By utilizing larger dilations, the convolution can produce larger feature maps than the inputs, thereby achieving upsampling. Deconvolution, used in the segment anything model (SAM) [77] , converts sparse features into dense features by learning from convolutional kernels. We conducted ablation experiments on the HV_NIR and FT_HRF datasets by modifying the upsampling method in the baseline, with results shown in Table 7 . On the HV_NIR dataset, our method surpassed the deconvolution method by 2.32%, 1.98%, and 2.29% in the AUC, Dice, and MCC metrics, respectively. On the FT_HRF dataset, DMTrans achieved improvements of 1.42%, 1.33%, and 1.79% compared with dilated convolution. It was found that the learnable upsampling method based on DMTrans still achieved the best results. This is because convolution is a window-based learning process; thus, it can only learn from the same layer features within a certain range window. However, blurring is a global issue, with all features affected by the blur kernel. Therefore, the upsampling process requires more long-range dependencies and global information. The proposed DMTrans establishes connections between multiscale features through the QTG and MLP modules, thereby obtaining more advanced results on blurred images. Fig. 8 further indicates the differences in using different learnable upsampling methods on the blurred blood vessel segmentation task. By zooming in areas in green boxes, although both dilated convolution and deconvolution can achieve competitive segmentation results, these methods are inherently limited to capturing features within a specific window range and cannot integrate global dependencies. As a result, the features learned during upsampling are less comprehensive and accurate than those learned by DMTrans, leading to issues such as broken blood vessels and misdetections. 4.5.5: 4.5.5 The influence of various blur conditions and methods In practical NIR imaging scenarios, blur can be caused by a variety of factors. To this end, the robustness and practicality of DMTrans was evaluated in multiple blurring conditions using an ablation study. Three representative models were selected as benchmarks: AttnUnet, TransUnet, and VMUnet, representing CNN-, transformer-, and Mamba-based techniques, respectively. During pretraining, datasets were generated with distinct types of simulated blur, including: 1 mm PSF, 3 mm PSF, and 5 mm PSF convolutions, as well as 5 × 5 Gaussian blur with standard deviations of 1, 2, and 4 and random-direction motion blur with lengths of 3 and 5. Notably, each simulated blur condition corresponded to a distinct DA_DRIVE dataset containing images with that specific blur type, excluding other types of blur. The models were subsequently fine-tuned and evaluated on the HV_NIR dataset to test the robustness and adaptability of DMTrans in comparison to other models under diverse blur conditions and methods. Table 8 shows Dice scores from four models applied to the HV_NIR dataset. These results demonstrate that DMTrans achieved superior performance in most simulated blur conditions, including a Dice score of 89.72% with 3 mm PSF convolution blur, outperforming the second-best model by 1.19%. Similarly, DMTrans produced a Dice score of 82.97% under 5 × 5 Gaussian blur with a standard deviation of 4, leading all other models by 0.52%. The table also highlights the performance of different models under varying degrees of blur. For instance, VMUnet performed well under mild blur conditions but deteriorated significantly as blur intensified, with Dice scores dropping by 1.82% and 3.92% under PSF convolutions (1–3 mm) and Gaussian blur (standard deviations of 1–2), respectively. In contrast, DMTrans exhibited greater robustness, with reductions of only 0.4% and 2.65%, under the same conditions. This disparity can be attributed to the Mamba-based VSS module in VMUnet, which effectively learns prior knowledge through long-range dependencies under mild blur. However, as the blur intensifies, the patch-expanding upsampling used in VMUnet fails to suppress blurred information, allowing the blur loss to propagate to upper layers, which negatively affects the final segmentation results. These findings confirm that learnable upsampling processes in the proposed model effectively handled prior knowledge from the domain. Unlike conventional bilinear interpolation followed by convolution or transformer-based feature processing, our method integrates learnable steps directly into the upsampling phase, preventing the amplification of feature noise during magnification. These results underscore the robustness and generalizability of DMTrans across diverse blur conditions, highlighting an ability to adapt to various blur types and perform optimally even in challenging conditions. 4.5.6: 4.5.6 The influence of model variants and the DA method An experiment was conducted to further validate the effectiveness of all core components in the proposed DMTrans model. Specifically, the generation of Q, K, and V tokens is critical, as these elements are responsible for aggregating features from upper and lower layers to provide all layer connections. It is thus important to note the DMTrans model and its variants used in this section follow the settings described in Section 4.3 , wherein Swin-S was employed as the encoder to extract features, while DMTrans served as the decoder for upsampling and reconstruction of the segmentation map. Table 9 shows variations in model performance across the four datasets (DA_CHASE, FT_CHASE, FT_CHUAC, and HV_NIR) when any of the token generators was missing. Specifically, DMTrans (no QTG) indicates the QTG module has been replaced by a 1 × 1 convolution used for channel alignment. DMTrans (no MLP) implies that a single linear layer was used to adjust channel dimensions for key token generation. DMTrans (traditional) signifies that traditional transformer self-attention was directly applied to the Z value i value features in Eq. (1) without a channel remodeling step. We also tested the original DMTrans model without the DA method, denoted as DMTrans (no DA), to further validate the improvement capabilities of core components. It is important to note that when DA was not used, the FT_CHASE, FT_CHUAC, and HV_NIR datasets were directly trained and validated on their respective datasets without pretraining. These results demonstrate that an absence of any model component significantly impacted performance. For example, when the QTG module was absent, the model lost detailed local information from the upper layers, leading to performance decreases of 1.50%, 2.14%, 3.72%, and 2.66% on the DA_CHASE, FT_CHASE, FT_CHUAC, and HV_NIR datasets, respectively. Similarly, when the MLP component was removed and the model no longer aggregated information from the lower layers, average Dice scores across the four datasets decreased by 2.54%. Replacing the DMTrans block with a traditional transformer block resulted in severe performance declines of 3.88%, 3.87%, 3.35%, and 4.60% on the four datasets. This is because conventional transformers apply self-attention in the spatial dimension rather than the channel dimension. However, the demerging operation in our technique supplements missing spatial information through channel dimensions. Without this inclusion, the model struggles to repair fragmented channel information, resulting in significant performance degradation. Additionally, the impact of the DA method was evaluated in a series of ablation tests. When training directly on standard splits of each dataset, removing the DA led to performance decreases across the CHASE, CHUAC, and HV_NIR datasets. As such, it became challenging to achieve model convergence with limited data, especially with transformer-based models. These ablation study results validate the effectiveness of each major component of the proposed DMTrans model. 4.6: 4.6 Visualization In this section, the blurred vessel segmentation results of three recent models, including FRUnet, TpUnet, and TransUnet, were visualized, showing the superiority of DMTrans (see Fig. 9 ). These images are organized vertically from top to bottom, representing simulations at different depths and in various conditions (i.e., DA_DRIVE with a 2 mm depth simulation, DA_CHASE with a 5 mm depth simulation, FT_CHASE with no blur simulation, FT_CHUAC with DA, HV_NIR without DA, and HV_NIR with DA). Horizontally, from left to right, the columns display the original images, segmentation outcomes for FRUnet, TpUnet, TransUnet, and DMTrans, as well as the ground truth. Due to the presence of thin vessels in the retinal vessel datasets, some areas are magnified for a clearer view, highlighted by red and green rectangular boxes. Although all models exhibited some detection and broken vessel problems, the proposed method outperformed the others in detecting thin-vessel pixels because the learnable decoder design enhanced the extraction ability of blurred vessels. Additionally, DMTrans showed strong learning and explanatory abilities for real NIR images, as observed in the HV_NIR dataset results. The presence of dark areas near vessels can confuse the models and degrade their performance. DA is crucial for overcoming these limitations in medical image segmentation tasks. By incorporating knowledge from the DA_DRIVE dataset, all models improved in distinguishing dark areas and minimizing false-positives. However, the performance improvements of other models were limited. Our DMTrans managed to leverage knowledge from related fields, effectively applying it to the target domain. These images indicate that the DMTrans benefits from the transformer design based on the DM operation, demonstrating a strong capability for blurred vessel image segmentation with the DA method. 4.7: 4.7 Discussion However, the proposed method still has some limitations. First and foremost is the computational complexity. Compared to the linear complexity of Mamba-based models, the proposed method has a quadratic time complexity. Training and inference speeds are efficient when image resolutions are small, but as image sizes increase, time efficiency deteriorates. We utilized the overlap patch method to split each image for efficient training (see Section 4.1.1 ), but this could lead to loss of contiguous information at the cropping boundaries, leading to less desirable outcomes. Second is the issue of the number of parameters. Although DMTrans reduced the number of required operation blocks to the extent possible, the transformer operations increase the number of parameters and computational complexity compared to other learnable convolution methods. This makes the method less favorable for deployment on small devices or in scenarios requiring high frame rates. Although this study did not involve an in-depth optimization for deployment on low-power devices, we acknowledge its importance for practical clinical applications. In addition, effective deployment requires dedicated techniques such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation, which are beyond the scope of this work. We consider this technique to be a valuable guide for future research and plan to investigate lightweight adaptations of our model in a subsequent study. Finally, the experiments primarily focused on simulated blurred vessel segmentation tasks and did not include a sufficient amount of real NIR transillumination images. Expanding the dataset to include more NIR blurred data and exploring more complex task transfers could further prove the strong generalizability of our proposed method under limited datasets. 5: 5 Conclusion Traditional decoders based on convolutions work well for many tasks that do not require high migratory learning capabilities. This study is among the first to use a transformer-based decoder for domain adaptation and blurred image segmentation. These tasks demand strong interpretive skills and the ability to learn knowledge for new tasks, especially regarding the crucial step of upsampling to restore lost spatial information. Our proposed technology shows that the attention mechanism and the learnability of DMTrans are beneficial for addressing these requirements. This method outperforms traditional upsampling techniques when solving problems associated with domain adaptation in blurred vessel image segmentation. To leverage the explanatory and learning abilities of the model, we introduce the DMTrans. This method restores the channel information lost during the DM operation, allowing the transformer to apply global attention and capture long-distance relationships in the decoder upsampling process. However, as described in the discussion, the proposed method still has some limitations in terms of time complexity, number of parameters, and universality. Our future work will also revolve around these three aspects, focusing on how to achieve learnable upsampling through lightweight models or other methods with lower complexity in more general domains. The current study has paved the way for training transformer-based networks with smaller datasets, thereby enhancing the precision of related image processing tasks. B.1: B.1 Experimental results for the ISIC2018 dataset with pretraining performed on the ISIC 2017 dataset As shown in Table B.10 , DMTrans achieved a Dice score of 90.46% and an mIoU of 83.82%, outperforming most baseline models. Notably, although GSCADE [8] achieved the highest Dice score (90.75%), it produced relatively low specificity and accuracy. VMUnet [36] , a lightweight Mamba-based model, achieved the highest sensitivity (91.08%), yet its specificity, accuracy, Dice, and mIoU scores remained lower than those of DMTrans by 0.38%, 0.93%, 0.65%, and 2.03%, respectively. In contrast, DMTrans achieved the highest specificity, accuracy, and mIoU (96.79%, 95.23%, and 83.82%) among all evaluated methods, demonstrating its robust discriminative capacity and low false positive rate for skin lesions. Its competitive Dice score and mIoU suggest the model offers strong spatial segmentation consistency after domain transfers. These results also indicate that DMTrans can be generalized well to non-vascular tasks when pretrained on semantically similar datasets, thereby extending its potential beyond the context of near-infrared vessel segmentation, which further supports its suitability as a universal medical image decoder in data-limited conditions. B.2: B.2 Results for extreme data imbalances This study compared the performance of the proposed DMTrans model to several SOTA methods in limited data conditions, wherein domain adaptation techniques were employed to transfer effective knowledge. However, model performance for extreme data imbalances (e.g., sparse vascular distributions) warrants further investigation. To this end, a series of ablation studies was conducted to evaluate model performance without the use of DA methods, instead training all models using vanilla mixed-dataset conditions. Each row in Table B.11 provides the Dice score (Dice), area under the curve (AUC), intersection over union (IoU), and accuracy (Acc) metrics produced by each model when trained on the data composition listed in the second column. Notably, all hyperparameters were strictly aligned with the settings outlined in Section 4.3 . GSCADE [8] and VMUnet [36] were re-trained on the vanilla mixed dataset using their official codebases to ensure consistency and reproducibility. Furthermore, when multiple datasets were involved in training, all input images were resized to 320 × 320 to facilitate unified training. The primary objective in these configurations was to examine the effect on DMTrans when training data were extremely imbalanced and DA methods were not applied. The results in Table B.11 indicate that performance for the HV_NIR dataset significantly decreased when multiple unrelated datasets were incorporated into the training process. For instance, when datasets (1), (2), and (3) were jointly trained, the Dice scores for HV_NIR decreased by 3.89%, 7.13%, and 4.25% for GSCADE, VMUnet, and DMTrans, respectively, compared to training on dataset (1) alone. The most pronounced degradation occurred with VMUnet, likely due to its relatively small parameter count, which limited its ability to process complex multi-task training steps. As more unrelated tasks were introduced, data from different domains exhibited distinct convergence directions, making it difficult to update parameters through backpropagation due to inconsistent optimization gradients across tasks, ultimately leading to performance degradation across all datasets. In contrast, performance remained relatively stable when datasets that were more closely related (e.g., real NIR-blurred images and simulated blurred images from datasets (1) and (2)) were jointly trained. This is because both datasets pertained to vascular segmentation, differing only in capture regions, which allowed for the sharing of knowledge and the mitigation of performance loss for HV_NIR. Regardless, joint training remained far less effective than the use of DA methods. For example, when datasets (1) and (2) are directly combined for training, the GSCADE Dice score for the HV_NIR dataset improved by −0.55% compared to using only dataset (1). In contrast, as shown in Table 5 , when applying a DA method (pretraining first on dataset (2) followed by transfer learning to dataset (1)), the improvement increased to 1.53%. Similarly, VMUnet improved from 0.22% to 1.75% and DMTrans improved from 0.64% to 3.12%. These findings further demonstrate that naively combining related datasets with the target dataset under limited data conditions did not yield substantial performance gains. In contrast, DA methods, through secondary transfer learning, can effectively extract useful knowledge from a pretraining stage, thereby suppressing misleading information and significantly improving performance. The inherent characteristics of transfer learning provide an effective solution to the challenge of extreme data imbalances. For tasks with limited available data, domain adaptation allows the model to achieve more stable results in the target dataset by leveraging knowledge transferred from related domains, thereby ensuring that learning is concentrated where it is most critical. C.1: C.1 The influence of bilinear shortcuts and skip connections Recent Unet-based studies have typically adopted a conventional upsampling strategy, in which features are enlarged using bilinear interpolation and fused with encoder features from a corresponding layer using skip connections. In this experiment, we investigated whether DMTrans, as a learnable upsampling method, could be effectively combined with traditional skip connections. Inspired by ResNet [43] , we designed two different residual pathways: bilinear shortcuts, in which bilinearly upsampled features were fused with DMTrans upsampled features through residual links, and skip connections, in which encoder features from the previous layer were fused with DMTrans upsampled features. It is important to note that this ablation study did not alter the internal structure of the DMTrans block, but instead explored its compatibility with a Unet decoder design. Table C.12 shows Dice scores from DA_DRIVE and DA_CHASE, in the case of pretraining and fine-tuning with HV_NIR. As shown, the proposed method outperformed both bilinear shortcuts and skip connections by 1.23% and 1.01%, respectively, on the HV_NIR dataset. However, even when combining these techniques, performance did not surpass that of the standalone DMTrans model. Furthermore, on simulated datasets ranging from 1–6 mm, our proposed method consistently achieved the best results, demonstrating its superiority in challenging blur conditions. Fig. C.10 presents the visualization results of the ablation study when pretraining on the DA_DRIVE dataset. By zooming into areas in red boxes, it can be observed that due to the non-learnability of the bilinear interpolation method and the identity mapping of the skip connections, segmentation results that incorporate these two methods will lead to the disappearance of some small branches of blood vessels. In contrast, our DMTrans model provided powerful and adaptive upsampling features. As such, non-learnable mapping methods (e.g., bilinear interpolation and skip connections) were observed to impair network performance. C.2: C.2 The effects of different activation functions and MLP ratios in dmtrans In Section 3.1 , we described how key tokens were generated from deeper layers using MLP and how query tokens were derived from upper layers using the QTG module. In this experiment, we further explore the impact of certain hyperparameters on these processes. Specifically, the MLP ratio controlled the expansion factor for features as they were passed through intermediate layers of the MLP. For instance, if the MLP ratio is set to 4, the number of channels in the intermediate layer of the MLP will be four times that of the input. Furthermore, a GELU activation function was employed in the QTG module, instead of more common alternatives such as ReLU or LeakyReLU. In this way, we conducted an ablation study to evaluate how these hyperparameters affected model performance. Table C.13 illustrates changes in output as the MLP ratio and QTG activation function were altered. In the table, MLP ratio refers to an expansion factor for intermediate channels used in key token generation, while QTG activation denotes the type of activation function used prior to fusion in the QTG module. Three representative activation functions were included in the experiment: ReLU, LeakyReLU, and ELU [80] . The table also includes the Dice scores for DMTrans applied to the DA_DRIVE, FT_CHASE, and HV_NIR datasets. It is important to note the results reported for the DA_DRIVE dataset are average Dice scores under simulated blur conditions ranging from 1–6 mm. It can be observed that an MLP ratio of 4 yielded the best performance across all three datasets, achieving Dice scores of 73.89%, 81.95%, and 89.94%, respectively. Performance suffered when this ratio was either reduced or increased. Additionally, the GELU activation function consistently delivered optimal results on most datasets, while LeakyReLU performed similarly. In contrast, ReLU and ELU resulted in average Dice score decreases of 3.24% and 1.80% across the three datasets, respectively. Notably, the performance drop associated with ReLU can be attributed to the dying ReLU problem [81] , in which negative weights are not updated, potentially leading to inactive network sections. Finally, GELU was selected as the activation function to avoid common activation issues and maintain consistency with most vision transformers, as is often done in other transformer-based models. C.3: C.3 The influence of demerge transformer block quantities In our proposed architecture, each layer incorporates a DMTrans block to perform learnable upsampling, gradually restoring abstract semantic information at the pixel level. This ablation study aims to evaluate the impact of demerge transformer block quantities on model performance. Dice scores across all datasets are summarized in Fig. C.11 . In the figure, the horizontal axis represents the number of DMTrans blocks used, where “1” indicates that a single DMTrans block was added in the deepest layer L = 5 . The other layers retained the structure of an AttnUnet [41] by using bilinear interpolation for resolution restoration, followed by a convolution with channel attention. In addition, “2” indicates that DMTrans blocks were added to both layers L and L − 1 , while “3” and “4” represent the addition of DMTrans blocks to three and four consecutive layers, respectively. These results clearly demonstrate that adding more DMTrans blocks generally improved segmentation performance. Furthermore, in the case of severe blur (i.e., 6 mm simulated blur in the DA_DRIVE dataset), performance improvements were more significant compared to milder blur conditions (e.g., 1 mm). These findings reinforce the validity of the DMTrans block design, confirming the model can suppress blur information while emphasizing clear features in the latent space through multi-layer learnable upsampling. This ultimately improved segmentation outcomes, particularly in highly blurred scenarios.

data.text: Title: A multi-expert deep learning framework with LLM-guided arbitration for multimodal histopathology prediction Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of computational pathology; however conventional model ensembling strategies often lack adaptability and interpretability hindering the clinical adaptability. While multiple artificial intelligence (AI) expert models can provide complementary perspectives, simply aggregating their outputs is often insufficient for handling inter-model disagreement and delivering interpretable decisions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel multi-expert framework that integrates diverse vision-based predictors and a clinical feature-based model, with a large language model (LLM) acting as an intelligent arbitrator. By leveraging the contextual reasoning and explanation capabilities of LLMs, our architecture dynamically synthesizes insights from both imaging and clinical data, resolving model conflicts, and providing transparent, rational decisions. We validate our approach on two cancer histopathology datasets, namely the HMU-GC-HE-30K which is a gastric cancer dataset containing pathology images only, and the BCNB which is a breast cancer biopsy dataset that is multimodal — contains pathology imaging and clinical information. Our proposed multi-expert, LLM arbitrated framework (MELLMA) outperforms convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and transformers, which are currently the de facto and state-of-the-art classification ensemble models, with better overall results. We test different LLMs as arbitrators, namely LLaMA, GPT variants, and Mistral. Further, our proposed framework outperforms strong single-agent CNN/ViT baselines on the datasets, and ablations show that learned per-agent trust materially improves the arbitrator’s decisions without altering prompts or data. These experimental results demonstrate that LLM-guided arbitration consistently provides more robust and explainable performance than individual models, conventional ensembling with majority vote, uniform average, and meta-learners. The results obtained highlight the promise of LLM-driven arbitration for building transparent and extensible AI systems in digital pathology.
