Noteworthy improvement in reconstruction accuracy and robustness, proving AHO’s potential as a very capable optimization tool for deep learning in challenging vision applications. 1: 1 Introduction The reconstruction of 3D shapes from 2D observations represents a leading edge of modern computer vision; therefore, it has far-reaching consequences across a variety of fields. For example, in robotics, 3D models are indispensable for autonomous navigation and manipulation of objects [1] . A robot would, in the end, assume an accurate 3D shaping of its environment in the IMS for obstacle avoidance and interaction with objects: as a planning rationale, 3D reconstruction from 2D images from CT or MRI greatly enhances medical diagnosis and surgical planning, giving surgeons 3D visualization of the anatomical structure before actual surgery [2] . Similarly, in industrial activities-interfaced with 3D printing and product development-3D shapes reconstructed from 2D sketches or images minimize the time taken from idea design to finished prototype, thus maximally compressing the development pipeline [3] . Reconstruction of 3D shapes from 2D observations is, however, fraught with difficulties. A crucial issue is occlusion, where some parts of the objects are occluded from view in the 2D image, giving rise to an incomplete data set on its geometry. For instance, from a 2D picture of a chair, if some legs are blocked from direct view by an object, assumptions regarding their shape will be complicated [4] . Moreover, the reconstruction process suffers acute inability thanks to noise that is introduced into 2D observations through various means, including constraints of the sensors and distortions inflicted by the external environment on the image features. Furthermore, ambiguity in 2D-to-3D mapping proves a key difficulty-a single 2D image may give rise to several different potential 3D configurations, and additional constraints or assumptions must be made in order to select the correct solution ( Table 1 ). Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have successfully addressed these obstacles and developed the ability to imitate humans through the learning process, understanding very complex feature representations of 2D images and inferring further once they are exposed to sufficient resources about what such images might be like in the third dimension. The ability of CNNs to identify patterns and generalize across dataset observations makes these neural networks capable of avoiding situations of occlusion and noisy features. Their functioning, however, highly depends on the parameter optimization of the architecture. The traditional optimization techniques such as gradient descent find themselves often stuck at such points in complex and high-dimensional search spaces in local minima and fail to fully exploit the potential of the CNN [5] . To overcome such limitations, metaheuristic algorithms have turned out to be promising alternatives for parameter optimization because they are exceptionally good at exploring various parts of the search space. These algorithms inspired by natural processes can discover better solutions where traditional approaches give up. In this work, we introduce the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer, which is a new modified metaheuristic algorithm modeled upon the social and territorial dynamics of hippopotamuses. The functionality of the design optimizer focuses on achieving an optimal balance between exploration and exploitation in the pursuit of improved convergence besides optimizing the CNN parameters for 3D shape reconstruction. The principal aim of this study is therefore to present an AI-based framework for 3D shape reconstruction from 2D observations, focusing mainly on CNN optimization through the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer. This will improve reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency while overcoming disadvantages that traditional optimization techniques suffer from and making CNN more robust to problems such as occlusion and noise. The contributions of this work are threefold: First, we develop an AI-based framework that harnesses a CNN to achieve accurate 3D shape reconstruction from 2D observations. In turn, we develop the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer, a new metaheuristic methodology for optimizing CNN parameters. Finally, we carry out a comprehensive evaluation of the presented framework and demonstrate that it is far more accurate and efficient than existing paradigms. To clarify the problems and aspirations of research, study the transformation from two-dimensional images, with their noise and obstruction, to a fully actualized three-dimensional model as depicted in Fig. 2 . 2: 2 Related works The inclination to reconstruct 3D shapes from 2D has advanced much due to the need for accuracy and efficiency to perform multiple applications in various fields, such as medical imaging, constructing or inspecting structures, and surgical planning. Established and current AI-based techniques have formulated foundational principles but are still limited when confronted with real challenges of occlusion, noise, and real-time processing requirements, thus warranting further innovation in this field. Here, we are reviewing some of the pioneering works towards 3D reconstruction from structured light systems to AI-based techniques that determine the challenges and opportunities inherent in our motivating research. Such analysis will identify gaps in existing solutions, especially on high-fidelity reconstruction from limited or imperfect 2D data, underscoring the need for a novel approach marrying deep learning and advanced optimization techniques. Shi et al. [6] suggested a 3D (three-dimensional) microscopic system that used structured light illumination to reconstruct a 3D image was. A 3D image of the object was created by measuring the change in the spatial pattern of the structured light, which varies depending on the object’s profile. One DMD (digital micro-mirror device) was used to create the structured light by allowing the system for recording 3D data in real time while controlling the structured light pattern to change at a kHz rate. In fact, the system’s working distance, resolution, and real-time 3D imaging made it possible to use it for structural defect identification of transportation infrastructures as well as for examining cracks in roads and bridges. Garcia-Granero et al. [7] demonstrated the use of a 3D image processing and reconstruction technique for D3-lymphadenectomy and complete mesocolic excision in cases of colon cancer. Both a right colon carcinoma with possible retroperitoneal invasion and a splenic flexure neoplasm were treated with it. The tumor’s corresponding vascularization and the 10 cm proximal and distal intestine margins were defined using 3D image processing and reconstruction. The location and precise measurements of the D3-lymphadenectomy region, as well as any potential retroperitoneal fascia infiltration, were displayed in the right colon cancer. Reconstruction and 3D image processing made it possible to extract useful information from CT scans. It might be used while planning a surgical strategy in order to decrease intraoperative problems and enhance oncological outcomes. Li et al. [8] presented a technique along with a miniature endoscopic 3D sensor. The sensor probe prototype was only 6 mm thick to fit in a small, confined area. They also suggested a calibration technique for a tiny line-structured light system based on specially made planar targets to guarantee the accuracy of the sensor measurement. The line-structured light system’s 3D extension depended on the translation stage’s motion. A high-precision translation stage direction calibration method based on joint multi-calibration position noise estimation was suggested, fully accounting for the sensor prototype’s characteristics. In order to confirm that the suggested measurement technique could accomplish high-precision 3D reconstruction in a constrained space and that the 3D reconstruction error was less than 10 μ m , the accuracy experiment was finally conducted on the gauge block. Fernandes et al. [9] assessed an AI (artificial intelligence) system that transformed 2D (two-dimensional) radiographs into three-dimensional (3D) bone models in terms of measurement accuracy, dependability, and repetition. To create 3D bone model reconstructions from 2D radiographs, an AI algorithm was created. When compared to measurements made using CT scanners and hand calipers, the AI algorithm’s accuracy was deemed good, with mean absolute errors of less than 2 mm in 9 out of 12 anatomical parameters. A high degree of measurement repeatability and reliability by both independent and identical observers was indicated by all intra-observer and inter-observer correlation coefficients being more than 0.90. This specific AI system was able to convert 2D radiographs into 3D bone reconstructions that resembled CT scans with a high degree of precision, dependability, and repeatability. The findings indicated that the AI algorithm might be used in preoperative surgery planning because of its time and cost-saving capabilities as well as its lower radiation exposure without the need for 3D imaging. Minhas et al. [10] investigated the viability of the present 3D reconstruction in order to determine the location of maxillary impacted canines using 2D panoramic X-rays. A total of 123 individuals’ pre-treatment CBCT data, 74 via impacted canines and 49 without, were used to construct a dataset. They produced a dataset with matched 2D panoramic X-rays and pseudo-3D photos from each of the 74 participants. The SSIM (structure similarity index measure) was really used to assess the reconstruction and provide a criterion for evaluating its quality. The two of the buccolingual and mesiodistal directions were used to evaluate the prediction of the position of the impacted canine. With 41% accuracy, the reconstruction method predicted the impacted canine’s position in the middle, buccal, or lingual position. It predicted the mesial and distal positions with 55% accuracy. The output’s SSIM ranged from 0.63 to 0.84, with a mean of 0.71. In order to diagnose and treat maxillary impacted canines, the study was the first to use AI reconstruction output for multidisciplinary care comprising periodontists, orthodontists, and maxillofacial surgeons. The emerging pattern from the above-discussed studies is forward movement in three-dimensional reconstructions with indications of areas still in need of development, which validates the proposition of our AI-based framework enhanced by the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer. For while Shi et al. show real-time three-dimensional imaging using structured light, their method requires controlled environments and multiple views, thus making it unfeasible for adaptive processing of many noisy or occluded 2D inputs. Garcia-Granero et al. and Li et al. addressed mostly medical applications or very confined spaces, yet most of their methods rely on highly accurate hardware and calibration whose generalization is questionable across various systems. Fernandes et al. and Minhas et al. take the advancement of AI-based techniques on 2D to 3D conversion quite further, presenting promising accuracies and repeatabilities; their needs of substantial training data, plus their mediocre quality of reconstruction (SSIM of 0.71, and positional accuracy of 41–55 percent) reveal a need for further advancements in robustness and precision. It is such shortcomings along with the computational inefficiencies of most traditional optimization techniques that lead us to the approach whereby a CNN is combined with a novel hippopotamus behavior-inspired metaheuristic optimizer for greater convergence, complexity acceptance, and improvement in reconstruction accuracy using very limited and simple 2D inputs against difficult conditions. 3: 3 Proposed framework This section presents the AI-based framework for 3D shape measurement and reconstruction from 2D observations. The framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer (AHO) to optimize the CNN parameters for improved 3D reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed framework is designed to transform 2D observations into accurate 3D shape reconstructions. The input to the system is a set of 2D images, which may be noisy or partially occluded. The framework processes these inputs through a CNN architecture that learns to infer the 3D structure from the 2D observations. The CNN parameters are optimized using the AHO algorithm, which balances exploration and exploitation to achieve faster convergence and better performance compared to traditional optimization techniques. The framework operates in the following stages: 1. Input Preprocessing: The 2D images are preprocessed to normalize the pixel intensities, resize the images to a standard size, and augment the dataset with synthetic variations to enhance robustness. 2. Feature Extraction: The CNN architecture, designed as an encoder-decoder network, extracts hierarchical features from the 2D images. The encoder compresses the input into a latent representation, while the decoder reconstructs the 3D shape from this representation. 3. Parameter Optimization: The AHO algorithm is employed to optimize the CNN parameters during training. The optimizer dynamically adjusts the learning rate and other hyperparameters to ensure convergence to the global optimum while avoiding local minima. 4. 3D Reconstruction: The optimized CNN generates a 3D mesh or voxel grid representing the reconstructed shape. Post-processing techniques, such as smoothing and refinement, are applied to enhance the quality of the output. Fig. 3 shows the proposed framework. 3.1: 3.1 Image preprocessing The three cornerstones upon which this rests are pixel intensity level normalization, rescaling to the same size dimensions, and data augmentation from synthetic transformations. Normalization is the process of scaling pixel values out to a common interval that stabilizes training and enhances convergence speed; normalization is generally in the range of [0, 1] or [−1,1]. Resizing will ensure that all images are of the same space dimensions which can allow for batch processing and fixed-size input requirements by the CNN. Data augmentation will add artificial variations such as rotation, flipping, brightness adjustments, and noise injection; these are great in making generalization to unseen data better as well as improving robustness to the imperfections of real-world like occlusion and lighting variations. Normalization is a vital preprocessing step preparing the input image pixel intensities into specific predefined range, making the CNN treat most images similarly regardless of the initial lighting or sensor parameters. In this work, pixel intensities are scaled into the range of [0, 1] by dividing into maximum possible intensity (255 for 8-bits image). This way, normalization will help stabilize the training process, preventing features with high magnitudes from dominating the learning dynamics. The mathematical expression for normalization is: (1) I normalized x , y = I x , y 255 where, I ( x , y ) defines the original pixel intensity at coordinates ( x , y ) ; I normalized x , y is the normalized intensity. This is done to each channel (RGB) of the image independently. To fit into a fixed input size as required by the CNN architecture, all images are resized to the size they are standardized to, for example, 256 × 256 pixels. Resizing is done using bilinear interpolation to maintain visual content while limiting spatial distortion. This step involves the CNN’s requirement for uniform sampled input sizes that allow batch processing and help with efficient memory usage. The resizing operation can be expressed as: (2) I resized = r e s i z e I normalized , t a r g e t s i z e where, resize refers to the bilinear interpolation resizing function and targetsize is set to 256 × 256 pixels in this framework. in the following, data augmentation has been provided. This process is a technique to artificially enlarge the training dataset by applying random transformations to the input frames. This is like random rotations, horizontal and vertical flipping, brightness changes, contrast changes, and Gaussian noise injection. The broadening exposure will improve generalization on the part of the model so that it will become well-acquainted with more data during training and thus become more robust for occlusion, lighting changes, and partial views. For example, because of providing random rotation from ±30 degrees, viewpoint changes can be simulated while brightness differentials would mimic different lighting scenarios. The augmentation process is usually implemented with affine transformation and intensity changes. An illustrative demonstration of the preprocessing steps on an example chair image is illustrated in Fig. 4 . Actually, normalization is a key preprocessing stage in order to prepare input 2D images for a 3D CNN-based reconstruction framework. The main purpose of normalization is to keep input constant for the network, which is key for gradient flow and faster convergence. If normalization is not performed, intensities of pixels across images would shamble idiosyncratically affecting the training quality and network generalization capability. Resizing serves the main purpose of maintaining the input size for uniform training purposes and guarantees the image batch is the same size as the fixed network input. Data augmentation is essential in this basis as its function is to enable the CNN to grasp features that remain invariable under changing conditions of illumination, pose, or occlusion to some extent. By these training techniques, you introduce many more variations of the picture into the training set. This will increase the model robustness and lower the chances of overfitting. 3.2: 3.2 The CNN architecture In fact, this CNN is an encoder-decoder architecture, designed especially for the purpose of reconstructing 3D shapes from 2D observations. This is the sort of CNN that can really help when it comes to working with things like spatial transformation and high-level feature learning; for example, from images to 3D reconstructions. The CNN is widely used for converting images to other images and other 3D reconstructions. Because, in this way, it is possible for the network to: - Encode the 2D input photograph into a concise representation of some compact latent space that supports spatial and semantic aspects. - Decode that compact latent space back into a 3D output, such as a voxel grid or mesh, which approximates the actual 3D shape. a) Encoder: The encoder of the CNN consists of a number of convolutional layers followed by batch normalization and ReLU activations. Each convolutional layer reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps and increases the number of channels (feature depth). This compression in hierarchy allows the network to build increasingly abstract representations of the input image. Mathematically, the encoder function E maps the input 2D image x into a latent representation z : (3) z = E x ; θ E where, x ∈ R H × W × C in would be the input image in height H , width W , and input channels C in , θ E are the learnable parameters of the encoder, x ∈ R h × w × C latent is the latent feature vector whose spatial dimensions are reduced by h × w and latent feature depth which is C latent. b) Decoder The upsampling structure of the decoder is constructed by the reverse of the encoder. Skip connections between the matching pairs of layers of the encoder and the decoder are introduced to help retain spatial information and therefore the flow of the gradients during training. These skip connections help to reduce the vanishing gradient problem and build a way for the network to keep details from the earlier layer fine-grained. This loss function encourages the CNN to learn accurate reconstructions while remaining generalizable to noisy or occluded 2D inputs. 3.3: 3.3 Advanced hippopotamus optimizer The hippopotamus optimizer derives its inspiration from 3 notable behavioral actions exhibited by the animals. The animal groups consist of many females, calves of the animals, several adult males, and a principal male, who serves as the herd leader. Young hippos and calves frequently exhibit a propensity to stray from the group due to their innate curiosity. Consequently, they may become alone and vulnerable to predators. The secondary behavioral style of individuals has been defensively activated when they face predation or once other animals approach onto their area. Spotted hyenas and lions are cognizant of the occurrence and deliberately avoids direct contact with the powerful jaws of an individual as a protection against damages. The personality characteristics of the hippopotamus includes an innate reaction of escaping hunters and intentionally avoiding regions of probable danger. The optimization of the parameters of the CNN is being performed via the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer (AHO) and not like the other traditional optimization techniques, including gradient descent, which gets stuck in local minima in high-dimensional space. AHO is a metaheuristic, inspired by the social and territorial behavior of hippos, and designed to manage balance between exploration and exploitation in the search space. The AHO algorithm ensures the movement of agents or hippos in the search space and dynamically adjusts weights and biases of the CNN. Each agent’s positional update is governed by the following equations: (25) v i t + 1 = w . v i t + c 1 . r 1 . p i - x i t + c 2 . r 2 . g - x i t (26) x i t + 1 = x i t + v i t + 1 where, v i t is the velocity of agent i at iteration t , x i t defines its position (representing a set of CNN parameters), p i is the best position found by agent i , g is the global best position found by the population, w is the inertia weight, c 1 and c 2 are acceleration coefficients, and r 1 and r 1 are random numbers between 0 and 1. By integrating AHO with the CNN, the framework achieves faster convergence and better performance, especially when dealing with complex, noisy, and occluded 2D inputs. 4: 4 Methodology This study presents the experiments on the proposed AI-based framework to reconstruct a 3D shape from a 2D view in terms of experimentation methodology. The methodology includes the dataset selection and preparation, evaluation metrics, establishment of baseline models for comparative analysis, technical setup for training and optimization, and design of experimental scenarios that simulate real-world conditions such as single-view and multi-view reconstruction, as well as robustness to noise and occlusion. 4.1: 4.1 Dataset and preprocessing To perform a complete evaluation, the ShapeNet dataset which is a well-known benchmark for 3D vision research, has been used for the experiments. ShapeNet has more than 50,000 3D CAD models organized into 55 object categories, each associated with multiple aligned 2D renderings viewed from different viewpoints. A subset of ShapeNet has been chosen that consists of some of the most common categories, e.g., chairs, tables, airplanes, and cars; this yields 15,000 models. For these models, 24 different RGB images are generated through the Blender rendering engine from a variety of viewpoints. These images were made into pairs with respective sets of 3D voxel grids of size 64 × 64 × 64, which together can be used as the ground truth for reconstruction. Typically, image preprocessing is performed to standardize input dimensions and enhance robustness before the images are ready for training works. The dimensions of images were equalized to 256 × 256 and normalized on the range of [1] . Another real-world imperfection was artificially incorporated to the input during the training of the model, by adding synthetic noise (Gaussian noise with μ = 0 , σ = 0.05 ) and partial occlusions (random rectangular masks covering up to 30% of the image) during the training. More augmentations were included to increase diversity and improve generalization in the dataset, like random rotation ( ± 30 ° ), brightness variations (±20%), and horizontal flipping. 4.2: 4.2 Evaluation metrics The proposed framework’s performance was evaluated using geometric and perceptual metrics that evaluated accuracy and fidelity regarding different aspects of the reconstructed 3D shapes. The primary evaluation metrics included: - Chamfer Distance (CD): Average Euclidean distance measurement among points in predicted point clouds and ground truth point cloud is defined as follows: (27) C D ( P , Q ) = 1 | P | ∑ PCP m i n q ⊂ Q ‖ p - q ‖ 2 2 + 1 | Q | ∑ q ⊂ Q m i n PCP ‖ q - p ‖ 2 2 where, P and Q represent the point clouds of the predicted and ground truth shapes, respectively. - Intersection over Union (loU): Assesses the volumetric overlap between the ground truth and predicted voxel grids and is mathematically defined as follows: (28) I o U V p , V g = V p ∩ V g V p ∪ V g where V p and V g describe the predicted and the ground truth voxel grids, respectively. - Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD): Measures the minimum cost required to transform one point cloud into another, providing a more perceptually meaningful metric for shape similarity. - F1 Score: A harmonic mean of precision and recall, used to evaluate the quality of surface reconstruction in terms of true positive, false positive, and false negative voxels. These metrics collectively provide a multi-faceted assessment of the framework’s ability to reconstruct accurate and detailed 3D shapes from 2D observations. 5: 5 Results and discussions In this section, an exhaustive analysis of the experimental findings from the proposed AI-based framework toward 3D shape reconstruction was presented from 2D observations. The evaluation of the performance of the proposed method, which integrates a CNN with the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer (AHO), is carried out in multiple dimensions quantifying both the qualitative and quantitative aspects where it is compared to standard optimization techniques and metaheuristic ones. The results are analyzed with respect to reconstruction accuracy, convergence behavior, resistance to occlusion and noise, and computational efficiency. The discussion further elucidates the strengths and weaknesses of the method we proposed in terms of applications in real-world scenarios involving robotics, medical imaging, and industrial design. This framework is implemented in Matlab R2019, relying on custom mfile code for integrating the AHO algorithm. The training is performed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090, 64 GB RAM, and Intel i9-12900 K processor. Training of the CNN is made with a batch size of 32 and learning rate 10 - 4 for the baseline optimizers. The AHO process is configured with 50 agents for the population size, up to 200 iterations at maximum; the inertia weight w initializes at 0.9 and decreases linearly until 0.4, while the acceleration coefficients c 1 and c 2 range over values from 1.5 to 2.0, respectively, by means of empirical tuning. The AHO algorithm was incorporated into the training cycle, where each agent was treated as a candidate solution for the weights of the CNN. In every iteration, the fitness of each agent was obtained using Chamfer Distance on the validation set. The agent with the best performance established the search direction, thereafter, positions (weights) were updated for the agents based on the AHO equations. This process was continued until a stopping criterion was satisfied. 5.1: 5.1 2D input sample and 3D ground truths In Fig. 8 , a representative collection of visual examples is given that illustrates the correspondence between a 2D input images and their related 3D ground truth voxel grids. The current example is taken from a randomly generated image downloaded from the Internet, and all images are used throughout the training and assessment phases of the proposed AI-based framework for 3D shape reconstruction. The figure acts as qualitative validation, providing a visual comparison between the 2D observations given to the CNN and the actual 3D structures that the model tries to reconstruct. The leftmost image shows one single RGB 2D image generated in a synthetic view and then the right part of the row presents the corresponding 3D voxel grid displayed as a three-dimensional binary occupancy map. The 2D image is pre-processed to a uniform size of 256 × 256 pixels and normalized to the intensity range [0, 1], while the 3D voxel grids are of dimensions 64 × 64 × 64, where each voxel indicates whether the spatial location is occupied (1) or empty (0) in an object’s internal structure. It shows the fact that a single 2D image is often not sufficient to contain complete geometric information about the shape because it may be occluded or viewed from a limited perspective. Specifically, in the case of a chair, you might see only the front view, with the backrest and legs partially or fully hidden. Despite this, the complete volumetric structure of the object is captured by the ground truth 3D model and provides the supervision required by the CNN for learning shape priors and inferring missing information during practice. Likewise, Item 8 embodies the important concept of accurate 3D shape learning with respect to variability in the geometry, scale, and pose of the object. The shapes are rendered with orthographic projections from many angles, which leads to an intuitive understanding of the way in which the object will structure itself in space. This vision not only supports a qualitative assessment in the model’s performance but also serves to show in which types of data the CNN must learn to be interpretable. 5.2: 5.2 Quantitative performance evaluation To evaluate the proposed framework, common 3D reconstruction metrics are used in terms of Chamfer distance (CD), intersection over Union (IoU), earth mover’s distance (EMD), and F1-Score. These metrics are considered across the ShapeNet dataset subsets for chairs, tables, airplanes, and cars, and their results are compared with the other four baselines − CNN trained with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), CNN with Adam optimizer, CNN with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and CNN with Genetic Algorithm (GA). Average performance across the categories is presented in Fig. 9 . The performance result indicates that AHO-optimized CNNs significantly surpass all baseline models using all metrics. In fact, the proposed framework shows 24.1% improvement in the Chamfer distance, 14.1% increase in IoU metric and 22.0% reduction in EMD when placed against the second-best method (GA). Currently, the F1 score has improved by 6.1% compared to that of the GA baseline, which indicates quality of surface reconstruction with lesser false negatives in the 3D shapes predicted. The improvements that are evident in these results arise from the effectiveness of the AHO in its exploratory and exploitative capabilities within the high-dimensional parameter space of the CNN, thus overcoming the local minima and leading to more favorable global solutions. On the other hand, AHO ensures that population diversity as well as adaptive search dynamics are maintained, unlike gradient-based methods such as SGD and Adam which have more chances of getting stuck in suboptimal regions due to the very complicated loss landscape of deep networks. 5.3: 5.3 Scenario-based analysis This section presents a thorough simulation and result analysis of the proposed AI-based framework for 3D shape reconstruction from 2D observations. The proposed framework integrates a CNN with the Advanced Hippopotamus Optimizer (AHO) and evaluates it under three different experimental scenarios: Single-View Reconstruction, Multi-View Reconstruction, and Noisy and Occluded Input Reconstruction. All these simulations are carried out on the ShapeNet dataset − the benchmark dataset widely used in 3D vision research. The architecture followed for the CNN is an encoder-decoder design having skip connections, as detailed in the proposed framework section, and is trained using the AHO algorithm. The performance evaluation is done through standard metrics which include Chamfer Distance (CD), Intersection over Union (IoU), Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD), and F1 Score. For comparative analysis, the framework’s performance has been benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods: CNN with Adam optimizer [11] , CNN with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [12] , and CNN with Genetic Algorithm (GA) [13] . All simulations in MATLAB R2020b are fully reproducible using the provided code snippets, which can be shared for other research purposes. Results confirm far superior performance by the AHO-optimized CNN in terms of reconstruction accuracy, rapid convergence, as well as robustness to imperfections of the real-world environments. a) Single-view reconstruction In such a training and evaluation setup, only a single 2D input image describing an object is used. This closely approximates a real-world application case in which truly only one view might be available, such as in robotic navigation or mobile-based 3D modeling. The training set contains 8,000 images, all caught from a single view, and samples randomly selected from 1,000 images, never before seen during the training of the model. These metrics are used to validate the recovered 3D shapes: Chamfer Distance and IoU. Fig. 9 shows the qualitative comparison between the ground truth 3D models and the predictions made by the AHO-optimized CNN and the baseline methods. The model by AHO achieved a value of Chamfer Distance of 6.3 × 10 −3 and an IoU value of 0.79. This is significantly ahead of the second-best method (GA with CD = 7.8 × 10 −3 and IoU = 0.75 ). Such superior performance is attributed to the fact that AHO explores the parameter space effectively while keeping away from the local minima. b) Multi-view reconstruction In this case, the framework is evaluated for its ability to reconstruct 3D shapes using multiple 2D views of each object, to eight views in total. The CNN learns to fuse information from different viewpoints in order to yield more accurate and complete 3D reconstructions. Both training and testing splits remain the same as in the single view case, but, in addition, each object is described by multiple images. The findings exhibited a massive surge in both Chamfer Distance and IoU where the AHO-optimized CNN finds improved convergence to 4.1 × 10 −3 and 0.85, respectively. This translates into a 23.7% increase in Chamfer Distance and 7.5% increase in IoU as compared to the GA baseline. A multi-view arrangement facilitates the model to reason about occluded regions and to refine shape details based on cross-view consistency. Reconstructed 3D shapes from different viewpoints, now with better structural fidelity, can be seen in Fig. 10 ( Fig. 11 ). c) Reconstructing the input from noise and occlusion The robustness of the proposed framework is tested on 2D images using synthetic noise and partial occlusions by the CNN. Images distorted with Gaussian noise whose mean is zero and standard deviation is 0.05 were further subjected to rectangular masks that occlude up to 30% of the image. Fig. 12 illustrates the F1 score comparison for noisy and occluded inputs. Despite the above shortcomings, this AHO-optimized ANN still managed to have a highly accurate reconstruction determined by a Chamfer Distance of 5.1 × 10 −3 and an IoU of 0.83, which is 26.1% better in terms of Chamfer Distance than the GA baseline. Robustness against noise and occlusion results from the global search capability of the AHO, which helps the CNN learn strong feature representations less sensitive to input distortion. Such types of reconstructions from noisy and occluded input examples with their sectional ground truth values are compared in Fig. 12 , asserting the model’s capability of structural detail preservation. d) Performance comparison across scenarios Fig. 13 summarizes average Chamfer distance, IoU, EMD, and F1 score in the framework under the three experimental conditions for providing a holistic view of average performance of each method across all scenarios. However, the most notable fact is that the CNN optimized by AHO performs better than the rest of baseline methods in every single experiment scenario concerning all performance metrics. Not only is the lowest reconstruction error achieved, but it also remains quite generalized. Strength and robustness in yielding results from very challenging input conditions are also apparent. This clearly shows the power of collaboration between AHO and a CNN for 3D reconstructions from 2D images. Each of the three experimental scenarios brought to light a particular aspect of the capabilities offered by the framework. In single-view reconstruction, the model demonstrates the ability to recover complete 3D structures from scant information, thereby demonstrating the strong prior learning of the CNN and the ability of an AHO to optimize parameters well. With respect to multi-view reconstruction, the present framework focuses on integrating evidence from multiple viewpoints thereby leading to the formation of a better and more accurate 3D model. This is alternatively crucial for applications such as autonomous navigation and augmented reality, where multiple camera viewpoints are available. Then in noisy occlusion, the reconstruction highlights the robustness of the model, since even degraded input images yield high accuracy. Hence the framework can be deployed in environments with noisy conditions. However, there are limitations to consider. While the AHO algorithm improves convergence and accuracy, it imposes an additional burden on computation compared to gradient-based methods. Also, the present implementation assumes voxel-based reconstruction, which may not be the best method for applications that require high-resolution surface detail. The next step will be to consider mesh-based representation and real-time optimization approaches to circumnavigate these limitations. 6: 6 Conclusions This study presented a new AI-based framework to achieve a 3D shape measurement and reconstruction from 2D observations. The method was based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture which is optimized by a newly advanced version of the Hippopotamus Optimizer (AHO) algorithm. The ongoing concerns of occlusion, noise, and ambiguity in 2D-to-3D mapping were dealt with the amalgamation of deep learning with some nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization techniques that can enhance both reconstruction accuracy and efficiency simultaneously. The proposed convolutional neural networks were based on encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections, learn hierarchal features from the 2D image and map them into accurate voxel grids or depth maps in 3D. The AHO algorithm draws inspiration from the territorial and social behavior of hippos and dynamically balances the exploration and exploitation objectives within the optimization of CNN parameters, resulting in quicker convergence and effective global search when compared with traditional gradient-based and other metaheuristic optimization approaches. Experimental validation on the ShapeNet dataset for single-view, multi-view, and noisy input scenarios proved that the proposed framework provides a significant advantage over baseline methods such as CNN trained with SGD, Adam, PSO, and GA in terms of Chamfer Distance, Intersection over Union (IoU), Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD), and, F1 Score, with Chamfer Distance of 5.9 × 10 −3 and IoU of 0.81 in the most difficult single-view case. Besides increasing CNN robustness to real-world imperfections like occlusion and sensor noise, AHO enhances CNN’s capability of generalization across object categories and input scenarios. The results provided an argument for the effectiveness of using deep learning with advanced metaheuristic optimization for complex vision tasks. The proposed framework has widespread real-world applications in robotics for autonomous navigation systems, in medical imaging for better diagnostic modeling, and in industrial design for rapid prototyping. Future works will focus on extending the framework towards mesh-based 3D output for high-resolution surface reconstruction, real-time implementation on embedded systems, and applying the AHO algorithm as a finetuning optimizer for other architectures in deep learning, like transformers and graph neural networks. The enhancement of hybrid optimization techniques that combine AHO with gradient-based fine-tuning could advance convergence speed and ultimately increase model performance. This has set the stage for bio-inspired computational intelligence in AI-driven 3D vision systems by proposing one novel optimizer that relied on biological behavior and validating it through deep learning.

Title: CLAV: clustering latent vector aggregation for whole slide image retrieval leveraging foundation models Abstract: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) is crucial in cancer diagnosis, assisting pathologists by providing similar image data from previous records for analysis, especially when there is uncertainty in diagnosing a case. This process supports decision-making by providing valuable reference points to guide the diagnostic process. Foundation models have become increasingly important in the medical field due to their ability to generalize across various tasks and datasets, offering valuable support to pathologists by enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of diagnostic processes. In this article, a foundation model pre-trained on histopathology data is leveraged as a feature extractor without the need for task-specific training, in contrast to existing models that require extensive training to learn significant data representations. The proposed method, Clustering Latent Vector Aggregation (CLAV), condenses the significant feature vectors into a unique representative vector for the Whole Slide Image (WSI). Using a unique feature vector offers the advantage of reducing the size of the memory bank, thereby making the process of querying and retrieving similar WSIs more efficient. The experimental results presented in this study demonstrate that the proposed method enhances performance in CBIR tasks. This article highlights the potential of foundation models to achieve superior retrieval metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods specifically trained for CBIR. This discipline, Digital Pathology, enables expert pathologists to examine, annotate, and share cases with other specialists [1] . This digitization enables their analysis through artificial intelligence (AI) models. This process allows large volumes of histological data to be accessed and manipulated efficiently. AI can leverage this digitization to perform complex tasks such as automated pattern recognition [2] , tissue classification [3] , and prediction of clinical outcomes [4] . These capabilities not only enhance the accuracy and speed of diagnosis but also provide additional tools for medical research, enabling the discovery of correlations that may be challenging to identify using traditional methods. The literature documents numerous applications of WSIs in histopathology, including segmentation [5] , classification [6] , anomaly detection [7] , and Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) [8] , among others. These applications demonstrate the versatility and potential of computational pathology (CPath) in revolutionizing traditional pathological practices. Among these, CBIR stands out as a valuable tool for assisting pathologists by retrieving similar cases based on visual patterns, particularly when facing ambiguous or rare diagnostic scenarios. However, most CBIR systems rely on patch-level comparisons or complex indexing of large feature sets, which can be computationally expensive and inefficient. This creates a need for methods that can summarize the information of an entire WSI into a compact and representative form without sacrificing retrieval accuracy. With the evolution of AI, foundation models are now being integrated into computational pathology [9] . These models have proven effective for multiple downstream tasks, thus providing an advantage over task-specific models. For example, in [10] , a model capable of performing tasks such as image zero-shot classification, segmentation, image captioning, cross-modal retrieval in histology has been trained. Some works in the literature, such as [11] , have integrated all these advances to develop a histopathological purpose AI assistant, offering better performance than other established models in the current landscape, such as GPT4V [12] . In the context of CBIR, the use of foundation models offers the opportunity to extract rich and generalizable features without requiring additional training or fine-tuning, making them ideal for scalable and task-agnostic retrieval pipelines. In this work, we propose a clustering method to obtain the unique feature vector representation of a WSI. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first use of a clustering-based method to compress the feature vectors of WSI patches into a unique feature vector using a task-agnostic foundation model (CONtrastive learning from Captions for Histopathology, CONCH [10] ) as the feature extractor. This approach aims to improve the efficiency and scalability of CBIR systems by reducing the memory and computational requirements while maintaining retrieval performance. Additionally, leveraging a task-agnostic foundation model eliminates the need for a training stage, which is typically time-consuming and resource-intensive. Therefore, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • Development of a clustering method for generating a compressed unique feature vector representation of WSIs. • Leveraging a task-agnostic foundation model (CONCH) as a feature extractor for the automated retrieval of WSIs. • Conducting comprehensive experiments and evaluations using Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) metrics, including measures like majority vote. • Integration of robust evaluation methodologies to validate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed clustering approach and feature extraction model. 2: 2 Related work 2.1: 2.1 Histopathological CBIR Traditional methods of CBIR in histopathology rely on extracting handcrafted features such as colour, texture, and shape from patches. Examples of these methods include Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [13] and Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) [14] for detecting and describing local features in images. However, these traditional methods often face the issue of a semantic gap, which refers to the disconnect between the low-level features that these algorithms extract and the high-level concepts that expert pathologists perceive and use in their diagnoses [15] . This gap can result in suboptimal retrieval performance, as the hand-crafted features may not fully capture the morphology and complex patterns that expert pathologists recognize. In this sense, deep learning methods offer a solution to this problem by automatically learning hierarchical features from the data to increase confidence in image understanding [15] . Patch retrieval methods have made significant advances in the field of image retrieval. For instance, Tabatabaei et al. [16] proposes a Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) network architecture specifically designed for patch retrieval tasks in prostate and breast cancer studies. This approach utilizes features extracted from the CAE’s bottleneck to perform content-based image retrieval (CBIR) efficiently. Similarly, Hegde et al. [17] introduces SMILY, a method leveraging a deep-ranking network [18] for feature extraction in patch retrieval scenarios. In contrast, Whole Slide Image (WSI) retrieval methods often focus on higher-level image understanding and processing. For example, Kalra et al. [19] employs a DenseNet architecture [20] for feature extraction from image patches without task-specific training, relying instead on a pre-trained model from the ImageNet dataset [21] . The approach includes a novel technique called mosaic generation, which selects the most representative patches from a WSI to accelerate the search for similar WSIs by reducing the number of patches considered. This method utilizes K-means clustering on RGB histograms and spatial coordinates to construct the mosaic, akin to the approach used in SISH [22] . While SISH relies on a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) [23] pre-trained on the TCGA dataset to aid retrieval, such approaches can suffer from suboptimal performance due to domain shifts between natural and histopathological images. Inspired by the concept of mosaic generation, RetCCL [8] introduces a novel method that combines clustering of feature vectors and spatial coordinates for mosaic construction, using a ResNet50 model [24] trained with contrastive learning. However, these methods still rely on handling a large number of patch-level features, which can be resource-intensive. In this context, our work addresses the challenges of managing large-scale feature vectors by proposing a method to obtain a unique feature vector representation for each WSI. By reducing the memory bank to a single feature vector per WSI, we significantly decrease resource consumption and improve efficiency in the retrieval process. 2.2: 2.2 Histopathological representation learning Deep-learning based representation learning pretends to extract high-level visual features from the images through different training paradigms. Convolutional neural networks based architectures pre-trained on ImageNet [25] under a fully-supervised learning paradigm have been used in CPath [26,27] . However, this dataset mostly contains natural images which limits the ability of ImageNet pre-trained models to extract discriminative features in images with a large domain shift, such as histopathological images. To address this limitation, extensive in-domain datasets encompassing multiple anatomical sites and conditions have been gathered to pursue in-domain pre-training and improved representation learning. Due to the challenges associated with the time-consuming and expert-dependent annotation of medical images, other pre-training paradigms, such as self- and vision-language supervision, have investigated other forms of supervision beyond fully supervised learning. These foundation models aims to learn discriminative data representation in a task-agnostic approach to later adapt to multiple downstream tasks. Vision-language supervision introduced by Radford et al. [28] has marked a big step in foundation model development by multimodal pre-training using image-captions pairs. In the field of CPath, some works, such as Lu et al. [10] , Huang et al. [29] , retrieved histopathology images and their descriptions in the form of natural text to fit this novel learning paradigm. Meanwhile, self-supervised learning (SSL) does not require any kind of supervision and aims to learn data representations from the images themselves. While CTransPath [30] combined the contrastive learning objectives with transformer architectures, other works, such as Chen et al. [31] , Xu et al. [32] , have used the popular DINO v2 algorithm [33] on large-scale datasets with data scales of tens of millions of patches from WSI of multiple anatomical sites and cancer subtypes. Similarly, RetCCL [8] follows a SSL pre-training scheme carefully designed for content-based WSI retrieval. KEEP [34] , in contrast, adopts a vision-language pretraining paradigm enhanced with structured medical knowledge from disease graphs. Although not designed specifically for CBIR, its strong zero-shot generalization across diagnostic tasks suggests that knowledge-aware models could offer new directions for retrieval tasks as well. We argue that this task-specific pretraining is not required if other foundational models offer great representation learning for diverse tasks such as slide classification, segmentation and image captioning [10] , while they are yet to be explored for CBIR. Our CLAV method is a lightweight, training-free aggregation strategy specifically designed for patch-based encoders, providing an efficient solution for scenarios where training data or computational resources are limited. 3: 3 Methodology This study presents a clustering-based method for CBIR of WSIs leveraging an existing task-agnostic feature extractor model, named CONCH. The following sections delve deeper into the theoretical underpinnings of this proposal. In Fig. 1 , a schematic of the framework for memory bank construction and query retrieval is presented. Specifically, the foundation model CONCH extracts the features from the patches that comprise a WSI. Subsequently, our clustering method is applied to obtain the centroids of the clusters, which, after aggregation, form the latent vector representing the WSI. After applying this process to all WSIs in the database, the memory bank is obtained. Finally, for the WSI Query Process, samples most similar to an input WSI query are retrieved from this memory bank. 3.1: 3.1 WSI latent representation generation Our framework aims to obtain a unique feature representation for each WSI, enabling the identification of similarities at the slide level. Compressing all information into a unique feature vector significantly reduces memory usage and speeds up the subsequent query process. Formally, we denote x i ∈ X N , with X N representing the set of N patches from a WSI and x i the i -patch of the slide. In this work, we rely on CONCH image encoder to extract patch-level features, and additionally evaluate other patch encoders such as KEEP and RetCCL. We obtain z i , the feature vector corresponding to the x i patch, as follows: z i = F I e ( x i ) where F I e represents the feature extraction performed by the image encoder on patch x i . This work proposes a Clustering and Latent Vector Aggregation (CLAV) to obtain a unique feature vector for each WSI. Specifically, three clustering algorithms, k-means, pc-means, and c-means, have been investigated. These clustering algorithms derive a set of Q centroids aggregated using either Batch Global Average Pooling (BGAP) or Batch Global Max Pooling (BGMP) aggregation methods to conform the WSI latent vector. First, note a clustering method denoted by γ , applied to all z i belonging to the set Z N (let’s denote this set as Z N = { z 1 , z 2 , … , z N } ). Applying the clustering method to all Z N , we obtain Q centroids { C 1 , C 2 , … , C Q } . Next, define an aggregation method denoted by A . Applying A to the Q centroids, we obtain z W S I : z w s i = A ( C 1 , C 2 , … , C Q ) The subsequent paragraphs describe the clustering algorithms employed. K-means++ : K-means is an iterative clustering algorithm that partitions a dataset into K clusters by minimizing the variance within each cluster. It starts by randomly initializing cluster centroids and then iteratively assigns data points to the nearest centroid, updating centroids based on the mean of the assigned points until convergence [35] . K-means++ is an enhanced version of the standard K-means algorithm, specifically designed to improve the initialization of cluster centroids. Unlike the standard K-means, which randomly initializes centroids, K-means++ selects initial centroids so that they are more likely to be spread out across the data. This method randomly chooses the first centroid, and each subsequent centroid is chosen from the remaining data points with a probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing centroid. This careful seeding helps accelerate the algorithm’s convergence and improves the overall quality of the clustering results [36] . C-means (Fuzzy C-means) : C-means is a fuzzy clustering algorithm that assigns membership degrees to data points across multiple clusters based on fuzzy set theory. Unlike k-means, which assigns data points exclusively to one cluster, c-means allows data points to belong to multiple clusters simultaneously based on their membership degrees. It iteratively updates cluster centroids and membership degrees until a convergence criterion is met [37] . PC-means (Possibilistic C-means) : PC-means is a variant of C-means clustering that allows for possibilistic assignments of data points to clusters, rather than strictly probabilistic assignments. Unlike traditional C-means, which assigns membership degrees based on probabilities, PC-means assigns a degree of belongingness to each cluster centroid based on a possibilistic approach, where data points can belong to multiple clusters simultaneously with varying degrees of membership. It iteratively updates cluster centroids and membership degrees until a convergence criterion is met. The formulation of PC-means provides flexibility in handling uncertainties and noise in data clustering tasks, making it suitable for applications where strict probabilistic assignments may not be appropriate [38] . 3.2: 3.2 WSI query process We computed the cosine similarity between the query image and all remaining samples in the memory bank after the leave-one-out strategy. Cosine similarity is formally defined as the cosine of the angle between two vectors in a multidimensional space, providing a measure of similarity that ranges from -1 (dissimilar) to 1 (similar), with 0 indicating orthogonality. Given an input query with its corresponding z wsi , and a memory bank M T consisting of all unique feature vectors from T WSIs, the cosine similarity for each m i ∈ M T is defined as follows: Cosine Similarity ( z w s i , m i ) = z w s i · m i ∥ z w s i ∥ ∥ m i ∥ After computing and sorting all cosine similarities, the k most similar results are retrieved. 4: 4 Materials This study utilised WSIs of gastrointestinal (GAST), pulmonary (PUL), and urinary (URI) anatomic sites. These WSIs were sourced from the TCGA database [39] . All WSIs are divided into patches measuring 1024 × 1024 pixels at 20 × magnification. Annotations specifying cancer subtypes are available at the WSI level. Table 1 displays the number of WSIs for each project, categorized by anatomical site. 5: 5 Experiments and results In this section, we present the experimental setup and detailed analysis of the results obtained from our study. 5.1: 5.1 Experimental setup To comprehensively evaluate the performance of different clustering methods, we tested all possible combinations of clustering methods, aggregation methods, and number of clusters. Specifically, the number of clusters Q was set to 10, 20, and 30. The aggregation methods employed were the maximum (max) and the mean (mean). The clustering methods used in the experiments are detailed in the Section 3 . We employed a leave-one-out evaluation method. This method involved systematically excluding one image from the dataset during each evaluation iteration, simulating its retrieval against the remaining images. Furthermore, to ensure robustness in our evaluation, we also excluded any images from the same patient as the query image from the dataset. This approach mitigates biases arising from intra-patient similarities. 5.2: 5.2 Evaluation metrics As an evaluation metric, we employed the majority vote method. This approach assesses whether the most frequent class among the k retrieved instances matches the ground truth class. The majority vote method provides a clear and reliable measure of the clustering method’s performance by determining if the predominant label in the retrieved set corresponds to the actual class. The majority vote is obtained by the following expression: (1) MV@k = 1 P ∑ i = 1 m δ ( y i , MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) ) where y i represents the ground truth label for the i -th instance, P represents the number of query WSIs and MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) denotes the majority vote result from the top k retrieved answers. δ ( ) is a discriminant function used to determine equality, as described earlier. For example, if MV ( a n s i [ : k ] ) = y i , then δ ( ) = 1 and 0 otherwise. In this article and following other studies in the literature, the results of this metric are reported for MV@5. 5.3: 5.3 Ablation experiments 5.3.1: 5.3.1 Clustering method selection via ablation analysis In this section, we present the content-based WSI retrieval results obtained for the three clustering methods employed. Table 2 displays the outcomes for K-means, Table 3 showcases those for PCMeans, and Table 4 illustrates the results for CMeans. Specifically, we evaluated three different initializations of centroid numbers and two aggregation methods, mean and maximum. The findings reveal that for the K-means++ algorithm, the optimal configuration consists of Q = 10 clusters with centroid aggregation using the maximum method. For PCMeans, superior results were achieved with Q = 30 clusters and maximum aggregation of centroids. Lastly, CMeans performed optimally with Q = 10 clusters and centroid aggregation using the mean method. Across these methods, employing CONCH as the feature extractor demonstrated that globally, the optimal configuration is to use K-means with Q = 10 clusters and maximum centroid aggregation, as it outperforms the best-performing setups in PCMeans and CMeans. 5.3.2: 5.3.2 Comparison with baseline aggregation methods This section presents the results of comparing our proposed CLAV method against two baseline methods. The baseline methods consist of aggregating all the feature vectors of the patches that make up a WSI using either BGAP or BGMP. The results, shown in Table 5 , indicate that our method achieves a higher overall mean compared to these aggregation methods. This demonstrates that our approach is more effective in condensing all the feature vectors from the patches of a WSI into a unique, representative vector. These evaluations were conducted using two different feature extractors: CONCH [29] and KEEP [34] . In both cases, CLAV consistently outperforms the baseline aggregation strategies, further validating the robustness of our method across different representation spaces. 5.3.3: 5.3.3 Performance comparison of RetCCL and CLAV In this section, we present the results for each anatomical site using the proposed method in RetCCL, along with the outcomes of our method when utilizing the RetCCL feature extractor combined with our clustering method. Additionally, we include the results of our approach that employs CONCH as the feature extractor in conjunction with our clustering method to obtain the feature vector representing each WSI. The results are summarized in Table 6 . It is important to note that the number of clusters used for the RetCCL + CLAV method is Q = 30 (see Appendix B.1 RetCCL + CLAV), and for the CONCH + CLAV method, it is Q = 10 (see Section 5.3.1 ). The clustering method used for both is kmeans++, as this has been shown in the previous sections to be the optimal configuration for each feature extractor and the optimal number of clusters. The results indicate that the combination of CONCH with our clustering method offers the best results regarding the average performance across the three anatomical sites. Furthermore, it can be observed that the average obtained using the RetCCL feature extractor and our clustering method is superior to that achieved by the authors of RetCCL. This demonstrates that our clustering method enhances the performance of the CBIR task. In addition to improving performance, using a unique latent vector per WSI significantly reduces the size of the database, making our clustering method much more efficient and scalable to a larger amount of data. These results highlight the ability of foundation models to extract rich features even without being trained on these specific data, facilitating the condensation of information from all patches of a WSI into a unique latent vector while preserving the information necessary to differentiate various WSIs for CBIR tasks. 5.4: 5.4 Comparison with literature This section presents the results obtained for the Yottixel, SISH and RetCCL methods on the dataset used in this study. The number of WSIs utilized in this work is similar to that employed in these methods. Table 7 reflects the results obtained for each method and subtype within each anatomical site. The results indicate that our method, CONCH + CLAV, achieves superior metrics in most cases compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Notable improvements are observed in the pulmonary and gastrointestinal anatomical sites. The enhancements in these metrics underscore the robustness and reliability of our approach. In most cases where our method has shown underperformance compared to existing literature, this is because the methods used for comparison were pre-trained on the same data used to evaluate the metrics, which may have conferred an advantage. Despite this, the macro-average MV@5 metric scores for Yottixel, SISH, RetCCL, and our CONCH + CLAV are 0.6471, 0.7241, 0.7927, and 0.8243, respectively, with our method achieving the highest macro-average score. Moreover, CLAV is fully compatible with any patch-based encoder and can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines. Its ability to produce high-quality WSI-level representations without supervision highlights its practical utility and opens the door to efficient deployment in diverse histopathological tasks. The innovative feature extraction leveraging CONCH and our CLAV is key to our method’s superior performance. This combination allows for a more accurate and meaningful representation of the WSIs. 5.5: 5.5 Qualitative results To further illustrate the effectiveness of our CBIR system based on the CLAV representation, we present a set of qualitative retrieval examples in Appendix A. These examples correspond to WSIs retrieved using our system for a variety of input queries across different anatomical sites. In each case, the objective is to retrieve WSIs associated with the same pathology, ideally from the same TCGA project as the query. The visual examples show that our method is able to retrieve a high proportion of relevant slides, indicating that the CLAV-based representation effectively captures the underlying pathological patterns in a compact and semantically meaningful way. This supports the quantitative findings reported in Section 5.3 , and in particular the retrieval metrics discussed in Section 5.3.3 . Notably, retrieval performance varies across anatomical sites. For most tissues, the retrieved sets contain a consistent number of slides with matching pathology and project. However, the GAST (stomach) site exhibits a noticeably higher number of retrieval errors. This is consistent with the lower quantitative performance observed for GAST in Section 5.3.3 , suggesting a higher level of intra-class variability or noise in the corresponding WSI data. Overall, the examples in Appendix A provide further evidence of the capacity of the CLAV method to generate discriminative and compact embeddings for WSIs, enabling reliable retrieval across a diverse set of pathological samples. 6: 6 Conclusion In conclusion, the CLAV method demonstrates substantial effectiveness in condensing features extracted from WSI patches into a single representative vector. Our results show that this approach improves retrieval performance compared to existing methods in the literature. Specifically, when applied to the RetCCL feature extractor, our method surpasses the retrieval outcomes achieved by its original technique. Similarly, using CONCH as a feature extractor also leads to enhanced performance, underlining that applying foundation models without task-specific training can still produce state-of-the-art results. The performance comparison across different feature extractors and clustering methods reveals that the combination of CLAV with CONCH and the K-means clustering method ( Q = 10 clusters) yields the best retrieval results, outperforming other setups like PCMeans and CMeans. Moreover, when combined with RetCCL and K-means with Q = 30 , our method also outperforms the baseline retrieval results from RetCCL, highlighting the advantage of our approach in improving retrieval accuracy. One of the key advantages of our method is its efficiency, as it eliminates the need for specific task-based training while still achieving competitive retrieval results. This greatly enhances its scalability and potential for integration into larger datasets and diagnostic support systems. Regarding future directions, clinical validation of this method through its application in diagnostic tools for expert pathologists could further validate its practical impact. Additionally, future work could address potential biases by ensuring that the model’s retrievals are based on the morphological and pathological characteristics of the samples, rather than the samples’ origin or color. This could be vital in ensuring the fairness and reliability of the system. Lastly, as foundation models continue to evolve, exploring newer feature extractors may further improve retrieval performance and lead to even more efficient diagnostic support systems. Title: Composite-metric deep learning for pathological complete response prediction from breast MRI Abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is commonly administered before surgery to reduce breast tumor size. Achieving a pathological complete response (pCR) after NACT is associated with improved prognosis. Early prediction of pCR help minimize unnecessary treatment related toxicity and facilitates personalized therapeutic strategies. This study introduces a deep learning approach for pCR prediction using 2D breast dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) data from the public I-SPY1 dataset. We focused on the pretreatment (T1) and early treatment (T2) time points and analyzed both the axial and sagittal planes. Variants of the VGG and ResNet architectures were trained and assessed. To provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s performance beyond accuracy alone, we developed a novel composite metric called the Global Performance Score (GPS). This metric combines accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity through a weighted summation. One-way ANOVA (F = 1.83, p = 0.127) confirmed GPS robustness across weighting schemes, with (0.4, 0.3, 0.3) chosen as the optimal configuration. Our findings show that VGG-11 and VGG-13 achieved the highest mean GPS scores (92.17 and 92.10, respectively), outperforming ResNet variants. In addition, sagittal views showed a significantly higher average GPS (95.08) compared to axial views (87.12). Similarly, the T2 time point outperformed the T1 time point (GPS: 91.32 vs. 90.89). These results highlight the effectiveness of deep learning in predicting pCR and support the GPS as a robust and interpretable evaluation metric for multi-objective assessment in breast cancer imaging.
