Patient outcomes and responses to standard therapies vary significantly, particularly in cases of locally advanced breast cancer (LABC), where neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is often administered before surgery. NACT aims to reduce tumor size and potentially downstage the disease, control metastasis, and increase the likelihood of breast-conserving surgery. Pathological complete response (pCR), defined as the complete absence of invasive disease, is as a crucial indicator of the effectiveness of NACT. It was evaluated at the end of chemotherapy and post-surgery. Studies have shown that patients who achieve pCR experience improved survival outcomes compared to those who do not. Accurate early prediction of pCR can help avoid unnecessary toxicity, optimize treatment plans and improve patient care. Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) plays a critical role in the diagnosis and monitoring of breast cancer. It is a noninvasive imaging technique that was initially designed to measure tumor vascularity and permeability[ 2–4 ]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows the visualization of anatomy in all three planes: axial, sagittal, and coronal [ 5 ]. However, no universal consensus exists regarding the most informative imaging plane for breast MRI protocols. This variability across institutions can affect diagnostic consistency and downstream predictive modeling [ 6 ]. To address this variability, we investigated both axial and sagittal DCE-MRI acquisitions at two clinically relevant time points: pretreatment (T1) and early treatment (T2). The primary objective of this study was to identify the optimal combination of a deep learning model, imaging orientation, and timing configuration that provides the most accurate and clinically meaningful prediction of pCR in breast cancer patients undergoing NACT. Deep learning approaches are increasingly applied to breast cancer imaging, yet many studies rely solely on accuracy for evaluation, overlooking clinically important trade-offs such as sensitivity and specificity, particularly problematic in imbalanced datasets.This limitation is particularly relevant in the context of imbalanced datasets, where misleading performance evaluations can result. To overcome this, we introduced a novel composite metric called the Global Performance Score (GPS), which combines accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity through weighted summation. This metric offers a more nuanced and clinically meaningful assessment of model performance and facilitates a fair comparison across different models, time points, and acquisition planes. The main contributions of this study are as follows: • We systematically compared VGG and ResNet models trained on axial and sagittal DCE-MRI slices acquired at T1 and T2 time points using the I-SPY1 dataset. • We introduced the GPS metric to assess model performance in a clinically meaningful way, integrating multiple metrics into a single composite measure. • We analyzed GPS weighting strategies and validate their stability through statistical analysis, enabling robust recommendations on model selection, imaging protocol, and time point configuration. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews the related work. Section III presents the proposed architecture. Section IV details the materials and methods. Section V reports the results. Section VI discusses the findings in comparison to prior work. Section VII concludes the study and outlines future research directions. 2: 2 Related works Machine learning techniques have gained significant traction in intelligent healthcare systems, especially for medical image classification and prediction tasks. Several studies have explored the use of deep learning to predict pCR to NACT in patients with breast cancer. Braman et al. [ 7 ] employed a CNN-based model on 2D dynamic contrast-enhanced MR images to predict response to HER2-targeted NACT. Comes et al. [ 8 ] applied a transfer learning approach combining pre- and early-treatment exams. They used a pre-trained CNN for low-level feature extraction and an SVM classifier, achieving an AUC of 0.90 and an accuracy of 92.3 % by integrating imaging and clinical data. These studies highlight the potential of early MRI features in pCR prediction. Several studies have focused on fully automated tumor detection using CNNs [ 9 , 10 ], but few have addressed whole-breast MRI for pCR prediction. El Adoui et al. [ 11 ] leveraged parametric response maps with deep learning on whole-breast MR images, emphasizing the early response assessment. Qu et al. [ 12 ] integrated pre- and post-NACT MRI in a deep learning model, outperforming models based on single time point data. Duanmu et al. [ 13 ] incorporated demographic and molecular data alongside CNN-extracted features from multi-phase DCE-MRI, yielding an AUC of 0.80 and accuracy of 0.83. Liu et al. [ 14 ] proposed a convolutional neural network (CNN) for predicting pCR to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer using data from the I-SPY1 Trial. Their model was trained on segmented post-contrast DCE-MRI tumor volumes from 131 patients and employed multiple data augmentation techniques such as flipping and rotation. The CNN consisted of six residual blocks and achieved a classification accuracy of 72.5 %, sensitivity of 65.5 %, specificity of 78.9 %, and AUC of 0.72. This study highlights the potential of deep learning for pCR prediction using breast MRI, although it primarily focuses on imaging data from a single time point. Ha et al. [ 15 ] utilized a VGG-16 network to classify breast tumors into three NACT response groups, achieving an accuracy of 88 %. Despite these advances, most studies have relied solely on either axial or sagittal acquisitions. Few studies have explored the combined potential of multiple orientations. In our previous study [ 16 ], we used axial DCE-MRI with deep learning, achieving accuracies of 92.22 % and 90.76 % using ResNet-50 and VGG-19, respectively, which were enhanced by data augmentation. Zeng et al. [ 17 ] developed a multimodal model combining deep features from HE-stained pathological images with clinical data using an SVM classifier. Their model achieved 73 % accuracy and 79 % specificity but was limited by a small patient cohort and the use of a single classifier. Using pretreatment multiparametric breast MRI and clinicopathological data, Xu et al. [ 18 ] proposed the creation of deep learning models to predict pCR to neoadjuvant systemic therapy in patients with triple-negative breast cancer. An AUC of 0.76 was obtained in the internal testing dataset by the top-performing deep learning model developed using pretreatment multiparametric breast MRI and clinicopathological data acquired from 282 patients with stage I to III triple-negative breast cancer enrolled in a prospective clinical trial. The deep learning model achieved an AUC of 0.72 in the external I-SPY 2 trial testing dataset. The model’s performance was affected by tumor volume preprocessing, whereas the 3D model frameworks, tumor ROI selection, and data inputs had minimal impact. A multimodal spatiotemporal deep learning framework (deep-NST) was proposed by Verma et al. [ 19 ] to predict the results of neoadjuvant systemic therapy before or at an early stage. Imaging data taken at different NST regimen timestamps, tumor molecular data, and patient demographic data were incorporated into the deep-NST model. Using the ISPY-1 dataset, the effectiveness of the proposed method was confirmed in terms of accuracy, area under the curve (AUC), and computational complexity. In this study, 121 patients from the ISPY-1 trial were divided into two groups: 84 patients with 182 data samples in the training set and 37 patients with 71 data samples in the test set. The results yielded an AUC of 0.88 and an accuracy of 0.85. Joo et al. [ 20 ] proposed a multimodal approach combining ResNet-50, 3D-CNN, and clinical data, trained on various MRI sequences. Their model achieved an accuracy of 85 % for pCR prediction. Massafra et al. [ 21 ] compared axial and sagittal acquisitions from two distinct datasets, reporting AUCs of 78.0 % and 80.3 % and accuracies of 77.3 % and 84.4 %, respectively. Although these studies have demonstrated promising results, few have directly compared the impact of MRI slice orientation or explored how imaging time points (T1 vs. T2) influence performance. This lack of standardization in MRI acquisition protocols represents a critical gap that our study addresses by systematically analyzing both axial and sagittal views across multiple time points within a unified deep learning framework. Furthermore, most prior studies assessed performance using accuracy or AUC alone, without accounting for clinically important trade-offs, such as sensitivity (to avoid false negatives) and specificity (to avoid overtreatment). Although composite metrics have been proposed in other domains, they remain rare in medical imaging applications. Brosch et al. [ 22 ] addressed severe class imbalance in lesion segmentation by using a weighted loss, combining sensitivity and specificity during CNN training. While conceptually similar, our study extends this idea by introducing a Global Performance Score (GPS) that integrates these metrics into a composite evaluation instead of a loss function, offering a novel and clinically interpretable method for assessing model performance. Furthermore, in educational chatbots, Alabbas et al. [ 23 ] introduced a weighted composite metric to assess the user experience by integrating effectiveness, engagement, and usability. Their approach, built on principal component analysis, demonstrated the value of multidimensional scoring over isolated metrics. Although their application domains differ, the underlying concept inspired our design of the GPS, which integrates accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity using configurable clinical weights. To our knowledge, no prior study in breast cancer imaging has introduced such a composite, statistically validated metric for evaluating deep learning models in a multi-objective context. 3: 3 Proposed architecture Our primary objective was to develop a model that can predict whether patients with breast cancer will achieve a pathological complete response or not to NACT. In our study, we considered pCR to be the medical ground truth. In addition, a preprocessing stepd was implemented to improve the performance of the proposed model. An intensity normalization step was applied, followed by the resizing of the MR images. This process can be considered atypical for CNN-based prediction approaches. Fig. 1 illustrates the proposed approach, which comprises the following steps: • Data preprocessing: Normalization is followed by cropping of the input images. All images had a uniform width and height of 256 pixels. • Splitting dataset into a training set (80 %) and a test set (20 %), and 20 % of the training set was further set aside as a validation set to monitor the generalization performance. • A data augmentation technique was utilized for increasing the number of input images. This involved horizontal and vertical flips, as well as positive and negative rotations of 20° and 30°, respectively. This technique is used to address the issue of limited data, overcome overfitting [ 24 , 25 ], and ensure efficient CNN training. • Training step: The proposed model was trained using the augmented dataset and two-dimensional input slices of each patient. • After training, the models were evaluated on the test set, and their predictions were assessed using multiple performance metrics, including accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. • To assess the model quality beyond conventional accuracy, a novel composite metric called GPS was computed. The GPS integrates accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity using weighted summation. This formulation ensures interpretability, robustness to class imbalance, and reflection of clinically relevant trade-offs, enabling a more meaningful evaluation than the accuracy metric alone. 4: 4 Materials and methods This section outlines the experimental setup, including a detailed description of the dataset, implementation details, and the evaluation metrics used to assess the model’s performance. While deep learning has been increasingly applied to breast MRI, few studies have systematically compared multiple architectures, imaging planes, and time points in predicting pCR using a composite evaluation metric. Our approach builds on prior studies but distinguishes itself by introducing the Global Performance Score (GPS) and validating its robustness across different weighting schemes, offering a more comprehensive and clinically relevant framework for performance assessment than previous studies. a. Dataset description The multi-site Investigation of Serial Studies to Predict Your Therapeutic Response with Imaging and Molecular Analysis (I-SPY1 TRIAL) dataset [ 26 , 27 ], which explores the potential of imaging and molecular analysis to predict therapeutic response through serial studies, is publicly available in The Cancer Imaging Archive [ 28 ]. This study was a collaborative effort by the American College of Radiology Imaging Network (ACRIN), Specialized Programs of Research Excellence (SPORE), and Cancer and Leukemia Group B (CALGB), and involved multiple centers. A total of 237 patients were enrolled, of whom 221 received neoadjuvant chemotherapy, while remaining patients have been excluded for various reasons. The patients included in this study had invasive breast tumors that were at least 3 cm in size and did not showed no signs of distant metastasis. Women were recruited for the study from 2002 to 2006 and underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy using an anthracycline-cyclophosphamide (AC) regimen. The treatment was administered as a standalone AC regimen or in combination with a taxane. As shown in Fig. 2 , MRI examinations were performed at most four time points: T1 is the first time point of MRI1 scans, obtained four weeks before the initiation of the anthracycline-cyclophosphamide chemotherapy; T2 is the second time point treatment, where MRI2 is received at least 2 weeks after the first cycle of AC and before the second cycle of AC; T3 is the third time point, corresponding to the MRI3 scans obtained between the AC treatment and taxane therapy, if taxane was administered; and T4 is the time point after the final chemotherapy treatment and before surgery to acquire MRI4 scans. MRI scans contain multiple images in the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format. b. Implementation details The proposed models consisted of multiple convolutional layers that used axial and sagittal 2D slices as inputs for each patient in the training dataset. Predictions of responders and non-responders were obtained from the outputs. Nonlinear activation function ReLU and max-pooling layers were employed. The dataset was divided into a training set (80 %) and a test set (20 %), and 20 % of the training set was further set aside as a validation set to monitor the generalization performance. Training was performed using a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.01, momentum of 0.9, a batch size of 32, and 100 epochs. To facilitate convergence, the learning rate was reduced by a factor of 10 after epoch 50. The models were compiled with a categorical cross-entropy loss function, and accuracy was used as the primary evaluation metric. The implementation was performed out using Python. PyTorch and NumPy were the machine learning libraries considered. An Intel Xeon CPU with 32 GB RAM and an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 4000 graphics card with 8 GB memory were used to expedite the training process and improve its efficiency. c. Evaluation Metrics The performance of the model prediction was evaluated based on its accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Each metric is shown with its corresponding equation. The accuracy metric measures the percentage of predictions made correctly by a the model. This is the proportion of correct results among the total number of cases examined, including the true positives and true negatives. The accuracy is mathematically presented by Eq. (1) . (1) A c c u r a c y = T P + T N TP + TN + FP + FN Sensitivity, also known as the true positive rate (TPR) or recall, quantifies the proportion of actual positive cases that a model correctly identifies as positives. The equation for sensitivity is given by Eq. (2) . (2) S e n s i t i v i t y = T P R = T P T P + F N Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), measures the proportion of actual negative cases correctly identified by the model. The specificity of the model is calculated as follows: (3) S p e c i f i c i t y = T N R = T N F P + T N We selected accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity as the key evaluation metrics owing to their established use and clinical relevance in breast cancer imaging research [ 29 ]. These metrics provide clear insights into the model’s ability to correctly identify positive and negative cases, making them essential for clinical decision-making. They were subsequently integrated into the GPS to provide a robust and clinically meaningful composite measure. The GPS is a composite metric that integrates three standard classification metrics: accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. It is defined as a weighted summation, as shown in Eq. (4) . (4) G P S = α · A c c u r a c y + β · S e n s i t i v i t y + γ · S p e c i f i c i t y This formulation offers several advantages. First, it ensures interpretability and flexibility by allowing the influence of each indicator to be explicitly controlled via the weighting factors α , β , and δ , where α + β + δ = 1 . This is particularly useful in clinical settings, where different performance criteria may have varying levels of importance. For example, when predicting pCR, sensitivity may be prioritized to avoid missing treatment responders, whereas specificity helps reduce unnecessary interventions. Second, the additive formulation avoids the drawbacks of multiplicative and geometric combinations. In contrast, a linear summation is more robust and stable, ensuring that high performance for one indicator can compensate, to some extent, for weaknesses for the other. This is consistent with real-world clinical decision-making, in which balanced trade-offs are often necessary. Finally, the summation approach offers statistical advantages: it allows simple comparisons and hypothesis testing (e.g., ANOVA) and can be effectively visualized using heat maps and box plots. Overall, the GPS provides a consistent and interpretable method for evaluating the performance of multi-objective models in medical imaging tasks. This metric enables a fine-tuned evaluation aligned with real-world diagnostic priorities. 5: 5 Results This section presents the experimental results, including a model performance comparison, evaluation of GPS weight stability, and detailed analyses across models, time points, and imaging views. a. Performance of ResNet and VGG models Tables 1 and 2 summarize the performance of the ResNet and VGG model variants in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity across different imaging time points (T1, T2) and views (axial, sagittal). Several observations emerge from these results: For ResNet models, ResNet-50 achieved the highest accuracy (90.25 %) and sensitivity (96.21 %) in the T1 axial setting, but with low specificity (63.49 %), indicating a high rate of false positives. ResNet-34 showed the highest sensitivity overall (98.48 % on T1 axial) but also the lowest specificity (65.07 %). ResNet-18 offered a more balanced performance across metrics, particularly for T1 sagittal images, with a good trade-off between sensitivity (93.05 %) and specificity (94.84 %). In contrast, the VGG models demonstrated stronger overall results. VGG-16 achieved an accuracy of 98.05 % for T2 sagittal images with high sensitivity (98.06 %) and specificity (94.11 %). VGG-11 and VGG-13 also produced consistently strong results, especially in sagittal views at both T1 and T2, with average accuracies exceeding 96 %. For better visualization, Fig. 3 provides comparative bar plots illustrating the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of ResNet-18, ResNet-34, and ResNet-50 across T1 and T2 imaging conditions, evaluated in both axial and sagittal views. While these metrics provide valuable insights, relying solely on accuracy or even pairwise comparisons of sensitivity and specificity can be misleading, particularly in imbalanced clinical datasets, where the cost of false negatives may differ from that of false positives. Therefore, a more comprehensive and interpretable evaluation approach is required. To address this, we introduced the Global Performance Score, a composite metric that integrates accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity through weighted summation. This metric enables multidimensional comparison across models, imaging views, and time points, offering a more holistic assessment of clinical relevance. For improved clarity, Fig. 4 provides comparative bar plots illustrating the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of VGG-11, VGG-13, VGG-16, and VGG-19 across T1 and T2 imaging conditions, evaluated in both axial and sagittal views. a. GPS Weight Stability Analysis To ensure the robustness of the GPS, we explored five different weighting combinations for accuracy (α), sensitivity (β), and specificity (γ) to reflect different clinical priorities. The combinations included (0.4, 0.3, 0.3), (0.33, 0.33, 0.34), (0.5, 0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.5, 0.25), and (0.25, 0.25, 0.5). We chose balanced weights (e.g., 0.33–0.33–0.34) to treat all metrics equally [ 30 ]. In addition, we chose weights focused on accuracy (e.g., 0.40–0.30–0.30) to reflect a standard emphasis on overall correct predictions, which is common in the radiomics literature for pCR tasks [ 21 ]. A heavy sensitivity weight was chosen (e.g., 0.25–0.50–0.25) to help avoid missing potential responders [ 14 ], while specificity-heavy choices (e.g., 0.25–0.25–0.50) aimed to reduce overtreatment risks [ 5 ]. Each weighting combination used in the GPS was designed as a convex linear combination (α + β + γ = 1), ensuring a normalized and interpretable integration of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity [ 23 ]. For each combination, the GPS scores were computed across all model variants and imaging conditions. We conducted a one-way ANOVA to assess whether the choice of weights significantly affected the GPS distribution. The results showed no statistically significant differences among the weight configurations ( F = 1.83, p = 0.127), indicating that the GPS remained stable regardless of the specific combination chosen. This robustness justifies the use of the GPS as a reliable composite metric. Additionally, the boxplot shown in Fig. 5 was generated to visually compare the distribution of GPS values for each weighting strategy. The combination (0.4, 0.3, 0.3) demonstrated a high median, low variance, and limited outliers, supporting its selection as the most balanced and interpretable configuration for subsequent analysis. These findings confirm that the GPS is both statistically robust and visually consistent across different weighting schemes, validating its utility for multi-objective model comparisons. To facilitate a multi-criteria assessment of model performance, we computed GPS using the weighting configuration (α=0.4, β=0.3, γ=0.3) applied to the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. The GPS was averaged and compared across different model architectures, treatment time points, and imaging planes. a. The mean GPS for each model m is presented in Eq. (6) : (6) G P S ‾ t = 1 | M | × | { axial , sagittal } | ∑ m ∈ M ∑ v ∈ { axial , sagittal } G P S m , t , v where | M | is the set of all models. For each view v ,as shown in Eq. (7) : (7) G P S ‾ v = 1 | M | × | { T 1 , T 2 } | ∑ m ∈ M ∑ t ∈ { T 1 , T 2 } G P S m , t , v • Comparison across models: Among all the tested architectures, the VGG variants achieved the highest average GPS. Specifically, VGG-11 (92.17) and VGG-13 (92.10) outperformed the ResNet models in terms of overall performance. ResNet-18 was the best-performing ResNet variant (91.70), while ResNet-50 had the lowest GPS (89.74), despite achieving high sensitivity in some cases ( Table 3 ). This suggests that while deeper ResNet models may excel in detecting positives, their balance across all metrics is suboptimal compared to that of VGG architectures. • Comparison Across time points (T1 vs. T2): Averaging across all models and views, images acquired at early treatment (T2) yielded a higher GPS (91.32) than those from pretreatment (T1, 90.89). This indicates that early treatment imaging provides richer or more discriminative information for the model-based prediction of pCR, likely because of the emerging treatment effects becoming visible in the tumor microenvironment. • Imaging views comparison (Axial vs. Sagittal): The sagittal view demonstrated a significantly higher average GPS (95.08) compared to the axial view (87.12). This trend was consistent across all models and both time points, highlighting the sagittal orientation as being more informative and reliable for capturing relevant features in breast DCE-MRI for pCR prediction. Fig. 6 shows a comparison of the GPS across deep learning architectures, both T1 and T2 time points, and imaging views (axial vs. sagittal). VGG-11 and VGG-13 achieved the highest GPS values, whereas sagittal views and T2 time points demonstrated superior performance. 6: 6 Comparison with the state-of-the-art and discussion A direct comparison between the state-of-the-art works is not possible because each of them applied different architectures with different orientation views and time points from the I-SPY1 dataset for a specific classification task, and the evaluation was performed using different metrics. The following discussion aims to highlight the advantages and limitations of the architecture in each cited work ( Table 4 ). Liu et al. [ 14 ] developed a CNN algorithm to predict NACT response utilizing the I-SPY TRIAL dataset. Despite promising results evaluated by accuracy, AUC ROC, sensitivity, and specificity, Liu et al .’s approach has some limitations. The model was trained on a relatively small dataset and relied solely on post-contrast DCE-MRI at a single time point, which limited its ability to capture temporal treatment effects. No composite evaluation metric was used; instead, only traditional metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, were reported, which may not fully reflect the performance trade-offs in clinically imbalanced settings. Comes et al. [ 8 ] proposed a transfer learning framework using pre-trained CNNs for early prediction of pCR to NACT in breast cancer patients, based on DCE-MRI images from the I-SPY1 trial. The authors extracted low-level convolutional features from MRI examinations at pretreatment and early treatment time points. They used a feature selection pipeline to identify the most stable features and trained SVM classifiers with or without clinical features (e.g., PgR, ER, HER2, and molecular subtype). The best results were achieved by combining both T1 and T2 features, yielding an accuracy of 91.4 % and an AUC of 0.93 on the fine-tuning dataset, with similar results on an independent test set. Despite achieving promising results using transfer learning and SVM classifiers, this study has some limitations. First, it relies solely on conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, without incorporating any composite metric that balances multiple clinical priorities, such as the proposed Global Performance Score (GPS). First, the dataset size was limited to 134 patients, which restricted generalizability. Second, the analysis does not explore the impact of different MRI acquisition planes (e.g., axial vs. sagittal) or assess multiple CNN architectures, and it focusing only on features extracted from AlexNet. Similarly, Kuramoto et al. [ 30 ] aimed to predict pCR in patients with breast cancer undergoing neoadjuvant pharmacotherapy using radiomic features extracted from MRI. Using data from 64 cases in the public I-SPY1 dataset, the authors extracted 371 radiomic features from the largest tumor slice and selected nine optimal features using the Lasso regression. The SVM classifier trained on these features achieved an AUC of 0.92, outperforming the linear discriminant analysis. This study had several limitations. First, the dataset was relatively small (only 64 patients), limiting the generalizability of the findings. Importantly, while the method showed a high AUC, no external validation set was used, raising concerns about overfitting. Moreover, only standard metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) were employed for evaluation, with no composite or clinically contextualized metrics (e.g., F1-score, balanced accuracy, or composite weighted scores such as GPS), which may limit the interpretability and clinical relevance of the findings in imbalanced datasets. Bahba et al. [ 16 ] introduced a deep learning–based framework aimed at predicting breast cancer tumor response to chemotherapy using dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI. Although this study presents a promising deep learning approach for predicting breast cancer response to chemotherapy, it has several important limitations. First, the dataset characteristics, including sample size, class balance, and data partitioning, were not clearly described, making it difficult to assess the robustness and generalizability of the model. Second, the lack of reported evaluation metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, limits the ability to compare the performance with existing methods. The study also relied on a single CNN architecture and did not explore alternative models or multiple imaging orientations, such as axial and sagittal views, which could enhance the predictive power. Additionally, no composite or multi-objective performance metric, such as a weighted score integrating sensitivity and specificity, was used to address potential class imbalances. Verma et al. [ 19 ] proposed a multimodal spatiotemporal deep learning framework (deep-NST) to predict the outcome of neoadjuvant systemic therapy before or early in treatment. Although the multimodal deep learning framework proposed by Verma et al . demonstrated promising results in predicting response to neoadjuvant therapy, the study's generalizability is constrained by a limited dataset size, lack of external validation, and reliance on manual tumor annotations, highlighting the need for larger multi-institutional studies with more robust and explainable models. Similarly, Dammu et al. [ 31 ] developed a novel deep-learning CNN to predict pCR, residual cancer burden, and progression-free survival in patients with breast cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy using molecular subtypes, longitudinal multiparametric MRI, and demographic data as inputs. They used pre- and post-neoadjuvant chemotherapy data that outperformed either method alone. The model was evaluated for accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and ROC AUC. Massafra et al. [ 21 ] compared axial and sagittal MRI acquisitions from different datasets, reporting accuracies of 77.3 % and 84.4 %, respectively. However, many of these studies suffer from methodological limitations, including the use of a single image orientation, limited dataset sizes, the absence of data augmentation [ 29 , 32 ], and multi-metric evaluation. In contrast, our study stands out for three key reasons. First, it systematically compared both axial and sagittal orientations across multiple time points (T1 and T2), offering a more comprehensive analysis of the effectiveness of the imaging protocol. Second, it applies modern deep learning architectures (VGG and ResNet variants) with augmentation strategies to mitigate data limitations. Third, and most distinctively, we introduced the Global Performance Score, a novel composite metric that integrates accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity through weighted summation. While previous studies have relied primarily on single metrics such as accuracy or AUC, none have adopted a composite metric to assess the multi-objective performance of models in this domain. The use of GPS enables a more clinically meaningful comparison to be made. It provides insights into the trade-offs between model sensitivity and specificity, which are especially critical in the context of imbalanced datasets and real-world clinical decisions. The primary limitation of our study was the small dataset size. In addition, the model was not evaluated on an external or private dataset, which restricted our ability to confirm its generalizability. Although data augmentation has been applied to mitigate overfitting, these methods only create synthetic variations of the same data and cannot fully represent real-world diversity. Finally, optimizing both accuracy and computational efficiency requires compromises that may limit performance improvements. 7: 7 Conclusion and future work In this study, we focused on predicting pCR to NACT using deep learning models trained on 2D DCE-MRI data from the public I-SPY1 dataset. Specifically, we used images taken at two time points: before (T1) and after the first chemotherapy cycle (T2), and from two orientations: axial and sagittal planes. These images targeted patients with tumors larger than 3 cm who were scheduled for NACT. Our experiments demonstrated that among all models, VGG-11 and VGG-13 achieved the highest mean GPS scores (92.17 and 92.10, respectively), outperforming the ResNet models. Additionally, sagittal views demonstrated a significantly higher average GPS (95.08) compared with axial views (87.12), and early treatment images outperformed pretreatment scans (GPS=91.32 vs. 90.89). Compared to prior studies, our approach yielded superior results and offered a more comprehensive assessment using GPS, particularly in evaluating the effects of imaging orientation and timing. The sagittal view and early treatment time points consistently demonstrated better predictive performance. The proposed Global Performance Score provides a comprehensive and flexible approach for evaluating deep learning models in pCR prediction, with potential applicability to other clinical imaging problems. In future work, we plan to expand our methodology to include the newer and larger I-SPY2 dataset, which features MRI data collected with updated imaging protocols. We will also focus on clinical validation to ensure the model’s reliability in real-world use. Additionally, we will explore the incorporation of non-imaging clinical data, such as molecular and demographic information, to improve the model’s predictive ability and work toward a solution that can be deployed in clinical settings.

Title: Diffusion models vs. DCGANs for class-imbalanced lung cancer CT classification: A comparative study Abstract: Effective lung cancer detection from CT scans remains critically challenged by class imbalance where benign and normal cases are underrepresented, leading to biased machine learning models with reduced sensitivity for minority classes and potentially missed diagnoses in cancer screening applications. We present a comprehensive comparative analysis of Diffusion Models and Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), both incorporating modern architectural enhancements including spectral normalization, self-attention mechanisms, and conditional generation, for addressing class imbalance in lung cancer CT classification. Using the IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset comprising 1097 CT images across normal, benign, and malignant categories with statistical validation across 10 independent runs, we evaluated both approaches through quantitative image quality metrics (Fréchet Inception Distance, Kullback-Leibler divergence, Kernel Inception Distance, and Inception Score) and downstream classification performance. While Diffusion models consistently outperformed DCGANs across most image quality measures, the clinical significance was confirmed through task-based validation. Both generative approaches successfully addressed class imbalance: DCGAN-augmented datasets achieved overall accuracy of 0.9760 ± 0.0116 with benign recall improvement from 0.833 to 0.933, while Diffusion-augmented datasets reached superior performance of 0.9959 ± 0.0068 with perfect benign recall (1.000 ± 0.000). Critically for cancer screening where false negatives carry severe consequences, Diffusion maintained the highest malignant detection sensitivity (0.997 ± 0.008) with substantially lower performance variance, demonstrating more consistent synthetic data quality. These findings establish that while both modern architectures can mitigate class imbalance, Diffusion models' superior recall performance and lower variability position them as the preferred approach for high-stakes clinical applications, demonstrating that ultimate validation must prioritize downstream clinical task performance over image quality metrics alone.
