Owing to its superior performance and computational efficiency, IlluC-Net is well-suited for integration into computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems and can be effectively deployed on edge devices for real-time diagnosis. 1: 1 Introduction Skin cancer is one of the most prevalent and potentially life-threatening diseases worldwide, with millions of new cases diagnosed each year [1] . The global incidence of skin cancer continues to rise, making early detection and accurate diagnosis essential for better treatment and reducing mortality rates [2] . Early stage identification of malignant lesions significantly improves successful treatment [3] , thereby underlining the importance of automated screening tools. In recent years, dermatological macro-photography has been used by clinicians and medical practitioners to diagnose skin cancer [4,5] . Macro-photographs are high-resolution close-up views of skin lesions captured with digital or mobile phone cameras. These macro-photographs provide detailed visual information of skin lesions at magnifications, enabling clinicians or automated tools to differentiate between benign and malignant skin conditions precisely [6–11] . Recently, clinicians have increasingly used dermatological macro-photographs and automated tools for skin cancer screening [12,13] . However, when capturing these images with digital cameras, variations in lighting conditions or the positioning of the camera can introduce uneven background illumination, commonly referred to as vignetting [14,15] . Vignetting is indicated by a gradual darkening toward the edges of an image, resulting in non-uniform illumination across the lesion and surrounding skin regions [16] . This variation in illumination can obscure critical lesion features and distort pixel intensity distributions, ultimately leading to inaccuracies in manual and automated diagnostic processes. Glaister et al. [17] , have shown that vignetting significantly hampers the performance of skin lesion analysis frameworks, particularly affecting segmentation and classification algorithms. Automated tools using vignetted macro-photographs often suffer from increased misclassification rates and inconsistent segmentation outputs. Researchers have used preprocessing techniques, such as histogram equalization [18] and color constancy algorithms [19] , to improve the contrast between the lesion and background skin, as well as to equalize background illumination. However, these methods often fall short when dealing with the complex and varied lighting conditions present in dermatological macro-photographs. As a result, their effectiveness in both clinical and automated skin cancer screening applications remains limited. Given these challenges, developing robust and adaptive illumination correction methods tailored particularly to dermatological macro-photographs is necessary. By correcting for vignetting and restoring consistent background illumination, such methods have the potential to significantly enhance lesion visibility, improve the reliability of segmentation and classification algorithms, and build trustworthy automated diagnostic systems [20] . 1.1: 1.1 Related work Venugopal et al. [21] introduced illumination equalization using counter-exponential transform (IECET), a method designed to correct vignetting in dermatological macro-photographs. Their approach displayed superior performance in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) on the University of Waterloo [22] and the MED-NODE [23] datasets. However, it fails to selectively equalize pixels in background skin regions, and computational inefficiency was noted as a limitation, highlighting the need for more robust illumination correction techniques. An adaptive image enhancement method was introduced by Wang et al. [24] , utilizing color-space transformation and multi-scale decomposition to enhance the brightness and contrast of low-light dermatological images. Their method significantly improved visual quality, information entropy, and average gradient but lacked an objective quality assessment aligned with human visual perception. This suggests the need for deep learning models that learn human-perceptible enhancement criteria rather than relying solely on the qualitative evaluation metrics. Li et al. [25] presented a U-Net-based deep fully convolutional encoder–decoder network to address the degradation of low- illumination images. Their method outperforms traditional enhancement algorithms by adaptively improving brightness and contrast without introducing edge artifacts. Although the model improves brightness and contrast adaptively, it may not explicitly handle complex and spatially varying background illumination. Ma et al. [26] proposed a novel bi-directional generative adversarial network (GAN) named Structure and illumination constrained GAN (StillGAN) that incorporates local structure and illumination constraints to enhance the quality of medical images without requiring paired data. The method outperforms conventional and deep learning-based approaches across different medical imaging modalities and improved clinical tasks such as segmentation, grading, localization, and classification. However, the complexity of bi-directional GAN training may result in increased computational demands and potential instability during optimization. Jiang et al. [27] introduce EnlightenGAN, an unsupervised GAN designed for low-light image enhancement without requiring paired low/normal-light training data. By incorporating a global–local discriminator, attention mechanisms, and a self-regularized perceptual loss, the model achieves strong generalization and superior visual quality across diverse panoramic images. Salvi et al. [28] introduced DermoCC-GAN, another GAN-based method incorporating a custom heuristic algorithm to address illumination variability in dermatological images. Their approach significantly enhanced segmentation and classification performance on the HAM10000 dataset, demonstrating low variance in diagnostic accuracy. However, they emphasized the need for improved color constancy and adaptation across different imaging conditions, underscoring the demand for illumination-correcting networks integrated with lesion segmentation pipelines. Recently, extensions of the U-Net architecture are used by researchers such as TransUNet and Swin-UNet to integrate the strengths of vision transformers (ViT). While these models have not yet been directly applied to illumination correction tasks, they have shown promise in related domains. For example, He et al. [29] utilized TransUNet in ghost imaging, an inverse problem closely resembling illumination correction, where target images are reconstructed from bucket signals and speckle patterns. Similarly, Shao et al. [30] applied Swin-UNet to enhance the quality of images captured in low-light environments, demonstrating its capability in addressing visibility and contrast challenges analogous to those encountered in uneven illumination scenarios. Li et al. [31] designed a pyramid transformer with cross-shaped windows (CSwin-P) for low-light image enhancement by effectively capturing both global and local contextual information. Featuring enhanced cross-shaped window (CSwin) transformer blocks [32] and spatial interaction units, CSwin-P outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both luminance correction and visual quality across various image sizes. The main limitation of their method is that the CSwin transformer architecture requires high computational resources. Finally, Hasan et al. [33] provided a comprehensive survey on skin lesion segmentation and classification, comparing traditional, machine learning, and deep learning methods. While their study outlined key strengths and trends, it identified gaps in dataset diversity and lack of performance benchmarks for specific techniques. This indicates a growing need for integrated frameworks that combine illumination correction with deep learning-driven segmentation and classification frameworks. Recently, Suchitra et al. [34] designed a luminance-based illumination correction algorithm for retinal fundus images. Their method uses a luminance scaling matrix obtained from Gaussian low-pass filter. The luminance scaling matrix is applied on to the original red, green, and blue channels to achieve balanced illumination. Contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) is thereafter applied to enhance image for improving contrast and structural details. However, since the method primarily relies on pixel-level luminance correction and CLAHE-based enhancement, it may lead to over-enhancement and the loss of fine structural details in regions with complex and uneven background illumination. 1.2: 1.2 Motivation, novelty, and highlights Motivation: Uneven background illumination in dermatological macro-photographs hampers both visual clarity and the performance of automated diagnostic systems. Existing methods like IECET correct background illumination but compromise the contrast between the lesion and the surrounding skin. While recently developed, GAN and transformer-based approaches are computationally inefficient and resource-intensive. Researchers have used deep learning models to enhance contrast of dermatological photographs; however, they do not adequately address the complex and inconsistent background illumination problem. This motivates the development of IlluC-Net, a lightweight U-Net-based model with attention mechanisms to ensure uniform illumination and improve lesion background distinction for accurate diagnosis of skin cancer. Novelty: The novelty of this work lies in the design of ‘IlluC-Net’, a lightweight U-Net-based architecture integrated with attention mechanisms, specifically tailored to correct uneven background illumination in dermatological macro-photographs—a challenge not adequately addressed in existing literature. Unlike traditional illumination correction methods that often degrade image contrast, or deep learning approaches such as GANs and transformers that overlook illumination inconsistencies and are computationally expensive for edge deployment. the proposed IlluC-Net model effectively corrects background illumination while preserving lesion features and contextual details. This is achieved through the use of attention gates embedded within skip connections, a design not employed in conventional attention U-Nets. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work, has systematically benchmarked attention-based illumination correction specifically for dermatological macro-photographs. Highlights: The key highlights of this work are as follows: • We propose IlluC-Net, a lightweight U-Net-based deep learning architecture with attention mechanisms to correct uneven background illumination in dermatological macro-photographs. • IlluC-Net effectively distinguishes lesions from surrounding skin by ensuring uniform illumination and improving feature visibility. • In qualitative and quantitative evaluations, the IlluC-Net demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning-based illumination correction techniques. • IlluC-Net serves as a robust preprocessing step that improves the reliability of downstream tasks such as lesion segmentation and classification, supporting more accurate clinical diagnosis. 1.3: 1.3 Contents of the paper The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the proposed methodology, including the architectural details of the IlluC-Net model, the dataset used, and the training strategies employed. Section 3 presents the experimental results, performance evaluation, and computational complexity analysis. Finally, Section 4 concludes the paper by summarizing the technical contributions and key research findings, along with a discussion of the limitations and insights into potential directions for future research. 2: 2 Methodology The proposed framework includes a preprocessing pipeline, a U-Net architecture integrated with attention mechanisms. The input consists of a source image with uneven illumination and a target ground-truth image with uniform illumination. Both images are passed through a preprocessing pipeline with pixel normalization and resizing. Image normalization ensures intensity values fall within the desired range, while resizing standardizes the image dimensions, a critical requirement for deep learning models with fixed input sizes. After preprocessing, the resized images are fed into the U-Net with Attention (UNA) block, which consists of an encoder–decoder architecture with skip connections. This architecture is suitable for equalizing the background illumination of macro-photographs. The UNA block effectively captures both low-level and high-level features through its encoder and decoder blocks, which are incorporated with skip connections that preserve spatial information. The integrated attention module further enhances the feature extraction process by enabling the model to focus selectively on pixels that are affected by uneven illumination. The UNA block in IlluC-Net effectively equalizes background illumination in the input images by removing shadows, glare, and non-uniform lighting artifacts. The clinical characteristics of the lesion, such as texture, color, and border features, are well-preserved in the equalized images. The IlluC-Net framework is evaluated using full-reference image quality assessment (IQA) metrics and no-reference IQA metrics. Corrected images produced by IlluC-Net are compared against ground-truth images based on pixel intensity and structural similarity. 2.1: 2.1 Dataset and preprocessing 2.1.1: 2.1.1 Dataset For the simulation of uneven illumination, 152 from the University of Waterloo skin cancer dataset [22] and 147 high-quality macro-photographs from the MED-NODE dataset [23] were selected for training and testing. Uneven background illumination was simulated following the procedure described by Xie et al. [35] . In total, 299 simulated images with uneven illumination were generated, with their corresponding original high-quality images serving as ground-truth references. Fig. 1 presents a sample dermatological macro-photograph under varying illumination conditions. Image (a) depicts the baseline with uniform background lighting. In contrast, images (b), (c), (d), and (e) illustrate different simulated uneven illumination patterns, introducing partial shadowing that can be misinterpreted as lesions by automated segmentation algorithms. These examples highlight how noticeable shadow artifacts can significantly reduce the contrast between the lesion and the background skin. This shows the critical need for efficient illumination correction techniques to ensure diagnostic accuracy in dermatological image analysis. 2.2: 2.2 IlluC-Net model architecture Fig. 2 illustrates the complete architecture of the IlluC-Net model, developed to equalize background illumination in dermatological macro-photographs. The architecture follows a symmetric encoder–decoder structure integrated with attention mechanisms. The encoder progressively learns feature representations through convolutional operations, followed by batch normalization and Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation. These operations are followed by max pooling layers that reduce spatial dimensions while increasing feature depth, enabling the model to capture coarse contextual features essential for understanding global illumination patterns. An input image of size 256 × 256 × 3 is processed through successive convolutional blocks with increasing channel depths of 64, 128, 256, and 512 before reaching the bridge layer, which contains 1024 channels. This bridge layer acts as the transition between the contracting and expanding paths, transferring rich, high-level features to the decoder for accurate image reconstruction. The decoder reconstructs the illumination-corrected image by iteratively upsampling the encoded features and fusing them with corresponding spatial features from the encoder via attention gates. Unlike a standard U-Net [36] , which passes features directly via skip connections, IlluC-Net incorporates attention gates into the skip connections. These gates ensure that only salient features are propagated to the decoder, thereby suppressing irrelevant background information and improving the process of illumination correction. Each decoder block includes an up-convolution layer to restore spatial resolution, followed by concatenation with the attention-weighted features. This is followed by convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU activation for feature refinement. The final output is constructed using a 1 × 1 convolution layer followed by a sigmoid activation function to normalize pixel intensities within the [ 0 , 1 ] range. The proposed architecture effectively removes shadows, glare, and uneven lighting artifacts while preserving key clinical features essential for accurate skin cancer diagnosis. 2.3: 2.3 Loss function and optimization strategy 2.3.1: 2.3.1 Mean squared error loss The loss function employed to train the IlluC-Net model is the mean squared error (MSE) [37] . This function quantifies the pixel-wise difference between the illumination-equalized image generated by IlluC-Net and the corresponding ground-truth image. By minimizing this error, the model learns to produce outputs that closely approximate the true uniform illumination. The MSE loss function is defined as: L MSE = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N I out ( i ) − I gt ( i ) 2 where I out ( i ) denotes the predicted intensity at pixel i , I gt ( i ) is the corresponding ground truth intensity, and N represents the total number of pixels. The use of MSE is well-suited for illumination correction task, as it directly penalizes large deviations in pixel intensity, encouraging the network to produce visually consistent outputs with minimal structural distortion. 2.3.2: 2.3.2 Optimization strategy IlluC-Net is trained using the adaptive moment estimation (Adam) optimizer [38] , which combines the benefits of adaptive gradient estimation and momentum-based updates. The parameter update rule is given by: θ t + 1 = θ t − η v ˆ t + ϵ m ˆ t Here, θ t refers to the model parameters at iteration t , η is the learning rate, and m ˆ t and v ˆ t are the bias-corrected estimates of the first and second moments of the gradients, respectively. The constant ϵ ensures numerical stability during division. 2.4: 2.4 Training of IlluC-Net For model development, 80% of the data is used for training and 20% for testing, with five-fold cross-validation employed to prevent overfitting. The reported results represent the average performance across all folds. The original image size in MED-NODE dataset [23] and University of Waterloo dataset [22] vary between 1024 × 768 and 2048 × 1536 pixels. In this study, images were resized to 256 × 256 to ensure training stability, uniformity across datasets, and computational feasibility, particularly given the deployment target of edge devices with limited memory and processing power. Given the limited size of the dataset, data augmentation techniques such as horizontal and vertical flipping, rotation, zooming, and cropping were applied to improve model generalization [39] . The IlluC-Net model is trained using the MSE loss [37] function, and the optimizer used is Adam [38] with an initial learning rate of 0.001. A learning rate scheduler is used to adjust the learning rate dynamically based on the validation loss plateau. Early stopping strategy is employed to prevent overfitting, terminating training if the validation loss does not improve over 50 consecutive epochs. The model is trained for 500 epochs with mini-batches of size 16. 3: 3 Results and discussion The proposed IlluC-Net model is comprehensively evaluated, both qualitatively and quantitatively, against 7 SOTA illumination correction methods: U-Net [25] , TransUNet [29] , GAN [26] , EnlightenGAN [27] , CSWin-P [31] , IECET [21] , and Suchitra et al. [34] . All experiments were conducted on a system with an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada generation GPU and an AMD Ryzen 9 4000 series CPU with 32 GB of RAM to accelerate computations. varying illumination conditions. 3.1: 3.1 Qualitative analysis The qualitative performance of the proposed IlluC-Net is evaluated and compared with 7 SOTA illumination correction methods, namely U-Net [25] , TransUNet [29] , StillGAN [26] , EnlightenGAN [27] , CSWin-P [31] , IECET [21] , and Suchitra et al. [34] . Figs. 3–5 show the illumination-corrected output images of all methods on three representative dermatological macro-photographs exhibiting varying degrees of uneven illumination. Fig. 3 shows the original image (a) exhibits noticeable uneven illumination, with shadowing along the left edge of the lesion. The ground-truth image (b) exhibits the uniform background lighting. The illumination-corrected image produced by U-Net (c) partially reduces vignetting but retains dark artifacts near the lesion boundary. TransUNet (d) provides slightly better overall brightness but introduces minor textural distortion across the lesion surface. The StillGAN (e) output is oversmoothed, resulting in the loss of fine textural information critical for accurate lesion assessment. The EnlightenGAN (f) output is over-enhanced and overly saturated, producing unnatural skin tone in the corrected image. The CSWin-P (g) equalized background illumination but smoothened the lesion boundaries. The approach developed by Suchitra et al. (i) produces an output image with high brightness. At the same time, IECET (h) overcorrects the image, giving it a yellowish color and loss of natural skin tone. The proposed IlluC-Net (j) produced an output image visually closest to the ground truth (b). The image produced by IlluC-Net effectively equalizes the background illumination, and the lesion color, boundary, and textural features are well preserved without over-saturation or introducing color artifacts. In Fig. 4 , the original image (a) suffers from dark shading across the lower region, obscuring lesion contrast. The U-Net (c) result enhanced the brightness but slightly overexposes the surrounding skin. TransUNet (d) improved over all illumination but highlights unwanted hair structures, reducing diagnostic clarity. The StillGAN (e) output smooths lesion boundaries overly, while EnlightenGAN (f) brightens the lesion center disproportionately, producing reddish hue at lesion center. The CSWin-P (g) method slightly reduced the sharpness of the lesion boundary. The traditional illumination correction methods of IECET (h) and Suchitra et al. (i) produced over-brightened images and altered skin tones, respectively, deviating from the natural appearance. The proposed IlluC-Net (j) effectively equalized the background illumination. The lesion edges and internal pigment structures remain distinct and natural, closely resembling the ground-truth image (b). Fig. 5 presents a more complex lesion with prominent uneven background illumination and shadowing artifacts. The U-Net (c) output shows improved brightness but produced over-enhancement near the lower-right area. TransUNet (d) introduces noise and contrast artifacts. The StillGAN (e) output is over-smoothed, losing the fine lesion borders. In contrast, EnlightenGAN (f) introduced color distortion and high saturation, producing a visually unpleasant image. The CSWin-P (g) and method by Suchitra et al. (i) failed to restore background illumination uniformly, leading to residual shading and unnatural skin color. The IECET (h) output shows washed-out regions in brighter areas. The proposed IlluC-Net (j) produced an output image with good color balance and uniform illumination across the lesion and surrounding skin. The corrected image produced by IlluC-Net closely resembles the ground-truth image (b), preserving both color and textural information required for clinical evaluation. Across all three representative test images, IlluC-Net consistently displays superior qualitative performance compared to traditional, GAN-based, and transformer-based methods. The attention-guided skip connections enable selective focus on illumination-affected regions while suppressing irrelevant background variations. Consequently, IlluC-Net produced illumination corrected images with natural skin tone without introducing any color artifacts, and diagnostically consistent outputs that closely resemble the uniformly illuminated ground-truth images. 3.2: 3.2 Quantitative analysis In this section, a quantitative evaluation of IlluC-Net is conducted against 7 SOTA illumination correction methods, namely U-Net [25] , TransUNet [29] , StillGAN [26] , EnlightenGAN [27] , CSWin-P [31] , IECET [21] , and Suchitra et al. [34] . The analysis is performed on 100 test images under similar experimental conditions. Seven widely used IQA metrics which includes 3 full-reference IQA and 4 no-reference IQA metrics were used to evaluate the performance of the illumination correction methods. Full-reference IQA metrics include Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and MSE. While no-reference IQA metrics include Entropy, Blind/ Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator (BRISQUE), Perception-based Image Quality Evaluator (PIQE), and Naturalness Image Quality Evaluator (NIQE). Higher the value of PSNR, SSIM, and Entropy values indicate better performance, whereas lower value of MSE, BRISQUE, PIQE, and NIQE scores correspond to superior perceptual quality and reduced artifacts in the corrected image [40] . As shown in Table 1 , the proposed IlluC-Net obtained the highest PSNR (35.99 ± 3.15 dB) and SSIM (0.98 ± 0.01) among all the compared methods. These results show that IlluC-Net produces illumination-corrected images that are structurally more consistent with the ground-truth image, effectively maintaining lesion boundaries, color consistency, and overall image fidelity. The significantly lower value of MSE (0.026 ± 0.002) further confirms that the pixel-wise intensity reconstruction error is minimal, highlighting the ability of IlluC-Net to accurately correct uneven background illumination without introducing color distortions. In terms of perceptual quality metrics, IlluC-Net obtained the lowest BRISQUE (27.09 ± 10.43), PIQE (44.39 ± 9.77), and NIQE (0.27 ± 0.02) scores, indicating that the corrected images appear more natural and visually closer to those captured under uniform illumination. These results outperform the transformer-based CSWin-P and TransUNet, as well as GAN-based methods such as StillGAN and EnlightenGAN, which exhibited higher BRISQUE and PIQE scores, suggesting the presence of illumination artifacts and texture inconsistencies. Although the baseline U-Net displayed a slightly higher entropy value (6.85 ± 0.14) compared to IlluC-Net (6.70 ± 0.25), this marginal difference suggests that U-Net retains a slightly broader intensity distribution. However, the perceptual quality and structural similarity achieved by IlluC-Net far surpass the baseline U-Net, indicating that its attention-guided feature fusion enables pixel wise illumination correction and improved preservation of the contrast of the image. Similarly, traditional approaches such as IECET and Suchitra et al. methods shown considerably lower PSNR and SSIM values, confirming their limitations in handling complex and spatially varying illumination patterns. Wang et al. [41] and Nemati et al. [40] , proposed patch-based training strategies for illumination correction in high-resolution images. However, given that IlluC-Net is designed as a lightweight architecture optimized for edge deployment. Venugopal et al. [42] have shown that a resolution of 256 × 256 adequately preserves dermatological features necessary for the diagnosis of skin lesions, while maintaining real-time inference efficiency. 3.3: 3.3 Computational complexity Table 2 shows the comparative analysis of model complexity and inference time per image for different illumination correction methods. The proposed IlluC-Net obtained an optimal trade-off between learnable parameters and inference time, indicating its suitability for real-time deployment in edge devices. With 31.3 million (M) parameters and an average inference time of 90 millisecond (ms) per image, IlluC-Net offers computational efficiency comparable to the baseline U-Net with better performance. In contrast, GAN-based architectures, such as StillGAN (42.4 M) and EnlightenGAN (36.2 M), require more computational resources due to their complex feature extraction and adversarial learning components, resulting in significantly higher inference times of 150 ms and 110 ms, respectively. Similarly, transformer-based models like TransUNet (41.4M) and CSwin-P (72.8M) require extensive self-attention computations and large parameter counts to capture global features. Traditional methods, like IECET (10.5 M) and the method developed by Suchitra et al. are relatively lightweight in terms of model size but computationally slower, with inference times of 170 ms and 110 ms, respectively. They take large inference time due to their pixel-wise or filter-based illumination equalization techniques. These results highlight that IlluC-Net produces superior illumination correction performance with a moderate requirement of computational resources, making it well-suited for integration into CAD systems and edge devices. 4: 4 Conclusion and future scope In this study, we proposed IlluC-Net, a novel deep learning-based framework for illumination correction in dermatological macro- photographs. The architecture effectively integrates local and global contextual features, using a U-Net backbone integrated with an attention mechanism to equalize background lighting effectively. The IlluC-Net model preserves critical structures such as lesion boundaries and texture features that the clinician uses to diagnose skin cancer. The IlluC-Net model was trained using a customized strategy incorporating MSE loss, dynamic learning rate scheduling, and early stopping to prevent overfitting. A curated set of images from the University of Waterloo skin cancer dataset and the MED-NODE dataset was used to evaluate the model’s performance under five-fold cross-validation. Quantitative evaluation showed that IlluC-Net consistently outperforms existing SOTA illumination correction methods, including U-Net, TransUNet, GAN, EnlightenGAN, CSWin-P, and IECET. Quantitative evaluation using PSNR and SSIM confirmed superior reconstruction accuracy and structural preservation, while perceptual quality metrics such as BRISQUE, PIQE, and NIQE validated the natural appearance of the illumination equalized images. Visual inspection further confirmed that the illumination-corrected images produced by IlluC-Net closely resemble the ground-truth, with minimal artifacts and lighting distortions, underscoring its effectiveness in clinical imaging applications. Although the attention module may slightly overcorrect regions with steep illumination gradients, future extensions incorporating multi-scale attention and perceptual loss functions could further mitigate this limitation. Overall, the proposed IlluC-Net framework demonstrates strong potential for integration into CAD systems for skin cancer detection and can be adapted for real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices in future work.

Title: Pixel-level annotations of context region for trustworthy diagnosis of Breast Lymph Node Metastasis from Histopathological WSI Abstract: There is a dearth of annotated images in digital pathology, and annotations are pivotal for supervised automated diagnosis. This work aims to create a set of data on breast lymph node metastatic whole slide images (WSI) that is truly valuable as it is annotated by the domain experts in a very precise and intensive manner. The annotations provided here are of rare kind that has pixel-level labels divided into three categories; first is based on the diagnostically significant tissue regions, second is background tissue and the third is artefacts present in breast lymph node metastatic WSI. High level annotations, as is provided in this work, for areas apart from the metastatic region is crucial for diagnosis as this is the context region which is critical for cancer diagnosis. Breast lymph node metastasis is a severe medical condition that requires significant efforts by pathologists to examine cancer under microscope using glass slides. Automated cancer diagnosis using WSI, the digitized versions of glass slides, needs to be trustworthy and responsible, which is ensured by involving domain experts in the process that begins with identifying diagnostically significant regions on a WSI. In this dataset, a two-stage high-value pixel-level annotation protocol is designed where selected 73 training images of Camelyon16 dataset are annotated by doctors and verified by pathologists for their accuracy. These annotations would help researchers to reliably prepare patches for further processing that can be used as training samples for extracting more such significant regions for data preparation from WSI for diagnosing metastasis. These reliable and trustworthy annotations would help to take it to the clinic from the research lab much quickly. These reliable and trustworthy annotations would help to take it to the clinic from the research lab much quickly. 1: 1 Value of the Data • High-quality, pixel-level labels of diagnostically relevant tissues, background tissues and artefacts are the most precise type of annotations created so far for breast lymph node histopathology WSI. As per the authors’ knowledge the annotations available in databases are either for two class annotations cancer vs normal tissues or multiclass annotations where various types of cancer tissues are annotated. In this dataset precise annotations for the above mentioned three categories are provided. • Pixel-level labels provided by experts are high-value data labels because of their accuracy and reliability. These characteristics are backbone of any supervised machine learning model for disease diagnosis. • These precise annotations are extremely helpful in determining the context region in the diagnosis, which is otherwise neglected due to high cost of annotating these regions. • The xml files can be used to create binary masks from the corresponding WSI to be downloaded from the dataset. The generated masks are used as template to extract patches from the corresponding regions and store them in respective folder to be used for classification enhanced by availability of context regions for classification. • This dataset is prepared in addition to the already available metastatic region annotations in the Camelon16 database. Thus the combined annotations from Camelyon16 and our annotations would help researchers to develop more reliable and trustworthy models for breast metastasis classification. 2: 2 Background Breast cancer is the second most common cancers among woman all over the world [ 1 ]. H&E stained histopathology is the gold standard for breast cancer diagnosis [ 2 ]. Recently, digital pathology has been becoming increasingly popular for automating the diagnosis process. Cancer diagnosis is done by identifying abnormal tissue regions and on these abnormal regions the deep learning diagnostic models are predominantly trained. Models are either trained for binary classification where images are divided into normal and abnormal classes, or multiclass where image regions are divided into multiple classes based on cancer stage or type. There is dearth of annotated data in which the context region which plays a significant role in validating the presence and severity of cancers is labelled at pixel-level. In breast lymph node histopathology, for a single whole slide image, the tissue region, apart from the main lymph node which is also termed as background tissue region holds invaluable information about the cancer its history and possible proliferation [ 3 ]. Thus, the context region is extremely important for making a trustworthy and reliable diagnostic model. The classification models built on context along with the abnormal tissues bear more weightage than the models trained solely on abnormal classes. 3: 3 Data Description The original Camelyon16 is an H&E stained histopathological WSI dataset of breast lymph node metastasis. From this dataset the training set of abnormal class are downloaded, which is available on GigaScience Database [ 4 ]. Out of the total images 73 images are selected from the dataset. The original WSI from the dataset are not included because of the ethical issues. However, link to the original dataset is provided in reference section [ 4 ]. The annotations for three categories, namely tissue, background tissue and artefacts are stored as separate .xml files in their respective folders, the number of xml files generated for each of the categories is mentioned in Table 1 . The annotation along with the masks when combined together can be used to generate patches for three different classes in addition to annotations provided in Camelyon16 dataset as shown in Fig. 1 . These patches can be used to train supervised learning model for further analysis. Tissue region is the portion of the slide that includes the cellular mass, lymphoid tissue and tumour cells. This region also contains small amounts of adipose or other connective tissue, which is present within the lymphoid tissue mass. All other types of tissue visible on the slide, mainly connective tissues like blood, blood vessels, adipose tissue, etc. are marked as 'background tissue'. White background of the WSI is not annotated and is excluded. Various blemishes in slide preparation, such as dirt, hair, crushed tissue, staining artefacts which appear as dark spots or dots or lines, folds in tissue, defocused tissue either due to folds in the tissue or improper focusing while capturing WSI are annotated as “artefact”. An example of annotation is shown in Fig. 2 . A few .tiff files of the binary masks generated using .xml files are provided for reference. The python code, adapted from Camelyon16 dataset, is used for generating this binary mask is also provided in this dataset. 4: 4 Experimental Design, Materials and Methods The annotations in the form of .xml files are obtained my providing domain experts with 73 original Camelyon16 WSI. ASAP which is a WSI viewer cum annotation tool was used, the whole experiment design is visually represented in Fig. 3 . 4.1: 4.1 Primary annotations Medical doctors, trained to identify various tissue types, used polygon annotation tool in the ASAP software to mark regions in three categories; tissue, background tissue, and artefacts. This step is crucial to delineate precise boundaries around specific regions of the slides. 4.2: 4.2 Reviewed annotations A trained pathologist verified all the annotations done by doctors using same ASAP software. This verification ensures the data is reliable as pathologist have thorough understanding of objects present on the slides. Pathologist also ensures the errors present in the primary annotation stage are minimized to make the annotations more accurate and robust for downstream processing. Limitations: Limitations In some images the tissue region lies totally inside the background tissue region. To extract masks for only background tissue region image subtraction is needed. This exhaustive annotation was done only on 73 WSI of abnormal class of training set. Only abnormal class is annotated because its background contains most of the context for classification. Artefacts for the WSI is not available because of the absence or negligible presence on the slides. The data size is small, this number maybe insufficient in dealing with various biases possibly present in the WSIs. Annotation subjectivity could be an issue because of inter-observer variability although minimised using standard protocols and terminologies. Large number of data points in annotation file take tremendous amount of time for mask generation. Users need to install python based multiresolutionImageInterface library for using the code provided in the repository. Although users can implement the same using open source libraries like openslide for the same. Title: Probabilistic smooth attention for deep multiple instance learning in medical imaging Abstract: The Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) paradigm is attracting plenty of attention in medical imaging classification, where labeled data is scarce. MIL methods cast medical images as bags of instances (e.g. patches in whole slide images, or slices in CT scans), and only bag labels are required for training. Deep MIL approaches have obtained promising results by aggregating instance-level representations via an attention mechanism to compute the bag-level prediction. These methods typically capture both local interactions among adjacent instances and global, long-range dependencies through various mechanisms. However, they treat attention values deterministically, potentially overlooking uncertainty in the contribution of individual instances. In this work we propose a novel probabilistic framework that estimates a probability distribution over the attention values, and accounts for both global and local interactions. In a comprehensive evaluation involving eleven state-of-the-art baselines and three medical datasets, we show that our approach achieves top predictive performance in different metrics. Moreover, the probabilistic treatment of the attention provides uncertainty maps that are interpretable in terms of illness localization. The Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) paradigm is attracting plenty of attention in medical imaging classification, where labeled data is scarce. MIL methods cast medical images as bags of instances (e.g. patches in whole slide images, or slices in CT scans), and only bag labels are required for training. Deep MIL approaches have obtained promising results by aggregating instance-level representations via an attention mechanism to compute the bag-level prediction. These methods typically capture both local interactions among adjacent instances and global, long-range dependencies through various mechanisms. However, they treat attention values deterministically, potentially overlooking uncertainty in the contribution of individual instances. In this work we propose a novel probabilistic framework that estimates a probability distribution over the attention values, and accounts for both global and local interactions. In a comprehensive evaluation involving eleven state-of-the-art baselines and three medical datasets, we show that our approach achieves top predictive performance in different metrics. Moreover, the probabilistic treatment of the attention provides uncertainty maps that are interpretable in terms of illness localization. 1: 1 Introduction Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a popular machine learning framework in which the model is trained on sets of instances, called bags, rather than individual instances [1] . Unlike the traditional supervised learning framework, which needs the label of each instance, in MIL only the label of the bag is required. This approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios where labelling many individual instances is impractical or prohibitively expensive. This is especially relevant in the context of medical imaging, where annotations are extremely costly [2] . Fig. 1 shows two illustrative examples of MIL problems within this context: (i) cancer detection from Whole Slide Images (WSIs), where the WSI represents the bag, and the patches are the instances; and (ii) intracranial hemorrhage detection from Computerized Tomographic (CT) scans, where the full scan represents the bag and the slices at different heights are the instances. Several methods have been proposed for learning in the MIL scenario, with Deep Learning (DL) approaches achieving remarkable results [2] . A seminal work in the area was the one by Ilse et al. [3] , which proposes the attention-based MIL (ABMIL) method. ABMIL features an attention mechanism with the ability to focus on the most relevant instances. The attention assigned to each instance can serve as a proxy to find instances with a positive label, i.e., those showing evidence of the disease or injury. With this in mind, the attention mechanism has been improved in various ways [4–6] . However, these methods have a major limitation: they are unable to capture interactions between instances because the attention mechanism treats them independently. Ultimately, this negatively affects the discriminative performance of these approaches. Based on the existing literature, two types of interactions among instances have been considered: global and local. Global interactions are those that may exist between any pair of instances in a bag. Shao et al. [7] showed that they can contain important information and proposed the TransMIL model, which includes a Transformer encoder to capture them. Note that the self-attention mechanism used in Transformers is a natural choice to model these interactions since it computes a similarity score between each pair of instances. For this reason, different variations of this mechanism were included to boost the performance of existing MIL models [8–10] . Local interactions are those that exist between neighboring instances. A natural way of modeling them is to treat each bag as a graph, where the instances are the nodes and the edges between them represent these local interactions. This is the approach followed by recent works, which have exploited them in combination with global interactions [9,11–13] and alone using Graph Neural Networks [14,15] . Note that an important difference between global and local interactions is that global interactions are learned from the data, while local interactions are known beforehand and encoded into the model. Recently, we proposed an interesting way of leveraging local interactions, called Smooth Attention (SA) [16] . It is based on the idea that, in CT scans, a slice is usually adjacent to slices with the same label, see Fig. 1 (b). Since the attention values act as a proxy to estimate these labels, they should inherit this property. To enforce this spatial constraint, SA proposes a novel regularization term based on the Dirichlet energy [17] , which is used to train the ABMIL model. It obtained very promising results in the intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) detection task, outperforming the vanilla ABMIL and other related approaches. However, SA does not account for global correlations, and it estimates attention values deterministically. The deterministic nature of SA and the other previously mentioned methods prevents them from expressing uncertainty in their predictions. However, the ability to model uncertainty is a crucial requirement in medical diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose the Probabilistic Smooth Attention (ProbSA) framework – a probabilistic generalization of SA – which introduces the following key contributions: 1. ProbSA provides a general probabilistic formulation. When a deterministic procedure is used for inference, we recover SA as a particular case. When Bayesian inference is leveraged instead, we obtain a new method that estimates attention values through a full probability distribution. As we will see, this yields enhanced predictive performance and allows for uncertainty estimation in the predictions. 2. ProbSA handles both local and global interactions. We explain how the local interactions in [16] can be combined with global interactions to yield a new method superior to the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, which usually leverage both types of interactions. 3. We provide a comprehensive evaluation as required for archival work. ProbSA is evaluated using three different datasets (two more than 16 ) covering two different medical imaging problems: cancer detection in WSIs and hemorrhage detection in CT scans. Also, ProbSA is compared against ten SOTA methods in MIL (six more than those used in [16] ). The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the foundations of our work (ABMIL and SA). Section 3 presents the novel ProbSA framework, discussing the probabilistic model and inference as well as the combination with global interactions. Section 4 discusses the empirical evaluation of the model, including dataset description, experimental setup, ablation study to understand ProbSA, and comparison against SOTA methods. Section 5 provides the main conclusions and limitations. 2: 2 Background Section 2.1 describes the MIL problem and reviews the attention-based MIL model (ABMIL) [3] , which is at the basis of the proposed approach. Section 2.2 describes our deterministic approach to introduce smoothness in the attention values, previously published as Smooth Attention (SA). 2.1: 2.1 Attention-based multiple instance learning In MIL, the training set consists of pairs of the form ( X , Y ) , where X ∈ R N × P is a bag of instances and Y ∈ { 0 , 1 } is the bag label. Each bag is composed of a variable number of instances, i.e., X = [ x 1 , … , x N ] T , where x n ∈ R P are the instances. Each instance x n has an unobserved label y n ∈ { 0 , 1 } which is not available during training. It is assumed that Y = max { y 1 , … , y N } , that is, a bag X is considered positive if and only if there is at least one positive instance in the bag. The goal is to learn a function that predicts the label of previously unseen bags. Attention-based MIL (ABMIL) was proposed by Ilse et al. [3] to learn in this scenario. This method maps the input bag X to a bag representation z ∈ R D , which is later used to predict the bag label. To compute this representation they use the attention-based pooling, which assigns an attention value f n to each instance x n . This value indicates its importance within the bag and can be used as a proxy to estimate the instance label y n . Formally, (1) z = H ⊤ Softmax ( f ) , where H = [ h ( x 1 ) , … , h ( x N ) ] ⊤ , h : R P → R D is a neural network applied to each instance, f = [ f 1 , … , f N ] ⊤ , and f n = w ⊤ tanh ( W h n ) , with W ∈ R D f × D and w ∈ R D f being trainable weights. Note that in ABMIL both the intermediate embeddings h n and the attention values f are obtained by applying a transformation independently to each instance. As a result, they will be the same regardless of what other instances are in the bag or what structure the bag has. In other words, the dependencies between the instances are neglected. 2.2: 2.2 Smooth attention (SA): Deterministic attention smoothing In order to take into account the dependencies between the instances during training, Smooth Attention (SA) [16] proposes to leverage the following property of medical images: if an instance shows evidence of a lesion, neighboring instances likely contain it too, see Fig. 1 . Therefore, for the attention maps to estimate the instance labels accurately, they should also exhibit this smoothing property: the attention value assigned to an instance should be similar to the values assigned to surrounding instances. SA restricts the solution space by discarding solutions with highly variable attention maps. This is achieved through the Dirichlet energy , a well-known functional that measures the variability of a function defined on a graph [17] . For a function f ∈ R N defined on a graph with adjacency matrix A = [ A i j ] ∈ R N × N , the Dirichlet energy of f is given by, (2) E D ( f , A ) = 1 2 ∑ i = 1 N ∑ j = 1 N A i j ( f i − f j ) 2 = f ⊤ L f , where L is the graph Laplacian matrix L = D − A , and D ∈ R N × N is the degree matrix, D = Diag ( D 1 , … , D N ) , D n = ∑ i A n i . SA treats the attention values as a function defined on the bag graph, which is defined by A i j > 0 if instances x i and x j are neighbors, and A i j = 0 otherwise. The Dirichlet energy is used to define a regularization term that penalizes solutions with highly variable attention maps. Formally, given a dataset of bags { X 1 , … , X B } , with corresponding bag labels { Y 1 , … , Y B } and adjacency matrices { A 1 , … , A B } , SA uses the architecture proposed in ABMIL and seeks to minimize the following objective, (3) ∑ b = 1 B { − log p ( Y b ∣ X b ) + λ E D ( f b , A b ) } , where p ( Y b ∣ X b ) = Bernouilli ( Y b ∣ ψ ( H b ⊤ Softmax ( f b ) ) ) , λ > 0 is an hyperparameter, ψ : R D → [ 0 , 1 ] is the bag classifier, H b and f b are as in Eq. (1) . SA achieved very promising results in the task of hemorrhage detection, and here we extend it in two ways. First, since its architecture is based on ABMIL, it does not include global interactions, which has proven successful in previous works. Second, like the rest of current SOTA deep MIL methods, it is a deterministic approach. By estimating a probability distribution over the attention values, we will achieve enhanced discriminative performance as well as interpretable uncertainty estimations. In the following section, we propose the Probabilistic Smooth Attention (ProbSA) framework, a generalization of SA that addresses these two aspects. 3: 3 Probabilistic smooth attention (ProbSA) In this section, we describe the novel Probabilistic Smooth Attention framework. Section 3.1 describes the Bayesian formulation of the model. In Section 3.2 we describe how to include global interactions in the architecture of the proposed methodology. Finally, Section 3.3 provides an overview of the different model variants proposed in this work. 3.1: 3.1 Model formulation We assume we are given a training set of bags X = { X 1 , … , X B } , with corresponding bag labels Y = { Y 1 , … , Y B } and adjacency matrices A = { A 1 , … , A B } . Recall that X b ∈ R N b × D , Y b ∈ { 0 , 1 } , and A b ∈ R N b × N b . Since we will be dealing with bags of different sizes, in the following we denote R N × D = ∪ m ∈ N R m × D , R N = ∪ m ∈ N R m , and ( 0 , + ∞ ) N = ∪ m ∈ N ( 0 , + ∞ ) m . Probabilistic model and inference. We model the attention values of each bag X b as an unobserved latent variable f b . The smoothing property is encoded as a prior distribution given by (4) p ( f b ∣ A b ) ∝ exp ( − E D ( f b , A b ) ) . This corresponds to the conditional and simultaneous autoregressive models in the statistics literature [18] . Following ABMIL [3] , the attention values are used to compute the bag label likelihood, (5) p ( Y b ∣ X b , f b ) = Bernouilli ( Y b ∣ ψ ( H b ⊤ Softmax ( f b ) ) ) , where H b = H ( X b ) , H : R N × P → R N × D is a bag transformation, and ψ : R D → [ 0 , 1 ] is the bag classifier. Note that in the original ABMIL and in SA the bag transformation H is implemented by applying a neural network independently to every instance. We will explain how to include global interactions in H in Section 3.2 . Finally, the joint probabilistic model is obtained assuming independence across bags, (6) p ( Y , F ∣ X , A ) = ∏ b = 1 B p ( Y b ∣ X b , f b ) p ( f b ∣ A b ) , where F = { f 1 , … , f B } . Making predictions in this model requires computing the posterior of the bag label given the observations. More precisely, given a new bag X * , the corresponding bag label Y * is obtained from, (7) p ( Y * ∣ X * , Y ) = ∫ p ( Y * ∣ X * , f * ) p ( f * ∣ X * , Y ) d f * . However, computing the posterior p ( f ∣ X , Y ) in closed form is not possible. To address this, we follow the Variational Inference (VI) [19] approach: we approximate it using a variational distribution q ( f ∣ X , Y ) , which we write as q ( f ∣ X ) in what follows. Using the variational distribution, we can make predictions using (8) p ( Y * ∣ X * , Y ) ≈ ∫ p ( Y * ∣ X * , f * ) q ( f * ∣ X * ) d f * = (9) = E q ( f * ∣ X * ) [ p ( Y * ∣ X * , f * ) ] . The optimal choice of q ( f ∣ X ) is obtained by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true posterior and the variational distribution [19] . This is equivalent to maximizing the following Evidence Lower BOund (ELBO), (10) ELBO = ∑ b = 1 B E q ( f b ∣ X b ) [ log p ( Y b ∣ X b , f b ) p ( f b ∣ A b ) q ( f b ∣ X b ) ] . Unfortunately, it is not possible to obtain the optimal variational distribution in closed form. Instead, we proceed as in [20] : we restrict q ( f ∣ X ) to belong to some parameterized family of distributions and adjust its parameters by maximizing the ELBO in Eq. (10) . In the following, we consider two choices for this family: as a Gaussian and as a Dirac delta. Modelling q ( f ∣ X ) as a Gaussian. In this case, we parameterize the variational distribution as a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a diagonal covariance matrix, (11) q ( f ∣ X ) = N ( f ∣ μ ( X ) , Σ ( X ) ) , Σ ( X ) = Diag ( σ ( X ) ) , where μ : R N × D → R N and σ : R N × D → ( 0 , + ∞ ) N are implemented using neural networks. With this choice, the ELBO in Eq. (10) can be written as (12) ELBO = ∑ b = 1 B { E q ( f b ∣ X b ) [ log p ( Y b ∣ X b , f b ) ] − KL [ q ( f b ∣ X b ) , p ( f b ∣ A b ) ] } . Since sampling from this distribution is very efficient, we can approximate the expectations in the first term and Eq. (9) – Eq. (10) using Monte Carlo sampling and the reparameterization trick [20] . Moreover, the KL divergence in the second term admits the following closed-form expression, (13) KL [ q ( f b ∣ X b ) , p ( f b ∣ A b ) ] = E D ( μ ( X b ) , A b ) + Tr ( L b Σ ( X b ) ) + (14) − 1 2 ( log ( | Σ ( X b ) | 2 | L b | ) − N b ) , which can be computed efficiently. Note that the KL divergence contains the Dirichlet energy used by SA plus a new term that regularizes the covariance matrix. Informally speaking, if we make the covariance matrix very small, Σ ( · ) → 0 , the KL divergence becomes the regularization term used by SA, see Eq. (3) . This can be formalized by modeling q ( f ∣ X ) as a Dirac delta, as follows. Recovering SA: q ( f ∣ X ) as a Dirac delta. We define the variational distribution as a deterministic distribution , i.e., a distribution with zero variance. To do so, we resort to the notion of Dirac delta [21] . However, since it is not a proper function we cannot use it to define our variational density. Fortunately, there exists mathematical machinery to use this concept rigorously [21,22] , see Appendix A for a precise justification of the following statements. We define (15) q ( f ∣ X ) = δ ( f − μ ( X ) ) = { ∞ if f = μ ( X ) , 0 otherwise , where δ ( · ) is the Dirac delta and μ : R N × D → R N is implemented using a neural network. Informally speaking, q ( f ∣ X ) assigns all the probability to one point which is determined by the output of μ . The ELBO becomes (16) ELBO = ∑ b = 1 B { log p ( Y b ∣ X b , f b = μ ( X b ) ) − E D ( μ ( X b ) , A b ) } , which is the negative of the objective used by SA with λ = 1 , recall Eq. (3) . Therefore, the probabilistic model ProbSA presented in this section has our previous SA [16] as a particular case. The loss objective. Whatever choice we make for q ( f ∣ X ) (as a Gaussian or as a Dirac delta), we must maximize the corresponding ELBO with respect to the parameters of the neural network. In both cases, the negative of the ELBO leads to the following minimization objective, (17) L ELBO = − ELBO = L LL + L KL , where L LL is the negative log-likelihood and L KL is a KL regularization term, see Table 1 . Previous works have introduced a balancing hyperparameter λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] to control the strength of the regularization and alleviate KL collapse [23] . Following this idea, we propose to minimize the following objective, (18) L = L LL + λ L KL . Note that by setting λ = 1 we recover the negative of the ELBO, and by setting λ = 0 we drop the KL regularization. To avoid the KL vanishing problem, some works have proposed to vary the value of λ during training, following different schedules [24] . We will use the cyclical annealing schedule proposed by Fu et al. [24] , and analyze its impact on the performance in Section 4.2 . Making predictions. To predict the bag label Y * of a new bag X * , we must approximate the integral in Eq. (9) . The variational posterior choices we have presented facilitate efficient sampling. Thus, we draw S samples { f 1 * , … , f S * } from q ( f * ∣ X * ) and compute (19) p ( Y * ∣ X * , Y ) ≈ 1 S ∑ s = 1 S p ( Y * ∣ X * , f s * ) . This process is illustrated in Fig. 2 . For a given input bag, one or more samples are drawn from the variational attention distribution and then used to compute the predicted bag label according to Eq. (19) . 3.2: 3.2 Incorporating global interactions Both SA and the proposed ProbSA take into account local interactions through a regularization term in the training objective, see Eq. (18) . However, previous works in deep MIL have demonstrated the benefits of including both global and local interactions [9,11] . Note that local interactions provide information about the environment of each instance but do not account for long-range dependencies. For example, detecting some types of tumors requires finding certain structures in distant regions within the WSI [7,9] . Next, we explain how we can include global interactions in the proposed ProbSA. As evidenced in Fig. 2 , one of the main advantages of ProbSA is that it is architecture agnostic . This means that we can choose any architecture to implement the bag transformation H , the bag classifier ψ , or the attention distribution networks ( μ , Σ ) , and still use the same training objective. Therefore, global interactions can be included by implementing H as a Transformer encoder, (20) H ( X ) = TransformerEnc ( X ) . At the core of the Transformer encoder module is the self-attention mechanism, which processes the input by calculating similarity scores between all pairs of instances in the bag. These scores determine how much attention each instance should pay to others, allowing the model to capture (global) contextual relationships effectively. Each layer of the Transformer encoder leverages multiple heads in the self-attention mechanism, along with skip-connections and pre-layer normalization [25] . More details can be found in Appendix B . 3.3: 3.3 Summary of the proposed models In the previous subsections, we introduced key design choices within the ProbSA framework that define different model variants. Specifically, there are two options for the variational posterior q ( f ∣ X ) and two for the bag transformation H . These choices can be naturally combined, resulting in four distinct model variants. Table 1 summarizes these variants and the fundamental differences between them. ABMIL and T-ABMIL stand for the two choices for the bag transformation H . Similarly, Σ = 0 and Σ = Diag refer to the two choices for the variational posterior q ( f ∣ X ) . Note that we write Σ = 0 for the Dirac delta variational posterior since we recover it by making the variance infinitely small in the Gaussian, Σ ( · ) → 0 . The variants with Σ = 0 can be regarded as an extension of the deterministic method proposed in our previous work [16] . They are deterministic because they learn a degenerate distribution for the attention values. In contrast, the variants with Σ = Diag learn a Gaussian distribution, from which we can sample and study its moments, see Section 4.4 . In the following section, we conduct extensive experimentation to evaluate these four variants. 4: 4 Experiments In this section, we evaluate the proposed method on three real medical image classification problems, comparing it against ten SOTA MIL methods. Our code will be made publicly available upon the acceptance of the paper at the following Github repository: . In Section 4.1 we describe the experimental framework. In Section 4.2 we perform an ablation study to better understand the proposed method. In Section 4.3 we compare our method against ten SOTA methods in MIL. Finally, Section 4.4 shows how the probabilistic treatment can help in by pointing out regions of the attention maps where the method may not be confident enough. 4.1: 4.1 Experimental framework Datasets. We evaluate the proposed method on three medical MIL datasets: RSNA [26] , PANDA [27] , and CAMELYON16 [28] . In RSNA the goal is to detect acute intracranial hemorrhage from CT scans. There are 1150 CT scans, each of them having from 24 to 57 slices. They are labeled as having hemorrhage (at least one slice shows evidence of hemorrhage) or not hemorrhage (no slice shows evidence of hemorrhage). In PANDA the goal is to detect prostate cancer from microscopy scans of prostate biopsy samples. It is composed of 10,616 WSIs at 10 × magnification. In CAMELYON16 the goal is to detect breast cancer metastasis. It consists of 400 WSIs at 20 × magnification. In both PANDA and CAMELYON16, we extract patches of size 512 × 512 using the method proposed by Lu et al. [4] . Each WSI is labeled as tumorous (at least one patch shows evidence of tumor) and non-tumorous (no patch shows evidence of tumor). For RSNA and CAMELYON16, we use the standard train/test partition. For PANDA, since the labels for the test set have not been released, we use the train/test split proposed by Silva-Rodriguez et al. [29] . We split the initial train data into five different train/validation splits. Every model is trained on each of these splits and then evaluated on the test set. We report the average performance on this test set. Metrics. Medical imaging datasets are typically imbalanced, containing more negative examples (those that do not show evidence of disease or lesion) than positive examples (those that show evidence of disease or lesion). For this reason, we analyze the performance of each method using the area under the ROC curve (AUROC) and the F1 score. We also report the average rank: we sort the different methods according to their performance on each tuple (metric, dataset), and report the average position. Feature extraction. Neither the proposed method nor the methods we compare with can be trained end-to-end alongside a feature extractor. This limitation arises because, for the datasets under consideration, almost no single bag can fit within the memory of commercially available GPUs. For this reason, we extract features from each instance using a pre-trained model. To choose this model, we note that previous works have pointed out the importance of using large-scale domain-aligned feature extractors [30,31] , with several improvements in MIL [6,7,9] . For pathology data (such as PANDA and CAMELYON16), the mentioned studies provide the weights of these models. However, we have not been able to find them for CT scans. For this reason, for the RSNA dataset, we use a ResNet50 pre-trained on Imagenet. For PANDA and CAMELYON16, we use a ResNet50 pre-trained using the Barlow Twins self-supervised learning method on a huge dataset of WSIs patches [30] , whose weights can be found online. 1 1 Weights available here Both choices transform the input instance into a vector of P = 2048 components. Finally, note that we use the same features for every MIL method, which ensures a fair comparison. MIL methods and architectures. We compare the proposed ProbSA with SOTA MIL methods. To ensure a fair comparison, we divide them into two groups, depending on whether or not they take into account global interactions through the self-attention mechanism. In the first group, we include those methods that do not account for these interactions: the proposed ABMIL+ProbSA, ABMIL [3] , CLAM [4] , DSMIL [6] , PatchGCN [15] , and DTFD-MIL [5] . In the second group we include those methods that do account for these interactions: the proposed T-ABMIL+ProbSA, TransMIL [7] , SETMIL [12] , GTP [11] , IIBMIL [32] , CAMIL [9] , and VMIL [10] . Note that the proposed ProbSA outperforms the related [13] , which uses the same datasets and metrics. For every method, we use the original implementation, which is publicly available on their GitHub repositories. We modify the number of layers and their dimensions to make the comparison under the same parameter budget. Every method first transforms the input instances using one fully connected layer with 512 units ( D = 512 ). The different variants of the attention pooling used by ABMIL, CLAM, DSMIL, PatchGCN, and DTFD-MIL are implemented with an inner dimension of D f = 128 . The different transformer encoders used by TransMIL, SETMIL, GTP, IIBMIL, and CAMIL have 2 transformer layers; key, query, and value dimensions of 512, and 8 attention heads. The bag-embedding classifier is implemented using one fully connected layer. The attention pooling used by ABMIL+ProbSA and T-ABMIL+ProbSA is the same as in ABMIL. The transformer encoder in T-ABMIL+ProbSA uses Pytorch’s implementation of dot product attention 2 2 Pytorch’s implementation of dot product attention is available here . The bag adjacency matrices (see Eq. (2) ) are constructed at the beginning of training and remain static throughout the process–that is, they are not learned or updated during optimization. Following the approach of [9] , we compute edge weights based on the inverse of the distance between corresponding instances in the feature space. This ensures that, if the feature space is appropriately structured, the weight between a positive and a negative instance will be close to zero, which suppresses attention smoothing across boundaries. Training setup. To ensure fair and reproducible conditions, we trained each method under the same setup. Since the authors of IIBMIL do not share their training code, we implemented the training procedure following the description in the original manuscript. The number of epochs was set to 100. We used the Adam optimizer with the default Pytorch configuration. The base learning rate was set to 10 − 4 . We adopted a slow training start using Pytorch’s LinearLR scheduler with start_factor=0.1 and total_iters=10 . During training, we monitored the bag AUROC in the validation set and kept the weights that obtained the best results in terms of bag AUROC. In RSNA and PANDA, the batch size was set to 32. In CAMELYON16, it was set to 4 for non-transformer methods, and to 1 for transformer-based methods. For SETMIL, however, we had to set it to 1 in PANDA and CAMELYON16 due to its high GPU memory requirements. In RSNA and PANDA, we weighted the loss function to account for the imbalance between positive and negative bags. All experiments were performed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090. 4.2: 4.2 Ablation study: Analyzing the novel ProbSA The aim of this subsection is to study the effect of three key components of our method: the baseline method on top of which it is implemented (ABMIL vs T-ABMIL), the hyperparameter λ , and the variational posterior q ( f ∣ X ) .
