However, the Gaussian posterior has an advantage over the Dirac delta: it naturally produces instance uncertainty maps, as will be discussed in Section 4.4 . 4.3: 4.3 Comparison against existing methods The goal of this subsection is to compare the proposed ProbSA with SOTA deep MIL methods. As we described in Section 4.1 , we categorize these methods into two families to ensure a fair comparison in terms of their architectural capabilities. The first group comprises methods that do not model global interactions within their architecture. This group includes our ABMIL+ProbSA. The second group consists of methods that incorporate global interactions, typically leveraging the self-attention mechanism. Our T-ABMIL+ProbSA falls into this category. Methods without global interactions. Table 2 shows the results in terms of AUROC and F1 for methods that do not account for global interactions. The average rank for each metric is shown in Fig. 4 (a). The proposed ProbSA with a Gaussian variational posterior ( Σ = Diag ) achieves the highest rank and the best result in four out of six (dataset, metric) pairs. We observe that PatchGCN achieves the best performance in PANDA and the second-best rank overall. This can be attributed to the fact that its architecture is the only one that incorporates local interactions through the graph convolutional layer. Methods with global interactions. Table 3 shows the results in terms of AUROC and F1 for methods that do not account for global interactions. The average rank for each metric is shown in Fig. 4 (b). The two variants of the proposed ProbSA are in the top 3. The Dirac delta variant ( Σ = 0 ) yields the best AUROC rank, while the Gaussian variant ( Σ = Diag ) yields the best F1 rank, see Fig. 4 (b). Interestingly, the Gaussian variant performs best in PANDA and is very competitive in CAMELYON16, where it obtains the highest F1, but falls short in RSNA. We observe that IIBMIL and VMIL perform notably worse on the CAMELYON16 dataset, despite achieving competitive results on RSNA and PANDA. This discrepancy can be attributed to the challenging nature of CAMELYON16. In this dataset, bags are significantly larger – containing, on average, approximately five times more instances per bag than PANDA – and the proportion of positive instances is very low. Since both IIBMIL and VMIL rely on an instance-level classifier that requires the identification of positive instances during training, the difficulty in locating positive instances in CAMELYON16 likely hampers the training process, leading to inaccurate predictions. Performance in RSNA. Finally, we observe that all methods perform significantly worse on the RSNA dataset compared to the other two. This discrepancy can be attributed to the feature extractor used for RSNA, which was not pretrained on data from this domain, resulting in a feature space with reduced representational capacity. 4.4: 4.4 Exploring instance predictions We conclude the experimental section by exploring the localization capabilities of each method. Recall that deep MIL methods usually assign a scalar to each instance that reflects its importance within the bag. For simplicity, we will refer to these scalars as attention values , although they can be obtained in different ways (e.g., using GradCam as in GTP [11] ). The proposed ProbSA, instead of assigning an attention value to each instance, outputs a probability distribution, denoted as q ( f ∣ X ) . In this section, we show that the first and second-order moments of the Gaussian variational posterior N ( μ ( X ) , Σ ( X ) ) provide important information for illness localization. To show this, we analyse the attention maps produced by ProbSA and compare them to those from other methods. We display the attention maps of a CT scan from RSNA in Fig. 5 , a WSI from PANDA in Fig. 7 , and a WSI from CAMELYON16 in Fig. 6 . Additional attention maps, including two more CT scans, two WSIs from PANDA, and two WSIs from CAMELYON16, are provided in C . In total, we present attention maps for methods from each family across three representative positive bags from each dataset. Notably, the instance labels displayed are used strictly for evaluation purposes and were not available during training. ProbSA is aligned with previous works. Previous works have shown that positive instances, i.e., those that are unhealthy, typically receive high attention values. This enables one to locate areas containing hemorrhage (in the case of RSNA) or cancerous regions (in the case of PANDA and CAMELYON16). Figs. 5–7 show that the attention maps generated by ProbSA also exhibit this desired pattern, demonstrating performance comparable to other leading methods, including DTFD-MIL, PatchGCN, GTP, and CAMIL. ProbSA reduces false positives. Other methods tends to produce undesirable medium-to-high intensity isolated red spots in healthy areas, falsely indicating unhealthy instances. A clear example of this phenomena is in Fig. 7 , where PatchGCN and DTFD-MIL assign high attention to healthy patches. Other examples are Figs. 5, C.3 , C.7 , and C.8 . Note that these spots do not appear on the maps generated by ProbSA. We attribute this behaviour to the training objective, which encourages the model to produce smooth attention maps, minimizing isolated high-attention regions in healthy areas. Attention variance flags wrong predictions. In practice, there are situations where the attention maps are not accurate. For example, in Fig. 6 none of the considered methods completely detects the cancerous area. Unlike the rest of the methods, the novel probabilistic ProbSA includes a mechanism to measure uncertainty, and one would expect that these wrong predictions are flagged with high variance. Indeed, in Fig. 6 we observe that ProbSA assigns high variance to these incorrectly predicted instances. Fig. C.2 and C.5 show a similar behaviour: as the other competing methods, ProbSA wrongly assigns high attention values to healthy instances but, unlike those baselines, it flags out these instances through a high variance value. 5: 5 Conclusion and limitations In this work, we have introduced ProbSA, a new attention-based deep MIL approach for medical imaging that accounts for both local and global interactions among instances in the bag. Local interactions, which refer to dependencies among neighbouring instances, are introduced by favouring smooth attention values within the bag. Global interactions, which are longer-range dependencies, are modelled using a Transformer encoder. Moreover, we propose a probabilistic formulation that estimates attention values through a probability distribution, instead of deterministically through a single numeric value. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method that tackles both types of interactions in a probabilistic manner. We show enhanced predictive performance against current SOTA deep MIL approaches, as well as interpretability of the attention uncertainty maps provided by the probabilistic treatment. There exist two main limitations to the proposed approach. First, we have only analyzed two possibilities for the variational attention distribution: a Dirac delta, which leads to a deterministic treatment, and a Gaussian distribution with a diagonal covariance matrix, which can be treated through the re-parametrization trick and is computationally tractable. However, more expressive variational distributions, possibly accounting for different modes, could be leveraged at a higher computational cost. Second, the proposed method does not solve the localization issues of current attention-based deep MIL approaches. Whereas the uncertainty maps are useful to highlight low-confidence regions, the mean of the attention does not accurately estimate the instance labels in every case, similar to existing methods. In future work, alongside addressing the aforementioned limitations, we will explore alternative priors to enforce smoothness in the attention maps. However, other approaches different than the one used in this study may render an intractable KL divergence term, and thus they would require careful handling.

Title: SKF-YOLO: An enhanced method for real-time blood cell detection Abstract: In biomedicine, accurate detection of blood cells in microscopic images is essential for disease diagnosis. However, challenges like cell adhesion and overlapping often lead to missed detections and lower accuracy with traditional methods. To address these issues, this paper introduces an algorithm called SKF-YOLO, which builds on enhancements made to YOLOv11n. The algorithm incorporates several innovative components: a P6 detection head to improve the detection of large blood cells; the Single-Head Self-Attention (SHSA) module embedded in the backbone’s C3K2 module to enhance small-target localization in complex backgrounds; the KernelWarehouse module, which reduces the size of convolutional kernels while increasing their number for better computational efficiency; and the Focaler-MPDIoU loss function, derived from Focaler-IoU and MPDIoU, that emphasizes difficult samples to increase the model’s robustness. Tests on the BCCD blood cell dataset demonstrate SKF-YOLO’s superior performance, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 94.1 % and an Average Precision (AP) of 96.1 % for platelets. Compared to the baseline YOLOv11n, SKF-YOLO improves mAP by 2.6 % and reduces computation by 2.5 GFLOPs. These results confirm that SKF-YOLO outperforms other algorithms in blood cell detection and recognition, fulfilling the needs of lightweight target detection and offering valuable insights for future blood cell analysis in medical imaging.

Title: Towards a cardiovascular magnetic resonance foundation model for multi-task cardiac image analysis Abstract: Background Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is a complex imaging modality requiring a broad variety of image processing tasks for comprehensive assessment of the study. Recently, foundation models (FM) have shown promise for automated image analyses in natural images (NI). In this study, a CMR-specific vision FM was developed and then finetuned in a supervised manner for nine different imaging tasks typical to a CMR workflow, including classification, segmentation, landmark localization, and pathology detection. Methods A ViT-S/8 model was trained in a self-supervised manner using DINO on 36 million CMR images from 27,524 subjects from three sources (UK Biobank and two clinical centers). The model was then finetuned for nine tasks: classification (sequence, cine view), segmentation (cine SAX, cine LAX, LGE SAX, Mapping SAX), landmark localization, pathology detection (LGE, cardiac disease), on data from various sources (both public and three clinical datasets). The results were compared against metrics from state-of-the-art methods on the same tasks. A comparable baseline model was also trained on the same datasets for direct comparison. Additionally, the effect of pretraining strategy, as well as generalization and few-shot performance (training on few labeled samples) was explored for the pretrained model, compared to the baseline. Results The proposed model obtained similar performance or moderate improvements to results reported in the literature in most tasks (except disease detection), without any task-specific optimization of methodology. The proposed model outperformed the baseline in most cases, with an average increase of 6.8% points (pp) for cine view classification, and 0.1 to 1.8 pp for segmentation tasks. The proposed method also obtained generally lower standard deviations in the metrics. Improvements of 3.7 and 6.6 pp for hyperenhancement detection from LGE and 14 pp for disease detection were observed. Ablation studies highlighted the importance of pretraining strategy, architecture, and the impact of domain shifts from pretraining to finetuning. Moreover, CMR-pretrained model achieved better generalization and few-shot performance compared to the baseline. Conclusions Vision FM specialized for medical imaging can improve accuracy and robustness over NI-FM. Self-supervised pretraining offers a resource-efficient, unified framework for CMR assessment, with the potential to accelerate the development of deep learning-based solutions for image analysis tasks, even with few annotated data available. Graphical abstract ga1 ga1 1: 1 Introduction Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is the reference standard for non-invasive assessment of cardiac structure, function, and viability. A typical CMR study involves multiple sequences and diverse image analysis tasks, such as segmentation of the ventricles and atria on cine images for functional assessment, and myocardial segmentation on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and mapping sequences for tissue characterization. Accurate analysis requires sequence selection, landmark detection, and integration of information across sequences, guided by the standardized American Heart Association (AHA) segment model [1] , which could in turn influence further image acquisition steps. These tasks are often complex and time-consuming due to image variability, anatomical differences, and scan artifacts. Several studies have explored each of these tasks individually or together, and deep learning (DL) techniques have emerged as the state-of-the-art (SoTA) across the various tasks. While deep learning (DL) techniques have become tSoTA for many of these tasks, existing studies are often limited in scope, sample size, or focus primarily on cine imaging in relatively healthy subjects. Additionally, most DL models address these tasks independently, without leveraging shared information across related analyses. Large-scale deep learning models known as foundation models (FM) have demonstrated impressive generalization across data distributions and tasks, achieving SoTA results with strong zero-shot and few-shot performance in natural image processing [2, 3] . By leveraging large-scale unlabeled data for pretraining, they enable downstream applications with minimal labeled data. Pretraining methods like self-distillation with no lables (DINO) [4] which uses contrastive learning for aligned representations, and masked autoencoders (MAE) [5] which reconstruct masked image regions, are particularly suited for training medical FM in applications where high-quality labeled data is scarce. While generalist FMs show promising transferability to medical domains [6] , they often underperform fully supervised training in terms of task-specific accuracies [7] . Medical imaging presents unique challenges such as diverse contrast properties, long-tailed distribution of pathologies, varying dimensionality, resolutions, and subtle anatomical differences. Consequently, task-specific models remain dominant for clinical metrics and diagnosis. A few studies have explored FM trained solely on medical images. Ghesu et al. [8] trained a medical FM with 100 million images, and reported a significant increase across multiple detection tasks in chest radiographs and brain MRI. Tang et al. [9] pretrained a UNetr model on 3D computed tomography images (CT) and obtained SoTA results on various segmentation tasks in CT images. Lu et al. [10] trained a vision-language FM on 1.17 M histopathological images, and showed SoTA results on various related downstream tasks with or without finetuning. More studies have explored FM in radiology [11] , for generalized prompt-based medical image segmentation [12] and applications of the same to specific modalities [13] . Recently, Fu et al. [14] trained a self-supervised autoencoder model on cine MRI images from a single center and demonstrated improved performance on a variety of tasks. This study presents the first known CMR-specific foundation model, trained in a task-agnostic manner on 36 million CMR images across multiple sequences ( Fig. 1 ). This model was then finetuned for classification, segmentation, regression, and detection tasks typical to a CMR image analyses workflow and showed performance improvements relative to a comparable model, with no other changes in the pipeline. Across 33 classes in 9 tasks, the model outperformed the baseline in 25, matched performance in 4, and underperformed in 4. Additionally, the model achieved performance comparable to SoTA for most tasks, with no task-specific optimization of methodology. The model also demonstrated strong generalization as evidenced through cross dataset testing. Ablation studies were also conducted to evaluate the effect of pretraining strategies in terms of method, architecture and type of pretraining data. It was observed that vision transformers, as compared to convolutional networks such as ResNet, are highly reliant on pretraining. Moreover, they are also more sensitive to domain shifts, emphasizing the importance of CMR-specific pretraining as compared to natural-image pretraining. In addition, the higher data efficiency of such a targeted FM was demonstrated by exploring its few-shot learning capabilities. 2: 2 Methods 2.1: 2.1 Data Data used for pretraining and finetuning in this study encompasses several publicly available collections and some non-public datasets detailed below. 2.1.1: 2.1.1 Public datasets UK Biobank [15] (Access application 2964): CMR imaging in the UKBB cohort was acquired on 1.5T scanner (MAGNETOM Aera, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). Three long axis cines (horizontal long axis—HLA, vertical long axis—VLA, and left ventricular outflow tract—LVOT cines both sagittal and coronal) and a complete short-axis (SAX) stack of balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) cines, covering the left ventricle (LV) and right ventricle (RV) are acquired. More details on demographics and acquisition can be found in Sudlow et al. [15] . This dataset consists of 16,230 patients with full imaging studies. ACDC [16] (not used for pretraining): “Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge” dataset is a publicly available and fully annotated dataset for the purpose of SAX cine CMR assessment. It consists of 150 patients with ground truth for LV, myocardium, and RV segmentations in ED and ES, as well as an expert-assigned disease label. The acquisitions were obtained using two MRI scanners of different magnetic strengths (1.5T (Siemens Area, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) and 3.0T (Siemens Trio Tim, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). EMIDEC [17] (not used for pretraining): This dataset provides LGE images and myocardial contours for 100 patients, with a third being normal, and rest being pathological. Images were acquired on 1.5T and 3T magnets (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany), using a T1-weighted phase-sensitive inversion recovery (PSIR) sequence. Ground truth masks are provided for myocardium, LV, and infarct. Kaggle [18] (not used for pretraining): The 2015 Kaggle Second Annual Data Science Bowl provided cine MR images for 700 patients, with the aim of detecting ED and ES volumes. Ground truth ED and ES volumes were provided, but no manually segmented contours. 2.1.2: 2.1.2 Clinical datasets Center 1: Data from this center constitutes of CMR studies performed on 1.5T scanners (MAGNETOM Aera, Siemens Healthineers AG, Erlangen, Germany) from 10,073 consecutive patients, acquired during 2016 to 2018. Long-axis and short-axis views covering the entire LV were obtained using balanced steady-state free-precession sequence (bSSFP). LGE images were acquired after injection of a bolus of gadolinium-based contrast agent (Dotarem, Guerbet, Villepinte, France, 0.1 mmol/kg). Stress perfusion imaging was performed using a saturation-prepared b-SSFP sequence. A series of six slices (four short-axis views, in addition to 2- and 4-chamber views) were acquired every other heartbeat. Single-breath-hold 3D T1-weighted inversion recovery gradient-echo sequence was acquired with the same prescriptions to detect hyperenhancement from cardiac LGE. The inversion time was individually adjusted to null normal myocardium. Other images in the dataset include those acquired with T2-weighted sequences such as half-Fourier acquisition single-shot turbo spin-echo (HASTE) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR), T2 star weighted, compressed sensing techniques, localizer scans, etc. Center 2: This included data for 1221 patients, acquired between 2013 and 2022, on 1.5T and 3T MRI systems (MAGNETOM Avanto and Skyra, Siemens Healthineers AG, Erlangen, Germany). CMR studies included cine bSSFP images in 2-, 3-, and 4-chamber LAX, and a stack of SAX slices. The protocol also included cine images focused on the LV outflow track and aorta, at various planes. LGE images, both single-shot and segmented, were acquired as single-breath-hold T1-weighted inversion-recovery gradient echo images acquired 10 min after contrast injection. The dataset also included first-pass myocardial perfusion imaging at rest and adenosine stress. The patient cohort includes both normal patients (41%), as well as patients with cardiomyopathies such as dilated cardiomyopathy (10%), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (13%), ischemic heart disease (32%), and myocarditis (4%). Center 3 (not used for pretraining): The data from this center includes 144 clinical subjects (52 normal, 49 myocarditis, 20 sarcoidosis, 23 systemic disease) who were scanned on a 1.5T MRI system (MAGNETOM Aera, Siemens Healthineers AG, Erlangen, Germany), acquired between 2016 and 2021. CMR studies included cine bSSFP images in 2-, 3-, and 4-chamber LAX, and a stack of SAX slices. The cine imaging included views of the LV outflow tract and aorta. LGE imaging consisted of Inversion Recovery fast low-angle shot (FLASH) acquired 10 min after contrast injection in several short-axis planes. Native and post-contrast T1 modified Look-Locker inversion recovery (MOLLI) and T2 prepared fast-low-angle shot maps were acquired. This dataset was not used in the pretraining stage. Patients in all three datasets were referred for clinical CMR at their respective institutions for evaluation of suspected cardiovascular disease. Due to the retrospective nature of the study, a waiver of informed consent was issued in accordance with the respective institutional review boards. All data were fully anonymized prior to inclusion in this study. 2.2: 2.2 Self-supervised pretraining A vision transformer-small (ViT-S/8) [19] model was trained using self-supervised learning (SSL) using DINO [4] on 36 million cardiac MRI images from 27,524 subjects from 3 sources: 2 clinical centers (henceforth referred to as Centers 1 and 2) and the UK Biobank (UKBB) [15] cohort. The combined dataset includes cine, LGE, T1, and T2 weighted imaging, flow imaging, black blood sequences, localizers, etc., from both healthy and diseased subjects, to encourage generalization across diverse image characteristics. The images focus on cardiac views and anatomies, with a large proportion being short-axis images, followed by long-axis (2, 3, and 4 chambers). All images were preprocessed by rescaling to a 1 mm × 1 mm resolution using cubic spline interpolation, and center-cropping to a size of 224 × 224, and repeated in the channel dimension to form 3-channel inputs. The self-supervised DINO method involves using contrastive learning to train the model on unlabeled images, by learning consistent representations across various image transformations, such as local and global crops, horizontal flips, rotations, solarization, and Gaussian blur. The method uses two networks—student and teacher—with identical architectures. The student network is trained to match the teacher’s output representations, and the teacher is updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student weights. The DINO loss is a cross-entropy loss between the softmax-normalized outputs of student and teacher networks, with teacher outputs sharpened using temperature scaling and centered to stabilize training. For efficient convergence, we initialized with DINO weights pretrained on natural images, and trained in two stages: the first half of training used half-resolution images (128 × 128) with batch size 1024, followed by training on the full resolution (224 × 224) with batch size of 512. The model was trained for a total of 7 days on 8 Nvidia Tesla H100 (80 GB) graphics processing units (GPUs), using a patch size of 8, the AdamW optimizer [20] , and a learning rate schedule identical to the original study: linearly ramped up during the first 10 epochs to the initial value ( lr = 0.0005 * batchsize / 256 ) and then decayed with a cosine schedule, with weight decay handled similarly. We used the LightlySSL [21] Python package for implementations of self-supervised methods and PyTorch Lightning [22] for distributed training. Values for hyperparameters such as teacher temperature, warmup epochs, and weight decay start/end were retained from the original DINO implementation [4] . An ablation study was also conducted on a subset of the data to analyze the effect of the choice of pretraining strategy and architecture. 2.3: 2.3 Downstream tasks—task definitions The model was finetuned and evaluated on nine tasks spanning classification, segmentation, landmark localization, and pathology detection across cine, LGE, and mapping images from multiple datasets. Tasks are illustrated in Fig. 2 , with data details summarized in Table 1 . When available, public datasets and labels were used; otherwise, clinical data from three centers were annotated by trained CMR experts. Data for each task was split into training, validation, and testing at the patient level. Classification tasks: 1. Image type classification: The model classified cine (bSSFP), T1 (MOLLI pre/post-contrast maps and T1-weighted images), T2 (single-shot SSFP maps and T2-weighted images), and LGE (PSIR acquisition, singleshot/segmented) images using image content alone, without DICOM tags. The classes were equally distributed. 2. Cine view classification: This task aimed to identify relevant cine views for automated CMR analysis. While SAX and LAX (2CH, 3CH, 4CH) views are standard, additional views, such as aorta-focused flow imaging and an "Others" category for less common acquisition planes were also included. Tasks 1 and 2 utilized data from Center 3. The class distribution was SAX (41%), 2CH (11%), 3CH (7%), 4CH (9%), Aorta (9%), Others (23%). Segmentation tasks: 3. Cine SAX segmentation: To segment the LV blood pool, myocardium, and RV blood pool in SAX cine bSSFP images from the ACDC challenge dataset. 4. Cine LAX segmentation: This task involved segmenting the four cardiac chambers and the myocardium in LAX 4-chamber view images from the Kaggle dataset. 5. LGE SAX segmentation: To segment myocardium and LV blood pool in LGE images. To explore the effect of dataset size on the same task, two subtasks were defined: task 5A was trained only on EMIDEC dataset, while task 5B used data from EMIDEC, Center 1, and center 2, amounting to a 10-fold increase in data. It is noted that this was an annotated subset of the larger dataset used from Centers 1 and 2 in the pretraining task; however, no labels were used during the pretraining phase. 6. Mapping segmentation: This involved myocardial segmentation on both T1 maps (pre- and post-contrast) and T2 maps using data from Center 3. Landmark-related tasks: 7. Landmark localization: This was performed on the UKBB dataset for the anterior and inferior right ventricular insertion points (ant. RVIP and inf. RVIP) in SAX cine bSSFP images. The ant. RVIP is typically used clinically for AHA segment initialization. Pathology Detection tasks: 8. LGE Detection: Both tasks 8A and 8B are designed as binary classification tasks aimed at detecting the presence/absence of hyperenhancement in LGE images. The reference labels (presence of hyperenhancement in LGE) in task 8A were extracted automatically from clinical reports (34% had reported positive LGE), while task 8B used the publicly provided annotations (67% had reported positive LGE, indicating the presence of infarct or microvascular obstruction) to infer the same. Both tasks used 3 image slices automatically extracted from the image stack at basal, mid, and apical levels, at ED, as the input, and predicted a binary label representing the presence or absence of LGE hyperenhancement. Task 8A uses data from center 2, and task 8B used data from the EMIDEC public dataset. 9. Disease Detection: This task used three frames from the cardiac cycle (ED, midway between ED and ES, and ES), extracted at the basal level from the image stack as the input, and predicts the patient as either normal (NORM), or assigned one of four disease labels: dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), abnormal RV (RV), and previous myocardial infarction (MINF). ACDC public dataset is used, and the classes were equally distributed. This specific choice of using only a single basal slice was primarily made to reduce computational complexity and standardize input dimensions. Using temporal frames allows the model to capture motion irregularities that are characteristic of these diseases, but restricting input to a single slice may have limited the model’s ability to detect disease manifestations appearing in other regions of the heart, potentially constraining performance on this complex multi-class task. Since the focus of the study was to evaluate the pretraining strategy, no further optimization was done in terms of incorporating additional spatial or temporal information, though that could potentially further improve the performance. Eight downstream tasks (tasks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5A, 6, 8B, 9) use datasets that were not seen during pretraining. Three tasks (5B, 7 and 8A) are in-distribution, where a small subset of the pretraining data with annotations is used. It is to be noted that GT annotations were not used in the pretraining stage. 2.4: 2.4 Downstream tasks—finetuning To enable a direct comparison on the same test data, two experiments were conducted: a) Baseline: ResNet50 [23] initialized with ImageNet pretrained weights (23 M parameters) b) The ViT-S/8 encoder pretrained on cardiac MR images (21 M parameters). ResNet50 is a commonly used architecture for medical image processing with a similar parameter count. For each task, both models were trained on the same labeled data and under identical conditions, differing only in network architecture. To adapt both encoders to classification and detection tasks, a single linear layer was added on top of the extracted features, as in [4] . Freezing/finetuning of the encoder was decided per-task and per-model, based on performance on the respective validation split. For the ResNet50, the feature vector was extracted and averaged along the spatial dimension, yielding a vector of size 2048. For ViT-S, the classification (CLS) token from the last 4 blocks and the mean of the patch tokens from the final block were concatenated to create a vector of size 1920. Both models were trained using cross-entropy loss. For segmentation and landmark tasks, the trained ResNet50 and ViT-S/8 encoders were combined with a UNet decoder to create either a ResNet50-Unet [24] (decoder parameters: depth = 5, feature sizes = [256, 128, 64, 32, 16]) or a UNETR [25] (decoder parameters: depth = 5, feature size=16, hidden size=384) respectively. The models were trained with the Jaccard loss [26] , with a Softmax final activation layer. Based on prior studies [6] as well as our empirical experiments that showed consistently superior performance through finetuning, both models were finetuned end-to-end (encoder included) for better accuracy. For landmark localization, the task was treated as a regression problem, with the network trained to predict a Gaussian heatmap centered on the landmark position, as in Xue et al. [27] . Table 2 summarizes the differences in experimental setup between the task groups. In all tasks (except for the detection tasks, as noted in Section 2.3 ), the model works on a single image, repeated in the channel dimension to create a 3-channel input. All images were resampled to 1 mm × 1 mm in-plane resolution using cubic spline interpolation, and center-cropped to 224 × 224. Intensities were capped at 98 percentile and then normalized to the range −1 to 1. The data were split into training, validation, and testing sets at the patient level ( Table 1 ). Data augmentations included rotations, translations, and Gaussian noise addition. All models were trained for 200 epochs using AdamW optimizer and cosine annealing of the learning rate (initial LR = 0.001). The best epoch was selected based on the validation metric averaged over classes for each split. Metrics used included Dice coefficient for segmentation, per-class accuracy for classification and detection, and absolute Euclidean distance error (in mm) for landmark localization. Statistical significance was assessed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for continuous metrics and McNemar’s test for classification accuracies, where applicable, with p <0.05 considered significant. 2.5: 2.5 Compared methods To benchmark our proposed CMR foundation model, we conducted a literature review to establish typical performance ranges for each task. In addition, for a more direct and controlled comparison, we selected four key tasks that span cine and parametric CMR: cine view classification, cine SAX segmentation, LGE segmentation, and myocardial mapping segmentation. The following models were used for comparison: Segmentation Tasks: • SAM2 [28] : A general-purpose vision foundation model pretrained on natural images. Click-prompting was used with 20 foreground clicks for the positive class and 20 background clicks for each negative class. • MedSAM2 [29] : A universal medical vision foundation model, prompted identically to SAM2. • UNETR [25] and SwinUNETR [30] : Two supervised segmentation baselines trained on our dataset using the same pipeline described in Section 2.4 . ViTS/8 [19] (∼21 M parameters) and Swin Tiny [31] (∼29 M parameters) encoders were used, respectively, selected for their comparable model sizes among available variants. • CineMA [14] : A domain-specific foundation model trained on standard cine MRI views (SAX, 2CH, 3CH, 4CH), evaluated only on cine-based tasks. For SAX segmentation, we used the publicly released finetuned weights. Results were averaged across the three officially released model checkpoints (initialized with different random seeds). Classification Tasks: • ViTS/8 [19] and SwinViT [31] , [32] classifiers: Supervised classifiers consisting of the respective transformer encoders, followed by a linear classifier layer, trained on our dataset. Both encoders were initialized with Imagenet-pretrained weights for improved performance. • CineMA [14] : For cine view classification, no pretrained weights were provided. We therefore finetuned the pretrained CineMA encoder on our classification dataset. 2.6: 2.6 Model investigations 2.6.1: 2.6.1 Generalization Deep learning-based CMR segmentation methods are known to exhibit performance degradation when applied directly to images from different scanners or sites different from those seen during training [33] . To evaluate generalization performance of the proposed CMR-SSL model, we follow the cross-testing methodology of this study [33] , where a model was trained solely on the UKBB cohort (with default settings) and tested directly on the ACDC dataset for the task of cine SAX segmentation. Both datasets were acquired on same-vendor scanners but differ in site, field strength, and acquisition protocol. Metrics are calculated per patient. 2.6.2: 2.6.2 Effect of encoder architecture and pretraining strategy To tease apart the effect of encoder architecture and pretraining method, we compared our proposed model to two other pretraining options: a ResNet50 pretrained through DINO and a ViTS/8 pretrained through MAE [5] . MAE is a popular reconstruction-based pretraining method (as opposed to contrastive learning/self-distillation in DINO) with strong performance in prior studies [6] , [34] . During training, 75% of input patches were randomly masked out from the input image, and the model was trained to predict the pixel values of the masked patches from the visible ones, forcing the encoder to learn meaningful latent representations. A lightweight transformer decoder, with half the depth and embedding size of the encoder (depth=6 blocks and embedding size=192), was used for reconstruction of the missing patches. Following the original study, MSE loss was used for the reconstruction of masked patches, AdamW [20] was used as the optimizer and default values were used for other hyperparameters. Data augmentations included random resized crops and horizontal flips. The method was implemented using LightlySSL [21] and Pytorch Lightning [22] . Only the encoder is retained for downstream tasks. For training the ResNet50 through DINO, we used an identical setup to the ViT-S/8, except for the model architecture. For efficiency, pretraining in this set of experiments was done on a subset of images, created from the original pretraining dataset by randomly selecting 10% of patients and 10% of images per patient, resulting in approximately 360,000 images. The models followed the same two-stage training schedule described earlier (initialized from NI weights, first trained on half-resolution images, then on full-resolution images, with the same batch sizes), but pretraining was shortened to 4 days. The models were then finetuned and evaluated on three representative tasks: cine view classification (task 2), LGE SAX segmentation (task 5B), and mapping SAX segmentation (task 6). For comparison, we also train both models with no pretraining i.e., starting from random weights. 2.6.3: 2.6.3 Effect of pretraining on CMR data An alternative to pretraining on CMR data is to pretrain the FM on natural images. To evaluate the benefit of training specifically on CMR data, the model was initialized with the weights of a ViT-S/8 pretrained on natural images [4] and then finetuned in the same framework. Three representative tasks were chosen for the comparison: cine view classification (task 2), LGE SAX segmentation (task 5 A) and mapping SAX segmentation (task 6). 2.6.4: 2.6.4 Few-shot performance To simulate a task with limited annotations, often encountered in medical image analysis settings, the few-shot performance of both the baseline and the proposed model was evaluated. The amount of training data was varied systematically between 1 and 512 samples per class, as available, in two representative tasks—cine view classification (task 1), and mapping SAX segmentation (task 6). View classification and segmentation are typical tasks that are often required to generalize to new centers and sequences, often with few samples available from the new set. Mapping segmentation provides more complexity, as compared to cine. The encoder was kept frozen across all experiments, to prevent overfitting. 3: 3 Results Table 3 provides the results direct comparison of the performance of the model against the baseline on the same test data. Out of 33 classes in the 9 tasks, the proposed model outperforms the baseline in 25, underperforms in 4 and achieves the same performance in 4. Both models perform well for task 1, distinguishing different CMR image types, with minor improvements from the SSL pretrained model, especially for the “Others” class. For the cine view classification task (task 2), an increase of 6.8% points (pp) was observed over all classes, ranging from 4.7 pp in SAX to 27.2 pp for the “2CH” class. For the segmentation tasks 3–6, improvements from 0.1 to 1.8 pp were obtained, depending on the class and task. For the landmark detection task 7, mixed results were achieved, with the proposed model outperforming the baseline for one landmark, and vice versa for the other. In both segmentation and landmark detection, generally lower standard deviations were observed in the metrics for the proposed method. Improvements of 3.7 and 6.6 pp for the LGE detection tasks (Tasks 8A, 8B) were observed, with the greater improvement in task 8B, with the smaller amount of data. For the disease detection (task 9), the proposed model outperformed the baseline by 14 pp. Tables 4 and 5 show comparison of the results against the literature. Table 4 compares the performance for each task against prior studies for the same task. Due to the fragmented nature of the field and the frequent use of non-public clinical datasets, prior results are reported as ranges. The performance of the proposed model (fine-tuned without any task-specific optimization of the methodology or hyperparameters), is comparable or superior in many tasks across classification, segmentation, and landmark localization. The model lags behind the SoTA in disease detection. This could potentially be due to the lack of comprehensive temporal/spatial information (captured through clinical metrics such as volumes, ejection fraction, and strain) in the experimental design for this study. Table 5 compares the performance of other methods on a few selected tasks. Out of the general foundation methods, SAM2 works fairly well for bright, blob-like structures (like the LV). For cine-based tasks, CineMA obtains almost comparable performance to the proposed model, underscoring the advantage of anatomy and modality-specific FMs. However, the method lags in non-standard views, which were not included in its pretraining. The proposed model outperforms other methods on most tasks. 3.1: 3.1 Model investigations 3.1.1: 3.1.1 Model generalization The proposed model showed improved generalization ability ( Table 6 ) in cross domain testing, achieving results comparable to the method presented by Chen et al. [33] , which involved carefully optimized network architecture, data normalization, and data augmentation techniques, and slightly larger training data. However, we note that while the training/testing splits are comparable, they differ from those used by the authors, as we did not have access to the exact same splits. 3.1.2: 3.1.2 Effect of encoder architecture and pretraining strategy As reported in Table 7 , DINO pretraining on CMR data sustains strong performance across both classification and segmentation tasks. While the MAE method performs well in segmentation, it falls short in classification, consistent with previous findings [6] . Additionally, ViT architectures outperform ResNet50. On the other hand, training from scratch causes both architectures to underperform, especially in classification, and more so for the ViT. 3.1.3: 3.1.3 Effect of pretraining on CMR data In most settings ( Table 8 ), the CMR pretrained model outperforms the ViT-S/8 model pretrained on natural images (NI-ViTS). Improvements of upto 70.7 pp were obtained in classification, and 9.1 pp in segmentation, when using the CMR-ViTS, compared to NI-ViTS. Generally, the CMR-ViTS scored higher than the ResNet baseline, which outperformed the NI-ViTS. The effect was particularly consistent for the segmentation tasks. 3.1.4: 3.1.4 Few-shot performanceg The few-shot performance is highlighted in Fig. 3 , which shows the test metric averaged across classes for cine view classification, and Mapping segmentation tasks. The performance is shown across repeated experiments where first very few, then gradually more and more labeled samples are used for training. The proposed model outperformed the baseline model in all configurations. It also reached convergence accuracy faster than the baseline model. 3.1.5: 3.1.5 Qualitative results Error analysis revealed several key factors contributing to performance limitations as follows: (a) Increased variability in apical slices, (b) Ambiguity in slices near valve levels leading to incorrect segmentation of additional/missing slices or over-/under-segmentation of the RV, (c) Image quality issues such as low contrast in LGE images or artifacts in mapping sequences, (d) Misplacement of contours in LGE images due to the presence of enhancement, and (e) Misclassification of cine views in cases where slices were at the boundary between typical categories. Representative failure cases are illustrated in Fig. 4 . 4: 4 Discussion In this study, a vision foundation model specific to CMR was introduced and evaluated on a wide variety of downstream tasks relevant to a clinical workflow. The proposed model achieved performance comparable or superior to the state-of-the-art for classification, segmentation, and landmark localization tasks, and promising results for disease detection, with no task-specific optimization. The model was also compared against a similar fully supervised DL network, without large-scale pretraining. It was observed that SSL pretraining using images of the relevant anatomy and modality can benefit all tasks in terms of accuracy and robustness, across a wide range of resource (labeled data) settings. Previous studies have explored individual CMR tasks with varying performance. Chauhan et al. [35] reported an accuracy of 0.90–0.95 for distinguishing between SAX and 3 LAX views, after training on an augmented, balanced dataset of 2000 images. Segmentation studies report Dice scores of 0.90 to 0.95 for LV, 0.88 to 0.91 for myocardium and 0.90–0.92 for RV [16] , [36–39] , in SAX cine MRI. Many of these studies were done on small, public datasets, made available as part of challenges, and involved extensive design of model architecture and postprocessing, which may potentially not generalize for new datasets. Bai et al. [38] achieved Dice scores of 0.94 (LV), 0.88 (myocardium), 0.95 (LA), and 0.96 (RA) in LAX cine MRI using 4875 UKBB subjects [15] . For LGE images, Dice scores of 0.84–0.88 have been reported for myocardium segmentation [40] , [41] , while scores of 0.85–0.86 were achieved for T1 and T2 mapping [42] , [43] . Kalapos et al. [42] trained a ResNet50-U-Net on 7000 T1 and T2 maps of differing etiologies, with contour-based postprocessing to obtain a dice score of 0.86. The proposed model achieved comparable or superior performance without task-specific optimization, often using fewer labeled data. For disease detection, Khened et al. [44] achieved an accuracy of 0.96 using a random forest classifier trained on clinical metrics such as ejection fraction, derived from temporal segmentations. In contrast, while the proposed model outperformed the baseline trained on the same data, both models underperformed relative to SoTA, likely due to the complexity of cardiomyopathy detection, which requires integrating spatial and temporal dynamics, as opposed to segmentation/classification tasks for which single images could suffice. A similar trend was observed in LGE hyperenhancement detection (task 8), where the CMR SSL model extracted more informative features, as evidenced by improvements over the baseline and performance gains with increased data (task 8A vs 8B). However, overall performance remained below SoTA [45] , potentially due to limited input (three spatial slices as opposed to the full stack). Patient-wise LGE hyperenhancement detection may benefit from incorporating full 3D information and hierarchical detection strategies (e.g., myocardium followed by infarct/no-reflow areas), as seen in prior work [45] . However, this study aimed to assess the information content of raw encoder features under a highly simplified method design. Future work could leverage pretrained ViT architectures to incorporate both temporal and comprehensive spatial information via linear probing over multiple frames, 3D architectures [46] processing volumetric stacks or video encoders initialized with pretrained ViTs [47] for temporal sequences such as cine. The current study offered some interesting observations. The improvement in performance relative to the baseline, was observed to be more substantial for more complex tasks, such as the detection tasks. Moreover, greater gains were observed in tasks with the smaller finetuning dataset, as seen in 5A vs 5B, or 8B vs 8A, both cases where the data size differed by approximately a factor of 10 for the same task. Notably, no performance differences were linked to class frequency. The CMR-SSL model also showed increased generalization performance in cross testing, similar to studies [33] which used carefully optimized strategies for the same. Ablation studies ( Table 7 ) also showed the differential importance of network architecture vs pretraining strategy. While both DINO and MAE are effective, prior studies suggest that task-specific preferences exist—segmentation tasks often benefit from masked image modeling methods like MAE, while instance discrimination methods like DINO excel in classification [48] . In our feasibility study, DINO outperformed MAE for classification and performed comparably for segmentation. Furthermore, vision transformers (ViTs) appeared to benefit more drastically from pretraining than convolutional models, likely due to their lack of spatial inductive bias. This is evidenced by the drop in performance for the ViT-S when trained from scratch, especially for classification task, possibly due to the weaker supervision signal in classification, the challenge of aggregating global information without pretraining, and the inherently data-hungry nature of ViTs. Furthermore, pretraining on CMR data was more beneficial compared to pretraining on natural images ( Table 8 ). Conversely, the ResNet50 baseline pretrained on natural images generally outperforms the ViT-S/8 model pretrained on natural images. Interestingly, the NI-ViT-S achieved competitive performance in the classification task on some classes, while consistently lagging behind both the proposed and the baseline methods in segmentation tasks, with a wider gap in the task with the smaller finetuning dataset (task 5A). This trend was also observed in the cardiac segmentation task by Baharoon et al. [6] and for general medical image classification in Huix et al. [49] . This might be explained by the fact that classification can be done on more global features while segmentation requires fine-grained features at a smaller scale. Pre-training on CMR images provides more CMR-relevant representations at the finer scale. These observations together underscore how the lack of inductive bias makes ViTs flexible and powerful architectures, but at the same time, increases their dependence on pretraining to learn feature priors. As a result, ViTs are more sensitive to domain shifts between pretraining and fine-tuning. In addition, diversity in the pretraining data is important even in domain-specific FMs. For instance, CineMA [14] , a more recently introduced cine-only CMR FM, shows comparable performance in specific views, while lagging in non-standard views which were not included in the pretraining ( Table 5 ). From the few shot experiments, it was seen that for the arguably easier tasks of view classification, and LV segmentation, the pretrained model achieved convergence and performance plateaued with relatively few labeled samples. The more linear improvement observed for myocardial segmentation likely reflects its higher complexity, as the thin myocardium is highly sensitive to small pixel-level errors (unlike the more robust LV blood pool), compounded by the variability introduced when combining multiple mapping contrasts (T1 pre, T1 post, and T2) in the same task. 5: 5 Limitations First, this study aimed to evaluate the benefits of a CMR-pretrained FM across various tasks without task-specific optimization, resulting in moderate improvements over the baseline. Not all observed differences reached statistical significance, possibly due to limited sample size in certain tasks. Task-specific designs, guided by clinical insights, could enhance performance, particularly in more complex tasks like pathology detection. In addition, the model can be improved using more advanced architectures and additional spatial and temporal frames. Second, the effect of size and type of pretraining data was not studied. Approximately 80% of the pretraining data was cine data, reflecting the typical distribution in a CMR study. Third, the model (or part of it) was finetuned for each task separately in this study. Zero-shot (true out-of-box) performance was not explored and constitutes future work. Lastly, this study was unimodal, focusing only on images, without incorporating other CMR-related data, such as clinical reports. Although we are unable to release the pretrained models due to institutional data agreements and the R&D setting, the methodological details provided should allow other researchers to replicate the training process using publicly available CMR datasets. 6: 6 Conclusions Targeted modality and organ-specific vision foundation models for medical imaging can improve accuracy and robustness over training on natural images. Self-supervised pretraining offers a resource-efficient, unified framework for CMR assessment, with the potential to accelerate the development of deep learning-based solutions for image analysis tasks, even with few annotated data available.
